supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a constitution $c$ with $C\ge1$ named species and its equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ from *Equilibrium state domains*. An interior composition is represented by

$$
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_{C-1})\in\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{C-1}:x_i>0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{C-1}x_i<1\},
$$

with $x_C:=1-\sum_{i<C}x_i>0$; for $C=1$, $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and $x_1=1$.

A **phase branch** $\alpha$ is model data consisting of an open chart $W_\alpha\subseteq(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R\times\Delta_{C-1}^{\circ}\times(0,\infty)$ with coordinates $(T,p,x,m)$ and a $C^1$ diffeomorphism $\sigma_\alpha:W_\alpha\to U_\alpha$ onto an open subset $U_\alpha\subseteq\mathbb R^{C+2}$ contained in the equilibrium state domain $D_c$. Here $T$ is in kelvins, $p$ is in pascals, $m$ is total amount in moles, and $C^1$ means continuous first coordinate derivatives as in *$C^k$ Euclidean maps and diffeomorphisms*. The chart dimension is $C+2$, matching the ambient dimension of $D_c$. The map $\sigma_\alpha$ takes values in numerical state coordinates; its physical SI state map is explicitly $\chi_\alpha=\Phi_c\circ\sigma_\alpha$, where $\Phi_c$ is the numerical-to-SI unit map of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials*. Thus the physical amounts at this point are $n_j=m x_j$, and the numerical amount coordinates in $\sigma_\alpha$ are $n_j/(1\,\mathrm{mol})$. Derivative-defined physical state functions are evaluated on $\chi_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$, or equivalently pulled back along $\Phi_c$ to $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$. At $\sigma_\alpha(T,p,x,m)$ in this precise pullback sense, the derivative-defined state functions of *Entropic temperature, pressure, and molar chemical potentials* give temperature $T$, pressure $p$, and mole fractions $x_j=n_j/m$; here $n_{\mathrm{tot}}:=\sum_{i=1}^C n_i=m$ uses the finite-sum convention of *Finite sums and finite products, by recursion*. An **intensive phase branch** additionally has each derivative-defined chemical potential $\mu_j(T,p,x,m)$ independent of $m$ throughout $W_\alpha$; write its value as $\mu_j^\alpha(T,p,x)$. This scale invariance is an explicit constitutive model property, not a consequence of *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling*. A valid local response chart and its inverse are as in *Thermodynamic response functions on valid local charts* and *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials*. Existence of $W_\alpha$ or $\sigma_\alpha$ is a model premise, not a consequence of the equations of thermodynamics.

On a branch with a valid natural-variable chart, $G^\alpha$ denotes the Gibbs potential of *Local thermodynamic Legendre potentials* restricted to the branch. For a one-component branch with amount $m_\alpha>0$, define $g_\alpha:=G^\alpha/m_\alpha$, $s_\alpha:=S_\alpha/m_\alpha$, and $v_\alpha:=V_\alpha/m_\alpha$, in $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively. These quotients need not be independent of amount, and $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ is not assumed by this definition. Such an equality requires a separate same-tag homogeneity hypothesis on the branch.

A **phase mixture** of a finite list of branches is a feasible separated compound whose positive phase amounts $m_\alpha$ have fractions $\lambda_\alpha:=m_\alpha/\sum_\beta m_\beta>0$ with $\sum_\alpha\lambda_\alpha=1$. Its extensive coordinates and entropy are those supplied by *Additive separated systems and tagged bulk scaling* and *Concave macroscopic fundamental entropy*, on the exact feasible set of *Isolated compound and feasible equilibrium set*. The mixture is in **coexistence** when it is an attained global entropy-maximizing endpoint under the declared totals and permitted exchanges, as in *Stable equilibrium requires an attained global entropy maximum*. This definition does not assert that a maximum exists, that all branches can exchange every coordinate, or that metastable states are global equilibria.

The bulk scaling postulate may send a material tag $c$ to a different tag $c^{(\lambda)}$. It therefore does not supply same-tag degree-one homogeneity of $G^\alpha$ or $U^\alpha$ on a phase branch. Any result using $g_\alpha=\mu^\alpha$ must state that additional hypothesis.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the explicitly declared feasible endpoint set of an isolated compound with the chosen independent separated macroscopic subsystem split and any explicitly modeled named auxiliaries, as defined in [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]. For this route, adopt the physical criterion that any endpoint tuple the model classifies as a stable equilibrium under these fixed totals, retained partitions, and permitted exchanges satisfies

$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})=\max_{x\in\mathcal F}S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x),\qquad S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}S_{c_i}(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}(y_j),$$

Here $\max$ means that $x^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathcal F$ and $S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x^{\mathrm{eq}})\ge S_{\mathrm{tot}}(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal F$, using maximum in the sense of [[def-max-min]]. Here $x=(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ is a complete endpoint tuple from [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]; $k=0$ gives the original thermodynamic-only formula. The finite sums are as in [[def-finite-sum]]. The macroscopic summands are those of the separated constituents under [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], and any auxiliary summands are the explicitly adopted endpoint entropy maps of the same complete compound model. This route assumes that these contributions add for the complete admitted split. A constant auxiliary entropy may be dropped as an additive constant when comparing maxima, whereas variable auxiliary entropy must be retained. Whenever the stable-equilibrium label is used, attainment is assumed: at least one maximizing endpoint lies in $\mathcal F$. If $\mathcal F$ is empty or the entropy supremum is not attained, this item supplies no equilibrium state.

“Global” refers to every endpoint in this exact $\mathcal F$, not just nearby states, states reachable by a restricted short-time dynamics, or states on a selected branch. A local maximum that is not global, or a long-lived preparation trapped by kinetic barriers, is not declared stable equilibrium by this postulate. No uniqueness or relaxation dynamics is assumed.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[post-td-entropy-maximum]] and [[def-td-isolated-compound-feasible-set]]: The adopted complete-compound entropy is the sum of the separated phase entropies and the explicitly supplied auxiliary entropies, and the stable endpoint is a global maximum on its exact feasible set. Along each stipulated curve, every auxiliary state is fixed, so its entropy contribution is constant.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite list of named subsystems $s_1,\ldots,s_m$, where $m\in\mathbb N$ and $m\ge1$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), each having its own equilibrium state domain $D_{c_i}$ as defined in [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. Their separated endpoint state space is the Cartesian product ([[def-cartesian-product]])

$$\mathcal D:=D_{c_1}\times\cdots\times D_{c_m}.$$

If the boundary also includes named auxiliaries or work devices $d_1,\ldots,d_k$ not already among the $s_i$, where $k\in\mathbb N$, supply endpoint state sets $Y_j$ and energy maps $E_j:Y_j\to\mathbb R$ with numerical values interpreted in joules. Supply also every coordinate map needed for their matter, volume, retained constraints and separately tracked mechanical or external-field energy. The complete endpoint space is

$$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}:=\mathcal D\times Y_1\times\cdots\times Y_k.$$

For $k=0$ use $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}=\mathcal D$. Write an endpoint as $(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)$ and obtain constituent states by coordinate projection. In the separated additive energy model, declare $E_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}U_{c_i}(x_i)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}E_j(y_j)\,\mathrm J$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the empty auxiliary sum zero. Every tracked endpoint energy contribution must be included in these maps or in an additional explicitly supplied contribution; an interacting model must supply its total-energy map on $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}$. For each entropy-bearing auxiliary supply $S_j^{\mathrm{aux}}:Y_j\to\mathbb R$ with values in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. If the complete separated split has an adopted additive entropy model, its total includes those maps as well as the $S_{c_i}$; omitting an auxiliary requires an explicitly constant entropy contribution or a supplied reduced total-entropy function.

An **isolated compound** consists of all these constituents inside a declared outer boundary, with no matter or energy transfer across that boundary during the admitted process, in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]]. Internal transfers may change auxiliary energy and entropy. On pairs admitted to the simple aggregate composition map of [[post-td-bulk-additivity]], totals and entropy satisfy that postulate and [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. A retained partition endpoint in $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}$ is not automatically such an admitted aggregate state: summing its coordinates can discard partition information. For endpoints outside that composition's admitted set, total-energy and total-entropy maps must be supplied separately; no aggregate entropy identity is inferred.

For specified totals and retained barriers, an **equilibrium feasible set** is the model-declared subset $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D_{\mathrm{all}}$ of complete endpoint tuples satisfying those totals and exactly the exchange permissions in the declared protocol. Its thermodynamic projection is $\Pi(\mathcal F):=\{\mathbf x\in\mathcal D:\exists\mathbf y\text{ with }(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\in\mathcal F\}$; that projection alone does not record variable auxiliary states, energy or entropy. When $k=0$ the original convention $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal D$ applies. Totals use all supplied endpoint maps and the dimensioned coordinate maps $U_c,V_c,n_{c,j}$ of [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]], rather than treating numerical coordinates as quantities with units. For two constituents without auxiliaries, thermal contact through [[def-td-thermal-contact-constraints]] at fixed volumes and mole amounts gives the model-declared allowed energy partitions with prescribed total energy and any further retained constraints. Volume or species exchange changes $\mathcal F$ only when explicitly permitted; retained walls fix the corresponding coordinates.

The set $\mathcal F$ may be empty, noncompact, or otherwise fail to contain an entropy-maximizing state. This definition imposes no existence, compactness, convexity, uniqueness, or attainment assumption.

Along each stipulated curve, every auxiliary state is fixed, so its entropy contribution is constant.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a material constitution $c$, with $r$ named species and dimensionless equilibrium state domain $D_c\subseteq\mathbb R^{r+2}$ from [[def-td-equilibrium-state-domain]]. For $x=(\hat U,\hat V,\hat n_1,\ldots,\hat n_r)\in D_c$, define the diagonal SI coordinate map

$$\Phi_c(x):=(U_c(x),V_c(x),n_{c,1}(x),\ldots,n_{c,r}(x))=(\hat U\,\mathrm J,\hat V\,\mathrm{m^3},\hat n_1\,\mathrm{mol},\ldots,\hat n_r\,\mathrm{mol}).$$

In SI numerical coordinates this is a diagonal linear bijection with a diagonal linear inverse, so it maps ambient open sets to open sets and its inverse is defined on its image.

Choose an open subset $O\subseteq D_c$ in the ambient dimensionless Euclidean coordinates that is designated as a single-phase chart, and set $\Omega:=\Phi_c(O)$, an open chart of physical SI coordinate values. Here $U$ is the internal-energy coordinate evaluated in the center-of-mass rest frame of [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]]. If $S_c:D_c\to\mathbb R$ is the entropy adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]], define its physical-coordinate representative on $\Omega$ by

$$S_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=S_c\circ\Phi_c^{-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R.$$

When its arguments are the physical coordinates $(U,V,n_1,\ldots,n_r)$, write this representative as $S_c(U,V,n)$ for brevity. On $\Omega$, assume the finite representative is $C^2$ and has $S_{c,U}>0$, as adopted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]]. Here $C^2$ means that all coordinate partial derivatives through order two exist and are continuous ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). A coordinate partial such as $S_{c,U}$ is the ordinary derivative in the physical $U$ coordinate while every other physical coordinate is held fixed, as in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]; in particular the conversion factor from $\hat U$ is included.

Explicitly, with the partial derivatives on the right taken in the dimensionless coordinates on $O$ while holding every other hatted coordinate fixed, the physical partials are

$$S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm J)^{-1}\partial_{\hat U}S_c,\qquad S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{m^3})^{-1}\partial_{\hat V}S_c,\qquad S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}=(1\,\mathrm{mol})^{-1}\partial_{\hat n_j}S_c,$$

using the coordinate-conversion convention of [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]].

Define the physical-coordinate representatives of the **absolute thermodynamic temperature**, **entropic pressure**, and **molar chemical potential** of species $j$ by

$$T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=\frac{1}{S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}},\qquad p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}:=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}},\qquad \mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}:=-T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}.$$

For a state-domain point $x\in O$, define the corresponding state functions by pullback, $T_c(x):=T_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, $p_c(x):=p_c^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$, and $\mu_{c,j}(x):=\mu_{c,j}^{\mathrm{SI}}(\Phi_c(x))$. When the argument is a physical tuple $(U,V,n)$, write $T_c(U,V,n)$, $p_c(U,V,n)$, and $\mu_{c,j}(U,V,n)$ for the physical-coordinate representatives. Thus both notations refer to the same state functions through $\Phi_c$.

The entropy unit is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, the energy $U$ is in joules, $V$ is in cubic metres, and $n_j$ is in moles ([[def-td-si-quantities]]). Thus $S_{c,U}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$, $T_c$ is finite and positive in kelvins, $S_{c,V}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$ and $p_c$ has units pascals, and $S_{c,n_j}^{\mathrm{SI}}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ and $\mu_{c,j}$ has units $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. If a microscopic model instead uses a dimensionless particle count $N_j=N_{\!A}n_j$, the corresponding per-particle chemical potential is $\mu_{c,j}/N_{\!A}$ joules, with the exact SI Avogadro constant from [[def-td-si-quantities]].

These are scalar state functions of the stated rest-frame equilibrium chart. The pressure in this definition is a derivative-defined conjugate; identifying it with force per area requires a separate adopted mechanical coupling. Neither an empirical thermometer calibration nor any equation of state is supplied by this definition.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]: On each single-phase chart, $S_{n_j}=-\mu_j/T$ at fixed energy, volume, and other species amounts; branch temperatures are positive.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $1\le q\le n$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^q$ be $C^1$ in the sense of [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]. Suppose $F(x_*)=0$ and some $q\times q$ minor of the derivative matrix $DF(x_*)$ is invertible. This nonsingular-minor hypothesis is the explicit full-row-rank condition used here. If $q<n$, then after permuting coordinates $x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{n-q}\times\mathbb R^q$, there are open neighborhoods $P$ of $u_*$ and $Q$ of $v_*$ and a unique $C^1$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$ such that

$$F(u,v)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v=\varphi(u)\qquad((u,v)\in P\times Q).$$

Its derivative is

$$D\varphi(u)=-D_vF(u,\varphi(u))^{-1}D_uF(u,\varphi(u)).$$

Thus the local zero set is a graph over $n-q$ free coordinates. If $q=n$, the zero is locally isolated, so the local graph dimension is zero. Here “local graph dimension $k$” means a local graph parameterized by an open subset of $\mathbb R^k$, with a singleton counted as dimension zero.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [[thm-tdmath-local-implicit-rank]]: If a C1 map $F:U\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, vanishes at $z_*$, and has an invertible $m\times m$ derivative minor there, then its local zero set is a graph of dimension $n-m$. This statement has no sign restriction on the coordinates of the open set; its current carrier is a draft with a complete conditional proof, not an independent acceptance stamp.

historical_case_scope.source_excerpt:
The branch theorems on this page require the stated smooth local charts. Here coexistence means equality of the declared intensive phase data at an admitted endpoint; it does not itself imply loss of chart regularity. The smooth-branch conclusions apply only on their specified C1 charts and interior composition domains. They supply no conclusion where a branch chart fails to be C1, a species amount reaches the composition boundary, or the specified coexistence-and-affinity Jacobian lacks its required nonsingular minor. In particular, [[pthm-td-clapeyron-local]] requires a nonzero molar-volume jump; when that jump vanishes, its local graph argument and quotient formula do not apply.

The compact-mixture result [[pthm-td-compact-continuous-phase-mixture]] requires a compact phase-generator domain, a continuous entropy map, a fixed barycenter, and feasibility of all probability mixtures with that barycenter. It supplies no attainment theorem for noncompact domains. Likewise, [[def-td-thermodynamic-limit-contract]] specifies the sequence and normalization for a limiting claim but proves no limit exists and no derivatives commute with that limit.

A finite-state partition sum is finite and positive at each finite system size. A singular phase behavior therefore needs a separately specified limit or another model with a separately established domain and regularity analysis. This page does not assert a universal thermodynamic-limit theorem, ensemble equivalence, critical exponent, or physical applicability of the van der Waals equation.

The local homogeneity used by [[pthm-td-clapeyron-local]] may be independently stipulated in a phase model or supplied on the separately designated common-law bulk branch under the local Euler theorem's inverse-chart and common-reference conditions. A constructed local Gibbs model need not be embedded in a global bulk cone to use the general conditional result. The added branch supplies no universal finite-size, long-range or gravitational extensivity and does not remove any smoothness, exchange or nonzero-volume-jump condition.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Let $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ be a basis of $V$, with dual basis
$e^1,\ldots,e^n$. Then the wedges

$$ e^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e^{i_k}\qquad (1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n) $$

form a basis of $\operatorname{Alt}^k(V)$.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

derivations.claim: For each increasing $I$, set $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$. By [F3], the $e^I$ form a basis, so this prescription extends uniquely by linearity to a map $\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$; its coefficients are constant, so it also defines a smooth map on the affine space.

For increasing $I,J$ of size $k$, $e^I\wedge e^{J^c}=0$ when $I\ne J$, because an index repeats. When $I=J$, $e^I\wedge\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$. The component pairing has $\langle e^I,e^J\rangle_\eta=0$ for $I\ne J$ and $\langle e^I,e^I\rangle_\eta=\epsilon_I$. Thus the characterizing identity holds on basis pairs and, by bilinearity, for every $\alpha,\beta$. Pairing with all complementary basis wedges also proves uniqueness.

The cycle integral in the Definition is a finite sum of the unique simplex integrals in [F7], so it is independent of how a finite chain is written after equal simplex coefficients are combined. The terms closed, exact, and $[\omega]=0$ have the quotient meanings in [F4] and [F5]. No physical assumption or choice principle is used.

A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $j:S\hookrightarrow M$ be an oriented embedded smooth $k$-submanifold, with boundary allowed. For a smooth $k$-form $\omega$ on $M$ such that $j^*\omega$ has compact support on $S$, define $\int_S\omega:=\int_Sj^*\omega$. If $F:T\to S$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism, this equals $\int_T(jF)^*\omega$. Compact support is required on $S$ itself.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

In ZF, let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be smooth, and let $a\in U$. If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is a diffeomorphism. Writing $g=(f|_V)^{-1}$,
$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$
No choice axiom is used.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and Jordan measurable, let $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded, and suppose $\{x\in E:f(x)\ne g(x)\}$ has content zero. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable over $E$ if and only if $g$ is, and when they are integrable their integrals are equal.

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

derivations.claim: The rectangle $D$ is a compact Jordan parameter region, and $\Phi$ is smooth on all of $\mathbb R^2$. Every point of $S^2$ is in its image: choose $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=p_3$; when $\sin\theta>0$, the pair $(p_1/\sin\theta,p_2/\sin\theta)$ is a unit-circle point and [F7] supplies $\phi\in[0,2\pi]$, while at a pole any $\phi$ works. More precisely, the interior image is $W=S^2\setminus\Phi(\partial D)$: for every point not on the poles or the longitude seam, the latitude is unique by strict decrease of cosine on $(0,\pi)$, and the longitude is unique by the bijection in [F7]. Direct differentiation gives $\Phi_\theta=(\cos\theta\cos\phi,\cos\theta\sin\phi,-\sin\theta)$ and $\Phi_\phi=(-\sin\theta\sin\phi,\sin\theta\cos\phi,0)$; substituting into the coordinate cross-product formula [F3] yields $\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\phi=(\sin^2\theta\cos\phi,\sin^2\theta\sin\phi,\sin\theta\cos\theta)=\sin\theta\,\Phi$. [F7] makes this nonzero for $0<\theta<\pi$, and its direction is outward because $\Phi$ is the unit radial vector. In any smooth chart on $S^2$, the coordinate derivative of $\Phi$ is therefore invertible; [F6] gives a smooth local inverse. The bijection onto $W$ and these local inverses make $\Phi|_{D^\circ}$ an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto the open set $W$. Thus [F1] applies, including the permitted seam and pole degeneracy on $\partial D$.

By [F2] and step 1.1, the flux integrand is $f(\theta,\phi)=\Phi\cdot(\sin\theta\,\Phi)=\sin\theta$, and the same coefficient is $\omega(\Phi_\theta,\Phi_\phi)$. This function is continuous on the compact Jordan rectangle $D$, so [F11] makes it Riemann integrable there; [F7] gives $0\le f\le1$. The bounded open rectangle $D^\circ$ has boundary $\partial D$, which has two-dimensional content zero by [F1], so [F10] makes $D^\circ$ Jordan measurable. Define $g:D\to\mathbb R$ by $g=f$ on $D^\circ$ and $g=0$ on $\partial D$. The functions $f,g$ are bounded and differ only on the content-zero set $\partial D$; [F9] therefore gives that $g$ is Riemann integrable on $D$ and $\int_Dg=\int_Df$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
A **compact Jordan parameter region** is a compact Jordan measurable set $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ that is the closure of its nonempty connected interior $D^\circ$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]). Its boundary has content zero ([[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]).

A regular parametrized surface patch is the image of a $C^1$ map from a compact Jordan parameter region whose parameter cross product is nonzero on the region's interior and for which no interior parameter point shares its image with a distinct point of the whole region. Seam identifications and rank failures may occur only on the boundary. Here $C^1$ is the Euclidean componentwise class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. More precisely, the parametrization $\varphi$ is defined on an open neighbourhood of $D$, $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ$, and no point of $D^\circ$ has the same image as a distinct point of $D$. The chosen pair $(D,\varphi)$ is part of the patch data.

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}$ be a bounded Jordan set and let $g:E\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Suppose that for all $x$ outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, the section $E_x$ is Jordan measurable and $g_x$ is integrable over it. Put $h(x)=\int_{E_x}g_x$ there and assign arbitrary bounded values to $h$ on $N$, with empty-section integral equal to $0$. Then $h$ is integrable on any rectangle containing the projection of $E$, its integral is independent of that rectangle and of the values on $N$, and
$$\int_Eg=\int h(x)\,dx.$$
The symmetric assertion holds for the other coordinate block.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. For $0\le k\le4$, give $\Lambda^kV^*$ the induced bilinear pairing $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}$, with indices raised by $\eta^{-1}$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.

For a smooth manifold $N$, an integer $1\le k\le\dim N$, a smooth closed $k$-form $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$, and a finite real smooth singular $k$-cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ with $\partial z=0$, define its period by $\operatorname{Per}_z(\omega):=\int_z\omega:=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$. The form $\omega$ is exact when $\omega=d\alpha$ for a globally defined smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha\in\Omega^{k-1}(N)$. These are mathematical definitions and use no physical constants.

derivations.claim: For any increasing $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$ of size $k$, apply [F1] twice to obtain $\star_\eta^2e^I=\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)e^I$.

The product $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}$ is $-1$, since the two complementary index sets contain the unique negative metric sign exactly once. Reversing the blocks $I,I^c$ uses $k(4-k)$ transpositions, so $s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)=(-1)^{k(4-k)}$. Thus the general square formula follows on the basis $e^I$. For $I=\{0,1\}$, the star is $-e^{23}$; for $I=\{2,3\}$, it is $e^{01}$, which gives the two displayed special cases.

For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.

For a smooth manifold $N$, an integer $1\le k\le\dim N$, a smooth closed $k$-form $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$, and a finite real smooth singular $k$-cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ with $\partial z=0$, define its period by $\operatorname{Per}_z(\omega):=\int_z\omega:=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$. The form $\omega$ is exact when $\omega=d\alpha$ for a globally defined smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha\in\Omega^{k-1}(N)$. These are mathematical definitions and use no physical constants.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

The real **de Rham cohomology** is $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^k(M)/B^k(M)$, with $Z^k,B^k$ as in [[def-closed-and-exact-differential-forms]].

This is [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]] in real vector spaces. Only a closed form $\omega$ represents a class $[\omega]$. For closed forms $\omega,\omega\prime$, equality $[\omega]=[\omega\prime]$ means precisely $\omega\prime-\omega=d\eta$ for some $(k-1)$-form $\eta$. Addition and real scalar multiplication are induced by those of forms. All groups on the empty manifold are zero.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that

is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. For $0\le k\le4$, give $\Lambda^kV^*$ the induced bilinear pairing $\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta:=\frac1{k!}\alpha_{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}\beta^{\mu_1\cdots\mu_k}$, with indices raised by $\eta^{-1}$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.

For a smooth manifold $N$, an integer $1\le k\le\dim N$, a smooth closed $k$-form $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$, and a finite real smooth singular $k$-cycle $z=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\sigma$ with $\partial z=0$, define its period by $\operatorname{Per}_z(\omega):=\int_z\omega:=\sum_\sigma c_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$. The form $\omega$ is exact when $\omega=d\alpha$ for a globally defined smooth $(k-1)$-form $\alpha\in\Omega^{k-1}(N)$. These are mathematical definitions and use no physical constants.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\geq1$, let $M^n$ be oriented, and let $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$. For $1\leq i\leq m$ let $D_i\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded open Jordan domains and $F_i:\overline D_i\to M$ continuous and smooth up to the boundary in target coordinates: near each parameter point, a target coordinate representative extends smoothly to a Euclidean neighborhood. Suppose $F_i|_{D_i}$ is an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism onto an open $W_i\subset M$, the $W_i$ are pairwise disjoint, and $\operatorname{supp}\omega\subset\bigcup_i\overline W_i$. Then
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{i=1}^m\int_{D_i}F_i^*\omega.$$
An empty family is allowed when the support is empty. No nonsingularity of $DF_i$ on $\partial D_i$, and no $M$-valued extension across a genuine target boundary, is assumed.

Let $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:\|p\|_2=1\}$ have its standard embedded smooth structure and outward orientation, let $X(p)=p$, and let $\omega$ be its outward area form, $\omega_p(v,w)=p\cdot(v\times w)$ for tangent vectors $v,w\in T_pS^2$. Put $D=[0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]$ and
$$
\Phi(\theta,\phi)=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta).
$$
The map $\Phi$ presents $S^2$ as a regular parametrized surface patch, with boundary seam and poles allowed by the patch convention. The outward flux of $X$ is
$$
\int_D (X\circ\Phi)\cdot(\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\phi)\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi.
$$
Equivalently, the oriented top-form integral is $\int_{S^2}\omega=4\pi$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open and star-shaped about $a\in U$, meaning $a+t(x-a)\in U$ for every $x\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$. For a smooth closed two-form $F=\frac12F_{\mu\nu}\,dx^\mu\wedge dx^\nu$ on $U$, define the smooth one-form $A=A_\mu dx^\mu$ by

$$A_\mu(x)=\int_0^1 t(x-a)^\nu F_{\nu\mu}(a+t(x-a))\,dt.$$

Then $dA=F$. On any smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, a smooth closed two-form $F$ has a globally defined smooth one-form potential $A$ with $dA=F$ if and only if its de Rham class $[F]\in H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)$ is zero. If a finite smooth singular two-cycle $z$ has nonzero period $\int_zF$, then $F$ is not globally exact.

derivations.claim: Writing $X=(x,y,z)/r^3$, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $d\beta=(\partial_x(xr^{-3})+\partial_y(yr^{-3})+\partial_z(zr^{-3}))\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. By [F2], $\partial_x(xr^{-3})=r^{-3}-3x^2r^{-5}$, with the analogous formulas for $y,z$; their sum is $3r^{-3}-3(x^2+y^2+z^2)r^{-5}=0$. Thus $d\beta=0$ throughout $r>0$.

Write the vertices as $v_0,v_1,v_2,v_3$. Their edge differences from $v_0$ are linearly independent: a relation $a(0,-2,-2)+b(-2,0,-2)+c(-2,-2,0)=0$ forces $b+c=a+c=a+b=0$, hence $a=b=c=0$. Also $v_0+v_1+v_2+v_3=0$, so $0$ is the barycenter with all four positive barycentric coefficients and is strictly inside the tetrahedron. Each face avoids the origin, so $q$ is smooth on a neighborhood of it. The intersection of the compact convex tetrahedron with any ray from $0$ is a bounded interval $[0,t_u]$ with $t_u>0$, so that ray meets $\partial T$ at exactly one point. Thus $q:\partial T\to S^2$ is a bijection. On a face in the plane $n\cdot p=h$ with outward unit normal $n$, one has $h>0$ and the inverse of $q$ is $u\mapsto hu/(n\cdot u)$; hence each face interior maps diffeomorphically to an open spherical patch, the four patch interiors are disjoint, and their closures cover $S^2$. The shared edges of the outward-oriented face simplices have opposite induced orientations, so their signed boundary cancels; since $q$ agrees on shared edges, [F3] gives $\partial z=0$. For face tangent vectors $v,w$, $Dq_p(v)=(v-(q\cdot v)q)/\|p\|_2$, and expanding the cross product after this substitution gives
$$
q\cdot(Dq_p(v)\times Dq_p(w))=\frac{p\cdot(v\times w)}{\|p\|_2^3}>0,
$$
because $p=h n+\text{(tangential part)}$ and [F7] gives $n\cdot(v\times w)>0$ in the outward face orientation. Thus $q$ preserves each face orientation. Expanding the coefficients of $\beta$ gives $\beta_p(v,w)=p\cdot(v\times w)/\|p\|_2^3$; on $S^2$ this is the outward area form $\omega$. By [F8], $\omega$ has compact support. By [F5], the integral over each smooth singular face is its pullback integral, and [F4] sums those integrals to $\int_z\beta$. The face interiors are disjoint and their closures cover $S^2$, so [F9] identifies their sum with $\int_{S^2}\omega$. This is exactly the top-form integral computed by [F10]; hence $\int_z\beta=4\pi$.
Step 1.2 gives $\int_z\beta=4\pi\ne0$. Since step 1.1 proved $d\beta=0$, [F11] makes $\beta$ nonexact on the punctured domain.
