citations.quote:
Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ (with the physical balance
interpretation conditional as in (d)) is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading with continuum coupling] For this clause additionally
adopt [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) for the empty-matter model on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the matter energy density
$w:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, energy flux
$Q:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, momentum density
$p:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ and momentum flux
$P:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ are all identically
zero, as are the source fields $\rho,J$. The adopted electromagnetic force
and power densities are then $f:=\rho E+J\times B=0$ and $J\cdot E=0$,
respectively; the zero matter balances are satisfied. Under this additional
interpretation premise the local identities of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]
and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $A,E,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be any fixed-time fields from the
compactly supported transverse Fourier construction: $A,E,B$ are real Schwartz
fields, $\operatorname{div}A=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$\operatorname{div}E=0$. Use the positively oriented laboratory coordinates
$x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and the fixed origin $0$. Every $\mathbb R^3$-valued
integrand below is integrated componentwise: on $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$, integrate each
of its three real components by the ordinary real Riemann integral. Its
whole-space integral is the finite componentwise cube-exhaustion limit specified
in the preceding Fourier-field Definition; the estimates in the Verification
establish absolute integrability in that definition's sense.
For each scalar component $A_i$, define
$(x\times\nabla)A_i$ to have components
$\sum_{m,j=1}^3\epsilon_{\ell m j}x_m\partial_jA_i$, where
$\epsilon_{\ell m j}$ is the right-handed Levi-Civita symbol in this chart.
Define the total kinetic angular-momentum functional and its Coulomb-gauge
canonical orbital and spin functionals by

$$J_{\mathrm{kin}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times(E\times B)\,d^3x,\qquad L_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\mathbb R^3}E_i(x\times\nabla)A_i\,d^3x,\qquad S_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}E\times A\,d^3x.$$

Each is a finite vector with SI units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The words “kinetic,”
“canonical orbital,” and “spin” are names for these functionals on this fixed
potential class; they do not identify three separately gauge-invariant local
densities. A generic gauge transform is outside this definition's domain.

Use a fixed positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with spatial coordinate
$x\in\mathbb R^3$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, Euclidean dot and cross products, and
the SI vacuum speed $c>0$. A smooth amplitude is a map
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ whose coordinate partial
derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. Require its support
$K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ to be compact and require the bilinear
transversality condition
$k\cdot a(k):=\sum_{j=1}^3 k_j a_j(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. The dot in this
condition is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. The zero extension of $a$
to $k=0$ is understood.

For $R>0$, put $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$. Integrals of continuous real scalar functions on
$Q_R$ are the ordinary real Riemann integrals, defined as the common lower and
upper Darboux value. For a continuous
$F:Q_R\to\mathbb C^m$, define its Riemann integral componentwise by
$$\left(\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3y\right)_j:=\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Re}F_j\,d^3y+i\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Im}F_j\,d^3y\qquad(1\le j\le m),$$
where $y$ denotes the cube coordinates.
This also defines integrals of real vector fields by taking their imaginary
components to be zero; a real scalar is the case $m=1$. For a continuous real
scalar or finite-dimensional real/complex vector field $F$ on $\mathbb R^3$, write
$\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\,d^3x$ for the finite componentwise limit
$\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3x$ when each real-valued component
$\operatorname{Re}F_j$ and $\operatorname{Im}F_j$ has a finite limit. For
$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^m$, say that $F$ is absolutely
integrable when the nonnegative real cube integrals
$$\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(|\operatorname{Re}F_j|+|\operatorname{Im}F_j|\bigr)\,d^3x$$
have a finite limit as $R\to\infty$. For a real scalar integrand this means
that the cube integrals of its absolute value have a finite limit. If this
absolute-integral limit is finite, every real or imaginary component integral
has a finite cube-exhaustion limit. For one such component $h$, set
$I_R:=\int_{Q_R}h$ and let $A_R$ denote the absolute component-sum cube integral
in the preceding display. Finite coordinate-slice additivity and the
absolute-value estimate give $|I_S-I_R|\le A_S-A_R$ for $S>R$. Since $A_R$
is nondecreasing by nonnegativity and additivity, if its limit is $A$ then
$0\le A_S-A_R\le A-A_R\to0$ uniformly for $S\ge R$. Thus these component
integrals are Cauchy as $R\to\infty$. The
integer-radius values form a Cauchy sequence and converge in $\mathbb R$; the
uniform tail bound then gives the same limit for all real radii, because an
integer radius can be chosen above any fixed real threshold. The argument uses
finite coordinate-slice additivity, the Riemann absolute-value estimate, and
completeness of $\mathbb R$. If $F$ is
continuous and compactly supported, its whole-space integral agrees with the
componentwise Riemann integral over any sufficiently large cube containing its
support and is independent of that cube. Every complex- or real-vector
integral below uses this convention. Define
the complex vector potential and its associated real fields by

$$A_+(x,t):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}a(k)\exp\!\bigl(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t)\bigr)\,d^3k,\qquad A:=2\operatorname{Re}A_+,\qquad \varphi:=0,\qquad E:=-\partial_tA,\qquad B:=\operatorname{curl}A.$$

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

derivations.claim:
Since $E_0>0$, $e\ne0$, and direct calculation gives
$k\cdot e=0$, $k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2=b$, and $\omega=c|k|$.
Therefore [F3] gives a smooth source-free Maxwell solution and [F1] makes it
nonzero. By [F2], its period-averaged energy density is
$\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$ and its total energy over $\mathbb R^3$ is infinite.

Every member of the Fourier-packet domain in [F4] has finite energy.
Thus the nonzero wave of step 1.1 does not belong to that domain, refuting the
universal statement. Componentwise formal cancellations do not make these
all-space functionals defined on this field.

Let $A,E,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be any fixed-time fields from the
compactly supported transverse Fourier construction: $A,E,B$ are real Schwartz
fields, $\operatorname{div}A=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$\operatorname{div}E=0$. Use the positively oriented laboratory coordinates
$x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and the fixed origin $0$. For every all-space integral below,
define it as the limit of the Riemann integrals over $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$ as
$R\to\infty$; the estimates in the Verification show absolute convergence.
For each scalar component $A_i$, define
$(x\times\nabla)A_i$ to have components
$\sum_{m,j=1}^3\epsilon_{\ell m j}x_m\partial_jA_i$, where
$\epsilon_{\ell m j}$ is the right-handed Levi-Civita symbol in this chart.

Use a fixed positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with spatial coordinate
$x\in\mathbb R^3$, time $t\in\mathbb R$, Euclidean dot and cross products, and
the SI vacuum speed $c>0$. A smooth amplitude is a map
$a:\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb C^3$ whose coordinate partial
derivatives of every order exist and are continuous. Require its support
$K\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ to be compact and require the bilinear
transversality condition
$k\cdot a(k):=\sum_{j=1}^3 k_j a_j(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. The dot in this
condition is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. The zero extension of $a$
to $k=0$ is understood.

For $R>0$, put $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$. Integrals of continuous real scalar functions on
$Q_R$ are the ordinary real Riemann integrals, defined as the common lower and
upper Darboux value. For a continuous
$F:Q_R\to\mathbb C^m$, define its Riemann integral componentwise by
$$\left(\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3y\right)_j:=\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Re}F_j\,d^3y+i\int_{Q_R}\operatorname{Im}F_j\,d^3y\qquad(1\le j\le m),$$
where $y$ denotes the cube coordinates.
This also defines integrals of real vector fields by taking their imaginary
components to be zero; a real scalar is the case $m=1$. For a continuous real
scalar or finite-dimensional real/complex vector field $F$ on $\mathbb R^3$, write
$\int_{\mathbb R^3}F\,d^3x$ for the finite componentwise limit
$\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{Q_R}F\,d^3x$ when each real-valued component
$\operatorname{Re}F_j$ and $\operatorname{Im}F_j$ has a finite limit. For
$F:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C^m$, say that $F$ is absolutely
integrable when the nonnegative real cube integrals
$$\int_{Q_R}\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(|\operatorname{Re}F_j|+|\operatorname{Im}F_j|\bigr)\,d^3x$$
have a finite limit as $R\to\infty$. For a real scalar integrand this means
that the cube integrals of its absolute value have a finite limit. If this
absolute-integral limit is finite, every real or imaginary component integral
has a finite cube-exhaustion limit. For one such component $h$, set
$I_R:=\int_{Q_R}h$ and let $A_R$ denote the absolute component-sum cube integral
in the preceding display. Finite coordinate-slice additivity and the
absolute-value estimate give $|I_S-I_R|\le A_S-A_R$ for $S>R$. Since $A_R$
is nondecreasing by nonnegativity and additivity, if its limit is $A$ then
$0\le A_S-A_R\le A-A_R\to0$ uniformly for $S\ge R$. Thus these component
integrals are Cauchy as $R\to\infty$. The
integer-radius values form a Cauchy sequence and converge in $\mathbb R$; the
uniform tail bound then gives the same limit for all real radii, because an
integer radius can be chosen above any fixed real threshold. The argument uses
finite coordinate-slice additivity, the Riemann absolute-value estimate, and
completeness of $\mathbb R$. If $F$ is
continuous and compactly supported, its whole-space integral agrees with the
componentwise Riemann integral over any sufficiently large cube containing its
support and is independent of that cube. Every complex- or real-vector
integral below uses this convention. Define
the complex vector potential and its associated real fields by

$$A_+(x,t):=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}a(k)\exp\!\bigl(i(k\cdot x-c|k|t)\bigr)\,d^3k,\qquad A:=2\operatorname{Re}A_+,\qquad \varphi:=0,\qquad E:=-\partial_tA,\qquad B:=\operatorname{curl}A.$$

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ (with the physical balance
interpretation conditional as in (d)) is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading with continuum coupling] For this clause additionally
adopt [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) for the empty-matter model on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the matter energy density
$w:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, energy flux
$Q:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, momentum density
$p:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ and momentum flux
$P:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ are all identically
zero, as are the source fields $\rho,J$. The adopted electromagnetic force
and power densities are then $f:=\rho E+J\times B=0$ and $J\cdot E=0$,
respectively; the zero matter balances are satisfied. Under this additional
interpretation premise the local identities of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]
and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

citations.quote:
Let $A,E,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be any fixed-time fields from the
compactly supported transverse Fourier construction: $A,E,B$ are real Schwartz
fields, $\operatorname{div}A=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$\operatorname{div}E=0$. Use the positively oriented laboratory coordinates
$x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and the fixed origin $0$. Every $\mathbb R^3$-valued
integrand below is integrated componentwise: on $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$, integrate each
of its three real components by the ordinary real Riemann integral. Its
whole-space integral is the finite componentwise cube-exhaustion limit specified
in the preceding Fourier-field Definition; the estimates in the Verification
establish absolute integrability in that definition's sense.
For each scalar component $A_i$, define
$(x\times\nabla)A_i$ to have components
$\sum_{m,j=1}^3\epsilon_{\ell m j}x_m\partial_jA_i$, where
$\epsilon_{\ell m j}$ is the right-handed Levi-Civita symbol in this chart.
Define the total kinetic angular-momentum functional and its Coulomb-gauge
canonical orbital and spin functionals by

$$J_{\mathrm{kin}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times(E\times B)\,d^3x,\qquad L_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\mathbb R^3}E_i(x\times\nabla)A_i\,d^3x,\qquad S_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}E\times A\,d^3x.$$

Each is a finite vector with SI units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The words “kinetic,”
“canonical orbital,” and “spin” are names for these functionals on this fixed
potential class; they do not identify three separately gauge-invariant local
densities. A generic gauge transform is outside this definition's domain.

(a) For the real Schwartz vacuum fields and the fixed Coulomb-gauge potential
defined in the preceding A-page item, let $J_{\mathrm{kin}}$,
$L_{\mathrm{can}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{can}}$ be the three global functionals in
that definition. Then

$$J_{\mathrm{kin}}=L_{\mathrm{can}}+S_{\mathrm{can}}.$$

(b) More generally, let $R>0$ and let $E,A:\overline{Q_R}\to\mathbb R^3$ be restrictions of
$C^1$ maps on a neighborhood of the cube $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$, let
$B=\operatorname{curl}A$. Interpret every $\mathbb R^3$-valued volume integral
below as the vector of its three ordinary real Riemann integrals, using the
componentwise convention in the preceding angular-momentum Definition. The
scalar integral over $\partial Q_R$ means the sum of the ordinary two-dimensional
Riemann integrals over its six faces, with their outward unit normals $n$.
Define
$$J_R:=\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}x\times(E\times B)\,d^3x,\quad L_R:=\varepsilon_0\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{Q_R}E_i(x\times\nabla)A_i\,d^3x,\quad S_R:=\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}E\times A\,d^3x.$$
For each component $\ell\in\{1,2,3\}$,

$$ (J_R)_\ell=(L_R)_\ell+(S_R)_\ell+\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}(\operatorname{div}E)(x\times A)_\ell\,d^3x-\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial Q_R}(n\cdot E)(x\times A)_\ell\,dS. $$

If the volume integrals converge absolutely in the componentwise convention of the preceding
Fourier-field Definition and this boundary term tends to zero as
$R\to\infty$, the corresponding whole-space identity retains the term
$\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}(\operatorname{div}E)(x\times A)\,d^3x$.
Thus the source-free Schwartz equality in (a) uses both
$\operatorname{div}E=0$ and the vanishing surface limit; it is not an equality
of local densities.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]]. No field equation is required to define the vocabulary; the existence theorem recalled in (a) has the additional hypotheses stated there.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. When $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped, $I$ is an interval with at least two elements, and the jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, satisfy $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ in the stated restriction convention, and smooth potentials for smooth data satisfying the same equations; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

derivations.claim: By [F5], $f$ and $g$ are smooth and compactly supported; $g=1$ on the support of $f$. Scaling shows that $f=1$ on the ball of radius $L$, so the cube $[-L/\sqrt3,L/\sqrt3]^3$ lies where $f=1$. Its positive volume and monotonicity of the Riemann integral [F7] imply $\int f\,d^3x>0$. The maps $E,A,B,\rho,J$ in the Example are smooth, and [F4] gives $E=-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$.

Direct differentiation gives $\operatorname{div}E=E_0\partial_1f=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and $\operatorname{div}B=0$, since mixed partial derivatives cancel in the divergence of a curl. Also $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$, because $\partial_tA=-E$, and $\partial_tE=0$. The definition $J=\mu_0^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$ gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Thus all four equations in [A1] hold, with continuous sources. Moreover $\partial_t\rho=0$ and $\operatorname{div}J=0$, so these sources satisfy continuity as well.

At $t=0$, all fields have compact support, so the boundary term in [F1] vanishes on sufficiently large cubes. Gauss's equation in [A1] identifies $\rho=\varepsilon_0\operatorname{div}E$, so [F1] leaves exactly the correction $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\,x\times A(x,0)\,d^3x$.

At $t=0$, $A=A_0g e_2$ and $x\times A=A_0g(-x_3,0,x_1)$ by [F6]. On the support of $f$ and $\partial_1f$, $g=1$ and $\partial_1g=0$. The FTC and iterated integration in [F7] give $\int x_3g\partial_1f\,d^3x=0$ and $\int x_1g\partial_1f\,d^3x=-\int f\,d^3x$. Rescaling $y=x/L$ gives $\int f(x)\,d^3x=L^3\int\chi(y)\,d^3y>0$. Hence $\int\rho\,x\times A(x,0)\,d^3x =-\varepsilon_0E_0A_0L^3(\int\chi(y)\,d^3y)e_3\ne0$.

(a) For the real Schwartz vacuum fields and the fixed Coulomb-gauge potential
defined in the preceding A-page item, let $J_{\mathrm{kin}}$,
$L_{\mathrm{can}}$, and $S_{\mathrm{can}}$ be the three global functionals in
that definition. Then

$$J_{\mathrm{kin}}=L_{\mathrm{can}}+S_{\mathrm{can}}.$$

(b) More generally, let $R>0$ and let $E,A:\overline{Q_R}\to\mathbb R^3$ be restrictions of
$C^1$ maps on a neighborhood of the cube $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$, let
$B=\operatorname{curl}A$. Interpret every $\mathbb R^3$-valued volume integral
below as the vector of its three ordinary real Riemann integrals, using the
componentwise convention in the preceding angular-momentum Definition. The
scalar integral over $\partial Q_R$ means the sum of the ordinary two-dimensional
Riemann integrals over its six faces, with their outward unit normals $n$.
Define
$$J_R:=\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}x\times(E\times B)\,d^3x,\quad L_R:=\varepsilon_0\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{Q_R}E_i(x\times\nabla)A_i\,d^3x,\quad S_R:=\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}E\times A\,d^3x.$$
For each component $\ell\in\{1,2,3\}$,

$$ (J_R)_\ell=(L_R)_\ell+(S_R)_\ell+\varepsilon_0\int_{Q_R}(\operatorname{div}E)(x\times A)_\ell\,d^3x-\varepsilon_0\int_{\partial Q_R}(n\cdot E)(x\times A)_\ell\,dS. $$

If the volume integrals converge absolutely in the componentwise convention of the preceding
Fourier-field Definition and this boundary term tends to zero as
$R\to\infty$, the corresponding whole-space identity retains the term
$\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}(\operatorname{div}E)(x\times A)\,d^3x$.
Thus the source-free Schwartz equality in (a) uses both
$\operatorname{div}E=0$ and the vanishing surface limit; it is not an equality
of local densities.

compactly supported transverse Fourier construction: $A,E,B$ are real Schwartz
fields, $\operatorname{div}A=0$, $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, and
$\operatorname{div}E=0$. Use the positively oriented laboratory coordinates
$x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ and the fixed origin $0$. Every $\mathbb R^3$-valued
integrand below is integrated componentwise: on $Q_R=[-R,R]^3$, integrate each
of its three real components by the ordinary real Riemann integral. Its
whole-space integral is the finite componentwise cube-exhaustion limit specified
in the preceding Fourier-field Definition; the estimates in the Verification
establish absolute integrability in that definition's sense.
For each scalar component $A_i$, define
$(x\times\nabla)A_i$ to have components
$\sum_{m,j=1}^3\epsilon_{\ell m j}x_m\partial_jA_i$, where
$\epsilon_{\ell m j}$ is the right-handed Levi-Civita symbol in this chart.
Define the total kinetic angular-momentum functional and its Coulomb-gauge
canonical orbital and spin functionals by

$$J_{\mathrm{kin}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times(E\times B)\,d^3x,\qquad L_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\sum_{i=1}^3\int_{\mathbb R^3}E_i(x\times\nabla)A_i\,d^3x,\qquad S_{\mathrm{can}}:=\varepsilon_0\int_{\mathbb R^3}E\times A\,d^3x.$$

Each is a finite vector with SI units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The words “kinetic,”
“canonical orbital,” and “spin” are names for these functionals on this fixed
potential class; they do not identify three separately gauge-invariant local
densities. A generic gauge transform is outside this definition's domain.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.
