supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a named positively oriented inertial laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$, spatial domain $\mathbb R^3$, and time domain $\mathbb R$. Adopt SI
units, a vacuum speed $c>0$, an angular frequency $\omega>0$, and
$k_0:=\omega/c$ (so $[k_0]=\mathrm{m}^{-1}$). Let
$\mathbf x_\perp:=(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. Use the unitary two-dimensional
Fourier transform $\mathcal F_2$ whose Schwartz-space convention is
$$\widehat f(\boldsymbol\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}f(\mathbf x_\perp) e^{-2\pi i\mathbf x_\perp\cdot\boldsymbol\xi}\,d^2\mathbf x_\perp,$$
and whose inverse is its unitary $L^2$ extension. The variable
$\boldsymbol\xi$ is in cycles per metre; its associated angular spatial
wavevector is $\mathbf q:=2\pi\boldsymbol\xi$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$, with
$|\mathbf q|^2:=q_x^2+q_y^2$.

Choose $0<\delta<1$ and $u_0\in L^2(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathcal F_2u_0$ supported, up to null sets, in
$D_\delta:=\{\boldsymbol\xi:|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|\le\delta k_0\}$.
For $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$ put
$$k_z(\boldsymbol\xi):=\sqrt{k_0^2-|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2},$$
which is real and strictly positive there. For each $z\in\mathbb R$, define the
exact multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=\begin{cases}e^{izk_z(\boldsymbol\xi)},&\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta,\\0,&\boldsymbol\xi\notin D_\delta,\end{cases}$$
and define the paraxial multiplier on all of $\mathbb R^2$ by
$$m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi):=e^{ik_0z}e^{-iz|2\pi\boldsymbol\xi|^2/(2k_0)}.$$
The exact scalar and paraxial scalar propagators are the $L^2$ equivalence
classes
$$u_{\mathrm{exact}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{exact}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right],\qquad u_{\mathrm{par}}(z):=\mathcal F_2^{-1}\!\left[m_{\mathrm{par}}(z,\boldsymbol\xi)\,\mathcal F_2u_0(\boldsymbol\xi)\right].$$
The associated real scalar fields are the real parts of these phasors multiplied
by $e^{-i\omega t}$. If $u_0$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, both propagated
fields carry the same unit. “Exact” here names the exact positive axial
dispersion multiplier inside this scalar model; it does not assert exact
Maxwell validity. Forward propagation is $z\ge0$; the formulas also define the
mathematical continuation to negative $z$.

At a fixed $\boldsymbol\xi\in D_\delta$, write
$\mathbf K(\boldsymbol\xi):=(2\pi\xi_x,2\pi\xi_y,k_z(\boldsymbol\xi))$.
A candidate monochromatic vector plane-wave mode at frequency $\omega$ has
complex amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$ in the real-field
encoding $e^{i(\mathbf K\cdot(x,y,z)-\omega t)}$. It is called an exact
source-free vacuum mode only when its associated real fields satisfy the
adopted source-free vacuum Maxwell equations. The longitudinal electric
coefficient is $e_z$, and
$\mathbf e_\perp:=(e_x,e_y)$ has norm
$|\mathbf e_\perp|^2:=|e_x|^2+|e_y|^2$. No scalar/vector polarization
factorization is part of this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j=1}^3k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. $$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of The derivative and the Riemann integral of a vector-valued function: an intrinsic derivative and a componentwise integral.

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5, The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.

derivations.claim: In positive dimension, if $M_ex=0$, then $x^TM_ex=0$, so positive definiteness gives $x=0$; the same argument applies to $M_b$. In dimension zero the unique square matrix is the identity map on the singleton space and is invertible. Thus both matrices are injective and hence invertible in their finite-dimensional domains, so their inverse operations used by consumers are defined in every allowed dimension.

For $u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$ and $v\in\ker C$, $\langle C^Tu,v\rangle=u^TCv=0$, hence $\operatorname{im}C^T\subseteq(\ker C)^\perp$. Also $z\in(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp$ exactly when $u^TCz=0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$, which is exactly $Cz=0$; therefore $(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp=\ker C$. By [F1], decompose any $w\in(\ker C)^\perp$ as $w=u+v$ with $u\in\operatorname{im}C^T$ and $v\in(\operatorname{im}C^T)^\perp=\ker C$. Both $w$ and $u$ are orthogonal to $v$, so $\lVert v\rVert^2=\langle w-u,v\rangle=0$ and $v=0$. Hence $(\ker C)^\perp=\operatorname{im}C^T$.
Assume $\operatorname{im}G=\ker C$. If $q=0$, then $G^TM_ee=0$, so $M_ee$ is orthogonal to every column of $G$ and hence to $\ker C$. By step 1.2, $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T$.

Conversely, if $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T$, then step 1.2 gives $M_ee\in(\ker C)^\perp$. Every column of $G$ lies in $\ker C$, so $G^TM_ee=0$ and therefore $q=0$. The two implications prove the stated characterization.

Let $n_e,n_b,n_c,n_g$ be nonnegative integers. For dimension zero, $\mathbb R^0$ has its single empty vector and its unique square matrix acts as the identity on that space. Choose real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, meaning $M_e^T=M_e$, $M_b^T=M_b$, $x^TM_ex>0$ for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and $y^TM_by>0$ for every nonzero $y\in\mathbb R^{n_b}$; these positivity conditions are vacuous on $\mathbb R^0$. Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. These are finite real matrix data; no mesh or continuum field is assumed.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

For bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, in the metric sense of [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], its **Jordan outer content** is the infimum of $\sum_{r<q}\operatorname{vol}(R_r)$ over finite axis-parallel rectangle covers of $E$. Its **Jordan inner content** is the supremum of the same sums over finite families of rectangles contained in $E$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint.

Metric boundedness always supplies a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. For
nonempty $E$, choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^m$ and $r>0$ with
$E\subseteq B(x_0,r)$. Since
$|x_j-(x_0)_j|\le d_\infty(x,x_0)\le d_2(x,x_0)<r$ for every coordinate
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, [[def-metric-ball]]), the nondegenerate box
$\prod_{j<m}[(x_0)_j-r,(x_0)_j+r]$ contains $E$. The empty set lies in
any fixed nondegenerate rectangle.

Thus the outer family is nonempty and the same bounding rectangle bounds the
inner sums; the empty family gives inner sum $0$. Refining all listed
endpoints into one grid and splitting the nested finite sums shows every
inscribed sum is at most every covering sum
([[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).
Completeness therefore supplies finite real extrema
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]],
[[lem-sup-unique]]).

The set is **Jordan measurable** when the contents agree, and their common value is its **Jordan content**. The empty set and every degenerate rectangle have content $0$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

derivations.claim: Put $z=(e,b)\in\mathbb R^{n_e+n_b}$ and define $A:=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}S&M_e^{-1}C^TM_b\\-C&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $f(t):=\begin{pmatrix}-M_e^{-1}j(t)\\0\end{pmatrix}$. The inverses exist by positive definiteness in [F1]: if $M_ex=0$, then $x^TM_ex=0$ forces $x=0$, and an injective square map in finite dimensions is invertible; the same holds for $M_b$. Thus the system is exactly $z'=Az+f(t)$.

Let $g(s):=e^{-(s-t_0)A}f(s)$ and $H(t):=\int_{t_0}^t g(s)\,ds$, interpreting each coordinate as a Riemann integral and using the oriented convention $\int_a^b=-\int_b^a$ when $b<a$ and $\int_a^a=0$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, then $g(s)$ and $H(t)$ are the unique empty vector for all $s,t$, so $H'=g$ vacuously. Otherwise, on every nondegenerate compact segment in $I$, each coordinate of $g$ is continuous, so [F3] gives integrability and [F4] defines $H$. For each coordinate $k$, the cut-additivity in [F6], together with the oriented convention, gives $H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)=\int_t^{t+h}g_k(s)\,ds$ whenever $t,t+h\in I$: positive-oriented additivity follows by splitting at an interior point, and reversing endpoints or using a zero-length interval gives the other endpoint orders. Thus, for $h\ne0$, $\frac{H_k(t+h)-H_k(t)}{h}-g_k(t)=\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds$, where [F7] evaluates the integral of the constant $g_k(t)$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, continuity of $g_k$ at $t$ gives $\delta>0$ such that $|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|<\varepsilon$ whenever $|s-t|<\delta$; since $I$ is open, reduce $\delta$ so $[t-\delta,t+\delta]\subset I$. If $0<|h|<\delta$, then on $J=[\min(t,t+h),\max(t,t+h)]$ the absolute-value estimate and monotonicity in [F6], followed by [F7], give $\left|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}(g_k(s)-g_k(t))\,ds\right|\le\frac1{|h|}\int_J|g_k(s)-g_k(t)|\,ds\le\varepsilon$. Therefore each coordinate has derivative $g_k(t)$ and $H'(t)=g(t)$ throughout $I$.

Define $z(t):=e^{(t-t_0)A}(z_0+H(t))$, where $z_0=(e_0,b_0)$. By [F2] and step 1.2, the product rule gives $z'=Az+f(t)$, since $e^{(t-t_0)A}e^{-(t-t_0)A}=I$ by the commuting-product identity in [F2]; also $z(t_0)=z_0$. Thus a $C^1$ solution exists on all of $I$. If $n_e+n_b=0$, every state is the unique empty vector, so the solution is unique. Otherwise, if $\widetilde z$ is another solution with the same initial value, then $\xi(t):=e^{-(t-t_0)A}(\widetilde z(t)-z(t))$ has derivative zero by [F2] and the two differential equations. Each coordinate of $\xi$ is constant by [F5] and vanishes at $t_0$, so $\widetilde z=z$.

Differentiate $W=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$ and substitute the system equations. Symmetry of $M_e,M_b$ gives $\dot W=e^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)+b^TM_b(-Ce)=-e^TSe-e^Tj$, because the real scalar cross terms $e^TC^TM_bb$ and $b^TM_bCe$ are equal and cancel.
The magnetic quantity satisfies $(Db)'=D\dot b=-DCe=0$ by [F1]; each coordinate is constant by [F5], and its value at $t_0$ is $Db(t_0)$.
Since $q=-G^TM_ee$, differentiation and the first system equation give $\dot q=-G^T(C^TM_bb-Se-j)=-(CG)^TM_bb+G^T(Se+j)=G^T(Se+j)$, using $CG=0$ from [F1]. This proves all three identities.

Choose $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, a symmetric positive semidefinite $S\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$, meaning $S^T=S$ and $x^TSx\ge0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^{n_e}$, and matrices $D\in\mathbb R^{n_c\times n_b}$ and $G\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_g}$ satisfying $DC=0$ and $CG=0$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ be continuous, and let candidate states $e:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ and $b:I\to\mathbb R^{n_b}$ be of class $C^1$. The **finite compatible matrix system** is

$$M_e\dot e(t)=C^TM_bb(t)-Se(t)-j(t),\qquad \dot b(t)=-Ce(t)\quad(t\in I).$$

Its quadratic **energy** is $W(e,b):=\tfrac12(e^TM_ee+b^TM_bb)$. Its magnetic constraint is the vector $Db\in\mathbb R^{n_c}$. For the chosen $G$, its weak-divergence coordinate is $q:=-G^TM_ee\in\mathbb R^{n_g}$. The term “weak-divergence” names this finite-dimensional quantity only. If the columns of $G$ form a basis of $\ker C:=\{v\in\mathbb R^{n_e}:Cv=0\}$, then $q=0$ exactly when $M_ee\in\operatorname{im}C^T:=\{C^Tu:u\in\mathbb R^{n_b}\}$.

Inputs are real matrices $M_e\in\mathbb R^{n_e\times n_e}$ and $M_b\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_b}$ that are symmetric positive definite, $C\in\mathbb R^{n_b\times n_e}$, and compatible matrices $D,G$ satisfying $DC=CG=0$, with $S=0$ and $j\equiv0$ in the finite compatible matrix system. $$b_{n+1/2}:=b_{n-1/2}-hCe_n,$$

derivations.claim: For a zero-dimensional mass space, the unique square matrix is the identity, its own inverse, and its root. In positive dimension, $M_e$ and $M_b$ are symmetric and therefore self-adjoint in the standard Euclidean inner product; by [F1] each has an orthonormal eigenbasis. If $v$ is a unit eigenvector of either matrix with eigenvalue $\lambda$, positive definiteness in [F6] gives $\lambda=v^TMv>0$. Define the square root to act by $\sqrt\lambda$ on the full $\lambda$-eigenspace, and its inverse to act by $1/\sqrt\lambda$ there. These definitions are independent of a basis choice within an eigenspace, satisfy $(M^{1/2})^2=M$ and $M^{-1/2}M^{1/2}=I$, and agree with the Statement's root convention.

Let $x_n=M_e^{1/2}e_n$ and $y_{n-1/2}=M_b^{1/2}b_{n-1/2}$. Multiplying the first update in [F7] by $M_b^{1/2}$ gives $y_{n+1/2}=y_{n-1/2}-hKx_n$. Multiplying the second update by $M_e^{1/2}$ and using the root identities from step 1.1 gives $x_{n+1}=x_n+hK^Ty_{n+1/2}$.

Write $x=x_n$, $y=y_{n-1/2}$, $y'=y_{n+1/2}$, and $x'=x_{n+1}$. From step 2.1, $x'=x+hK^Ty'$ and $y'=y-hKx$. Expanding gives $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2=\lVert x\rVert_2^2+2h(y')^TKx+h^2\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$, $\lVert y'\rVert_2^2=\lVert y\rVert_2^2-2hy^TKx+h^2\lVert Kx\rVert_2^2$, and $-h(y')^TKx'=-h(y')^TKx-h^2\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$.

Suppose $h\lVert K\rVert_2>2$. By the zero-domain clause of [F3], the domain is nonzero; [F2]–[F4] then give unit right and left singular vectors $v,u$ for $\sigma=\lVert K\rVert_2$, with $Kv=\sigma u$ and $K^Tu=\sigma v$. The recurrence in step 2.1 preserves the two-dimensional coefficient subspace $x=av$, $y=bu$ and sends $(a,b)^T$ by $T_\sigma:=\begin{pmatrix}1-h^2\sigma^2&h\sigma\\-h\sigma&1\end{pmatrix}$. Its trace is $2-h^2\sigma^2<-2$ and determinant is $1$. Its characteristic polynomial has two distinct real negative reciprocal roots, one with modulus greater than $1$. An eigenvector for that root is an expanding singular mode.

Adding the identities in step 3.1 cancels the $\lVert K^Ty'\rVert_2^2$ terms; substituting $y'=y-hKx$ in the remainder gives $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\lVert y'\rVert_2^2-h(y')^TKx'=\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2-hy^TKx$. Therefore $E_h(x',y')=E_h(x,y)$ at each update.

By [F5] and [F3]–[F4], $|y^TKx|\le\lVert y\rVert_2\lVert Kx\rVert_2\le\lVert K\rVert_2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$. Since $2\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2\le\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2$, the cross term in $E_h$ has absolute value at most $\tfrac12h\lVert K\rVert_2(\lVert x\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2)$. Substitution gives both displayed energy bounds, whose lower coefficient is strictly positive when $h\lVert K\rVert_2<2$.

For every update, [F7] and [F6] give $Db_{n+1/2}=Db_{n-1/2}-hDCe_n=Db_{n-1/2}$, so induction preserves $Db$. The loop in [F7] has exactly the finite index set $0,\ldots,N-1$; each exact mass solve is unique by [F6] and step 1.1. It therefore terminates after $N$ updates, including the case $N=0$.

$$\frac{1-h\lVert K\rVert_2/2}{2}\bigl(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n-1/2}\rVert_2^2\bigr)\le E_h(x_n,y_{n-1/2})\le\frac{1+h\lVert K\rVert_2/2}{2}\bigl(\lVert x_n\rVert_2^2+\lVert y_{n-1/2}\rVert_2^2\bigr).$$

Consequently this modified energy is positive definite under the strict CFL condition. The constraint $Db_{n-1/2}$ is preserved. If $h\lVert K\rVert_2>2$, an expanding singular mode exists. Equality at $h\lVert K\rVert_2=2$ is excluded from both assertions; no stability claim is made there.

derivations.claim: These one-dimensional data satisfy the matrix assumptions of the algorithm. Their positive mass roots equal $1$, so [F2] gives $K=[1]$ and $h\lVert K\rVert_2=2$, exactly the endpoint in the refuted extension.

Write $z_n:=(e_n,b_{n-1/2})^T$. By [F1], $z_{n+1}=Az_n$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}-3&2\\-2&1\end{pmatrix}$. Set $J:=A+I=\begin{pmatrix}-2&2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives $J\ne0$ and $J^2=0$, so $A=-(I-J)$ and the binomial formula yields $A^n=(-1)^n(I-nJ)$ for every integer $n\ge0$.

For the nonzero initial state $z_0=(1,0)^T$, one has $Jz_0=(-2,-2)^T\ne0$. The reverse triangle inequality therefore gives $\lVert z_n\rVert_2=\lVert z_0-nJz_0\rVert_2\ge n\lVert Jz_0\rVert_2-\lVert z_0\rVert_2=2\sqrt2\,n-1$. These outputs occur in the algorithm for each finite horizon $N\ge n$ and their norm ratio to $\lVert z_0\rVert_2$ is unbounded as $n$ grows. No constant $C$ independent of $N$ can satisfy the refuted estimate.

Let epsilon,mu:Omega -> Sym_3(R) be measurable, essentially bounded, time-independent coefficient fields with constants 0<a_epsilon<=b_epsilon<infinity and 0<a_mu<=b_mu<infinity such that almost everywhere

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^3).$$

Their units are F m^-1 and H m^-1. Pointwise inversion makes mu^-1 measurable, symmetric and essentially bounded, with eigenvalues between b_mu^-1 and a_mu^-1. These coefficient fields are explicit local model data; no material-realization or constitutive derivation is asserted. Let sigma:Omega -> Sym_3(R) be another measurable, essentially bounded, time-independent field with sigma(x) positive semidefinite almost everywhere and units S m^-1. Let J_ext:I -> L^2(Omega;R^3) be continuous in time and have units A m^-2.

Define the real matrices and current-load vector by

$$ (M_e)_{ij}:=\int_\Omega \phi_i\cdot\varepsilon\phi_j\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{\alpha\beta}:=\int_\Omega \psi_\alpha\cdot\mu^{-1}\psi_\beta\,dx,\qquad S_{ij}:=\int_\Omega\phi_i\cdot\sigma\phi_j\,dx,\qquad j_i(t):=\int_\Omega\phi_i\cdot J_{\rm ext}(x,t)\,dx.$$

All integrals are finite because the mesh is finite, its basis functions are piecewise polynomial, and the coefficient fields are essentially bounded. M_e and M_b are symmetric positive definite on nonzero basis spaces: their quadratic forms are the positive coefficient-weighted L^2 norms of the represented fields; if a basis space is zero-dimensional, the positive-definiteness condition is vacuous. S is symmetric positive semidefinite. The oriented matrices satisfy DC=CG=0. The edge coefficients e_i have units V and the edge basis functions units m^-1; the face coefficients b_alpha have units Wb and the face basis functions units m^-2. The incidence matrices C,D,G are dimensionless, M_e has units F, M_b has units H^-1, S has units S, and j has units A.

For C1 coefficient vectors e:I -> R^ne and b:I -> R^nb, define E_h(t):=sum_i e_i(t)phi_i and B_h(t):=sum_alpha b_alpha(t)psi_alpha, and put H_h:=mu^-1 B_h in L^2. The perfect-electric-conductor (PEC) semidiscrete model is the weak Galerkin system

$$\int_\Omega \bigl(\varepsilon\,\partial_t E_h+\sigma E_h+J_{\rm ext}\bigr)\cdot v_h\,dx=\int_\Omega H_h\cdot\operatorname{curl}v_h\,dx\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad \partial_t B_h=-\operatorname{curl}E_h\quad\text{in }M_h.$$

Here H_h is required only to be L^2; no H(curl) regularity or boundary trace for it is asserted. Testing the first identity against the edge basis and expanding the second in the face basis gives exactly M_e dot e=C^T M_b b-Se-j and dot b=-Ce, the finite compatible matrix system.

For the finite compatible matrix system on an open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, let $t_0\in I$, choose initial data $e(t_0)=e_0$ and $b(t_0)=b_0$, and assume the forcing $j:I\to\mathbb R^{n_e}$ is continuous. There is a unique $C^1$ solution $(e,b)$ on all of $I$. At every $t\in I$ it satisfies

$$\frac{d}{dt}W(e(t),b(t))=-e(t)^TSe(t)-e(t)^Tj(t),\qquad Db(t)=Db(t_0),\qquad \dot q(t)=G^T(Se(t)+j(t)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open and set
$$H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)}^{\,H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)},$$
where the norm is that of [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. This is the closure-defined zero-tangential subspace used on this page. Identifying this closure with the full kernel of a particular boundary trace map is not part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute in degrees zero through two on the homogeneous complex; the terminal degree-three differential is zero. In particular,
$$\pi_{h,0}^0:H_0^1(\Omega)\to W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\qquad \pi_{h,0}^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),\qquad \nabla\pi_{h,0}^0=\pi_{h,0}^1\nabla.$$
Here the zero tangential space uses [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Each family converges strongly in $L^2$ on every $L^2$ form, uniformly on compact $L^2$ subsets, and in the graph norm on its corresponding graph domain. The full and homogeneous families are separate operators. These are cochain projections; canonical edge moments are not asserted bounded on $H(\operatorname{curl})$.

For C1 coefficient vectors e:I -> R^ne and b:I -> R^nb, define E_h(t):=sum_i e_i(t)phi_i and B_h(t):=sum_alpha b_alpha(t)psi_alpha, and put H_h:=mu^-1 B_h in L^2. The perfect-electric-conductor (PEC) semidiscrete model is the weak Galerkin system

$$\int_\Omega \bigl(\varepsilon\,\partial_t E_h+\sigma E_h+J_{\rm ext}\bigr)\cdot v_h\,dx=\int_\Omega H_h\cdot\operatorname{curl}v_h\,dx\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad \partial_t B_h=-\operatorname{curl}E_h\quad\text{in }M_h.$$

Here H_h is required only to be L^2; no H(curl) regularity or boundary trace for it is asserted. Testing the first identity against the edge basis and expanding the second in the face basis gives exactly M_e dot e=C^T M_b b-Se-j and dot b=-Ce, the finite compatible matrix system.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

derivations.claim: The distributional graph of curl is closed: if v_j->v and curl v_j->w in L^2, then for every compactly supported smooth test field phi, integral(v dot curl phi)=lim_j integral(v_j dot curl phi)=lim_j integral(curl v_j dot phi)=integral(w dot phi); hence curl v=w distributionally. L^2 is complete under [A1] and [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], so H(curl;Omega) is Hilbert, and its graph-closed subspace H_0(curl;Omega) is Hilbert. Since ell_0 is fixed and positive, ||.||_{V,ell_0} is equivalent to the defining graph norm and gives the same complete space.

From [F1], the eigenvalues of mu^-1 lie between b_mu^-1 and a_mu^-1. Therefore a_s(v,v)>=b_mu^-1||curl v||_2^2+s^2a_epsilon||v||_2^2>=alpha||v||_{V,ell_0}^2. Cauchy-Schwarz and the upper coefficient bounds give |a_s(u,v)|<=a_mu^-1||curl u||_2||curl v||_2+s^2b_epsilon||u||_2||v||_2<=M||u||_{V,ell_0}||v||_{V,ell_0}. Since s has units s^-1, ell_0 has units m, and epsilon and mu have units F m^-1 and H m^-1 by [F1], both constants have units (H m)^-1; alpha>0 and M<infinity by the stated strict bounds.

Apply [F3] to the real Hilbert space and form of steps 1.1-1.2 to obtain the unique u. By [F6], each V_n is finite-dimensional and closed in V; restricting the same bounded coercive form and F to V_n gives the unique Galerkin solution u_n, including the zero-space case. If F=0, the zero vector is the solution on V and on every V_n by uniqueness.

Put e_n:=u-u_n. For any w_n in V_n, Galerkin orthogonality gives a_s(e_n,u_n-w_n)=0, so a_s(e_n,e_n)=a_s(e_n,u-w_n). Coercivity and boundedness from step 1.2 imply alpha||e_n||_{V,ell_0}^2<=a_s(e_n,e_n)<=M||e_n||_{V,ell_0}||u-w_n||_{V,ell_0}. If e_n=0 the asserted estimate is immediate; otherwise divide by alpha||e_n|| and take the infimum over w_n.

By [F4], pi_{h_n,0}^1 u belongs to V_n and converges to u in the unscaled H(curl) graph norm; equivalence of the fixed ell_0-scaled norm gives ||u-pi_{h_n,0}^1u||_{V,ell_0}->0. Thus the best-approximation infimum in step 3.1 tends to zero, and the error estimate proves u_n->u in V,ell_0. No interpolation by pointwise edge restrictions is used.
