The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ have a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T$ as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. The H(curl) and H(div) graph-space conventions used below carry their stated Countable Choice assumptions. Choose one orientation for every mesh edge and face and the ambient orientation for each tetrahedron, with incidence signs given by [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]]. Write $t_e$ for the unit tangent in the chosen direction of an edge $e$, and $n_F$ for the unit normal determined by the chosen orientation of a face $F$ and the ambient orientation. On a tetrahedron $K$ with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, list the vertices in any order and let $P_1(K)$ denote scalar polynomials of total degree at most one. For an ordered edge $[i,j]$, put $\phi_{ij}=\lambda_i\nabla\lambda_j-\lambda_j\nabla\lambda_i$; reversing its orientation changes the sign. Set
$$W_h^0:=\{q\in C^0(\overline\Omega):q|_K\in P_1(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The first-family lowest-order Nedelec space is
$$N_h^1:=\{u\in H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega):u|_K\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_{ij}:0\le i<j\le3\}\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global edge }e\text{ has one common oriented circulation }\int_e u|_K\cdot t_e\,ds\text{ for all }K\supset e\}.$$
The local Raviart–Thomas space is $RT_0(K)=\{a+c x:a\in\mathbb R^3,\ c\in\mathbb R\}$. With $H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ as defined by [[def-na-hdiv-space]], set
$$N_h^2:=\{v\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega):v|_K\in RT_0(K)\text{ for every }K\in\mathcal T,\text{ and every global face }F\text{ has one common oriented flux }\int_F v|_K\cdot n_F\,dS\text{ for all }K\supset F\},\qquad N_h^3:=\{q\in L^2(\Omega):q|_K\text{ is constant for every }K\in\mathcal T\}.$$
The covariant affine Piola map for $N_h^1$ and contravariant affine Piola map for $N_h^2$ use the orientation-preserving cell maps and conventions of [[def-covariant-contravariant-piola-maps-and-hdiv-hcurl]]. Their differential and moment identities are those of [[thm-affine-piola-differential-and-trace-moment-identities]]. The edge, face, and cell degrees of freedom are respectively the oriented edge circulation, oriented face-normal flux, and cell integral.

In the two conformity conditions above, each cellwise polynomial restriction has a unique polynomial representative on its closed cell, and those representatives define the displayed edge and face integrals. Thus the global edge and face moments are part of the assembled-space definition; their correspondence with all cochains is proved by the local unisolvence and commuting-moment items, not inferred from rough-field traces.

Assume Countable Choice for the H(curl), H(div), and real $L^2$ inner-product interfaces used here; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed. Let $\mathcal T$ be a finite matching tetrahedral mesh with realization $|\mathcal T|=\overline\Omega$. Define $C_k(\mathcal T;\mathbb R)$ by extending the oriented chain groups of [[def-oriented-simplicial-cell-chains]] to real coefficients, and put $C^k=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k,\mathbb R)$ with coboundary $\delta^k=\partial_{k+1}^*$. The degrees of freedom give a cochain isomorphism from
$$W_h^0\xrightarrow{\nabla}N_h^1\xrightarrow{\operatorname{curl}}N_h^2\xrightarrow{\operatorname{div}}N_h^3$$
to $C^0\xrightarrow{\delta^0}C^1\xrightarrow{\delta^1}C^2\xrightarrow{\delta^2}C^3$. Consequently the discrete cohomology in degree $k$ is naturally isomorphic to $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R),\mathbb R)$. If $\overline\Omega$ is nonempty, connected, and contractible, then the sequence is exact at every positive-degree space, $\ker\nabla$ consists of constants, and $\operatorname{div}:N_h^2\to N_h^3$ is onto. For general topology, define
$$\mathcal H_h^1:=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{N_h^1})\cap(\nabla W_h^0)^\perp,\qquad \mathcal H_h^2:=\ker(\operatorname{div}|_{N_h^2})\cap(\operatorname{curl}N_h^1)^\perp$$
using the $L^2$ inner product. Then $\ker\operatorname{curl}=\nabla W_h^0\oplus\mathcal H_h^1$ and $\ker\operatorname{div}=\operatorname{curl}N_h^1\oplus\mathcal H_h^2$, with $\dim\mathcal H_h^k=\dim H_k(|\mathcal T|;\mathbb R)$ for $k=1,2$.

Assume Countable Choice as in the real L^2 and weak-derivative conventions. Let I be a nonempty open interval in R, and let Omega be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in one SI laboratory frame under [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let T be a finite matching affine tetrahedral mesh with realization closure(Omega), with mesh and orientation conventions as in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Use the real graph space H(curl;Omega) of [[def-na-hcurl-space]] and define H_0(curl;Omega) by the closure of C_c^\infty(Omega;R^3) in that graph norm, as in [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Define H_0^1(Omega) as the closure of C_c^\infty(Omega;R) in W^{1,2}(Omega;R), using the norm and closure conventions of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]].

Let W_h^0 be the continuous piecewise P1 scalar space, where P1(K) is the real scalar-polynomial space of total degree at most one on tetrahedron K. On K with barycentric coordinates lambda_0,...,lambda_3, the lowest-order Whitney edge space is spanned by phi_ij=lambda_i grad(lambda_j)-lambda_j grad(lambda_i) for its six oriented edges. Globally N_h^1 consists of these piecewise fields with one common oriented circulation integral_e u dot t_e ds on each shared edge e, where t_e is its chosen unit tangent; it is H(curl)-conforming. The face space N_h^2 consists of piecewise RT0 fields, RT0(K)={x -> a+c x:a in R3,c in R}, with one common oriented flux integral_F u dot n_F dS on each shared face F, where n_F is its oriented unit normal; it is H(div)-conforming in the graph space [[def-na-hdiv-space]]. N_h^3 consists of cellwise constants. These spaces are the full spaces in [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Set S_h := W_h^0 intersect H_0^1(Omega), V_h := N_h^1 intersect H_0(curl;Omega), and M_h := N_h^2. The finite-dimensional map grad:S_h -> V_h is well-defined: for q in S_h, its weak gradient is L^2, curl(grad q)=0 distributionally, and a sequence from C_c^\infty converging to q in W^{1,2} has gradients converging to grad q in H(curl); also, on each tetrahedron grad q is constant and its common edge circulation is the endpoint difference of the single continuous function q. Take the canonical full-space nodal and edge reference bases from [[def-na-lowest-order-whitney-de-rham-spaces]]. Since S_h and V_h are finite-dimensional subspaces of the full nodal and edge spaces, choose any bases chi_1,...,chi_ng of S_h and phi_1,...,phi_ne of V_h obtained by dimensionless real linear combinations of those reference bases. Choose psi_1,...,psi_nb for M_h dual to all oriented face-flux degrees of freedom, and theta_1,...,theta_nc for N_h^3 dual to the cell-integral degrees of freedom, with theta_l=|K_l|^-1 on cell K_l and zero on the other cells. Thus chi_j is dimensionless, phi_i has units m^-1, psi_alpha has units m^-2, and theta_l has units m^-3. Define the real coordinate matrices C,D,G by curl(phi_i)=sum_alpha C_{alpha i} psi_alpha, div(psi_alpha)=sum_l D_{l alpha} theta_l, and grad(chi_j)=sum_i G_{ij} phi_i. These matrices are dimensionless representations of the oriented differentials; D is the face-to-cell incidence matrix in the face-moment basis, and changes of basis in S_h,V_h give the corresponding matrices for their PEC subspaces. Because curl grad=0 and div curl=0 on the full finite-element complex, DC=0 and CG=0. Here D denotes only the magnetic face-to-cell incidence matrix.

Write Sym_3(R) for the real symmetric 3 by 3 matrices. Let epsilon,mu:Omega -> Sym_3(R) be measurable, essentially bounded, time-independent coefficient fields with constants 0<a_epsilon<=b_epsilon<infinity and 0<a_mu<=b_mu<infinity such that almost everywhere

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2\quad(v\in\mathbb R^3).$$

Their units are F m^-1 and H m^-1. Pointwise inversion makes mu^-1 measurable, symmetric and essentially bounded, with eigenvalues between b_mu^-1 and a_mu^-1. These coefficient fields are explicit local model data; no material-realization or constitutive derivation is asserted. Let sigma:Omega -> Sym_3(R) be another measurable, essentially bounded, time-independent field with sigma(x) positive semidefinite almost everywhere and units S m^-1. Let J_ext:I -> L^2(Omega;R^3) be continuous in time and have units A m^-2.

Define the real matrices and current-load vector by

$$ (M_e)_{ij}:=\int_\Omega \phi_i\cdot\varepsilon\phi_j\,dx,\qquad (M_b)_{\alpha\beta}:=\int_\Omega \psi_\alpha\cdot\mu^{-1}\psi_\beta\,dx,\qquad S_{ij}:=\int_\Omega\phi_i\cdot\sigma\phi_j\,dx,\qquad j_i(t):=\int_\Omega\phi_i\cdot J_{\rm ext}(x,t)\,dx.$$

All integrals are finite because the mesh is finite, its basis functions are piecewise polynomial, and the coefficient fields are essentially bounded. M_e and M_b are symmetric positive definite on nonzero basis spaces: their quadratic forms are the positive coefficient-weighted L^2 norms of the represented fields; if a basis space is zero-dimensional, the positive-definiteness condition is vacuous. S is symmetric positive semidefinite. The oriented matrices satisfy DC=CG=0. The edge coefficients e_i have units V and the edge basis functions units m^-1; the face coefficients b_alpha have units Wb and the face basis functions units m^-2. The incidence matrices C,D,G are dimensionless, M_e has units F, M_b has units H^-1, S has units S, and j has units A.

For C1 coefficient vectors e:I -> R^ne and b:I -> R^nb, define E_h(t):=sum_i e_i(t)phi_i and B_h(t):=sum_alpha b_alpha(t)psi_alpha, and put H_h:=mu^-1 B_h in L^2. The perfect-electric-conductor (PEC) semidiscrete model is the weak Galerkin system

$$\int_\Omega \bigl(\varepsilon\,\partial_t E_h+\sigma E_h+J_{\rm ext}\bigr)\cdot v_h\,dx=\int_\Omega H_h\cdot\operatorname{curl}v_h\,dx\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad \partial_t B_h=-\operatorname{curl}E_h\quad\text{in }M_h.$$

Here H_h is required only to be L^2; no H(curl) regularity or boundary trace for it is asserted. Testing the first identity against the edge basis and expanding the second in the face basis gives exactly M_e dot e=C^T M_b b-Se-j and dot b=-Ce, the finite compatible matrix system. The quadratic semidiscrete energy is the finite Joule-valued quantity one-half times the integral of E_h dot epsilon E_h plus B_h dot mu^-1 B_h.

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz open set. There are bounded real linear maps $R:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $Q:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega)$ such that
$$u=Ru+\nabla Qu,\qquad \|Ru\|_{H^1}+\|Qu\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}.$$
No contractibility, connected boundary, or mesh hypothesis is required. The scalar estimate uses the full H(curl) norm; no estimate by curl alone is asserted.

There is also a boundary-corrected family of projections $\pi_{h,0}^k:L^2\Lambda^k(\Omega)\to E_{h,0}^k$, where $E_{h,0}^k=E_h^k\cap H_0\Lambda^k(\Omega)$ and $H_0\Lambda^k$ is the graph closure of compactly supported smooth forms. These have the same uniform bounds, are the identity on $E_{h,0}^k$, and commute in degrees zero through two on the homogeneous complex; the terminal degree-three differential is zero. In particular,
$$\pi_{h,0}^0:H_0^1(\Omega)\to W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega),\qquad \pi_{h,0}^1:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega),\qquad \nabla\pi_{h,0}^0=\pi_{h,0}^1\nabla.$$
Here the zero tangential space uses [[def-na-zero-tangential-hcurl]]. Each family converges strongly in $L^2$ on every $L^2$ form, uniformly on compact $L^2$ subsets, and in the graph norm on its corresponding graph domain. The full and homogeneous families are separate operators. These are cochain projections; canonical edge moments are not asserted bounded on $H(\operatorname{curl})$.

Assume AC, including its CC and DC consequences. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron and let $\{\mathcal T_h\}$ be a shape-regular family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes with $h=\max_K\operatorname{diam}K\to0$. Set $V_h=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $S_h=W_h^0\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$, and define
$$X_h=\{v_h\in V_h:(v_h,\nabla q_h)_{L^2}=0\text{ for every }q_h\in S_h\}.$$
Every sequence $v_h\in X_h$ bounded in $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. Moreover there is $C$ independent of $h$ such that $\|v_h\|_2\le C\|\operatorname{curl}v_h\|_2$ for all $v_h\in X_h$.

The precise harmonic-quotient version is as follows. On any bounded Lipschitz polyhedron for which the regular decomposition and relative commuting projections below are proved, put $K=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{H_0(\operatorname{curl})})$, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$ and
$$\mathcal H=K\cap(\nabla H_0^1)^\perp,\qquad\mathcal H_h=K_h\cap(\nabla S_h)^\perp.$$
Both harmonic spaces are finite dimensional. Discrete compactness still holds on $X_h$, while the uniform curl Poincare inequality holds on $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp=X_h\cap\mathcal H_h^\perp$. A nonzero vector of $\mathcal H_h$ prevents that inequality on all of $X_h$. These are the harmonic spaces of the relative boundary complex; the full-space absolute cohomology dimensions do not identify them.

derivations.claim: For the full clause, [F1] gives exactly the spaces and moment coordinates in [F2]. The finite mesh is matching, its realization is closure(Omega), and Countable Choice is [A1], so all hypotheses of the full discrete de Rham cohomology theorem are met. Applying [F2] gives dim_R H_h^1=beta_1 and dim_R H_h^2=beta_2. These are the full-complex spaces defined in the first clause, not PEC-relative spaces.

For the relative clause, [A2] supplies AC and its stated CC/DC consequences; the domain and refining-mesh hypotheses are those in the Statement; [F4] is the required full-Dirichlet regular decomposition and [F5] gives the exact relative commuting projections on these same spaces. Thus the hypotheses of [F6] hold. It gives discrete compactness on X_h and the mesh-uniform curl Poincare inequality on Z_h. Since B_h is a subspace of K_h and H_h^rel is its L^2-orthogonal complement within the finite-dimensional K_h, the finite-dimensional orthogonal decomposition gives K_h=B_h direct-sum H_h^rel and Z_h=X_h intersect (H_h^rel)^\perp.

If h in H_h^rel is nonzero, then h in K_h so curl h=0; also h is orthogonal to B_h, hence h belongs to X_h, and ||h||_2>0. Therefore no estimate ||v_h||_2<=C||curl v_h||_2 can hold on that X_h. This is the stated reason that removing only relative gradients can leave zero modes. It makes no claim that H_h^rel has the absolute dimensions beta_1 or beta_2; those numbers belong only to the full complex in step 1.1.

boundaries.evidence: Statement supplies the refining mesh family used in step 1.2. Zero Betti numbers and empty bases are allowed: step 1.1 gives zero-dimensional absolute harmonic spaces, and the relative orthogonal decomposition still includes zero.

Step 1.1 yields zero-dimensional absolute harmonic spaces when beta_1=beta_2=0. In steps 1.2 and 2.1 the zero relative harmonic space is harmless; an obstruction to a curl estimate requires a nonzero harmonic vector.

boundaries.reason: The claim compares cohomological dimensions and mesh families; it has no one-object exception.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.2–2.1 distinguish zero relative harmonic space from a nonzero zero-curl mode and apply the quotient inequality only on Z_h.

boundaries.reason: The family parameter h tends to zero but no endpoint of a time interval is involved.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 applies the relative theorem under the explicitly stated Axiom of Choice and its CC/DC consequences.

Assume Countable Choice for weak-derivative uniqueness and the real $L^2$ product below, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open. Here $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is the set of triples of real scalar $L^2$ classes from [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. Define
$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. On tests supported in a fixed compact $K\Subset\Omega$, the same estimate gives $|\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle|\le C_{u,K}\max_{|\alpha|\le1}\sup_K|D^\alpha\varphi|$ with a finite $C_{u,K}$. This proves continuity on each fixed-support test space; the LF universal property of [[lem-test-function-lf-topology-universal-property]], for the test topology of [[def-test-function-topology]], makes the pairing a vector distribution on $\Omega$.
If this vector distribution is represented by an $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ class, that class is unique almost everywhere componentwise by the injection of locally integrable functions into scalar distributions in [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], under the stated Countable Choice assumption.
Define
$$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\text{ is represented by an element of }L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)\}$$
with graph norm $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$. No boundary condition is imposed by this definition. Fields are real-valued; equality is equality of almost-everywhere classes.

$$ (u,v)_{L^2(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=1}^3\int_\Omega u_jv_j\,dx,\qquad \|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2:=\sum_{j=1}^3\|u_j\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2. $$
Each scalar pairing is well-defined and induces its quotient norm by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]; the finite sum is therefore a real inner product on the triple space with the displayed norm. A test field $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ means a triple of real-valued members of the test-function space $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ of [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Writing $\varphi=(\varphi_x,\varphi_y,\varphi_z)$, its classical curl is the coordinate expression of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]],
$$\operatorname{curl}\varphi=(\partial_y\varphi_z-\partial_z\varphi_y,\partial_z\varphi_x-\partial_x\varphi_z,\partial_x\varphi_y-\partial_y\varphi_x).$$
For $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the triple of scalar distributions whose action on a vector test field is the sum of the three component pairings, determined by
$$\langle \operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,dx,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$
The integral is finite because $u$ and the smooth compactly supported field $\operatorname{curl}\varphi$ are componentwise in $L^2$ and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz applies. Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]).
Use the statistical one-based coordinate labels: for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$
write $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le m$, so
$X_i(\omega)=X(\omega)(i-1)$. Each $X_i$ is a real random variable because
the coordinate projection $x\mapsto x(i-1)$ is continuous and therefore has
Borel preimages of Borel sets
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]).
For every integer $r\ge1$ and matrix
$A\in M_{r\times m}(\mathbb R)$, the notation $A_{ij}$ below means its
zero-based matrix entry
$A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i\le r$ and
$1\le j\le m$; likewise $\Sigma_{ij}$ means the entry at $(i-1,j-1)$ in
the covariance matrix below in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]]. These
are labels for the root library's zero-based function entries, not a different
matrix convention. If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, $h:U\to\mathbb R^r$
has all first partials at $a\in U$, and $A=Jh(a)$, then $A_{ij}$ in this
notation is $\partial_{j-1}h_{i-1}(a)$, with the zero-based Jacobian
convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
Assume $X$ is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For the random vector $X$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since the underlying measure is a
probability measure, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
gives $E|X_i|\le\tfrac12(1+E[X_i^2])<+\infty$ by monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence $X_i$
is integrable and $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is finite
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Also
$$(X_i-\mu_i)^2\le2X_i^2+2\mu_i^2,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable; the probability-space inequality
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\bigl(1+(X_i-\mu_i)^2\bigr)$$
then makes it integrable as well. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

For $M\in M_{m\times m}(\mathbb R)$ and $z\in\mathbb R^m$, write
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_iM_{ij}z_j.$$
For a real symmetric $m\times m$ matrix $M$, **positive semidefinite** means
$z^{\mathsf T}Mz\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$, and **positive definite**
means $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$. For a real
random variable $Z$, **almost surely constant** means that $Z=c$ outside a
measurable $\mathbb P$-null set for some $c\in\mathbb R$
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). If
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\operatorname{Var}(W)=0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\mathbb P(|W-E[W]|\ge1/r)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$; the union of these
events is $\{W\ne E[W]\}$, so $W=E[W]$ almost surely
([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]). Conversely, if $W=c$
almost surely, invariance of the integral under almost-everywhere equality
gives $E[W]=c$ and $E[(W-E[W])^2]=0$
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Hence
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely constant, and
$\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\ne0$ the random
variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Also
$$(X_i-\mu_i)^2\le2X_i^2+2\mu_i^2,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable; the probability-space inequality
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\bigl(1+(X_i-\mu_i)^2\bigr)$$
then makes it integrable as well. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

For $M\in M_{m\times m}(\mathbb R)$ and $z\in\mathbb R^m$, write
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_iM_{ij}z_j.$$
For a real symmetric $m\times m$ matrix $M$, **positive semidefinite** means
$z^{\mathsf T}Mz\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$, and **positive definite**
means $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$. For a real
random variable $Z$, **almost surely constant** means that $Z=c$ outside a
measurable $\mathbb P$-null set for some $c\in\mathbb R$
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). If
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\operatorname{Var}(W)=0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\mathbb P(|W-E[W]|\ge1/r)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$; the union of these
events is $\{W\ne E[W]\}$, so $W=E[W]$ almost surely
([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]). Conversely, if $W=c$
almost surely, invariance of the integral under almost-everywhere equality
gives $E[W]=c$ and $E[(W-E[W])^2]=0$
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Hence
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely constant, and
$\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\ne0$ the random
variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.
The trace itself is its boundary and has empty interior in the plane. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the real Gram identity
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] says
$|a\times d|^2>0$ exactly when $a,d$ are linearly independent. Thus
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

citations.quote:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim:
For $v=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T}$, the finite sum
$\overline{v_1}Z_1+\overline{v_2}Z_2$ has an integrable squared modulus,
because it is bounded by
$2(|v_1|^2|Z_1|^2+|v_2|^2|Z_2|^2)$. Expanding the finite matrix product
therefore gives $v^\dagger\Gamma v
=\mathbb E[|v^\dagger Z|^2]\ge0$. Hence $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite.

Write $\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\\overline c&b\end{pmatrix}$, where
$a,b\ge0$. If $a>0$, positivity applied to $v=(-c/a,1)^{\mathsf T}$ gives
$b-|c|^2/a\ge0$, hence $ab\ge|c|^2$. If $a=0$ and $c\ne0$, positivity at

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates
$(x,y,z,t)$ and angular frequency $\omega>0$. Adopt the SI constants and
coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.

two-component vector on a probability space and define
$\Gamma:=\mathbb E[ZZ^\dagger]$, with
$\Gamma_{ij}:=\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]$. Put
$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22}$,
$S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12}$, and

$$S_0\ge0,\qquad S_0^2\ge S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2.$$

realization $Z$ to $MZ$, then

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$

([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and

derivations.claim:
Expanding the squared modulus in [A1] gives
$|A_\zeta|^2=|A_2|^2+|A_1|^2+
\zeta A_1\overline{A_2}+\overline\zeta A_2\overline{A_1}$.
Taking expectations, using [F1] and [F3], yields
$I(\zeta)=I_1+I_2+2\operatorname{Re}(\zeta\Gamma_{12})$.

Put $S=I_1+I_2$ and $c=\Gamma_{12}$. Write
$\zeta=a+ib$ and $c=u+iv$. Since $\zeta\in\mathbb T$,
$a^2+b^2=1$. By [F4], $|c|^2=u^2+v^2$ and
$\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)=au-bv$. Therefore
$$|c|^2-\bigl(\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)\bigr)^2=(a^2+b^2)(u^2+v^2)-(au-bv)^2=(av+bu)^2\ge0,$$
so each $\operatorname{Re}(\zeta c)$ lies in $[-|c|,|c|]$. If $c\ne0$,
set $r:=|c|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}>0$ and $\zeta_0:=(u-iv)/r$. Then
$|\zeta_0|^2=(u^2+v^2)/r^2=1$, so $\zeta_0\in\mathbb T$, and direct
multiplication gives $\zeta_0c=r$ while $(-\zeta_0)c=-r$. Both endpoints
are therefore attained. If $c=0$, the cross term is identically zero. Hence
$I_{\max}=S+2|c|$ and $I_{\min}=S-2|c|$.

By [F2],
$S^2-4|c|^2=(I_1-I_2)^2+4(I_1I_2-|c|^2)\ge0$; since $S\ge0$, this gives
$2|c|\le S$. Under the given $S>0$ condition,
$I_{\max}+I_{\min}=2S>0$, so substitution of step 2.1 into the visibility
definition gives $V=2|c|/S\le1$.

For $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, let $n:=k/|k|$ and let the complex
transverse fibre be
$T_k:=\{v\in\mathbb C^3:\sum_j k_jv_j=0\}$. On $\mathbb C^3$ define
$C(k)v:=i\,n\times v$ and
$P_T(k)v:=v-n\sum_j n_jv_j$. Define
$P_\sigma(k):=\tfrac12(P_T(k)+\sigma C(k))$ for $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$.
Use the Hermitian product
$\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$. Then $P_T(k)$ is the
orthogonal projection onto $T_k$; $C(k)$ is Hermitian, vanishes on the
longitudinal line, and satisfies $C(k)^2=P_T(k)$. The restrictions of
$P_{+1}(k)$ and $P_{-1}(k)$ to $T_k$ are orthogonal rank-one projections with
sum $P_T(k)$. Their ranges are the two helicity eigenspaces, with eigenvalues
$+1$ and $-1$ for $C(k)$.

Here $k$ is a spatial wavevector with units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, $|k|$ is its
Euclidean norm, $t$ is in seconds, and $i^2=-1$; thus the phase is
dimensionless and real part is taken componentwise.
If $a$ carries units $\mathrm{T\,m^4}$, then $A$ carries $\mathrm{T\,m}$,
$E$ carries $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, and $B$ carries $\mathrm T$. These fields are
real and jointly smooth on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; at each fixed time
$A,E,B$ are Schwartz functions of $x$, and their spatial Schwartz seminorms are
bounded on every compact time interval. They satisfy the smooth source-free
vacuum Maxwell equations and the Coulomb condition
$\operatorname{div}A=0$ with the stated scalar potential $\varphi=0$. Their
total field energy
$W(t):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,d^3x$, with $u$ the vacuum
energy density, is finite for every $t$. The amplitudes are a classical Fourier
description; no photon state is defined.

Let $V=\mathbb R^4$ with ordered coframe $e^0=dx^0,e^1=dx^1,e^2=dx^2,e^3=dx^3$, bilinear form $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, inverse $\eta^{-1}=\eta$, and volume form $\mathrm{vol}_\eta=e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. The Lorentzian Hodge star is the unique linear map $\star_\eta:\Lambda^kV^*\to\Lambda^{4-k}V^*$ satisfying $\alpha\wedge\star_\eta\beta=\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_\eta\,\mathrm{vol}_\eta$ for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Lambda^kV^*$. For an increasing index set $I\subseteq\{0,1,2,3\}$, write $e^I$ for the corresponding wedge, $I^c$ for its increasing complement, $s(I,I^c)$ for the sign of the concatenation $(I,I^c)$ relative to $(0,1,2,3)$, and $\epsilon_I:=\prod_{i\in I}\epsilon_i$, where $\epsilon_0=-1$ and $\epsilon_1=\epsilon_2=\epsilon_3=1$. The equivalent basis formula is $\star_\eta e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$.

The globally defined form $\omega_{S^2,n}(X,Y)=n\cdot(X\times Y)$ is smooth because its coefficients are polynomial in the embedded coordinates and tangent vectors; since $\partial_\theta n=e_\theta$ and $\partial_\phi n=\sin\theta\,e_\phi$, it satisfies $\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, extend the real Euclidean dot and right-handed cross products complex-bilinearly, with coordinate formulas
$$u\cdot v:=\sum_{j=1}^3u_jv_j,\qquad u\times v:=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\ u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\ u_1v_2-u_2v_1).$$
The dot product in these formulas uses no complex conjugation; it differs from the Hermitian product $\langle u,v\rangle_H:=\sum_{j=1}^3\overline{u_j}v_j$. Write $\|z\|_H:=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle_H}$ for the associated nonnegative norm on $\mathbb C^3$.

Let $S^2:=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot n=1\}$ with the smooth structure given by the six graph charts solving $n_j=\pm\sqrt{1-\sum_{k\ne j}n_k^2}$ on the hemispheres $\pm n_j>0$. Orient it outward using the ordered spatial basis $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its tangent plane is $T_nS^2=\{X\in\mathbb R^3:n\cdot X=0\}$. Physically, $n=k/|k|$ for a nonzero spatial wavevector $k$ in the SI Fourier description, where $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; hence $n$ is dimensionless and the radial magnitude is discarded. Define the helicity fibre $L_\sigma(n):=\operatorname{range}P_\sigma(n)$ and the total space $L_\sigma:=\{(n,z):n\in S^2,\ z\in L_\sigma(n)\}$, projected to $S^2$ by $(n,z)\mapsto n$.

For an open set $U\subseteq S^2$, a unit frame of $L_\sigma$ over $U$ is a smooth map $v:U\to\mathbb C^3$ such that $v(n)\in L_\sigma(n)$ and $\langle v(n),v(n)\rangle_H=1$ for every $n\in U$. Since each fibre is a complex line, this vector spans that fibre. A local unit frame is such a map on an open neighborhood in $S^2$; a global unit frame is one defined on all of $S^2$.

Fibrewise addition and scalar multiplication are inherited from $\mathbb C^3$. A unit frame $v$ gives the local trivialization $(n,a)\mapsto(n,a v(n))$ from $U\times\mathbb C$ to $L_\sigma|_U$, with inverse $(n,z)\mapsto(n,\langle v(n),z\rangle_H)$. Its total flux is $\int_{S^2}F_\sigma=-4\pi\sigma$, so the flux divided by $2\pi$ is $-2\sigma$ in this convention. The line bundle has no globally smooth unit frame.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a real angular frequency $\omega\in\mathbb R$ and a bounded open region $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $C^1$ boundary in a material-rest frame. Here a material-rest frame is the inertial frame in which every modelled material element has fixed spatial coordinates, as stipulated by the framework's material-closure postulate. A map in $C^1(\overline\Omega)$ means the restriction of a $C^1$ map on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ be continuous coefficient fields with units $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$. They may be spatially varying and complex. Let $E_j,H_j\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ and $J_j\in C^0(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, for $j=1,2$, be phasor amplitudes with SI units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. The corresponding real fields use $e^{-i\omega t}$, for example $E_j^{\mathrm{real}}(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(E_j(x)e^{-i\omega t})$. Their displacement and magnetic-induction amplitudes are $D_j=\varepsilon E_j$ in $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$ and $B_j=\mu H_j$ in $\mathrm T$.

The fixed-frequency constitutive and source equations are

$$D_j=\varepsilon E_j,\qquad B_j=\mu H_j,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_j=i\omega B_j,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H_j=J_j-i\omega D_j.$$

All operators act componentwise on the spatial variable. For $u,v\in\mathbb C^3$, define the **bilinear** dot product $u\cdot v=\sum_{r=1}^3u_rv_r$ and the complex-bilinear cross product by the usual right-handed component formula. Neither product conjugates either input. The transpose $T$ is the ordinary matrix transpose, without complex conjugation. This definition calls the coefficient model **reciprocal** when $\varepsilon(x)^T=\varepsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)^T=\mu(x)$ at every $x\in\overline\Omega$. It places no Hermitian, positive-definite, or passivity condition on these complex matrices.

This is a fixed-frequency phasor data class. Its possibly complex coefficients are not inferred from the framework's real, instantaneous material branch; a separate response model is required to justify any such interpretation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded domain with $C^1$ boundary and outward unit normal $n$. Fix a real angular frequency $\omega$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Let $E_j,H_j\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ and $J_j\in C^0(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, for $j=1,2$, be phasor fields and electric-current densities in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, respectively. Suppose both pairs solve the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations there with the same continuous coefficient maps $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ and $\varepsilon(x)^T=\varepsilon(x)$, $\mu(x)^T=\mu(x)$ at every $x$. Use Euclidean volume measure $dV$ and boundary area measure $dS$. Then

$$\int_{\partial\Omega}n\cdot(E_1\times H_2-E_2\times H_1)\,dS=\int_\Omega(E_2\cdot J_1-E_1\cdot J_2)\,dV.$$

The dot and cross products in this identity are the complex-bilinear products defined in the reciprocal phasor model; no complex conjugation occurs. Both integrals have units W. In particular, the real symmetric positive permittivity tensor and positive scalar permeability of the lossless anisotropic plane-wave model satisfy these reciprocal-coefficient hypotheses, so the identity applies to any two such phasor solutions restricted to a bounded $C^1$ subdomain.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the finite-energy boundary model defined earlier on the nonempty open time interval $I$ and bounded Lipschitz polyhedron $\Omega$. Thus $\varepsilon,\mu$ are time-independent real symmetric essentially bounded coefficient fields with uniform positive lower bounds, $E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$, $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, and

$$\varepsilon\partial_tE=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad\mu\partial_tH=-\operatorname{curl}E$$

hold as $L^2$ identities for every $t\in I$. Define

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H\bigr)\,d\lambda_3.$$

For every $s<t$ in $I$, the closure-defined PEC branch satisfies

$$W(t)-W(s)=-\int_s^t\int_\Omega E\cdot J\,d\lambda_3\,dr.$$

For the Green-compatible impedance branch, where $H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)$, it satisfies

$$W(t)-W(s)=-\int_s^t\int_\Omega E\cdot J\,d\lambda_3\,dr-\int_s^t\int_{\partial\Omega}Y|E_\tau|^2\,dS\,dr.$$

Here $E_\tau,H_\tau$ and the Green identity are exactly the $L^2$ boundary data and admissibility condition in the model definition; no trace is inferred from H(curl) membership alone. The work density $E\cdot J$ has SI units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}$; the boundary term has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ per unit area and is nonnegative in the impedance branch. If $J=0$ and $E(t_0)=H(t_0)=0$ in $L^2$, the only admissible solution is zero for $t\ge t_0$. Uniqueness is forward from the specified initial time; no backward uniqueness is asserted for a dissipative boundary.

Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

Fix a real angular frequency $\omega>0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and use the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention and SI field units of the fixed-frequency reciprocal-phasor model. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded device region with $C^1$ boundary in one stationary material-rest frame. Its continuous phasor coefficient maps are $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. The complex phasor fields $\widetilde E,\widetilde H\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ have units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. They satisfy the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations of the reciprocal-phasor data class, with no impressed volume current or charge in $\Omega$. The corresponding real fields are $E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $H(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde H(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, with period $T=2\pi/\omega$. An **admissible port** consists of a bounded connected $C^1$ cross-section $\Sigma_j$ in a plane perpendicular to a fixed unit guide axis $\widehat z_j$, together with a uniform lossless straight reference guide extending from that section. The outward normal $n_j$ on the port points from $\Omega$ into the guide. The reference-guide phasor coefficients and wall conditions are independent of distance along $\widehat z_j$. A propagating channel mode is a pair of $C^1$ complex transverse profiles $(e_{j\alpha},h_{j\alpha})$ whose associated source-free phasor fields in the guide solve the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations and have longitudinal factor $e^{\pm i\beta_\alpha s_j}$ with real $\beta_\alpha>0$ in $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. The profiles are normalized per unit amplitude in $\mathrm{W^{1/2}}$, so the resulting fields have units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. The plus and minus signs are assigned according to whether energy travels toward or away from $\Omega$. At $\omega$, assume a finite list of $N$ propagating mode channels in total and that this list is complete for the propagating channels represented by the finite interface. Any outgoing radiation continuum or omitted propagating channel is separately recorded as nonnegative outward power $P_{\mathrm{other}}$. Evanescent modes may be required in the exact near-port matching field, but are not entries of the propagating amplitude vectors; no finite truncation of such matching modes is asserted to be exact.

Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)^T\in\mathbb C^N$ and $b=(b_1,\ldots,b_N)^T\in\mathbb C^N$ be the incoming and outgoing amplitudes. Choose the mode shapes and amplitude convention so that each coefficient has units $\mathrm{W^{1/2}}$, the Hermitian norm is $\|a\|_2^2=\sum_{\alpha=1}^N|a_\alpha|^2$ in W, and the total time-averaged outward power through the port sections is

$$P_{\mathrm{ports}}=\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2.$$

This equality, including the vanishing of cross terms in the real-power pairing, is a port-mode normalization hypothesis. For complex phasor fields the time-averaged Poynting vector is $\boldsymbol\Pi=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E\times\widetilde H^*)$ in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, where $*$ denotes componentwise conjugation before the bilinear cross product. This Hermitian power pairing is distinct from the unconjugated Lorentz bilinear pairing.

On the non-port wall $\Gamma_w$, the model prescribes either a smooth PEC condition $E_\tau(t)=0$, giving zero outward wall power, or a passive wall condition with explicitly specified nonnegative cycle-averaged outward power $P_\partial\ge0$. Here $E_\tau(t)=E(t)-(n\cdot E(t))n$ and $H_\tau(t)=H(t)-(n\cdot H(t))n$ are the classical tangential restrictions of the smooth real fields. This is a smooth-field model assumption; no $L^2$ trace is inferred from membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$.

The total cycle-averaged outward boundary power is the port contribution $\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2$, plus $P_\partial$ and any unlisted outgoing power $P_{\mathrm{other}}$. No unlisted incoming power is included.

derivations.claim: In the Lorentz branch set $J_{\mathrm{tot}}=J_f+\sum_{\ell=1}^M\partial_tP_\ell$, and in the Drude branch set $J_{\mathrm{tot}}=J_f+V$. From [L1] and [A1] or [A2], respectively, the field and constitutive equations give $\varepsilon_\infty\partial_tE=\operatorname{curl}H-J_{\mathrm{tot}}$ and $\mu\partial_tH=-\operatorname{curl}E$.

In the Lorentz branch, dot the $\ell$th oscillator equation [A1] with $\partial_tP_\ell/a_\ell$. Since $a_\ell>0$, the division is valid; the product rule in [F2] gives $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell=\partial_t\!\left((|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2)/(2a_\ell)\right)+(\gamma_\ell/a_\ell)|\partial_tP_\ell|^2$. The last term is nonnegative because $\gamma_\ell\ge0$.

In the Drude branch, dot $\partial_tV+\gamma V=aE$ from [A2] with $V/a$. The product rule and $a>0$ give $E\cdot V=\partial_t(|V|^2/(2a))+(\gamma/a)|V|^2$, whose last term is nonnegative because $\gamma\ge0$.

Define the field energy density $u_f:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ by $u_f=(\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2)/2$. Differentiate it componentwise using [F2] and the field equations of step 1.1. This gives $\partial_tu_f=E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H-E\cdot J_{\mathrm{tot}}-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E$. Applying [F1] yields $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-\sum E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ in the Lorentz branch and $-\operatorname{div}(E\times H)-E\cdot J_f-E\cdot V$ in the Drude branch.

Define the total field-plus-material energy density $u:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ branchwise: in the Lorentz branch, $u:=u_f+\sum_{\ell=1}^M\bigl(|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2\bigr)/(2a_\ell)$; in the Drude branch, $u:=u_f+|V|^2/(2a)$. All terms are nonnegative, have SI units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and are jointly smooth and $T$-periodic under the Statement's hypotheses. Substituting step 1.2 into the Lorentz field balance of step 2.1 cancels every $E\cdot\partial_tP_\ell$ term; substituting step 1.3 into its Drude balance cancels $E\cdot V$. Since the given source-free condition has $J_f=0$, each branch therefore satisfies $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-\ell$ with exactly the loss density $\ell$ in the Statement.

Integrate the local identity of step 3.1 over $\Omega$ at each time and apply [F3] to $E\times H$. Then integrate in time from $0$ to $T$. The integrand $\partial_tu$ is continuous and integrable on the finite product domain, so [F4] permits integration first in time: $\int_\Omega\int_0^T\partial_tu\,dt\,dV=\int_\Omega(u(x,T)-u(x,0))\,dV=0$ by periodicity. Hence the time-integrated outward boundary flux equals $-T P_{\mathrm{mat}}$.

Divide step 4.1 by $T$ and use the total boundary-flux decomposition [F5]. The port term is $\|b\|_2^2-\|a\|_2^2$, the wall term is $P_\partial\ge0$ by [A3], and the remaining outgoing term is $P_{\mathrm{other}}\ge0$. Rearrangement gives the power balance in the Statement.

Since each of $P_{\mathrm{mat}},P_\partial,P_{\mathrm{other}}$ is nonnegative, step 5.1 gives $\|Sa\|_2^2\le\|a\|_2^2$ for every $a$; taking nonnegative square roots proves contractivity. If all three powers vanish for every $a$, set $K:=I_N-S^\dagger S$. Then $K^\dagger=K$ because $(S^\dagger S)^\dagger=S^\dagger S$, and the power balance gives $a^\dagger Ka=\|a\|_2^2-\|Sa\|_2^2=0$ for every $a$. Let $e_j$ denote the $j$th coordinate vector of $\mathbb C^N$. Testing $a=e_j$ gives $K_{jj}=0$; for $j<k$, testing $a=e_j+e_k$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}K_{jk}=0$, while testing $a=e_j+i e_k$ gives $-2\operatorname{Im}K_{jk}=0$. Hence every entry of $K$ is zero, so $S^\dagger S=I_N$. The square matrix $S$ is injective, hence surjective by finite-dimensional rank-nullity; therefore $S^{-1}=S^\dagger$ and $SS^\dagger=I_N$ as well. Thus $S$ is unitary.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Its continuous phasor coefficient maps are $\varepsilon,\mu:\overline\Omega\to\mathbb C^{3\times3}$ in $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. The complex phasor fields $\widetilde E,\widetilde H\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$ have units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. They satisfy the fixed-frequency Maxwell equations of the reciprocal-phasor data class, with no impressed volume current or charge in $\Omega$. The corresponding real fields are $E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $H(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde H(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, with period $T=2\pi/\omega$. An **admissible port** consists of a bounded connected $C^1$ cross-section $\Sigma_j$ in a plane perpendicular to a fixed unit guide axis $\widehat z_j$, together with a uniform lossless straight reference guide extending from that section.
