The definition does not assert existence, uniqueness, a momentum constraint, or an asymptotically Euclidean or puncture solution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For the problem of *Bounded-domain charged conformal problem*, there are $\rho>0$, $\varepsilon_0>0$, and $C<\infty$ such that for each $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$ there is exactly one solution $u_\varepsilon\in X$ with $\|u_\varepsilon\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}<\rho$. The corresponding $\psi_\varepsilon=1+u_\varepsilon$ satisfies $\psi_\varepsilon\geq1$ on $\overline\Omega$. If $v\in X$ is the unique solution of $-8\Delta v=2S$ in $\Omega$, $v=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then

$$\|u_\varepsilon-\varepsilon^2v\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\leq C|\varepsilon|^4.$$

The constants may depend on $\Omega,\alpha,S$, and the uniqueness is only in the fixed neighborhood $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}<\rho$; no global uniqueness, asymptotically Euclidean solution, puncture solution, or non-CMC result is asserted. The $O(\varepsilon^4)$ statement means the displayed bound for all $|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty oriented smooth three-manifold without boundary. Let $\bar h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\psi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,(0,\infty))$, let $\bar E,\bar B$ be smooth contravariant vector fields, let $\bar A$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor with $\bar h^{ij}\bar A_{ij}=0$, let $\tau\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant. Let $c,G,\mu_0>0$ and $\kappa=8\pi G/c^4$ be the parameters of the inherited SI-to-geometric dictionary, and set $\alpha=\sqrt{\kappa/(2\mu_0)}>0$. Define

$$h:=\psi^4\bar h,\qquad K:=\frac{\tau}{3}h+\psi^{-2}\bar A,\qquad E:=\psi^{-6}\bar E,\qquad B:=\psi^{-6}\bar B.$$

The fields $E$ and $B$ are geometric-normalized spatial vectors: in length coordinates their components have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Their SI-convention counterparts are $e:=\alpha^{-1}E$ and $b:=\alpha^{-1}B$. In length coordinates, metric components and $\psi$ are dimensionless, $\tau$ and the covariant components of $\bar A$ and $K$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and $\Lambda$ has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. The tuple $(\Sigma,\bar h,\psi,\bar A,\tau,\bar E,\bar B,\Lambda)$ with these induced fields is called conformal electrovacuum seed data. This definition imposes no divergence, Hamiltonian, or momentum equation and asserts no existence, uniqueness, or spacetime development.

Use the smooth conformal seed data defined in this development on an oriented smooth three-manifold, and let $D$ and $\bar D$ be the Levi-Civita connections of $h=\psi^4\bar h$ and $\bar h$. Define $\Delta_{\bar h}\psi:=\bar h^{ij}\bar D_i\partial_j\psi$, with the Euclidean convention $\Delta=\sum_i\partial_i^2$ in Cartesian coordinates. Use the spatial curvature sign and scalar-curvature contraction fixed for induced data in the preceding Gauss-Codazzi convention. Let $e=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar E$ and $b=\alpha^{-1}\psi^{-6}\bar B$ be the SI-convention vector fields associated with the inherited constrained electrovacuum initial-data convention. Then the two Maxwell divergence constraints are equivalent to

$$\bar D_i\bar E^i=0,\qquad \bar D_i\bar B^i=0,$$

and the SI Hamiltonian constraint in that definition is equivalent to

$$-8\Delta_{\bar h}\psi+\bar R\,\psi-|\bar A|_{\bar h}^2\psi^{-7}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\tau^2-2\Lambda\right)\psi^5-2\left(|\bar E|_{\bar h}^2+|\bar B|_{\bar h}^2\right)\psi^{-3}=0.$$

Here $\bar R$ is the scalar curvature of $\bar h$ in the stated convention, and the barred norms use $\bar h$ to raise and lower indices. The exact vector divergence identities are $D_iE^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar E^i$ and $D_iB^i=\psi^{-6}\bar D_i\bar B^i$. The separate momentum constraint remains

$$D^jK_{ji}-D_i\tau=-2\psi^{-6}(\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B)_i,$$

where the cross product on the right is lowered with $\bar h$. In particular, if $K=0$ and $\bar E\times_{\bar h}\bar B=0$, the momentum equation holds. The transformed scalar equation alone does not impose the momentum constraint and gives no elliptic existence theorem.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty, smooth, oriented three-manifold without boundary. Let $h$ be a smooth Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $K$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor, and let $e,b$ be smooth vector fields tangent to $\Sigma$. For data induced on an embedded spacelike slice $i:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$, let $n$ be its future unit normal, let $F$ be the smooth two-form of [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]], and define spatial covectors $\mathcal E,\mathcal B\in\Omega^1(\Sigma)$ by $\mathcal E(X):=F(X,n)$ and $\mathcal B(X):=-({\star_gF})(X,n)$ for $X\in T\Sigma$. Identify these with vector fields using the positive metric $h$: $e:=\sharp_h\mathcal E$ and $b:=\sharp_h\mathcal B$, so in any coordinates $e^i=h^{ij}\mathcal E_j$ and $b^i=h^{ij}\mathcal B_j$. Equivalently, $\mathcal E$ is the restriction of the observer electric covector $E/c$ and $\mathcal B$ the restriction of the observer magnetic covector $B$ of [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]]. For an abstract data tuple not assumed to come from $F$, $e,b$ are simply the specified tangent vector fields. This fixes the convention without adding a potential or an existence assumption.

For the observer-covector comparison above, the smooth normal along $\Sigma$ has local smooth ambient extensions by [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]; shrinking and normalizing an extension gives an observer congruence to which [[lem-emg-observer-field-decomposition]] applies. The restrictions $\mathcal E,\mathcal B$ depend only on $n|_\Sigma$, so they are independent of the chosen extension.

Write $h^{ij}$ for the inverse matrix to $h_{ij}$ and use $h$ to raise every spatial index. Let $D$ and $R(h)$ denote the Levi-Civita connection and scalar curvature of $h$, set $\tau:=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell}$, and choose the induced spatial orientation so $\operatorname{vol}_g=\theta^0\wedge\operatorname{vol}_h=-n^\flat\wedge\operatorname{vol}_h$ in a positively oriented normal coframe with $\theta^0(n)=1$. Define the spatial cross product by $h(e\times_hb,w)=\operatorname{vol}_h(e,b,w)$ for each tangent vector $w$.

For the fixed parameters $(\kappa,\Lambda,\mu_0)$ of [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]], the tuple $(\Sigma,h,K,e,b)$ is **constrained electrovacuum initial data** when

$$D_ie^i=0,\qquad D_ib^i=0,$$

$$R(h)+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\bigl(|e|_h^2+|b|_h^2\bigr),$$

$$D^jK_{ji}-D_i\tau=-\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}(e\times_hb)_i.$$

Here the last display is an equality of covectors. The scalar-curvature form is the Gauss-Codazzi form of the normal projections in [[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]; the sign and $K$ convention are those of [[def-gr-spacelike-initial-data-and-constraints]] and [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]]. This definition asserts no existence or uniqueness of a spacetime development.

For the periodic high-regularity class, use the dimensionless coordinate $\theta^i$ and length coordinate $X^i=L_0\theta^i$ of [[def-emg-periodic-high-sobolev-state]], for a fixed $L_0>0$. The arrays $h_{ij}$ and $K_{ij}$ are the length-coordinate covariant components with $h_{ij}\in H^{s+1}$ and $K_{ij}\in H^s$. The Sobolev components of $e,b$ are $e_A=h(e,\mathsf e_A)$ and $b_A=h(b,\mathsf e_A)$ in the canonical positively oriented $h$-orthonormal frame $\mathsf e_A$ specified there; thus $e_A,b_A\in H^s$. If $\mathsf e_A=E_A^i\partial_{X^i}$, their coordinate components are $e^i=E_A^i e_A$ and $b^i=E_A^i b_A$. The coefficients $E_A^i$ are smooth functions of the positive matrix $h_{ij}$; on the compact range of each such metric, [[lem-gr-smooth-composition-and-commutator-estimates]] puts them in $H^{s+1}$ and [[lem-gr-periodic-sobolev-algebra]] makes the coordinate components $H^s$ as well.

For these representatives define the spatial connection coefficients by $\Gamma(h)^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12h^{k\ell}(\partial_{X^i}h_{j\ell}+\partial_{X^j}h_{i\ell}-\partial_{X^\ell}h_{ij})$, with $\partial_{X^i}=L_0^{-1}\partial_{\theta^i}$. On coordinate vector components put $D_i e^j=\partial_{X^i}e^j+\Gamma(h)^j{}_{ik}e^k$ and $D_i b^j=\partial_{X^i}b^j+\Gamma(h)^j{}_{ik}b^k$; on the covariant tensor $K$ put $D_iK_{jk}=\partial_{X^i}K_{jk}-\Gamma(h)^\ell{}_{ij}K_{\ell k}-\Gamma(h)^\ell{}_{ik}K_{j\ell}$. Define $R(h)$ by $R^a{}_{bij}=\partial_{X^i}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jb}-\partial_{X^j}\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ib}+\Gamma(h)^a{}_{ic}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{jb}-\Gamma(h)^a{}_{jc}\Gamma(h)^c{}_{ib}$, followed by the Ricci and scalar contractions of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Sobolev embedding gives $h\in C^{s-1}$ and $K,e,b\in C^{s-2}$; the uniform positive lower eigenvalue makes $h^{-1}$ well defined, and the smooth-composition and algebra suppliers give $\Gamma(h)\in H^s$, $R(h)\in H^{s-1}$, and $D K,D e,D b\in H^{s-1}$. Since $s\ge5$, these constraint terms have continuous representatives, and their displayed equalities mean pointwise equality of those representatives. In the SI interpretation, $K$ and $D$ carry one inverse-length factor, $R(h)$ and $\Lambda$ carry inverse-length squared, and the orthonormal components $e_A,b_A$ have units tesla; the factors $\kappa/\mu_0$ give matching units in the constraints. No numerical parameter values are assigned here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded smooth domain and choose $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset(-R,R)^3$. Write $H^1_0(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of the compactly supported smooth functions. Then $\|v\|_{L^2}\le2R\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. A function $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ represents an element of $H^1_0(\Omega)$ if and only if $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$ with $kp>n$. Then there is $C(n,p,k,\Omega)$ with
$$\|uv\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\|v\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u,v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega)),$$
so $W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ is a Banach algebra; the constants and the conclusion may depend on the choice of equivalent Sobolev norm only through $C$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p<\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then the set of restrictions
to $\Omega$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ is dense in
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|\varphi|_\Omega-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$.

The exponent range is $1\le p<\infty$; the result asserts no density in the
$W^{k,\infty}$ norm, and it does not hold on arbitrary open sets, as the
companion examples page shows.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: The base fields are smooth and $\partial_i\bar E_0^i=\partial_i\bar B_0^i=0$, so the source in [F1] is the constant $S=a^2$, and scaling them by $\varepsilon$ preserves their zero divergences. The units are consistent: $a^2$ and $\Delta$ have units of inverse length squared, while $\psi$ and $\varepsilon$ are dimensionless.

Smoothness bootstrap, initial gain. Set $u=u_\varepsilon=\psi_\varepsilon-1$ and $f=(\varepsilon^2a^2/4)\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, so $-\Delta u=f$ and $u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. The branch gives $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ and $\psi_\varepsilon\ge1$. The identities $\partial_i(\psi^{-3})=-3\psi^{-4}\partial_i\psi$ and $\partial_{ij}(\psi^{-3})=12\psi^{-5}(\partial_i\psi)(\partial_j\psi)-3\psi^{-4}\partial_{ij}\psi$ follow from [F11] and the product rule and show that $f\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$, with bounded derivatives through order two, hence $f\in H^2(\Omega)$ by integration by parts against compactly supported tests. By [F6], $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. Its classical equation tested against $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ gives the weak identity; continuity of both sides in the $H^1$ test norm and the defining density of $C_c^\infty$ in $H^1_0$ extend it to every test in $H^1_0$. Applying [F8] with $m=2$ yields $u\in H^4(\Omega)$.

On $B_R(0)$, define $v(x):=\frac{a^2}{24}(R^2-|x|^2)$. It vanishes on $\partial B_R$, and $\Delta |x|^2=6$ in $\mathbb R^3$, so $-8\Delta v=-8(-6a^2/24)=2a^2=2S$. By uniqueness of the zero-boundary solution in [F2], this is the coefficient in the branch expansion.

Smoothness bootstrap, composition and iteration. Fix an integer $m\ge4$ and suppose $\psi=1+u\in H^m(\Omega)$. Its continuous range is a compact interval $J\subset[1,\infty)$ by [F2] and [F9]. To verify $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$, use [F10] to choose smooth restrictions $\psi_n\to\psi$ in $H^m$; [F9] gives uniform convergence, so for all sufficiently large $n$ the values of $\psi_n$ lie in one compact interval $J'\subset(0,\infty)$ containing $J$. For each smooth $q$ with values in $J'$, repeated application of the total chain and product rules [F11] expresses every $D^\beta(q^{-3})$, $|\beta|\le m$, as a finite sum of bounded factors $G^{(r)}(q)$, $G(s)=s^{-3}$, times products $\prod_jD^{\gamma_j}q$ with $|\gamma_j|\ge1$ and $\sum_j|\gamma_j|=|\beta|$. Each product is in $L^2$ with a bound controlled by $\|q\|_{H^m}$: derivatives of order at most $m-2$ lie in $H^2$ or a higher Sobolev space and hence in $L^\infty$ by [F9]; a factor of order $m$ can occur only alone and is in $L^2$; a factor of order $m-1$ occurs at most once, lies in $H^1\subset L^6$, and any remaining factor has total derivative order at most one and lies in $L^\infty$. Thus $q\mapsto G'(q)$ is uniformly bounded in $H^m$ on the bounded smooth approximants and their line segments. The same difference identity applied to $G'$ shows $t\mapsto G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))$ is continuous in $H^m$, so its displayed integral exists as a Banach-valued Riemann integral. The identity $G(\psi_n)-G(\psi_\ell)=(\psi_n-\psi_\ell)\int_0^1G'(\psi_\ell+t(\psi_n-\psi_\ell))\,dt$, together with the Banach-algebra bound [F9], shows $G(\psi_n)$ is Cauchy in $H^m$. Its uniform limit is $G(\psi)$, proving $\psi^{-3}\in H^m$. Hence $f\in H^m$; [F8] gives $u\in H^{m+2}$. Starting with $m=4$ and repeating for $m=4,6,8,\ldots$ proves $u\in H^{2j}(\Omega)$ for every sufficiently large integer $j$. The same embeddings imply $u\in H^r(\Omega)$ for every finite integer $r$, and then $u\in C^k(\overline\Omega)$ for every $k$, so $\psi_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$.

Verification of the full constraints. On the oriented manifold without boundary $\Sigma=\Omega$, take the conformal seed data $\bar h=\delta$, $\bar A=0$, $\tau=0$, $\Lambda=0$, $\bar E=\varepsilon a e_1$, and $\bar B=0$. Smoothness and positivity of $\psi_\varepsilon$ follow from steps 1.2–2.2 and [F2], so [F3] defines smooth $h,K,E,B$ and gives $K=0$. The Maxwell constraints hold because $\partial_i\bar E^i=\partial_i\bar B^i=0$ by step 1.1 and the barred metric is Euclidean. Since $\bar R=0$ and $|\bar E|_\delta^2=\varepsilon^2a^2$, the transformed Hamiltonian constraint [F4] is exactly $-8\Delta\psi_\varepsilon=2\varepsilon^2a^2\psi_\varepsilon^{-3}$, the branch equation. Its transformed momentum equation has zero left side because $K=\tau=0$ and zero right side because $\bar E\times_\delta\bar B=0$. Thus all four constraints in [F5] hold. The data are smooth constrained time-symmetric data on this fixed ball; the Dirichlet boundary value is prescribed, and the proof makes no claim of an isolated asymptotically flat black hole or any other boundary-value problem.

boundaries.evidence: The ball is nonempty because R>0. If the seed amplitude a=0, S=0 and Verification2.1 gives v=0; psi=1 solves the branch equation/boundary data and agrees with the locally unique branch in F2.

At epsilon=0, F2 gives the reference branch psi=1, and Verification2.1 computes the quadratic coefficient v. At a=0 the branch PDE is homogeneous and psi=1 is the unique local branch. Current initial Sobolev gain1.2 and iteration2.2 never divide by a or epsilon.
Statement: a=1 is an allowed nonnegative inverse-length amplitude.
Step 2.1 includes a=0; the radius is required to be R>0.

boundaries.reason: The branch is asserted only for the open small-parameter interval from the theorem.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

derivations.claim: Extend $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by zero. For fixed $(x_2,x_3)$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-R}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$. Cauchy--Schwarz bounds its square by $2R\int_{-R}^R|\partial_1v|^2\,ds$. Integrating over the cube gives $\|v\|_2^2\le(2R)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2\le(2R)^2\|\nabla v\|_2^2$. Pass to an $H^1$-convergent compactly supported smooth approximation to obtain the same inequality on $H^1_0$.

Suppose $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ and $u=0$ on the boundary. Take a finite graph cover and a subordinate partition from [F3], with an additional interior term. In a boundary chart $\Psi(y',t)=(y',t+\varphi(y'))$, $t>0$ is the inward graph coordinate; its Jacobian is one and its differential and inverse differential are bounded on the compact chart. Each localized pullback $z$ is $C^1$, vanishes at $t=0$, and is supported away from artificial chart edges. The identity $z(y',t)=\int_0^t\partial_tz(y',s)\,ds$ gives $|z|\le Ct$. Choose a smooth $\eta_\delta(t)$ equal to zero for $t\le\delta$, one for $t\ge2\delta$, with $|\eta_\delta'|\le C/\delta$. The support of $z-z\eta_\delta$ is a layer of volume $O(\delta)$; both $Dz$ and $z\eta_\delta'$ are uniformly bounded there. Thus $\|z-z\eta_\delta\|_{H^1}=O(\delta^{1/2})$. Transport back and sum the finite partition. The resulting $C^1$ functions have compact support in $\Omega$, and ordinary mollification at a radius smaller than their distance to the boundary approximates each of them in $H^1$ by $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Hence $u\in H^1_0$.

Conversely, let $u\in C^1(\overline\Omega)\cap H^1_0$ and choose $u_j\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ converging in $H^1$. In a fixed smaller graph chart, for a $C^1$ pullback $w$ and $0<t<h$, the identity $w(y',0)=w(y',t)-\int_0^t\partial_tw(y',s)\,ds$ gives $|w(y',0)|^2\le2|w(y',t)|^2+2h\int_0^h|\partial_tw(y',s)|^2\,ds$. Average over $t\in(0,h)$ and integrate over a smaller fixed tangential base. Bounded chart Jacobians and differentials give $\|w(\cdot,0)\|_{L^2}^2\le C_h\|w\|_{H^1}^2$. Apply this to the localized pullback of $u-u_j$; its boundary value is the localized boundary value of $u$. The right side tends to zero, so that boundary value vanishes almost everywhere. Continuity makes it vanish everywhere: a nonzero value would persist on an open tangential disk of positive area. The finite cover proves $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$.

Steps 1.2 and 2.1 identify zero classical boundary values with the zero-boundary Sobolev closure for the stated $C^1$ representatives. Together with step 1.1 they establish both claims; no unproved trace-to-classical regularity upgrade has been used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f_k:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuously
differentiable: each $f_k$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ and each derivative
$f_k'$ is continuous there ([[def-continuity-real]]). Suppose there is
$c\in[a,b]$ such that the real
sequence $(f_k(c))$ converges to $A$, and suppose $f_k'\to g$ uniformly on
$[a,b]$. Then there is a differentiable function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ such
that

$$f_k\longrightarrow f\ \text{ uniformly},\qquad f'=g.$$

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be compactly
supported, meaning that it has a representative which vanishes outside a
compact set. Then $Nf$ is finite almost everywhere, belongs to
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, and depends only on the $L^1$ equivalence
class of $f$. Its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n).$$
The result includes $C_c$ data and compactly supported $L^p$ data for every
$1\le p\le\infty$. If $f=0$ almost everywhere outside a closed compact set
$K$, then $Nf$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^n\setminus K$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim: By scaling it suffices to prove the estimate for $R=1$. Direct differentiation gives $D_i\Phi(z)=-z_i/(4\pi|z|^3)$ and $K_{ij}(z)=D_{ij}\Phi(z)=(3z_iz_j|z|^{-5}-\delta_{ij}|z|^{-3})/(4\pi)$. Therefore $|D\Phi|\le C|z|^{-2}$, $|K|\le C|z|^{-3}$ and $|DK|\le C|z|^{-4}$. The spherical integrals satisfy $\int_{S^2}\theta_i\theta_j\,d\sigma=4\pi\delta_{ij}/3$ by coordinate reflections, permutations and $\sum_i\theta_i^2=1$. The divergence theorem consequently gives zero integral of $K_{ij}$ on every concentric annulus and the correction $-\delta_{ij}/3$ for the inner-sphere Hessian flux.

To justify the second derivatives for merely Hölder data, choose from [F5] a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_\varepsilon$ equal to zero in $B_\varepsilon$ and one outside $B_{2\varepsilon}$, with derivatives bounded by $C\varepsilon^{-j}$, and put $q_\varepsilon=\Phi\chi_\varepsilon$. For each fixed $\varepsilon>0$, [F3] differentiates $q_\varepsilon*g$. On any fixed compact set choose one large containing radius $M$ for all translated supports. Splitting off $g(x)$ inside $B_M(x)$ and using the boundary flux from step 1.1 gives
$$D_{ij}(q_\varepsilon*g)(x)=\int_{B_M(x)}D_{ij}q_\varepsilon(x-y)(g(y)-g(x))\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}3g(x).$$
The integral converges uniformly on that compact set to the same expression with $D_{ij}q_\varepsilon$ replaced by $K_{ij}$: the omitted ball and transition annulus are bounded by $C_\alpha[g]_\alpha\varepsilon^\alpha$, using $|g(y)-g(x)|\le[g]_\alpha|x-y|^\alpha$ and $\int_0^{2\varepsilon}r^{\alpha-1}\,dr$. The potentials and first derivatives likewise converge uniformly, with errors $O(\varepsilon^2\|g\|_\infty)$ and $O(\varepsilon\|g\|_\infty)$. Apply [F3] first to the functions and their first derivatives, then to the first and second derivatives on coordinate segments. This proves $Ng\in C^2$ and the absolutely convergent cancellation formula
$$D_{ij}Ng(x)=\int_{B_M(x)}K_{ij}(x-y)(g(y)-g(x))\,dy-\frac{\delta_{ij}}3g(x).$$

For the Hölder estimate take $x\ne x'$ in a fixed compact box, $d=|x-x'|$, and $m=(x+x')/2$. Choose a large ball $B_M(m)$ containing the support and both points with a positive margin and $M\ge2d$. The same divergence calculation on this fixed ball writes each Hessian as $\int_{B_M(m)}K_{ij}(x-y)(g(y)-g(x))\,dy-g(x)b(x)$, where $b(x)=\int_{\partial B_M(m)}D_i\Phi(x-y)\nu_j(y)\,dS(y)$. Reflection in $m$ and oddness of $D_i\Phi$ show $b(x)=b(x')$; its magnitude is bounded by a dimension constant since both poles remain a fixed fraction of $M$ away from the sphere.

Split the difference into $B_d(m)$ and its complement. The near integrals are at most $C_\alpha[g]_\alpha d^\alpha$. On the complement, $|K(x-y)-K(x'-y)|\le Cd|y-m|^{-4}$, so the part multiplied by $g(y)-g(x)$ is at most $C[g]_\alpha d\int_d^M r^{\alpha-2}\,dr\le C_\alpha[g]_\alpha d^\alpha$. The remaining part is $(g(x')-g(x))\int_{B_M(m)\setminus B_d(m)}K_{ij}(x'-y)\,dy$. This kernel integral is bounded uniformly: the divergence theorem expresses it as the difference of two $D_i\Phi$ boundary fluxes; each sphere stays at least half its radius from the pole and has area proportional to its radius squared. The boundary correction from step 3.1 is also at most $C[g]_\alpha d^\alpha$. Hence $[D^2Ng]_{\alpha}\le C_\alpha[g]_\alpha$ on the box. The convergent far radial integral uses $\alpha<1$.

For $x\in B_1$, the support is in $B_3(x)$. Integrating $|\Phi|$ and $|D\Phi|$ over that ball bounds $|Ng|$ and $|DNg|$ by $C\|g\|_\infty$. Step 2.1 with $M=3$ bounds $|D^2Ng|$ by $C_\alpha([g]_\alpha+\|g\|_\infty)$; step 4.1 supplies the seminorm. These are precisely the unit-radius scaled bounds. The identity $Ng(Rx)=R^2N(g(R\cdot))(x)$ proves the displayed estimate for arbitrary $R$.

By [F4] the distribution of $-\Delta Ng-g$ vanishes. Step 2.1 makes this difference continuous, so it vanishes everywhere: a nonzero value would persist on a ball of positive measure. Thus $-\Delta Ng=g$ classically. Empty support and zero data give the zero potential, and all bounds remain valid.

Step 6.1: zero data gives zero potential and all bounds.
Steps 1.1 and 5.1 prove unit-radius estimates then rescale.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For a set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with at least two points, write $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=\sup_{x,y\in A,\,x\ne y}|q(x)-q(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, using absolute value for scalar $q$ and Euclidean array norm for finite-dimensional vector- or tensor-valued $q$; set $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=0$ when $A$ has at most one point. For nonempty $A$, put $\|q\|_{\infty;A}:=\sup_A|q|$. Globally $\alpha$-Hölder means continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ with $[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}<\infty$; set $[g]_\alpha:=[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$, $\|g\|_\infty:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}$, and $\|g\|_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^3}:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}+[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$. For an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $C^{2,\alpha}(V)$ means that the function has continuous partial derivatives through order $2$ on $V$ and $[D^2q]_{\alpha;K}<\infty$ for every compact $K\subset V$; $C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ means this property on every such $V$. In derivative-array norms below, $|D^jq|$ is the Euclidean norm of the array of order-$j$ partial derivatives and $\|D^jq\|_{\infty;B_R}:=\sup_{B_R}|D^jq|$. Let $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, and let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be globally $\alpha$-Hölder with support in $B_{2R}(0)$. Put $Ng(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$. Then $Ng\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Ng=g$, and

$$\sum_{j=0}^2R^j\|D^jNg\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^{2+\alpha}[D^2Ng]_{\alpha;B_R}\le C_\alpha R^2\bigl(\|g\|_\infty+R^\alpha[g]_\alpha\bigr).$$

The estimate uses the displayed scaled norms and is uniform in $R$ and $g$.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

derivations.claim: Scale first to $R=1$. Write $x=(x',t)$, $t=x_3$. The boundary function $g(x')=f(x',0)$ on the closed unit disk is bounded by $M=\|f\|_\infty$ and has seminorm at most $H=[f]_\alpha$. Extend it to all $\mathbb R^2$ by taking $\inf_z(g(z)+H|x'-z|^\alpha)$ over the original disk and clamping to $[-M,M]$. The inequality $(a+b)^\alpha\le a^\alpha+b^\alpha$ shows that this infimum is $H$-Hölder; the original Hölder inequality and $z=x'$ show agreement on the disk. Clamping is one-Lipschitz and preserves this agreement. For $H=0$ take the constant extension. Thus no differentiability of the boundary forcing is assumed.

Choose a two-dimensional mollifier $\rho$ from [F2], set $g_t(x')=\int\rho(z)g(x'-tz)\,dz$ for $t>0$, and put $L(x',t)=t^2g_t(x')/2$. A derivative of total order $k\ge1$ in $(x',t)$ of the kernel $t^{-2}\rho((x'-y')/t)$ has integral zero and has the form $t^{-2-k}P((x'-y')/t)$, with $P$ smooth and compactly supported. Subtract $g(x')$ under that differentiated integral to obtain $|D^kg_t|\le C_kH t^{\alpha-k}$ for $k=1,2,3$, and $|g_t-g|\le CHt^\alpha$. Differentiation is legitimate on every compact positive-$t$ interval because the differentiated kernels are bounded and compactly supported there.

Set $L=DL=0$ on the face. For $i,j<3$, direct differentiation gives $L_{ij}=t^2(g_t)_{ij}/2$, $L_{it}=t(g_t)_i+t^2(g_t)_{it}/2$ and $L_{tt}=g_t+2t(g_t)_t+t^2(g_t)_{tt}/2$. Consequently $D^2L(x',t)$ differs by at most $CHt^\alpha$ from the boundary matrix whose sole nonzero entry is its normal-normal entry $g(x')$, and $|D^3L|\le CHt^{\alpha-1}$. These are actual boundary jets: $L/t^2\to g/2$, $L_t/t\to g$, and $L_i/t\to0$. For points $X=(x',t),Y=(y',s)$ at distance $d$, if $d<\min(t,s)/2$, integrate the third-derivative bound along their segment to get $CHd\min(t,s)^{\alpha-1}\le CHd^\alpha$. Otherwise $\min(t,s)\le2d$ and $\max(t,s)\le3d$; compare both Hessians to their boundary jets and use the Hölder bound of $g$. Thus $\|L\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2\times[0,1])}\le C_\alpha(M+H)$ and $(\Delta L)(x',0)=g(x')$.

Let $v=u-L$ and $F=f-\Delta L$. Then $v=0$ and $F=0$ on the flat face, $\Delta v=F$, and $\|F\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|L\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C_\alpha\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$. Because $v$ is $C^2$ up to the face and has zero face restriction, its tangential first and second derivatives vanish there. The continuous equation then gives $v_{tt}=0$ there. Its odd reflection $V(x',-t)=-v(x',t)$ is therefore $C^2$ across the face: tangential-tangential and normal-normal Hessian entries are odd with zero trace, and mixed entries are even with matching traces. Its equation is $\Delta V=F_o$, with $F_o$ the odd reflection of $F$. For opposite-side points $(x',t),(y',-s)$, the zero trace gives $|F_o(x',t)-F_o(y',-s)|\le[F]_\alpha(t^\alpha+s^\alpha)\le2^{1-\alpha}[F]_\alpha|(x',t)-(y',-s)|^\alpha$. Same-side pairs use the original bound. Hence $F_o\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_1)$ with controlled norm. The original forcing has not been reflected without first removing its possibly nonzero trace.

Choose a fixed radial $\eta$ equal to one on $B_{3/4}$ and supported in $B_{7/8}$, extend $G=\eta F_o$ by zero, and put $W=-NG$. The Hölder product inequality and the support buffer give $\|G\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\mathbb R^3)}\le C\|F_o\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(B_1)}$: a point in $B_{7/8}$ is at distance at least $1/8$ from the exterior of $B_1$. By [F1], $\Delta W=G$ and $\|W\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(B_{3/4})}\le C_\alpha\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$. The radial kernel and cutoff are even in the normal coordinate, so $W$ is odd, and on the upper half-space it is exactly the reflected Green potential $-\int_{y_3>0}(\Phi(x-y)-\Phi(x-y^*))\eta(y)F(y)\,dy$, with $y^*=(y',-y_3)$. This reflection uses the corrected zero-trace Hölder datum, not a discontinuous odd extension of $f$.

The remainder $H_0=V-W$ is harmonic in $B_{3/4}$ with $\|H_0\|_\infty\le\|u\|_\infty+C_\alpha\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}$. By [F3], its sphere averages equal its center value. Average those identities against a fixed smooth radial kernel supported in $B_{1/16}$. On $B_{5/8}$ this writes $H_0=\kappa*H_0$ using only values in $B_{3/4}$; differentiation falls on $\kappa$, giving $\|D^jH_0\|_{\infty;B_{1/2}}\le C_j\|H_0\|_\infty$ for $j\le3$. Integration along segments then bounds $[D^2H_0]_{\alpha;B_{1/2}}$. Combining these bounds with $u=L+W+H_0$ on the upper half-ball proves the unit-radius estimate, including its flat-face limits.

For general $R$, apply the unit result to $u_R(x)=u(Rx)$ and $f_R(x)=R^2f(Rx)$. Derivatives scale by $R^j$ and the Hessian Hölder seminorm by $R^{2+\alpha}$. Thus the displayed estimate follows with the same constant. Only the given $C^2$ boundary regularity was used to justify reflection; no bound on higher derivatives of $u$ or $f$ has entered.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume Countable Choice and fix $0<\alpha<1$. Put $B_R^+=B_R(0)\cap\{x_3>0\}$ and $T_R=B_R(0)\cap\{x_3=0\}$. For any nonempty set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with at least two points and any scalar or finite-dimensional array-valued $q$ on $A$, define $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=\sup_{x,y\in A,\,x\ne y}|q(x)-q(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, set $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=0$ when $A$ has at most one point, and define $\|q\|_{\infty;A}:=\sup_A|q|$, using the Euclidean norm for arrays. For a function $f$ on the closed half-ball, $C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})$ consists of continuous functions there with finite seminorm and norm $\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})}:=\|f\|_{\infty;\overline{B_R^+}}+[f]_{\alpha;\overline{B_R^+}}$; in this statement $[f]_\alpha$ and $\|f\|_\infty$ denote $[f]_{\alpha;\overline{B_R^+}}$ and $\|f\|_{\infty;\overline{B_R^+}}$. Suppose $u$ is bounded and has continuous partial derivatives through order $2$ in $B_R^+$ which extend continuously to every compact subset of $B_R\cap\{x_3\ge0\}$, $\Delta u=f$ in $B_R^+$, $u=0$ on $T_R$, and $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\overline{B_R^+})$. There is no condition on the curved boundary and no requirement that $f|_{T_R}=0$. Then

$$\sum_{j=0}^2R^j\|D^ju\|_{\infty;B_{R/2}^+}+R^{2+\alpha}[D^2u]_{\alpha;B_{R/2}^+}\le C_\alpha\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R^+}+R^2\|f\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_\alpha\bigr).$$

The derivatives extend Hölder continuously to the flat face. The constant is independent of $R$ and of any higher derivative of a smooth approximant.

Assume Countable Choice. For a set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with at least two points, write $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=\sup_{x,y\in A,\,x\ne y}|q(x)-q(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha$, using absolute value for scalar $q$ and Euclidean array norm for finite-dimensional vector- or tensor-valued $q$; set $[q]_{\alpha;A}:=0$ when $A$ has at most one point. For nonempty $A$, put $\|q\|_{\infty;A}:=\sup_A|q|$. Globally $\alpha$-Hölder means continuous on $\mathbb R^3$ with $[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}<\infty$; set $[g]_\alpha:=[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$, $\|g\|_\infty:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}$, and $\|g\|_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^3}:=\|g\|_{\infty;\mathbb R^3}+[g]_{\alpha;\mathbb R^3}$. For an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, $C^{2,\alpha}(V)$ means that the function has continuous partial derivatives through order $2$ on $V$ and $[D^2q]_{\alpha;K}<\infty$ for every compact $K\subset V$; $C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ means this property on every such $V$. In derivative-array norms below, $|D^jq|$ is the Euclidean norm of the array of order-$j$ partial derivatives and $\|D^jq\|_{\infty;B_R}:=\sup_{B_R}|D^jq|$. Let $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, and let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be globally $\alpha$-Hölder with support in $B_{2R}(0)$. Put $Ng(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g(y)/(4\pi|x-y|)\,dy$. Then $Ng\in C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Ng=g$, and

$$\sum_{j=0}^2R^j\|D^jNg\|_{\infty;B_R}+R^{2+\alpha}[D^2Ng]_{\alpha;B_R}\le C_\alpha R^2\bigl(\|g\|_\infty+R^\alpha[g]_\alpha\bigr).$$

The estimate uses the displayed scaled norms and is uniform in $R$ and $g$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

derivations.claim: Finite normalized charts. Near each boundary point rotate and translate so that the domain is $x_3>\varphi(x')$, with $\varphi(0)=0$ and $D\varphi(0)=0$. The shear $\Psi(y',t)=(y',t+\varphi(y'))$ maps the actual upper half-patch onto the domain portion of its image, and maps $t=0$ onto the boundary. Its inverse subtracts $\varphi$, its Jacobian determinant is one, and $J=D\Psi$ and $J^{-1}$ are bounded on smaller compact patches. Compactness of the smooth boundary permits a finite initial atlas. Further recenterings at nearby boundary points and rotations to their tangent planes have uniformly bounded derivatives on a common smaller radius: in each initial compact graph patch the normal derivative is bounded away from zero and the graph derivatives are bounded; solving the graph identity and differentiating gives these uniform bounds. Thus arbitrarily small radii $r$ can be used with one fixed bound on the first three chart derivatives, independent of the number of recentered patches.

For $v=u\circ\Psi$, the chain rule gives $D_yv=J^TD_xu$ and $D_y^2v=J^TD_x^2uJ+\sum_k u_{x_k}D_y^2\Psi_k$. Solving these identities expresses $\Delta_xu\circ\Psi=a^{ij}D_{ij}v+b^iD_iv$, with $a=J^{-1}J^{-T}$, $a(0)=I$, and bounded smooth $b$. On a radius-$r$ patch, $\|a-I\|_\infty\le C r$, while $[a]_\alpha$, $\|b\|_\infty$ and $[b]_\alpha$ are bounded uniformly for $r$ below the fixed atlas radius. Chain/product differences also give two-sided control of the local $C^{2,\alpha}$ norms. In particular the coefficient of the top-order seminorm in this comparison stays bounded as $r\downarrow0$; terms involving derivatives of charts and derivatives of $u$ of order at most two contribute a fixed-radius multiple of $\|u\|_{C^2}$. This follows from $[pq]_\alpha\le\|p\|_\infty[q]_\alpha+[p]_\alpha\|q\|_\infty$ and $[p\circ\Psi]_\alpha\le[p]_\alpha\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi)^\alpha$.

Local freezing. Write $f=\Delta u$. In a boundary half-patch, $\Delta_yv=f\circ\Psi+(I-a):D^2v-b\cdot Dv$ and $v=0$ on the flat face. Apply [F2], with outer radius $r$ and inner radius $r/2$. The seminorm part of the principal error is bounded by $C r[D^2v]_\alpha+C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$; its supremum contributes only $C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$ after rescaling. The drift product and its seminorm contribute only $C_r\|v\|_{C^2}$ because $Dv$ is Lipschitz on the convex half-ball. It follows, after the chart comparison in step 2.1, that $[D^2u]_{\alpha;\mathrm{inner\ patch}}\le C_0 r[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}+C_r(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$, where $C_0$ is independent of small $r$. For an interior ball, extend a cutoff times $f$ by zero, subtract its Newtonian potential, and bound the harmonic remainder by the averaging-kernel argument in [F3]. This gives the same bound without the $C_0r$ term. No regularity of a weak solution has been assumed in this use of a priori estimates.

Global seminorm absorption. At a fixed sufficiently small $r$, take boundary centers forming an $r$-net in the compact boundary and interior balls of comparable radii for points farther from the boundary. Use outer patches with fixed larger radii proportional to $r$ and controlled inner patches of radius proportional to $r$; the uniform bi-Lipschitz chart bounds of step 1.1 ensure that each point has a controlled inner patch containing its intersection with a Euclidean ball of radius $c r$, with $c>0$ independent of the number of centers. Compactness selects finitely many. A pair at distance below $c r$ is therefore in one controlled patch; a pair farther apart has Hessian difference quotient at most $2(c r)^{-\alpha}\|D^2u\|_\infty$. Taking a maximum of the local estimates, not a sum over patches, yields $[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}\le C_1r[D^2u]_{\alpha;\Omega}+C_r(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$. Choose $r$ with $C_1r<1/2$ and absorb. Thus $\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}\le C(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u\|_{C^2})$, with the radius now fixed solely by the domain and exponent.

Removing the lower derivative terms. If the stated estimate were false, normalize zero-boundary $C^{2,\alpha}$ functions to obtain $\|u_j\|_{C^{2,\alpha}}=1$ and $\|\Delta u_j\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u_j\|_\infty\to0$. The finite chart atlas makes the function and gradient fields uniformly equicontinuous from their bounded next derivatives; the Hessians are equicontinuous from their common Hölder bound. Apply [F4] to this finite list of derivative fields. A subsequence converges uniformly on $\overline\Omega$; integration on coordinate segments in interior balls identifies its derivative fields. Since $u_j\to0$ uniformly, its first and second derivative limits vanish in the interior and, by continuity, on the closure. Thus $\|u_j\|_{C^2}\to0$. Step 4.1 then gives $1\le C(\|\Delta u_j\|_{C^{0,\alpha}}+\|u_j\|_{C^2})\to0$, a contradiction. This proves the full a priori estimate with only the supremum of $u$ on the right.

All charts, radii and constants were fixed by $\Omega$ and $\alpha$ before the solution was chosen. Reflection and the Newtonian kernel enter through [F2], flattening and coefficient perturbation were derived in steps 1.1--3.1, and the finite-cover and compactness arguments in steps 4.1--5.1 complete the claimed global estimate. No published boundary or global Schauder theorem is an input.

Let $U$ be a nonempty, connected, simply connected, second-countable smooth
two-manifold without boundary. Let $q$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $U$ such that $q_y$ is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+)$
for every $y\in U$. Choose a smooth vector field $N$ on $U$ with
$q(N,N)<0$ everywhere; the **time orientation** is the choice of the
connected component containing $N_y$ in each timelike cone
$\{v\in T_yU:q_y(v,v)<0\}$. Choose an orientation of $U$, and let
$\epsilon_2$ be its metric volume form, characterized by
$\epsilon_2(e_0,e_1)=1$ on every positively oriented $q$-orthonormal frame
with $q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. Let $r:U\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth.
Take $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot p=1\}$ with the smooth structure and
induced round metric fixed by the earlier dyonic Reissner–Nordström data
definition cited below. Its tangent plane is
$T_pS^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot u=0\}$, its metric is
$\gamma_{S^2,p}(u,v)=u\cdot v$, and its outward area form is
$(\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(p,u,v)$. Write $\wedge$ for the exterior
product of alternating forms. In polar coordinates
$\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Put
$\mathcal M:=U\times S^2$ and define its projections by
$\pi_U(y,p):=y$ and $\pi_S(y,p):=p$. For a smooth map $F:X\to Y$ and a
smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $Y$, define its pullback by
$$(F^*h)_x(v,w):=h_{F(x)}(dF_xv,dF_xw),$$
where $x\in X$, $v,w\in T_xX$, and $dF_x:T_xX\to T_{F(x)}Y$ is the
derivative. This formula also defines pullback of a covariant $2$-form.
Define
$$g:=\pi_U^*q+(r\circ\pi_U)^2\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$
It has Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
The fibre over $y\in U$ is $S^2_y:=\pi_U^{-1}(\{y\})=\{y\}\times S^2$.
Its induced Riemannian metric is $r(y)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and its area form is
$r(y)^2\omega_{S^2}$; in polar angles $0<\theta<\pi$ and
$0\le\phi<2\pi$, its area is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi r(y)^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi r(y)^2$.
Thus $r(y)>0$ is the areal radius of this orbit sphere.
Choose the four-dimensional orientation so that its metric volume form is
$$\mathrm{vol}_g=-(r\circ\pi_U)^2\,\pi_U^*\epsilon_2\wedge\pi_S^*\omega_{S^2}.$$
In any chart $(x^0,r)$ for which $\epsilon_2=-dx^0\wedge dr$, this gives
$\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge r^2\omega_{S^2}$.

Define
$$SO(3):=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3,\ \det R=1\}.$$
Each $R\in SO(3)$ acts on $S^2$ by $p\mapsto Rp$ and defines the smooth
diffeomorphism $\rho_R:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M$,
$\rho_R(y,p)=(y,Rp)$, whose inverse is $\rho_{R^{\mathsf T}}$.
For nonnegative integers $a,b$, a smooth tensor field of type $(a,b)$ on
$\mathcal M$ is a smooth section of
$$T^a_b\mathcal M:=(T\mathcal M)^{\otimes a}\otimes(T^*\mathcal M)^{\otimes b};$$
at each $x\in\mathcal M$ its value is multilinear on $a$ covectors in
$T_x^*\mathcal M$ and $b$ vectors in $T_x\mathcal M$, where
$T_x^*\mathcal M:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(T_x\mathcal M,\mathbb R)$.
Smoothness means that the components of the section in every smooth product
chart are $C^\infty$. For such a field $T$, define its pullback by the
diffeomorphism $\rho_R$ by
$$(\rho_R^*T)_x(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a;v_1,\ldots,v_b)=T_{\rho_R(x)}(\alpha_1\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1},\ldots,\alpha_a\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1};(d\rho_R)_xv_1,\ldots,(d\rho_R)_xv_b)$$
where $\alpha_i\in T_x^*\mathcal M$, $v_j\in T_x\mathcal M$, and
$(d\rho_R)_x:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{\rho_R(x)}\mathcal M$ is the derivative
of $\rho_R$ at $x$.
A real two-form is a smooth alternating tensor field of type $(0,2)$.
The field $T$ is **rotationally invariant** if $\rho_R^*T=T$ for every
$R\in SO(3)$; a two-form $\mathcal F$ is rotationally invariant in exactly
this sense. This definition specifies a local warped-product model and a
group action. It asserts no global quotient, global potential, maximal
extension, or field equation.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

For flux integration, an **oriented embedded smooth sphere** means a compact smooth two-dimensional manifold $S$ without boundary, homeomorphic to the unit sphere $\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x\cdot x=1\}$, with a specified orientation in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] and a smooth inclusion $i:S\hookrightarrow M$. Here smooth embedding means an injective immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image with the subspace topology ([[def-smooth-embedding]]); identify $S$ with that image. The sphere orientation is specified independently of the spacetime orientation; for coordinate spheres used below it is the stated outward orientation.

For a smooth two-form $\eta$ on a neighborhood of $i(S)$, use the pullback convention of [[def-pullback-of-a-differential-form]],
$$(i^*\eta)_p(v,w)=\eta_{i(p)}(di_pv,di_pw),\qquad p\in S,\quad v,w\in T_pS.$$
By [[prop-pullback-of-forms-is-smooth-functorial-and-preserves-wedges]], this is a smooth top form on $S$. Its support is the closure in $S$ of its nonzero locus ([[def-compactly-supported-differential-form]]), hence is closed in compact $S$ and compact by [[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]. Thus $i^*\eta\in\Omega_c^2(S)$.

Write $\mathcal I_S$ for [[def-integral-of-a-compactly-supported-top-form-on-an-oriented-manifold]]: for a subordinate smooth partition $(\rho_j)$ and connected charts $\phi_j$, it sets $\mathcal I_S(\omega)=\sum_j I_{\phi_j}(\rho_j\omega)$, where $I_{\phi_j}$ is the signed chart integral of the compactly supported coefficient. Only finitely many terms are nonzero. The value is independent of charts, partition and refinement by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]]. Define the surface notation by
$$\int_S\eta:=\mathcal I_S(i^*\eta).$$
This agrees with [[prop-integration-over-an-oriented-embedded-submanifold]]; a reparametrization here means an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $F:T\to S$ of oriented smooth two-manifolds (a smooth bijection with smooth inverse and orientation-preserving differential). For such $F$, the same value is $\mathcal I_T((iF)^*\eta)$.
The integration definition and its independence theorem assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, already retained in the geometric background below. For $\eta=\mathcal F$ and $\eta=\star_g\mathcal F$, smoothness of the given field and Hodge map makes both pulled-back top forms admissible; their integrals are finite real numbers. Define the geometric electric and magnetic flux parameters by
$$q_e(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\star_g\mathcal F,\qquad q_m(S):=\frac1{4\pi}\int_S\mathcal F.$$
When $M$ and the coordinates have length units, these parameters have units of length. A magnetic flux need not have a global potential; no flux quantization is included. The background Lorentzian geometry and Hodge conventions carry the countable-choice assumption $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of their named suppliers; the algebraic identities in this definition require no additional choice principle.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Fix $p\in S^2$ and put $H_p:=2pp^{\mathsf T}-I_3$. This matrix fixes
$p$ and acts as $-I$ on $p^\perp=T_pS^2$; its eigenvalues are $1,-1,-1$,
so $H_p^{\mathsf T}H_p=I_3$ and $\det H_p=1$, hence $H_p\in SO(3)$. Its
lift fixes $(y,p)$, is the identity on $T_yU$, and is $-I$ on $T_pS^2$. The
decomposition
$\Lambda^2(T_y^*U\oplus T_p^*S^2)=\Lambda^2T_y^*U\oplus
(T_y^*U\otimes T_p^*S^2)\oplus\Lambda^2T_p^*S^2$ is preserved by the
lifted rotation, while the mixed summand changes sign. Invariance therefore
forces the mixed component of $\mathcal F_{(y,p)}$ to equal its negative, so
that component is zero. The first and last summands are one-dimensional,
with generators $\epsilon_2$ and $\omega_{S^2}$. The base form is preserved
because each lift is the identity on $U$, and
$(R^*\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(Rp,Ru,Rv)=\det(R)\det(p,u,v)
=\omega_{S^2,p}(u,v)$ for $R\in SO(3)$. To prove transitivity, take
$p,p'\in S^2$,
choose unit vectors $u\perp p$ and $u'\perp p'$, and set $v=p\times u$ and
$v'=p'\times u'$. The oriented orthonormal frames $(p,u,v)$ and $(p',u',v')$
are related by a unique orientation-preserving orthogonal map $R$, which lies
in $SO(3)$ and sends $p$ to $p'$. Thus invariance makes the coefficients of
$\epsilon_2$ and $\omega_{S^2}$ independent of $p$. For a fixed $p_*\in S^2$, the smooth section $j(y):=(y,p_*)$ gives
$j^*\mathcal F=E\epsilon_2$. In any base chart the coefficient of the
nowhere-vanishing smooth form $\epsilon_2$ is nonzero, so division by it
shows that $E$ is smooth locally, hence on $U$. To recover the vertical
coefficient instead, take $p_*=(0,0,1)$, $v=(1,0,0)$ and $w=(0,1,0)$ in
$T_{p_*}S^2$. Along $j$, the product tangent vectors $(0,v)$ and $(0,w)$
are smooth sections of $j^*T\mathcal M$: this follows in any fixed sphere
chart about $p_*$, and requires no frame on all of $S^2$. Smoothness of
$\mathcal F$ therefore makes $y\mapsto\mathcal F_{(y,p_*)}((0,v),(0,w))$
smooth. Since $\omega_{S^2,p_*}(v,w)=\det(p_*,v,w)=1$, this function is
exactly $B(y)$, proving its smoothness. Consequently, uniquely
$\mathcal F=E(y)\epsilon_2+B(y)\omega_{S^2}$.

Since $\epsilon_2$ and $\omega_{S^2}$ are top forms on their respective
two-dimensional factors, their exterior derivatives vanish, and
$d\mathcal F=dB\wedge\omega_{S^2}$. The form $\omega_{S^2}$ never vanishes, so
$d\mathcal F=0$ implies $dB=0$. A smooth function with zero differential is
constant on connected $U$ (differentiate along each smooth path in a
coordinate-ball chain); call this constant $q_m$.

In an oriented orthonormal coframe with $\epsilon_2=-e^0\wedge e^1$ and
$r^2\omega_{S^2}=e^2\wedge e^3$, the four-volume is
$e^0\wedge e^1\wedge e^2\wedge e^3$. The Lorentzian Hodge definition therefore
gives $\star_g\epsilon_2=r^2\omega_{S^2}$ and
$\star_g\omega_{S^2}=-r^{-2}\epsilon_2$. Hence
$\star_g\mathcal F=Er^2\omega_{S^2}-Br^{-2}\epsilon_2$, and
$d(\star_g\mathcal F)=d(Er^2)\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ because a base one-form
wedged with the base top form $\epsilon_2$ vanishes. The second Maxwell equation
implies $d(Er^2)=0$, so $q_e:=Er^2$ is constant on connected $U$. Restricting
$\mathcal F$ and its Hodge dual to $S_y$ gives $q_m\omega_{S^2}$ and
$q_e\omega_{S^2}$; since $\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$ and
$\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\int_0^{2\pi}d\phi=4\pi$, the stated flux
normalizations follow. This proves existence and uniqueness of both constants.
