Let $U$ be a nonempty, connected, simply connected, second-countable smooth
two-manifold without boundary. Let $q$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $U$ such that $q_y$ is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+)$
for every $y\in U$. Choose a smooth vector field $N$ on $U$ with
$q(N,N)<0$ everywhere; the **time orientation** is the choice of the
connected component containing $N_y$ in each timelike cone
$\{v\in T_yU:q_y(v,v)<0\}$. Choose an orientation of $U$, and let
$\epsilon_2$ be its metric volume form, characterized by
$\epsilon_2(e_0,e_1)=1$ on every positively oriented $q$-orthonormal frame
with $q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. Let $r:U\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth.
Take $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot p=1\}$ with the smooth structure and
induced round metric fixed by the earlier dyonic Reissner–Nordström data
definition cited below. Its tangent plane is
$T_pS^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot u=0\}$, its metric is
$\gamma_{S^2,p}(u,v)=u\cdot v$, and its outward area form is
$(\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(p,u,v)$. Write $\wedge$ for the exterior
product of alternating forms. In polar coordinates
$\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Put
$\mathcal M:=U\times S^2$ and define its projections by
$\pi_U(y,p):=y$ and $\pi_S(y,p):=p$. For a smooth map $F:X\to Y$ and a
smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $Y$, define its pullback by
$$(F^*h)_x(v,w):=h_{F(x)}(dF_xv,dF_xw),$$
where $x\in X$, $v,w\in T_xX$, and $dF_x:T_xX\to T_{F(x)}Y$ is the
derivative. This formula also defines pullback of a covariant $2$-form.
Define
$$g:=\pi_U^*q+(r\circ\pi_U)^2\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$
It has Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
The fibre over $y\in U$ is $S^2_y:=\pi_U^{-1}(\{y\})=\{y\}\times S^2$.
Its induced Riemannian metric is $r(y)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and its area form is
$r(y)^2\omega_{S^2}$; in polar angles $0<\theta<\pi$ and
$0\le\phi<2\pi$, its area is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi r(y)^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi r(y)^2$.
Thus $r(y)>0$ is the areal radius of this orbit sphere.
Choose the four-dimensional orientation so that its metric volume form is
$$\mathrm{vol}_g=-(r\circ\pi_U)^2\,\pi_U^*\epsilon_2\wedge\pi_S^*\omega_{S^2}.$$
In any chart $(x^0,r)$ for which $\epsilon_2=-dx^0\wedge dr$, this gives
$\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge r^2\omega_{S^2}$.

Define
$$SO(3):=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3,\ \det R=1\}.$$
Each $R\in SO(3)$ acts on $S^2$ by $p\mapsto Rp$ and defines the smooth
diffeomorphism $\rho_R:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M$,
$\rho_R(y,p)=(y,Rp)$, whose inverse is $\rho_{R^{\mathsf T}}$.
For nonnegative integers $a,b$, a smooth tensor field of type $(a,b)$ on
$\mathcal M$ is a smooth section of
$$T^a_b\mathcal M:=(T\mathcal M)^{\otimes a}\otimes(T^*\mathcal M)^{\otimes b};$$
at each $x\in\mathcal M$ its value is multilinear on $a$ covectors in
$T_x^*\mathcal M$ and $b$ vectors in $T_x\mathcal M$, where
$T_x^*\mathcal M:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(T_x\mathcal M,\mathbb R)$.
Smoothness means that the components of the section in every smooth product
chart are $C^\infty$. For such a field $T$, define its pullback by the
diffeomorphism $\rho_R$ by
$$(\rho_R^*T)_x(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a;v_1,\ldots,v_b)=T_{\rho_R(x)}(\alpha_1\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1},\ldots,\alpha_a\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1};(d\rho_R)_xv_1,\ldots,(d\rho_R)_xv_b)$$
where $\alpha_i\in T_x^*\mathcal M$, $v_j\in T_x\mathcal M$, and
$(d\rho_R)_x:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{\rho_R(x)}\mathcal M$ is the derivative
of $\rho_R$ at $x$.
A real two-form is a smooth alternating tensor field of type $(0,2)$.
The field $T$ is **rotationally invariant** if $\rho_R^*T=T$ for every
$R\in SO(3)$; a two-form $\mathcal F$ is rotationally invariant in exactly
this sense. This definition specifies a local warped-product model and a
group action. It asserts no global quotient, global potential, maximal
extension, or field equation.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let
$R$, $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ be as in
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Then the following
identities hold for all indices $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and at every point of
every smooth chart:

**(a) Skew-symmetries.** $R_{abcd}=-R_{bacd}$ and $R_{abcd}=-R_{abdc}$.
Equivalently, for smooth vector fields,
$$g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=-g\bigl(R(X,Y)W,Z\bigr) \quad\text{and}\quad g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=-g\bigl(R(Y,X)Z,W\bigr).$$

**(b) Exchange of the index pairs.** $R_{abcd}=R_{cdab}$, equivalently
$g\bigl(R(X,Y)Z,W\bigr)=g\bigl(R(Z,W)X,Y\bigr)$.

**(c) First Bianchi identity.** $R_{a[bcd]}=0$, that is,
$$R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}=0 .$$

**(d) Ricci symmetry.** $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=\operatorname{Ric}_{ba}$;
consequently the Einstein tensor is symmetric, $G_{ab}=G_{ba}$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Form the four-manifold $\widetilde M:=U\times\mathbb R^2$ with product
metric $\widetilde g:=q+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2$, product orientation, and the lift
of the chosen future timelike field on $U$. This is a smooth
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold. By [F2], its metric-selected
connection has the displayed Christoffel formula. In product coordinates its
base Christoffels are exactly $\Gamma[q]^A{}_{BC}$, every Christoffel with a
flat-factor index is zero, and its curvature components with all indices in
the base are exactly $R[q]^A{}_{BCD}$ by [F5]. Thus the base Ricci contraction
in the product equals the two-dimensional contraction in the Statement.
Moreover, in an oriented base chart,
$\epsilon_{01}=\pm\sqrt{|\det q|}$ and
$\Gamma^C{}_{AC}=\frac12q^{CD}\partial_Aq_{CD}
=\partial_A\log\sqrt{|\det q|}$. Substituting these identities in
$\nabla_A\epsilon_{BC}=\partial_A\epsilon_{BC}
-\Gamma^D{}_{AB}\epsilon_{DC}-\Gamma^D{}_{AC}\epsilon_{BD}$ gives
$\nabla^q\epsilon_2=0$; the only independent component is $BC=01$, for which
the connection terms sum to $\Gamma^C{}_{AC}\epsilon_{01}$ and cancel the
partial derivative.

At any point choose a $q$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1)$ with
$q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. In the product four-manifold the
algebraic symmetries [F4] and antisymmetry in each pair force every base
component of $R_{ABCD}$ to vanish unless both pairs are $(0,1)$ up to order.
Write $K:=R_{0101}$. Pair exchange and the two antisymmetries give
$R_{1010}=K$ and all components with repeated entries in either pair vanish.
Using [F3], $\operatorname{Ric}_{00}=q^{11}R_{1010}=K$,
$\operatorname{Ric}_{11}=q^{00}R_{0101}=-K$, and
$\operatorname{Ric}_{01}=\operatorname{Ric}_{10}=0$. Hence
$\operatorname{Ric}(q)=-Kq$ and $S_q=-2K$, so
$\operatorname{Ric}(q)=\tfrac12S_q q$. The point was arbitrary; together
with step 1.1 this proves both identities.

An exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum consists of the orbit
geometry specified above, a smooth rotationally invariant real two-form
$\mathcal F$, a constant $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
the equations
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ab}=\Lambda g_{ab}+2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F),$$
where
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c -\frac14g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd}.$$
This is a mathematical system of equations, not a physical postulate. For
$\Lambda=0$ it uses exactly the curvature, Hodge, and Maxwell normalization of
the previously defined geometric electrovac equations. For $\Lambda\ne0$ the extra constant
term is part of this local mathematical definition; it is not supplied by
that zero-$\Lambda$ item.

By the preceding Maxwell reduction lemma, the field has unique constant
flux parameters $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ and
$$\mathcal F=\frac{q_e}{r^2}\epsilon_2+q_m\omega_{S^2},\qquad Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2.$$
In geometric units, coordinates have length, $r,q_e,q_m$ have length, the
metric components are dimensionless, and $\Lambda$ has units of inverse
length squared. Define
$$z:=q^{-1}(dr,dr),\qquad \varpi:=\frac r2(1-z)+\frac{Q^2}{2r}-\frac{\Lambda r^3}{6}.$$
Thus $z$ is dimensionless and $\varpi$ has length. The scalar $\varpi$ is
called the charged spherical mass function; this definition does not assert
that it is constant. The field equations are local on $U\times S^2$ and
impose no global potential, bundle, horizon, asymptotic, completeness, or
extension condition.

The geometric-electrovacuum flux convention inherits only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
through the supplied geometric electrovac definition. No full axiom of choice is used
by this definition or by the subsequent local algebra.

Let $(U,q,\epsilon_2)$ be a connected, oriented, time-oriented smooth
two-dimensional Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+)$ with
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.
In local coordinates $y^0,y^1$, define
$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\frac12q^{AD} (\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}),$$
and use the resulting metric-selected derivative $\nabla^q$ and the
curvature convention
$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}.$$
Let $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=q^{AC}q_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD}$ and
$S_q:=q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}$. Then
$$\nabla^q\epsilon_2=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(q)=\frac12S_q\,q.$$
The only inherited choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from the
four-dimensional Levi-Civita supplier used below; no full axiom of choice is
used.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

derivations.claim: Use base indices $A,B,C$ and sphere indices $i,j,k$. The inverse metric is $g^{AB}=q^{AB}$ and $g^{ij}=r^{-2}\gamma^{ij}$. From [F4], the mixed Christoffels, in addition to the separate base and sphere Christoffels, are $$\Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-r(\nabla^q r)^A\gamma_{ij},\qquad \Gamma^i{}_{Aj}=r^{-1}(\partial_A r)\delta^i_j,$$ and all other mixed Christoffels vanish. The unit round sphere has $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\phi{}_{\theta\phi}=\Gamma^\phi{}_{\phi\theta}=\cot\theta$ on the polar chart of [F6]. Substitution in [F5] and contraction by [F3] give $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{\theta\theta} =-\partial_\theta\cot\theta-\cot^2\theta=1$ and $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{\phi\phi} =\partial_\theta(-\sin\theta\cos\theta)-\cos^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta =\sin^2\theta$, with mixed component zero. Thus $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)=\gamma$ on that chart and everywhere by smoothness.

In an oriented orthonormal coframe for the two-dimensional Lorentzian base and the round sphere, $\epsilon_{AB}\epsilon^{AB}=-2$ and the sphere area form has squared norm $2/r^4$. The two summands of $\mathcal F$ occupy orthogonal blocks, so $\mathcal F_{ab}\mathcal F^{ab}=2(q_m^2-q_e^2)/r^4$. The same two-dimensional contractions give $\mathcal F_{AC}\mathcal F_B{}^C=-q_e^2r^{-4}q_{AB}$ and $\mathcal F_{ik}\mathcal F_j{}^k=q_m^2r^{-4}g_{ij}$; mixed contractions vanish. Substituting these three identities into [F1]'s definition of $Q$ yields the stated base and sphere components.

In the coordinate Ricci formula, the terms in $\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{AB}$ with only base indices give $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}$. The remaining sphere-index terms are $$-\partial_B(2r_A/r)+(2r_C/r)\Gamma^C{}_{AB} -2r_Ar_B/r^2=-2r^{-1}(\partial_Br_A-\Gamma^C{}_{AB}r_C),$$ which is $-2r^{-1}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B$. For $\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ij}$, the pure-sphere terms give $\operatorname{Ric}(\gamma)_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}$. The base derivative terms are $-[\partial_A(rr^A)+\Gamma^C{}_{CA}rr^A]\gamma_{ij} =-(r\Delta_qr+z)\gamma_{ij}$. The mixed trace $\Gamma^k{}_{kA}\Gamma^A{}_{ij}=-2z\gamma_{ij}$ cancels the two mixed products $-\Gamma^k{}_{jA}\Gamma^A{}_{ik} -\Gamma^A{}_{jk}\Gamma^k{}_{iA}=2z\gamma_{ij}$. For $\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{Ai}$, the derivative $\partial_i\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha A}$ vanishes because $\Gamma^\alpha{}_{\alpha A}=\Gamma^B{}_{BA}+2r_A/r$ depends only on the base coordinates, and all derivatives $\partial_\alpha\Gamma^\alpha{}_{iA}$ vanish because the only nonzero such coefficients are $\Gamma^j{}_{iA}=(r_A/r)\delta^j_i$. In the remaining products, the term $\Gamma^\ell{}_{\ell k}\Gamma^k{}_{iA}=(r_A/r)\Gamma^\ell{}_{\ell i}$ is canceled by $-\Gamma^j{}_{ik}\Gamma^k{}_{jA}=-(r_A/r)\Gamma^j{}_{ij}=-(r_A/r)\Gamma^j{}_{ji}$; every other product contains a zero mixed Christoffel. Thus $\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{Ai}=0$. These identities give the three stated warped Ricci formulas.

The base Einstein equation, steps 2.1 and 1.2, and [F2] yield $$\frac12S_q q_{AB}-2r^{-1}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B =(\Lambda-Q^2/r^4)q_{AB}.$$ Its right-hand side and the first term are scalar multiples of $q$, so $\nabla^q dr$ is a scalar multiple of $q$. Taking its trace identifies that multiple as $\tfrac12\Delta_qr$. The sphere Einstein equation gives $1-z-r\Delta_qr=\Lambda r^2+Q^2/r^2$, which rearranges to the stated formula for $\Delta_qr$.

Differentiate $z=q^{AB}r_Ar_B$. Metric compatibility gives $dz=2(\nabla^q dr)(\nabla^q r,\cdot)=\Delta_qr\,dr$ by step 3.1. Therefore $$d\varpi=\frac12(1-z)dr-\frac r2dz -\frac{Q^2}{2r^2}dr-\frac{\Lambda r^2}{2}dr.$$ Substituting $\Delta_qr=(1-z)/r-\Lambda r-Q^2/r^3$ from step 3.1 makes the coefficient of $dr$ zero term by term. Thus $d\varpi=0$, completing the conditional calculation.

An exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum consists of the orbit
geometry specified above, a smooth rotationally invariant real two-form
$\mathcal F$, a constant $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
the equations
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ab}=\Lambda g_{ab}+2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F),$$
where
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c -\frac14g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd}.$$
This is a mathematical system of equations, not a physical postulate. For
$\Lambda=0$ it uses exactly the curvature, Hodge, and Maxwell normalization of
the previously defined geometric electrovac equations. For $\Lambda\ne0$ the extra constant
term is part of this local mathematical definition; it is not supplied by
that zero-$\Lambda$ item.

By the preceding Maxwell reduction lemma, the field has unique constant
flux parameters $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ and
$$\mathcal F=\frac{q_e}{r^2}\epsilon_2+q_m\omega_{S^2},\qquad Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2.$$
In geometric units, coordinates have length, $r,q_e,q_m$ have length, the
metric components are dimensionless, and $\Lambda$ has units of inverse
length squared. Define
$$z:=q^{-1}(dr,dr),\qquad \varpi:=\frac r2(1-z)+\frac{Q^2}{2r}-\frac{\Lambda r^3}{6}.$$
Thus $z$ is dimensionless and $\varpi$ has length. The scalar $\varpi$ is
called the charged spherical mass function; this definition does not assert
that it is constant. The field equations are local on $U\times S^2$ and
impose no global potential, bundle, horizon, asymptotic, completeness, or
extension condition.

The geometric-electrovacuum flux convention inherits only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
through the supplied geometric electrovac definition. No full axiom of choice is used
by this definition or by the subsequent local algebra.

For an exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum, let
$z=q^{-1}(dr,dr)$ and
$\Delta_qr:=q^{AB}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B$. The warped metric
$g=q+r^2\gamma_{S^2}$ has
$$\operatorname{Ric}(g)_{AB} =\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{AB}-2r^{-1}(\nabla^q_A dr)_B,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ij}=(1-z-r\Delta_qr)\gamma_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{Ai}=0.$$
Its Maxwell tensor satisfies
$$Q_{AB}(\mathcal F)=-\frac{Q^2}{2r^4}q_{AB},\qquad Q_{ij}(\mathcal F)=\frac{Q^2}{2r^4}g_{ij},\qquad Q_{Ai}(\mathcal F)=0.$$
Consequently the Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ equations imply
$$\nabla^q_A dr_B=\frac12(\Delta_qr)q_{AB},\qquad \Delta_qr=\frac{1-z}{r}-\Lambda r-\frac{Q^2}{r^3},\qquad d\varpi=0.$$

Let $(U,q,\epsilon_2)$ be a connected, oriented, time-oriented smooth
two-dimensional Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+)$ with
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.
In local coordinates $y^0,y^1$, define
$$\Gamma^A{}_{BC}:=\frac12q^{AD} (\partial_Bq_{DC}+\partial_Cq_{BD}-\partial_Dq_{BC}),$$
and use the resulting metric-selected derivative $\nabla^q$ and the
curvature convention
$$R^A{}_{BCD}:=\partial_C\Gamma^A{}_{DB}-\partial_D\Gamma^A{}_{CB} +\Gamma^A{}_{CE}\Gamma^E{}_{DB}-\Gamma^A{}_{DE}\Gamma^E{}_{CB}.$$
Let $\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}:=q^{AC}q_{AE}R^E{}_{BCD}$ and
$S_q:=q^{BD}\operatorname{Ric}(q)_{BD}$. Then
$$\nabla^q\epsilon_2=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(q)=\frac12S_q\,q.$$
The only inherited choice assumption is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ from the
four-dimensional Levi-Civita supplier used below; no full axiom of choice is
used.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map and let $p\in M$. If $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is
an isomorphism, then there are open neighbourhoods $U$ of $p$ and $V$ of
$F(p)$ such that $F|_U:U\to V$ is a diffeomorphism.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$), let $F$ be its integral function
(The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Let $U$ be a nonempty, connected, simply connected, second-countable smooth
two-manifold without boundary. Let $q$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $U$ such that $q_y$ is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+)$
for every $y\in U$. Choose a smooth vector field $N$ on $U$ with
$q(N,N)<0$ everywhere; the **time orientation** is the choice of the
connected component containing $N_y$ in each timelike cone
$\{v\in T_yU:q_y(v,v)<0\}$. Choose an orientation of $U$, and let
$\epsilon_2$ be its metric volume form, characterized by
$\epsilon_2(e_0,e_1)=1$ on every positively oriented $q$-orthonormal frame
with $q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. Let $r:U\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth.
Take $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot p=1\}$ with the smooth structure and
induced round metric fixed by the earlier dyonic Reissner–Nordström data
definition cited below. Its tangent plane is
$T_pS^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot u=0\}$, its metric is
$\gamma_{S^2,p}(u,v)=u\cdot v$, and its outward area form is
$(\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(p,u,v)$. Write $\wedge$ for the exterior
product of alternating forms. In polar coordinates
$\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Put
$\mathcal M:=U\times S^2$ and define its projections by
$\pi_U(y,p):=y$ and $\pi_S(y,p):=p$. For a smooth map $F:X\to Y$ and a
smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $Y$, define its pullback by
$$(F^*h)_x(v,w):=h_{F(x)}(dF_xv,dF_xw),$$
where $x\in X$, $v,w\in T_xX$, and $dF_x:T_xX\to T_{F(x)}Y$ is the
derivative. This formula also defines pullback of a covariant $2$-form.
Define
$$g:=\pi_U^*q+(r\circ\pi_U)^2\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$
It has Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
The fibre over $y\in U$ is $S^2_y:=\pi_U^{-1}(\{y\})=\{y\}\times S^2$.
Its induced Riemannian metric is $r(y)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and its area form is
$r(y)^2\omega_{S^2}$; in polar angles $0<\theta<\pi$ and
$0\le\phi<2\pi$, its area is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi r(y)^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi r(y)^2$.
Thus $r(y)>0$ is the areal radius of this orbit sphere.
Choose the four-dimensional orientation so that its metric volume form is
$$\mathrm{vol}_g=-(r\circ\pi_U)^2\,\pi_U^*\epsilon_2\wedge\pi_S^*\omega_{S^2}.$$
In any chart $(x^0,r)$ for which $\epsilon_2=-dx^0\wedge dr$, this gives
$\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge r^2\omega_{S^2}$.

Define
$$SO(3):=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3,\ \det R=1\}.$$
Each $R\in SO(3)$ acts on $S^2$ by $p\mapsto Rp$ and defines the smooth
diffeomorphism $\rho_R:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M$,
$\rho_R(y,p)=(y,Rp)$, whose inverse is $\rho_{R^{\mathsf T}}$.
For nonnegative integers $a,b$, a smooth tensor field of type $(a,b)$ on
$\mathcal M$ is a smooth section of
$$T^a_b\mathcal M:=(T\mathcal M)^{\otimes a}\otimes(T^*\mathcal M)^{\otimes b};$$
at each $x\in\mathcal M$ its value is multilinear on $a$ covectors in
$T_x^*\mathcal M$ and $b$ vectors in $T_x\mathcal M$, where
$T_x^*\mathcal M:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(T_x\mathcal M,\mathbb R)$.
Smoothness means that the components of the section in every smooth product
chart are $C^\infty$. For such a field $T$, define its pullback by the
diffeomorphism $\rho_R$ by
$$(\rho_R^*T)_x(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a;v_1,\ldots,v_b)=T_{\rho_R(x)}(\alpha_1\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1},\ldots,\alpha_a\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1};(d\rho_R)_xv_1,\ldots,(d\rho_R)_xv_b)$$
where $\alpha_i\in T_x^*\mathcal M$, $v_j\in T_x\mathcal M$, and
$(d\rho_R)_x:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{\rho_R(x)}\mathcal M$ is the derivative
of $\rho_R$ at $x$.
A real two-form is a smooth alternating tensor field of type $(0,2)$.
The field $T$ is **rotationally invariant** if $\rho_R^*T=T$ for every
$R\in SO(3)$; a two-form $\mathcal F$ is rotationally invariant in exactly
this sense. This definition specifies a local warped-product model and a
group action. It asserts no global quotient, global potential, maximal
extension, or field equation.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be smooth vector fields on $M$. Their **Lie bracket** is the
operator on smooth functions defined by

$$ [X,Y]f:=X(Yf)-Y(Xf). $$

The next results show that this commutator is again induced by a smooth vector
field on $M$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $d\varpi=0$. Any two points in a connected smooth manifold can be joined by a piecewise smooth path: the set reachable from a point by such paths and its complement are both unions of coordinate-ball neighborhoods, so connectedness makes the reachable set the whole patch. Along each smooth path segment $\sigma$, $(\varpi\circ\sigma)'=d\varpi(\sigma')=0$, so the one-variable mean-value theorem makes $\varpi$ constant along the segment. Thus $\varpi=m$ on the patch.

Let $X^A:=\epsilon_2^{AB}
abla^q_Br$, where indices on $\epsilon_2$ are raised with $q^{-1}$. The volume form is nondegenerate, so $X
e0$ because $dr
e0$. Antisymmetry gives $X(r)=0$. In an oriented orthonormal frame with $\epsilon_2=-e^0\wedge e^1$, direct contraction gives $q(X,X)=-(r_0)^2+(r_1)^2=-z$. By [F2] the Hessian is $
abla^q dr=	frac12(\Delta_qr)q$, and [F3] gives $
abla^q\epsilon_2=0$. Hence $
abla_A X_B=	frac12(\Delta_qr)\epsilon_{BA}$, which is antisymmetric in $A,B$. In local coordinates, [F9] and the Lie-derivative definition give $(\mathcal L_Xq)_{AB}=X^C\partial_Cq_{AB}+q_{CB}\partial_AX^C+q_{AC}\partial_BX^C$. Expanding $
abla^q_A X_B+
abla^q_B X_A$ with $X_B=q_{BC}X^C$ and the Christoffel formula for $
abla^q$ in [F3] gives the same expression: the coefficient of $X^C$ reduces to $\partial_Cq_{AB}$ by $2\Gamma^D{}_{AB}q_{DC}=\partial_Aq_{BC}+\partial_Bq_{AC}-\partial_Cq_{AB}$. Thus $\mathcal L_Xq=0$. Let $\widehat X_{(y,p)}:=(X_y,0)$ be the lift to $\mathcal M$; its local flow is $(y,p)\mapsto(\Phi_t(y),p)$, so $\mathcal L_{\widehat X}\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}=0$. Applying the defining Lie-derivative formula to the warped metric yields $\mathcal L_{\widehat X}g=\pi_U^*(\mathcal L_Xq)+2(r\circ\pi_U)(Xr)\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}=0$. Thus the lifted vector field is Killing for the full four-dimensional metric, and in the constructed coordinates it is the lift $K$ of $\partial_t$.

The smooth local flow theorem [F4] gives a local flow $\Phi_t$ of the nonvanishing field $X$. To construct a transverse curve, choose a chart $(y^0,y^1)$ with $\partial_{y^0}r\ne0$ at the point; the map $(y^0,y^1)\mapsto(r(y^0,y^1),y^1)$ has invertible differential there. The inverse function theorem [F5], after restricting the chart, therefore gives a smooth curve $\sigma(s)$ through the point with $r(\sigma(s))=s$. Define $\Psi(t,s):=\Phi_t(\sigma(s))$ on a sufficiently small product neighborhood. The identity $X(r)=0$ gives $r(\Psi(t,s))=s$. At the initial point the two derivatives of $\Psi$ are $X$ and $\sigma'(s)$; they are independent because $dr(X)=0$ and $dr(\sigma')=1$. Thus $d\Psi$ is invertible, and [F5] makes $(t,r)$ valid local coordinates with $X=\partial_t$.

Since $X=\partial_t$ and $\mathcal L_Xq=0$, each coordinate coefficient is independent of $t$, so $q=A(r)dt^2+2B(r)\,dt\,dr+C(r)dr^2$. From step 1.2, $A=q(X,X)=-z\ne0$. Both $A$ and $B$ are smooth functions of $r$, so $B/A$ is smooth on the local $r$-interval. Define $G(r):=\int_{r_0}^r B(s)/A(s)\,ds$. Applying [F6] on each compact subinterval containing $r_0$ and $r$ gives $G'=B/A$, first making $G$ continuously differentiable. Since its derivative $B/A$ is smooth, repeated differentiation shows $G$ is smooth. The coordinate change $(t,r)\mapsto(\widetilde t,r):=(t+G(r),r)$ and its inverse $(\widetilde t,r)\mapsto(\widetilde t-G(r),r)$ are therefore smooth. Substituting $dt=d\widetilde t-G'(r)dr$ makes the cross-term coefficient $2(B-AG')=0$. The coordinate $r$ is unchanged, so $q^{rr}=q^{-1}(dr,dr)=z$; for a diagonal two-metric this implies $q_{\widetilde t\widetilde t}=-z$ and $q_{rr}=z^{-1}$.

Solving $\varpi=m$ from step 1.1 for $z$ gives $z=1-2m/r+(q_e^2+q_m^2)/r^2-\Lambda r^2/3=:f(r)$. Substituting this in step 3.1 gives the stated metric; $f\ne0$ by [A2]. In these diagonal coordinates $\det q=-1$, so the metric volume form has the form $\epsilon_2=s\,d\widetilde t\wedge dr$ for a locally constant $s\in\{-1,1\}$. Raising indices gives $\epsilon_2^{\widetilde t r}=-s$, and hence $X^{\widetilde t}=\epsilon_2^{\widetilde t r}\partial_r r=-s$. Since the construction gives $X=\partial_{\widetilde t}$, it follows that $s=-1$. Thus $\epsilon_2=-d\widetilde t\wedge dr$ and the Maxwell form in [F1] is exactly the stated field. Since $q(\partial_{\widetilde t},\partial_{\widetilde t})=-f$, its causal character has the claimed sign. For $\Lambda=0$, this is precisely the signature and field normalization of [F7]. Renaming $\widetilde t$ as $t$ gives the coordinates in the Statement. No extension across $f=0$ or global uniqueness follows from these local coordinates.

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ carry its induced unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$ and outward area form $\omega_{S^2}$. Let $L>0$ have length units. Choose either (i) $f(z)=z^2$ on an open $J\subset(0,\infty)$, or (ii) $f(z)=1+z^2$ on an open $J\subset\mathbb R$. The coordinate $z$ and $\tau$ are dimensionless. On $\mathcal M_{L,f}=\mathbb R_\tau\times J_z\times S^2$, orient by $d\tau\wedge dz\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ and define

$$g_{L,f}=L^2\bigl(-f(z)d\tau^2+f(z)^{-1}dz^2+\gamma_{S^2}\bigr),\qquad \mathcal F_L=-L\,d\tau\wedge dz.$$

The smooth field $N=(L\sqrt{f})^{-1}\partial_\tau$ is unit timelike; it selects the future direction. This explicit metric-field tuple is the **Bertotti-Robinson product data** for this library. “Electrovac” refers to the equations in [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] and is not asserted by this definition. The product has sphere radius $L$ at every base point.

Every datum in [[def-emg-xs-br-products]] is a geometric electrovac datum of [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]]. With the oriented orthonormal coframe

$$e^0=L\sqrt f\,d\tau,\quad e^1=L f^{-1/2}dz,\quad e^2=L\,d\theta,\quad e^3=L\sin\theta\,d\phi,$$

the Ricci and quadratic Maxwell tensors are

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{AB}=L^{-2}\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)_{AB},\qquad Q_{AB}(\mathcal F_L)=\frac1{2L^2}\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,1)_{AB}.$$

All mixed base-sphere entries vanish. The statement is on the chosen open chart domains; it makes no maximal-extension or asymptotic-flatness claim.

Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ carry its induced unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$ and outward area form $\omega_{S^2}$. Let $L>0$ have length units. Choose either (i) $f(z)=z^2$ on an open $J\subset(0,\infty)$, or (ii) $f(z)=1+z^2$ on an open $J\subset\mathbb R$. The coordinate $z$ and $\tau$ are dimensionless. On $\mathcal M_{L,f}=\mathbb R_\tau\times J_z\times S^2$, orient by $d\tau\wedge dz\wedge\omega_{S^2}$ and define

$$g_{L,f}=L^2\bigl(-f(z)d\tau^2+f(z)^{-1}dz^2+\gamma_{S^2}\bigr),\qquad \mathcal F_L=-L\,d\tau\wedge dz.$$

The smooth field $N=(L\sqrt{f})^{-1}\partial_\tau$ is unit timelike; it selects the future direction. This explicit metric-field tuple is the **Bertotti-Robinson product data** for this library. “Electrovac” refers to the equations in [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]] and is not asserted by this definition. The product has sphere radius $L$ at every base point.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let an exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$
datum be given on a connected patch. Suppose $dr$ is nowhere zero and
$z=q^{-1}(dr,dr)$ is nowhere zero. Then the charged mass function $\varpi$ is
constant, say $m$. Around each point there are local
coordinates $(t,r)$ on the quotient in which
$$g=-f(r)\,dt^2+f(r)^{-1}\,dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad f(r)=1-\frac{2m}{r}+\frac{q_e^2+q_m^2}{r^2}-\frac{\Lambda r^2}{3},$$
and
$$\mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dt\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
For smooth vector fields $Y,V$ on an open set $O\subseteq\mathcal M$, define
their Lie bracket on $\varphi\in C^\infty(O)$ by
$[Y,V](\varphi):=Y(V(\varphi))-V(Y(\varphi))$. For a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $\mathcal M$ and smooth vector field $Y$,
define its Lie derivative by
$$(\mathcal L_Yh)(V,W):=Y(h(V,W))-h([Y,V],W)-h(V,[Y,W]),$$
for smooth vector fields $V,W$ on a common open set. A vector field is
**Killing** for $h$ when
$\mathcal L_Yh=0$. The quotient coordinate field $\partial_t$
has the product lift $K_{(y,p)}=(\partial_t|_y,0)$ to $\mathcal M$; this
lift is Killing for the full warped metric $g$ and has squared norm $-f$.
Where $f>0$, $K$ is timelike and is future- or past-directed according to the
given time orientation; where $f<0$, $K$ is spacelike and no future/past
designation is asserted. For $\Lambda=0$ this is the dyonic
Reissner–Nordström local form in the stated source convention.
Constant-radius and null-gradient patches, points with $f=0$, global
extensions, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, and black-hole uniqueness are
outside the claim.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Let $U$ be a nonempty, connected, simply connected, second-countable smooth
two-manifold without boundary. Let $q$ be a smooth symmetric covariant
$2$-tensor field on $U$ such that $q_y$ is nondegenerate of signature $(-,+)$
for every $y\in U$. Choose a smooth vector field $N$ on $U$ with
$q(N,N)<0$ everywhere; the **time orientation** is the choice of the
connected component containing $N_y$ in each timelike cone
$\{v\in T_yU:q_y(v,v)<0\}$. Choose an orientation of $U$, and let
$\epsilon_2$ be its metric volume form, characterized by
$\epsilon_2(e_0,e_1)=1$ on every positively oriented $q$-orthonormal frame
with $q(e_0,e_0)=-1$ and $q(e_1,e_1)=1$. Let $r:U\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth.
Take $S^2=\{p\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot p=1\}$ with the smooth structure and
induced round metric fixed by the earlier dyonic Reissner–Nordström data
definition cited below. Its tangent plane is
$T_pS^2=\{u\in\mathbb R^3:p\cdot u=0\}$, its metric is
$\gamma_{S^2,p}(u,v)=u\cdot v$, and its outward area form is
$(\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v)=\det(p,u,v)$. Write $\wedge$ for the exterior
product of alternating forms. In polar coordinates
$\omega_{S^2}=\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. Put
$\mathcal M:=U\times S^2$ and define its projections by
$\pi_U(y,p):=y$ and $\pi_S(y,p):=p$. For a smooth map $F:X\to Y$ and a
smooth covariant $2$-tensor field $h$ on $Y$, define its pullback by
$$(F^*h)_x(v,w):=h_{F(x)}(dF_xv,dF_xw),$$
where $x\in X$, $v,w\in T_xX$, and $dF_x:T_xX\to T_{F(x)}Y$ is the
derivative. This formula also defines pullback of a covariant $2$-form.
Define
$$g:=\pi_U^*q+(r\circ\pi_U)^2\pi_S^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$
It has Lorentzian signature $(-,+,+,+)$.
The fibre over $y\in U$ is $S^2_y:=\pi_U^{-1}(\{y\})=\{y\}\times S^2$.
Its induced Riemannian metric is $r(y)^2\gamma_{S^2}$ and its area form is
$r(y)^2\omega_{S^2}$; in polar angles $0<\theta<\pi$ and
$0\le\phi<2\pi$, its area is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi r(y)^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi r(y)^2$.
Thus $r(y)>0$ is the areal radius of this orbit sphere.
Choose the four-dimensional orientation so that its metric volume form is
$$\mathrm{vol}_g=-(r\circ\pi_U)^2\,\pi_U^*\epsilon_2\wedge\pi_S^*\omega_{S^2}.$$
In any chart $(x^0,r)$ for which $\epsilon_2=-dx^0\wedge dr$, this gives
$\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dr\wedge r^2\omega_{S^2}$.

Define
$$SO(3):=\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_3,\ \det R=1\}.$$
Each $R\in SO(3)$ acts on $S^2$ by $p\mapsto Rp$ and defines the smooth
diffeomorphism $\rho_R:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M$,
$\rho_R(y,p)=(y,Rp)$, whose inverse is $\rho_{R^{\mathsf T}}$.
For nonnegative integers $a,b$, a smooth tensor field of type $(a,b)$ on
$\mathcal M$ is a smooth section of
$$T^a_b\mathcal M:=(T\mathcal M)^{\otimes a}\otimes(T^*\mathcal M)^{\otimes b};$$
at each $x\in\mathcal M$ its value is multilinear on $a$ covectors in
$T_x^*\mathcal M$ and $b$ vectors in $T_x\mathcal M$, where
$T_x^*\mathcal M:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(T_x\mathcal M,\mathbb R)$.
Smoothness means that the components of the section in every smooth product
chart are $C^\infty$. For such a field $T$, define its pullback by the
diffeomorphism $\rho_R$ by
$$(\rho_R^*T)_x(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a;v_1,\ldots,v_b)=T_{\rho_R(x)}(\alpha_1\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1},\ldots,\alpha_a\circ(d\rho_R)_x^{-1};(d\rho_R)_xv_1,\ldots,(d\rho_R)_xv_b)$$
where $\alpha_i\in T_x^*\mathcal M$, $v_j\in T_x\mathcal M$, and
$(d\rho_R)_x:T_x\mathcal M\to T_{\rho_R(x)}\mathcal M$ is the derivative
of $\rho_R$ at $x$.
A real two-form is a smooth alternating tensor field of type $(0,2)$.
The field $T$ is **rotationally invariant** if $\rho_R^*T=T$ for every
$R\in SO(3)$; a two-form $\mathcal F$ is rotationally invariant in exactly
this sense. This definition specifies a local warped-product model and a
group action. It asserts no global quotient, global potential, maximal
extension, or field equation.

An exact spherical Einstein–Maxwell–$\Lambda$ datum consists of the orbit
geometry specified above, a smooth rotationally invariant real two-form
$\mathcal F$, a constant $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$, and
the equations
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}(g)_{ab}=\Lambda g_{ab}+2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F),$$
where
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c -\frac14g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd}.$$
This is a mathematical system of equations, not a physical postulate. For
$\Lambda=0$ it uses exactly the curvature, Hodge, and Maxwell normalization of
the previously defined geometric electrovac equations. For $\Lambda\ne0$ the extra constant
term is part of this local mathematical definition; it is not supplied by
that zero-$\Lambda$ item.

By the preceding Maxwell reduction lemma, the field has unique constant
flux parameters $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ and
$$\mathcal F=\frac{q_e}{r^2}\epsilon_2+q_m\omega_{S^2},\qquad Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2.$$
In geometric units, coordinates have length, $r,q_e,q_m$ have length, the
metric components are dimensionless, and $\Lambda$ has units of inverse
length squared. Define
$$z:=q^{-1}(dr,dr),\qquad \varpi:=\frac r2(1-z)+\frac{Q^2}{2r}-\frac{\Lambda r^3}{6}.$$
Thus $z$ is dimensionless and $\varpi$ has length. The scalar $\varpi$ is
called the charged spherical mass function; this definition does not assert
that it is constant. The field equations are local on $U\times S^2$ and
impose no global potential, bundle, horizon, asymptotic, completeness, or
extension condition.

The geometric-electrovacuum flux convention inherits only $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
through the supplied geometric electrovac definition. No full axiom of choice is used
by this definition or by the subsequent local algebra.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$; $o$ is the manifold orientation, $N$ is a smooth future timelike field, and the metric volume form is chosen to agree with $o$. Let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected connection, let $\mathcal F$ be a smooth real two-form on $M$, and use the curvature convention
$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$.
Define
$$Q_{ab}(\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where both raised indices use $g^{-1}$. A **geometric electrovac datum with zero cosmological constant** is the tuple $(M,g,N,o,\mathcal F)$ satisfying
$$d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(\mathcal F)$$
at every point of $M$. Here $\star_g$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$; on two-forms $\star_g^2=-1$. No material current, matter tensor, global potential, asymptotic flatness, positive mass, horizon, or extension condition is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Differentiating $g_\epsilon^{ac}g_{\epsilon cb}=\delta^a_b$ at $\epsilon=0$ gives $\dot g^{ab}=-h^{ab}$. In a positively oriented chart, $\mathrm{vol}_{g_\epsilon}=\sqrt{|\det(g_{\epsilon ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. Since $\det(g_\epsilon)=\det(g)\det(I+\epsilon g^{-1}h)+O(\epsilon^2)$ and the linear term of $\det(I+\epsilon A)$ is $\epsilon\operatorname{tr}A$, differentiation gives $\dot{\mathrm{vol}}_g=\tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\mathrm{vol}_g$.

Evaluating the defining identity in [F1] on increasing coordinate wedges gives the component formula $({\star_g\omega})_{b_1\ldots b_{4-k}}=\tfrac1{k!}(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{a_1\ldots a_k b_1\ldots b_{4-k}}\omega^{a_1\ldots a_k}$, with the same orientation sign as the displayed two-form case. Thus the component Hodge map is the oriented volume tensor times the $k$ inverse-metric factors that raise the indices of $\omega_\epsilon$. Differentiating the volume contributes $\tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\omega$ inside the Hodge map by step 1.1; differentiating each of the $k$ inverse metrics contributes $-h_{a_j}{}^b$ in its corresponding covariant slot by step 1.1; differentiating $\omega_\epsilon$ contributes $\tau$. Summing these $k+2$ terms yields $\dot\star\omega_\epsilon=\star_g(\tau+\tfrac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\omega-h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega)$, including $k=0$ where the slot sum is empty.

Substituting $\omega=\mathcal F$ and $\tau=f$ gives the displayed variation. The exterior derivative is independent of $\epsilon$ and linear, so differentiating $d(\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon)=0$ gives $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$. The closure equation differentiates to $df=0$ in the linearized definition.

Let $\Phi_\epsilon:V	o W$ be an orientation-preserving local flow map. Define its pulled-back connection by $(\Phi_\epsilon^*
abla)_XY:=\Phi_{\epsilon*}^{-1}(
abla_{\Phi_{\epsilon*}X}\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y)$. The coordinate Lie-bracket identity in [F3] and the chain rule give $[\Phi_{\epsilon*}X,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y]=\Phi_{\epsilon*}[X,Y]$, so this connection is torsion-free. For vector fields $X,Y,Z$, differentiating $(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)(Y,Z)=g(\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Z)\circ\Phi_\epsilon$ and using $
abla g=0$ shows it is compatible with $\Phi_\epsilon^*g$. Uniqueness in [F3] identifies it with $
abla^{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}$. Applying this definition twice in the curvature formula and using the same bracket identity gives $R[\Phi_\epsilon^*g](X,Y)Z=\Phi_{\epsilon*}^{-1}(R[g](\Phi_{\epsilon*}X,\Phi_{\epsilon*}Y)\Phi_{\epsilon*}Z)$; the trace defining Ricci is unchanged under conjugation by $D\Phi_\epsilon$, hence $\operatorname{Ric}[\Phi_\epsilon^*g]=\Phi_\epsilon^*\operatorname{Ric}[g]$. The formula for $Q$ uses only tensor products, the metric inverse and contractions; $(\Phi_\epsilon^*g)^{-1}(\Phi_\epsilon^*\alpha,\Phi_\epsilon^* eta)=\Phi_\epsilon^*(g^{-1}(\alpha, eta))$ by the inverse linear map, so $Q(\Phi_\epsilon^*g,\Phi_\epsilon^*\mathcal F)=\Phi_\epsilon^*Q(g,\mathcal F)$. In the defining Hodge identity, pullback commutes with alternating tensor evaluation and the inverse-metric pairing; it also carries $\mathrm{vol}_g$ to $\mathrm{vol}_{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}$ because the flow preserves orientation and the volume density transforms by the Jacobian determinant. Uniqueness of the Hodge map therefore gives $\star_{\Phi_\epsilon^*g}\Phi_\epsilon^*\mathcal F=\Phi_\epsilon^*(\star_g\mathcal F)$. Finally, write a $k$-form as $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I dx^I$. By [F4], $d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I$. The chain rule gives the terms where a derivative hits $\omega_I$; terms where it hits a coordinate derivative of $\Phi_\epsilon$ cancel in pairs because second partial derivatives commute while the exterior product is alternating. Hence $d\Phi_\epsilon^*\omega=\Phi_\epsilon^*d\omega$. Thus every exact residual of the pulled-back pair is the pullback of the corresponding zero residual.

For a smooth exact family $(g_\lambda,\mathcal F_\lambda)$ on a common open set, each of its three residuals in [F1] is identically zero as a smooth function of $(\lambda,x)$. Differentiating in $\lambda$ commutes with the finite coordinate derivatives and contractions in those residuals, so their derivatives at any $\lambda_0$ are exactly the linearized residuals of $(\partial_\lambda g,\partial_\lambda\mathcal F)|_{\lambda_0}$ and vanish.

Differentiating the residual identities of step 1.1 at $\epsilon=0$ gives zero linearized metric and Maxwell residuals; in the Hodge residual the varied tensor is the explicit $\delta(\star\mathcal F)$ of [F5]. By the definition of the Lie derivative through the local flow, the derivatives of the pulled-back fields are precisely $(\dot\Phi_0^*g,\dot\Phi_0^*\mathcal F)$, so this is the asserted pure-gauge solution.

The RN and KN data of [F6] are smooth in their displayed parameters on any fixed exterior domain satisfying the relevant strict chart inequalities. Restricting the parameter interval around the chosen values if necessary preserves those inequalities on the common domain. Both verification results establish the exact equations with $\Lambda=0$, so step 1.2 applies to each such parameter derivative in that fixed sector. The parameter derivatives are stationary because the displayed metric and field coefficients are independent of $x^0$. No inference is made that an arbitrary linearized solution lies on one of these families.

**(b) [first-order reduction]** Fix constants $\kappa>0$, $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ and a prescribed smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $T$ on the chart domain. Fix a chart $(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ with
$x^0=t$. Introduce the metric variables
$$u:=\bigl(g_{ab},\ p_{ab}:=\bar\nabla_0g_{ab},\ q_{abi}:=\bar\nabla_ig_{ab}\bigr)$$
(symmetry in $a,b$ understood) and the relation variables $\bar\nabla_0g_{ab}-p_{ab}=0$ and $\bar\nabla_0q_{abi}-\bar\nabla_ip_{ab}=\mathcal C_{abi}$, where $\mathcal C_{abi}=-\bar R^c{}_{a0i}g_{cb}-\bar R^c{}_{b0i}g_{ac}$. Second covariant derivatives include their derivative-slot connection. These known background-curvature terms are zeroth order in the first-order state and vanish for the flat coordinate background. Then the reduced Einstein equation can be solved for the second time derivatives in the form
$$\bar\nabla_0p_{ab}=-(g^{00})^{-1}\Bigl[2g^{0i}\bar\nabla_ip_{ab}+g^{ij}\bar\nabla_iq_{abj}+R_{ab}(x,u,T;\kappa,\Lambda,\bar g)\Bigr],$$
where the source is smooth in the first-order metric state and the prescribed matter data, with no derivatives of $T$, and includes $2\kappa(T_{ab}-\tfrac12(g^{cd}T_{cd})g_{ab})+2\Lambda g_{ab}$. The resulting first-order system for $u$ is symmetric hyperbolic on every
region where $g^{00}<0$ and the spatial block $(g^{ij})$ is positive definite:
the coefficient of $\bar\nabla_0u$ is the block diagonal
$\operatorname{diag}(I,-g^{00}I,g^{ij}I)$ (on the three slots
$g,p,q$), which is positive definite there, and the coefficients of the spatial
derivatives are symmetric. More generally, in a coupled reduction one may substitute a specified smooth algebraic stress map $T_{ab}=\mathcal T_{ab}(x,u,z)$, symmetric in $a,b$, where $z$ is a specified additional first-order matter state ranging in an open Euclidean set. This keeps the same metric principal matrices; symmetric hyperbolicity of the combined metric-matter system requires a separate check of the matter equations.

The six evolution equations for $(e,b)$ have principal part
$$n(e)-\operatorname{curl}_h b=\text{terms with no derivatives of }(e,b),\qquad n(b)+\operatorname{curl}_h e=\text{terms with no derivatives of }(e,b).$$
For a spatial covector $\xi$, let $C(\xi)v:=\xi^\sharp\times v$ in the oriented orthonormal frame. Set $\theta^0:=\alpha ds=-g(n,\cdot)$ and decompose any spacetime covector as $\zeta=\zeta(n)\theta^0+\zeta_\perp$, where $\zeta_\perp(n)=0$ and $|\zeta_\perp|_h$ is its spatial norm. The spatial principal block is the linear map on $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R^3$ defined by $S(\xi)(u,v)=(-C(\xi)v,C(\xi)u)$. It is real symmetric, has eigenvalues $0,0,|\xi|,|\xi|,-|\xi|,-|\xi|$, and satisfies $\|S(\xi)\|=|\xi|$. Therefore the principal symbol $P(\zeta)=\zeta(n)I_6+S(\zeta_\perp)$ is positive definite for every covector with $\zeta(n)>|\zeta_\perp|_h$. In the adapted coordinates its time matrix is $\alpha^{-1}I_6$, and every coordinate spatial matrix is symmetric. Derivatives of the frame and metric enter only as smooth lower-order coefficients depending on $(g,g^{-1},\partial g,e,b)$; in a first-order metric state they are zero-order terms. The remaining two Maxwell equations are the constraints $\operatorname{div}_h e=0$ and $\operatorname{div}_h b=0$.

Fix such a background on $U$. A **linearized perturbation** is a pair $(h,f)$ consisting of a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $h$ and a smooth real two-form $f$ on $U$. Its linearized metric residual is
$$\delta E_{(g,\mathcal F)}[h,f]:=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}\bigl(\operatorname{Ric}[g_\epsilon]-\Lambda g_\epsilon-2Q(g_\epsilon,\mathcal F_\epsilon)\bigr),$$
and its linearized Maxwell residuals are
$$df,\qquad d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F),\qquad \delta(\star\mathcal F):=\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0}\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon.$$
Here $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ and $\mathcal F_\epsilon=\mathcal F+\epsilon f+O(\epsilon^2)$ are smooth local families on the fixed domain, with dimensionless parameter $\epsilon$. The derivatives are the coordinatewise derivatives of these smooth finite-jet operators; the chain rule makes them depend only on $(h,f)$, not on the higher-order parts of the chosen families. The **linearized electrovacuum system** is the homogeneous system $\delta E_{(g,\mathcal F)}[h,f]=0$, $df=0$, and $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$.

Let $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of an oriented Lorentzian metric on a four-manifold, and let $\omega_\epsilon=\omega+\epsilon\tau+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of a $k$-form, $0\le k\le4$. Define $h_a{}^b:=g^{bc}h_{ac}$, $\operatorname{tr}_g h:=g^{ab}h_{ab}$, and
$$\bigl(h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\bigr)_{a_1\ldots a_k}:=\sum_{j=1}^k h_{a_j}{}^b\omega_{a_1\ldots a_{j-1}b a_{j+1}\ldots a_k},$$
with $h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega:=0$ for $k=0$. Then
$$\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_0\star_{g_\epsilon}\omega_\epsilon=\star_g\left(\tau+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\omega-h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\right).$$
In particular, for the geometric background $\mathcal F$ and perturbation $f$ of [[def-emg-fx-linearized-electrovac]],
$$\delta(\star\mathcal F)=\star_g\left(f+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\mathcal F-h^\sharp\!\cdot\mathcal F\right).$$
If $(h,f)$ satisfies the linearized Maxwell equation, then $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$; this last condition is exactly the derivative of $d(\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon)=0$, not a consequence of the variation formula alone.
