Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Fix real parameters $m>0$ and $q_e,q_m$ with $q_e^2+q_m^2=m^2$, and use the selected ingoing dyonic Reissner–Nordström metric on $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\times S^2$ with signature $(-,+,+,+)$:

$$g=-D(r)\,dv^2+2\,dv\,dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad D(r)=\left(1-\frac mr\right)^2.$$

Here $\gamma_{S^2}$ is the metric induced on the unit sphere $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ by the Euclidean metric, and $\omega_{S^2}$ is its outward area form. The coordinates $v,r$ and parameters $m,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres; angular coordinates are dimensionless. The displayed Maxwell two-form uses the supplied geometric normalization, with no additional SI normalization: its $vr$ coordinate component has units $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and its angular components have units $\mathrm m$. In the supplied ingoing RN background with mass parameter $M=m$, the fixed Maxwell two-form is

$$\mathcal F_{\mathrm{in}}=-q_e r^{-2}\,dv\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$

Use the unique torsion-free, $g$-compatible connection; in every smooth chart its coefficients are $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{ad}(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc})$ and are smooth. For the horizon-data result, set $M=m$, $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2=M^2$ and $f(r):=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2=D(r)$. It states that $\xi=\partial_v$ obeys $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$ and is normalized by $g(\xi,\xi)\to-1$ as $r\to\infty$; at $r=M$, $g^{-1}(dr,dr)=f(M)=0$, $\xi^\flat=dr$, and $\xi$ is tangent to the level. Thus $r=m$ is the local Killing horizon generated by $\xi$, with signed surface gravity fixed by $d(g(\xi,\xi))=-2\kappa_H\xi^\flat$ and equal to $\kappa_H=f'(M)/2=0$ (units $\mathrm m^{-1}$). No maximal-extension or global event-horizon assertion is included. The metric and displayed Maxwell field are fixed. A neutral test scalar has no electromagnetic gauge coupling or scalar coupling to that field, and does not source either background.

A reduced spherical scalar profile is a real function $\psi:\mathbb R_v\times(0,\infty)_r\to\mathbb R$ whose coordinate partial derivatives through total order three are continuous. Its full scalar on $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the spherical lift $\widetilde\psi(v,r,\omega):=\psi(v,r)$; in radial formulas we use $\psi(v,r)$ for the reduced profile, and the notation $\Box_g\psi=0$ means $\Box_g\widetilde\psi=0$. For a $C^3$ scalar lift, define the extension of the smooth-scalar wave operator by the trace of its $C^1$ scalar Hessian,

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi:=g^{ab}\bigl(\partial_a\partial_b\widetilde\psi-\Gamma^c{}_{ab}\partial_c\widetilde\psi\bigr).$$

The second-order chain rule and the connection-coefficient transformation law make these components a covariant $2$-tensor, so the trace is chart independent and $C^1$. This agrees with the supplied smooth-scalar definition when the lift is smooth. In every smooth chart, with $w=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}$, metric compatibility and the density formula give

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1w\partial_a\bigl(wg^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi\bigr).$$

For the spherical lift in an angular chart, $w=r^2\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{AB})}$ and this becomes

$$\Box_g\widetilde\psi=\frac1{r^2}\left[\partial_v(r^2\partial_r\psi)+\partial_r\!\left(r^2(\partial_v\psi+D\partial_r\psi)\right)\right].$$

The density identity used here is stated for smooth vector fields, but its coordinate proof uses only first derivatives of their components and the product rule; it therefore holds for $C^1$ vector fields as well. Here $g^{ab}\partial_b\widetilde\psi$ is $C^2$, so the formula is defined and $\Box_g\widetilde\psi$ is $C^1$. In particular the wave equation can be differentiated once in $r$ for a $C^3$ profile. Set $\phi(v,r)=r\psi(v,r)$ and take every $\partial_r$ derivative in this regular ingoing chart. If $[\psi]$ denotes the arbitrary scalar-field unit, then $[\phi]=[\psi]\,\mathrm m$.

Fix $m>0$ and real $q_e,q_m$ with $q_e^2+q_m^2=m^2$, and take the ingoing extremal RN metric and coordinates specified by the spherical test-scalar definition. Let $\psi$ be any admissible neutral spherical $C^3$ solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$, set $\phi=r\psi$, and define its spherical horizon charge by

$$H_\psi(v):=\partial_r\phi(v,m).$$

Then $H_\psi$ is constant for all $v\in\mathbb R$. If this constant is nonzero, the regular ingoing-chart transverse derivative $\partial_r\phi(v,m)$ is nonzero and does not tend to zero along the horizon. If $[\psi]$ is the scalar-field unit, then $[H_\psi]=[\psi]$. This is a local fixed-background statement and asserts no global decay or nonlinear instability.

Fix $m>0$ and real $q_e,q_m$ with $q_e^2+q_m^2=m^2$, and let $\psi$ be an admissible neutral spherical $C^3$ solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$ on the regular ingoing extremal RN metric. Put $\phi=r\psi$ and let $H=\partial_r\phi(v,m)$ be its constant spherical horizon charge. If $H\ne0$ and

$$\lim_{v\to+\infty}\phi(v,m)=0,$$

then

$$\lim_{v\to+\infty}\frac{\partial_r^2\phi(v,m)}{v}=-\frac{H}{m^2}.$$

Thus this transverse second derivative grows linearly in magnitude with rate $|H|/m^2$ under the stated horizon-trace decay hypothesis. Both sides of the limit have unit $[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The hypothesis is conditional: this proposition proves no global decay theorem, and it concerns neither coupled Einstein–Maxwell perturbations nor a nonlinear instability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The constant profile $\psi(v,r)=c$ has full lift $\widetilde\psi(v,r,\omega)=c$, is real and $C^3$, and has all first and second coordinate derivatives zero. Its scalar Hessian and metric trace therefore vanish, so $\Box_g\widetilde\psi=0$ and it is admissible by [F1]. The definition $\phi=r\psi$ gives $\phi(v,r)=cr$.
Differentiating $\phi=cr$ gives $\partial_r\phi=c$ and $\partial_r^2\phi=0$. Thus [F2] identifies its constant horizon charge as $H=c\ne0$, and its horizon trace is $\phi(v,m)=cm$.

Since $c\ne0$ and $m>0$, $cm\ne0$, so the horizon trace is constant nonzero and does not tend to zero. The extra hypothesis of [F3] therefore fails, while step 2.1 shows the second transverse derivative vanishes identically. The conditional proposition remains consistent with this example.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Let $M>0$, $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2>0$, and use
$f(r)=1-2M/r+Q^2/r^2$ on the selected ingoing RN model. If $M^2\ge Q^2$,
the positive roots
$$r_\pm=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2}$$
are null constant-$r$ hypersurfaces. For the Killing field $\xi=\partial_v$
normalized by the displayed coordinate for which
$g(\xi,\xi)\to-1$ as $r\to\infty$, each is a Killing horizon in the
local sense of
[[def-emg-causal-solution-and-horizon-vocabulary]], with signed surface
gravity
$$\kappa_\pm=\frac{f'(r_\pm)}2 =\frac{r_\pm-r_\mp}{2r_\pm^2}.$$
At extremality $M^2=Q^2$, the coincident root is $r_H=M$ and
$\kappa_H=0$. If $M^2<Q^2$, $f$ has no positive root and no constant-$r$
null hypersurface of this form. These are local properties of the selected
metric; they do not classify event horizons in a maximal spacetime.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $m>0$ and $q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters, put $Q^2=q_e^2+q_m^2$, and assume $Q^2<m^2$. Define
$$r_\pm:=m\pm\sqrt{m^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2m}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\quad(r>0).$$
On the fixed exterior $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$, use the exact dyonic Reissner–Nordström metric specified by the preceding mathematical definition with its mass parameter identified as $M=m$ and charges $q_e,q_m$, and set $t=x^0$. Define a real normalized spherical harmonic of degree $\ell\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ to mean a smooth real $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y,$$
where in the standard polar chart
$$\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta Y)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2Y.$$
Here $d\omega_{S^2}$ is the area measure of the unit round metric $\gamma_{S^2}$, and $f'(r)$ denotes the ordinary derivative of $f$ with respect to $r$. Since $r_+>0$, the basepoint $r_0:=2r_+$ lies in the exterior; define the tortoise coordinate by the oriented integral $r_*(r):=\int_{r_0}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho$. For any such $Y$, let $\psi(t,r,\omega)=\phi(t,r)Y(\omega)$ be a smooth real solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$, and put $U_\ell(t,r_*):=r\phi(t,r)$. Then $r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$, and
$$\partial_t^2U_\ell-\partial_{r_*}^2U_\ell+V_\ell(r_*)U_\ell=0,\qquad V_\ell(r_*):=f(r)\left(\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^2}+\frac{f'(r)}r\right).$$
The potential is smooth, bounded, and strictly positive on $\mathbb R$. If $U_\ell$ and its derivatives satisfy the decay assumptions of the positive matrix-potential wave-energy theorem on the time interval considered, then
$$E_\ell(t):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}\left((\partial_tU_\ell)^2+(\partial_{r_*}U_\ell)^2+V_\ell U_\ell^2\right)\,dr_*$$
is constant there. In the original radial coordinate, its radial derivative term is $\frac12\int_{r_+}^{\infty}f(r)|\partial_rU_\ell|^2\,dr$; this energy loses control of $\partial_rU_\ell$ as $r\downarrow r_+$. It asserts no nondegenerate horizon-crossing derivative estimate, decay estimate, or coupled Einstein–Maxwell stability result. The coordinates $t,r,r_*$ and parameters $m,q_e,q_m$ have unit metres, $f$ is dimensionless, and $V_\ell$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$. If $\psi,\phi$ have a common arbitrary field unit $\Phi$, then $Y$ is dimensionless, $U_\ell$ has unit $\Phi\,\mathrm m$, and $E_\ell$ has unit $\Phi^2\,\mathrm m$.

citations.quote:
Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Put $\varpi(r)=\omega-eQ/r$. Since $A_t$ is independent of $t$,
$D_t(e^{-i\omega t}uY/r)=-i\varpi(r)e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$ and
$D_t^2(e^{-i\omega t}uY/r)=-\varpi(r)^2e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$.
The angular term is $-\ell(\ell+1)e^{-i\omega t}uY/r$. Substitution into
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ and division only by the nonzero factor
$A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}$ gives $Y(\Omega)\,B(t,r)=0$, where
$$B(t,r)=\frac{\varpi(r)^2}{f(r)}\frac{u}{r}+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f(r)\partial_r\frac{u}{r}\right)-\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{r^3}u.$$
Multiplying by $Y$ and integrating over $S^2$ gives $B(t,r)=0$ because
$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1$; no division by $Y$ at its zeros is used.

Since $dr_*/dr=f^{-1}$, $\partial_{r_*}=f\partial_r$, so
$r^2f\partial_r(u/r)=r\,\partial_{r_*}u-fu$. Multiplying $B=0$ by $fr$,
the radial derivative term becomes
$$\frac f r\partial_r(r\partial_{r_*}u-fu)=\frac1r\partial_{r_*}(r\partial_{r_*}u-fu)=\partial_{r_*}^2u-\frac{ff'}r u,$$
where $\partial_{r_*}r=f$ and $\partial_{r_*}f=ff'$. The other terms become
$\varpi^2u$ and $-f\ell(\ell+1)u/r^2$. Their sum is the asserted radial
equation.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth

derivations.claim:
Differentiate $j=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,u')$. The radial equation
gives
$$j'=\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u'}u'+\overline u\,u'')=\operatorname{Im}(|u'|^2-K|u|^2)=0,$$
because both terms inside the last imaginary part are real by [F2]. Thus
$j$ is constant along the exterior.

At infinity, $\Theta'=\omega-eQf/r\to\omega$. Substitution of the
Definition's differentiated asymptotics into $j$ gives
$j_\infty=\omega(|R|^2-1)$: the incident and reflected diagonal terms are
$-\omega$ and $\omega|R|^2$, while the two cross terms have real sum. At the
horizon the asymptotics give $j_H=-\omega_H|T|^2$. Equating these limits by
step 1.1 and dividing by $\omega>0$ proves the identity. If
$0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ then $\omega_H<0$; when $T\ne0$ the identity yields
$|R|^2=1+(-\omega_H/\omega)|T|^2>1$. The unit incoming and reflected
asymptotic flux magnitudes are $\omega$ and $\omega|R|^2$, so the stated
radial-flux comparison follows.

$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

derivations.claim:
Write $x=r_*$ and use the choices in [A1]--[A2]. By [F3], $x$ ranges over
all of $\mathbb R$ and $dr/dx=f$. The charged radial
equation [F1] becomes
$$u''(x)+\bigl(\omega^2-V(x)\bigr)u(x)=0,\qquad
V(x):=\frac{f(r(x))f'(r(x))}{r(x)}.$$
The definition gives $dr/dx=f$ and $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2$. Since
$r_+>M>r_-$ and $r_+r_-=Q^2$, we have $f(r)>0$ and $Mr>Mr_+>Q^2$
for $r>r_+$, so $f'(r)=2(Mr-Q^2)/r^3>0$ and $V>0$. Thus $V$ is smooth
and real. Moreover,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}|V(x)|\,dx=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{f'(r)}r\,dr
=\int_{r_+}^{\infty}\frac{2(Mr-Q^2)}{r^4}\,dr<\infty.$$

Define $u_-$ by the Volterra equation
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+\frac1\omega\int_{-\infty}^{x}
\sin\!\bigl(\omega(x-y)\bigr)V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
Iteration gives a uniformly convergent Neumann series: the absolute value of
its $n$th iterated term is at most
$\|V\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}^n/(\omega^n n!)$, using $|\sin z|\le1$ for real $z$
and the ordered integration region. The sum is bounded on $\mathbb R$; differentiating
the integral equation shows it is a smooth solution of the equation in
step 1.1. The tail integrals tend to zero as $x\to-\infty$, and differentiation
under the integral gives
$$u_-(x)=e^{-i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega e^{-i\omega x}+o(1)\quad(x\to-\infty).$$

Since $V u_-\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, expanding the sine in step 2.1 into
exponentials and replacing the upper integration limit by $+\infty$ gives
$$u_-(x)=a e^{-i\omega x}+b e^{i\omega x}+o(1),\qquad
u_-'(x)=-i\omega a e^{-i\omega x}+i\omega b e^{i\omega x}+o(1)$$
as $x\to+\infty$, where
$$a=1-\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy,
\qquad b=\frac1{2i\omega}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-i\omega y}V(y)u_-(y)\,dy.$$
The same tail estimate after differentiating the integral equation proves the
displayed derivative asymptotic.

For $j=\operatorname{Im}(\overline{u_-}u_-')$, the real-coefficient
equation in step 1.1 gives $j'=0$. The horizon asymptotics in step 2.1 yield
$j=-\omega$, while step 3.1 yields $j=\omega(|b|^2-|a|^2)$ at infinity;
the two oscillatory cross terms have real sum and contribute no imaginary part.
Hence $|a|^2=|b|^2+1$, so $a\ne0$. Put $u=u_-/a$, $R=b/a$, and $T=1/a$.
Then $u$ has the asymptotics in [F3], with unit incoming amplitude and only
the ingoing branch at the horizon. The separated-wave substitution in the
proof of [F1] is reversible here: $Y$ is a nonzero constant, $A_{\mathrm{in}}$
and $fr$ are nonzero, and each displayed step is an equality. Therefore
$\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y u/r$ solves $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ and is
an admitted scattering solution for any fixed nonzero allowed
$A_{\mathrm{in}}$.

Apply [F2] to this constructed solution. Since $e=0$ and $T=1/a\ne0$,
$$|R|^2=1-|T|^2=1-|a|^{-2}<1.$$
Thus this nonzero-charge background admits a neutral mode whose reflected
radial flux is less than the incident flux, contradicting the universal
amplification statement.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $u$ be any scattering solution as defined on the fixed subextremal electric
RN exterior, with real $\omega>0$, real $e,Q$, unit incoming amplitude, and
reflection and transmission coefficients $R,T$. Then its radial Wronskian
flux $j:=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,\partial_{r_*}u)$ is constant and
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-eQ/r_+}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
Consequently, if $0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ and $T\ne0$, the reflected radial flux
magnitude exceeds the incident radial flux magnitude, since their ratio is
$|R|^2>1$. This is conditional on an admitted scattering solution and does not
assert its existence, a complex-frequency mode, or a nonlinear instability.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $P\to M$ be a smooth right principal
$G$-bundle with a principal connection $H$, and let
$\Phi\in\mathcal G(P)$. Then
$$\Phi_*H:=d\Phi(H)$$
is a principal connection. If $K_H$ and $K_{\Phi_*H}$ are the vertical-valued
curvatures from
[[def-principal-connection-and-vertical-curvature]], then for
$X,Y\in T_pP$,
$$K_{\Phi_*H}(d\Phi_pX,d\Phi_pY)=d\Phi_p(K_H(X,Y)).$$
Composition makes this a left action of $\mathcal G(P)$ on the set of
principal connections.
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Let $M^n$ be an oriented smooth manifold without boundary. For each compact set $K\subseteq M$ there are finitely many nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_i$ with compact supports contained in connected coordinate domains $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighbourhood of $K$. For $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$ define
$$\mathcal I_M(\omega)=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\chi_i\omega)\quad(K=\operatorname{supp}\omega),$$
using the signed chart integrals. This value is independent of the finite functions and charts. It defines a linear functional, is local under restriction to an open set containing the support, and for $n\ge1$ satisfies
$$\mathcal I_M(d\eta)=0\qquad(\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)).$$
For $n=0$ it is the finite signed sum $\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p)$. All assertions are choice-free: no partition on the entire manifold is required.

derivations.claim: On each overlap $U_i\cap U_j$, compatibility gives $\alpha_j=a_j'-a_j=(a_i'+\lambda(g_{ij}))-(a_i+\lambda(g_{ij}))=\alpha_i$. The forms therefore agree on overlaps and define one global smooth real one-form $\alpha$; uniqueness follows because the $U_i$ cover $M$. No global phase lift of any transition function is chosen.

Conversely, if $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$ is any smooth global real one-form, then $(a_i+\alpha|_{U_i})_i$ obeys $(a_j+\alpha|_{U_j})=(a_i+\alpha|_{U_i})+\lambda(g_{ij})$ because the restrictions of $\alpha$ agree on overlaps. Thus translation by $\alpha$ stays in the same bundle sector, and the set of representatives is affine over $\Omega^1(M)$.

By the curvature definitions in [F2], on every $U_i$ we have $f'-f=da_i'-da_i=d(a_i'-a_i)=d\alpha|_{U_i}$. Both sides are global, so the local equalities give $f'-f=d\alpha$ on $M$. Multiplying by the same constant $\kappa_0$ gives $F'-F=\kappa_0d\alpha$.

For a compact oriented smooth surface $S$ without boundary, pullback commutes with $d$ by [F4], so $\iota^*(F'-F)=\kappa_0d(\iota^*\alpha)$. The one-form $\iota^*\alpha$ has compact support because $S$ is compact; [F5] therefore gives $\int_S\iota^*(F'-F)=\kappa_0\int_Sd(\iota^*\alpha)=0$. Hence the physical curvature integrals agree.

On a trivializing chart, let $\Phi_h(x,z)=(x,h(x)z)$. Its inverse sends $(x,z)$ to $(x,h(x)^{-1}z)$. The connection form for the pushed-forward horizontal distribution is $(\Phi_h^{-1})^*\omega$, because its kernel is $d\Phi_h(\ker\omega)$. With $\omega=\eta+a_i$ from [F2] and $\eta=-iz^{-1}dz$, the product rule [F6] gives $(\Phi_h^{-1})^*\eta=\eta-\lambda(h)$ and hence $a_i'=a_i-\lambda(h)$. This is the pushforward sign; a pullback action by $\Phi_h$ instead has the opposite sign.

For a smooth real two-form $\mathcal F$, put
$$Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F):=\mathcal F_{ac}\mathcal F_b{}^c-\frac14 g_{ab}\mathcal F_{cd}\mathcal F^{cd},$$
where all raised indices use $g^{-1}$. Its length-coordinate components have unit $\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. Fix $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ with unit $\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. An **exact geometric electrovacuum background on $U\subseteq M$** is a smooth pair $(g,\mathcal F)$ on the same open set satisfying
$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}[g]-\Lambda g_{ab}=2Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F),\qquad d\mathcal F=0,\qquad d(\star_g\mathcal F)=0.$$
For $\Lambda=0$ this is the geometric normalization of [[def-emg-xs-geometric-electrovac]]. The symbol $\mathcal F$ here is geometric-normalized; it is not the SI-normalized field tensor used in [[def-emg-electrovacuum-cauchy-system]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $g_\epsilon=g+\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of an oriented Lorentzian metric on a four-manifold, and let $\omega_\epsilon=\omega+\epsilon\tau+O(\epsilon^2)$ be a smooth variation of a $k$-form, $0\le k\le4$. Define $h_a{}^b:=g^{bc}h_{ac}$, $\operatorname{tr}_g h:=g^{ab}h_{ab}$, and
$$\bigl(h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\bigr)_{a_1\ldots a_k}:=\sum_{j=1}^k h_{a_j}{}^b\omega_{a_1\ldots a_{j-1}b a_{j+1}\ldots a_k},$$
with $h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega:=0$ for $k=0$. Then
$$\left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\right|_0\star_{g_\epsilon}\omega_\epsilon=\star_g\left(\tau+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\omega-h^\sharp\!\cdot\omega\right).$$
In particular, for the geometric background $\mathcal F$ and perturbation $f$ of [[def-emg-fx-linearized-electrovac]],
$$\delta(\star\mathcal F)=\star_g\left(f+\frac12(\operatorname{tr}_g h)\mathcal F-h^\sharp\!\cdot\mathcal F\right).$$
If $(h,f)$ satisfies the linearized Maxwell equation, then $d\,\delta(\star\mathcal F)=0$; this last condition is exactly the derivative of $d(\star_{g_\epsilon}\mathcal F_\epsilon)=0$, not a consequence of the variation formula alone.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited from the smooth principal-connection convention. Fix an oriented, time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N,o)$ and a fixed normalized $U(1)$ connection sector as in the fixed-topology affine-sector result. Its connection variations are global smooth real one-forms $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^1(M)$, with components of unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ in length-coordinate charts. Length-coordinate charts use metre-valued coordinates, with $x^0=ct_{\mathrm{sec}}$ when time is recorded in seconds; $c$ is a coordinate unit-conversion scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$, with no numerical measured value or physical role asserted. Impose the fixed-background Maxwell operator equations $d\star_g d\alpha=0$ and $d\star_g d\beta=0$, where $\star_g$ is the oriented Lorentzian Hodge map of signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Define the real three-form

$$\omega_g(\alpha,\beta):=\alpha\wedge\star_g d\beta-\beta\wedge\star_g d\alpha.$$

Let $\iota_\Sigma:\Sigma\hookrightarrow M$ be an oriented smooth embedding of a possibly noncompact three-dimensional manifold, and require the induced metric $\gamma:=\iota_\Sigma^*g$ to be positive definite. Its oriented Riemannian volume form is the nowhere-vanishing three-form $\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$ whose expression in each positively oriented chart $y=(y^1,y^2,y^3)$ is $\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{ij})}\,dy^1\wedge dy^2\wedge dy^3$. Let $\mu_\gamma$ be the positive smooth density measure with coordinate expression $d\mu_\gamma=\sqrt{\det(\gamma_{ij})}\,d^3y$. The density-measure integration supplier listed below gives the chart-independent measure and integral; for a real $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$ function its signed integral is the finite difference of the integrals of its positive and negative parts, and its chart formula is absolutely convergent.

There is a unique smooth real function $u_{\alpha,\beta}$ on $\Sigma$ such that $\iota_\Sigma^*\omega_g(\alpha,\beta)=u_{\alpha,\beta}\,\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$. Define the pairing $\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha,\beta)$ precisely when $u_{\alpha,\beta}\in L^1(\Sigma,\mu_\gamma)$, meaning $\int_\Sigma|u_{\alpha,\beta}|\,d\mu_\gamma<\infty$, and then set $\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha,\beta):=\int_\Sigma u_{\alpha,\beta}\,d\mu_\gamma$. This absolute-integrability condition is the convergence convention on noncompact $\Sigma$ and makes the value independent of any exhaustion or ordering. In length coordinates on $\Sigma$, the coefficients of $d\alpha$ and $d\beta$ have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$, those of $\omega_g$ have units $\mathrm m^{-3}$, $u_{\alpha,\beta}$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3}$, and $d\mu_\gamma$ has volume units $\mathrm m^3$; thus the normalized integral is dimensionless. Replacing normalized variations by physical-potential variations $\kappa_0\alpha$ and $\kappa_0\beta$ multiplies the current by $\kappa_0^2$; an action prefactor is not fixed here.

This is a mathematical fixed-metric Maxwell-block definition. The equations are imposed on the normalized connection variations. The item does not identify $\kappa_0d\alpha$ with the geometric-normalized electrovac field of the coupled Einstein–Maxwell equations, prescribe a conversion between those normalizations, include metric variations, or claim to define the full coupled covariant phase-space current.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

derivations.claim: Applying the graded product rule to each term of [F1] gives $d\omega_g=d\alpha\wedge\star_g d\beta-\alpha\wedge d\star_g d\beta-d\beta\wedge\star_g d\alpha+\beta\wedge d\star_g d\alpha$. The first and third terms cancel because the two-form pairing in [F2] is symmetric, and the other two vanish by the stated equations. Hence $d\omega_g=0$.

Since $d^2\chi=0$ by [F2], the change in [F1] under $\alpha\mapsto\alpha+d\chi$ is exactly $d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta$. On the other hand, $d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta+\chi\,d\star_g d\beta=d\chi\wedge\star_g d\beta$. The current change is therefore the exact three-form $d(\chi\star_g d\beta)$.

Integrating the exact change over a finite smooth singular three-chain $c$ and applying [F3] gives $\int_c d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=\int_{\partial c}\chi\star_g d\beta$. This is zero when $c$ is a cycle, while for a chain with boundary it is the displayed boundary flux.

Now let $\Sigma$ be noncompact, assume both current pairings in the Statement are defined, and choose a compact Borel exhaustion with finite-chain representatives as in the Statement. Write $\iota_\Sigma^*(\omega_g(\alpha+d\chi,\beta)-\omega_g(\alpha,\beta))=u\,\mathrm{vol}_\gamma$. The two current coefficients are in $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$, so their difference $u$ is also in $L^1(\mu_\gamma)$ by $|u|\leq |u_{\alpha+d\chi,\beta}|+|u_{\alpha,\beta}|$. Since $K_n\uparrow\Sigma$, both $\mathbf1_{K_n}u^+$ and $\mathbf1_{K_n}u^-$ increase pointwise to $u^+$ and $u^-$. Applying [F4] separately to these nonnegative functions and subtracting their finite limits gives $\int_{K_n}u\,d\mu_\gamma\to\int_\Sigma u\,d\mu_\gamma$. By the defining property of $c_n$ and [F3], $\int_{\partial c_n}\chi\star_g d\beta=\int_{c_n}d(\chi\star_g d\beta)=\int_{K_n}u\,d\mu_\gamma$. This proves the stated flux identity. For the fixed $\beta$, the shift vanishes exactly when the limiting flux is zero; on a specified test space this must hold for every allowed $\beta$ for the gauge direction to be degenerate. No falloff condition is inferred from the field equations alone.

boundaries.evidence: The zero finite three-chain has empty support and both Stokes integrals in 2.1 are zero. Empty initial compact pieces K_n have zero integral in 3.1; an exhaustion of a nonempty Sigma cannot consist entirely of empty pieces.

If beta=0 then the current and its gauge change vanish in 1.1-1.2. If chi is constant, dchi=0 and d(chi*star d beta)=chi*d star d beta=0. A nonzero beta with alpha=0 does not by itself force the gauge shift to vanish.

boundaries.reason: The current is a three-form in four dimensions; no one-dimensional spacetime case is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The metric must be nondegenerate Lorentzian for the Hodge map. Separately, the gauge-degeneracy notion on the specified test solution space V is exactly the vanishing of every limiting boundary flux, by 3.1.

For finite chains 2.1 retains their actual boundary flux and annihilates it only for cycles. For noncompact Sigma, 3.1 uses absolute integrability and supplied chain representatives to obtain an exhaustion-independent limiting boundary flux, not an inferred falloff condition.

A1 carries AC_omega as background. The exhaustion and finite-chain representatives in 3.1 are hypotheses; monotone convergence applies to u positive and negative parts, without selecting an exhaustion or asserting it exists.

In 3.1 equality of pairing shift with the boundary-flux limit implies that zero shift forces zero limit for fixed beta. If the gauge direction is degenerate on V, this holds for every beta in V by the stated definition.

Conversely the same equality in 3.1 makes a zero flux limit imply zero shift for fixed beta; if all allowed beta have zero limit, the direction is degenerate on V. This is the actual public biconditional, not a classification of large gauge transformations.

Holonomy means the fibre multiplier of the horizontal lift around the indicated base loop; gauge trivial means gauge-equivalent to $\vartheta$ under a smooth bundle map $G_u(x,z)=(x,z u(x))$ covering the identity. Then $F=dA=0$ but holonomy around the circle is $e^{-2\pi ia}$, so this connection is gauge trivial exactly when $a\in\mathbb Z$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth tangent-bundle and principal-connection convention. Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold used for normalized circle-connection data. Fix a smooth right principal $U(1)$ bundle $P\to M$, one countable trivializing cover $(U_i)$ with transition functions $g_{ij}$ in the convention $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$, and one normalization constant $\kappa_0>0$ measured in webers. Let $(a_i)$ and $(a_i')$ be two smooth normalized connection representatives for this same atlas, each satisfying $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$ and $a_j'=a_i'+\lambda(g_{ij})$, where $\lambda(g):=-i g^{-1}dg$. In length-coordinate charts, the components of $a_i$ and $a_i'$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the physical potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ and $A_i'=\kappa_0a_i'$ have components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $\pi:P\to M$ be a smooth right principal $G$-bundle as in
[[def-smooth-principal-g-bundle]]. A **smooth gauge transformation** of $P$ is
a smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi:P\to P$ satisfying
$$\pi\circ\Phi=\pi,\qquad \Phi(pg)=\Phi(p)g\quad(p\in P,\ g\in G).$$
Here diffeomorphism has the meaning of
[[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]. The **gauge
group** $\mathcal G(P)$ is the set of these transformations under composition.
The identity is a smooth diffeomorphism and composites of smooth maps are
smooth by
[[prop-identity-maps-and-composites-of-smooth-maps-are-smooth]]; composites of
diffeomorphisms are diffeomorphisms because their inverses are composites of
the smooth inverses. The identity covers $M$ and commutes with the right
action. If $\Phi,\Psi\in\mathcal G(P)$, then $\Phi\circ\Psi$ covers $M$ and
$(\Phi\circ\Psi)(pg)=\Phi(\Psi(p)g)=\Phi(\Psi(p))g$, so the conditions are
closed under composition. The inverse of such a $\Phi$ also covers $M$: if
$q=\Phi(p)$ then $\pi(\Phi^{-1}(q))=\pi(p)=\pi(q)$. Equivariance gives
$$\Phi^{-1}(qg)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(p)g)=\Phi^{-1}(\Phi(pg))=pg.$$
Its smoothness is part of the diffeomorphism condition. Hence these maps form a
group under the composition law of [[def-group]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $P\to M$ be a smooth right principal
$G$-bundle with a principal connection $H$, and let

Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

For one update, the complex identities give
$D_2b_{n+1}=D_2b_n-\tau D_2D_1M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}=D_2b_n$ and

For a semidiscrete solution, symmetry of $M_2$ and $M_1^{-1}$ gives
$\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal E=\dot b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+\dot d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d
=-d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b=0$.
Therefore $\mathcal E$ is constant on the solution interval.

In positive dimensions set $x_n=M_2^{1/2}b_n$, $y_{n+1/2}=M_1^{-1/2}d_{n+1/2}$, and $S=M_2^{1/2}D_1M_1^{-1/2}$. By [F3], the update becomes $x_{n+1}=x_n-\tau Sy_{n+1/2}$ and $y_{n+3/2}=y_{n+1/2}+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x_{n+1}$. Write $x=x_n$, $y=y_{n+1/2}$, and $x'=x_{n+1}=x-\tau Sy$. Then
$\lVert y+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2
=\lVert y\rVert_2^2+2\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy+\tau^2\lVert S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2$
and
$-\tau x'^{\mathsf T}S(y+\tau S^{\mathsf T}x')
=-\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy-\tau^2\lVert S^{\mathsf T}x'\rVert_2^2$.
Adding these to $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2$ cancels the squared terms and leaves $\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\lVert y\rVert_2^2+\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy$. Finally,
$\lVert x'\rVert_2^2+\tau x'^{\mathsf T}Sy
=\lVert x-\tau Sy\rVert_2^2+\tau(x-\tau Sy)^{\mathsf T}Sy
=\lVert x\rVert_2^2-\tau x^{\mathsf T}Sy$,
so $Q_{n+1}=Q_n$. If either coordinate space is zero-dimensional, the cross term vanishes and the update leaves the squared Euclidean norm on the remaining state space unchanged.

By [F4] and [F5],
$|x^{\mathsf T}Sy|\leq\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert Sy\rVert_2\leq\sigma\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2

derivations.claim: If $n_1>0$, the initial trailing block $S_1=M_1$ is symmetric positive definite by [F1]. After eliminating the first $j-1$ columns without row swaps, the left augmented block has form $\begin{pmatrix}I_{j-1}&A\\0&S_j\end{pmatrix}$, where $S_j$ is the remaining Schur complement. Write $S_j=\begin{pmatrix}p&r^{\mathsf T}\\r&C\end{pmatrix}$. Since $S_j$ is positive definite, $p>0$, so the prescribed diagonal pivot is nonzero. The row operations in column $j$ replace the remaining block by $S_{j+1}=C-rp^{-1}r^{\mathsf T}$. For any nonzero $y$, put $x=-p^{-1}r^{\mathsf T}y$; then $(x,y)\neq0$ and $y^{\mathsf T}S_{j+1}y=(x,y)^{\mathsf T}S_j(x,y)>0$. Hence $S_{j+1}$ is positive definite. Induction proves that every no-row-swap pivot is positive and the error branch is unreachable. Each row operation is invertible; after the last column the left block is the identity, so the right block is exactly $M_1^{-1}$. For $n_1=0$, the inverse is the unique empty matrix and there are no pivot steps.

The input entries are rational. Each row operation uses addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division by a nonzero rational pivot from step 1.1, so every intermediate entry and the final inverse remain rational. The elimination loop has exactly $n_1$ finite iterations; consequently it terminates with an exact rational output.

Dense no-row-swap Gauss–Jordan elimination performs $O(n_1^2)$ row-entry updates per pivot column and hence $O(n_1^3)$ arithmetic operations. Each evolution step uses matrix-vector products with costs $O(n_1^2)$ for $M_1^{-1}d$, $O(n_1n_2)$ for each multiplication by $D_1$ or $D_1^{\mathsf T}$, and $O(n_2^2)$ for $M_2b$. There are exactly $N$ such steps. The matrices $D_0,D_1,D_2,M_1,M_2$ have respectively $n_1n_0,n_1n_2,n_3n_2,n_1^2,n_2^2$ entries; the inverse adds $n_1^2$, and the $N+1$ states add $(N+1)(n_1+n_2)$ entries. Their total is bounded by the stated storage order. When $N=0$, the initial state is returned without an update; when $n_1=0$ or $n_2=0$, the corresponding empty products and loops are finite and the same bounds remain valid. No bit-size or floating-point estimate follows from an arithmetic-operation count.

citations.quote:
Fix nonnegative integers $n_0,n_1,n_2,n_3$ and ordered coordinate bases, and put $C^k:=\mathbb R^{n_k}$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. The dual space $(C^k)^*$ is the vector space of linear functionals $C^k\to\mathbb R$, with the dual basis to the chosen coordinate basis. Let $D_0\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_0}$, $D_1\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_1}$, and $D_2\in\mathbb R^{n_3\times n_2}$ be linear maps satisfying $D_1D_0=0$ and $D_2D_1=0$. This data is a finite cochain complex. The transpose $D_k^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the representing matrix of the dual linear map in the dual bases. Let $M_1\in\mathbb R^{n_1\times n_1}$ and $M_2\in\mathbb R^{n_2\times n_2}$ be symmetric positive-definite matrices: $v^{\mathsf T}M_kv>0$ for each nonzero $v\in C^k$. They represent linear maps $M_1:C^1\to(C^1)^*$ and $M_2:C^2\to(C^2)^*$ in the chosen bases; in positive dimensions their inverses exist by the finite-dimensional positive-matrix result cited below, and the unique map on a zero-dimensional space is its own inverse.

The finite state space is $\mathcal X:=C^2\oplus(C^1)^*$, with state $(b,d)$, where $b$ is a column of $C^2$ coordinates and $d$ is a column in the dual basis of $(C^1)^*$. In this item, “phase space” means this finite-dimensional state space only; no symplectic form is asserted. On an open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a semidiscrete trajectory is a continuously differentiable map $t\mapsto(b(t),d(t))\in\mathcal X$ satisfying

$$\dot b(t)=-D_1M_1^{-1}d(t),\qquad \dot d(t)=D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b(t).$$

Its two discrete constraints are $D_2b(t)=0$ in $C^3$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d(t)=0$ in $(C^0)^*$. The associated quadratic energy is

$$\mathcal E(b,d):=\tfrac12\left(b^{\mathsf T}M_2b+d^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d\right).$$

All objects here are finite-dimensional real linear-algebra data. The term “Maxwell” names this algebraic model and does not identify it with a continuum Maxwell or Einstein–Maxwell solution.

Use the finite cochain data fixed by the preceding definition item, namely finite real coordinate spaces $C^0,C^1,C^2,C^3$, maps $D_0,D_1,D_2$ with $D_1D_0=D_2D_1=0$, and symmetric positive-definite mass maps $M_1,M_2$. Inputs are rational matrices $D_0,D_1,D_2,M_1,M_2$, rational initial coordinates $b_0\in C^2$ and $d_{1/2}\in(C^1)^*$, a positive rational step size $\tau$, and an integer $N\geq0$. The matrices and states use the fixed ordered bases and dual bases from that definition. All arithmetic is exact over $\mathbb Q$; floating-point arithmetic is not part of this algorithm.

First compute $R=M_1^{-1}$ once by fixed-order, no-row-swap Gauss–Jordan elimination of the augmented matrix $[M_1\mid I_{n_1}]$. For each pivot column $j=1,\ldots,n_1$, let $p$ be the current entry in position $(j,j)$. If $p=0$, return an inconsistency error. Otherwise divide row $j$ by $p$ and, for every $k\neq j$, replace row $k$ by row $k$ minus its current column-$j$ entry times row $j$. After all columns are processed, let $R$ be the right block. For $n_1=0$, take the unique empty matrix for $R$ and perform no elimination.

Set $(b,d):=(b_0,d_{1/2})$ and record this initial state. For each $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, in the stated order compute

$$b_{\mathrm{new}}:=b-\tau D_1Rd,\qquad d_{\mathrm{new}}:=d+\tau D_1^{\mathsf T}M_2b_{\mathrm{new}}.$$

Append $(b_{\mathrm{new}},d_{\mathrm{new}})$ to the output list and then set $(b,d):=(b_{\mathrm{new}},d_{\mathrm{new}})$. The output consists of the $N+1$ states $(b_n,d_{n+1/2})$ for $0\leq n\leq N$. The error branch is unreachable on admissible inputs; the separate finite-step termination lemma proves this and the exact inverse output.

Use the finite cochain data and exact update specified in the definition and algorithm items cited immediately below, with step size $\tau>0$. Every update preserves both constraints $D_2b=0$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d=0$. Every continuously differentiable semidiscrete solution conserves $\mathcal E(b,d)$. For the staggered sequence, define

$$Q_n:=b_n^{\mathsf T}M_2b_n+d_{n+1/2}^{\mathsf T}M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}-\tau b_n^{\mathsf T}M_2D_1M_1^{-1}d_{n+1/2}.$$

Then $Q_n$ is exactly invariant under the update. If $S:=M_2^{1/2}D_1M_1^{-1/2}$, set $\sigma:=0$ when the domain of $S$ is zero and otherwise set $\sigma:=\max_{\lVert y\rVert_2=1}\lVert Sy\rVert_2$; for a nonzero domain this is the largest singular value of $S$. Then $Q_n$ is positive definite whenever $\tau\sigma<2$.

derivations.claim: The matrices in [A1] are the signed boundary-incidence maps of one oriented tetrahedron, with edges ordered $01,02,03,12,13,23$, faces ordered $012,013,023,123$, and cell orientation $0123$. Matrix multiplication gives $D_1D_0=0_{4\times4}$ and $D_2D_1=0_{1\times6}$. Also $D_2x=-1+1=0$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d_{1/2}=0_{4\times1}$, so the initial state satisfies both constraints.

Put $c:=(-1,1,-1,1)^{\mathsf T}$, so $D_2=c^{\mathsf T}$. Direct multiplication gives
$$D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1&1\\1&3&1&-1\\-1&1&3&1\\1&-1&1&3\end{pmatrix}=4I_4-cc^{\mathsf T}.$$
For every $z\in\mathbb R^4$, this gives $\lVert D_1^{\mathsf T}z\rVert_2^2=4\lVert z\rVert_2^2-(c^{\mathsf T}z)^2\leq4\lVert z\rVert_2^2$. Hence, by Cauchy–Schwarz, $\lVert D_1v\rVert_2=\max_{\lVert z\rVert_2=1}|z^{\mathsf T}D_1v|\leq2\lVert v\rVert_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^6$. Since $c^{\mathsf T}x=0$, $e:=x/\sqrt2$ is unit and $D_1D_1^{\mathsf T}e=4e$; consequently $f:=D_1^{\mathsf T}e/2$ is unit and $D_1f=2e$. Thus the operator norm of $D_1$ is exactly $2$, attained at $f$. Here $M_1=M_2=I$, so the $\sigma$ defined in [F3] is $2$. For a state $b=ue$, $d=vf$, the update in [F2] with $\tau=2$ gives $u^+=u-4v$ and $v^+=v+4u^+=4u-15v$, hence the invariant two-dimensional subspace has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\4&-15\end{pmatrix}$. The initial state has modal coordinates $(u,v)=(\sqrt2,0)$.

The matrix in step 2.1 has trace $-14$, determinant $1$, and eigenvalues $\lambda_-=-7-4\sqrt3$ and $\lambda_+=-7+4\sqrt3$, found by solving $\lambda^2+14\lambda+1=0$. Since $6<4\sqrt3<7$, $\lambda_-<-1$ and $-1<\lambda_+<0$. Direct substitution gives eigenvectors $v_-=(1,2+\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$ and $v_+=(1,2-\sqrt3)^{\mathsf T}$; their determinant is $-2\sqrt3\neq0$, so write the initial modal vector as $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}=a v_-+b v_+$. The coefficient $a$ is nonzero, since otherwise $(\sqrt2,0)^{\mathsf T}$ would be a multiple of $v_+$, whose second coordinate $2-\sqrt3$ is nonzero. The first modal coordinate after $n$ steps is therefore $u_n=a\lambda_-^n+b\lambda_+^n$. If $u_n$ were bounded, then $b\lambda_+^n$ would be bounded because $|\lambda_+|<1$, so their difference $a\lambda_-^n$ would be bounded, contradicting $a\neq0$ and $|\lambda_-|>1$. Since $\lVert b_n\rVert_2\geq|u_n|$, the state orbit is unbounded.

By [F3], each update preserves both constraints, and step 1.1 sets them to zero initially. Explicitly, $D_2b^+=D_2b-\tau D_2D_1M_1^{-1}d=D_2b$ and $D_0^{\mathsf T}d^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d+\tau(D_1D_0)^{\mathsf T}M_2b^+=D_0^{\mathsf T}d$, so induction gives zero constraints at every iterate. Thus exact constraint preservation holds at every step although this rational finite-complex algorithm has an unbounded orbit for $\tau\sigma=4>2$. This refutes the stated bounded-orbit claim.

citations.quote: Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian structure and volume form of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. On decomposable $k$-covectors define the induced exterior pairing by

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.

Assume Countable Choice, meaning that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff second-countable oriented four-manifold without boundary. A continuous real top form is a continuous section of $\Lambda^4T^*M$: in every smooth coordinate chart it has the form $f(x)\,dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4$ with continuous real coefficient $f$, and the coefficients transform by the determinant of the coordinate-transition derivative. Its support is the closure in $M$ of its nonzero locus. Write $C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$ for these forms with compact support.

For $\omega\in C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$, put $K=\operatorname{supp}\omega$. If $K=\varnothing$, define its integral to be zero. Otherwise choose finitely many positively oriented charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$ and smooth functions $\chi_i:M\to[0,1]$ with compact support contained in $U_i$, such that $\sum_i\chi_i=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Write
$$
(\phi_i^{-1})^*(\chi_i\omega)=f_i\,dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4
$$
on $\phi_i(U_i)$ and extend $f_i$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$, obtaining $\widetilde f_i$. Define
$$
\mathcal I_M(\omega):=\sum_i\int_{\mathbb R^4}\widetilde f_i(x)\,dx,
$$
where each Euclidean integral is the Riemann integral over any closed nondegenerate rectangle whose interior contains its support. Such finite cutoffs exist, each zero extension is continuous and compactly supported, and the value is independent of the chosen charts, cutoffs and bounding rectangles. This is a linear functional on $C_c^0(\Lambda^4T^*M)$. For fixed cutoffs and bounding rectangles $Q_i$, it satisfies $|\mathcal I_M(\omega)|\le\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)\sup_{Q_i}|\widetilde f_i|$; thus uniform convergence of these finitely many zero-extended coefficients implies convergence of their integrals. If an open set $V\subseteq M$ contains $K$, then $\mathcal I_V(\omega|_V)=\mathcal I_M(\omega)$, with the restricted orientation. On smooth compactly supported top forms it equals the previously defined smooth manifold integral.

Countable Choice is retained to match that smooth integral's standing convention. The finite-cover construction and comparison for continuous coefficients below require no further choice principle, and do not assume the full Axiom of Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The compact-support integral on an oriented manifold is independent of the chart cover, coordinate maps, subordinate partition, and refinement. If $U\subset M$ is open and contains $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, with its restricted orientation, then $\int_U\omega|_U=\int_M\omega$.

derivations.claim: Each contraction defining $X$ and $Y$ is a scalar under changes of coordinates, because $g^{-1}$ and $\star_g$ are tensorial. Since $F$, $g$, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$ are smooth, $X,Y$ are smooth; $L_X(X,Y)$ and $L_Y(X,Y)$ are $C^1$. Therefore $H$ is a globally defined $C^1$ section of $\Lambda^2TM$, and the displayed action density is a globally defined $C^1$ top form.

For a permitted compactly supported variation $a$, [F3] gives $F_\epsilon-F=\epsilon da$, which vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}a$. Hence the difference of the two $L$ densities is compactly supported. Its coefficient is at least continuous, so the integral $\mathcal I_M$ in [F4] is finite without requiring a smooth density. On finitely many fixed chart rectangles near that support, the chain rule gives continuous parameter derivatives; their uniform convergence of difference quotients on compact rectangles allows passage to the integrals by the rectangle bound in [F4]. Hence its first variation is well-defined for $L\in C^2$, with no stronger regularity assumption. Thus the Definition specifies a relative action and stationarity predicate without assuming the unvaried action is finite or that a stationary connection exists.

def-emg-fx-nonlinear-lagrangian.definition_interface:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, independent orientation $o$, and the torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla$ selected by $g$. Fix a smooth principal $U(1)$ bundle sector and a smooth connection $\mathcal A$ in that sector. In the inherited physical-curvature normalization, its curvature is a smooth real two-form $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $dF=0$. A permitted variation is $\mathcal A_\epsilon=\mathcal A+\epsilon a$, where $a\in\Omega^1(M)$ is smooth and compactly supported; the same-sector convention gives $F_\epsilon=F+\epsilon da$. No global potential is required.

Raise indices with $g^{-1}$ and let $\star_g$ be the Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$. Define the scalar invariants
$X:=-\frac14 F_{ab}F^{ab},\qquad Y:=-\frac14F_{ab}(\star_gF)^{ab}.$
Let $L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and write $L_X,L_Y$ for its first partial derivatives evaluated at $(X,Y)$. Define the contravariant antisymmetric tensor
$H^{ab}:=L_XF^{ab}+L_Y(\star_gF)^{ab}.$
The source-free local action density is $L(X,Y)\,\mathrm{vol}_g$. Its relative action difference under a compact variation is the integral of $[L(X(F_\epsilon),Y(F_\epsilon))-L(X(F),Y(F))]\,\mathrm{vol}_g$; this difference has compact support even when the unvaried integral over $M$ is not finite. The connection is stationary when the derivative of this relative action at $\epsilon=0$ vanishes for every permitted $a$.

In the mathematical normalization, $L=X$ is the Maxwell quadratic term. If units are attached, the components of $F$ have a fixed unit $\mathfrak F$, $X,Y,L$ have unit $\mathfrak F^2$, and coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ in $L=X+\alpha X^2+\beta Y^2$ have unit $\mathfrak F^{-2}$, so $\alpha X$ and $\beta Y$ are dimensionless. This normalization is not an SI action prefactor. The coefficients are arbitrary parameters, not QED coefficients. This definition supplies no quantum origin, source coupling, characteristic-cone condition, hyperbolicity, causality, or solution-existence claim.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $M$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable oriented four-manifold, and let $(U_i,g_{ij},a_i;\kappa_0)$ be a normalized circle-connection datum as in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. Use the set-sized-object and quotient convention of [[def-emg-set-size-and-class-schema]]. Then the chart data construct a smooth Hausdorff second-countable right principal $U(1)$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ and a global smooth real connection one-form $\omega$ on $P$. Its curvature is basic: there is a smooth closed two-form $f\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $d\omega=\pi^*f$ and $f|_{U_i}=da_i$. The local potentials $A_i=\kappa_0a_i$ satisfy $dA_i=F$, where $F=\kappa_0 f$ is global. For two connections on the same fixed bundle with the same transition functions, their local-form differences are restrictions of one global base one-form; adding a global one-form to all local representatives stays in that bundle sector.
