Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of The derivative and the Riemann integral of a vector-valued function: an intrinsic derivative and a componentwise integral.

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5, The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

Let $d,n\in\mathbb N$ with $d,n\ge1$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is locally the graph of a smooth function. Here $C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$ means restriction of a smooth function on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Use the matrix spaces $M_n(\mathbb C)$ and ordinary matrix multiplication. For $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$, and write $\operatorname{tr}A:=\sum_{j<n}A_{jj}$. A matrix $\Phi$ is **positive definite Hermitian** when $\Phi^\dagger=\Phi$ and $v^\dagger\Phi v$ is a positive real number for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb C^n$. Define

$$\mathcal P_n:=\{\Phi\in M_n(\mathbb C):\Phi\text{ is positive definite Hermitian and }\det\Phi=1\}.$$

The determinant is the determinant over $\mathbb C$. Every $\Phi\in\mathcal P_n$ is invertible because $\det\Phi=1$ is a unit; its inverse is smooth when $\Phi$ is a smooth matrix field because the adjugate formula reduces to polynomial entries when $\det\Phi=1$.

For a smooth map $\Phi:\overline\Omega\to\mathcal P_n$, define the matrix-valued one-form $d\Phi=\sum_{a=1}^d(\partial_a\Phi)\,dx^a$ by differentiating entries, and put $J:=\Phi^{-1}d\Phi=\sum_{a=1}^d J_a\,dx^a$. Its **matrix harmonic-map equation** in this item means exactly

$$\operatorname{div}J:=\sum_{a=1}^d\partial_aJ_a=0\quad\text{on }\Omega.$$

The positive matrix boundary problem is to compare two such maps $\Phi_0,\Phi_1$ satisfying this equation and prescribed values on all of $\partial\Omega$. The Euclidean coordinates, matrix size, determinant normalization, and divergence convention are part of the definition. No spacetime metric, symmetry reduction, physical postulate, or spacetime uniqueness theorem is included.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the nonempty bounded connected smooth domain of [[def-emg-fx-matrix-harmonic-problem]]. Let $\Phi_0,\Phi_1\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathcal P_n)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}J_i=0$, where $J_i:=\Phi_i^{-1}d\Phi_i=\sum_{a=1}^dJ_{i,a}\,dx^a$ and $\operatorname{div}J_i:=\sum_a\partial_aJ_{i,a}$. Define

$$\Psi:=\Phi_1\Phi_0^{-1}-I_n,\qquad \Delta J_a:=J_{1,a}-J_{0,a}.$$

Then, pointwise on $\Omega$,

$$\Delta\operatorname{tr}\Psi=\sum_{a=1}^d\operatorname{tr}\!\left((\Delta J_a)^\dagger\Phi_1\Delta J_a\Phi_0^{-1}\right)\ge0,$$

where $\Delta=\sum_a\partial_a^2$ is the Euclidean Laplacian. If $\Phi_1=\Phi_0$ on the entire boundary $\partial\Omega$, then $\Phi_1=\Phi_0$ on $\overline\Omega$. This is an abstract bounded-domain uniqueness result for the stated positive matrix equation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with smooth future timelike time-orientation field $N$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be a nonempty connected open set. A **stationary field on $U$** is a specified smooth Killing field $k$ that is timelike on a specified nonempty open subset of $U$; no normalization or global timelikeness is inferred.

Here $U(1)=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ with complex multiplication and the smooth circle-group structure fixed in [[def-emg-local-potentials-and-circle-data]]. An **axial $U(1)$ action on $U$** is a specified smooth map $\rho:U(1)\times U\to U$ satisfying $\rho(1,p)=p$ and $\rho(z_1z_2,p)=\rho(z_1,\rho(z_2,p))$, with $\rho(z,\cdot)^*g=g$ for every $z$; effective means that only $z=1$ acts identically on all of $U$. Its generator is the smooth vector field $m$ defined by $m_p=\frac{d}{d\theta}|_{\theta=0}\rho(e^{i\theta},p)$; the parameter has period $2\pi$. Its **axis** is the fixed-point set $\mathcal A:=\{p\in U:\rho(z,p)=p\text{ for every }z\in U(1)\}$. For this page, an **axisymmetric region** is a region supplied with such an effective action and satisfying $g(m,m)>0$ on $U\setminus\mathcal A$. A stationary field and axial generator **commute** when their Lie bracket vanishes; in coordinates this means $\sum_a(k^a\partial_a m^b-m^a\partial_a k^b)=0$ for every component $b$.

Define

$$U_*:=\{p\in U\setminus\mathcal A:k_p,m_p\text{ are linearly independent and }g_p|_{\operatorname{span}\{k_p,m_p\}}\text{ is nondegenerate}\}.$$

Because $M$ is Hausdorff, each fixed set $\{p:\rho(z,p)=p\}$ is closed in $U$: it is the preimage of the closed diagonal in $U\times U$ under $p\mapsto(\rho(z,p),p)$. Their intersection $\mathcal A$ is closed, so $U\setminus\mathcal A$ is open. In a chart, linear independence is witnessed by a nonzero $2\times2$ minor of the $4\times2$ coordinate matrix with columns $k$ and $m$, and nondegeneracy is $\det G\ne0$ for the continuous Gram matrix $G_{ij}:=g(K_i,K_j)$, where $K_1:=k$ and $K_2:=m$. These are open conditions, so $U_*$ is open. On $U_*$ the matrix $G$ is invertible. Its inverse entries are smooth by the cofactor-over-determinant formula. The smooth map

$$\Pi_p(v):=\sum_{i,j=1}^2K_i(p)(G(p)^{-1})_{ij}g_p(K_j(p),v)$$

is a projection onto $\operatorname{span}\{k,m\}$, since it fixes each $K_i$ and $v-\Pi_p(v)$ is orthogonal to both generators. Therefore

$$\mathcal D_p:=\ker\Pi_p=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,k_p)=g_p(v,m_p)=0\}$$

is a smooth rank-two distribution on $U_*$: the projection has rank two in each tangent space, and its kernel has dimension $4-2=2$. The kernel varies smoothly because, locally, a nonzero two-by-two minor lets one solve its two linear equations smoothly for two components in terms of the other two.

Its generator is the smooth vector field $m$ defined by $m_p=\frac{d}{d\theta}|_{\theta=0}\rho(e^{i\theta},p)$; the parameter has period $2\pi$. For this page, an **axisymmetric region** is a region supplied with such an effective action and satisfying $g(m,m)>0$ on $U\setminus\mathcal A$. A stationary field and axial generator **commute** when their Lie bracket vanishes; in coordinates this means $\sum_a(k^a\partial_a m^b-m^a\partial_a k^b)=0$ for every component $b$.

Define

$$U_*:=\{p\in U\setminus\mathcal A:k_p,m_p\text{ are linearly independent and }g_p|_{\operatorname{span}\{k_p,m_p\}}\text{ is nondegenerate}\}.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Its smooth real $k$-forms are sections of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, written $\Omega^k(M)$, and $d$ is the exterior derivative of [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. A smooth two-form $F$ is **closed** when $dF=0$ and **exact** when $F=dA$ for some smooth real one-form $A$ on the whole base.

By [[def-de-rham-cohomology]], $H^2_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)=Z^2(M)/B^2(M)$, where $Z^2(M)$ is the vector space of closed smooth two-forms and $B^2(M)$ is the vector space of exact smooth two-forms. Thus, for closed $F$, the statement $[F]=0$ means exactly that $F=dA$ for a global smooth one-form $A$. This equivalence is the quotient definition; it does not assert that every closed form is exact.

Identify $\mathbb C$ with $\mathbb R^2$ by $z=x+iy$ and set $U(1)=S^1:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. Its topology is the subspace topology. Specify its smooth structure by the four charts

$$V_{x,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon x>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto y,\quad y\mapsto(\epsilon\sqrt{1-y^2},y),$$

and

$$V_{y,\epsilon}=\{(x,y)\in S^1:\epsilon y>0\},\quad (x,y)\mapsto x,\quad x\mapsto(x,\epsilon\sqrt{1-x^2}),$$

for $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, with each coordinate range $(-1,1)$. They cover $S^1$; their transition maps are restrictions of the positive square-root branch and coordinate projections, hence are smooth by [[lem-emg-positive-square-root-smoothness]] and [[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]]. In these coordinates multiplication is the restriction of $(x,y)(u,v)=(xu-yv,xv+yu)$ and inversion is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$, so both are smooth; they are also continuous for the stated topology. Thus this is a smooth Lie group and, in particular, a topological group as required by [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]].

Let $E:\mathbb R\to U(1)$ be $E(t)=e^{it}=(\cos t,\sin t)$; the Cartesian formula is [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The trigonometric derivative identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], iterated, show that $E$ is smooth in the $C^\infty$ sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: every derivative of either coordinate is $\pm\sin$ or $\pm\cos$, and these functions are continuous by [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]]. Surjectivity is [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]. If $E(t)\in V_{x,\epsilon}$, the chart coordinate $\sin t$ has derivative $\cos t=x\ne0$; if $E(t)\in V_{y,\epsilon}$, the coordinate $\cos t$ has derivative $-\sin t=-y\ne0$. The smooth inverse-function theorem [[lem-choice-free-smooth-inverse-function-theorem-in-euclidean-space]] therefore makes $E$ a diffeomorphism from some open interval about $t$ onto an open circle arc. Every smooth map from an open subset of $M$ to $U(1)$ consequently has, near each point, a smooth real phase lift obtained by composing with such a local inverse.

A **normalized circle-connection datum** on $M$ consists of a supplied countable open cover $(U_i)_{i\in I}$, smooth transition maps $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to U(1)$, smooth real one-forms $a_i\in\Omega^1(U_i)$, and a fixed constant $\kappa_0>0$. Require $g_{ii}=1$ and $g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}$ on every triple intersection. Around each point of $U_i\cap U_j$, take any smooth real phase lift $f_{ij}$ with $g_{ij}=e^{if_{ij}}$; require

$$
a_j=a_i+df_{ij}
$$

on every such phase-lift neighborhood. If $f$ and $\widetilde f$ are two lifts on a connected neighborhood, [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]] gives $f-\widetilde f\in2\pi\mathbb Z$ pointwise; continuity makes this difference constant, so $df=d\widetilde f$. Thus the compatibility condition is independent of the chosen lift. The globally defined form $\lambda(g):=-i\,g^{-1}dg$ is real, and [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]] together with [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] gives $\lambda(g)=df$ on every phase-lift neighborhood. Hence the equivalent lift-free condition is $a_j=a_i+\lambda(g_{ij})$.

The right principal $U(1)$-bundle convention is as defined in [[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]]: it has a continuous right action and locally trivial equivariant product charts, with free and transitive action on each fibre. The compatible transition functions are the gluing data for such a bundle, in the convention that a point with fibre coordinate $z_i$ in chart $i$ has coordinate $z_j=g_{ij}^{-1}z_i$ in chart $j$. No global real-valued angle on $U(1)$ is assumed.

The constant $\kappa_0$ is a chosen normalization with units of webers; it is not Planck's constant and is not a unit of electric charge. On a chart whose coordinates have length units, the normalized connection components $a_i$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$; the corresponding local potential $A_i:=\kappa_0a_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and its curvature $F_i:=dA_i=\kappa_0\,da_i$ has components $\mathrm{Wb}\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. This definition imposes no flux or charge quantization.

Let $d,n\in\mathbb N$ with $d,n\ge1$. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded connected open set whose boundary is locally the graph of a smooth function. Here $C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$ means restriction of a smooth function on an open neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$. Use the matrix spaces $M_n(\mathbb C)$ and ordinary matrix multiplication. For $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$, and write $\operatorname{tr}A:=\sum_{j<n}A_{jj}$. A matrix $\Phi$ is **positive definite Hermitian** when $\Phi^\dagger=\Phi$ and $v^\dagger\Phi v$ is a positive real number for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb C^n$. Define

$$\mathcal P_n:=\{\Phi\in M_n(\mathbb C):\Phi\text{ is positive definite Hermitian and }\det\Phi=1\}.$$

The determinant is the determinant over $\mathbb C$. Every $\Phi\in\mathcal P_n$ is invertible because $\det\Phi=1$ is a unit; its inverse is smooth when $\Phi$ is a smooth matrix field because the adjugate formula reduces to polynomial entries when $\det\Phi=1$.

For a smooth map $\Phi:\overline\Omega\to\mathcal P_n$, define the matrix-valued one-form $d\Phi=\sum_{a=1}^d(\partial_a\Phi)\,dx^a$ by differentiating entries, and put $J:=\Phi^{-1}d\Phi=\sum_{a=1}^d J_a\,dx^a$. Its **matrix harmonic-map equation** in this item means exactly

$$\operatorname{div}J:=\sum_{a=1}^d\partial_aJ_a=0\quad\text{on }\Omega.$$

The positive matrix boundary problem is to compare two such maps $\Phi_0,\Phi_1$ satisfying this equation and prescribed values on all of $\partial\Omega$. The Euclidean coordinates, matrix size, determinant normalization, and divergence convention are part of the definition. No spacetime metric, symmetry reduction, physical postulate, or spacetime uniqueness theorem is included.

Let $d,n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the nonempty bounded connected smooth domain of [[def-emg-fx-matrix-harmonic-problem]]. Let $\Phi_0,\Phi_1\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega,\mathcal P_n)$ satisfy $\operatorname{div}J_i=0$, where $J_i:=\Phi_i^{-1}d\Phi_i=\sum_{a=1}^dJ_{i,a}\,dx^a$ and $\operatorname{div}J_i:=\sum_a\partial_aJ_{i,a}$. Define

$$\Psi:=\Phi_1\Phi_0^{-1}-I_n,\qquad \Delta J_a:=J_{1,a}-J_{0,a}.$$

Then, pointwise on $\Omega$,

$$\Delta\operatorname{tr}\Psi=\sum_{a=1}^d\operatorname{tr}\!\left((\Delta J_a)^\dagger\Phi_1\Delta J_a\Phi_0^{-1}\right)\ge0,$$

where $\Delta=\sum_a\partial_a^2$ is the Euclidean Laplacian. If $\Phi_1=\Phi_0$ on the entire boundary $\partial\Omega$, then $\Phi_1=\Phi_0$ on $\overline\Omega$. This is an abstract bounded-domain uniqueness result for the stated positive matrix equation.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold structure, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla^g$, and length-coordinate convention of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Let $A\in\Omega^1(M)$ be a supplied smooth real one-form, let $e\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed real coupling, and let $\psi\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb C)$ be a smooth complex-valued function. In the length-coordinate convention, assign dimensionless components to $A_a$ and unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ to $e$, so $eA_a$ has derivative unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; assign $\psi$ an arbitrary fixed unit $[\psi]$. Define the complex covector

$$D_a\psi:=\nabla^g_a\psi-ieA_a\psi.$$

Since $\psi$ is a scalar, $\nabla^g_a\psi=\partial_a\psi$. Define the real symmetric covariant tensor

$$\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]:=\overline{D_a\psi}\,D_b\psi+\overline{D_b\psi}\,D_a\psi-g_{ab}g^{cd}\overline{D_c\psi}\,D_d\psi,$$

with indices raised using $g^{-1}$. Its covariant components have unit $[\psi]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$. This is a mathematical tensor assignment. Its interpretation as a stress-energy tensor, and any field equation or conservation law, require a separate physical model.

derivations.claim:
Since $A_t=-Q/r$ and $\omega>0$, the time derivative satisfies $D_t\psi=-i\omega\psi+o(r^{-1})$. Using $D^r=f\partial_r=\partial_{r_*}$ and $\partial_{r_*}(u/r)=u'/r-fu/r^2$, the differentiated asymptotics and $\Theta'\to\omega$ give
$$\psi=\frac{A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y}{r}\left(e^{-i\Theta}+Re^{i\Theta}\right)+o(r^{-1}),\qquad D^r\psi=\frac{A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y}{r}\left(-i\omega e^{-i\Theta}+i\omega Re^{i\Theta}\right)+o(r^{-1}).$$

Since $g^r{}_t=0$, [F2] gives $\mathsf T^r{}_t=2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{D^r\psi}D_t\psi)$. Substitution of step 1.1 gives the diagonal terms $\omega^2(1-|R|^2)$; the cross terms are $z-\overline z$ for $z=\omega^2R e^{2i\Theta}$ and have zero real part. Integrating $Y^2$ over the sphere and taking $r\to\infty$ therefore gives the net outward flux $\mathcal P(r)\to2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2(|R|^2-1)$.

For the incoming component, $D^r\psi_{\mathrm{in}}=-i\omega\psi_{\mathrm{in}}+o(r^{-1})$ and $D_t\psi_{\mathrm{in}}=-i\omega\psi_{\mathrm{in}}+o(r^{-1})$, so $\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi_{\mathrm{in}}]=2\omega^2|\psi_{\mathrm{in}}|^2+o(r^{-2})$; its positive inward magnitude is $2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2$ after sphere integration. For the reflected component, $D^r\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}=i\omega\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}+o(r^{-1})$ while $D_t\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}=-i\omega\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}+o(r^{-1})$, so its nonnegative outward magnitude is $2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2|R|^2$. Their ratio is $|R|^2$ because $\omega>0$ and $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ have the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold structure, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla^g$, and length-coordinate convention of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Let $A\in\Omega^1(M)$ be a supplied smooth real one-form, let $e\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed real coupling, and let $\psi\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb C)$ be a smooth complex-valued function. In the length-coordinate convention, assign dimensionless components to $A_a$ and unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ to $e$, so $eA_a$ has derivative unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; assign $\psi$ an arbitrary fixed unit $[\psi]$. Define the complex covector

$$D_a\psi:=\nabla^g_a\psi-ieA_a\psi.$$

Since $\psi$ is a scalar, $\nabla^g_a\psi=\partial_a\psi$. Define the real symmetric covariant tensor

$$\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]:=\overline{D_a\psi}\,D_b\psi+\overline{D_b\psi}\,D_a\psi-g_{ab}g^{cd}\overline{D_c\psi}\,D_d\psi,$$

with indices raised using $g^{-1}$. Its covariant components have unit $[\psi]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$. This is a mathematical tensor assignment. Its interpretation as a stress-energy tensor, and any field equation or conservation law, require a separate physical model.

On an open region of the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian spacetime and length-coordinate SI conventions of [[def-emg-matter-observables]], adopt a prescribed-background Maxwell model. The metric $g$ is fixed input. Choose a real $C^2$ electromagnetic two-form $F$ and either adopt the source-free equations $dF=0$ and $d(\star_gF)=0$, or supply a $C^1$ current $j$ and adopt $dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$, with the exact signs and units of that definition. The source current is prescribed independently of the probe; this postulate does not impose an Einstein equation, matter evolution equation, or field equation for the sources on the unchanged metric.

For a massive charged probe, use the adopted local action and finite-curve conditions of [[post-rpm-external-charge-action]]: $m>0$ and $q$ are constant, the path is a $C^2$ future-directed timelike segment parameterized by proper time, and its endpoints are fixed in variations supported in a local potential domain $V$ with a supplied $C^2$ one-form $A$ satisfying $dA=F$. The potential and metric are external data independent of the path. Under the exact hypotheses of [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]], action stationarity is equivalent to $m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U)$; that theorem's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption is inherited only when this equivalent force-law formulation is used. No global potential or trajectory is included.

The probe's own singular field and self-gravity are excluded. No radiation reaction, variable mass or charge, finite-body model, or backreaction estimate is adopted. In particular, calling $g$ or $F$ a test background records this model's omission of their response; it does not claim that the unchanged pair solves the coupled Einstein–Maxwell equations or is close to a coupled solution.

When geometric optics is invoked, it is restricted to the exact $C^4$ real phase, $C^3$ complex amplitudes, four pointwise ansatz constraints, and fixed compact-chart coefficient bounds of [[lem-emg-controlled-maxwell-wkb]]. That result supplies finite residual and leading-field estimates, local null rays, and a polarization quotient; it supplies no convergent series, global transport through caustics, exact-solution error estimate, or backreaction theorem.

This is a separately adopted physical model with no empirical premise. The Maxwell and probe assumptions are not deductions from one another, from mathematical axioms, or from source authority.

Let $M,q_e,q_m\in\mathbb R$ be length parameters and put
$Q^2:=q_e^2+q_m^2$. Let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and require
$$f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2}\ne0\qquad(r\in J).$$
On the smooth product $\mathcal M_J:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times J_r\times S^2$,
use $S^2=\{(X,Y,Z)\in\mathbb R^3:X^2+Y^2+Z^2=1\}$ with its subspace
topology ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]). Specify the smooth
structure by the sphere atlas of [[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]],
Definition (b): for $\varepsilon=\pm1$, delete $p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$
and use $\sigma_\varepsilon(X,Y,Z)=(X,Y)/(1-\varepsilon Z)$.
For $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $h=u_1^2+u_2^2$, its inverse is
$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=(2u_1,2u_2,\varepsilon(h-1))/(1+h)$;
the transition is $u\mapsto u/h$ on $h>0$. These rational maps are smooth
on their domains. The product atlas consists of
$(x^0,r,p)\mapsto(x^0,r,\sigma_\varepsilon(p))$ on
$\mathbb R\times J\times(S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\})$;
its transitions leave $x^0,r$ fixed and apply the displayed sphere transition.
The product is Hausdorff and second countable by the subspace topology from
$\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^3$, whose rational balls give a countable basis.
These charts specify its maximal smooth atlas, including when $J$ is empty.
The inclusion of $S^2$ into $\mathbb R^3$ is smooth with injective differential
in these parametrizations; its induced unit round metric is $\gamma_{S^2}$
([[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]).
Orient $S^2$ by its outward unit normal: for $p\in S^2$ and
$u,v\in T_pS^2$, define
$$ (\omega_{S^2})_p(u,v):=\det(p,u,v). $$
Thus $\omega_{S^2}$ is the positive area form of $\gamma_{S^2}$, and in the
polar chart $X=\sin\theta\cos\phi$, $Y=\sin\theta\sin\phi$,
$Z=\cos\theta$ it is $\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi$. The **dyonic RN
datum** is
$$g=-f(r)\,dx^0\otimes dx^0+f(r)^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\gamma_{S^2}, \qquad \mathcal F=-\frac{q_e}{r^2}\,dx^0\wedge dr+q_m\omega_{S^2}.$$
Here $x^0$ and $r$ have units of metres, angles on $S^2$ are dimensionless,
and $M,q_e,q_m$ have units of metres. The metric components are dimensionless
in length coordinates; the nonzero coordinate components of $\mathcal F$ have
units inherited from their coordinate Jacobians. Use the orientation
$dx^0\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$.

The set $J$ may have several connected components. On $\{f>0\}$ choose the
time orientation $\partial_{x^0}$; on $\{f<0\}$ choose $\partial_r$. These
are smooth timelike fields on their respective open subsets because
$g(\partial_{x^0},\partial_{x^0})=-f<0$ when $f>0$ and
$g(\partial_r,\partial_r)=f^{-1}<0$ when $f<0$. Since $f$ has no zero on
$\mathcal M_J$, this defines a smooth time orientation on the whole product.
The sphere area form and the displayed two-form are global on $S^2$.

Let $N,S$ denote the north and south poles. On
$U_N:=S^2\setminus\{S\}$ and $U_S:=S^2\setminus\{N\}$, respectively,
local potential one-forms are
$$\mathcal A_N=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0+q_m(1-\cos\theta)\,d\phi,\qquad \mathcal A_S=-\frac{q_e}{r}\,dx^0-q_m(1+\cos\theta)\,d\phi.$$
Each displayed potential extends smoothly over its named included pole:
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $N$ and
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi$ is smooth at $S$. Direct differentiation gives
$d\mathcal A_N=d\mathcal A_S=\mathcal F$ on the respective patches. Their
overlap difference is $2q_m\,d\phi$; it is local potential data, not a global
real gauge function on the entire sphere. The definition assumes no $U(1)$
bundle or charge quantization. To verify pole smoothness, use local coordinates
$u=X,v=Y$ near each pole. There
$d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(u^2+v^2)$. Near $N$,
$1-\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1+Z)$, so
$(1-\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1+Z)$ is smooth. Near $S$,
$1+\cos\theta=(u^2+v^2)/(1-Z)$, so
$(1+\cos\theta)d\phi=(u\,dv-v\,du)/(1-Z)$ is smooth. The denominators are
nonzero on the respective named patches.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with signature $(-,+,+,+)$, independent orientation $o$, and the torsion-free metric-compatible connection $
abla$ selected by $g$. Fix a smooth principal $U(1)$ bundle sector and a smooth connection $mathcal A$ in that sector. In the inherited physical-curvature normalization, its curvature is a smooth real two-form $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ with $dF=0$. A permitted variation is $mathcal A_\epsilon=\mathcal A+\epsilon a$, where $a\in\Omega^1(M)$ is smooth and compactly supported; the same-sector convention gives $F_\epsilon=F+\epsilon da$. No global potential is required.

Raise indices with $g^{-1}$ and let $\star_g$ be the Hodge map determined by $g$ and $o$. Define the scalar invariants
$$X:=-\frac14 F_{ab}F^{ab},\qquad Y:=-\frac14F_{ab}(\star_gF)^{ab}.$$
Let $L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and write $L_X,L_Y$ for its first partial derivatives evaluated at $(X,Y)$. Define the contravariant antisymmetric tensor
$$H^{ab}:=L_XF^{ab}+L_Y(\star_gF)^{ab}.$$
The source-free local action density is $L(X,Y)\,\mathrm{vol}_g$. Its relative action difference under a compact variation is the integral of $[L(X(F_\epsilon),Y(F_\epsilon))-L(X(F),Y(F))]\,\mathrm{vol}_g$; this difference has compact support even when the unvaried integral over $M$ is not finite. The connection is stationary when the derivative of this relative action at $\epsilon=0$ vanishes for every permitted $a$.

In the mathematical normalization, $L=X$ is the Maxwell quadratic term. If units are attached, the components of $F$ have a fixed unit $\mathfrak F$, $X,Y,L$ have unit $\mathfrak F^2$, and coefficients $\alpha,\beta$ in $L=X+\alpha X^2+\beta Y^2$ have unit $\mathfrak F^{-2}$, so $\alpha X$ and $\beta Y$ are dimensionless. This normalization is not an SI action prefactor. The coefficients are arbitrary parameters, not QED coefficients. This definition supplies no quantum origin, source coupling, characteristic-cone condition, hyperbolicity, causality, or solution-existence claim.

citations.quote:
Adopt the following classical test-scalar model in the geometric length-coordinate convention of the charged radial-scattering definition. Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|\le M$, put

$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad U:=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2.$$

On $U$ prescribe

$$g=-f(r)\,dt^2+f(r)^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad F=dA=-\frac{Q}{r^2}\,dt\wedge dr.$$

Here $\gamma_{S^2}$ is the unit round metric, $A_t\to0$ at infinity, and $r_+$ is the larger positive root; in the extremal case $Q^2=M^2$ both roots equal $M$. The factorization $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2$ makes $f>0$ on this open exterior. The larger root is a null constant-$r$ Killing horizon in the selected ingoing RN model; it is not an event-horizon assertion about a maximal spacetime. Orient the product by $dt\wedge dr\wedge\omega_{S^2}$, where $\omega_{S^2}$ is the outward area form of the unit round sphere; $\star_g$ denotes the corresponding Lorentzian Hodge map. Adopt the source-free background Maxwell branch $dF=0$ and $d(\star_gF)=0$ on $U$. The fields are prescribed on the open exterior only. No maximal extension, coupled Einstein equation, or actual astrophysical object is asserted by this postulate.

In the chosen global electric gauge, let $\psi:U\to\mathbb C$ be a smooth complex scalar and let $e\in\mathbb R$ be its fixed charge-coupling parameter. Define $D_a\psi:=\partial_a\psi-ieA_a\psi$, so $D_t=\partial_t+ieQ/r$. The scalar Laplace–Beltrami operator on the unit sphere is $\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}=\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta)+\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2$ in the standard polar chart, with smooth global extension. Adopt the massless, minimally coupled equation

$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi=0.$$

For its energy bookkeeping, adopt the symmetric tensor assignment $\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]$ defined by the exact mathematical stress-tensor formula linked below. The scalar's stress is omitted from the equations for the prescribed background, and no scalar source is added to its Maxwell equation. This is a test-field model: omission of the scalar response is a modeling choice, not an estimate that the response is small.

Coordinates $t,r,M,Q$ have unit metres; $f$ and $A_t$ are dimensionless; $e$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; $F_{tr}$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; and the scalar field has a specified but otherwise arbitrary unit $[\psi]$. The tensor assignment $\mathsf T_{ab}$ has component unit $[\psi]^2\mathrm m^{-2}$ in this geometric normalization. For the subextremal branch, define the gauge-normalized outer-root potential difference by $\Phi_H:=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)=Q/r_+$. The separate mathematical scalar model on the Einstein–Maxwell page uses SI bookkeeping and its own coupling parameters; no identification with those parameters is made here.

Let $M>0$ and $Q\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $0<|Q|<M$. Put
$$r_\pm:=M\pm\sqrt{M^2-Q^2},\qquad f(r):=1-\frac{2M}{r}+\frac{Q^2}{r^2},\qquad r>r_+.$$
Use the static exterior
$\mathcal M_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R_t\times(r_+,\infty)_r\times S^2$
with the electric specialization $q_e=Q$, $q_m=0$, and $t=x^0$ of the
Reissner--Nordström metric and potential fixed in the preceding definition.
Thus
$$g=-f\,dt^2+f^{-1}dr^2+r^2\gamma_{S^2},\qquad A=-\frac Qr\,dt,\qquad A_t\longrightarrow0\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty).$$
Here $r_+$ is the positive outer root in the selected local model, not a claim
about an event horizon in a maximal spacetime. Set
$\Phi_H:=Q/r_+=A_t(\infty)-A_t(r_+)$ for this gauge.

For a complex scalar function $\psi$ in this fixed trivialization and a real
coupling $e$, put $D_a\psi:=(\partial_a-ieA_a)\psi$. Define the massless
charged wave operator in the static chart by
$$\Box_{g,A}\psi:=-f^{-1}D_t^2\psi+\frac1{r^2}\partial_r\!\left(r^2f\,\partial_r\psi\right)+\frac1{r^2}\Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}\psi,\qquad D_t=\partial_t+\frac{ieQ}{r}.$$
The equation used here is $\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$; it is a fixed-background,
minimally coupled test-field equation and does not evolve or source $g$ or $A$.

Let $e\in\mathbb R$, $\omega>0$, and $\ell\in\mathbb N_0$. Supply a smooth
real function $Y:S^2\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\int_{S^2}Y^2\,d\omega_{S^2}=1,\qquad \Delta_{\gamma_{S^2}}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y.$$
No existence assertion about $Y$ is made. Use the tortoise coordinate
$$r_*(r):=\int_{2r_+}^{r}f(\rho)^{-1}\,d\rho,$$
which is strictly increasing because $f>0$ on the exterior. Under the
subextremal hypotheses the supplied RN scalar-coordinate result proves that
$r_*$ is a smooth coordinate from $(r_+,\infty)$ onto $\mathbb R$; hence
$r_*\to-\infty$ as $r\downarrow r_+$ and $r_*\to+\infty$ as $r\to\infty$.
A separated mode has the form
$$\psi(t,r,\Omega)=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)\frac{u(r_*)}{r},$$
where $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$ is a fixed incident amplitude with units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m$, and the normalized complex radial function $u$ and its
reflection and transmission coefficients are dimensionless.

Write $\omega_H:=\omega-e\Phi_H=\omega-eQ/r_+$ and, for any reference length
$L>0$, define the Coulomb phase
$$\Theta(r_*):=\omega r_*-eQ\log(r/L),\qquad \Theta'(r_*):=\omega-\frac{eQf(r)}r.$$
A normalized scattering solution is a smooth radial solution of
$\Box_{g,A}\psi=0$ for which, for some $R,T\in\mathbb C$,
$$u=e^{-i\Theta}+R e^{i\Theta}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\Theta'e^{-i\Theta}+i\Theta'R e^{i\Theta}+o(1)\quad(r\longrightarrow\infty),$$
and
$$u=T e^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1),\qquad \partial_{r_*}u=-i\omega_HTe^{-i\omega_Hr_*}+o(1)\quad(r\downarrow r_+).$$
The error terms tend to zero in the indicated limits. These boundary
conditions prescribe unit incoming amplitude at infinity and only the
ingoing branch at the future horizon. They define admissible scattering data;
they assert neither existence nor uniqueness of such a solution.

The logarithm in $\Theta$ is required by the long-range term
$-2\omega eQ/r$ in the asymptotic radial coefficient. Changing $L$ changes
constant phases, not flux magnitudes. A constant gauge shift changes the
frequency label, so the threshold uses the potential difference
$\Phi_H$, not an absolute value of $A_t$.

Use geometric units $G=c=1$ and length coordinates, with
$[t]=[r]=[r_*]=[M]=[Q]=[L]=\mathrm m$,
$[e]=[\omega]=\mathrm m^{-1}$, $f$ dimensionless, and $A_t$ dimensionless;
then $\Theta$ is dimensionless and each term in $\Box_{g,A}$ has units
$[\psi]\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. The coupling $e$ is the charge coupling in the
chosen field normalization; restoring SI units requires restoring the
corresponding field normalization and the charge-over-$\hbar$ coupling.
This definition excludes scalar mass, magnetic charge, mirrors, anti-de Sitter
boundaries, bound states, and complex-frequency quasinormal boundary conditions.
A scalar mass would change the propagating infinity wave number to
$\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$ and requires a different scattering normalization.
Complex-frequency quasinormal modes form a distinct non-self-adjoint spectral
problem and are not covered by the real-frequency Wronskian identity.

Let $u$ be any scattering solution as defined on the fixed subextremal electric
RN exterior, with real $\omega>0$, real $e,Q$, unit incoming amplitude, and
reflection and transmission coefficients $R,T$. Then its radial Wronskian
flux $j:=\operatorname{Im}(\overline u\,\partial_{r_*}u)$ is constant and
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-eQ/r_+}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
Consequently, if $0<\omega<eQ/r_+$ and $T\ne0$, the reflected radial flux
magnitude exceeds the incident radial flux magnitude, since their ratio is
$|R|^2>1$. This is conditional on an admitted scattering solution and does not
assert its existence, a complex-frequency mode, or a nonlinear instability.

Use the fixed subextremal electric Reissner–Nordström exterior, gauge, charged derivative, real normalized spherical harmonic $Y$, and mode conventions of [[def-emg-fx-charged-radial-scattering]]. Let $\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)u(r_*)/r$ be any admitted real-frequency scattering mode with $\omega>0$ and $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$, and let $R$ be its reflection coefficient. Form $\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]$ by the gauge-covariant scalar stress-tensor definition. With $\xi=\partial_t$, define the outward radial flux through the sphere of radius $r$ by

$$\mathcal P(r):=-\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi;g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2}.$$

Let $\psi_{\mathrm{in}}:=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y e^{-i\Theta}/r$ and $\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}:=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}YRe^{i\Theta}/r$ be the two leading asymptotic components. Define their nonnegative directional flux magnitudes by

$$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}:=\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi_{\mathrm{in}};g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2},\qquad \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}:=-\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi_{\mathrm{ref}};g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2}.$$

Then

$$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}=2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2,\qquad \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}=2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2|R|^2,\qquad \frac{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}}=|R|^2.$$

This is a conditional tensor calculation for the specified mode asymptotics; it asserts neither that such a mode exists nor that its flux has been observed.

derivations.claim:
By [F2] and $\Phi_H=Q/r_+$ from [F1],
$$|R|^2=1-\frac{\omega-e\Phi_H}{\omega}|T|^2=1+\frac{e\Phi_H-\omega}{\omega}|T|^2.$$
The band condition in [A2] makes both $(e\Phi_H-\omega)/\omega$ and $|T|^2$ strictly positive, so $|R|^2>1$.

By [F3], $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}/\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}=|R|^2>1$ and $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}>0$. Multiplying by the positive incident flux gives $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}>\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}$. This is a deduction in the stated fixed-background model.

boundaries.reason: The conclusion is conditional on a given admitted mode and nonzero transmission.

Statement assumes omega>0, incident amplitude nonzero and transmission T nonzero; its RN exterior has positive r_+. Proof 1.1 divides only by omega, and proof 2.1 uses P_in=2 omega^2 |A_in|^2>0. The zero-frequency or zero-incident limits are not asserted.

Proof 1.1 divides only by omega, and proof 2.1 uses P_in=2 omega^2 |A_in|^2>0. The zero-frequency or zero-incident limits are not asserted. The flagged surface expression does not introduce the excluded empty or zero case; this is an item-specific source-use review, not an independent proof acceptance.

boundaries.evidence: At threshold $omega=ePhi_H>0$, the Wronskian identity in [F2] gives $|R|^2=1$; the Statement excludes this endpoint.
When transmission is zero, [F2] gives unit reflection; the Statement requires nonzero transmission for a strict conclusion.
Step 1.1 uses the strict inequalities $0<omega<ePhi_H$; the lower endpoint is excluded and the threshold case has ratio one by [F2].
The Statement supplies an admitted mode conditionally; step 1.1 makes no choice and no existence claim is made.

No converse from amplification to frequency-band membership is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the fixed subextremal electric Reissner–Nordström exterior, gauge, charged derivative, real normalized spherical harmonic $Y$, and mode conventions of [[def-emg-fx-charged-radial-scattering]]. Let $\psi=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y(\Omega)u(r_*)/r$ be any admitted real-frequency scattering mode with $\omega>0$ and $A_{\mathrm{in}}\ne0$, and let $R$ be its reflection coefficient. Form $\mathsf T_{ab}[\psi;g,A,e]$ by the gauge-covariant scalar stress-tensor definition. With $\xi=\partial_t$, define the outward radial flux through the sphere of radius $r$ by

$$\mathcal P(r):=-\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi;g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2}.$$

Let $\psi_{\mathrm{in}}:=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}Y e^{-i\Theta}/r$ and $\psi_{\mathrm{ref}}:=A_{\mathrm{in}}e^{-i\omega t}YRe^{i\Theta}/r$ be the two leading asymptotic components. Define their nonnegative directional flux magnitudes by

$$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}:=\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi_{\mathrm{in}};g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2},\qquad \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}:=-\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2\mathsf T^r{}_t[\psi_{\mathrm{ref}};g,A,e]\,d\omega_{S^2}.$$

Then

$$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}=2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2,\qquad \mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}=2\omega^2|A_{\mathrm{in}}|^2|R|^2,\qquad \frac{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{in}}}=|R|^2.$$

This is a conditional tensor calculation for the specified mode asymptotics; it asserts neither that such a mode exists nor that its flux has been observed.

citations.quote:
On an open region of the oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian spacetime and length-coordinate SI conventions of [[def-emg-matter-observables]], adopt a prescribed-background Maxwell model. The metric $g$ is fixed input. Choose a real $C^2$ electromagnetic two-form $F$ and either adopt the source-free equations $dF=0$ and $d(\star_gF)=0$, or supply a $C^1$ current $j$ and adopt $dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$, with the exact signs and units of that definition. The source current is prescribed independently of the probe; this postulate does not impose an Einstein equation, matter evolution equation, or field equation for the sources on the unchanged metric.

For a massive charged probe, use the adopted local action and finite-curve conditions of [[post-rpm-external-charge-action]]: $m>0$ and $q$ are constant, the path is a $C^2$ future-directed timelike segment parameterized by proper time, and its endpoints are fixed in variations supported in a local potential domain $V$ with a supplied $C^2$ one-form $A$ satisfying $dA=F$. The potential and metric are external data independent of the path. Under the exact hypotheses of [[pthm-rpm-external-charge-action-equivalence]], action stationarity is equivalent to $m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U)$; that theorem's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption is inherited only when this equivalent force-law formulation is used. No global potential or trajectory is included.

The probe's own singular field and self-gravity are excluded. No radiation reaction, variable mass or charge, finite-body model, or backreaction estimate is adopted. In particular, calling $g$ or $F$ a test background records this model's omission of their response; it does not claim that the unchanged pair solves the coupled Einstein–Maxwell equations or is close to a coupled solution.

When geometric optics is invoked, it is restricted to the exact $C^4$ real phase, $C^3$ complex amplitudes, four pointwise ansatz constraints, and fixed compact-chart coefficient bounds of [[lem-emg-controlled-maxwell-wkb]]. That result supplies finite residual and leading-field estimates, local null rays, and a polarization quotient; it supplies no convergent series, global transport through caustics, exact-solution error estimate, or backreaction theorem.

This is a separately adopted physical model with no empirical premise. The Maxwell and probe assumptions are not deductions from one another, from mathematical axioms, or from source authority.

Let $U$ be a smooth Lorentzian four-dimensional chart domain with metric $g$ as in [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], and let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be constant. Write $\Omega^k(U)$ for the smooth real $k$-forms on $U$. Here $d:\Omega^k(U)\to\Omega^{k+1}(U)$, $0\le k\le3$, is the exterior derivative with coordinate formula $(d\beta)_{a_0\ldots a_k}=(k+1)\partial_{[a_0}\beta_{a_1\ldots a_k]}$, and $\star_g:\Omega^2(U)\to\Omega^2(U)$ is the Lorentzian Hodge map characterized by $\alpha\wedge\star_g\beta=\frac12\alpha_{ab}\beta^{ab}\,\operatorname{vol}_g$ for $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega^2(U)$, as in [[lem-emg-lorentz-hodge-calculus]]. Both operators are real-linear. Suppose $G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=0$. Let $F_1\in\Omega^2(U)$ satisfy $dF_1=0$ and $d(\star_gF_1)=0$. For any real dimensionless $\varepsilon$, put $F_\varepsilon:=\varepsilon F_1$ and define

$$T^{(1)}_{ab}:=\mu_0^{-1}\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F_1),\qquad \mathscr R_{ab}(g,F;\Lambda):=G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}-\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F),$$

using $\kappa,\mu_0,\mathcal Q$ of [[def-emg-geometric-scaling]] and [[thm-emg-field-normalization-equivalence]]. Then $F_\varepsilon$ remains an exact source-free Maxwell field on the fixed metric and

$$\mathscr R_{ab}(g,F_\varepsilon;\Lambda)=-\kappa\varepsilon^2T^{(1)}_{ab}.$$

For a smooth covariant two-tensor $S$ and compact $K\subset U$, define the chart component norm of its restriction by $\|S\|_{K}:=\max_{0\le a,b\le3}\sup_{p\in K}|S_{ab}(p)|$ when $K\ne\varnothing$. In this estimate and its applications, use $\sup_{p\in\varnothing}f(p):=0$ for nonnegative component functions $f$; equivalently, the empty restriction has $\|S\|_{\varnothing}:=0$. It is finite for smooth $S$ and satisfies

$$\|\mathscr R(g,F_\varepsilon;\Lambda)\|_K=\kappa\varepsilon^2\|T^{(1)}\|_K.$$

If $\varepsilon\ne0$ and $T^{(1)}$ is not identically zero on $K$, the fixed pair $(g,F_\varepsilon)$ is not an exact coupled Einstein–Maxwell solution on $K$. This is a residual estimate only; it gives no nearby metric, solution-distance bound, point-source solution or backreaction limit.

Use the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and arbitrary smooth real two-form $F$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. In a chart using the coordinate convention $x^0=ct$ with all four coordinates assigned metres, assign the SI component unit tesla to $F_{ab}$; the two-form $F=\frac12F_{ab}\,dx^a\wedge dx^b$ then has unit weber.

For this conversion dictionary, take $c>0$, $G>0$, and $\mu_0>0$ as numerical input parameters, with SI dimensions

$$[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad [G]=\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},\qquad [\mu_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m\,C^{-2}}.$$

Define the derived parameters

$$\varepsilon_0:=\frac{1}{\mu_0c^2},\qquad \kappa:=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},\qquad \alpha:=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\mu_0}},\qquad \mathcal F:=\alpha F.$$

Thus $\varepsilon_0$ has unit $\mathrm{C^2\,s^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $\kappa$ has unit $\mathrm{m\,J^{-1}}$, $\alpha$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,s\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$, and the components $\mathcal F_{ab}$ have unit $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. In modern SI, $c$ is fixed exactly by the definition of the metre; $\mu_0$ is not fixed exactly and its numerical value is determined experimentally. Here the equations use only the positive symbolic parameters above, not a selected numerical value.

For a physical mass $M_{\!p}>0$ in kilograms, signed charge $Q_e$ in coulombs, and angular momentum $J_{\mathrm{ang}}$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$, define the geometric length parameters

$$m_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{GM_{\!p}}{c^2},\qquad q_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\sqrt{\frac{G}{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4}}\,Q_e,\qquad a_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{J_{\mathrm{ang}}}{M_{\!p}c}.$$

For a supplied magnetic-flux parameter $\Phi_B$ in webers, also define $p_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\alpha\Phi_B/(4\pi)$ in metres. This is only a conversion of an already specified flux value; it asserts neither a global potential nor a magnetic source. The inverse parameter maps are $M_{\!p}=c^2m_{\mathrm{geo}}/G$, $Q_e=\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4/G}\,q_{\mathrm{geo}}$, $J_{\mathrm{ang}}=M_{\!p}c\,a_{\mathrm{geo}}$, and $\Phi_B=4\pi p_{\mathrm{geo}}/\alpha$.

The mass, charge, angular momentum and flux are inputs to this dictionary; their primitive or derived status in any physical model is framework-specific. No field equation, Maxwell postulate, matter law, or empirical value is part of this definition.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$, $F$, $\kappa$, $\mu_0$, $\alpha$ and $\mathcal F=\alpha F$ be as in [[def-emg-geometric-scaling]], with curvature tensors defined by [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a constant. Define the quadratic tensor

$$\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F):=F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd},$$

where indices are raised with $g^{-1}$. Then the following equations for the same metric and two-form are equivalent:

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F),$$

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g)-\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F).$$

These are algebraic equivalences between tensor equations. No Maxwell equation, matter model, limiting procedure or physical solution is assumed.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The hypotheses in [A3] and [A5] put the fixed pair in the scope of [F1]. Because $K_\tau=[0,\tau]\times K_0$ and there are finitely many components, the max-component norm on $K_\tau$ equals $\sup_{0\le t\le\tau}\|\mathscr R_\varepsilon(t)\|_{K_0}$. By [F1], this is $\kappa\varepsilon^2\|T^{(1)}\|_{K_\tau}=C\varepsilon^2$, with $C\ge0$ by [F2] and nonnegativity of the norm. The adopted model in [A1] leaves the metric and Maxwell field prescribed, while the vacuum and source-free conditions required by [F1] are stated separately in [A3]. [F3] and [F4] identify the same tensor and curvature normalizations. The only inherited choice convention is [A2]; this step uses the exact proposition as stated and introduces no stronger choice assumption.

For each $t\in[0,\tau]$, apply [A4] and then step 1.1:
$$\|z_\varepsilon(t)-\widetilde z_\varepsilon(t)\|_{\mathcal X}\le K(\tau)\int_0^t\|\mathscr R_\varepsilon(s)\|_{K_0}\,ds\le K(\tau)\int_0^t C\varepsilon^2\,ds=K(\tau)Ct\varepsilon^2\le K(\tau)C\tau\varepsilon^2.$$
Taking the supremum over the interval proves the stated bound. If $\varepsilon=0$ or $C=0$, the same inequality gives zero error under the assumed stability bound; no claim about the existence of that bound is made.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, metric signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and arbitrary smooth real two-form $F$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. In a chart using the coordinate convention $x^0=ct$ with all four coordinates assigned metres, assign the SI component unit tesla to $F_{ab}$; the two-form $F=\frac12F_{ab}\,dx^a\wedge dx^b$ then has unit weber.

For this conversion dictionary, take $c>0$, $G>0$, and $\mu_0>0$ as numerical input parameters, with SI dimensions

$$[c]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad [G]=\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}},\qquad [\mu_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m\,C^{-2}}.$$

Define the derived parameters

$$\varepsilon_0:=\frac{1}{\mu_0c^2},\qquad \kappa:=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4},\qquad \alpha:=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa}{2\mu_0}},\qquad \mathcal F:=\alpha F.$$

Thus $\varepsilon_0$ has unit $\mathrm{C^2\,s^2\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$, $\kappa$ has unit $\mathrm{m\,J^{-1}}$, $\alpha$ has unit $\mathrm{C\,s\,kg^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$, and the components $\mathcal F_{ab}$ have unit $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. In modern SI, $c$ is fixed exactly by the definition of the metre; $\mu_0$ is not fixed exactly and its numerical value is determined experimentally. Here the equations use only the positive symbolic parameters above, not a selected numerical value.

For a physical mass $M_{\!p}>0$ in kilograms, signed charge $Q_e$ in coulombs, and angular momentum $J_{\mathrm{ang}}$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$, define the geometric length parameters

$$m_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{GM_{\!p}}{c^2},\qquad q_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\sqrt{\frac{G}{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4}}\,Q_e,\qquad a_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\frac{J_{\mathrm{ang}}}{M_{\!p}c}.$$

For a supplied magnetic-flux parameter $\Phi_B$ in webers, also define $p_{\mathrm{geo}}:=\alpha\Phi_B/(4\pi)$ in metres. This is only a conversion of an already specified flux value; it asserts neither a global potential nor a magnetic source. The inverse parameter maps are $M_{\!p}=c^2m_{\mathrm{geo}}/G$, $Q_e=\sqrt{4\pi\varepsilon_0c^4/G}\,q_{\mathrm{geo}}$, $J_{\mathrm{ang}}=M_{\!p}c\,a_{\mathrm{geo}}$, and $\Phi_B=4\pi p_{\mathrm{geo}}/\alpha$.

The mass, charge, angular momentum and flux are inputs to this dictionary; their primitive or derived status in any physical model is framework-specific. No field equation, Maxwell postulate, matter law, or empirical value is part of this definition.

Let $(M,g,N,o)$, $F$, $\kappa$, $\mu_0$, $\alpha$ and $\mathcal F=\alpha F$ be as in [[def-emg-geometric-scaling]], with curvature tensors defined by [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]. Let $\Lambda\in\mathbb R$ be a constant. Define the quadratic tensor

$$\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F):=F_{ac}F_b{}^c-\frac14g_{ab}F_{cd}F^{cd},$$

where indices are raised with $g^{-1}$. Then the following equations for the same metric and two-form are equivalent:

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=\frac{\kappa}{\mu_0}\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,F),$$

$$G_{ab}(g)+\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F),$$

$$\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}(g)-\Lambda g_{ab}=2\mathcal Q_{ab}(g,\mathcal F).$$

These are algebraic equivalences between tensor equations. No Maxwell equation, matter model, limiting procedure or physical solution is assumed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
