Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M>0$, $0<|a|<M$, and use the length
coordinates of the subextremal Kerr datum. Use the smooth ingoing extension
with its proved compatible time orientation
$\overline N=\partial_v-(2Mr/\Sigma)\partial_r$ from
[[prop-gr-fx-kerr-horizon-generator]]. Set
$H^+:=\{r=r_+\}$ and let $P\subset H^+$ be a smooth open patch in the
hypersurface topology. Let $T$ and $\Phi$ be the stationary and axial Killing
fields restricted to $P$, and let
$\chi:=T+\Omega_H\Phi$ with
$\Omega_H:=a/(r_+^2+a^2)$ be the future null generator there; the supplier
proves $g(\chi,\overline N)=-1$ on $H^+$. A smooth
complex scalar $u\in C^\infty(P,\mathbb C)$ is an $(\omega,m)$ **horizon
mode** when $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $m\in\mathbb Z$, and

$$Tu=-i\omega u,\qquad \Phi u=im u.$$

Its **shifted horizon frequency** is
$\widetilde\omega:=\omega-m\Omega_H$. By linearity of $\chi$, every such
mode satisfies $\chi u=-i\widetilde\omega u$. The parameter $\omega$ has
units reciprocal to the Kerr time coordinate, $m$ is dimensionless, and
$\Omega_H$ has the same units as $\omega$. This is a local definition of
mode data only; it does not assert that a nonzero mode extends to a global
solution of the wave equation.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth
tangent-bundle conventions. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with metric-selected
connection $\nabla$ and inverse metric $g^{ab}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open,
let $\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ be a real scalar field, and let $X$ be a
smooth vector field on $U$. Define the wave operator
$\Box_g\psi:=g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b\psi$ and the symmetric covariant tensor

$$Q_{ab}[\psi]:=(\nabla_a\psi)(\nabla_b\psi)-\frac12 g_{ab}g^{cd}(\nabla_c\psi)(\nabla_d\psi).$$

Define the multiplier covector by $J^X_a[\psi]:=Q_{ab}[\psi]X^b$. The
associated energy-current vector is $j_X^a[\psi]:=-g^{ab}J^X_b[\psi]$; this
sign convention makes its flux through a future spacelike slice equal to the
density $Q_{ab}n^aX^b$ when $n$ is the future unit normal. The test-wave
equation is $\Box_g\psi=0$ on $U$. These objects are defined on the fixed
background $g$; $Q$ is not automatically an SI matter stress-energy tensor,
is not inserted into an Einstein equation here, and does not evolve $g$.

If $\psi$ is dimensionless and the coordinates have length units, the
components of $Q$ have units of inverse length squared. This dimensional fact
does not identify $Q$ with a physical stress tensor without an independently
specified field normalization and coupling.

Let $T=\partial_t$ be the stationary field and let $\Phi$ be the sphere
rotation field, extended to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm K}$. Both are Killing fields.
In a smooth ingoing extension across $r=r_+$, the hypersurface $H^+=\{r=r_+\}$
is null and its null normal direction is generated by
$\chi=T+\Omega_H\Phi$, where
$\Omega_H=a/(r_+^2+a^2)$. In the ingoing product coordinates $(v,r,p)$, the smooth field
$$\overline N:=\partial_v-\frac{2Mr}{\Sigma}\partial_r$$
is timelike on the extension and selects a time orientation agreeing with the
chosen exterior time orientation. On $H^+$ one has $g(\chi,\overline N)=-1$,
so $\chi$ is its future null generator. On the exterior polar chart, $T$ is spacelike
exactly for

$$r_+<r<r_{\mathrm s}(\theta),\qquad r_{\mathrm s}(\theta):=M+\sqrt{M^2-a^2\cos^2\theta}.$$

At the rotation axis $r_{\mathrm s}=r_+$, so the open ergoregion has zero
radial width there.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$. A smooth curve
$\gamma:I\to M$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, is an
**integral curve** of $X$ if

$$ \gamma'(t)=X_{\gamma(t)} $$

for every $t\in I$.

If $\gamma(0)=p$, then $\gamma$ is an integral curve of $X$ **through** $p$.

For every point $p\in M$ and every smooth vector field $X$ on $M$, there is a
unique maximal integral curve $\gamma_p:I_p\to M$ of $X$ with $\gamma_p(0)=p$.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim:
Since $\chi$ is normal to the null hypersurface $H^+$ and both $T$ and $\Phi$ are tangent to it by [F3], $g(\chi,T)=g(\chi,\Phi)=0$ on $H^+$. Hence the metric-trace term in [F2] vanishes when contracted with $\chi^aT^b$, so
$Q(\chi,T)=(\chi\psi)(T\psi)$.

Fix $p\in P_{\omega,T}$ and put $A:=u(p)$. Along its stationary integral-curve segment, $\frac{d}{d\tau}u(\gamma_p(\tau))=(Tu)(\gamma_p(\tau))=-i\omega u(\gamma_p(\tau))$ by [F4], so $u(\gamma_p(\tau))=Ae^{-i\omega\tau}$. The mode equations [F1] give
$T\psi=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega u)$ and
$\chi\psi=\operatorname{Re}(-i(\omega-m\Omega_H)u)$.

If $A=0$, both differentiated real fields vanish along this orbit and the displayed average identity is $0=0$. Otherwise put $\vartheta=\arg A-\omega\tau$. Then
$T\psi=\omega|A|\sin\vartheta$ and
$\chi\psi=(\omega-m\Omega_H)|A|\sin\vartheta$. Averaging their product over $\tau\in[0,2\pi/\omega]$ uses
$\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi/\omega}\sin^2(\arg A-\omega\tau)\,d\tau=\frac12$, and gives the displayed identity.

If $m\Omega_H>\omega>0$, the coefficient $\omega(\omega-m\Omega_H)/2$ is strictly negative. Since $|u|^2\ge0$, step 3.1 gives a nonpositive averaged density, with equality exactly at $u=0$ and strict negativity exactly at $u\ne0$. A mode that is not identically zero need not be nonvanishing at every point.

On the compact patch $D$, smoothness bounds $|u|^2$ and the induced area density, so both displayed integrals are finite. Integrating step 3.1 gives the formula for $\mathcal F_D$. If $u|_D$ is not identically zero, continuity and density of the interior give an interior point where $|u|^2>0$ and a smaller coordinate disk where $|u|^2\ge b>0$. The positive smooth area density has a positive lower bound $a>0$ on a still smaller closed disk; its positive Euclidean area makes $\int_D|u|^2d\mu_D\ge ab\,\operatorname{area}(\text{disk})>0$. Step 4.1 then makes $\mathcal F_D<0$. To find a patch near a point $p\in P_{\omega,T}$ with $u(p)\ne0$, cover the compact integral-curve segment $\gamma_p([0,2\pi/\omega])$ by finitely many neighborhoods supplied by [F6] and subdivide the parameter interval so each piece lies in one such neighborhood. Composing the corresponding local solution maps gives smooth dependence on initial data through the whole interval. Since $\gamma_p([0,2\pi/\omega])\subset P$ and $P$ is open, shrink the initial neighborhood of $p$ so all these curves remain in $P$; nearby points then also lie in $P_{\omega,T}$. By [F3], $T_pH^+=\chi_p^\perp$ for a nonzero null normal $\chi_p$. Nondegeneracy gives $v$ with $g(\chi_p,v)=-1$; then $k=v+\tfrac12g(v,v)\chi_p$ is null and $g(\chi_p,k)=-1$. The plane spanned by $\chi_p,k$ has one negative and one positive direction, so its orthogonal complement is a positive two-plane in $T_pH^+$. Choose a smooth hypersurface chart whose first two coordinate vectors span that plane at $p$, fix its third coordinate, and shrink a closed coordinate disk about $p$. Positivity persists by continuity of its metric matrix, and the disk can be chosen inside the neighborhood and the nonzero set. No integral over a full noncompact horizon is used.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum with $s>0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$, exterior coordinate $x^0$, and stationary
field $T=\partial_0$. Let $0<\delta<s/2$ and put
$K_\delta:=\{(x^0,r,\omega):|r-3s/2|\leq\delta\}$ for $\omega\in S^2$.
Then $K_\delta$ is contained in $r>s$. On the static slice
$\Sigma_{x^0}:=\{x^0=\text{constant}\}$ the future unit normal is
$n=f^{-1/2}T$. For a smooth real test wave $\psi$ with finite initial
stationary energy, define

$$E_T[\psi](x^0):=\int_{\Sigma_{x^0}}Q_{ab}[\psi]n^aT^b\,d\mu_{\Sigma_{x^0}},\qquad E_{T,\delta}[\psi](x^0):=\int_{\Sigma_{x^0}\cap K_\delta}Q_{ab}[\psi]n^aT^b\,d\mu_{\Sigma_{x^0}}.$$

A **nondegenerate integrated local energy estimate with no trapping loss**
on $K_\delta$ means that there is a finite constant $C$, independent of
$\psi$, such that every smooth solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$ with finite
$E_T[\psi](0)$ satisfies

$$\int_0^\infty E_{T,\delta}[\psi](x^0)\,dx^0\leq C E_T[\psi](0).$$

Here “nondegenerate” means that the estimate integrates the full unweighted
first-derivative density, with no weight vanishing at $r=3s/2$; “no trapping
loss” means that the right side contains only the initial first-derivative
stationary energy, with no additional derivatives or degenerating weights.
This definition asserts no existence or nonexistence of such a constant.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$ and
$f(r)=1-s/r$ ([[def-gr-schwarzschild-exterior-model]]), with
$f'=s/r^2$. Then:

For arbitrary $x^0_0,\varphi_0\in\mathbb R$, put
$\omega_0=(\cos\varphi_0,\sin\varphi_0,0)\in S^2$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$
define the rotation
$$R_\alpha(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(y_1\cos\alpha-y_2\sin\alpha,\ y_1\sin\alpha+y_2\cos\alpha,\ y_3),$$
and the global axial vector field $\Phi(y_1,y_2,y_3):=(-y_2,y_1,0)$ on $S^2$;
it is tangent because $y\cdot\Phi(y)=0$ for $y\in S^2$.
In every spherical-polar chart near the equator, $\Phi=\partial_\varphi$;
longitude expressions below are local chart expressions for the global sphere
curve $R_\alpha\omega_0$.

In this item, a **timelike circular geodesic** means a future timelike
geodesic whose areal radius $r$ is constant on an interval of positive length;
its angular orientation is unrestricted.

**(a) Existence of circular timelike geodesics.** Let $r_0>3s/2$ and choose
$\ell\in\mathbb R$ with

$$\ell^2=\frac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}>0,\qquad e:=\Bigl(f(r_0)\Bigl(c^2+\frac{\ell^2}{r_0^2}\Bigr)\Bigr)^{1/2} =\frac{c(r_0-s)\sqrt 2}{\sqrt{r_0(2r_0-3s)}}>0 .$$

Then the globally defined curve $\gamma:\mathbb R\to M$ is

$$\gamma(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr).$$
In each local polar chart along it, $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and the longitude is
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to a constant multiple of $2\pi$.

It is a future timelike geodesic of the datum, with $g(\gamma',\gamma')=-c^2$
and with the conserved quantities $e=-g(\gamma',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\gamma',\Phi)$ of
[[lem-gr-schwarzschild-timelike-geodesic-reduction]]; it is a **circular
orbit** at radius $r_0$. Its angular velocity in the coordinate $x^0$ is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\Bigl(\frac{s}{2r_0^3}\Bigr)^{1/2},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dt}\Bigr)^2=\frac{G_Nm_*}{r_0^3},$$

$t=x^0/c$.

**(b) The circular-orbit condition is necessary.** Conversely, if
$\gamma:I\to M$ is any future timelike geodesic parametrized by proper time with
$r(\tau)\equiv r_0>s$ constant on an interval of positive length, then
$r_0>\frac{3s}{2}$. If $\gamma$ is equatorial, its conserved angular
momentum additionally satisfies $\ell^2=\dfrac{c^2sr_0^2}{2r_0-3s}$.
Consequently no timelike circular geodesic, in any angular orientation, exists
with $s<r_0\le\frac{3s}{2}$.

**(c) Stability threshold of the radial potential.** For each radius
$r>\frac{3s}{2}$ set $\ell_r^2:=c^2sr^2/(2r-3s)$ and regard $\ell_r$ as a
constant in the function $V_{\ell_r}(x):=\tfrac12 f(x)(c^2+\ell_r^2/x^2)$.
Differentiate with respect to $x$ at fixed $\ell_r$, then evaluate at $x=r$.
The result, evaluated at the circular value $\ell_r$, is

$$V_{\ell_r}''(r)=\frac{c^2s(r-3s)}{r^3(2r-3s)},\qquad r>\frac{3s}{2},$$

so $V_\ell$ has a strict local minimum at the circular-orbit radius exactly
for $r>3s$, a strict local maximum exactly for $\frac{3s}{2}<r<3s$, and
$V_\ell''(3s)=0$; the radius $r=3s$ is the **innermost stable circular orbit
radius** of the restricted model in this potential sense.

**(d) The photon sphere at $r=3s/2$.** Let $\ell\neq0$ and put
$r_0=\frac{3s}{2}$ and $e_0:=\dfrac{\lvert\ell\rvert\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0}=\dfrac{2\lvert\ell\rvert}{3\sqrt3\,s}>0$.
Then the globally defined curve
$$\eta(\tau):=\bigl(x^0_0+\tfrac{e_0}{f(r_0)}\tau,\ r_0,\ R_{\ell\tau/r_0^2}\omega_0\bigr),\qquad \tau\in\mathbb R,$$
whose local polar expressions have $\vartheta=\pi/2$ and longitude
$\varphi_0+\ell\tau/r_0^2$ up to chart shifts, is a future null geodesic (a
**null circular orbit** or **photon sphere**
orbit) with conserved quantities $e_0=-g(\eta',\partial_0)$ and
$\ell=g(\eta',\Phi)$, and its angular velocity is

$$\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}=\frac{\ell f(r_0)}{r_0^2e_0}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\,\frac{\sqrt{f(r_0)}}{r_0},\qquad \Bigl(\frac{d\varphi}{dx^0}\Bigr)^2=\frac{f(r_0)}{r_0^2}=\frac{4}{27s^2}.$$

The **null effective potential** $W^{\mathrm n}_\ell(r):=f(r)\ell^2/r^2$
satisfies $(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)'(3s/2)=0$ and
$(W^{\mathrm n}_\ell)''(3s/2)=-\dfrac{32\ell^2}{81s^4}<0$, so the photon-sphere
radius is a strict local maximum of the null potential.

**(e) Scope.** All statements are exact data of the restricted model: the
orbits are ideal geodesics of the metric on the exterior domain, the
stability claim is the sign of the second derivative of the stated potential,
and no claim is made about nonlinear stability, about orbital decay, about
observations or about the interior region. The case $r_0=s$ is excluded, and
the reduction is stated only where $r>s$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. At a point $p$ of a time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold, let $n$ be a future-directed unit timelike vector, let
$X\in T_pM$ be future causal, and let $\psi$ be a smooth real scalar. Put
$\ell:=\sharp_g(d\psi)$, $a:=d\psi(n)$,
$b:=h_n(\ell)\in n^\perp$, and $|b|^2:=g(b,b)$, where $h_n$ is the spatial
projection relative to $n$. Then

$$Q(n,n)=\frac12\bigl(a^2+|b|^2\bigr),\qquad Q(n,X)\geq0.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Fix the Schwarzschild exterior datum with $s>0$, the stationary field $T=\partial_0$, and $0<\delta<s/2$. Let $K_\delta=\{|r-3s/2|\le\delta\}$ include the whole sphere factor, and use the stationary total and annular energies $E_T$ and $E_{T,\delta}$ defined for the real scalar test tensor. For every $H>0$ and every $0<\epsilon<1$, there is a real $\psi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2)$ solving $\Box_g\psi=0$, with compact smooth Cauchy data at $x^0=0$, such that

$$E_T[\psi](0)=1,\qquad E_{T,\delta}[\psi](x^0)\ge1-\epsilon\quad\text{for every }0\le x^0\le H.$$

The same solution works on the entire prescribed interval. Its stationary energy is finite and equal to one on every static slice. The frequency may depend on $H,\epsilon,s,\delta$; no infinite-time concentration, horizon extension, or concentration in a smaller angular neighborhood is asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

This item assumes the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through
the tangent-bundle structure used by
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (c)
([[def-countable-choice]]); no further choice principle is used.

**(a) Parameters and the Schwarzschild radius.** Let $c>0$ and $G_N>0$ be real
constants and let $m_*>0$ be a real **mass parameter**. Put

$$s:=\frac{2G_Nm_*}{c^2}>0 .$$

The number $s$ is the **Schwarzschild radius** of the datum. Neither $c$,
$G_N$ nor $m_*$ is measured here; the physical reading of $c$ and $G_N$ as the
framework's conversion and Newton constants and of $m_*$ as a mass is fixed by
the physical conventions of the framework, not by this definition.

**(b) The underlying manifold and its product charts.** Let $S^2:=S_2(0,1)=
\{y\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert y\rVert_2=1\}$ be the unit Euclidean sphere with the
subspace topology of [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Specify its
smooth structure as the maximal atlas generated by the following two charts
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). For $\varepsilon\in\{+1,-1\}$ put
$p_\varepsilon=(0,0,\varepsilon)$ and
$U_\varepsilon=S^2\setminus\{p_\varepsilon\}$, and define

$$\sigma_\varepsilon:U_\varepsilon\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad \sigma_\varepsilon(y)=\frac{(y_1,y_2)}{1-\varepsilon y_3}.$$

These open domains cover $S^2$. Each chart is a homeomorphism onto
$\mathbb R^2$, with inverse, for $u=(u_1,u_2)$ and $q=u_1^2+u_2^2$,

$$\sigma_\varepsilon^{-1}(u)=\left(\frac{2u_1}{1+q},\frac{2u_2}{1+q},\varepsilon\frac{q-1}{1+q}\right).$$

The two inverse identities follow by substitution; all displayed denominators
are nonzero on their domains. On the overlap both transition maps are
$u\mapsto u/(u_1^2+u_2^2)$ on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}$, hence smooth.
The subspace is Hausdorff and has a countable basis given by intersections
with Euclidean balls of rational centres and positive rational radii.
Thus these charts specify a smooth two-manifold without boundary. This is
the standard sphere structure used for the round metric below: the inclusion
has the displayed smooth local parametrizations, and their differentials
are injective because composition with $\sigma_\varepsilon$ is the identity.
Let $M$ be the product manifold

$$M:=\mathbb R\times(s,\infty)\times S^2$$

with the product smooth structure
([[prop-products-of-smooth-manifolds-have-a-canonical-product-smooth-structure]]);
it is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Write $x^0:M\to\mathbb R$ and
$r:M\to(s,\infty)$ for the first and second projections and $\iota:M\to S^2$
for the third. A **product chart** of $M$ is a smooth chart on the product
whose angular part is a smooth chart of $S^2$. In a **spherical-polar product
chart**, $0<\vartheta<\pi$ and the components of the round metric
$\gamma_{S^2}$ of [[ex-the-round-metric-on-the-sphere-as-an-induced-metric]]
are $\gamma_{22}=1$, $\gamma_{23}=\gamma_{32}=0$,
$\gamma_{33}=\sin^2\vartheta$. These polar charts omit the two poles; ordinary
smooth sphere charts around the poles complete the product atlas.

**(c) The metric.** Let $f:(s,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ be the smooth function

$$f(r):=1-\frac{s}{r} .$$

Define $g$ globally by the coordinate-free expression

$$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}.$$

In every spherical-polar product chart its component functions are

$$g_{00}:=-f(r),\qquad g_{11}:=\frac{1}{f(r)},\qquad g_{22}:=r^2,\qquad g_{33}:=r^2\sin^2\vartheta,$$

and $g_{ab}:=0$ whenever $a\ne b$, $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, with the index order
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)=(x^0,r,\vartheta,\varphi)$. This is a smooth symmetric
covariant $2$-tensor field on all of $M$
([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]); the component display is local
to spherical-polar charts, and $f>0$ because $r>s$. The pair $(M,g)$ is the **Schwarzschild exterior
metric of mass parameter $m_*$**; the datum of this definition is the
quadruple $(c,G_N,m_*,g)$. With these parameters fixed, write $(M,g,N)$
for its associated geometric datum, with $N$ as in clause (d). The geometric
datum depends on the parameters only through $s$ and does not retain $c$,
$G_N$ and $m_*$ separately. That $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not asserted here; it is proved in the companion metric-properties lemma of this page (its
justification record in the frontmatter), which also records the equivalent
coordinate-free description
$g=-f\,d(x^0)\otimes d(x^0)+f^{-1}\,dr\otimes dr+r^2\,\iota^*\gamma_{S^2}$.

**(d) Time orientation and the Schwarzschild chart.** The field
$N:=\partial_0$ is the smooth product vector field on $M$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); the chart components of $g$
are independent of $x^0$, so $N$ is the restriction of a global vector field,
and $g(N,N)=-f(r)<0$ at every point. The datum carries the time orientation
$N$. Spherical-polar product charts are **Schwarzschild charts** of the datum;
at the poles the same metric is represented in the smooth sphere charts of
the product atlas. We write $t$ for the coordinate $x^0/c$ when the datum is
read in the framework's unit conventions.

**(e) Scope.** The domain of the datum is the exterior region $r>s$; the
definition asserts nothing about $r=s$, about $r\le 0$, about any matter, or
about any equation satisfied by $g$. The horizon $r=s$ is not part of the
datum, and a continuation of the metric to $r=s$ requires the separate constructions recorded on this page, the
regularity lemma for the advanced chart and the Kruskal model-properties
lemma. Whether the datum is a solution of the
framework's field law is proved, not defined, in the Ricci-and-Einstein-tensor lemma of this
page.

Assume the axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth
tangent-bundle conventions. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth
Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with metric-selected
connection $\nabla$ and inverse metric $g^{ab}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open,
let $\psi\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ be a real scalar field, and let $X$ be a
smooth vector field on $U$. Define the wave operator
$\Box_g\psi:=g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b\psi$ and the symmetric covariant tensor

$$Q_{ab}[\psi]:=(\nabla_a\psi)(\nabla_b\psi)-\frac12 g_{ab}g^{cd}(\nabla_c\psi)(\nabla_d\psi).$$

Define the multiplier covector by $J^X_a[\psi]:=Q_{ab}[\psi]X^b$. The
associated energy-current vector is $j_X^a[\psi]:=-g^{ab}J^X_b[\psi]$; this
sign convention makes its flux through a future spacelike slice equal to the
density $Q_{ab}n^aX^b$ when $n$ is the future unit normal. The test-wave
equation is $\Box_g\psi=0$ on $U$. These objects are defined on the fixed
background $g$; $Q$ is not automatically an SI matter stress-energy tensor,
is not inserted into an Einstein equation here, and does not evolve $g$.

If $\psi$ is dimensionless and the coordinates have length units, the
components of $Q$ have units of inverse length squared. This dimensional fact
does not identify $Q$ with a physical stress tensor without an independently
specified field normalization and coupling.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g,N)$ be the Schwarzschild exterior
datum with $s>0$, $f(r)=1-s/r$, exterior coordinate $x^0$, and stationary
field $T=\partial_0$. Let $0<\delta<s/2$ and put
$K_\delta:=\{(x^0,r,\omega):|r-3s/2|\leq\delta\}$ for $\omega\in S^2$.
Then $K_\delta$ is contained in $r>s$. On the static slice
$\Sigma_{x^0}:=\{x^0=\text{constant}\}$ the future unit normal is
$n=f^{-1/2}T$. For a smooth real test wave $\psi$ with finite initial
stationary energy, define

$$E_T[\psi](x^0):=\int_{\Sigma_{x^0}}Q_{ab}[\psi]n^aT^b\,d\mu_{\Sigma_{x^0}},\qquad E_{T,\delta}[\psi](x^0):=\int_{\Sigma_{x^0}\cap K_\delta}Q_{ab}[\psi]n^aT^b\,d\mu_{\Sigma_{x^0}}.$$

A **nondegenerate integrated local energy estimate with no trapping loss**
on $K_\delta$ means that there is a finite constant $C$, independent of
$\psi$, such that every smooth solution of $\Box_g\psi=0$ with finite
$E_T[\psi](0)$ satisfies

$$\int_0^\infty E_{T,\delta}[\psi](x^0)\,dx^0\leq C E_T[\psi](0).$$

Here “nondegenerate” means that the estimate integrates the full unweighted
first-derivative density, with no weight vanishing at $r=3s/2$; “no trapping
loss” means that the right side contains only the initial first-derivative
stationary energy, with no additional derivatives or degenerating weights.
This definition asserts no existence or nonexistence of such a constant.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

derivations.claim:
Coordinates and angular functions. Put $r_0=3s/2$ and $x=r+s\log(r/s-1)-c$, with $c$ chosen so $x(r_0)=0$. Since $dx/dr=f^{-1}>0$ and the two endpoint limits are $-\infty,+\infty$, this is a smooth global radial coordinate with $r_x=f$. For an integer $l\ge1$ set $Y_l=c_l(\omega_1+i\omega_2)^l$, with the positive constant $c_l$ normalizing $\int_{S^2}|Y_l|^2=1$. This function is smooth at the poles by its polynomial expression. In polar coordinates it is $c_l\sin^l\vartheta\,e^{il\varphi}$; direct differentiation gives $\Delta_{S^2}Y_l=-l(l+1)Y_l$. Integration in $\varphi$ gives $\int Y_l^2=0$. Sphere integration by parts gives $\int|
abla Y_l|^2=l(l+1)$ and $\int
abla Y_l\cdot
abla Y_l=l(l+1)\int Y_l^2=0$. These identities can also be checked directly in the polar coordinates, where $\sin^l\vartheta$ removes the endpoint terms.

Exact scalar reduction. In $(t,x,\omega)$ the metric is $f(-dt^2+dx^2)+r^2\gamma_{S^2}$. Expanding $\Box_g$ in its volume density yields $\Box_g u=f^{-1}(-u_{tt}+r^{-2}\partial_x(r^2u_x))+r^{-2}\Delta_{S^2}u$. Substitution of $u=q(t,x)Y_l(\omega)/r(x)$ therefore gives precisely $q_{tt}-q_{xx}+W_lq=0$, with $W_l=f(l(l+1)/r^2+s/r^3)\ge0$. For each fixed $l$, $W_l$ and every $x$ derivative are bounded on $\mathbb R$: $\partial_x=f\partial_r$, the rational functions extend smoothly to $r=s$, and their derivatives decay at infinity. No uniform-in-$l$ bound is needed for existence.

Positive energy and real fields. For a compactly supported complex $q$ define $e_l[q]=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R}(|q_t|^2+|q_x|^2+W_l|q|^2)\,dx$. Use the sum of the real and imaginary scalar energies for a complex field. From [F2]--[F3], its energy density in $x,\omega$ is $\tfrac12(r^2|u_t|^2+r^2|u_x|^2+f|\nabla_{S^2}u|^2)$. For $qY_l/r$, integration over $S^2$ gives $\tfrac12(|q_t|^2+|q_x-bq|^2+fl(l+1)|q|^2/r^2)$, $b=f/r$. The identity $b'+b^2=fs/r^3$ and integration of $-b\partial_x|q|^2$, with zero endpoint terms, prove that its total energy equals $e_l[q]$. The zero bilinear angular integrals in step 1.1 give exactly $E_T[\operatorname{Re}(qY_l/r)]=e_l[q]/2$. The original local energy density is nonnegative on every radial subset. The factor $1/2$ for real fields also holds before the radial integration by parts, so no false boundary-term identity on a finite annulus is being used.

Global smooth radial Cauchy construction. For arbitrary compact smooth data $p,v$, solve the integral equation $q=q_0+\mathcal Kq$, where $q_0=(p(x+t)+p(x-t))/2+\tfrac12\int_{x-t}^{x+t}v(y)\,dy$ and $\mathcal Kq=-\tfrac12\int_0^t\int_{x-(t-a)}^{x+(t-a)}W_l(y)q(a,y)\,dy\,da$. On a slab of width $d$ its operator norm on bounded continuous functions is at most $\|W_l\|_\infty d^2/2$. Choose this below one. Picard iteration from $q_0$ then has geometrically summable successive sup-norm differences, so converges uniformly to the unique bounded continuous solution. Each iterate vanishes outside the unit-speed cone of the initial compact support. Spatial difference quotients of the integral equation inductively give continuous derivatives of every order: the highest differentiated unknown is acted on by the same $\mathcal K$, while all lower terms involve already known derivatives and bounded derivatives of $W_l$. Uniform convergence of these difference quotients follows from that same geometric estimate; the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies their limits as the derivatives. Differentiating the integral equation in time gives the initial velocity, $q_{tt}=q_{xx}-W_lq$, and all higher time derivatives. Thus the solution is jointly smooth. The fixed slab width depends on $l$ but not on the data size, so restart at successive endpoints and use uniqueness on overlaps to obtain a solution for every real time. Time reversal treats negative times. The iterates and their restarted solutions retain the compact unit-speed support cone. This is an actual Cauchy construction; global hyperbolicity or an unproved scalar-wave existence theorem has not been invoked.

Explicit Gaussian envelope. Let $h=(l+1/2)^{-1}$, $V_0=f/r^2$, $V_1=fs/r^3-V_0/4$. Then $W_l=h^{-2}V_0+V_1$. At $x=0$ direct differentiation gives $V_0(0)=\Omega^2$, $V_0'(0)=0$, $V_0''(0)/2=-\Omega^4$, where $\Omega=2/(3\sqrt3s)>0$. Indeed $\partial_rV_0=(-2r+3s)/r^4$, and $\partial_r^2V_0(r_0)=-3s/r_0^5$, with $\partial_x=f\partial_r$. Put $z(t)=\cosh(\Omega t)+i\sinh(\Omega t)$, $b(t)=\Omega^2(\cosh(\Omega t)-i\sinh(\Omega t))/z(t)$, and $a(t,y)=z(t)^{-1/2}e^{-b(t)y^2/2}$, using the smooth square-root branch equal to one initially. Since $\operatorname{Re}z>0$, it never vanishes. Calculation gives $\operatorname{Re}b=\Omega^2/|z|^2>0$, $b'=-i(b^2+\Omega^4)/\Omega$, and $(z^{-1/2})'/z^{-1/2}=-ib/(2\Omega)$. Therefore $2i\Omega a_t=-a_{yy}-\Omega^4y^2a$. On every fixed $|t|\le H$, all derivatives of $a$ are polynomials in $y$ with bounded coefficients times a Gaussian having $\operatorname{Re}b\ge c_H>0$; all required weighted $L^2$ norms are bounded uniformly there.

Frequency-independent energy stability. The same integral construction with an added d'Alembert forcing term treats smooth forcing on finite slabs. For a smooth spatially compact solution of $q_{tt}-q_{xx}+W_lq=F$, direct differentiation and integration by parts give $e_l'[q]=\operatorname{Re}\int F\overline{q_t}\,dx$. For nonzero $A=\|F\|_2$ and $B=\|q_t\|_2$, integration of $(|F|/A-|q_t|/B)^2\ge0$ gives $\int|Fq_t|\le AB$; zero-norm cases give the same inequality immediately. Since $W_l\ge0$, this bounds the energy derivative in absolute value by $\sqrt{2e_l[q]}\,\|F\|_2$. Apply this first to $\sqrt{e_l+\eta}$, integrate and let $\eta\downarrow0$ to obtain $\sqrt{e_l[q](t)}\le\sqrt{e_l[q](0)}+2^{-1/2}\int_0^t\|F(a)\|_2\,da$. In particular the energy of a homogeneous wave from step 3.2 is conserved. Compact support on every finite slab justifies all integrations, even though the full spatial line is noncompact.

Compact approximation and residual. Choose a real $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ from [F4], equal to one near $0$ and supported inside $\{|r(x)-r_0|<\delta\}$. Set $Q_h=h^{3/4}e^{-i\Omega t/h}\chi(x)a(t,x/\sqrt h)$. Its support and the support of each derivative lie in the exact annulus. In $R_h=(\partial_t^2-\partial_x^2+W_l)Q_h$, the $h^{-2}$ term cancels by $V_0(0)=\Omega^2$ and the $h^{-1}$ term cancels by the envelope equation in step 3.3. The remaining terms away from cutoff derivatives are $h^{3/4}e^{-i\Omega t/h}\chi$ times $a_{tt}+V_1a+h^{-2}(V_0(x)-\Omega^2+\Omega^4x^2)a$. Taylor's theorem on the fixed compact support bounds the last parenthesis by $C|x|^3$. With $dx=\sqrt h\,dy$, the amplitude prefactor changes an envelope $L^2$ norm by $h$. Thus the first two terms are $O_H(h)$ in $L^2_x$ and the cubic term is bounded by $Ch\,h^{-2}h^{3/2}\||y|^3a\|_2=O_H(\sqrt h)$. Cutoff commutators are $-2\chi'\partial_x$ of the uncut amplitude and $-\chi''$ times that amplitude. Their supports have $|x|\ge d_0>0$; Gaussian decay there makes their norms $O_{H,N}(h^N)$ for every $N$, despite any fixed derivative powers of $h^{-1}$. Consequently $\sup_{0\le t\le H}\|R_h(t)\|_2\le C_H\sqrt h$.

Positive normalization. At $t=0$, the substitution $x=\sqrt h\,y$ and Gaussian tail bounds show $e_l[Q_h](0)\to C_0=\Omega^2\int|a(0,y)|^2\,dy=\Omega\sqrt\pi>0$. More explicitly, the time derivative's leading term $-i\Omega Q_h/h$ contributes $\Omega^2\int|a_0|^2$ to the unhalved energy integral; $h^{-2}V_0|Q_h|^2$ contributes the same limit. Their cross/time-envelope terms are $O(h)$, the radial derivative energy is $O(h)$, and the $V_1$ term is $O(h^2)$. The factor $1/2$ in $e_l$ therefore gives $C_0+O(h)$. In particular this energy has a positive lower bound for sufficiently large integers $l$.

Exact correction. Use step 3.2 to solve the homogeneous radial equation with exactly the smooth compact initial data $Q_h(0),\partial_tQ_h(0)$, obtaining $q_h$ on all real times. Then $w_h=q_h-Q_h$ has zero initial data and forcing $-R_h$. Steps 4.1 and 4.2 give $\sup_{0\le t\le H}e_l[w_h](t)\le(H^2/2)\sup\|R_h(t)\|_2^2\le C_Hh$. Its compact support on finite slabs follows from the support of $q_h$ and $Q_h$. Define $U_h=\operatorname{Re}(q_hY_l/r)$. By steps 1.1--2.1 it is a real globally smooth exact scalar wave, including at the sphere poles, with compact smooth initial data. Its conserved stationary energy is exactly $e_l[Q_h](0)/2$ by steps 3.1 and 4.1.

Concentration on every required slice. Normalize $\psi_h=U_h/\sqrt{e_l[Q_h](0)/2}$; its stationary energy is exactly one on every slice. Outside $K_\delta$, the approximate field $\operatorname{Re}(Q_hY_l/r)$ and all its derivatives vanish. There the exact field equals the correction $\operatorname{Re}(w_hY_l/r)$. The original positive density of step 3.1 and the global energy identity consequently give $E_{T,\mathrm{outside}\ K_\delta}[\psi_h](t)\le e_l[w_h](t)/e_l[Q_h](0)\le C'_Hh$. The boundary spheres have measure zero, so total energy one implies $E_{T,\delta}[\psi_h](t)\ge1-C'_Hh$ simultaneously for all $t\in[0,H]$. Choose one sufficiently large integer $l$ with $C'_H/(l+1/2)<\epsilon$. This proves the exact quantifiers and real-field assertion. The construction uses the full specified radial annulus and makes no assertion about a smaller angular neighborhood or a frequency uniform in $H$.

boundaries.reason: The exterior and each specified annulus are nonempty because s>0 and delta>0; no empty-domain theorem is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes epsilon>0; step 5.1 proves a strictly positive initial energy limit before division, so zero initial data are never normalized.
Step 6.1 normalizes the real wave to total stationary energy exactly one; the factor one-half from taking a real field was computed in step 3.1.

Let $c>0$ be a fixed conversion constant in metres per second. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of physical time in seconds, and let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ have dimensionless angular coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its quotient charts are local lifts to $\mathbb R^3$; chart changes are translations by elements of $(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Give $M=I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the product smooth structure, so $M$ is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Here a **$C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum** means a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ with $C^2$ components in smooth charts, whose value at each point has inertia $(3,1,0)$, together with a smooth vector field $N$ satisfying $g(N,N)<0$ everywhere. This is the explicit $C^2$ variant of the pointwise signature and time-orientation conditions in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; that supplier's metric regularity itself is smooth. Choose positive $C^2$ functions $a_i:I\to(0,\infty)$, $i=1,2,3$, with values in metres, and set

$$g=-c^2\,dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3a_i(t)^2\,(dx^i)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_t.$$

In every lifted product chart, $g$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-c^2,a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)$, so it is symmetric, $C^2$, and has inertia $(3,1,0)$; $N$ is smooth and $g(N,N)=-c^2<0$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ is a $C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum in the stated sense. This diagonal, spatially homogeneous metric datum is called a diagonal Bianchi I datum here; homogeneity means its coefficients are independent of the torus coordinates, and no isotropy is required. Define the directional expansion rates, their mean, the spatial volume scale and the squared directional shear by

$$H_i:=\frac{\dot a_i}{a_i},\qquad H:=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3H_i,\qquad V:=a_1a_2a_3,\qquad \sigma^2:=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^3(H_i-H)^2.$$

Here $\dot a_i=d a_i/dt$; $H_i$ and $H$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $V$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3$, and $\sigma^2$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The symbol $\sigma^2$ denotes a nonnegative scalar defined by this formula, not a tensor norm on a spacetime frame. This is a geometric ansatz and makes no field-equation or observational claim. The product and quotient constructions carry the inherited axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and use no stronger choice principle.

For comparison with smooth Lorentzian geometry, use the curvature convention $R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z$ and the component order $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=R^a{}_{bcd}\partial_a$. The local connection and Ricci components for this $C^2$ metric are defined separately.

Let $c>0$ be a fixed conversion constant in metres per second. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of physical time in seconds, and let $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ have dimensionless angular coordinates $x^1,x^2,x^3$. Its quotient charts are local lifts to $\mathbb R^3$; chart changes are translations by elements of $(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Give $M=I\times\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ the product smooth structure, so $M$ is a smooth four-manifold without boundary. Here a **$C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum** means a symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field $g$ with $C^2$ components in smooth charts, whose value at each point has inertia $(3,1,0)$, together with a smooth vector field $N$ satisfying $g(N,N)<0$ everywhere. This is the explicit $C^2$ variant of the pointwise signature and time-orientation conditions in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; that supplier's metric regularity itself is smooth. Choose positive $C^2$ functions $a_i:I\to(0,\infty)$, $i=1,2,3$, with values in metres, and set

$$g=-c^2\,dt^2+\sum_{i=1}^3a_i(t)^2\,(dx^i)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_t.$$

In every lifted product chart, $g$ has matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-c^2,a_1^2,a_2^2,a_3^2)$, so it is symmetric, $C^2$, and has inertia $(3,1,0)$; $N$ is smooth and $g(N,N)=-c^2<0$. Thus $(M,g,N)$ is a $C^2$ time-oriented Lorentzian metric datum in the stated sense. This diagonal, spatially homogeneous metric datum is called a diagonal Bianchi I datum here; homogeneity means its coefficients are independent of the torus coordinates, and no isotropy is required. Define the directional expansion rates, their mean, the spatial volume scale and the squared directional shear by

$$H_i:=\frac{\dot a_i}{a_i},\qquad H:=\frac13\sum_{i=1}^3H_i,\qquad V:=a_1a_2a_3,\qquad \sigma^2:=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^3(H_i-H)^2.$$

Here $\dot a_i=d a_i/dt$; $H_i$ and $H$ have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $V$ has units $\mathrm{m}^3$, and $\sigma^2$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$. The symbol $\sigma^2$ denotes a nonnegative scalar defined by this formula, not a tensor norm on a spacetime frame. This is a geometric ansatz and makes no field-equation or observational claim. The product and quotient constructions carry the inherited axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and use no stronger choice principle.

The local connection and Ricci components for this $C^2$ metric are defined separately.

The Ricci components are

Let $a_i(t)=A_i(t/t_0)^{p_i}$ on a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq(0,\infty)$, where $A_i>0$ are lengths in metres, $t_0>0$ is a time in seconds, and $p_i\in\mathbb R$ are dimensionless exponents. These are exact statements about the specified finite-dimensional metrics; no singularity or generic cosmological conclusion follows.

Thus every $\dot H_i+H_i^2$ is zero and every product $H_iH_j$ with $i\ne j$ is zero; [F3] makes every independent Riemann component vanish, hence the full curvature tensor vanishes on $I$. Also $H=1/(3t)$, $V=A_1A_2A_3(t/t_0)$ and $\sigma^2=1/(3t^2)$. Since step 1.1 and [F2] give $\mathcal R=0$ and $G^i{}_i=0$, the equations in [F5] hold with $\Lambda=0$ and $Q_i=0$, yielding $V^2\sigma^2=(A_1A_2A_3)^2/(3t_0^2)$.

On the lifted chart, put $r=ct>0$ and $\eta=\alpha x^1$. Then $(T,X)=(r\cosh\eta,r\sinh\eta)$ satisfies $T>|X|$, and the inverse in its image is $t=\sqrt{T^2-X^2}/c$, $x^1=\operatorname{artanh}(X/T)/\alpha$, $x^2=z_2/A_2$, and $x^3=z_3/A_3$. Thus $\Phi$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathcal D$. The identities $-dT^2+dX^2=-dr^2+r^2d\eta^2=-c^2dt^2+a_1(t)^2(dx^1)^2$ and $(dz_2)^2+(dz_3)^2=a_2^2(dx^2)^2+a_3^2(dx^3)^2$ give $\Phi^*\eta=g$. The local lift does not define a global coordinate transformation of the periodic torus. Since all curvature components already vanish for every $t>0$, the collapse of $a_1$ at the excluded endpoint $t=0$ alone proves no curvature blowup.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix an integer $s\ge5$, a finite number $T>0$, the closed interval $J=[0,T]$, and the flat spatial torus $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Use the spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ and one fixed periodic symmetric-hyperbolic system as defined in [[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]: its state domain $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, its coefficient maps $A^\mu(t,x,z),B(t,x,z)$ are smooth on the stated time, torus and state domain, each $A^\mu$ is symmetric, and $A^0$ is positive definite. The fixed-gauge Einstein state is the finite vector $z=(g_{ab},p_{ab},q_{abi},w)$, where $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$, $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$, and $w$ is the complete matter and auxiliary state of one fixed reduction.

For the SI interpretation, the system's time parameter $t$ is the length coordinate $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ in metres, while $x^i$ are dimensionless angular coordinates on the torus. The metric components then have coordinate-dependent units: $g_{00}$ is dimensionless, $g_{0i}$ has units of metres, and $g_{ij}$ has units of square metres. Accordingly $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]$. The model-specific components of $w$ have the fixed units declared by that reduction. Divide each component by its fixed declared unit scale before forming the Euclidean-valued state and its Sobolev norm; the resulting numerical state is dimensionless. The coefficient and source fields are those of this same fixed normalized reduction. Thus $R_z$ is a bound on that normalized state, and $R_t$ is a separate bound on its derivative with respect to the length coordinate $x^0$ (units $\mathrm m^{-1}$). Neither is a unit-independent physical observable. If physical seconds are used instead, then $\partial_{x^0}=c^{-1}\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$; consequently the term $A^0\partial_{x^0}$ becomes $c^{-1}A^0\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$ unless the entire equation is multiplied by $c$.

A fixed-gauge finite-slab comparison context consists of one such coefficient family on an open time interval containing $J$, one coordinate gauge and reconstruction rule, compact state sets $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, separate finite nonnegative bounds $R_z,R_t$, and constants $0<a\le b<\infty$ such that

$$a|\zeta|^2\le \zeta^{\mathsf T}A^0(t,x,z)\zeta\le b|\zeta|^2$$

for every $t\in J$, $x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $z\in K_2$, and $\zeta\in\mathbb R^m$. The reference state takes values in $K_0$. Compared classical states take values in $K_1$, belong to $L^\infty(J;H^s)\cap C^0(J;H^{s-1})$, have $\partial_tz\in L^\infty(J;H^{s-1})$, and satisfy
$$\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|z(t)\|_{H^s}\le R_z,\qquad \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|\partial_tz(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le R_t.$$
The outer set $K_2$ supplies the positive coefficient margin for local existence restarted from data in compact subsets of $K_1$. Two states use the same chart grid, coefficient maps, gauge source functions, reconstruction rule, and fixed matter branch. Forcing terms, when included in a comparison, are continuous $H^{s-1}$-valued functions of the slab parameter; their size is controlled through the separate stated solution and time-derivative bounds when the comparison estimate is applied.

The Sobolev norms compare coordinate fields in this fixed gauge. They do not identify two arbitrary coordinate representatives by a diffeomorphism. The Einstein interpretation uses the same first-order reduction, full initial constraints, complete matter data, and local restart hypotheses throughout the finite slab.

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

derivations.claim:
The initialization uses a finite formula at each of the $N$ sites. The
outer index takes each of the finitely many values $1$ through $n_{\max}-1$
and has no data-dependent branch, so the procedure makes exactly
$n_{\max}-1$ update passes. Each pass writes the next $N$-tuple, giving the
output levels $u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}}$.

The initialization costs at most $C_0N$ scalar and array operations for a
fixed constant $C_0$. Each update pass costs at most $C_1N$ such operations
for a fixed $C_1$, because every site uses the same fixed stencil. Thus the
total is at most $C_0N+C_1N(n_{\max}-1)\le(C_0+C_1)Nn_{\max}$, proving the
claimed bound.

It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

derivations.claim: The period and zero-set facts in [F3, F5] make $e_\ell$ well-defined on $\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. Put $\theta_\ell=2\pi\ell/N$. Euler's formula and the addition formulas [F3, F4], together with the complex multiplication formulas [F2], give $e_\ell(j+1)=e^{i\theta_\ell}e_\ell(j)$ and $e_\ell(j-1)=e^{-i\theta_\ell}e_\ell(j)$. Therefore $$ (D_he_\ell)(j)=h^{-2}\bigl(e^{i\theta_\ell}-2+e^{-i\theta_\ell}\bigr)e_\ell(j) =-4h^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)e_\ell(j), $$ where the last equality uses [F3, F4]. Thus a mode sequence $u^n_j=a_ne_\ell(j)$ obeys $a_{n+1}-2c_\ell a_n+a_{n-1}=0$ for every update step.

For the constant mode, define $\bar u^n=N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u_j^n$. By [F8], a cyclic shift preserves a finite sum, so $\sum_j(D_hu^n)_j=0$. Averaging the update [F1] therefore gives $\bar u^{n+1}=2\bar u^n-\bar u^{n-1}$, and averaging the startup gives $\bar u^1=\bar u^0+k\bar v^0$. Induction yields $\bar u^n=\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$. If $0\le nk\le T$, then [F12, F13] give $|nk\bar v^0|=nk|\bar v^0|\le T|\bar v^0|$, and the real triangle inequality [F15] gives $|\bar u^n|\le|\bar u^0|+T|\bar v^0|$. If $\bar v^0\ne0$, then [F13] gives $|\bar v^0|>0$. Given any $M>0$, [F16] supplies a natural $n\ge1$ with $n>(M+|\bar u^0|)/(k|\bar v^0|)$; this quotient is defined because $k|\bar v^0|>0$. Since $nk\ge0$, [F12, F13] give $|nk\bar v^0|=nk|\bar v^0|$, and [F15] applied to $nk\bar v^0=(\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0)-\bar u^0$ yields $|\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0|\ge nk|\bar v^0|-|\bar u^0|>M$, proving unboundedness.

The derivative identities in [F3] give $\sin'=\cos$ and $\cos'=-\sin$ everywhere, so both functions are continuous and differentiable on the closed subintervals used here. By [F18], $\cos'<0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$; applying [F17] to cosine on any $[a,b]\subseteq[0,\pi/2]$ with $a<b$ shows $\cos b<\cos a$. For $0<x<\pi/2$, apply [F17] to sine on $[0,x]$ and $[x,\pi/2]$. Since [F3, F9] give $\sin0=0$ and $\sin(\pi/2)=1$, there are $c_1\in(0,x)$ and $c_2\in(x,\pi/2)$ with $\sin x/x=\cos c_1$ and $(1-\sin x)/(\pi/2-x)=\cos c_2$. The just-proved decrease gives $\sin x/x\ge(1-\sin x)/(\pi/2-x)$. Multiplying by the positive denominators and rearranging gives $\sin x\ge2x/\pi$. This also holds at $x=0,\pi/2$ by their stated values. For $1\le\ell<N$, let $m=\min\{\ell,N-\ell\}$, so $1\le m\le N/2$. Parity and the $\pi$ shift in [F4, F9] give $\sin(\pi\ell/N)=\sin(\pi m/N)>0$. Applying the chord bound at $x=\pi m/N$ gives $|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|\ge2m/N$. Consequently, since $h=2\pi/N$, one has $\omega_\ell=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|\ge2m/\pi\ge2/\pi$, uniformly in $N$. Taking successive minima over the finite list still gives an attained positive minimum on each grid. This proof is a frequency bound only and does not bound the initial-data-dependent coefficients of the two-root representation uniformly over arbitrary unscaled pairs.

Suppose $N$ is even and $\lambda=1$. Repeated $\pi$-shift use of [F9] gives $\sin(\pi j)=0$ and $\cos(\pi j)=(-1)^j$ for every grid index $0\le j<N$; Euler's formula [F3] identifies the Fourier character $e_{N/2}(j)$ with the alternating array $(-1)^j$. Its periodic neighbors are equal to its negative. By [F1], $(D_h((-1)^\cdot))_j=-4h^{-2}(-1)^j$, so the mode recurrence has coefficient $c=1-2\lambda^2=-1$ and characteristic polynomial $(z+1)^2$.

If $\ell\ne0$, [F5] gives $s:=\sin(\pi\ell/N)\ne0$, so $s^2>0$ by [F14]. Also $\cos^2(\pi\ell/N)\ge0$ by [F14] and the zero case, hence [F6] gives $s^2\le1$. As $0<\lambda<1$, it follows that $0<2\lambda^2s^2\le2\lambda^2<2$, so $-1<c_\ell<1$. Then $r_\ell:=\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2}$ exists and is positive by [F7]. Direct substitution shows that $z^2-2c_\ell z+1=0$ has roots $c_\ell\pm ir_\ell$; they are distinct. By [F10], their complex moduli are $\sqrt{c_\ell^2+r_\ell^2}=\sqrt1=1$, where the last equality uses uniqueness of the nonnegative square root [F7].

Since the roots are distinct, for any initial pair $a_0,a_1$ there are unique complex constants $A,B$ with $a_0=A+B$ and $a_1=Az_{\ell,+}+Bz_{\ell,-}$. The sequence $Az_{\ell,+}^n+Bz_{\ell,-}^n$ obeys the recurrence in step 1.1 and has that initial pair; induction on $n$ therefore identifies it with $a_n$. By multiplicativity in [F11], induction gives $|z_{\ell,\pm}^n|=|z_{\ell,\pm}|^n=1$. The complex triangle inequality and multiplicativity in [F11] then give $|Az_{\ell,+}^n+Bz_{\ell,-}^n|\le|A||z_{\ell,+}^n|+|B||z_{\ell,-}^n|=|A|+|B|$ for all $n$, so the mode is bounded on every finite slab.

Write $u_j^n=a_n(-1)^j$ and put $q_n:=(-1)^na_n$. The repeated-root recurrence from step 1.4 gives $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}=0$, so its first differences are constant and $q_n=a_0+n(-a_1-a_0)$. The startup in [F1] with $u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$ and $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ gives $a_1=-a_0+k\beta_0$, hence $a_n=(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0)$. For $\beta_0\ne0$ its magnitude grows linearly in $n$; for $\beta_0=0$ it is bounded.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, and suppose $f$ has derivatives through order $n+1$ on the closed interval between $a$ and $x$, with the usual endpoint continuity. If $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ throughout that interval, then
$$|R_{n,a}f(x)|\le \frac{M}{\iota((n+1)!)}|x-a|^{n+1}.$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

derivations.claim:
The set $[0,2\pi]\times[t_n-k,t_n+k]$ is a nonempty closed box in
$\mathbb R^2$: $k>0$ and the time interval lies in $I$. Thus [F4] makes it
compact. The function $(x,t)\mapsto u_{xxxx}(x,t)$ is continuous there because
$u\in C^6$; [F5] bounds it, so $M_n<\infty$ as claimed.

Apply [F2] to the spatial function $x\mapsto u(x,t_n)$ at $x_j$ with
increments $h$ and $-h$. Adding the two degree-three Taylor polynomials and
subtracting twice their common center value cancels their odd terms and leaves $h^2u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)$. By [F2], each remainder has absolute value at
most $M_nh^4/4!$; by [F7], the sum of the two remainders has absolute value
at most $2M_nh^4/4!$. After division by $h^2$,
$$
\left|\frac{U_{j+1}^n-2U_j^n+U_{j-1}^n}{h^2}-u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)\right| \le\frac{h^2}{12}M_n.
$$
Periodicity of $u$ and its derivatives extends the bound defining $M_n$ from
$[0,2\pi]$ to all real spatial coordinates, including a wrapped neighbor.

Apply the same estimate to $t\mapsto u(x_j,t)$ with increments $k$ and
$-k$. By [F3] and $u_{tt}=u_{xx}$, the fourth time derivative equals
$u_{tttt}=u_{xxxx}$, whose absolute value is bounded by $M_n$ on this time
window and all $x$. Thus
$$
\left|\frac{U_j^{n+1}-2U_j^n+U_j^{n-1}}{k^2}-u_{tt}(x_j,t_n)\right| \le\frac{k^2}{12}M_n.
$$

Subtract the two estimates of steps 1.2 and 1.3, use
$u_{tt}(x_j,t_n)=u_{xx}(x_j,t_n)$, and apply the real triangle inequality
[F7] to their error terms. The result is
$|\tau_j^n|\le(k^2+h^2)M_n/12$, as claimed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix an integer $s\ge5$, a finite number $T>0$, the closed interval $J=[0,T]$, and the flat spatial torus $\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$. Use the spaces $H^s(\mathbb T^3_{2\pi};\mathbb R^m)$ and one fixed periodic symmetric-hyperbolic system as defined in [[def-gr-periodic-symmetric-hyperbolic-system]]: its state domain $O\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, its coefficient maps $A^\mu(t,x,z),B(t,x,z)$ are smooth on the stated time, torus and state domain, each $A^\mu$ is symmetric, and $A^0$ is positive definite. The fixed-gauge Einstein state is the finite vector $z=(g_{ab},p_{ab},q_{abi},w)$, where $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$, $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$, and $w$ is the complete matter and auxiliary state of one fixed reduction.

For the SI interpretation, the system's time parameter $t$ is the length coordinate $x^0=ct_{\rm phys}$ in metres, while $x^i$ are dimensionless angular coordinates on the torus. The metric components then have coordinate-dependent units: $g_{00}$ is dimensionless, $g_{0i}$ has units of metres, and $g_{ij}$ has units of square metres. Accordingly $p_{ab}=\partial_0g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $q_{abi}=\partial_i g_{ab}$ has units $[g_{ab}]$. The model-specific components of $w$ have the fixed units declared by that reduction. Divide each component by its fixed declared unit scale before forming the Euclidean-valued state and its Sobolev norm; the resulting numerical state is dimensionless. The coefficient and source fields are those of this same fixed normalized reduction. Thus $R_z$ is a bound on that normalized state, and $R_t$ is a separate bound on its derivative with respect to the length coordinate $x^0$ (units $\mathrm m^{-1}$). Neither is a unit-independent physical observable. If physical seconds are used instead, then $\partial_{x^0}=c^{-1}\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$; consequently the term $A^0\partial_{x^0}$ becomes $c^{-1}A^0\partial_{t_{\rm phys}}$ unless the entire equation is multiplied by $c$.

A fixed-gauge finite-slab comparison context consists of one such coefficient family on an open time interval containing $J$, one coordinate gauge and reconstruction rule, compact state sets $K_0\subset\operatorname{int}K_1\subset\operatorname{int}K_2\subset O$, separate finite nonnegative bounds $R_z,R_t$, and constants $0<a\le b<\infty$ such that

$$a|\zeta|^2\le \zeta^{\mathsf T}A^0(t,x,z)\zeta\le b|\zeta|^2$$

for every $t\in J$, $x\in\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$, $z\in K_2$, and $\zeta\in\mathbb R^m$. The reference state takes values in $K_0$. Compared classical states take values in $K_1$, belong to $L^\infty(J;H^s)\cap C^0(J;H^{s-1})$, have $\partial_tz\in L^\infty(J;H^{s-1})$, and satisfy
$$\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|z(t)\|_{H^s}\le R_z,\qquad \operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in J}\|\partial_tz(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\le R_t.$$
The outer set $K_2$ supplies the positive coefficient margin for local existence restarted from data in compact subsets of $K_1$. Two states use the same chart grid, coefficient maps, gauge source functions, reconstruction rule, and fixed matter branch. Forcing terms, when included in a comparison, are continuous $H^{s-1}$-valued functions of the slab parameter; their size is controlled through the separate stated solution and time-derivative bounds when the comparison estimate is applied.

The Sobolev norms compare coordinate fields in this fixed gauge. They do not identify two arbitrary coordinate representatives by a diffeomorphism. The Einstein interpretation uses the same first-order reduction, full initial constraints, complete matter data, and local restart hypotheses throughout the finite slab.
