supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, and let $\Sigma\subseteq M$ be a smooth spacelike embedded hypersurface with future unit normal $n$, induced Riemannian metric $h$ and second fundamental form $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$ ([[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]], [[lem-gr-spacelike-hypersurface-normal-and-second-fundamental-form]]). Write $D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $h$, $R^h$ for its curvature operator in the same operator convention as the ambient curvature, and $S_h$ for its scalar curvature. Explicitly distinguish the lowered tensor from the operator pairing by setting
$$\mathcal R^g(A,B,C,D):=g(R^g(C,D)B,A),\qquad \mathcal R^h(A,B,C,D):=h(R^h(C,D)B,A).$$
Thus $\mathcal R^g_{abcd}=R_{abcd}$ in [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]]; in particular $g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=\mathcal R^g(W,Z,X,Y)$. Let $G$ be the Einstein tensor defined there. At every $p\in\Sigma$ and for all $X,Y,Z,W\in T_p\Sigma$:

**(a) Gauss equation.**
$$\mathcal R^g(X,Y,Z,W)=\mathcal R^h(X,Y,Z,W)+K(X,Z)K(Y,W)-K(X,W)K(Y,Z).$$
Equivalently, in operator order,
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,W)=h(R^h(X,Y)Z,W)+K(Y,Z)K(X,W)-K(X,Z)K(Y,W).$$

**(b) Codazzi equation.**
$$g(R^g(X,Y)Z,n)=(D_YK)(X,Z)-(D_XK)(Y,Z).$$

**(c) Normal projections.** Define $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)=h^{ij}(D_{e_i}K)(e_j,Y)$, $\tau=\operatorname{tr}_hK=h^{ij}K_{ij}$ and $|K|_h^2=h^{ik}h^{jl}K_{ij}K_{kl}$. Then
$$G(n,n)=\tfrac12(S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2),\qquad G(n,Y)=(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau.$$

**(d) Constraint equations.** If the tensor equation $G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ holds at $p$, for a smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor $T$ and real constants $\kappa,\Lambda$, then
$$S_h+\tau^2-|K|_h^2=2\Lambda+2\kappa T(n,n),\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=\kappa T(n,Y).$$
With $\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j(Y)=-T(n,Y)$, the second equation is $(\operatorname{div}_hK)(Y)-D_Y\tau=-\kappa j(Y)$.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: **Given:** The smooth Lorentzian manifold, spacelike embedded hypersurface, normal and tensors in the Statement; in (d), the field equation at the selected point.

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

For every admissible integer $N\ge3$, time-step count $n_{\max}\ge1$, real
step $k>0$, and pair of real periodic input arrays, the algorithm terminates
after exactly $n_{\max}-1$ update passes and outputs all levels through
$u^{n_{\max}}$. In the unit-cost exact-real-arithmetic model, where each scalar
arithmetic operation and each array read or write has bounded cost independent
of $N$ and $n_{\max}$, its operation count is $O(Nn_{\max})$.

Let $N\ge3$, $h=2\pi/N$, $k>0$, and $\lambda=k/h$. Complexify the real
linear recurrence of the periodic wave algorithm. For each discrete Fourier
index $\ell\in\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ define the mode
$$
e_\ell(j):=\exp(2\pi i\ell j/N),\qquad j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z.
$$
If $0<\lambda<1$, every nonconstant mode ($\ell\ne0$) has recurrence
coefficient
$$
c_\ell:=1-2\lambda^2\sin^2(\pi\ell/N)\in(-1,1)
$$
and two distinct amplification roots
$$
z_{\ell,\pm}:=c_\ell\pm i\sqrt{1-c_\ell^2},\qquad |z_{\ell,\pm}|=1.
$$
Consequently, each fixed nonconstant mode has bounded amplitude on every
finite slab. For arbitrary real initial arrays define their spatial means by
$$
\bar u^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}u^0_j,\qquad \bar v^0:=\frac1N\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}v^0_j.
$$
The constant mode has the repeated root $1$ and evolves exactly as
$\bar u^0+nk\bar v^0$; for any fixed $T\ge0$ it is bounded on the slab
$0\le nk\le T$ but has no uniform-in-time displacement bound when
$\bar v^0\ne0$. This statement
does not assert that the condition $0<\lambda<1$ alone proves convergence of a
numerical relativity scheme. Define the nonzero discrete frequencies $\omega_\ell:=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$. On this fixed torus they satisfy the mesh-independent lower bound
$$\omega_\ell\ge\frac2\pi\qquad(N\ge3,\ 1\le\ell<N).$$
In particular each fixed grid has a positive minimum. This frequency bound is not a mesh-independent amplitude bound for arbitrary unscaled two-step data $(a_0,a_1)$: the distinct-root coefficients in the mode solution can depend on the grid and the initial data. The constant-mode qualifications above are unchanged.
For even $N$, the alternating mode with Fourier index $\ell=N/2$ is called
the Nyquist mode. At the endpoint $\lambda=1$, if $N$ is even and
$u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$, $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ for real amplitudes $a_0,\beta_0$,
then each output level satisfies
$$
u_j^n=(-1)^j(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0).
$$
The Nyquist amplification root is repeated at $-1$, and a nonzero Nyquist
velocity amplitude $\beta_0$ gives linear growth in the step number.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Because $N$ is even, both periodic neighbors of $(-1)^j$ equal $-(-1)^j$. Hence $(D_hu^0)_j=-4h^{-2}(-1)^j$, and the startup in [F1] gives $a_0=1$ and $a_1=1-2(k/h)^2=c$. This mode has index $\ell=N/2$; it is outside the strict range of [F3].

Substitution of $u_j^n=a_n(-1)^j$ into the update [F1] gives $a_{n+1}-2ca_n+a_{n-1}=0$. Since $c<-1$, [F4] supplies $r=\sqrt{c^2-1}>0$. The two roots $z_{\rm grow}=c-r$ and $z_{\rm decay}=c+r$ satisfy $z_{\rm grow}z_{\rm decay}=1$; also $z_{\rm grow}<-1$ and $z_{\rm decay}=1/z_{\rm grow}\in(-1,0)$.

The sequence $(z_{\rm grow}^n+z_{\rm decay}^n)/2$ satisfies the recurrence because each root satisfies $z^2-2cz+1=0$, and its values at $n=0,1$ are $1,c$. Induction identifies it with $a_n$. For even $n$ the two powers are nonnegative, and for odd $n$ they are both negative; since $1/2>0$, their half-sum has the same sign. The piecewise definition [F5] therefore gives $|a_n|=(|z_{\rm grow}^n|+|z_{\rm decay}^n|)/2$, while induction using multiplicativity [F6] gives $|z_{\rm grow}^n|=|z_{\rm grow}|^n$ and $|z_{\rm decay}^n|=|z_{\rm decay}|^n$. Since $z_{\rm grow}<-1$, [F5] gives $|z_{\rm grow}|=-z_{\rm grow}>1$, while $|z_{\rm decay}|^n\ge0$ by [F6]; hence $|a_n|\ge|z_{\rm grow}|^n/2$.

$0\le nk\le T$ but has no uniform-in-time displacement bound when
$\bar v^0\ne0$. This statement
does not assert that the condition $0<\lambda<1$ alone proves convergence of a
numerical relativity scheme. For each fixed $N$, define the nonzero discrete
frequencies $\omega_\ell:=2h^{-1}|\sin(\pi\ell/N)|$, $1\le\ell<N$.
This finite list has a positive minimum; it is a fixed-grid fact and no bound
uniform in $N$ is asserted.
For even $N$, the alternating mode with Fourier index $\ell=N/2$ is called
the Nyquist mode. At the endpoint $\lambda=1$, if $N$ is even and
$u_j^0=a_0(-1)^j$, $v_j^0=\beta_0(-1)^j$ for real amplitudes $a_0,\beta_0$,
then each output level satisfies
$$
u_j^n=(-1)^j(-1)^n(a_0-nk\beta_0).
$$
The Nyquist amplification root is repeated at $-1$, and a nonzero Nyquist
velocity amplitude $\beta_0$ gives linear growth in the step number.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
For every $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \ge 0$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$n \ge 1$ there is a **unique** $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^n = a$
([[def-integer-power]]); we write

$$s = a^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{a}.$$

Moreover $a^{1/n} > 0$ when $a > 0$, and $a^{1/1} = a$.

**This generalises the published [[thm-of-square-roots]], and the case $n = 2$ is
not new.** That theorem already produces the unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with
$(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$, and it is cited as such throughout the library; the notation
$a^{1/2}$ introduced here is the same number. What is new is the passage to
general $n$: the completed square that drives the $n = 2$ argument has no direct
analogue, and its place is taken by the factorisation of $b^n - a^n$ and the
resulting Lipschitz estimate ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty compact smooth three-manifold without boundary. In
this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of [[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]].
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
[[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]].
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$
With $R(h)$ computed using $h$, define the Hamiltonian and momentum residuals
$$\mathcal H(h,K):=R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2,\qquad \mathcal M_j(h,K):=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}-D_j(\operatorname{tr}_hK).$$
The data satisfy the vacuum constraint equations when
$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

Tensoriality of curvature and basis-independent contraction make these scalar
curvatures independent of the chart.
For dimensional bookkeeping in the SI length convention, $[\tau]=\mathrm m^{-1}$,
$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

Use the first circle factor of the fixed periodic three-torus from the earlier
fixed-gauge data definition. This item is a separate nondimensionalized scalar
model: both the spatial coordinate $x$ and time $t$ are dimensionless, the
period is $2\pi$, and the model wave speed is $1$. Let $N\ge3$ be an integer,
$h:=2\pi/N$, and $x_j:=jh\pmod{2\pi}$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$. A
periodic grid function is an $N$-tuple $u=(u_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z}$ of
real numbers. Define the centered periodic second-difference operator
$$
(D_hu)_j:=\frac{u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}}{h^2},
$$
where subscripts are reduced modulo $N$.

The algorithm takes as input such arrays $u^0,v^0$, a real time step $k>0$,
and an integer $n_{\max}\ge1$. It sets
$$
u^1:=u^0+kv^0+\frac{k^2}{2}D_hu^0,
$$
then, for each integer $n=1,\ldots,n_{\max}-1$, computes
$$
u^{n+1}_j:=2u^n_j-u^{n-1}_j+k^2(D_hu^n)_j \qquad(j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z).
$$
It outputs $(u^0,u^1,\ldots,u^{n_{\max}})$. All operations here are exact real
arithmetic. No rounding-error model or claim about a floating-point
implementation is part of the definition.

Use the dimensionless angular coordinates $x^i$ and the periodic spatial
three-torus from the earlier fixed-gauge data definition. Choose integers
$N_i\ge3$, coordinate spacings $\Delta_i:=2\pi/N_i$, and the finite periodic
grid
$$
G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=\{(2\pi j_1/N_1,2\pi j_2/N_2,2\pi j_3/N_3): 0\le j_i<N_i\}\subset\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}.
$$
At each grid node $p$, supply a real symmetric positive-definite matrix
$h_{ij}(p)$ and its matrix inverse $h^{ij}(p)$ (so
$h^{ik}(p)h_{kj}(p)=\delta^i{}_j$), a real symmetric array $K_{ij}(p)$,
a scalar $\rho(p)$, a covector array $j_i(p)$, and real constants $\Lambda$
and $\kappa>0$. These are the sampled spatial metric, second fundamental
form, energy density and momentum density in the convention of
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]]: for a future unit normal $n$
and the coordinate basis $\partial_i$, $K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_Xn,Y)$,
$\rho=T(n,n)$ and $j_i=-T(n,\partial_i)$, where $T$ is a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor. The array definition itself needs only the listed
samples and does not assume the continuum field equation. The vacuum case is
$\rho=j_i=\Lambda=0$. In the SI angular-coordinate convention used here,
$[x^i]=1$, $[h_{ij}]=\mathrm m^2$, $[K_{ij}]=\mathrm m$,
$[\rho]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[j_i]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$,
$[\Lambda]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and
$[\kappa]=\mathrm{m^{-1}\,kg^{-1}\,s^2}$. Thus the scalar residual below
has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ and its covector components in this angular basis
have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ denote the real arrays indexed by
the grid. Choose and specify linear maps
$\delta_i:\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}\to
\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ with $\delta_i1=0$; apply them
componentwise to tensor arrays. Periodic index wrapping is used here. Define
the discrete connection components, curvature, Ricci array and scalar
curvature by nodewise operations, with every index $i,j,k,\ell,a,b$ ranging
over $1,2,3$ and repeated upper/lower indices summed:
$$
\Gamma^k{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \frac12h^{k\ell}(\delta_i h_{j\ell}+\delta_j h_{i\ell}-\delta_\ell h_{ij}),
$$
$$
R^a{}_{b i j,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \delta_i\Gamma^a{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\delta_j\Gamma^a{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta} +\Gamma^a{}_{i\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\Gamma^a{}_{j\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:=R^k{}_{i k j,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}.
$$
Set
$$
\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},
$$
$$
(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj}:= \delta_iK_{kj}-\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{\ell j} -\Gamma^\ell{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{k\ell}.
$$
The signed discrete Hamiltonian and momentum residuals are
$$
\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:= R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}^2 -|K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}-2\Lambda-2\kappa\rho,
$$
$$
\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,j}:= h^{ik}(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj} -\delta_j\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\kappa j_j.
$$
These signs match the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]] when its pointwise equation
$G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ is assumed. The displayed discrete formulas are array
operations: they do not define a coordinate-covariant discrete connection or
assume a discrete Leibniz rule. A reconstruction map has the exact type
$$
\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}\longrightarrow \mathcal C,
$$
where $\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ is the set of all grid arrays
$(h_{ij},K_{ij},\rho,j_i)$ with the pointwise symmetry and positive-definite
conditions above, and $\mathcal C$ is the set of pointwise assignments on
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ of a positive-definite symmetric covariant two-tensor
$h$, a symmetric covariant two-tensor $K$, a scalar $\rho$ and a covector
$j$, with the same units. No continuity or differentiability of a member of
$\mathcal C$ is implied; if continuum derivatives are used, the needed
regularity must be stated separately. Specify $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$
as part of each diagnostic, since it records which continuum field the grid
is intended to represent. For every reported diagnostic, also record the grid
norm and its weights, the mesh hierarchy, the units, the derivative maps, the
periodic boundary treatment, and $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$. A small
residual by itself does not assert closeness to an exact constraint-satisfying
development.

In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on $M$ in
the sense of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], and let $X,Y,Z$ be
smooth vector fields. With the sign convention used throughout this page, the
**curvature of $\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$

where $[X,Y]$ is the bracket of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. We usually write $R$ when the
connection is understood. The connection is **flat** or **curvature-free** when
$R(X,Y)Z=0$ for every triple of smooth vector fields.

The bracket correction is part of the definition. The raw commutator of two
covariant derivatives is not function-linear in its differentiating fields.
No metric or torsion hypothesis is imposed here. On an empty or
zero-dimensional manifold the condition is vacuous; on manifolds with boundary
the same formula uses the ambient tangent bundle supplied by the definition of
an affine connection.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Since $N/2$ is an integer, $\phi_N$ is $2\pi$-periodic. By [F6], $\phi_N\ge1-\varepsilon>0$. The flat seed metric is smooth positive-definite; $\widetilde\sigma=0$ is symmetric, trace-free and divergence-free, and $\tau=0$ is constant. Thus the data satisfy [F1] and $h=\phi_N^4\widetilde h$, $K=0$.

At each first-coordinate grid node $x^1_j=2\pi j/N$, [F6] gives $\phi_N(x_j)=1$. The sampled arrays therefore have $h_{ij}=L_*^2\delta_{ij}$, $h^{ik}=L_*^{-2}\delta^{ik}$, $K_{ij}=0$, $\rho=j=\Lambda=0$. Since the discrete derivatives annihilate these constant arrays, the discrete connection and curvature formulas of [F4] give zero; [F4] then gives $\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}=\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta}=0$ at every node. By [F8, F9], each scalar term $|\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}(\mathbf j)|^2=|0|^2=0$, and the covector term is zero because $\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta}=0$. The induced norm of this zero array is therefore zero. The specified piecewise-constant reconstruction of these samples is flat.

In the lifted angular coordinates the coefficients of $\widetilde h$ are constant. The Christoffel formula in [F5] therefore gives $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=0$, and the curvature formula in [F5] gives $\widetilde R=0$. Thus $\widetilde\Delta\phi_N=L_*^{-2}\partial_1^2\phi_N$. By [F7], $$ \widetilde\Delta\phi_N=-\frac{\varepsilon N^2}{4L_*^2}\sin(Nx^1/2). $$ At $x^1=\pi/N$, [F6] gives $\phi_N=1+\varepsilon$ and $\sin(Nx^1/2)=1$. Substituting $\widetilde\sigma=0$, $\tau=0$ and this Laplacian into [F2] gives $\mathcal H(h,K)=2\varepsilon N^2/[L_*^2(1+\varepsilon)^5]>0$.

Step 2.1 and step 2.2 exhibit identical grid data with zero discrete residuals and a smooth continuum representative with a nonzero exact Hamiltonian residual. The reconstruction and finite differences cannot identify the unresolved sine mode from these samples; the residual therefore does not certify continuum constraint satisfaction.

$[\rho]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, $[j_i]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$,
$[\Lambda]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and
$[\kappa]=\mathrm{m^{-1}\,kg^{-1}\,s^2}$. Thus the scalar residual below
has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$ and its covector components in this angular basis
have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ denote the real arrays indexed by
the grid. Choose and specify linear maps
$\delta_i:\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}\to
\mathbb R^{G_{\boldsymbol\Delta}}$ with $\delta_i1=0$; apply them
componentwise to tensor arrays. Periodic index wrapping is used here. Define
the discrete connection components, curvature, Ricci array and scalar
curvature by nodewise operations, with every index $i,j,k,\ell,a,b$ ranging
over $1,2,3$ and repeated upper/lower indices summed:
$$
\Gamma^k{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \frac12h^{k\ell}(\delta_i h_{j\ell}+\delta_j h_{i\ell}-\delta_\ell h_{ij}),
$$
$$
R^a{}_{b i j,\boldsymbol\Delta}:= \delta_i\Gamma^a{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\delta_j\Gamma^a{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta} +\Gamma^a{}_{i\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{jb,\boldsymbol\Delta} -\Gamma^a{}_{j\ell,\boldsymbol\Delta}\Gamma^\ell{}_{ib,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}:=R^k{}_{i k j,\boldsymbol\Delta}, \qquad R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}.
$$
Set
$$
\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},
$$
$$
(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj}:= \delta_iK_{kj}-\Gamma^\ell{}_{ik,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{\ell j} -\Gamma^\ell{}_{ij,\boldsymbol\Delta}K_{k\ell}.
$$
The signed discrete Hamiltonian and momentum residuals are
$$
\mathcal H_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:= R_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}^2 -|K|^2_{\boldsymbol\Delta}-2\Lambda-2\kappa\rho,
$$
$$
\mathcal M_{\boldsymbol\Delta,j}:= h^{ik}(D_i^{\boldsymbol\Delta}K)_{kj} -\delta_j\tau_{\boldsymbol\Delta}+\kappa j_j.
$$
These signs match the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints in
[[thm-gr-constraint-equations-in-normal-frame]] when its pointwise equation
$G+\Lambda g=\kappa T$ is assumed. The displayed discrete formulas are array
operations: they do not define a coordinate-covariant discrete connection or
assume a discrete Leibniz rule. A reconstruction map has the exact type
$$
\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}:\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}\longrightarrow \mathcal C,
$$
where $\mathcal D_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$ is the set of all grid arrays
$(h_{ij},K_{ij},\rho,j_i)$ with the pointwise symmetry and positive-definite
conditions above, and $\mathcal C$ is the set of pointwise assignments on
$\mathbb T^3_{2\pi}$ of a positive-definite symmetric covariant two-tensor
$h$, a symmetric covariant two-tensor $K$, a scalar $\rho$ and a covector
$j$, with the same units. No continuity or differentiability of a member of
$\mathcal C$ is implied; if continuum derivatives are used, the needed
regularity must be stated separately. Specify $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$
as part of each diagnostic, since it records which continuum field the grid
is intended to represent. For every reported diagnostic, also record the grid
norm and its weights, the mesh hierarchy, the units, the derivative maps, the
periodic boundary treatment, and $\mathcal I_{\boldsymbol\Delta}$. A small
residual by itself does not assert closeness to an exact constraint-satisfying
development.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty compact smooth three-manifold without boundary. In
this item, “vacuum” means that the stress-energy tensor is zero and the
cosmological constant is fixed at $\Lambda=0$. Let $\widetilde h$ be a smooth
Riemannian metric on $\Sigma$, let $\widetilde\sigma$ be a smooth symmetric
covariant two-tensor field, let $\tau\in\mathbb R$ be constant, and let
$\phi\in C^\infty(\Sigma,\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\phi(p)>0$ at every $p\in\Sigma$.
Use the positive scalar $\phi$ as a dimensionless conformal factor.

Write $\widetilde D$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $\widetilde h$ and
$D$ for that of the metric $h$ defined below. On covariant tensor fields, these
symbols also denote their induced product connections, with the dual and
tensor-factor rules of [[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]].
In a chart, $\widetilde h^{ij}$
denotes the inverse matrix to $\widetilde h_{ij}$. It is smooth because
$\det(\widetilde h_{ij})>0$ and the matrix inverse is the adjugate divided by
the determinant. For any smooth Riemannian metric $m$ on $\Sigma$, with
Levi-Civita connection $D^m$, define
$$R^m(X,Y)Z:=D^m_XD^m_YZ-D^m_YD^m_XZ-D^m_{[X,Y]}Z.$$
In a chart, $R[m]^a{}_{bij}$ denotes the components of
$R^m(\partial_i,\partial_j)\partial_b$. Define
$\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}:=R[m]^k{}_{ikj}$ and
$R(m):=m^{ij}\operatorname{Ric}(m)_{ij}$. In particular,
$\widetilde R:=R(\widetilde h)$, with the same curvature sign convention.
Define the scalar Laplacian by
$$\widetilde\Delta f:=\widetilde h^{ij} (\partial_i\partial_j f-\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}\partial_k f),$$
where $\widetilde\Gamma^k{}_{ij}$ are the Christoffel symbols of
$\widetilde D$, given by the Levi-Civita Christoffel formula
[[prop-christoffel-formula-for-the-levi-civita-connection]].
The curvature sign is the one displayed above. All traces, norms, raising of
indices and contractions in this item use the metric indicated by the
subscript. In particular,
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma:=\widetilde h^{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{ij},\qquad |\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde h^{j\ell}\widetilde\sigma_{ij}\widetilde\sigma_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_{\widetilde h}\widetilde\sigma)_j:=\widetilde h^{ik}\widetilde D_i\widetilde\sigma_{kj}.$$
The tensor $\widetilde\sigma$ is **transverse-traceless** (TT) with respect
to $\widetilde h$ when it is symmetric and both displayed trace and divergence
vanish. The input tensor in this definition is required to be TT.

Define
$$h:=\phi^4\widetilde h,\qquad K:=\phi^{-2}\widetilde\sigma+\frac{\tau}{3}h.$$
Because $\phi>0$, $h$ is a smooth Riemannian metric; because
$\widetilde\sigma$ and $h$ are symmetric, $K$ is a smooth symmetric tensor.
Here $h$ is the candidate induced Riemannian metric and $K$ is the candidate
second fundamental form, with the library convention
$K(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X n,Y)$ when the data are induced by a spacelike hypersurface
with future unit normal $n$. The pair is **vacuum conformal constraint data**.
It is abstract data on $\Sigma$; no embedding into a spacetime is part of this
definition. For its embedded Lorentzian interpretation assume the Axiom of
Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, as in the supplied smooth tangent-bundle
convention; the algebraic tensor definitions themselves use no choice
principle. Define the $h$-trace, squared norm and divergence by
$$\operatorname{tr}_hK:=h^{ij}K_{ij},\qquad |K|_h^2:=h^{ik}h^{j\ell}K_{ij}K_{k\ell},\qquad (\operatorname{div}_hK)_j:=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}.$$
With $R(h)$ computed using $h$, define the Hamiltonian and momentum residuals
$$\mathcal H(h,K):=R(h)+(\operatorname{tr}_hK)^2-|K|_h^2,\qquad \mathcal M_j(h,K):=h^{ik}D_iK_{kj}-D_j(\operatorname{tr}_hK).$$
The data satisfy the vacuum constraint equations when
$\mathcal H(h,K)=0$ and $\mathcal M(h,K)=0$. For an embedded hypersurface,
these are the normal and normal-tangential Einstein constraints in the
specified $K$ convention.

Tensoriality of curvature and basis-independent contraction make these scalar
curvatures independent of the chart.
For dimensional bookkeeping in the SI length convention, $[\tau]=\mathrm m^{-1}$,
$[R(h)]=[\widetilde R]=[|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2]
=[\widetilde\Delta]=\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $[\phi]=1$. Thus all terms in the
scalar constraint equation have units $\mathrm m^{-2}$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(h,K)$ be the vacuum conformal constraint data of the definition. Then
$\operatorname{tr}_hK=\tau$ and the momentum residual vanishes:
$$\mathcal M_j(h,K)=0.$$
The Hamiltonian residual is
$$\mathcal H(h,K)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -8\widetilde\Delta\phi+\widetilde R\,\phi-|\widetilde\sigma|_{\widetilde h}^2\phi^{-7} +\frac{2}{3}\tau^2\phi^5=0.$$
The displayed scalar equation is the **Lichnerowicz equation** for these
constant-mean-curvature (CMC) vacuum data. Here CMC means that the trace
$\operatorname{tr}_hK$ is spatially constant; its value is $\tau$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $\nabla$ be an affine connection on $M$ in
the sense of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], and let $X,Y,Z$ be
smooth vector fields. With the sign convention used throughout this page, the
**curvature of $\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$

where $[X,Y]$ is the bracket of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]]. We usually write $R$ when the
connection is understood. The connection is **flat** or **curvature-free** when
$R(X,Y)Z=0$ for every triple of smooth vector fields.

The bracket correction is part of the definition. The raw commutator of two
covariant derivatives is not function-linear in its differentiating fields.
No metric or torsion hypothesis is imposed here. On an empty or
zero-dimensional manifold the condition is vacuous; on manifolds with boundary
the same formula uses the ambient tangent bundle supplied by the definition of
an affine connection.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Define $F:(0,1)\times U\to U$ by $F(t,x)=a+t(x-a)$. By [F1] this map has image in $U$, and both its domain and target are boundaryless smooth manifolds, so [F3] applies to this restriction. In product coordinates decompose $F^*\alpha=\gamma_t+dt\wedge\eta_t$, where $\gamma_t$ is a $k$-form and $\eta_t$ a $(k-1)$-form on $U$. The same affine formula, viewed first as a map $\bar F:\mathbb R\times U\to\mathbb R^n$, has image in $U$ on a neighborhood of every $(t_0,x_0)$ with $0\le t_0\le1$, because $\bar F(t_0,x_0)\in U$ and $U$ is open. Thus the coefficient formulas for $\gamma_t$ and $\eta_t$ extend smoothly to $t=0,1$ locally in $(t,x)$.

The integrand defining $K\alpha$ is alternating and multilinear in $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$, so its integral is a $(k-1)$-covariant alternating tensor at each $x$. Its coefficient functions are smooth in $(x,t)$. Restricting $x$ to a compact coordinate rectangle inside $U$ and using [F4] on each coordinate derivative shows that parameter derivatives pass through the $t$-integral; iteration gives smooth coefficients, hence a smooth $(k-1)$-form $K\alpha$.

Since $d\alpha=0$, [F3] gives $d(F^*\alpha)=0$ on $(0,1)\times U$. In product coordinates $d=d_U+dt\wedge\partial_t$, so the coefficient of $dt$ is $\partial_t\gamma_t-d_U\eta_t=0$ for $0<t<1$. By the local smooth extension in step 1.1, this coefficient identity extends by continuity to $t=0,1$. The pullback formula [F2] gives $(\eta_t)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}) =t^{k-1}\alpha_{a+t(x-a)}(x-a,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})$ for interior $t$, and then also at the endpoints by continuity.

Thus $K\alpha=\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. By step 2.1 and [F4], $d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt=\int_0^1d_U\eta_t\,dt$. Apply [F5] to the coefficient functions of $\gamma_t$ and use step 2.2: $\gamma_1-\gamma_0=\int_0^1\partial_t\gamma_t\,dt =d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. Here $\gamma_1=\alpha$ because $F(1,x)=x$, while $\gamma_0=0$ because $F(0,x)=a$ is constant and $k\ge1$. Hence $d(K\alpha)=\alpha$.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: First consider integration on one simplex, using the zero extension in [F3] to a bounded nondegenerate rectangle $Q$. The Darboux definitions [F4] give linearity: for integrable $u,w$, choose grid partitions whose upper-minus lower sums for each are arbitrarily small, take a common refinement, and use $\inf(u+w)\ge\inf u+\inf w$ and $\sup(u+w)\le\sup u+\sup w$ on each cell. The upper-minus-lower gap for $u+w$ is therefore bounded by the sum of the chosen gaps, so $u+w$ is integrable. Its lower and upper integrals are squeezed between the sums of the lower integrals of $u,w$ and the sums of their upper integrals; letting the gaps tend to zero gives $\int_Q(u+w)=\int_Qu+\int_Qw$. For a scalar $c>0$, upper and lower sums scale by $c$; for $c<0$ they exchange after scaling, giving $\int_Q(cu)=c\int_Qu$, and $c=0$ gives zero. Also, if $|u|\le\varepsilon$ on $Q$, each lower sum is at least $-\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ and each upper sum at most $\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$, since cell volumes add to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ by [F5]. Thus $|\int_\sigma u|\le\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ for an integrable function on the simplex bounded by $\varepsilon$.

Fix a parameter chart and a point $p$. For one simplex $\sigma$ write $\sigma^*\alpha_p=f(p,z)\,dz_1\wedge dz_2\wedge dz_3$ on $T_3$. Choose a closed parameter rectangle $R$ around $p$ inside the chart. The displayed inequalities defining $T_3$ make it closed and bounded, hence compact by [F6]; [F2] identifies it as the integration domain. The product $R\times T_3$ is a closed bounded Euclidean set, hence compact by [F6], so $\partial_a f$ is uniformly continuous there by [F7]. For a small nonzero increment $h$ in coordinate $p^a$, [F8] gives $$\frac{f(p+he_a,z)-f(p,z)}{h}-\partial_af(p,z) =\frac1h\int_0^h\bigl(\partial_af(p+se_a,z)-\partial_af(p,z)\bigr)\,ds.$$ Uniform continuity makes the right side tend uniformly to zero on $T_3$ as $h\to0$. By step 1.1, the integral of this error tends to zero. Linearity therefore gives $$\partial_a\int_\sigma f(p,z)\,dz=\int_\sigma\partial_af(p,z)\,dz.$$ Applying the same argument to every parameter derivative of $f$ proves that all parameter partial derivatives of the simplex integral exist and are integrals of the corresponding derivatives. They are continuous: on a compact parameter rectangle, uniform continuity of each next derivative and step 1.1 bound the change in its integral by the uniform coefficient change times $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Hence this simplex integral is smooth.

By [F1], $\Sigma$ is a finite linear combination of such simplices. Linearity from step 1.1 makes $I$ the corresponding finite linear combination of their smooth integrals and gives the asserted derivative formula for every parameter coordinate. Linearity in the tangent vector then gives the formula for every $v\in T_pP$.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold and let $\pi:E\to M$ be a smooth fibre
bundle. A **field configuration** is a smooth section $\phi:M\to E$, so
$\pi\circ\phi=\operatorname{id}_M$. For a finite-dimensional smooth manifold
$P$, a **smooth field family** is a smooth map
$\Phi:P\times M\to E$ with $\pi(\Phi(p,x))=x$ for all $(p,x)$; it gives
configurations $\phi_p(x)=\Phi(p,x)$. For $u\in T_pP$, the **variation**
$\delta_u\phi_p$ at $x$ is the tangent vector
$d(r\mapsto\Phi(c(r),x))|_{r=0}$, where $c(0)=p$ and $c'(0)=u$. In a local
fibre chart this is the ordinary derivative of the field components with
respect to the parameter. For commuting parameter coordinates $s_1,s_2$,
$\delta_i\phi=\partial_{s_i}\phi$ and
$\delta_1\delta_2\phi=\delta_2\delta_1\phi$.

derivations.claim: Differentiate [A1] in direction $\delta_1$ with input $\delta_2\phi$ held fixed, and in direction $\delta_2$ with input $\delta_1\phi$ held fixed. The total derivatives of the Euler terms are respectively $(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]+E_\phi[\delta_1\delta_2\phi]$ and $(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi]+E_\phi[\delta_2\delta_1\phi]$ by the definition of $\delta_iE_\phi$ in [A1]. Subtract the second differentiated identity from the first. The second-variation terms cancel by [A2], and the left-hand sides cancel by commutation of mixed derivatives. Since $\omega(\delta_1,\delta_2)=\delta_2\theta(\delta_1)-\delta_1\theta(\delta_2)$, the remaining identity is $$0=(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]-(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi] -d_M\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi).$$
Rearranging step 1.1 gives $d_M\omega=(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]-(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi]$, with the stated sign fixed by the Iyer–Wald ordering in [A1].

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the

$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.
For every vector field $X$ and differential form $\omega$, $$\mathcal L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)+\iota_X(d\omega).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to $a\in U$, and let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(U)$ be a smooth closed
differential form with $1\le k\le n$. Define

$$(K\alpha)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}) :=\int_0^1 t^{k-1} \alpha_{a+t(x-a)}(x-a,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})\,dt .$$

Then $K\alpha$ is a smooth $(k-1)$-form on $U$ and $d(K\alpha)=\alpha$.

If $X$ has local flow $\Phi_t$ and $T$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(r,s)$, its Lie derivative is $$\mathcal L_XT=\left.\frac d{dt}\right|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*T,$$ on every local flow domain where this derivative is defined. Here the pullback by the local diffeomorphism $\Phi_t$ acts by $d\Phi_{-t}$ on each contravariant slot and by $d\Phi_t$ on each covariant slot.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Apply [F1] to the variation $\delta_\xi\phi$ supplied by [A1] and equate it with step 1.1: $E_\phi[\delta_\xi\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta_\xi\phi) =d_M(\iota_\xi\mathcal L)$. Rearranging gives $d_MJ_\xi=-E_\phi[\delta_\xi\phi]$.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field

coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $\mathcal L$ have a chosen first-variation decomposition with Euler
functional $E_\phi$. If $E_\phi=0$ and both variations satisfy the
linearized equations, so $\delta_iE_\phi=0$, then $d_M\omega=0$. For a finite
oriented smooth singular four-chain $C$ with
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

Thus on-shell closure alone gives independence between cuts only when the
side flux vanishes.

For a fixed smooth two-parameter family of commuting variations, replace the
Lagrangian and its selected potential by

$$\mathcal L'=\mathcal L+d_M\mu,\qquad \theta'(\phi;\delta\phi) =\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)+\delta\mu(\phi;\delta\phi) +d_MY(\phi;\delta\phi),$$

where $\mu$ is a local spacetime three-form and $Y$ is a local spacetime
two-form linear in the variation. Then

$$\omega'-\omega =d_M\bigl(\delta_2Y(\delta_1\phi)-\delta_1Y(\delta_2\phi)\bigr).$$

Consequently, for a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$,
the integrated form changes by the integral of this two-form over
$\partial\Sigma$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be a specified finite-dimensional smooth solution manifold
with specified admissible variations and boundary conditions, and let
$\Omega$ be a smooth closed two-form on $\mathcal S$, obtained by restricting
an integrated form $\Omega_\Sigma$ from the chosen covariant variation data.
The pair $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ is **presymplectic** when $\Omega$ is allowed
to be degenerate. At $p\in\mathcal S$, its pointwise null space is
$$\ker\Omega_p:=\{v\in T_p\mathcal S:\Omega_p(v,w)=0 \text{ for every }w\in T_p\mathcal S\}.$$
A **presymplectic reduction** is defined here only when there is a specified
smooth Hausdorff manifold $\mathcal R$ and a surjective submersion
$q:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$ with connected fibers such that
$$\ker(dq_p)=\ker\Omega_p\qquad(p\in\mathcal S),$$
where $\ker(dq_p)$ consists of tangent vectors mapped to zero by the
differential. This condition makes the quotient fibers exactly the connected
directions annihilated by $\Omega$. The reduction further requires a smooth
closed nondegenerate two-form $\bar\Omega$ on $\mathcal R$ satisfying
$q^*\bar\Omega=\Omega$. For a smooth vector field $X$ and smooth function
$H$ on a specified phase space, the Hamiltonian convention is
$\iota_X\Omega=dH$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $\mathcal L$ have a chosen first-variation decomposition with Euler
functional $E_\phi$. If $E_\phi=0$ and both variations satisfy the
linearized equations, so $\delta_iE_\phi=0$, then $d_M\omega=0$. For a finite
oriented smooth singular four-chain $C$ with
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

Thus on-shell closure alone gives independence between cuts only when the
side flux vanishes.

For a fixed smooth two-parameter family of commuting variations, replace the
Lagrangian and its selected potential by

$$\mathcal L'=\mathcal L+d_M\mu,\qquad \theta'(\phi;\delta\phi) =\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)+\delta\mu(\phi;\delta\phi) +d_MY(\phi;\delta\phi),$$

where $\mu$ is a local spacetime three-form and $Y$ is a local spacetime
two-form linear in the variation. Then

$$\omega'-\omega =d_M\bigl(\delta_2Y(\delta_1\phi)-\delta_1Y(\delta_2\phi)\bigr).$$

Consequently, for a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$,
the integrated form changes by the integral of this two-form over
$\partial\Sigma$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be a specified finite-dimensional smooth solution manifold
with specified admissible variations and boundary conditions, and let
$\Omega$ be a smooth closed two-form on $\mathcal S$, obtained by restricting
an integrated form $\Omega_\Sigma$ from the chosen covariant variation data.
The pair $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ is **presymplectic** when $\Omega$ is allowed
to be degenerate. At $p\in\mathcal S$, its pointwise null space is
$$\ker\Omega_p:=\{v\in T_p\mathcal S:\Omega_p(v,w)=0 \text{ for every }w\in T_p\mathcal S\}.$$
A **presymplectic reduction** is defined here only when there is a specified
smooth Hausdorff manifold $\mathcal R$ and a surjective submersion
$q:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$ with connected fibers such that
$$\ker(dq_p)=\ker\Omega_p\qquad(p\in\mathcal S),$$
where $\ker(dq_p)$ consists of tangent vectors mapped to zero by the
differential. This condition makes the quotient fibers exactly the connected
directions annihilated by $\Omega$. The reduction further requires a smooth
closed nondegenerate two-form $\bar\Omega$ on $\mathcal R$ satisfying
$q^*\bar\Omega=\Omega$. For a smooth vector field $X$ and smooth function
$H$ on a specified phase space, the Hamiltonian convention is
$\iota_X\Omega=dH$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

derivations.claim: The scalar-current formula from the chosen decomposition is $\omega=\delta_2\psi*d\delta_1\psi-\delta_1\psi*d\delta_2\psi$. Substitution of the displayed variations and Hodge map gives $$\omega=(x^2-t^2)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz -2tx\,dt\wedge dy\wedge dz.$$ By [F6], differentiating the first term gives $-2t\,dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$; differentiating the second gives $+2t\,dt\wedge dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$. The graded product rule [F5] justifies the coefficient differentiations. Thus $d_M\omega=0$, agreeing with [F2].

On a cut with orientation $dx\wedge dy\wedge dz$, $$\Omega_{\Sigma_t}=\int_0^L\int_0^1\int_0^1(x^2-t^2)\,dy\,dz\,dx =\frac{L^3}{3}-Lt^2.$$ Therefore $\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_2}}-\Omega_{\Sigma_{t_1}} =-L(t_2^2-t_1^2)$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

derivations.claim: Write the columns of $A$ as $u,v\in\mathbb C^2$. Since $\det A=1$, $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent. Put $r_{11}:=\|u\|>0$, $q_1:=u/r_{11}$, $\alpha:=q_1^\dagger v$, $w:=v-\alpha q_1$, and $r_{22}:=\|w\|>0$. Then $q_1^\dagger w=0$ and $q_2:=w/r_{22}$ makes $Q:=(q_1,q_2)$ unitary; with $R:=\begin{pmatrix}r_{11}&\alpha\\0&r_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ we have $A=QR$. By [F1]–[F2], $1=|\det A|=|\det Q|r_{11}r_{22}=r_{11}r_{22}$, and $\det A=\det Q\,r_{11}r_{22}=1$ then gives $\det Q=1$. Therefore $Q\in SU(2)$ and $R=\begin{pmatrix}r&z\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$ for $r>0$ and $z\in\mathbb C$.

If the first column of $Q$ is $(a,c)^{\mathsf T}$, its unit orthogonal vectors are $z(-\overline c,\overline a)^{\mathsf T}$ with $|z|=1$. The determinant of the matrix with these columns is $z(|a|^2+|c|^2)=z$; $\det Q=1$ therefore forces $z=1$. Thus $Q=\begin{pmatrix}a&-\overline c\\c&\overline a\end{pmatrix}$ and $|a|^2+|c|^2=1$. This identifies $SU(2)$ with the unit sphere $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. Under this identification use the standard Euclidean inner product $\cdot$ and norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ on $\mathbb R^4$. The sphere is path-connected: non-antipodal points are joined by normalizing their straight segment. For antipodal points $x,-x\in S^3$, at least one of the first two standard basis vectors $e_1,e_2$ is not parallel to $x$; choose such an $e_j$ and set
$$w:=\frac{e_j-(e_j\cdot x)x}{\lVert e_j-(e_j\cdot x)x\rVert_2}.$$
The denominator is nonzero because $e_j$ is not parallel to $x$; hence $w\in S^3$ and $w\cdot x=0$. The normalized straight segments from $x$ to $w$ and from $w$ to $-x$ give a path. Hence there is a continuous path $Q_t$ in $SU(2)$ from $I$ to $Q$.

For $R=\begin{pmatrix}r&z\\0&r^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, the path $R_t:=\begin{pmatrix}r^t&tz\\0&r^{-t}\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant one for every $t\in[0,1]$, with $R_0=I$ and $R_1=R$. Thus $A_t:=Q_tR_t$ is a continuous path in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ from $I$ to $A=QR$. Since $A$ was arbitrary, $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is path-connected.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$
