For $u\in\mathbb R^3$, set $\gamma:=\sqrt{1+|u|^2}$ and
$S:=I_3+\frac{uu^{\mathsf T}}{1+\gamma}$. Define
$B(u):=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&u^{\mathsf T}\\u&S\end{pmatrix}$. The identities
$|u|^2=\gamma^2-1$ and
$S^2=I_3+\bigl(\frac{2}{1+\gamma}+\frac{|u|^2}{(1+\gamma)^2}\bigr)uu^{\mathsf T}
=I_3+uu^{\mathsf T}$ give $B(u)^{\mathsf T}\eta B(u)=\eta$: the time-time entry is $-\gamma^2+|u|^2=-1$, the time-space block is $-\gamma u^{\mathsf T}+u^{\mathsf T}S=0$, and the spatial block is $-uu^{\mathsf T}+S^2=I_3$. Also $B(u)e_0=(\gamma,u)$ is future timelike. The continuous path $t\mapsto B(tu)$ consists of Lorentz maps and starts at the identity, so its determinant, which is always $\pm1$, stays $+1$. Since it sends the future vector $e_0$ to the future component, the Lorentz map preserves that component by [F2]. Thus $B(u)\in SO^+(1,3)$.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, write $\Lambda e_0=(\gamma,u)$. Preservation of $\eta$ and the future cone gives $\gamma=\sqrt{1+|u|^2}>0$, so the matrix in step 1.1 satisfies $B(u)e_0=\Lambda e_0$. Then $R:=B(u)^{-1}\Lambda$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map fixing $e_0$. Its first column is $e_0$, and preservation of $\eta$ makes its first row $e_0^{\mathsf T}$; therefore $R=\operatorname{diag}(1,R_3)$ with $R_3^{\mathsf T}R_3=I_3$ and $\det R_3=1$.

The real cubic characteristic polynomial of $R_3$ has a real root, and every real eigenvalue of an orthogonal matrix is $+1$ or $-1$. If there were no $+1$ eigenvalue, then either all three eigenvalues would be $-1$, giving determinant $-1$, or the other two would be a conjugate pair with product $1$, again giving determinant $-1$. Both contradict $\det R_3=1$. Choose a unit eigenvector $n$ for eigenvalue $+1$. Its orthogonal plane is invariant; the restriction to that plane is orthogonal with determinant $1$, hence is a two-dimensional rotation by an angle $\theta$. Choose a unit vector $m\perp n$ and then a unit vector $p\perp n,m$ so $(n,m,p)$ is positively oriented; such $m,p$ are obtained by finite orthogonalization in the two-dimensional plane. In this basis the matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\0&\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Replacing $\theta$ by $s\theta$ for $s\in[0,1]$ gives a continuous path $R_3(s)$ in $SO(3)$ from $I_3$ to $R_3$.

Use the path $B(2tu)$ for $0\le t\le \frac12$, followed by
$B(u)\operatorname{diag}(1,R_3(2t-1))$ for $\frac12\le t\le1$, where $R_3(s)$ is the path from step 3.1. This is a continuous path in $SO^+(1,3)$ from $I_4$ to $\Lambda=B(u)R$. Hence $SO^+(1,3)$ is path-connected.

In $O(1,3)$, the determinant takes only the values $+1,-1$, so the subset with determinant $+1$ is both open and closed. The continuous map $L\mapsto Le_0$ takes $O(1,3)$ into the timelike set; by [F2], the preimage of the future timelike component is also both open and closed. Their intersection is $SO^+(1,3)$ and contains $I_4$, so the connected component of $I_4$ in $O(1,3)$ lies in $SO^+(1,3)$. Step 4.1 joins every member of $SO^+(1,3)$ to $I_4$, giving the reverse inclusion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). Then there is an open
neighborhood $U\subseteq M$ of $p$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad field
$(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$
([[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]), i.e.
$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$ for all $q\in U$ with
$E_0(q)$ future-directed for every $q\in U$.

An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$. For $n>0$, a chart is oriented when its coordinate frame is in that ray. For $n=0$, the datum is a sign at each point; the unique empty frame does not encode both choices.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ and $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2,F_3)$ be two
future-directed tetrads at $p$ ([[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]).
Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Then there is a unique real
$4\times4$ matrix $\Lambda=(\Lambda^B{}_A)$ such that
$F_A=\sum_B\Lambda^B{}_AE_B$ for all $A$, and:

1. $\sum_{C,D}\Lambda^C{}_A\,\eta_{CD}\,\Lambda^D{}_B=\eta_{AB}$ for all
   $A,B$; equivalently $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$.
2. $\Lambda$ is invertible and $\det\Lambda=\pm1$.
3. $\Lambda^0{}_0>0$.
4. For every covariant $2$-tensor $T$ at $p$, its components in the two
   tetrads satisfy
   $T(F_A,F_B)=\sum_{C,D}\Lambda^C{}_A\Lambda^D{}_BT(E_C,E_D)$.
   More generally, for a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ each contravariant slot
   contributes a factor $(\Lambda^{-1})^A{}_B$ and each covariant slot a
   factor $\Lambda^A{}_B$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Let $G$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie group, $M$ a smooth manifold, and $P$
a smooth manifold. A **smooth right principal $G$-bundle** is a right principal
$G$-bundle $\pi:P\to M$ in the topological sense of
[[def-principal-g-bundle-and-associated-fiber-bundle]], with the following
additional smooth structure: $\pi$ and the right $G$-action are smooth, and
the principal-bundle charts can be chosen as equivariant diffeomorphisms
$\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times G$. Thus each chart respects the projection to
$U$ and the right action on the $G$ factor. The smoothness convention is that
of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]; boundaryless manifolds
are the default in this item.

The topological principal-bundle clause retains its free, transitive right
action on every fibre and its local triviality. Smoothness adds compatible
differentiable structure; it does not select a connection or assert that a
global trivialization exists. The empty-base case is allowed and then $P$ is
empty by the cited topological definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: For each point $p$, use [F1] to choose a neighborhood $U$ and a smooth future-directed tetrad $E$ there. In a local oriented coordinate frame, the determinant of the component matrix of $E$ is a smooth nonzero real function; shrink $U$ to a connected neighborhood of $p$, so its sign is constant. If that sign is negative, replace $E_1$ by $-E_1$. This preserves orthonormality and the future direction of $E_0$ and makes $E$ positively oriented by [F2]. Thus positively oriented future tetrads exist locally.

Let $u,v$ lie in a common fiber of $P^+_g(M)$. Since $u$ is an isomorphism, $A:=u^{-1}v$ is the unique real matrix with $v=u\circ A$. The isometry condition gives $A^{\mathsf T}\eta A=\eta$. Positivity of the two frame orientations gives $\det A>0$, while the Lorentz identity gives $\det A=\pm1$, hence $\det A=1$. Because $u(e_0)$ and $v(e_0)$ are future timelike, $A e_0$ is future timelike; so $A$ preserves the selected future component and belongs to $SO^+(1,3)$. This proves that the right action is transitive on each fiber; uniqueness of $A$ proves freeness.

For a local positively oriented future tetrad section $E$ on $U$, define $\Psi_E:U\times SO^+(1,3)\to(P^+_g(M))|_U$ by $\Psi_E(p,A)=E(p)\circ A$. Step 1.2 makes this map bijective. Its inverse sends a frame $u$ over $p$ to $(p,E(p)^{-1}\circ u)$; the matrix entries of this second component are smooth because they are obtained by applying the smooth dual coframe of $E$ to the smooth frame vectors of $u$. Thus $\Psi_E$ is a smooth local product chart.

If $E'$ is another such section on an overlap, write $E'(p)=E(p)\circ A(p)$. The coefficients of $A(p)$ are smooth by the same dual-coframe calculation in step 2.1, and step 1.2 places every value in $SO^+(1,3)$. The transition between the charts is $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)B)$, which is smooth; its inverse $(p,B)\mapsto(p,A(p)^{-1}B)$ is smooth because inversion is smooth in the Lie group of [F4]. The right action is smooth in these charts and the projection is the product projection.

The charts of step 2.1 and smooth transitions from step 3.1 give $P^+_g(M)$ local products $U\times SO^+(1,3)$. Different base points separate by the Hausdorff base [F6], and distinct frames over one point separate in the Hausdorff matrix group [F4], so the total space is Hausdorff. For second countability, let $\mathcal B$ be a countable base of $M$; for each $B\in\mathcal B$ contained in at least one local-section neighborhood, use [A1] to select one such neighborhood. The selected countable family covers $M$, and countable bases of each selected $U\times SO^+(1,3)$ give a countable base of the total space by [F4,F6]. Thus the local charts define a smooth manifold structure. Freeness and fiberwise transitivity were proved in step 1.2; by [F5], this is a smooth right principal $SO^+(1,3)$-bundle. The construction supplies local sections only, so no global tetrad is asserted.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For a complex matrix $A$, write $A^\dagger:=\overline A^{\mathsf T}$. On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle:=u^\dagger v$ and $\|u\|:=\sqrt{u^\dagger u}$, and set $SU(2):=\{Q:Q^\dagger Q=I,\det Q=1\}$. Give $M_2(\mathbb C)$ its Euclidean topology as $\mathbb R^8$, and define $SL(2,\mathbb C):=\{A\in M_2(\mathbb C):\det A=1\}$ with matrix multiplication. Then $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is path-connected.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ on $\mathbb R^4$ and let
$C^+:=\{(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3:t>|x|\}$. Give
$M_4(\mathbb R)$ its Euclidean topology and define
$O(1,3):=\{L\in M_4(\mathbb R):L^{\mathsf T}\eta L=\eta\}$ with the
induced subspace topology. Define
$SO^+(1,3):=\{L\in O(1,3):\det L=1,\ L(C^+)=C^+\}$ with the same induced
topology. The **identity component** means the connected component of $I_4$
in $O(1,3)$ for this topology. Then $SO^+(1,3)$ is path-connected and equals
that identity component.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the referenced cotangent and symplectic-action conventions. Work on affine Minkowski spacetime with inertial coordinates $x^0=ct,x^1,x^2,x^3$ in metres, metric matrix $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and cotangent coordinates $(x^a,p_a)$, where each $p_a$ has SI momentum units. Fix the future cone as the timelike component containing the positive $x^0$ axis, equivalently $v^0>\lvert\mathbf v\rvert$. Let $SO^+(1,3)$ denote the determinant-one, future-cone-preserving Lorentz subgroup. Define the proper orthochronous Poincaré group and its multiplication by

$$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3),\qquad (a,\Lambda)(b,L)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda L).$$

Its action on spacetime and the cotangent lift are $x'=\Lambda x+a$ and $p'=\Lambda^{-T}p$. The Lie algebra consists of pairs $(a,A)$ with $A^T\eta+\eta A=0$, bracket

$$[(a,A),(b,B)]=(Ab-Ba,[A,B]).$$

Use the library convention $\xi_M=\left.\frac d{ds}\right|_0\exp_G(-s\xi)\cdot z$. Thus the positive affine generator on spacetime is $Y_{(a,A)}(x)=a+Ax$, the fundamental field is its negative, and the cotangent-lifted positive field is $(a+Ax,-A^Tp)$. Pair the cotangent point with a Lie-algebra element by

$$\ell_{(a,A)}(x,p)=p_b(a^b+A^b{}_cx^c).$$

Define $P^a=\eta^{ab}p_b$ and $J^{ab}=x^aP^b-x^bP^a$. The equivalent dual pairing is $\ell_{(a,A)}=p_ba^b-\tfrac12J_{bc}A^{bc}$, where $A^{bc}=A^b{}_d\eta^{dc}$ and $J_{bc}=\eta_{bd}\eta_{ce}J^{de}$. Here $[P^a]=\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$ and $[J^{ab}]=\mathrm{J\,s}$. These are charge-space definitions on the full cotangent bundle; shell reduction and the moment-map identities are stated separately. No spin or particle model is included.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered $\eta$-orthonormal basis with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. For a linear map $K:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) with matrix $M$ in this basis, the following are
equivalent:

(a) $\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0$ for all $v,w\in V$;
(b) $M^{T}\eta_0+\eta_0M=0$;
(c) $M$ has the block form
$M=\begin{pmatrix}0&u^{T}\\ u&\Omega\end{pmatrix}$ with
$u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\Omega^{T}=-\Omega$.

The set
$\mathfrak g:=\{K:\eta(Kv,w)+\eta(v,Kw)=0\text{ for all }v,w\}$ is a
$6$-dimensional linear subspace of the space of linear maps $V\to V$. Define
the maps $M_{ab}$ for all $0\le a,b\le3$ by
$(M_{ab})^{\mu}{}_{\nu}=\delta^{\mu}_{a}\eta_{b\nu}
-\delta^{\mu}_{b}\eta_{a\nu}$. Thus $M_{aa}=0$ and $M_{ba}=-M_{ab}$; the six maps with $a<b$ form a basis of
$\mathfrak g$ and satisfy
$[M_{ab},M_{cd}]=\eta_{bc}M_{ad}-\eta_{ac}M_{bd}-\eta_{bd}M_{ac}
+\eta_{ad}M_{bc}$ for all $0\le a,b,c,d\le3$, where
$[K_1,K_2]:=K_1K_2-K_2K_1$ is the commutator. Here a real Lie algebra means a real vector space with a bilinear antisymmetric bracket satisfying $[K_1,[K_2,K_3]]+[K_2,[K_3,K_1]]+[K_3,[K_1,K_2]]=0$. The commutator makes $\mathfrak g$ such an algebra.
If $L:I\to O(V,\eta)$, with $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ an open interval containing $0$, is a
$\mathcal C^1$ curve in $O(V,\eta)$ with $L(0)=\operatorname{id}_V$, then its
derivative $K:=L'(0)$ belongs to $\mathfrak g$, and $L(s)=\operatorname{id}_V+sK+o(s)$ as $s\to0$. Here $\mathcal C^1$ means that each matrix entry is continuously differentiable on $I$, $K$ has entries $(L^a{}_b)\prime(0)$, and $o(s)$ denotes a matrix remainder each of whose entries divided by $|s|$ tends to $0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

A **finite-dimensional real Lie group** is a group $G$, in the sense of
[[def-group]], together with the structure of a finite-dimensional real smooth
manifold such that the maps

$$m:G\times G\longrightarrow G,\qquad m(g,h)=gh,$$

and

$$\operatorname{inv}:G\longrightarrow G,\qquad \operatorname{inv}(g)=g^{-1},$$

are smooth in the sense of
[[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]]. Its identity element is
denoted by $e$ (or occasionally $1$).

Unless an item explicitly says otherwise, every Lie group on this page is real,
finite-dimensional, and has no manifold boundary. Dimension zero is allowed;
for example, any countable discrete group with its discrete zero-dimensional
smooth structure is a Lie group. A Lie group cannot be empty because a group
contains its identity. The definition applies unchanged in dimension one,
uses no metric or nondegeneracy hypothesis, and makes no choice from a family
of sets.

derivations.claim:
Every Hermitian matrix has a unique form $X(x)$, since its two real diagonal entries determine $x^0,x^3$ and its complex off-diagonal entry determines $x^1,x^2$. Direct evaluation gives
$$X(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x^0+x^3&x^1-ix^2\\x^1+ix^2&x^0-x^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det X(x)=(x^0)^2-(x^1)^2-(x^2)^2-(x^3)^2.$$
Near its identity, the set $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ is a smooth real six-dimensional manifold: where the upper-left entry $a$ is nonzero, writing a matrix as $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, the equation $ad-bc=1$ uniquely gives $d=(1+bc)/a$, so $(a,b,c)$ are six real local coordinates. Left translates of this chart cover the group and have smooth transitions because left multiplication is a smooth invertible matrix map. The group product and inverse are smooth matrix operations, so [F8] makes $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ a Lie group.

For $A\in SL(2,\mathbb C)$, multiplicativity and the conjugate-transpose determinant identity in [F1] give $\det(AXA^\dagger)=\det X$. Thus the action defines a real linear Lorentz map $\rho(A)$; composition satisfies $\rho(AB)=\rho(A)\rho(B)$, and the coordinate entries are quadratic polynomials in the entries of $A$, so $\rho$ is smooth. Given any $A$, choose a path $A_t$ in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ from $I$ to $A$ by [F2]. Then $t\mapsto\rho(A_t)$ is a path of Lorentz maps from the identity to $\rho(A)$. By [F4], its endpoint is in $SO^+(1,3)$.

A tangent matrix at $I$ to $SL(2,\mathbb C)$ has trace zero: differentiating $ad-bc=1$ at $I$ gives $Z_{11}+Z_{22}=0$. Conversely, for any trace-zero $Z=\begin{pmatrix}z&b\\c&-z\end{pmatrix}$, the curve
$$A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1+tz&tb\\tc&(1+t^2bc)/(1+tz)\end{pmatrix}$$
has determinant one near $0$ and derivative $Z$ at $0$. Hence the real tangent space has dimension six. Differentiating the action gives
$$d\rho_I(Z)X=ZX+XZ^\dagger.$$
Since [F1] shows that the action preserves $-\det X$, differentiation places $d\rho_I(Z)$ in the tangent space of the Lorentz group. If it vanishes for every Hermitian $X$, then $X=I$ gives $Z^\dagger=-Z$, and the remaining equations give $ZX=XZ$ for every Hermitian $X$. Commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ makes $Z$ diagonal; commuting with $\sigma_1$ makes its diagonal entries equal. Its trace is zero, so $Z=0$. Thus $d\rho_I$ is injective. Every tangent $K$ to $SO^+(1,3)$ at $I$ is the derivative of a smooth curve $\Lambda(t)$ in that group. Differentiating $\Lambda(t)^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda(t)=\eta$ at $t=0$ gives $K^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta K=0$, so by [F6] the target tangent lies in the six-dimensional eta-skew space. By [F5] its own dimension is six, hence it equals that space. The injective differential between the six-dimensional source and target tangent spaces is therefore an isomorphism.

Apply [F7] in smooth coordinate charts at the identity, using step 3.1: after shrinking a neighborhood $U$ of $I$ in $SL(2,\mathbb C)$, $\rho$ maps $U$ diffeomorphically onto a neighborhood $V$ of the identity in $SO^+(1,3)$. Since $\rho$ is a homomorphism, its image is a subgroup containing $V$ and hence is open. Every coset of this subgroup is open; its complement is a union of open cosets, so the image is also closed. The target is connected by [F4], and the image is nonempty, so it is all of $SO^+(1,3)$.

If $A$ lies in the kernel, then $AXA^\dagger=X$ for every Hermitian $X$. Setting $X=I$ gives $AA^\dagger=I$, so $A$ is unitary and the same equations imply $AX=XA$. Commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $\sigma_1$ as in step 3.1 forces $A=zI$; $\det A=1$ gives $z^2=1$. Both $I$ and $-I$ act trivially, hence the kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$. Shrink $U$ from step 4.1 so that $U\cap(-U)=\varnothing$. If $\rho(B)\in V$, let $C\in U$ be the unique point with $\rho(C)=\rho(B)$; then $BC^{-1}$ is in the kernel, so $B=C$ or $B=-C$. Therefore $\rho^{-1}(V)=U\sqcup(-U)$ and both pieces map diffeomorphically to $V$. Translating this neighborhood by any target element gives evenly covered neighborhoods everywhere, proving that $\rho$ is a two-sheeted covering.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad
\omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad
F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$
For every differential form $\omega$, $d(d\omega)=0$.

derivations.claim:
For smooth vector fields $X,Y$ on $U$, evaluating exterior derivative and the wedge product gives $T^I(X,Y)=X(e^I(Y))-Y(e^I(X))-e^I([X,Y])+\omega^I{}_J(X)e^J(Y)-\omega^I{}_J(Y)e^J(X)$. Since $Y=e^J(Y)E_J$, the connection definition gives $e^I(
abla_XY)=X(e^I(Y))+\omega^I{}_J(X)e^J(Y)$; the corresponding formula with $X,Y$ exchanged shows $T^I(X,Y)=e^I(
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y])$. Thus all coframe torsion forms vanish exactly when the induced affine-connection torsion vanishes.

Write $\alpha:=d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}$ and $\bar\omega:=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}$, so $\omega'=\bar\omega-\alpha$. By [F3] applied componentwise and [F4], differentiating $\Lambda\Lambda^{-1}=I$ gives $d\Lambda^{-1}=-\Lambda^{-1}d\Lambda\Lambda^{-1}$ and then
$$d\alpha=d^2\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\wedge d\Lambda^{-1}=\alpha\wedge\alpha.$$
The same graded product rule gives
$$d\bar\omega=d\Lambda\wedge\omega\Lambda^{-1}+\Lambda d\omega\Lambda^{-1}-\Lambda\omega\wedge d\Lambda^{-1}=\alpha\wedge\bar\omega+\Lambda(d\omega)\Lambda^{-1}+\bar\omega\wedge\alpha.$$
Expanding $d\omega'+\omega'\wedge\omega'$ and substituting these identities cancels the $\alpha$ terms and leaves $\Lambda(d\omega+\omega\wedge\omega)\Lambda^{-1}$, hence $F'=\Lambda F\Lambda^{-1}$. Also [F3] gives $de'=d\Lambda\wedge e+\Lambda de$ and $\omega'\wedge e'=\Lambda\omega\wedge e-d\Lambda\wedge e$, hence $T'=\Lambda T$.

Restrict the unique Levi-Civita connection supplied by [F2] to $U$. Its connection coefficients in $E$ are smooth; metric compatibility and the constant frame metric $\eta_{IJ}$ give $\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. Its tangent torsion is zero, so step 1.1 makes every $T^I$ zero. This proves existence of an $\eta$-skew solution.

Conversely, an $\eta$-skew $\omega$ induces a metric-compatible connection. For $V=V^IE_I$ and $W=W^JE_J$, the connection terms in $g(\nabla_XV,W)+g(V,\nabla_XW)$ are $\omega_{KJ}V^JW^K+\omega_{IJ}V^IW^J=0$ after interchanging the summed indices in the first term and using $\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$; the remaining terms equal $X(g(V,W))$. If also $T^I=0$, step 1.1 gives zero tangent torsion. By uniqueness in [F2], this connection is the Levi-Civita connection. Hence the solution from step 2.1 is unique, and the displayed torsion equation is equivalent to torsion-freeness.
Steps 1.1–3.1 establish the torsion equivalence and unique Levi-Civita identification; step 1.2 establishes both transformation laws.

derivations.claim: From the Clifford relation, $\gamma^I\gamma^J\gamma^K=2\eta^{JK}\gamma^I-2\eta^{IK}\gamma^J+\gamma^K\gamma^I\gamma^J$. Subtracting $\gamma^K\gamma^I\gamma^J$ gives $[\gamma^I\gamma^J,\gamma^K]=2(\eta^{JK}\gamma^I-\eta^{IK}\gamma^J)$. This is an algebraic identity for every triple of indices, including repeated indices, and uses no group-representation covariance hypothesis.

Contract step 1.1 with $\frac14\omega_{IJ}$. Since $\omega_{IJ}\eta^{JK}=-\omega^K{}_I$ by antisymmetry and $\omega_{IJ}\eta^{IK}=\omega^K{}_J$, the two terms each contribute $-\frac12\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J$ after relabeling the summed index. Hence $[\Gamma,\gamma^K]=-\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J$. The contraction is valid because each $\omega_{IJ}$ is scalar-valued and the gamma matrices are constant in the chosen local frame.

Write $c(V)=V_K\gamma^K$. Then step 2.1 gives $dc(V)+[\Gamma,c(V)]=dV_K\gamma^K-V_K\omega^K{}_J\gamma^J=(dV_J-\omega^K{}_J V_K)\gamma^J=c(
abla V)$. For a spinor $\psi$, expand $D(c(V)\psi)=d(c(V)\psi)+\Gamma c(V)\psi$ and use
$\Gamma c(V)=c(V)\Gamma+[\Gamma,c(V)]$. The result is
$c(
abla V)\psi+c(V)(d\psi+\Gamma\psi)=c(
abla V)\psi+c(V)D\psi$, as asserted.

derivations.claim: Let $J$ be the stated generator, so $\Lambda=\exp(\theta J)$. Put $c=\cosh r$ and $s=\sinh r$. Multiplying the upper-left $2\times2$ block gives
$B(r)^{\mathsf T}\eta B(r)=\eta$, because $c^2-s^2=1$ and the off-diagonal time-space terms cancel. The determinant of that block is $1$, the remaining block is identity, and $B(r)e_0=(c,s,0,0)$ is future timelike since $c>|s|$. Hence $B(r)\in SO^+(1,3)$. For the Euclidean form, however,
$\delta(B(r)e_0,B(r)e_0)=c^2+s^2>1=\delta(e_0,e_0)$ for $r\ne0$, so $B(r)\notin SO(4)$. A map with codomain $SO(4)$ cannot lift this element through its covering map.

Write $A(r)=\cosh(r/2)I+\sinh(r/2)\sigma_1$. Its eigenvalues are $e^{r/2}$ and $e^{-r/2}$, so $\det A(r)=1$. Pauli multiplication gives
$AIA^\dagger=\cosh r\,I+\sinh r\,\sigma_1$,
$A\sigma_1A^\dagger=\sinh r\,I+\cosh r\,\sigma_1$, and

derivations.claim: The 1-skeleton of a connected CW complex is connected: attaching a cell of dimension at least two has connected attaching sphere, so it cannot join two components of the preceding skeleton. Since $K$ is finite, its 1-skeleton is a finite connected graph. The unique paths in $T$ contract it to $v_0$, supplying the contraction required by [F2]. The quotient that collapses $T$ to a point is a wedge with one circle for each 1-cell outside $T$, and [F3] gives the free basis represented by the loops $x_e$.

Suppose a 2-cell is attached to a path-connected finite subcomplex $X$ along $\alpha:S^1\to X$. In the attached space, the open sets consisting of $X$ together with an outer collar of the disk and the inner open disk cover the space; the first retracts to $X$, the second is contractible, and their overlap is an annulus retracting to $S^1$. Choose a basepoint on that annulus and connect it to $v_0$ and to the attaching basepoint by the collar and a path in $X$. Under the retraction to $X$, the once-around generator of the annulus maps to the resulting based attaching loop $\gamma*\alpha*\bar\gamma$; in the inner disk it maps to the identity. By [F4] and [F5], the pushout therefore imposes exactly that loop as a relation. The quotient by its normal closure has the same universal property: a homomorphism out of it is precisely a homomorphism out of $\pi_1(X,v_0)$ that sends the based attaching loop to the identity.

Attaching the finitely many 2-cells one at a time therefore quotients the free group from step 1.1 by the normal closure of all the words $r_f$. Replacing a connecting path conjugates the corresponding based loop, so its normal closure is unchanged.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. A **piecewise-smooth path** in $U$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ for which some finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ makes every restriction $\gamma|_{[t_{j-1},t_j]}$ smooth as a map of manifolds with boundary. Its source and target are $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$. The collection of all such paths is a set: it is a subset, defined by separation, of the function set from $[0,1]$ to $U$.

Two paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ with the same source $x$ and target $y$ are **thin-homotopic**, written $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$, if there is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to U$ and a finite subdivision of the square into compact curvilinear triangles such that $H$ is smooth up to each triangle's boundary, $H(0,t)=\gamma_0(t)$, $H(1,t)=\gamma_1(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$, $H(s,1)=y$, and $\operatorname{rank}(dH_{(s,t)})\le 1$ on every smooth triangle. A **curvilinear triangle** here is a compact region $D$ equipped with a specified homeomorphism $\psi:\Delta^2\to D$ from the standard closed two-simplex which is a smooth embedding on the interior, extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, and maps the three edges of $\Delta^2$ to the three boundary arcs of $D$. Saying $H$ is smooth up to $D$'s boundary means that $H\circ\psi$ extends smoothly from $\Delta^2$ to an open neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, with values in $U$; equivalently, it is a smooth singular $2$-simplex under the neighborhood-extension convention of [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. The rank is the dimension of the image of the differential from the two-dimensional tangent space of the triangle to $T_{H(s,t)}M$, computed through the interior chart $\psi$ and extended to boundary points by these smooth extensions. The quotient by this relation is used only after its equivalence and compatibility properties are proved.

A **binary relation** on a set $A$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times A$
([[def-relation-domain-range-and-field]], [[def-cartesian-product]]); we write
$a \sim b$ for $(a,b) \in R$ and read it "$a$ is related to $b$".

A binary relation $\sim$ on $A$ is an **equivalence relation** when it is reflexive
on $A$, symmetric and transitive ([[def-properties-of-a-relation-on-a-set]]), that
is, when it is

- **reflexive**: $a \sim a$ for every $a \in A$;
- **symmetric**: $a \sim b$ implies $b \sim a$, for all $a, b \in A$;
- **transitive**: $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$ imply $a \sim c$, for all
  $a, b, c \in A$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For $a \in A$, the **equivalence
class** of $a$ is the subset

$$[a] \;:=\; \{\, b \in A \;:\; a \sim b \,\} \;\subseteq\; A,$$

and any $b$ with $[b] = C$ is called a **representative** of the class $C$. The
**quotient set** is the set of all classes,

$$A/{\sim} \;:=\; \{\, [a] \;:\; a \in A \,\},$$

a subset of the power set of $A$ ([[def-power-set]]). The map
$\pi : A \to A/{\sim}$ ([[def-function]]) with $\pi(a) = [a]$ is the **quotient
map**; it is surjective by construction ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

In a category $\mathcal C$ ([[def-category]]), a morphism $f:A\to B$ is an
**isomorphism** if there is a morphism $g:B\to A$ with
$g\circ f=1_A$ and $f\circ g=1_B$. Such a $g$ is unique and is denoted
$f^{-1}$.

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism. A
category is **connected** when it is nonempty and any two objects can be joined
by a finite zigzag of morphisms, with successive arrows allowed to point in
either direction. In a groupoid this is equivalent to being nonempty and having
an isomorphism between every ordered pair of objects. Nonemptiness cannot be
dropped: the empty groupoid has an isomorphism between every ordered pair of its
objects, vacuously, and is not connected.

derivations.claim: The relation is reflexive because $H(s,t)=\gamma(t)$ has rank at most one and fixed endpoints; subdivide the square along each breakpoint of a finite smooth partition of $\gamma$ and triangulate the resulting strips. It is symmetric by replacing $s$ with $1-s$ and reflecting a witnessing subdivision. For transitivity, first take finite common refinements of the boundary subdivisions of $H_0$ and $H_1$ along their common path $\gamma_1$, then paste $H_0(2s,t)$ on $0\le s\le\tfrac12$ to $H_1(2s-1,t)$ on $\tfrac12\le s\le1$. The common boundary is the same path $\gamma_1$, so this paste is continuous; the scaled finite subdivisions on the two halves give a finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision after triangulating any resulting polygons. It fixes both path endpoints, and its differential has rank at most one on each triangle. Thus the relation is an equivalence relation.

If $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$ and $\delta_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1$ with matching endpoints, paste their homotopies on the first and second halves of the path parameter, scaling their finite subdivisions to those halves and taking a finite common refinement along their shared fixed endpoint. The shared endpoint is fixed throughout each homotopy, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth; on each triangle its differential has image contained in that of the corresponding homotopy differential, hence rank at most one. Therefore $\delta_0*\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1*\gamma_1$, and composition of classes is well-defined.

Let $\Gamma$ be the path obtained by placing the three given paths, in order, on the three consecutive thirds of $[0,1]$. Each parenthesized concatenation is $\Gamma\circ\phi_j$ for an increasing piecewise-linear homeomorphism $\phi_j:[0,1]\to[0,1]$. Put $u(s,t)=(1-s)\phi_0(t)+s\phi_1(t)$ and $H(s,t)=\Gamma(u(s,t))$. Refine the $t$-partition by all breakpoints of $\phi_0$ and $\phi_1$. On each resulting strip $u$ is smooth and piecewise bilinear. For every breakpoint $b$ of the piecewise-smooth path $\Gamma$, also subdivide along the level set $u^{-1}(b)$; on each strip these finitely many level sets are smooth arcs, with their finitely many endpoints and intersections included in the subdivision. The resulting regions have finitely many smooth boundary arcs and can be triangulated into curvilinear triangles. On each triangle, $u$ remains in one smooth piece of $\Gamma$, so $H$ is smooth there and both differential columns are scalar multiples of the single vector $\Gamma'$. Its rank is at most one. Thus the two parenthesizations are thin-homotopic. For the right identity law use $\rho_0(t)=2t$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $\rho_0(t)=1$ on $[\tfrac12,1]$, with $\rho_1(t)=t$; for the left identity law use $\rho_0(t)=0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $\rho_0(t)=2t-1$ on $[\tfrac12,1]$, again with $\rho_1(t)=t$. The corresponding homotopies $\gamma((1-s)\rho_0(t)+s\rho_1(t))$ have the required concatenated and unaltered paths as boundaries. Refine each square along the parameter-map breakpoints and the preimages of every breakpoint of $\gamma$; any region on which the argument is constant is already smooth. The same rank argument proves both identity laws.

Put $\lambda(t)=2t$ for $0\le t\le\tfrac12$ and $\lambda(t)=2(1-t)$ for $\tfrac12\le t\le1$. Then $t\mapsto\gamma(\lambda(t))$ traverses $\gamma$ and then its reverse. The map $H(s,t)=\gamma((1-s)\lambda(t))$ joins this path to the constant path at $\gamma(0)$ with both endpoints fixed. Subdivide first at $t=\tfrac12$, then along the preimages of every breakpoint of a finite smooth partition of $\gamma$ under $(s,t)\mapsto(1-s)\lambda(t)$; these are finitely many smooth arcs or constant regions on the two parameter strips. Triangulating the resulting finite curvilinear regions makes $H$ smooth on each triangle. Its differential has rank at most one because both derivatives are scalar multiples of $\dot\gamma$. Applying the same construction to $\bar\gamma$ contracts the reverse-then-forward path at $\gamma(1)$. Hence $[\bar\gamma]$ is a two-sided inverse of $[\gamma]$.

The tagged morphism set has well-defined domain and codomain by construction; step 2.1 makes composition independent of representatives, step 3.1 gives associativity, and step 3.2 gives the inverse axiom. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 also provide the two identity laws stated in [F3]. Thus the data form a category in which every morphism is invertible, which is a groupoid by [F4].

citations.quote: A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. For an open subset $U$ of a smooth manifold, the **thin path groupoid** $\Pi^{\mathrm{thin}}_1(U)$ is the category whose objects are the points of $U$ and whose morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are tagged triples $(x,y,[\gamma])$, where $[\gamma]$ is a thin-homotopy class of piecewise-smooth paths from $x$ to $y$; composition, identities, and inverses are those of Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-thin-path-quotient-groupoid]].

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge0$, put
$$A^k=\{(t_0,\ldots,t_k)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\textstyle\sum_i t_i=1\}.$$
A **smooth singular $k$-simplex** in $M$ is a map $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ for which there are an open set $O\subseteq A^k$ containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with $\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$. The simplex and its face maps are [[def-standard-topological-simplex-and-its-affine-face-maps]]. Smoothness into a boundary target is that of [[def-smooth-map-between-manifolds-with-boundary]].

The extension takes values in $M$ on all of $O$, including points outside the simplex. Merely extending its chart coordinates to a Euclidean space with values outside $M$ does not suffice. Nor is separate smoothness of the face restrictions the definition. For a boundaryless target this is the usual neighbourhood-extension convention.

Write $S_k^\infty(M)$ for this set of maps; the extension itself is not additional simplex data. Every such map is continuous. At $k=0$, $A^0=\Delta^0$ is a point, so every point of $M$ is a smooth zero-simplex. Constant maps are smooth in every degree, including maps to a boundary point, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. The empty manifold has no simplices. No simultaneous choice of extensions is part of this definition.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$

For a smooth map $F:M\to N$, pullback sends smooth differential forms on $N$ to
smooth differential forms on $M$, is functorial, and satisfies

$$ F^*(\alpha\wedge\beta)=F^*\alpha\wedge F^*\beta. $$

derivations.claim: The map $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ has derivative $(2x,2y)$, which is nonzero on $f^{-1}(1)$; thus $1$ is a regular value and [F2] makes $S^1$ a smooth one-dimensional submanifold. Let $\widetilde\alpha=x\,dy-y\,dx$ be the ambient one-form on $\mathbb R^2$, let $\iota:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^2$ be inclusion, and put $\alpha=\iota^*\widetilde\alpha$, which is defined by [F8] and smooth by [F9]. The global tangent field $X=(-y,x)|_{S^1}$ spans each tangent line and satisfies $\alpha(X)=x^2+y^2=1$. By [F4], $d\alpha(X,X)=X(\alpha(X))-X(\alpha(X))-\alpha([X,X])=0$; since $X$ spans each one-dimensional tangent space, this gives $d\alpha=0$ intrinsically on $S^1$. Along $\gamma$, $\dot\gamma(t)=2\pi X_{\gamma(t)}$, so [F6] gives $\int_\gamma\alpha=\int_0^1 2\pi\,dt=2\pi$; the constant loop has integral zero.

Suppose a thin homotopy $H:[0,1]^2\to S^1$ joined $\gamma$ to the constant loop while fixing the basepoint at the path endpoints. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. A **piecewise-smooth path** in $U$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ for which some finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ makes every restriction $\gamma|_{[t_{j-1},t_j]}$ smooth as a map of manifolds with boundary. Its source and target are $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$. The collection of all such paths is a set: it is a subset, defined by separation, of the function set from $[0,1]$ to $U$.

Two paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ with the same source $x$ and target $y$ are **thin-homotopic**, written $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$, if there is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to U$ and a finite subdivision of the square into compact curvilinear triangles such that $H$ is smooth up to each triangle's boundary, $H(0,t)=\gamma_0(t)$, $H(1,t)=\gamma_1(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$, $H(s,1)=y$, and $\operatorname{rank}(dH_{(s,t)})\le 1$ on every smooth triangle. A **curvilinear triangle** here is a compact region $D$ equipped with a specified homeomorphism $\psi:\Delta^2\to D$ from the standard closed two-simplex which is a smooth embedding on the interior, extends smoothly to a neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, and maps the three edges of $\Delta^2$ to the three boundary arcs of $D$. Saying $H$ is smooth up to $D$'s boundary means that $H\circ\psi$ extends smoothly from $\Delta^2$ to an open neighborhood of $\Delta^2$ in its affine span, with values in $U$; equivalently, it is a smooth singular $2$-simplex under the neighborhood-extension convention of [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. The rank is the dimension of the image of the differential from the two-dimensional tangent space of the triangle to $T_{H(s,t)}M$, computed through the interior chart $\psi$ and extended to boundary points by these smooth extensions. The quotient by this relation is used only after its equivalence and compatibility properties are proved.

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Let $F(t,x,\lambda)$ be jointly $C^\infty$ in $(t,x,\lambda)$ on an open time-state-parameter
domain. Near any base data $(t_0,x_0,\lambda_0)$ there are a compact time
interval $I$ and a neighbourhood $W$ of $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ such that, for every
$(y,\lambda)\in W$, the solution of

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t),\lambda),\qquad x(t_0)=y,$$

is defined on $I$, and the resulting solution map is smooth in the pair
$(y,\lambda)$.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $K$ be a finite connected CW complex, let $v_0$ be a vertex, and let $T$ be a maximal tree in its 1-skeleton. Choose one orientation of each 1-cell outside $T$. For each such edge $e:u\to v$, let $x_e$ be the based loop that follows $T$ from $v_0$ to $u$, traverses $e$, and returns along $T$ from $v$ to $v_0$. For every 2-cell $f$, choose a point on its attaching circle and a path in the 1-skeleton from $v_0$ to its image; the resulting based attaching loop has a unique reduced word $r_f$ in the free basis $(x_e)$. Then

$$\pi_1(K,v_0)\cong \langle x_e\ (e\notin T)\mid r_f\ (f\text{ a 2-cell})\rangle.$$

Cells of dimension at least three add no generators or relators. Changing the connecting path conjugates its relator, and reversing an edge orientation inverts the corresponding generator, so these choices do not change the presented group.

Let $F(X)$ be a free group and let $R\subseteq F(X)$ be a set of words, called
**relations**. The group with presentation

$$\langle X\mid R\rangle:=F(X)/\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_{F(X)}$$

is the quotient by the normal closure of $R$. The members of $X$ are its
**generators**. In this quotient, every relation in $R$ becomes the identity,
as do all consequences forced by normality.

Let $G$ be a group and $R\subseteq G$. Then

$$\langle\!\langle R\rangle\!\rangle_G=\left\{g_1r_1^{\varepsilon_1}g_1^{-1}\cdots g_nr_n^{\varepsilon_n}g_n^{-1}:n\in\mathbb N,\ g_i\in G,\ r_i\in R,\ \varepsilon_i\in\{1,-1\}\right\}.$$

For $n=0$ the displayed product is the identity. Replacing every conjugator
$g_i$ by $g_i^{-1}$ gives the equivalent convention
$g_i^{-1}r_i^{\varepsilon_i}g_i$.

derivations.claim: On one closed curvilinear triangle $\Delta$ of the subdivision, pull the connection back by the smooth restriction of $H$ and write its two coefficient matrices as $A_s=\omega(H_s)$ and $A_t=\omega(H_t)$. For a smooth family of paths inside $\Delta$, let $U_t=-A_tU$, $U(s,0)=I$, and put $K=U_s+A_sU$. Smooth dependence in [F4] permits this differentiation, and [F5] gives uniqueness for the linear equation satisfied by $K$. The product rule gives $K_t+A_tK=-(\partial_sA_t-\partial_tA_s+[A_s,A_t])U=-H^*F(\partial_s,\partial_t)U$. Here [F3] identifies the pulled-back two-form as the curvature of the supplier connection.

Since $\operatorname{rank}(dH)\le1$ on $\Delta$, $H_s,H_t$ are linearly dependent and the alternating two-form satisfies $H^*F(\partial_s,\partial_t)=F(H_s,H_t)=0$. Fix a vertex $q_0$ and join it to each $q\in\Delta$ by the image of the straight radial path in the standard-simplex parametrization. The associated transports $Q(q)$ exist globally by [F5] and depend smoothly on $q$: apply [F4] locally in the endpoint parameter and continue over finitely many subintervals of the compact path interval, using uniqueness on overlaps. For each radial path, [F3] and the ODE give $(Q^{\mathsf T}\eta Q)'=0$, hence $Q(q)^{\mathsf T}\eta Q(q)=\eta$ and $Q(q)$ is invertible. Step 1.1 on this radial family with fixed start gives $dQ=-H^*\omega\,Q$. Thus transport from $q_1$ to $q_2$ in $\Delta$ is $Q(q_2)Q(q_1)^{-1}$ by [F5], and the triangle boundary transport is identity.

The finite curvilinear-triangle subdivision is a finite connected CW complex $K$; choose the lower-left corner as basepoint and a maximal tree in its one-skeleton. The outer boundary loop contracts to that basepoint by the straight-line contraction of the parameter square, so [F6] makes its fundamental-group class the identity. By [F7], $\pi_1(K)$ has generators given by non-tree edge loops closed along the tree and relators given by based triangular face boundaries. For each free generator $x_e$, assign the inverse transport of its based edge loop and extend to a homomorphism $\Phi$ from the free group; [F2]'s path-composition law gives $\Phi(w)=U_w^{-1}$ for every edge word $w$. These transports are invertible because along each segment [F3] and the ODE give $(U^{\mathsf T}\eta U)'=-U^{\mathsf T}(\omega^{\mathsf T}\eta+\eta\omega)U=0$, hence $U^{\mathsf T}\eta U=\eta$; reversing the ODE gives $U_{\bar\alpha}=U_\alpha^{-1}$. A based face relator is a tree path, a triangular boundary and the reverse tree path, so step 2.1 makes its transport and its $\Phi$-image the identity. The boundary word is identity in the presentation by [F6]–[F8], and [F9] writes it as a finite product of conjugates of face relators and their inverses; all of these map to $I$, so $U_\lambda=I$. The side edges of the square are constant by fixed endpoints, giving $U_\lambda=U_{\gamma_1}^{-1}U_{\gamma_0}$ and $U_{\gamma_0}(1)=U_{\gamma_1}(1)$.

In a category $\mathcal C$ ([[def-category]]), a morphism $f:A\to B$ is an
**isomorphism** if there is a morphism $g:B\to A$ with
$g\circ f=1_A$ and $f\circ g=1_B$. Such a $g$ is unique and is denoted
$f^{-1}$.

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism. A
category is **connected** when it is nonempty and any two objects can be joined
by a finite zigzag of morphisms, with successive arrows allowed to point in
either direction. In a groupoid this is equivalent to being nonempty and having
an isomorphism between every ordered pair of objects. Nonemptiness cannot be
dropped: the empty groupoid has an isomorphism between every ordered pair of its
objects, vacuously, and is not connected.

For categories $\mathcal C,\mathcal D$ ([[def-category]]), a **covariant
functor** $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ assigns an object $FA$ to every object
$A$ and a morphism $Ff:FA\to FB$ to every $f:A\to B$, satisfying

$$F(1_A)=1_{FA},\qquad F(g\circ f)=Fg\circ Ff.$$

The **identity functor** acts identically on objects and morphisms. For
$F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ and $G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal E$, the
**composite functor** $GF$ has $(GF)A=G(FA)$ and $(GF)f=G(Ff)$.

A **contravariant functor** from $\mathcal C$ to $\mathcal D$ means a covariant
functor $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathcal D$, using
[[def-opposite-category]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

derivations.claim: On the constant path the coefficient $\omega(\dot\gamma)$ is zero, so the unique solution is $U(t)=I$. If $\gamma$ is followed by $\delta$, solve on the two parameter intervals with the terminal value from the first interval as initial value for the second. The second solution is $U_\delta(t)U_\gamma(1)$, so uniqueness gives $U_{\delta*\gamma}(1)=U_\delta(1)U_\gamma(1)$.

Write $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. Along each smooth segment the derivative is $\frac{d}{dt}(U^{\mathsf T}\eta U)=U^{\mathsf T}(-\omega^{\mathsf T}\eta-\eta\omega)U=0$ by [F4]; continuity across the finite segment endpoints gives $U(t)^{\mathsf T}\eta U(t)=\eta$ throughout. Since $\eta$ is nonsingular, each $U(t)$ is invertible.

Let $U(t)$ solve along $\gamma$. The matrix $V(s):=U(1-s)U(1)^{-1}$ starts at $I$ and, since $\dot{\bar\gamma}(s)=-\dot\gamma(1-s)$, satisfies $V'(s)=-\omega(\dot{\bar\gamma}(s))V(s)$. Hence uniqueness gives $U_{\bar\gamma}(1)=U(1)^{-1}$. By [F3], transport is independent of the representative of a thin class; [F1]–[F2] and the identities in steps 1.1–1.2 therefore give well-defined component maps on the thin path groupoid.

For $[\gamma]:x\to y$ and $[\delta]:y\to z$, the associated tangent arrows compose as $(E_zU_\delta E_y^{-1})\circ(E_yU_\gamma E_x^{-1})=E_zU_\delta U_\gamma E_x^{-1}=E_zU_{\delta*\gamma}E_x^{-1}$ by step 1.1. Constant paths give identity tangent maps, and reversed paths give inverse tangent maps by step 2.1. Thus the stated object and arrow assignments define a functor into $\mathcal T(U)$ by [F6], with arrows in the stated groupoid by [F5].

Put $\widetilde U(t)=\Lambda(\gamma(t))U(t)\Lambda(\gamma(0))^{-1}$. Differentiating and using $U'=-\omega(\dot\gamma)U$ gives $\widetilde U'(t)=(d\Lambda(\dot\gamma)\Lambda^{-1}-\Lambda\omega(\dot\gamma)\Lambda^{-1})\widetilde U(t)=-\omega'(\dot\gamma)\widetilde U(t)$ by the transformation law [F4]. Its initial value is $I$, so uniqueness identifies $\widetilde U$ with transport in the changed frame and gives the endpoint formula. Since $E'_x=E_x\Lambda(x)^{-1}$, the corresponding tangent map is frame independent:
$$E'_yU'_\gamma(1)(E'_x)^{-1}=E_yU_\gamma(1)E_x^{-1}.$$
This is a local frame covariance statement; it is a principal-bundle gauge action only when $\Lambda$ has the global extension required by the cited gauge-group definition.
