citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$ and let $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=1$ be a finite partition. For each $j$, let $A_j:[t_{j-1},t_j]\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous. There is a unique continuous function $U:[0,1]\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ that is $C^1$ on each partition interval, satisfies $U'(t)=-A_j(t)U(t)$ in its interior, and has $U(0)=I_n$. Derivatives at interval endpoints are the corresponding one-sided derivatives.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

For transport as in [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]], with composition convention $[\delta]\circ[\gamma]=[\delta*\gamma]$ meaning first traverse $\gamma$ and then $\delta$,

$$U_{\delta*\gamma}(1)=U_\delta(1)U_\gamma(1),\qquad U_{\bar\gamma}(1)=U_\gamma(1)^{-1}.$$

Let $E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be the tetrad of [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]]. For each $x\in U$, let $E_x:\mathbb R^4\to T_xM$ send the standard basis vector $\mathbf e_I$ to $E_I(x)$; because the tetrad vectors are a basis, $E_x$ is an invertible real-linear map, hence a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]). A groupoid is a category in which every morphism is an isomorphism ([[def-isomorphism-groupoid-and-connected-category]]). Define the target groupoid $\mathcal T(U)$ to have base-point-tagged objects $\tau_x:=(x,T_xM)$ for $x\in U$ and morphisms $\tau_x\to\tau_y$ the tagged triples $(\tau_x,\tau_y,L)$ where $L:T_xM\to T_yM$ is a real-linear isomorphism; identities and composition are tagged identity maps and ordinary composition ([[def-category]]). A covariant functor assigns objects and morphisms and preserves identities and composition ([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]]). The functor from the thin path groupoid [[def-gr-fx-thin-path-groupoid]] to $\mathcal T(U)$ sends $x$ to $\tau_x$ and sends $[\gamma]:x\to y$ to the tagged tangent-space arrow

$$\bigl(\tau_x,\tau_y,E_y\,U_\gamma(1)\,E_x^{-1}\bigr):\tau_x\longrightarrow\tau_y.$$

Here $U_\gamma(1)$ acts on tetrad components, while $E_y$ and $E_x^{-1}$ convert between components and tangent vectors. Under the supplier convention $e'=\Lambda e$, the component matrix in the changed local frame satisfies

$$U'_{\gamma}(1)=\Lambda(\gamma(1))U_\gamma(1)\Lambda(\gamma(0))^{-1}.$$

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

derivations.claim: Set $A=\omega_i(p)$ and $B=\omega_j(p)$. The integral equation $U(t)=I-\int_0^t\omega(\dot\gamma)U$ gives the positive-$i$ segment expansion $S_1=I-\varepsilon A+\tfrac12\varepsilon^2(A^2-\partial_iA)+O(\varepsilon^3)$. On the following positive-$j$ segment, Taylor expansion at $p+\varepsilon e_i$ gives $S_2=I-\varepsilon B+\varepsilon^2(\tfrac12B^2-\partial_iB-\tfrac12\partial_jB)+O(\varepsilon^3)$. In each case the second iterated integral contributes $\tfrac12\varepsilon^2\omega_k(p)^2$, and the first integral contributes the displayed derivative terms.

Along the negative-$i$ segment from $p+\varepsilon e_i+\varepsilon e_j$ to $p+\varepsilon e_j$ and the negative-$j$ segment from $p+\varepsilon e_j$ to $p$, the same integral expansion gives $S_3=I+\varepsilon A+\varepsilon^2(\tfrac12A^2+\tfrac12\partial_iA+\partial_jA)+O(\varepsilon^3)$ and $S_4=I+\varepsilon B+\tfrac12\varepsilon^2(B^2+\partial_jB)+O(\varepsilon^3)$. The derivative terms use starting points $p+\varepsilon e_j$ and $p$; reversing the tangent changes the first-order ODE coefficient's sign.

For any fixed $q$, uniqueness in [F1] shows that adjoining a segment with identity-initial transport $S$ to an already traversed path with transport $T$ gives total matrix $ST$: $S(t)T$ solves the next segment's ODE with its required initial value. Applying this successively gives total transport $S_4S_3S_2S_1$; for $q=4$ this agrees with [F3] using the same component ODE of [F4]. Its linear terms cancel. The within-segment quadratic terms sum to $A^2+B^2-\partial_iB+\partial_jA$; the six cross-products sum to $BA-B^2-BA-AB-A^2+BA=BA-AB-A^2-B^2$. The full coefficient is therefore $\partial_jA-\partial_iB+BA-AB=-(\partial_i\omega_j-\partial_j\omega_i+[A,B])=-F_{ij}(p)$ by [F2]. For a uniform remainder, choose a compact neighborhood $K'$ of $K$ contained in $V$ and containing the four square sides for $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$; the $C^2$ coefficients and derivatives are bounded there. Taylor remainders in single integrals are uniformly $O(\varepsilon^3)$, and if $M$ bounds coefficient norms in the fixed submultiplicative norm, iterated-integral terms of order $m\ge3$ are bounded by $M^m\varepsilon^m/m!$, whose sum is $O(\varepsilon^3)$. Multiplying four expansions preserves the uniform remainder order.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

A **topological group** is a group $G$ ([[def-group]]) with a topology such that multiplication $m:G\times G\to G$, $m(x,y)=xy$, and inversion $\iota:G\to G$, $\iota(x)=x^{-1}$, are continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) for the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]).

derivations.claim: If $Q,R\in SU(2)$, then $(QR)^\dagger QR=R^\dagger Q^\dagger QR=I_2$ and $\det(QR)=\det Q\det R=1$ by [F1]; $I_2$ is in the set. From $Q^\dagger Q=I_2$, the columns of $Q$ are linearly independent and hence $Q$ is invertible; therefore $Q^\dagger=Q^{-1}$ and $QQ^\dagger=I_2$. By [F1], $1=\det(I_2)=\det(QQ^\dagger)=\det Q\det(Q^\dagger)$, so $\det(Q^\dagger)=1$ and the inverse belongs to $SU(2)$. Associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication. The product entries are polynomials in real and imaginary entries and the inverse $Q\mapsto Q^\dagger$ is continuous, so these maps meet the topological-group definition [F4].

The equations $Q^\dagger Q=I_2$ and $\det Q=1$ are inverse images of closed points under continuous functions, so $SU(2)$ is closed in $\mathbb R^8$. Each unitary column has squared norm one, hence the sum of the squared absolute values of all four entries is $2$; this bounds the subset.
By [F2], the closed bounded subset is compact. Euclidean space is Hausdorff and every subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff, so $SU(2)$ is compact Hausdorff.

A **finite oriented graph** consists of finite vertex and edge sets $V,E$, source and target maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a fixed-point-free involution $e\mapsto\bar e$ with $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$. A **finite SU(2) graph configuration** assigns $g_e\in SU(2)$ to every oriented edge and requires $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$. A graph path is a finite composable edge word $e_1,\ldots,e_n$; its holonomy is the later-left product $g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1}$, and the empty path has holonomy $I_2$.

A vertex gauge assignment is a function $h:V\to SU(2)$. It acts on edge variables by

$$g_e\longmapsto g'_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1}.$$

A **finite-dimensional unitary representation** is a group homomorphism $\rho:SU(2)\to U(W)$ on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $W$ that is strongly continuous, meaning $g\mapsto\rho(g)w$ is continuous for each $w\in W$. Here

$$U(W):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}(W):\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle\text{ for all }v,w\in W\},$$

with the operator-norm topology inherited from $\operatorname{End}(W)$. In finite dimension, strong continuity is equivalent to continuity in this operator norm.

For a closed graph path $\ell=(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$, the associated **Wilson trace** is the basis-independent trace of the endomorphism of $W$ given by

$$\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(g_{e_n})\cdots\rho(g_{e_1})\bigr).$$

Here the trace of a finite-dimensional endomorphism is the trace of its matrix in any basis.

derivations.claim: The vertex action preserves the reverse-edge condition because $g'_{\bar e}=h_{s(e)}g_e^{-1}h_{t(e)}^{-1}=(h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1})^{-1}=(g'_e)^{-1}$. Thus the transformed variables are again a graph configuration.

If the path is empty, its product is $I_2$ before and after the gauge action, so its trace is unchanged. For the rest of the proof assume the closed path has $n\ge1$ edges and write it as $e_1:v_0\to v_1,\ldots,e_n:v_{n-1}\to v_n=v_0$.

The transformed product is $g'_{e_n}\cdots g'_{e_1}=h_{v_0}g_{e_n}h_{v_{n-1}}^{-1}h_{v_{n-1}}g_{e_{n-1}}\cdots h_{v_1}^{-1}h_{v_1}g_{e_1}h_{v_0}^{-1}=h_{v_0}(g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1})h_{v_0}^{-1}$; all adjacent intermediate factors cancel because $h_v^{-1}h_v=I$.

Applying the homomorphism $\rho$ carries this conjugation to conjugation by $\rho(h_{v_0})$. For finite matrices, $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$; take $A=\rho(h_{v_0})$ and $B=\rho(g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1})\rho(h_{v_0})^{-1}$ to obtain the same trace as before. Thus the Wilson trace is invariant.

Let $M_2(\mathbb C)$ have its Euclidean topology as $\mathbb R^8$, write $Q^\dagger:=\overline Q^{\mathsf T}$ for conjugate transpose, and define

$$SU(2)=\{Q\in M_2(\mathbb C):Q^\dagger Q=I_2,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

Under matrix multiplication, $SU(2)$ is a compact Hausdorff topological group.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ and $\sigma:G\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ be
finite-dimensional complex representations of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Their
**tensor product representation** $\rho\otimes\sigma$ is the representation of
$G$ on the complex tensor product $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ given on elementary
tensors by

$$g\cdot(v\otimes w):=\bigl(\rho(g)v\bigr)\otimes\bigl(\sigma(g)w\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ v\in V,\ w\in W).$$

**The action is well defined.** For fixed $g\in G$, the assignment
$(v,w)\mapsto\rho(g)v\otimes\sigma(g)w$ is additive in each variable and
$\mathbb C$-balanced, because $\rho(g)$ and $\sigma(g)$ are $\mathbb C$-linear:
$\rho(g)(v\lambda)\otimes\sigma(g)w=(\rho(g)v)\lambda\otimes\sigma(g)w$. By
[[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]] there is a unique
$\mathbb C$-linear map $\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g):V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W\to
V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ with the displayed value on every elementary tensor.
Because the two sides of
$g\cdot(h\cdot(v\otimes w))=(gh)\cdot(v\otimes w)$ agree on every elementary
tensor and the elementary tensors span $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$, the assignment
$g\mapsto\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g)$ is a group homomorphism into
$\operatorname{GL}(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)$, with
$\rho(1)\otimes\sigma(1)=\operatorname{id}$. The underlying space is
finite-dimensional: bases of $V$ and $W$ give the basis
$(v_i\otimes w_j)_{i,j}$, so $\dim(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)=(\dim V)(\dim W)$.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional complex
representation of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Its
**dual** or **contragredient** representation is the representation $\rho^{*}$
of $G$ on the algebraic dual space $V^{*}$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]) defined by

$$\bigl(g\cdot f\bigr)(v):=f\bigl(g^{-1}\cdot v\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ f\in V^{*},\ v\in V),$$

equivalently $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$.

Each operator $\rho^{*}(g)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear because $f$ and
$\rho(g^{-1})$ are. The inverse appears so that composition is
order-preserving: writing $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$,

$$(gh)\cdot f=f\circ\rho\bigl((gh)^{-1}\bigr)=f\circ\rho(h^{-1})\circ\rho(g^{-1})=g\cdot(h\cdot f),$$

and $1\cdot f=f\circ\operatorname{id}_V=f$. Hence $\rho^{*}$ is a group
homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V^{*})$, a representation of the same
degree as $\rho$.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $G$ be a topological group and $H$ a complex Hilbert space. A
**unitary representation** of $G$ on $H$ is a group homomorphism
$\pi:G\to U(H)$, where $U(H)$ is the group of bijective complex-linear
isometries of $H$, such that the orbit map $g\mapsto\pi(g)v$ is norm-continuous
for every $v\in H$. This condition is **strong continuity**. A closed linear
subspace $M\subseteq H$ is **invariant** if $\pi(g)M=M$ for every $g\in G$.
The representation is **irreducible** if $H\ne\{0\}$ and its only closed
invariant linear subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $H$.

For unitary representations $\pi$ on $H$ and $\rho$ on $K$, a **bounded
intertwiner** is a bounded linear operator $T:H\to K$ satisfying
$$T\pi(g)=\rho(g)T\qquad(g\in G).$$
The representations are **unitarily equivalent** if there is a unitary
intertwiner between them. The **commutant** of $\pi$ is
$$\pi(G)'=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):T\pi(g)=\pi(g)T\text{ for every }g\in G\}.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]). Under the assumed
Axiom of Choice the Axiom of Countable Choice holds as well
([[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]]).

Let $\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]),
and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). The pairing below is linear in the first
variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

**The scalar integrals.** Fix $v\in H$ and $w\in J$ and put

$$b_v(w):=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k).$$

The integrand is continuous on $K$. Indeed, $k\mapsto T\pi(k)^{-1}v$ is
continuous because $\pi$ is strongly continuous and $T$ is bounded, and for a
continuous map $\psi$ into $J$ the map $k\mapsto\sigma(k)\psi(k)$ is continuous
because every $\sigma(k)$ is an isometry: for fixed $k_0$,

$$\|\sigma(k)\psi(k)-\sigma(k_0)\psi(k_0)\|\le\|\psi(k)-\psi(k_0)\|+\|(\sigma(k)-\sigma(k_0))\psi(k_0)\|,$$

and both terms tend to zero as $k\to k_0$. A continuous complex function on the
compact space $K$ is bounded and Borel, so the displayed integral is a finite
complex number; and $\bigl|\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\bigr|\le
\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$ for every $k$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]), so
$|b_v(w)|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$. For fixed $v$ the assignment
$w\mapsto b_v(w)$ is conjugate-linear and $\|w\|\mapsto\|b_v(w)\|$ is bounded
by $\|T\|\,\|v\|$; hence

$$\varphi_v(w):=\overline{b_v(w)}=\int_K\langle w,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$

is a bounded linear functional on $J$ of norm at most $\|T\|\,\|v\|$.

**The definition.** Under Countable Choice the Hilbert space $J$ has the Riesz
representation property ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]): there
is a unique vector $A(T)v\in J$ with $\varphi_v(w)=\langle w,A(T)v\rangle$ for
every $w\in J$, equivalently

$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=b_v(w)=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)\qquad(v\in H,\ w\in J).$$

This determines $A(T)$ as a map $H\to J$, the **Haar average** of $T$ with
respect to the pair $(\sigma,\pi)$.

**Well-definedness.** For each $v$ the vector $A(T)v$ is unique, so $A(T)$ is a
well-defined function. It is linear: if $v=a v_1+b v_2$ then, by the
conjugate-linearity in $f$ of the representing vector recorded in
[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]], the vector representing
$\varphi_{av_1+bv_2}=\overline a\,\varphi_{v_1}+\overline b\,\varphi_{v_2}$ is
$aA(T)v_1+bA(T)v_2$; and $\|A(T)v\|=\|\varphi_v\|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|$ because the
Riesz representation is isometric, so $A(T)$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$. The assignment $A$ is itself linear in $T$: for fixed $v,w$
the integrand is linear in $T$, so the scalar integral is, and equality of the
weak matrix elements together with uniqueness of the Riesz vector gives
$A(aT+bT')=aA(T)+bA(T')$. Thus
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ is a well-defined map.

**This is a weak operator integral.** Only scalar functions are integrated in
the definition: for fixed $v$ and $w$, the continuous function
$k\mapsto\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle$ is integrated against the
scalar measure $\mu$, and the vector $A(T)v$ is then produced by the Riesz
representation theorem. No operator-norm continuity of the orbit
$k\mapsto\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}$ of an arbitrary bounded operator $T$ is assumed
or asserted. For finite-rank $T:H\to J$, it follows from
[[lem-conjugation-orbits-of-finite-rank-operators-are-norm-continuous]] as
follows. Equip $H\oplus J$ with the sum inner product; it is a Hilbert space
because Cauchy sequences converge in each coordinate. The representation
$\tau(k)(v,w)=(\pi(k)v,\sigma(k)w)$ is unitary and strongly continuous.
The bounded finite-rank operator $S(v,w)=(0,Tv)$ satisfies
$\tau(k)S\tau(k)^{-1}(v,w)=(0,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v)$.
The cited lemma makes this conjugation orbit norm continuous, and restriction
to $H\oplus\{0\}$ followed by projection onto $J$ does not increase operator
norm, proving the claimed continuity for $T$. Only
the Axiom of Choice is used, through normalized Haar measure and Countable
Choice. That $A$ is an idempotent contraction onto the bounded intertwiners,
with operator norm one exactly when $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, is the
content of [[lem-haar-averaging-projects-onto-the-intertwiner-space]], which
justifies the present definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]), and let
$\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]).
Write
$$\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J):=\{T\in\mathcal B(H,J):T\pi(g)=\sigma(g)T\text{ for every }g\in K\}$$
for the space of bounded intertwiners and let
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ be the Haar averaging operator of
[[def-haar-averaging-operator-on-hom-spaces]], so that
$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$
for all $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$, $v\in H$, $w\in J$. Then:

1. $A$ is idempotent, $A\circ A=A$, and its range is exactly
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)$: $A(T)$ intertwines for every bounded $T$, and
   $A(T)=T$ for every bounded intertwiner $T$;
2. $A$ is a contraction, $\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$ for every $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$,
   hence $\|A\|\le1$;
3. $\|A\|=1$ if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, and $\|A\|=0$ if
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)=\{0\}$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem (For a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space, $V=W\oplus W^\perp$) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

derivations.claim: For each dual factor, choose an orthonormal basis of $V_e$ and use its dual-basis inner product; this is basis-independent because a change between orthonormal bases preserves the Euclidean coefficient norm. The matrix of the dual action is the transpose of the inverse unitary matrix, hence is unitary. Tensor products of orthonormal bases are an orthonormal basis for the displayed tensor inner product, so the diagonal action is unitary by [F3]–[F4]. Its matrix entries are finite sums and products of continuous entries of the edge representations, so [F7] makes $R_v$ strongly continuous.

For fixed $w\in W_v$, define $T_w:\mathbb C\to W_v$ by $T_w(z)=zw$, with the trivial representation on $\mathbb C$. It is linear and bounded by [F8], with $\|T_w\|=\|w\|$. The intertwining equation $T_w(z)=R_v(g)T_w(z)$ for all $z$ is equivalent to $w\in W_v^{SU(2)}$.

By [F1], $SU(2)$ is compact Hausdorff; by [F2] and [F5], its normalized Haar probability exists under the stated full AC assumption. The hypotheses of [F9]–[F10] now hold for $H=\mathbb C$, $J=W_v$, and $T=T_w$, using [F6], [F7], and steps 1.1 and 2.1. Since the trivial representation acts as the identity, the weak Haar average of $T_w$ is $T_{P_vw}$, where the finite-dimensional vector integral is defined coordinatewise. The range clause of [F10] therefore gives $P_v^2=P_v$, $\|P_v\|\le1$, and $\operatorname{ran}P_v=W_v^{SU(2)}$.

If $x\in\operatorname{ran}P_v$ and $y\in\ker P_v$, then $P_v(x+ty)=x$ for every complex scalar $t$. Contractivity gives $\|x\|\le\|x+ty\|$. Squaring and taking real $t$ of both signs forces $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=0$; taking $t$ purely imaginary of both signs forces $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=0$. Hence range and kernel are orthogonal. Since an idempotent has $W_v=\operatorname{ran}P_v\oplus\ker P_v$, the kernel is the orthogonal complement of the range, and [F11] identifies $P_v$ as the orthogonal projection onto its invariant range.

On $W=\bigotimes_vW_v$, each vertex operator acts as $P_v$ on one factor and identity on the others. Operators on distinct tensor factors commute, so their product is an idempotent whose range is $\bigotimes_v\operatorname{ran}P_v$, the tensors invariant under every vertex action. It is the orthogonal projection onto this joint invariant subspace because tensor products of orthogonal projections are orthogonal projections in the product Hilbert structure. If the graph has no vertices, the empty product is the identity on $\mathbb C$, consistent with the statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

A **finite oriented graph** consists of finite vertex and edge sets $V,E$, source and target maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a fixed-point-free involution $e\mapsto\bar e$ with $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$. A **finite SU(2) graph configuration** assigns $g_e\in SU(2)$ to every oriented edge and requires $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$. A graph path is a finite composable edge word $e_1,\ldots,e_n$; its holonomy is the later-left product $g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1}$, and the empty path has holonomy $I_2$.

A vertex gauge assignment is a function $h:V\to SU(2)$. It acts on edge variables by

$$g_e\longmapsto g'_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1}.$$

A **finite-dimensional unitary representation** is a group homomorphism $\rho:SU(2)\to U(W)$ on a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $W$ that is strongly continuous, meaning $g\mapsto\rho(g)w$ is continuous for each $w\in W$. Here

$$U(W):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}(W):\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle\text{ for all }v,w\in W\},$$

with the operator-norm topology inherited from $\operatorname{End}(W)$. In finite dimension, strong continuity is equivalent to continuity in this operator norm.

For a closed graph path $\ell=(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$, the associated **Wilson trace** is the basis-independent trace of the endomorphism of $W$ given by

$$\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\rho(g_{e_n})\cdots\rho(g_{e_1})\bigr).$$

Here the trace of a finite-dimensional endomorphism is the trace of its matrix in any basis.

For every finite SU(2) graph configuration, continuous finite-dimensional unitary representation $\rho$, closed graph path $\ell$, and vertex gauge assignment $h$, the Wilson trace of $\ell$ is unchanged by $g_e\mapsto h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1}$.

$$W_v=\bigotimes_{t(e)=v}V_e\;\otimes\!\bigotimes_{s(e)=v}V_e^*,$$

Use the dual action $g\cdot\lambda=\lambda\circ\rho_e(g^{-1})$ on $V_e^*$, with the dual Hilbert inner product determined by any orthonormal basis of $V_e$. On elementary tensors use the tensor-product inner product $\langle\bigotimes_i u_i,\bigotimes_i w_i\rangle=\prod_i\langle u_i,w_i\rangle$, extended sesquilinearly. $$W_v^{SU(2)}:=\{w\in W_v:R_v(g)w=w\text{ for every }g\in SU(2)\}.$$

$$P_vw:=\int_{SU(2)}R_v(g)w\,d\mu(g)$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $u^*$ denote the continuous absolutely
continuous representative of a class in $H^1$ supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]], and write
$\|u\|=\|u\|_{L^2}$ and $\|u'\|=\|u'\|_{L^2}$ for the norms of

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with

subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

$\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$; moreover if $T\subseteq T^*$,
then $T$ is closable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

$$G(t,x):=\mathbf 1_{\{0<t<x<L\}}h(t)\varphi'(x),\qquad (t,x)\in(0,L)^2.$$
The function $q(t,x)=|h(t)||\varphi'(x)|$ is nonnegative and
product-measurable. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. The test derivative
$\varphi'$ is continuous with compact support in $(0,L)$, hence belongs to
$L^2(0,L)$; [F6] then gives $\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Tonelli [F8], applied only to
this nonnegative product, gives
$$\int_{(0,L)^2}q\,d(\lambda\times\lambda)=\left(\int_0^L|h(t)|\,dt\right)\left(\int_0^L|\varphi'(x)|\,dx\right)<\infty.$$
Since $|G|\le q$, this establishes $G\in L^1((0,L)^2)$ without using
Fubini to prove its own hypothesis. Its sections are integrable for every
parameter because $h,\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Fubini [F9] therefore gives
$$\int_0^L v(x)\varphi'(x)\,dx=\int_0^L\int_0^x h(t)\varphi'(x)\,dt\,dx=\int_0^Lh(t)\left(\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx\right)dt=-\int_0^Lh(t)\varphi(t)\,dt,$$
where [F7] applied to real and imaginary parts gives
$\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx=\varphi(L)-\varphi(t)=-\varphi(t)$, since
$\varphi$ vanishes near $L$. Hence $Dv=h$ weakly and $v\in H^1$.
The distribution $Du-v$ has derivative zero. For every test function
$\varphi$ of integral zero, its primitive
$\psi(x)=\int_0^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ is compactly supported in $(0,L)$, and hence
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(D\psi)=-(D(Du-v))(\psi)=0$. Obtain a test
function $\eta$ with integral one as follows. The constant function $1$ lies
in $L^2(0,L)$ with norm $\sqrt L$. By the density in [F3], choose
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ with $\|\chi-1\|_2<\sqrt L/2$; then
$\|\chi\|_2>\sqrt L/2$. Set $\eta=|\chi|^2/\|\chi\|_2^2$. It is a smooth
compactly supported test function and $\int_0^L\eta=1$. For arbitrary
$\varphi$,
$\varphi-(\int_0^L\varphi)\eta$ has integral zero, so
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(\eta)\int_0^L\varphi$. Therefore $Du-v$ is a constant
distribution, $Du=v+c\in L^2$, and $u\in H^2(0,L)$ by [F1].

If $g\in H^2(0,L)$, [F2] applied with a compactly supported test function
shows $\langle T_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-D^2g\rangle$; thus
$g\in D(T_c^*)$ and $T_c^*g=-D^2g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(T_c^*)$ and
$h=T_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2g=-h\in L^2$. Step 1.2
then gives $g\in H^2(0,L)$. Hence $T_c^*=T_{\max}$ with exactly the claimed
domain.

By [F5] and step 2.1, $T_{\min}=T_c^{**}=T_{\max}^*$. If
$u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$ and $h=T_{\max}^*u$, testing against
$C_c^\infty(0,L)\subset H^2(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2u=-h$.
Step 1.2 implies $u\in H^2(0,L)$. The adjoint identity for all
$g\in H^2(0,L)$ and [F2] now reads
$\langle\Gamma_1g,\Gamma_0u\rangle-\langle\Gamma_0g,\Gamma_1u\rangle=0$.
By step 1.3 the two traces of $g$ can be prescribed independently: first set
$\Gamma_0g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_1g$ to obtain $\Gamma_0u=0$; then set
$\Gamma_1g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_0g$ to obtain $\Gamma_1u=0$. Conversely, if
$u\in H^2$ has both traces zero, [F2] gives
$\langle T_{\max}g,u\rangle=\langle g,-D^2u\rangle$ for every
$g\in H^2$, so $u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$. Therefore
$D(T_{\min})=\{u\in H^2:\Gamma_0u=\Gamma_1u=0\}$ and its action is
$-D^2u$.

The preceding steps establish density, symmetry, the exact adjoint, the
closure domain, and trace surjectivity as stated.

citations.quote:
> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a positive scalar $E_*$ and write $I_H$ for the identity on $H$. The
**scaled deficiency subspaces** of $S$ at $E_*$ are
$N_+(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*-iE_*I_H)$ and
$N_-(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*+iE_*I_H)$. Their **deficiency indices** are
$n_\pm(S;E_*):=\dim N_\pm(S;E_*)$, where Hilbert dimension means the
cardinality of an orthonormal basis as in the standard deficiency-index
definition. The spaces are closed: if $g_k\in N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and $g_k\to g$,
then $S^*g_k=\pm iE_*g_k\to\pm iE_*g$, so closedness of $S^*$ gives
$g\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*g=\pm iE_*g$. The dimension convention is well defined
under Choice by the cited deficiency-index definition.

**Dimension convention and well-definedness.** An orthonormal basis exists
in each $K_\pm$ by [[thm-existence-of-a-maximal-orthonormal-family]], using
full AC. Its cardinality is independent of the basis, as follows. Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ be two orthonormal bases of the same
Hilbert space. By [[thm-bessel-inequality-for-an-arbitrary-orthonormal-family]],
for each $i$ and integer $n\ge1$ at most $n$ indices satisfy
$|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\ge1/n$. Thus the support in $J$ of each row is
countable. Each column has a nonzero entry: otherwise $f_j$ is orthogonal
to the dense span of all $e_i$, hence to itself, contradicting norm one.
Here orthogonality passes to the closure by
[[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]]. If $I$ is infinite, full AC lets
us enumerate the row supports and assign each $j$ to one row containing it;
this gives an injection $J\to I\times\mathbb N$. Cardinal absorption
[[cor-cardinal-absorption]] and cardinal comparison
[[lem-cardinal-arithmetic-basic-laws]] give $|J|\le|I|$.
If $I$ has finite size $n$, the residual
$f_j-\sum_{i\in I}\langle f_j,e_i\rangle e_i$ is orthogonal to the dense
span of the $e_i$ and so vanishes. Taking its norm gives
$\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=1$.
For every finite $F\subseteq J$, Bessel in the other direction yields
$$|F|=\sum_{j\in F}\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in F}|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\le n.$$
Hence $|J|\le n$. Exchanging the two bases proves equality of cardinalities
in all cases. In the finite case each basis also spans algebraically by the
same residual argument, so this is the ordinary linear dimension. For the
zero space the basis is empty and the dimension is zero. AC is used for
basis existence and the simultaneous choices in the infinite comparison.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a self-adjoint
operator on $H$. By
[[thm-self-adjoint-resolvent-estimate]] the points $\pm i$ lie in $\rho(T)$, so
$T+i$ and $T-i$ are bijections of $D(T)$ onto $H$ with bounded inverses, and
$$C_T:=(T-i)(T+i)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is a bounded everywhere defined operator, the **Cayley transform** of $T$. In
the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(z-T)^{-1}$ of
[[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]] one has
$$(T+i)^{-1}=-R_T(-i),\qquad C_T=I+2iR_T(-i)=I-2i(T+i)^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. The map $T\mapsto C_T=(T-i)(T+i)^{-1}$ is a bijection
from the set of self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of unitary operators
$U$ on $H$ with $\ker(I-U)=\{0\}$. The inverse map assigns to such a $U$ the
operator
$$D(T_U)=\operatorname{ran}(I-U),\qquad T_U(I-U)y=i(I+U)y\quad(y\in H).$$
For this $T_U$ both $T_U-i$ and $T_U+i$ map $D(T_U)$ onto $H$, so $T_U$ is
self-adjoint, and $C_{T_U}=U$.

**Dimension convention and well-definedness.** An orthonormal basis exists
in each $K_\pm$ by [[thm-existence-of-a-maximal-orthonormal-family]], using
full AC. Its cardinality is independent of the basis, as follows. Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ be two orthonormal bases of the same
Hilbert space. By [[thm-bessel-inequality-for-an-arbitrary-orthonormal-family]],
for each $i$ and integer $n\ge1$ at most $n$ indices satisfy
$|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\ge1/n$. Thus the support in $J$ of each row is
countable. Each column has a nonzero entry: otherwise $f_j$ is orthogonal
to the dense span of all $e_i$, hence to itself, contradicting norm one.
Here orthogonality passes to the closure by
[[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]]. If $I$ is infinite, full AC lets
us enumerate the row supports and assign each $j$ to one row containing it;
this gives an injection $J\to I\times\mathbb N$. Cardinal absorption
[[cor-cardinal-absorption]] and cardinal comparison
[[lem-cardinal-arithmetic-basic-laws]] give $|J|\le|I|$.
If $I$ has finite size $n$, the residual
$f_j-\sum_{i\in I}\langle f_j,e_i\rangle e_i$ is orthogonal to the dense
span of the $e_i$ and so vanishes. Taking its norm gives
$\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=1$.
For every finite $F\subseteq J$, Bessel in the other direction yields
$$|F|=\sum_{j\in F}\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in F}|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\le n.$$
Hence $|J|\le n$. Exchanging the two bases proves equality of cardinalities
in all cases. In the finite case each basis also spans algebraically by the
same residual argument, so this is the ordinary linear dimension. For the
zero space the basis is empty and the dimension is zero. AC is used for
basis existence and the simultaneous choices in the infinite comparison.
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets and let $f : A \to B$ be a function ([[def-function]]).

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

derivations.claim:
The graph of $A$ is the image of the graph of $S$ under the bounded
invertible map $(f,g)\mapsto(f,E_*^{-1}g)$ on $H\oplus H$, so it is closed;
real scaling preserves symmetry. If $g\in D(S^*)$, then for every
$f\in D(S)$,
$\langle Af,g\rangle=E_*^{-1}\langle Sf,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*^{-1}S^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(A^*)$ and
$A^*g=E_*^{-1}S^*g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(A^*)$, then
$\langle Sf,g\rangle=E_*\langle Af,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*A^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(S^*)$ and
$S^*g=E_*A^*g$. Therefore $D(A^*)=D(S^*)$ and
$A^*=E_*^{-1}S^*$. Since
$A^*\mp iI=E_*^{-1}(S^*\mp iE_*I)$, the ordinary deficiency spaces of
$A$ at $\pm i$ are exactly $N_\pm$.

Suppose $n_+=n_-$. Choose orthonormal bases $(e_j)_{j\in J_+}$ of $N_+$
and $(f_j)_{j\in J_-}$ of $N_-$. By [F6], choose a bijection
$\pi:J_+\to J_-$. The map $V_0e_j=f_{\pi(j)}$ preserves norms on finite
linear combinations by orthonormality, so it extends continuously to an
isometry $V:N_+\to N_-$. Its range contains the finite span of the $f_j$,
which is dense; the range of an isometry from the complete space $N_+$ is
closed, so $V$ is onto and unitary.

For $f\in D(A)$, symmetry makes $\langle Af,f\rangle$ real; expanding the
two norms gives
$\|(A\pm iI)f\|^2=\|Af\|^2+\|f\|^2$. Thus $A\pm iI$ are injective. If
$(A\pm iI)f_k$ converges, the norm identity applied to differences makes
$(f_k)$ Cauchy and then $(Af_k)$ Cauchy; closedness of $A$ shows the limit is
in the range. Hence $M_\pm:=\operatorname{ran}(A\pm iI)$ are closed. By [F2]
and [F3], $H=M_+\oplus N_+=M_-\oplus N_-$, with orthogonal sums.

Equip $D(A^*)$ with the graph inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle_{A^*}=\langle f,g\rangle+\langle A^*f,A^*g\rangle$.
It is complete by [F2, F4], and $D(A)$ is a closed subspace because $A$ is
closed and $A^*f=Af$ there. If $z\in D(A^*)$ is graph-orthogonal to $D(A)$,
then for every $f\in D(A)$,
$\langle Af,A^*z\rangle=-\langle f,z\rangle$. By the adjoint definition,
this means $A^*z\in D(A^*)$ and $A^{*2}z=-z$. Therefore
$z_+=(z-iA^*z)/2$ and $z_-=(z+iA^*z)/2$ satisfy
$A^*z_+=iz_+$ and $A^*z_-=-iz_-$, and $z=z_++z_-$. Conversely,
$D(A)$ is graph-orthogonal to both kernels: for $u\in N_+$,
$\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,A^*u\rangle
=\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,iu\rangle=0$ by the adjoint identity and
conjugate-linearity in the second argument, and the same computation with
$A^*u=-iu$ holds for $u\in N_-$. If $u\in N_+$ and $v\in N_-$, then
$\langle u,v\rangle+\langle A^*u,A^*v\rangle
=\langle u,v\rangle+\langle iu,-iv\rangle=0$. Thus the two kernels are
graph-orthogonal to each other. Applying [F3] in the graph Hilbert space proves the orthogonal
decomposition
$D(A^*)=D(A)\oplus N_+\oplus N_-$.

Define $C_A:M_+\to M_-$ by
$C_A((A+iI)f)=(A-iI)f$. Injectivity of $A+iI$ makes this well defined, the
norm identity in step 2.1 makes it an isometry, and it is onto $M_-$. Define
$W(m+u)=C_Am-Vu$ for $m\in M_+$ and $u\in N_+$. The decompositions from
step 2.1 make $W$ well defined; it is unitary because its two orthogonal summands
are mapped isometrically onto $M_-$ and $N_-$. For $f\in D(A)$,
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if$, so $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ is dense. If $Wz=z$, then
$z$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ by unitarity, hence to the
dense domain $D(A)$, so $z=0$. The Cayley correspondence [F5] therefore gives
a self-adjoint operator $A_V$ with Cayley transform $W$.

For $m=(A+iI)f$ and $u\in N_+$, direct calculation gives
$(I-W)(m+u)=2if+u+Vu$ and
$i(I+W)(m+u)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. The Cayley inverse is
$A_V=i(I+W)(I-W)^{-1}$ on $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$, so
$D(A_V)=\operatorname{ran}(I-W)=D(A)+\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\}$ and
$A_V(2if+u+Vu)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. Equivalently, after renaming $2if$ as $f$,
$A_V(f+u+Vu)=Af+iu-iVu$. The sum is direct: if $f=u+Vu\in D(A)$, then
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if=(I-W)(2iu)$; injectivity of $I-W$ gives
$(A+iI)f=2iu$. Its left side lies in $M_+$ and its right side in $N_+$,
whose intersection is zero, so $u=f=0$. Multiplication by $E_*$ gives the
displayed domain and action for $S_V=E_*A_V$. The two-way scalar-adjoint
calculation in step 1.1 applies to $A_V$ as well, so
$S_V^*=E_*A_V^*=S_V$. Thus $S_V$ is a self-adjoint
extension of $S$.

Conversely, let $T$ be any self-adjoint extension of $S$ and put
$R=E_*^{-1}T$. The two-way scalar-adjoint calculation in step 1.1 gives
$R^*=E_*^{-1}T^*=R$, so $R$ is a self-adjoint extension of $A$. Its Cayley transform $C_R$
is unitary by [F5] and agrees with $C_A$ on $M_+$, since $R$ equals $A$ on
$D(A)$. A unitary carrying $M_+$ onto $M_-$ carries their orthogonal
complements $N_+$ onto $N_-$ by step 2.1 and [F2]; hence
$C_R(N_+)=N_-$. Put $V=-C_R|_{N_+}$; this is unitary. The
unitary $W$ constructed from this $V$ agrees with $C_R$ on both orthogonal
summands of $H$, so uniqueness in [F5] gives $R=A_V$. This determines $V$
uniquely from $T$ and proves that every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$.

If $n_+=n_-$, step 1.2 supplies a unitary and step 4.1 supplies a
self-adjoint extension. If an extension exists, step 4.2 supplies a unitary
$N_+\to N_-$, so its orthonormal bases have bijective index sets and
$n_+=n_-$. This proves the existence equivalence and the complete
parameterization.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$0<L<\infty$, let $H=L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, and use the spaces $H^1(0,L)$ and
$H^2(0,L)$ and their continuous endpoint traces defined by the one-dimensional
Sobolev suppliers. Define $T_c f=-D^2f$ on $D(T_c)=C_c^\infty(0,L)$. Then
$T_c$ is densely defined and symmetric, its adjoint is
$T_{\max}f=-D^2f$ on exactly $D(T_{\max})=H^2(0,L)$, and its closure
$T_{\min}=\overline{T_c}=T_c^{**}$ has domain
$$D(T_{\min})=\{f\in H^2(0,L): f(0)=f'(0)=f(L)=f'(L)=0\},$$
with $T_{\min}f=-D^2f$. The trace map
$\gamma:H^2(0,L)\to\mathbb C^4$ defined by
$\gamma(f)=(f(0),f(L),f'(0),f'(L))$ is surjective.

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and $S:D(S)\to H$ a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear operator.
Fix $E_*>0$ and let $N_\pm=N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and
$n_\pm=\dim N_\pm$ be the scaled deficiency spaces and indices. For every
unitary map $V:N_+\to N_-$, the operator
$$D(S_V)=D(S)\oplus\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\},\qquad
S_V(f+u+Vu)=Sf+iE_*u-iE_*Vu$$
is a self-adjoint extension of $S$. Every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$ for one such $V$. Consequently $S$ has a self-adjoint
extension if and only if $n_+=n_-$.

We write $f : A \to B$, and say $f$ is a **function from $A$ to $B$**, when $f$
is a function with $\operatorname{dom} f = A$ and
$\operatorname{ran} f \subseteq B$ (Subset $x \subseteq y$, proper subset $x \subsetneq y$, and the separation notation $\{\, z \in x : \varphi(z) \,\}$); $A$ is the
**domain** of $f$ and $B$ is a **codomain** for $f$. Equivalently
$f \subseteq A \times B$ with $\operatorname{dom} f = A$
(The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Kuratowski ordered pair $(a,b) := \{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$).

- $f$ is **injective** (one-to-one) if $f(x) = f(y)$ implies $x = y$, for all
  $x, y \in A$.
- $f$ is **surjective** (onto) if for every $b \in B$ there is some $x \in A$
  with $f(x) = b$; equivalently, the image $f[A] := \{ f(x) : x \in A \}$ equals
  $B$.
- $f$ is **bijective** if it is both injective and surjective.

derivations.claim:
Let $T$ be any linear operator with $T_{\min}\subseteq T\subseteq T_{\max}$.
For this proof write $\gamma_b f=(\Gamma_0f,\Gamma_1f)\in
\mathbb C^2\times\mathbb C^2$. This is the four-coordinate trace map of
[F1] with the last coordinate sign reversed, so it is onto and has kernel
$D(T_{\min})$. Its image $M:=\gamma_b(D(T))$ is a linear subspace. Since
$\ker\gamma_b=D(T_{\min})\subseteq D(T)$, every $f\in H^2$ whose trace lies
in $M$ differs from a member of $D(T)$ by an element of $D(T_{\min})$; thus
$D(T)=\gamma_b^{-1}(M)$. Conversely, every linear subspace $M$ gives such a
domain because $\gamma_b$ is onto.

Define
$B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$M^\omega=\{z:B(m,z)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. By [F2], integration by
parts gives $T^*=T_{\gamma_b^{-1}(M^\omega)}$: indeed, since
$T_{\min}\subseteq T$, adjoint inclusion reversal puts $D(T^*)$ inside
$D(T_{\min}^*)=H^2$, and for $g\in H^2$ the adjoint identity for every
$f\in D(T)$ is exactly $B(\gamma_b f,\gamma_b g)=0$. Hence $T$ is self-adjoint
if and only if $M=M^\omega$.

Put $\gamma_\ell f=(a,b):=(\Gamma_0f,\ell\Gamma_1f)$ and let
$\widehat M=\gamma_\ell(D(T))$. Equivalently,
$\widehat M=\{(a,b):(a,b/\ell)\in M\}$, where $M$ is the unscaled trace
image from step 1.1. Define
$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}:=\{z:\widehat B(m,z)=0\text{ for all }m\in
\widehat M\}$.
Since $\widehat B=\ell B$ after undoing the derivative scaling and
$\ell>0$, step 1.2 gives $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ exactly
when $T$ is self-adjoint. The map $\gamma_\ell$ is onto because the trace map
in [F1] is onto and multiplying its derivative coordinates by $\ell>0$ is
invertible. For $x=a+ib$ and $y=a-ib$, direct expansion using
the first-variable-linear inner product gives
$$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\frac{\langle x,x'\rangle-\langle y,y'\rangle}{2i}.$$
Thus $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ implies that
$(a,b)\mapsto(x,y)$ sends $\widehat M$ to the graph of an
inner-product-preserving linear map $R:X\to\mathbb C^2$, where
$X=\{a+ib:(a,b)\in\widehat M\}$. It is well defined: if a member of
$\widehat M$ has $x=0$, isotropy gives $\|y\|^2=\|x\|^2=0$, so $y=0$.
Maximality forces
$X=\mathbb C^2$. Indeed, define $X^\perp=\{z:\langle x,z\rangle=0\text{ for every }x\in X\}$ with $\langle x,z\rangle=x_1\overline{z_1}+x_2\overline{z_2}$. Every proper complex linear subspace $X$ has a nonzero vector in $X^\perp$, by the following coordinate argument. If $X=\{0\}$, take $x_0=(1,0)$. Otherwise take $0\ne v=(v_1,v_2)\in X$. Every $w\in X$ is a multiple of $v$: if $v_1w_2-v_2w_1\ne0$, the inverse of the two-column matrix $(v,w)$ expresses both standard coordinate vectors as linear combinations of $v,w$, implying $X=\mathbb C^2$; if this determinant is zero, solving in a nonzero coordinate of $v$ gives $w=cv$. Thus for proper $X$ one has $X=\operatorname{span}\{v\}$, and $x_0=(-\overline{v_2},\overline{v_1})\ne0$ satisfies $\langle cv,x_0\rangle=c(-v_1v_2+v_2v_1)=0$. No closed-subspace decomposition or additional choice principle is used. If $X$ were proper, take this $x_0$ and set
$a=x_0/2$, $b=x_0/(2i)$, so $(x,y)=(x_0,0)$. The displayed identity makes
this boundary pair orthogonal for $\widehat B$ to all of $\widehat M$, hence it
lies in $\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}=\widehat M$; then
$x_0\in X\cap X^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore
$R$ is a linear isometry from $\mathbb C^2$ into $\mathbb C^2$. Let
$e_1,e_2$ be the standard basis and write $Re_1=(\alpha_1,\beta_1)$ and
$Re_2=(\alpha_2,\beta_2)$. Isometry gives
$$|\alpha_1|^2+|\beta_1|^2=|\alpha_2|^2+|\beta_2|^2=1,\qquad
\alpha_1\overline{\alpha_2}+\beta_1\overline{\beta_2}=0.$$
Direct expansion gives
$$|\alpha_1\beta_2-\alpha_2\beta_1|^2=(|\alpha_1|^2+|\beta_1|^2)(|\alpha_2|^2+|\beta_2|^2)-|\alpha_1\overline{\alpha_2}+\beta_1\overline{\beta_2}|^2=1.$$
Thus the matrix $U$ with columns $Re_1,Re_2$ is invertible, so these vectors
span $\mathbb C^2$ and $R$ is onto. Their orthonormality gives
$U^*U=I_2$; since $U$ is invertible, this implies $U^*=U^{-1}$ and hence
$UU^*=I_2$. Thus $U\in U(2)$, and its graph condition is
$U(a+ib)=a-ib$, equivalently
$(U-I_2)a+i(U+I_2)b=0$. This $U$ is unique because its value is fixed for
every $x\in\mathbb C^2$.

Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ and set
$\widehat M_U=\{(a,b):U(a+ib)=a-ib\}$ in the scaled boundary coordinates.
Every $x\in\mathbb C^2$ occurs, by taking
$a=(x+Ux)/2$ and $b=(x-Ux)/(2i)$. Unitarity gives
$\langle x,x'\rangle=\langle Ux,Ux'\rangle$ for every pair, so the
displayed formula in step 2.1 makes $\widehat M_U$ isotropic. If
$(a,b)\in\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$,
then for every $x'\in\mathbb C^2$ that formula gives
$\langle x',x\rangle=\langle Ux',y\rangle=\langle x',U^*y\rangle$, hence
$x=U^*y$ and $y=Ux$; therefore $(a,b)\in\widehat M_U$. Thus
$\widehat M_U=\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$. Since $\gamma_\ell$ is onto,
the restriction to $\gamma_\ell^{-1}(\widehat M_U)$ is self-adjoint by the
criterion in step 1.2 and the scaling equivalence in step 2.1. Its boundary equation is exactly
the Statement's equation, and its domain lies between $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}$ because it is a restriction of $T_{\max}$ whose domain contains
the zero-trace domain.

The preceding steps give a bijection from $U(2)$ to the entire set of
self-adjoint extensions between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$. By [F4], that same
extension set is uniquely parameterized by the abstract unitaries between
the deficiency subspaces. Composing the two bijections identifies the
boundary-matrix labels with the abstract deficiency labels and proves that
the displayed boundary family is exhaustive.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

(a) there is exactly one representative $u^*$ of the class $u$ that is
continuous on $[a,b]$, is absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$, and satisfies
$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xu'(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in[a,b],$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side means $-\int_x^yu'$;

(d) *Half-line and line.* If $u,v\in H^1(0,\infty)$, then
$\int_0^\infty u\overline{v'}=-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}-\int_0^\infty u'\overline v$, both integrals
being absolutely convergent. For $u,v\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ one instead has
$\int_{\mathbb R}u\overline{v'}=-\int_{\mathbb R}u'\overline v$,
with both integrals absolutely convergent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.
Then $T$ is closable if and only if $D(T^*)$ is dense in $H$. In that case
$\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$; moreover if $T\subseteq T^*$,
then $T$ is closable.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.
The complex exponential is entire, and

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and let $S:D(S)\to H$ be a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear
operator. The domain $D(S)$ is part of the operator data. Its adjoint is the
operator $S^*:D(S^*)\to H$ characterized by
$\langle Sf,g\rangle=\langle f,S^*g\rangle$ for every $f\in D(S)$ and
$g\in D(S^*)$, using an inner product linear in its first argument. A **graph
core** for $S$ is a linear subspace $C\subseteq D(S)$ dense for the graph norm
$\|f\|_S=(\|f\|^2+\|Sf\|^2)^{1/2}$; equivalently, the graph of the restriction
$S|_C$ is dense in the graph of $S$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and $S:D(S)\to H$ a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear operator.
Fix $E_*>0$ and let $N_\pm=N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and
$n_\pm=\dim N_\pm$ be the scaled deficiency spaces and indices. For every
unitary map $V:N_+\to N_-$, the operator
$$D(S_V)=D(S)\oplus\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\},\qquad
S_V(f+u+Vu)=Sf+iE_*u-iE_*Vu$$
is a self-adjoint extension of $S$. Every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$ for one such $V$. Consequently $S$ has a self-adjoint
extension if and only if $n_+=n_-$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

By [F5], the test functions are dense in $L^2(0,\infty)$. For
$f,g\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$, integration by parts [F1] gives
$\langle S_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,S_cg\rangle$ with no endpoint terms.
Thus $S_c$ is symmetric, so it is closable by [F2], and
$\overline S_c^{\,*}=S_c^*$.

If $g\in H^1(0,\infty)$, [F1] gives
$\langle S_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-iDg\rangle$ for every test $f$, so
$g\in D(S_c^*)$ and $S_c^*g=-iDg$. Conversely, if $g\in D(S_c^*)$ and
$h=S_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,\infty)$ says distributionally $Dg=i h\in L^2$.
Together with $g\in L^2$ this is exactly $g\in H^1$. Hence
$D(S_c^*)=H^1(0,\infty)$ and $S_c^*=-iD$.

By step 2.1, $g\in N_+(\overline S_c;1)$ exactly when
$g\in H^1$ and $-iDg=ig$, that is, $Dg=-g$. Its absolutely continuous
representative satisfies
$(e^xg(x))'=e^x(g(x)+g'(x))=0$ almost everywhere by the product rule in
[F3] and $g'=-g$. On each bounded subinterval the absolutely continuous
fundamental theorem in [F3] makes $e^xg(x)$ constant; overlap consistency
makes it one constant $c$ on the whole half-line. Thus $g(x)=ce^{-x}$. Since
$\int_0^\infty e^{-2x}\,dx=1/2$, this is in $L^2$ for every $c$, and
its classical derivative $-ce^{-x}$ is also in $L^2$ and is its weak
derivative by [F1]. Thus every such function is
in $H^1$ and satisfies the kernel equation, so
$N_+=\{ce^{-x}:c\in\mathbb C\}$ is one-dimensional.

A vector $g\in N_-(\overline S_c;1)$ satisfies $Dg=g$ by step 2.1, so
$(e^{-x}g(x))'=e^{-x}(g'(x)-g(x))=0$ almost everywhere by [F3] and
$g'=g$. On each bounded subinterval the absolutely continuous fundamental
theorem in [F3] makes $e^{-x}g(x)$ constant; overlap consistency gives
one $c\in\mathbb C$ on the whole half-line, so $g(x)=ce^x$. If $c\ne0$,
$\int_0^R|ce^x|^2dx=|c|^2(e^{2R}-1)/2\to\infty$, contradicting
$g\in L^2(0,\infty)$. Hence $c=0$, $N_- =\{0\}$ and $n_-=0$.
Combining step 3.1's positive-deficiency calculation with this result and the
common adjoint from step 1.1 gives the closure's indices $(1,0)$.

The indices are unequal, so [F4] implies that $\overline S_c$ has no
self-adjoint extension on $H$. This proves the Statement.

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
