Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use the unitary Fourier transform
$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$ on
$L^1\cap L^2$. Let $H_0=-\Delta$ be the self-adjoint multiplier
$\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$ with domain
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Put
$Q_0=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^3\langle \partial_j u,\partial_j v\rangle_{L^2}\quad(u,v\in Q_0),$$
where $\partial_j$ are weak derivatives. Then $q_0$ is dense, symmetric,
nonnegative, and closed; its associated self-adjoint operator is exactly $H_0$,
with $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\langle H_0u,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_0),\ v\in Q_0).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let
$q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its
first variable. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Suppose that for some $c\ge0$,
$q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in Q$, and that $Q$ is complete in the form
norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$. Then there is a unique self-adjoint
operator $H_q\ge-cI$ such that
$$D((H_q+cI)^{1/2})=Q,\qquad q(u,v)=\langle H_qu,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_q),\ v\in Q).$$
Equivalently, $D(H_q)$ consists exactly of those $u\in Q$ for which there is
$f\in H$ satisfying $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for all $v\in Q$, and then
$H_qu=f$. Under the $e^{tA}$ generator convention for associated forms, the
associated operator is $A=-H_q$. If $q_0$ is a densely defined closed symmetric
form with $q_0[u]\ge0$ and $v$ is a symmetric sesquilinear form on $Q(q_0)$
satisfying
$$|v[u,u]|\le a q_0[u]+b\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(q_0)),\qquad 0\le a<1,\ b\ge0,$$
then $q_0+v$ is closed and bounded below by $-b$ on the same domain. It has a
unique self-adjoint representing operator there. The form bound is not an
operator-relative bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$ and the unitary
extension $\mathcal F_2$. For $\kappa>0$, let
$$G_\kappa(x)=\frac{e^{-\kappa|x|}}{4\pi|x|}\quad(x\ne0),$$
with any value at $x=0$. Then $G_\kappa\in L^1\cap L^2$, and
$$\widehat G_\kappa(\xi)=\frac1{4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2}.$$
Consequently convolution by $G_\kappa$ is the bounded operator
$(-\Delta+\kappa^2)^{-1}$ on $L^2$, with its convolution integral interpreted
in the usual almost-everywhere $L^2$ sense.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Write
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of Lebesgue
(equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]), and write $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$
for the same construction over the product with Lebesgue measure; identify
Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^6$ with the completion of the product of
Lebesgue measures on the two $\mathbb R^3$ factors.

**Kernel data and sections.** Let $k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, an almost-everywhere equivalence class, and choose a finite-valued Lebesgue-measurable representative $k_0:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. When $f\in L^2$ is used, choose likewise a finite-valued Lebesgue-measurable representative $f_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$. For almost every $x\in\mathbb R^3$, the section $k_x(y):=k_0(x,y)$ is measurable, by applying the completed-product Fubini theorem to the positive and negative parts of the real and imaginary components of $k_0$ ([[thm-tonelli-and-fubini-for-completed-product-measures]]).

**Domain and action.** For $f\in L^2$ say that the integral defining $T_kf$
*exists at* $x\in\mathbb R^3$ if the section product
$y\mapsto k_0(x,y)f_0(y)$ is measurable and lies in $L^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, and at such points put
$$(T_kf)(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^3}k_0(x,y)f_0(y)\,dy .$$
Define
$$D(T_k):=\Bigl\{f\in L^2:\ x\mapsto(T_kf)(x)\ \text{exists for almost every }x\text{ and agrees a.e. with a class in }L^2\Bigr\},$$
and for $f\in D(T_k)$ let $T_kf$ denote that class. The assignment
$f\mapsto T_kf$ is called the *$L^2$-kernel operator with kernel $k$*.

This definition is independent of both representative choices. If $k_1$ is
another representative of $k$, its disagreement set with $k_0$ is null for the
completed product Lebesgue measure. Fubini applied to the indicator of that
set gives $k_0(x,\cdot)=k_1(x,\cdot)$ almost everywhere for almost every
$x$. For each such $x$ and any representative of $f$, the two section products
therefore have the same $L^1$ status and, when integrable, the same integral.
Replacing $f_0$ by another representative changes the section product only on
a null set of $y$, so it too preserves integrability and the integral.
Consequently the almost-everywhere sections, the subset $D(T_k)\subseteq L^2$,
and the resulting output class are unchanged by either representative choice.

**Hilbert-Schmidt operators.** A linear operator $T$ on $L^2$ is called a
*Hilbert-Schmidt operator* if there is
$k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $D(T)=D(T_k)$ and
$T=T_k$; such a $k$ is called an *$L^2$ kernel* of $T$.

This definition asserts nothing about whether $D(T_k)$ is all of $L^2$,
whether $T_k$ is bounded, or whether $T_k$ is compact; those properties are
proved in [[lem-nrqm-coulomb-ltwo-kernel-operators-bounded-and-compact]]. A
finite product kernel $\sum_{i=1}^nf_i(x)\overline{g_i(y)}$ with
$f_i,g_i\in L^2$ is also a class in $L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$,
as the same lemma records, so $T_k$ is defined for it whenever that membership
is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$L^2=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and let
$k\in L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, with $T_k$ the
$L^2$-kernel operator of [[def-nrqm-coulomb-ltwo-kernel-operators]]. Then:

(a) $D(T_k)=L^2$; $T_k$ is linear and bounded with
$\|T_kf\|_2\le\|k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\|f\|_2$ for every
$f\in L^2$, so $\|T_k\|\le\|k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}$;

(b) if $n\ge1$, $f_1,\dots,f_n,g_1,\dots,g_n\in L^2$ and
$k(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^nf_i(x)\overline{g_i(y)}$ a.e., then $k$ is a class in
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, the range of $T_k$ is contained
in $\operatorname{span}\{f_1,\dots,f_n\}$, and $T_k$ is compact;

(c) $T_k$ is compact; and

(d) for every sequence $(k_m)$ in
$L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with
$\|k_m-k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\to0$ one has
$T_{k_m}-T_k=T_{k_m-k}$ and
$\|T_{k_m}-T_k\|\le\|k_m-k\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R^3)}\to0$; in
particular $T_k$ is the operator-norm limit of finite-rank kernel operators.

No statement is made about the spectrum of $T_k$, about its singular values,
or about $L^2$ kernels of a given compact operator.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). The **discrete
spectrum** $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ is the set of eigenvalues of $A$ that are
isolated points of $\sigma(A)$ and whose eigenspace is finite dimensional; the
**essential spectrum** is
$$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A):=\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A),$$
with $\sigma(A)$ as in [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]].

For $H=\{0\}$ use its unique PVM directly: the spectrum and both parts
are empty and every projection has rank zero. Below suppose $H\ne\{0\}$,
as required by the cited spectral theorem.

**Spectral-projection description, with proofs.** Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and write
$P_\varepsilon:=E((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$ for
$\varepsilon>0$.

Here rank means the algebraic dimension of the range when finite; rank
$=\infty$ means the range is not finite dimensional. The calculus
[[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]] gives the support facts:
$E(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, and every open interval about a
spectral point has nonzero projection. Projections on disjoint sets have
orthogonal ranges, and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$
[[def-projection-valued-measure]].

1. *$E(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection onto $\ker(A-\lambda)$.* If
   $x=E(\{\lambda\})x$, its scalar measure $E_x$ is supported on
   $\{\lambda\}$ by the projection identity. Thus
   $\int\mu^2dE_x=\lambda^2\|x\|^2<\infty$, so $x\in D(A)$, and
   $$\|(A-\lambda)x\|^2=\int|\mu-\lambda|^2dE_x=0.$$
   The domain and norm identities are supplied by the unbounded calculus and
   [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]]. Hence $Ax=\lambda x$.
   Conversely, for an eigenvector (or the zero vector) the same norm identity
   gives zero integral. On $\{|\mu-\lambda|\ge1/n\}$ this bounds the measure
   by $n^2$ times that zero integral; taking the countable union shows
   $E_x(\mathbb R\setminus\{\lambda\})=0$.
   Since $\|(I-E(\{\lambda\}))x\|^2$ equals this scalar measure,
   $E(\{\lambda\})x=x$.
2. *A finite-rank interval contains only finitely many spectral points.*
   If $P_\varepsilon$ has rank $r<\infty$ and its interval contained $r+1$
   distinct spectral points, choose disjoint small open intervals about those
   finitely many points, all contained in the given interval. Each has a
   nonzero projection by support. Choose one unit vector in each range.
   They are orthonormal vectors in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$, hence
   linearly independent (take inner products with each vector), contradicting
   its dimension $r$. Thus there are at most $r$ spectral points there.
   In particular any $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$ with such a finite-rank
   $P_\varepsilon$ is isolated: take a smaller interval around $\lambda$
   excluding the other finitely many points. For that interval the projection
   is $E(\{\lambda\})$ by support, is nonzero by support, and has finite rank
   since its range lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$. By item 1,
   $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity.
3. *The two rank characterizations.* If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$,
   an isolating interval has projection $E(\{\lambda\})$, of finite rank
   by item 1. Conversely, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and some
   $P_\varepsilon$ has finite rank, item 2 proves it discrete. Hence
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue and some }P_\varepsilon\text{ has finite rank}.$$
   If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, item 2 excludes every finite-rank
   interval. Conversely, if every $P_\varepsilon$ has infinite rank, each is
   nonzero, so support puts $\lambda$ in $\sigma(A)$, and the just-proved
   discrete characterization excludes it from $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$.
   Therefore
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon=\infty\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0.$$
4. *$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ is closed.* If $\lambda_n\in
   \sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda$, then for every
   $\varepsilon>0$ some $n$ has $(\lambda_n-\varepsilon/2, \lambda_n+
   \varepsilon/2)\subseteq(\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon)$, so
   $\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon\ge\operatorname{rank}P_{\varepsilon/2}^{(n)}
   =\infty$ and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ by item 3.

The closure conclusion is in $\mathbb R$, and also in $\mathbb C$ since
$\mathbb R$ is closed there. A spectral accumulation point has infinitely
many spectral points in every surrounding interval, so item 2 forces infinite
rank. An isolated eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity has its infinite-dimensional
eigenspace inside every interval range by item 1. Consequently an accumulation point of $\sigma(A)$ and an isolated eigenvalue of
infinite multiplicity both lie in $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, and $\sigma(A)$
is the disjoint union of $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ and
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and
let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$. Let
$E_A$ be its spectral projection-valued measure, let
$Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$, and define the associated form by
$$q_A[u]=\|(A+cI)^{1/2}u\|^2-c\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(A)).$$
Set $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when the
essential spectrum is empty. For each integer $k\ge1$, put
$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],$$
where the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty$. Then $\lambda_k(A)$ is the
$k$th eigenvalue below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity, when at least $k$
such eigenvalues exist; otherwise $\lambda_k(A)=\alpha$. If the inclusion
$Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ is compact in the form norm
$\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then $A$ has a complete orthonormal
eigenbasis; every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and the only possible
accumulation is at $+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Write $M=\|W\|_{L^\infty}$. The multiplication operators $M_W$ and $M_s$ are bounded, nonnegative, and self-adjoint, with $\|M_W\|\le M$ and $\|M_s\|^2\le M$. Since $H_0\ge0$, Kato–Rellich makes $H=H_0-M_W$ self-adjoint on $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}$, and $H\ge-MI$. On $W^{1,2}$ define $q_H(u,v)=q_0(u,v)-\langle M_su,M_sv\rangle$. The perturbation has form bound $a=0$, $b=M$, because $\langle M_su,M_su\rangle=\langle M_Wu,u\rangle\le M\|u\|_2^2$; hence [F1] makes $q_H$ closed and bounded below by $-M$.

Let $\widetilde H$ be the self-adjoint operator representing $q_H$ from [F1]. For $u\in W^{2,2}$ and $v\in W^{1,2}$, the free-form identity [A1] and $\langle M_su,M_sv\rangle=\langle M_Wu,v\rangle$ give $q_H(u,v)=\langle(H_0-M_W)u,v\rangle$. Thus $H\subseteq\widetilde H$; self-adjointness gives $\widetilde H\subseteq H^*=H$, so $\widetilde H=H$. The representation theorem's square-root identity on the full form domain, with shift $M+1$, and [F3] then identify $q_H$ with the spectral form of $H$.

The resolvent convolution formula in [F2] gives, for a.e. $x$,
$(K_\kappa f)(x)=s(x)\int G_\kappa(x-y)s(y)f(y)\,dy$; thus the displayed
function is the integral kernel of $K_\kappa$. If $S$ is a compact set outside
which $W=0$ almost everywhere and $M=\|W\|_\infty$, then
$$\iint |s(x)G_\kappa(x-y)s(y)|^2\,dx\,dy\le M^2|S|\int_{S-S}|G_\kappa(z)|^2\,dz<\infty,$$
because $S-S$ is bounded and the $|z|^{-1}$ singularity of $G_\kappa$ is
square-integrable locally in three dimensions. This is an $L^2$ kernel, so
[F5] makes its integral operator $K_\kappa$ Hilbert–Schmidt and compact.

In the Fourier representation of [A1],
$$R_\kappa=(H_0+\kappa^2 I)^{-1}=\mathcal F_2^*M_{(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)^{-1}}\mathcal F_2.$$
The multiplier is real, strictly positive, and bounded by $\kappa^{-2}$; its positive square root is the bounded self-adjoint multiplier
$$R_\kappa^{1/2}=\mathcal F_2^*M_{(4\pi^2|\xi|^2+\kappa^2)^{-1/2}}\mathcal F_2.$$
Consequently $K_\kappa=(M_sR_\kappa^{1/2})(M_sR_\kappa^{1/2})^*$, so it is positive and self-adjoint.

If $Hu=-\kappa^2u$, then $(H_0+\kappa^2 I)u=M_Wu$. Put $f=M_su$. If $f=0$, invertibility of $H_0+\kappa^2 I$ forces $u=0$; hence a nonzero eigenvector gives $f\ne0$ and $$K_\kappa f=M_sR_\kappa M_s(M_su)=M_sR_\kappa M_Wu=M_su=f.$$ Conversely, if $K_\kappa f=f$ with $f\ne0$, set $u=R_\kappa M_s f$. Then $M_su=K_\kappa f=f$, so $(H_0+\kappa^2 I)u=M_s f=M_s^2u=M_Wu$ and $Hu=-\kappa^2u$. These maps are inverse because $R_\kappa M_Wu=u$ for an eigenvector and $M_sR_\kappa M_s f=f$ for a $1$-eigenvector; therefore the eigenspaces are isomorphic.

Let $A=(H_0+\kappa^2 I)^{1/2}$, which maps $W^{1,2}$ bijectively onto $L^2$ by [A1] and Fourier calculus, and put $T=M_sA^{-1}$. Then $TT^*=K_\kappa$. The compactness of $K_\kappa$ implies $T$ is compact: for finite-rank spectral projections $P_n$ of $K_\kappa$ increasing to its support, $$\|(I-P_n)T\|^2=\|(I-P_n)K_\kappa(I-P_n)\|\longrightarrow0,$$ so $T$ is an operator-norm limit of the finite-rank maps $P_nT$. Hence $C=T^*T$ is positive compact. For $v=Au$, $u\in W^{1,2}$, the exact form identity is $$q_H[u]+\kappa^2\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2-\|Tv\|^2 =\langle(I-C)v,v\rangle.$$ The maps $u\mapsto v$ and $v\mapsto A^{-1}v$ are inverse bijections.

The maximal dimension of a linear subspace on which the right side of the form identity in step 4.2 is strictly negative equals $\operatorname{rank}E_C((1,\infty))$: that spectral subspace is negative for $I-C$, and any subspace of larger dimension contains a nonzero vector orthogonal to it, where the spectral integral of $1-C$ is nonnegative. By [F4], this rank is the number of eigenvalues of $C$ above $1$, with multiplicity.

The same maximal negative dimension equals $\operatorname{rank}E_H(( -\infty,-\kappa^2))$ by [F3]: the spectral range below the threshold is supported in $[-M,-\kappa^2)$ by step 1.1, so it lies in the form domain and is strictly negative for the shifted form. Any larger subspace has a nonzero vector in its orthogonal complement, where the shifted form is nonnegative. Step 5.1 makes this rank finite; its finite-dimensional spectral range therefore consists of eigenvectors, so its dimension is the number of eigenvalues of $H$ below $-\kappa^2$, counted with multiplicity. No essential spectral point lies strictly below $-\kappa^2$: a sufficiently small interval around any such point has finite-rank projection as a subprojection of $E_H(( -\infty,-\kappa^2))$, contrary to [F6]. Hence the essential threshold is at least $-\kappa^2$ (or $+\infty$), and [F7] identifies the same count with the form min-max levels strictly below the cutoff. Finally, $T$ maps each positive eigenspace of $C=T^*T$ bijectively onto the same-eigenvalue eigenspace of $K_\kappa=TT^*$, with inverse $\mu^{-1}T^*$ at eigenvalue $\mu>0$. Thus the number above $1$ for $C$ equals that for $K_\kappa$, proving the asserted count.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$, with inner product linear in its first variable and
$\inf\sigma(H_0)>-\infty$. Let $g\in H$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and define
$P_g:H\to H$ by $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$. Put
$H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g$ on $D(H_\lambda)=D(H_0)$ and
$R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}$. Then $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint. For every
$z\in\rho(H_0)$ such that
$d_\lambda(z):=1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle\ne0$, one has
$z\in\rho(H_\lambda)$ and
$$R_\lambda(z):=(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}=R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle}.$$
For real $E<\inf\sigma(H_0)$ and $g\ne0$, $E$ is an eigenvalue of $H_\lambda$
if and only if $d_\lambda(E)=0$; in that case the eigenspace is one-dimensional.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,
Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and The recursion theorem applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
A nested sequence of nonempty closed bounded intervals has nonempty intersection, and the intersection is a single point exactly when the lengths tend to $0$ — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
On a closed interval of $\mathbb{Q}$ there is a continuous unbounded function, a bounded one with no maximum, and one without the intermediate value property, which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's

derivations.claim: By [F2], $H_0$ is self-adjoint. If $E<0$, multiplication by $(|p|^2-E)^{-1}$ is a bounded inverse of $H_0-EI$: it is bounded by $|E|^{-1}$, and $|p|^2/(|p|^2-E)\le1$ puts its range in $D(H_0)$. Therefore $\sigma(H_0)\subseteq[0,\infty)$. For $B_n=\{p:|p|<1/n\}$, [F3] gives $0<|B_n|<\infty$; the unit vectors $f_n=|B_n|^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{B_n}$ lie in $D(H_0)$ and satisfy $\|H_0f_n\|\le n^{-2}$. If $0\in\rho(H_0)$, then $1=\|f_n\|\le\|H_0^{-1}\|\,\|H_0f_n\|\to0$, a contradiction. Thus $\inf\sigma(H_0)=0$.

By [F3], $$\|g\|_2^2=4\pi|C|^2\int_0^\infty r^2e^{-r^2}\,dr<\infty.$$ For $E=-\kappa^2<0$, the rank-one scalar in [F1] is $$m(\kappa)=\langle(H_0+\kappa^2)^{-1}g,g\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|C|^2e^{-|p|^2}}{|p|^2+\kappa^2}\,dp.$$ By [F1] and step 1.1, its zeros in $1+\lambda m(\kappa)$ correspond exactly to negative eigenvalues, each with multiplicity one.

If $0<\kappa_1<\kappa_2$, then $(|p|^2+\kappa_1^2)^{-1}>(|p|^2+\kappa_2^2)^{-1}$ everywhere; since $|g(p)|^2>0$, integration gives $m(\kappa_1)>m(\kappa_2)$. On any compact interval $[a,b]\subset(0,\infty)$, the integrands are bounded by $|g(p)|^2/a^2\in L^1$, so dominated convergence [F4] gives continuity of $m$ there. Also $0<m(\kappa)\le\|g\|_2^2/\kappa^2$, hence $m(\kappa)\to0$ as $\kappa\to\infty$.

The integrands for $m(1/n)$ increase pointwise to $|g(p)|^2/|p|^2$ as $n\to\infty$. Monotone convergence [F4] gives $\lim_n m(1/n)=I_0$. Since step 3.1 makes $m$ strictly decreasing in $\kappa$, its limit as $\kappa\downarrow0$ equals this supremum. By [F3], $$I_0=4\pi|C|^2\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\,dr\in(0,\infty).$$

The function $1+\lambda m(\kappa)$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $(0,\infty)$ by step 3.1, with endpoint limits $1+\lambda I_0$ and $1$ by steps 3.1 and 4.1. When $1+\lambda I_0<0$, the endpoint limits give finite $0<a<b$ with $1+\lambda m(a)<0<1+\lambda m(b)$; [F5] on $[a,b]$ gives a positive zero, unique by strict increase. If $1+\lambda I_0\ge0$, then $m(\kappa)<I_0$ for every $\kappa>0$ by step 3.1 and the endpoint limit in step 4.1; because $\lambda<0$, this gives $1+\lambda m(\kappa)>1+\lambda I_0\ge0$, so no positive zero exists. Therefore a positive zero exists exactly when $1+\lambda I_0<0$. By step 2.1 and [F1], these zeros correspond exactly to negative eigenvalues.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ use the unitary Fourier transform
$\widehat u(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$ on
$L^1\cap L^2$. Let $H_0=-\Delta$ be the self-adjoint multiplier
$\mathcal F_2^*M_{4\pi^2|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2$ with domain
$D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Put
$Q_0=W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\sum_{j=1}^3\langle \partial_j u,\partial_j v\rangle_{L^2}\quad(u,v\in Q_0),$$
where $\partial_j$ are weak derivatives. Then $q_0$ is dense, symmetric,
nonnegative, and closed; its associated self-adjoint operator is exactly $H_0$,
with $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$ and
$$q_0(u,v)=\langle H_0u,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_0),\ v\in Q_0).$$

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and
let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$. Let
$E_A$ be its spectral projection-valued measure, let
$Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$, and define the associated form by
$$q_A[u]=\|(A+cI)^{1/2}u\|^2-c\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(A)).$$
Set $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when the
essential spectrum is empty. For each integer $k\ge1$, put
$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],$$
where the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty$. Then $\lambda_k(A)$ is the
$k$th eigenvalue below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity, when at least $k$
such eigenvalues exist; otherwise $\lambda_k(A)=\alpha$. If the inclusion
$Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ is compact in the form norm
$\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then $A$ has a complete orthonormal
eigenbasis; every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and the only possible
accumulation is at $+\infty$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

derivations.claim: In spherical coordinates [F4], $$J=\int_{\mathbb R^3}(1+|\xi|^2)^{-2}\,d\xi =4\pi\int_0^\infty\frac{r^2}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr.$$ The integrand is bounded by $r^2$ near zero and by $r^{-2}$ for $r\ge1$; thus $0<J<\infty$ and $c=J^{-1/2}$ is defined. By [F2], $\widehat f$ is the Fourier transform of an $L^2$ vector and its norm is $c^2J=1$.

Its formal kinetic form integral equals $$4\pi^2c^2\int_{\mathbb R^3} \frac{|\xi|^2}{(1+|\xi|^2)^2}\,d\xi =16\pi^3c^2\int_0^\infty\frac{r^4}{(1+r^2)^2}\,dr=+\infty,$$ because the radial integrand tends to $1$ as $r\to\infty$. By [F1], finite form energy is equivalent to this weighted integral being finite, so $f\notin H^1(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)=Q(H_0)$.

The vector is normalized in $L^2$ by step 1.1 but outside the exact form domain by step 2.1. Thus it cannot be inserted into the min-max variational family described in [F3], which requires its subspaces to lie in $Q(H_0)$; the universal trial-vector claim is false. This counterexample concerns domain admissibility and assigns no finite value to the divergent integral.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ and let $H_{\mathrm{pp}}$,
$H_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ be the subspaces of
[[def-pure-point-absolutely-continuous-and-singular-continuous-spectral-subspaces]].
Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually
orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with
$$H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}},$$
canonically determined by $T$; the restrictions of $T$ to them are
self-adjoint and their spectral measures are respectively purely atomic,
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and atomless and
singular. If $H$ is separable and $\mu$ is a maximal scalar spectral measure
with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$
of its discrete, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, then
$H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.

Here a support means a Borel carrier (zero mass off the set), not necessarily topological support. A maximal scalar spectral measure is a finite positive Borel measure mu with $E_x\ll\mu$ for every x (in particular a scalar spectral measure with this domination property qualifies). The last assertion is conditional on the supplied mu. On the zero Hilbert space use the unique PVM and full-domain zero operator directly.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set**
of $T$ is
$$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$
where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on
$H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is
$\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator
$$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used
throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of
[[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$.

**The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently
$T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for
$x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$.

**Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph
theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with
$R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$.
The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since
$\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$.
Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$
where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with
continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$
and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets
to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed.
No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here.

For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If two holomorphic functions on a complex domain agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain, then they agree everywhere on the domain.

Precisely, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be a complex domain (A complex domain is a nonempty connected open subset of $\mathbb C$), let $f,g:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ be holomorphic, and suppose that some $a\in\Omega$ is an accumulation point of $\{z\in\Omega:f(z)=g(z)\}$. Then $f=g$ on $\Omega$. The requirement $a\in\Omega$ is essential.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $H_0$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative. The Gaussian integral in [F2], applied in each coordinate and combined with Tonelli [F4], gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-|p|^2}\,dp=\pi^{3/2}$, so $\|g\|=1$. Polar coordinates [F3] and the resolvent multiplier therefore give
$m(z)=\frac{4}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{r^2e^{-r^2}}{r^2-z}\,dr$
for $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. The denominator is nonzero on the integration ray, and the integral is locally uniformly dominated on the upper half-plane, so it defines the stated resolvent matrix element.

For $\operatorname{Re}a>0$, put $I(a)=\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}(r^2+a^2)^{-1}\,dr$. When $a>0$ is real, the Laplace representation of $(r^2+a^2)^{-1}$ and Tonelli [F4] give $I(a)=\int_0^\infty e^{-a^2s}\int_0^\infty e^{-(1+s)r^2}\,dr\,ds=\frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-a^2s}}{\sqrt{1+s}}\,ds$ by [F2]. The substitutions $u=\sqrt{1+s}$ and $v=au$ then give $I(a)=\sqrt\pi e^{a^2}\int_1^\infty e^{-a^2u^2}\,du=\frac{\sqrt\pi e^{a^2}}a\int_a^\infty e^{-v^2}\,dv=\frac{\pi}{2a}e^{a^2}\mathcal E(a)$, using the horizontal-ray definition of $\mathcal E$ for real $a>0$.

Fix $a_0$ with $\operatorname{Re}a_0>0$ and a closed disk $K$ about $a_0$ contained in that half-plane. Choose $\eta>0$ and $A<\infty$ so that $\operatorname{Re}a\ge\eta$ and $|a|\le A$ on $K$. For $r\ge0$, $|r^2+a^2|=|a+ir||a-ir|\ge\eta^2$. For nonzero complex $\delta$ small enough that $a_0+\delta\in K$, the exact difference quotient of the integrand of $I$ is
$$\frac{e^{-r^2}}{\delta}\left(\frac1{r^2+(a_0+\delta)^2}-\frac1{r^2+a_0^2}\right)=-\frac{(2a_0+\delta)e^{-r^2}}{(r^2+(a_0+\delta)^2)(r^2+a_0^2)}.$$
For $|\delta|\le1$, its modulus is at most $(2A+1)\eta^{-4}e^{-r^2}$, an integrable majorant by [F2]. The quotients are measurable in $r$, and tend pointwise to $-2a_0e^{-r^2}/(r^2+a_0^2)^2$. Applying [F5] along every sequence of nonzero complex increments tending to zero proves that $I$ is complex differentiable at $a_0$, with derivative the integral of this limit. Thus $I$ is holomorphic on the right half-plane; this conclusion uses the actual difference quotients, not an assumption that dominated convergence is itself a differentiation theorem.
For $\mathcal E$, put $F(w,t)=e^{-(w+t)^2}$. Its exact segment identity is
$$\frac{F(w+\delta,t)-F(w,t)}{\delta}=\int_0^1-2(w+s\delta+t)e^{-(w+s\delta+t)^2}\,ds.$$
For completeness this identity follows by expanding the exponential series on the finite segment, differentiating each polynomial in $s$, and integrating it: the series and its derivative converge uniformly there, since for $|w+s\delta+t|\le B$ they are dominated respectively by $\sum B^{2n}/n!$ and $|\delta|\sum_{n\ge1}2n B^{2n-1}/n!$, both finite. Hence passage through the finite segment integral is justified by the uniform remainder bound. For $|w|\le R$, $|\delta|\le1$ and $0\le s\le1$, write $w+s\delta=u+iv$; then $|u|,|v|\le R+1$ and $(t+u)^2\ge t^2/2-u^2$. Consequently the segment derivative is bounded in modulus by $C_R(1+t)e^{-t^2/2}$, independently of $w,\delta,s$. This majorant is integrable: $(1+t)e^{-t^2/4}$ is bounded, and the remaining scaled Gaussian is integrable by [F2]. The original integrand is bounded the same way without the factor $1+t$. The measurable difference quotients therefore have one integrable majorant and tend pointwise, as complex $\delta\to0$, to $-2(w+t)e^{-(w+t)^2}$. Apply [F5] to every such sequence to obtain the complex derivative of $\mathcal E$ at every $w$. It is entire. Both sides of step 1.2 are therefore holomorphic on the connected half-plane $\operatorname{Re}a>0$; their agreement on the positive real axis has an accumulation point inside this domain, so [F6] extends the identity throughout the half-plane.

For $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, choose the square root $a=\sqrt{-z}$ with $\operatorname{Re}a>0$. Since $r^2/(r^2-z)=1+z/(r^2-z)$, $m(z)=2+\frac{4z}{\sqrt\pi}I(a)$; substituting the identity from step 2.1 and $z=-a^2$ gives $m(z)=2-2\sqrt\pi\,a e^{-z}\mathcal E(a)$.
On $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, the root $a$ equals $-ik(z)$: both square to $-z$, and $\operatorname{Re}(-ik(z))>0$. Substitution gives $m(z)=2+2i\sqrt\pi\,k(z)e^{-z}\mathcal E(-ik(z))$ there. The right hand side is holomorphic throughout $D$, so it is the required local continuation through $E_0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb C$. The function $f$ is **complex differentiable at $a$** if the limit

$$ \lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\ne0,\ a+h\in U}}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} $$

exists in the metric of [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. Its value is the **complex derivative** of $f$ at $a$, denoted $f'(a)$. The increments are nonzero and remain in the domain; because $U$ is open, all sufficiently small increments are allowed.

The function $f$ is **holomorphic on $U$** when it is complex differentiable at every point of $U$. A function holomorphic on all of $\mathbb C$ is **entire**. The word analytic is reserved for the local power-series notion.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $T$ be self-adjoint on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ whose inner product is linear in the first variable, use the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(T-zI)^{-1}$, and let $X\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a specified vector subspace. For $f,h\in X$, the scalar resolvent matrix element is

$$r_{f,h}(z):=\langle R_T(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

Given an open real interval $I$, a point $E_0\in I$, and a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$, a local analytic continuation of these matrix elements through $E_0$ is a specified family of holomorphic functions $\widetilde r_{f,h}:D\to\mathbb C$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, for the stated $f,h\in X$. A **meromorphic continuation** on $D$ is instead a specified family $\widetilde r_{f,h}$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, holomorphic on $D$ except for isolated poles. At every crossing point where no pole occurs it is a regular analytic continuation on a smaller neighborhood. For such a meromorphic continuation, if $z_0\in D$ is nonreal and for some $f,h\in X$ the continued function satisfies

$$\widetilde r_{f,h}(z)=(z-z_0)^{-k}q(z)$$

on a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$, for an integer $k\ge1$ and a holomorphic $q$ with $q(z_0)\ne0$, then $z_0$ is a pole of order $k$ of that continued matrix element. Such a pole is called a resonance matrix-element pole for the specified pair $(T,X)$ and continuation. This definition asserts neither that a continuation exists nor that a pole is an eigenvalue of $T$; the continuation and the chosen test vectors are part of the data.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$\widehat g(p)=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-ip\cdot x}g(x)\,dx,\qquad (F_0g)(E,\omega)=\frac{E^{1/4}}{\sqrt2}\widehat g(\sqrt E\,\omega).$$

For a compactly supported $g\in L^2$ and $E=k^2>0$, let $R_H(E\pm i0)g$
denote the local resolvent limits, and define the free trace on compact sources
and the two stationary transforms by

$$Z_0(E)g=\frac{\sqrt k}{4\pi^{3/2}}\int e^{-ik\omega\cdot x}g(x)\,dx,\qquad Z_\pm(E)g=Z_0(E)\bigl[g-VR_H(E\pm i0)g\bigr].$$

Then:

(a) $F_0$ is a unitary from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ onto
$\mathcal K=L^2((0,\infty),dE;\mathfrak h)$. The initially defined stationary
transforms extend to $Z_\pm=F_0\Omega_\pm^*$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$; their
restrictions to $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$ are unitary onto $\mathcal K$,
they vanish on the pure point subspace, and they diagonalize $H$ as
multiplication by $E$ on its absolutely continuous subspace.

(b) There is a measurable operator-valued unitary $S(E)$ on $\mathfrak h$
such that $F_0SF_0^*=M_{S(E)}$. No generic nonradial potential is assumed to
preserve individual spherical harmonic channels. For $R\in SO(3)$ set
$V_R(x)=V(R^{-1}x)$ and $(U_Ra)(\omega)=a(R^{-1}\omega)$. The covariance is
$S[V_R](E)=U_RS[V](E)U_R^{-1}$, not commutation with $U_R$ for a fixed
nonradial $V$.

(c) Let $u_{k,d}$ be the outgoing stationary solution restricted to a ball
$B$ containing the support of $V$:

$$u_{k,d}=(I+\chi_BR_0(k^2+i0)V)^{-1}\bigl(e^{ikd\cdot x}|_B\bigr),\qquad f_k(\omega,d)=-\frac1{4\pi}\int_Be^{-ik\omega\cdot x}V(x)u_{k,d}(x)\,dx.$$

Here $R_0(z)=(H_0-z)^{-1}$ and $\chi_B$ denotes restriction/localization;
the inverse is the inverse of **$I+K$**, not of $K$. Define
$(\mathcal A_ka)(\omega)=\int_{S^2}f_k(\omega,d)a(d)\,d\sigma(d)$. Then

$$S(E)=I-2\pi i\,Z_0(E)\bigl[V-VR_H(E+i0)V\bigr]Z_0(E)^*=I+\frac{ik}{2\pi}\mathcal A_k.$$

Adjoints $Z_0(E)^*$ and products in this formula are understood on the
compact interaction region, not as bounded maps into global $L^2$ plane waves.
The right side is norm-continuous on compact positive-energy intervals and
gives a unitary representative for every $E>0$.

(d) If in addition $V$ is radial, the energy-angular fiber decomposes in the
fixed countable spherical harmonic basis as
$S(E)Y_{lm}=S_l(E)Y_{lm}$. For the reduced radial equation

$$-\varphi_l''+\left(\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}+V(r)\right)\varphi_l=k^2\varphi_l,\qquad \varphi_l(r)/r^{l+1}\longrightarrow1,$$

let $f_l$ be the outgoing solution with
$f_l(r)=e^{i(kr-l\pi/2)}(1+O(r^{-1}))$ outside the interaction region and set
$W_l=W(\varphi_l,f_l)=\varphi_lf_l'-\varphi_l'f_l$. Then

$$S_l(E)=\frac{\overline{W_l(E)}}{W_l(E)},\qquad |S_l(E)|=1.$$

Equivalently, for the real normalized regular solution
$a_l=\sqrt{\rho_l}\,\varphi_l=c_lf_l+d_l\overline f_l$,
$\rho_l=k/(\pi|W_l|^2)$, the multiplier is
$(c_l/d_l)/(c_l^0/d_l^0)$, where the superscript $0$ denotes the corresponding
free normalization. The real regular transforms
$(T_lg)(E)=\int_0^\infty a_l(E,r)g(r)\,dr$ extend to unitaries from the
absolutely continuous reduced radial subspace onto $L^2((0,\infty),dE)$.
They implement the scalar channel statement with the incoming/outgoing phase
factors specified in the proof. No Coulomb continuum transform is used for a
compact potential.

No zero-energy nonresonance, absence of a zero eigenvalue, positivity of the
whole spectrum, finite bound-spectrum assumption, or radiality is imposed on
(a)-(c). The negative and any zero point spectrum are omitted by the
absolutely continuous restriction, rather than falsely declared nonexistent.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ and let $H_{\mathrm{pp}}$,
$H_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ be the subspaces of
[[def-pure-point-absolutely-continuous-and-singular-continuous-spectral-subspaces]].
Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually
orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with
$$H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}},$$
canonically determined by $T$; the restrictions of $T$ to them are
self-adjoint and their spectral measures are respectively purely atomic,
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and atomless and
singular. If $H$ is separable and $\mu$ is a maximal scalar spectral measure
with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$
of its discrete, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, then
$H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.

Here a support means a Borel carrier (zero mass off the set), not necessarily topological support. A maximal scalar spectral measure is a finite positive Borel measure mu with $E_x\ll\mu$ for every x (in particular a scalar spectral measure with this domination property qualifies). The last assertion is conditional on the supplied mu. On the zero Hilbert space use the unique PVM and full-domain zero operator directly.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H$ be separable complex Hilbert spaces, $H_0$ and $H$ self-adjoint operators on them, and $J:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H$ a bounded linear map. Write $E_{H_0}$ and $E_H$ for their spectral projection valued measures. The absolutely continuous subspace $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ consists of vectors $u$ for which the scalar measure $B\mapsto\|E_{H_0}(B)u\|^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure; $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ is its orthogonal projection. Define the two-space wave operators, when the pointwise strong limits exist on $\mathcal H_0$, by

$$\Omega_\pm(H,H_0;J):=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty} e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0),$$

where a strong limit means that for every $u\in\mathcal H_0$ the vector-valued expression converges in $\mathcal H$. The two signs are separate limits. When $J=I$ and $\mathcal H_0=\mathcal H$, write $\Omega_\pm(H,H_0)$. A wave operator is complete when its range is all of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$. When both wave operators exist and are isometries on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$, the scattering operator on that subspace is

$$S(H,H_0;J):=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

When both are complete with common range $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$, $S$ is unitary. For a fixed finite number $r\ge1$ of channels on an open energy interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, finite-channel data additionally consists of the standard space $\mathbb C^r$ and a matrix field $S:I\to U(r)$, where

$$U(r):=\{U\in M_r(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_r\}.$$

Here $U^*$ is conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{tr}U=\sum_{j=1}^r U_{jj}$, and $\det U$ is the usual alternating determinant. The fixed channel number means that $I$ contains no channel threshold. This finite-channel data is an explicit on-shell input; the abstract wave-operator definition alone does not assert that a given pair has finite-dimensional energy fibers.

derivations.claim: Differentiating $S(E)^*S(E)=I_r$ entrywise gives $S'(E)^*S(E)+S(E)^*S'(E)=0$. Thus $A:=S^*S'$ satisfies $A^*=-A$, and $Q^*=(-i\hbar A)^*=i\hbar A^*=-i\hbar A=Q$.

Since $S$ is unitary, $S^{-1}=S^*$ and $\det S\ne0$. Multilinearity of the alternating determinant gives $\det(I_r+hA+o(h))=1+h\operatorname{tr}(A)+o(h)$ for $A=S(E)^{-1}S'(E)$: terms linear in $h$ are exactly the $r$ choices of one diagonal entry, while every nonidentity permutation or two off-diagonal factors contributes $o(h)$. Applying this to $S(E+h)=S(E)(I_r+hS(E)^{-1}S'(E)+o(h))$ yields $(\det S)'(E)=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^{-1}S'(E))=\det S(E)\operatorname{tr}(S(E)^*S'(E))$. Multiplication by $-i\hbar/\det S(E)$ proves the trace formula.

For constant unitary $U_{\mathrm{in}},U_{\mathrm{out}}$, differentiation gives $(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{out}}^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, while $(S^\sharp)^*=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*U_{\mathrm{out}}$. Therefore $(S^\sharp)^*(S^\sharp)'=U_{\mathrm{in}}^*S^*S'U_{\mathrm{in}}$, proving the stated conjugation rule. Energy-dependent basis changes introduce derivatives of the basis matrices, so they are not covered by this claim.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes a fixed channel number r>=1, so the empty channel space is excluded. See the Statement.
If S is constant on I, then S prime is zero and Q=0 by its definition. See the Statement.
The theorem includes the one-channel case r=1, also computed in the companion example. See the Statement.
For any constant unitary field, the formula gives the zero Hermitian matrix and zero trace. See the Statement.
The energy interval I is open; derivative claims are only at interior energies. See the Statement.
The incoming and outgoing bases are fixed as part of the input; only constant unitary changes are covered. See the Statement.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_0$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex
Hilbert space $H$, with inner product linear in its first variable and
$\inf\sigma(H_0)>-\infty$. Let $g\in H$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and define
$P_g:H\to H$ by $P_gf=\langle f,g\rangle g$. Put
$H_\lambda=H_0+\lambda P_g$ on $D(H_\lambda)=D(H_0)$ and
$R_0(z)=(H_0-zI)^{-1}$. Then $H_\lambda$ is self-adjoint. For every
$z\in\rho(H_0)$ such that
$d_\lambda(z):=1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle\ne0$, one has
$z\in\rho(H_\lambda)$ and
$$R_\lambda(z):=(H_\lambda-zI)^{-1}=R_0(z)-\frac{\lambda R_0(z)P_gR_0(z)}{1+\lambda\langle R_0(z)g,g\rangle}.$$
For real $E<\inf\sigma(H_0)$ and $g\ne0$, $E$ is an eigenvalue of $H_\lambda$
if and only if $d_\lambda(E)=0$; in that case the eigenspace is one-dimensional.

Let $T$ be self-adjoint on a complex Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ whose inner product is linear in the first variable, use the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(T-zI)^{-1}$, and let $X\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a specified vector subspace. For $f,h\in X$, the scalar resolvent matrix element is

$$r_{f,h}(z):=\langle R_T(z)f,h\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

Given an open real interval $I$, a point $E_0\in I$, and a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$, a local analytic continuation of these matrix elements through $E_0$ is a specified family of holomorphic functions $\widetilde r_{f,h}:D\to\mathbb C$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, for the stated $f,h\in X$. A **meromorphic continuation** on $D$ is instead a specified family $\widetilde r_{f,h}$ agreeing with $r_{f,h}$ on $D\cap\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, holomorphic on $D$ except for isolated poles. At every crossing point where no pole occurs it is a regular analytic continuation on a smaller neighborhood. For such a meromorphic continuation, if $z_0\in D$ is nonreal and for some $f,h\in X$ the continued function satisfies

$$\widetilde r_{f,h}(z)=(z-z_0)^{-k}q(z)$$

on a punctured neighborhood of $z_0$, for an integer $k\ge1$ and a holomorphic $q$ with $q(z_0)\ne0$, then $z_0$ is a pole of order $k$ of that continued matrix element. Such a pole is called a resonance matrix-element pole for the specified pair $(T,X)$ and continuation. This definition asserts neither that a continuation exists nor that a pole is an eigenvalue of $T$; the continuation and the chosen test vectors are part of the data.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. On $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,dp;\mathbb C)$ with $\langle f,h\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f(p)\overline{h(p)}\,dp$, let $H_0=M_{|p|^2}$ on its maximal domain $\{f:|p|^2f\in L^2\}$, let $g(p)=\pi^{-3/4}e^{-|p|^2/2}$, and put

$$m(z):=\langle(H_0-zI)^{-1}g,g\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.$$

This is a dimensionless model; no physical units are assigned to $p$ or $z$.

For $w\in\mathbb C$, define the entire function

$$\mathcal E(w):=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_{\Gamma_w}e^{-\zeta^2}\,d\zeta,\qquad \Gamma_w=\{w+t:t\ge0\},$$

where $\Gamma_w$ is the horizontal ray oriented from $w$ toward $+\infty+w$. For any $E_0>0$, take a disk $D$ centered at $E_0$ with $0\notin D$, and the holomorphic square root $k:D\to\mathbb C$ with $k(E_0)=\sqrt{E_0}>0$. Then $m$ has the local analytic continuation through $E_0$

$$m_{\mathrm{cont}}(z)=2+2i\sqrt\pi\,k(z)e^{-z}\mathcal E(-ik(z)),\qquad z\in D.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then every nonreal number belongs to
$\rho(T)$: $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$. More precisely, for
$z=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $b\ne0$, and every $x\in D(T)$,
$$\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2 ,$$
and consequently $\|R_T(z)\|\le 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. In particular
$\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
