citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim:
The scaled oscillator eigenfunctions are polynomial multiples of $e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. To verify the core hypothesis of [[thm-nrqmx-quadratic-egorov]], take $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and set $L f=-\epsilon^2f''/2+x^2f/2\in L^2$. Integration by parts against each Hermite eigenfunction $\psi_n^\epsilon$, whose polynomial-Gaussian tails make the endpoint products vanish, gives
$ \langle Lf,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\langle f,L\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle. $
Parseval for the complete basis [F1] yields
$ \sum_{n\ge0}\epsilon^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle|^2 =\|Lf\|_2^2<\infty. $
Thus $f\in D(H_\epsilon)$. The coefficients of $H_\epsilon f$ in the Hermite basis are $\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle$, the same coefficients as $Lf$; completeness of that basis gives $H_\epsilon f=Lf$. The finite Hermite span is contained in $\mathcal S$ and is a graph core by [F1]; since $\mathcal S\subset D(H_\epsilon)$, $\mathcal S$ is also a core. This checks every operator hypothesis of [F4].

The Gaussian integral [F5] and the positive scaling in [F8] give $\|\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\|_2^2=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\int e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon}dx=1$. In its Wigner integral, the product of the two Gaussian factors is
$ (\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{\epsilon}-\frac{y^2}{4\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ipy}{\epsilon}\right). $
Multiplying by $e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}$ and applying [F3] with $\eta=\xi-p$ gives
$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon} 2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-(\xi-p)^2/\epsilon}, $
which is the stated nonnegative density. Its integral is $1$ by [F5] and [F8]. For its phase-space moments, apply [F8] to $x=q+\sqrt\epsilon s$ and $\xi=p+\sqrt\epsilon r$. The centered first moments vanish because $s e^{-s^2}$ and $r e^{-r^2}$ are odd; the cross-moment vanishes for the same reason. Integration by parts [F5] gives $\int s^2e^{-s^2}ds=\frac12\int e^{-s^2}ds$, so each centered variance is $\epsilon/2$. This verifies the mean and covariance definitions in the Statement.
For the operator uncertainties, direct differentiation gives $P\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=\bigl(p+i(x-q)\bigr)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$, while $Q\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}=x\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}$. Thus $\bar Q_\psi=q$, $\bar P_\psi=p$, and the two squared standard deviations are both $\int(x-q)^2|\psi|^2dx=\epsilon/2$ by the same Gaussian integration by parts. To prove the lower bound for every normalized $\varphi\in\mathcal S$, first note that $Q$ and $P$ are symmetric on $\mathcal S$: for $P$ this is [F5] applied to decaying Schwartz factors, and for $Q$ it follows from real multiplication. Hence $\bar Q_\varphi,\bar P_\varphi\in\mathbb R$. Put $A=Q-\bar Q_\varphi I$ and $B=P-\bar P_\varphi I$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F6], the commutator $[A,B]=[Q,P]=i\epsilon I$ from [F2], and symmetry give
$ \Delta_\varphi Q\,\Delta_\varphi P\ge|\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|\ge|\operatorname{Im}\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle|=\frac12|\langle[A,B]\varphi,\varphi\rangle|=\frac\epsilon2. $
Indeed, under the first-variable-linear convention, $\langle A\varphi,B\varphi\rangle=\langle BA\varphi,\varphi\rangle$ and its conjugate is $\langle AB\varphi,\varphi\rangle$. Thus the Gaussian attains the lower bound.

The classical Hamilton equations for $h(x,\xi)=(x^2+\xi^2)/2$ solve to
$ \Phi_t(x,\xi)=(x\cos t+\xi\sin t,\ \xi\cos t-x\sin t). $
This matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $\Phi_t(q,p)=(q_t,p_t)$. For $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, [F4] gives
$ \langle W_t,a\rangle =\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^2}a(\Phi_t z)W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](z)\,dz, $
where the last equality is [F2]. The integrand is in $L^1$ because $a$ is compactly supported and the Gaussian is integrable. Apply [F8] to the rotation $z'=\Phi_tz$; its determinant is $1$, so the resulting density is $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](\Phi_{-t}z')$. Orthogonality gives
$ |\Phi_{-t}(x,\xi)-(q,p)|^2 =|(x,\xi)-\Phi_t(q,p)|^2, $
so this density is exactly the displayed $W_t$. The same change of variables sends its mean $(q,p)$ to $(q_t,p_t)$ and transforms covariance as $R_t(\epsilon I_2/2)R_t^T=\epsilon I_2/2$, since $R_t$ is orthogonal. This proves the asserted exact transport and covariance for every compactly supported smooth test symbol and hence for the distributional Wigner functional defined in the Statement.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $0<\epsilon\le1$, and $V\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ with every partial derivative of total order at least $2$ bounded. Set
$$ h(x,\xi)=\frac{|\xi|^2}{2}+V(x),\qquad H_\epsilon^0=-\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}\Delta+V(x)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d). $$
Assume, as an explicit operator hypothesis, that for each $\epsilon$ a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_\epsilon$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_\epsilon^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for $H_\epsilon$. Let $U_\epsilon(t)$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$; for $t<0$ it is the adjoint of the forward propagator at time $-t$. Define the global Hamiltonian flow by
$$ \dot x=\xi,\qquad \dot\xi=-\nabla V(x),\qquad \Phi_0=I. $$
For every $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and finite $T>0$, there is $C_{T,V,a}<\infty$, independent of $0<\epsilon\le1$, such that
$$ \sup_{|t|\le T} \left\|U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_\epsilon(t) -\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\right\|_{L^2\to L^2} \le C_{T,V,a}\epsilon^2. $$
Only fixed finite times are covered by the first estimate. No Ehrenfest-time, caustic-uniformity, or physical measurement conclusion is asserted. If $V$ is a polynomial of degree at most two, the difference in that branch is identically zero.

There is also an exact statement for every real quadratic phase-space Hamiltonian. Let $z=(x,\xi)\in\mathbb R^{2d}$, let $G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{2d\times2d}$, $\ell\in\mathbb R^{2d}$ and $c\in\mathbb R$, and put
$$ h(z)=\tfrac12 z^TGz+\ell\cdot z+c. $$
Set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_d\\-I_d&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\widehat z=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_d,P_1,\ldots,P_d)$, where $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. On $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ define the Weyl realization by
$$ H_{\epsilon,h}^0:=cI+\sum_j\ell_j\widehat z_j+\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}G_{jk}(\widehat z_j\widehat z_k+\widehat z_k\widehat z_j). $$
For each $0<\epsilon\le1$, assume a densely defined self-adjoint operator $H_{\epsilon,h}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ extends $H_{\epsilon,h}^0$ and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ is a core for it. Let $U_{\epsilon,h}(t)$ be the strongly continuous unitary group for the constant generator $H_{\epsilon,h}/\epsilon$. The global Hamiltonian flow, defined by $\dot z=J\nabla h(z)=J(Gz+\ell)$ and $\Phi_0(z)=z$, is
$$ \Phi_t(z)=e^{tJG}z+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)JG}J\ell\,ds. $$
Here $e^{tJG}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^n(JG)^n/n!$ is the matrix exponential.
Then for every $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$$ U_{\epsilon,h}(t)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)U_{\epsilon,h}(t)=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t). $$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, and $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy $\|u\|_2=1$. With the definitions of [def-nrqmx-weyl-symbol-wigner], the Wigner distribution $W_\epsilon[u]$ is real and integrable, and

$$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,u\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{2d}}a(x,\xi)W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx\,d\xi , $$

$$ \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,d\xi=|u(x)|^2,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi)\,dx=|(\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi)|^2. $$

The Wigner distribution need not be nonnegative.

$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that

$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$

Write $A^2=2\epsilon^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}$. The product in the Wigner integrand is $$ \psi^\epsilon_1(x+y/2)\overline{\psi^\epsilon_1(x-y/2)} =A^2\left(x^2-\frac{y^2}{4}\right) e^{-x^2/\epsilon-y^2/(4\epsilon)}. $$ By [F4], $G_\epsilon''(\xi)=\int(-y^2/\epsilon^2)e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy$. Differentiating the explicit Gaussian in [F3] gives $$ \int y^2e^{-y^2/(4\epsilon)}e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}dy =-\epsilon^2G_\epsilon''(\xi) =(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi). $$ Substitution in the Wigner definition [F2] therefore yields $$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_1](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}A^2e^{-x^2/\epsilon} \left(x^2G_\epsilon(\xi)-\frac14(2\epsilon-4\xi^2)G_\epsilon(\xi)\right) =\frac1{\pi\epsilon} \left(\frac{2(x^2+\xi^2)}{\epsilon}-1\right) e^{-(x^2+\xi^2)/\epsilon}. $$ Every factor and sign follows from the displayed negative-sign Fourier convention.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

derivations.claim: Fix $x_0\in M$ and choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $\operatorname{ran}P(x_0)$. The vectors $P(x)e_j$ depend $C^2$ on $x$. Their Gram matrix is the identity at $x_0$, so its determinant remains positive on a neighborhood of $x_0$; hence the vectors remain linearly independent there. Applying the finite Gram–Schmidt formulas uses only sums, products, division by positive norms, and square roots of positive functions, so it gives a $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V(x)=(v_1(x),\ldots,v_r(x))$ for $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ on that neighborhood. The local bundle chart is $\Phi(x,z)=(x,V(x)z)$, with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(x,v)=(x,V(x)^*v)$; both maps are $C^2$. On an overlap, the frame change is $z\mapsto V_\beta(x)^*V_\alpha(x)z$, a $C^2$ map into the invertible complex matrices, so the transition maps are $C^2$. These charts make $E_P$ a rank-$r$ $C^2$ complex vector bundle. For $r=0$ the bundle is the zero bundle, and for $r=d$ every $P(x)=I_d$ and the bundle is trivial.

Along $\gamma$, abbreviate $P_\gamma$ by $P$. Differentiating $P^2=P$ gives $P'P+PP'=P'$ and $PP'P=0$. Therefore $K=P'P-PP'$ is $C^1$, $K^*=-K$, and $[K,P]=P'P+PP'=P'$. Let $M_K=\sup_{t\in[0,1]}\|K(t)\|$, set $V_0(t)=I_d$, and recursively set $V_{n+1}(t)=\int_0^tK(u)V_n(u)\,du$. Induction gives $\|V_n(t)\|\leq(M_Kt)^n/n!$, so $W=\sum_{n=0}^\infty V_n$ converges uniformly and satisfies $W(t)=I_d+\int_0^tK(u)W(u)\,du$. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $W'=KW$; since $K\in C^1$, also $W\in C^2$. If $Z$ is the difference of two solutions, iteration of $Z(t)=\int_0^tK(u)Z(u)\,du$ gives $\|Z(t)\|\leq\sup_{[0,1]}\|Z\|(M_Kt)^n/n!$ for every $n$, whose right side tends to zero, so $Z=0$.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], and write $E_P$ for its range family. Then $E_P\to M$ is a rank-$r$ $C^2$ complex vector bundle, and $\nabla s=P\,ds$ is a Hermitian connection on it. For every $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, the Kato equation $W'=[P_\gamma',P_\gamma]W$, $W(0)=I_d$, has a unique $C^2$ solution. That solution is unitary and satisfies $P_\gamma(t)W(t)=W(t)P_\gamma(0)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

derivations.claim: Differentiate $P^2=P$ in a tangent direction $X$ to obtain $(dP)(X)P+P(dP)(X)=(dP)(X)$. Multiplying on both sides by $P$ gives $P(dP)(X)P=0$. For a $C^1$ section $s$ with $Ps=s$, the curvature is $\nabla^2s(X,Y)=P(dP(X)\,ds(Y)-dP(Y)\,ds(X))$. Substituting $ds(X)=dP(X)s+P\,ds(X)$ and using $P(dP)P=0$ leaves $P(dP(X)dP(Y)-dP(Y)dP(X))Ps$. This is $P(dP\wedge dP)P\,s$, proving the projector formula.

In a local frame write a section as $s=Va$. Then $\nabla(Va)=P\,d(Va)=V(V^*dV\,a+da)=V(da+A a)$, where $A=V^*dV$. Differentiating $V^*V=I_r$ gives $(dV)^*V+V^*dV=0$, so $A^*=-A$. Applying $d+A$ twice gives $dA+A\wedge A$; expressing the already computed curvature in this frame gives $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=V^*FV=dA+A\wedge A$.

For $V'=Vg$, direct differentiation gives $A'=V'^*dV'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$, since $g^*=g^{-1}$. The frame-coordinate covariant derivative changes from $d+A$ to $g^{-1}(d+A)g$ on coefficient sections. Squaring this identity gives $dA'+A'\wedge A'=g^{-1}(dA+A\wedge A)g$, which is the claimed curvature covariance.

For a path the definitions give $W'=[P',P]W$; [F2] proves that its unique solution is unitary and satisfies $P(t)W(t)=W(t)P(0)$. This is projector parallel transport and uses no Schrödinger evolution.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

$$D(a,R)=\{\zeta\in\mathbb C:|\zeta-a|<R\}.$$

If $0<r<R$, $|z-a|<r$, and $\gamma(t)=a+r\exp(it)$ for $0\le t\le2\pi$, then

$$f(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\gamma\frac{f(\zeta)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected CW complex $B$ (or over one of the CW-type bases of
[[thm-integral-complex-projective-bundle-theorem]]). By that theorem there are
unique classes $a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, such that
$$x_E^{\,n}-a_1x_E^{\,n-1}+a_2x_E^{\,n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^na_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^{2n}(P(E);\mathbb Z),$$
where $x_E\in H^2(P(E);\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of the underlying real
bundle of the tautological line
([[def-complex-projective-bundle-and-tautological-complex-line]]). The
**Chern classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$c_i(E):=a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$
completed by the conventions $c_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb Z)$ and
$c_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Chern class** is the finite sum
$c(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}c_i(E)=1+c_1(E)+\cdots+c_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb Z)$.

For the zero bundle of rank $0$ the conventions give $c(0_B)=1$. The definition
depends only on the isomorphism class of $E$, because an isomorphism of
bundles induces an isomorphism of projective bundles pulling $x$ back to $x$
and hence preserves the unique relation. For a complex line bundle $L\to B$ one
has $P(L)\cong B$ over $B$ with $\gamma_L$ corresponding to $L$ under that
identification, so the relation is $x_L-c_1(L)=0$; since $x_L=e(L_{\mathbb R})$
under the identification, this gives
$$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R}).$$
This is the normalization used throughout the page: the first Chern class of a
complex line is the Euler class of its underlying real bundle in the complex
orientation, not a separately chosen normalization.

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, and $k\ge0$, define
$$I_M^k:\Omega^k(M)\longrightarrow C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R),\qquad I_M^k(\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega.$$
On $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ this means $I_M^k(\omega)(c)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$, a finite sum. In negative degrees $I_M^k$ is the zero map. Forms and the de Rham complex at a boundary use [[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]]. No orientation of $M$ is required: the domain simplex has the specified orientation. The name integration cochain map is justified by [[thm-de-rham-integration-is-a-cochain-map]].

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, the inclusion of smooth into continuous real singular chains induces an isomorphism
$$H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\longrightarrow H_k^{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$$
in every integer degree. This isomorphism is natural for smooth maps. The proof smooths only finitely many simplices at a time. For boundary targets it moves a finite compact set into the interior; it does not prescribe arbitrary boundary faces during smoothing.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For an oriented smooth manifold $M^n$, possibly with boundary, and $\omega\in\Omega_c^n(M)$, choose a smooth partition $(\rho_i)$ subordinate to connected interior or boundary charts $(U_i,\phi_i)$. For $n\geq1$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_i I_{\phi_i}(\rho_i\omega).$$
Each product has compact support in its chart and only finitely many are nonzero, by [[lem-a-locally-finite-sum-is-finite-near-the-compact-support-of-a-form]]. For $n=0$ set
$$\int_M\omega=\sum_{p\in\operatorname{supp}\omega}\varepsilon(p)\omega(p).$$
$\Lambda^0T_p^*M\cong\mathbb R$ has two orientations; define $\varepsilon(p)=+1$ when $1$ is positive in the chosen orientation and $\varepsilon(p)=-1$ when $-1$ is positive.
A zero-manifold is discrete; the singleton open cover of a compact subset has a finite subcover. Thus this sum too is finite. Empty support or empty $M$ gives zero. Independence of the choices is discharged by [[thm-global-form-integration-is-independent-of-the-atlas-partition-and-refinement]].

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. The compact-support integral on an oriented manifold is independent of the chart cover, coordinate maps, subordinate partition, and refinement. If $U\subset M$ is open and contains $\operatorname{supp}\omega$, with its restricted orientation, then $\int_U\omega|_U=\int_M\omega$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$

Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let

Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$

component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Assume AC. Let $E\to B$ be a numerable complex rank-$n$ bundle with $n\geq1$
over a path-connected CW complex $B$ (or over one of the CW-type bases of
[[thm-integral-complex-projective-bundle-theorem]]). By that theorem there are
unique classes $a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)$, $1\leq i\leq n$, such that
$$x_E^{\,n}-a_1x_E^{\,n-1}+a_2x_E^{\,n-2}-\cdots+(-1)^na_n=0\qquad\text{in }H^{2n}(P(E);\mathbb Z),$$
where $x_E\in H^2(P(E);\mathbb Z)$ is the Euler class of the underlying real
bundle of the tautological line
([[def-complex-projective-bundle-and-tautological-complex-line]]). The
**Chern classes** of $E$ are these coefficients:
$$c_i(E):=a_i\in H^{2i}(B;\mathbb Z)\qquad(1\leq i\leq n),$$
completed by the conventions $c_0(E):=1\in H^0(B;\mathbb Z)$ and
$c_i(E):=0$ for $i>n$, and the **total Chern class** is the finite sum
$c(E):=\sum_{i\geq0}c_i(E)=1+c_1(E)+\cdots+c_n(E)\in H^*(B;\mathbb Z)$.

For the zero bundle of rank $0$ the conventions give $c(0_B)=1$. The definition
depends only on the isomorphism class of $E$, because an isomorphism of
bundles induces an isomorphism of projective bundles pulling $x$ back to $x$
and hence preserves the unique relation. For a complex line bundle $L\to B$ one
has $P(L)\cong B$ over $B$ with $\gamma_L$ corresponding to $L$ under that
identification, so the relation is $x_L-c_1(L)=0$; since $x_L=e(L_{\mathbb R})$
under the identification, this gives
$$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R}).$$
This is the normalization used throughout the page: the first Chern class of a
complex line is the Euler class of its underlying real bundle in the complex
orientation, not a separately chosen normalization.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

The same lemma gives finitely many open-and-closed components $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ and the restriction isomorphism
$$H_n(M;R)\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^k H_n(M,M\setminus M_j;R).$$
The summand on the right identifies with $H_n(M_j;R)$: apply [[thm-excision-for-singular-homology]] to remove the closed set $M\setminus M_j$, which is the entire open relative subspace. The resulting pair is $(M_j,\varnothing)$. Under this identification $[M]$ corresponds to the finite tuple of the component fundamental classes.

If the orientation is negated on one component, its new fundamental-class summand is the negative of its old one. Indeed restriction is linear, so the negative class restricts to $-\mu_x$ at all points of that component, and uniqueness in the compact-set lemma identifies it with the new class. The other component summands are unchanged. In characteristic two this negation can leave the orientation and class unchanged; no distinction between $\mu$ and $-\mu$ is imposed when they are equal.

For empty $M$ the fundamental class is $0$ in the zero homology group, with an empty direct sum. For $R=0$ the unique orientation gives the zero class. A compact zero-manifold has finitely many singleton components, and its fundamental zero-cycle has at each point the coefficient prescribed by its local module generator. The definition requires a supplied orientation and uses no AC or simultaneous choice of one orientation per component.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, and $k\ge0$, define
$$I_M^k:\Omega^k(M)\longrightarrow C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R),\qquad I_M^k(\omega)(\sigma)=\int_\sigma\omega.$$
On $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ this means $I_M^k(\omega)(c)=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\int_\sigma\omega$, a finite sum. In negative degrees $I_M^k$ is the zero map. Forms and the de Rham complex at a boundary use [[lem-the-de-rham-complex-and-pullback-extend-to-manifolds-with-boundary]]. No orientation of $M$ is required: the domain simplex has the specified orientation. The name integration cochain map is justified by [[thm-de-rham-integration-is-a-cochain-map]].
