derivations.claim:
Choose a finite coordinate-chart cover of the compact surface $\Sigma$ and a smooth partition $\{\phi_j\}_{j=1}^N$ subordinate to it by [F3]. In each chart, every matrix entry of $\phi_jP$ is a $C^2$ function supported compactly inside the coordinate domain; extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^2$. Start with $\rho(y)=c\exp(-1/(1-|y|^2))$ for $|y|<1$ and $\rho(y)=0$ otherwise, where $c>0$ normalizes its integral to one. The extension is smooth because every derivative at the boundary is a finite sum of terms bounded by $t^{-m}e^{-1/t}$ as $t\downarrow0$, and these tend to zero. Put $\rho_\epsilon(y)=\epsilon^{-2}\rho(y/\epsilon)$ and convolve each real and imaginary entry with it. For every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\leq2$, $\partial^\alpha(\rho_\epsilon*f)=\rho_\epsilon*(\partial^\alpha f)$ and
$$\|\rho_\epsilon*(\partial^\alpha f)-\partial^\alpha f\|_\infty\leq\sup_{|y|\leq\epsilon}\|\partial^\alpha f(\,\cdot-y)-\partial^\alpha f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0,$$
because each compactly supported derivative is uniformly continuous. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the convolved supports remain inside their charts. Summing the finitely many pulled-back approximants gives a smooth matrix field $Q_\epsilon\to P$ in $C^2$; replacing it by $(Q_\epsilon+Q_\epsilon^*)/2$ keeps it smooth Hermitian and preserves this convergence.

Fix $\epsilon$ so $\delta:=\sup_\Sigma\|Q_\epsilon-P\|<1/4$. For each $x\in\Sigma$, define
$$R_\epsilon(x)=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|z-1|=1/2}(zI-Q_\epsilon(x))^{-1}\,dz.$$
On this contour $\|(zI-P(x))^{-1}\|=2$, so the Neumann series shows $zI-Q_\epsilon(x)$ is invertible and its inverse has norm at most $4$. The finite-dimensional spectral theorem [F4] diagonalizes $Q_\epsilon(x)$. For an eigenvalue $\lambda$ inside the circle, the Cauchy integral formula [F4] gives $\oint_\Gamma(z-\lambda)^{-1}\,dz=2\pi i$. For an exterior eigenvalue put $c=1$, $R=1/2$, and $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. On $\Gamma$, the geometric expansion
$$\frac1{z-\lambda}=-\sum_{k=0}^N\frac{(z-c)^k}{(\lambda-c)^{k+1}}+r_N(z),\qquad \sup_\Gamma|r_N|\leq\frac{q^{N+1}}{|\lambda-c|(1-q)}$$
has a remainder whose contour integral tends to zero, since the circle has length $2\pi R$. Each polynomial term integrates to zero, as the parametrization $z=c+Re^{it}$ gives $\oint_\Gamma(z-c)^k\,dz=iR^{k+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(k+1)t}\,dt=0$. Thus the exterior eigenvalue contributes zero. Applying these two scalar calculations to the diagonalization shows that $R_\epsilon(x)$ is the orthogonal spectral projection onto eigenvalues inside the circle. The same contour is valid for $Q_t=P+t(Q_\epsilon-P)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, so these projections vary continuously with $t$; their integer-valued ranks are constant and equal the rank one of $P$. The resolvent identity gives
$$\|R_\epsilon-P\|_\infty\leq\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\pi\,(4)\delta(2)=4\delta<1.$$
The contour integral also shows $R_\epsilon$ is smooth in $x$.

The restriction $R_\epsilon(x)|_{\operatorname{ran}P(x)}$ is injective: if $R_\epsilon v=0$ and $P v=v$, then $\|v\|=\|(P-R_\epsilon)v\|\leq\|P-R_\epsilon\|\,\|v\|$, which forces $v=0$. Both ranges are one-dimensional, so these restrictions form a continuous complex line-bundle isomorphism $E_P\cong E_{R_\epsilon}$ and [F6] gives $c_1(E_P)=c_1(E_{R_\epsilon})$. The compact surface has finitely many components by [F6]; apply the disconnected line-class convention of [F5] on each component and sum the pairings using the fundamental-class direct sum. In a local unit frame $u$ for $E_{R_\epsilon}$, its connection form is $A=u^*du$ and its scalar curvature is $dA$. The rank-one curvature matrix is $F_{R_\epsilon}=u(dA)u^*$, hence $\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}=dA=\Omega_{\nabla_\epsilon}$. The smooth integral here is the chart-partition integral [F10], agreeing with the continuous convention [F11]; its coordinate independence uses the common-refinement change-of-variables argument [F8]. Applying [F5] to the smooth Hermitian line bundle $E_{R_\epsilon}$ and its projected Hermitian connection, then evaluating on $[\Sigma]$ using [F6] and [F7], gives
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}=\langle c_1(E_{R_\epsilon}),[\Sigma]\rangle=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$

The contour formula for $R_\epsilon$ and its first two coordinate derivatives show $R_\epsilon\to P$ in $C^2$: differentiating $(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}$ once gives $(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}(\partial_jQ_\epsilon)(zI-Q_\epsilon)^{-1}$, and differentiating twice gives a finite sum of products of uniformly bounded resolvents with first and second derivatives of $Q_\epsilon$. Thus in each chart of the fixed finite partition, $R_\epsilon$ and its first derivatives converge uniformly to $P$ and its first derivatives. On the compact supports of that partition, let $\delta_0$ and $\delta_1$ be the largest of the zeroth- and first-coordinate-derivative errors, and choose $M\ge1$ bounding all first derivatives of $P$ and $R_\epsilon$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. For the coordinate coefficient $F_{12}(P)=P(\partial_1P\,\partial_2P-\partial_2P\,\partial_1P)P$, submultiplicativity and $\|P\|=\|R_\epsilon\|=1$ give $\|F_{12}(R_\epsilon)-F_{12}(P)\|\le4M^2\delta_0+4M\delta_1$; the trace difference is at most $d$ times this bound. Hence the continuous coefficients in the fixed finite chart-partition formula [F11] converge uniformly. Put each compact chart support in the interior of a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q_j$. By [F12], both real and imaginary parts of each continuous zero-extended coefficient and its difference are Riemann integrable there. For a real continuous $h$ on $Q_j$, put $c=\sup_{Q_j}|h|$. Every Darboux sum of the constant functions $\pm c$ is $\pm c\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)$, since the cell volumes sum to the rectangle volume. Monotonicity in [F9] applied to $-c\le h\le c$ therefore gives $|\int_{Q_j}h|\le c\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)$. Applying this separately to the real and imaginary parts of a complex coefficient $g$ and using $|\operatorname{Re}g|,|\operatorname{Im}g|\le|g|$ gives $|\int_{Q_j}g|\le2\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)\sup_{Q_j}|g|$. Finite linearity then gives $\left|\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_{R_\epsilon}-\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F_P\right|\leq2\sum_j\operatorname{vol}(Q_j)\sup_{Q_j}|\widetilde f_j^\epsilon-\widetilde f_j|\longrightarrow0$. The continuous-integral convention [F11] and this estimate show that the limit is the integral in the Statement. Step 2.1 gives the same integer for every sufficiently small $\epsilon$, so taking the limit proves the stated equality for $P$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional Hausdorff
second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$L\to M$ be a smooth complex line bundle with a supplied Hermitian metric and
Hermitian connection $\nabla$. Write $\Omega_\nabla$ for its curvature and
$c_1(L):=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for the published integral line class, using the
complex orientation on the underlying real plane. Let
$$\rho_M:H^2(M;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow H^2(M;\mathbb R)$$
be induced by $\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Under the natural de Rham
isomorphism $J_M$,
$$J_M\left[ -\frac{\Omega_\nabla}{2\pi i}\right]=\rho_M(c_1(L)).$$
For a disconnected base the same line-class convention is understood on each
component; the global class is the Euler class displayed above.

If $\nabla'$ is any complex connection on $L$, not necessarily metric
compatible, then
$$\left[-\frac{\Omega_{\nabla'}}{2\pi i}\right]=\iota_M\!\left(J_M^{-1}\rho_M(c_1(L))\right)\quad\text{in }H^2_{\rm dR}(M;\mathbb C),$$
where $\iota_M$ is induced by including real-valued forms into complex-valued
forms. Thus the arbitrary-connection class is identified with the same real
class by the degree-one transgression.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

Let $\gamma$ lie in one frame patch with unit frame $u$. A section is $u c$, and $\nabla(uc)=u(dc+A c)$ for $A=u^*du$; therefore a parallel section satisfies $c'=-A(\gamma')c$. Since this is a scalar equation, its transport factor on that segment is $\exp(-\int_\gamma A)$. The compact path has a finite subdivision into local frame patches by compactness and the open-cover property; uniqueness on each segment follows from the Kato ODE in [F1].

At a frame change $u_{j+1}=u_jg_j$, equality of the represented section $u_jc_j=u_{j+1}c_{j+1}$ gives $c_{j+1}=g_j^{-1}c_j$. Composing the local scalar transport equations from step 1.2 with these coefficient changes gives exactly the product in the Statement. Refining the subdivision inserts a segment and its inverse transition at the same point, so the product is unchanged; equivalently, it is the unique transport from the Kato ODE in [F1].

In the two-subsurface decomposition, set $A_N=u_N^*du_N$ and $A_S=u_S^*du_S$. From $u_S=u_Ng$ and $g^{-1}g=1$, the product rule gives $A_S=A_N+g^{-1}dg$. For a line, $A\wedge A=0$, so the scalar curvature on each patch is $dA$. The common boundary has opposite induced orientations on the two subsurfaces. Applying [F4] gives
$\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\int_\Gamma A_N+\int_{-\Gamma}A_S=\int_\Gamma(A_N-A_S)=-\int_\Gamma g^{-1}dg.$
For one oriented component parameterized by $t\in[0,2\pi]$, $|g(t)|=1$ implies $g^{-1}g'=ia(t)$ for a real continuous function $a$. Put $\theta(t)=\int_0^t a(s)\,ds$; differentiating shows $g(t)e^{-i\theta(t)}$ is constant, so $g(t)=g(0)e^{i\theta(t)}$. Since $g(2\pi)=g(0)$, $\theta(2\pi)\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, and hence $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int g^{-1}dg\in\mathbb Z$. Summing components shows $\operatorname{wind}(g)\in\mathbb Z$. Multiplying the curvature identity by $i/(2\pi)$ and using step 1.1 proves the claimed Chern-number formula, with the sign fixed by the orientation of $\partial\Sigma_N$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$H:[0,1]\to\operatorname{Herm}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a map of class $C^2$ into the
Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices, let $P(s)$ be the spectral projection of $H(s)$
for a spectral cluster $\sigma_P(s)$ that is separated from the complementary
spectrum by a uniform gap: $\operatorname{dist}(\sigma_P(s),\sigma(H(s))\setminus\sigma_P(s))\ge g>0$
for all $s\in[0,1]$. Require that the cluster is followed coherently:
$P(s)$ is continuous in operator norm (equivalently, it follows the local
Riesz continuation of its initial cluster). Fix $T>0$. Let $U_T$ solve
$i\,\partial_sU_T(s)=TH(s)U_T(s)$, $U_T(0)=I$
by the finite matrix construction below, and let
$U_A$ solve $i\,\partial_sU_A(s)=\bigl(TH(s)+i[P'(s),P(s)]\bigr)U_A(s)$,
$U_A(0)=I$ (equivalently $U_A'=(-iTH+K)U_A$ with $K=[P',P]$). Then:

(a) $P\in C^2([0,1];\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d))$ and $K=[P',P]$ is
anti-Hermitian of class $C^1$ with $[K,P]=P'$.

(b) There is a $C^1$ Hermitian $X:[0,1]\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ with
$[H(s),X(s)]=K(s)$ for all $s$.

(c) *Intertwining.* $P(s)U_A(s)=U_A(s)P(0)$ for all $s$.

(d) *Adiabatic estimate.* With
$C:=2\sup_s\|X(s)\|+\int_0^1\bigl(\|X'(s)\|+\|K(s)\|\|X(s)\|\bigr)ds$ one has
$$\bigl\|(I-P(s))U_T(s)P(0)\bigr\|\le\frac CT\qquad(s\in[0,1]).$$

The estimate is finite-dimensional and conditional on the uniform positive gap;
gap-closing families and unbounded families are not covered.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

derivations.claim: Divide the evolution equation by $\hbar$ and set $\tau=T/\hbar>0$. Then $i\,\partial_sU_T=\tau H(s)U_T$, exactly the scale convention of [F1], with the same $H$, $P$, $K$, and $X$. The supplier's hypotheses hold: $H$ is $C^2$, the cluster is coherently followed, and its complementary spectral distance is uniformly at least $g>0$. Therefore its estimate gives $\|(I-P(s))U_T(s)P(0)\|\leq C/\tau=\hbar C/T$.

Suppose $\operatorname{rank}P=1$ and $HP=EP$. By [F2], $W'=KW$, $P(s)W(s)=W(s)P(0)$, and $W$ is unitary. Set $V(s)=W(s)\exp(-i\tau\int_0^sE(u)\,du)$. For $v\in\operatorname{ran}P(0)$, intertwining gives $W(s)v\in\operatorname{ran}P(s)$, so $H(s)W(s)v=E(s)W(s)v$. Differentiating therefore gives $V'(s)v=(-i\tau H(s)+K(s))V(s)v$, with $V(0)v=v$. The defined $U_A$ satisfies the same matrix initial-value equation $U_A'=(-i\tau H+K)U_A$; uniqueness of finite-dimensional linear ODE solutions yields $U_A(s)v=V(s)v$ for every such $v$, which is the stated factorization.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

Assume full AC. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ rank-one orthogonal projection family. Let $E_P$ be its complex line bundle, $\nabla=P\,d$, and $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
For any $C^2$ closed path $\gamma$ subdivided into local unit frames $u_j$, with $A_j=u_j^*du_j$ and transition $u_{j+1}=u_jg_j$ for $g_j$ valued in $U(1)$ at the crossing points, the holonomy is the scalar by which parallel transport acts on its one-dimensional initial fiber. This scalar is the product of the local factors $\exp(-\int_{\gamma_j}A_j)$ and the transition factors $g_j^{-1}$. Thus geometric holonomy includes the frame-transition scalars whenever one frame does not cover the path.

In addition, suppose $\Sigma=\Sigma_N\cup\Sigma_S$ is a decomposition into compact oriented subsurfaces with disjoint interiors and common finite boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Sigma_N=-\partial\Sigma_S$, a finite union of oriented smooth circles. If $E_P$ has supplied $C^2$ unit frames $u_N,u_S$ on these subsurfaces and $u_S=u_Ng$ on $\Gamma$ for a $C^2$ map $g:\Gamma\to U(1)$, then
$$\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle=\operatorname{wind}(g):=\sum_{\Gamma_j\subset\Gamma}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma_j}g^{-1}dg\in\mathbb Z,$$
where each component $\Gamma_j$ has the orientation induced by $\partial\Sigma_N$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth surface with boundary. Let $D\subseteq M$ be a compact oriented region with the following local regularity: its interior points have disk charts, its smooth boundary points have half-disk charts, and each of its finitely many corners has a chart in which it is a quadrant or the complement of an open quadrant. Its boundary is a finite union of embedded $C^2$ arcs with pairwise disjoint interiors; each arc is the image of an injective $C^2$ parametrization with nonzero derivative, including one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Arcs meet only at their common endpoints, and at every corner their one-sided tangent vectors are linearly independent. Let $\eta=a\,dx+b\,dy$ be a complex-valued $C^1$ one-form on a neighborhood of $D$ in each local chart, where $C^1$ means its coefficients and first partial derivatives are continuous up to the boundary. Define $d\eta=(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)\,dx\wedge dy$ in each chart; the chain rule and symmetry of second derivatives make this expression coordinate-independent. Orient every open boundary arc outward-normal-first: $(\nu_{\rm out},\tau)$ is a positive basis of $TD$, where $\nu_{\rm out}$ is outward and $\tau$ is the positive boundary tangent. Integrals over $D$ use oriented coordinate Riemann integrals, and the boundary integral is the sum of the line integrals over its finitely many oriented arcs. Then
$$\int_D d\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta.$$

Assume full AC. Let $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$ have its outward area form $\omega$. Let $D^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|\leq1\}$ have orientation $dx\wedge dy$; $C^2$ maps on $D^2$ have derivatives through order two extending continuously to the boundary. Set
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_+(n)=\frac{I+n_x\sigma_x+n_y\sigma_y+n_z\sigma_z}{2}.$$
For any two $C^2$ maps $f_0,f_1:D^2\to S^2$ from an oriented disk, with the same boundary map and its induced boundary orientation, the two oriented solid-angle integrals differ by a multiple of $4\pi$:
$$\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega\in4\pi\mathbb Z.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: Matrix multiplication gives $(n\cdot\sigma)^*=(n\cdot\sigma)$ and $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=I$, while $\operatorname{tr}(n\cdot\sigma)=0$. Hence $P_+^*=P_+^2=P_+$ and $\operatorname{tr}P_+=1$, so it is a rank-one orthogonal projection. Direct multiplication gives $(n\cdot\sigma)u_N=u_N$ and $u_N^*u_N=1$, so $u_N$ is a normalized local frame of its positive eigenline.

Differentiating the displayed spinor gives $u_N^*du_N=i\sin^2(\theta/2)\,d\phi=i(1-\cos\theta)d\phi/2$. Taking the exterior derivative yields $dA_N=i\sin\theta\,d\theta\wedge d\phi/2$, which is the curvature in this frame by [F1]. Both the projector curvature and the spherical area form are global smooth two-forms, so their equality on the northern chart gives $F=(i/2)\omega_{S^2}$ globally.

Integrating the area form gives $\int_{S^2}\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi=4\pi$, hence $\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}F=\frac{i}{2\pi}\frac{i}{2}(4\pi)=-1$. By [F2] this is the integral first Chern number with the stated anti-Hermitian connection convention.

A southern frame is $u_S=(e^{-i\phi}\cos(\theta/2),\sin(\theta/2))^T=e^{-i\phi}u_N$; it is regular at the south pole and together with $u_N$ covers $S^2$. Along the equator the transition is $g(\phi)=e^{-i\phi}$, so $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}g^{-1}dg=-1$. The two-hemisphere clutching clause in [F2] therefore gives Chern number $-1$, matching the direct curvature integral in step 3.1 and fixing the orientation sign. Pull these frames back to the standard closed parameter disk filling $S$. Their inverse images form an open cover of the disk; by [F5] it has a Lebesgue number $\delta>0$. Choose $N$ with $\sqrt2/N<\delta$, set $h=1/N$, and intersect the disk with the closed axis-aligned squares $[i h,(i+1)h]\times[j h,(j+1)h]$. Retain only intersections $C_{ij}$ with nonempty interior. There are finitely many; their interiors are disjoint and their closures cover the disk, since every disk point is a limit of interior points off the grid lines and a subsequence lies in one of finitely many retained cells. Each cell has diameter at most $\sqrt2h<\delta$, so it lies in one frame patch. Each is a compact convex region whose boundary, after zero-length pieces are discarded, is a finite union of regular straight or circular arcs meeting at finitely many corners; the C1 Stokes item [F3] applies. On a cell $C_{ij}$, its frame connection $A_{ij}$ is $C^1$ because the filling is $C^2$, and [F3] gives $\int_{\partial C_{ij}}A_{ij}=\int_{C_{ij}}F$. Since one frame covers the cell, its boundary holonomy is $\exp(-\int_{\partial C_{ij}}A_{ij})=\exp(-\int_{C_{ij}}F)$. Choose a unit vector at each vertex of this finite cell decomposition and write each oriented edge transport as its unit-modulus scalar in those endpoint vectors. In the product of the cell-boundary holonomies every internal edge occurs once in each direction, so its scalar and inverse cancel; only the outer boundary loop remains. Thus $\operatorname{Hol}(C)=\exp(-\int_SF)=\exp(-i\Omega/2)$. If a second filling is chosen, [F4] says its solid angle differs by $4\pi k$ for some integer $k$, so this exponential is independent of the filling. For a latitude circle the north-cap integral is $\Omega=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\theta\sin u\,du\,d\phi=2\pi(1-\cos\theta)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $H\in C^2([0,1],\operatorname{Herm}(\mathbb C^d))$ be a finite Hermitian family with energy unit joules, and let $\hbar>0$ have unit joule-seconds. A spectral cluster at $s$ is a subset $\sigma_P(s)$ of the finite spectrum of $H(s)$, and $P(s)$ is the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. Coherently followed means that $s\mapsto P(s)$ is continuous in operator norm (equivalently, it agrees locally with the Riesz continuation of its initial cluster). Assume the distance from $\sigma_P(s)$ to the complementary spectrum is at least a uniform $g>0$ in joules. Let $T>0$ be a total duration in seconds, let $s=t/T$ be dimensionless, and let $U_T(0)=I$ solve
$$i\hbar\,\partial_sU_T(s)=T H(s)U_T(s).$$
Put $K(s)=[P'(s),P(s)]$. There is a $C^1$ Hermitian matrix $X(s)$ solving $[H(s),X(s)]=K(s)$. With
$$C=2\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|X(s)\|+\int_0^1\bigl(\|X'(s)\|+\|K(s)\|\,\|X(s)\|\bigr)\,ds,$$
the leakage satisfies
$$\|(I-P(s))U_T(s)P(0)\|\leq\frac{\hbar C}{T}\qquad(0\leq s\leq1).$$
The supplier provides a $C^1$ Hermitian $X$ solving the displayed commutator equation. For that $X$, $C$ has unit joule-inverse, so $\hbar C/T$ is dimensionless. If the cluster has rank one, with $H(s)P(s)=E(s)P(s)$, define $U_A(0)=I$ by
$$i\,\partial_sU_A(s)=\left(\frac{T}{\hbar}H(s)+iK(s)\right)U_A(s).$$
For Kato transport $W'(s)=K(s)W(s)$, $W(0)=I$, the comparison evolution factors exactly on the initial eigenspace:
$$U_A(s)P(0)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iT}{\hbar}\int_0^sE(u)\,du\right)W(s)P(0).$$
The leakage estimate is finite-dimensional and conditional on the stated uniform positive gap.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb C^2$, let $e_\uparrow=(1,0)^T$, $e_\downarrow=(0,1)^T$, and $H(s)=E_0(2s-1)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ for $s\in[0,1]$. For $s<1/2$ the ordered upper eigenvalue is $E_0(1-2s)$ and its projection is $P_{\rm up}(s)=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$; for $s>1/2$ it is $E_0(2s-1)$ and its projection is $P_{\rm up}(s)=e_\uparrow e_\uparrow^*$. At $s=1/2$, $H(s)=0$, so the degenerate upper eigenspace is all of $\mathbb C^2$ and its spectral projection is $I_2$; the one-sided rank-one projections therefore have no continuous rank-one extension. The gap between the two eigenvalues is $2E_0|2s-1|$, which closes at $s=1/2$.

The propagator from $s=0$ solves $i\hbar U_T'(s)=T H(s)U_T(s)$ and is
$$U_T(s)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{iTE_0}{\hbar}(s^2-s)\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\right),$$
as direct differentiation verifies. In particular $U_T(1)=I_2$.

At the endpoints, $P_{\rm up}(0)=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$ and $P_{\rm up}(1)=e_\uparrow e_\uparrow^*$. Therefore
$$\bigl\|(I-P_{\rm up}(1))U_T(1)P_{\rm up}(0)\bigr\|=\|e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*\|=1$$
for every $T>0$. No finite constant $C$ independent of $T$ can bound this leakage by $C/T$. The ordered projection fails the continuity and uniform-gap hypotheses in [F1].

The constant projection $P_\downarrow=e_\downarrow e_\downarrow^*$ commutes with every $H(s)$ and has zero leakage for all $T$. At the crossing it is not the spectral projection onto the degenerate eigenspace, which is all of $\mathbb C^2$; it is a continuous invariant rank-one subspace, not a coherently followed gapped spectral cluster. Thus the example refutes a gap-free uniform tracking claim for the ordered branch; it does not assert that every choice of state at a crossing causes transitions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A boundary chart is a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb H^n$, where $U\subseteq M$ is open and $V$ is relatively open. Two charts are compatible if each transition map is smooth in the local-extension sense. A smooth atlas is a compatible covering atlas; its smooth structure is its maximal compatible atlas.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

For an oriented manifold with boundary, orient $T_p\partial M$ by the **outward-normal-first** rule: an outward vector first, followed by a positive boundary determinant, is a positive determinant of $T_pM$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

derivations.claim: By compactness and [F2], choose finitely many $C^2$ straightening neighborhoods of $D$ with compact coordinate closures, using the local models in the Statement at points on $\partial M$. At an interior boundary arc with parametrization $\gamma(s)$, choose a transverse vector $v$ and use $(s,t)\mapsto\gamma(s)+tv$; its derivative is invertible, so [F8] gives a $C^2$ inverse chart. At a corner in an interior chart, the independent tangent vectors of the two incident arcs make $(s,t)\mapsto\gamma_1(s)+\gamma_2(t)-\gamma_1(0)$ a $C^2$ local diffeomorphism by [F8]; it straightens the boundary to coordinate axes and the region to a quadrant or its reentrant complement. Add $M\setminus D$ to this finite open cover and use [F3] for a smooth subordinate partition of unity. On $D$, only finitely many localized forms $\eta_i=\rho_i\eta$ contribute, each with compact support in one straightening chart.

In an oriented coordinate plane, a compactly supported $C^1$ form $a\,dx+b\,dy$ satisfies $\int_{\mathbb R^2}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=0$, $\int_{y\geq0}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=\int_{\mathbb R}a(x,0)\,dx$, and $\int_{x,y\geq0}(\partial_xb-\partial_ya)=\int_0^\infty a(x,0)\,dx-\int_0^\infty b(0,y)\,dy$. For complex coefficients, apply the calculation to real and imaginary parts. Put the support in a rectangle; [F9] makes the coefficients and their first derivatives Riemann integrable, and [F10] makes them uniformly continuous. Double Riemann sums and iterated one-dimensional Riemann sums have the same limit, since their difference is bounded by the rectangle area times the modulus of continuity at the mesh diameter. Then [F7] evaluates the one-dimensional integrals of $\partial_xb$ and $\partial_ya$ at their endpoints, and the compact support removes the artificial outer edges. The half-plane and quadrant boundary signs are exactly the outward-normal-first convention [F6]. On the reentrant model, subtract the missing open quadrant from the plane; the two axis integrals have the opposite orientation, so the same identity holds.

A $C^2$ straightening map preserves the exterior derivative of a $C^1$ one-form by the chain rule: the terms involving its second derivatives cancel by symmetry. The compact-support change-of-variables formula [F4] carries each local area identity to $D$, while [F6] carries the axis orientations to the oriented boundary arcs. Summing over the partition from step 1.1 gives $\int_Dd\eta=\int_{\partial D}\eta$. The empty region and empty boundary give zero on both sides.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. Write $U(r)=\{g\in\mathbb C^{r\times r}:g^*g=gg^*=I_r\}$ for the unitary group. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], with constant rank $r$. The curvature of the projected connection $\nabla=P\,d$, as an endomorphism-valued two-form on $\mathbb C^d$, is
$$F=P(dP\wedge dP)P.$$
For any local $C^2$ orthonormal frame $V:U\to\mathbb C^{d\times r}$ with $V^*V=I_r$ and $P=VV^*$, its connection matrix $A=V^*dV$ is anti-Hermitian and its curvature matrix is $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=dA+A\wedge A=V^*FV$. If $V'=Vg$ for a $C^2$ map $g:U\to U(r)$, then $A'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$ and $F'_{\mathrm{fr}}=g^{-1}F_{\mathrm{fr}}g$. Along every $C^2$ path, Kato transport is unitary and intertwines the endpoint projectors.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact boundaryless oriented smooth surface, let $d\geq1$, and let $P:\Sigma\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ family of rank-one orthogonal projections. Let $E_P\to\Sigma$ be the complex line bundle with fibers $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$, let $\nabla=P\,d$, and let $F=P(dP\wedge dP)P$ be the curvature of this projected connection. Then
$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$
Here $c_1(E_P)$ is the first integral Chern class of the underlying topological complex line bundle, and $[\Sigma]$ is the fundamental class for the stated orientation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be smooth manifolds, let $F:M\to N$ be a map, let $p\in M$ and
let $r\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$, where $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$.
For $m,q\in\mathbb N_0$ and an open set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, a map
$g:E\to\mathbb R^q$ is **of class $C^r$** as follows. When $m=0$, every such
map is declared $C^r$. When $m\ge1$, each component $g_l$ with $l<q$ must be
$C^r$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]; when $q=0$ this
component condition is vacuous.
Suppose $F$ is continuous at $p$. Then $F$ is **of class $C^r$ at $p$** when
there are smooth charts $(U,\varphi)$ of $M$ at $p$ and $(V,\psi)$ of $N$ at
$F(p)$ with $F(U)\subseteq V$ such that the coordinate representative

$$\psi\circ F\circ\varphi^{-1}:\varphi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V)$$

([[def-coordinate-representation-of-a-map]]) is of class $C^r$ on a
neighbourhood of $\varphi(p)$ in this componentwise Euclidean sense. By
[[lem-chart-independence-of-c-r-smoothness]], this condition is independent of
the chosen charts: if one such representative is $C^r$, then every one is, so
"some charts" may be read as "any charts". A map is **$C^r$ on an open set**
$W\subseteq M$ when it is continuous on $W$ and $C^r$ at every point of $W$. A
map that is $C^r$ for every finite $r$ — equivalently $C^\infty$ — is called
**smooth**; the term **$C^r$ map between smooth manifolds** is reserved for the
case where $F$ is continuous and the representative condition holds at every
point of $M$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

derivations.claim:
Write $n=(\sin\theta\cos\phi,\sin\theta\sin\phi,\cos\theta)$ and use
$$\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Direct multiplication of the displayed matrices gives $\sigma_j^2=I$ and $\sigma_j\sigma_k+\sigma_k\sigma_j=0$ for $j\ne k$, while each $\sigma_j$ has trace zero. Hence $(n\cdot\sigma)^2=(n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2)I=I$ and $\operatorname{tr}(n\cdot\sigma)=0$, so $P_+$ is a rank-one orthogonal projector. On the northern chart, $u_N=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\phi}\sin(\theta/2))^T$ is a unit frame and $A_N=u_N^*du_N=i(1-\cos\theta)d\phi/2$, giving $dA_N=(i/2)\omega$. On the southern chart $u_S=e^{-i\phi}u_N$ is regular, and $A_S=A_N-i\,d\phi=-i(1+\cos\theta)d\phi/2$, so $dA_S=(i/2)\omega$ there as well. By [F1], these local calculations identify the global curvature trace as $\operatorname{tr}F_+=(i/2)\omega$.

Use orientation-preserving disk coordinates to identify each $D^2$ with $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:|x|\leq1\}$ oriented by $dx\wedge dy$. The explicit collar is $(q,t)\mapsto(1-t)q$, where $q=e^{i\theta}\in S^1$ and $t=1-r\geq0$ is inward radial distance. Since $dx\wedge dy=r\,d\theta\wedge dt$, the induced boundary orientation at $t=0$ is increasing $\theta$ (counterclockwise). Define $h(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $h(s)=0$ for $s\leq0$. For $0\leq t\leq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=h(t)/(h(t)+h(\epsilon/2-t))$, and for $t\geq\epsilon/2$ set $\chi_0(t)=1$. Every derivative of $h$ vanishes at $0$, so $\chi_0$ is smooth, flat at $0$, positive for $t>0$, at most $1$, and equal to $1$ near $\epsilon$; hence $\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0(t)\,dt<\epsilon$. Put $b(t)=h(t-\epsilon/4)h(3\epsilon/4-t)$, a nonnegative smooth function supported in $[\epsilon/4,3\epsilon/4]$ with positive integral, and define $\chi=\chi_0+c b$ where $c=(\epsilon-\int_0^\epsilon\chi_0)/\int_0^\epsilon b>0$. Then $\chi$ is positive for $t>0$, flat at $0$, equals $1$ near $\epsilon$, and has integral $\epsilon$. Set $\rho(t)=\int_0^t\chi(s)\,ds$. Thus $\rho(0)=\rho'(0)=\rho''(0)=0$, $\rho'(t)>0$ for $t>0$, and $\rho(t)=t$ near $\epsilon$. Replace $f_j(q,t)$ by $f_j(q,\rho(t))$ in each collar. This preserves area integral: the pullback coefficient is multiplied by $\rho'(t)$, and substitution $s=\rho(t)$ gives the original integral. Now form $X=D_0^2\cup_{S^1}(-D_1^2)$ by gluing the standard boundary circles with the identity; the first disk has orientation $dx\wedge dy$, the second has its negative, and their induced boundary orientations are opposite. Use the signed collar coordinates $s=t$ on the first disk and $s=-t$ on the second as seam charts; together with the two disk interiors they define the smooth structure on $X$. Both sides have orientation $d\theta\wedge ds$. The modified maps have the same boundary trace and all normal derivatives through order two vanish at the seam, while their tangential derivatives through order two agree there. They therefore glue to a $C^2$ map $g:X\to S^2$. The double is compact, smooth and boundaryless, and its chosen orientation gives $\int_Xg^*\omega=\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega$.

The projector $P_+\circ g$ is $C^2$ and rank one. Its projected curvature is $g^*F_+$: applying [F1] to $P_+\circ g$, the chain rule and [F4] give $d(P_+\circ g)=g^*dP_+$ and preserve the ordered wedge product. Thus [F2] gives
$$-\frac1{4\pi}\left(\int_{D^2}f_0^*\omega-\int_{D^2}f_1^*\omega\right)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\int\operatorname{tr}F_{P_+\circ g}\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the coefficient is $-1/(4\pi)$ because $i\cdot i=-1$. Rearranging proves the stated $4\pi$ period. This is a topological ambiguity statement for the same boundary loop; no physical observation is involved.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a set and write $\mathcal{P}(X)$ for its power set. A **topology** on
$X$ is a family $\mathcal{T} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ such that

- **(T1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{T}$ and $X \in \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T2)** $\bigcup \mathcal{S} \in \mathcal{T}$ for every $\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$;
- **(T3)** $U \cap V \in \mathcal{T}$ for all $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$.

A **topological space** is a pair $(X, \mathcal{T})$ consisting of a set $X$ and
a topology $\mathcal{T}$ on it; the elements of $X$ are its **points**. When only
one topology is in play we write $X$ for the pair; when several are, the topology
is always named.

The members of $\mathcal{T}$ are the **open** sets of $(X,\mathcal{T})$. A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed** when its complement $X \setminus F$ is open, and
**clopen** when it is both open and closed. By (T1) both $\varnothing$ and $X$
are clopen. *Open and closed are not opposites*: a set may be neither, and it may
be both, so "not open" is never a synonym for "closed".

**Finite intersections, and the empty one.** Axiom (T3) is stated for two sets
because that is all that is ever needed: if $n \ge 1$ and
$U_1, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{T}$, then $U_1 \cap \dots \cap U_n \in \mathcal{T}$
follows by iterating (T3) $n-1$ times. The intersection of the **empty** family
of subsets of $X$ is $X$, since the condition "lies in every member of the empty
family" is vacuous; that case is covered by (T1) rather than by (T3), which is
one of the two reasons $X \in \mathcal{T}$ is demanded outright. The other is
that (T2) alone gives only $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$.

**The closed sets, and the dual axiomatisation.** Put
$\mathcal{C} := \{\, X \setminus U : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\}$, the family of closed
sets. Then

- **(C1)** $\varnothing \in \mathcal{C}$ and $X \in \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C2)** $\bigcap \mathcal{D} \in \mathcal{C}$ for every **nonempty**
  $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$;
- **(C3)** $C \cup D \in \mathcal{C}$ for all $C, D \in \mathcal{C}$.

Conversely, if a family $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{P}(X)$ satisfies (C1),
(C2) and (C3), then $\mathcal{T} := \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$
is a topology on $X$ whose closed sets are exactly the members of $\mathcal{C}$.
So a topology may be presented equally well by its open sets or by its closed
sets, and this library uses whichever is shorter.

*Both directions are one computation, and it is carried out here rather than
assumed.* The map $U \mapsto X \setminus U$ is an involution of
$\mathcal{P}(X)$, hence a bijection, and it carries the two De Morgan identities

$$X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing), \qquad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad (I \ne \varnothing)$$

term by term into each other. Given (T1)–(T3): $\varnothing = X \setminus X$ and
$X = X \setminus \varnothing$ lie in $\mathcal{C}$, which is (C1); for nonempty
$\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ the family
$\mathcal{S} = \{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{D} \,\}$ lies in $\mathcal{T}$
and $\bigcap \mathcal{D} = X \setminus \bigcup \mathcal{S}$ is closed by (T2),
which is (C2); and $C \cup D = X \setminus ((X \setminus C) \cap (X \setminus D))$
is closed by (T3), which is (C3). Given (C1)–(C3) the same three lines run
backwards, the empty-union case $\bigcup \varnothing = \varnothing$ being supplied
by (C1) rather than by (C2); and $\{\, X \setminus C : C \in \mathcal{C} \,\}$ has
$\mathcal{C}$ as its family of complements because complementation is an
involution.

**Comparison of topologies.** If $\mathcal{T}_1$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ are
topologies on the same set $X$ and $\mathcal{T}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{T}_2$, then
$\mathcal{T}_1$ is **coarser** than $\mathcal{T}_2$ and $\mathcal{T}_2$ is
**finer** than $\mathcal{T}_1$; the comparison is **strict** when the inclusion
is. Inclusion is a partial order on the set of topologies on $X$
([[def-partial-order]]), and it is not a total one: two topologies on the same
set may be incomparable.
