supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and let
$S \subseteq X$. The **subspace topology** (also *relative topology*) on $S$ is

$$\mathcal{T}_S := \{\, U \cap S : U \in \mathcal{T} \,\},$$

the family of **traces** on $S$ of the open sets of $X$. The pair
$(S, \mathcal{T}_S)$ is a **subspace** of $X$. A subset of $S$ that lies in
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is said to be **open in $S$**, and *relatively open* where the
ambient space needs emphasis.

**$\mathcal{T}_S$ is a topology, and this is discharged here.** (T1):
$\varnothing = \varnothing \cap S$ and $S = X \cap S$ are traces. (T2): if
$\mathcal{S}' \subseteq \mathcal{T}_S$, choose for each member a set of
$\mathcal{T}$ tracing to it — no choice principle is needed, since
$U' := \bigcup \{\, U \in \mathcal{T} : U \cap S \subseteq W \,\}$ is a canonical
such set for $W \in \mathcal{T}_S$, being open by (T2) in $X$ and satisfying
$U' \cap S = W$ — and then
$\bigcup_i (U_i \cap S) = (\bigcup_i U_i) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by (T2) in
$X$. (T3): $(U \cap S) \cap (V \cap S) = (U \cap V) \cap S \in \mathcal{T}_S$ by
(T3) in $X$.

**Closed sets of a subspace are the traces of the closed sets.** A set
$C \subseteq S$ is closed in $S$ if and only if $C = F \cap S$ for some closed
$F \subseteq X$. Indeed $S \setminus (U \cap S) = (X \setminus U) \cap S$ and
$S \setminus (F \cap S) = (X \setminus F) \cap S$, so complementation inside $S$
matches complementation inside $X$ under tracing.

**Bases and subbases trace as well.** If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}$ ([[def-topology-basis-subbasis]]) then
$\mathcal{B}_S := \{\, B \cap S : B \in \mathcal{B} \,\}$ is a basis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$: its members are open in $S$, and for $W = U \cap S$ open in $S$
and $x \in W$ there is $B \in \mathcal{B}$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, whence
$x \in B \cap S \subseteq W$. The same computation with a subbasis $\mathcal{S}$
shows that $\{\, S_0 \cap S : S_0 \in \mathcal{S} \,\}$ is a subbasis for
$\mathcal{T}_S$, since tracing commutes with finite intersections and with
unions.

**The inclusion is continuous.** The inclusion map $\iota : S \to X$,
$\iota(s) = s$, satisfies $\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$ for every $U \subseteq X$,
so preimages of open sets are open and $\iota$ is continuous
([[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]], clause (b)). Moreover
$\mathcal{T}_S$ is the **coarsest** topology on $S$ making $\iota$ continuous: any
topology on $S$ for which $\iota$ is continuous must contain every
$\iota^{-1}[U] = U \cap S$, hence contain $\mathcal{T}_S$.

**Characteristic property of a map into a subspace.** Let $(Z, \mathcal{T}_Z)$ be
a topological space and let $g : Z \to S$ be a function. Then

$$g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (S,\mathcal{T}_S) \iff \iota \circ g \text{ is continuous as a map } Z \to (X,\mathcal{T}) .$$

*Proof.* For $U \in \mathcal{T}$ one has
$(\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U] = g^{-1}[\iota^{-1}[U]] = g^{-1}[U \cap S]$. If $g$ is
continuous then each $g^{-1}[U \cap S]$ is open, so $\iota \circ g$ is continuous;
conversely if $\iota \circ g$ is continuous then for any $W = U \cap S$ open in
$S$ the set $g^{-1}[W] = (\iota \circ g)^{-1}[U]$ is open, so $g$ is continuous.
Both directions use only clause (b) of [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]].

**Restriction of a continuous map.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous and
$S \subseteq X$, then $f|_S : S \to Y$ is continuous, since
$(f|_S)^{-1}[V] = f^{-1}[V] \cap S$ is open in $S$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]]).

**When relative and ambient agree.** If $S$ is open in $X$ then a subset of $S$
is open in $S$ if and only if it is open in $X$: a trace $U \cap S$ is then an
intersection of two open sets of $X$, and conversely an open subset of $X$
contained in $S$ is its own trace. The same statement with "closed" throughout
holds when $S$ is closed in $X$. Both are used in the pasting lemma of the next
item, and both fail without the hypothesis: $S$ itself is always open and closed
in $S$, and need be neither in $X$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. For each $n\ge0$, let $F_n:=R\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}\rangle$ be the free associative unital $R$-algebra on the indicated symbols ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]). When $n=0$ or $n=1$, the symbol set is empty and $F_n=R$.

Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

Thus its defining relations are $u_i^2=\delta u_i$, $u_i u_{i\pm1}u_i=u_i$, and $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$. The definition of a presented $R$-algebra and its universal property are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]].

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim:
On a word $w=u_{i_1}\cdots u_{i_k}$ define
$w^*=u_{i_k}\cdots u_{i_1}$, extend by
$(\sum_w c_w w)^*=\sum_w\overline{c_w}w^*$, and set $1^*=1$. Reversal of
words and [F2] give $(xy)^*=y^*x^*$ and $(x^*)^*=x$ in the free algebra.
Thus this is a conjugate-linear anti-involution before taking the quotient.

The star fixes each relation $u_i^2-2u_i$ and each palindromic relation
$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i$ and $u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}$. It sends a distant
commutator $u_i u_j-u_j u_i$ to its negative. Hence the star sends every
generator of the defining ideal into that ideal.

Every element of the ideal is a finite sum of terms $x r y$ with $r$ a
displayed defining relation; its star is $y^*r^*x^*$, which is again in the
ideal by step 2.1. The ideal is therefore star-invariant, so the operation
descends to the quotient and remains conjugate-linear, anti-multiplicative,
and involutive there. If $N\leq1$ there are no generators or relations, and
the same construction is just coefficient conjugation.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $n\ge0$. Write
$\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the $\mathbb C$-vector space of all linear maps
$V\to V$, and $\operatorname{GL}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the
invertible ones
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
All tensor products below are over $\mathbb C$.

**The tensor power.** For $n\ge1$ fix the parenthesization
$$E_n\;:=\;V^{\otimes n}\;:=\;\underbrace{V\otimes_{\mathbb C}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb C}V}_{n\text{ factors}},\qquad V^{\otimes0}\;:=\;\mathbb C,$$
and write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for the elementary tensor of
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in V^n$; for $n=0$ the unique elementary tensor is $1\in\mathbb C$.
By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] the
assignment $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ is
$\mathbb C$-multilinear and every element of $E_n$ is a finite
$\mathbb C$-linear combination of elementary tensors; for $n=0$ this means
$c=c\cdot1$ for $c\in\mathbb C$. If $e_1,\dots,e_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis of
$V$, then by iterating [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]] the $d^n$ tensors
$e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $E_n$, so
$E_n$ is finite-dimensional.

**Place permutations: the left $S_n$-action.** Let $S_n$ be the symmetric
group of the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]). For
$\sigma\in S_n$ define, on elementary tensors,
$$\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}.$$
The right-hand side depends $\mathbb C$-multilinearly on
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)$, so by the universal property in
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] there is a
unique $\mathbb C$-linear map $E_n\to E_n$ with this value on every elementary
tensor. Uniqueness is what makes the rule well defined on all of $E_n$, since
the elementary tensors span. The identity permutation acts trivially, and for
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$ and every elementary tensor,
$$(\sigma\tau)\cdot\bigl(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\bigr)=v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(n)}=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))},$$
while $\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\tau^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(n)}$
and hence
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))}.$$
The two agree, so the assignments constitute a left action of the group $S_n$
on $E_n$; equivalently $E_n$ is a left module over $S_n$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
For $n=0$ the group $S_0$ is trivial and acts on $E_0=\mathbb C$ by the
identity.

**Diagonal linear action.** For $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ define, on
elementary tensors,
$$g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n,$$
again first on elementary tensors by multilinearity and then uniquely on
$E_n$. Since $g$ and $h$ are linear, the two assignments compose in the
expected way: on elementary tensors,
$$(gh)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=g(hv_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes g(hv_n)=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(h^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
and $(\mathrm{id}_V)^{\otimes n}$ is the identity. In particular
$(g^{-1})^{\otimes n}$ is the inverse of $g^{\otimes n}$. For $n=0$ every
diagonal operator is the identity on $\mathbb C$.
Thus $g\mapsto g^{\otimes n}$ is a group homomorphism
$\operatorname{GL}(V)\to\operatorname{GL}(E_n)$, that is, a finite-dimensional
representation of the group $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ on $E_n$.

**The two actions commute.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$
and an elementary tensor,
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=gv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
so the two linear maps $\sigma\cdot(-)$ and $g^{\otimes n}\cdot(-)$ commute;
equivalently, every $g^{\otimes n}$ is an $S_n$-equivariant endomorphism of
$E_n$ ([[def-intertwiner-equivalent-and-faithful-representations]]).

**The diagonal infinitesimal operator.** For $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ put
$$\Delta(T)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\ \in\ \operatorname{End}(E_n),$$
where $\mathbf 1=\mathrm{id}_V$ and the sum is $0$ for $n=0$. Each summand
lies in $\operatorname{End}(E_n)$, and $\Delta:\operatorname{End}(V)\to
\operatorname{End}(E_n)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. It is the first coefficient of
the diagonal action along the line $t\mapsto\mathbf 1+tT$. In this polynomial
calculation, $(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}$ is the tensor power of the
endomorphism $\mathbf 1+tT$; it agrees with the $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ action
whenever that endomorphism is invertible. For every $t\in\mathbb C$ one
computes, on elementary tensors,
$$(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}t^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}w_{i_1,\dots,i_k},\qquad (w_{i_1,\dots,i_k})_j=\begin{cases}Tv_j,&j\in\{i_1,\dots,i_k\},\\ v_j,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
the coefficient of $t$ being $\Delta(T)\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$
(zero when $n=0$); both sides
are polynomials in $t$ with values in the finite-dimensional space $E_n$
described on a spanning set. Finally let
$$A_n\;:=\;\text{the unital }\mathbb C\text{-subalgebra of }\operatorname{End}(E_n)\text{ generated by }\{\Delta(T):T\in\operatorname{End}(V)\};$$
this is the image of the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
$U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$ on $E_n$, defined here as that generated algebra, with
no Lie-theoretic input.

For every $n\ge0$, the modules $\{S^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ form a
complete irredundant list, up to isomorphism, of finite-dimensional irreducible
complex $S_n$-representations.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space of dimension $d\ge0$,
let $n\ge0$, and let $E:=V^{\otimes n}$ carry the commuting left place action
of $S_n$ and diagonal action of $\operatorname{GL}(V)$
([[def-commuting-symmetric-and-linear-actions-on-tensor-power]]). Let
$B:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{g^{\otimes n}:g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)\}$,
and for $\lambda\vdash n$ put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_n}\bigl(S^\lambda,E\bigr),$$
on which $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ acts by postcomposition
$(g\cdot\psi)(s):=g^{\otimes n}\psi(s)$ and $B$ acts by
$b\cdot\psi:=b\circ\psi$. Then:

1. **(Decomposition.)** There is an isomorphism of
   $(S_n\times\operatorname{GL}(V))$-modules
   $$E\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n,\ \ell(\lambda)\le d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda,$$
   where $S_n$ acts on the first factor and trivially on $M_\lambda$ and
   $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ acts on $M_\lambda$ by postcomposition and trivially
   on $S^\lambda$. The sum runs over exactly the partitions $\lambda\vdash n$
   with at most $d$ rows.
2. **(Nonzero irreducible factors.)** For every $\lambda\vdash n$ with
   $\ell(\lambda)\le d$ the space $M_\lambda$ is nonzero and irreducible as a
   module over $B$ by postcomposition, hence also irreducible as a
   $\operatorname{GL}(V)$-module and as a $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$-module under
   $x\mapsto\Delta(x)$
   ([[def-irreducible-completely-reducible-and-faithful-lie-algebra-representation]]);
   for $\ell(\lambda)>d$ one has $M_\lambda=0$.
3. **(Pairwise inequivalence of the nonzero factors.)** If $\lambda\ne\mu$
   are partitions of $n$ with $\ell(\lambda)\le d$ and $\ell(\mu)\le d$, then
   $M_\lambda$ and $M_\mu$ are non-isomorphic as $B$-modules, as
   $\operatorname{GL}(V)$-modules and as $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$-modules. Thus the
   nonzero factors in the decomposition of claim 1 are pairwise inequivalent,
   and a nonzero $M_\lambda$ is not isomorphic to a zero $M_\mu$ with
   $\ell(\mu)>d$ because their dimensions differ; no assertion is made about
   two zero factors.
4. **(Highest weight $\lambda$.)** For every $\lambda\vdash n$ with
   $\ell(\lambda)\le d$, writing $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$, the
   module $M_\lambda$ has highest weight $\lambda$ with respect to the Borel
   of upper triangular matrices: it contains a nonzero vector $\varphi$ with
   $\Delta(E_{ii})\circ\varphi=\lambda_i\varphi$ for all $i$ and
   $\Delta(E_{ij})\circ\varphi=0$ for all $i<j$, and every nonzero
   $\psi\in M_\lambda$ killed by all raising operators $\Delta(E_{ij})$,
   $i<j$, and satisfying $\Delta(E_{ii})\circ\psi=\mu_i\psi$ for scalars
   $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d$ satisfies $\mu=\lambda$ and lies in
   $\mathbb C\varphi$.
5. **(Homogeneous polynomial module of degree $n$.)** Fix a basis
   $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $V$ and write $ge_j=\sum_ig_{ij}e_i$ for the matrix
   entries of $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ with
   $\ell(\lambda)\le d$ and every basis of $M_\lambda$, each matrix
   coefficient $g\mapsto\langle\psi^*,g\cdot\psi\rangle$ of the action on
   $M_\lambda$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$ in the entries
   $g_{ij}$.

All statements are over $\mathbb C$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be irreducible representations of a group $G$ over a field $k$.
Then every nonzero intertwiner $f:V \to W$ is an isomorphism. Consequently
$\operatorname{End}_G(V)$ is a division ring.

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field, let $G$ be a group, and let $V$ be an
irreducible representation of $G$ over $k$. Then every $T \in \operatorname{End}_G(V)$
is of the form $T=\lambda \operatorname{id}_V$ for some $\lambda \in k$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces (Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **permutation** of $X$ is a bijection $f : X \to X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **symmetric group of $X$** is the
set of all permutations of $X$,

$$\operatorname{Sym}(X) \;:=\; \{\, f : X \to X \;:\; f \text{ is a bijection} \,\},$$

equipped with **composition** as its operation,

$$(f \circ g)(x) \;=\; f(g(x)) \qquad (x \in X),$$

and with the identity map $\mathrm{id}_X$, given by $\mathrm{id}_X(x) = x$, as
distinguished element.

Composition of two bijections of $X$ is again a bijection of $X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), so $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ is closed
under $\circ$ and $\circ$ is a binary operation on it
([[def-binary-operation]]); and $\mathrm{id}_X$ is a bijection of $X$, so it is an
element of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, and it is a two-sided identity for
composition ([[def-identity-element]]) because
$f \circ \mathrm{id}_X = f = \mathrm{id}_X \circ f$ holds pointwise for every
$f$. That $(\operatorname{Sym}(X), \circ, \mathrm{id}_X)$ is a group is
[[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]].

**Cycle notation for a finite list of distinct points.** For distinct elements
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of $X$ with $k \ge 2$, the symbol
$(x_0\,x_1\,\cdots\,x_{k-1})$ denotes the permutation sending $x_i$ to
$x_{i+1}$ for $i < k-1$, sending $x_{k-1}$ to $x_0$, and fixing every element of
$X$ outside $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$. It is a bijection, because the map
described sends the set $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$ onto itself by a rule with an
evident inverse (send each $x_{i+1}$ back to $x_i$ and $x_0$ back to $x_{k-1}$)
and fixes the complement pointwise. A **transposition** is such a symbol with
$k = 2$, that is $(a\,b)$ with $a \ne b$: it exchanges $a$ and $b$ and fixes
everything else, and it satisfies $(a\,b) \circ (a\,b) = \mathrm{id}_X$.

A product of cycle symbols means their composite, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b) \circ (c\,d)$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,

$$|S_n| = n!.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim:
On elementary tensors, applying $\rho(\pi)$ after $\Delta_N(U)$ gives
$Uv_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes Uv_{\pi^{-1}(N)}$, which is also the
result of applying $\Delta_N(U)$ after $\rho(\pi)$. The product formula and
[F6] make $\rho(\pi)$ unitary because it permutes the factors, and make
$U^{\otimes N}$ unitary because $\langle Uv,Uw\rangle_V=\langle v,w\rangle_V$
for every factor. For $N=0$ both actions are the identity on $\mathbb C$.

The normalized trace formula is an inner product on $M_\lambda$. Choose
an orthonormal basis $(s_k)_{k=1}^{d_\lambda}$ of $S^\lambda$ using [F9].
The adjoint identity [F7], conjugate symmetry, and the diagonal trace formula
[F12] give
$$d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f) =d_\lambda^{-1}\sum_k\langle f(s_k),g(s_k)\rangle_{H_N}.$$
This expression is linear in $f$, conjugate-linear in $g$, conjugate
symmetric, and for $g=f$ is a sum of nonnegative squared norms. If it is
zero, every $f(s_k)=0$, hence $f=0$; so it is positive definite. The product
inner product on $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ is well-defined by its finite
product basis from [F6] and the tensor basis theorem, and is positive definite
by the same coordinate formula.

By [F2] and [F3], the irreducible $S_N$-types occurring in $H_N$ are
exactly the modules $S^\lambda$ with $\lambda\vdash N$ and
$\ell(\lambda)\leq d$. Their multiplicity spaces are
$M_\lambda=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N)$, and the algebraic
Schur–Weyl decomposition places $S_N$ on the Specht factor and $GL(V)$ on
the multiplicity factor. This gives the algebraic partition and factor-
placement inputs for the local evaluation argument.

By [F6], $H_N$ is finite-dimensional. In any nonzero invariant subspace
of the current remainder, choose an invariant subspace $W$ of least positive
dimension; it is irreducible. Its orthogonal complement in that remainder is
invariant: for $x\perp W$ and $w\in W$,
$\langle\rho(\pi)x,w\rangle=\langle x,\rho(\pi)^{-1}w\rangle=0$ because
$W$ is invariant under $\rho(\pi)^{-1}$ and the action is unitary. [F8]
gives the orthogonal splitting at each stage. Repeating in the complement,
whose dimension strictly decreases, yields a finite orthogonal decomposition
of all $H_N$ into irreducible copies. By [F2], each copy has a unique Specht
type. The orthogonal projection onto one copy commutes with $S_N$, since that
copy and the sum of the other invariant copies are invariant. Its restriction
to an inequivalent irreducible copy is an intertwiner, so [F4] forces it to
vanish. Hence copies of distinct Specht types are orthogonal.

Since $S_N$ is finite by [F11], choose a basis $(v_j)$ of the finite-
dimensional $S^\lambda$ and define its coordinate product
$\langle\sum a_jv_j,\sum b_jv_j\rangle_0:=\sum a_j\overline{b_j}$.
Average this product over $S_N$ by
$\langle v,w\rangle:=|S_N|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_N}
\langle\rho(\pi)v,\rho(\pi)w\rangle_0$. Each summand on $(v,v)$ is
nonnegative and the identity term is positive for $v\ne0$, while right
multiplication reindexes the finite sum; hence this is a positive definite
invariant Hermitian product. This proves existence; now use the invariant
product fixed in the Statement. For each irreducible copy $K_a$ of type
$S^\lambda$, choose an equivariant isomorphism $j_a:S^\lambda\to K_a$.
Its adjoint exists by [F10], and $j_a^*j_a$ commutes with $S_N$: the
adjoint identity [F7], equivariance of $j_a$, and unitarity of both
representations give $\rho(\pi)^{-1}j_a^*j_a\rho(\pi)=j_a^*j_a$. By [F5]
this is $c_aI$; injectivity gives $c_a>0$, so replacing $j_a$ by
$c_a^{-1/2}j_a$ makes it unitary. For any $f\in M_\lambda$, decompose
$f=\sum_b P_bf$ using the orthogonal projections onto all irreducible copies
in $H_N$; each $P_bf$ is an intertwiner because $P_b$ commutes with $S_N$ by
step 2.1. If $K_b$ has type different from $S^\lambda$, then $P_bf=0$ by
[F4] and [F2]. If $K_b$ has type $S^\lambda$, then
$j_b^{-1}P_bf:S^\lambda\to S^\lambda$ is an intertwiner, hence is a scalar
by [F5]. Thus the maps $j_a$ span $M_\lambda$. Their ranges are orthogonal,
so $d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(j_b^*j_a)=\delta_{ab}$; they are an
orthonormal basis in the stated normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.
By [F9], take an orthonormal basis of each $S^\lambda$; evaluation sends the tensor
product basis to the union of the corresponding orthonormal bases of all
copies $K_a$. This union is an orthonormal basis of $H_N$, so $\Phi$ is
unitary.

For $\pi\in S_N$, evaluation gives
$\Phi(\rho_\lambda(\pi)s\otimes f)=f(\rho_\lambda(\pi)s)
=\rho(\pi)f(s)=\rho(\pi)\Phi(s\otimes f)$ because $f$ is an intertwiner.
For $U\in U(d)$, $\Delta_N(U)\circ f$ is again an intertwiner by [F1], and
evaluation gives
$\Phi(s\otimes(\Delta_N(U)\circ f))=\Delta_N(U)f(s)
=\Delta_N(U)\Phi(s\otimes f)$. Thus the actions have the asserted factor
placement. Since $\Delta_N(U)$ is unitary and $\Phi$ is unitary, the
postcomposition action is unitary on each multiplicity factor: on the
orthogonal summand $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ the operator is
$I\otimes T_U$, and evaluating on any unit vector of the nonzero
$S^\lambda$ factor shows that $T_U$ preserves inner products; $T_{U^{-1}}$
is its inverse.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex vector space and let $n\ge0$. Write
$\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the $\mathbb C$-vector space of all linear maps
$V\to V$, and $\operatorname{GL}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{End}(V)$ for the
invertible ones
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
All tensor products below are over $\mathbb C$.

**The tensor power.** For $n\ge1$ fix the parenthesization
$$E_n\;:=\;V^{\otimes n}\;:=\;\underbrace{V\otimes_{\mathbb C}\cdots\otimes_{\mathbb C}V}_{n\text{ factors}},\qquad V^{\otimes0}\;:=\;\mathbb C,$$
and write $v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for the elementary tensor of
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)\in V^n$; for $n=0$ the unique elementary tensor is $1\in\mathbb C$.
By [[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] the
assignment $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ is
$\mathbb C$-multilinear and every element of $E_n$ is a finite
$\mathbb C$-linear combination of elementary tensors; for $n=0$ this means
$c=c\cdot1$ for $c\in\mathbb C$. If $e_1,\dots,e_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-basis of
$V$, then by iterating [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]] the $d^n$ tensors
$e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $E_n$, so
$E_n$ is finite-dimensional.

**Place permutations: the left $S_n$-action.** Let $S_n$ be the symmetric
group of the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]). For
$\sigma\in S_n$ define, on elementary tensors,
$$\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;v_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}.$$
The right-hand side depends $\mathbb C$-multilinearly on
$(v_1,\dots,v_n)$, so by the universal property in
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]] there is a
unique $\mathbb C$-linear map $E_n\to E_n$ with this value on every elementary
tensor. Uniqueness is what makes the rule well defined on all of $E_n$, since
the elementary tensors span. The identity permutation acts trivially, and for
$\sigma,\tau\in S_n$ and every elementary tensor,
$$(\sigma\tau)\cdot\bigl(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n\bigr)=v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{(\sigma\tau)^{-1}(n)}=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))},$$
while $\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\tau^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(n)}$
and hence
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(\tau\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(1))}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\tau^{-1}(\sigma^{-1}(n))}.$$
The two agree, so the assignments constitute a left action of the group $S_n$
on $E_n$; equivalently $E_n$ is a left module over $S_n$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]).
For $n=0$ the group $S_0$ is trivial and acts on $E_0=\mathbb C$ by the
identity.

**Diagonal linear action.** For $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$ define, on
elementary tensors,
$$g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\;:=\;gv_1\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_n,$$
again first on elementary tensors by multilinearity and then uniquely on
$E_n$. Since $g$ and $h$ are linear, the two assignments compose in the
expected way: on elementary tensors,
$$(gh)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=g(hv_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes g(hv_n)=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(h^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
and $(\mathrm{id}_V)^{\otimes n}$ is the identity. In particular
$(g^{-1})^{\otimes n}$ is the inverse of $g^{\otimes n}$. For $n=0$ every
diagonal operator is the identity on $\mathbb C$.
Thus $g\mapsto g^{\otimes n}$ is a group homomorphism
$\operatorname{GL}(V)\to\operatorname{GL}(E_n)$, that is, a finite-dimensional
representation of the group $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ on $E_n$.

**The two actions commute.** For $\sigma\in S_n$, $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$
and an elementary tensor,
$$\sigma\cdot\bigl(g^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr)=gv_{\sigma^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes gv_{\sigma^{-1}(n)}=g^{\otimes n}\cdot\bigl(\sigma\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)\bigr),$$
so the two linear maps $\sigma\cdot(-)$ and $g^{\otimes n}\cdot(-)$ commute;
equivalently, every $g^{\otimes n}$ is an $S_n$-equivariant endomorphism of
$E_n$ ([[def-intertwiner-equivalent-and-faithful-representations]]).

**The diagonal infinitesimal operator.** For $T\in\operatorname{End}(V)$ put
$$\Delta(T)\;:=\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf 1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes T\otimes\mathbf 1^{\otimes(n-i)}\ \in\ \operatorname{End}(E_n),$$
where $\mathbf 1=\mathrm{id}_V$ and the sum is $0$ for $n=0$. Each summand
lies in $\operatorname{End}(E_n)$, and $\Delta:\operatorname{End}(V)\to
\operatorname{End}(E_n)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear. It is the first coefficient of
the diagonal action along the line $t\mapsto\mathbf 1+tT$. In this polynomial
calculation, $(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}$ is the tensor power of the
endomorphism $\mathbf 1+tT$; it agrees with the $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ action
whenever that endomorphism is invertible. For every $t\in\mathbb C$ one
computes, on elementary tensors,
$$(\mathbf 1+tT)^{\otimes n}\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}t^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}w_{i_1,\dots,i_k},\qquad (w_{i_1,\dots,i_k})_j=\begin{cases}Tv_j,&j\in\{i_1,\dots,i_k\},\\ v_j,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
the coefficient of $t$ being $\Delta(T)\cdot(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$
(zero when $n=0$); both sides
are polynomials in $t$ with values in the finite-dimensional space $E_n$
described on a spanning set. Finally let
$$A_n\;:=\;\text{the unital }\mathbb C\text{-subalgebra of }\operatorname{End}(E_n)\text{ generated by }\{\Delta(T):T\in\operatorname{End}(V)\};$$
this is the image of the diagonal action of the universal enveloping algebra
$U(\mathfrak{gl}(V))$ on $E_n$, defined here as that generated algebra, with
no Lie-theoretic input.

   $\operatorname{GL}(V)$-modules and as $\mathfrak{gl}(V)$-modules. Thus the
   nonzero factors in the decomposition of claim 1 are pairwise inequivalent,
   and a nonzero $M_\lambda$ is not isomorphic to a zero $M_\mu$ with
   $\ell(\mu)>d$ because their dimensions differ; no assertion is made about
   two zero factors.
4. **(Highest weight $\lambda$.)** For every $\lambda\vdash n$ with
   $\ell(\lambda)\le d$, writing $\lambda_i:=0$ for $i>\ell(\lambda)$, the
   module $M_\lambda$ has highest weight $\lambda$ with respect to the Borel
   of upper triangular matrices: it contains a nonzero vector $\varphi$ with
   $\Delta(E_{ii})\circ\varphi=\lambda_i\varphi$ for all $i$ and
   $\Delta(E_{ij})\circ\varphi=0$ for all $i<j$, and every nonzero
   $\psi\in M_\lambda$ killed by all raising operators $\Delta(E_{ij})$,
   $i<j$, and satisfying $\Delta(E_{ii})\circ\psi=\mu_i\psi$ for scalars
   $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_d$ satisfies $\mu=\lambda$ and lies in
   $\mathbb C\varphi$.
5. **(Homogeneous polynomial module of degree $n$.)** Fix a basis
   $e_1,\dots,e_d$ of $V$ and write $ge_j=\sum_ig_{ij}e_i$ for the matrix
   entries of $g\in\operatorname{GL}(V)$. For every $\lambda\vdash n$ with
   $\ell(\lambda)\le d$ and every basis of $M_\lambda$, each matrix
   coefficient $g\mapsto\langle\psi^*,g\cdot\psi\rangle$ of the action on
   $M_\lambda$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $n$ in the entries
   $g_{ij}$.

All statements are over $\mathbb C$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a set. A **permutation** of $X$ is a bijection $f : X \to X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **symmetric group of $X$** is the
set of all permutations of $X$,

$$\operatorname{Sym}(X) \;:=\; \{\, f : X \to X \;:\; f \text{ is a bijection} \,\},$$

equipped with **composition** as its operation,

$$(f \circ g)(x) \;=\; f(g(x)) \qquad (x \in X),$$

and with the identity map $\mathrm{id}_X$, given by $\mathrm{id}_X(x) = x$, as
distinguished element.

Composition of two bijections of $X$ is again a bijection of $X$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]), so $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ is closed
under $\circ$ and $\circ$ is a binary operation on it
([[def-binary-operation]]); and $\mathrm{id}_X$ is a bijection of $X$, so it is an
element of $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$, and it is a two-sided identity for
composition ([[def-identity-element]]) because
$f \circ \mathrm{id}_X = f = \mathrm{id}_X \circ f$ holds pointwise for every
$f$. That $(\operatorname{Sym}(X), \circ, \mathrm{id}_X)$ is a group is
[[lem-symmetric-group-is-a-group]].

**Cycle notation for a finite list of distinct points.** For distinct elements
$x_0, x_1, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of $X$ with $k \ge 2$, the symbol
$(x_0\,x_1\,\cdots\,x_{k-1})$ denotes the permutation sending $x_i$ to
$x_{i+1}$ for $i < k-1$, sending $x_{k-1}$ to $x_0$, and fixing every element of
$X$ outside $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$. It is a bijection, because the map
described sends the set $\{x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\}$ onto itself by a rule with an
evident inverse (send each $x_{i+1}$ back to $x_i$ and $x_0$ back to $x_{k-1}$)
and fixes the complement pointwise. A **transposition** is such a symbol with
$k = 2$, that is $(a\,b)$ with $a \ne b$: it exchanges $a$ and $b$ and fixes
everything else, and it satisfies $(a\,b) \circ (a\,b) = \mathrm{id}_X$.

A product of cycle symbols means their composite, so $(a\,b)(c\,d)$ is
$(a\,b) \circ (c\,d)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Give $\mathbb R^4$ its Euclidean topology, whose basic open sets are the
Euclidean open balls, and write a point as an ordered pair $(x,y)$ with
$x,y\in\mathbb R^2$. The **ordered configuration space** is the subspace
$$F_2(\mathbb R^2):=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2:x\ne y\}$$
with the subspace topology. The transposition acts by $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$.
The **unordered configuration space of two distinct planar points** is
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2):=F_2(\mathbb R^2)/\bigl((x,y)\sim(y,x)\bigr)$$
with the quotient topology of the canonical projection
$q:F_2(\mathbb R^2)\to C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. We write its points as unordered
sets $\{x,y\}$; equality in this set means equality up to transposition.
The diagonal $x=y$ is excluded, so collisions are not points of this space.

The topology on each finite Cartesian coordinate space used below is its
Euclidean topology; on a finite product it is equivalently the topology with
basis the products of open sets in the factors.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

$\operatorname{Deg}:\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,[0])\to(\mathbb Z,+)$ is an isomorphism. Its inverse is

$$n\longmapsto[\omega_n].$$

Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

Let

$$C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$$

with the Euclidean subspace topology. The function

$$h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow C,\qquad h([t])=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),$$

is a homeomorphism. Thus $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle and sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$.

Let $q : X \to Y$ be a quotient map ([[def-quotient-topology]]). Then:

1. **Characteristic property.** For every space $W$ and every function
   $k : Y \to W$,
   $$k \text{ is continuous } \iff k \circ q \text{ is continuous} .$$
2. **Factorisation.** Let $f : X \to W$ be continuous and **constant on the
   fibres of $q$**, that is $q(x) = q(x')$ implies $f(x) = f(x')$. Then there is
   exactly one function $\bar f : Y \to W$ with $\bar f \circ q = f$, and it is
   continuous.
3. **Composites.** If $q : X \to Y$ and $p : Y \to Z$ are quotient maps then
   $p \circ q : X \to Z$ is a quotient map.

derivations.claim:
For an ordered pair put $c=(x+y)/2$ and $z=(x-y)/2$. This is an
invertible linear coordinate change, with inverse $(c,z)\mapsto(c+z,c-z)$;
the collision-free condition is $z\ne0$. In polar coordinates write
$z=ru$ with $r=\|z\|>0$ and $u\in S^1$. These formulas and their inverses
are continuous, so they give a homeomorphism
$F_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times S^1$. Transposition
fixes $c,r$ and sends $u$ to $-u$. If $A:=S^1/(u\sim-u)$ has quotient
topology, the map $(c,r,u)\mapsto(c,r,[u])$ is an open quotient map: the
circle quotient is open because the saturation of an open set is its union
with its antipodal image, and products of open rectangles show the same for
the product map. Its fibers are exactly the transposition orbits. Thus it
induces a homeomorphism
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong X:=\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times A.$$

Let $\eta:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to S^1$ be the homeomorphism
$\eta([t])=(\cos2\pi t,\sin2\pi t)$ from [F5]. The antipodal map on $S^1$
corresponds under $\eta$ to $[t]\mapsto[t+1/2]$. The continuous map
$D_2:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, $D_2([t]):=[2t]$,
is well-defined and continuous by [F6] applied to $t\mapsto[2t]$ on
$\mathbb R$; its fibres are exactly the pairs $[t],[t+1/2]$. Hence
$\psi:A\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, $\psi([\eta([t])]):=[2t]$, is well-defined
and continuous by the quotient topology. Its inverse is
$[s]\mapsto[\eta([s/2])]$; changing $s$ by an integer changes $s/2$ by a
half-integer, which is the same class in $A$. This inverse is continuous by
[F6] applied to the continuous map $s\mapsto[\eta([s/2])]$ on $\mathbb R$;
the two formulas compose to the identity, so $\psi$ is a homeomorphism.
Under the homeomorphism of step 1.1, $q_0$ is
$(0,1,[(1,0)])$, which $\psi$ sends to $[0]$.

On $X$ define $r(c,\rho,a):=\psi(a)$ and
$i([t]):=(0,1,\psi^{-1}([t]))$. These maps are continuous, preserve the
specified basepoints, and $r\circ i$ is the identity. The maps
$$H_s(c,\rho,a):=((1-s)c,(1-s)\rho+s,a),\qquad 0\leq s\leq1,$$
are a continuous based homotopy from $\operatorname{id}_X$ to $i\circ r$:
the radius is positive since $(1-s)\rho+s>0$, and the basepoint
$(0,1,[(1,0)])$ is fixed for every $s$.

By [F3], $(r\circ i)_*=r_*i_*=\operatorname{id}$ and the based homotopy
in step 3.1 gives $(i\circ r)_*=i_*r_*=\operatorname{id}$ on the based-loop
classes of [F2]. Thus $r_*$ and $i_*$ are inverse isomorphisms. The pointed
homeomorphism of step 1.1 transports this isomorphism back to
$C_2(\mathbb R^2)$; applying [F4] gives
$\pi_1(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0)\cong\mathbb Z$.

In the coordinates of step 1.1, $\gamma$ keeps $c=0$ and $r=1$ and has
$u(t)=(\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t)$. Its image under $r$ is $[t]=\omega_1(t)$,
which is the positive generator by [F4]. Replacing $\pi t$ by $2\pi t$
describes a full turn of the relative direction; its image is $[2t]=\omega_2(t)$,
so its class is twice $[\gamma]$. This identifies exchange and winding
orientation without using a diagram.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $f:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ be a continuous map with $f(x_0)=y_0$. Then

$$f_*([\alpha])=[f\circ\alpha]$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism. For pointed continuous maps,

$$\operatorname{id}_*=\operatorname{id},\qquad (g\circ f)_*=g_*\circ f_*.$$

If $f_0,f_1:(X,x_0)\to(Y,y_0)$ are homotopic through a homotopy that keeps
$x_0$ at $y_0$, then $(f_0)_*=(f_1)_*$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let

$$C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$$

with the Euclidean subspace topology. The function

$$h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow C,\qquad h([t])=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),$$

is a homeomorphism. Thus $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle and sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $q : X \to Y$ be a quotient map ([[def-quotient-topology]]). Then:

1. **Characteristic property.** For every space $W$ and every function
   $k : Y \to W$,
   $$k \text{ is continuous } \iff k \circ q \text{ is continuous} .$$
2. **Factorisation.** Let $f : X \to W$ be continuous and **constant on the
   fibres of $q$**, that is $q(x) = q(x')$ implies $f(x) = f(x')$. Then there is
   exactly one function $\bar f : Y \to W$ with $\bar f \circ q = f$, and it is
   continuous.
3. **Composites.** If $q : X \to Y$ and $p : Y \to Z$ are quotient maps then
   $p \circ q : X \to Z$ is a quotient map.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions:
[F6] [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]: a continuous map constant on the
fibres of a quotient map factors uniquely as a continuous map out of the
quotient.

Let $N\geq1$ be an integer. The finite spin-half tensor chain is the complex
inner-product space $\mathcal H_N:=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$. On each factor
use the inner product
$$\langle (z_0,z_1),(w_0,w_1)\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}:=z_0\overline{w_0}+z_1\overline{w_1},$$
which is linear in its first argument, and let $|0\rangle=(1,0)$ and
$|1\rangle=(0,1)$. By the finite tensor-product basis theorem, for
$\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$ the words
$|\alpha\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_N\rangle$ form a basis of
$\mathcal H_N$. For $u=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ and
$v=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}d_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, define
$$\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}:=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha\overline{d_\alpha}.$$
This is a positive-definite inner product because
$\langle u,u\rangle=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$, and it makes the tensor words
orthonormal. Expanding each factor in $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ gives its
elementary-tensor product formula
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Let $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ be the Pauli matrices of the finite-spin
matrix supplier, and for $1\leq k\leq N$ define
$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$
For $1\leq i<N$, define the adjacent swap $s_i$ on elementary tensors by
$$s_i(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i+1}\otimes v_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N.$$
Write
$$|\omega\rangle:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle),\qquad P_i:=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P_\omega\otimes I^{\otimes(N-i-1)},$$
where $P_\omega v:=\langle v,\omega\rangle\,\omega$ on the adjacent two
factors. Also put $e_i:=I_{\mathcal H_N}-s_i$ for $1\leq i<N$. If $N=1$,
these bond-indexed families are empty.

This is a mathematical definition of finite-dimensional tensor spaces and
operators; it makes no physical claim about a material, a particle species, or
an adopted statistics sector.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. For each $n\ge0$, let $F_n:=R\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}\rangle$ be the free associative unital $R$-algebra on the indicated symbols ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]). When $n=0$ or $n=1$, the symbol set is empty and $F_n=R$.

Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

Thus its defining relations are $u_i^2=\delta u_i$, $u_i u_{i\pm1}u_i=u_i$, and $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$. The definition of a presented $R$-algebra and its universal property are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]].

For each integer $N\geq0$, let $P_N(\mathbb C,2)$ be the quotient of the free
unital associative complex algebra on $u_1,\ldots,u_{N-1}$ by the relations
$$u_i^2=2u_i,\qquad u_iu_j=u_ju_i\ (|i-j|>1),\qquad u_iu_{i+1}u_i=u_i,\quad u_{i+1}u_iu_{i+1}=u_{i+1}.$$
This complex Temperley–Lieb algebra has a
conjugate-linear anti-involution $*$ determined by
$$c^*=\overline c\quad(c\in\mathbb C),\qquad u_i^*=u_i\quad(1\leq i<N),\qquad (xy)^*=y^*x^*.$$
For $N=0$ or $N=1$ this is complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$.

Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

derivations.claim:
On $\mathbb C^2\otimes\mathbb C^2$, direct application to the four basis
vectors gives
$$s=\tfrac12\left(I+\sigma_x\otimes\sigma_x+\sigma_y\otimes\sigma_y+ \sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z\right).$$
For $|00\rangle$ and $|11\rangle$, the sum of the three Pauli products is
the vector itself; for $|01\rangle$ it is $2|10\rangle-|01\rangle$, and
for $|10\rangle$ it is $2|01\rangle-|10\rangle$, so the displayed operator
is the factor swap in all four cases. The symmetric three-dimensional
subspace and antisymmetric line are an orthogonal decomposition; $s$ is $+I$
on the former and $-I$ on the latter, whose unit vector is $\omega$.
Therefore $I-s=2P_\omega$, and $(I-s)^2=4P_\omega^2=4P_\omega=2(I-s)$.
Tensoring with identities gives $e_i=2P_i$, self-adjointness, and
$e_i^2=2e_i$ for every bond.

On three adjacent factors, $P_{12}$ has image spanned by
$|\omega\rangle_{12}\otimes|0\rangle$ and
$|\omega\rangle_{12}\otimes|1\rangle$. Applying $P_{23}$ and then $P_{12}$
to these two vectors gives, respectively,
$$P_{12}P_{23}P_{12}(|\omega\rangle_{12}|0\rangle_3) =\tfrac14|\omega\rangle_{12}|0\rangle_3,\qquad P_{12}P_{23}P_{12}(|\omega\rangle_{12}|1\rangle_3) =\tfrac14|\omega\rangle_{12}|1\rangle_3.$$
For example, the first intermediate vector is
$P_{23}(|\omega\rangle_{12}|0\rangle_3)=(-|001\rangle+|010\rangle)/(2\sqrt2)$;
$P_{12}$ kills $|001\rangle$ and sends $|010\rangle$ to
$|\omega\rangle_{12}|0\rangle_3/\sqrt2$. The second computation is the
explicit calculation
$P_{23}(|\omega\rangle_{12}|1\rangle_3)=(-|101\rangle+|110\rangle)/(2\sqrt2)$;
$P_{12}$ kills $|110\rangle$ and sends $|101\rangle$ to
$-|\omega\rangle_{12}|1\rangle_3/\sqrt2$, again giving the coefficient
$1/4$. Since
$P_{12}P_{23}P_{12}$ first projects into the displayed image, it follows on
all eight basis vectors that $P_{12}P_{23}P_{12}=P_{12}/4$. Reversing the
three tensor factors exchanges $P_{12}$ and $P_{23}$ (the singlet line is
unchanged by reversing its two entries), so also
$P_{23}P_{12}P_{23}=P_{23}/4$. Hence
$e_i e_{i+1}e_i=8P_iP_{i+1}P_i=2P_i=e_i$ and the reversed relation holds.
Operators on disjoint tensor factors commute, giving the distant relation.

The relations proved in steps 1.1 and 2.1 and [F3] give an algebra
homomorphism from the presented quotient, since every defining relation has
zero image. Each $e_i$ is self-adjoint by step 1.1, so the operator adjoint
of a word reverses its factors and fixes its generator images; conjugating
coefficients agrees with the algebra involution [F4]. Thus the representation
preserves $*$.

The adjacent swap is the place action of the transposition
$(i,i+1)$, since that transposition is its own inverse in the left-place
convention. Therefore $e_i=I-\rho((i,i+1))$. Applying the factor placement in
[F5] shows that on each summand $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ it is
$\bigl(I-\rho_\lambda((i,i+1))\bigr)\otimes I_{M_\lambda}$, as claimed.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. For each $n\ge0$, let $F_n:=R\langle u_1,\ldots,u_{n-1}\rangle$ be the free associative unital $R$-algebra on the indicated symbols ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]). When $n=0$ or $n=1$, the symbol set is empty and $F_n=R$.

Let $I_n$ be the two-sided ideal generated by

$$u_i^2-\delta u_i\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad u_i u_j-u_j u_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$

and

$$u_i u_{i+1}u_i-u_i,\qquad u_{i+1}u_i u_{i+1}-u_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2).$$

The abstract **rank-$n$ Temperley–Lieb algebra** is the presented $R$-algebra

$$P_n(R,\delta):=F_n/I_n.$$

Thus its defining relations are $u_i^2=\delta u_i$, $u_i u_{i\pm1}u_i=u_i$, and $u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$. The definition of a presented $R$-algebra and its universal property are those of [[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]].

$u_i u_j=u_j u_i$ for $|i-j|>1$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For each integer $N\geq0$, let $P_N(\mathbb C,2)$ be the quotient of the free
unital associative complex algebra on $u_1,\ldots,u_{N-1}$ by the relations
$$u_i^2=2u_i,\qquad u_iu_j=u_ju_i\ (|i-j|>1),\qquad u_iu_{i+1}u_i=u_i,\quad u_{i+1}u_iu_{i+1}=u_{i+1}.$$
This complex Temperley–Lieb algebra has a
conjugate-linear anti-involution $*$ determined by
$$c^*=\overline c\quad(c\in\mathbb C),\qquad u_i^*=u_i\quad(1\leq i<N),\qquad (xy)^*=y^*x^*.$$
For $N=0$ or $N=1$ this is complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions:
Using the conventions of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]], the standard
Temperley–Lieb diagram for $e_i$ has a cap joining the two
adjacent upper boundary points and a cup joining the corresponding lower
points, with all other strands vertical. Boundary points are numbered from
left to right and diagrams are composed by stacking the left factor above the
right factor. In the spin representation each cap/cup contraction uses the
unnormalized tensor $\sqrt2\,|\omega\rangle$; a closed loop therefore
contributes $2$. The proof above uses tensor contractions, not the diagram.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

acts on $S^\lambda$ and as identity on $M_\lambda$, while the diagonal
$U(2)$ action acts on the multiplicity factor.

Let $N\geq1$ be an integer. The finite spin-half tensor chain is the complex
inner-product space $\mathcal H_N:=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$. On each factor
use the inner product
$$\langle (z_0,z_1),(w_0,w_1)\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}:=z_0\overline{w_0}+z_1\overline{w_1},$$
which is linear in its first argument, and let $|0\rangle=(1,0)$ and
$|1\rangle=(0,1)$. By the finite tensor-product basis theorem, for
$\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$ the words
$|\alpha\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_N\rangle$ form a basis of
$\mathcal H_N$. For $u=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ and
$v=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}d_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, define
$$\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}:=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha\overline{d_\alpha}.$$
This is a positive-definite inner product because
$\langle u,u\rangle=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$, and it makes the tensor words
orthonormal. Expanding each factor in $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ gives its
elementary-tensor product formula
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Let $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ be the Pauli matrices of the finite-spin
matrix supplier, and for $1\leq k\leq N$ define
$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$
For $1\leq i<N$, define the adjacent swap $s_i$ on elementary tensors by
$$s_i(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i+1}\otimes v_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N.$$
Write
$$|\omega\rangle:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle),\qquad P_i:=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P_\omega\otimes I^{\otimes(N-i-1)},$$
where $P_\omega v:=\langle v,\omega\rangle\,\omega$ on the adjacent two
factors. Also put $e_i:=I_{\mathcal H_N}-s_i$ for $1\leq i<N$. If $N=1$,
these bond-indexed families are empty.

operators; it makes no physical claim about a material, a particle species, or
an adopted statistics sector.

Let $N\geq1$, $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the standard

$|\omega\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$,

bond,
$$e_i=I-s_i=2P_i,\qquad e_i^*=e_i,\qquad e_i^2=2e_i.$$

S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$. Each $e_i$ acts on the Specht factor as

derivations.claim:
Since $S_i^a=\hbar\sigma_i^a/2$, the factors $\hbar^2$ cancel and
$$\hbar^{-2}\sum_aS_i^aS_{i+1}^a=\tfrac14\sum_a\sigma_i^a\sigma_{i+1}^a.$$
On the ordered basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the
operator $\frac12(I+\sum_a\sigma_a\otimes\sigma_a)$ sends these four
vectors respectively to $|00\rangle,|10\rangle,|01\rangle,|11\rangle$:
for the middle two, the Pauli sum is $2|10\rangle-|01\rangle$ and
$2|01\rangle-|10\rangle$. This is exactly the swap, so
$s_i=\frac12(I+\sum_a\sigma_i^a\sigma_{i+1}^a)$. Rearranging gives
$\frac12s_i-\frac14I$, and substituting $e_i=I-s_i$ gives
$\frac14I-\frac12e_i$. This proves the bond identity including its
normalization.

Each $e_i$ is self-adjoint by [F3], $I$ is self-adjoint, and every
$\mathcal J_i$ is real; hence their finite real linear combination $H$ is
self-adjoint. By [F3] each $e_i$ lies in the represented Temperley–Lieb
algebra, so the displayed expression for $H$ is an element of that algebra's
image.

An adjacent swap commutes with the diagonal action $U^{\otimes N}$ for
every $U\in U(2)$: on an elementary tensor, swapping the two entries after
applying $U$ to each gives the same tensor as applying $U$ after the swap.
Thus $e_i=I-s_i$ and $H$ commute with that action. By [F4], the decomposition
places the permutation operators on $S^\lambda$ and the collective unitary
action on $M_\lambda$; therefore the formula for $H$ acts on $S^\lambda$ and
as identity on $M_\lambda$. When $N=1$ there are no bonds and all displayed
sums are zero.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $N\geq1$ be an integer. The finite spin-half tensor chain is the complex
inner-product space $\mathcal H_N:=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$. On each factor
use the inner product
$$\langle (z_0,z_1),(w_0,w_1)\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}:=z_0\overline{w_0}+z_1\overline{w_1},$$
which is linear in its first argument, and let $|0\rangle=(1,0)$ and
$|1\rangle=(0,1)$. By the finite tensor-product basis theorem, for
$\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$ the words
$|\alpha\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_N\rangle$ form a basis of
$\mathcal H_N$. For $u=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ and
$v=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}d_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, define
$$\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}:=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha\overline{d_\alpha}.$$
This is a positive-definite inner product because
$\langle u,u\rangle=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$, and it makes the tensor words
orthonormal. Expanding each factor in $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ gives its
elementary-tensor product formula
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Let $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ be the Pauli matrices of the finite-spin
matrix supplier, and for $1\leq k\leq N$ define
$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$
For $1\leq i<N$, define the adjacent swap $s_i$ on elementary tensors by
$$s_i(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i+1}\otimes v_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N.$$
Write
$$|\omega\rangle:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle),\qquad P_i:=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P_\omega\otimes I^{\otimes(N-i-1)},$$
where $P_\omega v:=\langle v,\omega\rangle\,\omega$ on the adjacent two
factors. Also put $e_i:=I_{\mathcal H_N}-s_i$ for $1\leq i<N$. If $N=1$,
these bond-indexed families are empty.

This is a mathematical definition of finite-dimensional tensor spaces and
operators; it makes no physical claim about a material, a particle species, or
an adopted statistics sector.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $N\geq1$, $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the standard
orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ on each factor, and for
$1\leq i<N$ define $s_i$ to swap factors $i,i+1$. Put
$|\omega\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$,
$P_\omega v=\langle v,\omega\rangle\omega$, let $P_i$ act as $P_\omega$ on
factors $i,i+1$ and identity on all others, and set $e_i=I-s_i$. For every
bond,
$$e_i=I-s_i=2P_i,\qquad e_i^*=e_i,\qquad e_i^2=2e_i.$$
For $1\leq i<N-1$,
$$e_i e_{i+1}e_i=e_i,\qquad e_{i+1}e_i e_{i+1}=e_{i+1},$$
and $e_i e_j=e_j e_i$ when $|i-j|>1$. Consequently the assignment
$u_i\mapsto e_i$ defines a star-preserving algebra representation
$$P_N(\mathbb C,2)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_N).$$
For $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most two rows, put
$M_\lambda=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,\mathcal H_N)$ and use the
unitary Schur–Weyl decomposition
$\mathcal H_N\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\,\ell(\lambda)\le2}
S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$. Each $e_i$ acts on the Specht factor as
$I-\rho_\lambda((i,i+1))$ and as identity on the multiplicity factor. No
faithfulness assertion is made.
