supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $q_0:=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}\in C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. There is a pointed
homeomorphism
$$\bigl(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0\bigr)\cong \bigl(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, (0,1,[0])\bigr),$$
and
$$\pi_1(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$
Under the isomorphism specified in the proof, the counterclockwise exchange
loop
$$\gamma(t):=\{(\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t),(-\cos\pi t,-\sin\pi t)\},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1,$$
is a positive generator. The loop in which the relative direction makes one
full counterclockwise turn is $[\gamma]^2$, so it represents twice the
generator.

A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.

A **universal covering space** of $B$ is a covering map $p:\widetilde B\to B$ whose total space $\widetilde B$ is simply connected ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]], [[def-simply-connected]]).

For a covering $p:E\to B$, a **deck transformation** is an isomorphism $h:E\to E$ over $B$, so $p\circ h=p$ ([[def-map-and-isomorphism-of-covering-spaces]]). Deck transformations form the **deck group** $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ under composition, and this group acts on $E$ by evaluation ([[def-group]], [[def-group-action]]).

Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.

**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

Use the pointed coordinate identification
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,$$
which sends $q_0=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}$ to $(0,1,[0])$, to write
$$X:=C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z.$$
Put $\widetilde X:=\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ and define
$$p(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,[t])\in X,\qquad T_n(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,t+n)\quad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$
Define $U(1):=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ under complex multiplication. Let
$\chi:\mathbb Z\to U(1)$ satisfy
$\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(m+n)=\chi(m)\chi(n)$ for all $m,n\in\mathbb Z$.
Let $\mathbb Z$ act on
$\widetilde X\times\mathbb C$ by
$$n\cdot((c,\rho,t),z):=((c,\rho,t+n),\chi(n)^{-1}z).$$
The homomorphism law for $\chi$ makes this a group action, and its orbits
define the quotient relation.
Define the **character quotient** and its projection by
$$L_\chi:=(\widetilde X\times\mathbb C)/\mathbb Z, \qquad \Pi_\chi([\widetilde x,z]):=p(\widetilde x),$$
with the quotient topology on $L_\chi$. Since $p(T_n\widetilde x)=p(\widetilde x)$,
it induces a continuous map $\Pi_\chi:L_\chi\to X$. Once $p$ is known to be
a covering map, the **monodromy** of this quotient around a based loop means
the fiber map obtained by lifting the loop and keeping its complex coordinate
$z$ constant along the lift.

For this item, a **unitary flat complex line bundle** over a space $X$ means a
continuous surjection $\Pi:L\to X$ with local trivializations
$\Pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb C$ over open sets $U$, whose changes of fiber
coordinate on overlaps are multiplication by functions $g:U\cap V\to U(1)$
that are locally constant (constant on some neighbourhood of each point).
The definition above names the quotient data; the following theorem verifies
that $L_\chi$ has these line-bundle and flatness properties.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.

Let $p:E\to B$ be a covering, let $\alpha:I\to B$ be a path, and let $e_0\in E$ satisfy $p(e_0)=\alpha(0)$. There is a unique path $\widetilde\alpha:I\to E$ with $\widetilde\alpha(0)=e_0$ and $p\circ\widetilde\alpha=\alpha$.

derivations.claim:
The projection $p(c,\rho,t)=(c,\rho,[t])$ is continuous and surjective.
For any $[t_0]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$, choose an open interval
$I=(a,b)$ around a representative of $[t_0]$ with $b-a<1$. Its image is an
open arc because its full preimage $\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb Z}(I+n)$ is open
by [F5, F7]; the translates are disjoint by $b-a<1$. On each sheet $I+n$,
the quotient map $t\mapsto[t]$ is a homeomorphism onto that arc: it is a
continuous bijection and maps open subsets to open subsets by the same
saturation check. Taking products with the other two coordinate factors
gives evenly covered open neighborhoods in $X$, so [F2] makes $p$ a covering
map.

By [F4], a deck transformation $D$ satisfies $pD=p$. Hence $D$ fixes
the $\mathbb R^2$ and $(0,\infty)$ coordinates and has last coordinate
$t+k(c,\rho,t)$ for an integer-valued continuous function $k$, by [F5].
The space $\widetilde X$ is connected because it is convex: its radius
coordinate stays positive on every line segment. Therefore $k$ is constant;
thus $D=T_n$ for some
$n\in\mathbb Z$. Conversely each $T_n$ preserves $p$ and is a homeomorphism,
so these are exactly the deck transformations.

The space $\widetilde X$ is nonempty and convex in $\mathbb R^4$ because
the radius coordinate remains positive along every line segment. For any
basepoint $x_0\in\widetilde X$ and based loop $\alpha$, the straight-line
homotopy $H_s(t)=(1-s)\alpha(t)+s x_0$ remains in $\widetilde X$ and fixes
both endpoints. Thus every based loop from [F9] is null-homotopic, so [F6]
makes $\widetilde X$ simply connected. By [F3], $p$ is a universal covering
map.

The action in [F8] is a group action: composing the $m$ and $n$ actions
adds the shifts and multiplies the fiber coordinate by
$\chi(m)^{-1}\chi(n)^{-1}=\chi(m+n)^{-1}$. The action is free because
$T_n\widetilde x=\widetilde x$ implies $n=0$. If $U$ is an evenly covered
neighborhood as in step 1.1 and $V$ is one chosen sheet, every orbit over
$U$ has exactly one representative in $V\times\mathbb C$. The quotient
topology therefore identifies $\Pi_\chi^{-1}(U)$ homeomorphically with
$U\times\mathbb C$: the restriction from $V\times\mathbb C$ is bijective,
and it is open because the saturation of an open subset is the union of its
translates under the homeomorphisms in [F8]. The fiber coordinate is the
unique representative's complex coordinate. This gives a local trivialization
with one-dimensional complex fibers.

On an overlap, two chosen sheets differ locally by a fixed translation
$T_n$, because the sheets of a covering are disjoint and indexed by the
discrete integers. The corresponding fiber coordinate changes by
$z\mapsto\chi(n)z$ or its inverse, according to the direction of the chart
change. Since $|\chi(n)|=1$ and $n$ is locally constant, these transition
functions are locally constant $U(1)$-valued functions. By [F8], this is a
unitary flat complex line bundle.

Let a based loop have a lift from $\widetilde x$ to $T_n\widetilde x$;
the path-lifting theorem [F10] supplies a unique lift from every prescribed
starting point. Keeping $z$ constant along this lift gives endpoint class
$[T_n\widetilde x,z]$. The defining equivalence in [F8] gives
$[T_n\widetilde x,z]=[\widetilde x,\chi(n)z]$, so monodromy is multiplication
by $\chi(n)$. The explicit positive exchange path has lifted angle coordinate
$t\mapsto t$ from $0$ to $1$, while the full relative turn has $t\mapsto2t$
from $0$ to $2$, by the homeomorphism in [F1]. Thus their monodromies are
$\chi(1)$ and $\chi(2)$.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show that the cover is surjective and its total space is nonempty; q₀ supplies a base point.
For χ(n)=1 the action and transitions in steps 2.2–3.1 have phase 1, giving the product bundle.
Step 4.1 computes the deck translate T₁ and its monodromy χ(1).
Steps 1.1 and 2.1 keep ρ>0, so the collision boundary is outside the covering space.
Step 1.1 gives the open arc sheet ranges; step 4.1 lifts the exchange path from t=0 to t=1.
Steps 1.1 and 2.2 use local sheets and the unique representative in a selected sheet; no global section is asserted.

The public deck-group classification is two-sided: in 1.2 pD=p forces the deck map to fix c,rho and shift t by a continuous integer-valued function, constant since the covering space is connected; thus every deck map is T_n.

Conversely 1.2 verifies each T_n is a homeomorphism preserving p, so every integer shift is a deck transformation.4.1 then calculates its character monodromy; no converse classification of arbitrary line bundles is asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: A **covering map** is a continuous surjection $p:E\to B$ such that every $b\in B$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ for which $p^{-1}(U)$ is a disjoint union of open sets $V_j$, called **sheets**, and each restriction $p|_{V_j}:V_j\to U$ is a homeomorphism ([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]], [[def-disjoint-union-topology]]). Such a $U$ is **evenly covered**, and $p^{-1}(b)$ is the **fibre** over $b$. A covering is **trivial** when it is isomorphic over $B$ to a product projection $B\times F\to B$ with $F$ discrete.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

of $t\mapsto[t]$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
A topological space $X$ is **simply connected** when it is nonempty and
path-connected ([[def-path-connected]]) and, for every $x_0\in X$, the group
$\pi_1(X,x_0)$ has exactly one element.

Requiring every basepoint avoids presuming a change-of-basepoint theorem. For a
path-connected space that later theorem shows that checking one basepoint is
equivalent, but no such result is needed for this definition. The empty space
is path-connected under the published convention, but it is not simply
connected here because nonemptiness is explicit.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions:
[F6] [[def-simply-connected]]: a nonempty path-connected space is simply
connected when every based fundamental group is trivial.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is
independent of representatives and that $[c_{x_0}]$ and $[\bar\alpha]$ are the
identity and inverse required by the group axioms.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions:
[F9] [[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]: based loops are identified
under endpoint-fixed path homotopy, and a loop class is the input to its
covering lift and monodromy.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**The quotient topology.** Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]), let $Y$ be a set and let $q : X \to Y$ be a
surjection ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). The **quotient topology** on
$Y$ induced by $q$ is the final topology of the one-element family $(q)$
([[def-initial-and-final-topology]]):

$$\mathcal{T}_q \;:=\; \{\, V \subseteq Y : q^{-1}[V] \in \mathcal{T} \,\} .$$

That this is a topology is discharged in [[def-initial-and-final-topology]],
where every final topology is verified to satisfy (T1), (T2) and (T3). Dually,
$C \subseteq Y$ is closed in $\mathcal{T}_q$ exactly when $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed
in $X$, because $q^{-1}[Y \setminus V] = X \setminus q^{-1}[V]$.

**Quotient map.** A surjection $q : X \to Y$ between topological *spaces* is a
**quotient map** (also *identification map*) when the topology of $Y$ is the
quotient topology of $q$, that is when

$$V \text{ is open in } Y \iff q^{-1}[V] \text{ is open in } X \qquad (V \subseteq Y).$$

The implication from left to right is exactly continuity of $q$
([[def-continuous-map-top]], [[thm-continuity-characterisations-top]] clause
(b)), so a quotient map is a continuous surjection with the extra property that
its topology is as *fine* as continuity permits. Equivalently, and this form is
used as often: $C$ is closed in $Y$ if and only if $q^{-1}[C]$ is closed in $X$.

**Saturated sets.** Let $q : X \to Y$ be a surjection. A subset $A \subseteq X$ is
**saturated** with respect to $q$ when

$$A \;=\; q^{-1}\big[\,q[A]\,\big] ,$$

equivalently when $A$ is a union of fibres $q^{-1}[\{y\}]$, equivalently when
$x \in A$ and $q(x') = q(x)$ imply $x' \in A$. The set $q^{-1}[q[A]]$ is the
**saturation** of $A$, and it is the smallest saturated set containing $A$. The
map $V \mapsto q^{-1}[V]$ is a bijection from $\mathcal{P}(Y)$ onto the saturated
subsets of $X$, with inverse $A \mapsto q[A]$, since $q$ is surjective; under it
the open sets of the quotient topology correspond exactly to the **saturated open
subsets of $X$**. That correspondence is the working description of the quotient
topology: to know the open sets of $Y$ is to know which open subsets of $X$ are
saturated.

**Quotient by an equivalence relation.** Let $\sim$ be an **equivalence relation**
on $X$, that is a relation that is reflexive ($x \sim x$), symmetric
($x \sim x'$ implies $x' \sim x$) and transitive ($x \sim x'$ and $x' \sim x''$
imply $x \sim x''$). Write $[x] := \{\, x' \in X : x' \sim x \,\}$ for the
**equivalence class** of $x$; distinct classes are disjoint and their union is
$X$. The **quotient set** is $X/\!\sim\ := \{\, [x] : x \in X \,\}$ and the
**canonical projection** is

$$\pi : X \to X/\!\sim, \qquad \pi(x) := [x] ,$$

which is a surjection by construction. The set $X/\!\sim$ always carries the
quotient topology of $\pi$, and $(X/\!\sim,\ \mathcal{T}_\pi)$ is called an
**identification space**. A subset of $X$ is saturated for $\pi$ exactly when it
is a union of equivalence classes.

**A convenient special case: collapsing a subset.** For $\varnothing \ne B \subseteq X$
let $\sim_B$ be the relation whose classes are $B$ itself and the singletons
$\{x\}$ for $x \notin B$; this is an equivalence relation, its classes being a
partition of $X$. The resulting quotient is written $X/B$, and its canonical
projection is a surjection identifying all of $B$ to a single point and doing
nothing else. Saturated sets for $\sim_B$ are the sets $A$ with $A \cap B \in
\{\varnothing, B\}$.

**Two conventions used throughout.** First, "quotient map" is a property of a map
*together with the two topologies*, never of the map alone. Second, a quotient
topology is determined by $q$ together with the topology on its domain, and not by
the underlying pair of sets $(X,Y)$: two different surjections onto the same set
can give different topologies, the same surjection gives different topologies when
its domain is retopologised, and where more than one is in play the map is named.

citations.quote:
Let $q_0:=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}\in C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. There is a pointed
homeomorphism
$$\bigl(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0\bigr)\cong \bigl(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, (0,1,[0])\bigr),$$
and
$$\pi_1(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$
Under the isomorphism specified in the proof, the counterclockwise exchange
loop
$$\gamma(t):=\{(\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t),(-\cos\pi t,-\sin\pi t)\},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1,$$
is a positive generator. The loop in which the relative direction makes one
full counterclockwise turn is $[\gamma]^2$, so it represents twice the
generator.

Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

Let

$$C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$$

with the Euclidean subspace topology. The function

$$h:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\longrightarrow C,\qquad h([t])=(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t),$$

is a homeomorphism. Thus $[t]\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ to the unit circle and sends $[0]$ to $(1,0)$.

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

Let $n\ge 0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Use the left action of
$S_n$ on tableaux, tabloids, and $M^\lambda$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). For each
$\gamma\in C_t$, let $\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)$ be its inversion sign in
$S_n$. The order-preserving relabelling
$\iota_n:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $i\mapsto i-1$, carries each
inversion pair $(i,j)$ bijectively to $(i-1,j-1)$; thus this sign is exactly
the published inversion sign on the finite ordinal
([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). For $n=0$, both groups are
trivial and the sign is $1$.

The **column antisymmetrizer**, **polytabloid**, and **Specht space** are
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma\quad\in\mathbb C[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}\quad\in M^\lambda,\qquad S^\lambda:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_s:s\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}.$$
The elements of the sum are in the finite subgroup $C_t$, and each acts by the
declared left action on the tabloid basis, so these are well-defined finite
expressions.

For every tableau, $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a permutation in both stabilizers
preserves the row and column of each entry, and each row-column intersection
contains at most one node. Thus $\gamma\{t\}$ are distinct as $\gamma$ ranges
over $C_t$, and the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. In particular,
$e_t\ne0$. When $n=0$, the empty tableau has $C_t=\{1\}$, so
$\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$, and $S^\varnothing=\mathbb C$.

For every character $\chi:\mathbb Z\to U(1)$, the coordinate covering
$p:\widetilde X\to X$ and quotient $\Pi_\chi:L_\chi\to X$ defined by the
character-quotient construction have the following properties:

1. $p$ is a universal covering map and its deck transformations are exactly
   $T_n(c,\rho,t)=(c,\rho,t+n)$, $n\in\mathbb Z$.
2. $\Pi_\chi$ is a unitary flat complex line bundle, meaning its local
   transition phases are locally constant.
3. Parallel transport defined by keeping the lifted fiber coordinate fixed
   has monodromy $\chi(n)$ on a based loop whose lift ends at $T_n\widetilde x$.

In particular, a positive planar exchange has monodromy $\chi(1)$ and a full
relative winding has monodromy $\chi(2)$.

derivations.claim:
Write $g=[\gamma]$. By [F1], every element of the fundamental group is
uniquely $ng$ for $n\in\mathbb Z$. A homomorphism $\chi$ is therefore
determined by $z:=\chi(g)$: the homomorphism law gives
$\chi(ng)=z^n$, including negative $n$ because $z^{-1}$ is the group inverse
in $U(1)$. Conversely, for any $z\in U(1)$ this formula preserves addition
of integer exponents and defines a homomorphism. By [F3], the pair
$(\operatorname{Re}z,\operatorname{Im}z)$ lies on the unit circle. By [F2]
there is a unique $[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ for which
$z=\cos(2\pi t)+i\sin(2\pi t)$. Put $\theta:=2\pi t$ modulo $2\pi$.
Repeated application of [F4] gives
$z^n=\cos(n\theta)+i\sin(n\theta)$ for $n\geq0$; for $n<0$, use
$z^{-1}=\overline z=\cos(-\theta)+i\sin(-\theta)$ by [F5], and the same
induction.
This proves the full character classification and the displayed formula.

Write $S_2=\{e,\tau\}$ with $\tau=(12)$ and $\tau^2=e$. The
permutation quotient $q:\mathbb Z\to S_2$, $q(n)=\tau^n$, is onto and has
kernel $2\mathbb Z$. A character factors through that quotient exactly when
$z^2=1$, where
$z=\chi(g)$. By [F6], this forces $z=1$ or $z=-1$. The parameterization
[F2] is unique modulo $2\pi$; [F7] identifies these points with angles
$0$ and $\pi$, respectively. The resulting generator values are $+1$ and
$-1$. For shape $(2)$ the unique tableau has trivial
column stabilizer, so its column antisymmetrizer is the identity and the
one-dimensional Specht module is trivial; for shape $(1,1)$ the column
antisymmetrizer is $1-(12)$, whose image is the sign line. This direct use of
the Specht definition [F9] identifies the two factors.

By [F1], one full relative turn represents $2g$. The homomorphism law
then gives $\chi(2g)=z^2=\cos(2\theta)+i\sin(2\theta)=e^{2i\theta}$ by
[F4].

On $(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes2}$ the swap fixes $|00\rangle$ and sends
$|\omega\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$ to $-|\omega\rangle$.
Thus both exchange eigenspaces are nonzero. They are the $+1$ and $-1$
Specht factors in the Schur–Weyl decomposition [F8, F9], so the two permutation
characters occur algebraically. This establishes occurrence only; it does
not select a physical statistics sector.

Apply [F10] to $\chi_\theta$. The positive exchange is the loop class
$g$ from [F1], whose lift shifts the normalized angle coordinate by $1$;
therefore its monodromy is $\chi_\theta(1)=e^{i\theta}$. A full relative
turn shifts by $2$, so its monodromy is $\chi_\theta(2)=e^{2i\theta}$ by
step 2.1.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Give $\mathbb R^4$ its Euclidean topology, whose basic open sets are the
Euclidean open balls, and write a point as an ordered pair $(x,y)$ with
$x,y\in\mathbb R^2$. The **ordered configuration space** is the subspace
$$F_2(\mathbb R^2):=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^2:x\ne y\}$$
with the subspace topology. The transposition acts by $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$.
The **unordered configuration space of two distinct planar points** is
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2):=F_2(\mathbb R^2)/\bigl((x,y)\sim(y,x)\bigr)$$
with the quotient topology of the canonical projection
$q:F_2(\mathbb R^2)\to C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. We write its points as unordered
sets $\{x,y\}$; equality in this set means equality up to transposition.
The diagonal $x=y$ is excluded, so collisions are not points of this space.

The topology on each finite Cartesian coordinate space used below is its
Euclidean topology; on a finite product it is equivalently the topology with
basis the products of open sets in the factors.

Let $q_0:=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}\in C_2(\mathbb R^2)$. There is a pointed
homeomorphism
$$\bigl(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0\bigr)\cong \bigl(\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z, (0,1,[0])\bigr),$$
and
$$\pi_1(C_2(\mathbb R^2),q_0)\cong(\mathbb Z,+).$$
Under the isomorphism specified in the proof, the counterclockwise exchange
loop
$$\gamma(t):=\{(\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t),(-\cos\pi t,-\sin\pi t)\},\qquad 0\leq t\leq1,$$
is a positive generator. The loop in which the relative direction makes one
full counterclockwise turn is $[\gamma]^2$, so it represents twice the
generator.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions:
[F8] [[thm-nrqmx-schur-weyl-exchange-blocks]]: on
$(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes2}$ the transposition acts on the Specht factor and as
identity on the multiplicity factor; the collective $U(2)$ action acts on
the multiplicity factor.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the canonical copy of $\mathbb Z$ inside $\mathbb R$ fixed in
[[lem-integer-part]]. For $x,y\in\mathbb R$, put

$$x\sim y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

This is an equivalence relation. Indeed, $x-x=0\in\mathbb Z$; if
$x-y\in\mathbb Z$, then $y-x=-(x-y)\in\mathbb Z$; and if
$x-y,y-z\in\mathbb Z$, then $x-z=(x-y)+(y-z)\in\mathbb Z$. The closure facts
used here are part of the additive-group structure supplied by
[[thm-int-comm-ring]], and the quotient-set construction is that of
[[def-quotient-topology]].

Let $[x]$ denote the equivalence class of $x$. Let
$p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the canonical projection,
$p(x)=[x]$. Thus

$$p(x)=p(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x-y\in\mathbb Z.$$

Let $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ carry the quotient topology induced by $p$.
The circle is $S^1:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with the quotient topology induced by $p(x)=[x]$ and basepoint $[0]$; moreover $p^{-1}([0])=\mathbb Z$ and $p(x+n)=p(x)$ for every real $x$ and integer $n$.

The last assertions follow directly from the displayed fibre criterion:
$p(x)=[0]$ exactly when $x\in\mathbb Z$, while
$(x+n)-x=n\in\mathbb Z$.

field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n\ge 0$, let $\lambda\vdash n$, and let $t$ be a $\lambda$-tableau
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]],
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]). Use the left action of
$S_n$ on tableaux, tabloids, and $M^\lambda$
([[def-young-subgroup-tabloid-and-permutation-module]]). For each
$\gamma\in C_t$, let $\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)$ be its inversion sign in
$S_n$. The order-preserving relabelling
$\iota_n:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, $i\mapsto i-1$, carries each
inversion pair $(i,j)$ bijectively to $(i-1,j-1)$; thus this sign is exactly
the published inversion sign on the finite ordinal
([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). For $n=0$, both groups are
trivial and the sign is $1$.

The **column antisymmetrizer**, **polytabloid**, and **Specht space** are
$$\kappa_t:=\sum_{\gamma\in C_t}\operatorname{sgn}(\gamma)\gamma\quad\in\mathbb C[S_n],\qquad e_t:=\kappa_t\cdot\{t\}\quad\in M^\lambda,\qquad S^\lambda:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{e_s:s\text{ is a }\lambda\text{-tableau}\}.$$
The elements of the sum are in the finite subgroup $C_t$, and each acts by the
declared left action on the tabloid basis, so these are well-defined finite
expressions.

For every tableau, $C_t\cap R_t=\{1\}$: a permutation in both stabilizers
preserves the row and column of each entry, and each row-column intersection
contains at most one node. Thus $\gamma\{t\}$ are distinct as $\gamma$ ranges
over $C_t$, and the coefficient of $\{t\}$ in $e_t$ is $1$. In particular,
$e_t\ne0$. When $n=0$, the empty tableau has $C_t=\{1\}$, so
$\kappa_t=1$, $e_t=\{\varnothing\}$, and $S^\varnothing=\mathbb C$.

the Specht module of shape $(1,1)$ is the one-dimensional sign module, by
applying the column antisymmetrizer to the unique tableau of each shape.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the pointed coordinate identification
$$C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z,$$
which sends $q_0=\{(1,0),(-1,0)\}$ to $(0,1,[0])$, to write
$$X:=C_2(\mathbb R^2)\cong\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R/\mathbb Z.$$
Put $\widetilde X:=\mathbb R^2\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ and define
$$p(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,[t])\in X,\qquad T_n(c,\rho,t):=(c,\rho,t+n)\quad(n\in\mathbb Z).$$
Define $U(1):=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ under complex multiplication. Let
$\chi:\mathbb Z\to U(1)$ satisfy
$\chi(0)=1$ and $\chi(m+n)=\chi(m)\chi(n)$ for all $m,n\in\mathbb Z$.
Let $\mathbb Z$ act on
$\widetilde X\times\mathbb C$ by
$$n\cdot((c,\rho,t),z):=((c,\rho,t+n),\chi(n)^{-1}z).$$
The homomorphism law for $\chi$ makes this a group action, and its orbits
define the quotient relation.
Define the **character quotient** and its projection by
$$L_\chi:=(\widetilde X\times\mathbb C)/\mathbb Z, \qquad \Pi_\chi([\widetilde x,z]):=p(\widetilde x),$$
with the quotient topology on $L_\chi$. Since $p(T_n\widetilde x)=p(\widetilde x)$,
it induces a continuous map $\Pi_\chi:L_\chi\to X$. Once $p$ is known to be
a covering map, the **monodromy** of this quotient around a based loop means
the fiber map obtained by lifting the loop and keeping its complex coordinate
$z$ constant along the lift.

For this item, a **unitary flat complex line bundle** over a space $X$ means a
continuous surjection $\Pi:L\to X$ with local trivializations
$\Pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb C$ over open sets $U$, whose changes of fiber
coordinate on overlaps are multiplication by functions $g:U\cap V\to U(1)$
that are locally constant (constant on some neighbourhood of each point).
The definition above names the quotient data; the following theorem verifies
that $L_\chi$ has these line-bundle and flatness properties.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For every character $\chi:\mathbb Z\to U(1)$, the coordinate covering
$p:\widetilde X\to X$ and quotient $\Pi_\chi:L_\chi\to X$ defined by the
character-quotient construction have the following properties:

1. $p$ is a universal covering map and its deck transformations are exactly
   $T_n(c,\rho,t)=(c,\rho,t+n)$, $n\in\mathbb Z$.
2. $\Pi_\chi$ is a unitary flat complex line bundle, meaning its local
   transition phases are locally constant.
3. Parallel transport defined by keeping the lifted fiber coordinate fixed
   has monodromy $\chi(n)$ on a based loop whose lift ends at $T_n\widetilde x$.

In particular, a positive planar exchange has monodromy $\chi(1)$ and a full
relative winding has monodromy $\chi(2)$.

Let $N\geq1$ be an integer. The finite spin-half tensor chain is the complex
inner-product space $\mathcal H_N:=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$. On each factor
use the inner product
$$\langle (z_0,z_1),(w_0,w_1)\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}:=z_0\overline{w_0}+z_1\overline{w_1},$$
which is linear in its first argument, and let $|0\rangle=(1,0)$ and
$|1\rangle=(0,1)$. By the finite tensor-product basis theorem, for
$\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$ the words
$|\alpha\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_N\rangle$ form a basis of
$\mathcal H_N$. For $u=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ and
$v=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}d_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, define
$$\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}:=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha\overline{d_\alpha}.$$
This is a positive-definite inner product because
$\langle u,u\rangle=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$, and it makes the tensor words
orthonormal. Expanding each factor in $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ gives its
elementary-tensor product formula
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Let $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ be the Pauli matrices of the finite-spin
matrix supplier, and for $1\leq k\leq N$ define
$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$
For $1\leq i<N$, define the adjacent swap $s_i$ on elementary tensors by

The identity commutes with every endomorphism, so in particular
$I_{H_2}s=sI_{H_2}$. By [F1], $s|00\rangle=|00\rangle$. Also
$s|\omega\rangle=(|10\rangle-|01\rangle)/\sqrt2=-|\omega\rangle$;

to both one-zero/one-one basis vectors. By [F2], this swap is exactly the
left place action of the transposition. Thus both exchange eigenspaces in

step 1.1 shows that its underlying space is contained in neither single
exchange eigenspace. This is a counterexample to the universal claim. The
Schur–Weyl decomposition [F3] records both exchange factors and their
multiplicity spaces; it does not add a rule that removes one of them.

Hermitian inner product, and give $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$ its standard
tensor-product inner product. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I\}$ use the diagonal action
$\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$. For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

citations.quote:
Let $N\geq1$ be an integer. The finite spin-half tensor chain is the complex
inner-product space $\mathcal H_N:=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$. On each factor
use the inner product
$$\langle (z_0,z_1),(w_0,w_1)\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}:=z_0\overline{w_0}+z_1\overline{w_1},$$
which is linear in its first argument, and let $|0\rangle=(1,0)$ and
$|1\rangle=(0,1)$. By the finite tensor-product basis theorem, for
$\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_N)\in\{0,1\}^N$ the words
$|\alpha\rangle:=|a_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|a_N\rangle$ form a basis of
$\mathcal H_N$. For $u=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$ and
$v=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}d_\alpha|\alpha\rangle$, define
$$\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}:=\sum_{\alpha\in\{0,1\}^N}c_\alpha\overline{d_\alpha}.$$
This is a positive-definite inner product because
$\langle u,u\rangle=\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha|^2$, and it makes the tensor words
orthonormal. Expanding each factor in $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ gives its
elementary-tensor product formula
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{\mathcal H_N}=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Let $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ be the Pauli matrices of the finite-spin
matrix supplier, and for $1\leq k\leq N$ define
$$\sigma_k^a:=I^{\otimes(k-1)}\otimes\sigma^a\otimes I^{\otimes(N-k)},\qquad J_k^a:=\tfrac12\sigma_k^a\quad(a\in\{x,y,z\}).$$
For $1\leq i<N$, define the adjacent swap $s_i$ on elementary tensors by
$$s_i(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{i+1}\otimes v_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N.$$
Write
$$|\omega\rangle:=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle\otimes|1\rangle-|1\rangle\otimes|0\rangle),\qquad P_i:=I^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P_\omega\otimes I^{\otimes(N-i-1)},$$
where $P_\omega v:=\langle v,\omega\rangle\,\omega$ on the adjacent two
factors. Also put $e_i:=I_{\mathcal H_N}-s_i$ for $1\leq i<N$. If $N=1$,
these bond-indexed families are empty.

This is a mathematical definition of finite-dimensional tensor spaces and
operators; it makes no physical claim about a material, a particle species, or
an adopted statistics sector.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $N\geq1$, $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the standard
orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$ on each factor, and for
$1\leq i<N$ define $s_i$ to swap factors $i,i+1$. Put
$|\omega\rangle=(|01\rangle-|10\rangle)/\sqrt2$,
$P_\omega v=\langle v,\omega\rangle\omega$, let $P_i$ act as $P_\omega$ on
factors $i,i+1$ and identity on all others, and set $e_i=I-s_i$. For every
bond,
$$e_i=I-s_i=2P_i,\qquad e_i^*=e_i,\qquad e_i^2=2e_i.$$
For $1\leq i<N-1$,
$$e_i e_{i+1}e_i=e_i,\qquad e_{i+1}e_i e_{i+1}=e_{i+1},$$
and $e_i e_j=e_j e_i$ when $|i-j|>1$. Consequently the assignment
$u_i\mapsto e_i$ defines a star-preserving algebra representation
$$P_N(\mathbb C,2)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H_N).$$
For $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most two rows, put
$M_\lambda=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,\mathcal H_N)$ and use the
unitary Schur–Weyl decomposition
$\mathcal H_N\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\,\ell(\lambda)\le2}
S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$. Each $e_i$ acts on the Specht factor as
$I-\rho_\lambda((i,i+1))$ and as identity on the multiplicity factor. No
faithfulness assertion is made.

Let $N\geq1$, let $\hbar>0$, and let real couplings
$\mathcal J_i\in\mathbb R$ be given for $1\leq i<N$. On
$\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$, let $\sigma_i^a$ be the Pauli
matrix $\sigma^a$ acting on factor $i$ and identity on all other factors,
where
$$\sigma^x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma^y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \sigma^z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Let $s_i$ swap factors $i,i+1$ and put $e_i=I-s_i$. Set
$S_i^a:=\hbar\sigma_i^a/2$ for $a\in\{x,y,z\}$, and define the finite-chain
operator
$$H:=\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}\mathcal J_i\hbar^{-2}\sum_{a=x,y,z}S_i^aS_{i+1}^a.$$
For every bond,
$$\hbar^{-2}\sum_a S_i^aS_{i+1}^a=\tfrac12s_i-\tfrac14I =\tfrac14I-\tfrac12e_i.$$
Thus $H=\sum_i\mathcal J_i(\tfrac14I-\tfrac12e_i)$ is self-adjoint, belongs
to the represented Temperley–Lieb algebra, and on each summand of the unitary
decomposition
$$\mathcal H_N\cong\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\,\ell(\lambda)\le2} S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda,\qquad M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,\mathcal H_N),$$
acts on $S^\lambda$ and as identity on $M_\lambda$. For $N=1$ the sum is
empty and $H=0$.

Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

derivations.claim:
The coefficient vectors of $a_+$ and $b_+$ in the ordered one-down
subspace $(|001\rangle,|010\rangle,|100\rangle)$ are
$(0,1,-1)/\sqrt2$ and $(2,-1,-1)/\sqrt6$; their squared norms are $1$ and
their inner product is $0$. The one-up pair $a_-,b_-$ has coefficient vectors
$(0,-1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $(-2,1,1)/\sqrt6$ in the ordered basis
$(|110\rangle,|101\rangle,|011\rangle)$, again with norm $1$ and inner
product $0$. Each $q$-vector has norm $1$; the two three-term $q$-vectors
are orthogonal to the corresponding $a,b$ vectors because their coefficient
vectors are constant while the latter have coefficient sum zero. Vectors
with different numbers of entries equal to $1$ are orthogonal. Thus the eight
vectors are orthonormal, and [F1] says the ambient space has dimension eight;
they are a basis.

Applying $K_z$ counts $+1/2$ for each $0$ and $-1/2$ for each $1$,
which gives the subscripts in the statement. By [F2], $K_+$ changes one $1$
to $0$ with coefficient $1$. Summing over positions gives
$$K_+q_{1/2}=\sqrt3q_{3/2},\quad K_+q_{-1/2}=2q_{1/2},\quad K_+q_{-3/2}=\sqrt3q_{-1/2},\quad K_+a_-=a_+,\quad K_+b_-=b_+;$$
the top states $q_{3/2},a_+,b_+$ are killed because their coefficients
cancel or they contain no $1$. The lowering actions are the adjoints of these
raising actions because the displayed basis is orthonormal and each local
lowering matrix is the adjoint of its raising matrix by [F2]. This verifies
both ladder directions.

The swaps fix every symmetric $q$-vector. On both magnetic pairs,
$s_{12}$ changes the sign of $a_\pm$ and fixes $b_\pm$, by their displayed
coefficients. For the upper pair,
$$s_{23}a_+=(|001\rangle-|100\rangle)/\sqrt2 =\tfrac12a_++\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}b_+,$$
and direct substitution gives
$s_{23}b_+=(\sqrt3/2)a_+-(1/2)b_+$. On the lower pair the same
substitution gives
$$s_{23}a_-=(|011\rangle-|110\rangle)/\sqrt2 =\tfrac12a_-+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}b_-,\qquad s_{23}b_-=(\sqrt3/2)a_--(1/2)b_-.$$
These are exactly the two matrices stated.

The two matrices act on the same coordinate pair $(a_+,b_+)$ and
$(a_-,b_-)$, while $K_z$ and $K_\pm$ act on the magnetic labels with the
same coefficients for either exchange coordinate. The two-dimensional
exchange representation is irreducible: the only invariant lines of
$s_{12}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ are the two coordinate axes, and
$s_{23}$ mixes both axes because its off-diagonal entries are nonzero.
Thus this basis displays a spin-$3/2$ block with trivial exchange and a
two-dimensional exchange factor repeated over the two spin-$1/2$ magnetic
states, in the factor placement of [F5].

By [F3]–[F4], each bond contributes $\mathcal J(I/4-e/2)$.
On the quartet both swaps are $I$, so both $e$'s vanish and the total is
$(\mathcal J_{12}+\mathcal J_{23})I/4$. On either doublet pair,
$$e_{12}=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad e_{23}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&-\sqrt3/2\\-\sqrt3/2&3/2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Therefore the two bond matrices are
$$\begin{pmatrix}-3/4&0\\0&1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad \begin{pmatrix}0&\sqrt3/4\\\sqrt3/4&-1/2\end{pmatrix},$$
and their real-coupled sum is the displayed doublet matrix, identical for
$+$ and $-$. For $a=\mathcal J_{12}$ and $b=\mathcal J_{23}$, its trace is
$-(a+b)/2$ and determinant is $-3(a-b)^2/16$; solving the quadratic
characteristic equation gives
$-(a+b)/4\pm\frac12\sqrt{a^2-ab+b^2}$. This proves the exact block
decomposition and multiplicity of these eigenvalues.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $d\geq1$ and $N\geq0$ be integers. Let $V=\mathbb C^d$ with standard
coordinate basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ and inner product
$$\langle z,w\rangle_V:=\sum_{r=1}^d z_r\overline{w_r},$$
linear in its first argument. Put $H_N:=V^{\otimes N}$, with $H_0:=\mathbb C$.
For $N\geq1$ equip $H_N$ with the sesquilinear form linear in its first
argument specified on elementary tensors by
$$\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_N\rangle_{H_N}:=\prod_{j=1}^N\langle v_j,w_j\rangle_V,$$
and extended sesquilinearly; for $N=0$ use $\langle z,w\rangle_{H_0}:=z\overline w$
(the empty product is $1$). Let
$$U(d):=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A^*A=I_d\},$$
where $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. For $\pi\in S_N$ use the left place action
$$\rho(\pi)(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N):=v_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(N)},$$
and for $U\in U(d)$ use the diagonal action $\Delta_N(U):=U^{\otimes N}$.
For a partition $\lambda\vdash N$ with at most
$d$ rows, let $S^\lambda$ be the corresponding complex Specht module and put
$$M_\lambda:=\operatorname{Hom}_{S_N}(S^\lambda,H_N),\qquad d_\lambda:=\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\lambda.$$
Equip $S^\lambda$ with any $S_N$-invariant Hermitian inner product and equip
$M_\lambda$ with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{M_\lambda}:=d_\lambda^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(g^*f).$$
Equip each $S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with the product inner product,
defined on elementary tensors by
$\langle s\otimes f,s'\otimes g\rangle=
\langle s,s'\rangle\langle f,g\rangle$ and extended sesquilinearly, and give
the direct sum the orthogonal direct-sum inner product.
Then the evaluation map
$$\Phi:\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash N,\ \ell(\lambda)\leq d}S^\lambda\otimes M_\lambda\longrightarrow H_N,\qquad \Phi(s\otimes f):=f(s),$$
is unitary. Under this decomposition every permutation acts on $S^\lambda$
and as the identity on $M_\lambda$, while every diagonal $U(d)$ action acts
as the identity on $S^\lambda$ and by postcomposition on $M_\lambda$. The
multiplicity spaces in the sum are nonzero; partitions with more than $d$
rows have zero multiplicity space.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.
