derivations.claim: The two parenthesizations of a triple product in $G_d$ have the same central coordinate, since both give $\theta+\theta'+\theta''-v'\cdot a-v''\cdot a-v''\cdot a'$. The identity is $(0,0,0)$ and the inverse of $(a,v,\theta)$ is $(-a,-v,-\theta-v\cdot a)$. Multiplying by $(0,0,\eta)$ on either side adds $\eta$ to the central coordinate and leaves $(a,v)$ fixed, so $Z$ is central; the quotient forgets $\theta$ and is the additive group $\mathbb R^{2d}$. The product and inverse maps are continuous in the product Euclidean topology: their coordinates are sums and the polynomial expression $\theta+\theta'-v'\cdot a$ or $-\theta-v\cdot a$. Thus $G_d$ is a topological group.
By [A2] and [F1], $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx;\mathbb C)$ with the stated pairing is a complex Hilbert space, so the operator definitions act on the required Hilbert space.

Translation is well-defined on almost-everywhere classes by [F2], and $\|T(a)f\|_2^2=\int |f(x-a)|^2dx=\int |f(x)|^2dx$ by [F3]. The map is linear with inverse $T(-a)$; hence it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.

The multiplier $e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}=\exp(imv\cdot x/\hbar)$ is continuous, hence measurable, by [F15], and has modulus one by [F16]. Therefore $B_m(v)$ preserves the norm. It is linear, and the addition law [F14] gives $B_m(v)B_m(-v)=I$; hence $B_m(-v)$ is its inverse and it is unitary by [F5] and step 1.2.

For almost every $x$, $(B_m(v)T(a)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}f(x-a)$ while $(T(a)B_m(v)f)(x)=e^{imv\cdot(x-a)/\hbar}f(x-a)$. By the addition law [F14], $e^{imv\cdot x/\hbar}=e^{imv\cdot(x-a)/\hbar}e^{imv\cdot a/\hbar}$, proving the commutation identity. Multiplying it on the right by $B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$ gives the displayed loop identity.

Let $g=u+iw\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$. For the unitary families established in steps 2.1 and 2.2, [F10] gives $u,w\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$; applying [F9] to each component and using $\|h+ik\|_2^2=\|h\|_2^2+\|k\|_2^2$ yields $\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2\to0$ as $a\to a_0$. If $v_n\to v_0$, continuity of the scalar exponential [F15] gives pointwise convergence $|e^{im(v_n-v_0)\cdot x/\hbar}-1|^2|g(x)|^2\to0$; by [F16] and the triangle inequality [F4], this is bounded by $4|g(x)|^2$, which is integrable. Dominated convergence [F12] gives $\|B_m(v_n)g-B_m(v_0)g\|_2\to0$. Since Euclidean parameter spaces are metric, both orbit maps are continuous on this dense smooth subspace.

For arbitrary $f\in\mathcal H$, approximate it in $L^2$ by $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ using [F8]. Unitarity in steps 2.1 and 2.2 gives $\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2\le2\|f-g\|_2+\|T(a)g-T(a_0)g\|_2$, and the analogous estimate for $B_m(v)$; letting the approximation error be arbitrarily small extends both continuities to every $f$. The scalar phase $e^{im\theta/\hbar}$ is continuous in $\theta$ by [F15]. Moreover,
$$\|\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)f-\Pi_m(a_0,v_0,\theta_0)f\|_2\le |e^{im\theta/\hbar}-e^{im\theta_0/\hbar}|\|f\|_2+\|T(a)f-T(a_0)f\|_2+\|(B_m(v)-B_m(v_0))T(a_0)f\|_2,$$
so the orbit map of $\Pi_m$ is norm-continuous on the product Euclidean group.

Using $T(a)B_m(v')=e^{-imv'\cdot a/\hbar}B_m(v')T(a)$ from step 3.1 and the translation law together with the exponential addition law [F14], multiplication gives $\Pi_m(a,v,\theta)\Pi_m(a',v',\theta')=\Pi_m(a+a',v+v',\theta+\theta'-v'\cdot a)$. By step 1.1 this is the group law; the operators are unitary by steps 2.1 and 2.2, and their orbit maps are continuous by step 4.1. Thus $\Pi_m$ is a unitary representation by [F5], and $\Pi_m(0,0,\eta)=e^{im\eta/\hbar}I$ is its central character.

For a finite direct sum the central subgroup acts as $\bigoplus_j e^{im_j\eta/\hbar}I_j$. If $m_j\ne m_k$, equality of the two central characters as functions would imply $\exp(im_j\eta/\hbar)=\exp(im_k\eta/\hbar)$ for every real $\eta$. By [F13], $\exp(0)=1$; by the derivative at zero from [F15], for every nonzero real $\alpha$ we have $\lim_{\eta\to0}(\exp(i\alpha\eta)-1)/\eta=i\alpha$, since factoring $i\alpha$ reduces this limit to the complex derivative of $\exp$ at $0$. Applying this with $\alpha=m_j/\hbar$ and $\alpha=m_k/\hbar$ would give $im_j/\hbar=im_k/\hbar$, contrary to $m_j\ne m_k$. Therefore the central characters are pairwise distinct.

Substituting $p=mv$ into the displayed Weyl formula gives $W(a,mv)=e^{-imv\cdot a/(2\hbar)}B_m(v)T(a)$. Direct multiplication, using the exponential addition law [F14], gives $W(a,p)W(a',p')=e^{-i\omega((a,p),(a',p'))/(2\hbar)}W(a+a',p+p')$. The published model result [F7] verifies this system is irreducible and regular, and [F6] gives unitary equivalence for every other system with the same finite phase space and nonzero parameter $1/\hbar$.

derivations.claim: We use real-parameter differentiation in the finite orthonormal basis supplied by [F1]. For a complex scalar $f=a+ib$ with real components, its derivative is $a'+ib'$: convergence of the complex difference quotient is equivalent to convergence of its two real coordinates, since $|x|,|y|\le|x+iy|\le|x|+|y|$. Expanding $(a+ib)(c+id)=(ac-bd)+i(ad+bc)$ transfers [F11] to complex scalar products, and conjugation differentiates by conjugating the derivative. Finite sums then give the scalar-vector and matrix product rules entry by entry, and $(M^*)'=(M')^*$. These entry derivatives are the finite-dimensional vector or operator derivatives: in an orthonormal basis the squared vector norm is the finite sum of squared coordinate moduli, while for a $d\times d$ matrix $A$, each coordinate of $Ax$ has modulus at most $d\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|\,\|x\|$ by the finite triangle inequality and $|x_k|\le\|x\|$. Thus $\|Ax\|^2\le d^3(\max_{j,k}|A_{jk}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus entrywise difference-quotient remainders tending to zero also tend to zero in the corresponding norm. Direct calculation for each displayed Pauli matrix gives $\sigma_i^*=\sigma_i$, $\sigma_i^2=I$, $\operatorname{tr}\sigma_i=0$, and $\det\sigma_i=-1$. With $c=\cos(t/2)$ and $s_t=\sin(t/2)$, direct $2\times2$ matrix calculations and the Pythagorean identity [F8] give $A_i(t)^*A_i(t)=(c^2+s_t^2)I=I$ and $\det A_i(t)=c^2+s_t^2=1$, so each $A_i(t)$ lies in $SU(2)$. Its entries are differentiable by [F9]. The addition formulas [F10] and $\sigma_i^2=I$ give $A_i(t+h)=A_i(t)A_i(h)$ for each $i$, and [F9] gives $A_i(0)=I$; thus each map $t\mapsto A_i(t)$ is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb R,+)$ to $SU(2)$. Differentiating $D(A_i(t))^*D(A_i(t))=I$ at $0$ and using $\frac{d}{dt}D(A_i(t))|_{t=0}=-iJ_i$ gives $J_i^*=J_i$. For $i=z$, the Euler formula [F7] and parity [F8] give $A_z(t)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-it/2),\exp(it/2))$. Set $U(t):=D(A_z(t))$. Since $D$ is a differentiable representation, $U$ is differentiable, $U(t+h)=U(t)U(h)=U(h)U(t)$, and the generator convention gives $U'(0)=-iJ_z$. Differentiating the two products with respect to $h$ at $0$ yields $U'(t)=U(t)(-iJ_z)=(-iJ_z)U(t)$.

By [F1], the irreducibility hypothesis leaves one spin-$s$ block, with orthonormal basis $v_k$, $k=0,\ldots,2s$, and $J_zv_k=(s-k)v_k$. Write $\mu_k=s-k$ and $u_k(t)=U(t)v_k$. Step 1.1 gives $u_k'(t)=-i\mu_k u_k(t)$. From [F5] and [F6], the scalar map $t\mapsto\exp(i\mu_k t)$ has derivative $i\mu_k\exp(i\mu_k t)$: its difference quotient at $t$ factors as $\exp(i\mu_k t)(\exp(i\mu_k h)-1)/h$ and the second factor tends to $i\mu_k$. The coordinate product rule established in step 1.1 gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\exp(i\mu_k t)u_k(t))=0$. To justify constancy, write this vector in the fixed finite orthonormal basis of [F1]. Every real and imaginary coordinate has zero derivative on $\mathbb R$ and is continuous (its increment is its difference quotient times the real increment). For arbitrary $a<b$, apply [F12] separately to these real coordinate functions on $[a,b]$; each has equal endpoint values. All coordinates, and hence the vector, are therefore constant on $\mathbb R$ and equal $v_k$ at $t=0$. Consequently $U(t)v_k=\exp(-i\mu_k t)v_k$.

Put $N=2s\in\mathbb N_0$. For every $k=0,\ldots,2s$, $2(s-k)=N-2k$ is an integer and [F5], [F7] give $\exp(-i2\pi(s-k))=\exp(-i\pi N)\exp(i2\pi k)=(-1)^N$. Indeed, $\exp(-i\pi)=-1$ follows from $\exp(i\pi)=-1$ and $\exp(-i\pi)\exp(i\pi)=\exp(0)=1$ by the power-series definition [F4]; also $\exp(i2\pi)=\exp(i\pi)^2=1$. Repeated use of [F5] gives the displayed integer powers. Thus step 2.1 implies $U(2\pi)v_k=(-1)^{2s}v_k$ for every basis vector.

By the diagonal form in step 1.1 and [F7], $A_z(2\pi)=\operatorname{diag}(\exp(-i\pi),\exp(i\pi))=-I$. Hence $D(-I)=U(2\pi)$; step 3.1 evaluates this operator on an orthonormal basis and proves $D(-I)=(-1)^{2s}I_V$.

By [F2], every $R\in SO(3)$ has exactly two lifts $W$ and $-W$. The representation law gives $D(-W)=D(-I)D(W)=(-1)^{2s}D(W)$ by step 4.1. The scalar has modulus one by [F7], so the projective class $[D(W)]\in PU(V)$ is independent of the lift. If $R_1=\rho(W_1)$ and $R_2=\rho(W_2)$, then $W_1W_2$ lifts $R_1R_2$, and $[D(W_1W_2)]=[D(W_1)][D(W_2)]$; hence the ray map is a homomorphism. The map is continuous: on any evenly covered neighborhood for $\rho$, its local section $s$ is continuous and the descended map there is $q\circ D\circ s$, a composition of continuous maps.

If $s$ is integer, $(-1)^{2s}=1$, so $D(W)$ is independent of the lift; defining $\widetilde D(R)=D(W)$ gives a unitary representation because products of lifts lift the product, as in step 5.1, and it is continuous by the same local-section argument. If $s$ is half-integer, $(-1)^{2s}=-1$, so the two lifts $I$ and $-I$ of the identity have images $I_V$ and $-I_V$; these differ since $V\ne\{0\}$. Therefore $D$ cannot factor as a unitary representation through $\rho$, although its projective class from step 5.1 does factor.

Let $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx;\mathbb C)$. On the path space $\mathbb C^2$ set $|0\rangle=(1,0)^T$, $|1\rangle=(0,1)^T$, and $\langle j|:=|j\rangle^*$. Its orthogonal projectors are $|0\rangle\langle0|=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $|1\rangle\langle1|=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, so they are self-adjoint, square to themselves, have zero product and sum to $I_2$. Interpret the finite path-system product as $\mathcal H\oplus\mathcal H$ with $|0\rangle\otimes f=(f,0)$, $|1\rangle\otimes f=(0,f)$ and squared norm $\|(f,g)\|^2=\|f\|^2+\|g\|^2$; completeness follows componentwise from that of $\mathcal H$. In this explicit product model define the controlled loop $C=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes L+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes I$, where $L=B_m(v)T(a)B_m(v)^*T(a)^*$. By step 1.1, $C=U_\theta\otimes I$ with $U_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},1)$. Equip the path space with inner product $u^*w$ and put $u_+=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2$. The recombining path overlap is $u_+^*U_\theta u_+=(1+e^{i\theta})/2$. The addition law [F3] and Euler formula with parity [F4, F6] give $(1+e^{i\theta})/2=e^{i\theta/2}(e^{-i\theta/2}+e^{i\theta/2})/2=e^{i\theta/2}\cos(\theta/2)$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; the following well-definedness lemma establishes that the trace pairing makes $S^*$ well-defined and that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

Let $d,e\geq1$. For $A\in M_{e\times d}(\mathbb C)$ and $B\in M_{d\times e}(\mathbb C)$,
$$ \operatorname{Tr}_e(AB)=\operatorname{Tr}_d(BA), $$
where $\operatorname{Tr}_r$ is the diagonal-sum trace on $M_r(\mathbb C)$. This includes cyclicity for square matrices. For $C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the bilinear trace pairing is nondegenerate: if $\operatorname{Tr}_d(XC)=0$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, then $C=0$. No adjoint is inserted in this pairing.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: For Hermitian $A,B$, $\overline{\operatorname{Tr}(AB)}=\operatorname{Tr}((AB)^*)=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ by [F2]. The trace is additive and real-homogeneous, so the pairing is real-valued, symmetric, and real-bilinear.

Diagonalize $A\in\mathsf H_d$ by [F3] with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$. Then $\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)=\sum_j\lambda_j^2\ge0$, with equality exactly when all $\lambda_j=0$, hence exactly when $A=0$. This proves positive definiteness and the displayed square-root formula.

For $c\in\mathbb R^m$, bilinearity gives $c^\mathsf T Gc=\operatorname{Tr}((Sc)^2)=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\ge0$. For $X\in\mathsf H_d$, the vector $v$ with coordinates $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aX)$ satisfies $\langle Sc,X\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}=c^\mathsf Tv$ for every $c$, so it is $S^*X$. By [F2], $v_a=\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)$; hence the matrix of $S^*S$ is precisely $G$. The equality $\langle c,Gc\rangle=\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ implies $\ker G=\ker S$: $Sc=0$ gives $Gc=0$, while $Gc=0$ gives $\|Sc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=0$ and hence $Sc=0$ by step 2.1. By [F4], $|\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$; expanding $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$ and applying this bound gives $\|A+B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}+\|B\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$. Thus the formula is a norm.

Step 2.1 handles A=0, and step 3.1 gives G=0 and matching kernels for a zero family.
Steps 1.1–3.1 apply to a singleton family without a separate case assumption.
Step 3.1 proves the Gram/kernel identities for arbitrary finite families, including linearly dependent families.

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

derivations.claim: Summing the product law [A1] over the other $n-1$ coordinates gives $\mathbb P(X_k=1)=p\prod_{j\ne k}(p+(1-p))=p$, so $\mathbb E X_k=p$. Put $S=\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-p)$. By [F1], $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(X_k-p)}\le e^{\lambda^2/8}$ for every real $\lambda$. Expanding the finite expectation over $\{0,1\}^n$ and using [A1] factors it into the product of these $n$ expectations. Hence $\mathbb E e^{\lambda S}\le e^{n\lambda^2/8}$.

For $\lambda>0$, $S\ge nt$ implies $e^{\lambda S}\ge e^{\lambda nt}$. For any nonnegative $W$ and $c>0$, $W\ge c\,\mathbf1_{\{W\ge c\}}$, so $\mathbb P(W\ge c)\le\mathbb EW/c$. Apply this to $W=e^{\lambda S}$ and then step 1.1 to get $\mathbb P(f-p\ge t)\le e^{-\lambda nt+n\lambda^2/8}$. Setting $\lambda=4t$ gives $e^{-2nt^2}$.

Apply the same argument to $-S$, using step 1.1 at $-4t$; it gives $\mathbb P(p-f\ge t)\le e^{-2nt^2}$. The union bound follows from $\mathbf1_{A\cup B}\le\mathbf1_A+\mathbf1_B$, so adding the two tails proves the claim. Endpoints $p=0,1$ are included by [A1]: then every $X_k=p$ almost surely and the left side is zero for $t>0$.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each $I_a$ is completely positive in the finite matrix sense. Apply [F2] to obtain a finite Kraus family $(K_{a,r})_r$ for it, allowing the empty family for a zero map. Since $\mathcal A$ is finite, these finitely many choices require only finite choice. Put $q=\sum_aq_a$, where $q_a$ is the number of Kraus operators for outcome $a$.

The combined map $\sum_aI_a$ has Kraus family $(K_{a,r})_{a,r}$ and is trace-preserving by [A1] and [F1]. Thus [F2] gives $\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}^*K_{a,r}=I_d$. Since $d\ge1$, this identity implies $q\ge1$.

Let $(e_{a,r})_{a,r}$ be the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^q$ indexed by these labels. Define $Vx=\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}x\otimes e_{a,r}$ and $Q_a=\sum_r|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,r}|$. Then $V^*V=\sum_{a,r}K_{a,r}^*K_{a,r}=I_d$, so $V$ is an isometry. Disjoint label sets make the $Q_a$ pairwise orthogonal and their sum $I_q$.

Expanding the sandwich gives $\sum_{r,s}K_{a,r}XK_{a,s}^*\otimes|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,s}|$ with both labels restricted to outcome $a$. The partial trace sends each register matrix unit $|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{a,s}|$ to $\delta_{rs}$, leaving $\sum_rK_{a,r}XK_{a,r}^*=I_a(X)$ by step 1.1. This proves the claimed formula.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$, $p\ge1$, of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** here is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{1\le a\le p,\,1\le r\le q_a}$ of endomorphisms of $H$, where each $q_a$ is a non-negative integer; its outcome operators and update maps are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a:\operatorname{End}(H)\to\operatorname{End}(H)$, $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$, with empty sums equal to zero. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

(d) *Non-determination.* Effects alone do not determine the update: there are two normalized instruments on $\mathbb C^2$ with the same outcome effects $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $F_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ whose updates differ on the same input.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: Suppose all $P_i$ commute with all $Q_j$. Then $G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$ is self-adjoint, since $(P_iQ_j)^*=Q_jP_i=P_iQ_j$, and is idempotent, since $(P_iQ_j)^2=P_i^2Q_j^2=P_iQ_j$. For any $x$, $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\langle G_{ij}x,G_{ij}x\rangle\ge0$, so each is positive; the sum identity makes each bounded above by $I_H$. Finite summation gives $\sum_{i,j}G_{ij}=(\sum_iP_i)(\sum_jQ_j)=I_H$, and the two marginal sums are $P_i$ and $Q_j$. So this family is a joint POVM.

Conversely, suppose a joint POVM $(G_{ij})$ exists. For each pair, $0\le G_{ij}\le P_i$ because $P_i-G_{ij}=\sum_{k\ne j}G_{ik}\ge0$, and similarly $0\le G_{ij}\le Q_j$. If $x\in\ker P_i$, then $0\le\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle\le\langle P_ix,x\rangle=0$. By [F2], $\langle G_{ij}x,x\rangle=\|G_{ij}^{1/2}x\|^2$, hence $G_{ij}x=0$ and $G_{ij}(I-P_i)=0$. Taking adjoints gives $(I-P_i)G_{ij}=0$, so $G_{ij}=P_iG_{ij}P_i$. The same argument yields $G_{ij}=Q_jG_{ij}Q_j$.

Using $P_i=\sum_kG_{ik}$ and $Q_j=\sum_\ell G_{\ell j}$, we obtain $P_iQ_j=\sum_kG_{ik}Q_j$. The support relation $G_{ik}=Q_kG_{ik}Q_k$ from step 1.2 makes every term with $k\ne j$ zero, and the $k=j$ term is $G_{ij}$. Therefore $P_iQ_j=G_{ij}$. Since $G_{ij}$ is self-adjoint, taking adjoints gives $Q_jP_i=G_{ij}=P_iQ_j$. This proves commutation and uniqueness.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires finite nonempty I,J, so I times J is nonempty. In step 1.2 a marginal remainder sum may be empty for a singleton index set and equals zero; in step 2.1 the excluded-index terms vanish. The zero-dimensional Hilbert space is also harmless: all effects and identity are zero.
Zero projections are permitted; the product construction in step 1.1 and support argument in step 1.2 still apply.
A one-outcome PVM has its sole projection equal to I_H, and the construction in step 1.1 gives the joint.
Zero projections and zero joint effects are covered by the support relations in steps 1.2–2.1.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; the following well-definedness lemma establishes that the trace pairing makes $S^*$ well-defined and that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$ span $\mathsf H_d$ over $\mathbb R$, and form $S$, $G=S^*S$, $G^+$, and $D_a$ as in the preceding finite-frame definition. If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)D_a.
$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

Let $n\ge1$, $p\in[0,1]$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n:\Omega\to\{0,1\}$ be measurable on a probability space with
$$\mathbb P(X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_n=x_n)=\prod_{k=1}^n b_p(x_k)\quad\text{for every }(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n.$$
Here $b_p(1)=p$ and $b_p(0)=1-p$, including $p=0$ and $p=1$. Thus the variables have the stated independent Bernoulli product law. For their frequency $f=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$ and every $t>0$,
$$
\mathbb P(|f-p|\ge t)\le2e^{-2nt^2}.
$$
No axiom of choice is assumed.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Input integers $d,m\ge1$, a finite POVM $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ on $\mathbb C^d$ that spans the real Hermitian matrices, and real frequencies $f_a\ge0$ with $\sum_af_a=1$. Form the Gram matrix $G_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$, compute its Moore–Penrose inverse $G^+$, set $D_a=\sum_b(G^+)_{ba}F_b$, and return
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m f_aD_a.
$$
All sums and matrices are finite. The output is Hermitian. The procedure does not project $X$ onto the positive cone, and it makes no positivity claim for finite frequency inputs.

$$
No axiom of choice is assumed.

It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

Let $d,e\ge1$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A finite completely positive instrument from $\mathbb C^d$ to $\mathbb C^e$ is a family of completely positive complex-linear maps $I_a:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$, indexed by $a\in\mathcal A$, whose sum is trace-preserving. Then there are an integer $q\ge1$, an isometry $V:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e\otimes\mathbb C^q$, and pairwise orthogonal projections $Q_a$ on $\mathbb C^q$ with $\sum_aQ_a=I_q$ such that, for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$,
$$
I_a(X)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left[(I_e\otimes Q_a)VXV^*(I_e\otimes Q_a)\right].
$$
Here $E=\mathbb C^q$ is the finite register space with its displayed orthonormal basis, and the partial trace is defined on its matrix units by $\operatorname{Tr}_E(Y\otimes|e_{a,r}\rangle\langle e_{b,s}|)=\delta_{(a,r),(b,s)}Y$, extended linearly. The register basis is indexed by the Kraus labels $(a,r)$; a zero outcome map has no labels and corresponds to $Q_a=0$.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

derivations.claim: Since $P_a^*=P_a=P_a^2$, the Lüders Kraus operators have $M^{L*}_aM^L_a=P_a$. For the other family, $M^{R*}_aM^R_a=(|a\rangle\langle+|)(|+\rangle\langle a|)=\langle+|+\rangle P_a=P_a$, since the displayed normalized vector satisfies $\langle+|+\rangle=1$. Thus both families are normalized, with the same outcome effects, because $P_0+P_1=I$.

By [F3], the one-operator Kraus forms give completely positive maps, and their sum is trace-preserving because the combined adjoint products sum to identity by step 1.1. Hence both are finite instruments in the sense of the A-page theorem, and each admits its stated outcome-register dilation by [F2].

On $\rho=P_0$, the Lüders update for outcome $0$ is $I^L_0(P_0)=P_0$, whereas the other update is $I^R_0(P_0)=|+\rangle\langle+|$. These matrices differ: $P_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $|+\rangle\langle+|=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$. The outcome probabilities are nevertheless identical, $\operatorname{Tr}(P_0P_0)=1$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(P_0P_1)=0$. This refutes the statement.

Let $d,m,n\ge1$, let $(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite POVM on $\mathbb C^d$ whose real span is $\mathsf H_d$, and let $\rho\in\mathsf H_d$ satisfy $\rho\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Put $p_a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_a)$, form the canonical dual $D_a$ from the Gram pseudoinverse, and write $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$ for $D c=\sum_ac_aD_a$. Let $X(f)=\sum_af_aD_a$ be the linear-inversion output and use the induced operator norm $\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}=\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\|Dc\|_{\mathrm{HS}}$.

Then exact probabilities reconstruct the state: $X(p)=\rho$. For every real frequency vector $f\in\mathbb R^m$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\|f-p\|_2.
$$
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,m\}$ be measurable with the independent product law $\mathbb P(Y_1=a_1,\ldots,Y_n=a_n)=\prod_kp_{a_k}$ for every outcome tuple. Define $f_a=n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{Y_k=a\}}$. Then for every $0<\delta<1$,
$$
\mathbb P\!\left(\max_{1\le a\le m}|f_a-p_a|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}\right)\ge1-\delta.
$$
Consequently, with probability at least $1-\delta$,
$$
\|X(f)-\rho\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\|D\|_{2\to\mathrm{HS}}\sqrt m\sqrt{\frac{\log(2m/\delta)}{2n}}.
$$
These are conditional mathematical statements under the specified product sampling law; no empirical data or calibrated apparatus is asserted.

Let $d,m\ge1$, let $F_1,\ldots,F_m\in\mathsf H_d$ span $\mathsf H_d$ over $\mathbb R$, and form $S$, $G=S^*S$, $G^+$, and $D_a$ as in the preceding finite-frame definition. If $G=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda P_\lambda$ is its finite spectral resolution, then $G^+=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda^{-1}P_\lambda$. Moreover, every $X\in\mathsf H_d$ is reconstructed by
$$
X=\sum_{a=1}^m\operatorname{Tr}(XF_a)D_a.
$$
This holds for redundant families as well as bases; $G$ need not be invertible.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; the following well-definedness lemma establishes that the trace pairing makes $S^*$ well-defined and that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $\sigma_j^2=I$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j)=0$, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, and $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$; reversing the order negates each mixed product. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_j\sigma_k)=2\delta_{jk}$. Since a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix has two real diagonal entries and one complex off-diagonal entry, $\dim_{\mathbb R}\mathsf H_2=4$; the four nonzero orthogonal matrices $I,\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z$ form a basis. Every trace-one Hermitian $\rho$ therefore has the stated form with $r_j=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\sigma_j)\in\mathbb R$. Positivity [A2] restricts $|r|\le1$, since $(r_x\sigma_x+r_y\sigma_y+r_z\sigma_z)^2=|r|^2I$ and the eigenvalues of $\rho$ are $(1\pm|r|)/2$.

Each $\sigma_j$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $1,-1$ by step 1.1, so $F_{j,\pm}$ has eigenvalues $1/3,0$ and is positive. For each $j$, $F_{j,+}+F_{j,-}=I/3$; summing over $x,y,z$ gives $I$. Also $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, so each $\sigma_j$ lies in the real span of the effects. Since $I$ is their sum, the basis in step 1.1 shows that the effects span $\mathsf H_2$.

In the coordinate order $(x+,x-,y+,y-,z+,z-)$, direct multiplication and step 1.1 give $G_{(j,s),(k,t)}=\frac1{36}\operatorname{Tr}((I+s\sigma_j)(I+t\sigma_k))=\frac1{18}(1+st\,\delta_{jk})$ for $s,t\in\{+1,-1\}$. Thus the diagonal entries are $1/9$, opposite outcomes on one axis have entry $0$, and distinct axes have entry $1/18$. Let $u=(1,1,1,1,1,1)$ and $v_j=e_{j+}-e_{j-}$. Then $Gu=u/3$, $Gv_j=v_j/9$, and $G$ vanishes on vectors $(s_x,s_x,s_y,s_y,s_z,s_z)$ with $s_x+s_y+s_z=0$. These mutually orthogonal subspaces have dimensions $1,3,2$ and span $\mathbb R^6$.

By [F2] and the eigenspaces in step 3.1, $G^+=3P_u+9\sum_jP_{v_j}$, where $P_u=uu^\mathsf T/6$ and $P_{v_j}=v_jv_j^\mathsf T/2$. The $e_{j+}$ column of $G^+$ is $u/2+9v_j/2$. Applying the canonical-dual formula [F3], using $\sum_{k,\pm}F_{k,\pm}=I$ and $F_{j,+}-F_{j,-}=\sigma_j/3$, gives $D_{j,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_j$; similarly $D_{j,-}=\frac12I-\frac32\sigma_j$. The probabilities are $p_{j,\pm}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F_{j,\pm})=(1\pm r_j)/6$, so $\sum_{j,\pm}p_{j,\pm}D_{j,\pm}=\frac12I+\frac12\sum_jr_j\sigma_j=\rho$, in agreement with [F1].

The frequency vector with $f_{x,+}=1$ and all other entries zero is nonnegative and sums to one. Its output is $D_{x,+}=\frac12I+\frac32\sigma_x$, whose eigenvalues are $2$ and $-1$. It is Hermitian but not positive, so the linear-inversion procedure does not preserve positivity for every frequency vector.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

citations.quote:
Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a family of finite quantum channels indexed by $t\geq0$, where “finite quantum channel” has the meaning in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. The family obeys the **semigroup law** when $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{M_d(\mathbb C)}$ and $\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s$ for every $s,t\geq0$.

The family is **CP-divisible** when for every $0\leq s\leq t$ there exists a finite quantum channel $V_{t,s}:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi_t=V_{t,s}\circ\Phi_s$. CP-divisibility is this specified factorization property; the definition does not assert that it is a universal meaning of “Markovian”.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: By [F3], choose an orthonormal environment eigenbasis $(|k\rangle)_{k=1}^m$ with $\eta=\sum_{k=1}^mp_k|k\rangle\langle k|$, $p_k\geq0$, and $\sum_kp_k=1$. Choose any system orthonormal basis $(|\alpha\rangle)_{\alpha=1}^d$ and use their ordered product basis. By [F2], this basis change leaves the finite partial trace in [F1] unchanged. For environment indices $j,k$ define the system matrix $K_{jk}$ by $(K_{jk})_{\alpha\beta}:=\sqrt{p_k}(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,k)}$. Expanding $X\otimes\eta$, conjugating by $U_t$, and applying the coordinate formula [F1] gives, entry by entry, $\Phi_t(X)=\sum_{j,k=1}^mK_{jk}XK_{jk}^*$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$.

For a two-qubit instance take $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, $g>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $H_{\mathrm{tot}}=\hbar g\,Z\otimes Z$ with $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, and $\eta=|+\rangle\langle+|$ where $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ in the chosen environment $Z$ eigenbasis. By [F3], the finite spectral exponential gives $U_t=e^{-igtZ\otimes Z}=\sum_{b=\pm1}V_b(t)\otimes|b\rangle\langle b|$, with $V_b(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ibgt},e^{ibgt})$. The partial trace in [F1] therefore gives $\Phi_t(X)=\frac12(V_{+1}(t)XV_{+1}(t)^*+V_{-1}(t)XV_{-1}(t)^*)$, so for $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\w&c\end{pmatrix}$ the diagonal entries are unchanged and the off-diagonal entries are multiplied by $\kappa(t)=\frac12(e^{-2igt}+e^{2igt})=\cos(2gt)$, using [F7], [F8], and [F9].

By [F10], choose $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ with $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=1$; hence $\theta>0$. Set $s=\theta/(2g)>0$. Euler's identity [F9] gives $e^{i\theta}=i$, and [F7]–[F8] give $e^{-i\theta}=(e^{i\theta})^{-1}=-i$. Applying [F8] again yields $\kappa(s)=0$ and $\kappa(2s)=\frac12(e^{-2i\theta}+e^{2i\theta})=-1$.

For system basis indices $\beta,\delta$, unitarity of $U_t$ gives $(\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk})_{\beta\delta}=\sum_{k=1}^mp_k\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{\alpha=1}^d\overline{(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,k)}}(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\delta,k)}=\sum_kp_k\delta_{\beta\delta}=\delta_{\beta\delta}$. Thus $\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk}=I_d$, so [F5] makes the Kraus map in step 1.1 completely positive and trace-preserving; by [F4], $\Phi_t$ is a finite channel.

Let $X_{\!P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\rho_\pm=(I\pm X_{\!P})/2$. Since $X_{\!P}=X_{\!P}^*$ and $X_{\!P}^2=I$, each $\rho_\pm$ is a projection; since $\operatorname{Tr}X_{\!P}=0$, each has trace one. Steps 1.2 and 1.3 give $\Phi_s(\rho_+)=\Phi_s(\rho_-)=I/2$, while $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)=\rho_-$ and $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_-)=\rho_+$. Consequently $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)\ne\Phi_s(\Phi_s(\rho_+))=I/2$, so the semigroup law in [F6] fails. If a channel $V_{2s,s}$ satisfied $\Phi_{2s}=V_{2s,s}\circ\Phi_s$, it would send the equal matrices $\Phi_s(\rho_+)$ and $\Phi_s(\rho_-)$ to equal outputs, contradicting the two distinct outputs at $2s$. By step 2.1, the family consists of channels, so this contradiction proves it is not CP-divisible by [F6].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Direct multiplication in [F1] gives $\mathcal L(E_{00})=0$, $\mathcal L(E_{11})=\gamma(E_{00}-E_{11})$, $\mathcal L(E_{01})=(i\omega-\gamma/2)E_{01}$, and $\mathcal L(E_{10})=(-i\omega-\gamma/2)E_{10}$.

The matrix space is finite-dimensional and complete by [F2]. The trace-ideal estimate [F4] applied to the finitely many left and right multiplications in [F1] bounds $\|\mathcal L(X)\|_1$ by a finite constant times $\|X\|_1$, so $\mathcal L$ is bounded; [F2] therefore gives $e^{t\mathcal L}=\sum_{n\geq0}t^n\mathcal L^n/n!$. Put $D=E_{00}-E_{11}$. Step 1.1 gives $\mathcal L(D)=-\gamma D$ and $\mathcal L(E_{11})=\gamma D$; induction therefore gives $\mathcal L^n(E_{11})=\gamma(-\gamma)^{n-1}D$ for $n\geq1$. Applying these four identities linearly to $\rho(0)=\sum_{j,k}\rho_{jk}(0)E_{jk}$ gives all four formulas in the Statement.

By [F5] and [F6], the full evolution map is completely positive and trace-preserving for $t\geq0$, so it carries each initial density matrix to a density matrix. These formulas are deductions within the selected approximation and assert no microscopic bath limit.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first.
