citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge0$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and use the symplectic
form $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$ on $\mathbb R^{2n}$. On
$L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ define

$$\big(S_\lambda(q,p,t)f\big)(x) =e^{i\lambda t+i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q).$$
Then $S_\lambda$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation of [[def-heisenberg-group-of-a-symplectic-vector-space]], has central character $t\mapsto e^{i\lambda t}$, and its Weyl operators form an irreducible regular Weyl system with phase $e^{-i\lambda\omega/2}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real
symplectic vector space of dimension $2n$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ be
nonzero, and let $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ be a nonzero irreducible regular
Weyl system with

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w).$$
Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, so there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of irreducible regular Weyl systems with the fixed parameter $\lambda$. In a symplectic basis the model is
$$\big(W_\lambda(q,p)f\big)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q),$$
for $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. The statement assumes finite-dimensional phase space, irreducibility, strong continuity, and a fixed nonzero central parameter. It makes no claim about algebraic modules, nonregular representations, $\lambda=0$, or infinitely many modes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

derivations.claim:
On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, multiplication by real $x_j$ is symmetric. If $g$
lies in its adjoint domain with adjoint value $h$, testing against compactly
supported functions on each box where $x_j$ is bounded gives $h=x_jg$ almost
everywhere there; the boxes exhaust $\mathbb R^r$, so $x_jg\in L^2$ and the
adjoint domain is exactly $D(M_{x_j})$. Thus $M_{x_j}$ is self-adjoint. Let
$Dg(k):=(2\pi)^{-r/2}g(k/(2\pi))$. The $L^1$ Fourier definition in [F2] gives,
for $f\in\mathcal S$, $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f=D\mathcal F_{2\pi}f$ by
substitution in the defining integrals. For every $g\in L^2$, [F2] and the
change-of-variables formula in [F2] give
$$\|Dg\|_2^2=(2\pi)^{-r}\int|g(k/(2\pi))|^2\,dk=\int|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi,$$
so $D$ is an isometry; its inverse is $D^{-1}h(\xi)=(2\pi)^{r/2}h(2\pi\xi)$,
so it is unitary. For Schwartz seminorms
$p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)=\sup_k|k^\alpha\partial^\beta g(k)|$,
$$p_{\alpha,\beta}(Dg)=(2\pi)^{|\alpha|-|\beta|-r/2}p_{\alpha,\beta}(g),$$
and the corresponding inverse formula has finite reciprocal factors. Hence
$D$ and $D^{-1}$ are continuous on Schwartz space. Together with [F2] this
proves that $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$ is unitary on $L^2$ and a topological
automorphism of Schwartz space. Conjugating $M_{k_j}$ by it defines the
self-adjoint operator $-i\partial_{x_j}$; on Schwartz functions the kernel
formula and integration by parts give
$\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}(-i\partial_{x_j}f)=k_j\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f$.
Schwartz functions are a core for multiplication: truncate by smooth compact
cutoffs and then mollify on the resulting bounded support; dominated
convergence controls $f$ and $x_jf$, and boundedness of $x_j$ on that support
controls the mollification error. Fourier invariance of Schwartz space gives
the same core assertion for the derivative. Conjugation by $\mathcal U$
therefore defines the stated self-adjoint quadratures and common core.

On that core, [F1] gives $Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*)$ and
$P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$. The creation and annihilation CCR in
[F1] imply the displayed quadrature commutators by bilinearity; all products are defined on
the finite Hermite span. Direct multiplication of the formula for $W$ gives
the phase $e^{-i\hbar(q\cdot p'-p\cdot q')/2}$, which is
$e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}$ in interleaved notation. Its strong continuity and
irreducibility follow from [F3] after the parameter-preserving change
$(q_0,p_0)=(-\sqrt\hbar p,q/\sqrt\hbar)$ in the root Schrödinger formula.
The real symplectic form is unchanged by that map and the central parameter
is $\hbar\ne0$. Applying [F5] proves the representation-equivalence clause
with precisely its hypotheses.

The positive trace-class spectral expansion in [F6] has weights summing
to one. For any eigenvalue $w>0$, changing the orthonormal basis of its
eigenspace changes the sum of squared norms $\sum\|R_j\psi\|^2$ by a unitary
finite-dimensional change of basis when the eigenspace is finite-dimensional;
positive trace-class compactness makes each nonzero eigenspace finite
dimensional. The same basis invariance holds for the sesquilinear cross sum
by polarization, and the zero eigenspace contributes nothing. Cauchy–Schwarz
then gives absolute convergence of each first-moment series and of each
cross-moment series under the stated second-moment bound. Thus the definitions
of $d,V$ are finite and basis independent; taking the real part makes
$V_{jk}=V_{kj}\in\mathbb R$. Finally, every finite-dimensional cutoff of
Fock space has finite matrix dimension, and for square matrices $A,B$,
$\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$ by expanding the diagonal entries, whereas the
identity has positive trace. Hence a finite cutoff cannot satisfy the exact
CCR $[Q_j,P_j]=i\hbar I$.

The formula for $W$ is a unitary composition of translation and a
modulus-one multiplier; its inverse is $W(-q,-p)$. Direct substitution gives
$$W(q,p)W(q',p')=e^{-i\hbar(q\cdot p'-p\cdot q')/2}W(q+q',p+p').$$
For a real symmetric $X$, the chirp
$$[C_Xf](x)=e^{ix^TXx/2}f(x)$$
is unitary, and substitution in the Weyl formula gives
$C_X^*W(q,p)C_X=W(q+Xp,p)$, the upper shear. For invertible real $A$,
$$[D_Af](x)=|\det A|^{1/2}f(Ax)$$
is unitary by [F5] applied to the diffeomorphism $x\mapsto Ax$ and the
integrable function $|f|^2$; direct
substitution gives
$D_A^*W(q,p)D_A=W(A^{-T}q,Ap)$, an invertible coordinate change.

Let $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$ be the exact angular-frequency unitary of
[F3]. Substitution into the Fourier integral on Schwartz functions gives
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}W(q,p)f](k)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,p\cdot(k-\sqrt\hbar q/2)}[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k-\sqrt\hbar q),$$
which is exactly $[W(p,-q)\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)$. Both sides are
bounded operators, and Schwartz functions are dense, so this identity holds
on all of $L^2$. Applying it to selected coordinates gives partial Fourier
rotations. Conjugating an upper shear by the full or partial
Fourier rotation gives every lower shear, since the matrix identity is
$\begin{pmatrix}0&-I\\I&0\end{pmatrix}
U_X\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}=L_{-X}$.
Thus each generator and inverse in [F2] has a unitary Weyl implementer.

Each generator unitary maps Schwartz space onto itself: this follows from
the product rule for the smooth quadratic chirp, the chain rule for an
invertible linear coordinate change, and Fourier invariance of Schwartz
space. On any connected parameter neighborhood on which $A$ remains
invertible, the chirp and coordinate formulas vary continuously in every
Schwartz seminorm; the Fourier factor is fixed. If
$G_1^*W(z)G_1=W(T_1z)$ and $G_2^*W(z)G_2=W(T_2z)$, then
$(G_1G_2)^*W(z)(G_1G_2)=W(T_2T_1z)$. Therefore, for any finite factorization
$T=T_k\cdots T_1$ supplied by [F2], multiplying the corresponding generator
unitaries in the order $G_1\cdots G_k$ gives a unitary $M_T$ with
$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)$ for every label $z$. This proves existence and does not
invoke a general metaplectic existence theorem.

Suppose $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $T$. Then
$X=M_2M_1^*$ commutes with every $W(z)$ by applying their two covariance
identities. Since the Weyl system is irreducible by [F1], every spectral
projection of either bounded self-adjoint operator
$\operatorname{Re}X=(X+X^*)/2$ and
$\operatorname{Im}X=(X-X^*)/(2i)$ commutes with every $W(z)$ and has invariant
range. Irreducibility forces each such projection to be $0$ or $I$. The
spectral measure in [F4] then implies each self-adjoint part is scalar: if a
bounded self-adjoint operator had two distinct spectral values, disjoint
neighborhoods of those values would yield a nonzero proper spectral
projection. Hence $X=\lambda I$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$; since $X$ is
unitary, $|\lambda|=1$. Thus $M_1,M_2$ differ only by a phase.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain. Fix the
angular-frequency Fourier unitary by
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int_{\mathbb R^r}e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\quad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)),$$
and define $-i\partial_{x_j}:=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}M_{k_j}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$, where $M_{k_j}$ is multiplication by $k_j$ on its maximal domain. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, for $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$,
define the Weyl unitaries in grouped label order $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^r\oplus
\mathbb R^r$ by
$$[W(q,p)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
For $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, every
$T\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ has a unitary $M_T$ such that
$$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$
Any two such unitaries differ by a scalar of modulus one. The covariance
identity holds on all of $L^2$; the corresponding unbounded quadrature
identities hold on the common transported Schwartz domain. This is an
individual existence and phase-uniqueness result; it does not identify the
global topology or kernel of a continuously chosen implementer family.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $a\le b$ and $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]). The function $f$ is
**absolutely continuous** on $[a,b]$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$\delta>0$ such that every finite family of subintervals
$[u_j,v_j]\subseteq[a,b]$, indexed by $j<m$, whose open interiors are pairwise
disjoint and which satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}(v_j-u_j)<\delta$$

also satisfies

$$\sum_{j<m}|f(v_j)-f(u_j)|<\varepsilon.$$

Finite sums and the empty sum are those of [[def-finite-sum]] and
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. For $m=0$ both sums are $0$, so the condition is
automatic. On $[a,a]$ every permitted interval is a singleton and every endpoint
increment is $0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), so every function on that singleton is
absolutely continuous. Absolute continuity implies ordinary continuity
([[def-continuity-real]]); that implication is proved next rather than built into
the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Fix a measurable integrable representative, also denoted by $f$, if $L^1([a,b])$ is interpreted as a space of almost-everywhere equivalence classes. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then there is a measurable set $E\subseteq(a,b)$ whose complement in $(a,b)$ has Lebesgue measure zero such that $F$ is differentiable at every $x\in E$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)\qquad(x\in E).$$
The primitive $F$ is independent of the chosen representative; the almost-everywhere derivative identity holds for every fixed measurable integrable representative.

derivations.claim: Put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$. For $f\in\mathcal S$, the $L^1$ definitions give the exact dilation identity $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f(k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}(\mathcal F_{2\pi}f)(k/(2\pi))$. The change-of-variables formula with $k=2\pi\xi$ proves this dilation is unitary on $L^2$; differentiating its argument shows $p_{\alpha,\beta}(Dg)=(2\pi)^{|\alpha|-|\beta|-r/2}p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)$, and the inverse dilation has the reciprocal seminorm factors, so it is a Schwartz automorphism. Integration by parts in the angular kernel gives $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}(-i\partial_{x_j}f)=k_j\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f$. Thus the angular transform is precisely the required unitary, derivative and Schwartz-space consequence of the imported $2\pi$ transform, rather than a differently normalized Plancherel claim. Near the identity the block $A$ is invertible with positive determinant. For the factorization in [F2] define $C_Yf(x)=e^{ix^TYx/2}f(x)$, $E_Af(x)=(\det A)^{-1/2}f(A^{-1}x)$ and $T_X=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}e^{-ik^TXk/2}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$. Each is unitary by change of variables or [F4]. The product rule and linear change of variables show that each factor and its inverse act continuously on Schwartz space and depend smoothly on their parameters there. For example every derivative of a chirp is a polynomial times the same chirp, giving bounds by finitely many Schwartz seminorms, uniformly on compact parameter sets; differentiation in a parameter inserts only another polynomial or a first-order differential operator. The same argument applies in Fourier coordinates to $T_X$ by [F4]. Direct differentiation or substitution gives $C_Y^*R_gC_Y=L_YR_g$, $E_A^*R_gE_A=D_AR_g$, and $T_X^*R_gT_X=U_XR_g$. The same substitutions in the explicit Weyl formula give covariance on all $L^2$. Thus $L(S):=C_YE_AT_X$ is a smooth local unitary Schwartz lift of $S$, with $L(I)=I$. Shrink the neighborhood so $A$ is sufficiently close to $I$; then replacing $(Y,A,X)$ by $(\tau Y,I+\tau(A-I),\tau X)$, $0\le\tau\le1$, gives a smooth operator path from $I$ to $L(S)$ within these formulas.

Along an absolutely continuous local parameter path the three logarithmic generators $i\hbar\dot C_YC_Y^{-1}$, $i\hbar\dot E_AE_A^{-1}$ and $i\hbar\dot T_XT_X^{-1}$ are respectively $-\hbar x^T\dot Yx/2$, $-i\hbar((\dot AA^{-1}x)\cdot\partial_x+\operatorname{tr}(\dot AA^{-1})/2)$ and $\hbar p^T\dot Xp/2$. These identities hold almost everywhere by finite-dimensional differentiation at the points where the parameters have derivatives. The half-trace in the middle expression is exactly the symmetric ordering of the mixed position-momentum term. Product differentiation conjugates and adds these expressions. The covariance from step 1.1 replaces each quadrature by a real linear combination, so a symmetrically ordered homogeneous quadratic stays exactly such a quadratic, with no extra scalar. If its coefficient matrix is $K_L$, differentiating the covariance and using $[R_j,R_k]=i\hbar(J_0)_{jk}$ gives $\dot S=J_0K_LS$, hence $K_L=-J_0\dot SS^{-1}$. Equality of the quadratic coefficients is literal: the coefficients of second derivatives, of $x_j\partial_k$, and of $x_jx_k$ determine the three real blocks, including the symmetric-order half-trace.

Put $V(t)=J_0K(t)$ and $m(t)=\int_0^t\|V(s)\|\,ds$. The iterated-integral series for the matrix equation has $n$th term bounded by $m(t)^n/n!$: the scalar product integrand is symmetric in its $n$ variables and the ordered simplex is one of the $n!$ equal regions of their product cube, up to null diagonals. Thus the series converges uniformly, with sum bounded by $e^{m(T)}$. It satisfies $S(t)=I+\int_0^tV(s)S(s)\,ds$, since the series under that integral is dominated by $\|V(s)\|e^{m(T)}$. For any integrable scalar $f$, choose $M$ with $\int_{|f|>M}|f|<\varepsilon/2$; then $\int_E|f|\le M\lambda(E)+\varepsilon/2$, proving absolute continuity of its primitive by the finite disjoint-interval definition. Applied entrywise to the integral equation, this proves absolute continuity of $S$, and [F6] gives $\dot S=VS$ almost everywhere. If two solutions have the same initial value, their continuous difference obeys $\Delta(t)=\int_0^tV(s)\Delta(s)\,ds$. Iterating this equation $n$ times gives $\|\Delta(t)\|\le\sup_s\|\Delta(s)\|m(T)^n/n!$, which tends to zero. This proves uniqueness of the classical absolutely continuous solution. Product differentiation gives $(S^TJ_0S)'=0$ almost everywhere, so [F5] and its initial value give symplecticity at every time. A finite subdivision, using uniform continuity and invertibility of $S$, makes each $S(t)S(t_j)^{-1}$ lie in the neighborhood of step 1.1. Set $U(t)=L(S(t)S(t_j)^{-1})U(t_j)$, with $U(0)=I$. To justify the Schwartz calculus, restrict each parameter path to a small compact neighborhood where the local factors are smooth. The seminorm estimates of step 1.1, also for their parameter derivatives, imply $p((L(\alpha)-L(\beta))f)\le C_{p,q}|\alpha-\beta|q(f)$ there and $p(\partial_t L(\alpha(t))f)\le C_{p,q}|\alpha'(t)|q(f)$ almost everywhere, for some Schwartz seminorm $q$. One can obtain the first bound by integrating along the straight parameter segment inside that neighborhood; finite smaller neighborhoods suffice. Matrix inversion and the local factor parameters have bounded derivatives on those sets, and $|S'|\le e^{m(T)}\|V\|$ is integrable. A finite-dimensional smooth map with bounded derivative on the small convex parameter neighborhood is Lipschitz there, hence takes an absolutely continuous parameter curve to an absolutely continuous curve; at points of differentiability of that curve, its differentiability gives the chain rule directly. The same derivative estimate in each seminorm proves this assertion for the explicit Schwartz-valued factors. Products are covered by the two-variable version of those bounds. Thus these estimates prove absolute continuity in every seminorm, the chain and product rules almost everywhere, and the same assertions for the inverse factors. Step 2.1 therefore gives $i\hbar\dot U=H_KU$ almost everywhere, with continuous matching at joins and covariance from step 1.1. If two such evolutions have the same initial vector, their difference $w(t)$ is absolutely continuous in $L^2$ and satisfies the same equation. Its squared norm is absolutely continuous and has derivative $2\operatorname{Re}\langle-iH_Kw/\hbar,w\rangle=0$ almost everywhere, because the real symmetrically ordered expression is symmetric on Schwartz space by integration by parts. By [F5] the difference remains zero. Density and unitarity extend uniqueness to all $L^2$. Thus existence, uniqueness, inverse continuity and covariance hold for the full integrable coefficient class in the Statement.

Write $K=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b^T&d\end{pmatrix}$ with $a,d$ real symmetric, and $S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$. Set $F=A+iB$ and $G=C+iD$. The symplectic block relations give $F^*G-G^*F=2iI$ and $F^TG=G^TF$. If $Fv=0$, multiplying the first identity by $v^*$ and $v$ forces $\|v\|^2=0$; thus $F$ is invertible at every time, even at a singular generating chart. Consequently $Z:=GF^{-1}$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{Im}Z=(Z-Z^*)/(2i)=F^{-*}F^{-1}>0$. The classical equation gives $\dot F=(b^T+dZ)F$ and $\dot Z=-a-bZ-Zb^T-ZdZ$, with $F(0)=I$ and $Z(0)=iI$.

Let $c(0)=1$ and $\dot c/c=-\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(b+dZ)$, defining $c$ by the exponential of the indefinite integral of this $L^1$ coefficient; it is integrable because $b,d$ are integrable and $Z$ is continuous and bounded on the compact time interval. By the primitive estimate in step 3.1, [F6] and the smooth chain rule on the bounded range of this integral, $c$ is absolutely continuous and satisfies that equation almost everywhere. It never vanishes. Define $g(t,x)=\pi^{-r/4}c(t)\exp(ix^TZ(t)x/2)$. Positive definiteness of $\operatorname{Im}Z$ makes $g$ Schwartz. On the compact time interval $\operatorname{Im}Z$ has a uniform positive lower eigenvalue. Every parameter derivative of this Gaussian is a polynomial times a Gaussian, so the same seminorm estimates as in step 3.1 make $g$ absolutely continuous in each Schwartz seminorm and justify the almost-everywhere derivatives below. In these dimensionless coordinates $H_K/\hbar=\tfrac12(x^Tax+x^Tbp+p^Tb^Tx+p^Tdp)$. Applying this differential expression to $g$ gives $H_Kg/\hbar=\bigl(x^T(a+bZ+Zb^T+ZdZ)x/2-i\operatorname{tr}(b+dZ)/2\bigr)g$. Steps 4.1 and the equation for $c$ identify this with $i\partial_tg$. As $g(0)=g_0:=\pi^{-r/4}e^{-|x|^2/2}$, the uniqueness in step 3.1 gives $U(t)g_0=g(t)$. No physical-coordinate factor of $\hbar$ is missing: both the Schrödinger equation and the quadratic contain that common factor.

Differentiating the determinant by its finite polynomial formula gives $(\det F)'=(\det F)\operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}\dot F)$. Since the trace of $b^T$ equals the trace of $b$, steps 4.1 and 5.1 give $(c^2\det F)'=0$ almost everywhere. Put $h:=c^2\det F=u+iv$ with real and imaginary parts $u,v$. The entries of $F$ and $c$ are absolutely continuous and bounded on $[0,T]$, so their finite polynomial products $h,u,v$ are absolutely continuous. On the full-measure set where the displayed derivative identity holds and $h$ is differentiable, $h'=0$ implies $u'=v'=0$; hence both real derivatives vanish almost everywhere. By the real-valued theorem [F5], $u$ and $v$ are constant on $[0,T]$. Since $h(0)=1$, $h(t)=1$ for every $t$, including all subdivision joins. It uses neither a choice of a global square root nor a real generating-chart denominator.

For the two endpoint propagators of the Statement, step 3.1 supplies the same Weyl covariance at their common $S$. By [F3], $U_2=\lambda U_1$ with $|\lambda|=1$. Step 4.1 gives the same endpoint $Z$ for both Gaussian vectors, and step 6.1 gives $c_2^2=c_1^2=1/\det(A+iB)$. Since $c_1\ne0$, $\lambda=c_2/c_1$ and $\lambda^2=1$, so $U_2=\pm U_1$. This proves the required invertible-$B$ claim and in fact the same phase conclusion at every endpoint. Multiplying both unitaries by any fixed normalized quadratic propagator preserves their relative sign, proving the final clause.

boundaries.evidence: Statement fixes r>=1 and supplies two normalized evolutions on compact intervals with the same endpoint. Step 7.1 compares their nonzero Gaussian scalar factors; the mode and comparison carriers are nonempty.

Steps 3.1 through 6.1 internally allow K=0, giving S=I, Z=iI and c=1; that endpoint has B=0 and is outside the Statement's invertible-B terminal chart. Step 4.1 nevertheless proves A+iB invertible throughout the path, so all actual determinant divisions in steps 5.1 through 7.1 are valid. No false K=0 witness for the terminal chart is asserted.
For r=1, steps 4.1–7.1 give the scalar identity c^2(A+iB)=1 and hence the same two possible phases; the determinant calculation does not require multiple modes.

Although the Statement requests det B nonzero, step 4.1 proves A+iB invertible even when either real block is singular; the sign calculation therefore does not divide by a singular real generating block.
Step 3.1 constructs continuous absolutely continuous paths from the identity, step 6.1 extends the determinant identity to every time by scalar FTC, and step 7.1 compares the common endpoint.

Statement explicitly inherits AC from the finite-mode definition. Facts F4–F6 invoke the pinned Fourier and absolutely continuous calculus with their CC/DC hypotheses, consequences of that same AC; finite subdivision adds no stronger choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(V,\omega)$ be a finite-dimensional real
symplectic vector space of dimension $2n$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ be
nonzero, and let $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ be a nonzero irreducible regular
Weyl system with

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w).$$
Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent to the Schrödinger Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, so there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of irreducible regular Weyl systems with the fixed parameter $\lambda$. In a symplectic basis the model is
$$\big(W_\lambda(q,p)f\big)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q),$$
for $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. The statement assumes finite-dimensional phase space, irreducibility, strong continuity, and a fixed nonzero central parameter. It makes no claim about algebraic modules, nonregular representations, $\lambda=0$, or infinitely many modes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, let $(V,\omega)$ be a real vector space of dimension $2n$ with a nondegenerate alternating bilinear form, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A unitary operator on $\mathcal H$ means a bijective complex-linear isometry. Suppose $W:V\to U(\mathcal H)$ satisfies $W(0)=I$ and

$$W(v)W(w)=e^{-i\lambda\omega(v,w)/2}W(v+w)\qquad(v,w\in V),$$

is regular in the sense that $t\mapsto W(tv)\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $v\in V$ and $\xi\in\mathcal H$, and is irreducible in the sense that its only closed invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$. Choose a symplectic basis identifying $(V,\omega)$ with $\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ and $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. Then $W$ is unitarily equivalent, meaning that there is a unitary map $U:\mathcal H\to L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ intertwining the two Weyl actions, to the Schrödinger system

$$\bigl(W_\lambda(q,p)f\bigr)(x)=e^{i\lambda p\cdot(x-q/2)}f(x-q)$$

on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$. Consequently, there is exactly one unitary-equivalence class of nonzero irreducible regular Weyl systems with this fixed finite-dimensional phase space and parameter. No conclusion is asserted for infinite-dimensional phase spaces, nonregular systems, or zero central parameter.

Let $r\ge1$, $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$, and
$$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)=\{S\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R):S^TJ_0S=J_0\}.$$
Every $S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is a finite product of matrices
of the following three types and their inverses:
$$U_X=\begin{pmatrix}I&X\\0&I\end{pmatrix},\quad L_Y=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\Y&I\end{pmatrix},\quad D_A=\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\0&A^{-T}\end{pmatrix},$$
where $X,Y$ are real symmetric and $A$ is real invertible. Partial Fourier
rotations, which act by $(q_j,p_j)\mapsto(-p_j,q_j)$ on any selected set of
coordinates and fix the others, are also products of these matrices.
In addition, for every $S$ there is a product $G$ of these generators such
that the upper-left block of $SG$ is invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$, for $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$,
define the Weyl unitaries in grouped label order $(q,p)\in\mathbb R^r\oplus
\mathbb R^r$ by
$$[W(q,p)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
For $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, every
$T\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ has a unitary $M_T$ such that
$$M_T^*W(z)M_T=W(Tz)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}).$$
Any two such unitaries differ by a scalar of modulus one. The covariance
identity holds on all of $L^2$; the corresponding unbounded quadrature
identities hold on the common transported Schwartz domain. This is an
individual existence and phase-uniqueness result; it does not identify the
global topology or kernel of a continuously chosen implementer family.

Use the finite-mode conventions, including their Axiom of Choice assumption, of the finite-mode symplectic-data definition. Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and put $J_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix}$. In grouped order $(q,p)$, write
$$S=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R),\qquad A,B,C,D\in M_r(\mathbb R),\qquad S^TJ_0S=J_0,$$
and assume its upper-right block $B$ is invertible. Define
$$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T.$$
Fix a compact interval $I=[0,T]$ with $T>0$. For each $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $K_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ have Lebesgue-integrable entries in grouped order and satisfy $K_j(t)=K_j(t)^T$ for every $t$. Let $S_j:I\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ be absolutely continuous with $S_j(0)=I_{2r}$, $\dot S_j(t)=J_0K_j(t)S_j(t)$ almost everywhere, and $S_j(T)=S$. Define the real symmetrically ordered quadratic operator on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ by
$$H_{j,t}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}(K_j)_{ab}(t)((R_g)_a(R_g)_b+(R_g)_b(R_g)_a),$$
with no linear or scalar term. Assume $U_j:I\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ is a path of unitary Schwartz automorphisms with $U_j(0)=I$ such that, for each $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$, the path $t\mapsto U_j(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in every Schwartz seminorm and satisfies
$$i\hbar\,\partial_tU_j(t)f=H_{j,t}U_j(t)f$$
almost everywhere. Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism is a unitary on $L^2$ whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of $\mathcal S$ with continuous inverse, and the Schwartz seminorms are $p_{\alpha,\beta}(f)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$ for multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$. Absolute continuity of each trajectory means the usual finite disjoint-interval condition for its increments in every seminorm. These hypotheses include piecewise-smooth Hamiltonian paths.
Then
$$U_2=U_1\quad\text{or}\quad U_2=-U_1.$$
The same conclusion holds after multiplying both propagators by a fixed
normalized quadratic propagator, provided the resulting endpoint lies in a
chart with invertible upper-right block.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

derivations.claim: Reorder interleaved coordinates by the fixed permutation $P(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$, and write $R_g:=PR$ and $W_g(w)=W(P^Tw)$ for grouped labels. Then $J_0=PJP^T$ and $S_g=PSP^T$ obeys $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$. Apply [F3] directly to the grouped Weyl system on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ with label matrix $S_g^T$; this matrix is symplectic because $S_g^TJ_0S_g=J_0$ also implies $S_gJ_0S_g^T=J_0$. Since $S_g^TP=PS^T$, converting labels back gives $$M_S^*W(z)M_S=M_S^*W_g(Pz)M_S=W_g(S_g^TPz)=W(S^Tz).$$ Differentiating the bounded one-parameter Weyl identity on the common Schwartz core gives $M_S^*RM_S=SR$. For the rest of the proof abbreviate $R_g$ to $R$ and $S_g$ to $S$, so $R$, $K$, and $J_0$ all use grouped order.

Use exactly the endpoint definition and trajectory class in the Statement, on arbitrary compact intervals $[0,T]$ with $T>0$. Reordering by the fixed permutation of step 1.1 sends $K$ to $PKP^T$ and preserves entrywise integrability, reality and symmetry, so [F4] constructs and uniquely determines these evolutions in grouped order with $H_t=\tfrac14\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}(t)(R_jR_k+R_kR_j)$ and no linear or scalar term. The operator acts on the common Schwartz space, and each trajectory is absolutely continuous in every seminorm and solves the equation almost everywhere. Concatenation gives products: first evolve by $U_2$ on $[0,T_2]$, then evolve by $U_1$ on $[0,T_1]$ with initial vector $U_2(T_2)f$, obtaining endpoint $U_1(T_1)U_2(T_2)$. The concatenated coefficient is integrable and symmetric on $[0,T_2+T_1]$, and the two absolutely continuous trajectories match at the join. The reversed evolution $U(T-t)U(T)^{-1}$ starts at $I$, ends at $U(T)^{-1}$, and is generated almost everywhere by $-H_{T-t}$, whose symmetric coefficient is again integrable. Thus inverses also belong to the set. By [F4], each endpoint implements the symplectic solution $\dot S=J_0K(t)S$. If two matrices had the same implementing unitary, differentiating their Weyl covariances on Schwartz space would give $(S-S')R=0$. Applied to the vacuum, $Q_kg_0=\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ and $P_kg_0=i\sqrt{\hbar/2}g_{e_k}$ by [F6]; the reality of the rows forces both their position and momentum coefficients to vanish. Thus the endpoint is unique. For two lifts, $\pi(M_1M_2)=\pi(M_1)\pi(M_2)$ by conjugating the quadratures, so $\pi$ is a homomorphism.

If $M_1,M_2$ implement the same $S$, then [F3] makes $M_2M_1^*=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. For any other representation $W'$ in [F1], choose a unitary $V$ with $VW'(z)V^*=W(z)$ by the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem. Then $M'_S=V^*M_SV$ is unitary and $$M_S'^*W'(z)M'_S=V^*M_S^*W(z)M_SV=W'(S^Tz).$$ Conjugating the phase-uniqueness statement by $V$ proves the same result in that representation.

Every generator from [F2] is a path endpoint of a homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonian. A symmetric shear is joined to the identity by scaling its symmetric block, and a partial Fourier rotation is joined by varying the oscillator angle. If $\det A>0$, polar decomposition writes $A=OP$ with $O\in SO(r)$ and $P$ positive definite. The path $P_t=(1-t)I+tP$ stays positive definite, and an orthogonal matrix in $SO(r)$ is a product of plane rotations, each joined to the identity by varying its angle. These paths connect the coordinate change to the identity. If $\det A<0$, factor one coordinate reflection from a positive-determinant change; that reflection is a $\pi$ oscillator rotation on that mode. This gives a piecewise-smooth symplectic path for each generator. Along any such path $S_t$, the matrix $X_t=\dot S_tS_t^{-1}$ satisfies $X_t^TJ_0+J_0X_t=0$; hence $K_t=-J_0X_t$ is symmetric and $\dot S_t=J_0K_tS_t$. The symmetrically ordered quadratic with matrix $K_t$ therefore has this classical endpoint. Thus [F2] supplies, for every $S$, a product of normalized quadratic propagators whose endpoint is $S$, proving $\pi$ is onto. The one-parameter paths also show that each such product belongs to the identity component of $\operatorname{Mp}$.

If two normalized lifts lie over the same grouped matrix $S$, the Gaussian determinant calculation in [F5] makes them differ by sign. This already holds for every $S$: the matrix $A+iB$ used there is invertible by symplecticity, including when either real block is singular. In particular it supplies the required invertible-$B$ chart argument without an imported Maslov-index parity formula. Thus every fiber has at most two elements.

The identity has two distinct lifts. The constant zero Hamiltonian gives $I$. On the first mode (and as the identity on the other modes if $r>1$), take the canonical Schwartz evolution of $H=\hbar(N+1/2)$ constructed in [F4]. For each Hermite vector, $e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$ solves the same Schrödinger equation with that initial vector, so uniqueness in [F4] identifies $U(t)|n\rangle=e^{-it(n+1/2)}|n\rangle$. Its classical endpoint is the identity at $t=2\pi$, because its Hamilton equations are $\dot Q=P$, $\dot P=-Q$ and make one full rotation, while by [F6] $$U(2\pi)|n\rangle=e^{-2\pi i(n+1/2)}|n\rangle=-|n\rangle$$ for every $n$. Completeness of the Hermite basis gives $U(2\pi)=-I$. For any $S$, choose a normalized lift $\widetilde M_S$ supplied by step 3.1. Then $\widetilde M_S$ and $-\widetilde M_S$ are two distinct lifts; step 3.2 proves there are no others. The kernel is exactly $\{I,-I\}$.

Fix $S_0$ and a normalized lift $M_0$. On a matrix neighborhood $\mathcal B$ of $S_0$ small enough that $SS_0^{-1}$ lies in the local neighborhood of [F4], put $\sigma(S)=L(SS_0^{-1})M_0$. The parameter path $(Y,A,X)\mapsto(\tau Y,I+\tau(A-I),\tau X)$ in [F4] joins each local factor lift to $I$ smoothly, with homogeneous quadratic logarithmic generator. Thus the local factors are endpoints of the piecewise-smooth subclass of the integrable class defining this group, so $\sigma(S)$ belongs to $\operatorname{Mp}$ and has endpoint $S$. Conversely the construction of [F4] writes any integrable-coefficient propagator endpoint as a finite product of these same local lifts. Hence allowing the broader integrable temporal class in the parity lemma introduces no additional endpoint operators or phases. It depends continuously on $S$, as does its inverse, pointwise in the Schwartz topology: the explicit chirp and linear-coordinate factors have uniformly bounded seminorm estimates on compact parameter neighborhoods, and the Fourier factors are fixed continuous maps. These estimates also justify continuity when composing such a varying local factor with a varying Schwartz vector. Step 4.1 shows every lift over $S$ is exactly $\sigma(S)$ or $-\sigma(S)$.

The endpoint map is continuous for the specified operator topology, without assuming joint continuity of arbitrary Schwartz-operator composition. For each row $j$ and mode $k$, covariance and [F6] give $\langle R_jMg_0,Mg_{e_k}\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(S_{j,Q_k}+iS_{j,P_k})$, where the pairing is linear in its first argument. On the left $R_j$ is continuous on Schwartz space, its inclusion into $L^2$ is continuous, and only the two fixed input vectors $g_0,g_{e_k}$ are used. Thus every real matrix entry of $\pi(M)$ is continuous. Over $\mathcal B$, the scalar $\varepsilon(M):=\langle Mg_0,\sigma(\pi(M))g_0\rangle$ is continuous, takes exactly the values $+1,-1$, and distinguishes the two lifts since $\|g_0\|=1$. Therefore the two inverse images $\varepsilon^{-1}(1)$ and $\varepsilon^{-1}(-1)$ in $\pi^{-1}(\mathcal B)$ are disjoint open sheets; on each, $\pi$ and $\pm\sigma$ are continuous inverse maps onto $\mathcal B$. This proves the two-fold covering in the given topology.

The same charts make the set a topological group. Locally its elements are $\varepsilon\sigma(S)$. Products and inverses of their explicit finite-parameter factors depend continuously on the matrix parameters and on each Schwartz vector, by the uniform seminorm bounds in step 5.1; their endpoint matrices multiply and invert continuously. The sign relative to a local section at the resulting endpoint is recovered by the continuous vacuum pairing in step 6.1. Hence multiplication and inversion are continuous in these charts, which have precisely the operator topology by step 6.1. Finally every defining normalized path is continuous in that topology by [F4], including its inverse path, so it joins its endpoint to $I$. Consequently the group is path connected. Together with step 4.1 this proves the connected double cover with kernel $\{I,-I\}$ and its defining unitary action, retaining the unrestricted phase ambiguity only for arbitrary individual Weyl implementers.

whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and

$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$

nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,

derivations.claim:
First diagonalize $V$ by the Rayleigh-quotient induction in [F1]: a
maximizer of $x^TVx$ on the unit sphere is an eigenvector, because the
derivative at zero of the quotient at $e+tv$ vanishes for every $v\perp e$;
the orthogonal complement is invariant under a symmetric matrix, so induction
gives an orthonormal eigenbasis. Positivity makes each eigenvalue positive,
and replacing it by its positive square root constructs the real symmetric
positive definite $M=V^{1/2}$. Now let $K=MJM$. Then $K^T=-K$, and $K$ is
invertible because both $M$ and $J$ are. The matrix $B=-K^2=K^TK$ is real
symmetric positive definite. Apply the same Rayleigh-quotient argument to $B$
to choose a unit eigenvector $e$ with eigenvalue $\nu^2>0$ and put
$f=-Ke/\nu$. Since
$\|Ke\|^2=e^TBe=\nu^2$, $f$ is unit; since $K$ is skew,
$e^Tf=0$. Also $Ke=-\nu f$ and
$Kf=-K^2e/\nu=\nu e$. Thus in the orthonormal ordered pair $(e,f)$,
$$\begin{pmatrix}e^TKe&e^TKf\\f^TKe&f^TKf\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}0&\nu\\-\nu&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
For any $x$ orthogonal to both $e,f$, skew-symmetry gives
$e^TKx=-(Ke)^Tx=\nu f^Tx=0$ and
$f^TKx=-(Kf)^Tx=-\nu e^Tx=0$, so their orthogonal complement is
$K$-invariant. Repeating the argument on this complement gives an
orthogonal matrix $O$ and positive $\nu_j$ with
$O^TKO=JD$, where $D=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r,\nu_r)$.

Set $S=MO D^{-1/2}$. Then
$$SDS^T=MO D^{-1/2}D D^{-1/2}O^TM=M^2=V,$$
and
$$S^TJS=D^{-1/2}O^TMJM O D^{-1/2} =D^{-1/2}(JD)D^{-1/2}=J,$$
because $D$ commutes with $J$. This proves the Williamson factorization and
symplecticity of $S$.

For symplectic $S$, congruence by $S^{-1}$ maps
$V+i\hbar J/2$ to $D+i\hbar J/2$, since
$S^{-1}JS^{-T}=J$. In each $(Q_j,P_j)$ block the latter matrix is
$$\begin{pmatrix}\nu_j&i\hbar/2\\-i\hbar/2&\nu_j\end{pmatrix},$$
whose eigenvalues are $\nu_j+\hbar/2$ and $\nu_j-\hbar/2$. Congruence by an
invertible matrix preserves nonnegative quadratic forms, so the full matrix
is positive semidefinite exactly when every $\nu_j\ge\hbar/2$.
