Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad
V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n
\langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))=
\exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume Countable Choice, let $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, and use the
Schrödinger quadratures of [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Put
$$D=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^r):x_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^r),\ \partial_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^r)\text{ for every }j\}.$$
For
$$\|f\|_{\mathrm{quad}}:=\|f\|_2+\sum_{j=1}^r(\|x_jf\|_2+\|\partial_jf\|_2),$$
the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ is dense in $D$. The weak
derivatives in this definition are taken in the distributional sense and
agree with the Fourier-defined momentum
domains in the cited quadrature definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain. Fix the
angular-frequency Fourier unitary by
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int_{\mathbb R^r}e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\quad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)),$$
and define $-i\partial_{x_j}:=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}M_{k_j}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$, where $M_{k_j}$ is multiplication by $k_j$ on its maximal domain. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator is defined on a compact interval $[0,T]$ with $0<T<\infty$. Its coefficient path $K:[0,T]\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ has Lebesgue-integrable entries and is symmetric, $K(t)=K(t)^T$ for every $t$; an almost-everywhere symmetric integrable path is understood through a symmetric representative. In the displayed interleaved quadrature order put
$$H_t=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}K_{ab}(t)(R_aR_b+R_bR_a)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r),$$
with no linear or scalar term. The path $U:[0,T]\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ consists of unitary Schwartz automorphisms, has $U(0)=I$, and for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ its trajectory $U(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in each Schwartz seminorm $p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta g(x)|$ and satisfies $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)f=H_tU(t)f$ almost everywhere. Absolute continuity in a seminorm means the finite disjoint-interval condition for the seminorms of the increments. The construction below proves existence, uniqueness and continuity of the inverse path in the same pointwise Schwartz topology. Precisely, $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is the set of all endpoint operators $U(T)$ for this integrable-coefficient class, over all such $T$ and $K$. Piecewise-smooth coefficient paths are included and yield the same endpoint set, as proved below; the definition does not restrict the admissible propagators to that subclass.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.

There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order.

Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
For every real symmetric positive definite $2r\times2r$ matrix $V$, there
are an interleaved symplectic matrix $S$ ($S^TJS=J$) and positive numbers
$\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r$ such that
$$V=S D S^T,\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r,\nu_r).$$
Moreover,
$$V+i\hbar J/2\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nu_j\ge\hbar/2\ \text{for every }j.$$
Here $A\succeq0$ means the Hermitian matrix $A$ has nonnegative quadratic
form on every complex vector.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad
P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.
For every $n\ge1$, $V_n(1)=\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(n/2+1)$. Here $n$ is an integer.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Write $X_j=R_j-d_jI$ and
$G_{jk}=\sum_nw_n\langle X_j\psi_n,X_k\psi_n\rangle$. The series converge
absolutely by Cauchy–Schwarz and the second-moment bounds. On compactly
supported smooth functions, integration by parts gives
$$\langle R_jf,R_kf\rangle-\langle R_kf,R_jf\rangle =-i\hbar J_{jk}\|f\|^2.$$
For the same-mode $Q_j,P_j$ pair, this is
$i\hbar\int x_j\partial_j|f|^2=-i\hbar\|f\|^2$ after the vanishing
boundary term; distinct coordinate pairs and equal-type pairs give zero.
The joint graph-norm density in [F2] extends the identity to each
$\psi_n$ in the common domain. Centering by the real scalars $d_j$ does not
change the antisymmetric difference. Summing with weights yields
$G-G^T=-i\hbar J$, while $\operatorname{Re}G=V$ by definition; hence
$G=V-i\hbar J/2$. For any $c\in\mathbb C^{2r}$,
$$\sum_nw_n\left\|\sum_jc_jX_j\psi_n\right\|^2 =\overline c^{\,T}G^Tc\ge0.$$
Since $G^T=V+i\hbar J/2$, the uncertainty matrix is positive
semidefinite.

Now suppose the target $V+i\hbar J/2$ is positive semidefinite. For real
$x$, $x^TVx=x^*(V+i\hbar J/2)x\ge0$, so $V$ is nonnegative. If a nonzero
real $x$ had $x^TVx=0$, put $H=V+i\hbar J/2$. For every complex $y$ and
real $t$, positivity gives
$(x+ty)^*H(x+ty)=2t\operatorname{Re}(y^*Hx)+t^2y^*Hy\ge0$. Allowing both
signs of $t$ forces $\operatorname{Re}(y^*Hx)=0$; replacing $y$ by $iy$
forces the imaginary part to vanish as well. This holds for every $y$, so
take $y=Hx$ to obtain $\|Hx\|^2=0$ and hence $Hx=0$. Its real and imaginary
parts give $Vx=0$ and
$Jx=0$, contradicting invertibility of $J$. Thus $V$ is positive definite.
Apply [F5] to obtain $V=SD S^T$ with
$D=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r,\nu_r)$ and
$\nu_j\ge\hbar/2$.

For one mode and $\bar n\ge0$, set
$$\eta=\frac{\bar n}{1+\bar n},\qquad \rho_{\bar n}=(1-\eta)\sum_{m=0}^\infty \eta^m|m\rangle\langle m|,$$
with $\rho_0=|0\rangle\langle0|$. The geometric series makes this a
positive trace-class operator of trace one. For $\bar n>0$, define
$$|\alpha\rangle=e^{- |\alpha|^2/2}\sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{\alpha^m}{\sqrt{m!}}|m\rangle.$$
Its norm is one by the exponential series. The vector
$\psi_\alpha:=W(q_0,p_0)g_0$, with
$\alpha=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(-p_0+iq_0)$, is a scalar phase times $|\alpha\rangle$:
the differential formula gives $a\psi=\alpha\psi$, and comparing
coefficients in the complete number basis gives the displayed series up to
one constant phase. In Schrödinger coordinates
$$\psi_\alpha(x)=\pi^{-1/4} e^{i\sqrt\hbar q_0(x+\sqrt\hbar p_0/2)} e^{-(x+\sqrt\hbar p_0)^2/2}.$$
Set $y=x+\sqrt\hbar p_0+\sqrt\hbar p/2$. In
$\langle W(q,p)\psi_\alpha,\psi_\alpha\rangle$, the Gaussian factor is
$e^{-y^2-\hbar p^2/4}$ and the phase is
$\sqrt\hbar qy-\hbar q p_0+\hbar q_0p$. For $\alpha_0>0$ and real
$\beta$, [F9] gives
$$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-\alpha_0 y^2+i\beta y}\,dy=\sqrt{\frac\pi{\alpha_0}}e^{-\beta^2/(4\alpha_0)}$$
by the explicit substitutions $t=\alpha_0/\pi$ and $\xi=-\beta/(2\pi)$
in the supplier's $2\pi$-frequency formula. Taking $\alpha_0=1$ and
$\beta=\sqrt\hbar q$ gives the normalized factor
$\pi^{-1/2}\int e^{-y^2+i\sqrt\hbar qy}\,dy=e^{-\hbar q^2/4}$.
Therefore, for $u=\operatorname{Re}\alpha$ and $v=\operatorname{Im}\alpha$,
$$\langle W(q,p)\psi_\alpha,\psi_\alpha\rangle =\exp\!\left(i\sqrt{2\hbar}(qu+pv) -\frac{\hbar}{4}(q^2+p^2)\right).$$
The phase is the mean $d=(\sqrt{2\hbar}u,\sqrt{2\hbar}v)$. The geometric
weights have mean occupation
$\sum_m m(1-\eta)\eta^m=\eta/(1-\eta)=\bar n$. For a number vector,
$$Q|m\rangle=\sqrt{\hbar/2}\big(\sqrt{m+1}|m+1\rangle+\sqrt m|m-1\rangle\big),$$
and $P|m\rangle=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(\sqrt m|m-1\rangle-\sqrt{m+1}|m+1\rangle)$
by [F8]. Orthogonality of number vectors gives zero means and
$\langle m,Q^2m\rangle=\langle m,P^2m\rangle=\hbar(m+1/2)$. Also
$QP+PQ=-i\hbar(a^2-(a^*)^2)$, whose diagonal matrix entries vanish because
$a^2$ and $(a^*)^2$ change number by two. Thus the diagonal state has zero
symmetrized cross covariance. Summing against the geometric weights gives
$$\langle Q^2\rangle=\langle P^2\rangle =\frac{\hbar}{2}(2\bar n+1)=\nu.$$
Thus its quadrature second moments are finite and its covariance is $\nu I_2$.
The probability density $(\pi\bar n)^{-1}e^{-(u^2+v^2)/\bar n}$ on the
complex plane is normalized because [F9] at zero frequency gives
$\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-u^2/\bar n}du=\sqrt{\pi\bar n}$ in each coordinate,
and [F12] factors the absolutely integrable product integral.
By [F12] and two applications of [F9] with $\alpha_0=1/\bar n$,
$\beta_u=\sqrt{2\hbar}q$ and $\beta_v=\sqrt{2\hbar}p$, its characteristic
factor is
$$\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{e^{-|\alpha|^2/\bar n}}{\pi\bar n}e^{i\sqrt{2\hbar}(qu+pv)}\,du\,dv=e^{-\hbar\bar n(q^2+p^2)/2}.$$
To identify the mixture with $\rho_{\bar n}$, the $(m,n)$ matrix entry of
$|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|$ is
$e^{-|\alpha|^2}\alpha^m\bar\alpha^n/\sqrt{m!n!}$ by the coherent-state
series. Under a planar rotation $\alpha\mapsto e^{i\theta}\alpha$,
Lebesgue measure and the radial density are invariant by [F11], while
$\alpha^m\bar\alpha^n$ gains the factor $e^{i(m-n)\theta}$; choosing
$\theta$ with this factor unequal to $1$ shows that every off-diagonal entry
vanishes. For $m=n$, the polar formula [F11] and $\sigma(S^1)=2\pi$ give
$$\int_{\mathbb C}|\alpha|^{2m}e^{-a|\alpha|^2}\,du\,dv=2\pi\int_0^\infty r^{2m+1}e^{-ar^2}\,dr=\pi\int_0^\infty x^me^{-ax}\,dx,$$
where $x=r^2$. For $a>0$, the last integral is $m!/a^{m+1}$: its value
at $m=0$ is $1/a$, and integration by parts on $[0,R]$ followed by
$R\to\infty$ gives $I_m(a)=(m/a)I_{m-1}(a)$; the boundary term vanishes
by [F10]. Thus the $m$th diagonal entry of the mixture is
$$\frac{1}{\pi\bar n m!}\int_{\mathbb C}|\alpha|^{2m}e^{-(1+1/\bar n)|\alpha|^2}\,du\,dv=\frac{\bar n^m}{(1+\bar n)^{m+1}}=(1-\eta)\eta^m.$$
Let
$P_K=\sum_{m=0}^K|m\rangle\langle m|$ and integrate the finite-rank operators
$P_K|\alpha\rangle\langle\alpha|P_K$. Their diagonal entries just computed
give $\sum_{m=0}^K(1-\eta)\eta^m|m\rangle\langle m|$, which converges in trace norm
to $\rho_{\bar n}$. Also $P_K|\alpha\rangle\to|\alpha\rangle$ in norm for
each $\alpha$, and
$|\langle W(q,p)P_K\alpha,P_K\alpha\rangle|\le1$. Dominated convergence
[F6] therefore passes the characteristic function through the mixture.
Multiplying the two scaled Gaussian Fourier factors just computed by the
vacuum factor in the coherent formula gives
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{\bar n}W(q,p)) =e^{-\hbar(2\bar n+1)(q^2+p^2)/4} =e^{-\nu(q^2+p^2)/2},\qquad \nu=\hbar(\bar n+1/2).$$
For $\bar n=0$, the same formula and covariance follow from [F9] with
$\alpha_0=1$ and $\beta=\sqrt\hbar q$ (and the $p$ coordinate).

Let $M_S$ be an implementer from [F3] and set $\rho_S=M_S\rho M_S^*$.
The Weyl identity and cyclicity of trace against a bounded operator give
$$\chi_{\rho_S}(z)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_S^*W(z)M_S) =\chi_\rho(S^Tz).$$
For a coordinate vector $e_j$, the explicit Weyl formula gives
$W(te_j)=e^{itR_j}$. Therefore
$M_S^*e^{itR_j}M_S=W(tS^Te_j)$; its derivative on Schwartz functions at zero
is $i\sum_kS_{jk}R_k$. By [F7], the two strongly continuous groups have
unique self-adjoint generators, so
$M_S^*R_jM_S=\overline{\sum_kS_{jk}R_k}$. The left side has Schwartz as a
core because every generator unitary in [F3] preserves Schwartz. By [F2],
Schwartz is dense in the joint quadrature graph norm, so every vector with all
quadrature second moments lies in the domain of these finite sums and the
identity acts there as written. Applying it to the eigenvectors of $\rho$
and using the absolutely convergent form sums in [F1] gives $d_S=Sd$ and
$V_S=SVS^T$. For transformations arising from finite Bogoliubov matrices,
these are exactly the core and Weyl interfaces of [F4].

Put $\bar n_j=\nu_j/\hbar-1/2\ge0$ and take the finite tensor product
of the one-mode states $\rho_{\bar n_j}$. In the occupation basis it is
positive trace class with trace one, and its characteristic function is the
product of the one-mode functions from step 1.3, namely
$\exp(-z^TDz/2)$. Conjugate this product state by an implementer $M_S$ from
[F3]; step 2.1 gives characteristic function
$\exp(-z^TSDS^Tz/2)=\exp(-z^TVz/2)$. Finally set

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form
$$q_{A,V}(u,v)=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\langle\Pi_j^A u,\Pi_j^A v\rangle+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(x)u(x)\overline{v(x)}\,dx,$$
and write $q_{A,V}[u]=q_{A,V}(u,u)$. Each integral is finite: the test
functions and their magnetic derivatives are bounded with compact support,
and $V$ is integrable on compact sets. The form is Hermitian, densely
defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

For $\varepsilon_0>0$ define its shifted form norm by
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=q_{A,V}[u]+(v_0+\varepsilon_0)\|u\|_2^2.$$
The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the
choice of $\varepsilon_0>0$. When it holds, the **closed form closure** is the
completion of $\mathscr D$ in this norm, identified with its $L^2$ limits;
the corresponding closed form is denoted $\overline q_{A,V}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix
$\hbar>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$, and work in the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\overline g$ linear in the first
argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**Weak derivatives.** For $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and
$j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$, say that the $j$-th weak derivative of $f$ exists in
$L^2$ when there is a class $g\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,D_j\varphi=(-1)\int_{\mathbb R^d}g\,\varphi \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d),$$
where $D_j\varphi$ is the classical partial derivative and the pairing is
bilinear without conjugation ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]).
Such a $g$ is unique as an $L^2$ class
([[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]]); write $D_jf:=g$.
The Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of classes
$f\in L^2$ for which $D_1f,\dots,D_df$ all exist in $L^2$, and
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ is the set of $f\in W^{1,2}$ with
$D_jf\in W^{1,2}$ for every $j$, with $D_jD_kf$ written for the iterated
derivative ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

**(a) Position operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(Q_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ x\mapsto x_jf(x)\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)\},\qquad (Q_jf)(x):=x_jf(x).$$
Thus $Q_jf$ is the class of the pointwise product with the $j$-th coordinate
function.

**(b) Momentum operators.** For $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ define
$$D(P_j):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C):\ D_jf\text{ exists in }L^2\},\qquad P_jf:=-i\hbar\,D_jf .$$

Both $Q_j$ and $P_j$ are densely defined $\mathbb C$-linear operators in
$L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$: for $Q_j$ the compactly supported smooth
classes lie in the domain because $x_j$ is bounded there, and for $P_j$ they
lie in the domain because their classical derivatives are weak derivatives in
$L^2$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]).

For density, the classes of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ are dense in
$W^{0,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ by
[[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]] and
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. Since these classes lie in each domain
as above, both operator domains are dense.

For a class
$f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ one has $Q_jf=x_jf$ and
$P_jf=-i\hbar\,\partial_jf$ pointwise. The self-adjointness of these operators
and their Fourier representation are proved in
the companion self-adjointness lemma on this page, not
asserted here; for $d=1$ the domain $D(P)$ of the single momentum operator
coincides with $W^{1,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice and let $d\ge1$ be an integer. Work in
$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first
variable, using the quotient and complex-function conventions of the linked
Euclidean $L^2$ definitions. Fix real scalars $m>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $q$.
Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy
$V\ge-v_0$ almost everywhere for some finite $v_0\ge0$. Put
$\mathscr D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ and, for $u\in\mathscr D$,
define
$$\Pi_j^A u=-i\hbar\,\partial_j u-qA_j u\qquad (1\le j\le d).$$
For $u,v\in\mathscr D$ define the sesquilinear form

defined, and bounded below by $-v_0\|u\|_2^2$.

The form is **closable** when every sequence $(u_n)\subset\mathscr D$ with
$\|u_n\|_2\to0$ and
$\|u_n-u_m\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$ as $n,m\to\infty$ also satisfies
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$. This condition is independent of the

derivations.claim:
Fix $\varepsilon_0>0$ and put $W=V+v_0$. For every $u\in C_c^\infty$,
$$\|u\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}^2=\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^d\|\Pi_j^A u\|_2^2+\|W^{1/2}u\|_2^2+\varepsilon_0\|u\|_2^2.$$
This identity shows that if $(u_n)$ is Cauchy in the shifted form norm,
then each sequence $(\Pi_j^A u_n)$ and $(W^{1/2}u_n)$ is Cauchy in $L^2$.

Suppose additionally that $\|u_n\|_2\to0$. Let $w_j$ be the $L^2$
limit of $\Pi_j^A u_n$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty$, symmetry [F2]
and Cauchy–Schwarz give
$$\langle w_j,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle\Pi_j^A u_n,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle u_n,\Pi_j^A\phi\rangle=0.$$
Density in [F1] implies $w_j=0$. If $w_0$ is the $L^2$ limit of
$W^{1/2}u_n$, then [F3] and Cauchy–Schwarz similarly give
$$\langle w_0,\phi\rangle=\lim_n\langle u_n,W^{1/2}\phi\rangle=0$$
for every test function $\phi$, so density gives $w_0=0$.

Every term on the right side of the norm identity in step 1.1 therefore
tends to zero, including $\varepsilon_0\|u_n\|_2^2$. Thus
$\|u_n\|_{q,v_0,\varepsilon_0}\to0$, which is exactly the closability
criterion in [[def-nrqmx-magnetic-form-data]]. The completion is densely
embedded in $L^2$ because it contains the dense core, and the criterion makes
that embedding injective; its form is closed by construction and retains the
lower bound $-v_0$.

boundaries.reason: The test core is nonempty and no empty-set case is claimed.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 identifies every limiting component as zero when tested against the dense core; step 3.1 applies the closability criterion.

boundaries.reason: There is no cardinality parameter.
No spectral multiplicity is asserted.
The form is on R^d and has no endpoint parameter.
No arbitrary family is selected; the Choice axioms are stated in A1.
The claim is a one-way closability result.
The claim is a one-way closability result.

$H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with
$\langle u,v\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^d}u\overline v$, linear in the first

Let $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$ be real and
let $V\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R)$ satisfy

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F,G\in AC[a,b]$,
$$\int_a^bFG'+\int_a^bF'G=F(b)G(b)-F(a)G(a).$$

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every

On the dense tensor core $a(x)b(y)$ with $a,b\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$,
$\mathcal F_y$ is the identity on the first factor and the unitary Fourier
transform on the second, by [F2] and the Euclidean $L^2$ product identification
in [F2]. It extends uniquely to a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$. For each
$k$, translation $x=\xi+x_0(k)$ preserves the $x$-integral by [F4]; Fubini
then shows that $Wg(\xi,k)=g(\xi+x_0(k),k)$ is an isometry with inverse
$W^{-1}h(x,k)=h(x-x_0(k),k)$. Hence $U=W\mathcal F_y$ is unitary.

Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ and write
$F(\xi,k)=Uu(\xi,k)$. For each fixed $k$, $F(\cdot,k)$ is smooth and
compactly supported in $\xi$. Plancherel in $y$, the derivative identity
in [F2], and the substitution $x=\xi+x_0(k)$ give
$$q_B[u]=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}|\partial_\xi F|^2+\frac{(qB)^2}{2m}\xi^2|F|^2\right)d\xi\,dk.$$
For a compactly supported smooth $g(\xi)$, put
$Lg=-\hbar^2g''/(2m)+m\omega_c^2\xi^2g/2\in L^2$. Integrating by parts
twice on a finite interval containing the support of $g$ gives
$\langle Lg,\psi_n\rangle=E_n\langle g,\psi_n\rangle$, since
$L\psi_n=E_n\psi_n$ and the boundary terms vanish. Completeness and Parseval
therefore give
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n^2|\langle g,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\|Lg\|_2^2<\infty.$$
The exact domain characterization in [F3] now implies
$g\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$, and its diagonal action gives
$H_{\mathrm{osc}}g=Lg$. Hence
$$\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}g,g\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^\infty E_n|\langle g,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
Integration by parts also identifies the left side with
$$\frac1{2m}\left(\hbar^2\|g'\|_2^2+(qB)^2\|\xi g\|_2^2\right).$$
Apply this identity to $F(\cdot,k)$ for almost every $k$. Tonelli [F6]
permits integrating the nonnegative series, so the displayed core form is
the coefficient form on every transformed core vector.

For $N<\infty$ and $f_0,\ldots,f_N\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R_k)$,
$F_N(\xi,k)=\sum_{n=0}^Nf_n(k)\psi_n(\xi)$ has inverse
$$U^{-1}F_N(x,y)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\sum_{n=0}^N\int_{\mathbb R}e^{iky}f_n(k)\psi_n\!\left(x-\frac{\hbar k}{qB}\right)dk.$$
Write $v:=U^{-1}F_N$. The integrands have compact $k$-support and are Schwartz in $x$ uniformly
there by the Hermite form in [F3]; differentiating under the integral and
integrating by parts in $k$ show rapid decay in $y$, so the inverse is
Schwartz. Define
$$\chi_R(x,y)=\prod_{s\in\{x,y\}}\sigma(2-s/R)\sigma(2+s/R),$$
using [F5]. These cutoffs are one on $[-R,R]^2$, vanish outside
$[-2R,2R]^2$, and have $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. For each covariant
derivative,
$$\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv)=\chi_R\Pi_j^Av-i\hbar(\partial_j\chi_R)v.$$
Take integer $R\ge1$. The step-function bounds in [F5] give $0\le\chi_R\le1$, and for every fixed $(x,y)$, $\chi_R(x,y)=1$ once $R\ge\max\{|x|,|y|\}$, so $\chi_R\to1$ pointwise. Since $v$ is Schwartz and $A=(0,Bx)$ is linear, $\Pi_1^Av=-i\hbar\partial_xv$ and $\Pi_2^Av=-i\hbar\partial_yv-qBxv$ are Schwartz and belong to $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$. For each $w\in\{v,\Pi_1^Av,\Pi_2^Av\}$, the functions $|(\chi_R-1)w|^2$ are measurable, tend pointwise to zero, and are bounded by the single measurable $L^1$ majorant $|w|^2$. Applying [F9] on the Lebesgue measure space $\mathbb R^2$ gives $\|(\chi_R-1)w\|_2\to0$. The derivative-cutoff term separately satisfies $\|\hbar(\partial_j\chi_R)v\|_2\le C\hbar\|v\|_2/R\to0$. Thus the displayed product identity and the triangle inequality give $\|\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv-v)\|_2\to0$ for both $j$, as well as $\|\chi_Rv-v\|_2\to0$.
The form identity of step 2.1 also holds for Schwartz functions: the Fourier and shear maps preserve Schwartz regularity, and for each Schwartz $g(\xi)$ one has $Lg\in L^2$; its integration-by-parts pairings with the polynomial-Gaussian $\psi_n$ have vanishing boundary terms at both infinities. The same Parseval calculation and exact diagonal operator-domain criterion in [F3] therefore give $g\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and the same oscillator energy identity. All resulting nonnegative energies can again be integrated by [F6]. Apply this extended identity to the Schwartz difference $\chi_Rv-v$. Its weighted coefficient norm squared is exactly $\frac1{2m}\sum_{j=1}^2\|\Pi_j^A(\chi_Rv-v)\|_2^2$, which tends to zero by the preceding bounds. Since $\chi_Rv\in C_c^\infty$, each $F_N$ therefore lies in the weighted-norm closure of the transformed original core, without assuming closability in advance. Finite coefficient families are dense
in the weighted target: truncate its convergent nonnegative series, then
approximate the remaining finitely many $L^2(k)$ coefficients by
$C_c^\infty(k)$ using [F7].

Let $\mathcal K_E$ be the coefficient space
$\{(f_n):\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2<\infty\}$ with squared norm
$\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2$, and let
$J:\mathcal K_E\hookrightarrow L^2(\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb R,d\#\,dk)$
be the identity inclusion. Step 2.1 maps the transformed core isometrically
into $\mathcal K_E$. Since $E_n\ge E_0=\hbar\omega_c/2>0$, $J$ is
continuous and injective, with
$\|Jf\|_2^2\le E_0^{-1}\sum_nE_n\|f_n\|_2^2$. The coefficient map is
unitary on the underlying $L^2$ space by [F2] and [F3]. Thus
$q_B[u]\ge E_0\|u\|_2^2$ on the core. For every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$q_B[u]\le q_B[u]+\varepsilon\|u\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon/E_0)q_B[u],$$
so each shifted form norm is equivalent to $q_B[u]^{1/2}$. Suppose a core
sequence is Cauchy in $q_B[u]^{1/2}$ and tends to zero in $L^2$. Its
weighted coefficient image converges in $\mathcal K_E$ to
some $f$; unweighted $L^2$ convergence and continuity of $J$ give $Jf=0$.
Injectivity of $J$ gives $f=0$, so $q_B[u]\to0$ along that sequence.
The equivalence above then gives convergence to zero in the defining shifted
form norm, proving closability of the core form. By [F8] the
target is complete, so the isometric image of the form completion is
closed there. Step 3.1 places a dense subspace of that target in the image;
hence the image is the whole weighted space and the form closure is exactly
the stated one.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,

> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of

makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let
$S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ with angular coordinate $\phi$, and identify
$L^2(S^1;\mathbb C)$ with $L^2((0,2\pi),d\phi;\mathbb C)$; the omitted
endpoint has measure zero. Let $H^2(0,2\pi)$ be the interval Sobolev space whose elements and first two weak derivatives are in $L^2$. For $f\in H^2(0,2\pi)$ use the continuous endpoint representatives of $f$ and $f'$, and denote their traces by $f^*(0),f^*(2\pi)$ and $(f')^*(0),(f')^*(2\pi)$. Define
the periodic second-order domain
$$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)=\{f\in H^2(0,2\pi):f^*(0)=f^*(2\pi),\ (f')^*(0)=(f')^*(2\pi)\}.$$
It is the domain used for the periodic realization of the second derivative;
it imposes no boundary at the angular seam beyond periodic matching.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$0<L<\infty$, let $H=L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, and let $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}=T_{\min}^*$ be the minimal and maximal realizations of
$-D^2$ from the preceding interval-domain lemma. Fix a positive reference
length $\ell$. For $f\in H^2(0,L)$ define
$\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(L))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(L))$. Let
$U(2)=\{U\in M_2(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_2\}$, where $U^*$ is conjugate
transpose. For each $U\in U(2)$ define
$$D(T_U)=\{f\in H^2(0,L):(U-I_2)\Gamma_0f+i\ell(U+I_2)\Gamma_1f=0\},\qquad T_Uf=-D^2f.$$
Then $T_{\min}\subseteq T_U\subseteq T_{\max}$, each $T_U$ is self-adjoint,
and every self-adjoint realization between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$ equals
exactly one $T_U$. The reference length makes the value and scaled derivative
boundary vectors have the same units if the interval coordinate is assigned
units; in the dimensionless mathematical model they are numerical vectors.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axioms of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice
([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]).
Use the spaces of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] and the
absolutely continuous representatives supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]].

(a) *Bounded intervals.* Let $0<L<\infty$ and $u,v\in H^1(0,L)$. Then
$\int_0^Lu\,\overline{v'}=u^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}
-\int_0^Lu'\,\overline v .$

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

(c) *Second-order identity.* For $u,v\in H^2(0,L)$,
$\int_0^L\bigl(u''\overline v-u\,\overline{v''}\bigr)
=\bigl[u'^*\overline{v^*}-u^*\overline{v'^*}\bigr]_0^L,$
where the bracket denotes
$u'^*(L)\overline{v^*(L)}-u^*(L)\overline{v'^*(L)}
-u'^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}+u^*(0)\overline{v'^*(0)}$.

(d) *Half-line and line.* If $u,v\in H^1(0,\infty)$, then
$\int_0^\infty u\overline{v'}=-u^*(0)\overline{v^*(0)}-\int_0^\infty u'\overline v$, both integrals
being absolutely convergent. For $u,v\in H^1(\mathbb R)$ one instead has
$\int_{\mathbb R}u\overline{v'}=-\int_{\mathbb R}u'\overline v$,
with both integrals absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim:
Set $A_0=-\kappa\partial_\phi^2$ on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$. In the
boundary coordinates $\Gamma_0f=(f(0),f(2\pi))$ and
$\Gamma_1f=(f'(0),-f'(2\pi))$, the unitary swap matrix in [F1] makes the
boundary equation equivalent to $f(0)=f(2\pi)$ and
$f'(0)=f'(2\pi)$: adding and subtracting its two scalar equations gives
these two equalities. Hence $-\partial_\phi^2$ is self-adjoint on this
domain, and multiplication by the positive real $\kappa$ shows that $A_0$
is self-adjoint. Let $P=-i\partial_\phi$.
Integration by parts [F5] and equality of the endpoint traces show that $P$ is
symmetric on $H^2_{\mathrm{per}}$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$ in this domain,
integration by parts gives $\langle Pf,e_n\rangle=nc_n$ and
$\langle A_0f,e_n\rangle=\kappa n^2c_n$. Parseval for [F2] therefore
implies $\|Pf\|_2^2=\sum_n n^2|c_n|^2$ and
$\|A_0f\|_2^2=\kappa^2\sum_n n^4|c_n|^2$.

On $D(A_0)$ write
$T_\alpha=A_0+B_\alpha$ with
$B_\alpha=-2\kappa\alpha P+\kappa\alpha^2I$. This operator is symmetric
because $P$ is symmetric and $\alpha,\kappa$ are real. For every
$\varepsilon>0$ and integer $n$,
$|n|\le\varepsilon n^2+(4\varepsilon)^{-1}$; the coefficient identities
in step 1.1 and the triangle inequality give
$\|B_\alpha f\|_2\le a\|A_0f\|_2+b\|f\|_2$ with any prescribed $a>0$
after choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small and then a finite $b$.
Applying [F3] with $a<1$ proves that $T_\alpha$ is self-adjoint on the
stated periodic domain.

Each $e_n$ lies in the periodic domain and direct differentiation gives
$T_\alpha e_n=\kappa(n-\alpha)^2e_n$. Completeness [F2] makes this the full
orthonormal eigenbasis. The associated spectral projections are therefore
the sums of the character projections whose eigenvalues lie in the chosen
Borel set, so every scalar spectral measure is supported on
$\{\kappa(n-\alpha)^2:n\in\mathbb Z\}$. This set has no finite accumulation
point because $\kappa>0$ and $|n-\alpha|\to\infty$. If $z$ is outside it,
$\inf_n|\lambda_n-z|>0$. For $f=\sum_nc_ne_n$, where
$c_n=\langle f,e_n\rangle$, the diagonal map
$R_zf=\sum_n c_n(\lambda_n-z)^{-1}e_n$ is bounded on $H$. Also
$\sup_n|\lambda_n/(\lambda_n-z)|<\infty$, so the domain characterization
in [F4] shows that $R_z$ maps into $D(T_\alpha)$. Coefficientwise,
$(T_\alpha-z)R_z=I$ and $R_z(T_\alpha-z)=I$ on $D(T_\alpha)$, so $z$ is
in the resolvent. If $z=\lambda_n$ then $e_n$ is a nonzero kernel vector.
Hence the spectrum is exactly the
displayed set and there is no continuous spectral measure.

Let $j\in\mathbb Z$ and $U_jf=e^{ij\phi}f$. It is unitary, preserves
the periodic $H^2$ domain, and
$(P-\alpha-j)U_jf=U_j(P-\alpha)f$ by differentiation; squaring gives
$T_{\alpha+j}U_j=U_jT_\alpha$. If a smooth periodic unit-modulus function
$u$ satisfies the displayed conjugacy, then $(P-\alpha)u=0$, or
$u'=i\alpha u$.
The solutions are $u(\phi)=c e^{i\alpha\phi}$ with $|c|=1$, which are
periodic exactly when $e^{2\pi i\alpha}=1$, equivalently $\alpha\in\mathbb Z$.
Conversely, for integral $\alpha$ this multiplier is single-valued and
periodic.
