The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Adopt the static ring model of a spinless particle of mass $m>0$ kilograms
and charge $q\ne0$ coulombs constrained to a circle of radius $R>0$ metres.
Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, flux $\Phi$ in webers, and energies in joules.
The angular coordinate is $\phi\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$; the
single-valued wavefunction belongs to the periodic domain
$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$; the scalar potential is zero; and a static
tangential vector potential $A_\phi=\Phi/(2\pi R)$ has circulation
$\oint A\cdot d\ell=\Phi$, where $\Phi$ is flux in webers. Under the SI
minimal-coupling assignment, the Hamiltonian is
$$H_\Phi=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mR^2}\left(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha\right)^2,\qquad \alpha=\frac{q\Phi}{2\pi\hbar},$$
on that periodic domain. Its energies are
$$E_n(\Phi)=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mR^2}(n-\alpha)^2,\qquad n\in\mathbb Z,$$
with a complete periodic Fourier eigenbasis. For every $j\in\mathbb Z$,
$\Phi\mapsto\Phi+2\pi\hbar j/q$ gives a unitarily equivalent Hamiltonian;
a noninteger $\alpha$ cannot be removed by a single-valued periodic gauge
phase. These are conditional deductions of the ideal ring model.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice, and Dependent Choice. Let
$\kappa>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$. On
$H=L^2(S^1;\mathbb C)=L^2((0,2\pi),d\phi;\mathbb C)$ use the periodic domain
$H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1)$ defined by periodic endpoint traces and define
$$T_\alpha f=\kappa(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha)^2f,\qquad D(T_\alpha)=H^2_{\mathrm{per}}(S^1).$$
Then $T_\alpha$ is self-adjoint and the normalized characters
$e_n(\phi)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{in\phi}$, $n\in\mathbb Z$, form a complete
orthonormal eigenbasis with eigenvalues $\lambda_n=\kappa(n-\alpha)^2$.
Its spectrum is the closed set $\{\lambda_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$ and its
spectral measures are purely atomic on that set. For every $j\in\mathbb Z$,
multiplication by $e^{ij\phi}$ unitarily intertwines $T_\alpha$ with
$T_{\alpha+j}$. A smooth periodic unit-modulus function $u$ satisfying
$u^{-1}(-i\partial_\phi-\alpha)u=-i\partial_\phi$ exists exactly when
$\alpha\in\mathbb Z$.

At $\alpha=1/2$, $E_n=\kappa(n-1/2)^2$. The nearest integers to $1/2$
are exactly $0$ and $1$, and both have squared distance $1/4$; every other
integer has distance at least $3/2$. Therefore $E_0=E_1=\kappa/4$ is the
ground energy and no other Fourier label attains it. The complete basis in
[F1] makes the ground eigenspace exactly two-dimensional, conditional on the ideal ring assumptions.

At $\alpha=0$, $E_n=\kappa n^2\ge0$, with equality exactly at the
integer $n=0$. The eigenbasis in [F1] then gives a one-dimensional ground
eigenspace, spanned by $e_0(\phi)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}$, again conditional on the ideal ring assumptions.

derivations.claim: For finitely supported $\psi$, each shift $\psi_n\mapsto\psi_{n-\delta}$ preserves the $\ell^2$ norm, so the triangle inequality gives $\|H_0\psi\|_2\le(\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|)\|\psi\|_2$. Hence $H_0$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator $H$. For finitely supported $\psi,\phi$, reindexing the finite sum gives $\langle H_0\psi,\phi\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle T_\delta\psi_m,\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle\psi_m,T_\delta^*\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\langle\psi,H_0\phi\rangle$, because $T_\delta^*=T_{-\delta}$ and $S=-S$. Density and boundedness extend symmetry to all of $\mathcal H$, so $H=H^*$.

Under $k=2\pi x$, the functions $e^{-ik\cdot n}$ are the characters $e_{-n}(x)$. For each internal coordinate $a$, the corresponding scalar character family is complete and Parseval by [F1] and [F2]; summing the $r$ coordinate norm identities proves $\|\mathcal F_0\psi\|_{\mathcal K}=\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H}$. This norm identity agrees with the conjugate-linear-first pairings fixed in the Definition. The range contains every vector-valued trigonometric polynomial, a dense subspace of $\mathcal K$ by [F1] coordinatewise. Hence $\mathcal F_0$ extends uniquely to an isometry $\mathcal F:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$. Its range is closed because $\mathcal H$ is complete, and contains a dense subspace, so it is all of $\mathcal K$. Therefore $\mathcal F$ is unitary.

Direct substitution and the change of index $m=n-\delta$ give, for finitely supported $\psi$, $\mathcal F_0(H_0\psi)(k)=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta e^{-ik\cdot\delta}\sum_m\psi_m e^{-ik\cdot m}=h(k)\mathcal F_0\psi(k)$. The finite sum defining $h$ is continuous and satisfies $\sup_k\|h(k)\|\le\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|$, so multiplication by $h$ is bounded on $L^2$. Extending the identity from the dense finitely supported sequences proves the claimed unitary equivalence. Also, $h(k)^*=\sum_\delta T_\delta^*e^{ik\cdot\delta}=\sum_\delta T_{-\delta}e^{-ik\cdot(-\delta)}=h(k)$, and its entries are trigonometric polynomials, hence smooth.

Write the eigenvalues of $h(k)$ in nondecreasing order as $\lambda_1(k)\le\cdots\le\lambda_r(k)$. For a Hermitian matrix $A$ with eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, its $j$th eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_j(A)=\max_{\dim L=r-j+1}\min_{\|v\|=1,\,v\in L}\langle Av,v\rangle$: every such $L$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_j)$ nontrivially, while $L=\operatorname{span}(e_j,\ldots,e_r)$ attains the value. Since every unit-vector Rayleigh quotient changes by at most $\|A-B\|$ when $A$ is replaced by $B$, this formula gives $|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|$. Thus each $\lambda_j(k)$ is continuous.

Fix $k_0$. The gap and continuity in step 1.4 let us choose disjoint small circles around the distinct eigenvalues in the selected block at $k_0$ so that, on some neighborhood of $k_0$, all selected eigenvalues stay inside their union and all complementary eigenvalues stay outside. The inverse matrix $(zI-h(k))^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ in $k$ on this fixed contour: differentiating the inverse gives $\partial_j(zI-h)^{-1}=(zI-h)^{-1}(\partial_jh)(zI-h)^{-1}$, and repeated differentiation gives finite sums of products of smooth matrices. Therefore its contour integral is $C^\infty$. At each $k$, [F3] diagonalizes $h(k)$ and [F4] gives $2\pi i$ for an eigenvalue inside a component circle. For an exterior eigenvalue $\lambda$, write that circle as $z=c+Re^{it}$ and put $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. The finite geometric identity gives $(z-\lambda)^{-1}=-\sum_{j=0}^N(z-c)^j/(\lambda-c)^{j+1}+r_N(z)$ with $\sup|r_N|\le q^{N+1}/(|\lambda-c|(1-q))$. Each polynomial term integrates to zero because $\oint(z-c)^jdz=iR^{j+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(j+1)t}dt=0$, and the remainder integral is bounded by $2\pi R\sup|r_N|\to0$. Thus the scalar exterior integral is zero. Summing the component circles gives coefficient $1$ on the selected eigenvalues and $0$ on their complement, proving that the matrix contour integral is exactly the selected orthogonal projector. On overlaps the local definitions project onto the same selected eigenspaces, so they agree and define the asserted global projector.

Consequently $[(\bigwedge^mT)^*]_{I,J}=\overline{\det T_{J,I}}=\det (T^*)_{I,J}$, so $(\bigwedge^mT)^*=\bigwedge^m(T^*)$. Applying this to $P=P^*$ shows $Q=Q^*$.

Functoriality [F2] gives $Q^2=\bigwedge^m(P^2)=\bigwedge^mP=Q$. Hence $Q$ is a Hermitian idempotent by step 1.1; for $x=Qy$ and $Qz=0$, $\langle x,z\rangle=\langle Qy,z\rangle=\langle y,Qz\rangle=0$, so its range and kernel are orthogonal and it is the orthogonal projection onto its range.

Every decomposable wedge in the image of $Q$ is a wedge of $m$ vectors in $\operatorname{im}P$, so the full image lies in $\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P$. Conversely, for a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ of the $m$-dimensional range of $P$, $Q(v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m)=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m\ne0$. The increasing-wedge basis theorem [F4], applied to this basis of the range, says $\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P$ is one-dimensional; thus it equals $\operatorname{im}Q$ and $Q$ has rank one.

Differentiating by the product rule gives $dw=\sum_j v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dv_j\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$. The projected connection applies $P$ to each differentiated factor. Since $P\,dv_j=\sum_a v_a A_{aj}$, each term with $a\ne j$ vanishes from a repeated wedge factor, while the $a=j$ term is $A_{jj}w$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Let $f:M\to N$ be continuous, where $M,N$ are **nonempty connected closed integrally oriented $n$-manifolds** of the same dimension. Closed means compact and boundaryless. Write $[M],[N]$ for their specified fundamental classes from [[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]]. The **degree** of $f$ is the integer $d=\deg(f)$ determined by
$$f_*[M]=d[N]\quad\text{in }H_n(N;\mathbb Z).$$

Let $M$ be a compact boundaryless $n$-manifold with a specified $R$-orientation $\mu$, where $R$ is a commutative unital ring. Its **fundamental class** is
$$[M]=[M]_M\in H_n(M,M\setminus M;R)=H_n(M;R),$$
using [[lem-compatible-local-orientation-classes-exist-over-compact-subsets]] with the compact support $K=M$. The final equality holds at the chain-complex level: $C_*(\varnothing;R)=0$, so quotienting by it leaves $C_*(M;R)$. The cited lemma proves existence and uniqueness of this class with point restriction $\mu_x$ at every $x\in M$. Thus the notation denotes a class determined by the supplied orientation, not an arbitrary generator chosen afterward.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every finite-dimensional Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, integration on smooth simplices followed by the inverse of restriction from continuous to smooth singular cohomology gives a natural isomorphism of unital graded real algebras
$$J_M:H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\xrightarrow{\cong}H^*_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R).$$
The source product is wedge of form classes, the target product is the front/back singular cup product, and both stars denote direct sums of the homogeneous groups. Naturality is for smooth maps. No compactness assumption is imposed.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The Kronecker rule $\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c)$ is independent of both cocycle and cycle representatives and is additive in both variables. For a continuous $f:X\to Y$, $\alpha\in H^n(Y;G)$ and $z\in H_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, it satisfies
$$\langle f^*\alpha,z\rangle=\langle\alpha,f_*z\rangle.$$
For a coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$, it satisfies $\langle u_*\alpha,z\rangle=u\langle\alpha,z\rangle$. The same representative-independence argument gives the $R$-bilinear pairing for $R$-linear cochains on chains over a commutative ring $R$.

$m$-manifold and let $\alpha\in\Omega^m(M)$ be a smooth real or complex top form.
Let $J_M:H^m_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\to H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb R)$ be the de Rham
comparison of [[thm-de-rham-theorem]] for real forms, extended
complex-linearly with codomain $H^m_{\mathrm{sing}}(M;\mathbb C)$ for complex
forms. Use the smooth-orientation normalization: a positively oriented affine
$m$-simplex represents the positive local homology generator at each interior
point. Let $[M]\in H_m(M;\mathbb R)$ be the real fundamental class of
[[def-fundamental-class-of-a-compact-oriented-manifold]], and let
$\langle\,,\rangle$ be the Kronecker evaluation pairing
([[def-kronecker-evaluation-pairing]]). Then

For a topological space $X$ and an abelian group $G$, the singular chain groups
and boundary maps of [[def-singular-boundary-operator]] form the
**singular chain complex**
$$C_\bullet(X;G):=\bigl(\cdots\to C_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\partial_n}C_{n-1}(X;G)\to\cdots\bigr),$$
because [[thm-the-singular-boundary-squares-to-zero]] gives
$\partial_{n-1}\partial_n=0$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces. For each $n\geq 0$,
the **induced singular chain map in degree $n$** is the homomorphism
$$f_{\#,n}:C_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to C_n(Y;\mathbb Z)$$
defined on a singular simplex $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ by
$$f_{\#,n}(\sigma):=f\circ\sigma,$$
and extended $\mathbb Z$-linearly.

For each abelian group $G$, the assignments
$$X\mapsto C_\bullet(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto f_\#$$
and
$$X\mapsto H_n^{\mathrm{sing}}(X;G),\qquad f\mapsto H_n(f_\#)$$
define covariant functors from topological spaces to chain complexes and to
abelian groups, respectively. Equivalently,
$$\operatorname{id}_{X,\#}=\operatorname{id}_{C_\bullet(X;G)},\qquad (g\circ f)_\#=g_\#\circ f_\#,$$
and for every $n\geq 0$,
$$H_n((g\circ f)_\#)=H_n(g_\#)\circ H_n(f_\#),\qquad H_n(\operatorname{id}_{X,\#})=\operatorname{id}_{H_n(X;G)}.$$

Let $X$ be any topological space and $G$ an abelian group. Its **singular cochains with coefficients in $G$** are
$$C^n(X;G)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(C_n(X;\mathbb Z),G)\quad(n\ge0),\qquad C^n(X;G)=0\quad(n<0),$$
where the chains are those of [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. Addition and negatives of homomorphisms are pointwise. The **coboundary** is
$$\delta^n:C^n(X;G)\to C^{n+1}(X;G),\qquad \delta^n\varphi=\varphi\circ\partial_{n+1}$$
for $n\ge0$, and is zero for $n<0$. Composition with the homomorphism [[def-singular-boundary-operator|$\partial_{n+1}$]] is additive, so this is a homomorphism. The sign convention is positive: there is no extra degree sign on this composite. On a singular $(n+1)$-simplex it says
$$\delta^n\varphi(\sigma)=\sum_{i=0}^{n+1}(-1)^i\varphi(\sigma\circ\delta_i),$$
where $\delta_i$ denotes the affine face map, distinct from the superscripted coboundary. In particular $\delta^0\varphi$ on an oriented path is its endpoint value minus its initial value.

By [[def-singular-simplex-and-singular-chain-group-with-coefficients]], the integer chains are finite sums on the specified simplex set $S_n(X)$. Thus a cochain is equivalently an arbitrary function $S_n(X)\to G$: the extension sends $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ to $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$. The sum is finite and the formal coefficients are unique. The cochain need not have finite support.

For a commutative unital ring $R$ and an $R$-module $G$, there is a canonical identification

A homomorphism $\varphi$ on integer chains defines an $R$-linear map by $c\otimes r\mapsto r\varphi(c)$; the defining additive and integer-balanced tensor relations are preserved. Conversely evaluate an $R$-linear map on $c\otimes1$. These operations are inverse since $c\otimes r=r(c\otimes1)$, and they intertwine the two coboundaries because the coefficient boundary is $\partial\otimes1$. The construction also covers the zero ring with its unital zero module.

The resulting graded group and coboundary are called the **singular cochain complex**. The square-zero identity follows by precomposition with $\partial^2=0$ in the chain complex and is spelled out in the next lemma. If $X$ is empty there are no singular simplices, so every cochain group is zero; if $G=0$ the same is true. The extension and tensor formulas are uniquely specified and require no AC.

Fix a space $X$, abelian group $G$ and integer $n\ge0$. For a singular cocycle $\varphi\in Z^n(X;G)$ and an integral singular cycle $c\in Z_n(X;\mathbb Z)$, define their **evaluation** to be $\varphi(c)\in G$, using [[def-singular-cohomology-with-coefficients]] and [[def-singular-chain-complex-and-singular-homology]]. If $c=\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\sigma$ is its finite formal expansion, this value is $\sum_\sigma a_\sigma\varphi(\sigma)$.

The **Kronecker pairing** on quotient classes is the rule
$$\langle[\varphi],[c]\rangle=\varphi(c),\qquad H^n(X;G)\times H_n(X;\mathbb Z)\to G.$$
Its descent through both quotients, biadditivity and naturality are justified by the following lemma [[lem-the-kronecker-pairing-is-independent-of-cocycle-and-cycle-representatives]], before any use of the quotient pairing. It is not an assertion that evaluation gives an isomorphism to the full dual of homology.

For negative $n$, the two groups are zero and the pairing is the zero map. Empty $X$ and zero $G$ also give zero evaluation. When $G$ is an $R$-module, the cohomology variable is $R$-linear and the integral homology variable is additive; an $R$-bilinear pairing instead uses chains and homology over $R$ with $R$-linear cochains. No representative-selection function is included in the definition.

A continuous map $f:X\to Y$ induces $f^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and abelian group $G$, by $f^*[\varphi]=[\varphi f_\#]$. These maps satisfy $(1_X)^*=1$ and $(g\circ f)^*=f^*\circ g^*$. A coefficient homomorphism $u:G\to G'$ induces $u_*:H^n(X;G)\to H^n(X;G')$, covariantly functorial in coefficients and commuting with $f^*$.

For the projector of [[def-nrqmx-determinant-line-projector]], $Q(x)=\bigwedge^mP(x)$ is a $C^2$ orthogonal projector of rank one. Its range is exactly $\det E_P(x)=\bigwedge^m\operatorname{im}P(x)$, so these ranges form the determinant line bundle.

Write $E_P=\{(x,v):P(x)v=v\}$ and give it the projected connection $\nabla s=P\,ds$. For $x\in M$ and $X,Y\in T_xM$, define the curvature two-form with values in $M_r(\mathbb C)$ by

$$F_x(X,Y):=P(x)\bigl(dP_x(X)dP_x(Y)-dP_x(Y)dP_x(X)\bigr)P(x).$$

Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let $V:U\to\mathbb C^{r\times m}$ be a $C^2$ orthonormal frame, meaning $V(x)^*V(x)=I_m$ and $V(x)V(x)^*=P(x)$ for all $x\in U$. Put $A=V^*dV$ and $w=v_1\wedge\cdots\wedge v_m$, where $v_1,\ldots,v_m$ are the columns of $V$. The induced projected connection on $\det E_P$ has local connection one-form $a=\operatorname{tr}A$ in the unit frame $w$, and its scalar curvature is

$$da=\operatorname{tr}(V^*FV)=\operatorname{tr}F.$$

Thus the curvature of the determinant line is the trace of the original bundle curvature, with the same orientation and sign convention.

$$\frac{i}{2\pi}\int_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}F=\langle c_1(E_P),[\Sigma]\rangle\in\mathbb Z.$$

Thus geometric holonomy includes the frame-transition scalars whenever one frame does not cover the path.

be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $a\in\mathbb C$, let $R>0$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on the disc

Applying [F3] to $Q_t$ proves the displayed equality and integrality, with $c_1$ interpreted by [F5].

For a jointly $C^2$ family, the coefficient function $g(k,t)$ of the two-form $\operatorname{tr}(P_t(dP_t\wedge dP_t)P_t)$ is continuous on the compact set $\mathbb T^2_{2\pi}\times[0,1]$, so it is uniformly continuous. Ordered eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix depend continuously on its entries: the min-max formula gives $|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|$, by the same Rayleigh-quotient argument as in [F6]. At any $(k_0,t_0)$, choose disjoint small positively oriented circles around the distinct eigenvalues in the selected block of $h(k_0,t_0)$, with their closed disks separated from the complementary eigenvalues. Joint continuity of $h$ and its eigenvalues keeps the selected eigenvalues inside this fixed contour union and the complementary eigenvalues outside on a neighborhood of $(k_0,t_0)$. On the contours, $(zI-h(k,t))^{-1}$ is jointly $C^2$, since matrix inversion is smooth on invertible matrices and the contour remains in the resolvent set. Its contour integral is therefore jointly $C^2$. For completeness, on any component circle $z=c+Re^{it}$ an exterior eigenvalue $\lambda$ has $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. The finite geometric identity gives $(z-\lambda)^{-1}=-\sum_{k=0}^N(z-c)^k/(\lambda-c)^{k+1}+r_N(z)$ with $\sup|r_N|\le q^{N+1}/(|\lambda-c|(1-q))$. Each polynomial term has zero circle integral, since $\oint(z-c)^k dz=iR^{k+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(k+1)t}dt=0$, while the remainder integral has modulus at most $2\pi R\sup|r_N|\to0$. Thus an exterior eigenvalue contributes zero. The interior formula in [F7] and this exterior calculation, applied in a finite orthonormal eigenbasis at each fixed $(k,t)$, give coefficient $1$ on each selected eigenspace and $0$ on its complement. Thus the contour integral is exactly the selected orthogonal projector. The local contour projectors agree on overlaps because they select the same ordered block, so $P(k,t)$ is jointly $C^2$ on the whole product. The general homotopy argument above now applies.

If $V$ is a global $C^2$ periodic orthonormal frame, then $A=V^*dV$ is a globally defined $C^1$ matrix-valued one-form. By [F2] and its proof, $\operatorname{tr}F=d\operatorname{tr}A$ (the trace of $A\wedge A$ vanishes). Fix $M$ outside the closing set and let $N=(0,0,1)\in S^2$. The preimages of $N$ under $n_M=d_M/|d_M|$ are exactly the four candidate points above for which the third component is positive. The derivative matrix is diagonal with entries $\cos k_1/d_3$ and $\cos k_2/d_3$, where $d_3=M+\cos k_1+\cos k_2>0$; its determinant is nonzero. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Let $H$ be an arbitrary complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ a nonempty compact interval, $\hbar>0$, and $\mathcal H:I\to\mathcal B(H)$ a norm-continuous family of bounded self-adjoint operators. Put $A(t)=-i\mathcal H(t)/\hbar$ and $K=\sup_{t\in I}\|A(t)\|<\infty$. For every $s,t\in I$ define $U_0(t,s)=I_H$ and, recursively, the oriented Bochner integrals
$$U_{n+1}(t,s)=\int_s^t A(r)U_n(r,s)\,dr,$$
where $\int_s^t=-\int_t^s$ when $t<s$. Equivalently, for $s\le t$ these are the **latest-time-left** ordered integrals
$$U_n(t,s)=\Bigl(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\Bigr)^n\int_{s<t_1<\cdots<t_n<t}\mathcal H(t_n)\cdots\mathcal H(t_1)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n,$$
with the simplex integral meaning the nested integral with $t_n$ outermost and $t_1$ innermost. For arbitrary $s,t$ its unambiguous nested form is $\int_s^t dr_1\int_s^{r_1}dr_2\cdots\int_s^{r_{n-1}}dr_n\,A(r_1)\cdots A(r_n)$. Then:

(a) $\|U_n(t,s)\|\le(K|t-s|)^n/n!$ for all $n\ge0$ and all $s,t\in I$.

(b) $U(t,s)=\sum_{n\ge0}U_n(t,s)$ converges in operator norm uniformly on $I\times I$, is jointly norm-continuous, satisfies $U(s,s)=I_H$, and obeys $\|U(t,s)-I_H\|\le e^{K|t-s|}-1$. In particular all original forward-time convergence claims hold.

(c) For every $s,t\in I$,
$$U(t,s)=I_H-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_s^t\mathcal H(r)U(r,s)\,dr.$$
For fixed $s$ this is the unique continuous $\mathcal B(H)$-valued solution on $I$. More generally, the solution with initial value $C\in\mathcal B(H)$ at $s$ is $U(t,s)C$. For $a<b$, the operator-norm derivatives are
$$\partial_tU(t,s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\mathcal H(t)U(t,s),\qquad \partial_sU(t,s)=+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(t,s)\mathcal H(s),$$
with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Therefore, for every $\psi\in H$, $U(t,s)\psi$ is strongly continuously differentiable in either variable and satisfies the same equations applied to $\psi$, with the common bounded-generator domain equal to all of $H$.

(d) Every $U(t,s)$ is unitary, $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)=U(t,s)^{-1}$, and
$$U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)\qquad(r,s,t\in I).$$
These conclusions include both orientations of the time interval and intervals containing positive and negative times. If $a=b$, all terms with $n\ge1$ vanish and $U(a,a)=I_H$; the derivative assertions then have no nontrivial interval on which to apply.

No separability hypothesis on $H$, invariant domain for an unbounded operator, differentiability of $\mathcal H$, spectral theorem or physical interpretation is required.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A=A^*$ be an endomorphism of $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $\hbar>0$. For real $t$, define $E_A(t):=e^{-itA/\hbar}$ by the finite-dimensional matrix exponential defined on this page. Then $E_A(t)$ is unitary, $E_A(t+s)=E_A(t)E_A(s)$ for all real $s,t$, and its operator-norm derivative is
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_A(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}AE_A(t)= -\frac{i}{\hbar}E_A(t)A.$$

derivations.claim: On any compact interval, $H$ is a norm-continuous bounded self-adjoint family, so [F1] supplies the unique unitary propagator there. On overlapping compact intervals the propagators agree by uniqueness; hence $U(t,s)$ is consistently defined for all real $s,t$. For each fixed $t$, the curves $r\mapsto U(r+T,T)$ and $r\mapsto U(r,0)$ solve the same differential equation because $H(r+T)=H(r)$, and both equal $I_d$ at $r=0$. Uniqueness in [F1] gives $U(t+T,T)=U(t,0)$.

Put $M=U(T,0)$. By [F1], $M$ is unitary, so [F2] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $v_j$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of modulus one. Write $\lambda_j=x_j+iy_j$; then $(x_j,-y_j)$ lies on the real unit circle. By [F3], choose $\theta_j\in[0,2\pi)$ with $x_j=\cos\theta_j$ and $-y_j=\sin\theta_j$, so $\lambda_j=e^{-i\theta_j}$. Set $\varepsilon_j=\hbar\theta_j/T$ and define $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$. Each $\varepsilon_j$ is real, hence $H_F$ is Hermitian, and [F5] gives $e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}v_j=e^{-i\theta_j}v_j=\lambda_jv_j$. Equality on the basis proves $e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}=U(T,0)$.

If $\varepsilon'_j$ gives the same eigenphase as $\varepsilon_j$, then $\exp(-iT(\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j)/\hbar)=1$. By [F4], $T(\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j)/\hbar\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, so $\varepsilon'_j-\varepsilon_j\in\hbar\omega\mathbb Z$. Conversely adding $n\hbar\omega$ multiplies the phase by $e^{-i2\pi n}=1$. Thus the class stated is independent of the real lift.

Define $P(t)=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}$. Both factors are unitary by [F1] and [F5], so $P(t)$ is unitary, and the group law in [F5] gives $P(t)e^{-itH_F/\hbar}=U(t,0)$. By composition and step 1.1, $U(t+T,0)=U(t+T,T)U(T,0)=U(t,0)e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}$. Therefore
$$P(t+T)=U(t,0)e^{-iTH_F/\hbar}e^{i(t+T)H_F/\hbar}=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}=P(t),$$
where the middle cancellation follows from [F5]. This proves the factorization and periodicity.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Put
$D_\theta:=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(L)=e^{i\theta}u^*(0)\},\qquad
P_\theta u:=-i\,Du,$
with $H^1$ and the trace $u^*$ of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]
and [[lem-nrqm-intervals-integration-by-parts]] clause (b). Then:

(a) $D_\theta$ is dense in $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, $P_\theta$ is symmetric and
self-adjoint;

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, each
$\varphi_n\in D_\theta$, and $P_\theta\varphi_n=\kappa_n\varphi_n$ with
$\kappa_n:=\frac{2\pi n+\theta}{L};$
the eigenvalues $\kappa_n$ are simple and
$\sigma(P_\theta)=\{\kappa_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$;

(c) $P_\theta$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of the symmetric operator
$P_\theta$ restricted to the finite linear span of the $\varphi_n$, and its
domain is exactly
$D_\theta=\Bigl\{\sum_nc_n\varphi_n:\sum_n\kappa_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix complex
scalars. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, bounded or
unbounded, and write $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of
Lebesgue (equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with the inner
product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_Iu\overline v$ linear in the first argument
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**First-order space.** Define
$H^1(I):=\{u\in L^2(I;\mathbb C):\ \text{the weak derivative }Du\text{ of the class }u\text{ exists and }Du\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)\},$
where $Du$ is the weak derivative of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a class
$Du\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;\mathbb C)$ with
$\int_Iu\,\varphi'=(-1)\int_I(Du)\varphi\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I),$
an identity that is choice-free
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). Equip
$H^1(I)$ with the sesquilinear form
$\langle u,v\rangle_{H^1}:=\int_Iu\overline v+\int_I(Du)\overline{Dv},$
whose associated norm is $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$;
the symbol $u'$ denotes the same weak derivative $Du$ throughout the page.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

**Endpoint-vanishing first-order space and the Dirichlet form.** For the
bounded interval $(0,L)$, $L>0$, define
$H^1_0(0,L):=\overline{C_c^\infty(0,L)}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{H^1}},$
the closure of the test functions in $H^1(0,L)$, and define the **Dirichlet
form** on it by $q_D[u]:=\|Du\|_{L^2(0,L)}^2=\int_0^L|Du|^2$.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\hbar>0$, $\omega=2\pi/T$, and let $H:\mathbb R\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be continuous, $T$-periodic, and Hermitian at every time. Let $U(t,s)$ be the unitary propagator solving $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t,s)=H(t)U(t,s)$ and $U(s,s)=I_d$. There are an orthonormal basis $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ and real numbers $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_d$ such that
$$U(T,0)v_j=e^{-iT\varepsilon_j/\hbar}v_j\qquad(1\le j\le d).$$
Define the Hermitian matrix $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$ and the quasienergy classes $\varepsilon_j+\hbar\omega\mathbb Z$. With $P(t):=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}$, $P(t)$ is a $T$-periodic unitary matrix and
$$U(t,0)=P(t)e^{-itH_F/\hbar}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
The real representative $\varepsilon_j$ may be changed by any integer multiple of $\hbar\omega$ without changing its eigenphase; no preferred real branch is asserted.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A=A^*$ be an endomorphism of $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $\hbar>0$. For real $t$, define $E_A(t):=e^{-itA/\hbar}$ by the finite-dimensional matrix exponential defined on this page. Then $E_A(t)$ is unitary, $E_A(t+s)=E_A(t)E_A(s)$ for all real $s,t$, and its operator-norm derivative is
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_A(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}AE_A(t)= -\frac{i}{\hbar}E_A(t)A.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix complex
scalars. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, bounded or
unbounded, and write $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$ for the complex Hilbert space of
Lebesgue (equivalence classes of) square-integrable functions with the inner
product $\langle u,v\rangle=\int_Iu\overline v$ linear in the first argument
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]],
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]).

**First-order space.** Define
$H^1(I):=\{u\in L^2(I;\mathbb C):\ \text{the weak derivative }Du\text{ of the class }u\text{ exists and }Du\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)\},$
where $Du$ is the weak derivative of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]: a class
$Du\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(I;\mathbb C)$ with
$\int_Iu\,\varphi'=(-1)\int_I(Du)\varphi\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(I),$
an identity that is choice-free
([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]). Equip
$H^1(I)$ with the sesquilinear form
$\langle u,v\rangle_{H^1}:=\int_Iu\overline v+\int_I(Du)\overline{Dv},$
whose associated norm is $\|u\|_{H^1}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$;
the symbol $u'$ denotes the same weak derivative $Du$ throughout the page.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

**Endpoint-vanishing first-order space and the Dirichlet form.** For the
bounded interval $(0,L)$, $L>0$, define
$H^1_0(0,L):=\overline{C_c^\infty(0,L)}^{\,\|\cdot\|_{H^1}},$
the closure of the test functions in $H^1(0,L)$, and define the **Dirichlet
form** on it by $q_D[u]:=\|Du\|_{L^2(0,L)}^2=\int_0^L|Du|^2$.

**Elementary consequences, recorded for reuse.** Weak derivatives are unique
as locally integrable classes under Countable Choice, are additive and
$\mathbb C$-homogeneous, and classical derivatives of continuously
differentiable functions are weak derivatives. The cited published items
supply these facts, so $H^1(I)$ and $H^2(I)$ are well-defined linear
subspaces of $L^2(I;\mathbb C)$. No claim is made here that $H^1_0(0,L)$
equals the set of classes with vanishing endpoint values; that identification
is proved on this page from the trace estimates.

For $d$ components, the finite orthogonal direct sum is self-adjoint: testing the adjoint identity against vectors with only one nonzero component gives the scalar adjoint domain in each component, hence the full adjoint domain is exactly the componentwise domain. Its orthonormal eigenbasis is $T^{-1/2}e^{in\omega t}e_a$ with eigenvalue $n\hbar\omega$, where $e_a$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb C^d$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A=A^*$ be an endomorphism of $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $\hbar>0$. For real $t$, define $E_A(t):=e^{-itA/\hbar}$ by the finite-dimensional matrix exponential defined on this page. Then $E_A(t)$ is unitary, $E_A(t+s)=E_A(t)E_A(s)$ for all real $s,t$, and its operator-norm derivative is
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_A(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}AE_A(t)= -\frac{i}{\hbar}E_A(t)A.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $H_D$ is Hermitian because $P=P^*$, $P^\perp=(P^\perp)^*$, and $H=H^*$. Also $PH_DP^\perp=P^\perp H_DP=0$, so $H_D$ preserves both $\operatorname{ran}P$ and $\operatorname{ran}P^\perp$. Its power-series exponential therefore preserves those subspaces and commutes with $P$, giving $P^\perp e^{-itH_D/\hbar}P=0$. The vectors $Px$ and $P^\perp x$ are orthogonal because $PP^\perp=0$ and $P=P^*$; hence $\|x\|^2=\|Px\|^2+\|P^\perp x\|^2$, so $\|P\|,\|P^\perp\|\le1$.

For $s$ between $0$ and $t$, set $F(s)=e^{-i(t-s)H/\hbar}e^{-isH_D/\hbar}$. By [F1] and the product rule,
$$F'(s)=\frac{i}{\hbar}e^{-i(t-s)H/\hbar}(H-H_D)e^{-isH_D/\hbar}=\frac{i}{\hbar}e^{-i(t-s)H/\hbar}Ve^{-isH_D/\hbar}.$$
Integrating this continuous matrix curve from $0$ to $t$ by [F2] gives
$$e^{-itH_D/\hbar}-e^{-itH/\hbar}=\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^t e^{-i(t-s)H/\hbar}Ve^{-isH_D/\hbar}\,ds.$$
This oriented integral identity holds also for $t<0$.

The two exponentials in the integrand of step 1.2 are unitary by [F1], so its integrand has norm at most $\|V\|$ by [F2]. Taking norms in that identity and using the interval length $|t|$ proves the first bound.

Step 1.1 gives $P^\perp e^{-itH_D/\hbar}P=0$. Hence $P^\perp e^{-itH/\hbar}P=P^\perp(e^{-itH/\hbar}-e^{-itH_D/\hbar})P$. The contraction bounds for $P$ and $P^\perp$ from step 1.1 and the first estimate in step 2.1 yield the claimed leakage bound.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\omega=2\pi/T$, $\hbar>0$, and let $H:\mathbb R\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be $C^1$, $T$-periodic, and Hermitian at every time. On $\mathscr H_T=L^2((0,T),dt;\mathbb C^d)$ define
$$D(K)=\{f=(f_1,\ldots,f_d): f_a\in H^1(0,T)\text{ for every }a,\ f(0)=f(T)\},\qquad (Kf)(t)=H(t)f(t)-i\hbar f'(t).$$
Here each $H^1(0,T)$ function is represented by its unique absolutely continuous representative, so endpoint values are its traces, and $f'$ is its componentwise weak derivative. Then $K$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(K)$. Choose $v_j$ and $\varepsilon_j$ from [[thm-nrqmx-finite-floquet-normal-form]], so $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$ and $P(t)$ is its periodic unitary. The functions
$$\phi_{jn}(t)=T^{-1/2}e^{in\omega t}P(t)v_j\qquad(1\le j\le d,\ n\in\mathbb Z)$$
form an orthonormal basis of $\mathscr H_T$ and satisfy $K\phi_{jn}=(\varepsilon_j+n\hbar\omega)\phi_{jn}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $0<L<\infty$ and $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Put
$D_\theta:=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(L)=e^{i\theta}u^*(0)\},\qquad
P_\theta u:=-i\,Du,$
with $H^1$ and the trace $u^*$ of [[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]
and [[lem-nrqm-intervals-integration-by-parts]] clause (b). Then:

(a) $D_\theta$ is dense in $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, $P_\theta$ is symmetric and
self-adjoint;

(b) the functions
$\varphi_n(x):=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{i(2\pi n+\theta)x/L}\qquad(n\in\mathbb Z)$
form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(0,L;\mathbb C)$, each
$\varphi_n\in D_\theta$, and $P_\theta\varphi_n=\kappa_n\varphi_n$ with
$\kappa_n:=\frac{2\pi n+\theta}{L};$
the eigenvalues $\kappa_n$ are simple and
$\sigma(P_\theta)=\{\kappa_n:n\in\mathbb Z\}$;

(c) $P_\theta$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of the symmetric operator
$P_\theta$ restricted to the finite linear span of the $\varphi_n$, and its
domain is exactly
$D_\theta=\Bigl\{\sum_nc_n\varphi_n:\sum_n\kappa_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $b,N\ge0$, and real numbers $\hbar>0$, $\omega>0$, and $\tau>0$. Let $H_k\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ for $-b\le k\le b$ satisfy $H_{-k}=H_k^*$; set $H_k=0$ when $|k|>b$. Thus $H(t)=\sum_{k=-b}^{b}H_ke^{ik\omega t}$ is a finite Fourier polynomial with period $T=2\pi/\omega$. Put $q=(2N+1)d$. Let $S_\tau$ be a caller-supplied total classical routine on $\{M\in M_q(\mathbb C):M=M^*\}$ whose declared interface, on input $M$, returns real numbers $\widetilde\lambda_1,\ldots,\widetilde\lambda_q$, an orthonormal basis $x_1,\ldots,x_q$ of standard $\mathbb C^q$, and residuals $r_j=\|Mx_j-\widetilde\lambda_jx_j\|\le\tau$ for $1\le j\le q$. This algorithm returns that finite record unchanged and does not independently certify its residual claims.

The algorithm takes $(d,b,N,\hbar,\omega,(H_k)_{|k|\le b},\tau,S_\tau)$ and returns a matrix $K_N$ and the eigensolver's output record:

1. Order the Fourier indices as $-N,-N+1,\ldots,N$ and allocate a $(2N+1)d$ by $(2N+1)d$ block matrix.

2. For each ordered pair $n,m\in\{-N,\ldots,N\}$, assign the $d$ by $d$ block
$$ (K_N)_{nm}:=H_{n-m}+n\hbar\omega\,\delta_{nm}I_d,$$
where $\delta_{nm}=1$ if $n=m$ and $0$ otherwise.

3. Set $R:=S_\tau(K_N)$ by one call, then return $(K_N,R)$.

derivations.claim: For $-N\le m\le N$ and $v\in\mathbb C^d$, $e_m(t)v=T^{-1/2}e^{im\omega t}v$ is smooth and periodic, so it lies in $D(K)$ by [F1]. Multiplication by $H(t)$ gives $\sum_kT^{-1/2}e^{i(m+k)\omega t}H_kv$; its coefficient in harmonic $n$ is $H_{n-m}v$. The derivative term is $-i\hbar\,\partial_t(e_m v)=m\hbar\omega e_m v$, which contributes only when $n=m$. Thus $\Pi_NK(e_m v)$ has $n$th coefficient $(H_{n-m}+n\hbar\omega\delta_{nm}I_d)v$.

For every pair $n,m$, [F3] gives $(K_N)_{nm}^*=H_{n-m}^*+n\hbar\omega\delta_{nm}I_d=H_{m-n}+m\hbar\omega\delta_{mn}I_d=(K_N)_{mn}$, since $H_{-k}=H_k^*$ and the diagonal term is present only when $n=m$. Hence $K_N$ is Hermitian.

The coefficient just computed is precisely the block assigned by [F3] in row $n$, column $m$. Since the ordered Fourier basis spans $\mathcal S_N$, equality of all its matrix blocks proves that $K_N$ is exactly the matrix of $\Pi_NK|_{\mathcal S_N}$.

There are $(2N+1)^2$ ordered pairs $(n,m)$, each assignment fills one finite $d$ by $d$ block, so the block assembly terminates after exactly that many assignments. By step 1.2, $K_N$ is Hermitian, and it has dimension $q=(2N+1)d$; hence it is in the domain of the total routine $S_\tau$ in [F4]. The algorithm makes one call $R:=S_\tau(K_N)$ after assembly, and totality gives a returned finite record. Thus the complete procedure is well-defined and terminates. This exact compression and termination argument proves no convergence as $N\to\infty$, spectral accuracy, or residual claim beyond the routine's stipulated interface.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an arbitrary complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ a nonempty compact interval, $\hbar>0$, and $\mathcal H:I\to\mathcal B(H)$ a norm-continuous family of bounded self-adjoint operators. Put $A(t)=-i\mathcal H(t)/\hbar$ and $K=\sup_{t\in I}\|A(t)\|<\infty$. For every $s,t\in I$ define $U_0(t,s)=I_H$ and, recursively, the oriented Bochner integrals
$$U_{n+1}(t,s)=\int_s^t A(r)U_n(r,s)\,dr,$$
where $\int_s^t=-\int_t^s$ when $t<s$. Equivalently, for $s\le t$ these are the **latest-time-left** ordered integrals
$$U_n(t,s)=\Bigl(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\Bigr)^n\int_{s<t_1<\cdots<t_n<t}\mathcal H(t_n)\cdots\mathcal H(t_1)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n,$$
with the simplex integral meaning the nested integral with $t_n$ outermost and $t_1$ innermost. For arbitrary $s,t$ its unambiguous nested form is $\int_s^t dr_1\int_s^{r_1}dr_2\cdots\int_s^{r_{n-1}}dr_n\,A(r_1)\cdots A(r_n)$. Then:

(a) $\|U_n(t,s)\|\le(K|t-s|)^n/n!$ for all $n\ge0$ and all $s,t\in I$.

(b) $U(t,s)=\sum_{n\ge0}U_n(t,s)$ converges in operator norm uniformly on $I\times I$, is jointly norm-continuous, satisfies $U(s,s)=I_H$, and obeys $\|U(t,s)-I_H\|\le e^{K|t-s|}-1$. In particular all original forward-time convergence claims hold.

(c) For every $s,t\in I$,
$$U(t,s)=I_H-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_s^t\mathcal H(r)U(r,s)\,dr.$$
For fixed $s$ this is the unique continuous $\mathcal B(H)$-valued solution on $I$. More generally, the solution with initial value $C\in\mathcal B(H)$ at $s$ is $U(t,s)C$. For $a<b$, the operator-norm derivatives are
$$\partial_tU(t,s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\mathcal H(t)U(t,s),\qquad \partial_sU(t,s)=+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(t,s)\mathcal H(s),$$
with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Therefore, for every $\psi\in H$, $U(t,s)\psi$ is strongly continuously differentiable in either variable and satisfies the same equations applied to $\psi$, with the common bounded-generator domain equal to all of $H$.

(d) Every $U(t,s)$ is unitary, $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)=U(t,s)^{-1}$, and
$$U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)\qquad(r,s,t\in I).$$
These conclusions include both orientations of the time interval and intervals containing positive and negative times. If $a=b$, all terms with $n\ge1$ vanish and $U(a,a)=I_H$; the derivative assertions then have no nontrivial interval on which to apply.

No separability hypothesis on $H$, invariant domain for an unbounded operator, differentiability of $\mathcal H$, spectral theorem or physical interpretation is required.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $z\in\mathbb C$. Define the finite-dimensional matrix exponential by
$$e^{zA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^kA^k}{k!},\qquad A^0=I_d.$$
Every matrix $B=(b_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ is bounded on $\mathbb C^d$: since $|x_j|\le\|x\|$ for the standard Euclidean norm, $\|Bx\|^2\le\sum_{i=1}^d(\sum_{j=1}^d|b_{ij}|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus its operator norm is defined by the unit-ball supremum in [[def-operator-norm]]. For $B,C\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $\|x\|\le1$, that definition and the bound $\|By\|\le\|B\|\|y\|$ give $\|BCx\|\le\|B\|\|Cx\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$; taking the supremum over the unit ball proves $\|BC\|\le\|B\|\|C\|$. Since $d\ge1$, the standard unit ball contains a unit vector and $\|I_d\|=1$. Hence $\|A^0\|=1$, while induction using submultiplicativity gives $\|A^k\|\le\|A\|^k$ for every $k\ge1$. The terms are therefore dominated by the convergent scalar exponential series $\sum_{k\ge0}(|z|\|A\|)^k/k!$; the displayed series converges absolutely in operator norm. The scalar exponential uses the convention $\exp z=\sum_{k\ge0}z^k/k!$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $A=A^*$ be an endomorphism of $\mathbb C^d$ with its standard complex inner product, and let $\hbar>0$. For real $t$, define $E_A(t):=e^{-itA/\hbar}$ by the finite-dimensional matrix exponential defined on this page. Then $E_A(t)$ is unitary, $E_A(t+s)=E_A(t)E_A(s)$ for all real $s,t$, and its operator-norm derivative is
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_A(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}AE_A(t)= -\frac{i}{\hbar}E_A(t)A.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\hbar>0$, $\omega=2\pi/T$, and let $H:\mathbb R\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be continuous, $T$-periodic, and Hermitian at every time. There are an orthonormal basis $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ and real numbers $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_d$ such that
$$U(T,0)v_j=e^{-iT\varepsilon_j/\hbar}v_j\qquad(1\le j\le d).$$
Define the Hermitian matrix $H_Fv_j=\varepsilon_jv_j$ and the quasienergy classes $\varepsilon_j+\hbar\omega\mathbb Z$. With $P(t):=U(t,0)e^{itH_F/\hbar}$, $P(t)$ is a $T$-periodic unitary matrix and
$$U(t,0)=P(t)e^{-itH_F/\hbar}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
The real representative $\varepsilon_j$ may be changed by any integer multiple of $\hbar\omega$ without changing its eigenphase; no preferred real branch is asserted.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be an arbitrary complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ a nonempty compact interval, $\hbar>0$, and $\mathcal H:I\to\mathcal B(H)$ a norm-continuous family of bounded self-adjoint operators. Put $A(t)=-i\mathcal H(t)/\hbar$ and $K=\sup_{t\in I}\|A(t)\|<\infty$. For every $s,t\in I$ define $U_0(t,s)=I_H$ and, recursively, the oriented Bochner integrals
$$U_{n+1}(t,s)=\int_s^t A(r)U_n(r,s)\,dr,$$
where $\int_s^t=-\int_t^s$ when $t<s$. Equivalently, for $s\le t$ these are the **latest-time-left** ordered integrals
$$U_n(t,s)=\Bigl(\frac{-i}{\hbar}\Bigr)^n\int_{s<t_1<\cdots<t_n<t}\mathcal H(t_n)\cdots\mathcal H(t_1)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n,$$
with the simplex integral meaning the nested integral with $t_n$ outermost and $t_1$ innermost. For arbitrary $s,t$ its unambiguous nested form is $\int_s^t dr_1\int_s^{r_1}dr_2\cdots\int_s^{r_{n-1}}dr_n\,A(r_1)\cdots A(r_n)$. Then:

(a) $\|U_n(t,s)\|\le(K|t-s|)^n/n!$ for all $n\ge0$ and all $s,t\in I$.

(b) $U(t,s)=\sum_{n\ge0}U_n(t,s)$ converges in operator norm uniformly on $I\times I$, is jointly norm-continuous, satisfies $U(s,s)=I_H$, and obeys $\|U(t,s)-I_H\|\le e^{K|t-s|}-1$. In particular all original forward-time convergence claims hold.

(c) For every $s,t\in I$,
$$U(t,s)=I_H-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_s^t\mathcal H(r)U(r,s)\,dr.$$
For fixed $s$ this is the unique continuous $\mathcal B(H)$-valued solution on $I$. More generally, the solution with initial value $C\in\mathcal B(H)$ at $s$ is $U(t,s)C$. For $a<b$, the operator-norm derivatives are
$$\partial_tU(t,s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\mathcal H(t)U(t,s),\qquad \partial_sU(t,s)=+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(t,s)\mathcal H(s),$$
with the corresponding one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. Therefore, for every $\psi\in H$, $U(t,s)\psi$ is strongly continuously differentiable in either variable and satisfies the same equations applied to $\psi$, with the common bounded-generator domain equal to all of $H$.

(d) Every $U(t,s)$ is unitary, $U(t,s)^*=U(s,t)=U(t,s)^{-1}$, and
$$U(t,s)U(s,r)=U(t,r)\qquad(r,s,t\in I).$$
These conclusions include both orientations of the time interval and intervals containing positive and negative times. If $a=b$, all terms with $n\ge1$ vanish and $U(a,a)=I_H$; the derivative assertions then have no nontrivial interval on which to apply.

No separability hypothesis on $H$, invariant domain for an unbounded operator, differentiability of $\mathcal H$, spectral theorem or physical interpretation is required.

derivations.claim: Take the constant zero Hamiltonian $H(t)=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Its propagator is $U(t,0)=1$ by [F3]. For each integer $n$, the Hermitian scalar $H_F^{(n)}=n\hbar\omega$ satisfies $e^{-iTH_F^{(n)}/\hbar}=e^{-i2\pi n}=1=U(T,0)$, so each is a valid logarithm of the same monodromy.

In dimension one the only eigenvalue of $H_F^{(n)}$, and hence its least quasienergy representative, is $n\hbar\omega$. It varies with $n$, while all representatives have the same class modulo $\hbar\omega$ by [F1, F2]. Therefore the period unitary determines a quasienergy class but no branch-independent least real quasienergy.
