citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). The **discrete
spectrum** $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ is the set of eigenvalues of $A$ that are
isolated points of $\sigma(A)$ and whose eigenspace is finite dimensional; the
**essential spectrum** is
$$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A):=\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A),$$
with $\sigma(A)$ as in [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]].

For $H=\{0\}$ use its unique PVM directly: the spectrum and both parts
are empty and every projection has rank zero. Below suppose $H\ne\{0\}$,
as required by the cited spectral theorem.

**Spectral-projection description, with proofs.** Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and write
$P_\varepsilon:=E((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$ for
$\varepsilon>0$.

Here rank means the algebraic dimension of the range when finite; rank
$=\infty$ means the range is not finite dimensional. The calculus
[[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]] gives the support facts:
$E(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, and every open interval about a
spectral point has nonzero projection. Projections on disjoint sets have
orthogonal ranges, and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$
[[def-projection-valued-measure]].

1. *$E(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection onto $\ker(A-\lambda)$.* If
   $x=E(\{\lambda\})x$, its scalar measure $E_x$ is supported on
   $\{\lambda\}$ by the projection identity. Thus
   $\int\mu^2dE_x=\lambda^2\|x\|^2<\infty$, so $x\in D(A)$, and
   $$\|(A-\lambda)x\|^2=\int|\mu-\lambda|^2dE_x=0.$$
   The domain and norm identities are supplied by the unbounded calculus and
   [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]]. Hence $Ax=\lambda x$.
   Conversely, for an eigenvector (or the zero vector) the same norm identity
   gives zero integral. On $\{|\mu-\lambda|\ge1/n\}$ this bounds the measure
   by $n^2$ times that zero integral; taking the countable union shows
   $E_x(\mathbb R\setminus\{\lambda\})=0$.
   Since $\|(I-E(\{\lambda\}))x\|^2$ equals this scalar measure,
   $E(\{\lambda\})x=x$.
2. *A finite-rank interval contains only finitely many spectral points.*
   If $P_\varepsilon$ has rank $r<\infty$ and its interval contained $r+1$
   distinct spectral points, choose disjoint small open intervals about those
   finitely many points, all contained in the given interval. Each has a
   nonzero projection by support. Choose one unit vector in each range.
   They are orthonormal vectors in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$, hence
   linearly independent (take inner products with each vector), contradicting
   its dimension $r$. Thus there are at most $r$ spectral points there.
   In particular any $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$ with such a finite-rank
   $P_\varepsilon$ is isolated: take a smaller interval around $\lambda$
   excluding the other finitely many points. For that interval the projection
   is $E(\{\lambda\})$ by support, is nonzero by support, and has finite rank
   since its range lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$. By item 1,
   $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity.
3. *The two rank characterizations.* If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$,
   an isolating interval has projection $E(\{\lambda\})$, of finite rank
   by item 1. Conversely, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and some
   $P_\varepsilon$ has finite rank, item 2 proves it discrete. Hence
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue and some }P_\varepsilon\text{ has finite rank}.$$
   If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, item 2 excludes every finite-rank
   interval. Conversely, if every $P_\varepsilon$ has infinite rank, each is
   nonzero, so support puts $\lambda$ in $\sigma(A)$, and the just-proved
   discrete characterization excludes it from $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$.
   Therefore
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon=\infty\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0.$$
4. *$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ is closed.* If $\lambda_n\in
   \sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda$, then for every
   $\varepsilon>0$ some $n$ has $(\lambda_n-\varepsilon/2, \lambda_n+
   \varepsilon/2)\subseteq(\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon)$, so
   $\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon\ge\operatorname{rank}P_{\varepsilon/2}^{(n)}
   =\infty$ and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ by item 3.

The closure conclusion is in $\mathbb R$, and also in $\mathbb C$ since
$\mathbb R$ is closed there. A spectral accumulation point has infinitely
many spectral points in every surrounding interval, so item 2 forces infinite
rank. An isolated eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity has its infinite-dimensional
eigenspace inside every interval range by item 1. Consequently an accumulation point of $\sigma(A)$ and an isolated eigenvalue of
infinite multiplicity both lie in $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, and $\sigma(A)$
is the disjoint union of $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ and
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and
let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$. Let
$E_A$ be its spectral projection-valued measure, let
$Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$, and define the associated form by
$$q_A[u]=\|(A+cI)^{1/2}u\|^2-c\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(A)).$$
Set $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when the
essential spectrum is empty. For each integer $k\ge1$, put
$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],$$
where the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty$. Then $\lambda_k(A)$ is the
$k$th eigenvalue below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity, when at least $k$
such eigenvalues exist; otherwise $\lambda_k(A)=\alpha$. If the inclusion
$Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ is compact in the form norm
$\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then $A$ has a complete orthonormal
eigenbasis; every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and the only possible
accumulation is at $+\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space whose inner product is linear in its first argument. Let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let $q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its first argument. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Assume $q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for some real $c\ge0$, and assume $Q$ is complete in the form norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$; this is the meaning of a closed semibounded form here.

For an integer $n\ge1$, let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\in Q$ be linearly independent. The exact input matrices are the Gram matrix $G$ and form matrix $A$ with entries

$$G_{ij}=\langle\phi_j,\phi_i\rangle,\qquad A_{ij}=q(\phi_j,\phi_i)\qquad(1\le i,j\le n).$$

For every nonzero coefficient vector $z\in\mathbb C^n$, $z^*Gz=\|\sum_jz_j\phi_j\|^2>0$, so $G$ is positive definite; the symmetry of $q$ makes $A$ Hermitian.

The procedure is:

1. Form $G$ and $A$ from the supplied vectors and form, using exact entries.
2. Diagonalize the positive definite Hermitian matrix $G$ and form its unique positive inverse square root $G^{-1/2}$. Set $B=G^{-1/2}AG^{-1/2}$.
3. Diagonalize the Hermitian matrix $B$, listing its real eigenvalues $\rho_1\le\cdots\le\rho_n$ with multiplicity and selecting an orthonormal eigenbasis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. For each $j$, set $c_j=G^{-1/2}y_j$ and return $(\rho_j,c_j)$.

Each returned vector satisfies $Ac_j=\rho_jGc_j$ and $c_j^*Gc_k=\delta_{jk}$. Repeated eigenvalues may return any orthonormal basis of the corresponding eigenspace. The procedure uses trial vectors in $Q$ and does not require them to lie in the operator domain of an associated self-adjoint operator. It operates on exact matrix entries: if quadrature or an approximate eigensolver supplies numerical data, this procedure alone supplies no error enclosure or certification for those approximations.

derivations.claim: Fix $V$ with $m=\dim V\ge k$. The algorithm in [F6] gives the eigenvalues $\rho_1\le\cdots\le\rho_m$ of the Hermitian form matrix relative to its positive Gram matrix and coefficient vectors $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. Their linear combinations $e_j:=\sum_{i=1}^m(c_j)_i\phi_i$ form an orthonormal eigenbasis of $V$: Gram normalization gives orthonormality, and the coefficient eigenvalue equation gives $q_A(e_j,e_i)=\rho_j\delta_{ij}$. For any $k$-dimensional $L\subseteq V$, the dimension formula forces $L\cap\operatorname{span}\{e_k,\ldots,e_m\}\ne\{0\}$; a unit vector in this intersection has form value at least $\rho_k$. The subspace $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}$ has supremum exactly $\rho_k$. Hence $\theta_k(V)=\rho_k$, the $k$th generalized Ritz eigenvalue.

Suppose $\lambda_k(A)<\alpha$. By [F2], $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_k=\lambda_k(A)$ are the first $k$ isolated eigenvalues below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity. Each corresponding eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F1]. If $x\ne0$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$, self-adjointness gives $\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle Ax,x\rangle=\langle x,Ax\rangle=\overline\lambda\|x\|^2$, so $\lambda$ is real. For $x\in\ker(A-\lambda_i I)$ and $y\in\ker(A-\lambda_j I)$ with $\lambda_i\ne\lambda_j$, this reality and self-adjointness give $\lambda_i\langle x,y\rangle=\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle=\lambda_j\langle x,y\rangle$, so the eigenspaces are orthogonal. Within each finite-dimensional eigenspace choose an orthonormal basis and take as many vectors as its multiplicity among $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$; concatenating these finite lists gives orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in D(A)$ with $Au_j=\lambda_j u_j$.

Every $k$-dimensional subspace of $V$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $Q(A)$, so the infimum defining $\theta_k(V)$ is over a subfamily of the one defining $\lambda_k(A)$. Therefore $\theta_k(V)\ge\lambda_k(A)$.

For $u=\sum_{j=1}^k c_ju_j$ with $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, orthonormality gives $\|u\|=1$, while [F3] gives $q_A(u_j,u_i)=\langle Au_j,u_i\rangle=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}$. Hence $q_A[u]=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2\le\lambda_k(A)$.

For nested $V_n$, every $k$-subspace of $V_n$ is a $k$-subspace of $V_{n+1}$; thus $\theta_k(V_{n+1})\le\theta_k(V_n)$. By step 2.1 this sequence is bounded below by $\lambda_k(A)$, so it has a limit at least $\lambda_k(A)$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and put $M=(\sum_{j=1}^k\|u_j\|_{Q(A)}^2)^{1/2}$. For each $j$, density gives an approximation from some $V_{n_j}$; taking $N=\max_jn_j$ and using nesting, choose all $w_j\in V_N$ with $\|w_j-u_j\|_{Q(A)}<\delta$. For coefficients $c$ with $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, put $w=\sum_jc_jw_j$ and $u=\sum_jc_ju_j$. Then $\|w-u\|_{Q(A)}\le\sqrt{k}\delta$ and $\|u\|=1$, so $\|w\|\ge1-\sqrt{k}\delta$; taking $\sqrt{k}\delta<1/2$ ensures the $w_j$ are linearly independent. Writing $a(x,y)=q_A(x,y)+(c+1)\langle x,y\rangle$, [F5] and $a[x]\ge\|x\|^2$ give $|q_A(x,y)|\le(c+2)\|x\|_{Q(A)}\|y\|_{Q(A)}$. Since $\|u\|_{Q(A)}\le M$ and $\|w\|_{Q(A)}\le M+\sqrt{k}\delta$, this yields $|q_A[w]-q_A[u]|\le(c+2)\sqrt{k}\delta(2M+\sqrt{k}\delta)$ uniformly in $c$. Also $|\|w\|^2-1|\le\sqrt{k}\delta(2+\sqrt{k}\delta)$ uniformly, so for sufficiently small $\delta$, $\|w\|^2\ge1/2$. The bound just proved for $q_A[w]-q_A[u]$ and the uniform bound $|q_A[u]|\le\max_j|\lambda_j|$ then show that $q_A[w]/\|w\|^2$ converges uniformly to $q_A[u]$. The values $q_A[u]=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2$ are at most $\lambda_k(A)$ by step 2.2; hence choose $\delta$ small enough that every such $w$ satisfies $q_A[w]/\|w\|^2\le\lambda_k(A)+\varepsilon$.

The span of $w_1,\ldots,w_k$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $V_N$, so step 3.2 gives $\theta_k(V_N)\le\lambda_k(A)+\varepsilon$. By monotonicity from step 3.1 the same upper bound holds for all $n\ge N$. As $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the limit in step 3.1 is at most $\lambda_k(A)$; combined with its lower bound from step 2.1 it equals $\lambda_k(A)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$
on the complex Hilbert space $H$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be $\Sigma$-measurable. Then the
operator $f(E)$ of [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]] is densely defined
and closed, and it is normal, in the sense $D(f(E))=D(f(E)^*)$ and equal norms for the operator and its adjoint; in particular $D(f(E))=D(\overline f(E))$ and
$\|f(E)x\|=\|\overline f(E)x\|$ for all such $x$. Moreover
$$\|f(E)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x,\qquad \langle x,f(E)x\rangle=\int\overline f\,dE_x\qquad(x\in D(f(E))),$$
and $(f(E))^*=\overline f(E)$; in particular $f(E)$ is self-adjoint whenever
$f$ takes real values. Finally, if $(g_n)$ are bounded $\Sigma$-measurable functions with
$|g_n|\le C|f|$ pointwise and $g_n\to f$ pointwise, then $g_n(E)x\to f(E)x$
for every $x\in D(f(E))$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the Borel product rule in [F3], $r=(x\mapsto x-\lambda)(T)u$. The norm identity in [F3] therefore gives $\|r\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|x-\lambda|^2\,d\mu_u(x)$. The measure $\mu_u$ has total mass one by [F2].

By [F3], $\mu_u$ is supported on $\sigma(T)$. Set $d=\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\sigma(T))$. For every $x\in\sigma(T)$, $|x-\lambda|\ge d$ by the definition of infimum, so step 1.1 yields $\|r\|^2\ge d^2\mu_u(\sigma(T))=d^2$. Both sides are nonnegative, hence $d\le\|r\|$.

Since $I-P_\Delta=E_T(\mathbb R\setminus\Delta)$, the PVM norm identity gives $\|(I-P_\Delta)u\|^2=\mu_u(\mathbb R\setminus\Delta)=\mu_u(\sigma(T)\setminus\Delta)$ by support from [F3]. On this set $|x-\lambda|\ge g$, so step 1.1 implies $\|r\|^2\ge g^2\|(I-P_\Delta)u\|^2$. Taking nonnegative square roots and dividing by $g>0$ proves the cluster estimate. If $\sigma(T)\setminus\Delta$ is empty, [F3] directly gives $\mu_u(\mathbb R\setminus\Delta)=0$, yielding the stated zero bound.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $s$ in the compact segment joining $t_0$ to $t$, put $W(\tau)=e^{i\tau T}$ and $U(s)=W((s-t_0)/\hbar)$, and define $w(s)=U(s)v(s)$. For $h$ with $s+h$ in the interval, the group law gives $\frac{w(s+h)-w(s)}h=U(s+h)\frac{v(s+h)-v(s)}h+U(s)\frac{W(h/\hbar)-I}{h}v(s)$. By [F1], $U$ is strongly continuous and unitary, the first term tends to $U(s)v'(s)$, and since $v(s)\in D(T)$ the second tends to $\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)$ by the derivative of $W$ at zero and the scalar chain rule. Thus $w$ is differentiable and $w'(s)=U(s)v'(s)+\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)Tv(s)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}U(s)r(s)$, after substituting $i\hbar v'=Tv+r$. The derivative is continuous because $v'$, $Tv$, and hence $r$ are continuous and $U$ is strongly continuous.

If $t\ge t_0$, apply [F3] on $[t_0,t]$; if $t<t_0$, apply it on $[t,t_0]$ and negate the resulting identity. In either case $w(t)-w(t_0)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_{t_0}^{t}U(s)r(s)\,ds$, using step 1.1. Then [F4] gives $\|w(t)-w(t_0)\|\le\frac1\hbar\int_{\min(t,t_0)}^{\max(t,t_0)}\|U(s)r(s)\|\,ds=\frac1\hbar\int_{\min(t,t_0)}^{\max(t,t_0)}\|r(s)\|\,ds$; the equality uses unitarity of $U(s)$. Since $w(t_0)=v(t_0)$ and $w(t)=U_T(t,t_0)^*v(t)$, unitarity also gives $\|w(t)-w(t_0)\|=\|v(t)-U_T(t,t_0)v(t_0)\|$. This is the required estimate, including $t=t_0$ and either time orientation.

Fix real parameters $m>0$, $\omega>0$, $\hbar>0$, put $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}>0$, and let $g_0,P,(g_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be the Hermite data of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$, so that $(g_n)$ is a complete orthonormal family by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-completeness]]. Define

$$D:L^2(\mathbb R,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R,dx),\qquad (Df)(x):=\ell^{-1/2}f(x/\ell),$$

and let $A$ be the self-adjoint diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the complete orthonormal family $(g_n)$ and the eigenvalues $\lambda_n=2n+1$, with the core $P$ and spectrum $\{2n+1:n\in\mathbb N\}$ ([[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]).

Then:

(a) $D$ is a linear isometry of $L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ onto $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$ with two-sided inverse $(D^{-1}g)(y)=\ell^{1/2}g(\ell y)$; the functions $\psi_n:=Dg_n$, $\psi_n(x)=\ell^{-1/2}g_n(x/\ell)$, form a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R,dx)$;

(b) the operator

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}:=\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\,DAD^{-1},\qquad D(H_{\mathrm{osc}}):=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R,dx):D^{-1}f\in D(A)\},$$

is self-adjoint, satisfies $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)\psi_n$ for every $n$, and has

$$D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\Bigl\{f:\sum_n\hbar^2\omega^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|c_n|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=\sum_n\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)c_n\psi_n,$$

where $c_n:=\langle D^{-1}f,g_n\rangle=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$; its spectrum is $\sigma(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=\{\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12):n\in\mathbb N\}$, its ground energy is $\hbar\omega/2$ with eigenvector $\psi_0$, and $\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}f,f\rangle\ge\frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\|f\|^2$ for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$;

(c) $D(P)=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_n\}$ is a core for $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and for every polynomial $p$ the function $f:=D(pg_0)$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R$ with

$$H_{\mathrm{osc}}f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}f''+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2f$$

pointwise on $\mathbb R$;

(d) for every $f\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ and every test function $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R}(H_{\mathrm{osc}}f)(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\varphi''(x)+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2\varphi(x)\Bigr)dx,$$

so $H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is the self-adjoint realization of the differential expression $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}+\frac{m\omega^2}{2}x^2$ in the weak sense; no identification of $D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$ with a separately defined maximal differential-operator domain is asserted.

All parameters enter as positive real numbers; no physical identification of $m,\omega,\hbar$ with measured quantities is made.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $A=A^*$ satisfy $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$, and set $Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$. Define the associated closed form by

$$q_A(u,v)=\langle(A+cI)^{1/2}u,(A+cI)^{1/2}v\rangle-c\langle u,v\rangle\qquad(u,v\in Q(A)).$$

Let $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ be the essential spectrum, the complement in $\sigma(A)$ of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, and put $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when this set is empty. For $k\ge1$, define

$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],\qquad q_A[u]=q_A(u,u),$$

where the infimum over an empty family is $+\infty$. For a finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V\subseteq Q(A)$ and $1\le k\le\dim V$, define its $k$th Ritz value

$$\theta_k(V)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq V\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u].$$

Then $\theta_k(V)\ge\lambda_k(A)$. If $V_1\subseteq V_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq Q(A)$ are finite-dimensional subspaces whose union is dense in $Q(A)$ in the form norm $\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then for every fixed $k$ with $\lambda_k(A)<\alpha$ the values $\theta_k(V_n)$, defined once $\dim V_n\ge k$, decrease to $\lambda_k(A)$, the $k$th isolated eigenvalue below the essential spectrum counted with multiplicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $A=A^*$ satisfy $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$, and set $Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$. Define the associated closed form by

$$q_A(u,v)=\langle(A+cI)^{1/2}u,(A+cI)^{1/2}v\rangle-c\langle u,v\rangle\qquad(u,v\in Q(A)).$$

Let $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ be the essential spectrum, the complement in $\sigma(A)$ of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, and put $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when this set is empty. For $k\ge1$, define

$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],\qquad q_A[u]=q_A(u,u),$$

where the infimum over an empty family is $+\infty$. For a finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V\subseteq Q(A)$ and $1\le k\le\dim V$, define its $k$th Ritz value

$$\theta_k(V)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq V\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u].$$

Then $\theta_k(V)\ge\lambda_k(A)$. If $V_1\subseteq V_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq Q(A)$ are finite-dimensional subspaces whose union is dense in $Q(A)$ in the form norm $\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then for every fixed $k$ with $\lambda_k(A)<\alpha$ the values $\theta_k(V_n)$, defined once $\dim V_n\ge k$, decrease to $\lambda_k(A)$, the $k$th isolated eigenvalue below the essential spectrum counted with multiplicity.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each $\psi_j\in D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$, the family is orthonormal, and $H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_j=E_j\psi_j$. By [F3], each $\psi_j$ lies in $Q(H_{\mathrm{osc}})=D(S)$. The product rule gives $S^2=H_{\mathrm{osc}}$ with $D(S^2)=D(H_{\mathrm{osc}})$; since $S$ is self-adjoint, for $i,j<n$ we have $q(\psi_j,\psi_i)=\langle S\psi_j,S\psi_i\rangle=\langle S^2\psi_j,\psi_i\rangle=\langle H_{\mathrm{osc}}\psi_j,\psi_i\rangle=E_j\delta_{ij}$. Thus the Gram matrix on $V_n$ is the identity and its form matrix is diagonal with entries $E_0,\ldots,E_{n-1}$.

Since $\hbar\omega>0$, $E_0<\cdots<E_{n-1}$. The generalized matrix eigenproblem therefore returns exactly these $n$ ordered Ritz values by [F4], and the oscillator eigenvalue equations in [F1] give $(H_{\mathrm{osc}}-E_jI)\psi_j=0$ for each $j<n$.
Hence this conforming Hermite trial space attains the first $n$ oscillator eigenvalues exactly and every corresponding continuum residual vanishes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $T=T^*$ be self-adjoint on $H$, with spectral projection-valued measure $E_T$. Let $u\in D(T)$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$, let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and define the residual $r=(T-\lambda I)u$. For a Borel set $\Delta\subseteq\mathbb R$, write $P_\Delta=E_T(\Delta)$. If $g>0$ and $|x-\lambda|\ge g$ for every $x\in\sigma(T)\setminus\Delta$, then

$$\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,\sigma(T))\le\|r\|,\qquad \|(I-P_\Delta)u\|\le\frac{\|r\|}{g},$$

where $\operatorname{dist}(\lambda,S)=\inf_{x\in S}|x-\lambda|$. If $\sigma(T)\setminus\Delta=\varnothing$, the second conclusion is $\|(I-P_\Delta)u\|=0$.

derivations.claim: On $H=\mathbb C^2$ with its standard inner product, set $T=\operatorname{diag}(0,100)$ on all of $H$, $u=(0,1)$, and $\lambda=100$. Then $T$ is self-adjoint and bounded below, $\|u\|=1$, $\sigma(T)=\{0,100\}$, the lowest eigenvalue is $E_0=0$, and $(T-100I)u=0$.

The ground eigenspace is $\ker T=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0)\}$, while $u=(0,1)$ is orthogonal to it and $\lambda=100\ne E_0$. Thus the zero residual verifies a spectral point, as in [F1], but refutes the asserted ground-state label.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain and
$-i\partial_{x_j}$ is defined by conjugating that multiplication operator by
the unitary Fourier transform. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and the finite-mode Fock conventions of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Let $U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ obey
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
where $^*$ is conjugate transpose and $^T$ is transpose without conjugation.
On the finite Hermite core define
$$a'_j=\sum_k(U_{jk}a_k+V_{jk}a_k^*).$$
Then the $a'_j$ satisfy $[a'_j,(a'_k)^*]=\delta_{jk}I$ and
$[a'_j,a'_k]=0$ on that core. The real matrix
$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\ \operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$
is symplectic in grouped coordinate order $(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$.
There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order. The transformed vacuum
$M\Omega$ has finite mean number
$$\sum_j\|a_jM\Omega\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(VV^*).$$
No infinite-mode implementability assertion is made.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Q^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ with $a,b,c,d\in\mathbb Q$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. For a rational power $q$, dimension powers mean $[X]^q=\ell^{qa}\tau^{qb}\mu^{qc}\vartheta^{qd}$ when $[X]=\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$. Rational exponents include the half-integer wave-function dimensions in clause (d); the integer-exponent dimensions form the subgroup $\mathbb Z^4$. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

For extensions using temperature, adjoin an independent dimension symbol $\Theta$: the enlarged group is $\mathbb Q^4\times\mathbb Q$, written $\ell^a\tau^b\mu^c\vartheta^d\Theta^e$, with the same componentwise rules. The preceding group embeds by $e=0$, so all previously assigned dimensions are preserved. Temperature has dimension $\Theta$, the Boltzmann constant has dimension $\mu\ell^2\tau^{-2}\Theta^{-1}$, and entropy in joules per kelvin has that same dimension; a dimensionless entropy remains dimensionless. This convention does not assign a temperature or an entropy to any system.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres. In the temperature extension the reference unit of $\Theta$ is the kelvin (K), so the general reference unit gains a factor $\mathrm K^e$.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. These are real scalar constants with dimensions and units $[h]=[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (J s), $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (m s$^{-1}$), and $[e]=\vartheta$ (C). The vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is a positive real scalar that is experimentally determined in the current SI, with $[\mu_{0}]=\mu\ell\vartheta^{-2}$ (N A$^{-2}$ = H m$^{-1}$); $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$ is a positive real scalar with $[\varepsilon_{0}]=\mu^{-1}\ell^{-3}\tau^{2}\vartheta^{2}$ (F m$^{-1}$). These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

**(d) Dimensions and types of the framework's quantities.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities.

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: in the ordinary continuous-field regime, fix an integer $d\ge1$, an open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and an open time interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$. A **probability current density** is a declared continuous map $j:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^d$, whose spatial components have dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$ and reference unit $\mathrm m^{1-d}\mathrm s^{-1}$. At fixed time it is a spatial vector field; its signed normal component is read as probability transported per unit spatial $(d-1)$-area and time. Explicitly, for a flat face $S=\{x:x_k=a,\ a_i\le x_i\le b_i\ (i\ne k)\}\subset\Omega$, with $a_i<b_i$ and chosen normal $n=\epsilon e_k$, $\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, define its **signed probability flux** at $t\in I$ as $\Phi_S(t):=\epsilon\int_{\prod_{i\ne k}[a_i,b_i]}j_k(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},a,x_{k+1},\ldots,x_d,t)\prod_{i\ne k}dx_i$. Here $e_k$ is the $k$th coordinate unit vector and the integral uses $(d-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure; for $d=1$ this means $\Phi_{\{a\}}(t)=\epsilon j(a,t)$. The flux has dimension $\tau^{-1}$ and unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$; positive sign means transport in the chosen normal direction. Fluxes through curved surfaces, or currents with weaker regularity, require separately specified surface measures or traces. This fixes the quantity type and flux convention; it supplies neither a current associated to an arbitrary $L^2$ state nor a conservation or detector law. Each dynamical model supplies its current construction and balance hypotheses.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Adopt the state postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) and the ideal conditional-measurement postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-ideal-conditional-measurement]] (P3) for the declared system, whose state space is $D(H)$ for the assigned nonzero separable complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis of the cited mathematics. Here the projective outcome law is supplied directly by P3(ii), and the finite-effect law by P2(iv); no spectral PVM is constructed from an assigned self-adjoint observable. The additional Axiom of Choice required by P2(ii) for that construction is therefore not used here. The following vocabulary is used by this page.

**(a) Declared ideal sharp measurement.** A **declared ideal sharp measurement** of the system is a finite or countably infinite family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ of bounded orthogonal projections on $H$ ([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]) that are **mutually orthogonal**, $P_{a}P_{b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and whose **strong sum** is the identity,
$$\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}x=x\qquad(x\in H).$$
The index $a$ is the **outcome label** and the family $(P_{a})_{a\in A}$ is the **outcome structure** of the declared measurement; it is part of the declared apparatus model, not a quantity computed from the state. This is clause (i) of P3.

**(b) The Lueders instrument of a declared ideal sharp measurement.** For a preparation $\rho$ the **outcome probabilities** are
$$p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_{a})\ge0,\qquad \sum_{a}p_{a}=1,$$
and for a pure preparation of the unit ray $[\psi]$ they are $p_{a}=\|P_{a}\psi\|^{2}$ (clause (ii) of P3). If $p_{a}>0$ the **conditional state** after the outcome $a$ is the selective Lueders update
$$\rho_{a}:=\frac{P_{a}\rho P_{a}}{p_{a}};$$
it is a state with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{a}P_{a})=1$ and $P_{a}\rho_{a}P_{a}=\rho_{a}$ ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], clause (iii) of P3). If the outcomes are recorded but not selected, the **discarded-outcome state** is
$$\Phi(\rho):=\sum_{a\in A}P_{a}\rho P_{a},$$
the trace-norm convergent series of [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]]; it is a state with $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{a:p_{a}>0}p_{a}\rho_{a}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\Phi(\rho)P_{a})=p_{a}$ (clause (iv) of P3).

**(c) Declared ideal filter.** A **declared ideal filter** is a declared ideal sharp measurement with exactly two outcomes $a=1,2$: the filter **passes** the component in the range of $P_{1}$ and **blocks** the component in the range of $P_{2}=I-P_{1}$. Repeated use of the filter in series means the sequential application of the conditional updates of clause (b).

**(d) Declared instrument.** A **declared finite or countable instrument** for an outcome set $A$ consists of a finite or countable family $(M_{a,r})_{\substack{a\in A\\r\in R_{a}}}$ of bounded operators on $H$ with
$$\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r}=I$$
in the strong sense ([[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]]), the **effects**
$$F_{a}:=\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}^{*}M_{a,r},$$
where each subseries converges strongly, independently of its enumeration. An **effect** on general $H$ is a bounded self-adjoint operator $F$ with $0\le\langle Fx,x\rangle\le\|x\|^2$ for all $x\in H$; the **order** $F\le G$ means $\langle(G-F)x,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x$. Here $\langle F_a x,x\rangle=\sum_r\|M_{a,r}x\|^2\le\|x\|^2$, so $0\le F_a\le I$. In particular the positive partial sums $S_N$ of any subseries are contractions and have convergent quadratic forms. For a positive tail $D=S_N-S_m$, expanding $\langle D(x+ty),x+ty\rangle\ge0$ with $t=-\langle Dx,y\rangle/\langle Dy,y\rangle$ when $\langle Dy,y\rangle>0$, and varying $t\in\mathbb C$ when $\langle Dy,y\rangle=0$, gives $|\langle Dx,y\rangle|^2\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\langle Dy,y\rangle$. Since $0\le D\le I$, taking $y=Dx$ yields $\|Dx\|^4\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\langle D(Dx),Dx\rangle\le\langle Dx,x\rangle\|Dx\|^2$, hence $\|Dx\|^2\le\langle Dx,x\rangle$ (also when $Dx=0$). The partial sums therefore converge on every $x$ and their limit defines $F_a$. The **outcome probabilities** are $p_{a}:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_{a})$. For finite $A$ this is clause (iv) of P2, even if an outcome has countably many Kraus operators. For countably infinite $A$ outside the projective case of (a)-(b), we explicitly adopt this same probability law as an additional assumption of the declared apparatus model; P2(iv) does not state that extension. The Kraus-normalization lemma establishes that these numbers are nonnegative and sum to one, not that they describe physical outcomes. The model also explicitly stipulates the **conditional updates**
$$\rho\longmapsto\frac{1}{p_{a}}\sum_{r\in R_{a}}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}\qquad(p_{a}>0),$$
and the **discarded-outcome map** $\rho\mapsto\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}\rho M_{a,r}^{*}$. These update series converge in trace norm by the Kraus-normalization lemma, with grouping permitted by absolute trace-norm convergence for positive inputs. Their interpretation as post-measurement states is part of the instrument declaration; P3 supplies that interpretation only for its projective Lueders case. The family $(M_{a,r})$, called the **Kraus family** of the instrument, is part of the declared apparatus model. The effects $(F_{a})$ alone do not determine the conditional updates: distinct normalized Kraus families can share the same effects while defining different updates ([[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]] clause (d); clause (v) of P3). More generally, on a specified measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$, a **declared abstract instrument** is a map $J:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal S_{1}(H))$ into bounded complex-linear maps of trace-class operators satisfying: each $J_B$ is completely positive, meaning every finite matrix amplification preserves positive trace-class block operators; for disjoint $B_n$ with union $B$, $J_B(T)=\sum_nJ_{B_n}(T)$ in trace norm for every trace-class $T$; and $J_X$ preserves trace. Its outcome effect $F_B$ is the unique effect with $\operatorname{tr}(J_B(T))=\operatorname{tr}(TF_B)$, its probability is $p(B)=\operatorname{tr}(J_B(\rho))$, and its conditional state is $J_B(\rho)/p(B)$ only when $p(B)>0$. The interpretation of these formulas as an outcome law and a post-measurement state is likewise an explicitly adopted assumption of this abstract apparatus model. [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]] establishes the effect duality, countably additive normalization and well-definedness of the positive-probability conditional state, not this physical interpretation. The Kraus case above is a concrete instance on $(A,2^A)$, with $J_B(T)=\sum_{a\in B,r}M_{a,r}TM_{a,r}^*$ in trace norm. This declaration does not assert that every abstract instrument has a Kraus representation or that a laboratory apparatus realizes it.

**(e) Declaration discipline.** A model of an apparatus that is used to predict post-measurement states must declare both an outcome structure (effects) and an update rule; the outcome law of P2 alone does not supply the update, and the update is not a mathematical consequence of the effects. The special case in which the Kraus family consists of the projections $P_{a}$ themselves (with a single $r$ per outcome) is the Lueders instrument of clauses (a)-(b). The claim that a concrete laboratory device realizes a particular declared measurement, filter or instrument is a physical identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 ([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]), not a consequence of this definition.

**(f) Limits.** Declared ideal sharp measurements are idealizations of apparatus that are idealized as repeatable and projection-valued; the framework does not assert that every apparatus, or any particular apparatus, is of this form (clause (v) of P3). The following are outside the declared class and require their own models: a measurement of an exact value of a quantity whose spectrum is continuous (no normalization of a delta symbol is intended; clauses (iii) of P2 and (v) of P3); a photon-absorption or other destructive detector, whose declared instrument need not leave an outgoing state of the same form (clause (v) of P3); and a unitary system-apparatus interaction, which by itself produces conditional correlations without selecting a unique recorded outcome or a preferred outcome family (clause (v) of P3).

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(c) read the projective rules of P3, and the finite-outcome law in (d) reads P2(iv). Clause (d) additionally stipulates the countably infinite nonprojective outcome law, generalized conditional and discarded-outcome updates, and abstract-instrument law and updates as assumptions of each declared apparatus model, as permitted by P3(v)'s requirement for separate models outside its projective class. These are not consequences of P1-P3 alone. Clauses (e)-(f) fix the declaration discipline and limits used by the page's later items. The cited mathematical items ([[lem-nrqm-measurement-selective-luders-update]], [[lem-nrqm-measurement-nonselective-luders-map]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-finite-effects-and-instruments]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-countable-kraus-normalization]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-general-trace-class-instrument-and-effect-duality]]) are conditional mathematics about the displayed formulas; no physical process, outcome uniqueness or empirical fact is deduced here.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
**(a) Finite oscillator-mode data.** Choose an integer $M\ge1$, the one-particle mode space $\mathfrak h=\mathbb C^M$ with a declared orthonormal mode basis $e_1,\ldots,e_M$, and the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}\mathfrak h^{\otimes_s n}$ with vacuum $\Omega$. Here $\mathfrak h^{\otimes_s n}$ is the range of the orthogonal symmetrizer in the completed $n$-fold Hilbert tensor product, with the zero-particle sector $\mathbb C\Omega$. For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_M)\in\mathbb N_0^M$, let $|\mathbf n\rangle$ be the normalized occupation vector. Define the finite-particle subspace $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}:=\{\psi=(\psi^{(n)})_{n\ge0}\in\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h):\psi^{(n)}=0\text{ for all but finitely many }n\}=\operatorname{span}\{|\mathbf n\rangle:\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^M\}$. The mode operators are dimensionless and on $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$ satisfy $a_j|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j}|\mathbf n-\mathbf e_j\rangle$ and $a_j^*|\mathbf n\rangle=\sqrt{n_j+1}|\mathbf n+\mathbf e_j\rangle$, with the first expression zero if $n_j=0$. The Fock space is infinite-dimensional for each $M\ge1$; no particle-number cutoff or tensor factorization of an individual photon into position and spin is part of this assignment.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and countable choice wherever the finite-mode Fock, quadrature, and implementability suppliers require them. These are mathematical hypotheses of the assignment, not physical postulates.

**Mode-frequency data.** Use $\hbar>0$ for the reduced Planck constant in joule-seconds under the framework's SI convention. For each selected mode $j$, choose a positive angular frequency $\omega_j>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$; the assigned one-quantum energy scale is $\hbar\omega_j$ joules. These are parameters of the finite-mode model, not measured frequencies.

**(b) Finite atom and dipole data.** Choose $d\ge1$, an atomic Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A=\mathbb C^d$, a Hermitian atomic energy matrix $H_A$ in joules, Hermitian compressed dipole matrices $D_j$ in coulomb-metres, and real mode field scales $\mathcal E_j$ in volts per metre. The matrix elements of $G_j:=\mathcal E_jD_j/\hbar$ have units seconds$^{-1}$, where $\hbar>0$ is retained in joule-seconds. The finite matrices and scales are chosen model data. If they are obtained by compressing a larger atomic model, that compression's error is a separate model input and is not bounded here.

Write $\mathcal H_{AF}:=\mathcal H_A\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)$ for the completed ordered Hilbert tensor product, with the atom factor first, and let $\kappa:\mathcal H_A\odot\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)\to\mathcal H_{AF}$ be the canonical isometric inclusion. Let $I_A$ and $I_F$ denote the identity operators on $\mathcal H_A$ and $\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)$. Let $\mathcal D_0:=\kappa[\mathcal H_A\odot\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}]\subseteq\mathcal H_{AF}$ be the algebraic product domain. If $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ is the standard orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_A=\mathbb C^d$, then the vectors $\kappa(f_\alpha\otimes|\mathbf n\rangle)$ form a complete orthonormal basis by the Hilbert tensor product and finite-mode Fock product-basis conclusions for this ordered pair. Hence $\mathcal D_0$ is dense in $\mathcal H_{AF}$.

The assigned dipole interaction is the linear operator $V_{\mathrm{dip}}:\mathcal D_0\to\mathcal H_{AF}$ defined on elementary tensors by $V_{\mathrm{dip}}(\kappa(\phi\otimes\psi)):=-\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathcal E_j\kappa(D_j\phi\otimes(a_j+a_j^*)\psi)$ for $\phi\in\mathcal H_A$ and $\psi\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$, and extended linearly to $\mathcal D_0$. Each map $(\phi,\psi)\mapsto\kappa(D_j\phi\otimes(a_j+a_j^*)\psi)$ is bilinear, so it descends to the algebraic tensor product; $a_j,a_j^*$ preserve $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$. Each summand has units joules. This is the declared algebraic product domain of the finite-core expression; no graph-core assertion for a closed realization is made. The assignment does not assert that an arbitrary such sum has a self-adjoint realization or generates an evolution; any dynamical use must state and justify its operator domain. The Jaynes–Cummings supplier below gives one specific self-adjoint direct-sum realization.

**(c) Mode transformations.** A finite mode-coordinate change is assigned only when its finite Bogoliubov matrices satisfy the exact hypotheses of the finite-mode implementability statement: for $U,V\in M_M(\mathbb C)$, $UU^*-VV^*=I_M$ and $UV^T=VU^T$. The resulting unitary acts on this finite-mode Fock space. The statement assumes the Axiom of Choice; this is a mathematical assumption, not a physical law. No infinite-mode implementability follows.

**(d) Detector outcome models.** A detector's outcome space $(X,\Sigma)$ and POVM $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{AF})$ are declared model data: each $E(B)$ is bounded and positive, $E(X)=I$, and $E$ is countably additive in the weak operator topology. For a density operator $\rho$ on $\mathcal H_{AF}$ (a positive trace-class operator of trace one), the assigned probability is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ under the framework's stated measurement convention. An ideal number-resolving model on the field has outcomes $\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^M$ and effects $I_A\otimes|\mathbf n\rangle\langle\mathbf n|$; these are bounded tensor maps and projections on $\mathcal H_{AF}$ by the tensor-map adjoint and composition rules. For ideal homodyne of mode $j$ at phase $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $R_j(\theta)|\mathbf n\rangle=e^{i\theta n_j}|\mathbf n\rangle$ and $X_{j,\theta}:=\hbar^{-1/2}R_j(\theta)Q_jR_j(\theta)^*$, where $\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^M)\to L^2(\mathbb R^M)$ is the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary and $Q_j:=\mathcal U^{-1}M_{\sqrt\hbar x_j}\mathcal U$. Here $M_{\sqrt\hbar x_j}$ multiplies by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ on its maximal domain $\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^M):x_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^M)\}$. Thus $X_{j,\theta}$ is self-adjoint by unitary conjugation and on $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{fin}}$ equals $(e^{-i\theta}a_j+e^{i\theta}a_j^*)/\sqrt2$. Its spectral PVM $B\mapsto I_A\otimes\mathbf1_B(X_{j,\theta})$ is defined by the same bounded tensor maps and is the ideal homodyne POVM on the product space. These are ideal outcome assignments, not claims about a detector's optical local oscillator, efficiency, bandwidth, calibration or state update. If a state update or a finite detector environment is modeled, declare its instrument separately. The finite product-preparation/unitary/partial-trace assignment described by the finite open-system postulate is for $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$ with a fixed environment state and a declared joint unitary; it may be used for a separately selected finite-dimensional subsystem but does not cover the Fock field. A reduced-dynamics model involving the Fock field must separately specify a trace-class joint preparation and joint unitary on $\mathcal H_{AF}$. The trace-class partial trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h)}:\mathcal S_1(\mathcal H_{AF})\to\mathcal S_1(\mathcal H_A)$ is defined for arbitrary Hilbert factors, is trace-norm contractive, and preserves positivity and trace by the mathematical partial-trace result listed below. No Fock-field reduced dynamics or reservoir limit is adopted here.

**(e) Optional approximation regimes.** A long-wavelength identification with a spatial electromagnetic mode requires a separately declared atomic extent $L$ and wave number $k_j$ and the scale regime $k_jL\ll1$; no error bound is supplied. A rotating-wave choice keeps only the excitation-exchange terms. For a two-level transition of frequency $\omega_0$ coupled to a mode of frequency $\omega$, its usual low-excitation regime is $|g|\sqrt{n+1}\ll\omega,\omega_0$ on the declared photon-number sectors; it is not uniform over the full Fock space. A Markov/GKSL approximation is another separate model choice and must state its rates, reservoir correlation time $\tau_B$, system time scale $\tau_S$, and regime $\tau_B\ll\tau_S$. None of these optional approximations is derived from this assignment or from the finite system-environment model.

The matrix elements of $G_j:=\mathcal E_jD_j/\hbar$ have units seconds$^{-1}$, where $\hbar>0$ is retained in joule-seconds. The finite matrices and scales are chosen model data. If they are obtained by compressing a larger atomic model, that compression's error is a separate model input and is not bounded here.

The Jaynes–Cummings supplier below gives one specific self-adjoint direct-sum realization.

**(c) Mode transformations.** A finite mode-coordinate change is assigned only when its finite Bogoliubov matrices satisfy the exact hypotheses of the finite-mode implementability statement: for $U,V\in M_M(\mathbb C)$, $UU^*-VV^*=I_M$ and $UV^T=VU^T$. The resulting unitary acts on this finite-mode Fock space. The statement assumes the Axiom of Choice; this is a mathematical assumption, not a physical law. No infinite-mode implementability follows.

**(d) Detector outcome models.** A detector's outcome space $(X,\Sigma)$ and POVM $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H_A\otimes\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h))$ are declared model data: each $E(B)$ is bounded and positive, $E(X)=I$, and $E$ is countably additive in the weak operator topology. Thus $X_{j,\theta}$ is self-adjoint by unitary conjugation and on the finite-particle core equals $(e^{-i\theta}a_j+e^{i\theta}a_j^*)/\sqrt2$. Its spectral PVM $B\mapsto I_A\otimes\mathbf1_B(X_{j,\theta})$ is the ideal homodyne POVM on the product space. These are ideal outcome assignments, not claims about a detector's optical local oscillator, efficiency, bandwidth, calibration or state update. If a state update or a finite detector environment is modeled, declare its instrument separately; the optional finite product-preparation/unitary/partial-trace assignment has the exact scope of the finite open-system postulate and implies no reservoir limit.

**(e) Optional approximation regimes.** A long-wavelength identification with a spatial electromagnetic mode requires a separately declared atomic extent $L$ and wave number $k_j$ and the scale regime $k_jL\ll1$; no error bound is supplied. A rotating-wave choice keeps only the excitation-exchange terms. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathbb H:=\mathbb C$ with its standard inner product (linear in the first
argument), let $F(\mathbb C)$ be its Fock space as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], let
$e_n\in F(\mathbb C)$ be the unit vector supported in coordinate $n$ (so
$(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $F(\mathbb C)$),
let $N$ be the number operator and let $A_\pm(1)$ be the maximal creation and
annihilation operators of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]] for the vector
$1\in\mathbb C$. Then:

(a) *oscillator coefficients*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$A_+(1)e_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1},\qquad A_-(1)e_n=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\ (n\ge1),\qquad A_-(1)e_0=0;$$

(b) *coherent vectors*: for every $z\in\mathbb C$ the series
$$\psi_z:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\frac{z^n}{\sqrt{n!}}\,e_n$$
converges absolutely in $F(\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]]),
$\|\psi_z\|=1$, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ with
$$A_-(1)\psi_z=z\,\psi_z,$$
and for all $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w};$$

(c) *number law*: for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
$$\bigl|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\frac{|z|^{2n}}{n!},$$
and $\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=1$.

The numbers in (c) are squared moduli of overlaps of unit vectors; identifying
them with outcome probabilities of a number measurement requires a separately
adopted measurement postulate, and no such physical claim is made here.
