citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable smooth $n$-manifold without boundary. In a smooth chart $x=(x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, a smooth density is written $\phi_x(x)|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$. On a coordinate change $y=\psi(x)$ its coefficient transforms by
$$ \phi_y(y)=\phi_x(\psi^{-1}(y))\,|\det D\psi^{-1}(y)|. $$
A compactly supported smooth density is one whose support is compact in $M$. Give their space $\mathcal D(M;|\Lambda^nT^*M|)$ the locally convex test-density topology obtained from the usual fixed-compact derivative seminorms in charts and the corresponding LF inductive limit. A scalar distribution on $M$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on this test-density space, with bilinear pairing $\langle u,\omega\rangle$. Write $\mathcal D'(M)$ for these distributions and $\mathcal E'(M)$ for those with compact support. On a product manifold use the same definition with product densities. In a chart this definition is the ordinary distribution definition on an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$; the displayed Jacobian law is the coordinate compatibility condition.

Give $C^\infty(\Omega)$ the topology generated by $q_{K,m}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_K|\partial^\alpha f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $m\ge0$. A compactly supported distribution $u$ has a unique continuous complex-linear extension to this space, given by
$$\widetilde u(f)=u(\chi f),$$
where $\chi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is any cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}u$. The result is independent of $\chi$. The extension vanishes on every smooth function zero near the support. No Hahn–Banach or choice axiom is needed.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. Here $g$ is a smooth symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each tangent space with one negative and $n-1$ positive directions; in charts its signature is $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in each tangent space. A time orientation selects one of the two components of $\{v\ne0:g(v,v)<0\}$ as future. A tangent vector is causal when $g(v,v)\le0$, and is future or past causal when it belongs to the closure of the selected future or past timelike cone. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A nonzero cotangent vector is future or past causal, or future or past null, when its metric dual under $g^{-1}$ has the corresponding tangent property.

Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. It is coordinate-independent: under $y=\psi(x)$, $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det g_y|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det g_x|^{1/2}$, the density transformation law. Functional-kernel pairings and contractions on this page use $\mu_g$ in each integrated variable; no physical units are assigned.

For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. Two nonzero future-null cotangent vectors $(p,\xi)$ and $(q,\zeta)$ are related, written $(p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta)$, if $p=q$ and $\zeta=\xi$, or if there are a nonconstant future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic $\gamma:I\to M$, parameters $s,t\in I$ in either order, and a common scale $\lambda>0$ such that
$$p=\gamma(s),\qquad q=\gamma(t),\qquad \xi=\lambda g_p(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot),\qquad \zeta=\lambda g_q(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot).$$
These covectors are the metric-dual tangents to that geodesic and are related by induced covector parallel transport. There is no requirement $s\le t$: the future-frequency choice concerns the covectors, not an ordering of the two base points. The coincident case includes every nonzero future-null covector with $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. Write $W^{\mathsf T}=\tau^*W$ for the pullback by $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$. A fixed antisymmetric part means the equality $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for one specified distribution $E$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

For a distribution $u$ on a smooth manifold, the chartwise rapid-decay definition of its wavefront set is independent of the chart: if $y=\psi(x)$, its covector coordinates satisfy $\eta=(D\psi(x))^{-T}\xi$. The resulting $\operatorname{WF}(u)$ is closed and conic in $T^*M\setminus0$. For distributions $u,v$ and a smooth diffeomorphism $\psi$, one has $\operatorname{WF}(u+v)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup\operatorname{WF}(v)$ and $\operatorname{WF}(\psi^*u)=\psi^*\operatorname{WF}(u)$. Finally, $\operatorname{WF}(u)=\varnothing$ exactly when $u$ is represented by a smooth scalar function in every chart.

A complex-linear functional $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is a distribution if and only if, for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, there are an integer $m_K\ge0$ and a finite constant $C_K\ge0$ such that
$$|u(\varphi)|\le C_K p_{m_K}(\varphi)\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D_K).$$
The quantifiers are $\forall K\,\exists(m_K,C_K)$; no simultaneous selection of witnesses is asserted or needed. The equivalence holds in ZF.

Assume Countable Choice.  Let $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ have compact
support, let $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'$ be its canonical extension, and let
$\chi\in\mathcal D$ equal one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}v$.
Then $\mathcal F\widetilde v$ is the regular tempered distribution represented
by

$$V(\xi)=\left\langle v_x,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\right\rangle.$$

The function $V$ is independent of $\chi$, is smooth, and for every
multi-index $\alpha$ there are $C_\alpha,m_\alpha$ with
$|\partial^\alpha V(\xi)|\leq C_\alpha(1+|\xi|)^{m_\alpha}$.  Consequently
multiplication by $V$ is continuous on $\mathcal S$ and, by transpose, on
$\mathcal S'$ in both dual topologies.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

For $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, the map

$$x\longmapsto T_x\varphi,\qquad (T_x\varphi)(y)=\varphi(x-y),$$

is $C^\infty$ as a map from $\mathbb R^n$ to Schwartz space, with
$\partial_x^\gamma T_x\varphi=T_x(\partial^\gamma\varphi)$.  This clause holds
in ZF.

Assume Countable Choice for the following integral clause.  Let $r\geq1$ and
let $H:\mathbb R^r\to\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ be continuous in every Schwartz
seminorm.  Suppose each $\partial_y^\beta H(t,y)$ is jointly measurable and,
for every $\alpha,\beta$, there is $g_{\alpha\beta}\in L^1(\mathbb R^r)$ such
that

$$p_{\alpha\beta}(H(t))\leq g_{\alpha\beta}(t)$$

for almost every $t$.  Then
$G(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^r}H(t,y)\,dt$ belongs to $\mathcal S$, derivatives pass
under the integral, and every $u\in\mathcal S'$ satisfies

$$\left\langle u,\int H(t)\,dt\right\rangle =\int\langle u,H(t)\rangle\,dt.$$

All integrals in this clause are Lebesgue integrals.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $v\in\mathcal D'(V)$ the tensor candidate is a distribution on $U\times V$, uniquely determined by $(u\otimes v)(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$. Its two iterated pairing orders agree, and $\operatorname{supp}(u\otimes v)=\operatorname{supp}u\times\operatorname{supp}v$. Three-factor pairings associate. Moreover $\partial_x^\alpha(u\otimes v)=(\partial^\alpha u)\otimes v$ and $\partial_y^\beta(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(\partial^\beta v)$. All claims hold in ZF.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

derivations.claim: In a pair of coordinate charts, localize compactly supported $u$ and $v$. By [F5], the localized tensor transform factors as $\widehat{u\otimes v}(\xi,\zeta)=\widehat u(\xi)\widehat v(\zeta)$. If both covectors are regular, each factor decreases faster than every power on a conic neighborhood; if only one is singular, the other factor still supplies rapid decay in that block. The finite-order bounds [F3] control the remaining factor polynomially. Thus $\operatorname{WF}(u\otimes v)\subseteq(\operatorname{WF}(u)\times\operatorname{WF}(v))\cup(\operatorname{WF}(u)\times0_M)\cup(0_M\times\operatorname{WF}(v))$. Finite chart covers and cutoffs [F7] give the same inclusion on manifolds.

For a compactly supported test density $\omega$ on $N$, localize $u$ by a cutoff equal to one near $f(\operatorname{supp}\omega)$ and set $T_\omega(\eta):=\int_N e^{2\pi i f(x)\cdot\eta}\omega(x)$. In coordinates define $\langle f^*u,\omega\rangle=\int\widehat u(\eta)T_\omega(\eta)\,d\eta$, where $m=\dim M$. The conormal condition and compactness give a cone $V$ around the directions where $df_x^T\eta$ can vanish, disjoint from the localized wavefront directions of $u$. On $V$, $\widehat u$ is rapidly decreasing and $T_\omega$ is bounded by $\int|\omega|$. On the complementary cone, $|df_x^T\eta|\ge c|\eta|$ on $\operatorname{supp}\omega$ for some $c>0$; repeated integration by parts with the operator $(df_x^T\eta\cdot\nabla_x)/(2\pi i|df_x^T\eta|^2)$ gives $|T_\omega(\eta)|\le C_N(1+|\eta|)^{-N}$ for every $N$. Combining these bounds with [F3] makes the integral absolutely convergent and bounded by finitely many seminorms of $\omega$, so it defines a distribution. For smooth $u$, [F4] and [F6] identify the integral with $\int_Nu(f(x))\omega(x)$. To obtain the wavefront estimate, localize the output at $x_0$ and Fourier transform in $x$; the coefficient is the same double integral with phase $2\pi(f(x)\cdot\eta-x\cdot\xi)$, whose stationary equation is $\xi=df_x^T\eta$. If $(x_0,\xi_0)$ is outside the displayed pullback of $\operatorname{WF}(u)$, choose smaller cones so that either the stationary $\eta$ lies in a regular cone of $u$, or the phase gradient is bounded below by $c(|\eta|+|\xi|)$. The first region is controlled by rapid decay of $\widehat u$; in the second, repeated integration by parts gives arbitrary powers of decay in $|\xi|+|\eta|$. Integrating the polynomial bound from [F3] proves rapid output decay near $\xi_0$.

For the diagonal $\Delta:M\to M\times M$, $d\Delta_x^T(\eta,\zeta)=\eta+\zeta$ and $N_\Delta=\{(x,x;\eta,-\eta):\eta\ne0\}$. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{WF}(u\otimes v)$ can meet $N_\Delta$ only if $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ for a common nonzero $\eta$. The hypothesis excludes this, so step 1.2 defines $\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$. When both factors are smooth, the Fourier pullback formula in step 1.2 gives their ordinary pointwise product.

On a compact chart patch, the pullback formula in step 1.2 and the factorization in [F5] give the local Fourier-convolution expression $\widehat{uv}(\xi)=\int\widehat u(\eta)\widehat v(\xi-\eta)\,d\eta$. The no-opposite-covector hypothesis separates the closed conic directions of $\widehat u$ and $\widehat v$ from cancellation. On a compact base patch their unit directions have a positive angular separation, so when both frequencies lie in their singular cones, $|\eta|+|\xi-\eta|\le C|\xi|$. In the tail $|\eta|>2|\xi|$, the two directions are nearly opposite, hence at least one factor is outside its singular cone and is rapidly decreasing; [F3] bounds the other polynomially. The integral is absolutely convergent and has polynomial growth, using [F6]. If $\xi$ lies outside $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup(\operatorname{WF}(u)+\operatorname{WF}(v))$, choose a smaller cone still outside that union; the same split makes at least one factor rapidly decreasing in every part of the convolution, proving rapid decay there. This proves the displayed wavefront inclusion and shows that the convolution product is exactly the diagonal pullback from step 2.1. Cutoffs from [F7] and coordinate invariance [F2] glue these local products.

For the projection $\pi$ and smooth positive density $
u$, define $\pi_{*,
u}t$ by pairing $t$ with $\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes
u)$, where $\chi=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}t$. A change of cutoff pairs $t$ with a test density zero near its support, so the value is independent of $\chi$; the support lies in the compact set $\pi(\operatorname{supp}t)$. In a product chart, multiplication by the smooth coefficient of $
u$ does not enlarge the wavefront set by step 3.1, and the localized Fourier transform in the base variables is the full transform of $\chi t$ evaluated at vertical frequency zero. Therefore rapid decay can fail only if $(x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)$ for some $y$, giving the stated estimate. Finite chart covers and cutoffs [F7] give the manifold statement.

boundaries.evidence: For zero input the tensor product and pullback are zero; the product agrees with this convention in steps 2.1–3.1.
Multiplication by the zero smooth distribution gives zero under the smooth-factor clause in step 2.1.
When both factors are smooth, step 2.1 identifies the diagonal pullback with ordinary multiplication.
A map with nonzero conormal intersection is excluded by the stated hypothesis; step 1.2 constructs the pullback only under that condition.

boundaries.reason: The pullback and product statements are local on manifolds and do not involve an interval endpoint parameter.

boundaries.evidence: A1 records ACω for Fourier inversion and integrable parameter pairing used in steps 1.2 and 3.1.

boundaries.reason: The theorem gives sufficient transversality and wavefront bounds; it asserts no converse criterion.
No converse to the sufficient wavefront product or pullback condition is claimed.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$, with signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. A cotangent vector is future or past causal when its metric dual belongs to the corresponding closed causal tangent cone. For $r\ge1$, let $\overline V_\pm^r\subset T^*M^r\setminus0$ consist of tuples $(x_1,\ldots,x_r;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r)$ such that every $\xi_j$ is either zero or future causal for $+$, respectively past causal for $-$, and the total tuple is nonzero. The wavefront set used below is the set of nonzero cotangent tuples where compactly localized Fourier transforms fail rapid decay in every conic neighborhood.

A compactly supported polynomial functional is a finite expression
$$ F(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left\langle f_m,\phi^{\otimes m}\mu_g^{\otimes m}\right\rangle, $$
where $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, $f_m\in\mathcal E'(M^m)$ is symmetric under permutations of its $m$ variables, $\mu_g$ is the metric density fixed by the Lorentzian metric, and the pairing is defined by inserting a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ in the smooth factor. Its $r$th functional derivative $F^{(r)}(\phi)\in\mathcal E'(M^r)$ is specified, for a test density $\omega$ on $M^r$, by
$$ \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi),\omega\right\rangle =\sum_{m=r}^{N}\frac{m!}{(m-r)!} \left\langle f_m,\omega\otimes\phi^{\otimes(m-r)}\mu_g^{\otimes(m-r)}\right\rangle, $$
where a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ is inserted in the smooth $\phi$ factors. Expanding the finite polynomial shows that this kernel represents the directional derivative in smooth compactly supported real directions. The functional is microcausal when
$$ \operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\cap(\overline V_+^r\cup\overline V_-^r)=\varnothing $$
for every $r\ge1$ and every $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$. Write $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$ for this class, including constants.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. $$p=\gamma(s),\qquad q=\gamma(t),\qquad \xi=\lambda g_p(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot),\qquad \zeta=\lambda g_q(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot).$$
These covectors are the metric-dual tangents to that geodesic and are related by induced covector parallel transport. There is no requirement $s\le t$: the future-frequency choice concerns the covectors, not an ordering of the two base points. The coincident case includes every nonzero future-null covector with $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$

derivations.claim: Fix a contraction order $r\ge1$, a field $\phi$, and put $A=F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi)$ and $B=W^{\otimes r}$. By [F3], each wavefront component of $B$ is either zero or a Hadamard pair $(k_i,-\ell_i)$ with both $k_i,\ell_i$ future null. If a nonzero covector of $\operatorname{WF}(A)$ cancelled one of $B$, then in the $F$ block every contracted entry would be past null or zero and in the $G$ block every contracted entry would be future null or zero. Both full tuples would lie in the forbidden cones of [F1], contrary to microcausality. Hence $\operatorname{WF}(A)$ has no covector opposite to $\operatorname{WF}(B)$, and [F3] defines $A\cdot B$. Its support is compact because it is contained in $\operatorname{supp}A$.

Push the product distribution forward over the $r$ contracted pairs, integrating against $\mu_g^{\otimes2r}$. The projection is proper on its compact support, so [F3] makes the result a compactly supported distribution in the remaining variables. Differentiating this finite expression in $\phi$ uses the polynomial product rule: for any order $s$, each term assigns a subset of the $s$ labeled directions to $F$ and the rest to $G$, producing contractions of $F^{(r+a)}(\phi)$ and $G^{(r+s-a)}(\phi)$ with the same $W^{\otimes r}$. This defines every output derivative as a finite sum of the same proper pushforwards. Since the polynomial degrees are finite, all contractions with $r>\min(\deg F,\deg G)$ vanish and the displayed sum is finite.

Fix an output derivative order $s\ge1$ and one term from step 2.1, with $a$ external directions assigned to $F$ and $s-a$ to $G$. Put $A=F^{(r+a)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r+s-a)}(\phi)$ and $B=W^{\otimes r}$. Suppose a nonzero wavefront covector of the pushed-forward term were entirely future causal. By [F3] it lifts to a covector of $A\cdot B$ with zero covectors in all contracted directions. The product wavefront bound in [F3] has three cases. A contribution from $\operatorname{WF}(A)$ alone would give an all-future nonzero tuple in one of the two functional derivatives, forbidden by [F1]; a contribution from $\operatorname{WF}(B)$ alone has zero external covectors and cannot give the nonzero output. In a sum contribution from $\operatorname{WF}(A)+\operatorname{WF}(B)$, the vertical zero condition makes each contracted $F$ entry past null or zero and each contracted $G$ entry future null or zero. The external entries of both blocks are the assumed future output entries. The full $G$ tuple is therefore nonzero and all future, forbidden by [F1]. If the output covector were all past, the same vertical equations make the full $F$ tuple nonzero and all past. Thus every output derivative kernel avoids both forbidden cones. The case $r=0$ is covered by the $\operatorname{WF}(A)$-alone case.

If $K$ is smooth, multiplying $F^{(2)}(\phi)$ by $K$ is allowed by the smooth-factor case of [F3] and adds no wavefront directions. Pairing the result against the cutoff metric density $\chi\mu_g^{\otimes2}$ is defined because the distribution has compact support. For each output derivative, the corresponding wavefront covectors of $F$ have zero entries in the two contracted slots; if the output had an all-future or all-past nonzero covector, adjoining those zeros would put $F^{(s+2)}(\phi)$ in a forbidden cone from [F1]. Hence $\Gamma_KF$ is microcausal. Its degree is at most $\deg F-2$ because two functional derivative slots were contracted; constants and degree-one functionals give zero.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by

If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and

where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $\hbar$ be a formal indeterminate. Let $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ be a scalar Hadamard bisolution. For $F,G\in\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$, let $\deg F$ be the largest degree with nonzero coefficient kernel, with $\deg 0=0$, and define, coefficientwise in $\hbar$,
$$ F\star_W G =\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)} \frac{\hbar^r}{r!} \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),\,W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle. $$
Each term is formed by the distribution product on the $r$ contracted variable pairs and proper pushforward over those pairs, as in [[thm-qftx-wavefront-product]], integrating with the metric density $\mu_g$ in each contracted variable. The sum is finite and defines a member of $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$. If $K\in C^\infty(M\times M)$ is symmetric, then
$$ \Gamma_KF(\phi)=\left\langle F^{(2)}(\phi),\chi K\mu_g^{\otimes2}\right\rangle $$
is also a compactly supported polynomial microcausal functional and lowers polynomial degree by two; here $\chi$ is any compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}F^{(2)}(\phi)$.

Let $X=\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, and let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be
any continuous complex bidistribution. For a real formal parameter $\eta$
and $F,G\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)$, define
$$ F\star_W G=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\eta^k}{k!}\left\langle W^{\otimes k},F^{(k)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(k)}(\phi)\right\rangle . $$
The pairing is over $k$ independent pairs of variables; $W^{\otimes k}$
is formed by iterated distributional tensor products, not by multiplying
distributions at coincident points. The sum is finite because the inputs are
polynomial. It defines an element of
$\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$, and $\star_W$ is associative.
Here complex conjugation is $\overline{a+ib}=a-ib$ for $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
If $W$ is Hermitian in the sense
$\overline{\langle W,\overline g\otimes\overline f\rangle}
=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle$, then
$(F\star_W G)^*=G^*\star_W F^*$, where $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.
For $\ell_f(\phi)=\int_X f(x)\phi(x)\,dx$,
$$ [\ell_f,\ell_g]_{\star_W}=\eta\bigl(W(f,g)-W(g,f)\bigr), \qquad W(f,g):=\langle W,f\otimes g\rangle . $$

Let $W\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$, $X=\mathbb R^d$, and let
$K\in\mathcal D'(X\times X)$ be symmetric under interchange of its
variables. Define
$$ \Gamma_KF(\phi)=\langle K,F^{(2)}(\phi)\rangle,\qquad \alpha_K=\exp\!\left(\frac{\eta}{2}\Gamma_K\right) =\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{(\eta/2)^j}{j!}\Gamma_K^j $$
on $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{reg}}(X)[\eta]$. Each sum is finite on each
polynomial because $\Gamma_K$ lowers degree by two. Then $\alpha_K$ is
invertible with inverse $\alpha_{-K}$, and
$$ \alpha_K(F\star_W G)=\alpha_K(F)\star_{W+K}\alpha_K(G) $$
for all regular polynomial functionals $F,G$. Thus the change from $W$
to $W+K$ is an exact algebra isomorphism on this regular class.

derivations.claim: Put $K=W'-W$. The common antisymmetric part gives $K-K^{\mathsf T}=0$, so $K$ is symmetric. By [F1]–[F2], $\operatorname{WF}(K)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(W)\cup\operatorname{WF}(W')=\mathcal C_g^+$. Symmetry also gives $\operatorname{WF}(K)=\tau^*\operatorname{WF}(K)\subseteq\mathcal C_g^-$, where $\mathcal C_g^-$ has past-directed first covectors. A nonzero null covector cannot be both future and past, so $\mathcal C_g^+\cap\mathcal C_g^-=\varnothing$ and $\operatorname{WF}(K)=\varnothing$. By [F2], $K$ is smooth.

By [F3], $\Gamma_K$ is defined on the class and preserves microcausality. On a polynomial of degree $d$, $\Gamma_K^jF=0$ for $2j>d$, so $\alpha_KF$ and $\alpha_{-K}F$ are finite sums. The coefficient of $\Gamma_K^q$ in either composition is multiplied by $\sum_{j=0}^{q}\binom qj(-1)^{q-j}=(1-1)^q$, which is zero for $q>0$ and one for $q=0$. Hence $\alpha_K\alpha_{-K}=\alpha_{-K}\alpha_K=I$.

On the regular polynomial subspace of a Euclidean chart, [F4]–[F5] fix the contraction ordering and the factor $\hbar/2$. For the general class, label the two functional arguments by $1,2$ and define $D_L(F\otimes G)$ by multiplying their first derivative distributions by $L$ and integrating the contracted pair with $\mu_g^{\otimes2}$. Let $\Gamma_K^{(1)}$ and $\Gamma_K^{(2)}$ contract two derivative slots within the first and second arguments using the same density. The finite Leibniz expansion of the second derivative gives
$$ \Gamma_K\circ m =m\circ(\Gamma_K^{(1)}+\Gamma_K^{(2)}+2D_K), $$
where $m$ is pointwise multiplication. The factor $2$ consists of the two cross terms, equal because $K$ is symmetric. Every term is defined by [F3].

Each contraction acts on distinct labelled derivative slots; the finite tensor-pairing construction in [F3] makes their order immaterial, and finite polynomial degree makes every coefficient sum finite. Thus $\alpha_K(F\star_WG)=m\,e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(\Gamma_K^{(1)}+\Gamma_K^{(2)}+2D_K)}e^{\hbar D_W}(F\otimes G)=m\,e^{\frac{\hbar}{2}(\Gamma_K^{(1)}+\Gamma_K^{(2)})}e^{\hbar D_{W+K}}(F\otimes G)=\alpha_KF\star_{W+K}\alpha_KG$. Here $D_{W+K}=D_W+D_K$ by bilinearity and $W+K=W'$. These are coefficientwise identities of finite sums, not analytic convergence claims. Together with step 1.2 this proves the stated intertwiner and bijectivity.

The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. Here $g$ is a smooth symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each tangent space with one negative and $n-1$ positive directions; in charts its signature is $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in each tangent space. A time orientation selects one of the two components of $\{v\ne0:g(v,v)<0\}$ as future. A tangent vector is causal when $g(v,v)\le0$, and is future or past causal when it belongs to the closure of the selected future or past timelike cone. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A nonzero cotangent vector is future or past causal, or future or past null, when its metric dual under $g^{-1}$ has the corresponding tangent property.

Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. It is coordinate-independent: under $y=\psi(x)$, $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det g_y|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det g_x|^{1/2}$, the density transformation law. Functional-kernel pairings and contractions on this page use $\mu_g$ in each integrated variable; no physical units are assigned.

For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. Two nonzero future-null cotangent vectors $(p,\xi)$ and $(q,\zeta)$ are related, written $(p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta)$, if $p=q$ and $\zeta=\xi$, or if there are a nonconstant future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic $\gamma:I\to M$, parameters $s,t\in I$ in either order, and a common scale $\lambda>0$ such that
$$p=\gamma(s),\qquad q=\gamma(t),\qquad \xi=\lambda g_p(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot),\qquad \zeta=\lambda g_q(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot).$$
These covectors are the metric-dual tangents to that geodesic and are related by induced covector parallel transport. There is no requirement $s\le t$: the future-frequency choice concerns the covectors, not an ordering of the two base points. The coincident case includes every nonzero future-null covector with $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. Write $W^{\mathsf T}=\tau^*W$ for the pullback by $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$. A fixed antisymmetric part means the equality $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for one specified distribution $E$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

A radial mollifier family is $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$ as in [[def-mollifier-family-generated-by-a-unit-mass-smooth-bump]], where $\rho\ge0$, $\int\rho=1$, $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$, $\rho(x)=q(|x|)$, and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset B_1(0)$. Thus $\operatorname{supp}\rho_\varepsilon\subset B_\varepsilon(0)$.

derivations.claim: Choose a compactly supported smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $0$. By [F1], $\chi\delta_0=\delta_0$ and $\widehat{\chi\delta_0}(\xi)=\langle\delta_0,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\rangle=1$ for every $\xi$. This constant function is not rapidly decreasing in any open cone about a nonzero covector, so [F2] gives $(0,\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}(\delta_0)$ for every $\xi\ne0$.

Since $\rho\ge0$ and $\int\rho=1$ by [F4], it is positive at some point. Continuity gives a ball on which $\rho^2$ is bounded below by a positive constant, so $\int\rho^2>0$. Compact support and smoothness make $\rho$ bounded, and $0\le\rho^2\le\|\rho\|_\infty\rho$ with $\int\rho=1$ gives $\rho^2\in L^1$.

For every $\xi\ne0$, both $(0,\xi)$ and $(0,-\xi)$ belong to $\operatorname{WF}(\delta_0)$ by step 1.1. The hypothesis of the product criterion [F3] therefore fails for $(u,v)=(\delta_0,\delta_0)$; the theorem does not define $\delta_0^2$.

Let $f\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ equal one on a neighborhood of $0$. Since $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subset B_1(0)$, for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, $f(\varepsilon y)=1$ on $\operatorname{supp}\rho$. Substitution $x=\varepsilon y$ in the Lebesgue integral of the smooth compactly supported square gives $\langle\rho_\varepsilon^2,f\rangle=\int \varepsilon^{-2n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)^2f(x)\,dx=\varepsilon^{-n}\int\rho(y)^2\,dy$. By step 1.2 this tends to $+\infty$, whereas convergence in $\mathcal D'$ would make the pairing with the fixed test $f$ converge to a finite scalar. Thus these unrenormalized squares have no distributional limit.

boundaries.reason: The counterexample is specifically on R^n with n≥1 and uses the nonempty base point 0.

boundaries.evidence: The Dirac distribution has Fourier transform 1 in step 1.1, so it is nonzero and the excluded product is not a zero-input case.
The computation uses only n≥1 and the Jacobian power ε−n; step 3.1 includes n=1.

boundaries.reason: The mollifier is a nonnegative unit-mass smooth function; no degenerate or zero-mass mollifier is part of the stated example.

boundaries.evidence: The family is considered for ε>0 and its limit as ε decreases to zero diverges by step 3.1; ε=0 is not an admissible smooth member.
A1 records ACω for the Fourier convention; the distributional and mollifier calculations themselves use the explicit witnesses in steps 1.1 and 1.2.

boundaries.reason: This is a one-way counterexample to universal definability, not an equivalence statement.
No converse criterion is stated; the example only shows failure of the sufficient product hypothesis.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, with operator spectrum $\sigma(T)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then:

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;
2. conversely, if $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb C$ is nonempty and compact and $E$ is
   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of
   $\Lambda$, then $T_E:=\int z\,dE(z)=\Phi_E(z)$ is a bounded normal operator
   with $\sigma(T_E)\subseteq\Lambda$ and $\|T_E\|\le\max_{z\in\Lambda}|z|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For $u\in D(A)$, [F5] and nonnegativity give $\|(I+A)u\|\,\|u\|\ge|\langle(I+A)u,u\rangle|=\|u\|^2+\langle Au,u\rangle\ge\|u\|^2$. Hence $I+A$ is injective and bounded below by $1$. To prove $A$ is closed, suppose $u_n\in D(A)$, $u_n\to u$, and $Au_n\to v$. For every $w\in D(A)$, self-adjointness gives $\langle Aw,u\rangle=\lim_n\langle Aw,u_n\rangle=\lim_n\langle w,Au_n\rangle=\langle w,v\rangle$; by the defining criterion for the adjoint, $u\in D(A^*)$ and $A^*u=v$. Self-adjointness, including equality of domains, yields $u\in D(A)$ and $Au=v$. Thus $A$ is closed. For $w\in D((I+A)^*)$, subtracting the identity term from the defining adjoint relation gives $w\in D(A^*)$ and $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Conversely, if $w\in D(A^*)$, then $\langle(I+A)u,w\rangle=\langle u,w+A^*w\rangle$ for every $u\in D(A)$, so $w\in D((I+A)^*)$ with $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Thus $(I+A)^*=I+A^*=I+A$ with domain $D(A)$, so $I+A$ is self-adjoint. If $u_n\in D(A)$ and $(I+A)u_n$ converges, the lower bound makes $(u_n)$ Cauchy; closedness then puts the limit in the range, so the range of $I+A$ is closed. A vector orthogonal to that range lies in $\ker(I+A)^*=\ker(I+A)$, which is zero by the same lower bound; the range is therefore dense and hence all of $H$. Thus $B=(I+A)^{-1}$ exists everywhere, is bounded with norm at most $1$, is injective, and has range $D(A)$, which is dense.

If $x=(I+A)u$ and $y=(I+A)v$, then $\langle Bx,y\rangle=\langle u,(I+A)v\rangle=\langle(I+A)u,v\rangle=\langle x,By\rangle$, so $B$ is self-adjoint. Also $\langle Bx,x\rangle=\langle u,(I+A)u\rangle=\|u\|^2+\langle Au,u\rangle\ge0$, so $B$ is positive. For nonreal $z$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] and self-adjointness give $\|(B-zI)w\|\ge|\operatorname{Im}z|\,\|w\|$ and the same lower bound for its adjoint, so its range is closed and dense. For real $z<0$, positivity and [F5] give $\|(B-zI)w\|\ge(-z)\|w\|$, again giving closed and dense range. For real $z>1$, the Neumann series $(zI-B)^{-1}=z^{-1}\sum_{n\ge0}(B/z)^n$ converges in operator norm, so $B-zI$ is invertible as well. Hence $\sigma(B)\subseteq[0,1]$.

By [A1] and [F1], $B$ has its regular spectral PVM $E_B$ on $\sigma(B)$. If $x=E_B(\{0\})y$, then [F4] gives $Bx=\Phi_{E_B}(b\mathbf1_{\{0\}})y=0$, so $E_B(\{0\})H\subseteq\ker B$. Conversely, if $Bx=0$, [F3] gives $0=\|Bx\|^2=\int b^2\,dE_x(b)$. Since $\{b>0\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]$ and $b^2\ge n^{-2}$ on each such interval, $E_x([1/n,1])=0$ for every $n$. Strong countable additivity and $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$ then imply $x=E_B(\{0\})x$. Since $B$ is injective, $E_B(\{0\})=0$. This is a zero spectral projection; it does not remove $0$ from the operator spectrum.

The map $\phi(b)=b^{-1}-1$ on $\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}$ is Borel. For a Borel set $S\subseteq[0,\infty)$ set $E_A(S):=E_B(\{b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}:\phi(b)\in S\})$. Inverse images preserve disjoint unions and intersections, so [F2] makes $E_A$ a PVM; its total value is $E_B(\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\})=I$ because $E_B(\{0\})=0$. The defining identity on indicator functions, extended first to simple functions and then by uniform approximation, gives $\Phi_{E_A}(f)=\Phi_{E_B}(g)$ for every bounded Borel $f$ on $[0,\infty)$, where $g(b)=f(\phi(b))$ for $b>0$ and $g(0)=0$.

Write $\mu_x^B(S)=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle$. From the definition in step 4.1, $\mu_x(S)=\mu_x^B(\{b>0:\phi(b)\in S\})$, so $\int\lambda^2\,d\mu_x(\lambda)=\int\phi(b)^2\,d\mu_x^B(b)$. If $x=By$, multiplicativity and the star-homomorphism identity [F4] give $d\mu_x^B(b)=b^2d\mu_y^B(b)$; hence $\int\phi(b)^2\,d\mu_x^B(b)=\int_{(0,1]}(1-b)^2\,d\mu_y^B(b)\le\|y\|^2$. Thus $x$ lies in the domain defining $T_A$. Conversely, if $\int\phi^2\,d\mu_x^B<\infty$, then $\int_{(0,1]}b^{-2}\,d\mu_x^B=\int(\phi+1)^2\,d\mu_x^B\le2\int\phi^2\,d\mu_x^B+2\|x\|^2<\infty$. The bounded truncations $y_N:=\Phi_{E_B}(b^{-1}\mathbf1_{[1/N,1]})(x)$ are Cauchy by the quadratic identity [F3], since their squared tails are tails of this finite integral, and converge to some $y\in H$. Multiplying by $B$ gives $By_N=E_B([1/N,1])x\to x$ by strong countable additivity and $E_B(\{0\})=0$, so $By=x$. Hence $D(T_A)=\operatorname{Ran}B=D(A)$. For $x=By$, the truncation in the definition of $T_A$ is, by step 4.1, $\Phi_{E_B}((1-b)\mathbf1_{[1/(N+1),1]})(y)$. These bounded multipliers converge pointwise off $\{0\}$ to $1-b$ and are uniformly bounded by $1$; [F4] gives strong convergence to $\Phi_{E_B}(1-b)y=(I-B)y=y-x=Ax$. Thus $T_A=A$ on the common domain, proving the operator identity.

If $f$ is bounded Borel on $[0,\infty)$, step 4.1 gives $f(A)=\Phi_{E_B}(g)$ for $g(b)=f(\phi(b))$ on $b>0$ and $g(0)=0$. By [F3], $\|f(A)\|\le\|g\|_\infty\le\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|f(\lambda)|$, and $\|f(A)u\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_u$. This proves the bounded Borel calculus claims.

boundaries.evidence: Public statement and its supplied argument: H is nonzero, so the normalized total PVM is not zero and σ(B) is nonempty. Empty Borel sets are nevertheless allowed and have E_A(∅)=E_B(∅)=0; empty/disjoint zero contributions in the PVM additivity argument cause no difficulty. The union in the proof is not an arbitrary empty operator family.
Step 3.1 proves E_B({0})=0; step 5.1 uses it in the inverse-domain truncation.
Step 4.1 maps b=1 to λ=0 and step 5.1 includes this endpoint.
The allowed A=0 case gives B=I and E_A concentrated at λ=0; steps 1.1–6.1 still apply.
Steps 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1 treat b=0 and b=1 explicitly.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $d\ge1$. For each $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ put $K_j^y:=L^2(\mathbb R,dy_j)$ and take a copy $(g^{(j)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of the Hermite family of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-hermite-recurrence]] in $K_j^y$. Define the left-associated completed tensor products by $\mathcal K_1^y:=K_1^y$ and $\mathcal K_r^y:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^y\widehat\otimes K_r^y$ for $2\le r\le d$. Let $\Theta_y^{(1)}:K_1^y\to L^2(\mathbb R,dy_1)$ be the identity; recursively, for $2\le r\le d$, let

$$\Theta_y^{(r)}:=\Theta_{r-1,1}^y\circ\bigl(\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}\bigr):\mathcal K_r^y\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy),$$

where $\Theta_{r-1,1}^y:L^2(\mathbb R^{r-1},dy)\widehat\otimes K_r^y\to L^2(\mathbb R^r,dy)$ is the two-factor Euclidean product unitary of [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]], and $\Theta_y^{(r-1)}\otimes I_{K_r^y}$ is the bounded tensor map of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Thus $\Theta_y^{(r)}$ is a specified unitary, with $\Theta_y^{(r)}(u\otimes v)(y',y_r)=\Theta_y^{(r-1)}u(y')v(y_r)$ almost everywhere. For $N=(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d$, set $G_N^{y,1}:=g^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{y,r}:=G_N^{y,r-1}\otimes g^{(r)}_{n_r}$; define $g_N:=\Theta_y^{(d)}G_N^{y,d}\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$.

Let $\varphi:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N^d$ list the multi-indices by increasing total degree $M=\sum_jn_j$ and, within each finite level, in lexicographic order. By [[thm-stars-and-bars]] each level is finite and the levels exhaust $\mathbb N^d$, so this specifies a bijection. All sums indexed by $\mathbb N^d$ below are taken in this order; nonnegative sums equivalently mean the supremum of finite subsums.

The functions $g_N$ have smooth product representatives from the recursive construction. These representatives are unique: a continuous difference that is nonzero at a point remains nonzero on a ball of positive Lebesgue measure. The coordinate derivatives in (b) and (c) are taken on these representatives and their scaled products.

Then:

(a) $(g_N)_{N\in\mathbb N^d}$ is a complete orthonormal family of $L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$: $\langle g_N,g_M\rangle=\delta_{NM}$ and every $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)$ has $f=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\langle f,g_N\rangle g_N$ with $\|f\|^2=\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2$, the sum being the supremum over finite subfamilies ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]);

(b) with the eigenvalues $\lambda_N:=\sum_{j=1}^d(2n_j+1)=2M+d$, $M:=\sum_jn_j$, let $A_d$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $e_m:=g_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $\lambda_{\varphi(m)}$. Then $A_d$ is self-adjoint with

$$A_dg_N=\lambda_Ng_N,\qquad D(A_d)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_{N\in\mathbb N^d}\lambda_N^2|\langle f,g_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(A_d)=\{2M+d:M\in\mathbb N\}$$

(the spectrum by [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-spectrum]]); the algebraic span of the $g_N$ is a core, and on that span

$$A_d=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(-\partial_{y_j}^2+y_j^2\bigr)$$

as operators, the $j$-th summand acting in the $j$-th coordinate;

(c) for real $m_j,\omega_j,\hbar>0$ put $\ell_j:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}$ and let $D_j:K_j^y\to K_j^x:=L^2(\mathbb R,dx_j)$ be the one-dimensional unitary of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]]. Define $\mathcal K_1^x:=K_1^x$ and $\mathcal K_r^x:=\mathcal K_{r-1}^x\widehat\otimes K_r^x$ for $2\le r\le d$, and define $\Theta_x^{(1)}$ and $\Theta_x^{(r)}$ by the same recursion as $\Theta_y^{(r)}$, using the two-factor Euclidean product unitaries on the $x$-coordinate spaces. Let $\mathcal D_1:=D_1$ and recursively $\mathcal D_r:=\mathcal D_{r-1}\otimes D_r:\mathcal K_r^y\to\mathcal K_r^x$; each $\mathcal D_r$ is unitary by [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]]. Put $D_d:=\Theta_x^{(d)}\mathcal D_d(\Theta_y^{(d)})^{-1}:L^2(\mathbb R^d,dy)\to L^2(\mathbb R^d,dx)$. For $N\in\mathbb N^d$, define $G_N^{x,1}:=D_1g^{(1)}_{n_1}=:\psi^{(1)}_{n_1}$ and recursively $G_N^{x,r}:=G_N^{x,r-1}\otimes\psi^{(r)}_{n_r}$; then $\psi_N:=D_dg_N=\Theta_x^{(d)}G_N^{x,d}$. Let $H$ be the diagonal operator of [[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]] for the enumerated family $\psi_{\varphi(m)}$ and eigenvalue sequence $E_{\varphi(m)}$, where $E_N:=\hbar\sum_{j=1}^d\omega_j(n_j+\frac12)$. Then $H$ is self-adjoint with

$$H\psi_N=E_N\psi_N,\qquad D(H)=\Bigl\{f:\sum_N E_N^2|\langle f,\psi_N\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad \sigma(H)=\overline{\{E_N:N\in\mathbb N^d\}},$$

the span of the $\psi_N$ is a core, and on that core

$$H=\sum_{j=1}^d\Bigl(-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_j}\partial_{x_j}^2+\frac{m_j\omega_j^2}{2}x_j^2\Bigr);$$

(d) if $\omega_1=\cdots=\omega_d=\omega$, then $\sigma(H)=\{\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2):M\in\mathbb N\}$, and the eigenvalue $\hbar\omega(M+\frac d2)$ has multiplicity

$$\bigl|\{(n_1,\dots,n_d)\in\mathbb N^d:n_1+\cdots+n_d=M\}\bigr|=\binom{M+d-1}{d-1};$$

in particular for $d=3$ the multiplicity is $(M+1)(M+2)/2$ ([[thm-stars-and-bars]]). All parameters are positive real numbers; no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L^2=L^2(\mathbb R,dy)$ be the complex Lebesgue space with inner product $\langle\varphi,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi(y)\overline{\psi(y)}\,dy$ linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); this pairing makes $L^2$ a complex Hilbert space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For complex-valued functions, smoothness and derivatives use the componentwise convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Write $g_0$ for the function $g_0(y):=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-y^{2}/2}$ and also for its class in $L^2$. Put

$$P:=\{p\,g_0:\ p\in\mathbb C[y]\}\subseteq L^2 ,$$

the set of classes of polynomial multiples of $g_0$. Each class in $P$ has a unique representative of the form $p g_0$: if $p g_0=qg_0$ almost everywhere, the continuous function $(p-q)g_0$ vanishes almost everywhere and therefore everywhere, and $g_0(y)>0$ for every $y$, so $p=q$. Let $Y$ be multiplication by $y$ and $\partial_y$ the derivative, acting on this unique smooth representative. Set $g_{-1}:=0$ for use in the recurrence formulas at $n=0$. Define

$$a:=\frac{Y+\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad a^\dagger:=\frac{Y-\partial_y}{\sqrt2},\qquad g_n:=\frac{(a^\dagger)^ng_0}{\sqrt{n!}}\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then:

(a) $g_0\in L^2$ with $\|g_0\|=1$; more generally $y^kg_0\in L^2$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$, so $P$ is a linear subspace of $L^2$ all of whose members are represented by $C^\infty$ functions;

(b) $Y,\partial_y,a,a^\dagger$ map $P$ into $P$, and $\partial_y(pg_0)=(p'-yp)g_0$ for every polynomial $p$;

(c) for all $\varphi,\psi\in P$, $\langle a^\dagger\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a\psi\rangle$ and $\langle a\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,a^\dagger\psi\rangle$;

(d) $a^\dagger a-a a^\dagger=-I$ on $P$, i.e. $[a,a^\dagger]=aa^\dagger-a^\dagger a=I$ on $P$, and $ag_0=0$;

(e) for every $n\in\mathbb N$: $ag_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}$ (with $ag_0=0$), $a^\dagger g_n=\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}$, $a^\dagger ag_n=ng_n$ and $aa^\dagger g_n=(n+1)g_n$;

(f) the polynomials

$$H_n(y):=(-1)^ne^{y^2}\frac{d^n}{dy^n}e^{-y^2}$$

are polynomials of degree $n$ with leading coefficient $2^n$, $H_0=1$, $H_1(y)=2y$, $H_n(-y)=(-1)^nH_n(y)$, and they satisfy

$$H_n'=2nH_{n-1},\qquad H_{n+1}=2yH_n-2nH_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1);$$

moreover

$$g_n=\frac{H_ng_0}{\sqrt{2^nn!}};$$

(g) consequently

$$\sqrt2\,y\,g_n=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}+\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1},\qquad \sqrt2\,g_n'=\sqrt n\,g_{n-1}-\sqrt{n+1}\,g_{n+1}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

derivations.claim: With these parameters, $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=1$, $m_j\omega_j^2/2=1$, and $\ell_j=\sqrt{\hbar/(m_j\omega_j)}=1$. The parameter substitution in the inspected proof of [F1] uses precisely this scaling; [F2] specifies the resulting unscaled product basis $h_\alpha=g_{\alpha_1}(x_1)g_{\alpha_2}(x_2)$ and its eigenvalue $\lambda_\alpha=\sum_{j=1}^2(2\alpha_j+1)=2|\alpha|+2$.

By [F3] each Hermite factor is a polynomial times $e^{-x_j^2/2}$, so $h_\alpha$ and all its derivatives decay rapidly enough for integration by parts against any Schwartz function. The operator $H^r$ is a finite sum of polynomial-coefficient derivatives and maps Schwartz space continuously to itself, hence $H^r f\in L^2$. Repeated integration by parts in $x_1$ and $x_2$ has no boundary terms; it gives $\langle H^r f,h_\alpha\rangle=\langle f,H^r h_\alpha\rangle=\lambda_\alpha^r\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle$.

Parseval for the complete orthonormal basis [F1]–[F2] is supplied by [F4] and gives $\|H^r f\|_2^2=\sum_\alpha|\langle H^r f,h_\alpha\rangle|^2=\sum_\alpha(2|\alpha|+2)^{2r}|\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle|^2$. Since $1+|\alpha|\le2|\alpha|+2$, the asserted weighted bound follows.

Each $H^r$ is a finite differential expression with polynomial coefficients, so its Schwartz seminorms bound the pointwise polynomially weighted derivatives in that expression. In two dimensions, $\|u\|_2\le C\sup_x(1+|x|)^2|u(x)|$ because $(1+|x|)^{-4}$ is integrable. Thus $f\mapsto\|H^r f\|_2$ is a continuous seminorm on Schwartz space, and the weighted coefficient map is continuous.
