citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ be the space of smooth complex-valued functions $f$ for which $\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^2}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|<\infty$ for every pair of multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^2$. Let $(h_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^2}$ be the product Hermite basis of $L^2(\mathbb R^2)$ obtained from the multidimensional oscillator at $\hbar=1$, $m_1=m_2=1/2$, and $\omega_1=\omega_2=2$, and write $|\alpha|=\alpha_1+\alpha_2$. For $H=-\partial_{x_1}^2-\partial_{x_2}^2+|x|^2$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$, every integer $r\ge0$ and every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C)$ satisfy

$$\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^2}(1+|\alpha|)^{2r}|\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle_{L^2}|^2\le\|H^r f\|_{L^2}^2<\infty.$$

Consequently the map $f\mapsto(\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle)_\alpha$ is continuous from Schwartz space to each weighted square-summable sequence space with norm $\bigl(\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^{2r}|c_\alpha|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Assume countable choice. For $f,g\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$,
$$\int\widehat f(\xi)\overline{\widehat g(\xi)}\,d\xi=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx.$$
The pairing is complex-linear in the first variable. In particular $\|\widehat f\|_2=\|f\|_2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Let $I=\mathbb N_0^2$, enumerated by total degree and lexicographic order. For each finite $F\subset I$, let $\mu_F$ have density $\prod_{\alpha\in F}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x_\alpha^2/2}$ on $\mathbb R^F$. [F5] makes these probability laws; integrating out coordinates with [F6] proves their consistency. Each coordinate space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is standard Borel by [F4]. Applying [F1] with [A1] yields $\Omega=\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder $\sigma$-algebra and a probability $\mathbb P$ having these finite marginals. The coordinate variables $\xi_\alpha(\omega)=\omega_\alpha$ are therefore independent standard normals.

For $p\in\mathbb R^2$ put $w_m(p)=(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1/2}$. Since $m>0$, $w_m$ is smooth, and every derivative is bounded: its derivatives are finite sums of polynomial factors divided by positive powers of $|p|^2+m^2$, bounded near the origin and decaying at infinity. The product rule therefore shows multiplication by $w_m$ maps Schwartz space continuously to itself. Define $T_mf=\mathcal F_{2\pi}^{-1}\bigl(w_m(2\pi\cdot)\mathcal F_{2\pi}f\bigr)$. By [F8], $T_mf$ is Schwartz; because $w_m$ is real and even, $T_mf$ is real for real $f$. Under the exact convention in the Statement, $\widehat f(p)=\mathcal F_{2\pi}f(p/(2\pi))$, and the change of variables $p=2\pi\xi$ gives $\widehat{T_mf}(p)=w_m(p)\widehat f(p)$.

For a finite initial segment $I_N$ of the fixed enumeration set $S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2$. The density in [F5] is normalized, and integration by parts using $(-xe^{-x^2/2})'=(x^2-1)e^{-x^2/2}$ gives $\mathbb E\xi_\alpha^2=1$. Hence $\mathbb E S_N=\sum_{\alpha\in I_N}(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\le\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)(n+1)^{-4}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)^{-3}=:C<\infty$: grouping $n+1$ in dyadic blocks $[2^j,2^{j+1})$ bounds each block by $2^j2^{-3j}=2^{-2j}$, a summable geometric series. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{S_N>M\}}\le S_N/M$, gives $\mathbb P(S_N>M)\le C/M$. Since the events increase to $\{S:=\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^{-4}\xi_\alpha^2>M\}$, countable additivity gives $\mathbb P(S>M)\le C/M$; letting integer $M\to\infty$ shows $S<\infty$ on a common event $\Omega_0$ of probability one.

For $f\in\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ put $c_\alpha(f)=\langle f,h_\alpha\rangle$. On $\Omega_0$, [F11] and [F3] give $\sum_\alpha|\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)|\le S^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_\alpha(1+|\alpha|)^4|c_\alpha(f)|^2\bigr)^{1/2}<\infty$. Thus $W_0(f):=\sum_\alpha\xi_\alpha c_\alpha(f)$ converges absolutely for every $f$ on the same event, is real-linear, and satisfies $|W_0(f)|\le S^{1/2}\|H^2f\|_2$. The last quantity is a continuous Schwartz seminorm by [F3], so each sample is a tempered distribution. Set $W_0=0$ outside $\Omega_0$. Every evaluation $W_0(f)$ is measurable as the almost-sure limit of measurable finite sums, hence $W_0$ is measurable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra.

The partial sums for $W_0(f)$ converge in $L^2(\Omega,\mathbb P)$ as well: independence, unit variance, and Parseval in [F10] make their squared $L^2$ tail equal to the corresponding tail of $\sum_\alpha|c_\alpha(f)|^2=\|f\|_2^2$. For any finite real combination $\sum_j t_jW_0(f_j)$, a finite partial sum is a linear combination of independent standard normals, with characteristic function $\prod_\alpha e^{-t^2c_\alpha^2/2}=e^{-t^2\sum_\alpha c_\alpha^2/2}$; by [F10] its variance converges to $\|\sum_jt_jf_j\|_2^2$. If $X_N\to X$ in $L^2$, then $|\mathbb E e^{itX_N}-\mathbb E e^{itX}|\le|t|\,\mathbb E|X_N-X|\le|t|\|X_N-X\|_2\to0$, so the limit has the centered normal characteristic function with that variance. Hence the family is jointly Gaussian, centered, and $\mathbb E[W_0(f)W_0(g)]=\int f(x)g(x)\,d^2x$.

Set $\Phi(f)=W_0(T_mf)$. Each sample in $\Omega_0$ is a continuous real-linear functional of $f$ because both $W_0$ and $T_m$ are continuous on Schwartz space; outside $\Omega_0$ it is zero. Thus $\Phi$ is a measurable $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R$-valued random variable for the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra. From step 4.1 its covariance is $\mathbb E[\Phi(f)\Phi(g)]=\int T_mf(x)T_mg(x)\,d^2x$. Applying [F9] and changing variables $p=2\pi\xi$ gives $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\widehat{T_mf}(p)\overline{\widehat{T_mg}(p)}\,d^2p$. Since $f,g$ are real, $\widehat f(-p)=\overline{\widehat f(p)}$ and $\widehat g(-p)=\overline{\widehat g(p)}$; the substitution $p\mapsto-p$ changes this to $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\overline{\widehat f(p)}\widehat g(p)w_m(p)^2\,d^2p=C_m(f,g)$ by step 1.2. The finite-dimensional distributions remain centered Gaussian by step 4.1 and linearity of $T_m$.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.
The Euclidean inclusion of $S^n$ induces its round metric. In spherical coordinates on $S^2$, $g=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].

Let $n\ge1$. For $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, its **support** is
$$\operatorname{supp}f:=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\ne0\}}.$$
The function is **compactly supported** if $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact.

A compactly supported $f$ is **compactly supported Riemann integrable** if there is a nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq\operatorname{int}Q$ such that $f|_Q$ is Riemann integrable. Its integral over Euclidean space is defined by
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f:=\int_Qf.$$
The value is independent of $Q$ by [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]]. When the support is empty, $f=0$ and the value is $0$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
 $C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb R$ is continuous and compactly
supported, then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: In $\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ set $L_i=(J_i+iK_i)/2$ and $R_i=(J_i-iK_i)/2$. Expanding the stated brackets gives $[L_i,L_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$, $[R_i,R_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}R_k$, and $[L_i,R_j]=0$. The real span $\mathfrak k=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{L_i,R_i\}$ has compact Lie-algebra bracket: with $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_3=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, the basis $-i\sigma_i/2$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ has the same $\epsilon_{ijk}$ brackets. The two summands commute, and $\mathfrak k\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C=\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ because $J_i=L_i+R_i$ and $K_i=(L_i-R_i)/i$.

Let $G=\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2)$, whose Lie algebra is $\mathfrak k$. The matrices $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-\overline b&\overline a\end{pmatrix}$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$ identify $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with the unit quaternions and hence with $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$, so $G$ is compact. To prove simple connectivity in the form needed here, take any piecewise-smooth based loop in $S^3$. Uniform continuity gives a finite subdivision on which each subarc lies in an open hemisphere. If $\delta(t)$ is the short great-circle arc between its endpoints, then $H(s,t)=((1-s)\gamma(t)+s\delta(t))/\|(1-s)\gamma(t)+s\delta(t)\|$ is defined throughout that hemisphere, fixes the endpoints, and homotopes the subarc to $\delta$. Each great-circle arc lies in the intersection of $S^3$ with a proper two-dimensional linear subspace $P_j\subset\mathbb R^4$. A finite union of proper linear subspaces cannot cover $\mathbb R^4$: induct on their number; after choosing $x$ outside $P_1,\ldots,P_{n-1}$, if $x\notin P_n$ we are done, and otherwise choose $y\notin P_n$; the line $x+ty$ meets each $P_j$ in at most one parameter value, so a real $t$ outside the finite forbidden set gives a point outside all $P_j$. Thus the resulting polygonal loop omits some $q\in S^3$. Stereographic projection identifies $S^3\setminus\{q\}$ with $\mathbb R^3$; straight-line contraction there to the basepoint fixes the loop endpoints and is piecewise smooth. Hence every piecewise-smooth based loop contracts through piecewise-smooth based loops. Applying this factorwise proves the required property for $G$.

Complexify $\rho$ and $c$ and, on $W=V\oplus\mathbb C$, define $\widetilde\rho(X)(v,z)=(\rho(X)v+zc(X),0)$ for $X\in\mathfrak k$. The representation identity for $\rho$ and the cocycle identity for $c$ give $[\widetilde\rho(X),\widetilde\rho(Y)](v,z)=([\rho(X),\rho(Y)]v+z(\rho(X)c(Y)-\rho(Y)c(X)),0)=\widetilde\rho([X,Y])(v,z)$, so $\widetilde\rho$ is a finite-dimensional Lie-algebra representation.

Reparameterize each smooth path segment to $[0,1]$. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma$ put $a(t)=\gamma(t)^{-1}\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathfrak k$ and $A(t)=\widetilde\rho(a(t))$. Solve $U'=UA$, $U(0)=I$, separately on each segment and concatenate. On a segment with $\|A\|\le M$, the Picard series has $n$th term $\int_{0\le t_1\le\cdots\le t_n\le t}A(t_1)\cdots A(t_n)\,dt_1\cdots dt_n$, bounded by $M^n/n!$; it converges uniformly and termwise integration verifies the integral equation. If $D$ is the difference of two solutions with $D(0)=0$, then $\|D(t)\|\le M\int_0^t\|D(r)\|dr$; iterating gives $\|D(t)\|\le\sup\|D\|M^nt^n/n!\to0$, proving uniqueness. Solving $V'=-AV$, $V(0)=I$, by the same series gives $(UV)'=0$ and $UV=I$, so each transport matrix is invertible. Concatenating paths multiplies their transports in order, since on the second segment the solution with initial value $U_1$ is $U_1$ times the solution with initial value $I$. For a piecewise-smooth endpoint-fixed homotopy $\Gamma(s,t)$, the series terms and their $s$-derivatives are uniformly bounded by $M^n/n!$ and $nLM^{n-1}/n!$, respectively, where $L=\sup\|\partial_sA\|$ and we enlarge $M$ so $M\ge1$. Both series converge uniformly; integrating the derivative series in $s$ shows the limit $U$ is differentiable in $s$. Put $a=\Gamma^{-1}\partial_t\Gamma$ and $b=\Gamma^{-1}\partial_s\Gamma$. Direct differentiation yields $\partial_sa-\partial_tb=[a,b]$. The matrix-valued form $\theta=g^{-1}dg$ satisfies $d\theta=-\theta\wedge\theta$, by differentiating $g^{-1}g=I$; equivalently $d\theta+\frac12[\theta,\theta]=0$. Applying the representation from step 2.1 gives $A_s-B_t=[A,B]$, where $B=\widetilde\rho(b)$. For $K=U_s-UB$, differentiation now gives $K_t=KA+U(BA+A_s-AB-B_t)=KA$, and $K(s,0)=0$ because the initial endpoint is fixed. The uniqueness just proved gives $K=0$; at the fixed terminal endpoint $B(s,1)=0$, so $U_s(s,1)=0$. Thus transport is invariant under these homotopies. If $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ run from $e$ to the same $g$, the loop $\gamma_1$ followed by the reverse of $\gamma_2$ contracts by step 1.2, so its transport is $I$; the analogous loop using $\gamma_2$ shows the two transports agree. Hence transport is path-independent. Locally near $g_0$, choose paths from $e$ to $g_0^{-1}g$ varying smoothly with $g$ in a coordinate ball; the same uniform-series bounds imply continuous dependence on $g$, so $U$ is continuous. Finally, left-translating a path from $e$ to $h$ and concatenating it after a path from $e$ to $g$ gives $U(gh)=U(g)U(h)$, since left translation preserves $\gamma^{-1}\dot\gamma$. Thus $U$ is a continuous group representation.

The block form of $\widetildeho$ makes $U(g)= egin{pmatrix}R(g)&b(g)\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, and its group law gives $b(hg)=R(h)b(g)+b(h)$. Identify each $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with the unit quaternions and regard $S^3$ as the unit quaternions. For an explicit normalized round-volume integral, let $\chi(t)=0$ for $t\le1/3$ and $\chi(t)=e^{-1/(t-1/3)}$ for $t>1/3$. For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_4)\in S^3$, put $D(x)=\sum_{j=1}^4(\chi(x_j)+\chi(-x_j))$ and $\psi_{j,\pm}(x)=\chi(\pm x_j)/D(x)$. Since some $|x_j|\ge1/2$, $D(x)>0$; these eight smooth nonnegative functions sum to $1$ and have supports compactly contained in $U_{j,\pm}=\{\pm x_j>1/4\}$. In the chart given by the other three coordinates $y$, the sphere is $x_j=\pm\sqrt{1-|y|^2}$, the metric matrix is $G=I+yy^{\mathsf T}/(1-|y|^2)$, and therefore $\sqrt{\det G}=(1-|y|^2)^{-1/2}$. By [L1], integrate each complex chart integrand and each finite-dimensional $V$-valued function coordinatewise in any basis. Define
$$I(f)=\sum_{j,\pm}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\psi_{j,\pm}(x(y))f(x(y))(1-|y|^2)^{-1/2}\,dy,$$
extending each integrand by zero outside its chart. Each real and imaginary part is continuous with compact support inside the chart, so [F1]–[F2] make each coordinate integral finite. The chart weights are nonnegative, and their partition-of-unity sum gives $I(1)$; applying the triangle inequality to the complex Riemann sums and passing to their limits gives $|I(h)|\le\sup_{S^3}|h|\,I(1)$. The number $I(1)$ is finite and positive: at $x=(1,0,0,0)$ one partition function is positive on a neighborhood, and on a small coordinate cube there the integrand has a positive lower bound. Thus $
u(h):=I(h)/I(1)$ is complex-linear, normalized, positive on nonnegative real functions, and satisfies $|
u(h)|\le\sup_{S^3}|h|$. Its chart definition is independent of a finite subordinate chart partition: insert the second partition into each summand; each product has compact support in the chart overlap, and the metric identity $G(x)=DT(x)^{\mathsf T}G(Tx)DT(x)$ gives $\sqrt{\det G(x)}=|\det DT(x)|\sqrt{\det G(Tx)}$. Apply [F3] to real and imaginary parts separately to transfer each compactly supported integral; summing the finite terms gives equality. Quaternion left multiplication $L_q(x)=qx$ is real-linear; using $q ar q=|q|^2$, $\overline{qx}= ar x ar q$, and associativity gives $|qx|^2=(qx)\overline{qx}=q(x ar x) ar q=|x|^2|q|^2=|x|^2$ for unit $q$, so $L_q$ is orthogonal and an isometry of the induced metric; using the transported charts and partition in the same identity gives $
u(h\circ L_q)=
u(h)$. Extend $
u$ to continuous $V$-valued maps by the same coordinatewise rule and call this extension $
u_V$. Define the product functional on continuous $F:G	o V$ by $\mu(F)=
u_V(q\mapsto
u_V(r\mapsto F(q,r)))$. For continuity, fix $q_0\in S^3$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $r\in S^3$, continuity of the finitely many coordinate functions of $F$ at $(q_0,r)$ gives neighborhoods in both factors on which their values differ from $F(q_0,r)$ by less than $\varepsilon/3$. Compactness of the second $S^3$ selects finitely many such neighborhoods; intersecting their first-factor neighborhoods gives $U
i q_0$ with $\sup_r|F_j(q,r)-F_j(q_0,r)|<2\varepsilon/3$ for each coordinate $j$ and $q\in U$. The scalar bound for $
u$ therefore makes each coordinate of $q\mapsto
u_V(r\mapsto F(q,r))$ continuous. The product functional is linear, normalized, and left invariant by applying the factor identity twice. Since $b$ is continuous on compact $G$ and $V$ is finite-dimensional, $ ar v:=\mu(b)$ exists coordinatewise. Left invariance and the cocycle formula give $R(h) ar v+b(h)=\mu(g\mapsto b(hg))= ar v$ for every $h\in G$.

Differentiate the fixed-point identity of step 4.1 at $h=\exp(tX)$ and $t=0$. The path equation defining $U$ gives $dR_e(X)=\rho(X)$ and $db_e(X)=c(X)$: these are the upper-left and upper-right blocks of $\widetilde\rho(X)$ in step 2.1. Hence $\rho(X)\bar v+c(X)=0$ for $X\in\mathfrak k$. Set $v=-\bar v$. The identity $c(X)=\rho(X)v$ extends complex-linearly from $\mathfrak k$ to $\mathfrak l_{\mathbb C}$ by step 1.1, and hence holds for every original $X\in\mathfrak l$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first variable, and let $A:D(A)\subseteq H\to H$ be densely defined, self-adjoint, and nonnegative, meaning $\langle Au,u\rangle\ge0$ for every $u\in D(A)$. Here self-adjoint means equality with the Hilbert-space adjoint, including equality of domains. A projection-valued measure (PVM) on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ is a map $E:\Sigma\to\mathcal B(H)$ such that every $E(S)$ is a bounded orthogonal projection ($E(S)^2=E(S)=E(S)^*$), $E(\varnothing)=0$, $E(X)=I$, $E(S\cap T)=E(S)E(T)$, and $E(\bigcup_n S_n)u=\sum_nE(S_n)u$ in norm for each disjoint sequence $(S_n)$ and each $u\in H$. On a locally compact Hausdorff Borel space, such a PVM is regular when each finite scalar measure $\mu_u(S):=\langle E(S)u,u\rangle$ is inner regular on Borel sets and outer regular by open supersets. Then $I+A:D(A)\to H$ is bijective. Its inverse $B:=(I+A)^{-1}$ is a bounded positive (meaning $\langle Bx,x\rangle\ge0$ for all $x\in H$) self-adjoint injection with $\|B\|\le1$ and dense range $D(A)$. For a bounded operator, its spectrum $\sigma(B)$ is the set of complex $z$ for which $B-zI$ has no bounded two-sided inverse. Let $E_B$ be the regular spectral PVM on the Borel subsets of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(B)$ satisfying $B=\int_{\sigma(B)}b\,dE_B(b)$. Then $\sigma(B)\subseteq[0,1]$ and $E_B(\{0\})=0$. Define $\phi(b)=b^{-1}-1$ for $b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}$ and, for every Borel $S\subseteq[0,\infty)$, define

$$E_A(S):=E_B(\{b\in\sigma(B)\setminus\{0\}:\phi(b)\in S\}).$$

This is a PVM on the Borel subsets of $[0,\infty)$. For each $u\in H$ put $\mu_u(S):=\langle E_A(S)u,u\rangle$. The unbounded integral $\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)$ denotes the operator $T_A$ with domain

$$D(T_A):=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\mu_u(\lambda)<\infty\right\}$$

and action

$$T_Au:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_{E_A}(\lambda\mathbf1_{[0,N]})(u),$$

where $\Phi_{E_A}(g)$ is the bounded Borel PVM integral of $g$. Then $A=T_A$ and hence

$$A=\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda),\qquad D(A)=\left\{u\in H:\int_{[0,\infty)}\lambda^2\,d\langle E_A(\lambda)u,u\rangle<\infty\right\}.$$

For every bounded Borel function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb C$, $f(A):=\Phi_{E_A}(f)$ is bounded, satisfies $\|f(A)\|\le\sup_{\lambda\ge0}|f(\lambda)|$, and obeys $\|f(A)u\|^2=\int|f|^2\,d\mu_u$. The condition $E_B(\{0\})=0$ does not assert that $0\notin\sigma(B)$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: On $H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with standard basis $(e_n)_{n\ge1}$ define $D(A)=\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2|x_n|^2<\infty\}$ and $(Ax)_n=nx_n$. Finite sequences lie in $D(A)$ and are dense. For $x\in D(A)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F2] gives $\sum n|x_n|^2\le(\sum n^2|x_n|^2)^{1/2}(\sum|x_n|^2)^{1/2}<\infty$, so $\langle Ax,x\rangle=\sum n|x_n|^2\ge0$ and $A$ is nonnegative.

The operator is self-adjoint. If $y\in D(A^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ with $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every finite sequence $x$; choosing $x=e_n$ gives $z_n=ny_n$, so $\sum n^2|y_n|^2=\|z\|^2<\infty$ and $y\in D(A)$. Conversely, if $y\in D(A)$ then $z=(ny_n)\in\ell^2$ satisfies the adjoint identity for every $x\in D(A)$: both inner-product series converge by [F2] because $Ax,y,x,z\in\ell^2$, and their terms agree. Thus $D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $A^*=A$.

The inverse of $I+A$ is the bounded diagonal operator $B e_n=(n+1)^{-1}e_n$. Indeed for any $x\in\ell^2$, $y_n=x_n/(n+1)$ satisfies $\sum n^2|y_n|^2\le\sum|x_n|^2$, and $(I+A)y=x$. The operator $B$ is positive and injective, but it is not bounded below because $\|Be_n\|=(n+1)^{-1}\to0$ for unit vectors $e_n$. The vector $y=(1/n)_{n\ge1}$ belongs to $\ell^2$: for $n\ge2$, $n^{-2}\le(n-1)^{-1}-n^{-1}$, so $\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}\le2$. It is not in $\operatorname{Ran}B$, since $Bx=y$ would require $x_n=(n+1)/n>1$ for every $n$, which is not square-summable. Hence $B$ is not surjective and $0\in\sigma(B)$.

Define $E_B(S)x=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}x_ne_n$ for Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$. Its values are orthogonal coordinate projections, and the coordinate definition gives $E_B(\varnothing)=0$, $E_B(\sigma(B))=I$, and $E_B(S)E_B(T)=E_B(S\cap T)$. For disjoint Borel $S_k$, each coordinate $n$ occurs in at most one projection, so the partial sums $\sum_{k\le N}E_B(S_k)x$ converge in $\ell^2$ to $E_B(\bigcup_kS_k)x$: the squared norm of the omitted coordinates is a tail of the convergent nonnegative series $\sum_n|x_n|^2$. Thus $E_B$ is strongly countably additive. It integrates the coordinate function to $B$, because its integral acts diagonally by $(n+1)^{-1}$ on each $e_n$. For every $x$, its finite scalar measure is $\mu_x(S):=\langle E_B(S)x,x\rangle=\sum_{n:(n+1)^{-1}\in S}|x_n|^2$. For any Borel $S\subseteq\sigma(B)$, the finite set $K_N:=\{(n+1)^{-1}:n\le N,\ (n+1)^{-1}\in S\}$ is compact and contained in $S$, and $\mu_x(K_N)\uparrow\mu_x(S)$ because $\sum_n|x_n|^2<\infty$. Hence $\mu_x$ is inner regular on every Borel set. Since $\sigma(B)$ is compact, for any Borel $S$ and $\varepsilon>0$, inner regularity of $S^c$ gives a compact $K\subseteq S^c$ with $\mu_x(S^c\setminus K)<\varepsilon$; then the open set $\sigma(B)\setminus K$ contains $S$ and its excess measure is less than $\varepsilon$. Thus $\mu_x$ is also outer regular, so $E_B$ is a regular PVM. Hence [F1] identifies it with the bounded-resolvent spectral PVM. Since no atom is at zero, $E_B(\{0\})=0$, although step 3.1 proves $0\in\sigma(B)$. This refutes the asserted implication and shows why a zero spectral projection must be distinguished from a spectral value.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, using the local distribution convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. For $p\in\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, call $(p,\xi)$ regular for $u$ if there are $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\chi=1$ near $p$ and an open cone $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ containing $\xi$ such that for every integer $N\ge0$,
$$ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}(1+|\eta|)^N\left|\left\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|\right\rangle\right|<\infty. $$
The local wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_\Omega(u)$ is the complement of these regular pairs in $T^*\Omega\setminus0$, with the standard cotangent coordinates $(p,\xi)$. A cone is invariant under multiplication by positive scalars. This is a chart-level definition; this item makes no assertion about its behavior under a change of coordinates.

Let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$, with signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. A cotangent vector is future or past causal when its metric dual belongs to the corresponding closed causal tangent cone. For $r\ge1$, let $\overline V_\pm^r\subset T^*M^r\setminus0$ consist of tuples $(x_1,\ldots,x_r;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r)$ such that every $\xi_j$ is either zero or future causal for $+$, respectively past causal for $-$, and the total tuple is nonzero. The wavefront set used below is the set of nonzero cotangent tuples where compactly localized Fourier transforms fail rapid decay in every conic neighborhood.

A compactly supported polynomial functional is a finite expression
$$ F(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left\langle f_m,\phi^{\otimes m}\mu_g^{\otimes m}\right\rangle, $$
where $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, $f_m\in\mathcal E'(M^m)$ is symmetric under permutations of its $m$ variables, $\mu_g$ is the metric density fixed by the Lorentzian metric, and the pairing is defined by inserting a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ in the smooth factor. Its $r$th functional derivative $F^{(r)}(\phi)\in\mathcal E'(M^r)$ is specified, for a test density $\omega$ on $M^r$, by
$$ \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi),\omega\right\rangle =\sum_{m=r}^{N}\frac{m!}{(m-r)!} \left\langle f_m,\omega\otimes\phi^{\otimes(m-r)}\mu_g^{\otimes(m-r)}\right\rangle, $$
where a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ is inserted in the smooth $\phi$ factors. Expanding the finite polynomial shows that this kernel represents the directional derivative in smooth compactly supported real directions. The functional is microcausal when
$$ \operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\cap(\overline V_+^r\cup\overline V_-^r)=\varnothing $$
for every $r\ge1$ and every $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$. Write $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$ for this class, including constants.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. Here $g$ is a smooth symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each tangent space with one negative and $n-1$ positive directions; in charts its signature is $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in each tangent space. A time orientation selects one of the two components of $\{v\ne0:g(v,v)<0\}$ as future. A tangent vector is causal when $g(v,v)\le0$, and is future or past causal when it belongs to the closure of the selected future or past timelike cone. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A nonzero cotangent vector is future or past causal, or future or past null, when its metric dual under $g^{-1}$ has the corresponding tangent property.

Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. It is coordinate-independent: under $y=\psi(x)$, $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det g_y|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det g_x|^{1/2}$, the density transformation law. Functional-kernel pairings and contractions on this page use $\mu_g$ in each integrated variable; no physical units are assigned.

For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. Two nonzero future-null cotangent vectors $(p,\xi)$ and $(q,\zeta)$ are related, written $(p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta)$, if $p=q$ and $\zeta=\xi$, or if there are a nonconstant future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic $\gamma:I\to M$, parameters $s,t\in I$ in either order, and a common scale $\lambda>0$ such that
$$p=\gamma(s),\qquad q=\gamma(t),\qquad \xi=\lambda g_p(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot),\qquad \zeta=\lambda g_q(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot).$$
These covectors are the metric-dual tangents to that geodesic and are related by induced covector parallel transport. There is no requirement $s\le t$: the future-frequency choice concerns the covectors, not an ordering of the two base points. The coincident case includes every nonzero future-null covector with $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. Write $W^{\mathsf T}=\tau^*W$ for the pullback by $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$. A fixed antisymmetric part means the equality $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for one specified distribution $E$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

derivations.claim: Expand the finite polynomial in the definition of $F$ after substituting $\phi+\sum_jt_jh_j$ and take the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_r$. Each resulting term has the form $\int a(x)\prod_{j=1}^{r}\partial^{\alpha_j}h_j(x)\,d^4x$ with $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M)$. Its distribution kernel is $(-1)^{\sum_j|\alpha_j|}\partial_{x_1}^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_{x_r}^{\alpha_r}[a(x_r)\prod_{j<r}\delta(x_j-x_r)]$. Indeed, pairing this derivative distribution with a product test gives the displayed integral by the definition of distributional differentiation. The derivatives cannot in general all be moved to the smooth coefficient: derivatives of the relative diagonal deltas remain. The kernel is a finite derivative of a smooth compact diagonal distribution and is supported on $\Delta_r$.

In coordinates $x=x_r$ and $z_j=x_j-x_r$ for $j<r$, multiply the kernels from step 1.1 by any compact smooth localization and expand the derivatives by Leibniz's rule. Each term is a smooth compact coefficient in $x$ times a finite derivative of $\prod_{j<r}\delta(z_j)$, allowing also finitely many $x$-derivatives. Its Fourier transform is therefore a finite sum of polynomials in $(\kappa,\zeta)$ times Fourier transforms of smooth compact $x$-coefficients. These coefficient transforms decrease faster than every power of $\kappa$. On a cone $|\kappa|\ge\epsilon|(\kappa,\zeta)|$ this arbitrary decay absorbs every finite polynomial factor. Thus every nonconormal direction is regular and every wavefront covector has $\kappa=0$. In the original coordinates this is exactly $\sum_j\xi_j=0$.

If $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r$ are all future causal covectors in this Minkowski chart, their metric-dual time components have one weak sign, and a nonzero causal covector has a strictly nonzero time component. Thus $\sum_j\xi_j=0$ forces every $\xi_j=0$. The same argument applies to past causal covectors. By step 2.1 the wavefront set is conormal, so it contains no nonzero tuple in either forbidden cone of [F3]. This proves microcausality.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, the space $\mathcal D_K$ is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete for
$$d(f,g)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(f-g)).$$
This metric induces exactly its derivative-seminorm topology. Multiplying the metric by two gives the equivalent convention with weights $2^{-m}$. These assertions require no choice axiom.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ($\mathrm{DC}$). If a nonempty metric space $X$ is complete, then it is not the union of a sequence of closed sets each having empty interior. Equivalently, the intersection of countably many open dense subsets of $X$ is dense.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, using the local distribution convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. For $p\in\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, call $(p,\xi)$ regular for $u$ if there are $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\chi=1$ near $p$ and an open cone $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ containing $\xi$ such that for every integer $N\ge0$,
$$ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}(1+|\eta|)^N\left|\left\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|\right\rangle\right|<\infty. $$
The local wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_\Omega(u)$ is the complement of these regular pairs in $T^*\Omega\setminus0$, with the standard cotangent coordinates $(p,\xi)$. A cone is invariant under multiplication by positive scalars. This is a chart-level definition; this item makes no assertion about its behavior under a change of coordinates.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

Assume Countable Choice.  Let $v\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ have compact
support, let $\widetilde v\in\mathcal S'$ be its canonical extension, and let
$\chi\in\mathcal D$ equal one on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}v$.
Then $\mathcal F\widetilde v$ is the regular tempered distribution represented
by

$$V(\xi)=\left\langle v_x,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\right\rangle.$$

The function $V$ is independent of $\chi$, is smooth, and for every
multi-index $\alpha$ there are $C_\alpha,m_\alpha$ with
$|\partial^\alpha V(\xi)|\leq C_\alpha(1+|\xi|)^{m_\alpha}$.  Consequently
multiplication by $V$ is continuous on $\mathcal S$ and, by transpose, on
$\mathcal S'$ in both dual topologies.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

derivations.claim: Fix one factor $u$ and a positive exponent $s>\max(0,\operatorname{sd}_0(u))$. Multiply $u$ by a compact cutoff equal to one near zero and denote the result by $v$. Multiplication by this cutoff preserves the scaling upper bound: the tests acquire the factor $\psi(\rho x)$, a bounded smooth family on every fixed compact, and the uniform estimate established next applies to it. For any fixed compact test support $K$, the continuous linear functionals $L_\rho=\rho^s v_\rho$, $0<\rho\le T<\infty$, are pointwise bounded: convergence at zero follows from [F1], and away from zero the dilation tests vary continuously on compact scale intervals. To justify the uniform estimate without assuming it, apply [F2] first to $\rho^s u_\rho$ on a compact containing all small-scale supports. The closed sets $E_N=\{\varphi:\sup_\rho|L_\rho(\varphi)|\le N\}$ cover the fixed-support space. One has interior, so subtracting two elements of that interior and rescaling gives $|L_\rho(\varphi)|\le C p_m(\varphi)$ uniformly in $\rho$, with $p_m=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\|\partial^\alpha\varphi\|_\infty$. The same argument then applies to $v$ and to every fixed compact scale interval.

Choose slightly enlarged closed frequency cones $K_j$ around the $C_j$ such that the joint no-cancellation condition still holds for the $K_j$. This is possible by compactness of tuples with $\sum_j|\xi_j|=1$: the set of tuples in $\prod_j(C_j\cup\{0\})$ is compact there and its sum stays away from zero. If $C_j$ is empty use the empty cone. Closedness of the wavefront set permits localization to a sufficiently small common neighborhood so that all singular directions of each localized $v_j$ lie strictly inside $K_j$. Choose a smooth Fourier cutoff $q_j$ supported in $K_j$ outside a bounded ball and equal to one around those singular directions at large frequencies. Then $(1-q_j)\widehat v_j$ is Schwartz. In fact [F3] gives rapid decay on its unbounded support, while each frequency derivative is a localized Fourier transform with a coordinate monomial inserted, so has the same regular-cone bounds by [F3]–[F4]. Bounded frequencies cause no problem. Thus $v_j=b_j+c_j$, with $b_j$ Schwartz and the Fourier transform of $c_j$ supported in $K_j$ together with a bounded ball.

The family $L_\rho=\rho^s v_\rho$ is uniformly bounded on Schwartz space by one Schwartz seminorm. Indeed, decompose a Schwartz test into a fixed ball and smooth dyadic annuli of radii $R=2^k\ge1$. On an annulus write $\varphi_R(x)=\theta(x/R)\varphi(x)$ with one fixed annular cutoff. Dilation gives
$$\langle\rho^s v_\rho,\varphi_R\rangle=R^{D-s}\langle(\rho R)^s v_{\rho R},\theta(y)\varphi(Ry)\rangle.$$
If $\operatorname{supp}v\subset B(0,M)$, annuli with $\rho R>2M$ give zero, after increasing $M$ to accommodate the fixed annular radii. For $0<\rho R\le2M$, step 1.1 on the one fixed annulus bounds this by $C R^{D-s+m-L}P_{m,L}(\varphi)$, where $P_{m,L}(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_x(1+|x|)^L|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|$. Choose $L>D-s+m+1$; the geometric sum over $R=2^k$ is finite uniformly in $\rho$. The fixed ball is controlled by step 1.1. This proves $|\langle L_\rho,\varphi\rangle|\le C'P_{m',L'}(\varphi)$ for fixed $m',L',C'$ independent of $\rho$. By transposition [F5] the Fourier transforms are likewise uniformly tempered.

For $s_j>a_j\ge0$, step 2.1 makes $\rho^{s_j}(v_j)_\rho$ uniformly tempered. The Schwartz part $\rho^{s_j}(b_j)_\rho$ is also uniformly tempered, since $b_j(\rho x)$ and each of its derivatives are bounded uniformly for $0<\rho\le1$, and its local smooth seminorms tend to zero. Consequently the Fourier family of $\rho^{s_j}(c_j)_\rho$ is uniformly tempered and supported in $K_j$ together with a fixed bounded ball: dilation shrinks that ball in frequency. Let $V$ be a closed cone disjoint from a slightly larger cone around $K_j$, and let $\chi$ be any fixed compact smooth test cutoff. Evaluate the localized Fourier transform by pairing this Fourier family with $\widehat\chi(\xi-\eta)$ times a smooth cutoff equal to one on its support. On the unbounded conic support, separation gives $|\xi-\eta|\ge c(|\xi|+|\eta|)$ for $\xi\in V$; on the bounded part use $1+|\xi-\eta|\ge c'(1+|\xi|)$ for large $\xi$. Every Schwartz seminorm of this test kernel is therefore $O((1+|\xi|)^{-N})$ for arbitrary $N$. The uniform tempered bound gives
$$\sup_{0<\rho\le1}\sup_{\xi\in V}(1+|\xi|)^N\left|\widehat{\chi\rho^{s_j}(v_j)_\rho}(\xi)\right|<\infty.$$
The Schwartz part has the same estimate by integration by parts on the fixed support of $\chi$. An intermediate exponent between $a_j$ and $s_j$ even makes each displayed seminorm tend to zero. Ordinary weak convergence follows from [F1]. Since $v_j=u_j$ near zero, every fixed output localization uses these same dilates for all sufficiently small $\rho$. This proves the required directional control rather than inferring it from pointwise wavefront inclusion of the rescaled family.

Shrink the cones and localization neighborhoods as in step 1.2, retaining a little angular margin. The product exists there by [F3], iterated over the finitely many factors. For a fixed compactly supported test $\varphi$, its pairing with the product of the localized scaled factors is the absolutely convergent Fourier integral of $\widehat\varphi(-\sum_j\eta_j)$ times the factor transforms. Here is a uniform integrable bound. Compactness of normalized frequency tuples and the joint no-cancellation condition imply that either $|\sum_j\eta_j|\ge c\sum_j|\eta_j|$, or some $\eta_j$ lies in a regular cone and $|\eta_j|\ge c\sum_k|\eta_k|$, for a fixed $c>0$, apart from bounded frequencies. In the first region the Schwartz decay of $\widehat\varphi$ controls the total frequency size; in the second region step 3.1 supplies arbitrarily high decay from that factor. All other localized factor transforms have fixed uniform polynomial bounds by step 1.1 and [F4]. Choosing the decay power larger than the total polynomial degree plus $Dr+1$ gives an integrable majorant independent of $\rho$. Each localized factor transform tends pointwise to zero by weak convergence. Dominated convergence therefore proves $\rho^{\sum_j s_j}\prod_j(u_j)_\rho\to0$. Dilation commutes with the locally defined product by the pullback formula [F3], so this is precisely the scaling estimate for the product. Let every $s_j$ decrease to $a_j$ to obtain the claimed bound.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement assumes a finite nonempty list of factors; empty wavefront cones are allowed and give Schwartz regular parts in step 1.2.
A zero factor makes the product zero and the scaling upper bound in the Statement holds.
For one factor the no-cancellation condition is automatic and the Statement recovers its given upper bound.
The Statement allows a_j=0 and empty singular cones; the strictly positive exponents in step 3.1 control the smooth Fourier parts.
The claimed bound follows by decreasing strictly larger exponents to a_j in step 4.1; no convergence at the endpoint exponent is assumed.
The Statement assumes AC for complete-metric Baire and Countable Choice for Fourier inversion; step 1.1 names those uses.
