The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim: Polarize each homogeneous field-degree-$r$ jet polynomial into $r$ field slots. Commutativity of the scalar fields identifies it with a polynomial in the formal derivative variables $p_a$, invariant under slot permutations. The invertible linear change $p_a=q_a+P/r$ identifies the full polynomial algebra with $\mathbb C[P]\otimes\mathbb C[q_1,\ldots,q_r]/(\sum_aq_a)$. Slot permutations fix $P$ and act only on the relative factor. Expanding in the independent monomials of $P$, invariance holds if and only if every relative coefficient is invariant. Thus the invariant space is exactly $\mathbb C[P]\otimes\mathcal B_r$. In each finite degree choose a basis by ordinary finite Gaussian elimination on the real coefficient polynomials; the monomial ordering gives compatible choices across degrees. The Leibniz rule identifies multiplication by $P_\mu$ with the total derivative $\partial_\mu$ of the local field polynomial. This is a direct tensor decomposition, so has no hidden relations between total and balanced derivatives.

Expand a density using step 1.1 as a finite sum $p(\partial)B_b$. In its integral against $f$, move $p(\partial)$ onto the compact coefficient by integration by parts, obtaining $p(-\partial)f$ multiplying $B_b$. This gives existence of the displayed representation and preserves compact support. Degree zero gives the scalar $c=F(0)$ and is separated from the positive field degrees. To prove uniqueness, suppose a balanced expression represents zero. Separate its field degrees by replacing $\phi$ by $t\phi$, polarize, and evaluate its $r$ slots on the smooth exponential fields $e^{2\pi i k_a\cdot x}$; complex exponentials are permitted by complex multilinear extension from real configurations. The resulting identity is a finite sum of $\widehat f_{r,b}(-\sum_a k_a)$ times the balanced polynomial $b(2\pi ik_1,\ldots,2\pi ik_r)$. For fixed total momentum, vary freely the relative momenta. Independence of the basis polynomials on $\sum_aq_a=0$ makes every coefficient Fourier transform zero at that total momentum. Since that momentum is arbitrary, [F2] gives every $f_{r,b}=0$; also $c=0$.

The same uniqueness is local. In center and relative coordinates for the polarized variational kernel on the thin diagonal, balanced differential operators differentiate only the relative delta variables; their coefficients are the $f_{r,b}$ in the center variable, up to fixed nonzero coordinate constants. Test with a center test times a relative monomial times a cutoff equal to one near the relative origin. Starting at the highest relative order and descending isolates every independent relative delta-jet coefficient. Thus vanishing of the kernel over an open center set forces each $f_{r,b}$ to vanish there. If $F$ is unchanged by all variations supported in an open set $U$, its polarized kernels vanish where any one field slot lies in $U$; near their thin diagonal this is precisely the preceding situation. Conversely, if every coefficient vanishes on $U$, no variation supported in $U$ changes $F$. This proves equality with the functional support. Under the action defined in the Statement, a Lorentz transformation substitutes $p_a\mapsto\Lambda^{\mathsf T}p_a$ and transforms each coefficient by $f(x)\mapsto f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$; $\det\Lambda=1$ preserves $d^4x$. Thus $P$ and all $q_a$ transform by the same linear map and the tensor decomposition is preserved. Translations act on coefficients by the same formula with $\Lambda=I$, and, because the chosen basis is real, complex conjugation sends each coefficient to its complex conjugate. Hence the decomposition is equivariant as stated.

For a general polynomial label write its unique tensor decomposition as $\sum_{\beta,b}c_{\beta,b}\partial^\beta B_b$, and define its coefficient by $\sum_{\beta,b}c_{\beta,b}\partial_{x_i}^\beta K(\ldots,B_b,\ldots)$, independently in every entry. Commutativity of coordinate derivatives and the direct decomposition in step 1.1 make this consistent, linear, and the unique extension satisfying the displayed derivative identity. Smearing and integrating by parts gives exactly the coefficient normal form of step 2.1, so equivalent functional presentations yield the same map. The construction respects the equivariance and support statements of step 3.1. Finally, dilation of a distributional derivative gives $(\partial^\beta T)_\rho=\rho^{-|\beta|}\partial^\beta T_\rho$, so the added derivative increases a scaling upper bound by at most $|\beta|$. All sums and derivative orders here are finite.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. $$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. First write every local density in its unique balanced-jet representative, in which the derivative variables at a degree-$r$ vertex are the relative combinations $q_a=p_a-r^{-1}\sum_bp_b$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. The allowed counterterms must also satisfy the stated linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. A differentiated coefficient is not required to retain the exact scaling degree of a punctured linear combination that vanishes: total differentiation may force a contact term at the diagonal.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Assume Countable Choice. Set $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and let $SO^+(1,3)$ consist of the matrices $\Lambda\in GL_4(\mathbb R)$ satisfying $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preserving the future cone $\{v\in\mathbb R^4:v^0\ge|\mathbf v|\}$. For $a\in\mathbb R^4$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, let $\gamma$ be the affine map $x\mapsto\Lambda x+a$ and define
$$(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),\qquad (\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi).$$
Complex conjugation is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$.

For field degree $r\ge1$, let $p_1,\ldots,p_r\in\mathbb R^4$ be formal commuting derivative variables, put $P=\sum_a p_a$ and $q_a=p_a-P/r$, and let $\mathcal B_r$ be the vector space of permutation-invariant polynomials in the $q_a$, subject to $\sum_aq_a=0$. A balanced degree-$r$ jet polynomial is
$$B_b(\phi)(x)=\left.b(\partial_{x_1},\ldots,\partial_{x_r})\prod_{a=1}^r\phi(x_a)\right|_{x_1=\cdots=x_r=x},\qquad b\in\mathcal B_r.$$
Thus only relative derivative combinations occur in $b$. Choose a real homogeneous basis of each finite-degree part of $\mathcal B_r$. Every off-shell compactly supported local polynomial functional has a unique expression
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{r\ge1}\sum_b\int f_{r,b}(x)B_b(\phi)(x)\,d^4x,$$
with $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_{r,b}\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$, and only finitely many nonzero coefficients. The union of the supports of these coefficient functions equals the functional support, apart from the constant $c$, whose support is empty. With each $p_a$ viewed as a column of coordinate derivative components, the induced Lorentz substitution is $p_a\mapsto\Lambda^{\mathsf T}p_a$, so $P$ and all $q_a$ transform by the same linear map. The balanced decomposition is equivariant for the translation/Lorentz action and complex conjugation specified above.

Distribution-valued multilinear coefficients prescribed linearly on balanced labels extend consistently to all polynomial jet labels by imposing, in each vertex entry,
$$K(\ldots,\partial_\mu A,\ldots)=\partial_{x_i^\mu}K(\ldots,A,\ldots).$$
After smearing, integration by parts therefore makes the resulting maps independent of the chosen local density presentation. Differentiation adds only a finite derivative order to any finite scaling upper bound.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

For $a\in\Omega$ and $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\{a\}$ if and only if
$$u=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}c_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta_a$$
for some finite $m\ge0$ and complex coefficients. The coefficients, with absent higher terms interpreted as zero, are unique. A nonzero such combination has support exactly $\{a\}$; the zero combination has empty support. This holds in ZF.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

For a distribution $u$ on a smooth manifold, the chartwise rapid-decay definition of its wavefront set is independent of the chart: if $y=\psi(x)$, its covector coordinates satisfy $\eta=(D\psi(x))^{-T}\xi$. The resulting $\operatorname{WF}(u)$ is closed and conic in $T^*M\setminus0$. For distributions $u,v$ and a smooth diffeomorphism $\psi$, one has $\operatorname{WF}(u+v)\subseteq\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup\operatorname{WF}(v)$ and $\operatorname{WF}(\psi^*u)=\psi^*\operatorname{WF}(u)$. Finally, $\operatorname{WF}(u)=\varnothing$ exactly when $u$ is represented by a smooth scalar function in every chart.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

derivations.claim:
Define the positive-frequency massless distribution by
$$w(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-i|\mathbf k|t+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}}{2|\mathbf k|(2\pi)^3}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
This is a distribution: pairing a compact smooth spacetime test gives its rapidly decreasing Fourier transform on the null mass shell, and $|\mathbf k|^{-1}d^3\mathbf k$ is integrable at zero and has polynomial growth at infinity. The mass-shell relation gives $Pw=0$. The measure is the restriction of $\theta(k^0)\delta((k^0)^2-|\mathbf k|^2)d^4k$, hence is invariant under the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; its reflection gives $w^*=w(-t,-\mathbf x)$. Scaling $\mathbf k$ shows that $w$ is nonzero homogeneous of degree $-2$. With a damping factor $e^{-\epsilon|\mathbf k|}$, angular integration and the elementary Laplace integral give
$$w_\epsilon(t,\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{4\pi^2}\frac{1}{|\mathbf x|^2-(t-i\epsilon)^2}.$$
The damped spectral integrals converge to $w$ on tests by the preceding absolute Fourier bound.

This datum has precisely the required wavefront condition. At any nonzero point of the null cone, the preceding formula is, in a normal coordinate to that cone, a nonvanishing smooth multiple of a one-sided boundary value $(s\pm i0)^{-1}$. Its Laplace representation has Fourier support in one half-line and nonzero constant magnitude there; convolution with a compact cutoff therefore gives precisely that one-sided conormal direction. The sign selected by $t-i\epsilon$ makes the covector future null under the contract's metric-dual convention. Away from the cone the formula is smooth. At the origin, convolution of the null-shell measure with the rapidly decreasing transform of a test cutoff decreases arbitrarily fast in every cone separated from the future null cone: on that cone the frequency difference is bounded below by a fixed positive multiple of the sum of the two frequency magnitudes, and the mass-shell measure has polynomial growth. Thus no other origin directions occur. Every future null origin direction does occur, by closedness of the wavefront set and approach along nonzero null points with that conormal direction. In the two-point lift $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$ the covectors are $(\xi,-\xi)$ by [F4], giving exactly the specified relation. The boundary-value difference $w-w(-t,-\mathbf x)$ is supported on the null cone, so $E=(W-W^{\mathsf T})/i$ has causal support. This verifies the free $W$ conditions in [F1].

Define the time-ordered distribution by its spatial Fourier representation
$$h_F(t,\mathbf x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-i|\mathbf k||t|+i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}}{2|\mathbf k|(2\pi)^3}\,d^3\mathbf k.$$
It acts continuously on tests by first taking their spatial Fourier transform, which decreases rapidly uniformly on compact time intervals; the same polynomial measure bound as in step 1.1 is integrable after this decay. It is symmetric under $(t,\mathbf x)\mapsto(-t,-\mathbf x)$, equals the required ordering of $w$, and is homogeneous of degree $-2$, hence has scaling degree $2$. Off zero, time ordering and step 2.1 give exactly the permitted Feynman wavefront directions. At zero every relative covector is allowed by [F1]. Lorentz transformations preserve its off-zero ordering, since time order is preserved on causal pairs and the two orderings agree on spacelike pairs; the transformed distribution is another degree-$2$ extension of the same punctured kernel. Uniqueness from [F3] gives Lorentz invariance globally. Translation invariance of $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ is immediate. Thus $(W,H_F)$ is an admissible free datum, with all its stated hypotheses checked.

For a fixed spatial frequency $\mathbf k\ne0$, $e^{-i|\mathbf k||t|}/(2|\mathbf k|)$ is continuous at $t=0$, and its first derivative has jump $-i$. Twice differentiating it as a one-dimensional distribution therefore gives
$$\left(\partial_t^2+|\mathbf k|^2\right)\frac{e^{-i|\mathbf k||t|}}{2|\mathbf k|}=-i\delta(t).$$
The integrable small-frequency bound and the rapidly decreasing spatial test transform justify this differentiation inside the pairing; the value at the single frequency zero is immaterial. Fourier inversion [F4] yields $Ph_F=-i\delta_0$ in four spacetime dimensions. Its punctured restriction is zero, of degree $-\infty$, while the forced contact term has degree $4$. Two undifferentiated linear vertices have a contraction of degree $2<4$, whose unique degree-preserving extension is $h_F$. Replacing the first vertex $\int(Pf)\phi$ by the equal functional $\int fP\phi$ in [F2] forces its differentiated contraction to be $Ph_F=-i\delta_0$. Requiring instead that the zero punctured differentiated coefficient extend with degree $-\infty$ forces zero, giving different values for the same input functional. This refutes the Statement. The engineering bound is $2+2=4$, which permits precisely this contact term and is compatible with the corrected contract.

citations.quote: For a rooted tree $t$, an admissible cut is a subset $C$ of its edges meeting every root-to-leaf path in at most one edge. Removing the edges of $C$ leaves one component containing the root; denote it by $R_C(t)$. The components on the child side of the cut edges form a forest denoted by $P_C(t)$.

derivations.claim: A rooted-tree isomorphism bijects admissible edge subsets and preserves the isomorphism classes of their pruned forests and root components, so the cut sum is well-defined on $\mathcal T$. Each cut partitions the vertices between $P_C$ and $R_C$, hence every coproduct term has the same total degree as $t$; multiplicative extension makes $\Delta$ a graded algebra map. For nonempty $t$, only the empty cut contributes after applying $\varepsilon$ to the first factor, and only the virtual full cut $t\otimes1$ contributes after applying $\varepsilon$ to the second factor. Thus both counit identities hold on tree generators and, since both maps are algebra maps, on all forests.

Adjoin the empty cut $(P,R)=(1,t)$ and the virtual root cut $(P,R)=(t,1)$. A term of either iterated coproduct is equivalently a labeling of every vertex by its tensor position $1$, $2$, or $3$, with labels nonincreasing along every parent-to-child edge: the root-side trunk has label $3$, any middle components have label $2$, and the detached crown has label $1$. In $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta(t)$, the first cut separates the label-$3$ trunk and the second cuts the pruned forest into labels $1$ and $2$; in $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta(t)$, the first cut separates the label-$1$ crown and the second cuts the root component into labels $2$ and $3$. Conversely, any such labeling determines these cuts uniquely: cut each edge where the label drops, and use the empty or virtual root cut when a layer is absent. Jumps from $3$ directly to $1$ are represented by the same edge cut in both iterates, with the missing middle factor supplied by the corresponding extreme cut. Thus both iterates sum over exactly the same finite vertex labelings, and each labeling gives the same three forests with the same multiplicity even when distinct labelings yield isomorphic forests. Coassociativity holds on $t$. Both iterated maps are algebra maps, so the identity holds on all forests.

The degree-zero part is exactly $\mathbb Q1$, and the counit and grading checked in steps 1.1 and 2.1 make $H$ a connected graded bialgebra. For linear maps $f,g:H\to H$, define convolution $f*g=m(f\otimes g)\Delta$; coassociativity of $\Delta$ and associativity of multiplication make this product associative with unit $u\varepsilon$, where $u$ is the algebra unit map. Put $\pi=\mathrm{id}-u\varepsilon$.

If $h$ is homogeneous of degree $n$, then $\pi^{*k}(h)=0$ for $k>n$: the iterated coproduct has $k$ nonnegative homogeneous tensor degrees summing to $n$, so for $k>n$ at least one factor has degree zero and is killed by $\pi$. Therefore $S=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k\pi^{*k}$ is a finite sum on each homogeneous input. Multiplying its finite partial sum on either side by $\mathrm{id}=u\varepsilon+\pi$ telescopes to $u\varepsilon$, because the remaining power of $\pi$ vanishes above degree $n$. Thus $S$ is a two-sided convolution inverse of $\mathrm{id}$; uniqueness follows by multiplying any two-sided inverse expressions in the associative convolution algebra.

For a positive-degree tree $t$, expand $(S*\mathrm{id})(t)=0$ using the coproduct in [F1]. The two extreme cuts contribute $S(t)$ and $t$, and each nonempty ordinary cut contributes $S(P_C(t))R_C(t)$. Rearranging gives the displayed recursion. For every such cut both the root component and each tree in the pruned forest have fewer vertices than $t$, so induction on degree terminates.

Let $m:H\otimes H\to H$ be multiplication and define $g(a\otimes b)=S(b)S(a)$. In the convolution algebra $\operatorname{Hom}(H\otimes H,H)$, both $S\circ m$ and $g$ are two-sided inverses of $m$: for example, $(g*m)(a\otimes b)=\sum S(b_{(1)})(S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)})b_{(2)}=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$, and $(m*g)(a\otimes b)=\sum a_{(1)}(b_{(1)}S(b_{(2)}))S(a_{(2)})=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b)1$; the analogous two products for $S\circ m$ are $(S*\mathrm{id})(ab)$ and $(\mathrm{id}*S)(ab)$. Uniqueness of a two-sided inverse gives $S(ab)=S(b)S(a)$. Since $H$ is commutative, $S(b)S(a)=S(a)S(b)$, so the antipode is multiplicative.

citations.quote: Let $H=\mathbb Q[\mathcal T]$ be the commutative polynomial algebra generated by $\mathcal T$; its monomial basis consists of forests, and the degree of a forest is its total number of vertices.

The algebra $H$ is a connected graded bialgebra. Let $u$ be the algebra unit map and $m$ forest multiplication; use convolution $f*g=m(f\otimes g)\Delta$ on endomorphisms of $H$, with unit $u\varepsilon$. It has a unique two-sided convolution inverse $S$ of its identity map.
Then $A=A_-\oplus A_+$ as a $K$-module, and both summands are subalgebras, with $1\in A_+$. Define $R:A\to A_-$ by retaining exactly the strictly negative powers; $1-R$ is the projection onto $A_+$.
For all $x,y\in A$, $R$ satisfies $$R(x)R(y)=R\bigl(R(x)y+xR(y)-xy\bigr).$$

derivations.claim: For homogeneous $h$ of degree $n>0$, every term $h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}$ in $\widetilde\Delta(h)$ has both factors of positive degree strictly less than $n$, because $H$ is connected and graded by [F2]. There are finitely many terms by [F1], so induction on $n$ defines $B_\phi(h)$ and $\phi_-(h)$ without circularity; extend linearly and set $\phi_-(1)=1$.

Let $x,y$ be positive-degree homogeneous elements with total degree $d$, and assume inductively that $\phi_-(uv)=\phi_-(u)\phi_-(v)$ whenever $\deg u+\deg v<d$. Expand $\Delta(xy)=\Delta(x)\Delta(y)$. In $(\phi_-*\phi)(x)(\phi_-*\phi)(y)$, every summand except the unique pair $(x\otimes1)(y\otimes1)$ has left-factor product degree less than $d$; for those terms the induction hypothesis factors $\phi_-(x_{(1)}y_{(1)})$, while the character property factors $\phi(x_{(2)}y_{(2)})$. Thus these lower-degree summands agree term-by-term with those in $(\phi_-*\phi)(xy)$. The only remaining terms are the top pair $\phi_-(x)\phi_-(y)$ in the product and $\phi_-(xy)$ in the convolution of $xy$. Since $B_\phi(xy)=(\phi_-*\phi)(xy)-\phi_-(xy)$ and $(\phi_-*\phi)(x)=\phi_-(x)+B_\phi(x)$, subtracting the top pair gives
$$B_\phi(xy)=(\phi_-*\phi)(x)(\phi_-*\phi)(y)-\phi_-(x)\phi_-(y)=\phi_-(x)B_\phi(y)+B_\phi(x)\phi_-(y)+B_\phi(x)B_\phi(y).$$
The equality uses commutativity of $A$.

If either $x$ or $y$ has degree zero, multiplicativity follows from $\phi_-(1)=1$. Otherwise write $X=B_\phi(x)$ and $Y=B_\phi(y)$. By the recursion and the identity in [F4],
$$\phi_-(xy)=-R B_\phi(xy)=R\bigl(R(X)Y+XR(Y)-XY\bigr)=R(X)R(Y)=\phi_-(x)\phi_-(y).$$
Thus degree induction proves that $\phi_-$ is a character on all of $H$.

For positive-degree $h$, expanding its full coproduct gives $(\phi_-*\phi)(h)=\phi_-(h)+B_\phi(h)=-RB_\phi(h)+B_\phi(h)=(1-R)B_\phi(h)\in A_+$; also $(\phi_-*\phi)(1)=1\in A_+$. For $x,y\in H$, the character properties already proved and multiplicativity of $\Delta$ give
$$ (\phi_-*\phi)(xy)=\sum\phi_-(x_{(1)})\phi_-(y_{(1)})\phi(x_{(2)})\phi(y_{(2)})=(\phi_-*\phi)(x)(\phi_-*\phi)(y),$$
where commutativity of $A$ permits the middle factors to be regrouped. Thus $\phi_+=\phi_-*\phi$ is a character with the stated range.

For $h\in H$, multiplicativity and unitality of $\phi_-$ and the antipode identities in [F2] give
$$((\phi_-\circ S)*\phi_-)(h)=\sum\phi_-(S(h_{(1)}))\phi_-(h_{(2)})=\phi_-\bigl(\sum S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}\bigr)=\phi_-(u\varepsilon(h))=u_A\varepsilon(h),$$
and likewise
$$ (\phi_-*(\phi_-\circ S))(h)=\sum\phi_-(h_{(1)})\phi_-(S(h_{(2)}))=\phi_-\bigl(\sum h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)})\bigr)=u_A\varepsilon(h).$$
Hence $\phi_-^{-1}=\phi_-\circ S$. From $\phi_+=\phi_-*\phi$, associativity and cancellation by this inverse give $\phi=\phi_-^{-1}*\phi_+$.

Use the smooth off-shell coordinate model $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$, with $x^0=c_{\mathrm{light}}t$ in SI coordinates, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, increasing $x^0$ as the future direction, and standard orientation. The scalar time-ordering convention sets $c_{\mathrm{light}}=1$, so $x^0$ is the length coordinate in that convention as well. Here off shell means that no field equation is imposed. Take smooth real components $a_\mu\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ and a smooth commuting matter field $\psi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C^4)$. Use the normalized real potential $a=a_\mu dx^\mu$ and dimensionless coupling $g=q\sqrt{\mu_0c_{\mathrm{light}}/\hbar}$ of the charged-gauge-data convention; $a_\mu$ has units $\mathrm m^{-1}$, $g$ is dimensionless, and $\psi$ has units $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$. The exact supplier convention is $a'_\mu=a_\mu+\partial_\mu\alpha$, $\psi'=e^{ig\alpha}\psi$, for a smooth dimensionless real infinitesimal gauge parameter $\alpha$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be the free graded-commutative $\mathbb C$-algebra over $C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$ generated by the finite jets of $a_\mu$, $\psi$, an odd ghost $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$, an odd antighost $\bar c$, and an even auxiliary variable $B$. Every element of $\mathcal P$ is a polynomial in finitely many jet coordinates. The fields $a_\mu$ and $\psi$ have Grassmann parity $0$ and ghost number $0$; $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$ has parity $1$ and ghost number $1$; $\bar c$ has parity $1$ and ghost number $-1$; and $B$ has parity $0$ and ghost number $0$. The ghost and nonminimal variables are formal algebraic generators; no state-space or positivity claim is made. The generators $c_{\mathrm{gh}},\bar c,B$ carry no physical unit assignment, and the differential below is dimensionless. The subscript distinguishes the ghost from the speed of light $c_{\mathrm{light}}$.

Define the odd derivation $s:\mathcal P\to\mathcal P$ of ghost number $1$ by
$$
sa_\mu=\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}},\qquad sc_{\mathrm{gh}}=0,\qquad s\bar c=B,\qquad sB=0,\qquad s\psi=igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi .
$$
Extend $s$ by the graded Leibniz rule $s(XY)=(sX)Y+(-1)^{|X|}X(sY)$ for homogeneous $X$, where $|X|$ is Grassmann parity, and by $s(\partial^\beta X)=\partial^\beta(sX)$ for every multi-index $\beta$. This is an off-shell local algebraic differential for the Abelian gauge transformations; it is not a BRST charge on a Hilbert space and it does not assert existence of a gauge-invariant quantum theory.

derivations.claim: On the gauge and nonminimal generators, $s^2a_\mu=s(\partial_\mu c_{\mathrm{gh}})=\partial_\mu(sc_{\mathrm{gh}})=0$, $s^2c_{\mathrm{gh}}=0$, $s^2\bar c=sB=0$, and $s^2B=0$. Commutation of $s$ with spacetime derivatives gives the same equality on every jet of these generators.

Since $c_{\mathrm{gh}}$ is odd in a graded-commutative algebra over $\mathbb C$, $c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2=-c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2$ and hence $c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2=0$. The graded Leibniz rule therefore gives
$$s^2\psi=s(igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi)=-igc_{\mathrm{gh}}(igc_{\mathrm{gh}}\psi)=g^2c_{\mathrm{gh}}^2\psi=0.$$

The square of an odd derivation is an even derivation: the two mixed terms in $s^2(XY)$ cancel by the graded Leibniz rule. It vanishes on every generator and every jet by steps 1.1–1.2, so it vanishes on each finite polynomial in $\mathcal P$.

Now $s^2=0$ by step 2.1, so $s$ is a differential. It preserves the number of the selected doublet variables: its action on the other generators is independent of them, and each term $v^j\partial_L/\partial u^j$ replaces one $u^j$ by one $v^j$. Thus $[N,s]=0$. On each pair, $hu^j=0$, $hv^j=u^j$, $su^j=v^j$, and $sv^j=0$, so $(sh+hs)u^j=u^j$ and $(sh+hs)v^j=v^j$. Both $sh+hs$ and $N$ are even derivations and vanish on the doublet-independent generators; equality on generators proves $sh+hs=N$ on the polynomial algebra.

Let $a_k$ be $s$-closed and homogeneous of doublet number $k>0$. Since $[N,s]=0$, the homogeneous components of any $s$-closed polynomial are separately $s$-closed. Applying $sh+hs=N$ to $a_k$ gives $s(ha_k)=ka_k$ because $sa_k=0$; division by the nonzero integer $k$ yields $a_k=s(ha_k/k)$.

Every polynomial has a finite decomposition $a=\sum_{k\ge0}a_k$. For an $s$-closed $a$, step 4.1 makes every $a_k$ with $k>0$ exact, while $a_0$ is closed by $[N,s]=0$. Therefore every extended cohomology class has a representative in the doublet-independent subalgebra.

If a doublet-independent closed polynomial $a_0$ is $s b$ in the extended algebra, take the doublet-number-zero component $b_0$ of the finite decomposition of $b$. Because $s$ preserves $N$, the number-zero component of $sb=a_0$ is $s b_0=a_0$. Thus a class from the minimal subalgebra becomes exact in the extension only if it was already exact there, proving injectivity as well as the surjectivity in step 5.1.

citations.quote:
The Abelian jet derivation $s$ defined in the local BRST algebra satisfies $s^2=0$. More generally, take any finite set of jet doublets $u^j,v^j$ with $|v^j|=|u^j|+1\pmod 2$, $\operatorname{gh}(v^j)=\operatorname{gh}(u^j)+1$, $su^j=v^j$, and $sv^j=0$, and suppose the transformations of all other generators are independent of these doublets. Define the doublet-number operator
$$N=\sum_j\left(u^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial u^j}+v^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial v^j}\right)$$
and the odd homotopy $h=\sum_j u^j\frac{\partial_L}{\partial v^j}$, using left graded derivatives. Then $[N,s]=0$ and $sh+hs=N$. Consequently the inclusion of the doublet-independent polynomial subalgebra induces an isomorphism on polynomial BRST cohomology. In particular, if $sa_k=0$ and $Na_k=ka_k$ for a positive integer $k$, then $a_k=s(ha_k/k)$.

For a ghost-number grading, write this cohomology as
$$H^r(s,\mathcal P)=\ker(s:\mathcal P^r\to\mathcal P^{r+1})/\operatorname{im}(s:\mathcal P^{r-1}\to\mathcal P^r).$$

Use the four-dimensional coordinate and jet algebra and nilpotent differential $s$ fixed by the earlier Abelian local BRST definition and nilpotence lemma. For integers $r$ and $0\le p\le4$, a compactly supported local horizontal $p$-form of ghost number $r$ is a finite sum of terms
$$f_{i_1\ldots i_p}(x,z)\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_p},$$
where each coefficient is smooth and compactly supported in $x\in\mathbb R^4$, polynomial in finitely many field-jet coordinates $z$, and homogeneous of ghost number $r$. Denote this space by $\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}$. A left derivative is used for odd jet coordinates.

For each spacetime index $\mu$, define the total derivative on a local coefficient by
$$D_\mu=\frac{\partial}{\partial x^\mu}+\sum_{i,\alpha}z^i_{\alpha+e_\mu}\frac{\partial_L}{\partial z^i_\alpha},$$
where $\alpha$ ranges over multi-indices, $i$ over the field and ghost generators, and $e_\mu$ is the multi-index with one derivative in direction $\mu$. The horizontal exterior derivative is $d_H=dx^\mu\wedge D_\mu$. It satisfies $d_H^2=0$. Extend $s$ to a homogeneous $p$-form by $s\omega=(-1)^p s_{\mathrm{coeff}}\omega$, where $s_{\mathrm{coeff}}$ acts on its coefficient by the earlier local BRST definition; then $s^2=0$ and $s d_H+d_Hs=0$.

Set $\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}=0$ for $p<0$ or $p>4$. Evaluation of a compactly supported local four-form on any smooth off-shell configuration is a finite integral.

For a graded subcomplex $\mathcal K^{r,p}\subseteq\Omega^{r,p}_{\mathrm{loc},c}$ stable under $s$ and $d_H$, define
$$Z^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=\{a_p\in\mathcal K^{r,p}:\ s a_p+d_Ha_{p-1}=0\text{ for some }a_{p-1}\in\mathcal K^{r+1,p-1}\}$$
and
$$B^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=\{s b_p+d_Hc_{p-1}:\ b_p\in\mathcal K^{r-1,p},\ c_{p-1}\in\mathcal K^{r,p-1}\}.$$
The relative local BRST cohomology is $H^{r,p}(s|d_H;\mathcal K)=Z^{r,p}/B^{r,p}$. In four dimensions, $H^1(s|d_H)$ is shorthand for $H^{1,4}(s|d_H)$. For compactly supported coefficients, $\int_{\mathbb R^4}d_Hc_3=0$ by the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus in each coordinate and Fubini's theorem, so the quotient by $d_H$ identifies densities that define the same integrated local functional.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix any admissible flat scalar free datum and local scalar polynomial class as defined by the local time-ordered product contract. Then there exists a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps $T_n$ satisfying that contract at every finite perturbative order. At order $n$, each numerical graph distribution has a finite upper scaling bound in the $4(n-1)$ relative coordinates. At the analytic extension stage, independent balanced coefficients admit extensions preserving their actual scaling degree; total-derivative labels and the final local normalizations obey the engineering scaling upper bounds prescribed by the contract. For a fixed punctured coefficient with bound $B_\Gamma$, the extension ambiguity is contained in the finite span of derivatives of the diagonal delta distribution of order at most $\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and is zero when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$, subject also to the linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, one can use its actual degree in place of $B_\Gamma$. Thus the coefficients form a formal series only; no convergence in the coupling, adiabatic limit, positivity claim, or gauge/Ward identity is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Under the hypotheses of [F3], including [A3] and [A4], the scalar time-ordering input exists as a formal coefficientwise scheme. Fix such a scheme as background. The additional operator $\mathcal W_\hbar$, its nilpotence, and the locality premise in [A1]–[A2] are separate hypotheses not supplied by [F3].

Apply $\mathcal W_\hbar$ to the expansion in [A1]. Since $\mathcal W_\hbar^2X=0$, its order-$\hbar^n$ coefficient is the leading operator $s$ applied to $\mathcal A$; all terms from the positive powers of $\hbar$ in $\mathcal W_\hbar$ have order at least $n+1$. Hence $s\mathcal A=0$ in $\mathscr F_n^2$.

Since $\mathcal A=[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ and $s\mathcal A=0$ in $\mathscr F_n^2$, the quotient definition in [F2] gives $s a_4=d_Hc_3$ for some $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{2,3}$, after absorbing a sign into $c_3$. Thus $a_4$ is a cocycle in the specified relative local cohomology.

If $[a_4]_{s|d_H}=0$, the quotient definition in [F2], restricted to $\mathcal K_n$, supplies $b_4\in\mathcal K_n^{0,4}$ and $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}$ such that $a_4=s b_4+d_Hc_3$. This uses the cocycle conclusion of step 3.1 so the relative class is defined.

The counterterm class $[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ is admissible by [A2]. Replacing $X$ by $X-\hbar^n[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ changes the order-$n$ breaking by $-s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, because the leading term of $\mathcal W_\hbar$ is $s$. Step 4.1 gives $[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}=s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$, since $d_Hc_3$ is zero in that quotient, so the breaking is canceled.

Conversely, if an admissible local counterterm class $[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}$ cancels the order-$n$ breaking in $\mathscr F_n^1$, then $[a_4]_{\mathscr F_n}-s[b_4]_{\mathscr F_n}=0$. By the quotient definition in [F2], $a_4-sb_4=d_Hc_3$ for some $c_3\in\mathcal K_n^{1,3}$. This is exactly the relative coboundary condition; step 3.1 ensures that $[a_4]_{s|d_H}$ is the class under discussion.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. Let $\kappa:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bilinear form that is invariant, meaning
$$\kappa([U,V],W)=\kappa(U,[V,W])\qquad(U,V,W\in\mathfrak g).$$
No nondegeneracy, positivity, simplicity, or compactness assumption is imposed. Put $S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and $\mathcal L\mathfrak g=C^\infty(S^1,\mathfrak g)$, with pointwise bracket $[X,Y](\theta)=[X(\theta),Y(\theta)]_{\mathfrak g}$. For $Y\in\mathcal L\mathfrak g$, write $Y'=\partial_\theta Y$ in the indicated periodic coordinate.

A Lie-algebra $2$-cocycle for the trivial scalar action is an alternating bilinear map $\omega:\mathcal L\mathfrak g\times\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\omega([X,Y],Z)+\omega([Y,Z],X)+\omega([Z,X],Y)=0.$$
Define the candidate current cocycle and its candidate central-term bracket by
$$\omega(X,Y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\kappa(X(\theta),Y'(\theta))\,d\theta,\qquad \widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}=\mathcal L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb R,$$
$$[(X,a),(Y,b)]=([X,Y],\omega(X,Y)).$$
The real coordinates $a,b$ are central coordinates and do not enter the right-hand side. A one-dimensional central extension means a short exact sequence of Lie algebras $0\to\mathbb R\to\widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}\to\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to0$ whose kernel is central. The proposition on this page verifies that the displayed operation has this Lie-algebra structure. The normalization is fixed as written; no integer level, integration to a loop group, or representation-theoretic existence or unitarity follows from this definition.

derivations.claim:
Bilinearity of $\kappa$ and differentiation makes $\omega$ bilinear. By symmetry and the product rule,
$$\omega(X,Y)+\omega(Y,X)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\bigl(\kappa(X,Y')+\kappa(X',Y)\bigr)\,d\theta=\frac1{2\pi}\bigl[\kappa(X,Y)\bigr]_{0}^{2\pi}=0.$$
The endpoint values agree because $X$ and $Y$ are smooth maps on $S^1$, so $\omega$ is skew-symmetric; over $\mathbb R$, this implies $\omega(X,X)=0$.

Invariance and symmetry give
$$\kappa([X,Y],Z')=\kappa(X,[Y,Z']),\quad \kappa([Y,Z],X')=\kappa(X',[Y,Z]),\quad \kappa([Z,X],Y')=\kappa(X,[Y',Z]).$$
The product rule and $[Y,Z]'=[Y',Z]+[Y,Z']$ therefore yield
$$\kappa([X,Y],Z')+\kappa([Y,Z],X')+\kappa([Z,X],Y')=\partial_\theta\kappa(X,[Y,Z]).$$
Integrating over one period makes the right-hand side zero. By the definition of $\omega$, this is the required cyclic cocycle identity.

The displayed operation is bilinear and skew-symmetric by the pointwise Lie bracket and step 1.1. The vector component of its Jacobi sum is the pointwise Jacobi sum in $\mathfrak g$, hence vanishes at every $\theta$. Its real component is the cyclic sum in step 1.2, hence also vanishes. Thus the operation satisfies Jacobi and is a Lie bracket.

The maps $i(a)=(0,a)$ and $p(X,a)=X$ are Lie-algebra homomorphisms: the bracket of any two elements in $\operatorname{im}i$ is zero, and $p([(X,a),(Y,b)])=[X,Y]$. The projection is surjective because $p(X,0)=X$, and $\ker p=\{(0,a):a\in\mathbb R\}=\operatorname{im}i$. Moreover $[(0,a),(Y,b)]=(0,\omega(0,Y))=(0,0)$ by bilinearity of $\omega$, so the kernel is central. This proves the asserted central extension.

Apply [F2] with $m(p)=p^2$ on the sigma-finite positive-measure space $(\mathbb R,dp)$; sigma-finiteness follows from $\mathbb R=\bigcup_{n\ge1}[-n,n]$ and $[-1,1]$ has positive finite measure. It gives the self-adjoint nonnegative multiplication operator $A$ with the displayed domain and spectral calculus. The multiplier $(M^2+p^2)^{-1}$ is bounded by $M^{-2}$ and maps $H$ into $D(A)$ because $p^2/(M^2+p^2)\le1$; pointwise multiplication then shows it is the two-sided inverse of $M^2I+A$. For $u$ with bounded support, every $A^ru$ is in $H$. Pointwise finite geometric division gives
$$
(M^2+p^2)^{-1}-M^{-2}\sum_{r=0}^{N}(-p^2/M^2)^r=r_N(p^2),
$$
so the remainder on such $u$ is multiplication by $r_N(p^2)$.

The target coefficient $C_N:=M^{-2}(E^2/M^2)^{N+1}$ is finite and is strictly less than $M^{-2}$. If $N=0$, $|r_0(q)|=M^{-2}(q/M^2)/(1+q/M^2)\to M^{-2}>C_0$ as $q\to\infty$. If $N\ge1$, $|r_N(q)|=M^{-2}(q/M^2)^{N+1}/(1+q/M^2)\to\infty$. In either case choose $P>0$ so that $|r_N(p^2)|>C_N$ for every $p\in[P,P+M]$, and put $u=M^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{[P,P+M]}$. The interval has Lebesgue measure $M$, so $\|u\|_2^2=M^{-1}\int_P^{P+M}1\,dp=1$; its bounded support puts it in every $D(A^r)$, while
$$\|r_N(A)u\|_2^2=M^{-1}\int_P^{P+M}|r_N(p^2)|^2\,dp>C_N^2.$$
Thus the full-space bound fails. The restriction $E<M$ is precisely what makes the proposed low-energy coefficient smaller than the $N=0$ high-momentum limit; the example does not contradict the band-limited theorem.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\zeta)$ when both covectors are nonzero null and cotangent to the same null straight line, with parallel transport carrying $\xi$ to $\zeta$. Precisely, for $x\ne y$ there must be a future-directed nonconstant affinely parametrized null straight line $\gamma$ and parameters $s,t$ in either order with $x=\gamma(s)$, $y=\gamma(t)$ and a real $\lambda\ne0$ such that $\xi=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(s),\cdot)$ and $\zeta=\lambda\eta(\dot\gamma(t),\cdot)$. When $x=y$, require $\xi=\zeta$ and allow every nonzero null covector. This relation is unsigned: the future first-covector condition below selects $\lambda>0$, while the Feynman past branch selects $\lambda<0$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition is imposed compatibly with integration by parts in the local functionals. First write every local density in its unique balanced-jet representative, in which the derivative variables at a degree-$r$ vertex are the relative combinations $q_a=p_a-r^{-1}\sum_bp_b$. At the extension stage, numerical coefficients on independent balanced labels admit extensions across the total diagonal preserving their actual scaling degree; the final normalization conditions below are imposed within the engineering upper bounds. General jet labels are recovered by total coordinate differentiation of the already extended full coefficients and by linearity; this includes differentiation of the remaining field jets. For a primitive differentiated graph the required upper scaling bound is the engineering degree
$$B_\Gamma=2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_e|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph containing proper subgraphs, use a finite upper bound obtained by causal block induction from the edge degrees and the finite derivative orders of the chosen lower-order local counterterms; total derivatives add their orders to that bound. Any two extensions of a fixed punctured coefficient with upper bound $B_\Gamma$ differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor B_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $B_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $B_\Gamma<4(n-1)$. The allowed counterterms must also satisfy the stated linearity and derivative identities. For the analytic degree-preserving extension family of an independent balanced coefficient, its actual degree replaces $B_\Gamma$ in this ambiguity bound. A differentiated coefficient is not required to retain the exact scaling degree of a punctured linear combination that vanishes: total differentiation may force a contact term at the diagonal.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Assume Countable Choice. For two scalar time-ordered systems $T$ and $T'$ satisfying the local scalar contract for the same free data and with $T_0=T'_0=1$, $T_1=T'_1=\operatorname{id}$, define their normalized formal S-maps by
$$\mathcal S(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V),\qquad \mathcal S'(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}T'_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
There is a unique formal map $Z(V)=V+O(V^2)$ from local polynomial functionals to local polynomial functionals such that $Z(0)=0$, $dZ_0=\operatorname{id}$, $Z$ preserves supports and scalar Poincare covariance, and
$$\mathcal S'(V)=\mathcal S(Z(V))$$
coefficientwise. Such maps compose, and each has a recursively defined formal inverse; hence they form a group under composition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have Minkowski metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$. A scalar local polynomial functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_j(x)P_j(j^{s_j}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $N$ is a finite nonnegative integer, $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$, $c\in\mathbb C$, and $f_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$. For a finite integer $s_j\ge0$, the $s_j$-jet is $j^{s_j}\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{\alpha\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}^4,\,|\alpha|\le s_j}$; each $P_j$ is a complex polynomial in these finitely many jet coordinates. This is the local functional class used by the supplied scalar time-ordered system.

For every mass label $m\ge0$, suppose a normalized scalar time-ordered system $T_n^{(m)}$ with the same local scalar contract is supplied. Define its coefficientwise formal S-map by
$$\mathcal S_m(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}T_n^{(m)}(V,\ldots,V),\qquad T_0^{(m)}=1,\quad T_1^{(m)}=\operatorname{id}.$$
The series is formal in the interaction degree; no analytic convergence is asserted.

Use units $c=\hbar=1$, so the mass label $m$ has mass dimension one. The scale parameter $\rho>0$ is dimensionless. On scalar field configurations put
$$(C_\rho\phi)(x)=\rho^{-1}\phi(\rho^{-1}x),$$
the engineering scaling of a four-dimensional scalar field. For a mass-indexed family of functionals $F=(F_m)_{m\ge0}$, define
$$(\sigma_\rho F)_m=C_\rho^*F_{\rho^{-1}m},\qquad (C_\rho^*F)(\phi)=F(C_{\rho^{-1}}\phi).$$
Thus the component at mass $m$ is pulled back from the component at mass $\rho^{-1}m$; equivalently the mass label scales as $m\mapsto\rho m$. If $A=(A_m)_{m\ge0}$ is instead a family of maps from local functionals (or their formal series) to local or microcausal functionals (or their formal series), define its induced scale conjugate, denoted $\sigma_\rho A\sigma_\rho^{-1}$, by
$$(\sigma_\rho A\sigma_\rho^{-1})_m=C_\rho^*\circ A_{\rho^{-1}m}\circ(C_\rho^*)^{-1},\qquad (C_\rho^*)^{-1}=C_{\rho^{-1}}^*.$$
Here the rightmost pullback acts on the input, the leftmost pullback acts on every output coefficient, and formal indeterminates are fixed. In particular the mass-$m$ component of the scale-conjugated formal S-map is
$$ (\sigma_\rho\mathcal S\sigma_\rho^{-1})_m=C_\rho^*\circ\mathcal S_{\rho^{-1}m}\circ(C_\rho^*)^{-1}.$$
These functional and map actions are extended coefficientwise to formal series. They obey $\sigma_1=\operatorname{id}$ and $\sigma_{\rho\tau}=\sigma_\rho\sigma_\tau$; the dilation sends compact supports to compact supports and normalizes the proper orthochronous Poincare action.

For $m\ge0$, $\rho>0$ and each $n\ge0$, define the conjugated sequence of multilinear maps componentwise by
$$T'^{(m)}_{n,\rho}(F_1,\ldots,F_n):=C_\rho^*\!\left[T_n^{(\rho^{-1}m)}\bigl((C_\rho^*)^{-1}F_1,\ldots,(C_\rho^*)^{-1}F_n\bigr)\right].$$
For $n=0$ this means $T'^{(m)}_{0,\rho}=C_\rho^*1=1$; for $n=1$ it gives $T'^{(m)}_{1,\rho}=\operatorname{id}$. Assume for every $m\ge0$ and $\rho>0$ that this sequence, as well as the supplied sequence $(T_n^{(m)})_{n\ge0}$, satisfies the normalized local scalar time-ordered-system contract for the same free data at mass $m$, after transporting the free data at mass $\rho^{-1}m$ by the stated pullback. This is the scale-admissibility condition on the sequences. Their formal S-maps are distinct objects: by multilinearity and coefficientwise pullback, the S-map of $(T'^{(m)}_{n,\rho})_{n\ge0}$ is exactly $(\sigma_\rho\mathcal S\sigma_\rho^{-1})_m$ displayed above. Define $Z_\rho=(Z_{\rho,m})_{m\ge0}$ by the componentwise equations
$$C_\rho^*\circ\mathcal S_{\rho^{-1}m}\circ(C_\rho^*)^{-1}=\mathcal S_m\circ Z_{\rho,m}\qquad(m\ge0),$$
where each $Z_{\rho,m}$ is the unique formal local map with identity linear term, supplied by the finite-renormalization comparison proposition under these hypotheses. The notation $Z_{\rho,m}(V)=V+O(V^2)$ means that all terms after the linear term have interaction degree at least two. This is a conditional definition: no existence of a time-ordered system for any particular model is asserted.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Under [A1], [F1] fixes $t=\log\rho$ as the dimensionless scale coordinate and the vector field is the prescribed $F(t,g)=bg^2$. If $c=0$, the constant function $g(t)=g_0$ has derivative zero and $bg_0^2=0$, so it solves the IVP on all of $\mathbb R$. If $c\ne0$, set $\gamma(t)=g_0/(1-ct)$ on the interval specified in the Statement. For every interior $t$,
$$\frac{\gamma(t+h)-\gamma(t)}{h}=\frac{g_0c}{(1-ct)(1-c(t+h))}\longrightarrow\frac{g_0c}{(1-ct)^2}=b\gamma(t)^2,$$
and $\gamma(0)=g_0$, so it solves the IVP.

The vector field $F(t,x)=bx^2$ is continuous on the open domain $D=\mathbb R^2$. On any compact time-state cylinder with $|x|,|y|\le R$,
$$|F(t,x)-F(t,y)|=|b||x-y||x+y|\le2|b|R|x-y|,$$
so it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable by [F3]. Uniqueness from [F4] shows that every solution through $(0,g_0)$ agrees with step 1.1 on its common interval. If $c\ne0$, any strictly larger interval containing the stated interval must contain $c^{-1}$. A solution $G$ on such an interval would be continuous at $c^{-1}$, while uniqueness forces $G=\gamma$ on the original interval and $|\gamma(t)|\to\infty$ as $t$ approaches $c^{-1}$ from within it, a contradiction. When $c=0$, the constant solution already exists on all of $\mathbb R$. These facts establish the stated maximal intervals.

Termwise differentiation in $\mathbb R[ [u] ]$ gives $\Phi'(u)=1+2au+O(u^2)$. Since $\Phi$ has linear term $u$, recursive coefficient matching gives $\Phi^{-1}(\widetilde u)=\widetilde u+O(\widetilde u^2)$, hence $u^2=\widetilde u^2+O(\widetilde u^3)$. Therefore $\Phi'(u)\beta(u)=bu^2+O(u^3)$ and re-expression in $\widetilde u$ yields $\widetilde\beta(\widetilde u)=b\widetilde u^2+O(\widetilde u^3)$. The coefficient $b$ is unchanged; no coefficient at higher order is determined here.

Let $\rho>0$ be a dimensionless scale and put $t=\log\rho\in\mathbb R$. Take $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ to be an interval containing $0$. Let $g:I\to\mathbb R$ be a differentiable real coupling and let $b,g_0\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless constants; require $g$ to satisfy the truncated scalar initial-value problem
$$\frac{dg}{dt}=bg^2,\qquad g(0)=g_0.$$
A solution through $(0,g_0)$ is **maximal** if there is no strictly larger interval $J\supsetneq I$ and solution $G:J\to\mathbb R$ of the same initial-value problem with $G|_I=g$. If $c:=bg_0=0$, the unique maximal real solution is $g(t)=g_0$ on $\mathbb R$. If $c\ne0$, the unique maximal solution through $t=0$ is
$$g(t)=\frac{g_0}{1-bg_0t}$$
on $(-\infty,c^{-1})$ when $c>0$ and on $(c^{-1},\infty)$ when $c<0$.

For the formal beta-series calculation, let $u$ be an indeterminate and work in $\mathbb R[ [u] ]$. Write $\beta(u)=bu^2+O(u^3)$ and let $\Phi(u)=u+au^2+O(u^3)$ be an invertible formal change of dimensionless coupling, with dimensionless $a\in\mathbb R$. The notation $O(u^k)$ means an element of $u^k\mathbb R[ [u] ]$, so its terms have degree at least $k$; the real trajectory $g(t)$ is distinct from the formal indeterminate $u$. Put $\widetilde u=\Phi(u)$, let $\Phi'$ be the termwise formal derivative, and define the transformed formal vector field in $\mathbb R[ [\widetilde u] ]$ by
$$\widetilde\beta(\widetilde u)=\bigl(\Phi'(u)\beta(u)\bigr)\big|_{u=\Phi^{-1}(\widetilde u)}.$$
The quadratic coefficient of $\widetilde\beta$ is $b$. The real ODE is exact only for the displayed truncation; neither it nor the formal scheme-change statement determines $b$ from a QFT graph or bounds omitted higher-order terms. Its pole is a property of this truncated equation, not a theorem about an ultraviolet completion.
