citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), with the pointwise causal

[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]. All curves below
take values in $M$; the physical reading of the model is not part of this
definition.

**(a) The curve class.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a continuous map,
where $I$ has its relative topology. A **chart representative** on a parameter
neighborhood $J\subseteq I$ is $x\circ\gamma|_J$, where $(U,x)$ is a smooth
chart and $\gamma(J)\subseteq U$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). The map $\gamma$ is
**locally absolutely continuous** when for each $t\in I$ there are
$\delta>0$ and a chart $(U,x)$ such that
$\gamma(I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta))\subseteq U$ and every coordinate of
$x\circ\gamma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of
$I\cap(t-\delta,t+\delta)$ in the sense of
[[def-absolutely-continuous-function]]. This includes one-sided neighborhoods
at included endpoints. Equivalently, for every compact subinterval
$[a,b]\subseteq I$ and every chart $(U,x)$ with
$\gamma([a,b])\subseteq U$, the coordinates of $x\circ\gamma$ are
absolutely continuous on $[a,b]$. The equivalence and independence of the
chart and smooth atlas are proved in [[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]]
clause (a); continuity is part of both formulations.

**(b) Velocity and causal curves.** Let $\gamma$ be locally absolutely
continuous and let $t$ be an interior point of $I$ at which some — equivalently
every — chart representative is differentiable. The **velocity**
$\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the derivation whose components in a chart
$(U,x)$ around $\gamma(t)$ are
$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}(x^a\circ\gamma)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)}$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]],
[[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]); it is independent of the
chart by the chain rule, as recorded in
[[lem-gr-causal-curve-calculus]] clause (b). A **future causal curve** is a
locally absolutely continuous $\gamma$ such that the set of $t\in I$ for which
$\gamma'(t)$ exists, is nonzero and is future causal is of full measure in
$I$ (its complement meets every compact subinterval of $I$ in a set of
Lebesgue measure zero). A **future timelike curve** (also called future
chronological) is defined in the same way with "future causal" replaced by
"future timelike". Past-directed versions are defined with $g_p(v,N_p)>0$.
Since a future causal nonzero vector is nonzero by definition, the velocity is
required to be nonzero at almost every parameter value; in particular no
nondegenerate subinterval of $I$ can be mapped to a single point: a
constant chart representative has derivative zero everywhere in its interior,
contradicting the full-measure nonzero-velocity requirement.

**(c) Reachability.** For events $p,q\in M$ define:

- $p\le q$, read "$q$ is in the future of $p$", when $p=q$, or when there are
  $a<b$ and a future causal curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$;
- $p\ll q$, read "$p$ chronologically precedes $q$", when there are $a<b$ and
  a future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=p$ and
  $\gamma(b)=q$.

The **causal future** and **chronological future** of a subset $S\subseteq M$
are
$$J^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}J^+(p),\qquad I^+(S):=\bigcup_{p\in S}I^+(p),$$
where $J^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\le q\}$ and $I^+(p):=\{q\in M:p\ll q\}$; past
versions are $J^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ q\in J^+(p)\}$ and
$I^-(S):=\{p:\exists q\in S,\ p\ll q\}$. By the displayed definition
$p\in J^+(p)$ for every $p$. Whether $p\in I^+(p)$ is a property of the
model, not a convention: $p\ll p$ holds exactly when there are $a<b$ and a
future timelike curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)=p$, that
is, exactly when a closed future timelike curve through $p$ exists. No
irreflexivity of $\ll$ is asserted, and closed timelike curves are not
excluded by the definition.

**(d) Inextendibility.** A locally absolutely continuous causal curve
$\gamma:I\to M$ is **future-inextendible** when $\gamma$ does not converge to
any point of $M$ as its parameter tends to $\sup I$, that is, there is no
$x\in M$ with $\gamma(t)\to x$ as $t\to\sup I$; in particular a curve whose
parameter range is unbounded above is future-inextendible exactly when it does
not converge as $t\to+\infty$. **Past-inextendible** is defined dually with
$\inf I$, and $\gamma$ is **inextendible** when it is both. This is the
convention of Minguzzi's Definition 2.16; for causal curves parametrized by
arclength of a complete auxiliary Riemannian metric it agrees with "the domain
cannot be extended", and a causal curve that converges at an endpoint can be
extended by a short geodesic segment, as proved in
[[lem-gr-maximal-geodesics-and-extension]] clauses (a) and (b). A causal
curve **passes through** $p$ when $p\in\gamma(I)$.

**(e) Scope.** The definitions are mathematical. They record no postulate
about nature, no measurement and no dynamical law; the physical reading of
$(M,g,N)$ and of the causal structure as the model's signalling structure is
adopted in the framework postulates and is not asserted here.

derivations.claim: If $O_1\subseteq O_2$, every real compact test supported in $O_1$ is also supported in $O_2$. Thus the generating set for $\mathfrak W_M(O_1)$ is included in the generating set for $\mathfrak W_M(O_2)$, so the generated unital $*$-subalgebra is included.

Let $f,g$ be real compact tests supported in $O_1,O_2$, respectively. By causal disjointness and [F1], $\operatorname{supp}f\cap\operatorname{supp}(Eg)=\varnothing$. Therefore [F2] gives $\sigma_M([f],[g])=\int_M f(Eg)\,\mu_g=0$. The Weyl relation [F3] now gives
$$W_M([f])W_M([g])=W_M([f]+[g])=W_M([g])W_M([f]),$$
because the same argument gives $\sigma_M([g],[f])=0$. The adjoints of these generators are $W_M(-[f])$ and $W_M(-[g])$, whose test functions have the same supports, so they commute across the two regions as well. Finite sums and products of mutually commuting cross-generators still commute, by distributivity and associativity; these sums and products are exactly the generated algebraic local subalgebras. Hence every pair of elements of the two local algebras commutes.

boundaries.evidence: If either open set is empty its generated local algebra is the scalar unit algebra, and the claims in steps 1.1–2.1 are immediate.
The zero test gives W(0), which commutes with every generator by step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: The statement has no one-dimensional-space or single-generator hypothesis.
No degeneracy case for the operator or symplectic space is part of the locality implication.
The result has no interval endpoint or limiting parameter.

boundaries.evidence: The assumptions are recorded in Fact A1 and are used to pass the Green-data supplier hypotheses in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: The lemma proves isotony and a one-way locality implication, not an iff.
No converse from commuting algebras to causal disjointness is claimed.

finite_checks.calculation: For f=0, W([f])=W(0), the unit, so it commutes with every local generator by the Weyl relation in step 2.1.
finite_checks.disposition: Exact specialization of step 2.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For a Green-data background of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]], let $(V(M),\sigma_M)$ be the real symplectic vector space of [[lem-qftx-green-propagator-symplectic-quotient]]. Define its **algebraic Weyl $*$-algebra** $\mathfrak W(M)$ to be the complex vector space of finite formal sums of basis symbols $W_M(v)$, $v\in V(M)$, with bilinear product and conjugate-linear involution specified on generators by

$$W_M(v)W_M(w):=e^{-i\sigma_M(v,w)/2}W_M(v+w),\qquad W_M(v)^*:=W_M(-v).$$

The unit is $W_M(0)$. This is the algebraic Weyl algebra: this definition assigns no norm, Hilbert-space representation, or $C^*$-completion. For an open set $O\subseteq M$, define the local algebra $\mathfrak W_M(O)$ as the unital $*$-subalgebra generated by the symbols $W_M([f])$ with real $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ and $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq O$. No norm closure is taken.

An **admissible Green-background morphism** $\iota:(U,g_U,N_U,P_U,E^U_+,E^U_-)\to(M,g_M,N_M,P_M,E^M_+,E^M_-)$ is an orientation-preserving, time-orientation-preserving isometric smooth embedding with open causally convex image, for which $P_M\iota_*f=\iota_*P_Uf$ on compact smooth real tests. Here $\iota_*f$ is extension by zero from the open image, which is smooth and compactly supported because $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compact in $U$. The morphism is **Cauchy** when its image contains a Cauchy hypersurface of $(M,g_M,N_M)$, meaning a spacelike embedded hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve, as in [[def-gr-spacelike-hypersurfaces-and-cauchy-sets]]. The associated quotient map, when well-defined, sends $[f]\in V(U)$ to $[\iota_*f]\in V(M)$, and the Weyl map is required to send $W_U([f])$ to $W_M([\iota_*f])$.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $\iota:U\hookrightarrow M$ be a Cauchy morphism between Green-data backgrounds of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]], with $U$ identified with its open image in $M$. Thus $U$ is globally hyperbolic and causally convex in $M$, and it contains a Cauchy hypersurface of $M$. For every $f\in\mathcal D_g(M)$ there is $g\in\mathcal D_g(U)$ such that

$$[f]=[\iota_*g]\quad\text{in }V(M)=\mathcal D_g(M)/P_M\mathcal D_g(M).$$

The conclusion is conditional on the Green maps and Cauchy uniqueness in the stated interfaces.

Assume Countable Choice and let $\iota:U\to M$ be an admissible Green-background morphism of [[def-qftx-free-weyl-net]], with Green data of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]]. The extension map $[f]\mapsto[\iota_*f]$ is a well-defined real symplectic linear map $S_\iota:V(U)\to V(M)$. The generator assignment $W_U(v)\mapsto W_M(S_\iota v)$ extends to a unital $*$-homomorphism $\alpha_\iota:\mathfrak W(U)\to\mathfrak W(M)$, and identity and composition of admissible embeddings are preserved. For every open $O\subseteq U$, the map also sends $\mathfrak W_U(O)$ into $\mathfrak W_M(\operatorname{im}(\iota|_O))$.

derivations.claim: Let $W_M([f])$ be any basis generator of $\mathfrak W(M)$. By [F2] there is $g\in\mathcal D_g(U)$ with $[f]=[\iota_*g]$. Hence $W_M([f])=W_M(S_\iota[g])=\alpha_{\iota}\bigl(W_U([g])\bigr)$ by [F3]. Every element of $\mathfrak W(M)$ is a finite linear combination of basis generators by [F1], so every element has a preimage under $\alpha_\iota$. This proves surjectivity.

Suppose $S_\iota$ is injective. If $\sum_{j=1}^n c_jW_U(v_j)$ maps to zero, first combine any repeated $v_j$ so the remaining $v_j$ are distinct. Their images $S_\iota v_j$ are then distinct, and $\alpha_\iota$ sends the sum to $\sum_{j=1}^n c_jW_M(S_\iota v_j)$. The latter can be zero only if every $c_j=0$, since the $W_M(w)$ are a formal vector-space basis by [F1]. Thus $\alpha_\iota$ is injective. Together with step 1.1 it is bijective; the inverse of a bijective algebra homomorphism preserves products, the unit and involution, so it is an isomorphism.

boundaries.evidence: The zero class has the zero test representative and its Weyl generator lies in the image by step 1.1.
The zero generator is included by the surjectivity argument in step 1.1.
The unit W(0) is preserved by the homomorphism supplier used in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate quotient or symplectic form case is asserted.
The theorem is stated for a Cauchy embedding, not an interval endpoint problem.

boundaries.evidence: The statement and Fact A1 declare Countable Choice and Dependent Choice; the image argument is in step 1.1.
Step 2.1 proves that injectivity of S_iota implies that alpha_iota is an isomorphism.

boundaries.reason: The theorem does not claim that an isomorphism forces S_iota to be injective.

finite_checks.calculation: For U=M and iota=id, every class is represented by itself; the induced map is the identity.
finite_checks.disposition: Exact specialization of the statement and step 1.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal B(H)$ for the bounded linear operators on $H$ ([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); for $M\in\mathcal B(H)$, $M^*$ is its Hilbert adjoint, characterized by $\langle Mx,y\rangle=\langle x,M^*y\rangle$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

Under this same $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis, [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]] gives $M^*\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $\|M^*\|=\|M\|$.

A **finite bounded Kraus instrument datum** on $H$ consists of an integer $m\ge1$, integers $q_a\ge0$ for $a=1,\ldots,m$, and bounded operators $M_{a,r}\in\mathcal B(H)$ for $r=1,\ldots,q_a$. It is **normalized** when

$$\sum_{a=1}^{m}\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I_H.$$

Empty inner sums are zero. For each outcome $a$, define its outcome operator and operation by

$$E_a:=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r},\qquad \mathcal J_a(X):=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*\quad(X\in\mathcal B(H)).$$

These formulas take values in $\mathcal B(H)$: the adjoint theorem above makes each $M_{a,r}^*$ bounded, and $\|M_{a,r}XM_{a,r}^*x\|\le\|M_{a,r}\|\,\|X\|\,\|M_{a,r}^*\|\,\|x\|=\|M_{a,r}\|^2\,\|X\|\,\|x\|$; the sums are finite. This definition specifies only the displayed finite Kraus form; it is not a representation theorem for arbitrary instruments and does not assert that an apparatus realizes these data.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ carry a normalized finite bounded Kraus instrument datum as defined in [[def-qft-finite-bounded-kraus-instrument]], and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]], [[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). For each outcome $a$, put $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))$. Then each $E_a$ is an effect ($E_a\ge0$ and $I_H-E_a\ge0$), each $\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is positive trace class, and

$$p_a=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal J_a(\rho))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1],\qquad \sum_{a=1}^{m}p_a=1.$$

The nonselective output $\sum_a\mathcal J_a(\rho)$ is a density operator. If $p_a>0$, the normalized conditional state $\rho_a:=\mathcal J_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator; when $p_a=0$, this normalized update is undefined. For a unit vector $\psi\in H$, the rank-one density operator $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ has outcome probability $p_a=\sum_{r=1}^{q_a}\|M_{a,r}\psi\|^2$. These are conditional mathematical identities; they do not assert that an apparatus realizes the instrument or supply a physical measurement postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]].
Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ be open. For real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O)$ define
$$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2K_\mu f),$$
where the Segal normalization is exactly
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2$ on the finite-particle
domain, as in [[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]]. This scale makes the self-adjoint generator
of $t\mapsto W_\mu(tf)$ equal to the closure $\overline{\Phi_\mu(f)}$,
whose restriction to $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is the real scalar field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the unital norm-closed operator
algebra
$$\mathfrak A_\mu(O)= \overline{\operatorname{alg}}^{\|\cdot\|} \{I,W_\mu(f),W_\mu(f)^*:f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)\}.$$
Then $O_1\subseteq O_2$ implies
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. If every difference
$x-y$, with $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, is spacelike, then every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_1)$ commutes with every element of
$\mathfrak A_\mu(O_2)$. These are algebraic properties of the constructed
representation; they are not empirical signaling or measurement claims.

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $(M,g,N,P,E_+,E_-)$ be a Green-data background of [[def-qftx-green-hyperbolic-interface]], and let $\mathfrak W_M(O)$ be the algebraic local Weyl subalgebra assigned to an open set $O\subseteq M$ by [[def-qftx-free-weyl-net]]. If $O_1\subseteq O_2$, then $\mathfrak W_M(O_1)\subseteq\mathfrak W_M(O_2)$. If $O_1$ and $O_2$ are causally disjoint, meaning that no point of either set is causally related in either direction to a point of the other, then every element of $\mathfrak W_M(O_1)$ commutes with every element of $\mathfrak W_M(O_2)$.

derivations.claim:
Fix $C\in\mathcal B$. Since $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ commute elementwise and $M_r^*\in\mathcal A$, both $M_rC=CM_r$ and $M_r^*C=CM_r^*$ hold. Therefore
$$M_r^*CM_r=M_r^*M_rC.$$
Summing this equality over the finite family and using [F1] gives
$$\sum_{r=1}^nM_r^*CM_r=\left(\sum_{r=1}^nM_r^*M_r\right)C=I_HC=C.$$
This is an equality in $\mathcal B(H)$.

By linearity of $\omega$ and the finite sum in the definition, step 1.1 yields
$$\omega'(C)=\sum_{r=1}^n\omega(M_r^*CM_r)=\omega\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^nM_r^*CM_r\right)=\omega(C).$$
When $\omega(X)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho X)$ for a density operator, put $\rho':=\sum_rM_r\rho M_r^*$. The cyclic trace identity [F3] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho' C)=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\rho M_r^*CM_r)=\omega'(C)$, and [F2] identifies $\rho'$ as the normalized one-outcome output of the finite instrument. Fact [F4] gives a flat scalar local-algebra instance of the commuting hypothesis; [F5] gives the corresponding abstract Green-background locality statement. Whenever a $*$-representation of those algebras is defined, it preserves the commutation equality because it preserves products.

No converse from preservation of expectations to commutation or normalization is asserted.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be unital $*$-subalgebras (each contains $I_H$ and is closed under adjoints and linear combinations) such that $AC=CA$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $C\in\mathcal B$. Let $M_1,\ldots,M_n\in\mathcal A$ be a finite family, $n\ge1$, satisfying
$$\sum_{r=1}^n M_r^*M_r=I_H.$$
For any state $\omega$ on $\mathcal B(H)$, meaning a complex-linear functional with $\omega(I_H)=1$ and $\omega(X^*X)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $X\in\mathcal B(H)$, define the nonselective expectation on $C\in\mathcal B$ by
$$\omega'(C):=\sum_{r=1}^n\omega(M_r^*CM_r).$$
Then $\omega'(C)=\omega(C)$ for every $C\in\mathcal B$. This is an algebraic conditional deduction; it does not assert that a physical apparatus realizes these operators.

For the finite flat scalar mass-shell representation of [[lem-qft-scalar-local-weyl-algebra]], open regions whose point differences are all spacelike have commuting local Weyl algebras, so the proposition applies to those two algebras. The proposition itself only assumes the stated commutation relation and does not require a tensor-product factorization of $H$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

The four vectors $|ab\rangle$ are orthonormal, so $\|\psi\|^2=(1+1)/2=1$. By [F1], $\omega$ is complex-linear and $\omega(I_H)=1$. For every $X\in\mathcal B(H)$, adjointness [F5] and conjugate symmetry give $\omega(X^*X)=\langle X^*X\psi,\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle\psi,X^*X\psi\rangle}=\overline{\langle X\psi,X\psi\rangle}=\|X\psi\|^2\ge0$, so $\omega$ is a state in the sense of [F2]. The projections satisfy $M_0^*=M_0$, $M_1^*=M_1$, $M_0M_1=0$, and $M_0+M_1=I_H$. Hence $\sum_{j=0}^1M_j^*M_j=I_H$, and
$$M_0\psi=\frac{|00\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad M_1\psi=\frac{|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}.$$
The outcome probabilities are $p_j=\|M_j\psi\|^2=1/2$, so both normalized conditional vectors are defined.

Dividing the branch vectors in step 1.1 by $\sqrt{p_j}=1/\sqrt2$ gives $\psi_0=|00\rangle$ and $\psi_1=|11\rangle$. Since $Z_B|00\rangle=|00\rangle$ and $Z_B|11\rangle=-|11\rangle$, their conditional expectations are respectively $\omega_0(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi_0,\psi_0\rangle=+1$ and $\omega_1(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi_1,\psi_1\rangle=-1$. Also
$$Z_B\psi=\frac{|00\rangle-|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},\qquad \omega(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi,\psi\rangle=\left\langle\frac{|00\rangle-|11\rangle}{\sqrt2},\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}\right\rangle=0,$$
because the cross terms vanish by orthogonality.

Let $\mathcal A:=\{A\otimes I_2:A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^2)\}$ and $\mathcal B:=\{I_2\otimes B:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb C^2)\}$. For every elementary tensor $u\otimes v$, $(A\otimes I_2)(I_2\otimes B)(u\otimes v)=Au\otimes Bv=(I_2\otimes B)(A\otimes I_2)(u\otimes v)$; elementary tensors span $H$, so these unital $*$-algebras commute. The two projections lie in $\mathcal A$ and the normalization was checked in step 1.1. Applying [F2] to the state proved in step 1.1 and $C=Z_B$ gives the nonselective expectation $\sum_j\omega(M_j^*Z_BM_j)=\sum_j\langle M_j^*Z_BM_j\psi,\psi\rangle=\omega(Z_B)=\langle Z_B\psi,\psi\rangle=0$. Thus post-selection changes the conditional remote expectation in either branch, while retaining and averaging the outcomes leaves the original remote marginal unchanged.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

For the seminorms of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]], a basic neighbourhood of $f_0\in\mathcal S$ is
$$\{f:p_{\alpha_r\beta_r}(f-f_0)<\varepsilon_r\ (1\le r\le m)\},\qquad m<\infty,\quad\varepsilon_r>0.$$
The empty intersection is the whole space. The topology consists of unions of these neighbourhoods. A sequence $f_k$ converges to $f$ precisely when $p_{\alpha\beta}(f_k-f)\to0$ for every pair of multi-indices: necessity follows from the one-condition neighbourhoods, and sufficiency follows by taking the maximum of the finitely many convergence thresholds in a basic neighbourhood.

A complex topological vector space is called locally convex here when zero has a base of convex balanced sets; balanced means $|c|\le1$ implies $cV\subseteq V$. The displayed sets about zero are convex and balanced by the seminorm inequalities. They also show addition is continuous, by halving each tolerance. Scalar multiplication is jointly continuous: near $(c_0,f_0)$, restrict $|c-c_0|<1$ and use
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(cf-c_0f_0)\le (|c_0|+1)p_{\alpha\beta}(f-f_0)+|c-c_0|p_{\alpha\beta}(f_0).$$
There are finitely many bounds to enforce. Finally $p_{00}(f-g)>0$ for distinct functions; balls of radius less than half this number separate them. Thus this is a Hausdorff locally convex topological vector space. All these verifications use only finite choices.

Fix an integer $n\geq1$.  A **tempered distribution** on $\mathbb R^n$ is a
continuous complex-linear functional

$$u:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)\longrightarrow\mathbb C,$$

where Schwartz space and its locally convex topology are those of
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] and
[[def-schwartz-topology-and-convergence]].  The space of all such functionals
is denoted $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.

We write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$.  This pairing is bilinear:
the test variable is not conjugated.  Thus $u(a\varphi+b\psi)=
a\langle u,\varphi\rangle+b\langle u,\psi\rangle$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C$.
The zero functional is tempered.  Continuity is topological continuity, and,
because the Schwartz topology is generated by a countable cofinal family of
seminorms, it is equivalently continuity on every convergent sequence.  No
choice principle is used in this definition.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

For integers $p,q\ge 1$ and open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, $V\subseteq\mathbb R^q$, every $\Phi\in\mathcal D(U\times V)$ is a limit in the LF test topology of finite sums of products $f(x)g(y)$ with $f\in\mathcal D(U)$ and $g\in\mathcal D(V)$. All approximating supports and the target support lie in one compact product inside $U\times V$. This holds in ZF.

For $u\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $v\in\mathcal D'(V)$ the tensor candidate is a distribution on $U\times V$, uniquely determined by $(u\otimes v)(\varphi\otimes\psi)=u(\varphi)v(\psi)$. Its two iterated pairing orders agree, and $\operatorname{supp}(u\otimes v)=\operatorname{supp}u\times\operatorname{supp}v$. Three-factor pairings associate. Moreover $\partial_x^\alpha(u\otimes v)=(\partial^\alpha u)\otimes v$ and $\partial_y^\beta(u\otimes v)=u\otimes(\partial^\beta v)$. All claims hold in ZF.

derivations.claim: By continuity [F3], there is a basic neighbourhood $V_u$ of zero such that $|u(f)|<1$ on $V_u$. Write $V_u=\{f:p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f)<\varepsilon_j,\ 1\le j\le k\}$ using [F2], and let $M_u$ be the largest component of these finitely many multi-indices. Put $P_{M_u}(f)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le M_u}p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$ and $c_u=2\max_j\varepsilon_j^{-1}$. If $P_{M_u}(f)>0$, then $f/(2\max_j(p_{\alpha_j\beta_j}(f)/\varepsilon_j))\in V_u$, so linearity gives $|u(f)|\le c_uP_{M_u}(f)$. If the denominator vanishes, every positive scalar multiple of $f$ lies in $V_u$, forcing $u(f)=0$ and the same bound. The same argument gives $|v(g)|\le c_vP_{M_v}(g)$ for some finite $M_v,c_v$.

For fixed $\Phi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$, the map $x\mapsto\Phi(x,\cdot)$ is smooth with values in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^q)$: Taylor's formula in the $x$ coordinates, with its remainder differentiated in $y$, tends to zero in each $p_{\gamma\delta}$ on every compact $x$ set because every mixed Schwartz seminorm of $\Phi$ is finite. Continuity of $v$ therefore makes $h(x):=v(\Phi(x,\cdot))$ smooth and gives $\partial_x^\beta h(x)=v(\partial_x^\beta\Phi(x,\cdot))$. For every $\alpha,\beta$, [F3] and step 1.1 yield $\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial_x^\beta h(x)|\le c_v\max_{|\gamma|,|\delta|\le M_v}\sup_{x,y}|x^\alpha y^\gamma\partial_x^\beta\partial_y^\delta\Phi(x,y)|<\infty.$ Thus $h\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^p)$.

Define $w(\Phi)=u(h)$. Applying the bound in step 1.1 to the finitely many $x$ seminorms with indices at most $M_u$, and then the displayed estimate in step 2.1, bounds $|w(\Phi)|$ by a finite constant times the maximum of finitely many product Schwartz seminorms of $\Phi$. Hence $w$ is continuous on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. For $\Phi=\varphi\otimes\psi$, the inner pairing is $\varphi(x)v(\psi)$, giving the claimed product value; on compactly supported tests the formula is the same iterated pairing as [F6].

Finite sums of Schwartz product tests are dense in $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{p+q})$. Indeed, choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^p)$ and $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^q)$ equal to one near the unit balls by [F4], and set $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ and $\eta_R(y)=\eta(y/R)$. The product rule and rapid decay show $\chi_R(x)\eta_R(y)\Phi(x,y)\to\Phi(x,y)$ in every product Schwartz seminorm: the undifferentiated tails lie outside balls of radius proportional to $R$, and each differentiated cutoff contributes a factor $R^{-j}$ on the same tails. For fixed $R$, [F5] approximates this compactly supported smooth function by finite sums of product tests with common compact support; on that support, uniform convergence of all derivatives implies convergence in every Schwartz seminorm. Thus any two continuous functionals with the same product values agree on a dense subspace and hence everywhere. The same density argument, iterated over finitely many factors, shows that different parenthesizations of the constructed tensor product agree; this also agrees with the compact-test associativity in [F6].

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, write Euclidean space as $E_d=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with coordinates $x=(t,\mathbf x)$, and put $S_d=\mathcal S(E_d;\mathbb C)$ and $S_{d,n}=\mathcal S(E_d^n;\mathbb C)$ for $n\ge1$, with $S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$, $\mathbb R^0$ is the one-point vector space with unit measure. A Schwinger hierarchy is a sequence $S=(S_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $S_0=1$ and each $S_n\in S_{d,n}'$; its moments on elementary tests are $\langle S_n,f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n\rangle$. The associated unital algebraic test algebra is $T_d=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}^{\rm alg}S_d^{\otimes_{\rm alg}n}$ with concatenation multiplication, unit $1\in S_{d,0}=\mathbb C$, and involution $(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)^*=\overline f_n\otimes\cdots\otimes\overline f_1$ and $(c1)^*=\overline c1$. The moments define $\omega_S:T_d\to\mathbb C$ by linear extension. At $d=4$ this is the same four-dimensional algebra and moment convention used by the positive-tempered-moment definition.

Ordinary moment positivity means $\omega_S(1)=1$ and $\omega_S(a^*a)\ge0$ for every $a\in T_d$. It is distinct from reflection positivity. Let $\vartheta(t,\mathbf x)=(-t,\mathbf x)$ and $E_{d,+}=\{(t,\mathbf x):t>0\}$. The positive-time polynomial algebra $T_{d,+}$ is the unital star subalgebra generated by tests in $C_c^\infty(E_{d,+};\mathbb C)$. Define the antilinear reflection $\Theta$ by $\Theta f=\overline{f\circ\vartheta}$ on degree one, $\Theta(c1)=\overline c1$, and $\Theta(ab)=\Theta(b)\Theta(a)$. Reflection positivity is $\omega_S(\Theta a\,a)\in[0,\infty)$ for every $a\in T_{d,+}$. The same formula applies to finite-site test algebras with an involution exchanging the sites.

A regulated hierarchy is a family $S^\lambda=(S^\lambda_n)_{n\ge0}$ indexed by a nonempty directed set $(\Lambda,\preceq)$, where directed means every two indices have a common upper bound. A distributional continuum limit is a hierarchy $S$ such that for every fixed $n$ and every $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$, $\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle\to\langle S_n,\Phi\rangle$ as $\lambda$ advances in $\Lambda$. A limit contract records these pairings, the regulator family, and any additional uniform estimates; pointwise-in-$n$ convergence by itself asserts no uniform bound as $n$ varies.

For explicit comparison, define the Schwartz seminorm $P_k(\Phi)=\max_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le k}\sup_{x\in E_d^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\Phi(x)|$ on $S_{d,n}$. A per-order uniform continuity record is a choice, for each fixed $n$, of $r_n\in\mathbb N_0$ and $C_n\ge0$ such that $|\langle S^\lambda_n,\Phi\rangle|\le C_nP_{r_n}(\Phi)$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $\Phi\in S_{d,n}$. Symmetry of the support weights gives $\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[Y]=0$, and $X^2=Y^2=1$ at every support point, so the covariance diagonal is $(1,1)$. The equal-sign outcomes have total probability $(1-r)/2$ and product $XY=1$; the opposite-sign outcomes have total probability $(1+r)/2$ and product $XY=-1$. The covariance matrix is $C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-r\\-r&1\end{pmatrix}$. For real $u,v$, $(u,v)C(u,v)^{\mathsf T}=(u-rv)^2+(1-r^2)v^2,$ which is strictly positive unless $(u,v)=(0,0)$ because $0<r<1$. Reflection positivity would require $\mathbb E[(\Theta F)F]=\mathbb E[XY]\ge0$, but this is $-r<0$. Hence the statement is false.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every real polynomial $P$ in $Q$ satisfies $\mathbb E|P(Q)|<\infty$, and its expectation $\mathbb E[P(Q)]$ is computed by expanding $P$ into monomials and applying finitely many covariance pairings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.

derivations.claim: In the formal power-series ring $\mathbb R\llbracket s,t\rrbracket$, set $M(s,t)=\sum_{a,b\ge0}\mathbb E[X^aY^b]s^at^b/(a!b!)$. By [F1], a pairing with $j$ $X$-self-pairs, $k$ $Y$-self-pairs, and $\ell$ cross-pairs can occur only when $a=2j+\ell$ and $b=2k+\ell$. The number of such pairings is $a!b!/(2^j j!\,2^k k!\,\ell!)$: choose the $\ell$ cross-indices on each side, match them in $\ell!$ ways, then pair the remaining indices on each side. Thus coefficient-by-coefficient $M(s,t)=\exp(\sigma^2s^2/2)\exp(cst)\exp(\tau^2t^2/2)$. This is an identity of formal series, so no moment-generating-function convergence is assumed.

Multiplying the series in step 1.1 by $\exp(-\sigma^2s^2/2)\exp(-\tau^2t^2/2)$ leaves $\exp(cst)=\sum_{r\ge0}c^r s^rt^r/r!$. By [F2], the coefficient of $s^nt^m$ on the multiplied left side is $\mathbb E[:X^n:_{\sigma^2}:Y^m:_{\tau^2}]/(n!m!)$. The right side has zero coefficient when $n\ne m$ and coefficient $c^n/n!$ when $n=m$, giving the claimed formula. For $n=m=0$ the constant coefficient is $1$, including when $c=0$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $m>0$. Write $\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ for the real-valued Schwartz test functions and define $\widehat f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^2x$; this convention has inverse factor $(2\pi)^{-2}$. For real $f,g\in\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ set

$$C_m(f,g):=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\frac{\overline{\widehat f(p)}\,\widehat g(p)}{|p|^2+m^2}\,\frac{d^2p}{(2\pi)^2}.$$

Let $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ be the continuous real-linear dual of $\mathcal S_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$, and give it the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $u\mapsto u(f)$. There is a probability measure on this cylinder $\sigma$-algebra, equivalently a measurable $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$-valued random variable $\Phi$, such that every finite vector $(\Phi(f_1),\ldots,\Phi(f_k))$ is centered jointly Gaussian and $\mathbb E[\Phi(f)\Phi(g)]=C_m(f,g)$. The construction gives tempered-distribution samples on one common full-measure set; it makes no pointwise-sample-field or interaction-measure claim.

Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $t>0$, and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\mathcal F(e^{-\pi t|x|^2})(\xi)=t^{-n/2}e^{-\pi|\xi|^2/t}.$$
Every polynomial times a positive real Gaussian is absolutely integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $I$ and $J$ be intervals, possibly open at finite or infinite singular ends, and let $\phi:I\to J$ be a monotone differentiable surjection. Assume $\phi'$ is locally Riemann integrable and the proper change-of-variable hypotheses hold on every compact truncation. If $f$ is locally Riemann integrable on $J$, then
$$\int_J f(x)\,dx\quad\text{and}\quad\int_I f(\phi(t))|\phi'(t)|\,dt$$
converge simultaneously and, when convergent, are equal. At several singular ends this assertion is applied separately to the corresponding ends; orientation is retained for decreasing parametrizations.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: For $a>0$ and $T>0$, substitute $u=-at$ by [F6]. The function $u\mapsto\exp(u)$ is continuous and has derivative $\exp(u)$ by [F7], and this derivative is Riemann integrable on $[-aT,0]$ by [F12]; hence [F10] gives $\int_0^T\exp(-at)dt=a^{-1}(1-\exp(-aT))$. By [F9] with power $1$ and scale $a$, $T/\exp(aT)\to0$; for $T\ge1$, [F8] gives $0<\exp(-aT)\le T/\exp(aT)$, so $\exp(-aT)\to0$. Thus $\int_0^\infty\exp(-at)dt=1/a$ as a nonnegative improper Riemann integral, and as a Lebesgue integral by [F11]. Next, [F2] and [F14] with $s=t/\pi$ and $\xi=-z/(2\pi)$ give $(2\pi)^{-2}\int e^{ip\cdot z}e^{-t|p|^2}d^2p=(2\pi)^{-2}(\pi/t)e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}=(4\pi t)^{-1}e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}=:h_t(z)$. Its integral is one: [F5] in each coordinate and $x=2\sqrt t\,u$ by [F6] give $\int h_t(z)d^2z=1$. For every $p$, the Laplace identity gives $(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1}=\int_0^\infty e^{-t(|p|^2+m^2)}dt$. If $\psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$, the displayed inverse-kernel formula and Fubini give $\int h_t(z)\psi(z)d^2z=(2\pi)^{-2}\int e^{-t|p|^2}\widehat\psi(-p)d^2p$; the exchanges are absolute because $e^{-t|p|^2}\in L^1$ and $\psi\in L^1$. Therefore $\int_0^\infty e^{-m^2t}\int h_t(z)|\psi(z)|d^2zdt\le\|\psi\|_\infty/m^2$, while the Fourier-side integral is absolutely convergent since [F13] makes $\widehat\psi$ Schwartz and $m>0$. Integrating the Fourier identity over $t$ and applying Fubini [F3] in $(t,z)$ and $(t,p)$ gives the heat-kernel superposition's pairing $(2\pi)^{-2}\int\widehat\psi(-p)(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1}d^2p$; reflection $p\mapsto-p$ preserves Lebesgue measure by [F15] and yields the covariance pairing. For real Schwartz $f,g$, set $\Psi(z)=\int\overline{f(y+z)}g(y)d^2y$. Differentiation under this integral is justified locally in $z$ by bounded derivatives of $f$ and the integrability of $g$. For multiindices $\alpha,\beta$, write $x=y+z$ and expand $z^\alpha=(x-y)^\alpha$; each term of $z^\alpha\partial^\beta\Psi(z)$ is bounded uniformly in $z$ by a finite product of seminorms $\sup_x|x^\gamma\partial^\beta f(x)|$ and integrals $\int|y^{\alpha-\gamma}g(y)|d^2y$, which are finite because $f,g$ are Schwartz. Thus $\Psi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^2)$. Absolute Fubini and the substitution $x=y+z$ give $\widehat\Psi(-p)=\int\!\!\int e^{ip\cdot(x-y)}\overline{f(x)}g(y)d^2x\,d^2y=\overline{\widehat f(p)}\widehat g(p)$; absolute integrability follows from $\|f\|_1\|g\|_1<\infty$. Applying the just-proved kernel pairing to this Schwartz test $\Psi$ recovers exactly the covariance $C_m(f,g)$ in [F1]. Thus the heat-kernel superposition is the a.e. spatial density of the covariance distribution, and its value for each $z\ne0$ is the defining integral for $G_m(z)$.

For $0<r=|z|\le1$, the part of the defining $t$-integral over $t\ge1$ is bounded by $\int_1^\infty e^{-m^2t}dt<\infty$ by step 1.1. On $0<t<1$, drop $e^{-m^2t}\le1$ and substitute $u=r^2/(4t)$ by [F6] to bound the remaining integral by $\int_{r^2/4}^\infty e^{-u}du/u\le\log(4/r^2)+\int_1^\infty e^{-u}du/u$; the last tail is finite because $1/u\le1$ and step 1.1 gives $\int_1^\infty e^{-u}du<\infty$. This gives $|G_m(z)|\le K_m(1+|\log r|)$. For $r\ge1$, substitute $t=(r/(2m))e^v$ in [F6]; then $m^2t+r^2/(4t)=mr\cosh v$ and $dt/t=dv$. Define $\cosh v=(\exp(v)+\exp(-v))/2$. The exponential power series gives $\cosh v=\sum_{j\ge0}v^{2j}/(2j)!\ge1+v^2/2$. [F5] and a further scaling substitution from [F6] give $G_m(z)\le (4\pi)^{-1}e^{-mr}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-mr v^2/2}dv\le K_m e^{-mr}/\sqrt{mr}$. Together with the almost-everywhere density from step 1.1, this proves that $G_m$ is a locally integrable representative of the covariance distribution.

For every finite $p\ge1$ and $0<s\le1$, the same annuli scaled to $s$ show $\int_{|z|\le s}(1+|\log|z||)^p d^2z\le K_p s^2(1+|\log s|)^p$: on $s2^{-j-1}<|z|\le s2^{-j}$ the area is at most $\pi s^22^{-2j}$ and the logarithmic factor is at most $(1+|\log s|+(j+1)\log2)^p$. Put $A=1+|\log s|\ge1$; then this factor is at most $A^p(1+(j+1)\log2)^p$. The ratio of successive terms $4^{-j}(1+(j+1)\log2)^p$ tends to $1/4$, so after an index depending only on $p$ it is at most $1/2$; the remaining series is bounded by its finite initial sum plus a geometric tail. This proves the bound with $K_p$ independent of $s$, hence $G_m^p\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The integral formula is continuous for $z\ne0$: for any sequence $z_k\to z\ne0$, choose $c>0$ so $|z_k|^2/4\ge c$ for all sufficiently large $k$. On $0<t\le1$, substitution $u=c/t$ by [F6] gives $\int_0^1t^{-1}e^{-c/t}dt=\int_c^\infty u^{-1}e^{-u}du<\infty$; the finite interval up to $1$ is bounded and the tail is at most $\int_1^\infty e^{-u}du$, finite by step 1.1. On $t\ge1$, $t^{-1}e^{-m^2t}\le e^{-m^2t}$, integrable by step 1.1. Thus [F4] applies and gives sequential continuity.

Let $R_\rho>0$ satisfy $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq B(0,R_\rho)$. For $f_{\epsilon,x}(u)=\rho_\epsilon(x-u)$ and $f_{\delta,y}(v)=\rho_\delta(y-v)$, the Gaussian covariance [F1] and the kernel representation in steps 1.1–2.1 give $\mathbb E[\Phi_\epsilon(x)\Phi_\delta(y)]=\int\!\!\int f_{\epsilon,x}(u)f_{\delta,y}(v)G_m(u-v)d^2u\,d^2v$. This integral is absolute because the tests are bounded and compactly supported and $G_m\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Put $z=x-y$, $a=x-u$, and $b=y-v$; [F15] preserves Lebesgue measure and yields $\int\!\!\int\rho_\epsilon(a)\rho_\delta(b)G_m(z-a+b)d^2a\,d^2b$. With $w=a-b$, Fubini [F3] gives this as $\int G_m(z-w)\kappa_{\epsilon,\delta}(w)d^2w=C_{\epsilon,\delta}(z)$. The nonnegative correlation kernel $\kappa_{\epsilon,\delta}$ has integral one, support in a disk of radius $2R_\rho q$ for $q=\max(\epsilon,\delta)$, and $\|\kappa_{\epsilon,\delta}\|_\infty\le\|\rho\|_\infty q^{-2}$. Its support shrinks to zero, so continuity of $G_m$ away from zero gives $C_{\epsilon,\delta}(z)\to G_m(z)$ for each $z\ne0$. To get the uniform bound, fix bounded $|z|\le R$. If $|z|$ exceeds twice the support radius, then $|z-w|\ge|z|/2$ throughout the convolution and step 2.1 bounds the integrand by $K_{m,R}(1+|\log|z||)$. Otherwise $|z|\le4R_\rho q$ and $|z-w|\le6R_\rho q$; the scaled dyadic-annulus estimate in step 3.1 gives $\int_{|u|\le6R_\rho q}|G_m(u)|d^2u\le K_mq^2(1+|\log q|)$. Multiplying by $\|\kappa\|_\infty$ bounds the convolution by $K_m(1+|\log q|)\le K_{m,R}(1+|\log|z||)$ because $q\ge|z|/(4R_\rho)$. Choose $\epsilon_{m,R}$ small enough that $6R_\rho q\le1$. This proves the uniform estimate for all $0<\epsilon,\delta\le\epsilon_{m,R}$.

> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

statement.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, its countable-family consequence, and $m>0$. Let $\Phi$ be the real centered Gaussian random tempered distribution on $\mathbb R^2$ with covariance $C_m(f,g)=(2\pi)^{-2}\int_{\mathbb R^2}\overline{\widehat f(p)}\widehat g(p)(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1}\,d^2p$ for real Schwartz tests and $\widehat f(p)=\int e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^2x$. Write $\mu_C$ for the Gaussian probability measure on the cylinder $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathcal S'_\mathbb R(\mathbb R^2)$ supplied by [[thm-qftx-tempered-massive-gaussian-field]], equivalently the law of $\Phi$; all expectations below are with respect to $\mu_C$. Fix one nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ with $\int\rho(x)\,d^2x=1$, set $\rho_\epsilon(x)=\epsilon^{-2}\rho(x/\epsilon)$ for $\epsilon>0$, and define $\Phi_\epsilon(x)=\Phi(u\mapsto\rho_\epsilon(x-u))$. For each $n\ge0$, define the finite-cutoff Wick polynomial $:\!\Phi_\epsilon(x)^n\!:$ by

$$\exp\!\left(t\Phi_\epsilon(x)-\tfrac12t^2\mathbb E[\Phi_\epsilon(x)^2]\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:\!\Phi_\epsilon(x)^n\!:\,\frac{t^n}{n!}$$

as an identity of formal power series. For a bounded measurable $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$ that vanishes outside a bounded set, define its cutoff smearing by the samplewise Lebesgue integral $W_{\epsilon,n}(f)=\int f(x):\!\Phi_\epsilon(x)^n\!:\,d^2x$. Every tempered sample gives a smooth $x\mapsto\Phi_\epsilon(x)$, so this integral is finite for each sample; its $L^2(\mu_C)$ limit as $\epsilon\downarrow0$ is a separate theorem, not part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, its countable-family consequence, $m>0$, and the fixed mollifier from the earlier cutoff definition. Let $C_m$ be the translation-invariant covariance distribution whose Fourier multiplier is $(|p|^2+m^2)^{-1}$ in the convention $\widehat f(p)=\int e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,d^2x$. It is represented by the even locally integrable function

$$G_m(z)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_0^\infty t^{-1}\exp\!\left(-m^2t-\frac{|z|^2}{4t}\right)dt,\qquad z\ne0.$$

There are constants $K_m,K_{m,R}<\infty$ such that $|G_m(z)|\le K_m(1+|\log|z||)$ for $0<|z|\le1$, $|G_m(z)|\le K_m e^{-m|z|}/\sqrt{m|z|}$ for $|z|\ge1$, and $G_m^q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^2)$ for every finite $q\ge1$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and its countable-family consequence, fix $m>0$, and let $P(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{2k}a_js^j$ be a real polynomial of even degree $2k\ge2$ with $a_{2k}>0$. An exhaustion $\Lambda\nearrow\mathbb R^2$ means a directed family of such sets whose union is $\mathbb R^2$ and such that every compact subset of $\mathbb R^2$ is contained in some member.
