The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space, let $e\in H$ have norm one, and put
$K=e^\perp=\{v\in H:\langle e,v\rangle_2=0\}$. For
$\psi_m\in K_s^{(m)}$ and $k,m\ge0$, write
$|k\rangle:=e^{\otimes k}\in(\mathbb Ce)_s^{(k)}$ (with $|0\rangle=1$),
and define

$$J_{k,m}(|k\rangle\otimes\psi_m) =\sqrt{\binom{k+m}{k}}\, P_{s,k+m}(e^{\otimes k}\otimes\psi_m).$$

The map $J_{k,m}$ extends over the sector Hilbert tensor products and the
orthogonal direct sums to a unitary

$$J:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb Ce)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(K) \longrightarrow\mathcal F_s(H).$$

Under this unitary, bosonic creation and annihilation by $e$ act on the first
factor as the one-mode ladder maps
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k+1}|k+1\rangle$ and
$|k\rangle\mapsto\sqrt{k}|k-1\rangle$, respectively, tensored with the
identity on $\mathcal F_s(K)$, on finite-particle vectors.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]] and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear convention of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ define the bosonic
creation and annihilation maps $a^\dagger(h)$ and $a(h)$ and the fermionic maps
$c^\dagger(h)$ and $c(h)$ as in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. Write $a_n(h)$ and $a_n^\dagger(h)$ for
their restrictions to the $n$th bosonic sector. For bosons set

$$D(a(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge1}\|a_n(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\},\qquad D(a^\dagger(h))=\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n\ge0}\|a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}.$$

Then $\mathcal F_s(H)$ and $\mathcal F_a(H)$ are Hilbert spaces,
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is dense, and it is a graph core for both maximal
bosonic sector maps. The bosonic operators on their displayed domains are
closed and mutually adjoint, and on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ satisfy

$$[a(h),a^\dagger(k)]=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad [a(h),a(k)]=[a^\dagger(h),a^\dagger(k)]=0.$$

The fermionic $c(h)$ and $c^\dagger(h)$ extend to bounded operators on the
whole Fock space, with norms $\|h\|$, and satisfy on the whole space

$$\{c(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=\langle h,k\rangle_2I,\qquad \{c(h),c(k)\}=\{c^\dagger(h),c^\dagger(k)\}=0.$$

This is a mathematical construction of the two Fock representations; it does
not assign particle statistics to a physical species.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Throughout this page $H$ is a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with
inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

derivations.claim: Under the unitary $J_u$ of [F2], the one-dimensional $n$th sector of $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$ is spanned by the unit vector $e_n$. Therefore $Q_n$ are mutually orthogonal projections and their strong sum is the identity on $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$. Tensoring with the identity on $\mathcal F_s(K)$ and conjugating by $J_u$ shows that each $P_n$ is an orthogonal projection, $P_nP_m=0$ for $n\ne m$, and $\sum_{n\ge0}P_n\Psi=\Psi$ in norm for every $\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H)$.

For Borel $B$, the orthogonal sum defining $E_u(B)$ converges strongly because $\sum_n\|P_n\Psi\|^2=\|\Psi\|^2$. It is an orthogonal projection, $E_u(\varnothing)=0$, $E_u(\mathbb R)=I$, and orthogonality gives $E_u(B)E_u(C)=E_u(B\cap C)$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $B_j$, their intersections with $\mathbb N_0$ partition $B\cap\mathbb N_0$, so the corresponding orthogonal series gives $E_u(\bigcup_jB_j)\Psi=\sum_jE_u(B_j)\Psi$ in norm. Thus $E_u$ is a PVM supported on $\mathbb N_0$, and $E_u(\{n\})=P_n$.

Under $J_u$, $N_u$ is the diagonal operator $(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}\mapsto(n\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}$ with domain $\sum_n n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty$. It is symmetric because every diagonal coefficient $n$ is real. If $\Phi$ lies in its adjoint domain with adjoint value $\Xi$, testing the adjoint identity on vectors supported in a single sector forces $\Xi_n=n\Phi_n$ for every $n$. Since $\Xi$ is square-summable, $\sum_n n^2\|\Phi_n\|^2<\infty$, so $\Phi\in D(N_u)$. Conversely, for $\Phi\in D(N_u)$, Cauchy–Schwarz on the sector sum gives the adjoint identity with value $N_u\Phi$. Hence $D(N_u^*)=D(N_u)$ and $N_u^*=N_u$, and its projections are the constructed $E_u(\{n\})=P_n$.

By [F2], on a one-mode occupation vector $e_n\otimes\phi$ one has $a(u)(e_n\otimes\phi)=\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}\otimes\phi$ and $a^\dagger(u)(e_n\otimes\phi)=\sqrt{n+1}\,e_{n+1}\otimes\phi$; thus $a^\dagger(u)a(u)=N_u$ on finite-particle vectors, including the $n=0$ sector. On the same invariant subspace, [F3] gives $a(u)a^\dagger(u)=a^\dagger(u)a(u)+I$. Consequently
$$N_u(N_u-I)=a^\dagger(u)a(u)a^\dagger(u)a(u)-a^\dagger(u)a(u)=a^\dagger(u)^2a(u)^2$$
on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, by substitution of the CCR and cancellation of the two $a^\dagger(u)a(u)$ terms.

Let $\Psi$ lie in the domain of $N_u(N_u-I)$ and truncate its one-mode occupation to $\Psi^{(M)}=\sum_{n=0}^{M}P_n\Psi$. The tail of the squared graph norm is $\sum_{n>M}(1+n^2(n-1)^2)\|P_n\Psi\|^2$, which tends to zero by the domain condition. For fixed $M$, write each $P_n\Psi$ under $J_u^{-1}$ as $e_n\otimes\phi_n$ with $\phi_n\in\mathcal F_s(K)$. Finite-particle vectors are dense in $\mathcal F_s(K)$ by [F1]; approximate each of the finitely many $\phi_n$ by such a vector. The one-mode unitary preserves norm, and on $n\le M$ the multiplier $n(n-1)$ is bounded, so these approximations also converge in graph norm. Their images under $J_u$ have finite total particle number. Thus $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for $N_u(N_u-I)$, and the finite-core normal-ordered identity of step 3.1 determines this closed extension.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and use the positive transverse free-photon model whose one-particle space is $\mathcal H_T=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)$ with its transverse condition and whose state space is the bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. In the unit convention where $\mathbf k$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, let $u\in\mathcal H_T^\nu$ be a normalized transverse wavepacket for the invariant measure $d\nu=d^3\mathbf k/(2|\mathbf k|)$, so that $u(\mathbf k)$ has unit metre and $\int|u|^2d\nu=1$. Let $v=Wu$, where $Wf(\mathbf k)=f(\mathbf k)/\sqrt{2|\mathbf k|}$; then $v\in\mathcal H_T$, $v(\mathbf k)$ has unit $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, and $\|v\|_2=1$. In the Fock factorization $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)\cong\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C v)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(v^\perp)$, $P_n(v)$ is the orthogonal projection onto mode occupation $n$ tensored with the identity on the orthogonal-mode Fock factor. These projections are mutually orthogonal and have strong sum $I$; their count PVM is $E_v(B)=\sum_{n\in B\cap\mathbb N_0}P_n(v)$, and $N_v=\sum_n nP_n(v)$ on the domain $\sum_n n^2\|P_n(v)\Psi\|^2<\infty$. A density operator $\rho$ means a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, using the trace pairing obtained from the Fock space's second-variable-linear convention by conjugation. For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, put $p_n=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_n(v))$. The mathematical density/PVM result makes $(p_n)$ a countably additive probability law under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis.

Adopt as the ideal detector postulate that this law is the model probability for recording exactly $n$ photons in the selected mode. The detector is number resolving, has unit mode efficiency, and has no mode mismatch, background counts or dark counts. This is an additional physical measurement assumption; it is not deduced from the CCR or from the free-field equations.

When $\sum_n np_n<\infty$ and $\sum_n n(n-1)p_n<\infty$, define the first number moment and normally ordered second factorial moment by
$$\mu_v(\rho):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}np_n,\qquad F^{(2)}_v(\rho):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n-1)p_n.$$
The PVM sums define the unbounded-state moments. In this ideal mode model, define the normally ordered second-mode correlation to be the spectral factorial expectation $F^{(2)}_v(\rho)$. The self-adjoint closure of the finite-particle operator $a^\dagger(v)^2a(v)^2$ is $N_v(N_v-I)$ by [[lem-qftx-mode-number-pvm]], so this definition agrees with the normally ordered operator on its finite-particle core and uses the spectral expectation for states outside that core. It does not assert a trace product of $\rho$ with an unbounded operator. If $\mu_v(\rho)>0$, define the dimensionless same-mode zero-delay statistic
$$g_v^{(2)}(0):=\frac{F^{(2)}_v(\rho)}{\mu_v(\rho)^2}.$$
Here $0$ is the conventional zero-delay label for this same-mode statistic; no temporal detector response or pointwise product of electric-field distributions is defined.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with the second-variable-linear pairing used for bosonic Fock space, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Put $K=u^\perp$. Let $J_u:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_s(K)\to\mathcal F_s(H)$ be the one-mode Fock unitary, and for $n\in\mathbb N_0$ let $e_n=u^{\otimes n}\in(\mathbb C u)_s^{(n)}$, with $e_0=1$. On $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C u)$ define $Q_n z=\langle e_n,z\rangle_2e_n$, and on $\mathcal F_s(H)$ put
$$P_n:=J_u(Q_n\otimes I)J_u^{-1}.$$
For every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, define the strong sum
$$E_u(B):=\sum_{n\in B\cap\mathbb N_0}P_n.$$
Define the mode number operator
$$N_u:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}nP_n,\qquad D(N_u):=\left\{\Psi\in\mathcal F_s(H):\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n^2\|P_n\Psi\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Then $(P_n)_{n\ge0}$ are mutually orthogonal projections with strong sum $I$, $E_u$ is a projection-valued measure supported on $\mathbb N_0$, and $N_u$ is self-adjoint with these spectral projections. The diagonal operator $N_u(N_u-I)$ has domain $\{\Psi:\sum_n n^2(n-1)^2\|P_n\Psi\|^2<\infty\}$, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a graph core for it. On the finite-particle subspace,
$$N_u=a^\dagger(u)a(u),\qquad N_u(N_u-I)=a^\dagger(u)^2a(u)^2.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

derivations.claim:
The coefficients of $\psi_\alpha$ are square-summable because their squared norms sum to $Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_n\lambda^n/n!=1$ by [F2]; the orthogonal one-mode sectors therefore make $\psi_\alpha$ a unit vector and [F6] makes its rank-one state a density operator. Its count probabilities are $p_n=Z_\lambda^{-1}\lambda^n/n!$ by [A1] and [F1]. Shifting indices in the nonnegative exponential series gives
$$\mu=Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n\lambda^n}{n!}=\lambda,\qquad F_2=Z_\lambda^{-1}\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{n(n-1)\lambda^n}{n!}=\lambda^2,$$
so $g_v^{(2)}(0)=1$. The same calculation shows both required moments are finite.
For $\psi_m$, [F1] gives $p_n=\mathbf1_{n=m}$, hence $\mu=m$ and $F_2=m(m-1)$. Since $m\ge1$, the denominator is positive, and substitution into [A1] gives $g_v^{(2)}(0)=m(m-1)/m^2=1-1/m$.

The weights $(1-r)r^n$ are nonnegative and sum to one by [F4], so [F6] makes $\rho_r$ a density operator and [A1] gives the geometric count law $p_n=(1-r)r^n$. By Tonelli [F5],
$$\left(\sum_{j\ge0}r^j\right)^2=\sum_{i,j\ge0}r^{i+j}=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+1)r^n.$$
Therefore $\sum_{n\ge0}nr^n=(1-r)^{-2}-(1-r)^{-1}=r/(1-r)^2$. Applying Tonelli to the triple product and counting the $(i,j,k)\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with $i+j+k=n-2$ gives
$$r^2\left(\sum_{j\ge0}r^j\right)^3=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{n(n-1)}2r^n,$$
because that finite set has $\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i)=n(n-1)/2$ elements. Hence $\sum_{n\ge0}n(n-1)r^n=2r^2/(1-r)^3$. Multiplying by $1-r$ gives $\mu=r/(1-r)>0$ and $F_2=2r^2/(1-r)^2<\infty$, so [A1] yields $g_v^{(2)}(0)=2$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

For each $j\le n$, factorization gives $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})X_{n,j}(x)=\eta$, and for distinct $i,j\le n$ it gives $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})X_{n,i}(x)X_{n,j}(x)=\eta^2$. Since $K(n,x)=\sum_{j=1}^nX_{n,j}(x)$ and $K(n,x)(K(n,x)-1)=\sum_{i\ne j}X_{n,i}(x)X_{n,j}(x)$ for zero-one coordinates, it follows that $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})K(n,x)=n\eta$ and $\sum_xQ_n(\{x\})K(n,x)(K(n,x)-1)=n(n-1)\eta^2$. For $n=0$ or $n=1$ the relevant sums are empty and the same formulas hold.

Using the Statement's encoding, identify $\Omega$ with a subset of $\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb N_0$. For either $Y=K$ or $Y=K(K-1)$, extend $f_Y(n,m):=p_nQ_n(\{x\})Y(n,x)$ by zero outside that subset. Counting measure on $\mathbb N_0$ is sigma-finite, so [F2] applied to the product of the two counting-measure spaces permits the nonnegative sum to be regrouped over the finite fibers. Assume the ideal wavepacket-counting postulate for a selected mode $v\in\mathcal H_T$ with $\|v\|=1$, and let $\rho$ be the incoming density operator on $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ (a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator with trace one). By that postulate, $P_n(v)$ are the mode-count projections and $p_n=\operatorname{tr}(\rho P_n(v))$ are the count probabilities, so $p_n\ge0$ and $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}p_n=1$. Define the incoming mean and second factorial moment by
$$\mu:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}np_n,\qquad F_2:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n(n-1)p_n,$$
and assume $0<\mu<\infty$ and $F_2<\infty$. Define $g_N^{(2)}(0):=F_2/\mu^2$; for this input state $\rho$, the postulate denotes the same statistic by $g_v^{(2)}(0)$.

Let $0<\eta\le1$ be a dimensionless fixed efficiency and assume no background or dark counts. To specify independent recording, put $b_\eta(0)=1-\eta$, $b_\eta(1)=\eta$, and
$$\Omega:=\{(n,x):n\in\mathbb N_0,\ x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{0,1\}^n\},\qquad \mathcal A:=\mathcal P(\Omega).$$
This is countable under the explicit encoding $(n,x)\mapsto(n,\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j2^{j-1})$. Give the space the point masses
$$\mathbb P(\{(n,x)\}):=p_n\prod_{j=1}^{n}b_\eta(x_j),$$
where the empty product for $n=0$ is $1$. For each fixed $n$, the product factors define the conditional product law $Q_n$ on $\{0,1\}^n$; hence its coordinates are independent Bernoulli variables with success probability $\eta$. Since $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}Q_n(\{x\})=(\eta+(1-\eta))^n=1$, these point masses sum to one and define a probability measure $\mathbb P$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal A)$. Define $N(n,x):=n$ and $K(n,x):=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$. For every nonnegative random variable $Y$ on this space, use the expectation
$$\mathbb E Y:=\sum_{(n,x)\in\Omega}Y(n,x)\,\mathbb P(\{(n,x)\}).$$
The marginal law of $N$ is $(p_n)$, and the conditional count law of $K$ given $N=n$ is the binomial law induced by $Q_n$. If $\mathbb E K>0$, define $g_K^{(2)}(0):=\mathbb E[K(K-1)]/(\mathbb E K)^2$. Then
$$\mathbb E K=\eta\mu,\qquad \mathbb E[K(K-1)]=\eta^2F_2.$$
Consequently the normalized zero-delay factorial correlation is unchanged:
$$g_K^{(2)}(0)=\frac{\mathbb E[K(K-1)]}{(\mathbb E K)^2}=\frac{F_2}{\mu^2}=g_N^{(2)}(0)=g_v^{(2)}(0).$$

A **multitensor category over $k$** is a locally finite $k$-linear abelian,
rigid monoidal category whose tensor product is $k$-bilinear in both variables.
A **tensor category** is a multitensor category for which
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbf1)\cong k$ as $k$-algebras.

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided monoidal category and let $X$ be an object of
$\mathcal C$. Each **formal canonical composite** on $X^{\otimes n}$ built
from associators, unitors, braidings, and their inverses has an underlying
braid in $B_n$. If two such formal composites have equal underlying braids,
then their interpreted morphisms in $\mathcal C$ are equal. Different formal
braids may, of course, have the same interpretation in a particular braided
category.

For $n\ge2$, the **braid group** $B_n$ is the group with generators
$\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations

$$\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\qquad(1\le i\le n-2),$$

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

interpreted in the sense of [[def-group-presentation]] and
[[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]].

For $n=0$ and $n=1$, there are no generators, and $B_n$ is the trivial group
given by the empty presentation.

Let $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ be a presentation, let $H$ be a group, and let
$u:X\to H$ be a function. If the evaluation of every $r\in R$ under $u$ is
$e_H$, then there is a unique homomorphism

$$\overline u:\langle X\mid R\rangle\longrightarrow H$$

with $\overline u([x])=u(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Moreover, $\overline u$ is
surjective if and only if $u(X)$ generates $H$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra over a field with bijective antipode, and let $(h_i)$ and $(f_i)$ be dual bases of $H$ and $H^*$. In the factor order $D(H)=H^{*\mathrm{op}}\otimes H$, the tensor

$$R=\sum_i(f_i\otimes1_H)\otimes(\varepsilon_H\otimes h_i)$$

is basis-independent and invertible, with

$$R^{-1}=\sum_i(f_i\otimes1_H)\otimes(\varepsilon_H\otimes S^{-1}(h_i)).$$

It is quasitriangular in the convention

$$R\Delta_D(d)=\Delta_D^{\mathrm{op}}(d)R,\qquad(\Delta_D\otimes\operatorname{id})R=R_{13}R_{23},\qquad\alpha^{-1}_{D,D,D}(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Delta_D)R=R_{13}R_{12}.$$

On every pair of left $D(H)$-modules, $\tau\circ R$ is the Yetter–Drinfeld braiding of [[thm-hh-double-modules-and-yetter-drinfeld-modules]].

derivations.claim: By the canonical rebracketing property in [F3], there is a canonical isomorphism $\rho_{n,i}:P_n(X)\to Q_{n,i}(X)$ built from the associators and unitors; every factor is invertible, so the composite is invertible. The map $\operatorname{id}\otimes c_{X,X}\otimes\operatorname{id}$ is an endomorphism of $Q_{n,i}(X)$, because $c_{X,X}$ is an isomorphism from $X\otimes X$ to the same ordered object $X\otimes X$. Conjugating gives the displayed endomorphism $B_i^X$ of $P_n(X)$.

If $\rho_{n,i}$ and $\rho'_{n,i}$ are two such canonical rebracketings, then $\rho'_{n,i}\rho_{n,i}^{-1}$ has trivial underlying braid. Inserting the same local $c_{X,X}$ gives formal composites with underlying braid $\sigma_i$; [F3] makes the resulting endomorphisms equal. Thus $B_i^X$ is independent of the rebracketing path.

The two composites $B_i^XB_{i+1}^XB_i^X$ and $B_{i+1}^XB_i^XB_{i+1}^X$ have underlying braid words $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i$ and $\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$, equal in $B_n$; operators with $|i-j|>1$ have the equal underlying words $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$. By [F3] the corresponding morphisms are equal.

Each $B_i^X$ is invertible by step 1.1 and [F2]. The relations in step 3.1 therefore satisfy the Artin presentation [F4], and [F5] gives the unique homomorphism $\varrho_n:B_n\to\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(P_n(X))$ with $\varrho_n(\sigma_i)=B_i^X$.

In the Hopf-module convention, the coproduct supplies the tensor-product module action, while [F6]'s intertwining identity $R\Delta_D(d)=\Delta_D^{\mathrm{op}}(d)R$ makes $\tau\circ R$ the exchange braiding; [F6] fixes the factor order $H^{*\mathrm{op}}\otimes H$. This supplies the category braiding only when the relevant module objects and category structure are supplied. No semisimplicity, unitarity, modularity, or physical realization follows from [F6] alone.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $\mathbb C$, so it is finite semisimple, rigid, monoidal, and has simple unit [[def-fusion-and-multifusion-category]]. Let $a,b,c$ be simple objects and let $n\ge0$. Fix one representative of each simple isomorphism class for the internal path labels; the external objects $a,b,c$ need not equal their representatives. Set $T_0=b$ and recursively fix the left-associated parenthesization $T_{j+1}:=T_j\otimes a$. The **fixed-boundary anyonic path space** is

$$H_{a,n;b,c}:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(c,T_n).$$

For simple labels $x,y$, define the split multiplicity space $W_{x,a}^y:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(y,x\otimes a)$. For $n\ge1$, a fusion path is a sequence of simple labels $x_0=b,x_1,\ldots,x_n=c$, with $x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1}$ drawn from the fixed representative set, together with, for every $1\le j\le n$, one basis index $\mu_j$ in a chosen basis $B_{x_{j-1},a}^{x_j}$ of $W_{x_{j-1},a}^{x_j}$. The basis index is retained even when distinct indices have the same adjacent labels. Fusion rules are the nonnegative integers $N_{x a}^{y}$ in $[x][a]=\sum_yN_{x a}^{y}[y]$ [[def-fusion-rules]].

For $n=0$, there is no path if $b\not\cong c$. If $b\cong c$, fix an isomorphism $u_{c,b}:c\to b$ and take it as the single empty-path vector (use $u_{b,b}=\operatorname{id}_b$ when the objects coincide). In the unitary setting choose this isomorphism unitary.

For $n\ge1$, if $i_j\in B_{x_{j-1},a}^{x_j}$ is the selected inclusion $x_j\to x_{j-1}\otimes a$, define the path composite by $\gamma_0:=\operatorname{id}_b$ and $\gamma_j:=(\gamma_{j-1}\otimes\operatorname{id}_a)\circ i_j:x_j\to T_j$. For $x_n=c$, $\gamma_n$ is a vector in $H_{a,n;b,c}$. The next lemma proves these composites form a basis and computes the dimension. No Hilbert-space or physical Hamiltonian structure is part of this definition.

Fix a fusion-path space with repeated simple site charge $a$, a position $i$ with two adjacent $a$-labels, and a simple output $s$ of $a\otimes a$, chosen from the fixed internal representative set of [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]]. Choose bases in the split spaces $\operatorname{Hom}(z,x\otimes y)$ at every vertex of the trees used below, retaining the fixed path vertex bases on the fixed tree. In the tree basis where this adjacent pair is fused first, let $\Pi_s$ be the projection onto the direct summand with pair output $s$, acting as the identity on every multiplicity index inside that channel and as zero on all other pair outputs. Let $A_i:T_{\mathrm{fixed}}\to T_{\mathrm{pair}}$ be a typed composite of associators and their inverses carrying the fixed path tree to this pair-first tree, without permuting the ordered inputs (including the boundary charge). In the split-tree bases of $\operatorname{Hom}(c,T)$, let $F_i$ be the matrix of $h\mapsto A_i\circ h$, with target coordinates as rows and source coordinates as columns. The proof below constructs these bases and proves invertibility in any complex fusion category. Define the **local channel projector** in the fixed path basis by

$$P_{i,s}:=F_i^{-1}\Pi_sF_i.$$

This is an idempotent for any fusion category because $F_i$ is invertible. In a unitary fusion category with orthonormal tree bases, $F_i$ is unitary and $P_{i,s}$ is an orthogonal projection. The channel projection includes every multiplicity coordinate; the definition has no multiplicity-free restriction. The split Hom convention here is $\operatorname{Hom}(c,T)$, as in [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]]. In the unitary case with adjoint vertex bases, each local left-to-right split recoupling matrix is the entrywise conjugate of the QC25 inverse-precomposition F matrix, as proved below; they agree for the displayed real Fibonacci and Ising blocks.

Let $a,b,c,d$ be simple charges in a unitary fusion category, and put
$P_L=((a\otimes b)\otimes c)$ and $P_R=a\otimes(b\otimes c)$. The local
fusion-tree basis result [[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]] identifies

$$\mathcal H_L:=\bigoplus_e V_{ab}^e\otimes V_{ec}^d \quad\text{with}\quad\operatorname{Hom}(P_L,d),$$

and

$$\mathcal H_R:=\bigoplus_f V_{bc}^f\otimes V_{af}^d \quad\text{with}\quad\operatorname{Hom}(P_R,d),$$

by the corresponding tree compositions. These direct sums carry the
orthonormal left- and right-tree bases. If $\mu:a\otimes b\to e$ and
$\nu:e\otimes c\to d$ are vertex basis maps, write
$L_{e,\mu,\nu}:=\nu\circ(\mu\otimes\operatorname{id}_c):P_L\to d$. If
$\rho:b\otimes c\to f$ and $\sigma:a\otimes f\to d$ are vertex basis maps,
write $R_{f,\rho,\sigma}:=\sigma\circ(\operatorname{id}_a\otimes\rho):P_R\to d$.
Let $\alpha_{a,b,c}:P_L\to P_R$ be the associator. Define the **F-symbol
matrix** $F_d^{abc}$ by

$$L_{e,\mu,\nu}\circ\alpha_{a,b,c}^{-1} =\sum_{f,\rho,\sigma}F_d^{abc}[(f,\rho,\sigma),(e,\mu,\nu)]R_{f,\rho,\sigma}.$$

Rows index target-tree labels and multiplicity indices; columns index
source-tree labels and multiplicity indices. The sums retain every fusion
channel and every multiplicity coordinate.
If the fixed-total fusion space is zero-dimensional, the F-symbol is the unique
empty $0\times0$ matrix.

Let $b,c,a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be simple objects of a unitary fusion category, with $n\ge2$, and let $T_{\mathrm{fixed}}$ be a fixed parenthesization of $b\otimes a_1\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n$. Equip $H=\operatorname{Hom}(c,T_{\mathrm{fixed}})$ with the split Hom inner product $g^\dagger h=\langle h,g\rangle\operatorname{id}_c$ and choose orthonormal split vertex bases in the trees below. Fix $1\le i<n$. Let $A_i:T_{\mathrm{fixed}}\to T_{\mathrm{pair}}$ be a composite of associators and inverses to a tree fusing $a_i,a_{i+1}$ first, without permuting inputs. Let $F_i$ be the matrix of $h\mapsto A_i\circ h$, with target rows and source columns, and let $\Pi_s$ project onto all pair-first coordinates of simple pair output $s$, retaining every multiplicity index. Define $P_{i,s}:=F_i^{-1}\Pi_sF_i$, extending the repeated-charge construction of [[def-anyonic-local-channel-projector]] to these arbitrary simple site charges. Then $(P_{i,s})_s$ is pairwise orthogonal, self-adjoint, and idempotent, and its sum over all simple outputs of $a_i\otimes a_{i+1}$ is the identity on $H$.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary spherical fusion category over $\mathbb C$, with pivotal structure and spherical dimension as in [[def-pivotal-structure]], [[def-spherical-structure]], and [[def-the-dimension-of-an-object-relative-to-a-pivotal-structure]]. Let $a$ be a self-dual simple object with $N_{aa}^{\mathbf1}=1$. Choose a unit vector $v:\mathbf1\to a\otimes a$ spanning the one-dimensional vacuum split space and let $d_a>0$ be its positive spherical dimension.

A **normalized vacuum-channel self-duality datum** is a supplied pair of maps $\operatorname{coev}:\mathbf1\to a\otimes a$ and $\operatorname{ev}:a\otimes a\to\mathbf1$ of the form

$$\operatorname{coev}=\sqrt{d_a}\,v,\qquad \operatorname{ev}=\kappa_a\sqrt{d_a}\,v^\dagger,$$

where $\kappa_a\in\{+1,-1\}$ and the two duality zig-zag identities hold after the self-duality identification, using the left-dual convention of [[def-left-dual-and-right-dual-object]]. We call $\kappa_a$ the **Frobenius–Schur sign in this normalized cup/cap convention**. It is not a braiding or $R$-symbol phase.

This item records supplied normalized duality data; it does not assert that every self-dual simple object admits the displayed gauge or prove a trace, ribbon, or category-equivalence theorem. An example must supply the datum or compute the sign from coherent normalized F-data; fusion rules alone do not specify it.

Let $a$ and $(v,\operatorname{ev},\operatorname{coev},d_a,\kappa_a)$ be as in [[def-anyonic-frobenius-schur-sign]]. In the multiplicity-free vacuum-normalized gauge of [[def-qc-tqc-f-symbol]],

$$\left(F^{aaa}_a\right)_{\mathbf1,\mathbf1}=\frac{\kappa_a}{d_a},\qquad \delta_a:=\frac{1}{\left((F^{aaa}_a)^{-1}\right)_{\mathbf1,\mathbf1}}=\kappa_a d_a.$$

For fixed ordered tensor inputs and fixed source and target parenthesizations, any two sequences of canonical associator F-moves between them induce the same coordinate map. Consequently, conjugating a fixed pair-channel projection by either sequence gives the same operator on the fusion-path space.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category, and use orthonormal bases in each split space $W_{x,a}^y=\operatorname{Hom}(y,x\otimes a)$, equivalently the adjoints of orthonormal bases of $V_{x a}^y=\operatorname{Hom}(x\otimes a,y)$. Give $H_{a,n;b,c}=\operatorname{Hom}(c,T_n)$ the Hom-space inner product linear in the first variable, determined by $g^\dagger f=\langle f,g\rangle\operatorname{id}_c$. For $n=0$ use the unitary empty-path isomorphism specified in [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]]. Then the path composites of [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]] are an orthonormal basis of $H_{a,n;b,c}$.

derivations.claim: Choose a parenthesization grouping the three sites $a_i,a_{i+1},a_{i+2}$ and decompose the split-tree basis by their simple total charge $y$ and the spectator labels. If the first pair fuses to $\mathbf1$, then its fusion with the third $a$ has total charge $y=\mathbf1\otimes a\cong a$; the same is true if the last pair fuses to $\mathbf1$. On the $y=a$ block each vacuum-channel subspace has dimension $N_{aa}^{\mathbf1}N_{\mathbf1 a}^{a}=1$, since $N_{aa}^{\mathbf1}=1$ and the tensor unit acts as the identity. On every $y\not\cong a$ block both projectors vanish. Each fixed spectator label and multiplicity coordinate gives a copy of this local block, where $P_i$ and $P_{i+1}$ act as rank-one orthogonal projections onto unit vectors $e$ and $f$, by [F4].

By the F-symbol coordinate convention in [F3], the vacuum-to-vacuum entry of the three-site F-move is the coordinate of one unit basis vector in the other tree basis. Therefore $|\langle e,f\rangle|=|(F^{aaa}_a)_{\mathbf1,\mathbf1}|=|\kappa_a/d_a|=1/d_a$ by [F5] and [F6], so $|\langle e,f\rangle|^2=d_a^{-2}$.

For unit vectors $e,f$, the linear-first convention in [F8] gives the rank-one projections $P_e x=\langle x,e\rangle e$ and $P_f x=\langle x,f\rangle f$. Hence $P_fP_eP_f x=\langle x,f\rangle\langle f,e\rangle\langle e,f\rangle f=|\langle e,f\rangle|^2P_f x$. Therefore $P_{i+1}P_iP_{i+1}=d_a^{-2}P_{i+1}$ on each $y=a$ spectator copy; on every other block both sides are zero. Tensoring with the spectator identities and transporting to the fixed path parenthesization preserves the relation by [F7].

Since $\delta_a=\kappa_ad_a$ and $\kappa_a^2=1$, $\delta_a^2=d_a^2$. Thus $U_{i+1}U_iU_{i+1}=\delta_a^3P_{i+1}P_iP_{i+1}=\delta_a^3d_a^{-2}P_{i+1}=\delta_aP_{i+1}=U_{i+1}$. The sign is retained in the final equality.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary spherical fusion category over $\mathbb C$. Let $a,b,c$ be simple objects, with $a$ self-dual, $N_{aa}^{\mathbf1}=1$, and supply the normalized vacuum-channel self-duality datum with sign $\kappa_a\in\{+1,-1\}$ and positive spherical dimension $d_a$. For $n\ge3$, take the fixed-boundary repeated-$a$ path space $H_{a,n;b,c}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(c,T_n)$ with $T_0=b$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j\otimes a$, as in [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]]. Let $P_i=P_{i,\mathbf1}$ be the orthogonal local vacuum-channel projectors and put $U_i=\delta_aP_i$, where $\delta_a=\kappa_ad_a$. Then, for every $1\le i\le n-2$,

$$U_{i+1}U_iU_{i+1}=U_{i+1}.$$

This supplies the reverse adjacent relation for the repeated-charge Temperley–Lieb family.

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, with $S_0=\{1\}$ as in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]. Let $A:=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]$ be the ring of Laurent polynomials in one
indeterminate $v$ over $\mathbb Z$. For $n\ge2$ the **generic type-A Hecke
algebra** $H_v(n)$ is the associative unital $A$-algebra presented by generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ and the relations
$$T_i^2=(v-1)T_i+v\quad(1\le i<n),\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}\quad(1\le i\le n-2),\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(1\le i,j<n,\ |i-j|>1),$$
that is, the quotient of the free unital associative $A$-algebra on
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ by the two-sided ideal generated by these relators. The
first relation is written in the **RG-13 quadratic normalization**
$(T_i-v)(T_i+1)=0$, equivalent to the displayed form over $A$. For $n\le1$ there
are no generators and we set $H_v(n):=A$.

**Standard basis elements.** Let $S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ with
simple transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$
([[def-symmetric-group]]), and let $w\in S_n$ have inversion length $\ell(w)=\ell$
([[def-weyl-group-and-length-for-finite-gl-n]]). Choose a reduced expression
$w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_\ell}$, that is, a word of the minimal length $\ell(w)$
representing $w$, and put
$$T_w:=T_{i_1}\cdots T_{i_\ell}\in H_v(n),$$
the empty product when $w$ is the identity of $S_n$, so that $T_w=1$ for that
element. That $T_w$ is independent of the chosen reduced expression, and that
the elements $T_w$ form an $A$-basis of $H_v(n)$, is proved in the
standard-basis theorem below
([[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]); the notation
distinguishes the generator $T_i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$ from $T_w$ for the group
element $w$.

**Specializations.** Let $R$ be a commutative $A$-algebra with structure map
$\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1}]\to R$, $v\mapsto v_0$, and suppose $v_0\in R^\times$. The
**specialization** of $H_v(n)$ at $v_0$ is the $R$-algebra
$R\otimes_AH_v(n)$; it is presented over $R$ by the images of $T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$
subject to the same relations with $v$ replaced by $v_0$, and we write $H_{v_0}(n)$
for it. Two specializations are used on this page: $v\mapsto1$, where the
quadratic relation becomes $T_i^2=1$ together with the braid and commutation
relations, and $v\mapsto q$, where $q$ is the prime power defining
$\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_q)$; the latter specializes the generic algebra to
the Hecke algebra attached to the finite general linear group. The condition
$v_0\in R^\times$ is part of the definition of a specialization and, for a nonzero coefficient ring $R$, excludes $v_0=0$. The zero ring
is allowed: its unique element is a unit and its specialization is the zero algebra.

Let $H(n)$ be the Hecke tower over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1},z]$ of
[[def-markov-trace-on-the-type-a-hecke-tower]]. Then: (1) the elements
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ are units of $H(n)$ with
$T_i^{-1}=v^{-1}T_i+(v^{-1}-1)$; (2) the assignment $\sigma_i\mapsto T_i$
descends to a group homomorphism
$$\pi_n:B_n\longrightarrow H(n)^{\times},\qquad \pi_n(\sigma_i)=T_i,$$
where $H(n)^{\times}$ is the group of units of $H(n)$; (3) for every Artin word
$\beta=\sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_k}^{\varepsilon_k}$ one has
$\pi_n(\beta)=T_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots T_{i_k}^{\varepsilon_k}$, and
$\pi_{n+1}(\iota_n^{\mathrm{Br}}(\beta))=\iota_n(\pi_n(\beta))$ for all
$\beta\in B_n$ under the standard inclusion of braid groups $B_n\to B_{n+1}$.

For $n\ge2$, the **braid group** $B_n$ is the group with generators
$\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations

$$\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\qquad(1\le i\le n-2),$$

$$\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\qquad(1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1).$$

Equivalently,

$$B_n=\langle \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\mid \sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\ (1\le i\le n-2),\ \sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i\ (1\le i,j\le n-1,\ |i-j|>1)\rangle,$$

interpreted in the sense of [[def-group-presentation]] and
[[def-relators-relations-and-finite-presentations]].

For $n=0$ and $n=1$, there are no generators, and $B_n$ is the trivial group
given by the empty presentation.

Let $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ be a presentation, let $H$ be a group, and let
$u:X\to H$ be a function. If the evaluation of every $r\in R$ under $u$ is
$e_H$, then there is a unique homomorphism

$$\overline u:\langle X\mid R\rangle\longrightarrow H$$

with $\overline u([x])=u(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Moreover, $\overline u$ is
surjective if and only if $u(X)$ generates $H$.

derivations.claim: Since $U_i^2=\delta U_i$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, $(qI_V-U_i)(q^{-1}I_V-U_i)=I_V-(q+q^{-1})U_i+U_i^2=I_V$. The product in the reverse order is the same polynomial in $U_i$, so $B_i^{-1}=q^{-1}I_V-U_i$.

For adjacent $i,i+1$, expansion and the square and adjacent Temperley–Lieb relations give $(qI_V-U_i)(qI_V-U_{i+1})(qI_V-U_i)-(qI_V-U_{i+1})(qI_V-U_i)(qI_V-U_{i+1})=-(q^2-q\delta+1)(U_i-U_{i+1})=0$, since $q\delta=q^2+1$. Thus the adjacent braid relation holds.
We have $B_i-qI_V=-U_i$ and $B_i+q^{-1}I_V=\delta I_V-U_i$; hence $(B_i-qI_V)(B_i+q^{-1}I_V)=-\delta U_i+U_i^2=0$.
If $|i-j|>1$, then $B_iB_j-B_jB_i=U_iU_j-U_jU_i=0$. Together with step 1.1, the $B_i$ are units satisfying all relators of [F5].
By [F6] applied to [F5] and the assignment $\sigma_i\mapsto B_i$, step 2.2 supplies a unique homomorphism $\rho_n:B_n\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ with $\rho_n(\sigma_i)=B_i$.

Let $\widetilde T_i:=qB_i$. They satisfy the braid and distant relations by steps 1.2–2.2, and $(\widetilde T_i-q^2I_V)(\widetilde T_i+I_V)=q^2(B_i-qI_V)(B_i+q^{-1}I_V)=0$. Consequently the generator map from the free unital algebra kills every defining relator of $H_{q^2}(n)$, so its defining ideal lies in the kernel and the map factors through the quotient $H_{q^2}(n)$. This gives the stated unital Hecke-algebra representation.

Apply the coefficient map $\mathbb Z[v^{\pm1},z]\to\mathbb C$, $v\mapsto q^2$, $z\mapsto0$, to the Hecke tower in [F4]. By its defining scalar-extension construction and the specialization in [F3], the resulting algebra is $H_{q^2}(n)$; base change carries [F4]'s braid homomorphism to $\eta_n:B_n\to H_{q^2}(n)^\times$ with $\eta_n(\sigma_i)=T_i$. Composing with $\Phi_n$ from step 3.2 sends $\sigma_i$ to $qB_i$, identifying the chosen normalization against the standard Hecke generator assignment. No Markov trace or link-invariant claim is used.

If $V$ is a complex Hilbert space, $U_i$ is bounded self-adjoint, $\delta\in\mathbb R$, and $|q|=1$, then for all $x,y\in V$ self-adjointness and $U_i^2=\delta U_i$ give $\langle B_ix,B_iy\rangle=|q|^2\langle x,y\rangle-(q+\overline q)\langle x,U_iy\rangle+\delta\langle x,U_iy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, since $q^{-1}=\overline q$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$. Thus $B_i$ preserves the inner product; it is surjective by its inverse in step 1.1, and so it is unitary by the convention in the Statement. For the repeated-$a$ anyonic path family, [F1] and [F2] supply both adjacent relations, the square relation, and distant commutation with the signed $\delta_a=\kappa_ad_a$; whenever $q+q^{-1}=\delta_a$, it therefore meets the operator hypotheses of this theorem. No sign is replaced by $+1$.

$$(B_i-qI_V)(B_i+q^{-1}I_V)=0.$$

Thus $\sigma_i\mapsto B_i$ defines a group homomorphism $B_n\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$. derivations.claim: At $q=1$, the parameter relation gives $\delta=2$. For every $i$, $B_i^2=(I_V-U_i)^2=I_V-2U_i+U_i^2=I_V$, using $U_i^2=2U_i$ from [F1].

The composite $\widetilde\rho_n\circ\pi_n$, with $\pi_n$ from [F4], and the braid representation $\rho_n$ from [F1] agree on every generator $\sigma_i$, since both send it to $B_i$. The generators determine a homomorphism from $B_n$, so $\rho_n=\widetilde\rho_n\circ\pi_n$.

Fix a fusion-path space with repeated simple site charge $a$, a position $i$ with two adjacent $a$-labels, and a simple output $s$ of $a\otimes a$, chosen from the fixed internal representative set of [[def-anyonic-fusion-path-space]]. Choose bases in the split spaces $\operatorname{Hom}(z,x\otimes y)$ at every vertex of the trees used below, retaining the fixed path vertex bases on the fixed tree. In the tree basis where this adjacent pair is fused first, let $\Pi_s$ be the projection onto the direct summand with pair output $s$, acting as the identity on every multiplicity index inside that channel and as zero on all other pair outputs. derivations.claim: For fixed $z\in\mathcal Z$, an object of the iterated fiber is $(y,\beta:q(y)\to z,x,\alpha:p(x)\to y)$. The functor $(y,\beta,x,\alpha)\mapsto(x,\beta\circ q(\alpha))$ maps it to $(\mathcal X)_z$. A quasi-inverse sends $(x,\gamma:q(p(x))\to z)$ to $(p(x),\gamma,x,\operatorname{id}_{p(x)})$. The composite on $(\mathcal X)_z$ is the identity. For any iterated object, the isomorphism $\alpha:p(x)\to y$ and $\operatorname{id}_x$ give a natural isomorphism from the quasi-inverse image back to that object. Hence the functor is an equivalence.

Fix an isomorphism class $[e]$ of $\mathcal E$, set $y=b(e)$, and write $A=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal Y}(y)$, $B=\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal E}(e)$, $I=\operatorname{im}(B\to A)$, and $N=\ker(B\to A)$. The classes in the homotopy fiber $\mathcal E_y$ represented by this $[e]$ are the orbits of $I$ on the $A$-torsor of isomorphisms $b(e)\cong y$, so there are $|A|/|I|$ of them; each has automorphism group $N$. Their contribution after the outer factor $1/|A|$ is $f([e])/(|I||N|)=f([e])/|B|$, by the finite homomorphism counting identity $|B|=|I||N|$. Summing over $[e]$ proves $\int_{y\in\mathcal Y} b_!f(y)=\int_{e\in\mathcal E} f(e)$.

Compose spans $\mathcal X\xleftarrow{a}\mathcal E\xrightarrow{b}\mathcal Y$ and $\mathcal Y\xleftarrow{c}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal Z$, and let $P=\mathcal E\times^h_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal F$ with projections $\pi_E,\pi_F$. For fixed $z\in\mathcal F$, the homotopy fiber of $\pi_F$ over $z$ has objects $((e,f',\alpha),\tau:f'\cong z)$. The functor to $\mathcal E_{c(z)}$ sends this object to $(e,c(\tau)\circ\alpha)$ and sends an arrow $(u,v)$ to $u$. Such an arrow satisfies $\tau'\circ v=\tau$ and $c(v)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ b(u)$, so its image satisfies $\beta'\circ b(u)=\beta$. Conversely, for any such $u$ between images $(e,\beta)$ and $(e',\beta')$, the only possible lift has $v=(\tau')^{-1}\circ\tau:f'\to f''$; the equation $\beta'\circ b(u)=\beta$ implies $c(v)\circ\alpha=\alpha'\circ b(u)$, so this lift exists and is unique. The functor is fully faithful; every object $(e,\beta)$ is its image from $((e,z,\beta),\operatorname{id}_z)$, so it is essentially surjective. It is therefore an equivalence. By [F1], equivalent fibers have equal finite integrals, giving $c^*b_!g=(\pi_F)_!\pi_E^*g$ for every invariant function $g$ on $\mathcal E$. Applying step 1.1 to $\pi_F$ and $d$ now gives $d_!c^*b_!a^*f=(d\circ\pi_F)_!(a\circ\pi_E)^*f$, which is the push-pull map of the homotopy-pullback composite span.

Put $\phi([e]):=\overline{f([a(e)])}g([b(e)])$, which is invariant on $\pi_0(\mathcal E)$. Expanding the left inner product by the definition of $b_!$ gives $\langle b_!a^*f,g\rangle_{\mathcal Y}=\sum_{[y]}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal Y}(y)|}\sum_{[(e,\eta)]\in\pi_0(\mathcal E_y)}\frac{\overline{f([a(e)])}g([y])}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal E_y}(e,\eta)|}$. Since $\eta:b(e)\cong y$ and $g$ is invariant, $g([y])=g([b(e)])$, so this is $\int_{y\in\mathcal Y}b_!\phi(y)=\int_{e\in\mathcal E}\phi(e)=\sum_{[e]}\frac{\phi([e])}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal E}(e)|}$ by step 1.2. On the other side, expanding $a_!b^*g$ and using $\xi:a(e)\cong x$ to replace $\overline{f([x])}$ by $\overline{f([a(e)])}$ gives $\langle f,a_!b^*g\rangle_{\mathcal X}=\sum_{[x]}\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal X}(x)|}\sum_{[(e,\xi)]\in\pi_0(\mathcal E_x)}\frac{\phi([e])}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal E_x}(e,\xi)|}=\int_{x\in\mathcal X}a_!\phi(x)=\int_{e\in\mathcal E}\phi(e)$, again by step 1.2. derivations.claim: For each connected component $K_j$, start with any flat assignment and set the root gauge value at $v_j$ to the identity. Along the unique tree paths in $T_j$ from $v_j$, choose the gauge value at each new vertex so that the transformed label on the traversed tree edge is the identity; when that edge is traversed against its chosen orientation, use its inverse label. This recursively produces a tree-normalized assignment on every component. It is unique among gauges whose value at each $v_j$ is the identity, since the condition that each transformed tree label remain $1$ determines each next vertex value.

In a tree-normalized assignment on $K_j$, every edge of $T_j$ has label $1$. Assign to each generator $x_e$ of $\pi_1(K_j,v_j)$ the inverse of the label on its oriented non-tree edge. By [F4], this is a homomorphism for the traversal-first product on loops: holonomy of a concatenation is the reverse-ordered product, and reversing the path in the Statement reverses that order. Flatness says exactly that every relator $r_f$ maps to $1$. By the presentation in [F2], the normalized assignments on $K_j$ are in bijection with homomorphisms $\rho:\pi_1(K_j,v_j)\to G$.

For a connected subcomplex $L_i\subseteq K_{j(i)}$ and base data as in the Statement, the pointed inclusion at $v_i$ induces a well-defined homomorphism on fundamental groups by [F5]. The base-path change map $c_{\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}:\pi_1(K_{j(i)},v_i)\to\pi_1(K_{j(i)},w_{j(i)})$, given by $[\alpha]\mapsto[\gamma_i*\alpha*\bar\gamma_i]$, is a well-defined isomorphism: endpoint-fixed homotopies remain endpoint-fixed after adjoining $\gamma_i,\bar\gamma_i$, insertion of the retraced path $\bar\gamma_i*\gamma_i$ contracts in a product of loop classes, and $c_{\bar\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}$ is its inverse. Thus $\jmath_{\gamma_i,*}=c_{\gamma_i}^{K_{j(i)}}\circ\jmath_*$ is well defined. For a flat assignment $A$ and an edge loop $\ell$ in $L_i$, the edge-product convention gives $\Phi_{K_{j(i)}}(A)(\jmath_{\gamma_i,*}[\ell])=H_A(\bar\gamma_i)H_A(\bar\ell)H_A(\gamma_i)=H_A(\bar\gamma_i)\Phi_{L_i}(A|_{L_i})([\ell])H_A(\bar\gamma_i)^{-1}$. If a gauge arrow $h:A\to A'$ is applied, its path-product rule gives $H_{A'}(\bar\gamma_i)=h(w_{j(i)})H_A(\bar\gamma_i)h(v_i)^{-1}$; this is exactly the naturality condition for the stated conjugation arrows. Hence inverse path holonomy intertwines restriction with the componentwise precomposition functor up to that natural isomorphism.

On a fixed component $K_j$, a gauge transformation taking one tree-normalized assignment to another must have equal values at the two endpoints of every edge of $T_j$, because both edge labels are $1$. Since $T_j$ is connected, it is constant on all vertices of $K_j$. Conversely, each constant gauge value $a\in G$ preserves tree normalization and conjugates every generator label by $a$. Thus the full subgroupoid on tree-normalized objects over $K_j$ is identified with $\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K_j,v_j),G)//G$. Step 1.1 makes its inclusion into the full flat-connection groupoid essentially surjective, and the inclusion is fully faithful because it is full. The root-one gauge used in step 1.1 leaves inverse path holonomy at $v_j$ unchanged, so the object map $\Phi_{K_j}$ in the Statement agrees with normalization followed by this identification. For any gauge arrow $h:A\to A'$, the gauge factors telescope along each based edge loop $\delta$ at $v_j$ to give $H_{A'}(\bar\delta)=h(v_j)H_A(\bar\delta)h(v_j)^{-1}$, so $\Phi_{K_j}(A')=h(v_j)\Phi_{K_j}(A)h(v_j)^{-1}$. Conversely, after normalizing $A$ and $A'$ by root-one gauges, each conjugating arrow between their representations is the unique constant gauge arrow between the normalized assignments; conjugating back gives the unique gauge arrow between $A$ and $A'$ with that value at $v_j$. Hence the stated functor is fully faithful as well as essentially surjective, and is an equivalence.

For each connected component $K_j$, the subgroup of vertex gauges equal to $1$ at $v_j$ acts freely and transitively on each fiber of the map from flat assignments to their tree-normalized representative, by step 1.1 and its uniqueness. Its order is $|G|^{|(K_j)_0|-1}$, so $|\operatorname{Flat}(K_j,G)|=|G|^{|(K_j)_0|-1}|\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K_j,v_j),G)|$. Substituting this count into [F1] gives the connected normalization. Equivalently, the action-groupoid cardinality in step 4.1 sums $1/|\operatorname{Stab}(\rho)|$ over conjugacy classes; no freeness of the conjugation action is assumed.

For $K=K_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup K_m$, the defining edge-label and vertex-gauge data split componentwise, so $\mathcal C_G(K)=\prod_j\mathcal C_G(K_j)$. Applying step 4.1 on each component gives the product equivalence $\Phi_K:\mathcal C_G(K)\simeq\mathcal R_G(K)$, and applying step 3.1 componentwise gives the stated restriction naturality. Automorphism orders multiply in a product groupoid and its isomorphism classes are componentwise tuples, so its groupoid cardinality is the product of the connected cardinalities from step 5.1. When $m=0$, the empty product is terminal with cardinality $1$.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and a finite group $G$. A **triangulated $d$-bordism** $M:\Sigma_0\to\Sigma_1$ is a compact oriented piecewise-linear $d$-manifold with product collars on its boundary, where $\Sigma_0$ and $\Sigma_1$ are closed oriented $(d-1)$-manifolds with finite triangulations and the incoming boundary is identified with $-\Sigma_0$ while the outgoing boundary is identified with $\Sigma_1$. The boundary triangulations agree with the induced triangulation of $M$.

For a closed $(d-1)$-manifold $\Sigma$, define the state space

$$V_G(\Sigma):=\operatorname{Fun}(\pi_0(\mathcal C_G(\Sigma)),\mathbb C), \qquad \langle f,g\rangle_\Sigma :=\sum_{[A]\in\pi_0(\mathcal C_G(\Sigma))} \frac{\overline{f([A])}g([A])}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C_G(\Sigma)}(A)|}.$$

The orientation reversal $-\Sigma$ has the same underlying triangulated cell complex and the same chosen directions on its edges, with only the manifold orientation reversed. Since the flat-connection groupoid uses the cell complex, directed edge labels, flatness equations, and vertex gauge action, not the manifold orientation, the identity on these data gives $\mathcal C_G(-\Sigma)=\mathcal C_G(\Sigma)$ and hence the same function set for their state spaces. For a complex vector space $W$, write $\overline W$ for its conjugate vector space, with the same addition and scalar multiplication $\lambda\cdot_{\overline W}w:=\overline\lambda w$. The map $J_\Sigma:V_G(-\Sigma)\to\overline{V_G(\Sigma)}$ given by $J_\Sigma(f)=\overline f$ pointwise is complex-linear. Reversing the manifold orientation does not replace any fixed directed edge label by its inverse; inversion occurs only when a chosen edge direction itself is reversed.

The specified boundary triangulation identifications induce restriction functors. On the incoming end, $r_0$ is restriction to $\partial_{\mathrm{in}}M$, transport through its identification with $-\Sigma_0$, and then the identity on the common underlying cell data $\mathcal C_G(-\Sigma_0)=\mathcal C_G(\Sigma_0)$. The outgoing functor $r_1$ is defined by restriction and its specified identification with $\Sigma_1$. In either transport, a chosen edge mapped to the opposite chosen direction uses the inverse-edge rule from the flat-connection Definition. These functors give a span of finite groupoids

$$\mathcal C_G(\Sigma_0)\xleftarrow{r_0}\mathcal C_G(M)\xrightarrow{r_1}\mathcal C_G(\Sigma_1).$$

The associated linear map is

$$Z_M:=(r_1)_!r_0^*:V_G(\Sigma_0)\to V_G(\Sigma_1),$$

where pullback and pushforward are the finite homotopy-fiber operations just defined. For empty boundary, the amplitude is $Z_G(M)=|\mathcal C_G(M)|$.

The identity boundary isomorphism makes this a triple in the homotopy pullback defined by [F3]. Restriction of a global vertex gauge transformation gives a compatible pair, so restriction defines a functor from the global groupoid.

Conversely, let $(A_2,A_1,\alpha)$ be a homotopy-pullback object as in [F3], where $\alpha:r_2(A_2)\to r_1(A_1)$ is a boundary gauge isomorphism. Its finite vertex values on the boundary extend to the vertices of $M_2$ by setting every non-boundary value to the identity. Applying this gauge transformation to $A_2$ makes its boundary edge labels equal to those of $A_1$. The two edge labelings then glue to a unique labeling on the union; every 2-cell lies in one of the pieces or their common boundary, so each flatness equation remains satisfied. This proves essential surjectivity.

By [F3], a morphism in the homotopy pullback is a pair of gauge transformations on $M_2$ and $M_1$ satisfying the boundary compatibility equation. After the boundary representatives are aligned as in step 2.1, this equation says exactly that the two vertex gauge values agree at every identified boundary vertex. They therefore glue to a unique gauge transformation on $M_2\cup_\Sigma M_1$. Conversely, every global gauge transformation restricts to such a compatible pair. The boundary isomorphism $\alpha$ is load-bearing. For the one-object groupoid $BG$ of a finite group $G$, an object of the homotopy pullback of two identity functors is an element $\alpha\in G$. By [F3], a morphism $(u,v):\alpha\to\alpha'$ satisfies $v\alpha=\alpha'u$, so every $\alpha$ is isomorphic to $1$ and the automorphisms of $1$ are the diagonal pairs $(u,u)$. Thus the homotopy pullback has one isomorphism class with automorphism group isomorphic to $G$ and cardinality $1/|G|$. The ordinary set-theoretic fiber product has one object with trivial automorphism group and cardinality $1$. Let $\mathcal R_G(K)$ be the product over $j$ of the action groupoids whose objects are homomorphisms $\rho:\pi_1(K_j,v_j)\to G$ and whose arrows $\rho\to\rho'$ are elements $a\in G$ satisfying $\rho'(\gamma)=a\rho(\gamma)a^{-1}$ for every loop class $\gamma$; identity arrows are labeled by $1$, and if $a:\rho\to\rho'$ and $b:\rho'\to\rho''$, then their composite $b\circ a$ is labeled by $ba$. For $K=\varnothing$, this empty product is the terminal groupoid. Choosing a maximal tree in each component, inverse path holonomy defines an equivalence $\Phi_K:\mathcal C_G(K)\simeq\mathcal R_G(K)$: for an edge path traversing $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ with signs $\epsilon_k$, its holonomy is $H_A(e_1^{\epsilon_1}\cdots e_n^{\epsilon_n})=g_{e_n}^{\epsilon_n}\cdots g_{e_1}^{\epsilon_1}$, and $\Phi_K(A)$ sends a loop class represented by an edge loop $[\gamma]$ to $H_A(\bar\gamma)$; a gauge arrow $h$ maps to the conjugating arrow $h(v_j)$ on component $K_j$. In particular, for connected $K$,

$$|\mathcal C_G(K)|=\frac{|\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K,v_1),G)|}{|G|},$$

and for arbitrary finite $K$,

$$|\mathcal C_G(K)|=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\frac{|\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(K_j,v_j),G)|}{|G|}.$$

The action retains all conjugation stabilizers. For a subcomplex inclusion $\jmath:L\hookrightarrow K$, choose a base vertex $v_i$ in each component $L_i$, a base vertex $w_{j(i)}$ in its containing component $K_{j(i)}$, and an edge path $\gamma_i$ in $K_{j(i)}$ from $w_{j(i)}$ to $v_i$. The associated based map is $\jmath_{\gamma_i,*}([\ell])=[\gamma_i*\jmath(\ell)*\bar\gamma_i]$. Under $\Phi_K$ and $\Phi_L$, restriction corresponds to precomposition by these maps, up to the natural isomorphism whose component at a flat assignment $A$ is conjugation by $H_A(\bar\gamma_i)$. Write $\Sigma=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^m\Sigma_j$ and let $C_j=\Sigma_j\times[0,1]$. For each $j$ and $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$, choose $v_j\in\Sigma_j$ and base the end inclusion $i_\epsilon:\Sigma_j\to C_j$ at $(v_j,\epsilon)$. The projection $p_j:C_j\to\Sigma_j$ satisfies $p_j i_\epsilon=\operatorname{id}$, and $i_\epsilon p_j$ is based-homotopic to the identity through $H_s^{(0)}(x,t)=(x,(1-s)t)$ for $\epsilon=0$ and $H_s^{(1)}(x,t)=(x,(1-s)t+s)$ for $\epsilon=1$. By [F6], these maps induce inverse isomorphisms on fundamental groups. Precomposition with a group isomorphism is an equivalence of representation action groupoids, with inverse precomposition by its inverse and the identity map on conjugating arrows. The componentwise representation equivalence and restriction naturality in [F3] therefore make both end restriction functors $\mathcal C_G(C_j)\to\mathcal C_G(\Sigma_j)$ equivalences; taking products gives the same conclusion for disconnected $\Sigma$. Choose an edge path in each connected cylinder 1-skeleton joining its two end base vertices. The base-path naturality in [F3] gives a natural isomorphism between the two restriction functors. Hence the cylinder span is equivalent to the identity span. Each homotopy fiber of either end equivalence has one isomorphism class and trivial automorphism group, while the natural isomorphism identifies the two boundary values; its weighted push-pull map is therefore the identity on $V_G(\Sigma)$.

For a disjoint union, a flat assignment and a vertex gauge transformation are exactly independent assignments on its components. Hence the bulk and boundary groupoids are products. Since the component sets are finite, the indicator functions of pairs of isomorphism classes form the tensor-product basis of the functions on their product. The automorphism weights multiply and the finite fiber sums factor, so the state spaces and maps identify with tensor products.

By the corrected orientation convention in [F1], reversing the manifold orientation leaves each fixed directed edge label and its gauge action unchanged; it only exchanges the incoming and outgoing restriction functors. Thus the span of $\overline M$ is the transposed span with the same underlying finite groupoids, so [F2] gives $Z_{\overline M}=Z_M^\dagger$ on those function spaces. Every coefficient of these push-pull maps in the isomorphism-class indicator bases is a finite sum of positive reciprocal automorphism orders, hence is real; the identity on underlying groupoids therefore yields $Z_{\overline M}\circ c_{\Sigma_1}=c_{\Sigma_0}\circ Z_M^\dagger$. Pointwise conjugation is the only anti-linear operation, since this model has no cocycle phase.

The push-pull composition identity in [F2] identifies the linear map of that composite span with $Z_{M_2}\circ Z_{M_1}$. Equivalent finite groupoids give the same weighted fiber sums, so this map is $Z_{M_2\cup_{\Sigma_1}M_1}$.

For empty boundary the amplitude is $|\mathcal C_G(M)|$ by [F1]. Applying [F3] to connected $M$ gives $Z_G(M)=|\operatorname{Hom}(\pi_1(M),G)|/|G|$, with all conjugation stabilizers retained. The gluing, identity, disjoint-union, and orientation statements above establish the asserted finite state-sum rules.
