Define $S_{abcd}$ to be the right-hand side of the displayed formula. Symmetry of $g$ and $\operatorname{Ric}$ gives antisymmetry of $S$ in each index pair and symmetry under exchanging the pairs. Substitution into $S_{abcd}+S_{acdb}+S_{adbc}$ cancels the Ricci and scalar terms pairwise, so $S$ satisfies the first Bianchi identity and is an algebraic curvature tensor. Contracting the first and third indices gives
$$g^{ac}S_{abcd}=3\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}-\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}-\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}+\operatorname{Scal}\,g_{bd}-\tfrac12\operatorname{Scal}(3g_{bd}-g_{bd})=\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}.$$
Thus $W:=R-S$ is an algebraic curvature tensor with zero Ricci contraction.

In the basis of [A1], an algebraic curvature tensor is represented by a symmetric $3\times3$ matrix on the basis bivectors $e_0\wedge e_1,e_0\wedge e_2,e_1\wedge e_2$. Write its diagonal entries as $x=W_{0101}$, $y=W_{0202}$, and $z=W_{1212}$. The three diagonal zero-Ricci equations are $x+y=0$, $-x+z=0$, and $-y+z=0$. They imply $2x=0$, hence $x=y=z=0$.

The three off-diagonal zero-Ricci equations are $\operatorname{Ric}(W)_{01}=W_{0212}=0$, $\operatorname{Ric}(W)_{02}=-W_{0112}=0$, and $\operatorname{Ric}(W)_{12}=-W_{0102}=0$. They set the three off-diagonal entries of the same symmetric bivector matrix to zero. Therefore $W=0$, so $R=S$ and the displayed identity holds. If $\operatorname{Ric}=0$, then its scalar contraction is zero and the formula gives $R=0$; conversely $R=0$ implies its Ricci contraction vanishes.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth three-manifold, possibly with smooth boundary, and fix a trivialization of a principal $G$-bundle over $M$, where $G$ has finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Give $\mathfrak g$ its Lie bracket $[\ ,\ ]_{\mathfrak g}$ and a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathfrak g}$ satisfying $\langle[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g},Z\rangle_{\mathfrak g}=\langle X,[Y,Z]_{\mathfrak g}\rangle_{\mathfrak g}$. Write $\Omega^p(M;\mathfrak g)=\Gamma(M,\wedge^pT^*M\otimes\mathfrak g)$ for smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $p$-forms. Extend the Lie bracket and pairing to homogeneous simple tensors by $[X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta]=[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g}\otimes(\alpha\wedge\beta)$ and $\langle X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta\rangle=\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathfrak g}\,\alpha\wedge\beta$, then extend bilinearly.

A connection in the chosen trivialization is a form $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$. Its curvature and covariant exterior derivative are $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A,A]$ and $D_AX=dX+[A,X]$. Define the local Chern–Simons functional and the BF functional, for $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, by

$$\operatorname{CS}(A)=\int_M\left\langle A\wedge dA+\tfrac13A\wedge[A,A]\right\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{BF}(B,A)=\int_M\langle B\wedge F_A\rangle.$$

These are integrals of smooth top forms on a compact oriented manifold. The Chern–Simons formula is the local expression in the fixed trivialization; it does not define a globally gauge-invariant exponentiated action on arbitrary nontrivial bundles without additional characteristic-class and level data. No path-integral measure, quantization, or identification with a Reshetikhin–Turaev amplitude is part of this definition.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

derivations.claim: Differentiate the Chern–Simons integrand along $A+s\alpha$. The quadratic term contributes $\langle\alpha\wedge dA+A\wedge d\alpha\rangle$. For the cubic term, the graded bracket and invariant pairing give the cyclic identities $\langle A\wedge[\alpha,A]\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ and $\langle A\wedge[A,\alpha]\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ for degree-one $A,\alpha$. Thus the three differentiated terms in $\tfrac13\langle A\wedge[A,A]\rangle$ are equal, and their average is $\langle\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$. The full unintegrated variation is $\langle\alpha\wedge dA+A\wedge d\alpha+\alpha\wedge[A,A]\rangle$.

Differentiate $F_{A+s\alpha}$ at $s=0$; bilinearity of the bracket gives $\delta F_A=D_A\alpha$. Thus the BF variation before integration by parts is $\int_M\langle\beta\wedge F_A+B\wedge D_A\alpha\rangle$.

The graded Leibniz rule gives $d\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle=\langle dA\wedge\alpha\rangle-\langle A\wedge d\alpha\rangle$. Since a two-form commutes with a one-form under wedge, $\langle A\wedge d\alpha\rangle=\langle\alpha\wedge dA\rangle-d\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle$. Substitute this into step 1.1, combine $2dA+[A,A]=2F_A$, and apply [F2] to obtain the stated Chern–Simons formula, including its boundary sign.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth three-manifold, possibly with smooth boundary, and fix a trivialization of a principal $G$-bundle over $M$, where $G$ has finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$. Give $\mathfrak g$ its Lie bracket $[\ ,\ ]_{\mathfrak g}$ and a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_{\mathfrak g}$ satisfying $\langle[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g},Z\rangle_{\mathfrak g}=\langle X,[Y,Z]_{\mathfrak g}\rangle_{\mathfrak g}$. Write $\Omega^p(M;\mathfrak g)=\Gamma(M,\wedge^pT^*M\otimes\mathfrak g)$ for smooth $\mathfrak g$-valued $p$-forms. Extend the Lie bracket and pairing to homogeneous simple tensors by $[X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta]=[X,Y]_{\mathfrak g}\otimes(\alpha\wedge\beta)$ and $\langle X\otimes\alpha,Y\otimes\beta\rangle=\langle X,Y\rangle_{\mathfrak g}\,\alpha\wedge\beta$, then extend bilinearly.

A connection in the chosen trivialization is a form $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$. Its curvature and covariant exterior derivative are $F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A,A]$ and $D_AX=dX+[A,X]$. Define the local Chern–Simons functional and the BF functional, for $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, by

$$\operatorname{CS}(A)=\int_M\left\langle A\wedge dA+\tfrac13A\wedge[A,A]\right\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{BF}(B,A)=\int_M\langle B\wedge F_A\rangle.$$

These are integrals of smooth top forms on a compact oriented manifold. The Chern–Simons formula is the local expression in the fixed trivialization; it does not define a globally gauge-invariant exponentiated action on arbitrary nontrivial bundles without additional characteristic-class and level data. No path-integral measure, quantization, or identification with a Reshetikhin–Turaev amplitude is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be a compact oriented smooth three-manifold with boundary, $\mathfrak g$ a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra with invariant nondegenerate symmetric pairing, and $A\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$ a smooth connection in a fixed trivialization. For an arbitrary smooth variation $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$, the Chern–Simons first variation is

$$\delta\operatorname{CS}_A(\alpha)=2\int_M\langle\alpha\wedge F_A\rangle-\int_{\partial M}\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle,$$

where $\partial M$ has the outward-normal-first orientation. Thus the boundary term is part of the variation; the bulk Euler equation is $F_A=0$ when variations are compactly supported in $\operatorname{int}M$ (or when boundary data make the boundary variation vanish). For $B\in\Omega^1(M;\mathfrak g)$ the BF action has first variation

$$\delta\operatorname{BF}_{(B,A)}(\beta,\alpha)=\int_M\langle\beta\wedge F_A\rangle+\int_M\langle\alpha\wedge D_AB\rangle-\int_{\partial M}\langle B\wedge\alpha\rangle,$$

so interior-compact variations give the equations $F_A=0$ and $D_AB=0$. No boundary condition is imposed by these bulk equations.

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ fixed, the boundary potential current of $\lambda\operatorname{CS}$ is $\theta_A(\alpha)=-\lambda\langle A\wedge\alpha\rangle$. On a compact oriented smooth surface $\Sigma$ (with smooth boundary allowed), put $\mathcal A_\Sigma=\Omega^1(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$ and identify each tangent space with $\Omega^1(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$. For $a\in\mathcal A_\Sigma$ define $\Theta_\Sigma|_a(\alpha)=\int_\Sigma\theta_a(\alpha)$, and let $\Omega_\Sigma=d_{\mathcal A_\Sigma}\Theta_\Sigma$. The restriction to the flat-connection solution space, wherever it is smooth, is the possibly degenerate presymplectic form. Explicitly, on tangent vectors $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ it is the constant closed form

$$\Omega_\Sigma(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)=-2\lambda\int_\Sigma\langle\alpha_1\wedge\alpha_2\rangle.$$

At a flat connection $a$ ($F_a=0$), tangent variations $\alpha$ to the flat-connection equations satisfy $D_a\alpha=0$. For an infinitesimal gauge parameter $\epsilon\in C^\infty(\Sigma;\mathfrak g)$, the gauge direction is $D_a\epsilon$ and

$$\Omega_\Sigma(D_a\epsilon,\alpha)=-2\lambda\int_{\partial\Sigma}\langle\epsilon,\alpha\rangle.$$

Consequently gauge parameters vanishing on $\partial\Sigma$ generate null directions on the linearized flat locus. If $\epsilon$ is field-independent, the displayed boundary variation is $\delta Q_\epsilon$ for $Q_\epsilon(a)=-2\lambda\int_{\partial\Sigma}\langle\epsilon,a\rangle$. For $\lambda\ne0$, nonzero boundary parameters need not be null and can carry such charges when the boundary conditions permit them; no charge algebra or integrability assertion for field-dependent parameters is made. If $\lambda=0$, the displayed $\Theta_\Sigma$, $\Omega_\Sigma$ and $Q_\epsilon$ vanish identically, and every gauge direction on the linearized flat locus is null.

Let $V$ be a three-dimensional real vector space with Lorentzian inner product $g$ of signature $(-,+,+)$. Let $R_{abcd}$ be an algebraic curvature tensor: it is antisymmetric in $a,b$ and in $c,d$, symmetric under exchange of the pairs, and satisfies $R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}=0$. Define $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}=g^{ac}R_{abcd}$ and $\operatorname{Scal}=g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$. Then

$$R_{abcd}=g_{ac}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}-g_{ad}\operatorname{Ric}_{bc}-g_{bc}\operatorname{Ric}_{ad}+g_{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{ac}-\tfrac12\operatorname{Scal}(g_{ac}g_{bd}-g_{ad}g_{bc}).$$

In particular, $\operatorname{Ric}=0$ if and only if $R_{abcd}=0$.

Let $\mathrm{vol}$ be the oriented volume form of $(V,\eta)$. The displayed $J$ satisfies $\eta(J(v)w,z)=\mathrm{vol}(v,w,z)$, so it takes values in $\mathfrak{so}(V,\eta)$ and has zero kernel. Both vector spaces have dimension three: $\eta A$ is an antisymmetric $3\times3$ matrix for $A\in\mathfrak{so}(V,\eta)$, giving three independent entries. Thus $J$ is an isomorphism. For such $A$, $\operatorname{tr}A=0$ and the alternating-form identity
$$\mathrm{vol}(Av,w,z)+\mathrm{vol}(v,Aw,z)+\mathrm{vol}(v,w,Az)=(\operatorname{tr}A)\mathrm{vol}(v,w,z)=0$$
follows by expanding on an oriented basis. Hence
$$\eta([A,J(v)]w,z)=-\mathrm{vol}(v,w,Az)-\mathrm{vol}(v,Aw,z)=\mathrm{vol}(Av,w,z)=\eta(J(Av)w,z),$$
which proves $J(Av)=[A,J(v)]$ by nondegeneracy of $\eta$. This also makes the pairing $\langle J(v),J(w)\rangle=\eta(v,w)$ invariant and nondegenerate. Since $J$ is constant, the identity gives $D_\omega(Je)=J(D_\omega e)$ as two-forms, by evaluating on each pair of tangent vectors. $$2g_e(
abla_XY,Z)=Xg_e(Y,Z)+Yg_e(Z,X)-Zg_e(X,Y)-g_e(X,[Y,Z])+g_e(Y,[Z,X])+g_e(Z,[X,Y]).$$
It follows by adding the metric-compatibility identities for $(X,Y,Z)$ and $(Y,X,Z)$, subtracting the one for $(Z,X,Y)$, and replacing each antisymmetric difference $
abla_XY-
abla_YX$ by $[X,Y]$. Nondegeneracy of $g_e$ makes this formula determine $

Using the curvature operator defined in the Statement and expanding the vector covariant derivative gives
$$e(R^\nabla(X,Y)Z)=(D_X^\omega D_Y^\omega-D_Y^\omega D_X^\omega-D_{[X,Y]}^\omega)(eZ)=F_\omega(X,Y)eZ.$$
The derivative terms in $eZ$ cancel; the remaining coefficient is $d\omega(X,Y)+[\omega(X),\omega(Y)]=F_\omega(X,Y)$. Thus $F_\omega=0$ exactly when $R^\nabla=0$ on a coframe region. For the precise tensor interface in [F3], metric compatibility, applied twice to $g_e(Z,W)$ and subtracting the commutator derivative, gives $g_e(R(X,Y)Z,W)=-g_e(Z,R(X,Y)W)$. Torsion-freeness and the Jacobi identity give $R(X,Y)Z+R(Y,Z)X+R(Z,X)Y=0$. Together with antisymmetry in $X,Y$, these identities give pair-exchange symmetry by rearranging the cyclic identity. Therefore $R_{abcd}=g_e(E_a,R(E_c,E_d)E_b)$ is antisymmetric in $a,b$ and in $c,d$, symmetric under pair exchange, and obeys $R_{abcd}+R_{acdb}+R_{adbc}=0$. Its first/third contraction is exactly the $\operatorname{Ric}_{bd}$ in the Statement, so [F3] applies with the same convention.

The metric trace of $G=0$ in dimension three is $-	frac12\operatorname{Scal}=0$, hence $\operatorname{Scal}=0$ and $\operatorname{Ric}=0$. By [F3], this is equivalent to $R^

abla=0$, and step 4.1 then gives $F_\omega=0$. Their composite is $\Phi_B$, hence $\Phi_B$ is an isomorphism. Duality gives $\sum_a x_a B(x^a,y)=y$ for every $y$, so $\Phi_B(\Omega)=I_{\mathfrak g}$.

Invariance and symmetry [F1] imply $B([x,u],v)=-B(u,[x,v])$: indeed $B(u,[x,v])=B([u,x],v)=-B([x,u],v)$. Thus $\Phi_B(( [x,\cdot]\otimes 1)\Omega)(y)=[x,y]$, while $\Phi_B((1\otimes[x,\cdot])\Omega)(y)=-\sum_a x_aB(x^a,[x,y])=-[x,y]$, using step 1.1's dual-basis identity.

The two images in step 2.1 sum to zero for every $y$. Since $\Phi_B$ is injective by step 1.1, the sum of tensors is zero. The tensor itself is independent of the dual bases by [F2], so this is the diagonal adjoint invariance of the canonical Casimir tensor.

The trace is taken on the finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak g$. This is the invariant form used to define dual bases, the root-theoretic vectors $H_\alpha$, and the quadratic Casimir element on this page.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Killing form $B$. A **Cartan subalgebra** here means a maximal toral subalgebra: a maximal abelian subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ all of whose adjoint operators are diagonalizable. Such subalgebras exist, and every one is self-centralizing. There is a decomposition
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha,\qquad \mathfrak g_\alpha=\{x:[h,x]=\alpha(h)x\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\},$$
where the nonzero weights $\Phi$ are finite, span $\mathfrak h^*$, and each root space has dimension one. The form is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak h$, pairs $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ perfectly with $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$, and all other weight-space pairings are zero. Define $H_\alpha\in\mathfrak h$ by $B(H_\alpha,h)=\alpha(h)$. Then $c_\alpha=\alpha(H_\alpha)\ne0$, and $h_\alpha=2H_\alpha/c_\alpha$ admits root vectors $e_\alpha,f_\alpha$ with $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=h_\alpha$, $[h_\alpha,e_\alpha]=2e_\alpha$, $[h_\alpha,f_\alpha]=-2f_\alpha$.

The real span $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ of the $h_\alpha$ is a real form of $\mathfrak h$ on which $B$ is positive definite. On $E=\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}^*$ with the dual form, $\Phi$ is a finite reduced crystallographic root system and $h_\alpha$ is its coroot. In particular the preceding abstract finite-Weyl conventions apply. For nonproportional roots $\alpha,\beta$, the root spaces with roots $\beta+k\alpha$ form one simple rank-one module: the integers occurring are a consecutive interval, reflection in $\alpha$ reverses it, and raising or lowering between adjacent spaces is nonzero with the positive $fe,ef$ coefficients of $V_m$. The adjoint operators of all root vectors are nilpotent. For any positive system, normalized triples $e_i,f_i,h_i$ of its simple roots generate $\mathfrak g$, and the $h_i$ form a basis of $\mathfrak h$. All assertions include $\mathfrak g=0$ and use no AC.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and let $B$ be the Killing form from [[def-killing-form-of-a-semisimple-lie-algebra]]. Choose dual bases $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $x^1,\dots,x^n$ with respect to $B$, so $B(x_i,x^j)=\delta_i^j$. The **quadratic Casimir element** is

$$C:=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x^i \in U(\mathfrak g).$$

By [[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]], this element is independent of the chosen dual bases.

Fix a positive root system $\Phi^+$ as in [[thm-triangular-decomposition-from-a-chosen-positive-root-system]]. The **Weyl vector** for that choice is

$$\rho:=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in \Phi^+} \alpha \in \mathfrak h^*.$$

This is the shift used in the dot action and in the quadratic Casimir eigenvalue formula on this page.

$$ (\lambda,\lambda+2\rho), $$

where the pairing on $\mathfrak h^*$ is induced by the Killing form and $\rho$ is the Weyl vector from [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, so that $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ is the set of its
predecessors ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and let $X$ be a topological space
([[def-topological-space]]). Write

$$X^n:=\prod_{k<n}X$$

for the $n$-fold product, carrying the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]),
and display its points as $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$: the **label** $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
names the coordinate of index $i-1$ in the sense of that definition. The
**ordered configuration space** of $n$ points in $X$ is the subspace

$$F_n(X):=\{\,(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in X^n\;:\;x_i\neq x_j\ \text{whenever}\ i\neq j\,\}$$

with the subspace topology inherited from $X^n$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Equivalently

$$F_n(X)=X^n\setminus\bigcup_{i\neq j}\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in X^n:x_i=x_j\},$$

since a tuple lies in $F_n(X)$ exactly when its entries are pairwise distinct:
the **collision diagonals** $x_i=x_j$, $i\neq j$, are removed from the product.
Points of $F_n(X)$ are called **ordered configurations** of $n$ points in $X$.

**The label set.** The labels $1,\dots,n$ are part of the data, and throughout
this page they are identified with the set $n=\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$ by the
bijection $\kappa(i):=i-1$. It is through $\kappa$ that the symmetric group
$S_n=\operatorname{Sym}(n)$ acts on $F_n(X)$, in
[[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]].

**Elementary cases.** For $n=0$ the product $X^0$ is a one-point space
([[def-product-topology]]), and the defining condition is vacuous, so

$$F_0(X)=\{\,\text{the empty tuple}\,\}$$

for every $X$, including $X=\varnothing$. For $n=1$ there is no pair $i\neq j$,
so single-coordinate evaluation $(x_1)\mapsto x_1$ is a canonical
homeomorphism $F_1(X)\cong X$. For $n\geq2$ and any $X$ one has

$$F_n(X)\neq\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X\ \text{has at least } n \text{ distinct points}.$$

if $X$ has at least $n$ points, an injection $\{1,\dots,n\}\to X$ is exactly a
tuple of pairwise distinct points of $X$, and conversely such a tuple displays
$n$ distinct points. In particular $F_n(X)=\varnothing$ when $X$ is empty and
$n\geq1$.

**Based configurations.** A **base configuration** in $F_n(X)$ is a point
$q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ of $F_n(X)$. Such a $q$ is fixed once and for all only when
$F_n(X)$ is nonempty; when $n\ge1$, $F_n(X)\ne\varnothing$, and $X$ is
infinite, $F_n(X)$ is infinite: from any one configuration, keep coordinates
$2,\dots,n$ fixed and vary the first coordinate among the infinitely many
points of $X\setminus\{q_2,\dots,q_n\}$. The choice of $q$ is part of the data
of every construction below. All base configurations on this page are chosen in the ordered space
$F_n(X)$; the corresponding basepoint of the unordered quotient is its orbit
([[def-unordered-configuration-space]]).

**Separation of distinct coordinates.** If $X$ is Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $q\in F_n(X)$, then the finitely many points
$q_1,\dots,q_n$ are pairwise distinct, and for each pair $i\neq j$ Hausdorffness
supplies disjoint open sets separating $q_i$ from $q_j$; a finite intersection
over the finitely many pairs $j\neq i$ therefore gives, for every $i$, an open
neighbourhood $U_i$ of $q_i$ with $U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $i\neq j$.
This is used in
[[lem-disjoint-coordinate-neighborhoods-evenly-cover-unordered-configurations]].

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and let $B$ be the Killing form from [[def-killing-form-of-a-semisimple-lie-algebra]]. Choose dual bases $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $x^1,\dots,x^n$ with respect to $B$, so $B(x_i,x^j)=\delta_i^j$. The **quadratic Casimir element** is

Changing the $B$-dual bases leaves $\Omega$ unchanged by [F3], and applying $\rho_i\otimes\rho_j$ and identities on the other factors therefore leaves $\Omega_{ij}$ unchanged. On $F_n(\mathbb C)$ the scalar $z_i-z_j$ is never zero by [F1]. Hence its reciprocal is smooth, so $\eta_{ij}=(dz_i-dz_j)/(z_i-z_j)$ is a globally defined smooth one-form; the finite sum $A=\kappa^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}$ is a smooth $\operatorname{End}(V)$-valued one-form.

For a smooth section $s:F_n(\mathbb C)	o V$ and smooth scalar function $f$, $
abla(fs)=d(fs)-A(fs)=df\otimes s+f(ds-As)=df\otimes s+f
abla s$, because each endomorphism coefficient in $A$ acts $\mathbb C$-linearly on $s$. Thus $

A connection on a finite-rank smooth vector bundle $E\to M$ is flat if and
only if every point of $M$ has a neighborhood carrying a local frame
$(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ of parallel sections, meaning $\nabla_Xe_a=0$ for every
local vector field $X$ and every $a$.

For a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ and $v\in E_{\gamma(a)}$, let $V_v$ be the unique continuous piecewise parallel section with $V_v(a)=v$, supplied by [[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-parallel-sections]]. Its **parallel transport** is
$$P_\gamma:E_{\gamma(a)}\to E_{\gamma(b)},\qquad P_\gamma(v)=V_v(b).$$
More generally, $P_{\gamma;s,t}$ sends initial data at $s$ to its value at $t$, allowing either order of the parameters. The same theorem gives independence from frames and subdivisions. On a singleton, $P_\gamma$ is the identity of its fibre. An empty curve has no endpoint fibres and is not assigned such a map. particular such isomorphism is fixed here. For $n=0$ the space $F_0(D^2)$ is a
point, so $PB_0$ is the one-element group; for $n=1$ single-coordinate
evaluation gives $F_1(D^2)\cong D^2$ and $PB_1$ is trivial.

**Scope.** This is the configuration-space definition of the pure braid group,
stated before any comparison with geometric strands or with the Artin
presentation: no presentation of $PB_n$ is asserted here. The description by
geometric braids and the Artin presentation, and the configuration braid short
exact sequence relating $PB_n$ to the unordered configuration braid group,
belong to the later items on braids, which consume this definition.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $X$ be a topological space
([[def-ordered-configuration-space]], [[def-topological-space]]). The label
permutation action

$$S_n\times F_n(X)\longrightarrow F_n(X),\qquad(\sigma,x)\longmapsto\sigma\cdot x,\qquad(\sigma\cdot x)_i=x_{\sigma^{-1}(i-1)+1},$$

is a continuous free left action
([[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]]). Its set of
orbits $S_n\cdot x=\{\sigma\cdot x:\sigma\in S_n\}$
([[def-orbit-and-stabilizer]]) is the **unordered configuration space** of $n$
points in $X$, written

$$C_n(X):=F_n(X)/S_n=\{S_n\cdot x:x\in F_n(X)\},$$

and it carries the **quotient topology** of the canonical projection

$$p_n:F_n(X)\longrightarrow C_n(X),\qquad p_n(x):=S_n\cdot x,$$

in the sense of [[def-quotient-topology]]: a subset $V\subseteq C_n(X)$ is open
exactly when $p_n^{-1}(V)$ is open in $F_n(X)$. This projection is a quotient
map, hence continuous and surjective, and points of $C_n(X)$ are written
$[x]:=p_n(x)$.

**Basepoint.** For a base configuration $q\in F_n(X)$ in the sense of
[[def-ordered-configuration-space]], the **basepoint** of $C_n(X)$ is the orbit

$$[q]=p_n(q)=S_n\cdot q,$$

and $C_n(X)$ is nonempty exactly when $F_n(X)$ is, in which case a basepoint can
be fixed. The unordered space is based by the orbit of the ordered base
configuration, and this is the basepoint used in every later construction on
this page.

**Elementary cases.** $C_0(X)$ is the quotient of the one-point space $F_0(X)$
by the trivial group $S_0$, hence is a one-point space. Since $S_1$ is trivial,
$p_1:F_1(X)\to C_1(X)$ is a bijective quotient map and hence a
homeomorphism: for every open $U\subseteq F_1(X)$, the equality
$p_1^{-1}(p_1(U))=U$ makes $p_1(U)$ open by the quotient topology.
Thus $C_1(X)$ is canonically homeomorphic to $X$ by $[(x)]\mapsto x$,
using the single-coordinate homeomorphism $F_1(X)\to X$.
These are canonical identifications, not literal equalities of the orbit set
with the original set.

**Elements are $n$-element subsets, as a set.** Because the coordinates of a
configuration are pairwise distinct, two ordered configurations $x,y\in F_n(X)$
lie in the same orbit exactly when their underlying sets of coordinates agree:
if $y=\sigma\cdot x$ then the coordinates of $y$ are those of $x$ in a different
order, and conversely, if $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}=\{y_1,\dots,y_n\}$, then for every
label $i$ there is exactly one label $\sigma(i)$ with $y_i=x_{\sigma(i)}$, and
$i\mapsto\sigma(i)$ is a bijection of $\{1,\dots,n\}$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); composing with the identification
$\kappa(i)=i-1$ of labels with $n$, the permutation
$\tau=\kappa\circ\sigma^{-1}\circ\kappa^{-1}\in S_n$ takes $x$ to $y$:
$(\tau\cdot x)_i=x_{\tau^{-1}(i-1)+1}=x_{\sigma(i)}=y_i$. Hence

$$C_n(X)\longrightarrow\{\,S\subseteq X:S \text{ has exactly } n \text{ elements}\,\},\qquad [x]\longmapsto\{x_1,\dots,x_n\},$$

is a bijection of sets, the inverse sending an $n$-element subset $S$ to the
orbit of any enumeration of $S$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]). This identifies
the *elements* of $C_n(X)$ with $n$-element subsets of $X$; the topology on
$C_n(X)$ is the quotient topology displayed above, and no topology on a set of
subsets is asserted here. In particular the quotient topology is not defined
through any metric or hyperspace structure.

Let $M$ be a nonempty connected Hausdorff topological $d$-manifold with boundary, possibly empty boundary, in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-with-boundary]], of dimension $d\ge2$, and let $n\in\mathbb N$. Write $p:F_n(M)\to C_n(M)$ for the quotient map from the ordered to the unordered configuration space ([[def-ordered-configuration-space]], [[def-unordered-configuration-space]]). Then:

1. $p$ is a covering map in the sense of [[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]; every fibre of $p$ has exactly $n!$ elements, so $p$ is an $n!$-sheeted covering, and each point of $C_n(M)$ has an evenly covered neighbourhood of the form supplied by [[lem-disjoint-coordinate-neighborhoods-evenly-cover-unordered-configurations]].
2. $F_n(M)$ is path-connected, and so is $C_n(M)$; in particular $F_n(M)$ is connected and is a connected covering space of $C_n(M)$.
3. The deck group $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$ ([[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]) is isomorphic to $S_n$: the map $\sigma\mapsto\tau_\sigma$, $\tau_\sigma(x):=\sigma\cdot x$, is an isomorphism of groups from $S_n$ onto $\operatorname{Deck}(p)$, where $S_n$ acts on $F_n(M)$ by permuting the labels $1,\dots,n$ ([[prop-the-symmetric-group-acts-freely-on-ordered-configurations]]).
4. $p$ is a regular covering in the sense of [[def-regular-covering]]: its deck group acts transitively on every fibre.

For $n=0$ the spaces $F_0(M)$ and $C_0(M)$ are one-point spaces and $p$ is their unique homeomorphism, so the assertions hold with $0!=1$. No choice principle, paracompactness or second countability beyond the manifold definition is used.

Fix $n\in\mathbb N$ and the same base configuration $q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ of
pairwise distinct points of $\operatorname{int}D^2$ that is used in
[[def-pure-braid-group-from-ordered-configurations]], with $D^2$ the closed unit
disc. Write $p:F_n(D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ for the quotient of the ordered by the
unordered configuration space, so that $p(q)=[q]$ is the orbit of $q$
([[def-unordered-configuration-space]]). The **configuration braid group** on
$n$ strands is the fundamental group
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]])

$$B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\pi_1\big(C_n(D^2),[q]\big),$$

the group of based-loop classes at the orbit $[q]$ in the unordered
configuration space of the closed disc, with the first-then-second loop product.

**The open-disc model.** The inclusion-induced map
$\iota^C:C_n(\operatorname{int}D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ of
[[lem-interior-and-closed-disk-configuration-spaces-are-homotopy-equivalent]]
induces an isomorphism
$$\pi_1\big(C_n(\operatorname{int}D^2),[q]\big)\longrightarrow\pi_1\big(C_n(D^2),[q]\big)$$
at the same basepoint (claim 3 of that lemma,
[[def-induced-homomorphism-on-fundamental-groups]]), so $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$
may be computed from either disc model exactly as $PB_n$ may. Both groups in
this definition and in
[[def-pure-braid-group-from-ordered-configurations]] are taken at the
basepoints $[q]$ and $q$ coming from the same tuple $q$, which is what makes the
comparison map of the configuration braid short exact sequence, proved in a
later item on this page, a map of based fundamental groups.

**The basepoint.** Since $F_n(D^2)\to C_n(D^2)$ is surjective every basepoint of
$C_n(D^2)$ is an orbit, and since $C_n(D^2)$ is path-connected (claim 2 of
[[thm-ordered-configurations-cover-unordered-configurations-regularly]]) the
groups at different orbits are isomorphic by conjugation along a path
([[lem-path-conjugation-isomorphism-of-fundamental-groups]]); no particular
isomorphism is fixed. For $n=0$ the space $C_0(D^2)$ is a point and
$B_0^{\mathrm{conf}}$ is the one-element group.

**The superscript.** The decoration $\mathrm{conf}$ records that the group is
defined here through configuration spaces, and it is retained until the later
geometric identification of $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$ with the braid group given by
strand diagrams and with its Artin presentation. No such identification and no
presentation is asserted on this page; neither is any identification of
$B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}$ with a group of self-homeomorphisms of the disc.

derivations.claim: If $\{i,j\}$ and $\{k,l\}$ are disjoint pairs, then $\Omega_{ij}$ and $\Omega_{kl}$ act on disjoint tensor factors. Each factorwise operator commutes with every operator on the other factors, so $[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{kl}]=0$.

For three distinct indices $i,j,k$, write $\Omega=\sum_a x_a\otimes x^a$. Apply [F2] with $x=x_b$, place its two tensor factors in slots $i,j$, apply $\rho_i\otimes\rho_j$, multiply on slot $k$ by $\rho_k(x^b)$, and sum over $b$. The first resulting sum is $- [\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}]$ and the second is $-[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{jk}]$, because $[x_b,x_a]=-[x_a,x_b]$ and $[x_b,x^a]=-[x^a,x_b]$. Hence $[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}+\Omega_{jk}]=0$.

Set $u=z_i-z_j$ and $v=z_j-z_k$, so $z_i-z_k=u+v$. Then $\eta_{ij}=du/u$, $\eta_{jk}=dv/v$, and $\eta_{ik}=(du+dv)/(u+v)$. Direct expansion gives $\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{jk}+\eta_{jk}\wedge\eta_{ik}+\eta_{ik}\wedge\eta_{ij}=\left(1/(uv)-1/(v(u+v))-1/(u(u+v))\right)du\wedge dv=0$, since the numerator after taking a common denominator is $(u+v)-u-v=0$.

Put $B_0:=\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}$, so $
abla=d-\kappa^{-1}B_0$. Each $\eta_{ij}$ is closed because $d(dw/w)=0$ on $w
e0$, hence $dB_0=0$, and the curvature is $R^
abla=\kappa^{-2}B_0\wedge B_0$. Expanding the wedge product groups terms by disjoint pairs and by triples. The disjoint terms vanish by step 1.1. For $i<j<k$, the triple contribution is $C_{ijk}(\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{ik}-\eta_{ij}\wedge\eta_{jk}+\eta_{ik}\wedge\eta_{jk})$, where $C_{ijk}:=[\Omega_{ij},\Omega_{ik}]$: step 1.2 gives the other two commutators as $-C_{ijk}$ and $C_{ijk}$. This form is the negative of the zero Arnold sum in step 1.3, so every triple contribution vanishes and $R^
abla=0$.

By [F3], every point has a neighborhood with a parallel frame. A parallel section has constant coordinates in that frame. On an overlap, if one parallel frame is the other times a smooth matrix $G(x)$, the connection equation gives $dG=0$, so $G$ is constant on each connected component of the overlap. These charts therefore define a locally constant sheaf of horizontal sections; define its transport along a continuous path by subdividing the path into chart intervals and retaining the same frame coordinates. For a piecewise smooth path this agrees with differential parallel transport by [F4] and uniqueness in [F5].

Suppose $V_i=V_0$ and $\rho_i=\rho_0$ for every $i$. The coordinate-permutation action from [F7] lifts to the same permutation of tensor factors. Since $\eta_{ij}$ is symmetric in $i,j$, and the factor permutation sends $\Omega_{ij}$ to the correspondingly relabeled $\Omega$, it preserves the connection. The action is free on $F_n(\mathbb C)$ by [F7]. The usual $\mathbb C$ is a connected Hausdorff real 2-manifold, so [F10] makes the quotient map a regular covering.

Given $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in F_n(\mathbb C)$, choose pairwise disjoint open discs $D_i\subset\mathbb C$ about $z_i$ and put $\widetilde U:=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. This is an open connected subset of $F_n(\mathbb C)$, and its $S_n$-translates are pairwise disjoint because the $D_i$ are disjoint. By [F10] these sheets evenly cover their open image $U$ in the quotient; write $p(z)=[z]$ for the orbit quotient, so $p|_{\widetilde U}:\widetilde U\to U$ is a homeomorphism. These product charts give the quotient its smooth-manifold structure: on overlaps the change of ordered representative is locally one fixed coordinate permutation, hence smooth. The map $(p(z),v)\mapsto[(z,v)]$, for the unique $z\in\widetilde U$ over $p(z)$, is a local trivialization of $(F_n(\mathbb C)\times V_0^{\otimes n})/S_n$ over $U$. On each connected component of an overlap, changing the chosen sheet acts on the fiber by one fixed $\tau_\sigma$, a linear isomorphism, so these are smooth vector-bundle transition maps. In these local trivializations the connection is obtained by restricting the KZ connection to the chosen sheet. If a different sheet is chosen, the connection agrees under the transition $\tau_\sigma$ because the KZ connection is equivariant. Thus the quotient is a vector bundle and its connection descends, with fiber identified with $V_0^{\otimes n}$ at $[q]$ by the representative $q$.

For an endpoint-fixed homotopy of paths, pull back the parallel-frame neighborhoods to the compact square. A finite subcover has a positive Lebesgue number: choose finitely many smaller metric balls covering the square whose doubled balls lie in cover members, and take the minimum radius $\delta$ of those smaller balls. Choose a rectangular grid whose cell diameters are less than $\delta$; every cell then maps into one parallel-frame neighborhood. Transport around each cell is the identity because its four edges use one constant frame. Multiplying the cell identities cancels every interior edge with its reverse, so the boundary paths have identical local-system transport. By concatenating the unique parallel sections on successive path segments, [F5] gives $P_{\alpha*\beta}=P_\beta P_\alpha$; reversing a parallel section gives $P_{\bar\alpha}=P_\alpha^{-1}$. The same composition and inverse rules hold for local-system transport by its subdivision definition.

Let $T_\gamma$ denote the local-system transport for a continuous path. Step 4.2 makes it depend only on the path-homotopy class. Under [F6], the first-then-second product satisfies $T_{\alpha*\beta}=T_\beta T_\alpha$, so $\rho([\gamma]):=T_\gamma^{-1}$ is a left representation because $\rho([\alpha][\beta])=(T_\beta T_\alpha)^{-1}=T_\alpha^{-1}T_\beta^{-1}$. On piecewise smooth loops $T_\gamma=P_\gamma$ by step 3.1. The map $h(z)=z/(1+|z|)$ has inverse $h^{-1}(w)=w/(1-|w|)$ from $D^\circ$ to $\mathbb C$; its coordinatewise product is a homeomorphism of ordered configuration spaces and takes $q$ to $\widetilde q$. It induces a based isomorphism on fundamental groups, and the inclusion $D^\circ\hookrightarrow D^2$ induces the based isomorphism in [F8]. Hence the ordered monodromy representation is based at $\widetilde q$ when identified with $PB_n=\pi_1(F_n(D^2),\widetilde q)$.

The descended connection is flat because its pullback is the flat connection of step 2.1. Applying the local-system monodromy construction of steps 3.1 and 5.1 on the quotient gives its left monodromy representation of $\pi_1(C_n(\mathbb C),[q])$. The coordinatewise homeomorphism $h$ is $S_n$-equivariant, so it descends to a homeomorphism of unordered configuration spaces and takes $[q]$ to $[\widetilde q]$. The inclusion-induced isomorphism at $[\widetilde q]$ in [F11] then identifies this based fundamental group with $B_n^{\mathrm{conf}}=\pi_1(C_n(D^2),[\widetilde q])$. No identification with any quantum-group ribbon representation follows from this construction.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with Killing form $B_{\mathrm{Kill}}$. Choose a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and a positive root system $\Phi^+$ with highest root $\theta$, and put $\rho:=\tfrac12\sum_{\alpha\in\Phi^+}\alpha$. For each $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$ let $H_{\lambda,\mathrm{Kill}}\in\mathfrak h$ be the unique vector satisfying $B_{\mathrm{Kill}}(H_{\lambda,\mathrm{Kill}},H)=\lambda(H)$ for every $H\in\mathfrak h$, and define the induced form on $\mathfrak h^*$ by $(\lambda,\mu)_{\mathrm{Kill}}:=B_{\mathrm{Kill}}(H_{\lambda,\mathrm{Kill}},H_{\mu,\mathrm{Kill}})$. This extends the supplied convention $B_{\mathrm{Kill}}(H_{\alpha,\mathrm{Kill}},H)=\alpha(H)$ for roots $\alpha$. Set $c:=2/(\theta,\theta)_{\mathrm{Kill}}$ and $B_0:=B_{\mathrm{Kill}}/c$. For each $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, let $H_{\lambda,0}\in\mathfrak h$ satisfy $B_0(H_{\lambda,0},H)=\lambda(H)$ for every $H\in\mathfrak h$, and put $(\lambda,\mu)_0:=B_0(H_{\lambda,0},H_{\mu,0})$. Then $(\theta,\theta)_0=2$. Define the coroot $\theta^\vee:=2H_{\theta,0}/(\theta,\theta)_0=H_{\theta,0}$ and the dual Coxeter number $h^\vee:=1+\rho(\theta^\vee)$. Then

$$B_{\mathrm{Kill}}=2h^\vee B_0.$$

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Killing form $B$, let $n\ge2$, and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be finite-dimensional complex vector spaces. A representation here is a complex-linear Lie algebra homomorphism $ho_i:\mathfrak g	o\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_i)$, so $[ho_i(x),ho_i(y)]=ho_i([x,y])$. Let $F_n(\mathbb C)=\{(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\in\mathbb C^n:z_i
e z_j	ext{ for }i
e j\}$ be the ordered configuration space and put $V:=V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_n$ in the indicated factor order. For any pair of $B$-dual bases $(x_a),(x^a)$ define $\Omega_{ij}:=\sum_aho_i(x_a)^{(i)}ho_j(x^a)^{(j)}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, where each superscript means that the operator acts on that tensor factor and as the identity on all other factors. For $i<j$ put $\eta_{ij}:=(dz_i-dz_j)/(z_i-z_j)$, a globally defined complex-valued one-form on $F_n(\mathbb C)$. For $\kappa\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, the **Casimir Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov connection** on the trivial vector bundle $F_n(\mathbb C)	imes V	o F_n(\mathbb C)$ is

$$
abla^{\mathrm{KZ}}_\kappa:=d-\kappa^{-1}\sum_{i<j}\Omega_{ij}\eta_{ij}.$$

Here a connection on this trivial bundle is a complex-linear operator on smooth $V$-valued sections satisfying $
abla(fs)=df\otimes s+f
abla s$ for every smooth scalar function $f$ and section $s$. The associated quadratic Casimir is $C_B:=\sum_a x_ax^a$ in the universal enveloping algebra; with the Killing-form convention above it is central, and $\Omega_{ij}$ is its tensor-level Casimir counterpart.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional real Lie algebra. Let $\kappa:\mathfrak g\times\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bilinear form that is invariant, meaning
$$\kappa([U,V],W)=\kappa(U,[V,W])\qquad(U,V,W\in\mathfrak g).$$
No nondegeneracy, positivity, simplicity, or compactness assumption is imposed. Put $S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and $\mathcal L\mathfrak g=C^\infty(S^1,\mathfrak g)$, with pointwise bracket $[X,Y](\theta)=[X(\theta),Y(\theta)]_{\mathfrak g}$. For $Y\in\mathcal L\mathfrak g$, write $Y'=\partial_\theta Y$ in the indicated periodic coordinate.

A Lie-algebra $2$-cocycle for the trivial scalar action is an alternating bilinear map $\omega:\mathcal L\mathfrak g\times\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\omega([X,Y],Z)+\omega([Y,Z],X)+\omega([Z,X],Y)=0.$$
Define the candidate current cocycle and its candidate central-term bracket by
$$\omega(X,Y)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\kappa(X(\theta),Y'(\theta))\,d\theta,\qquad \widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}=\mathcal L\mathfrak g\oplus\mathbb R,$$
$$[(X,a),(Y,b)]=([X,Y],\omega(X,Y)).$$
The real coordinates $a,b$ are central coordinates and do not enter the right-hand side. A one-dimensional central extension means a short exact sequence of Lie algebras $0\to\mathbb R\to\widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}\to\mathcal L\mathfrak g\to0$ whose kernel is central. The proposition on this page verifies that the displayed operation has this Lie-algebra structure. The normalization is fixed as written; no integer level, integration to a loop group, or representation-theoretic existence or unitarity follows from this definition.

For the finite-dimensional real Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, invariant symmetric form $\kappa$, smooth loop algebra $\mathcal L\mathfrak g$, and bilinear form $\omega$ defined in [[def-qftx-loop-current-cocycle]], the form $\omega$ is alternating and satisfies
$$\omega([X,Y],Z)+\omega([Y,Z],X)+\omega([Z,X],Y)=0\qquad(X,Y,Z\in\mathcal L\mathfrak g).$$
Consequently the candidate bracket on $\widehat{\mathcal L\mathfrak g}$ is a Lie bracket and gives a one-dimensional central extension of $\mathcal L\mathfrak g$ by $\mathbb R$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $\mathcal C$ be a locally finite $k$-linear abelian rigid monoidal category whose tensor product is $k$-bilinear. For each object $Y$ write $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y):=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Y,Y)$. The tensor unit $\mathbf1$ is assumed to satisfy $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(\mathbf1)\cong k$ as $k$-algebras. Here rigid means every object has left and right duals with evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfying the two snake identities. Equip $\mathcal C$ with a braiding $c_{Y,Z}:Y\otimes Z\to Z\otimes Y$, natural in $Y,Z$, satisfying the two hexagon identities with the associator $\alpha$. Fix $X\in\mathcal C$, put $P_0(X)=\mathbf1$, $P_1(X)=X$, and recursively put $P_{m+1}(X)=P_m(X)\otimes X$.

For any object $Y$, let $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ be the group under composition of those $g\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ for which some $h\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(Y)$ satisfies $g\circ h=h\circ g=\operatorname{id}_Y$.

For each $n\ge2$ and $1\le i<n$, let $Q_{n,i}(X)$ be the parenthesized product $\bigl(P_{i-1}(X)\otimes(X\otimes X)\bigr)\otimes P_{n-i-1}(X)$, with the unit factors at either end removed by the fixed unitors when an exponent is zero. Choose a canonical rebracketing isomorphism $\rho_{n,i}:P_n(X)\to Q_{n,i}(X)$ made from associators, unitors, and their inverses, without permuting the ordered tensor factors. Define

$$B_i^X:=\rho_{n,i}^{-1}\circ\bigl(\operatorname{id}_{P_{i-1}(X)}\otimes c_{X,X}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{P_{n-i-1}(X)}\bigr)\circ\rho_{n,i}\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(P_n(X)).$$

**Physical interpretation boundary.** A physical adiabatic-exchange interpretation needs additional model data; the categorical data below supply none of the analytic or physical data. For a densely defined operator $K$, its adjoint $K^*$ is defined by $y\in\mathcal D(K^*)$ exactly when some $z\in\mathcal H$ satisfies $\langle Kx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in\mathcal D(K)$, with $K^*y=z$; self-adjoint means $\mathcal D(K^*)=\mathcal D$ and $K^*x=Kx$ there. The spectrum $\sigma(K)$ is the set of $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ for which $K-\lambda I$ has no bounded, everywhere-defined inverse.

For each $s$, supply a projection-valued measure $E_s$ on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R$: each $E_s(A)$ is an orthogonal projection, $E_s(\mathbb R)=I$, and for pairwise disjoint Borel sets $A_j$, $E_s(\bigcup_j A_j)x=\sum_jE_s(A_j)x$ with norm convergence for every $x\in\mathcal H$. For a Borel set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$, define its spectral projection by $P(s):=E_s(\Omega)$. Require $\operatorname{ran}P(s)$ to be finite-dimensional and $\operatorname{dist}(\Omega,\sigma(K(s))\setminus\Omega)\ge\gamma>0$ uniformly in $s$, where $\operatorname{dist}(A,B):=\inf\{|a-b|:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ and $\inf\varnothing:=+\infty$.

Require $s\mapsto P(s)$ to be continuously differentiable in operator norm. $$\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\|U_\varepsilon(s,0)P(0)-\iota_sW(s,0)P(0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le r(\varepsilon),$$

Let $\mathcal C$ be a complex finite semisimple rigid tensor category with simple unit $\mathbf 1$ and a finite set $I$ of isomorphism classes of simple objects. Its trace is $\operatorname{tr}_j(f)=\operatorname{Tr}_L(j_Xf)$ for $f\in\operatorname{End}(X)$.

Write $0$ for the unit label and $i^*$ for the dual of $i$. Put $N_{ij}^k=\dim_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Hom}(k,i\otimes j)$, $d_i=\operatorname{tr}_j(1_i)$, and $s_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}_j(c_{j,i}c_{i,j})$. Define $D^2=\sum_{i\in I}d_i^2$. When $D^2\ne0$, either square root $D$ defines the normalized matrix $S=s/D$; for a modular category, [[lem-modular-hopf-matrix-squared]] proves this nonvanishing. Let $\ell\ge3$, $q=e^{\pi i/\ell}$, and let $\mathcal C_\ell$ be the standard ribbon semisimplification of finite-dimensional integrable type-1 tilting modules for Lusztig's divided-power $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, using the positive-trace quantum ribbon convention. $$u_X:X\to X^{\vee\vee},$$

$$X\xrightarrow{1_X\otimes\operatorname{coev}_{X^\vee}}X\otimes X^\vee\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{c_{X,X^\vee}\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^\vee\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee\vee}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_X\otimes1_{X^{\vee\vee}}}X^{\vee\vee}.$$

monoidality obstruction.

Let $Q$ be any finite acyclic quiver over $\mathbb F_q$, including wild
quivers, and let $Z_-$ and $Z_+$ be any two assignments of upper-half-plane
charges $z_i\in\mathbb H$. In the dimension completion of the subobject-first
Hall algebra,
$$A_{\mathrm{all}}=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z\ \mathrm{decreasing}}S_Z(\phi),\qquad \Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):0\ne\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}\}.$$
The product is degreewise finite and includes all semistable objects, whether
stable or strictly semistable. Applying either Euler integration $I$ or skew
integration $J$ gives equal completed ordered products for $Z_-$ and $Z_+$.
Each integrated ordered product has constant term $1$ and is a unit in its
completed quantum torus; conjugation by the two equal products therefore gives
the same continuous automorphism.
No generic-stability, finite-type, 3-Calabi–Yau, orientation-data, or analytic
convergence assumption is used.

Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, where $Q_0,Q_1$ are finite
sets and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ are the source and target maps. Let $k=\mathbb F_q$
with $q>1$, and assign to each vertex $i\in Q_0$ a charge
$z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$. A
finite-dimensional representation $M$ assigns a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $M_i$ to each vertex and a linear map
$M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each arrow; its dimension vector is
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_k M_i)_{i\in Q_0}$. Put
$Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ and, for nonzero
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, put
$\phi_Z(\mathbf d)=\arg Z(\mathbf d)/\pi$ using the principal argument. For
$M\ne0$, set $\phi_Z(M)=\phi_Z(\mathbf d(M))$. Call $M$
$Z$-semistable when every nonzero subrepresentation has phase at most
$\phi_Z(M)$. Include the zero representation as semistable with no assigned
phase.

Use the small finitary abelian skeleton of these representations. Its Hall
algebra has basis $\delta_M$ indexed by isomorphism classes, and the
subobject-first convention is
$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L}f(U)g(L/U)$, with distinct embedded
subobjects counted separately. Its dimension completion is the product of
the finite-dimensional homogeneous components. For integer dimension
vectors define the bilinear Euler form and its skew-symmetrization by
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,\qquad \langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d).$$

For a phase $\phi$, let
$$S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\ne[0]\\M\ Z\text{-semistable}\\\phi_Z(M)=\phi}}\delta_M,$$
where $\delta_M$ is the characteristic function of the isomorphism class
$[M]$ and $\delta_0$ is the Hall unit. The Euler and skew integrations are
the continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad t=\sqrt q>0,$$
as proved for this finite-field category by the Euler and skew integration
theorem. Their completed targets have bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$ and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$

Write $\Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0},\
\mathbf e\ne0\}$ and order its elements decreasingly. Define the Euler and
skew Hall spectrum generators by
$$P_Z^{E}:=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow} I(S_Z(\phi)),\qquad P_Z^{\mathrm{sk}}:=\mathop{*}_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow}J(S_Z(\phi)).$$
In each product the largest phase is the leftmost factor and multiplication
is in the corresponding completed torus. In any fixed total-dimension degree
$D$, only dimension vectors with $\sum_i d_i\le D$ and their finitely many
phases can contribute. Thus these are degreewise formal products in the
specified completion; no analytic convergence is asserted.

These generators describe the Euler or skew integration of finite-field
semistable representation groupoids. Calling such data protected BPS indices,
dimensions of physical state spaces, or spectra of a four-dimensional
supersymmetric model is an additional dictionary, not part of this
mathematical definition.

skeleton of $\mathcal A_Q$, so $\mathcal A_Q$ is essentially small.

For $\mathbf d,\mathbf e\in\mathbb Z^{Q_0}$ define the bilinear form
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,$$
and its skew-symmetrization
$\langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)$.
The next lemma proves that $\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(N))$ is the
Hom-minus-Yoneda-Ext$^1$ dimension for this arrow convention.

Fix $z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ for each
vertex and extend $Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ additively. If
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$ is nonzero, then
$\operatorname{Im}Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i\operatorname{Im}z_i>0$; thus its
principal argument lies in $(0,\pi)$. For a nonzero representation $M$, put
$\phi_Z(M)=\arg Z(\mathbf d(M))/\pi\in(0,1)$. Call
$M$ **$Z$-semistable** if every nonzero subrepresentation $U\subseteq M$
satisfies $\phi_Z(U)\le\phi_Z(M)$, and **$Z$-stable** if the inequality is
strict for every proper nonzero subrepresentation.

For the semistable groupoids and stacks below, include the zero representation
as semistable without assigning it a phase. Stable objects and HN factors
remain nonzero.

For a dimension vector $\mathbf d$, let
$$\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf d}(Q)=\prod_{a:i\to j} \operatorname{Hom}_k(k^{d_i},k^{d_j}),\qquad G_{\mathbf d}=\prod_{i\in Q_0}\operatorname{GL}_{d_i,k}.$$
The group $G_{\mathbf d}$ acts by change of bases. Define
$\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)$ geometrically: its points over an
algebraic closure $\bar k$ are representations for which every nonzero
$\bar k$-subrepresentation satisfies the semistability inequality. The
associated quotient stack is
$\mathfrak M^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)=[\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}(Q,Z)/G_{\mathbf d}]$.
For $\mathbf d=0$, set $\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf0}=\operatorname{Rep}_{\mathbf0}=\operatorname{Spec}k$.
The group $G_{\mathbf0}$ is trivial, so its rational-point groupoid has one
zero object, trivial automorphism group, and cardinality $1$.
Here $[X/G]$ denotes the groupoid-valued quotient: over a scheme $S$ its
objects are $G$-torsors on $S$ with equivariant maps to $X$, and its arrows
are equivariant isomorphisms over $S$. The openness lemma below proves that
$\operatorname{Rep}^{ss}_{\mathbf d}$ is open.

For a finite groupoid $\mathcal G$, define its groupoid cardinality by
$$|\mathcal G|=\sum_{[x]\in\operatorname{Iso}(\mathcal G)} \frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal G}(x)|}.$$
The rational-point groupoid of $\mathfrak M^{ss}_{\mathbf d}$ is finite, and
the finite-field descent lemma identifies it with the groupoid of finite-field
semistable representations and their isomorphisms. No Calabi–Yau structure,
potential, orientation data, vanishing cycles, or physical state-counting
identification is part of this definition.

Fix $Q$, $k=\mathbb F_q$, and $Z$ as in
[[def-finite-acyclic-quiver-stability-data]]. For a representation $M$, write
$a_M=|\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal A_Q}(M)|$ and let $\delta_M$ be the basis
function of its isomorphism class. Let $\mathcal S_Q$ be the small finitary
abelian skeleton constructed in
[[lem-finite-acyclic-quiver-representations-are-finitary-hereditary-with-euler-form]].
Define $H_Q:=H_{\mathcal S_Q,\mathbb Q}$, identifying its basis with the
isomorphism classes of $\mathcal A_Q$. Fullness and transport of subobjects
and cokernels along isomorphisms preserve the Hall coefficients. Thus $H_Q$ is
the direct sum over those classes, with rational
coefficients and the quotient-first untwisted Hall product of
[[def-untwisted-hall-algebra]]. In that convention $[A]*_{qf}[B]$ counts
sequences $0\to B\to L\to A\to0$, and identify the basis symbol $[M]$ with
the characteristic function $\delta_M$. Define the **subobject-first** product
by $f\star g:=g*_{qf}f$. Then
$$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L} f(U)g(L/U),$$
where the sum is over subobject classes of $L$: monomorphisms into $L$ modulo
isomorphisms of their domains commuting with the monomorphism. Distinct
embedded subobjects are counted separately even when their domains are
isomorphic. Put
$\kappa_M=a_M\delta_M$.

For $\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, let $H_{Q,\mathbf d}$ be the span of
classes of dimension vector $\mathbf d$. It is finite-dimensional: the
representation set on the standard spaces $k^{d_i}$ is finite. Define the
dimension completion
$$\widehat H_Q=\prod_{\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}}H_{Q,\mathbf d}.$$
The product is extended degreewise; each coefficient uses finitely many
decompositions $\mathbf d=\mathbf a+\mathbf b$. There is no analytic
convergence assertion. The all-object and phase factors are
$$A_{\mathrm{all}}=\sum_{[M]}\delta_M,\qquad S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\\M\ne0,\ \phi_Z(M)=\phi,\ M\ Z\text{-semistable}}}\delta_M.$$
Each is an element of $\widehat H_Q$ because each homogeneous component has
finite support.

Let $t=\sqrt q>0$ and $K_q=\mathbb Q(\sqrt q)$. Take the completed Euler
torus and skew torus over $K_q$, with bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$, respectively, and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$
Their completions use the same dimension product. The next theorem proves
associativity and gives the continuous Euler and skew integration maps.

Let $\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ and define
$\phi(z)=\arg(z)/\pi\in(0,1)$. For $z,w\in\mathbb H$, the phase of $z+w$
lies between $\phi(z)$ and $\phi(w)$, strictly between them when they are
unequal and equal to their common value when they coincide.

Let $Q$ be finite and acyclic, let $k=\mathbb F_q$, and give every vertex an
arbitrary charge $z_i\in\mathbb H$. Over any field extension $K/k$, every
finite-dimensional representation has a unique filtration
$$0=M_0\subsetneq M_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq M_r=M$$
whose nonzero factors $M_j/M_{j-1}$ are $Z$-semistable and have strictly
decreasing phases. If $M$ is defined over $k$, the unique filtration of its
scalar extension $M_{\bar k}=M\otimes_k\bar k$ is Frobenius invariant and
descends to $k$. Consequently geometric
semistability of an $\mathbb F_q$-representation is equivalent to
semistability tested only on its $\mathbb F_q$-subrepresentations. Write
$|\mathbf d|=\sum_i d_i$ for total dimension.

Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver over $k=\mathbb F_q$, let
$t=\sqrt q>0$, and use the subobject-first completion and tori from
[[def-subobject-first-completed-finite-quiver-hall-algebra-and-tori]]. The
degree-completed Hall product is associative and unital. The continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))} \frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)}$$
are unital algebra homomorphisms to the completed tori with products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}, \qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$
These are separate normalizations: the first is the Euler form target, while
the second uses the skew-symmetrized form and the diagonal factor
$t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf d)}$.

Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1,s,t)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, where $Q_0,Q_1$ are finite
sets and $s,t:Q_1\to Q_0$ are the source and target maps. Let $k=\mathbb F_q$
with $q>1$, and assign to each vertex $i\in Q_0$ a charge
$z_i\in\mathbb H:=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$. A
finite-dimensional representation $M$ assigns a finite-dimensional
$k$-vector space $M_i$ to each vertex and a linear map
$M_a:M_{s(a)}\to M_{t(a)}$ to each arrow; its dimension vector is
$\mathbf d(M)=(\dim_k M_i)_{i\in Q_0}$. Put
$Z(\mathbf d)=\sum_i d_i z_i$ and, for nonzero
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb N^{Q_0}$, put
$\phi_Z(\mathbf d)=\arg Z(\mathbf d)/\pi$ using the principal argument. For
$M\ne0$, set $\phi_Z(M)=\phi_Z(\mathbf d(M))$. Call $M$
$Z$-semistable when every nonzero subrepresentation has phase at most
$\phi_Z(M)$. Include the zero representation as semistable with no assigned
phase.

Use the small finitary abelian skeleton of these representations. Its Hall
algebra has basis $\delta_M$ indexed by isomorphism classes, and the
subobject-first convention is
$(f\star g)(L)=\sum_{U\subseteq L}f(U)g(L/U)$, with distinct embedded
subobjects counted separately. Its dimension completion is the product of
the finite-dimensional homogeneous components. For integer dimension
vectors define the bilinear Euler form and its skew-symmetrization by
$$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)=\sum_{i\in Q_0}d_i e_i-\sum_{a:i\to j}d_i e_j,\qquad \langle\mathbf d,\mathbf e\rangle=\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf e)-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d).$$

For a phase $\phi$, let
$$S_Z(\phi)=\delta_0+\sum_{\substack{[M]\ne[0]\\M\ Z\text{-semistable}\\\phi_Z(M)=\phi}}\delta_M,$$
where $\delta_M$ is the characteristic function of the isomorphism class
$[M]$ and $\delta_0$ is the Hall unit. The Euler and skew integrations are
the continuous maps
$$I(f)=\sum_{[M]}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}X^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad J(f)=\sum_{[M]}t^{\chi_Q(\mathbf d(M),\mathbf d(M))}\frac{f(M)}{|\operatorname{Aut}(M)|}x^{\mathbf d(M)},\qquad t=\sqrt q>0,$$
as proved for this finite-field category by the Euler and skew integration
theorem. Their completed targets have bases $X^{\mathbf d}$ and
$x^{\mathbf d}$ and products
$$X^{\mathbf d}X^{\mathbf e}=q^{-\chi_Q(\mathbf e,\mathbf d)}X^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e},\qquad x^{\mathbf d}*x^{\mathbf e}=t^{-\langle\mathbf e,\mathbf d\rangle}x^{\mathbf d+\mathbf e}.$$

Write $\Phi_Z=\{\phi_Z(\mathbf e):\mathbf e\in\mathbb N^{Q_0},\
\mathbf e\ne0\}$ and order its elements decreasingly. Define the Euler and
skew Hall spectrum generators by
$$P_Z^{E}:=\prod_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow} I(S_Z(\phi)),\qquad P_Z^{\mathrm{sk}}:=\mathop{*}_{\phi\in\Phi_Z}^{\searrow}J(S_Z(\phi)).$$
In each product the largest phase is the leftmost factor and multiplication
is in the corresponding completed torus. In any fixed total-dimension degree
$D$, only dimension vectors with $\sum_i d_i\le D$ and their finitely many
phases can contribute. Thus these are degreewise formal products in the
specified completion; no analytic convergence is asserted.

These generators describe the Euler or skew integration of finite-field
semistable representation groupoids. Calling such data protected BPS indices,
dimensions of physical state spaces, or spectra of a four-dimensional
supersymmetric model is an additional dictionary, not part of this
mathematical definition.

Let $Q$ be any finite acyclic quiver over $k=\mathbb F_q$, with no
finite-representation-type restriction, and let $Z_-$ and $Z_+$ assign a charge in
$\mathbb H=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$ to every vertex. Use the
subobject-first dimension completion and the Euler and skew integrations
defined on this A page. Then
$$P_{Z_-}^E=P_{Z_+}^E,\qquad P_{Z_-}^{\mathrm{sk}}=P_{Z_+}^{\mathrm{sk}}.$$
Each is a unit with constant term $1$ in its own completed quantum torus.
Consequently conjugation by the two generators defines the same continuous
automorphism on each corresponding completed torus. The products and
automorphisms are formal in the dimension completion. This is a finite-field
Hall identity only; it makes no physical state-counting identification.

derivations.claim:
After choosing bases at both vertices, a representation of dimension
$(1,1)$ is the scalar arrow $a\in k$. A change of bases
$(g_1,g_2)\in k^\times\times k^\times$ sends it to $g_2ag_1^{-1}$.
Therefore zero remains zero and every nonzero $a$ is isomorphic to $1$.
For $M_0$, every pair $(g_1,g_2)$ is an automorphism, so
$|\operatorname{Aut}(M_0)|=(q-1)^2$. For $M_1$, the automorphism condition
is $g_2=g_1$, so $|\operatorname{Aut}(M_1)|=q-1$.

A proper nonzero subrepresentation of a $(1,1)$ representation can
only have dimension $(1,0)$ or $(0,1)$. The latter is always preserved by
the arrow, whereas the former is preserved exactly when $a=0$. Hence the
subobject-first product counts one $S_1$ subobject in $M_0$ and none in
$M_1$, while it counts one $S_2$ subobject in each. The corresponding
quotients are $S_2$ for the first count and $S_1$ for the second; this gives
the two displayed Hall products.

Each $S_i$ is stable because it has no proper nonzero subobject. The
phase of $M_a$ is the phase of $z_1+z_2$, strictly between the two simple
phases by [F3] when they differ. If
$\phi_Z(S_1)>\phi_Z(S_2)$, the only proper nonzero subobject $S_2$ of $M_1$
has lower phase, so $M_1$ is stable; $M_0$ has both simples as
subobjects and its unique HN factors are $S_1,S_2$. If
$\phi_Z(S_2)>\phi_Z(S_1)$, $S_2$ destabilizes $M_1$ and
$0\subset S_2\subset M_1$ has factors $S_2,S_1$; the split object $M_0$
has the same ordered factors. If the phases are equal, all proper
nonzero subobjects of both objects have the same phase as the object, so
both objects are semistable in the same phase factor. The uniqueness in
[F4] shows that these are exactly their HN placements.

For either unequal-phase chamber, the Hall product has coefficient one
on each of $M_0,M_1$ in degree $\mathbf d$ by steps 2.1 and 3.1; on the
wall both occur in one semistable factor. Since
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=
\chi_Q(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2)=1$,
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)=0$, and
$\chi_Q(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=-1$, [F5] and step 1.1 give
$$I(\delta_{M_0}+\delta_{M_1})=\left(\frac1{(q-1)^2}+\frac1{q-1}\right)X^{\mathbf d}=\frac q{(q-1)^2}X^{\mathbf d},$$
while the reversed product of simple factors has the same coefficient
because $X^{\mathbf e_2}X^{\mathbf e_1}
=qX^{\mathbf d}$. For the skew integration,
$\chi_Q(\mathbf d,\mathbf d)=1$ and
$\langle\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2\rangle=-1$; hence
$$J(\delta_{M_0}+\delta_{M_1})=\left(\frac t{(q-1)^2}+\frac t{q-1}\right)x^{\mathbf d}=\frac{t^3}{(q-1)^2}x^{\mathbf d},$$
and the reversed simple-factor product has coefficient
$t^2t/(q-1)^2=t^3/(q-1)^2$ as well, using $q=t^2$. This proves the
stated finite-degree comparison and its wall case without assigning a
physical interpretation.

boundaries.reason: The example fixes the nonempty one-arrow quiver and dimension vector (1,1); it does not claim a formula for an empty quiver.

boundaries.evidence: The zero arrow M_0 and its two proper nonzero subobjects are counted in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
The one nonzero-arrow orbit M_1, its diagonal automorphisms, and its unique S_2 subobject are counted in steps 1.1 and 2.1.
The equal-phase wall is checked explicitly in step 3.1; both classes are semistable in one phase factor.
The charges lie in the open upper half-plane and the phase-sum lemma keeps all nonzero phases inside (0,1), as stated in the Example.

boundaries.reason: The two vertex bases and finite arrow set use only finite choices; no choice axiom occurs.
The example gives explicit counts and phase cases, not a biconditional.
The example gives explicit counts and phase cases, not a biconditional.

finite_checks.calculation: The two arrow scalars are 0 and 1, and both automorphism groups have order 1. For phi_1>phi_2 the Euler coefficient is 1+1=2 and the skew coefficient is t+t=2t. For phi_2>phi_1 the simple-factor Euler twist is q=2 and the skew twist is t=sqrt(2), giving 2 and t^3=2t.
finite_checks.disposition: Direct enumeration of all arrow maps over F_2 and substitution into the proved general formulas.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $n\ge2$, let $R=\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ with $\deg x_j=2$, and let $S_n$ act on $R$ by permuting variables. Let $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ be the idempotent-complete additive monoidal category of graded $(R,R)$-Soergel bimodules generated by the unit bimodule $R$, the bimodules $B_i=R\otimes_{R^{s_i}}R(1)$ for the adjacent transpositions $s_i=(i\ i+1)$, internal grading shifts, finite direct sums, tensor products over $R$, and direct summands. Use the shift convention $M(1)_d=M_{d+1}$; on the split Grothendieck ring it is recorded by $v[M]=[M(1)]$. Let $K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ denote the category of bounded cochain complexes in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ with chain maps modulo chain homotopy.

For $1\le i<n$, let $F_i=[B_i\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_i}R(1)]$ in cohomological degrees $0,1$ and $F_i^{-1}=[R(-1)\xrightarrow{\eta_i}B_i]$ in degrees $-1,0$, with the maps and grading conventions of the positive and negative Rouquier generator complexes. For a signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, $\epsilon_k\in\{+1,-1\}$, let $F(\sigma)=F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_R F_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$, using signed tensor totalization and left-to-right bracketing; the empty word gives $R$ in degree zero. If $\beta\in B_n$ is the braid represented by $\sigma$, the **Rouquier categorified line operator** $F(\beta)$ is this complex considered up to the canonical homotopy equivalence between words representing $\beta$. Tensor product is the categorical stacking operation. The comparison maps give the unit and coherent multiplication maps $F(\beta)\otimes_R F(\gamma)\simeq F(\beta\gamma)$; equivalently, left tensoring defines the coherent braid-group action on $K^b(R\text{-grmod})$.

A **physical defect realization** is additional data. A monoidal category $\mathcal D$ here means a category with a tensor bifunctor, a unit object, associator and unit isomorphisms satisfying the pentagon and unit triangles; its objects are declared line-defect types, its morphisms are declared junction maps, and its tensor product is the chosen stacking operation. The realization is a strong monoidal functor $\mathcal R:K^b(\mathrm{SBim}_n)\to\mathcal D$, meaning a functor with natural product and unit isomorphisms satisfying those same coherence equations and assigning images to every morphism, including junction maps, in its domain. Calling $\mathcal D$ a category of defects in a particular quantum field theory also requires an independently specified physical model. The Soergel and Rouquier data alone supply neither $\mathcal D$ nor this functor.

**Setting.** Fix $n\ge2$ and the two graded additive monoidal categories of this
page: the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$, the idempotent completion of
the category of Bott–Samelson bimodules
([[def-the-type-a-soergel-category]]), and the Karoubi envelope
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ of the type-A diagrammatic category
$D$ ([[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]).
Both are graded: an object $X$ has a shift $X(1)=X\{-1\}$, and both are monoidal
with unit the one-object bimodule $R$ respectively the empty word. Both are
additive in the sense of [[def-additive-category]].

**The split Grothendieck group.** For such a category $C$ choose a *small
skeleton*, that is, a set $\operatorname{sk}(C)$ of representative objects
meeting every isomorphism class exactly once — for $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ one may take
the graded direct summands of finite direct sums of shifts of Bott–Samelson
bimodules with a fixed underlying set of words, and for
$\operatorname{Kar}(D)$ the idempotents in finite direct sums of shifts of words,
so that the representatives form a set rather than a proper class. Define
$$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C):=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{X\in\operatorname{sk}(C)}\mathbb Z[X]\Bigr)\Big/\,\bigl\langle[X]-[X']-[X'']\ :\ X\cong X'\oplus X''\ \text{in }C\bigr\rangle,$$
the free abelian group on the isomorphism classes of representative objects
modulo the relations $[X]=[X']+[X'']$ whenever $X$ is isomorphic to a direct sum
of $X'$ and $X''$.

**Ring structure.** For representatives $X,Y$ the tensor product $X\otimes Y$
is again an object of $C$, whose isomorphism class is represented by a unique
element of the skeleton; the assignment $(X,Y)\mapsto X\otimes Y$ is additive in
each variable up to isomorphism, so $[X][Y]:=[X\otimes Y]$ descends to a
well-defined bilinear product on $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$, with the unit
$1:=[\mathbf 1]$ the class of the monoidal unit $R$ (respectively the empty
word). Associativity and unitality of the tensor product make
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ a ring; it is not commutative in general, and
$K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ is not commutative for $n\ge3$, since
the classes of two adjacent one-color products do not commute. The grading
shift is an additive
autoequivalence commuting with the tensor product, so setting
$$v[X]:=[X(1)]=[X\{-1\}]$$
equips $K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(C)$ with the structure of a
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-algebra, with $v^{-1}[X]=[X(-1)]=[X\{1\}]$.

**The two charts.** For the bimodule category the classes are those of the
Bott–Samelson products, $[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$, and for
every object $X$ the shift rule is $[X\{k\}]=v^{-k}[X]$; for the diagrammatic
category the class of a word is $[B_{\underline i}]$, with the same shift rule.
The standard bimodules $R_x$, $\Delta_x(d)$ and $\nabla_x(d)$ with $x\ne e$ are
not objects of $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ — they occur only as the successive quotients
of the support flags of its objects — so this definition attaches no object
class to them; the Hecke algebra's basis elements indexed by $x$ are written
$T_x,\widetilde T_x,H_x$, as in
[[def-type-a-hecke-algebra-in-soergel-normalization]]. Under the
dictionary of [[def-type-a-diagrammatic-soergel-category-and-its-bimodule-functor]]
the two rings are compared by sending $[B_{\underline i}]$ to
$[B_{i_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RB_{i_r}]$; the comparison is an isomorphism only
after the equivalence of the two categories is proved later on this page.

Let $C,D$ be bounded cochain complexes of graded $(R,R)$-bimodules whose terms
lie in the type-A Soergel category $\mathrm{SBim}_n$ (for instance Rouquier
word complexes), and define the alternating class
$$\chi(C):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^m[C^m]\ \in\ K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n),$$
the cochain indexing being translated to the chain indexing of
[[def-mapping-cone-of-a-chain-map]] by $C_m:=C^{-m}$. Then:

1. $\chi$ is a homotopy invariant: if $C\simeq D$ in $K^b$, then
   $\chi(C)=\chi(D)$, so $\chi$ is well defined on isomorphism classes of the
   homotopy category;
2. $\chi$ is multiplicative: $\chi(C\otimes_RD)=\chi(C)\chi(D)$ for the signed
   tensor totalization and more generally for every finite tensor product;
3. for every chain map $f\colon C\to D$ one has
   $\chi(\operatorname{Cone}(f))=\chi(D)-\chi(C)$, and $\chi$ is additive on
   distinguished triangles of the homotopy category, so it descends to a
   homomorphism $K_0^{\mathrm{tri}}\to K_0^{\mathrm{split}}(\mathrm{SBim}_n)$ on
   the triangulated Grothendieck group of the full triangulated subcategory of
   complexes with terms in $\mathrm{SBim}_n$;
4. for every signed word $\sigma=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$,
   the iterated signed tensor totalization
   $F_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RF_{i_r}^{\epsilon_r}$ (the word
   complex $F(\sigma)$ once that notation is introduced) satisfies
   $\chi(F(\sigma))=\prod_{k=1}^r\chi(F_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k})$.

In particular the alternating class of a Rouquier complex depends only on its
homotopy class and is compatible with tensor products.

**Additive setting.** Fix an additive category $\mathcal A$
([[def-additive-category]]): every hom-set is an abelian group, finite
biproducts exist, and every object has an identity morphism. All morphisms below
are morphisms of $\mathcal A$, sums and negatives are taken in the hom-groups,
and $0$ denotes the zero morphism between the indicated objects.

**Cochain complexes.** A **cochain complex** $C^\bullet=(C^n,d^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$
consists of objects $C^n$ of $\mathcal A$ and morphisms $d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$
with
$$d^{n+1}d^n=0\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
The morphisms $d^n$ are the **differentials** of $C^\bullet$. No boundedness,
finiteness or nonvanishing condition is imposed on the family of objects.

**Cochain maps.** A **cochain map** $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of
morphisms $f^n:C^n\to D^n$ with
$$f^{n+1}d^n_C=d^n_Df^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Identities and composites of cochain maps are cochain maps, so cochain complexes
and cochain maps form a category; this category is written
$\operatorname{Ch}^\bullet(\mathcal A)$ when the ambient category needs to be
recorded.

**Homotopies.** A **homotopy** $h:f\simeq g$ between cochain maps
$f,g:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to D^{n-1}$, one
in each degree, such that
$$f^n-g^n=d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
Thus $h$ has degree $-1$, and the right-hand side is the $n$-th component of the
graded map
$$dh+hd:=(d^{n-1}_Dh^n+h^{n+1}d^n_C)_{n\in\mathbb Z},$$
written with $d$ on both sides. A **null
homotopy** of a cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a homotopy
$f\simeq0$ to the zero map with the same source and target; $D^\bullet$
need not be the zero complex. A map admitting such a homotopy is
**null-homotopic**.

**Homotopy equivalence.** A cochain map $f:C^\bullet\to D^\bullet$ is a
**homotopy equivalence** when there is a cochain map
$g:D^\bullet\to C^\bullet$ with $gf\simeq1_{C^\bullet}$ and
$fg\simeq1_{D^\bullet}$; the complexes are then **homotopy equivalent**. The maps
$f$ and $g$ are homotopy inverses of one another.

**Contractibility.** A cochain complex $C^\bullet$ is **contractible** when its
identity is null-homotopic, $1_{C^\bullet}\simeq0$: that is, when there is a
family of morphisms $h^n:C^n\to C^{n-1}$ with
$$1_{C^n}=d^{n-1}h^n+h^{n+1}d^n\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb Z .$$
A complex is contractible exactly when it is homotopy equivalent to the zero
complex, since a homotopy equivalence onto the zero complex is a pair of
null-homotopies of the identities.

**Degreewise biproducts.** If $C^\bullet$ and $D^\bullet$ are cochain complexes,
then defining
$$(C\oplus D)^n:=C^n\oplus D^n,\qquad d^n_{C\oplus D}:=d^n_C\oplus d^n_D$$
gives a cochain complex, because
$(d^{n+1}_C\oplus d^{n+1}_D)(d^n_C\oplus d^n_D)=0\oplus0=0$. The degreewise
injections and projections are cochain maps, and the biproduct identities hold in
each degree and are therefore identities of cochain maps; hence $C\oplus D$ is a
biproduct of $C$ and $D$. Iterating, finite direct sums of cochain complexes are
formed degreewise, and finite direct sums of cochain maps and of homotopies are
formed degreewise as well. Under the reindexing below this is the additive
structure on complexes over an additive category recorded in
[[thm-the-category-of-complexes-in-an-additive-category-is-additive]].

**Dictionary with the published chain convention.** Reindex by
$C_n:=C^{-n}$ and $d_n:=d^{-n}$. Then $d_n:C_n\to C_{n-1}$ and
$$d_{n-1}d_n=d^{-(n-1)}d^{-n}=d^{-n+1}d^{-n}=0,$$
so $(C_\bullet,d_\bullet)$ is an ordinary chain complex. A cochain map $f$
becomes the chain map with components $f_n:=f^{-n}$, and a homotopy
$h:f\simeq g$ becomes the chain homotopy $s_n:=h^{-n}:C_n\to D_{n+1}$, because
substituting $n\mapsto-n$ into the displayed homotopy equation produces exactly
$$f_n-g_n=d^D_{n+1}s_n+s_{n-1}d^C_n .$$
Consequently, when $\mathcal A$ is abelian, these definitions restrict under this
dictionary to the published [[def-chain-homotopy]] and
[[def-contractible-complex]], which are stated for chain complexes in an abelian
category. Reindexing reverses the sign of the differential degree ($+1$ for
cochains, $-1$ for chains) and of the homotopy degree ($-1$ for cochains, $+1$
for chains), and introduces no further sign.

**What is not asserted.** The definitions use only zero morphisms, addition,
negatives, composition and identities. No kernel, cokernel, image, homology
object or exactness is assumed or defined, no linear structure on the hom-groups
beyond the additive one is used, and no homology object is attached to a complex
in an arbitrary additive category; contractibility is the existence of the
displayed family $h$, not the vanishing of homology.
