Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathcal H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space
with inner product $(\cdot,\cdot)$ linear in its first argument. Use
$p\cdot a:=p^0a^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf a$ on $\mathbb R^4$, the convention
of the proper-orthochronous Poincaré supplier, and put
$$\overline V_+:=\{p=(p^0,\mathbf p)\in\mathbb R^4:p^0\ge|\mathbf p|\},\qquad
V_+:=\{b=(b^0,\mathbf b)\in\mathbb R^4:b^0>|\mathbf b|\}.$$
For estimates only, write
$|p|_{\mathrm E}:=\sqrt{(p^0)^2+|\mathbf p|^2}$.

Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^4$:
each $E(S)$ is an orthogonal projection, $E(\varnothing)=0$,
$E(\mathbb R^4)=I$, $E(S\cap T)=E(S)E(T)$, and for every disjoint sequence
$(S_n)$, $E(\bigcup_nS_n)\xi=\sum_nE(S_n)\xi$ in norm for each
$\xi\in\mathcal H$. For a bounded Borel function $g$, write
$\Phi_E(g):=\int g(p)\,dE(p)$ for its bounded spectral integral, defined by
uniform simple-function approximation. Let
$U:\mathbb R^4\to\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ be a strongly continuous unitary
representation of translations: $U(0)=I$, $U(a+a')=U(a)U(a')$, every $U(a)$
is a surjective linear isometry, and $a\mapsto U(a)\xi$ is norm-continuous for
each $\xi\in\mathcal H$. The **positive-energy joint spectral input** is the
additional data and condition
$$U(a)=\Phi_E\bigl(p\mapsto e^{ip\cdot a}\bigr),\qquad
E(\mathbb R^4\setminus\overline V_+)=0.$$

Fix a translation-invariant unit vector $\Omega\in\mathcal H$, so $U(a)\Omega=\Omega$ for every $a\in\mathbb R^4$, and a specified unital $*$-subalgebra
$\mathfrak A\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ such that
$\overline{\{A\Omega:A\in\mathfrak A\}}=\mathcal H$; this is the meaning of
cyclic vacuum here. If local bounded operators are used, their assignment
$O\mapsto\mathfrak A(O)\subseteq\mathfrak A$ for bounded open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ is separately specified. This input asserts no
locality, isotony, covariance, or field-domain property for that assignment.
The PVM and its joint support are input; separate generators or a
matrix-coefficient Fourier-support condition do not replace this additional
data.

Assume Countable Choice and the positive-energy joint spectral input of
[[def-qftx-joint-spectrum-input]] on $\mathcal H$. Put
$\mathcal T_+:=\{a+ib:a\in\mathbb R^4,\ b\in V_+\}$ and, for
$z=a+ib\in\mathcal T_+$, define
$$U(z):=\Phi_E\bigl(p\mapsto\mathbf1_{\overline V_+}(p)e^{ip\cdot z}\bigr),
\qquad p\cdot z:=p^0z^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf z.$$
Then $U(z)$ is a bounded operator with $\|U(z)\|\le1$; the same formula
extends it to a strongly continuous contraction-valued map on
$\mathbb R^4+i\overline V_+$ and agrees with the given $U(a)$ when $b=0$.
Holomorphic means complex differentiable as a map of the full complex
coordinate vector, with a complex-linear total derivative and remainder
$o(\|h\|)$.

For every integer $n\ge1$, every $B_1,\ldots,B_{n-1}\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$,
and every $\psi,\phi\in\mathcal H$, the matrix coefficient
$$F(z_1,\ldots,z_n):=
\bigl(U(z_1)B_1U(z_2)\cdots B_{n-1}U(z_n)\psi,\phi\bigr)$$
is holomorphic on $\mathcal T_+^n$, where each
$\operatorname{Im}z_j\in V_+$. No locality assumption on the bounded
insertions is used. This result concerns bounded operators; it asserts no
domain, product, or holomorphy claim for unbounded Wightman fields.

derivations.claim:
For Borel sets $S,T$, $E_p(S)$ is diagonal with entries in $\{0,1\}$,
$E_p(\mathbb R^4)=I$, and
$E_p(S\cap T)=E_p(S)E_p(T)$. For a disjoint sequence, each of the distinct
points $0,p$ belongs to at most one set, so the coordinatewise sum of the
projections is $E_p(\bigcup_n S_n)$ and is finite on every vector. Thus $E_p$
is a strongly countably additive PVM supported on $\{0,p\}\subseteq\overline
V_+$. The diagonal operators $U_p(a)$ form a unitary representation because
$|e^{ip\cdot a}|=1$ and $U_p(a+a')=U_p(a)U_p(a')$; continuity is ordinary
continuity of the exponential. Put $P_0:=E_p(\{0\})=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$
and $P_p:=E_p(\{p\})=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$. Since $p\ne0$, these are the
two spectral projections and $E_p$ vanishes off their supports. Therefore the
bounded Borel multiplier $q\mapsto e^{iq\cdot a}$ has integral
$$\Phi_{E_p}(q\mapsto e^{iq\cdot a})=e^{i0\cdot a}P_0+e^{ip\cdot a}P_p
=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{ip\cdot a})=U_p(a),$$
by the finite-support PVM integral formula. Also $U_p(a)\Omega=\Omega$. For every
$(x,y)\in\mathbb C^2$, the matrix
$\begin{pmatrix}x&0\\y&0\end{pmatrix}$ sends $\Omega$ to $(x,y)$, so
$\Omega$ is cyclic for $\mathfrak A$.

The cone-restricted multiplier has values $1$ at $0$ and
$e^{ip\cdot(a+ib)}=e^{ip\cdot a}e^{-p\cdot b}$ at $p$; hence its PVM integral
is $\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{ip\cdot a-p\cdot b})$. For $b\in V_+$,
$p\cdot b\ge p^0(b^0-|\mathbf b|)>0$, since nonzero $p\in\overline V_+$
has $p^0>0$. Therefore the $e_1$ eigenvalue has modulus
$e^{-p\cdot b}<1$, while the $e_0$ eigenvalue is $1$. The operator norm is
$1$, in agreement with [F2].

On the $e_1$ component the reversed-sign continuation is
$e^{-ip\cdot(a+ib)}=e^{-ip\cdot a+p\cdot b}$, of modulus
$e^{p\cdot b}>1$ for $b\in V_+$. For $b\in -V_+$, $p\cdot b<0$, so its
modulus is less than $1$. The $e_0$ vacuum component stays $1$ in both
continuations. Thus the nonzero frequency's damping direction reverses with
the Fourier sign.

citations.quote:
The Cook condition is
that $t\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is norm-$C^1$ on
$[1,\infty)$ and, for constants $C_{\eta,f}\ge0$ and
$\epsilon_{\eta,f}>0$,
$$\left\|\frac{d}{dt}\Psi_t^\eta(f)\right\|\le C_{\eta,f}(1+t)^{-1-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\qquad(t\ge1).$$

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $1\le s\le t$. If $s=t$ the increment inequality is immediate.
If $s<t$, restrict $r\mapsto\Psi_r^\eta(f)$ to $[s,t]$. By [F1] this is a
continuous curve into the Banach space $\mathcal H$, differentiable on $(s,t)$
with derivative extending continuously to $[s,t]$.
The contract's Countable Choice premise satisfies the hypothesis of [F3], so
the Banach-valued fundamental theorem gives
$\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)=\int_s^t\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\,dr$.
The derivative is continuous and hence Bochner integrable on this compact
interval; [F4] then gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le\int_s^t
\|\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\|\,dr$.

Apply the derivative bound in [F1] and integrate the scalar power:
$$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigl((1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}-(1+t)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigr)\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}(1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}.$$
As $s\to\infty$, the last expression tends to zero uniformly for $t\ge s$.
Thus $\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is Cauchy as $t\to\infty$; completeness gives a limit
$W_\eta f\in\mathcal H$. Taking $t\to\infty$ in the first inequality gives
the claimed rate, and taking $s=1$ gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)\|\le\|\Psi_1^\eta(f)\|+
C_{\eta,f}/\epsilon_{\eta,f}$ for every $t\ge1$.

For $f,g\in\mathcal D_\sigma$, linearity of each $\Psi_t^\eta$ and norm
convergence from 2.1 imply
$W_\eta(af+bg)=aW_\eta f+bW_\eta g$ for all scalars $a,b\in\mathbb C$:
apply the triangle inequality to the finite linear combination and pass to
the limit. Hence $W_\eta$ is linear on $\mathcal D_\sigma$.

By continuity of the Hilbert inner product and the assumed limit [A1],
$(W_\eta f,W_\eta g)=\lim_{t\to\infty}
(\Psi_t^\eta(f),\Psi_t^\eta(g))=(f,g)_{\mathcal F,1}$.
Setting $g=f$ proves preservation of norm, so $W_\eta$ is an isometry on
$\mathcal D_\sigma$.

If $(f_n)$ in $\mathcal D_\sigma$ converges in its Hilbert-space closure,
then $(W_\eta f_n)$ is Cauchy because
$\|W_\eta f_n-W_\eta f_k\|=\|f_n-f_k\|$. Completeness of $\mathcal H$
defines a limit independent of the approximating sequence; the same equality
passes to the limit. This is the unique isometric extension to
$\overline{\mathcal D_\sigma}$. No surjectivity onto $\mathcal H$ follows.

derivations.claim:
By [F3], the bounded linear isometry $\Omega_+$ has a bounded Hilbert
adjoint. For any $z$ in a Hilbert space,
$\|z\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(z,x)|$: Cauchy–Schwarz gives the upper bound, and
if $z\ne0$ the choice $x=z/\|z\|$ attains it. For $y\in\mathcal H$, the
adjoint identity and [F2] therefore give
$\|\Omega_+^*y\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(\Omega_+^*y,x)|
=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|(y,\Omega_+x)|\le\|y\|$, since $\|\Omega_+x\|=\|x\|$.
Therefore
$\|Sx\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|\le\|\Omega_-x\|=\|x\|$ for every
$x\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$, so $S$ is a contraction.

By [F3], the bounded maps $\Omega_\pm$ and $S$ have bounded Hilbert
adjoints with the stated adjoint identities. For either isometry $\Omega$,
the adjoint identity gives
$(x,\Omega^*\Omega y)=(\Omega x,\Omega y)=(x,y)$ for all $x,y$; nondegeneracy
therefore gives $\Omega^*\Omega=I$. For $P=\Omega\Omega^*$ the same identity
gives $(Px,y)=(\Omega^*x,\Omega^*y)=(x,Py)$, so $P^*=P$, and
$\Omega^*\Omega=I$ gives $P^2=P$. Also $P$ fixes each $\Omega x$ and its
image is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}\Omega$, so $P$ is the orthogonal
projection onto the closed range. If
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-=:R$, both products
are the same projection $P_R$. For all $x,z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$,
$(Sx,z)_{\mathrm{as}}=(\Omega_-x,\Omega_+z)_{\mathcal H}
=(x,\Omega_-^*\Omega_+z)_{\mathrm{as}}$, so uniqueness of the adjoint gives
$S^*=\Omega_-^*\Omega_+$. It follows that
$S^*S=\Omega_-^*P_R\Omega_-=\Omega_-^*\Omega_-=I$ and
$SS^*=\Omega_+^*P_R\Omega_+=\Omega_+^*\Omega_+=I$, so $S$ is unitary.

Conversely, suppose $S$ is unitary and put
$P_+=\Omega_+\Omega_+^*$. By [F3] and step 1.2 this is a bounded
orthogonal projection.
For each $x$,
$\|P_+\Omega_-x\|=\|\Omega_+^*\Omega_-x\|=\|Sx\|=\|x\|
=\|\Omega_-x\|$. For an orthogonal projection $P$, the identity
$\|Py\|=\|y\|$ implies
$\|y\|^2=\|Py\|^2+\|(I-P)y\|^2$ and hence $(I-P)y=0$; therefore
$\Omega_-x\in\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$ for every $x$, proving
$\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_-\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}\Omega_+$. Since $S$
is onto, for every $z\in\mathcal H_{\mathrm{as}}$ choose $x$ with $Sx=z$.
Then $\Omega_+z=\Omega_+Sx=P_+\Omega_-x=\Omega_-x$, which gives the reverse
range inclusion. Thus the ranges coincide.

derivations.claim:
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$(\Omega_-(z),\Omega_-(w))=z\overline w=(z,w)$ and
$(\Omega_+(z),\Omega_+(w))=z\overline w=(z,w)$ in the standard
first-variable-linear inner products, so both maps are isometries.
Their ranges are $\mathbb C\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times\mathbb C$,
respectively, and are distinct proper subspaces of $\mathbb C^2$.

The Hilbert adjoint is $\Omega_+^*(x,y)=y$, since
$(\Omega_+z,(x,y))=(z,y)$ for all $z,x,y$. Hence
$\Omega_+^*\Omega_-(z)=\Omega_+^*(z,0)=0$ for every $z$. The zero map is
not unitary because it does not preserve the norm of $1\in\mathbb C$ and is
not surjective. This refutes the unqualified claim and shows that isometry
and limit existence do not imply full asymptotic completeness.

def-csm-frontier-local-topologies.definition_interface:
Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

def-csm-frontier-vague-topology.definition_interface:
Fix $d\ge1$. A locally finite counting measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is a measure of the form $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, where $I$ is finite or countable, repetitions among the points $x_r\in\mathbb R^d$ are allowed, and every compact set contains only finitely many listed points, counting repetitions. The empty sum is allowed and is the zero measure. For a Borel set $B$, $\xi(B)$ is the number of listed points in $B$, with multiplicity. Write $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the set of these measures. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the point mass $\delta_x$ assigns mass $1$ to a Borel set containing $x$ and mass $0$ otherwise.

The vague topology on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is the coarsest topology for which $\xi\mapsto\int f\,d\xi$ is continuous for every nonnegative continuous compactly supported function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$. Thus $\xi_n\to_{\mathrm v}\xi$ exactly when $\int f\,d\xi_n\to\int f\,d\xi$ for every such $f$.

Here a random locally finite counting measure means a measurable random element for which $\Xi_n(B)$ is a random variable for every bounded Borel set $B$. If $(\Xi_n)$ is a sequence of such measures on a common probability space and $K$ is compact, its local counts are uniformly integrable on $K$ when

$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E\!\left[\Xi_n(K)\mathbf1_{\{\Xi_n(K)>R\}}\right]=0.$$

This is the count-tail condition used when an argument needs control of unbounded observables supported in $K$. The definition asserts no convergence of expectations without the exact test-function, support, and tail hypotheses of the result being applied.

def-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain.finite_checks_disposition: No finite computation applies to this definition; its complete interface is recorded in definition_interface.
def-csm-frontier-finite-generator-chain.definition_interface:
Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $\nu$ on $E$ and put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and the associated realization is the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim\nu$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $\nu$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. A local existence result proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The result is immediate when $T=0$. Suppose $T>0$, fix $n\ge0$, and let $t_k=kT/2^n$ for $0\le k\le2^n$. Put $S_n=\max_{0\le k\le2^n}|M_{t_k}|$, which is square-integrable because it is bounded by the finite sum $\sum_k|M_{t_k}|$. For $r>0$, let $\tau$ be the first grid index $k$ with $|M_{t_k}|\ge r$, or leave it undefined if no grid value reaches $r$. Each event $\{\tau=k\}$ belongs to $\mathcal F_{t_k}$. By [F1] and [F2], $|M_{t_k}|=|\mathbb E[M_T\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]|\le\mathbb E[|M_T|\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}]$ almost surely. Multiplying by $\mathbf1_{\{\tau=k\}}$ and taking expectations gives $\mathbb E[|M_T|\mathbf1_{\{\tau=k\}}]\ge r\mathbb P(\tau=k)$. Summing over the finite grid yields $$ r\,\mathbb P(S_n\ge r)\le\mathbb E[|M_T|\mathbf1_{\{S_n\ge r\}}]. $$

Apply [F4] to $S_n^2$, use $\mathbb P(S_n>r)\le\mathbb P(S_n\ge r)$ and integrate the bound from step 1.1. [F5] for the nonnegative indicator $\mathbf1_{\{S_n\ge r\}}$ gives $$ \mathbb E S_n^2=\int_0^\infty2r\,\mathbb P(S_n>r)\,dr\le2\,\mathbb E[|M_T|S_n]. $$ By [F3], the right side is at most $2(\mathbb E|M_T|^2)^{1/2}(\mathbb E S_n^2)^{1/2}$. If $\mathbb E S_n^2=0$ the desired finite-grid bound is immediate; otherwise divide by its square root and square to obtain $\mathbb E S_n^2\le4\mathbb E|M_T|^2$.

The dyadic grids are nested, so $S_n\uparrow S_*:=\sup_{t\in D_T}|M_t|=S_T$. For every $\omega\in\Omega_0$ and each $t<T$, there are dyadic grid times decreasing to $t$, and right-continuity makes their process values converge to $M_t(\omega)$; time $T$ is in every grid. Hence $S_*$ equals the pathwise supremum on $[0,T]$ almost surely. Apply [F6] to $S_n^2$ and take limits in the finite-grid estimate from step 2.1 to obtain the stated inequality.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Write $p_x=P_X(x)$ and $q_x=Q_X(x)$. Strict positivity of $Q$ gives $q_x>0$ and $Q_{Y|x}(y)>0$ for each $x,y$. If $P(x,y)>0$, then $p_x>0$ and
$$\ln\frac{P(x,y)}{Q(x,y)}=\ln\frac{p_x}{q_x}+\ln\frac{P_{Y|x}(y)}{Q_{Y|x}(y)}$$
by [F2]. Multiply by $P(x,y)$ and sum over positive joint atoms. For each $x$ with $p_x>0$, summing the first term over $y$ gives $p_x\ln(p_x/q_x)$, and summing the second gives $p_xD(P_{Y|x}\|Q_{Y|x})$. Atoms with $p_x=0$ contribute no terms. This is exactly the claimed chain rule.

If $C$ is empty or all of $I\times J$, then $P(C)=Q(C)$ is respectively $0$ or $1$, so the binary divergence is $0$ under the stated zero-weight convention. The grouping bound is then $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $P=Q$ by [F1]. For a nonempty proper $C$, strict positivity gives $0<Q(C)<1$. Put $a=P(C)$ and $b=Q(C)$. When $a>0$, the conditional laws on $C$ are $P_C(z)=P(z)/a$ and $Q_C(z)=Q(z)/b$; the latter is strictly positive on $C$. The logarithmic identity $\ln(P(z)/Q(z))=\ln(a/b)+\ln(P_C(z)/Q_C(z))$ for each $z\in C$ with $P(z)>0$ yields
$$\sum_{z\in C:P(z)>0}P(z)\ln\frac{P(z)}{Q(z)}=a\ln\frac ab+aD(P_C\|Q_C).$$
If $a=0$, both the sum and the weighted conditional term are zero, so the same identity holds with that term omitted. Applying the identical calculation to $C^c$ and adding gives $D(P\|Q)=d(a\|b)+aD(P_C\|Q_C)+(1-a)D(P_{C^c}\|Q_{C^c})$, with zero-weight conditional terms omitted. Both weighted conditional divergences are nonnegative by [F1], which proves the grouping inequality, including $a=0$ or $1$. Equality holds precisely when every conditional divergence with positive weight vanishes; by the equality clause of [F1], this is equivalent to agreement of the conditional probability vectors on each positive-$P$-mass block. Zero-$P$-mass blocks impose no conditional-law condition.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

derivations.claim: If $\sigma\ne\eta$, some coordinate differs, so $\rho(\sigma,\eta)>0$; symmetry is immediate, and the coordinatewise triangle inequality gives the triangle inequality after summing. If two configurations agree on $x_1,\ldots,x_N$, then $\rho\le\sum_{k>N}2^{-k}=2^{-N}$. Conversely, if $\rho(\sigma,\eta)<2^{-N}$, no coordinate among $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ differs, because a mismatch at $x_k$ contributes at least $2^{-N}$. These bounds show that metric balls and finite-coordinate basic neighborhoods generate the same topology.

If $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$, every cylinder indicator is bounded and continuous by [F2], so its integrals converge. Every bounded function depending on finitely many coordinates is a finite linear combination of cylinder indicators, and its integrals therefore converge as well.

Suppose an open cover of $\Omega$ has no finite subcover. Let $C_0=\Omega$. Recursively, if $C_{N-1}$ is the cylinder fixing the first $N-1$ spins and has no finite subcover, its finitely many children obtained by assigning $\sigma_{x_N}=s$ cannot all have finite subcovers; otherwise their finite union would cover $C_{N-1}$. Choose the least $s$ in the fixed order whose child still has no finite subcover and call that child $C_N$. These nested cylinders determine a configuration $\sigma$. A cover member containing $\sigma$ contains a basic neighborhood fixing finitely many sites; for sufficiently large $N$, $C_N$ lies inside that neighborhood and hence has a one-member subcover, a contradiction. Thus every open cover has a finite subcover and $\Omega$ is compact.

Each cylinder is clopen by [F2], and cylinders form a countable basis: $\mathbb Z^d$ has countably many finite subsets, and each finite coordinate set has finitely many spin assignments. Therefore every open set is a countable union of cylinders and belongs to the cylinder sigma-algebra, while every cylinder is Borel. Hence the two sigma-algebras are equal.

Fix a bounded continuous $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $\sigma$, continuity and the cylinder basis give a cylinder neighborhood $C_\sigma$ of $\sigma$ on which $|g(\eta)-g(\sigma)|<\varepsilon/3$. Compactness from step 2.1 gives a finite subcover $C_1,\ldots,C_r$. Let $F$ be the union of the finitely many coordinate sets fixed by these cylinders. If $\eta,\zeta$ agree on $F$, choose a $C_i$ containing $\eta$; because $C_i$ depends only on a subset of $F$, it also contains $\zeta$, so $|g(\eta)-g(\zeta)|<2\varepsilon/3$. Choose $N$ with $F\subseteq\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}$ and fix one default spin $s_0\in S$. Replace all coordinates after $x_N$ by $s_0$ to define a canonical extension $\widehat\sigma$ of each first-$N$ prefix, and set $g_N(\sigma)=g(\widehat\sigma)$. Then $g_N$ depends only on the first $N$ coordinates and $\sup_\sigma|g(\sigma)-g_N(\sigma)|<\varepsilon$.

For every $n$, $|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g_N\,d\mu_n|\le\varepsilon$ and the same bound holds for $\mu$. Step 1.2 gives $\int g_N\,d\mu_n\to\int g_N\,d\mu$, so the limit superior of $|\int g\,d\mu_n-\int g\,d\mu|$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, weak convergence follows. Conversely, if $\mu_n$ converges weakly, indicators of all cylinders are bounded continuous by [F2], so their probabilities converge; finite sums give every finite marginal, hence local weak convergence by [F1].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $\nu$ on $E$ and put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and the associated realization is the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim\nu$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $\nu$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. A local existence result proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Put $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$ and $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, all off-diagonal entries vanish and the zero row sums force $L=0$. On the finite probability space $(E,2^E,\nu)$ put $Y_0(\omega)=\omega$ and $X_t=Y_0$ for all $t$. Then $N_t=0$, paths are constant, the conditional transition is the identity, and $e^{tL}=I$, giving the conclusion in this case.

Suppose $q>0$. For $i\ne j$, $R_{ij}=L_{ij}/q\ge0$, while $R_{ii}=1-\lambda_i/q\ge0$; each row sums to $1$. Let $\mu_q(dw)=q e^{-qw}\,dw$ on $(0,\infty)$, a probability measure because its density integrates to $1$. On $E\times(0,\infty)$ use initial law $\nu\otimes\mu_q$ and transition kernel $K((i,w),\{j\}\times B)=R_{ij}\mu_q(B)$ for Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. For any Borel subset of the product, its kernel value is the finite sum over $j$ of $R_{ij}$ times the $\mu_q$-measure of the corresponding section; thus it is measurable, nonnegative and has total mass $1$.

Apply [F2] to this initial law and kernel, and write the resulting coordinates as $Z_n=(Y_n,W_{n+1})$. Their finite-prefix law factors as the Markov-chain prefix law for $Y$ times $\prod_{k=1}^{n+1}\mu_q(dW_k)$, because every transition kernel chooses the next state with probabilities $R_{ij}$ and the next waiting time with the same factor $\mu_q$, independently of the current waiting time. Cylinder events generate the two coordinate sigma-algebras, so [F3] extends this factorization to independence of the full sequence $Y$ from the iid family $(W_k)$. The first coordinate is an $R$-Markov sequence with initial law $\nu$, as required by [F1].

Each $W_k$ has probability $e^{-1}$ of being at least $q^{-1}$. For any fixed $r$, independence gives $\mathbb P(W_k<q^{-1}\text{ for }r\le k\le n)=(1-e^{-1})^{n-r+1}\to0$. Continuity of probability for decreasing events, obtained by applying [F4] to complements, shows that the probability of no such event after $r$ is zero. A countable union over $r$ shows that $W_k\ge q^{-1}$ occurs infinitely often almost surely, and therefore $\sum_kW_k=\infty$ almost surely. On every bounded time interval there are consequently finitely many event times; the convention $X_t=Y_{N_t}$ makes paths right-continuous with left limits.

For $n\ge1$, convolution of the exponential densities gives the arrival-time density $$ f_{T_n}(u)=\frac{q^n u^{n-1}e^{-qu}}{(n-1)!},\qquad u>0. $$ Indeed the formula holds for $n=1$, and convolving it with $q e^{-q(t-u)}$ gives $q^{n+1}e^{-qt}\int_0^t u^{n-1}du/(n-1)!=q^{n+1}t^ne^{-qt}/n!$. Since $W_{n+1}$ is independent of $T_n$, for $n\ge1$, $$ \mathbb P(N_t=n)=\int_0^t f_{T_n}(u)\mathbb P(W_{n+1}>t-u)\,du=e^{-qt}\frac{(qt)^n}{n!}; $$ for $n=0$ the probability is $\mathbb P(W_1>t)=e^{-qt}$.

The event process has independent rate-$q$ Poisson increments. To see the conditional assertion needed here, on $\{N_s=n\}$ the event-clock history gives $T_n\le s<T_{n+1}$; by the exponential memoryless identity $\mathbb P(W_{n+1}-(s-T_n)>u\mid W_{n+1}>s-T_n)=e^{-qu}$, the residual time after $s$ is rate-$q$ exponential independent of that history. The later waiting times are independent rate-$q$ exponentials as well. Repeating the calculation in step 3.2 shows that, conditional on the clock history up to $s$, $N_{s+h}-N_s$ has probabilities $e^{-qh}(qh)^k/k!$, independent of that history. The clock is independent of $Y$ by step 2.1 and the uniformized convention [F1].

Let $H_s=(Y_0,\ldots,Y_{N_s})$ be the finite embedded-state prefix and put $\mathcal G_s=\sigma(N_u:0\le u\le s,H_s)$. Since $N_u\le N_s$ for $u\le s$, the construction filtration $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is contained in $\mathcal G_s$. Given $\mathcal G_s$ and $X_s=i$, $k$ further clock events have probability $e^{-qh}(qh)^k/k!$ by step 4.1, and the embedded chain has $k$-step transition matrix $R^k$. Hence $$ \mathbb P(X_{s+h}=j\mid\mathcal G_s)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-qh}\frac{(qh)^k}{k!}(R^k)_{ij}=\bigl(e^{-qh}e^{qhR}\bigr)_{ij}=(e^{hL})_{ij}, $$ since $q(R-I)=L$. This conditional law depends on $\mathcal G_s$ only through $X_s$; conditioning down to $\mathcal F_s$ gives the required identity for all $s\le t$. The matrix series converges absolutely because $E$ is finite.

The constructed $X$ is adapted to $\mathcal F_t$ by definition. Step 3.1 gives nonexplosion and càdlàg paths; step 5.1 gives its all-pairs conditional transition matrices. Thus it is a uniformized realization for every finite rate matrix, including reducible matrices and states with $\lambda_i=0$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be a nonempty finite set, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$ with nonnegative off-diagonal entries and zero row sums, and let $\nu$ be an initial probability vector. Then there exists a uniformized realization under the conventions stated below. Its paths are càdlàg and almost surely have only finitely many event times on each bounded interval (nonexplosion), and, for all $0\le s\le t$,
$$\mathbb P(X_t=j\mid\mathcal F_s)=(e^{(t-s)L})_{X_sj}\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is the construction filtration. In particular, $e^{tL}$ is the transition matrix from any initial state.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $D=(D_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous martingale relative to a
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)$, with $D_0=0$. Suppose each path has finite total
variation $V_T(D)$ and $\mathbb E V_T(D)<\infty$. Then $D$ is indistinguishably
zero on $[0,T]$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], for $h\ge0$ and $g=Lf$, $\mathbb E[g(X_{s+r})\mid\mathcal F_s]=(e^{rL}g)(X_s)$. The paths are piecewise constant with finitely many jumps on bounded intervals, so the bounded integrand is jointly measurable and [F5] applies. Testing against each event in $\mathcal F_s$ gives $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\int_s^{s+h}g(X_u)\,du\middle|\mathcal F_s\right] =\int_0^h(e^{rL}Lf)(X_s)\,dr=(e^{hL}f-f)(X_s), $$ where the last equality follows by termwise differentiation of the absolutely convergent finite-matrix exponential series. Also $\mathbb E[f(X_{s+h})\mid\mathcal F_s]=(e^{hL}f)(X_s)$. Subtracting proves $\mathbb E[M_{s+h}-M_s\mid\mathcal F_s]=0$ for every $s,h$. On $[0,T]$, $|M_t|\le2\|f\|_\infty+T\|Lf\|_\infty$, so every $M_t$ is square-integrable and the all-pairs martingale assertion follows from [F2].

Since $\sum_jL_{ij}=0$, $$ \Gamma_f(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2\ge0. $$ Thus $A$ is increasing and bounded on $[0,T]$. It is adapted because it is the time integral of the bounded adapted process $\Gamma_f(X_s)$. It is continuous. For each $n$, the step process equal to $A_{kT/2^n}$ on $(kT/2^n,(k+1)T/2^n]$ and zero at time zero is predictable by [F4]; these processes converge pointwise to $A$ by continuity. Therefore $A$ is predictable.

Fix $u$ and condition on $\mathcal F_u$, writing $X_u=i$. For $0<h\le1$, the number of uniformization events during $(u,u+h]$ is Poisson with rate $q=\max_i\lambda_i$ by the exponential-clock construction in [F1]. If there is no event, $\Delta M:=M_{u+h}-M_u=-h g(i)$, whose square is $O(h^2)$. If there is exactly one event and the new state is $j\ne i$, its probability is $e^{-qh}qhR_{ij}=e^{-qh}hL_{ij}=hL_{ij}+O(h^2)$, and $\Delta M=f(j)-f(i)+O(h)$ uniformly because the drift integral has magnitude at most $h\|g\|_\infty$. Its contribution to the conditional second moment is therefore $hL_{ij}(f(j)-f(i))^2+O(h^2)$. A one-event self-transition contributes $O(h^3)$. The probability of at least two events is $O(h^2)$ and $\Delta M$ is uniformly bounded for $h\le1$, so its contribution is $O(h^2)$. Since $E$ is finite, all error bounds are uniform in $i$, and $$ \mathbb E[(\Delta M)^2\mid\mathcal F_u]=h\Gamma_f(i)+O(h^2). $$ Also $\mathbb P(X_{u+r}\ne i\mid\mathcal F_u)\le qr$, so boundedness of $\Gamma_f$ gives $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv\middle|\mathcal F_u\right]=h\Gamma_f(i)+O(h^2). $$ Consequently $\left|\mathbb E[(\Delta M)^2-\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv\mid\mathcal F_u]\right|\le C h^2$ for a finite constant $C$ depending only on $L,f,T$.

Let $D_t=M_t^2-A_t$. On any interval $[u,u+h]$, $D_{u+h}-D_u=2M_u\Delta M+(\Delta M)^2-\int_u^{u+h}\Gamma_f(X_v)\,dv$. The conditional mean-zero increment from step 1.1 makes the first term's conditional expectation zero, while step 2.1 bounds the conditional expectation of the remaining terms by $Ch^2$. For fixed $s<t$, divide $[s,t]$ into $n$ equal intervals of length $h=(t-s)/n\le1$. The tower property and the preceding bound imply $|\mathbb E[D_t-D_s\mid\mathcal F_s]|\le nCh^2=C(t-s)^2/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves $\mathbb E[D_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=D_s$. Thus $M^2-A$ is a martingale.

In this item, a continuous predictable bracket means a continuous predictable increasing process $B$ with $B_0=0$, $\mathbb E B_T<\infty$, and $M^2-B$ a martingale. Steps 1.2 and 3.1 show that $A$ has these properties. If $B$ is another such process, then $B-A$ is a continuous martingale starting at zero, and its total variation on $[0,T]$ is at most $B_T+A_T$, which is integrable. By [F6], $B-A$ is indistinguishably zero. Therefore $A$ is the unique bracket in this stated continuous predictable compensator class, and it has the displayed formula.

Fix $d\ge1$. Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ be the $\sigma$-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, and understand all measures below as defined on $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d))$. A measure here is a countably additive map from $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ to $[0,\infty]$ that assigns $0$ to the empty set. A locally finite counting measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is a measure of the form $\xi=\sum_{r\in I}\delta_{x_r}$, where $I$ is finite or countable, repetitions among the points $x_r\in\mathbb R^d$ are allowed, and every compact set contains only finitely many listed points, counting repetitions. The empty sum is allowed and is the zero measure. For a Borel set $B$, $\xi(B)$ is the number of listed points in $B$, with multiplicity. Write $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ for the set of these measures. For $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the point mass $\delta_x$ assigns mass $1$ to a Borel set containing $x$ and mass $0$ otherwise.

The vague topology on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$ is the coarsest topology for which $\xi\mapsto\int f\,d\xi$ is continuous for every nonnegative continuous compactly supported function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$. Thus $\xi_n\to_{\mathrm v}\xi$ exactly when $\int f\,d\xi_n\to\int f\,d\xi$ for every such $f$.

Given a probability space $(\Theta,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$, meaning that $\mathcal A$ is a $\sigma$-algebra on $\Theta$ and $\mathbb P$ is a countably additive probability measure on $\mathcal A$ with $\mathbb P(\Theta)=1$, a random locally finite counting measure is an $(\mathcal A,\mathcal B_{\mathrm v})$-measurable map $\Xi:\Theta\to\Gamma_{\mathrm{lf}}(\mathbb R^d)$, where $\mathcal B_{\mathrm v}:=\sigma\{U:U\text{ is open in the vague topology just defined}\}$. We require that, for every bounded Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the evaluation $\Xi(B):\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ given by $\Xi(B)(\theta)=\Xi(\theta)(B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable; it is finite by local finiteness. Write $\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}$ for integration with respect to $\mathbb P$. A sequence $(\Xi_n)$ of such measures on a common probability space uses this same domain and target for every $n$. If $K$ is compact, its local counts are uniformly integrable on $K$ when

$$\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}\!\left[\Xi_n(K)\mathbf1_{\{\Xi_n(K)>R\}}\right]=0.$$

This is the count-tail condition used when an argument needs control of unbounded observables supported in $K$. The definition asserts no convergence of expectations without the exact test-function, support, and tail hypotheses of the result being applied.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a finite nonempty alphabet $S$ with the discrete topology, and a bijective enumeration $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ of $\mathbb Z^d$. Let $\Omega=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ be the set of all configurations $\sigma:\mathbb Z^d\to S$ with the product topology, the smallest topology that makes each coordinate map $\sigma\mapsto\sigma_x$ continuous. For a finite set $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and assignment $a\in S^F$, the cylinder set determined by $(F,a)$ is $[F,a]=\{\sigma\in\Omega:\sigma|_F=a\}$. The cylinder sigma-algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated by these sets.

For each finite $F$, let $\pi_F:\Omega\to S^F$ be restriction to $F$. For probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal C)$, local weak convergence $\mu_n\to_{\mathrm{loc}}\mu$ means that $(\pi_F)_*\mu_n(B)\to(\pi_F)_*\mu(B)$ for every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and every $B\subseteq S^F$. Equivalently, all finite-coordinate cylinder probabilities converge. The cylinder sigma-algebra is shown below in a local result to equal the Borel sigma-algebra, with local weak convergence equal to ordinary weak convergence on this space.

derivations.claim: For any fixed site $x\in S_n$, exactly $(2n-1)!$ of the $(2n)!$ bijections send label $1$ to $x$. Thus $U_n$ is uniform on $S_n$ under $\mathbb P_n$. The inverse label $\pi_n^{-1}(0)$ is also uniform on $L_n$, because exactly $(2n-1)!$ bijections assign any prescribed label to site $0$. Exactly $n$ labels carry each mark, so $\mathbb P_n(V_n=0)=\mathbb P_n(V_n=1)=1/2$.

Let $K=\operatorname{supp}f$. Since $K$ is compact, it is bounded and $K\cap\mathbb Z$ is finite; write $c_K=|K\cap\mathbb Z|$. Uniformity of $U_n$ gives $\mathbb P_n(U_n\in K)=|K\cap S_n|/(2n)\le c_K/(2n)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [F1] gives
$$\mathbb P_n\!\left(\left|\int f\,d\Xi_n\right|>\varepsilon\right)\le\mathbb P_n(U_n\in K)\le\frac{c_K}{2n}\longrightarrow0.$$
Thus each compactly supported vague test tends to zero in probability, while step 1.1 shows that selecting by the fixed spatial site $0$ retains a nondegenerate mark law. This is a statement about spatial point-measure tests; finite-coordinate local convergence on spin configurations is a separate notion by [F2]. These two statements concern different selection rules and do not contradict one another.

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, $H:S\to\mathbb R$, and $\beta>0$. Define $Z=\sum_{s\in S}e^{-\beta H(s)}$ and $\gamma(s)=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta H(s)}$. For every probability vector $p$ on $S$, with $0\log0=0$, its Shannon entropy $H_{\rm Sh}(p)=-\sum_s p(s)\log p(s)$ and relative entropy $D(p\Vert\gamma)=\sum_{p(s)>0}p(s)\log(p(s)/\gamma(s))$ satisfy
$$D(p\Vert\gamma)=-H_{\rm Sh}(p)+\beta\sum_s p(s)H(s)+\log Z\geq0.$$
Equality holds exactly when $p=\gamma$. Equivalently, $\gamma$ is the unique minimizer of $\sum_s p(s)H(s)-\beta^{-1}H_{\rm Sh}(p)$, and the minimum is $-\beta^{-1}\log Z$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim: For every $t\in\mathbb R$, each $e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$ is positive and finite, and $E$ is finite nonempty, so $0<Z(t)<\infty$ by [F1]. Thus $\gamma_t$ is a probability vector, and both $Z(t)$ and $N_F(t):=\sum_xF(x)e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$ are finite sums with nonzero denominator $Z(t)$.

Since $H_t(x)=H_0(x)-tM(x)$, [F2] and [F4] give $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-\beta H_t(x)}=\beta M(x)e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$. Differentiating the finite sums term by term with [F3] therefore gives $Z'(t)=\beta\sum_xM(x)e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$ and $N_F'(t)=\beta\sum_xF(x)M(x)e^{-\beta H_t(x)}$.

The denominator $Z(t)$ is nonzero by step 1.1. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the product-measure extension framework of [[def-countable-choice]] and [[lem-csm-lattice-product-and-measure-compactness]]. Work in the finite-alphabet configuration space $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with its cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra. Let the finite-range interaction and its conditional energy be as in [[def-csm-finite-range-lattice-interaction]], and fix $\beta>0$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$ and exterior configuration $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$, put
$$Z_\Lambda^\eta=\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)},\qquad \gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in A^\Lambda}f(\tau\eta)e^{-\beta E_\Lambda(\tau\mid\eta)}}{Z_\Lambda^\eta}$$
for bounded measurable $f:X\to\mathbb R$. Here $\gamma_\Lambda f$ denotes the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)$, composition is operator composition, and $\mu\gamma_\Lambda(f)=\int\gamma_\Lambda(f\mid\eta)\,d\mu(\eta)$. A proper kernel leaves every exterior-measurable event fixed. A specification is a family $(\gamma_\Lambda)_{\Lambda\text{ finite}}$ of proper probability kernels satisfying $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ whenever $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$. A DLR state is a probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ satisfying $\mu\gamma_\Lambda=\mu$ for every finite $\Lambda$.

For the existence and uniqueness results below, a specification has **finite range** when for every finite $\Delta$ and every cylinder event $C$ the function $\eta\mapsto\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_C\mid\eta)$ depends on only finitely many coordinates of $\eta$. The displayed finite-range Gibbs formula has this property because only finitely many interaction terms meet $\Delta$, and a cylinder indicator depends on only finitely many additional coordinates.

The formula is the candidate Gibbs specification; [[lem-csm-lattice-specification-consistency]] establishes its positive finite normalization, measurability, properness and consistency under the stated hypotheses. The Countable Choice assumption is used for the product-measure construction, not for any finite conditional sum.

Let $d\geq1$, let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=S^{\mathbb Z^d}$ with the $\sigma$-algebra generated by finite-coordinate cylinders. A specification on $X$ is a family $\gamma=(\gamma_\Lambda)$ of probability kernels indexed by finite $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d$. It is proper when each kernel leaves every exterior-measurable event fixed, and consistent when $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ for all finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, write $\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)$ for its one-site conditional probability vector on $S$, where $\eta\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on $S$, define their total-variation distance by $\lVert p-q\rVert_{\rm TV}:=\frac12\sum_{s\in S}|p(s)-q(s)|$. The influence coefficient of site $j$ on the conditional law at site $i$ is

$$c^\gamma_{ij}:=\begin{cases}0,&i=j,\\[2pt]\displaystyle\sup_{\substack{\eta,\eta'\in S^{\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{i\}}\\ \eta_k=\eta'_k\ \text{for every }k\notin\{i,j\}}}\lVert\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta)-\gamma_i(\cdot\mid\eta')\rVert_{\rm TV},&i\ne j.\end{cases}$$

The matrix $C^\gamma=(c^\gamma_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb Z^d}$ is the Dobrushin influence matrix of $\gamma$. Its coefficients lie in $[0,1]$; a supremum need not be attained. The Dobrushin row constant is $c_\gamma:=\sup_i\sum_j c^\gamma_{ij}$, with value $+\infty$ allowed. A common uniform finite influence radius $R$ means $c^\gamma_{ij}=0$ whenever $\lVert i-j\rVert_\infty>R$.

For probability vectors $p,q$ on a finite set $A$, there is a coupling $(X,Y)$ with $\Pr(X\ne Y)=\tfrac12\sum_{a\in A}|p(a)-q(a)|$. For a finite region $\Lambda$ with strictly positive single-site Gibbs conditionals, the random-scan heat-bath chain has the finite-volume Gibbs law as its unique stationary distribution. This chain is an auxiliary finite-state proof device, not a physical time evolution.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Here consistency means $\gamma_\Lambda\gamma_\Delta=\gamma_\Lambda$ for finite $\Delta\subseteq\Lambda$, properness means $\gamma_\Lambda(r_\Lambda^{-1}(D)\mid\eta)=\mathbf1_D(\eta)$ for each exterior-measurable event $D\subseteq A^{\Lambda^c}$ and $\eta\in A^{\Lambda^c}$, where $r_\Lambda:X\to A^{\Lambda^c}$ is coordinate restriction; in compositions and integrals against measures on $X$, every kernel takes the appropriate exterior restriction of the global configuration as its argument, and finite range means each $\gamma_\Delta(\mathbf1_C\mid\cdot)$ for finite $\Delta$ and cylinder event $C$ depends on only finitely many exterior coordinates. Also assume a uniform finite integer radius $R\geq0$ such that each one-site kernel $\gamma_{\{i\}}$ depends only on exterior spins $j$ with $\|i-j\|_\infty\leq R$. For each pair of sites define $c_{ij}$ as the supremum of the half-total-variation change in the one-site conditional law at $i$ when only exterior spin $j$ is changed, where half-total variation for probability vectors $p,q$ on $A$ is $\frac12\sum_{a\in A}|p(a)-q(a)|$, and set $c_{ii}=0$. If
$$c=\sup_i\sum_jc_{ij}<1,$$
then the DLR state is unique. Moreover, for a finite region $\Lambda$ and two exterior conditions $\xi,\zeta$, couple the random-scan finite-volume heat-bath chains by choosing the same uniformly random site and using a maximal coupling of its two single-site conditional laws. A stationary joint law of this pair chain exists. If the distance $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(i,\Lambda^c):=\inf_{j\notin\Lambda}\|i-j\|_\infty$ is at least $r(R+1)$ for a nonnegative integer $r$, then its disagreement probability at $i$ is at most $c^r/(1-c)$.
