Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite, let $p$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$, and set $S:=\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{a\in\mathcal A:p(a)>0\}$. Then $S$ is finite nonempty and $p(a)>0$ on $S$. For each $n\ge1$, use the finite product law $p^{\otimes n}$ from [[def-it-finite-alphabet-product-law]] and [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]] on $\mathcal A^n$, and let $X_1^{(n)},\ldots,X_n^{(n)}$ be its coordinate maps. Let $\widehat P_n$ be the empirical type of this coordinate word, viewed as a $\Delta(\mathcal A)$-valued map. Identify the support simplex
$$\Delta(S):=\{q\in[0,1]^S:\sum_{a\in S}q(a)=1\}$$
with the face of $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ whose coordinates outside $S$ vanish. Then $\widehat P_n\in\Delta(S)$ almost surely under $p^{\otimes n}$. For any set $\Gamma\subseteq\Delta(S)$, let $\Gamma^\circ$ and $\overline\Gamma$ denote its interior and closure in the relative topology induced by $\|\cdot\|_1$.
With $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\ge-\inf_{q\in\Gamma^\circ}D(q\|p),$$
and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le-\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p).$$
For every $n\ge1$ the finite upper bound
$$p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le(n+1)^{|S|-1}\exp\!\left(-n\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p)\right)$$
also holds. If the two infima agree, the limit exists and equals their negative common value. Equivalently, when $S\ne\mathcal A$, one may restrict the product sample space to $S^n$ without changing these event probabilities, since every word outside $S^n$ has zero product mass.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and let $p$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$. Then $q\mapsto D(q\|p)$ is finite and continuous on the probability simplex $\Delta(\mathcal A)$.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), with
subspaces as in [[def-subspace-topology-top]] and compactness as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **Closed in compact is compact.** If $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact and
   $F \subseteq X$ is closed in $X$, then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$.
2. **Finite unions.** If $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $K_0, \dots, K_n$ are compact
   subsets of $X$, then $K_0 \cup \dots \cup K_n$ is a compact subset of $X$. The
   union of the empty list is $\varnothing$, which is a compact subset of every
   space.

Claim 1 needs $X$ to be compact and claim 2 does not; no hypothesis of any kind
is placed on $X$ in claim 2. **No choice principle is used**: claim 1 selects
nothing, taking a least index where a selection would be natural, and claim 2
makes finitely many selections through [[lem-finite-choice]], a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim:
Enumerate $\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_d\}$, with $d\geq1$, and identify $\mathbb R^{\mathcal A}$ with Euclidean $\mathbb R^d$. Write $\|x\|_1:=\sum_{i=1}^d|x_i|$ and $\|x\|_2:=(\sum_{i=1}^dx_i^2)^{1/2}$; the declared $\ell^1$ topology on the simplex is the topology from $\|\cdot\|_1$. The simplex is closed because it is the intersection of the closed coordinate constraints $0\leq q(a_i)\leq1$ and the closed affine constraint $\sum_iq(a_i)=1$; these are closed since coordinate maps and their finite sum are continuous. It is bounded because $\|q\|_2^2=\sum_iq(a_i)^2\leq\sum_iq(a_i)=1$. By [F6] it is compact in the Euclidean topology. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, $\|x\|_2\leq\|x\|_1$ because $(\sum_i|x_i|)^2\geq\sum_ix_i^2$, and $\|x\|_1\leq d\|x\|_2$ because $\sum_i|x_i|\leq d\max_i|x_i|\leq d\|x\|_2$. These inequalities show that the Euclidean and $\ell^1$ metrics have the same open sets, so the simplex is compact in its declared topology. By continuity of $h$ and $D$, each fiber $h^{-1}(\{u\})$ and each sublevel set $\{q:D(q\|p)\leq r\}$ is closed in the simplex and hence compact by [F7]. The continuous-image and extreme-value conclusions in [F8] therefore apply to these sets. In particular, [F4] makes $q\mapsto D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)$ continuous on the compact simplex, so it attains a finite minimum $m_\beta$. The rate $D$ is nonnegative by [F5]. The empirical macrostate law under $p^{\otimes n}$ has rate $D(q\|p)$ by [F2]. For every Borel $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$, the canonical macrostate probability is exactly
$$p_{n,\beta}(L_n\in B)=\frac{\int_Be^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)}{\int_{\Delta(\mathcal A)}e^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)},$$
where $\mu_n$ is the base law of $L_n$; this follows by summing the word weights in [F1] over the fiber $L_n^{-1}(B)$. Thus it is the tilt in [F3] with $F=-\beta h$, and its rate is $D+\beta h-m_\beta$. Its zero set is $\mathcal M_\beta$. Let $U$ be any open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_\beta$ and put $C:=\Delta(\mathcal A)\setminus U$. If $C=\varnothing$, the probability of the complement is zero. Otherwise $C$ is a nonempty closed subset of the compact simplex, hence compact by [F7]. The continuous rate is positive at every point of $C$ because its zero set is $\mathcal M_\beta\subset U$; by [F8] it attains a strictly positive minimum on $C$, and the LDP upper bound makes the canonical macrostate probability of that complement exponentially small.

Let $q\in\mathcal M_\beta$ and put $u=h(q)$. If $r\in H_u$, then $D(r)+\beta u\geq D(q)+\beta u$, so $q\in\mathcal M_u$ and $D(q)=d(u)$. For any $v$ in the energy range, minimizing over $H_v$ gives $d(v)+\beta v\geq d(u)+\beta u$, equivalently $s(v)-\beta v\leq s(u)-\beta u$. Thus $u$ maximizes the stated entropy-minus-energy expression.

The fiber $H_u:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u\}$ is nonempty and closed, hence compact by step 1.1 and [F7], because $u$ is in the range of continuous $h$. By [F4] and [F8], $D$ attains its finite minimum $d(u)$ on $H_u$, so $\mathcal M_u$ is nonempty. For fixed $\delta>0$, put $B_\delta:=\{q:|h(q)-u|<\delta\}$; it is open and contains $H_u$. By [F2],
$$-\inf_{B_\delta}D\leq\liminf_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq\limsup_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq-\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D.$$
For each matching radius $\delta_j$ in the Statement the two infima agree, so the inner limit exists and equals their negative common value. The lower bound is finite because $B_{\delta_j}$ contains a finite-rate point of $H_u$; hence the conditioning event has positive probability for all sufficiently large $n$.

Write $d_\delta:=\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D$ for any $\delta>0$; since $H_u\subseteq\overline B_\delta$, $d_\delta\leq d(u)$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and let $K_\varepsilon:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):D(q\|p)\leq d(u)-\varepsilon\}$. By [F4], this set is closed and hence compact by [F7]; it is disjoint from $H_u$ by the definition of $d(u)$. Thus its compact image $h(K_\varepsilon)$ does not contain $u$ by [F8]. If it is nonempty, the continuous function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ on that compact image attains a positive minimum by [F8]; continuity follows from $\big||v-u|-|w-u|\big|\leq|v-w|$. Therefore the image is separated from $u$; if it is empty the conclusion is immediate. For every sufficiently small $\delta$, the closed shell $\overline B_\delta$ misses $K_\varepsilon$, so $d_\delta\geq d(u)-\varepsilon$. Together with $d_\delta\leq d(u)$, this proves $d_\delta\to d(u)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, in particular along the matching sequence $\delta_j$. Step 2.1 now gives the iterated shell limit $-d(u)=s(u)$.

Let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_u$ and put $C:=\Delta(\mathcal A)\setminus U$, which is closed and hence compact by step 1.1 and [F7]. If $C\cap H_u=\varnothing$, then $h(C)$ is compact by [F8] and does not contain $u$; if $C$ is nonempty, the continuous function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ attains a positive minimum there by [F8], using $\big||v-u|-|w-u|\big|\leq|v-w|$. Thus sufficiently small shells miss $C$; this is also immediate when $C=\varnothing$. Otherwise, $C\cap H_u$ is a nonempty closed subset of the compact simplex and is compact by [F7]. Continuity of $D$ and [F8] give $d_C:=\min_{C\cap H_u}D>d(u)$, since $C$ contains no constrained minimizer. Choose $0<\eta<d_C-d(u)$ and set $K:=\{q\in C:D(q\|p)\leq d(u)+\eta\}$; it is closed and hence compact by [F4] and [F7], and it is disjoint from $H_u$. Therefore $h(K)$ is compact by [F8] and does not contain $u$. If empty it is already separated from $u$; otherwise, the continuous distance function $v\mapsto|v-u|$ attains a positive minimum there by [F8], so $h(K)$ is separated from $u$. Hence for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $\inf_{C\cap\overline B_\delta}D\geq d(u)+\eta$. For every sufficiently small matching radius $\delta_j$, we also have $d_{\delta_j}<d(u)+\eta/2$. The LDP upper bound [F2] on the closed set $\overline{C\cap B_{\delta_j}}\subseteq C\cap\overline B_{\delta_j}$ bounds the numerator's logarithmic limsup exponent by $-d(u)-\eta$. By step 2.1 the denominator's logarithmic limit exponent is $-d_{\delta_j}$, so subtracting gives a conditional logarithmic limsup at most $d_{\delta_j}-d(u)-\eta<-\eta/2$. Thus for every sufficiently large $j$ the conditional probability tends to zero exponentially as $n\to\infty$, which gives the asserted iterated concentration limit.

Conversely, let $u$ maximize $s(v)-\beta v$ and let $q\in\mathcal M_u$. For any $r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, put $v=h(r)$. Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. By [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]], this mass assignment is normalized and is a probability law; explicitly, $\sum_{x^n\in\mathcal A^n}\prod_{i=1}^np(x_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p(a)=1$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$

$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Write $q(+1)=(1+m)/2$ and $q(-1)=(1-m)/2$. Substituting into [F1] with $p(+1)=p(-1)=1/2$ gives
$$D(q\|p)=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m),$$
with the zero-mass endpoint term omitted. Since $q$ depends continuously on $m\in[-1,1]$ and [F8] makes $D(q\|p)$ continuous on the whole simplex, adding $\beta h(q)=-\beta Jm^2/2$ shows that $\Phi_\beta$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$; [F8] supplies the boundary limit $t\ln t\to0$ behind the convention $0\ln0=0$. The formula is even in $m$.

For $|m|<1$ define $a(m):=\operatorname{atanh}(m):=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+m}{1-m}$. By [F3]–[F5] and direct differentiation, $$a'(m)=\frac1{1-m^2},\qquad \Phi_\beta'(m)=a(m)-\beta Jm.$$ For $0<m<1$ put $g(m):=a(m)/m$ and define $r:[0,1)\to\mathbb R$ by $r(m):=m/(1-m^2)-a(m)$. Then $g'(m)=r(m)/m^2$, $r(0)=0$, and $r'(m)=2m^2/(1-m^2)^2>0$ for $0<m<1$. The mean value theorem [F6] applies to $r$ on $[0,m]$ because $r$ is continuous there and differentiable on $(0,m)$; it gives $r(m)>0$, hence $g'(m)>0$.

The same theorem [F6] applied to $a$ on $[0,m]$ gives $g(m)=a'(c_m)$ for some $c_m\in(0,m)$; as $m\downarrow0$, $c_m\downarrow0$ and $a'(c_m)\to1$, so $\lim_{m\downarrow0}g(m)=1$. As $m\uparrow1$, $(1+m)/(1-m)\to+\infty$, and the increasing onto logarithm [F3] gives $a(m)\to+\infty$, hence $g(m)\to+\infty$. Thus $g$ is continuous, strictly increasing from limiting value $1$ to $+\infty$ on $(0,1)$.

If $\beta J\leq1$, then for $0<m<1$, $\Phi_\beta'(m)=m(g(m)-\beta J)>0$ by step 2.1. The mean value theorem [F6] on each subinterval of $[0,1]$ makes $\Phi_\beta$ strictly increasing there; continuity includes the endpoint $m=1$. Evenness then shows $\Phi_\beta(m)>\Phi_\beta(0)$ for every $m\neq0$, so $0$ is the unique global minimizer.

If $\beta J>1$, the limits in step 2.1 give $a,b$ with $0<a<b<1$, $g(a)<\beta J<g(b)$. Continuity of $g$ on $[a,b]$ and the intermediate value theorem [F7] give an $m_\beta\in(a,b)$ with $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$; strict increase of $g$ makes it unique on $(0,1)$. The derivative formula in step 1.2 is negative for $0<m<m_\beta$ and positive for $m_\beta<m<1$. By [F6], $\Phi_\beta$ strictly decreases on $[0,m_\beta]$ and strictly increases on $[m_\beta,1]$, including the endpoint by continuity. Evenness proves that the only global minimizers on $[-1,1]$ are $\pm m_\beta$; in particular the stationary point $m=0$ is not a minimizer.

The equation $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$ is $\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)=\beta Jm_\beta$. If $r=(1+m_\beta)/(1-m_\beta)$, then $e^{2\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)}=e^{\ln r}=r$ by [F3], so the stated formula for $\tanh$ gives $\tanh(\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta))=(r-1)/(r+1)=m_\beta$. Hence $m_\beta=\tanh(\beta Jm_\beta)$. Conversely, any $m\in(0,1)$ solving this fixed-point equation yields $e^{2\beta Jm}=(1+m)/(1-m)$ by rearrangement of the stated $\tanh$ formula; applying $\ln$ and [F3] gives $g(m)=\beta J$. Strict increase of $g$ therefore proves uniqueness of the positive fixed point. By [F2], the global minimizers just classified are exactly the canonical equilibrium magnetizations.

differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals

differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and

If $0<u\leq1$, then $h(q)=u$ forces $q(1)=u^4$ and $q(0)=1-u^4$, again a singleton fiber. The relative-entropy formula in [F1] gives $D(q\|p)=u^4\ln(2u^4)+(1-u^4)\ln(2(1-u^4))=\ln2-H_2(u^4)$; hence $s(u)=H_2(u^4)-\ln2$.

On $0<u\leq1/9$, $R(u):=(1-u^4)/u^4=u^{-4}-1$ decreases and $1/(1-u^4)$ increases, so $B(u)$ decreases. At $u=1/9$, $R(u)=6560$ and $B(1/9)=12\ln6560-16\cdot6561/6560$. By applying [F6] first to $s'$ and then to $s$, positive second derivative makes $s'$ strictly increasing and every interior chord lie strictly above the graph; hence $s$ is strictly convex on $(0,1/9)$.

Fix an integer $n$. Congruence modulo $n$ is an equivalence relation on
$\mathbb Z$ by [[lem-congruence-is-an-equivalence-relation]]. The
**congruence class of $a$ modulo $n$** is

$$[a]_n:=\{\,b\in\mathbb Z:b\equiv a\pmod n\,\},$$

and the **integers modulo $n$** form the quotient set

$$\mathbb Z/n:=\{\,[a]_n:a\in\mathbb Z\,\}.$$

This is the quotient-set construction of [[def-equivalence-relation]]. By
[[lem-equivalence-classes-partition]], two classes are equal exactly when their
representatives are congruent:

$$[a]_n=[b]_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\equiv b\pmod n.$$

At $n=0$ each class is a singleton because congruence modulo $0$ is equality.
At $n=1$ there is one class, namely $\mathbb Z$ itself.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every class in $\mathbb Z/n$
([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) contains exactly one integer $r$ with
$0\le r<n$. Consequently the map

$$r\longmapsto[r]_n\qquad(0\le r<n)$$

is a bijection from the von Neumann natural $n$ to $\mathbb Z/n$, and
$|\mathbb Z/n|=n$. This includes $n=1$, where the only representative is $0$.
For $n=0$, the map $a\mapsto[a]_0$ is a bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, including $n=0$ and $n=1$. For classes in
$\mathbb Z/n$ ([[def-integers-modulo-n]]) define

$$[a]_n+[b]_n:=[a+b]_n,\qquad [a]_n[b]_n:=[ab]_n.$$

These are binary operations in the sense of [[def-binary-operation]]. Indeed,
if $[a]_n=[a']_n$ and $[b]_n=[b']_n$, then
$a\equiv a'\pmod n$ and $b\equiv b'\pmod n$, so

$$a+b\equiv a'+b'\pmod n,\qquad ab\equiv a'b'\pmod n$$

by [[lem-congruence-respects-integer-arithmetic]]. Thus the two displayed
classes do not depend on the representatives chosen.

For $n=0$, every class is a singleton and these operations reproduce integer
addition and multiplication under the bijection $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/0$. For
$n=1$, the quotient has one element, so $[0]_1=[1]_1$ and both operations are
the unique binary operation on a one-element set.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$, with addition and multiplication as in
[[def-addition-and-multiplication-modulo-n]]:

1. $(\mathbb Z/n,+,[0]_n)$ is an abelian group ([[def-group]]), with
   $-[a]_n=[-a]_n$;
2. $(\mathbb Z/n,\cdot,[1]_n)$ is a commutative monoid
   ([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]);
3. multiplication distributes over addition on both sides.

The assertions include $n=0$ and $n=1$. At $n=1$, the two distinguished
identities coincide because $[0]_1=[1]_1$.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $k,\ell\in\mathbb Z$. Then

$$\sum_{x=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}=\begin{cases}N,&k\equiv\ell\pmod N,\\\\ 0,&k\not\equiv\ell\pmod N.\end{cases}$$

At $N=1$ the congruence holds for all $k,\ell$ and the sum is $1$. The sum is the finite sum of the complex family $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i(k-\ell)x/N}$ over the von Neumann natural $N=\{0,\dots,N-1\}$ ([[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]]), and $N$ on the right is the natural number $N$ read in $\mathbb C$ as the additive multiple $N\cdot1_{\mathbb C}$, that is, the value at $N$ of the canonical embedding $\mathbb N\to\mathbb C$ ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]).

Let $(M,+,0)$ be a commutative monoid and let all index sets below be finite.

1. If $h:T\to S$ is a bijection and $a:S\to M$, then $\sum_{t\in T}a_{h(t)}=\sum_{s\in S}a_s$.
2. If $S$ and $T$ are disjoint and $a:S\cup T\to M$, then $\sum_{u\in S\cup T}a_u=\sum_{s\in S}a_s+\sum_{t\in T}a_t$.
3. If $a:S\times T\to M$, then
   $$\sum_{(s,t)\in S\times T}a_{s,t}=\sum_{s\in S}\left(\sum_{t\in T}a_{s,t}\right)=\sum_{t\in T}\left(\sum_{s\in S}a_{s,t}\right).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

$$\ker(\exp)=2\pi i\mathbb Z,$$
and $\exp z=\exp w$ exactly when $z-w\in2\pi i\mathbb Z$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]], [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\Lambda_{d,L}$ and put $a_j=\widetilde x_j$. By [F1]–[F2], the $j$th representative of $x+e_j$ is $a_j+1-L\epsilon_j$, where $\epsilon_j=1$ if $a_j=L-1$ and $0$ otherwise; the $j$th representative of $x-e_j$ is $a_j-1+L\eta_j$, where $\eta_j=1$ if $a_j=0$ and $0$ otherwise. All other representatives are unchanged. Substitution into the definition of $\chi_r$, followed by the exponential addition law and $\exp(2\pi i n)=1$ for integers $n$ from [F5], gives $\chi_r(x+e_j)=e^{2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$ and $\chi_r(x-e_j)=e^{-2\pi i r_j/L}\chi_r(x)$. This also holds for $L=1$ and $L=2$.

For $r,s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, finite-sum factorization [F4] and the conjugation identity [F8] give $\langle\chi_r,\chi_s\rangle=\prod_{j=1}^d L^{-1}\sum_{u=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i(r_j-s_j)u/L}$. By [F1], distinct canonical representatives are incongruent modulo $L$, so [F3] makes each factor $1$ when $r_j=s_j$ and $0$ otherwise. This is the inner-product identity stated above.

Substituting the shift identities of step 1.1 into $-\Delta$ gives $-\Delta\chi_r=\sum_{j=1}^d(2-e^{2\pi i r_j/L}-e^{-2\pi i r_j/L})\chi_r$. By [F6]–[F7], each coefficient equals $2-2\cos(2\pi r_j/L)=4\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)$, proving the eigenvalue formula.

For any $f:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb C$, set $\widehat f(r)=L^{-d}\sum_{y\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(y)\overline{\chi_r(y)}$. By [F4] and [F8], the frequency sum factors as $\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\sum_{r_j=0}^{L-1}e^{2\pi i r_j(\widetilde x_j-\widetilde y_j)/L}$. The canonical-representative theorem [F1] and orthogonality [F3] make this product $L^d$ if $x=y$ in $\Lambda_{d,L}$ and $0$ otherwise. Therefore $\sum_r\widehat f(r)\chi_r(x)=L^{-d}\sum_y f(y)\sum_r\chi_r(x)\overline{\chi_r(y)}=f(x)$ for every $x$. If a linear combination $\sum_r c_r\chi_r$ vanishes, taking its inner product with $\chi_s$ and applying step 1.2 gives $c_s=0$ for each $s$, so the expansion is unique.

For every real $f$, the translations $x\mapsto x+e_j$ are bijections with inverses $x\mapsto x-e_j$, so reindexing the finite sums [F4] gives $\sum_xf(x)(-\Delta f)(x)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2\ge0$. Thus $-\Delta$ is positive semidefinite; its matrix is symmetric because every shift term is paired with its inverse shift. For nonzero $f$, $$f^{\mathsf T}(m^2I+\kappa(-\Delta))f=m^2\sum_xf(x)^2+\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_x(f(x+e_j)-f(x))^2>0,$$ since $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$. By steps 2.1 and 2.2, the spanning functions $\chi_r$ satisfy the eigenvalue equations in the Statement, so the combined operator has the displayed eigenvalues.

citations.quote:
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Powers are those of Integer powers $a^m$, and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ (Finite sums and finite products, by recursion). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ (Integer powers $a^m$), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]].

derivations.claim: On $[0,\pi/2]$ define $h(t)=\sin t-t\cos t$. By [F1]–[F3] and the product rule, $h$ is differentiable and continuous, with $h(0)=0$ and $h'(t)=t\sin t\ge0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$. For $0<t\le\pi/2$, the mean value theorem on $[0,t]$ gives $h(t)-h(0)=h'(c)t\ge0$ for some $c\in(0,t)$; at $t=0$ equality holds.
For $|u|\le\pi/2$, apply the mean value theorem to $\sin$ between $0$ and $|u|$. Its derivative has modulus at most $1$ by [F1] and [F5], so $|\sin |u||\le|u|$; parity gives $|\sin u|\le|u|$.

For $0<t<\pi/2$, put $r(t)=\sin t/t$. The quotient rule and step 1.1 give $r'(t)=(t\cos t-\sin t)/t^2=-h(t)/t^2\le0$. Applying the mean value theorem to $r$ on $[t,\pi/2]$ yields $r(t)\ge r(\pi/2)=2/\pi$ by [F1] and the quarter-turn value in [F1]; the endpoint $t=\pi/2$ is equality, and $t=0$ is immediate. Parity in [F5] extends the lower bound to negative $u$.

If $u\ne v$, apply the mean value theorem to $\sin$ on the closed interval with endpoints $u,v$. For some interior $c$, $|\sin u-\sin v|=|\cos c|\,|u-v|\le|u-v|$ by [F1], [F4], and [F5]; if $u=v$, both sides are zero.

boundaries.evidence: At u=0 the chord bounds are equalities, and for u=v the Lipschitz bound has both sides zero; steps 1.2–3.1 cover these cases.
Step 2.1 explicitly includes t=0 and step 1.2 gives equality at u=0.
At |u|=π/2 the lower chord bound is equality; step 2.1 includes the endpoint by continuity and the quarter-turn value.
When u=v the Lipschitz inequality is 0≤0 by step 3.1.
The proof treats t=π/2 directly and extends to negative endpoints by parity in step 2.1.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$ and every real matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$,
$$A\text{ is invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det(A)\ne0.$$

derivations.claim: For nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^s$, the vector $(0,z)$ is nonzero, so $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=(0,z)^{\mathsf T}K(0,z)>0$. Thus $C$ is symmetric positive definite. By the Cholesky statement in [F1], $C=LL^{\mathsf T}$ with positive diagonal; by the determinant laws in [F1], $\det C=(\det L)^2=(\prod_iL_{ii})^2>0$, so the invertibility criterion in [F1] gives that $C$ is invertible.

Since $C$ is symmetric and invertible, $C^{-1}$ is symmetric. Expanding the quadratic form on the right gives $x^{\mathsf T}(A-BC^{-1}B^{\mathsf T})x+2x^{\mathsf T}By+y^{\mathsf T}Cy$, which is the quadratic form on the left; this proves the displayed completion-of-the-square identity.

If $r\ge1$ and $x\ne0$, choose $y=-C^{-1}B^{\mathsf T}x$ in step 2.1. The second term vanishes and $(x,y)\ne0$, so positive definiteness of $K$ gives $x^{\mathsf T}Sx>0$. Symmetry of $S$ follows from symmetry of $A,C^{-1}$; hence $S$ is symmetric positive definite. If $r=0$, the claimed empty-matrix convention holds by definition.

The empty retained block r=0 is the degenerate boundary and is handled separately in step 3.1.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For $k\ne0$, apply [F1] to $u=k_j/2$ in each coordinate and square the bounds. Summing yields
$$\frac{4}{\pi^2}|k|_2^2\le D_d(k)\le |k|_2^2,$$
where $|k|_2^2=\sum_jk_j^2$. The denominator is positive off the origin, so its reciprocal is continuous on the cube with the origin removed. Extending it by the stated value at the closed singleton $\{0\}$ makes it Borel measurable: each open-set preimage is the union of a Borel subset of that complement and, when applicable, the singleton. The cosine numerator is continuous, so all nonnegative comparison integrands below are measurable by [F4].

For $j\ge0$, let $Q_j=[-2^{-j},2^{-j}]^d\setminus[-2^{-(j+1)},2^{-(j+1)}]^d$. The sets are pairwise disjoint, are contained in $[-1,1]^d$, and by [F2] have measure $(2^d-1)2^{-jd}$. On $Q_j$, $|k|_2\ge\|k\|_\infty>2^{-(j+1)}$, so step 1.1 gives $(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\le (\pi^2/(4\kappa))2^{2j+2}$. Hence
$$\int_{Q_j}(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\,d\lambda_d(k)\le \frac{\pi^2}{\kappa}(2^d-1)2^{(2-d)j}.$$
For $d>2$, these upper bounds sum to a finite geometric series by [F4]. On the remaining part of $[-\pi,\pi]^d$ outside $[-1,1]^d$, $|k|_2\ge1$, so step 1.1 bounds $(\kappa D_d)^{-1}$ by $\pi^2/(4\kappa)$; that part has finite measure by [F2]. Countable additivity and monotone convergence in [F3] therefore show that $(\kappa D_d)^{-1}$ is integrable on the whole cube.

For $1\le d\le2$, step 1.1 gives $(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\ge(\kappa|k|_2^2)^{-1}$ on every $Q_j$. There $|k|_2\le\sqrt d\,2^{-j}$, and hence
$$\int_{Q_j}(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\,d\lambda_d(k)\ge \frac{1}{\kappa d}(2^d-1)2^{(2-d)j}.$$
The right side is bounded below by the positive constant $(2^d-1)/(\kappa d)$ for all $j\ge0$ when $d\le2$. Since the $Q_j$ are disjoint, finite additivity in [F3] shows that the integral over their first $M+1$ layers is at least $(M+1)(2^d-1)/(\kappa d)$; letting $M\to\infty$ and using monotonicity gives $\int(\kappa D_d)^{-1}=+\infty$.

If $d>2$, then $|\cos(k\cdot x)|(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}\le(\kappa D_d(k))^{-1}$ away from the origin by [F5], and step 2.1 proves $\int |h_x|\,d\lambda_d<+\infty$; hence the signed integral in the Statement is finite by [F6], and multiplication by the finite constant $(2\pi)^{-d}$ preserves it. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice from [[def-countable-choice]]. Let integers $d,L\ge1$ specify the periodic lattice $\Lambda_{d,L}=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$ and let $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$ be dimensionless real parameters in lattice units. On the real coordinate space $\mathbb R^{\Lambda_{d,L}}$, let

$$K_{d,L,m,\kappa}:=m^2I+\kappa(-\Delta),$$

where $-\Delta$ is the periodic Laplacian of [[lem-csm-frontier-periodic-laplacian-spectrum]]. Its eigenvalues are

$$m^2+4\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L),\qquad r\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d,$$

so it is symmetric positive definite. The finite periodic Gaussian lattice field is the centered probability $\gamma_{K_{d,L,m,\kappa}}$ of [[def-csm-frontier-finite-gaussian-precision]], with density proportional to $\exp(-z^{\mathsf T}K_{d,L,m,\kappa}z/2)$ against Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^{L^d}$ and covariance $K_{d,L,m,\kappa}^{-1}$ by [[thm-csm-examples-quadratic-covariance]] at $\beta=1$.

The lattice coordinates $z_x$ and the quadratic exponent are dimensionless. A physical model may set $z_x=\Phi_x/\Phi_*$ and divide its energy by $k_BT$, where $\Phi_*$ is a declared field unit and $T>0$ is temperature; this definition itself makes no empirical claim. At $m^2=0$, the constant field is a zero mode and the unrestricted normalizer diverges by [[lem-csm-frontier-massless-torus-normalization-diverges]], so the full-space positive-precision definition does not apply. A finite-volume massless model must first specify a restriction such as the subspace $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{d,L}}z_x=0$ before inverting the Laplacian.

Positive definiteness and $\beta>0$ are essential for this normalized full-space Gaussian. The unrestricted identity $\mathbb E[x\,H'(x)]=\beta^{-1}$ is false without a boundary hypothesis: on $[-L,L]$ with $L>0$ and $H\equiv0$, the normalized expectation on the left is $0$.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

where the simple integral on the right is the one from

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero

$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Initially $K_0$ is positive definite. At any later stage with nonempty $E_j$, the current $K_{j-1}$ is positive definite by induction, so its principal block $C_j$ is positive definite. The Schur identity in [F2] then gives exactly the algorithm's $K_j=A_j-B_jC_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}$ and proves it positive definite when $R_j$ is nonempty. If $R_j$ is empty, the empty-matrix convention applies. Stages with $E_j=\varnothing$ leave $K_j=K_{j-1}$. The algorithm is consequently well-defined at every one of its finitely many stages.

Fix one stage with $E_j\ne\varnothing$ and fix its retained coordinates $x$. By step 1.1 the current matrix is well-defined and positive definite. Reordering the coordinates is a linear permutation with Jacobian determinant of absolute value $1$, so the change-of-variables formula in [F3] preserves the integral. With eliminated coordinates denoted by $y$, [F2] gives
$$\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}K_{j-1}\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix} =x^{\mathsf T}K_jx+(y+C_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}x)^{\mathsf T}C_j(y+C_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}x).$$
For fixed $x$, the translation $y\mapsto y+C_j^{-1}B_j^{\mathsf T}x$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of Euclidean space with Jacobian $1$. The change-of-variables formula [F3] and the Gaussian normalizer [F1] therefore give
$$\int_{\mathbb R^{E_j}}e^{-\frac12(x,y)^{\mathsf T}K_{j-1}(x,y)}\,dy =\frac{(2\pi)^{|E_j|/2}}{\sqrt{\det C_j}}e^{-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_jx} =e^{\ell_j}e^{-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_jx}.$$
The last equality follows from the definition of $\ell_j$ and positivity of $\det C_j$. If $E_j=\varnothing$, the same identity holds with factor $1=e^{\ell_j}$ by definition.

Apply step 2.1 successively for the finite stages. At each stage the integrand is nonnegative, so Tonelli [F3] permits the iterated eliminations in the stated order. Multiplying the one-stage factors yields, for each fixed final retained vector $x$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^{\bigcup_j E_j}}e^{-\frac12\widetilde z(x,y)^{\mathsf T}K_0\widetilde z(x,y)}\,dy =\left(\prod_{j=1}^qe^{\ell_j}\right)e^{-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_qx} =e^{\sum_j\ell_j}e^{-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_qx},$$
using exponential addition in [F4]. For $q=0$ the equality is the identity with an empty product.

Integrating step 3.1 over the retained vector and using Tonelli [F3] gives $Z_{K_0}=e^{\sum_j\ell_j}Z_{K_q}$. Each nonempty $K_q$ is positive definite by step 1.1, so [F1] makes $Z_{K_q}$ finite and positive; for empty $R_q$ it equals $1$ by convention. Dividing step 3.1 by $Z_{K_0}$ gives the retained density $Z_{K_q}^{-1}e^{-x^{\mathsf T}K_qx/2}$, exactly $\gamma_{K_q}$. Taking natural logarithms of the positive normalizer identity and using [F4] proves the logarithmic formula, including the empty-space case.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The exact Gaussian block-elimination algorithm has input:

- an integer $N\ge1$ and a real matrix $K_0\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ satisfying $K_0^{\mathsf T}=K_0$ and $v^{\mathsf T}K_0v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^N$. - an integer $q\ge0$ and nested retained coordinate sets
  $$R_0=\{1,\ldots,N\}\supseteq R_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq R_q,$$
  each given in increasing coordinate order.

It starts at stage $0$ with the ordered coordinates $R_0$ and matrix $K_0$. For each $j=1,\ldots,q$, let $E_j=R_{j-1}\setminus R_j$ be the coordinates to eliminate at that stage.

1. If $E_j=\varnothing$, set $K_j=K_{j-1}$ and $\ell_j=0$.
2. If $E_j\ne\varnothing$, reorder the current coordinates as the increasing list of $R_j$ followed by the increasing list of $E_j$, and write the correspondingly permuted matrix
   $$K_{j-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A_j&B_j\\B_j^{\mathsf T}&C_j\end{pmatrix}.$$
   Solve the nonsingular system $C_jX_j=B_j^{\mathsf T}$, set
   $$K_j:=A_j-B_jX_j,\qquad \ell_j:=\frac{|E_j|}{2}\ln(2\pi)-\frac12\ln(\det C_j).$$
   Interpret $K_j$ in the increasing coordinate order on $R_j$.

The output is $(K_q,\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_q)$, with the accumulated log normalization $\sum_{j=1}^q\ell_j$. If $q=0$, this output means $K_0$ and an empty list of increments. When $R_j=\varnothing$, $K_j$ is the unique empty $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is defined to be $1$. This is an exact-arithmetic procedure on finite matrices.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. For $N\ge1$, a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ (meaning $z^{\mathsf T}Kz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^N$) defines the finite centered Gaussian probability $\gamma_K$ on $\mathbb R^N$ by

$$Z_K:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z),\qquad \gamma_K(dz):=Z_K^{-1}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z).$$

Under the stated Axiom of Countable Choice, $Z_K=(2\pi)^{N/2}(\det K)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbb E_{\gamma_K}[z]=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}_{\gamma_K}(z)=K^{-1}$; these identities are the positive-quadratic-form Gaussian theorem of the mathematical supplier. Here $K$ is called the precision matrix because it appears in the quadratic exponent, and the covariance is its inverse. For $N=0$, define $\mathbb R^0$ to be the singleton containing the empty vector and define $\gamma_{\varnothing}$ to put mass one on that point; its partition factor and empty determinant are both $1$.

The variables $z_i$ and exponent $z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2$ are dimensionless in this mathematical definition. In a physical quadratic model, if $\Phi_i$ has field unit $\Phi_*$ and $H(\Phi)=\frac12\Phi^{\mathsf T}K_{\rm phys}\Phi$, then each entry of $K_{\rm phys}$ has units $\mathrm J/(\Phi_*)^2$. With $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$ and $z_i=\Phi_i/\Phi_*$, the dimensionless precision is $K=\beta\Phi_*^2K_{\rm phys}$. This dimensional conversion does not assert an empirical model.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

derivations.claim:
The map $T(x')=b x'$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$ with Jacobian determinant $b^d$. By [F2], each partial derivative satisfies
$$\partial_{x_j}\varphi_b(x)=b^{-(d-2)/2}b^{-1}(\partial_{x'_j}\varphi')(x/b)=b^{-d/2}(\partial_{x'_j}\varphi')(x/b).$$
Thus $|\nabla\varphi_b(x)|^2=b^{-d}|\nabla\varphi'(x/b)|^2$. Applying [F1] with $T$ to this nonnegative integrand gives
$$S_2[\varphi_b]=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^d}b^{-d}|\nabla\varphi'(x')|^2b^d\,d\lambda_d(x')=S_2[\varphi'].$$
The compact support and smoothness assumptions make these integrands measurable and finite.

The same change of variables gives
$$Q_4[\varphi_b]=\frac1{4!}\int_{\mathbb R^d}b^{-2(d-2)}\varphi'(x/b)^4\,d\lambda_d(x) =b^{d-2(d-2)}Q_4[\varphi']=b^{4-d}Q_4[\varphi'].$$
Therefore $gQ_4[\varphi_b]=g'Q_4[\varphi']$ with $g'=b^{4-d}g$, as claimed.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the hypotheses of [[alg-csm-frontier-gaussian-block-rg]] with input $K_0$ and retained sets $R_0,\ldots,R_q$. Let $K_j,C_j,\ell_j$ be the algorithm outputs. At each stage write $E_j=R_{j-1}\setminus R_j$, and use the empty-set conventions of the algorithm. Then the algorithm terminates after $q$ stages, every nonempty retained precision $K_j$ is positive definite, and for every fixed retained vector $x\in\mathbb R^{R_q}$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^{\bigcup_{j=1}^q E_j}}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 \widetilde z(x,y)^{\mathsf T}K_0\widetilde z(x,y)\right)\,d\lambda(y)
=\exp\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^q\ell_j\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac12x^{\mathsf T}K_qx\right),$$

where $y$ lists the eliminated coordinates in increasing order, $\widetilde z(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{R_0}$ is the unique full coordinate vector agreeing with $x$ on $R_q$ and with $y$ on $R_0\setminus R_q$, and $\lambda$ is Euclidean Lebesgue measure in that finite-dimensional space. If $R_q\ne\varnothing$, the normalized marginal law of the retained coordinates under $\gamma_{K_0}$ is exactly $\gamma_{K_q}$; if $R_q=\varnothing$, the final retained space is the singleton $\mathbb R^0$ and the identity gives $Z_{K_0}=\exp(\sum_j\ell_j)$. In all cases,

$$\ln Z_{K_0}=\sum_{j=1}^q\ell_j+\ln Z_{K_q},$$

with $Z_{K_q}=1$ under the empty-space convention. These are exact finite-dimensional Gaussian identities and make no approximation or empirical claim.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets has a function $f$ with $f(n)\in X_n$ for every $n$. For $N\ge1$, a real symmetric positive-definite matrix $K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}$ (meaning $z^{\mathsf T}Kz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^N$) defines the finite centered Gaussian probability $\gamma_K$ on $\mathbb R^N$ by

$$Z_K:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z),\qquad \gamma_K(dz):=Z_K^{-1}e^{-z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2}\,d\lambda_N(z).$$

Under the stated Axiom of Countable Choice, $Z_K=(2\pi)^{N/2}(\det K)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbb E_{\gamma_K}[z]=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}_{\gamma_K}(z)=K^{-1}$; these identities are the positive-quadratic-form Gaussian theorem of the mathematical supplier. Here $K$ is called the precision matrix because it appears in the quadratic exponent, and the covariance is its inverse. For $N=0$, define $\mathbb R^0$ to be the singleton containing the empty vector and define $\gamma_{\varnothing}$ to put mass one on that point; its partition factor and empty determinant are both $1$.

The variables $z_i$ and exponent $z^{\mathsf T}Kz/2$ are dimensionless in this mathematical definition. In a physical quadratic model, if $\Phi_i$ has field unit $\Phi_*$ and $H(\Phi)=\frac12\Phi^{\mathsf T}K_{\rm phys}\Phi$, then each entry of $K_{\rm phys}$ has units $\mathrm J/(\Phi_*)^2$. With $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm J^{-1}$ and $z_i=\Phi_i/\Phi_*$, the dimensionless precision is $K=\beta\Phi_*^2K_{\rm phys}$. This dimensional conversion does not assert an empirical model.

derivations.claim:
For $x\in\mathbb R^n$ and $y\in\mathbb R$, expansion and completion of the scalar square give
$$\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix}^{\mathsf T}K_n\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\end{pmatrix} =(y+\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}x)^2+2n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\right)^2.$$
Expanding the finite sum shows
$$n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i\right)^2 =\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}(x_i-x_j)^2\ge0.$$
Consequently the remaining part is $n\sum_i x_i^2+\sum_{i<j}(x_i-x_j)^2$, which is positive when $x\ne0$; when $x=0$ and $(x,y)\ne0$, the first square is $y^2>0$. Hence $K_n$ is symmetric positive definite and the Gaussian law is defined by [F2].

Use one retained set consisting of the $n$ leaves and eliminate the final central coordinate. The eliminated block is $C=[1]$, and the cross block is $B=\mathbf1_n$. The algorithm and its correctness theorem [F1] therefore return
$$2nI_n-\mathbf1_n[1]^{-1}\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}=2nI_n-\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}.$$
For $i\ne j$, the identity matrix contributes zero and $(\mathbf1_n\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})_{ij}=1$, so the resulting precision entry is $-1$. In the original $K_n$, the leaf block is $2nI_n$ and its distinct-leaf entries are zero. This verifies the stated generation of all pair couplings.
