Let $d,L\ge1$ be integers and let $\Lambda_{d,L}:=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, where $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$ is the quotient set of integers modulo $L$. Use the quotient addition $[a]_L+[b]_L=[a+b]_L$ and additive inverse $-[a]_L=[-a]_L$, and define these operations coordinatewise on $\Lambda_{d,L}$. For $x\in\Lambda_{d,L}$, write $\widetilde x=(\widetilde x_1,\ldots,\widetilde x_d)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$ for its unique coordinate representatives. For $1\le j\le d$, let $e_j\in\Lambda_{d,L}$ have coordinate $[1]_L$ in position $j$ and $[0]_L$ elsewhere. Count the two terms $x+e_j$ and $x-e_j$ separately even when they coincide for $L=1$ or $L=2$.

For a real-valued function $f:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb R$, define

$$(-\Delta f)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(2f(x)-f(x+e_j)-f(x-e_j)\bigr).$$

For a complex-valued function, use the same formula for $-\Delta$, which is its complex-linear extension. Write $\mathbb C^{\Lambda_{d,L}}$ for the complex-valued functions on $\Lambda_{d,L}$ with pointwise vector operations. For $r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, define the function $\chi_r:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb C$ by

$$\chi_r(x):=\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i}{L}\sum_{j=1}^d r_j\widetilde x_j\right).$$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle:=L^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(x)\overline{g(x)}$. Identify real functions with coordinate vectors using the lexicographic order on the representatives $\widetilde x$, and let $I_{\Lambda_{d,L}}$ be the identity operator on those functions. A real matrix $A$ is symmetric when $A^{\mathsf T}=A$; a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when $v^{\mathsf T}Av\ge0$ for every real vector $v$, and positive definite when $v^{\mathsf T}Av>0$ for every nonzero real vector $v$. For all $r,s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, the inner products satisfy $\langle\chi_r,\chi_s\rangle=1$ if $r=s$ and $0$ otherwise; every complex-valued function on $\Lambda_{d,L}$ is a unique linear combination of the functions $\chi_r$.

For each $r$, the equation $-\Delta\chi_r=\lambda_r\chi_r$ holds with $\lambda_r:=4\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)$; this scalar is the eigenvalue associated with $\chi_r$.

Consequently $-\Delta$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite, and for real $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$ the matrix $m^2I_{\Lambda_{d,L}}+\kappa(-\Delta)$ is real symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues $m^2+4\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)>0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
The integral of a nonnegative simple function.

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple (Nonnegative simple measurable functions).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $K\mathbf1=0$ and $K$ is symmetric. Hence the quadratic form is unchanged by adding any constant multiple of $\mathbf1$: for every $z$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $(z+t\mathbf1)^{\mathsf T}K(z+t\mathbf1)=z^{\mathsf T}Kz$.

If $N=1$, then $K=0$ by step 1.1, and the integrand is identically $1$ on $\mathbb R$. Its integral is infinite because the intervals $[-M,M]$ have measure $2M$ for every integer $M\ge1$ by [F4], and [F5] bounds the full integral below by each of these unbounded values.

Suppose $N\ge2$ and enumerate the lattice sites as $x_1,\ldots,x_N$. Define the linear map $T:\mathbb R^{N-1}\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^N$ by $T(w,t)=(w_1+t,\ldots,w_{N-1}+t,t)$. Its matrix is triangular with all diagonal entries $1$, so it is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism with determinant $1$. For $\widetilde w=(w_1,\ldots,w_{N-1},0)$, one has $T(w,t)=\widetilde w+t\mathbf1$. By step 1.1, $T(w,t)^{\mathsf T}KT(w,t)=\widetilde w^{\mathsf T}K\widetilde w$, which is independent of $t$. Applying [F2] changes the original integral to
$$\int_{\mathbb R^{N-1}\times\mathbb R}f(w)\,d\lambda_N(w,t),\qquad f(w):=\exp\!\left(-\frac12\widetilde w^{\mathsf T}K\widetilde w\right).$$

The function $f$ is continuous and positive. On $[-1,1]^{N-1}$, $|\widetilde w^{\mathsf T}K\widetilde w|\le M$, where $M:=\sum_{i,j=1}^{N-1}|K_{ij}|<\infty$; hence $f(w)\ge e^{-M/2}$ there. By [F4] and [F5], $\int_{\mathbb R^{N-1}}f(w)\,d\lambda_{N-1}(w)\ge2^{N-1}e^{-M/2}>0$. By [F3], Tonelli factors the nonnegative integral in step 2.2 as $\int f(w)\,dw\int_{\mathbb R}1\,dt$. The second factor is infinite because each interval $[-M',M']$ has measure $2M'$ for integer $M'\ge1$ by [F4], and [F5] bounds the full-line integral below by each such value. Thus the original normalizer is infinite, proving the claim.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d,L\ge1$ be integers and let $\Lambda_{d,L}:=(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, where $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$ is the quotient set of integers modulo $L$. Use the quotient addition $[a]_L+[b]_L=[a+b]_L$ and additive inverse $-[a]_L=[-a]_L$, and define these operations coordinatewise on $\Lambda_{d,L}$. For $x\in\Lambda_{d,L}$, write $\widetilde x=(\widetilde x_1,\ldots,\widetilde x_d)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$ for its unique coordinate representatives. For $1\le j\le d$, let $e_j\in\Lambda_{d,L}$ have coordinate $[1]_L$ in position $j$ and $[0]_L$ elsewhere. Count the two terms $x+e_j$ and $x-e_j$ separately even when they coincide for $L=1$ or $L=2$.

For a real-valued function $f:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb R$, define

$$(-\Delta f)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(2f(x)-f(x+e_j)-f(x-e_j)\bigr).$$

For a complex-valued function, use the same formula for $-\Delta$, which is its complex-linear extension. Write $\mathbb C^{\Lambda_{d,L}}$ for the complex-valued functions on $\Lambda_{d,L}$ with pointwise vector operations. For $r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, define the function $\chi_r:\Lambda_{d,L}\to\mathbb C$ by

$$\chi_r(x):=\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i}{L}\sum_{j=1}^d r_j\widetilde x_j\right).$$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle:=L^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(x)\overline{g(x)}$. Identify real functions with coordinate vectors using the lexicographic order on the representatives $\widetilde x$, and let $I_{\Lambda_{d,L}}$ be the identity operator on those functions. A real matrix $A$ is symmetric when $A^{\mathsf T}=A$; a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite when $v^{\mathsf T}Av\ge0$ for every real vector $v$, and positive definite when $v^{\mathsf T}Av>0$ for every nonzero real vector $v$. For all $r,s\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, the inner products satisfy $\langle\chi_r,\chi_s\rangle=1$ if $r=s$ and $0$ otherwise; every complex-valued function on $\Lambda_{d,L}$ is a unique linear combination of the functions $\chi_r$.

For each $r$, the equation $-\Delta\chi_r=\lambda_r\chi_r$ holds with $\lambda_r:=4\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)$; this scalar is the eigenvalue associated with $\chi_r$.

Consequently $-\Delta$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite, and for real $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$ the matrix $m^2I_{\Lambda_{d,L}}+\kappa(-\Delta)$ is real symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues $m^2+4\kappa\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)>0$.

Write $e_j$ for the $j$th coordinate class, and count the two terms $x+e_j$ and $x-e_j$ separately even when they coincide for $L=1$ or $L=2$. For a real function $f$ on $\Lambda_{d,L}$, define

$$(-\Delta f)(x):=\sum_{j=1}^d\bigl(2f(x)-f(x+e_j)-f(x-e_j)\bigr).$$

Extend $-\Delta$ complex-linearly. For $r=(r_1,\ldots,r_d)\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^d$, define $\chi_r(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,r\cdot x/L)$. With inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=L^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_{d,L}}f(x)\overline{g(x)}$, the $L^d$ characters $\chi_r$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C^{\Lambda_{d,L}}$ and satisfy

$$-\Delta\chi_r=\lambda_r\chi_r,\qquad \lambda_r=4\sum_{j=1}^d\sin^2(\pi r_j/L).$$

Consequently $-\Delta$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite, and for $m^2>0$ and $\kappa>0$ the matrix $m^2I_{\Lambda_{d,L}}+\kappa(-\Delta)$ is real symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues $m^2+4\kappa\sum_j\sin^2(\pi r_j/L)>0$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
(Lebesgue outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, Assuming countable choice, Lebesgue outer measure is an outer measure that restricts to elementary volume
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of Carathéodory measurable sets.

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume, which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

def-csm-frontier-finite-potts-fk.finite_checks_disposition: The listed exact finite checks cover the stated boundary conventions; the general result is established by the carrier argument.
def-csm-frontier-finite-potts-fk.definition_interface:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

def-csm-frontier-fk-boundary-wiring.finite_checks_disposition: These direct finite calculations verify the discrete, wired, and isolated-boundary conventions; the definition specifies the general finite partition polynomial.
def-csm-frontier-fk-boundary-wiring.definition_interface:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, and give each edge a finite activity $v_e\geq0$. Choose a set $B\subseteq V$ of boundary vertices and an equivalence relation $\xi$ on $B$. The relation $\xi$ specifies which boundary vertices are identified before any edges are occupied. For $A\subseteq E$, let $\sim_{\xi,A}$ be the least equivalence relation on $V$ containing every pair in $\xi$ and both endpoints of every edge in $A$. Write $k_\xi(A):=|V/{\sim_{\xi,A}}|$ and $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. Define
$$w^\xi_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_\xi(A)}v_A,\qquad Z^\xi_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w^\xi_{FK}(A).$$
The free boundary choice is the discrete relation on $B$ (each boundary vertex is a singleton); the wired classes are the equivalence classes of $\xi$, with a fully wired boundary given by one class when $B\neq\varnothing$. Thus $k_\xi(A)$ counts components after the prescribed identifications and occupied edges, including isolated vertices and boundary classes. The sum is finite and positive because its empty-edge term is $Q^{k_\xi(\varnothing)}>0$. For discrete $\xi$, $k_\xi(A)=k_G(A)$ and $Z^\xi_{FK}=Z_{FK}$. This is a mathematical partition polynomial; no wired Potts spin marginal is asserted.

For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

derivations.claim: For fixed $\sigma$, summing $W(\sigma,A)$ over all $A\subseteq E$ chooses, independently for each edge, either its absent factor $1$ or its present factor $v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}$. Distributivity of the finite product therefore gives $\sum_AW(\sigma,A)=w_P(\sigma)$. Summing this equality over the finite set $[Q]^V$ gives $\sum_{\sigma,A}W(\sigma,A)=Z_P$.

Fix $A\subseteq E$. The product $W(\sigma,A)$ is zero unless the spins agree across every edge in $A$. Equality propagates along each finite path, so the admissible configurations are exactly those constant on each connected component of $G_A$. Assigning one of $Q$ colors independently to each of its $k_G(A)$ components gives exactly $Q^{k_G(A)}$ such configurations, each with weight $\prod_{e\in A}v_e$. Hence $\sum_\sigma W(\sigma,A)=w_{FK}(A)$, including when this weight is zero. Summing over $A$ gives $\sum_{\sigma,A}W(\sigma,A)=Z_{FK}$.

The common total is positive by [F1], so dividing $W$ by it defines a probability law. The finite marginal sums in steps 1.1 and 1.2 show that its spin and edge marginals are respectively $w_P/Z_P$ and $w_{FK}/Z_{FK}$, and that $Z_P=Z_{FK}$.

For a fixed $A$ with positive FK probability, every spin assignment constant on its components has the same joint weight $\prod_{e\in A}v_e$. By step 1.2 there are $Q^{k_G(A)}$ such assignments, so the conditional law is uniform on them; this is equivalent to assigning independent uniform colors to the components.

If $x,y$ are connected in $G_A$, step 2.2 makes their colors equal with conditional probability $1$. If they are in distinct components, their independent uniform colors agree with probability $1/Q$. Averaging over the FK marginal from step 2.1 yields $\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y)+Q^{-1}\mathbb P_{FK}(x\not\leftrightarrow y)=Q^{-1}+(1-Q^{-1})\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y)$.

alg-csm-frontier-fk-connectivity-transfe.definition_interface:
Input a finite simple graph $G=(V,E)$, integer $Q\geq2$, finite activities $v_e\in[0,\infty)$, a total edge order $e_1,\ldots,e_m$, and boundary data consisting of a set $B\subseteq V$ and an equivalence relation $\xi$ on $B$. The relation $\xi$ identifies prescribed boundary vertices before any edge is processed; its singleton classes give free boundary and its non-singleton classes give the wired classes. A vertex incident to no edge is isolated. Put $n_0:=|\{x\in V\setminus B:x\text{ is isolated}\}|$. At time $t$, the **active frontier** consists of the initially active boundary vertices $B$ together with vertices introduced at a processed edge, minus those already forgotten. A state is a set partition of the active frontier. Its blocks record equivalence generated by the initial boundary relation $\xi$ and processed present edges. A coefficient vector assigns a nonnegative real weight to each such partition.

Initialize the frontier as $B$ with partition $\xi$ and coefficient $Q^{n_0}$; if $B=\varnothing$, this is the empty partition. For $t=1,\ldots,m$, perform the following operations in order.

1. Introduce each endpoint of $e_t$ that is not yet active as a singleton block.
2. For each state $\pi$ of coefficient $c$, add $c$ to the same state (the edge is absent) and add $c v_{e_t}$ to $J_{uv}\pi$ (the edge is present), where $e_t=\{u,v\}$ and $J_{uv}\pi$ merges the blocks containing $u$ and $v$ and leaves all other blocks unchanged. If $u,v$ already share a block, $J_{uv}\pi=\pi$. Thus $J_{uv}^2=J_{uv}$ and the edge operator is $I+v_{e_t}J_{uv}$.
3. Forget vertices whose last incident edge is $e_t$. When removing a vertex empties its block, delete that block and multiply its coefficient by $Q$ once; otherwise just remove the vertex from its block. If several vertices in a block are forgotten at this step, the factor $Q$ is applied only when the last active member is removed.

After all edges are processed, forget any remaining active vertices by the same rule and return the coefficient of the empty partition. This includes boundary vertices with no incident edge; each surviving wired component is then counted once. Discrete $\xi$ gives free boundary, while non-singleton classes implement the stated wired boundary condition. A planar-strip annotation consists of a plane embedding, an ordered frontier list at every update, a noncrossing initial relation $\xi$, and the condition that every reachable connectivity partition is noncrossing. For an ordered frontier, “noncrossing” means that no two different blocks contain alternating points $a<b<c<d$ with $a,c$ in one block and $b,d$ in the other. When $u,v$ are adjacent frontier points $i,i+1$, write $J_i$ for $J_{uv}$; these are the noncrossing connectivity states and adjacent-block joins used for planar transfer. The general procedure stores all set partitions when no such annotation is supplied. All arithmetic is exact; each input has finitely many edge updates and finitely many partitions at every frontier.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, and give each edge a finite activity $v_e\geq0$. Choose a set $B\subseteq V$ of boundary vertices and an equivalence relation $\xi$ on $B$. The relation $\xi$ specifies which boundary vertices are identified before any edges are occupied. For $A\subseteq E$, let $\sim_{\xi,A}$ be the least equivalence relation on $V$ containing every pair in $\xi$ and both endpoints of every edge in $A$. Write $k_\xi(A):=|V/{\sim_{\xi,A}}|$ and $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. Define
$$w^\xi_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_\xi(A)}v_A,\qquad Z^\xi_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w^\xi_{FK}(A).$$
The free boundary choice is the discrete relation on $B$ (each boundary vertex is a singleton); the wired classes are the equivalence classes of $\xi$, with a fully wired boundary given by one class when $B\neq\varnothing$. Thus $k_\xi(A)$ counts components after the prescribed identifications and occupied edges, including isolated vertices and boundary classes. The sum is finite and positive because its empty-edge term is $Q^{k_\xi(\varnothing)}>0$. For discrete $\xi$, $k_\xi(A)=k_G(A)$ and $Z^\xi_{FK}=Z_{FK}$. This is a mathematical partition polynomial; no wired Potts spin marginal is asserted.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$

derivations.claim:
Let $E_t=\{e_1,\ldots,e_t\}$ and let $n_0$ count vertices outside $B$ that are isolated in $G$. For each edge subset $C\subseteq E_t$, form the graph on the initially present boundary vertices and the endpoints introduced by time $t$, impose $\xi$, and retain the present edges in $C$. Let $\pi_t(C)$ be the resulting equivalence partition restricted to the active frontier, and let $c_t(C)$ count its equivalence classes containing no active vertex. The coefficient vector after time $t$ satisfies
$$W_t(\pi)=Q^{n_0}\sum_{\substack{C\subseteq E_t\\\pi_t(C)=\pi}}Q^{c_t(C)}\prod_{e\in C}v_e.$$
At $t=0$ the only subset is empty, every boundary vertex is active, their partition is $\xi$, and $c_0=0$. The initialized coefficient is $Q^{n_0}$, so the invariant holds.

Assume the invariant after $t-1$ edges. Introducing a new endpoint as a singleton agrees with adding that previously unseen vertex to the partial graph; a boundary endpoint is already present in the initial relation $\xi$. For each partial subset $C\subseteq E_{t-1}$, the two subsets at the next edge are exactly $C$ and $C\cup\{e_t\}$. The absent choice preserves the partition and weight; the present choice multiplies by $v_{e_t}$ and merges precisely the endpoint blocks. Thus $I+v_{e_t}J_{uv}$ gives the two required contributions, even when $u,v$ were already equivalent through $\xi$ or previous edges.

When vertices at their last incident edge are forgotten, no future edge is incident to them. If their block still has an active vertex, that equivalence class can connect to future edges through that vertex and is not yet closed. If removing a vertex empties its block, every boundary vertex in its $\xi$-class was already initially active and is now absent as well; no future edge can meet any member of the class. The class is therefore final, and the algorithm multiplies by $Q$ exactly once at this first emptying. This updates $c_t(C)$ and preserves the invariant. After the last edge, terminal cleanup applies the same criterion to the remaining blocks, which have no future incident edges.

For each full present-edge subset $C$, let $r_m(C)$ be the number of blocks still active just before terminal cleanup. Every equivalence class generated by $\xi$ and $C$ is counted exactly once: isolated vertices outside $B$ contribute $n_0$, classes closed earlier contribute $c_m(C)$, and the $r_m(C)$ remaining blocks each contribute one factor $Q$ in cleanup. Therefore $n_0+c_m(C)+r_m(C)=k_\xi(C)$, and summing the invariant from step 1.1 with these cleanup factors over $C\subseteq E$ gives the returned scalar $\sum_C Q^{k_\xi(C)}v_C=Z^\xi_{FK}$.

Each of the finitely many $m$ edges is processed once; every active frontier is finite and has finitely many set partitions, and terminal cleanup removes finitely many vertices. Hence the procedure terminates. For discrete $\xi$, [F3] identifies $Z^\xi_{FK}$ with $Z_{FK}$.

A **plane graph** is a finite simple graph ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]) together with distinct points of $\mathbb R^2$ for its vertices and a polygonal arc ([[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]]) for each edge, joining its endpoints, such that an edge interior contains no vertex and two edge arcs meet only at a common endpoint. A finite simple graph is **planar** if it is isomorphic to the abstract graph underlying some plane graph.

A **face** is a region of the complement of the drawing ([[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]). The **boundary subgraph** of a face consists of the vertices and whole edges lying in its frontier; this is a subgraph in the sense of [[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]].

For a connected plane graph, walking once around a face with that face locally on the same side gives its **facial boundary walk**. Its **length** is the number of edge traversals, not the number of distinct edges: an edge incident with the same face on both local sides is traversed twice. For a disconnected plane graph a face may have several boundary walks; its boundary length is the sum of their lengths. No boundary walk is assumed to be a cycle unless a later connectivity result proves it.

Let $G$ be a connected plane graph with face set $F(G)$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]). Its **dual multigraph** $G^*$ has vertex set $F(G)$ and one edge $e^*$ for every primal edge $e$. If the two local sides of $e$ belong to faces $f$ and $g$, then $e^*$ has endpoints $f,g$.

By [[lem-plane-edge-face-incidence]], a bridge has the same face on both local sides, so its dual edge is a loop. Different primal edges may have the same incident face pair, so their duals may be parallel. These are permitted by [[def-multigraph-loop-and-digraph]]. The definition is attached to the fixed plane embedding: different embeddings of the same abstract planar graph may have nonisomorphic dual multigraphs.

Every connected plane graph $G$ admits a polygonal plane embedding of its dual multigraph [[def-plane-dual-multigraph]] in which each dual edge crosses its corresponding primal edge exactly once and crosses no other primal or dual edge. In this reciprocal embedding, if $G^*$ is itself simple — equivalently, if $G$ has no bridge and no two faces share more than one edge — then $G^*$ is a plane graph in the sense of [[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]] and $(G^*)^*$ is isomorphic to $G$ in the sense of [[def-graph-isomorphism-and-complement]]. The simplicity hypothesis is necessary and not a convenience: a plane graph is a finite **simple** graph here, while [[def-plane-dual-multigraph]] may produce loops and parallel edges, so the double dual is otherwise not formed at all. For $G=K_2$ the single edge is a bridge and $G^*$ is one vertex with a loop, which is not a plane graph and has no dual under these definitions. Face finiteness is [[lem-plane-graph-faces-are-finite-with-one-unbounded-face]], local incidence is [[lem-plane-edge-face-incidence]], and polygonal separation is [[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]].

If a plane graph has $c$ connected components, then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=1+c.$$

This includes the null graph, for which $c=0$ and the complement is its single face. Component sets and their finite cardinalities are those of [[cor-connected-components-partition-the-vertex-set]] and [[def-finite-cardinality]], and face finiteness is [[lem-plane-graph-faces-are-finite-with-one-unbounded-face]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.

derivations.claim: Fix $A\subseteq E$. The drawing of $G_A$ is a finite union of points and closed line segments, hence is closed in $\mathbb R^2$. Its complement is open, so each of its face components is open and polygonally connected by [F7]. The original faces are vertices of $G^*$. Two such faces lie in the same face of $G_A$ exactly when they are connected by dual edges corresponding to $E\setminus A$. A dual path crosses only absent primal edges and therefore stays in the complement of $G_A$. Conversely, a path between two original face points inside one face of $G_A$ can be chosen polygonal; perturb its finitely many segments to avoid primal vertices and to cross edge interiors transversely. Because it avoids $G_A$, every crossed edge lies in $E\setminus A$, so the crossed dual edges form a path in $(F(G),A^*)$. Thus the faces of $G_A$ correspond bijectively to the components counted by $k^*(A)$.

Apply [F4] to the spanning plane subgraph $G_A$. Its vertex set is $V$, its edge set is $A$, its component count is $k(A)$, and by step 1.1 its face count is $k^*(A)$. Therefore $|V|-|A|+k^*(A)=1+k(A)$, or $k(A)-k^*(A)=|V|-|A|-1$.

View the fixed embedding on the sphere $S^2$ by adding the point at infinity. By [F4] the plane subgraph $G_A$ has finitely many faces; choose one point in each. For every vertex $x\in V$, including each vertex isolated in $G_A$, choose a closed polygonal disk $D_x$ so that the disks are pairwise disjoint and avoid all the chosen face points. Choose pairwise disjoint attachment intervals on each $\partial D_x$, one for each edge incident to $x$ and in the cyclic order of the embedding. For each $e\in A$, choose a closed polygonal rectangular band around the part of its polygonal arc outside its endpoint disks; make the bands pairwise disjoint, disjoint from all nonendpoint disks, and attach them to the corresponding intervals. These choices are possible with sufficiently small radii and widths because the graph is finite and edge arcs meet only at shared endpoints. Let $N_A$ be the union of these disks and bands. Each band joins exactly its two endpoint disks, and distinct bands otherwise remain disjoint, so the connected components of $N_A$ correspond exactly to those of $G_A$, including isolated-vertex disks; hence there are $k(A)$. Its boundary is a finite disjoint union of simple polygonal circles. In particular, the one-vertex graph with no edges gives one disk and one boundary loop. At a primal-dual crossing, the two sides of an occupied-edge band join the medial half-edges as $(h_4,h_1)$ and $(h_2,h_3)$; when the edge is absent, there is no band there and the two face-side sectors join as $(h_1,h_2)$ and $(h_3,h_4)$. The cyclic ordering of the attachment intervals fixes these local continuations, so $\partial N_A$ gives exactly the smoothings in the Statement and has $\ell(A)$ loops. Inside each face $U$ of $G_A$, the disk-and-band pieces form collars along the facial boundary side occurrences: each band side is a polygonal strip, and intervening vertex-disk sectors join consecutive strips in cyclic order. Repeated vertices or edges in a facial boundary walk are treated as separate side occurrences, so a bridge's two sides remain distinct; an isolated vertex gives a punctured-disk collar in its unique incident face. Choose all radii and widths small enough that distinct collars meet only at their prescribed continuations within the same face. Trimming them leaves a nonempty core $U_A=U\setminus N_A$, since the selected point of $U$ lies outside $N_A$. The core is connected: for finite points use the polygonal path in the plane face $U$ supplied by [F7], perturb the path to meet the finitely many polygonal collar sides transversely, and replace each excursion into a collar by a parallel path just outside $N_A$ along that collar's connected $U$-facing boundary, with the vertex-disk sector prescribing the continuation at each turn. Thus the same connected core includes infinity. Each face therefore leaves exactly one nonempty component of $S^2\setminus N_A$. Since $N_A$ contains $G_A$, these trimmed faces are all the components of $S^2\setminus N_A$; by step 1.1 their number is $k^*(A)$. The regions of $S^2\setminus\partial N_A$ are the interiors of the $k(A)$ components of $N_A$ together with those $k^*(A)$ complementary components, so there are $k(A)+k^*(A)$ regions.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, let $Q\geq2$ be an integer, and let each edge activity $v_e$ be finite and nonnegative. Use the Potts weight $w_P(\sigma)=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}}(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}})$ and FK weight $w_{FK}(A)=Q^{k_G(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e$ from the finite definitions. Define
$$W(\sigma,A):=\prod_{e\notin A}1\prod_{e\in A}v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}},\qquad (\sigma,A)\in[Q]^V\times2^E.$$
The normalized joint law $\nu(\sigma,A):=W(\sigma,A)/\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$ has Potts marginal $w_P/Z_P$ and FK marginal $w_{FK}/Z_{FK}$, with $Z_P=Z_{FK}=\sum_{\tau,B}W(\tau,B)$. Conditional on an edge set $A$ of positive probability, the colors of its connected components are independent and uniform on $[Q]$. Thus for every $x,y\in V$,
$$\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=\frac1Q+\left(1-\frac1Q\right)\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y),$$
where $x\leftrightarrow y$ means that $x$ and $y$ lie in the same component of $G_A$.

derivations.claim: There are two edge subsets. The empty subset has two isolated components and weight $Q^2$; the occupied subset has one component and weight $Qv$. Thus $Z_{FK}=Q^2+Qv$ and $\mathbb P_{FK}(x\leftrightarrow y)=Qv/(Q^2+Qv)=v/(Q+v)$, also when $v=0$.
Substitution in [F2] gives $\mathbb P(\sigma(x)=\sigma(y))=Q^{-1}+(1-Q^{-1})v/(Q+v)=(1+v)/(Q+v)$.

Direct spin enumeration checks the same result: $Q$ equal-color assignments each have weight $1+v$, and $Q(Q-1)$ unequal-color assignments each have weight $1$, so $Z_P=Q(1+v)+Q(Q-1)=Q^2+Qv$ and the same-color probability is $Q(1+v)/(Q^2+Qv)=(1+v)/(Q+v)$.

derivations.claim: A finite connected graph has a spanning tree: start with one vertex and, while the current vertex set is not $V$, add an edge from that set to its complement together with the new endpoint. Such an edge exists because otherwise no path could join the current set to its complement. Finiteness makes this process terminate; each added edge attaches one new vertex, so the resulting spanning subgraph is connected and has no cycle.

We prove by induction on the number of vertices that the $k$-element subsets of any finite tree are connected for every admissible $k$. The assertion holds for a one-vertex tree, since its $0$- and $1$-element subset graphs each have one vertex. For a tree $T$ with at least two vertices, choose a simple path of maximum length; either endpoint is a leaf, because an additional neighbor outside the path would extend it, while an additional neighbor on the path would create a cycle. Let $v$ be a leaf. Removing a leaf leaves a connected acyclic graph, hence a smaller tree: the unique path between two remaining vertices cannot have the leaf as an interior vertex. If two configurations $A,B$ have the same occupancy at $v$, removing $v$ leaves two subsets of the same cardinality in $T-v$; by induction a sequence of legal moves there connects them, and the same moves in $T$ keep the occupancy at $v$ fixed.

Suppose $v\in A$ and $v
otin B$. Since $k<m$, choose a vacant vertex $w
otin A$ and let $v=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_r=w$ be the unique simple path in $T$ from $v$ to $w$. Existence follows from connectedness, and two distinct simple paths would contain a cycle, so the path is unique. Let $j$ be the first index with $v_j
otin A$; then $v_0,\ldots,v_{j-1}$ are occupied. Move the particle at $v_{j-1}$ to the vacancy $v_j$, then the particle at $v_{j-2}$ to the new vacancy $v_{j-1}$, and continue until the particle at $v_0$ has moved to $v_1$. These are legal edge moves and leave $v$ vacant. The resulting configuration and $B$, restricted to $T-v$, both have $k$ particles; induction connects them without using $v$.

Suppose $v\notin A$ and $v\in B$. Since $k>0$, choose an occupied vertex $w\in A$ and use the unique path $v=v_0,\ldots,v_r=w$. Let $j$ be the first index with $v_j\in A$; all earlier vertices are vacant. Move the particle from $v_j$ to $v_{j-1}$, then from $v_{j-1}$ to $v_{j-2}$, and continue until $v_0=v$ is occupied. The moves are legal along the path. The resulting configuration and $B$, restricted to $T-v$, both have $k-1$ particles; induction connects them without using $v$. This proves the claim for trees, including the cases $k=0$ and $k=m$ already covered by their singleton configuration graphs.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

$$\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_t(x)G(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb T^d}\rho_0(x)G(x)\,dx+\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb T^d}u_s(x)\Delta G(x)\,dx\,ds$$

for every $0\le t\le T$. Here $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{x_i}^2$ is the periodic Laplacian; equality of function classes means equality almost everywhere with respect to $dx$. For the Fourier convention on this torus, set $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and $\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dx$ for $f\in L^1(\mathbb T^d,dx)$.

derivations.claim: Since $0\le\rho_0\le1$ and $dx(\mathbb T^d)=1$, $\rho_0\in L^1$ and $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ for every $k$. For any smooth $G$ and integer $m\ge1$, periodic integration by parts gives $(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^m\widehat G(k)=\widehat{(1-\Delta)^mG}(k)$, hence $|\widehat G(k)|\le\|(1-\Delta)^mG\|_{L^1}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)^{-m}$. If $q\ge0$ is fixed, choose $m>(d+q)/2$; grouping lattice points by $r=\|k\|_\infty$ gives at most $(2r+1)^d-(2r-1)^d\le C_dr^{d-1}$ points in shell $r$. The shell contribution to $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|$ is at most $C r^{d-1+q-2m}$. Grouping shells into dyadic blocks $2^j\le r<2^{j+1}$ bounds the $j$th block by $C'2^{j(d+q-2m)}$, a convergent geometric series since $2m>d+q$. Thus $\sum_k(1+|k|)^q|\widehat G(k)|<\infty$.

For each $t>0$ and each fixed derivative order, multiplication of the coefficients by any corresponding polynomial in $k$ still leaves an absolutely summable sequence, because $|\widehat\rho_0(k)|\le1$ and the Gaussian factor $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ dominates every inverse power on lattice shells. Therefore the heat series and all fixed-order differentiated series converge uniformly on $\mathbb T^d$ for $t\ge\varepsilon>0$. Pairing the $k$ and $-k$ terms shows $\rho_t$ is real. Termwise differentiation is valid on every such compact time interval; both $\partial_t$ and $\Delta$ multiply the $k$th term by $-4\pi^2|k|^2$, so $\partial_t\rho_t=\Delta\rho_t$.

The decay estimate in step 1.1 makes the Fourier series for $G$ and for each fixed space or time derivative of $P_tG$ uniformly absolutely convergent even at $t=0$. By [F2], the series at $t=0$ equals $G$ in $L^2$; both are continuous, so equality almost everywhere implies equality everywhere. Uniform convergence of the differentiated series proves smoothness and uniform derivative bounds on $[0,T]\times\mathbb T^d$. Also $\|P_tG-G\|_\infty\le\sum_k|\widehat G(k)|\,|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|\to0$ by splitting into a finite set of modes and an absolutely summable tail. Termwise differentiation gives $\partial_tP_tG=\Delta P_tG$.

Absolute convergence permits termwise integration against $\rho_0\in L^1$. Reindexing $k\mapsto-k$ and using the even multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}$ gives $\int\rho_tG=\sum_k e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)\widehat G(-k)=\int\rho_0P_tG$. By step 2.2 this pairing tends to $\int\rho_0G$ as $t\downarrow0$. Differentiating the pairing for $t>0$ and using $\Delta P_tG=P_t\Delta G$ yields $\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho_tG=\int\rho_t\Delta G$; integration from $0$ proves the weak identity in [F3]. Thus the constructed family is a weak heat solution.

Parseval and the heat coefficients give $\|\rho_t-\rho_0\|_2^2=\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2|e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}-1|^2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$: choose a finite set whose tail in the convergent series $\sum_k|\widehat\rho_0(k)|^2$ is small, then take the limit on that finite set. For $\epsilon>0$ put $a_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1-z/\sqrt{z^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Phi_\epsilon(z)=\int_0^z\int_0^r a_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. Then $\Phi_\epsilon$ is smooth and convex, $\Phi_\epsilon(0)=\Phi_\epsilon'(0)=0$, and $0\le\Phi_\epsilon(z)\le z^2/2$. On any interval $[a,b]\subset(0,T]$, the heat equation, chain rule, and periodic integration by parts give $\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_b)-\int\Phi_\epsilon(\rho_a)=-\int_a^b\int\Phi_\epsilon''(\rho_s)\sum_{i=1}^d|\partial_{x_i}\rho_s|^2\,dx\,ds\le0$. For each real $z$, the defining double integral tends to $\frac12(z^-)^2$, where $z^-:=\max\{-z,0\}$; dominated convergence on the bounded range of $\rho$ over $[a,b]\times\mathbb T^d$ gives the same monotonicity for $\|\rho_t^-\|_2^2$. Letting $a\downarrow0$, the $L^2$ continuity just proved and $\rho_0\ge0$ imply $\rho_t^-=0$. The assumed datum already gives the required bound when $T=0$.

For the upper bound put $b_\epsilon(z)=\frac12(1+(z-1)/\sqrt{(z-1)^2+\epsilon^2})$ and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)=\int_1^z\int_1^r b_\epsilon(q)\,dq\,dr$. This is smooth and convex with $\Psi_\epsilon(1)=\Psi_\epsilon'(1)=0$ and $0\le\Psi_\epsilon(z)\le(z-1)^2/2$. The same integration by parts gives $\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_b)\le\int\Psi_\epsilon(\rho_a)$ for $0<a<b$, and $\Psi_\epsilon(z)\to\frac12((z-1)^+)^2$, where $r^+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Dominated convergence and $L^2$ continuity at zero, together with $\rho_0\le1$, give $(\rho_t-1)^+=0$. The zero Fourier coefficient is unchanged by the heat multiplier, so $\int\rho_t=\widehat\rho_0(0)=\int\rho_0$. The assumed datum already gives the bound when $T=0$.

Let $(u_t)$ be any weak heat solution in the sense of [F3]. Testing its weak identity with $e_{-k}$ shows $g_k(t):=\widehat u_t(k)$ is continuous and satisfies $g_k(t)=\widehat\rho_0(k)-4\pi^2|k|^2\int_0^t g_k(s)\,ds$. Hence $g_k$ is differentiable and solves $g_k'=-4\pi^2|k|^2g_k$, so $g_k(t)=e^{-4\pi^2|k|^2t}\widehat\rho_0(k)$, the coefficient of the constructed $\rho_t$. For each $t$, both functions are in $L^2$; equality of all Fourier coefficients and completeness in [F2] imply $u_t=\rho_t$ almost everywhere. Thus the weak heat solution is unique.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let
$\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its normalized Haar integral
$dm_{\mathbb T}$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).

**Characters.** For $k\in\mathbb Z$ define $e_k:\mathbb T\to\mathbb C$ by
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\,\widetilde x)$ for $x=[\widetilde x]\in\mathbb T$,
where $\exp$ is the complex exponential ([[def-complex-exponential]]). The
definition is independent of the representative $\widetilde x$: replacing
$\widetilde x$ by $\widetilde x+n$ with $n\in\mathbb Z$ adds the period
$2\pi kn$ to the argument of sine and cosine. Each $e_k$ is continuous, hence
Borel, and satisfies

$$e_k(x)e_l(x)=e_{k+l}(x),\qquad |e_k(x)|=1,\qquad \overline{e_k(x)}=e_{-k}(x) ,$$

the last two by the cartesian form $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of
[[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]. In particular $e_0=1$ and every
$e_k$ is bounded and nonzero everywhere.

**Fourier coefficients.** Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]), that is, a class
of Borel functions with $\int_{\mathbb T}|f|\,dm_{\mathbb T}<+\infty$. Define the
**Fourier coefficient** of $f$ at $k\in\mathbb Z$ by

$$\widehat f(k):=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)e_{-k}(x)\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}f(x)\exp(-2\pi ikx)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$

This is well defined: $|f\,e_{-k}|=|f|$ because $|e_{-k}|=1$, so
$f\,e_{-k}\in L^1(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and its integral is finite; and the
integral depends only on the class of $f$, because it is unchanged when $f$ is
modified on a null set
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). The map
$f\mapsto\widehat f(k)$ is complex-linear for each $k$
([[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]).

**Trigonometric polynomials.** A **trigonometric polynomial** on $\mathbb T$ is
a finite complex linear combination of characters, $p=\sum_{k\in F}c_ke_k$, for
a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z$ and scalars $c_k\in\mathbb C$. The set of all
trigonometric polynomials is the span of $\{e_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; it is closed
under addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication and complex conjugation
(by the identities for $e_ke_l$ and $\overline{e_k}$), and it contains $e_0=1$.
Nothing is claimed here about uniqueness of the coefficients in an expansion,
nor about the size of $\widehat p$; those are properties of the characters
proved below.

**The finite torus.** On $\mathbb T^n$, $n\ge1$, the characters are
$e_k(x):=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, where $k\cdot x$ is the
Euclidean dot product of a representative tuple; trigonometric polynomials are
finite complex linear combinations of these, and Fourier coefficients of
$f\in L^1(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ are
$\widehat f(k)=\int_{\mathbb T^n}f\,e_{-k}\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}$. Fubini computes
integrals of products of characters on the product measure
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); for
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T^n;\mathbb C)$ Hölder's inequality makes $f\,e_{-k}$
integrable ([[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]],
[[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]]).

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The Ionescu–Tulcea construction [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] supplies the countable random sequence under the stated Choice assumption. The theorem on this page proves nonexplosion, identifies the transition semigroup, and establishes the positive reversible spectral gap. This is a finite mathematical rate model, not a derivation of rates from Hamiltonian mechanics.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $E=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for a finite integer $m\ge1$. A rate matrix on $E$ is a real matrix $L=(L_{ij})_{i,j\in E}$ such that $L_{ij}\ge0$ for $i\ne j$ and $\sum_{j\in E}L_{ij}=0$ for every $i$. Write $\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}L_{ij}$, so $L_{ii}=-\lambda_i$. The row convention acts on a column observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$ by $(Lf)(i)=\sum_jL_{ij}f(j)$; a row probability vector evolves by right multiplication.

Fix an initial probability vector $\nu$ on $E$ and put $q=\max_i\lambda_i$. If $q=0$, then $L=0$ and the associated realization is the constant process $X_t=Y_0$ with $Y_0\sim\nu$. If $q>0$, put $R=I+L/q$, a stochastic matrix. A uniformized realization consists of a probability space carrying a discrete-time Markov sequence $(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ with initial law $\nu$ and transition matrix $R$, and independent random variables $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ that are independent of the entire sequence $Y$ and satisfy $\mathbb P(W_n>u)=e^{-qu}$ for $u\ge0$. Here a discrete-time Markov sequence with transition matrix $R$ means that
$$\mathbb P(A\cap\{Y_{n+1}=j\})=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_A R_{Y_nj}]$$
for every $n\ge0$, $j\in E$, and $A\in\sigma(Y_0,\ldots,Y_n)$. Each $W_n$ therefore has the exponential distribution of rate $q$; in particular its mean is $q^{-1}$. Require $\sum_{n\ge1}W_n=+\infty$ almost surely. Put $T_0=0$, $T_n=\sum_{k=1}^nW_k$, and, on this probability-one event, $N_t=\max\{n:T_n\le t\}$ and $X_t=Y_{N_t}$. On its null complement set $N_t=0$ and $X_t=Y_0$. The construction filtration is $\mathcal F_t=\sigma(N_s,X_s:0\le s\le t)$; it records event counts and states through time $t$ and is not completed or made right-continuous by this definition.

This uniformized construction permits reducible rate matrices and states with zero exit rate. A local existence result proves that every finite rate matrix and initial law admit such a realization and that its conditional transition matrices are $e^{tL}:=\sum_{n=0}^\infty t^nL^n/n!$.

Then there exists a uniformized realization under the conventions stated below. Its paths are càdlàg and almost surely have only finitely many event times on each bounded interval (nonexplosion), and, for all $0\le s\le t$,
$$\mathbb P(X_t=j\mid\mathcal F_s)=(e^{(t-s)L})_{X_sj}\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\mathcal F_s=\sigma(N_u,X_u:0\le u\le s)$ is the construction filtration. In particular, $e^{tL}$ is the transition matrix from any initial state.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, meaning every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and an integer $N\ge3$. Let $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$, with each coordinate represented by $0,1,\ldots,N-1$, and let $\mathcal E_N$ be the set of unordered nearest-neighbor bonds $\{x,x+e_i\}$, where $1\le i\le d$ and addition is modulo $N$. The condition $N\ge3$ makes this a simple graph with each bond listed once as $x$ ranges over $\Lambda_N$. The site graph is connected because any two coordinate tuples are joined by finitely many steps of $+e_i$ or $-e_i$.

The configuration space is $\Omega_N=\{\eta:\Lambda_N\to\{0,1\}\}$, ordered lexicographically by its binary occupation vector in the fixed site order; this labels it as a finite set $\{1,\ldots,2^{N^d}\}$. The occupation $\eta_x$ is $1$ for an occupied site and $0$ for a vacant site. For $b=\{x,y\}\in\mathcal E_N$, let $\eta^b$ be the configuration obtained by swapping $\eta_x$ and $\eta_y$.

The coordinates $x/N$ have dimensionless spacing $1/N$ on the unit torus, and $t$ is dimensionless diffusive time: it is the microscopic unit-rate bond clock accelerated by the factor $N^2$. Thus the continuum heat equation below has normalized diffusion coefficient $D=1$.

Define a rate matrix $L_N$ on $\Omega_N$ by giving each distinct state change $\eta\to\eta^b\ne\eta$ rate $N^2$ and setting the diagonal entry to the negative sum of the off-diagonal row. If the two occupations on a bond agree, swapping them produces no state change and contributes no off-diagonal transition. On a column observable $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb R$, use the row-generator convention $(L_Nf)(\eta)=\sum_{\xi\ne\eta}L_N(\eta,\xi)(f(\xi)-f(\eta))$; a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pL_N$. The **symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP)** is the uniformized finite-state chain with rate matrix $L_N$ and any specified initial probability vector. The finite-generator existence result supplies its all-pairs transition matrices $e^{tL_N}$ and càdlàg paths. Every jump conserves $\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x$.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N^d$, the fixed-occupancy sector is $\Omega_{N,k}=\{\eta\in\Omega_N:\sum_x\eta_x=k\}$. When $0<k<N^d$, this sector has at least two states and its transition graph is connected by the fixed-occupancy connectivity lemma. Setting every sector energy to $0$, $\beta=1$, and each allowed transition rate to $N^2$ makes this sector a finite reversible stochastic rate model with uniform stationary weights. The sectors $k=0$ and $k=N^d$ are singleton constant chains. The full SSEP state graph is reducible across particle-number sectors; the generic finite rate-matrix construction, not the irreducible reversible-model definition, defines the full process.

Let $\mathbb T^d=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^d$ with normalized Haar measure $dx$. For $x\in\Lambda_N$, write $x/N\in\mathbb T^d$ for the point with coordinates represented in $[0,1)$. The empirical measure and its action on a smooth periodic test function $G$ are

$$\pi_t^N:=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)\,\delta_{x/N},\qquad \langle\pi_t^N,G\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb T^d}G\,d\pi_t^N=N^{-d}\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\eta_x(t)G(x/N).$$

Here $\delta_y$ denotes unit point mass at $y$. Thus $\pi_t^N$ is a finite positive measure of total mass at most $1$, not necessarily a probability measure. For a smooth periodic $G$, define its discrete Laplacian on grid points by

$$\Delta_NG(x/N):=N^2\sum_{i=1}^d\bigl[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)\bigr].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E$ be finite and nonempty, let $L$ be a rate matrix on $E$, let $X$ be its uniformized realization from the preceding existence result, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Put $g=Lf$ and
$$M_t=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t g(X_s)\,ds,\qquad \Gamma_f(i)=L(f^2)(i)-2f(i)Lf(i).$$For every finite $T$, $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ is a square-integrable martingale relative to the construction filtration, and$$A_t:=\int_0^t\Gamma_f(X_s)\,ds$$
is its continuous predictable bracket: $A_0=0$, $A$ is increasing and predictable, and $M_t^2-A_t$ is a martingale. The bracket is understood in the continuous predictable increasing compensator convention stated in the proof.

derivations.claim: Put $f_G(\eta)=N^{-d}\sum_x\eta_xG(x/N)$. For the bond $\{x,x+e_i\}$, $f_G(\eta^{x,x+e_i})-f_G(\eta)=N^{-d}(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)(G(x/N)-G((x+e_i)/N))$. Summing its rate-$N^2$ contribution over all $x,i$ and reindexing the terms containing $\eta_{x+e_i}$ gives $L_Nf_G(\eta)=N^{-d}\sum_x\eta_xN^2\sum_i[G((x+e_i)/N)+G((x-e_i)/N)-2G(x/N)]=\langle\pi^N(\eta),\Delta_NG\rangle$. Thus the finite-chain martingale in [F2], applied to $f_G$, is exactly $M_t^{N,G}$ and has bracket given by the sum of rates times squared jumps.

A bond with equal endpoint occupations has zero jump; otherwise its squared jump is $N^{-2d}(G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N))^2$. Substituting these jumps and rate $N^2$ into [F2] gives the displayed bracket. By the fundamental theorem of calculus along the coordinate segment, $|G((x+e_i)/N)-G(x/N)|\le N^{-1}\|\partial_iG\|_\infty$, while $(\eta_{x+e_i}-\eta_x)^2\le1$. There are $N^d$ bonds in each coordinate direction, so the bracket is increasing, continuous, predictable, and bounded by $TN^{-d}\sum_i\|\partial_iG\|_\infty^2$. The finite state space makes $f_G$ bounded, hence [F2] also gives square integrability.
