citations.quote:
Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph: $V$ and the edge-label set $E$ are finite, and each $e\in E$ has a singleton or two-element endpoint set $\partial e\subseteq V$. Distinct labels may have the same endpoint set. Let $B\subseteq V$ be a designated boundary set and let $\xi$ be an equivalence relation on $B$; vertices in each $\xi$-class are wired together, while vertices outside $B$ remain separate. For $A\subseteq E$, let $k_\xi(A)$ be the number of connected components, including isolated vertices, after wiring the $\xi$-classes and opening exactly the edges in $A$. A loop does not join distinct vertices.

For $q\in[1,\infty)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK weight of $A$ and its partition function are

$$w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)},\qquad Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}:=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A).$$

The finite FK random-cluster probability is $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)/Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$. Every weight is positive and finite, and the finite sum $Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ is positive and finite. The free boundary condition is the identity partition on $B$; the wired boundary condition identifies all vertices of $B$ in one class.

When $G$ is a finite simple graph with the Potts/FK convention of the earlier finite Potts definition, $\xi$ is free, $q=Q$ is an integer at least two, and every activity equals $v=p/(1-p)$, this definition gives the same normalized FK law, since $w_{FK}(A)=(1-p)^{-|E|}w_{G,p,Q}^{\xi}(A)$.

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

For an integer $m\geq1$, let $T_m$ be the labelled square cellulation obtained by quotienting the unit square cellulation of $\mathbb R^2$ by $m\mathbb Z^2$. Its vertices are $V=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$. For every $(i,j)\in V$, retain a horizontal edge label $h(i,j)$ from $(i,j)$ to $(i+1,j)$, a vertical edge label $v(i,j)$ from $(i,j)$ to $(i,j+1)$, and a square face label $f(i,j)$. All indices are modulo $m$. Distinct labels remain distinct even when their endpoints agree: for $m=2$ this retains parallel edges, and for $m=1$ it retains two loops. In a face boundary retain its four edge occurrences before reducing coefficients modulo two. Thus $|V|=|F|=m^2$ and $|E|=2m^2$. The dual has vertices $f(i,j)$ and a separate label $e^*$ crossing each primal label $e$; specifically $h(i,j)^*$ joins $f(i,j-1)$ to $f(i,j)$ and $v(i,j)^*$ joins $f(i-1,j)$ to $f(i,j)$. Its faces correspond to primal vertices and use the dual square cellulation.

Let $\mathbb F_2=\{0,1\}$ be the field with addition and multiplication modulo two. Let $C_0=\mathbb F_2^V$, $C_1=\mathbb F_2^E$, and $C_2=\mathbb F_2^F$ have the indicated labelled bases. Define $\partial_1:C_1\to C_0$ by summing the two endpoint occurrences of each edge, so a loop has zero boundary, and define $\partial_2:C_2\to C_1$ by

$$\partial_2 f(i,j)=h(i,j)+v(i+1,j)+h(i,j+1)+v(i,j).$$

Then $\partial_1\partial_2=0$ and $H:=\ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2$ has dimension two. For $A\subseteq E$, let $C_1(A)$ be the coordinate subspace generated by its labels, put $Z(A)=C_1(A)\cap\ker\partial_1$, and define

$$r(A):=\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\operatorname{im}\bigl(Z(A)\longrightarrow H\bigr).$$

Let $k(A)$ count all components of the spanning graph $(V,A)$, including isolated vertices. Let $A^*=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, and let $k^*(A^*)$ count all components of this dual spanning graph. Define $r^*(A^*)$ by the same matrix construction on the dual cellulation. Then

$$r(A)\in\{0,1,2\},\qquad k^*(A^*)-1=|A|-|V|+k(A)-r(A),\qquad r^*(A^*)=2-r(A).$$

For every real $q\geq1$, set $p=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. Give both primal and dual graphs the finite FK law with parameter $(p,q)$ and identity boundary partition. Write $w(A)$ and $w^*(A^*)$ for their unnormalized weights, $\phi$ and $\phi^*$ for their laws, and $\nu$ for the image of $\phi$ under $A\mapsto A^*$. Then

$$\frac{w(A)}{w^*(A^*)}=q^{r(A)-1}.$$

For every dual configuration $B\subseteq E^*$, the two partition functions are equal and the exact normalized likelihood is

$$\frac{\nu(B)}{\phi^*(B)}=q^{1-r^*(B)}.$$

In particular this likelihood lies in $[q^{-1},q]$, and hence also in $[q^{-2},q^2]$. For every event $\mathcal E\subseteq2^{E^*}$,

$$q^{-2}\phi^*(\mathcal E)\leq\nu(\mathcal E)\leq q^2\phi^*(\mathcal E).$$

The same event bounds hold after any labelled graph isomorphism identifying the dual torus with the primal torus.

Let $P$ have vertices $(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2$ with $u\equiv v\pmod2$ and straight edges with displacement $(\pm1,\pm1)$. For a positive integer $m$, quotient its labelled cellulation by the periods $(m,m)$ and $(-m,m)$, retaining distinct edge labels even if endpoints agree. Give this torus the finite FK law $\phi$ with identity boundary partition, real $q\geq1$, and $p=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. A closed coordinate rectangle means its induced primal graph on the indicated integer vertices. A horizontal crossing joins its extreme left and right coordinate layers; a vertical crossing joins its extreme bottom and top layers, using only its edges. Paths may be stopped at their first target-layer visit.

Put

$$r(q)=\frac1{1+\sqrt q},\qquad a_0(q)=\frac1{1+q^2},\qquad a(q)=r(q)a_0(q),\qquad b(q)=\frac{a(q)^3}{2(1+q^2)}.$$

For every positive integer $N$ divisible by four and every $m>N$, the closed square $[0,N]^2$ has horizontal and vertical crossing probabilities at least $a(q)$. If additionally $m>3N/2$, the closed rectangle $[0,3N/2]\times[0,N]$ has horizontal crossing probability at least $b(q)$, and the corresponding vertical crossing bound holds for $[0,N]\times[0,3N/2]$. The same bounds hold after every translation by a vertex of $P$. Every rectangle in these conclusions embeds in the torus under its stated size condition. No restriction on $q$ beyond real $q\geq1$ is imposed.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

derivations.claim: The invertible linear map $u=x+y$, $v=y-x$ sends the ordinary square lattice to $P$ and its nearest-neighbor edges to the diagonal edges. Its inverse is $x=(u-v)/2$, $y=(u+v)/2$. Ordinary periods $(m,0),(0,m)$ become $(m,-m),(m,m)$, generating exactly the diagonal-period lattice in [F4]. It is therefore a labelled graph isomorphism, preserving the weights in [F1]. A rotated patch with both coordinate spans less than $m$ embeds: every nonzero period has at least one coordinate of absolute value at least $m$. We may compute probabilities of such patches in these coordinates. The cellular torus comparison [F3] is the likelihood input used in [F4], not an unproved planar substitution for torus topology.

A closed rotated vertical rectangle of width $S\in4\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and height $2S$ has crossing probability at least $d=b^2a$ if $2S<m$. Indeed take the vertical crossings of $[0,S]\times[0,3S/2]$ and $[0,S]\times[S/2,2S]$, and a horizontal crossing of their overlap square $[0,S]\times[S/2,3S/2]$. The vertical bounds are [F4] after coordinate interchange; the shift $S/2$ is even and preserves $P$. The square bound is also [F4]. Each horizontal path intersects both vertical paths by [F5], so their union gives the required vertical crossing. FKG [F2] gives $b^2a$. Translation by any integer vector with even coordinate sum preserves the lattice, the periodic FK law, and this estimate. Restricting a taller crossing at its first hit of any intermediate integer height gives a crossing of the truncated rectangle.

Suppose $n\geq32$. Set $k=\lfloor n/32\rfloor$, $L=16k$, $h=4k=L/4$, $W=\lceil\alpha n\rceil$ and $J=\lceil W/h\rceil$. For $0\leq j\leq J$ put $a_j=jh$, $b_j=-jh$, and take the closed squares
$$Q_j=[a_j,a_j+L]\times[b_j,b_j+L].$$
For $0\leq j<J$ take the closed connectors
$$C_j=[a_j+h,a_j+L]\times[b_j-h,b_j+L].$$
Each connector has width $12k$ and height $20k$. Since $a_j+b_j=0$, every vertex of every square and connector has original coordinate $0\leq y=(u+v)/2\leq L\leq n$. The corner translations $(jh,-jh)$ preserve $P$. Every square embeds and has horizontal crossing probability at least $a$ by [F4], since $L<m$. A vertical aspect-two rectangle of the same connector width $S=12k$, starting at its bottom, has height $24k<n<m$. Step 1.2 bounds its vertical crossing probability below by $d$. Truncation at height $20k$ implies a vertical crossing of $C_j$, so that event too has probability at least $d$. Its witness may use the taller box to establish the numerical bound, but the event being intersected below is supported on $C_j$ itself.

Require horizontal crossings of all $Q_j$ and vertical crossings of all $C_j$. In $Q_j\cap C_j$ the horizontal path has a subpath crossing its width-$12k$ span, while the vertical path has a subpath crossing its full height-$L$ span. They intersect by [F5]. The same applies to $Q_{j+1}\cap C_j$, whose height-$L$ span is shifted down by $h$. Thus the union is a connected actual-open-edge set. Their joined path stays in $0\leq y\leq n$ by step 2.1. Truncate this path between its last vertex on $x=0$ before its first hit of $x=W$. It gives the required ordinary-grid crossing of $\{0,\ldots,W\}\times\{0,\ldots,n\}$. The patches need not jointly embed: lift the periodic configuration to the plane and choose the guaranteed crossings in these fixed lifts. Their adjacent overlaps are literal planar overlaps. The final target itself embeds, since $W<m$ and $n<m$, so its projected crossing is unambiguous.

By finite FKG [F2], the joint event in step 3.1 has probability at least $a^{J+1}d^J\geq\min(a,d)^{2J+1}$. Because $k\geq n/64$ for $n\geq32$, $h\geq n/16$ and $h\geq4$. This proves the stronger ceiling-width statement for all stated sizes.

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph: $V$ and the edge-label set $E$ are finite, and each $e\in E$ has a singleton or two-element endpoint set $\partial e\subseteq V$. Distinct labels may have the same endpoint set. Let $B\subseteq V$ be a designated boundary set and let $\xi$ be an equivalence relation on $B$; vertices in each $\xi$-class are wired together, while vertices outside $B$ remain separate. For $A\subseteq E$, let $k_\xi(A)$ be the number of connected components, including isolated vertices, after wiring the $\xi$-classes and opening exactly the edges in $A$. A loop does not join distinct vertices.

For $q\in[1,\infty)$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK weight of $A$ and its partition function are

$$w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)},\qquad Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}:=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A).$$

The finite FK random-cluster probability is $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A):=w_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)/Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$. Every weight is positive and finite, and the finite sum $Z_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ is positive and finite. The free boundary condition is the identity partition on $B$; the wired boundary condition identifies all vertices of $B$ in one class.

When $G$ is a finite simple graph with the Potts/FK convention of the earlier finite Potts definition, $\xi$ is free, $q=Q$ is an integer at least two, and every activity equals $v=p/(1-p)$, this definition gives the same normalized FK law, since $w_{FK}(A)=(1-p)^{-|E|}w_{G,p,Q}^{\xi}(A)$.

Let $n\ge2$ be an integer and let $C\subseteq[0,1]^n$ be coordinatewise increasing and a finite union of axis-parallel boxes, with specified open or closed endpoint conventions. Degenerate boxes are allowed. Let $v_r$ denote elementary $r$-dimensional box volume: a box has the product of its side lengths as volume, and finite unions are evaluated by a common coordinate-endpoint subdivision, with coordinate faces assigned volume zero. Put $f=\mathbf1_C$, $a=v_n(C)$, and

$$F_i=v_{n-1}\{x_{-i}\in[0,1]^{n-1}:f(x_{-i},1)-f(x_{-i},0)=1\},\qquad M=\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i.$$

If $M=0$, then $a(1-a)=0$. If $M>0$, then

$$a(1-a)\le\frac{2\sum_{i=1}^nF_i}{1+\log(1/M)}.$$

In every case,

$$\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i\ge\frac14a(1-a)\frac{\log n}{n}.$$

Logarithms are natural. Endpoint influence uses the actual values on the faces. The assertion and proof use only finite box volumes, finite probability spaces and elementary real calculus; they require no countable product measure or choice principle.

derivations.claim: We first establish two conditional comparisons. Fix some coordinates and change one prescribed value from zero to one. The resulting laws $\mu_0,\mu_1$ on the unprescribed coordinates are strictly positive and associated by [F1]. For $z\le z'$, apply log-supermodularity to the incomparable configurations $(z',0)$ and $(z,1)$ to obtain $\mu_1(z')\mu_0(z)\ge\mu_0(z')\mu_1(z)$; normalizing constants cancel. Thus $R=\mu_1/\mu_0$ is increasing, $\mathbb E_{\mu_0}R=1$, and association gives $\mathbb E_{\mu_1}h=\mathbb E_{\mu_0}(hR)\ge\mathbb E_{\mu_0}h$ for every increasing $h$. Successively changing prescribed coordinates proves conditional monotonicity for ordered assignments on the same prescribed set. Separately, in any fixed-prefix conditional law, association gives $\operatorname{Cov}(h,X_j)\ge0$, whence $\mathbb E[h\mid X_j=0]\le\mathbb E h\le\mathbb E[h\mid X_j=1]$ for increasing $h$. Strict positivity makes both conditional expectations defined. This second comparison allows an additional coordinate to be prescribed.

Label the edges $1,\ldots,n$. For a prefix $\eta$ put $a_r(\eta)=\phi(X_r=1\mid X_s=\eta_s,\ s<r)$ and $t_r(\eta)=1-a_r(\eta)$; positivity gives $0<t_r<1$. For $U\in[0,1]^n$ define recursively $\Phi_r(U)=\mathbf1_{\{U_r>t_r(\Phi_{<r}(U))\}}$. The first comparison in step 1.1 makes each $a_r$ increasing, so induction makes $\Phi$ coordinatewise increasing. For every $\omega\in\{0,1\}^n$, its exact inverse image is the box $Q_\omega=\prod_r I_r(\omega)$, where $I_r(\omega)=(t_r(\omega_{<r}),1]$ if $\omega_r=1$ and $I_r(\omega)=[0,t_r(\omega_{<r})]$ if $\omega_r=0$. Indeed membership in these intervals recursively forces exactly the prefix $\omega_{<r}$ and then bit $\omega_r$. These boxes form a disjoint partition of the entire cube, including all threshold values and endpoint faces. Their elementary volumes are $v_n(Q_\omega)=\prod_r a_r(\omega_{<r})^{\omega_r}(1-a_r(\omega_{<r}))^{1-\omega_r}=\phi(\omega)$ by the finite chain rule. Consequently $C=\Phi^{-1}(A)=\bigcup_{\omega\in A}Q_\omega$ is an increasing finite-box set of elementary volume $\phi(A)$.

Fix $j$ and use the same uniforms attached to the same edge labels to construct $\Psi$ in order $j,1,\ldots,j-1,j+1,\ldots,n$. First set $U_j=1$. Both outputs have $j$th bit one. For $r<j$, suppose inductively $\Psi_{<r}\ge\Phi_{<r}$. The two comparisons in step 1.1 give
$$\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Psi_{<r},X_j=1)\ge\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r},X_j=1)\ge\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r}).$$
The common $U_r$ therefore gives $\Psi_r\ge\Phi_r$. After coordinate $j$, both constructions condition on the same set of previous labels, including $j=1$, with ordered values, so the first comparison alone continues the induction for $r>j$. Thus $\Psi(U_{-j},1)\ge\Phi(U_{-j},1)$ pointwise. With $U_j=0$, both $j$th bits are zero. For $r<j$, induction and the same two comparisons instead give
$$\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Psi_{<r},X_j=0)\le\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r},X_j=0)\le\phi(X_r=1\mid X_{<r}=\Phi_{<r}),$$
provided $\Psi_{<r}\le\Phi_{<r}$. For $r>j$ the first comparison continues this reversed order. Hence $\Psi(U_{-j},0)\le\Phi(U_{-j},0)$ pointwise as well.

Since $A$ is increasing, the pointwise comparisons in step 3.1 imply, by elementary $(n-1)$-dimensional box integration,
$$F_j(C)\le\int\mathbf1_A(\Psi(U_{-j},1))\,dU_{-j}-\int\mathbf1_A(\Psi(U_{-j},0))\,dU_{-j}=I_A(j).$$
The equality follows from the finite conditional chain rule: after the first, forced bit $j$, the reordered algorithm samples the successive conditional probabilities given that bit. Its output inverse images and their sections are finite boxes, exactly as in step 2.1, so the displayed integrals are finite volume sums. These are literal endpoint evaluations of the defined maps, not conditioning a uniform variable on a null-probability event.

Apply [F3] to $C$ from step 2.1, with $n=|E|\ge2$ and $a=\phi(A)$. For some $j$ its endpoint influence is at least $\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\log n/(4n)$. Step 4.1 bounds that influence above by $I_A(j)$, proving the stated inequality with $c(q,\varepsilon)=1/4$. All conditional laws used exist for every real $q\ge1$ and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]\subset(0,1)$.

Let $q\geq1$ be a finite real number. On the nearest-neighbor square lattice let $\Lambda_n=\{-n,\ldots,n\}^2$, let $E_n$ consist of edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_\infty=n\}$. Write $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ for the free partition when $b=0$ and the one-class wired partition when $b=1$.

For every event $C$ determined by finitely many edge coordinates, the numerical limits
$$\pi^b_{p,q}(C):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(C),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},$$
exist. They are consistent, nonnegative normalized finite-coordinate probability families, invariant under translations and quarter-turns. On increasing cylinder events they are increasing in $p$, with $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$. Every cylinder-probability limit of arbitrary boundary partitions lies between these two families on increasing cylinder events. There is an at most countable set $D_q\subset(0,1)$ such that $\pi^0_{p,q}(C)=\pi^1_{p,q}(C)$ for every cylinder event $C$ whenever $p\notin D_q$.

Let $D_r$ be the event that actual open edges inside $\Lambda_r$ join $0$ to $B_r$, and define the real numbers
$$\Theta_b(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^b_{p,q}(D_r).$$
Then $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$ for $0<p<p'<1$, and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^1_{n,p,q}(0\leftrightarrow B_n)=\Theta_1(p,q).$$
Connections here use actual edges, not artificial boundary-identification paths. These are statements about real limits and finite probability tables; existence of a countably additive probability on the infinite configuration space is not asserted.

For each $q\geq1$ and aspect ratio $\alpha>1$, there is a constant $c(\alpha,q)>0$ such that the following holds. The probability of a horizontal open crossing of the vertex rectangle $\{0,\ldots,\lceil\alpha n\rceil\}\times\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is at least $c(\alpha,q)$, uniformly in $n$ and $m$.

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph, let $B\subseteq V$ have boundary partition $\xi$, fix $q\geq1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$, and let $\phi=\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ be the finite FK law. For every increasing event $A\subseteq2^E$ with $0<\phi(A)<1$ and $|E|\geq2$, define the conditional influence of edge $e$ by

$$I_A(e):=\phi(A\mid \omega_e=1)-\phi(A\mid\omega_e=0).$$

There is a constant $c(q,\varepsilon)>0$ such that

$$\max_{e\in E}I_A(e)\geq c(q,\varepsilon)\,\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\frac{\log|E|}{|E|}.$$

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected plane graph with a fixed embedding and $|V|\geq1$. Use the free partition on all primal vertices, $B=V$. Its plane dual multigraph $G^*$ has one vertex for each face, including the unbounded face, and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; use the identity partition on the dual face-vertices. The unbounded face is one dual vertex, so this convention retains the exterior-face connection in the dual. For a primal open set $A\subseteq E$, let $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, so a dual edge is open exactly when its crossing primal edge is closed. For $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$ define $p^*\in(0,1)$ by

$$\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}=q\frac{1-p}{p}.$$

Then complementing the primal edges sends the finite FK law $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$ to the dual FK law $\phi_{G^*,p^*,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$: the random dual edge set $A^*$ has exactly that distribution. The unnormalized weight ratio is the configuration-independent factor $q^{|V|-1}((1-p)/p^*)^{|E|}$; the exponent $|V|-1$ includes the exterior-face contribution under this identity-partition convention.

Let $a,b\geq1$ be integers and let $Q_{a,b}=\{0,\ldots,a\}\times\{0,\ldots,b\}$ have its nearest-neighbor square-grid edges, drawn as unit horizontal and vertical segments. A left-to-right path is a finite edge path whose endpoints lie on the sides $x=0$ and $x=a$; a bottom-to-top path is defined analogously using $y=0$ and $y=b$. Every left-to-right path and every bottom-to-top path in $Q_{a,b}$ share a vertex.

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

derivations.claim: For an increasing event $B$ on a finite graph, differentiation of its finite FK weights gives $\phi'_p(B)=\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_B,|\omega|)/[p(1-p)]$. Writing $u_e=\phi_p(e\text{ open})$ and $I_B(e)=\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ open})-\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ closed})$ yields $\phi'_p(B)=\sum_e u_e(1-u_e)I_B(e)/[p(1-p)]$. By [F1] the coefficients have a positive lower bound on a compact parameter interval inside $(0,1)$. On an $L$-torus a translation-invariant $B$ has equal influences on each of the two edge orbits, each of size $L^2$. Thus [F4] implies $\phi'_p(B)\geq c\phi_p(B)(1-\phi_p(B))\log L$. Integrating its logistic derivative between $p_s$ and fixed $p>p_s$ shows that $\phi_{p_s}(B)\geq b>0$ implies $1-\phi_p(B)\leq C L^{-\eta}$, with constants independent of $L$.

We specify the finite stopping operation used for an outer circuit. In a finite ambient box list all simple circuits disjoint from $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$, strictly inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, and surrounding the inner square. For a candidate $\gamma$, let $I(\gamma)$ be the edges whose relative interiors lie in its bounded component, including edges entering that component from circuit vertices. Let $O(\gamma)$ contain all other ambient edges, including circuit edges. The event selecting $\Gamma=\gamma$ is: every edge of $\gamma$ is open and there is no surrounding open circuit in $O(\gamma)$ whose bounded interior strictly contains that of $\gamma$. These tests involve only $O(\gamma)$. To verify that exactly one candidate is selected whenever a surrounding circuit exists, splice any exterior excursion of another surrounding circuit with the outer arcs of $\gamma$, keeping the unbounded face on the outside, and erase subloops not surrounding the inner square. This gives a surrounding circuit in the union, on or outside $\gamma$, with strictly larger interior if that excursion protrudes. Applying this finite operation to all candidates yields an outermost circuit; two different maximal circuits would enlarge each other by the same surgery. Equal interiors have the same Jordan boundary. Thus the selected candidate is unique. For each output $(\gamma,\tau)$, where $\tau$ is the full assignment on $O(\gamma)$, the output fiber is precisely the fixed-exterior cylinder $\{\omega|_{O(\gamma)}=\tau\}$ if $\tau$ passes the tests, and is empty otherwise. Every interior assignment is admitted. This fiber identity, rather than a claim about a particular probing order, certifies that conditioning on the output never conditions an interior edge.

For $m\geq r$, reaching $\partial\Lambda_m$ entails $D_r$, and wired domain comparison gives $a_m\leq\phi^1_{m,p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. In particular $a_n$ decreases, so $\Theta^1=\inf_n a_n$ exists. Taking $m\to\infty$ in the displayed inequalities gives $\Theta^1\leq\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. Infimizing over $r$ proves $\Theta^1=\inf_r\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)$. This is a pair of real inequalities, not an exchange of two limits.

On a finite edge set and for an increasing event $D$, its Hamming distance $H_D$ is the minimum number of closed edges to open to enter $D$. Opening one coordinate lowers it by zero or one; hence $|\omega|+H_D$ is increasing, $H_D$ is decreasing, and $H_D\mathbf1_D=0$. Finite differentiation and FKG give $\frac{d}{dp}\phi_p(D)=\{\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_D,|\omega|+H_D)+\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D\}/[p(1-p)]\geq4\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D$. Integrate from $p$ to $t>p$ and use monotonicity of the decreasing $H_D$ to obtain $\phi_p(D)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_tH_D\}$. Apply this to $D_n$ in wired $\Lambda_m$ with $m>n$ and take $m\to\infty$. Both sides involve only fixed finite cylinder sums, proving the claimed Hamming inequality.

We derive the exact numerical free/wired duality from a concrete free plane graph. Let $H_m$ be the free rectangular grid on the $(2m)^2$ unit-cell centers of $\Lambda_m$. Each bounded face of $H_m$ surrounds one interior vertex of $\Lambda_m$; its one unbounded face represents all vertices of $B_m$ identified together. A dual edge of $H_m$ crosses exactly one nonperimeter edge of $\Lambda_m$, with precisely those interior-vertex or boundary-class endpoints. Thus $H_m^*$ is the wired quotient graph with the perimeter edge labels omitted. Each omitted perimeter edge is a loop after wiring, so its open/closed weight sums to $p+(1-p)=1$ independently and changes no retained-edge law. Apply [F5] to the connected free plane graph $H_m$ at parameter $t^*$, whose dual parameter is $t$. The inverse complement bijection sends the wired retained-edge law at $t$ to the free law on $H_m$ at $t^*$. This proves the finite identity before taking any limit; the exterior face is one of the wired-quotient vertices, not an additional cell-center vertex. The cell-center grids exhaust the translated dual lattice, and, after its fixed half-unit identification with $\mathbb Z^2$, lie between centered boxes with radii differing by a fixed constant. Finite domain comparison and [F2] therefore give, for every dual cylinder $E$, $\pi^1_{t,q}(\text{dual-complement }E)=\pi^0_{t^*,q}(E)$. This is a numerical cylinder identity, not a claim of an unconstructed infinite law.

To turn this estimate into a bound for one specified rectangle, first take width $2u$, height $2bu$ with integer $b\geq1$, and torus side $L=16b^2u$. Let $B$ mean that some translate of a width-$u$, height-$L/2$ rectangle has a vertical crossing. It is translation invariant and has self-dual probability bounded below by [F3], since its fixed aspect is $8b^2$ and its height is strictly less than $L$. Every such narrow strip is contained horizontally in one of the width-$2u$ strips starting on the $u$-grid, and its height interval contains a full height-$2bu$ band starting on the $2bu$-grid. Its crossing therefore crosses one of $M=(L/u)(L/(2bu))$ fixed translates of the target rectangle. Wrapping translates are lifted to the plane for this containment. If their crossing events are $B_i$, positive association of their decreasing complements gives $(1-\phi_p(B_1))^M\leq\phi_p(\bigcap_iB_i^c)\leq\phi_p(B^c)$. Step 1.1 proves $\phi_p(B_1)\geq1-Cu^{-\eta/M}$. The number $M$ is independent of $u$.

For a rectangle of width $w$ and height $h$ with $1\leq h/w\leq\beta$, take $u=\lfloor w/2\rfloor$ and a fixed integer $b$ depending only on $\beta$ with $2bu\geq h$. A crossing of the narrower, taller rectangle restricts to a crossing of the target. Rotating handles the other orientations. A fixed enlargement of $L/u$ in step 2.1 preserves the proof and accommodates any surrounding planar box of size comparable to $w$. Condition that torus law on all edges outside the box; its induced partition is bounded above by the wired partition. Hence the wired box gives the specified rectangle a crossing probability at least $1-Cw^{-\delta}$. The finitely many small widths are absorbed into $C$.

Fix $\alpha>1$. For large $k$ put $a=r_k+2$, $b=r_{k+1}-2$, $R=r_{k+2}$. Use vertical crossings of $[a,b]\times[-b,b]$ and $[-b,-a]\times[-b,b]$, horizontal crossings of $[-b,b]\times[a,b]$ and $[-b,b]\times[-b,-a]$, and a horizontal crossing of $[-R,R]\times[-b,b]$. In each corner square the adjacent side crossings intersect by [F6]; their union contains a surrounding closed walk, from which erasing nonsurrounding loops gives a simple circuit. The last crossing intersects the two vertical sides and connects that circuit to the outer boundary. All widths are comparable to $\alpha^k$ and all aspects are fixed. Step 3.1 and a union bound give $\phi^1_{r_{k+2},p,q}(A_k)\geq1-d_k$ with $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}$. Enlarge $K$ until $b>a$ and $d_k<1/2$ for $k\geq K$.

Suppose $A_{k+1},\ldots,A_n$ hold. Apply step 1.2 to the next annulus. The selected $\Gamma$ has an outgoing open connection to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+3}}$: an outgoing path from any surrounding circuit meets $\Gamma$. These outer events are measurable in its returned exterior data. For $A_{k+1}$ one may use $\Gamma$ itself, and any path excursion inside it can be replaced by an open circuit arc; circuits of $A_j$ for $j\geq k+2$ are outside it. On each output fiber, [F1] gives the interior FK law with all vertices of $\Gamma$ wired together by its actual open edges. Its connection then follows the already exposed outgoing path through $\Gamma$ to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, giving $A_k$. Averaging the exterior fibers proves $P(A_k\mid A_{k+1},\ldots,A_n)\geq1-d_k$. No square boundary is asserted to be wired in the random configuration.

Start in wired $\Lambda_{r_{n+2}}$, where $A_n$ has probability at least $1-d_n$, and descend using step 5.1. This proves the finite product bound for $\bigcap_{k=N}^n A_k$, and hence for $\bigcap_{k=N}^m A_k$. For fixed $m$, take the deterministic outer-box limit along $n\to\infty$; finite additivity and $\prod_{k=N}^n(1-d_k)\geq1-\sum_{k=N}^n d_k$ prove the stated cylinder lower bound. No probability of an infinite intersection or measure extension is used.

For $p>p_s$ choose $N\geq K$ with $\sum_{k\geq N}d_k\leq1/2$. Finite FKG and step 6.1 give $\phi^1_{r_{n+2},p,q}(T\cap\bigcap_{k=N}^m A_k)\geq\rho^{M_0}/2$ for $n\geq m\geq N$. Consecutive circuits connect because an outgoing path meets the next surrounding circuit. For any prescribed $R$, take the least $m\geq N$ with $r_{m+2}>R$; this finite chain and the tree imply $D_R$. Taking only the outer-box limit gives $\pi^1_{p,q}(D_R)\geq\rho^{M_0}/2$ for every $R$, with the same constant. Step 1.3 proves $\Theta^1(p,q)>0$.

Fix $0<s<p_s$ and choose one $t\in(s,p_s)$ such that $t^*\notin J_q$. The preimage of $J_q$ under the explicit dual bijection is countable. A point outside it can be specified without Countable Choice: enumerate that exceptional set, start with a rational closed interval inside $(s,p_s)$, and recursively take the first smaller rational closed interval in a fixed enumeration which avoids the next exceptional point and has diameter at most half the previous diameter. Its unique limit lies outside the exceptional set. Since $t^*>p_s$, step 6.1 at the dual parameter, for any chosen $\alpha>1$, supplies $N$ such that every finite intersection of dual annulus events with indices from $N$ onward has numerical wired weight at least $1/2$. By equality of the free/wired cylinder weights at $t^*$ and step 1.5, the same finite dual-circuit intersections have primal wired cylinder weight at least $1/2$ at $t$.

Retain every other annulus, so its dual circuits have disjoint edge supports. Among the annuli strictly inside $\Lambda_{n-2}$ there are at least $(\log n)/(2\log\alpha)-O(N+1)$ retained circuits; the fixed dual-lattice translation changes only the cutoff. Every primal path realizing $D_n$ must cross each such circuit at a distinct closed primal edge. On the finite cylinder supporting these circuits and $H_n$, multiply this pointwise inequality by its nonnegative atom weights and sum. Step 7.2 gives $\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{t,q}}H_n\geq(\log n)/(8\log\alpha)$ for large $n$. Taking $\log\alpha=(t-s)/(4d+8)$ in step 1.4 gives $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq n^{-(2d+4)}$ for sufficiently large $n$, proving the claimed bound after enlarging $C_d$. In particular these probabilities tend to zero, so step 1.3 yields $\Theta^1(s,q)=0$. All intersections and expectations used here are finite.

Every parameter strictly above $p_s$ belongs to the set defining the numerical threshold by step 7.1, and none strictly below belongs by step 8.1. Its infimum is therefore $p_s$. The proof never assigns a value at $p_s$ and never invokes an infinite-volume probability measure or Countable Choice.

citations.quote: A measure space is a triple $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ where $\Sigma$ contains $\varnothing,X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (a $\sigma$-algebra) of subsets of $X$ and $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive with $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function $f:X\to[-\infty,\infty]$ has measurable inverse images of Borel sets, where $[-\infty,\infty]$ has its order topology: finite open intervals and the endpoint neighborhoods $[-\infty,a)$ and $(a,\infty]$ form a basis. Its Borel sigma-algebra is generated by these open sets. A complex-valued function is measurable exactly when its finite real and imaginary parts are measurable, equivalently for the usual Borel structure of $\mathbb C$. Almost-everywhere assertions mean outside a measurable $\mu$-null set; completeness of $\mu$ is not assumed. Nonnegative extended addition uses $a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty$ for $a\in[0,\infty]$; positive scalars multiply $\infty$ to $\infty$, while $0\cdot\infty=0$. Signed expressions $\infty-\infty$ remain undefined and are not used in signed integrals. A nonnegative simple function has the form $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$ with finitely many disjoint $A_j\in\Sigma$ and finite $c_j\ge0$. Define $c\mu(A)=+\infty$ if $c>0$ and $\mu(A)=+\infty$, define $0\cdot\infty:=0$, and define the finite sum of these extended nonnegative terms to be $+\infty$ if any term is $+\infty$ and otherwise the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Then $\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_j c_j\mu(A_j)$; using canonical level sets $\{s=c\}$ makes this value representation-independent. For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\{\int s\,d\mu: s\text{ is simple and }0\le s\le f\}$, using [[def-complete-ordered-field]] for a bounded set of finite values and setting the supremum to $+\infty$ when the values are unbounded or one is infinite. A real measurable $f$ is integrable when $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, and then $\int f:=\int f^+-\int f^-$, where $f^+=\max(f,0)$ and $f^-:=\max(-f,0)$. Complex integrability and integration are defined by integrable real and imaginary parts.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.

derivations.claim: Every supremum defining $M_z$ is measurable because the roots are countable and each $S_y$ has countably many possible finite values. Translation of the common set law and [F2] give $\sum_yP(z\in S_y,|S_y|>u)=\mathbb E[|S_0|\mathbf1_{\{|S_0|>u\}}]$. This tail tends to zero: for example it is at most $u^{-1}\mathbb E|S_0|^2$. The union bound therefore shows $P(M_z>u)\to0$, hence $M_z<\infty$ almost surely. At least $S_z$ contains $z$, and every size is a positive integer, so a finite supremum is attained. Taking the countable union of the null exceptional events proves this simultaneously for all $z$. No independence of the $M_z$ is asserted.

We first prove the assertion for the independent field $X$. Suppose sites are independently marked with probability $r$. If an animal of size at most $m$ contains $k$ distinct marked sites, a depth-first traversal of a spanning tree of that animal, rooted at $0$, visits them in some order using at most $2m$ steps. The successive displacement vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb Z^2$, starting at $0$, have total $\ell^1$ length at most $2m$. There are at most $2^{2k}\binom{2m+2k}{2k}\leq(Cm/k)^{2k}$ such ordered lists for $1\leq k\leq m$: choose signs of their two coordinates and distribute at most $2m$ units among $2k$ nonnegative coordinate magnitudes. Repeated sites and zero coordinates only cause overcounting. For a list of distinct visited sites, all its sites are marked with probability $r^k$. Thus $P(\text{some animal of size at most }m\text{ has }k\text{ marked sites})\leq(C' r m^2/k^2)^k$. This counts marked-site lists rather than all animals and is uniform over all their shapes.

Put $m=2^l$, $r_j=P(X_0\geq2^j)$ and fix $\epsilon=1/4$. Choose a deterministic $a$ such that $C'/a^2\leq e^{-2}$, and a fixed $B\geq2$. For $0\leq j\leq\lfloor\epsilon\log_2m\rfloor$ set $k_j=\lceil\max\{am\sqrt{r_j},B\log m\}\rceil$. If $k_j>m$ the corresponding forbidden event is empty; otherwise step 1.2 bounds its probability by $e^{-2k_j}\leq m^{-2B}$. The union over these $O(\log m)$ values of $j$ is summable along dyadic $m$. For a moment order $Q>2/\epsilon$, the elementary inequality $P(X_0>v)\leq v^{-Q}\mathbb E X_0^Q$ and the fact that every size-at-most-$m$ animal lies in $\Lambda_m=[-m,m]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$ give $P(\max_{\Lambda_m}X_y>m^\epsilon)\leq(2m+1)^2\mathbb E X_0^Q m^{-\epsilon Q}$, also summable in $l$.

If events $E_l$ have summable probabilities, then $P(\bigcup_{l\geq L}E_l)\leq\sum_{l\geq L}P(E_l)\to0$; countable additivity implies that only finitely many $E_l$ occur almost surely. Apply this elementary argument to the failures in step 2.1. Almost surely, for every sufficiently large dyadic $m$, all weights in $\Lambda_m$ are at most $m^\epsilon$, and every size-at-most-$m$ animal has fewer than $k_j$ sites with $X_y\geq2^j$ at each relevant level. The pointwise layer bound $X_y\leq1+\sum_{j\geq0}2^{j+1}\mathbf1_{\{X_y\geq2^j\}}$ then gives, for every animal with $m/2<|\Gamma|\leq m$, $|\Gamma|^{-1}\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq1+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}+O(m^{\epsilon-1}\log m)$. Levels above $\epsilon\log_2m$ contribute zero; the error comes from the additive $B\log m+1$ in $k_j$. The constants are deterministic.

A fixed moment order $Q>2$ gives $\sqrt{r_j}\leq(\mathbb E X_0^Q)^{1/2}2^{-Qj/2}$, so the series in step 3.1 converges. Its value is deterministic, and the error tends to zero. Choose $K$ larger than $2+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}$. Every sufficiently large animal belongs to one of the dyadic size ranges in step 3.1. Thus almost surely its average $X$-weight is at most this same $K$, proving the general independent-field assertion.

Apply step 4.1 to $X_y=|S_y|^2$, which is an independent identically distributed field with all moments. Work on the probability-one event where its large-animal bound holds and all $M_z$ are finite. Let $\Gamma$ be any sufficiently large animal, $m=|\Gamma|$, $A=\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z$, and $t=A/(2m)>0$. For each of the finitely many $z\in\Gamma$ with $M_z>t$, choose a root $y(z)$ attaining its maximum; to avoid even a selection convention take the first such root in a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb Z^2$. Let $Y$ be the distinct chosen roots, $s_y=|S_y|$, $U=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y^2$, and $V=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y$. Low-weight sites contribute at most $A/2$, and at most $s_y$ sites can be assigned to a given $S_y$. Hence $U\geq A/2=mt$. Since $s_y>t$ for chosen roots, $V\leq U/t$.

The set $\Delta=\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{y\in Y}S_y$ is a finite connected animal containing every root in $Y$, because every chosen set meets $\Gamma$ and is connected. Its size is at least $m$ and at most $m+V$. Therefore the same large-animal bound gives $U\leq\sum_{y\in\Delta}|S_y|^2\leq K|\Delta|\leq K(m+U/t)$. If $t>2K$, this would imply $U<2Km$ while step 5.1 gives $U\geq mt>2Km$, a contradiction. Thus $t\leq2K$ and $A\leq4Km$. Taking the deterministic constant $K_0=4K$ proves the envelope assertion uniformly over every sufficiently large animal. Only the given probability laws and countable additivity were used, without constructing any new infinite family.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

For every $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$, the free finite-volume FK laws on $\Lambda_n$ are stochastically increasing under restriction as $n$ grows, and the wired finite-volume FK laws are stochastically decreasing under restriction. The probabilities of every finite-coordinate atom therefore have unique nonnegative normalized consistent numerical limits. Under Countable Choice, each limiting family extends uniquely to a probability measure on the cylinder-generated Borel sigma-algebra of $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$. Thus the free and wired infinite-volume states exist under this measure-extension hypothesis.

Let $q\geq1$ be a finite real number. On the nearest-neighbor square lattice let $\Lambda_n=\{-n,\ldots,n\}^2$, let $E_n$ consist of edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_\infty=n\}$. For $p\in(0,1)$ and a partition $\xi$ of $B_n$, give $A\subseteq E_n$ probability proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)}$, where $k_\xi$ counts components after the partition classes are identified. Write $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ for the free partition when $b=0$ and the one-class wired partition when $b=1$.

For every event $C$ determined by finitely many edge coordinates, the numerical limits
$$\pi^b_{p,q}(C):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(C),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},$$
exist. They are consistent, nonnegative normalized finite-coordinate probability families, invariant under translations and quarter-turns. On increasing cylinder events they are increasing in $p$, with $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$. Every cylinder-probability limit of arbitrary boundary partitions lies between these two families on increasing cylinder events. There is an at most countable set $D_q\subset(0,1)$ such that $\pi^0_{p,q}(C)=\pi^1_{p,q}(C)$ for every cylinder event $C$ whenever $p\notin D_q$.

Let $D_r$ be the event that actual open edges inside $\Lambda_r$ join $0$ to $B_r$, and define the real numbers
$$\Theta_b(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^b_{p,q}(D_r).$$
Then $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$ for $0<p<p'<1$, and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^1_{n,p,q}(0\leftrightarrow B_n)=\Theta_1(p,q).$$
Connections here use actual edges, not artificial boundary-identification paths. These are statements about real limits and finite probability tables; existence of a countably additive probability on the infinite configuration space is not asserted.

Let $E_\infty$ be the nearest-neighbor edge set of $\mathbb Z^2$, and let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$. Let $E_n$ contain the edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $\partial\Lambda_n$ be the vertices of $\Lambda_n$ adjacent to a vertex outside it. Fix $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$. For each boundary partition $\xi_n$ on $\partial\Lambda_n$, let $\phi_{n,p,q}^{\xi_n}$ be the finite FK law on $(\Lambda_n,E_n)$ with mass proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_{\xi_n}(A)}$ for $A\subseteq E_n$, where $k_{\xi_n}(A)$ counts components after wiring the partition classes and extend its configurations to $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ by setting all edges outside $E_n$ closed.

An **infinite-volume FK state** at $(p,q)$ is any probability measure on $\{0,1\}^{E_\infty}$ that is a cylinder-probability limit of such extended finite-volume laws along a sequence $n_j\to\infty$ and boundary partitions $\xi_{n_j}$. Cylinder-probability convergence means convergence of the probability of every assignment on every finite set of edges. When they exist, the **free FK state** and **wired FK state** are the cylinder limits for the identity and one-class partitions, respectively, at every $n$. Their existence and uniqueness as probability-measure cylinder limits are established by a later A-page lemma under its stated measure-extension hypothesis. For either state $\phi^b_{p,q}$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, define $\theta^b(p,q):=\phi^b_{p,q}(0\leftrightarrow\infty)$, where $0\leftrightarrow\infty$ means that the open cluster of the origin is not contained in any finite box, and define

$$p_c^b(q):=\inf\{p\in(0,1):\theta^b(p,q)>0\}.$$

No equality of free and wired states at $p=p_c$ is part of this definition.

For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

Let $q\geq1$ be real, $p\in(0,1)$, $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$, and $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ the finite square-lattice FK law with free boundary partition $b=0$ or wired partition $b=1$. All paths below use actual open lattice edges, not artificial wiring edges. For each cylinder event $A$ let $\pi^b_{p,q}(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(A)$ be its numerical cylinder limit. Put $p_s=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $D_r$ be the cylinder event that $0$ connects inside $\Lambda_r$ to its vertex boundary. Then $a_n(p,q)=\phi^1_{n,p,q}(D_n)$ decreases, and
$$\Theta^1(p,q):=\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r).$$
For $p>p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)>0$; for $p<p_s$, $\Theta^1(p,q)=0$. Consequently $\inf\{p\in(0,1):\Theta^1(p,q)>0\}=p_s$. No value at $p_s$ is asserted. These numerical conclusions do not require Countable Choice or the extension of cylinder weights to an infinite-volume measure.

More precisely, fix $p>p_s$ and any real $\alpha>1$. Put $r_k=\lfloor\alpha^k\rfloor$. For all sufficiently large $k$, let $A_k$ be the cylinder event that an actual open simple circuit surrounds $\Lambda_{r_k}$, lies outside $\Lambda_{r_k}$ and strictly inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$, and is connected inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$ to its vertex boundary. There are $C,\varepsilon>0$ and an integer $K$ such that $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}<1/2$ for $k\geq K$ and, for every $n\geq m\geq N\geq K$,
$$\phi^1_{r_{n+2},p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq\prod_{k=N}^{n}(1-d_k),\qquad \pi^1_{p,q}\left(\bigcap_{k=N}^{m}A_k\right)\geq1-\sum_{k=N}^{\infty}d_k.$$
For $0<p<t<1$ and $H_n$ the finite Hamming distance to $D_n$, the finite cylinder expectation satisfies
$$\pi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{t,q}}H_n\}.$$
For every $0<s<p_s$ and every $d>0$, there are $C_d,n_d$ such that $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq C_d n^{-(2d+4)}$ for $n\geq n_d$. The expectation here is a finite sum of cylinder atom weights.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a given probability space. For each $y\in\mathbb Z^2$, let $S_y$ be a measurable random finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $y$, with the discrete sigma-algebra on the countable collection of such sets. Assume the sets $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed and that $\mathbb E|S_0|^r<\infty$ for every real $r>0$. A lattice animal is a finite nearest-neighbor-connected vertex set containing $0$. Define the extended measurable envelope
$$M_z=\sup\{|S_y|:y\in\mathbb Z^2,\ z\in S_y\}.$$
Almost surely every $M_z$ is a finite maximum, and there is a deterministic finite constant $K_0$ such that, almost surely, every sufficiently large lattice animal $\Gamma$ satisfies
$$\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|.$$
More generally, for any given independent identically distributed field $X_y\geq1$ with finite moments of every positive order, there is a deterministic finite $K$ such that almost surely $\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq K|\Gamma|$ for every sufficiently large lattice animal. The random cutoff may depend on the realization. This result assumes the stated random family on a probability space; it does not construct an infinite product law or require a choice axiom to supply that law.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, let $A$ be a finite nonempty set, and put $X=A^{\mathbb Z^d}$. Fix a bijection $(i_n)_{n\geq1}:\mathbb N_{>0}	o\mathbb Z^d$ and give $X$ the metric
$$d_X(\sigma,\eta)=\sum_{n\geq1}2^{-n}\mathbf 1_{\{\sigma_{i_n}
e\eta_{i_n}\}}.$$
For a finite $F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ and $B\subseteq A^F$, write $[F,B]=\{\sigma\in X:\sigma|_F\in B\}$ and let $\mathcal C=\{[F,B]:F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite},\ B\subseteq A^F\}$ be the cylinder algebra. A family $(
u_F)_{F\subseteq\mathbb Z^d	ext{ finite}}$ of probability measures on $A^F$ is **consistent** if $(\pi_E^F)_*
u_F=
u_E$ whenever $E\subseteq F$, where $\pi_E^F:A^F	o A^E$ is restriction. Such a family defines $\mu_0([F,B])=
u_F(B)$; consistency makes this a well-defined normalized finitely additive probability on $\mathcal C$. Then $X$ is compact, the Borel sigma-algebra is $\sigma(\mathcal C)$, and $\mu_0$ extends uniquely to a probability on $\sigma(\mathcal C)$. Moreover, every sequence of probabilities on this sigma-algebra has a subsequence whose cylinder probabilities converge to those of a probability measure; along that subsequence integrals of every continuous $f:X	o\mathbb R$ converge.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable with $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ and $f_n\to f$ pointwise. Then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, including infinite values. Also, for measurable $f,g\ge0$, $\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu$. For every $c\ge0$, $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$; the integral is also linear on real integrable functions.
Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable. Then $\int\liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

derivations.claim: Fix any $0<s<p_s:=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $R_x=\sup\{\lVert z-x\rVert_\infty:z\in C_x\}$, allowing infinity initially. The event $R_x\geq n$ is the translate of $D_n$: a path reaching that distance has an initial segment inside the centered box to its boundary. Its probability under the wired law is its numerical cylinder weight by [F1]. Thus [F3], with arbitrarily large $d$, gives polynomial tails of arbitrarily high order for $R_x$. Since $|C_x|\leq(2R_x+1)^2$, nonnegative monotone convergence applied to successive integer layers proves $\mathbb E_s^1|C_x|^d<\infty$ for every $d>0$; explicitly the layer bound for $R_x^{2d}$ is a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}n^{2d-1}P(R_x\geq n)$, which converges after choosing [F3] with that $d$. Every $C_x$ is finite almost surely, simultaneously at all countably many vertices. Translation invariance follows from the numerical cylinder identities in [F1] and uniqueness in [F5].

We establish a conditional cluster comparison before constructing a new law. Enumerate the vertices deterministically. Suppose a finite number of complete finite clusters have been discovered, with union $E$. Revealing their vertex sets says that each discovered set is connected by its internal open edges and every edge from it to its complement is closed. These are finite-edge events. In each finite FK box, after all edges between $E$ and its complement are fixed closed, the component factors and edge weights internal to $E$ factor from the remaining weights; summing over allowed internal configurations preserves that factorization. Hence the law outside $E$ depends on the discovered sets only through the closed boundary edges. Passing fixed finite-cylinder conditional probabilities to the wired limit proves the same identity there. A positive-probability history has a positive denominator because its defining finite edge event does; null histories may be assigned arbitrary normalized kernels and are never reached.

If the next vertex $y$ is outside $E$, its conditional cluster law is dominated, by inclusion of vertex sets, by the unconditional wired cluster law of $y$. Indeed in a finite box compare the original wired law with the same law constrained to close every edge from $E$ to its complement. The common-uniform heat-bath update in [F2] preserves order; fixed-closed coordinates stay below the upper chain, and all other conditional edge probabilities remain ordered. Taking stationary limits gives an ordered finite-box coupling. Apply [F5] to the pair of binary edge fields along growing boxes and take a joint cylinder limit. Its upper marginal is the wired law; its lower marginal outside $E$ is the conditional law in step 2.1, since conditioning a fixed positive-probability cylinder commutes with these limits. The order event is a countable intersection of coordinatewise closed conditions and holds in the limit. Project to the two clusters of $y$. Both are finite almost surely, by the upper marginal and step 1.1. This proves existence of an ordered coupling on pairs of finite connected vertex sets for each possible positive-probability history.

The possible finite histories, finite connected lattice sets, and pairs of such sets have explicit countable encodings by integer vertex lists. Apply [A1] to the fixed countable family of nonempty sets of coupling kernels from step 3.1, choosing one kernel for every history in advance. At a stage whose vertex $y$ is already discovered, its actual-cluster output is its earlier cluster and the second output is a fresh independent set with the unconditional cluster law of $y$. At an undiscovered $y$, use its selected ordered kernel: its first marginal is the conditional cluster law from step 2.1 and its second marginal is again that fixed unconditional law. Each kernel is a probability on a countable set of pairs of finite sets. The product of the successive kernels defines normalized consistent finite-prefix atomic probabilities; summing the last kernel's mass one verifies consistency. A kernel's second marginal is fixed for every history, including the earlier second outputs, so these second outputs have product marginals for every finite list of stages. Countable Choice here selects kernels for a countable set fixed in advance, rather than successive unspecified choices from a relation.

Here is an explicit extension of the process, to avoid assuming a countable-alphabet extension theorem. Enumerate each stage's possible output pairs by integers $j\geq0$, and encode $j$ by a bit row consisting of $j$ ones, a zero, and then zeros. For every finite set of coordinates in the countable array of bits, sum the appropriate finite-prefix atomic probabilities from step 4.1. All sums are nonnegative countable sums over explicitly enumerated finite tuples of integers. Summing the last kernel verifies consistency of the binary finite-dimensional laws. Identify the bit array with the countable coordinates in [F5] and extend under [A1]. For a given row the weight of its first $K$ bits being all ones is the atomic tail $P(j\geq K)$, tending to zero, so the all-ones row has probability zero by countable additivity. Each finite pattern having a one after its first zero also has prescribed probability zero. A countable union shows that almost surely every row is a valid integer code. Decode on this measurable full-probability set, assigning a fixed default on its null complement. The resulting process has exactly the specified finite-prefix laws. This constructs the required law without an additional invocation of a process-extension or independent-uniform theorem.

Write $S_y$ for the second output at the stage of $y$, and $\widehat C_z$ for the actual cluster assigned by the first outputs. Step 4.1 shows that the $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed as the translated wired cluster; their sizes have all moments by step 1.1. The first outputs have precisely the original wired cluster-exploration laws by induction on every finite prefix. The complete cluster at each fixed $z$ is assigned by the stage reaching $z$, so all finite lists of complete cluster sets have the actual wired joint law. Equality of the whole countably indexed cluster-set law follows as well: unary encode these finite-set labels; its binary cylinder values determine its law uniquely by [F5]. Whenever a new cluster is discovered at $y$, it is a subset of $S_y$ by the ordered kernel. Every $z$ in that cluster therefore satisfies $|\widehat C_z|\leq M_z:=\sup\{|S_y|:z\in S_y\}$. The enumeration eventually assigns every vertex. This coupled object is a cluster partition, not an edge configuration reconstructed from clusters.

Apply [F4] to the given independent family $S_y$ on the constructed probability space. There is a deterministic finite $K_0$ such that almost surely all sufficiently large animals $\Gamma$ satisfy $\sum_{z\in\Gamma}|\widehat C_z|\leq\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|$. This countably measurable property of the cluster partition transfers to the actual wired law by step 6.1. An animal is a finite connected vertex set containing $0$, so this applies simultaneously to every sufficiently long self-avoiding path starting at $0$. No claim that the dependent envelope variables are independent is made.

In any edge configuration with such a cluster partition, let $\gamma$ be a self-avoiding path from $0$ to $\partial\Lambda_n$, with $m$ vertices. It has $m\geq n+1$. If it visits $J$ distinct open clusters, its number $T(\gamma)$ of closed edges is at least $J-1$. Each visited cluster $C$ contributes at most one to $\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}$, because the path visits distinct vertices. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives $T(\gamma)+1\geq\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}\geq m^2/(\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|)\geq m/K_0$ for all sufficiently long paths, by step 7.1. The subtraction of one is necessary even for a path contained in a single cluster. Since this inequality holds for every edge configuration with that partition, transferring the partition law was sufficient; no internal open edges had to be selected in the coupling.

A path minimizing the number of closed edges in the finite box may be taken self-avoiding by erasing loops without increasing that number. The uniform large-animal cutoff in step 7.1 and step 8.1 give $H_n\geq(n+1)/K_0-1$ for all sufficiently large $n$, almost surely in the actual wired law at $s$. Fatou's inequality from [F6], applied to the nonnegative measurable variables $H_n/n$, gives $\liminf_n\mathbb E_s^1H_n/n\geq1/K_0$. Thus for all sufficiently large deterministic $n$, $\mathbb E_s^1H_n\geq n/(2K_0)$. This expectation conclusion does not assume a deterministic bound on the random almost-sure cutoff.

Now fix the parameter $p$ in the statement and choose $s\in(p,p_s)$. The preceding moment, coupling, and Hamming-expectation arguments apply at this $s$. Since $H_n$ is a finite-coordinate function, its expectation under the wired Borel law is exactly the finite sum of its numerical cylinder atom weights in [F3]. That supplier's Hamming inequality therefore gives $\phi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-2(s-p)n/K_0\}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Increasing a prefactor covers all $n\geq1$. In particular the probability of an infinite cluster at $0$ is zero: that event is contained in every $D_n$, whose probabilities tend to zero.

By translation invariance, the same one-arm bound holds at every center. If $x\ne y$ and $r=\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty$, any finite open path from $x$ to $y$ has an initial segment from $x$ to the vertex boundary of $x+\Lambda_r$ inside that box. Thus its wired connection probability is at most the translated one-arm bound at radius $r$. Since $r\geq\lVert x-y\rVert_2/\sqrt2$, changing constants proves $\phi^1_{p,q}(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}$, also for $x=y$ after enlarging $C$.

Let $\phi$ be any cylinder limit in the statement. An increasing event supported on a fixed inner box has finite-volume conditional laws with boundary partitions at most wired; passing its cylinder probabilities to the limit bounds them above by the wired inner-box law. Then increase that inner box to infinity, using the wired cylinder limit in [F1], to obtain domination by the wired state on increasing cylinder events. The event that $x$ connects $y$ by a path in a fixed box is such an event. These events increase to $\{x\leftrightarrow y\}$ as boxes grow; countable additivity, or [F6] applied to their indicators, therefore gives the identical upper bound in step 11.1 for $\phi$. Similarly the translated $D_n$ events dominate any infinite cluster at their center, giving probability zero. Constants depend only on $p,q$, not on the cylinder-limit state. The proof has made no assertion at $p_s$ and has used Countable Choice exactly in the stated extensions and kernel selection.

step 12.1 covers every arbitrary-boundary cylinder-limit state.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Its weighted value is $Y=(Z_0/Z_1)R=\pi_1/\pi_0$, and finite summation gives $\mathbb E_{\pi_0}Y=(Z_0/Z_1)\mathbb E_{\pi_0}R=1$. supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X,\mu)$ be a measure space. An **unnormalized target density** is a measurable function $\tilde p:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$Z_p:=\int_{\mathsf X}\tilde p\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
The target probability measure is $\pi(dx)=\tilde p(x)\mu(dx)/Z_p$. A **proposal density** is a measurable $q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\int q\,d\mu=1$; write $Q(dx)=q(x)\mu(dx)$. The input integrand $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and the input sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ is IID with law $Q$, in the sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]. The normalizing constant $Z_p$ is known for this algorithm.

**Admissible conditions for an unbiased estimate:** $n\ge1$, $q>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{x:f(x)\tilde p(x)\ne0\}$, and the random variable
$$Y:=\begin{cases}f(X_1)\tilde p(X_1)/(Z_pq(X_1)),&q(X_1)>0,\\0,&q(X_1)=0\end{cases}$$
is integrable under $Q$. The support condition makes the value on $q=0$ immaterial to the target integral.

**Well-defined weights:** The reciprocal map $r(s)=1/s$ for $s>0$ and $r(s)=0$ for $s\le0$ is Borel. Its composition with $q$, multiplied by the measurable inputs, makes the piecewise weight and weighted integrand measurable ([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]], [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

**Procedure and output:** For each supplied draw $X_i$, set $Y_i=f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i))$ when $q(X_i)>0$ and set $Y_i=0$ otherwise. Return
$$\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i.$$
Separate variance and central limit claims require the corresponding weighted second-moment hypothesis.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the hypotheses and notation of [[thm-ordinary-importance-sampling-is-unbiased]]. Define
$$Y_i:=\begin{cases}f(X_i)\tilde p(X_i)/(Z_pq(X_i)),&q(X_i)>0,\\0,&q(X_i)=0\end{cases},\qquad \theta:=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad \sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}_Q(Y_1).$$
If $\mathbb E_Q[Y_1^2]<\infty$, then $\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}$ has finite variance and
$$\operatorname{Var}_Q(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}})=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}=\frac1n\left(\frac1{Z_p^2}\int_{\{q>0\}}\frac{f(x)^2\tilde p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,d\mu(x)-\theta^2\right).$$
This finite-sample conclusion is choice-free. For the central limit conclusion, let $(X_i)_{i\ge1}$ be an IID sequence with law $Q$, and apply the estimator to its first $n$ draws for each $n\ge1$. If, in addition, AC holds, then
$$\sqrt n\bigl(\hat\mu_{\mathrm{IS}}-\theta\bigr)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2).$$
No finite variance or normal-limit claim is made when the weighted second moment is infinite.

Let $\mathsf X$ be a finite nonempty set equipped with counting measure. For $a\in\{0,1\}$, let $w_a:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$ be a finite positive weight, define $Z_a=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_a(x)$, and define the probability mass function $\pi_a(x)=w_a(x)/Z_a$. For an integer $n\geq1$, let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent random variables with common law $\pi_0$. Define $R(x)=w_1(x)/w_0(x)$, $\widehat r_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nR(X_j)$, and $\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}\pi_0(x)(\pi_1(x)/\pi_0(x)-1)^2$. Then

$$\mathbb E_{\pi_0}[\widehat r_n]=\frac{Z_1}{Z_0},\qquad \frac{\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_0}(\widehat r_n)}{(Z_1/Z_0)^2}=\frac{\chi^2(\pi_1\Vert\pi_0)}{n}.$$

The estimator uses only the finite raw-weight ratios $w_1(X_j)/w_0(X_j)$; the partition sums define the target ratio and probability laws but are not inputs to its computation.

Input a finite nonempty state space $\mathsf X$, an integer $K\geq1$, positive finite weights $w_0,\ldots,w_K:\mathsf X\to(0,\infty)$, positive integers $n_0,\ldots,n_{K-1}$, and arrays of supplied random samples $X_{k,1},\ldots,X_{k,n_k}$ such that for each $k$ the samples are IID with law $\pi_k(x)=w_k(x)/Z_k$, where $Z_k=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}w_k(x)$, and all samples across distinct stages are mutually independent. These exact IID draws are inputs, not outputs of this procedure; approximate Gibbs draws, correlated trajectories, and adaptively chosen bridges are outside its contract.

For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, compute $\overline R_k=n_k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_k}w_{k+1}(X_{k,j})/w_k(X_{k,j})$. Return $\widehat R=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\overline R_k$. The procedure evaluates only raw-weight ratios; it neither computes nor requires any $Z_k$ as a numeric input.

derivations.claim: For each $k$, apply [F1] to $(w_k,w_{k+1})$ and the $n_k$ exact IID samples from $\pi_k$. With $r_k=Z_{k+1}/Z_k$, the stage mean $\overline R_k$ satisfies $\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=r_k$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)/r_k^2=\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. Since $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\overline R_k)+(\mathbb E[\overline R_k])^2$, it follows that $\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2=1+\chi^2(\pi_{k+1}\Vert\pi_k)/n_k$. All moments are finite because $\mathsf X$ is finite and the weights are positive and finite.

By [F2] and independence across stages, $\mathbb E[\widehat R]=\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}\mathbb E[\overline R_k]=\prod_k(Z_{k+1}/Z_k)=Z_K/Z_0$. The same independence factors second moments, so $\mathbb E[\widehat R^2]/(Z_K/Z_0)^2=\prod_k\mathbb E[\overline R_k^2]/r_k^2$. Substituting step 1.1 gives the stated product; subtracting one yields the relative variance.

citations.quote:
Input a finite nonempty set $\mathsf X$ with an explicit enumeration, an exact positive finite weight $w(x)$ and a real observable $f(x)$ for each $x\in\mathsf X$, a finite rational interval $W_x=[a_x,b_x]$ containing $w(x)$, a finite rational interval $F_x=[c_x,d_x]$ containing $f(x)$, and a selected finite dyadic format $\mathbb F$ with directed roundings. The interval assertions are certified input premises; this procedure does not derive them from energies or evaluate an exponential or logarithm.

For each input interval, convert its lower rational endpoint by directed rounding down and its upper rational endpoint by directed rounding up into $\mathbb F$. If any conversion overflows, return unresolved-overflow and no finite enclosure claim. Using the resulting dyadic intervals and the outward-rounded operations, construct the finite expression DAG for

$$\mathcal Z=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}W_x,\qquad \mathcal N=\sum_{x\in\mathsf X}W_xF_x.$$

Every addition and multiplication uses the outward-rounded interval operations; division is used only for a denominator interval excluding zero. If any operation returns a non-finite status, return unresolved-operation and no finite enclosure claim. Otherwise return the finite intervals $\mathcal Z$ and $\mathcal N$. If the lower endpoint of $\mathcal Z$ is strictly positive, also return the outward interval quotient $\mathcal E=\mathcal N/\mathcal Z$; if that endpoint is nonpositive, return unresolved-denominator and no normalized-expectation enclosure.

This is finite enumeration and can require exponentially many operations in the model size. It certifies arithmetic from supplied weight intervals; it does not certify how those intervals were obtained.

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with integers $e,k$ satisfying
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with integer $k$ satisfying $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. Set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(0)=0$.
For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. For $x>N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(N_{\max},+\infty)$; for
$x<-N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(-\infty,-N_{\max})$.
In either overflow case set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=+\infty$ and report
`overflow`, even when the selected directed endpoint is finite.
The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of the
extended endpoint set $\mathbb F\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.
