It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Let $X,Y$ be normed spaces over the same field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $\mathcal B(X,Y)$, the bounded scalar-linear operators of [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]], define:

- The **strong operator topology** (SOT) is the initial topology of all maps $T\mapsto Tx$ to normed $Y$, for $x\in X$.
- The **weak operator topology** (WOT) is the initial topology of all scalar maps $T\mapsto f(Tx)$, for $x\in X$ and $f\in Y^*$.

These topologies exist by [[def-initial-and-final-topology]]. Equivalently WOT is initial for $T\mapsto Tx$ with the weak topology on $Y$ from [[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]]. At $T$, basic neighborhoods impose finitely many inequalities $\|(S-T)x_j\|<\varepsilon$ for SOT, or $|f_j((S-T)x_j)|<\varepsilon$ for WOT, with $\varepsilon>0$. Empty lists give the whole operator space.

For a net of bounded operators with specified limit $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$, SOT convergence means $\|(T_i-T)x\|\to0$ for every fixed $x$, and WOT convergence means $f(T_ix)\to f(Tx)$ for every fixed $x,f$. Both equivalences follow by testing one coordinate and then using a common upper bound for the finitely many eventual indices in a basic neighborhood. No uniformity in $x$ is part of either definition. These are choice-free constructions, also when one space is zero and the operator space is a singleton.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For $\xi\in H$, the real numbers
$q_i(\xi):=\langle x_i\xi,\xi\rangle$ increase and satisfy
$0\le q_i(\xi)\le C\|\xi\|^2$. Define
$q(\xi):=\sup_{i\in I}q_i(\xi)$. For each $i$, the complex polarization
identity gives
$$\langle x_i\xi,\eta\rangle =\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^k q_i(\xi+i^k\eta).$$
Each term on the right converges as $i$ increases, so the left-hand side
converges for every $\xi,\eta$. Let $b(\xi,\eta)$ be its limit. The forms
$\langle x_i\xi,\eta\rangle$ are sesquilinear and uniformly bounded by
$C\|\xi\|\|\eta\|$, so their pointwise limit $b$ is sesquilinear with the
same bound. For fixed $\xi$, Riesz representation applied to
$\eta\mapsto\overline{b(\xi,\eta)}$ gives a unique vector $x\xi$ with
$b(\xi,\eta)=\langle x\xi,\eta\rangle$. Sesquilinearity and uniqueness
make $\xi\mapsto x\xi$ linear, and the bound gives $\|x\xi\|\le C\|\xi\|$;
thus $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and $\|x\|\le C$. Since each $x_i$ is self-adjoint,
$b(\xi,\eta)=\overline{b(\eta,\xi)}$, hence
$\langle x\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle\xi,x\eta\rangle$ and $x=x^*$. Also
$\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle=q(\xi)\ge0$, so $x$ is positive. By [F2],
$x_i\to x$ weakly. Since $M$ is weakly closed by [F1], $x\in M$.

For every $\xi$, $q_i(\xi)\le q(\xi)=\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$, so
$x_i\le x$. If $y\in M_+$ is any other upper bound, then
$q_i(\xi)\le\langle y\xi,\xi\rangle$ for every $i,\xi$; taking the supremum
over $i$ gives $\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle\le\langle y\xi,\xi\rangle$ for every
$\xi$, hence $x\le y$. Thus $x=\sup_i x_i$ in $M_+$.

Fix $\xi\in H$ and put $D_i=x-x_i$. Then $0\le D_i\le x\le CI$ and
$\langle D_i\xi,\xi\rangle=q(\xi)-q_i(\xi)\to0$. Positivity gives the
Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the form
$(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\langle D_i\alpha,\beta\rangle$: applying positivity to
$\xi+z\eta$ for arbitrary $z\in\mathbb C$ yields the nonnegative quantity
$$u+2\operatorname{Re}(\overline z a)+|z|^2v,$$
where $u=\langle D_i\xi,\xi\rangle$, $a=\langle D_i\xi,\eta\rangle$,
and $v=\langle D_i\eta,\eta\rangle$. If $v>0$, taking $z=-a/v$ gives
$$|a|^2\le uv.$$
If $v=0$ and $a\ne0$, taking $z=-t a$ for sufficiently large real $t>0$
makes the quantity negative; hence $a=0$ and the same inequality holds.
Therefore
$$|\langle D_i\xi,\eta\rangle|^2 \le\langle D_i\xi,\xi\rangle\langle D_i\eta,\eta\rangle \le C\|\eta\|^2\langle D_i\xi,\xi\rangle.$$
Taking the supremum over unit $\eta$ gives
$\|D_i\xi\|^2\le C\langle D_i\xi,\xi\rangle\to0$. Therefore
$\|(x_i-x)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi$, which is strong-operator convergence.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. All inner products are linear in their first
argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

For complex Hilbert spaces $H_1,H_2$, a linear operator $A$ is a linear map
$A:D(A)\to H_2$ on a linear domain $D(A)\subseteq H_1$. Its graph is
$\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}\subseteq H_1\oplus H_2$, with the direct-sum
Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define
$D(A^*)$ to consist of those $y\in H_2$ for which
$x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}$ is bounded on $D(A)$ in the $H_1$ norm.
The bounded functional extends uniquely to $H_1$; its Riesz vector
$A^*y\in H_1$ is specified by
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_{H_1} \qquad(x\in D(A)).$$
This defines the linear adjoint $A^*:D(A^*)\subseteq H_2\to H_1$.

An operator $S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ is **antilinear** when
$S(ax+by)=\overline a\,Sx+\overline b\,Sy$. Its associated linear operator
$\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ is
$D(\widetilde S)=c_H(D(S))$ and
$\widetilde S(\overline x)=Sx$. For densely defined antilinear $S$, define
$$S^*:=c_H^{-1}\widetilde S^*,$$
on the domain $D(S^*)=D(\widetilde S^*)$. Thus $S^*$ is antilinear and
$$\langle Sx,y\rangle_H=\langle S^*y,x\rangle_H \qquad(x\in D(S),\ y\in D(S^*)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$ be a linear operator with dense domain and closed
graph. Define $A^*$ as in the local Hilbert-space adjoint convention. Then
$T:=A^*A$, on
$D(T)=\{x\in D(A):Ax\in D(A^*)\}$, is positive and self-adjoint. Its positive
square root $P:=T^{1/2}$ has domain $D(P)=D(A)$ and satisfies
$\|Px\|=\|Ax\|$ for every $x\in D(A)$. There is a unique partial isometry
$U:H_1\to H_2$ such that
$$A=UP,\qquad \ker U=\ker A.$$
Its initial space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P}=(\ker A)^\perp$ and its
final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$. If $A$ is injective and has
dense range, then $U$ is unitary.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$R\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital star subalgebra. Its strong-operator
closure is $R''$. If $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ is a concrete von Neumann
algebra and $\Omega\in H$, then $\Omega$ is cyclic for $M$ exactly when it is
separating for $M'$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Throughout this page $H$ is a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with
inner product linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

A **(possibly unbounded) linear operator on $H$** is a linear map
$T:D(T)\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]) whose **domain** $D(T)\subseteq H$ is a linear
subspace ([[def-linear-subspace]]). The domain is part of the data: $T=S$ means
$D(T)=D(S)$ and $Tx=Sx$ for all $x\in D(T)$. One writes $T\subseteq S$, and
calls $S$ an **extension** of $T$, when $D(T)\subseteq D(S)$ and $Sx=Tx$ for
every $x\in D(T)$.

The **graph** of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T):=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}\subseteq H\oplus H .$$
The direct sum $H\oplus H$ is read as the complex vector space of pairs with
coordinatewise operations and the inner product
$\langle (x,y),(u,v)\rangle=\langle x,u\rangle+\langle y,v\rangle$, whose induced
norm is
$$\|(x,y)\|=(\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2)^{1/2};$$
it is complete because $H$ is ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). The **graph norm**
on $D(T)$ is
$$\|x\|_T:=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2},$$
so that $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$
onto $\Gamma(T)$ with the norm restricted from $H\oplus H$.

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

**Notation.** No boundedness of $T$ is assumed, and $T$ is frequently called
*unbounded* to stress this; a bounded everywhere defined operator on $H$ is the
special case $D(T)=H$ in which $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subspace by continuity.
The letter $I$ denotes the identity operator on $H$ with domain $H$.

**Completeness of $H\oplus H$.** If $(x_n,y_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in
$H\oplus H$, then $\|x_n-x_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ and
$\|y_n-y_m\|\le\|(x_n-x_m,y_n-y_m)\|$ show that $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are Cauchy
in $H$; let $x,y$ be their limits. Then
$\|(x_n,y_n)-(x,y)\|^2=\|x_n-x\|^2+\|y_n-y\|^2\to0$, so $H\oplus H$ is
complete. Consequently a sequence in $H\oplus H$ converges exactly when its two
coordinate sequences converge in $H$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H_1,H_2$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$ be a linear operator with dense domain and closed
graph. Define $A^*$ as in the local Hilbert-space adjoint convention. Then
$T:=A^*A$, on
$D(T)=\{x\in D(A):Ax\in D(A^*)\}$, is positive and self-adjoint. Its positive
square root $P:=T^{1/2}$ has domain $D(P)=D(A)$ and satisfies
$\|Px\|=\|Ax\|$ for every $x\in D(A)$. There is a unique partial isometry
$U:H_1\to H_2$ such that
$$A=UP,\qquad \ker U=\ker A.$$
Its initial space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}P}=(\ker A)^\perp$ and its
final space is $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$. If $A$ is injective and has
dense range, then $U$ is unitary.

derivations.claim: Put $C=c_H$ and $T=\overline S$. The definition of graph closure above makes $A:=\widetilde T$ a closed densely defined complex-linear operator $\overline H\to H$. By [F2], write $A=U B$, where $B=(A^*A)^{1/2}$ is positive self-adjoint with $D(B)=D(A)$ and $U$ is a partial isometry with initial space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}B}=(\ker A)^\perp$, final space $\overline{\operatorname{ran}A}$, and kernel $\ker A$. Set $J:=UC$ and $P:=C^{-1}BC$, with domain $D(P)=C^{-1}D(B)$. The composition $P$ is linear. If $E$ is the spectral measure of $B$, then $F(\Lambda):=C^{-1}E(\Lambda)C$ is a spectral measure of orthogonal projections on $H$, and its spectral integral is $P$; hence $P$ is positive self-adjoint. More explicitly, $D(T^*T)=\{x:Cx\in D(A),\ ACx\in D(A^*)\}=C^{-1}D(A^*A)$, and the adjoint convention [F1] gives $T^*T=C^{-1}A^*AC$ there. Also $D(P^2)=C^{-1}D(B^2)$ and $P^2=C^{-1}B^2C=C^{-1}A^*AC=T^*T$ on that domain; uniqueness of the positive self-adjoint square root gives $P=(T^*T)^{1/2}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $M \le X$ be a closed linear subspace. Then
$X/M$ is Banach for the quotient norm.

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Let $X$ be normed and $M\le X$ closed. With quotient norm $\|x+M\|=\inf_{m\in M}\|x+m\|$ and $q(x)=x+M$, the map $$Q:(X/M)^*\longrightarrow M^\perp,\qquad Qh=h\circ q$$ is a linear isometric bijection.

Let $X$ be a normed space and let $M \le X$ be a linear subspace. For a coset
$x+M \in X/M$, define

$$\|x+M\|_{X/M} := \inf_{m \in M}\|x+m\|.$$

Equivalently, this is the distance from $x$ to $M$ inside the ambient normed
space:

$$\|x+M\|_{X/M} = \operatorname{dist}(x,M).$$

The formula is representative-independent by
[[lem-quotient-seminorm-is-representative-independent]], so it is a
well-defined seminorm on the quotient vector space.

Let $X$ be a normed space and let $M \le X$ be a linear subspace. The
underlying quotient vector space is the one already defined in
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]], with cosets written

$$x+M := \{x+m : m \in M\}.$$

On this page the canonical projection is written

$$q:X\to X/M,\qquad q(x):=x+M.$$

By [[prop-quotient-vector-space-operations-and-projection]], $q$ is a
surjective linear map and $\ker q = M$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over the scalar field $\mathbb{K}$, where
$\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, using [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] over $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] over $\mathbb C$. The
**dual space** of $X$ is

$$X^*:=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K}),$$

the space of bounded linear functionals on $X$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]).

Each $f \in X^*$ is in particular a linear functional in the algebraic sense,
so $X^*$ is a subspace of the algebraic dual from
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]].

The **dual norm** on $X^*$ is the operator norm:

$$\|f\|_{X^*}:=\|f\| =\sup\{|f(x)|:\|x\| \le 1\}.$$

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. For a normed $X$ and arbitrary subsets $M\subseteq X$, $N\subseteq X^*$, define $$M^\perp=\{f\in X^*:f(m)=0\text{ for all }m\in M\},\qquad {}^\perp N=\{x\in X:f(x)=0\text{ for all }f\in N\}.$$ Here $X^*$ is [[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]. The first notation agrees with [[def-continuous-annihilator-of-a-subspace]] on $\operatorname{span}M$, since linearity makes vanishing on $M$ equivalent to vanishing on its span. The preannihilator lies in $X$, not in $X^{**}$. Empty sets impose no conditions: $\varnothing^\perp=X^*$ and ${}^\perp\varnothing=X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ a concrete von Neumann algebra. Let $I$ be a
nonempty directed set, and let $(x_i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $M$ such that each
$x_i$ is positive, $x_i\le x_j$ whenever $i\le j$, and
$\|x_i\|\le C$ for some finite $C\ge0$. Here $A\le B$ means that $A,B$ are
self-adjoint and $\langle A\xi,\xi\rangle\le\langle B\xi,\xi\rangle$ for every
$\xi\in H$. Then the net has a least upper bound $x=\sup_i x_i$ in $M_+$, and
$x_i\to x$ in the strong operator topology.

**Assume the ultrafilter lemma.**  If $X$ is a real or complex normed space,
then its closed dual unit ball $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology
$\sigma(X^*,X)$.  Completeness of $X$ is not required.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal B(H)$ denote
its bounded linear operators. Applying AC to a family indexed by the natural numbers
supplies Countable Choice, the hypothesis of
[[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]], which provides adjoints on $\mathcal B(H)$.
A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a
unital $*$-subalgebra $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ that is closed in the
weak operator topology (WOT). Here unital means $I_H\in\mathcal A$; the zero
Hilbert space is allowed, with $I_H=0$ and sole unital algebra $\{0\}$. This is
the only use of AC in this definition.

For any set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, its **commutant** and
**double commutant** are
$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):TS=ST\text{ for every }S\in\mathcal S\},\qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$
Commutants are taken inside $\mathcal B(H)$. The **von Neumann algebra
generated by $\mathcal S$** is
$$W^*(\mathcal S):=\overline{\operatorname{Alg}^*(\mathcal S\cup\{I_H\})}^{\,\mathrm{WOT}},$$
the WOT closure in $\mathcal B(H)$ of the unital $*$-algebra generated by
$\mathcal S$. No bicommutant theorem is part of these definitions.

Two elementary properties will be used. For fixed $S\in\mathcal B(H)$,
$$\langle TS\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T(S\xi),\eta\rangle,\qquad \langle ST\xi,\eta\rangle=\langle T\xi,S^*\eta\rangle$$
are WOT-continuous matrix coefficients as functions of $T$. Thus each equation
$TS=ST$ defines a WOT-closed set, and so $\mathcal S'$ is WOT-closed. If
$\mathcal S$ is self-adjoint, then $\mathcal S'$ is a unital $*$-subalgebra:
products preserve commutation with every $S$, and taking adjoints of $TS=ST$
gives $ST^*=T^*S$. These facts do not identify $W^*(\mathcal S)$ with
$\mathcal S''$.

Let $X,Y$ be normed spaces over the same field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $\mathcal B(X,Y)$, the bounded scalar-linear operators of [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]], define:

- The **strong operator topology** (SOT) is the initial topology of all maps $T\mapsto Tx$ to normed $Y$, for $x\in X$.
- The **weak operator topology** (WOT) is the initial topology of all scalar maps $T\mapsto f(Tx)$, for $x\in X$ and $f\in Y^*$.

These topologies exist by [[def-initial-and-final-topology]]. Equivalently WOT is initial for $T\mapsto Tx$ with the weak topology on $Y$ from [[def-weak-topology-on-a-normed-space]]. At $T$, basic neighborhoods impose finitely many inequalities $\|(S-T)x_j\|<\varepsilon$ for SOT, or $|f_j((S-T)x_j)|<\varepsilon$ for WOT, with $\varepsilon>0$. Empty lists give the whole operator space.

For a net of bounded operators with specified limit $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$, SOT convergence means $\|(T_i-T)x\|\to0$ for every fixed $x$, and WOT convergence means $f(T_ix)\to f(Tx)$ for every fixed $x,f$. Both equivalences follow by testing one coordinate and then using a common upper bound for the finitely many eventual indices in a basic neighborhood. No uniformity in $x$ is part of either definition. These are choice-free constructions, also when one space is zero and the operator space is a singleton.

In particular, for $\xi\in H$ the vector functional is represented by $[R_{\xi,\xi}]$, since $\operatorname{Tr}(R_{\xi,\xi}x)=\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$; it is positive and therefore normal as well.

Steps 1.1–1.3 and 2.1–2.2 prove the quotient predual, its weak-star compact dual ball, normality of positive functionals in the quotient, and normality of vector functionals. The positive-functional normality proof uses trace-norm approximation by finite-rank operators; it does not assume a positive trace-class lift for every positive functional on $M$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Throughout, $H$ and $K$ are real or complex Hilbert spaces with the pairing
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-hilbert-space]]), $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]) of
operator norm $\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]), and $E$ is a **Hilbert basis**
of $H$, that is, a complete orthonormal subset of $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]).
The basis $E$ is **supplied as data**; the definitions below are stated
relative to it.

**The Hilbert–Schmidt square-sum.** The family $(\|Te\|^2)_{e\in E}$ consists of
nonnegative real numbers and is indexed by the arbitrary set $E$. Its sum is the
supremum of the finite subsums,

$$s_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2 \;:\; F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty],$$

in the finite-subset-supremum convention of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]; the empty finite
subset contributes the empty sum $0$, so the supremum is over a nonempty
set and exists in $[0,+\infty]$. No enumeration, ordering or countability of
$E$ is used or asserted, and no choice is performed: the supremum ranges over
the set of finite subsets of the fixed index set $E$. For finite $E$ the
supremum is the ordinary finite sum over $E$, because all terms are
nonnegative.

**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a basis.** The operator $T$ is
**Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$** when $s_E(T)<+\infty$, that is, when the
finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$. In that case the
**Hilbert–Schmidt norm of $T$ relative to $E$** is the nonnegative square root

$$\|T\|_{HS,E}:=\Bigl(\sum_{e\in E}\|Te\|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,+\infty).$$

When $s_E(T)=+\infty$, no Hilbert–Schmidt norm relative to $E$ is defined, and
$T$ is not Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**Degenerate and extreme cases.** The zero operator satisfies $s_E(0)=0$ for
every basis $E$, so it is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to every basis with norm
$0$. If $H=\{0\}$ then the empty family is a Hilbert basis of $H$, the only
finite subset is empty, and $s_\varnothing(T)=0$ for the only linear operator
$T:\{0\}\to K$; that operator is Hilbert–Schmidt relative to the empty basis
with norm $0$. If $H$ is finite dimensional and $E$ is finite, $s_E(T)$ is an
ordinary finite sum of the squared norms $\|Te\|^2$, and $T$ is automatically
Hilbert–Schmidt relative to $E$.

**The basis is part of the notation.** The symbol $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ keeps the
basis in the subscript on purpose. Until the next result is proved, the phrase
"$T$ is Hilbert–Schmidt" is never used without a specified Hilbert basis, and
nothing here asserts that a Hilbert basis of $H$ exists: the existence of $E$
is a hypothesis of the definition, and the question of whether the finiteness
of $s_E(T)$ and the value $\|T\|_{HS,E}$ depend on $E$ is taken up in
[[thm-hilbert-schmidt-norm-is-basis-independent]]. In particular this
definition makes no basis-existence claim and no comparison with the operator
norm $\|T\|$; every such statement is proved later, where its own hypotheses
are displayed.

**Notation.** For a finite $F\subseteq E$ we write
$s_F(T):=\sum_{e\in F}\|Te\|^2$ for the finite subsum, so that
$s_E(T)=\sup\{s_F(T):F\subseteq E \text{ finite}\}$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: Let $(e_j)_{j=1}^n$ be the standard orthonormal basis. If $T\in M'$, then commuting with each coordinate projection $P_j$ forces $Te_j=\lambda_j e_j$. Commuting with each matrix unit $E_{ij}$ gives $\lambda_i=\lambda_j$, hence $T=\lambda I$. Conversely scalar matrices commute with every element of $M$. Thus $M'=\mathbb C I$ and $M''=(\mathbb C I)'=\mathcal B(H)=M$, so $M$ is concrete.

Fix $\xi\ne0$. For any $\eta\in H$, define $a_\eta z:=\langle z,\xi\rangle\eta/\|\xi\|^2$. This is a linear matrix operator and $a_\eta\xi=\eta$, so $M\xi=H$ and $\xi$ is cyclic. If $\xi\ne0$, the orthogonal projection onto $\xi^\perp$ is nonzero since $n>1$, and it annihilates $\xi$. If $\xi=0$, the identity is nonzero and annihilates $\xi$. Hence no vector is separating for $M$.

Direct matrix-unit calculation gives $\langle E_{ij},E_{kl}\rangle_2=\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}$, so the units are an orthonormal basis of $K$. For $X=(x_{ij})$, $\|X\|_2^2=\sum_{i,j}|x_{ij}|^2$, proving positive definiteness. If $(X_m)$ is Cauchy, then each entry is Cauchy because $|x_{ij}^{(m)}-x_{ij}^{(k)}|\le\|X_m-X_k\|_2$. Their finitely many limits form a matrix $X$, and the finite sum formula gives $\|X_m-X\|_2\to0$. Thus $K$ is complete and hence a Hilbert space; [F3] makes every matrix Hilbert–Schmidt.

For $a,b\in M$, the coordinate formulas are $(aX)_{ij}=\sum_k a_{ik}x_{kj}$ and $(Xb)_{ij}=\sum_k x_{ik}b_{kj}$. Finite Cauchy–Schwarz, summed over $i,j$, gives $\|aX\|_2^2\le\bigl(\sum_{i,k}|a_{ik}|^2\bigr)\|X\|_2^2$ and $\|Xb\|_2^2\le\|X\|_2^2\bigl(\sum_{k,j}|b_{kj}|^2\bigr)$. Thus $L_a,R_b\in\mathcal B(K)$ by [F5] and [F6]. Also $L_aL_b=L_{ab}$, $L_I=I_K$, and $\langle L_aX,Y\rangle_2=\operatorname{Tr}(Y^*aX)=\langle X,L_{a^*}Y\rangle_2$, so $L_a^*=L_{a^*}$. Since $L_aI=a$, the map $a\mapsto L_a$ is injective. If $S\in\{L_a:a\in M\}'$ and $b=S(I)$, then every $X=L_X(I)$ satisfies $S(X)=S(L_XI)=L_XS(I)=Xb$; hence $S=R_b$. Conversely every right multiplication commutes with every left multiplication. If $T\in\{R_b:b\in M\}'$ and $a=T(I)$, then every $X=R_X(I)$ satisfies $T(X)=R_XT(I)=aX$, so $T=L_a$; the converse commutation also holds. Therefore $\{L_a:a\in M\}''=\{L_a:a\in M\}$, proving that the left representation is concrete.

By [F2], $\rho^{1/2}$ is invertible and $\|\Omega\|_2^2=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=1$. For every $X\in K$, $a=X\rho^{-1/2}$ satisfies $L_a\Omega=X$, so $M\Omega=K$ and $\Omega$ is cyclic. If $L_a\Omega=0$, then $a\rho^{1/2}=0$; right multiplication by $\rho^{-1/2}$ gives $a=0$, so $\Omega$ is separating. Finally, $\langle L_a\Omega,\Omega\rangle_2=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1/2}a\rho^{1/2})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho a)$ by cyclicity of finite matrix trace [F2].

Steps 1.1–1.2 establish the defining-representation assertions; steps 1.3, 2.1, and 3.1 construct the Hilbert–Schmidt left representation and verify its faithful cyclic-separating vector. The two representations act on different Hilbert spaces.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $t_n\to t$. For every $\lambda>0$, $\lambda^{it_n}\to\lambda^{it}$, while $|\lambda^{it_n}-\lambda^{it}|^2\leq4$. Since $\mu_\xi((0,\infty))=\|\xi\|^2<\infty$, [F1] and [F2] give
$$\|A^{it_n}\xi-A^{it}\xi\|^2=\int_{(0,\infty)}|\lambda^{it_n}-\lambda^{it}|^2\,d\mu_\xi(\lambda)\longrightarrow0.$$
Thus the orbit is sequentially continuous.
The real parameter space and Hilbert-space norm topology are metric, so sequential continuity is equivalent to continuity. Therefore $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $\xi\in H$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital $*$-subalgebra closed in the weak operator topology. Then $M''=M$, and $M$ is also closed in the strong operator topology. Consequently the concrete von Neumann algebras of [[def-von-neumann-algebra-and-commutant]] are exactly the unital $*$-subalgebras that are closed in either of these topologies. For an arbitrary set $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ one has $W^*(\mathcal S)''=W^*(\mathcal S)$.

Here a complex C$^*$-algebra is a complex Banach algebra with associative bilinear multiplication, submultiplicative norm, and a conjugate-linear involution satisfying $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$; **unital** means that it has a nonzero identity $I$ ([[def-c-star-algebra]]). A $*$-automorphism is a bijective complex-linear map preserving multiplication and involution. Let $t\mapsto\alpha_t$ be a strongly continuous one-parameter group of such automorphisms, so $\alpha_0$ is the identity and $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$. It is **strongly continuous** when $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for each fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. A **state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$; this is the state convention of [[def-qsm-infinite-algebraic-state]].

Fix absolute temperature $T>0$ in kelvins and Boltzmann's constant $k_B>0$ in J K$^{-1}$; the inverse-temperature parameter is $\beta:=(k_BT)^{-1}>0$, measured in J$^{-1}$. Let the reduced Planck constant $\hbar>0$ have units J s. Write $b:=\beta\hbar$, measured in seconds, and

$$S_b:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le b\},\qquad S_b^\circ:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0<\operatorname{Im}z<b\}.$$

A state $\omega$ is a **$\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in physical time** when for every $A,B\in\mathcal A$ there is a bounded function $F_{A,B}:S_b\to\mathbb C$ (that is, $\sup_{z\in S_b}|F_{A,B}(z)|<\infty$) that is continuous on $S_b$, complex-differentiable at every point of $S_b^\circ$, and satisfies

$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega\!\left(A\alpha_t(B)\right),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+ib)=\omega\!\left(\alpha_t(B)A\right)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

For the assigned quantum spin model, $\mathcal A$ is the norm-completed quasi-local algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] and $\alpha$ is the thermodynamic dynamics of [[thm-qsm-finite-range-spin-dynamics]], under that theorem's stated hypotheses. The strip width is $\beta\hbar$ in physical seconds; setting $\hbar=1$ is a separate natural-unit convention. This is a mathematical equilibrium criterion for the specified algebra and dynamics. It does not assert that a model describes a material, that a system has dynamically relaxed, or that all stationary states are KMS.

derivations.claim: Let $M=\{L_A:A\in M_n(\mathbb C)\}$ on $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, where $L_A X=AX$. The Hilbert-Schmidt adjoint satisfies $L_A^*=L_{A^*}$, so $M$ is a unital star subalgebra. The ambient operator space $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\rm HS})$ is finite dimensional; hence $M$ is weak-operator closed. By [F2], $M$ is a concrete von Neumann algebra. Since $\rho^{1/2}$ is invertible, every $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$ equals $L_{X\rho^{-1/2}}\Omega$, so $\Omega$ is cyclic. If $L_A\Omega=0$, then $A\rho^{1/2}=0$ and invertibility gives $A=0$, so $\Omega$ is separating. Finally, $$\langle L_A\Omega,\Omega\rangle_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1/2}A\rho^{1/2})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),$$ using finite trace cyclicity.

For $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho A e^{izH/\hbar}Be^{-izH/\hbar}\right).$$ Finite matrix exponentials are entire, so $F_{A,B}$ is entire. If $0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\hbar$, the real-time factors are unitary and the two imaginary-time factors have norms at most $e^{\beta\|H\|}$ each. Since $\|\rho\|_1=1$, $|F_{A,B}(z)|\leq\|A\|\|B\|e^{2\beta\|H\|}$ uniformly on that strip. The group $\alpha_s$ is norm-continuous because its matrix entries are continuous.

Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $\rho$, with eigenvalues $p_j>0$, and write $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$. Then $E_{ij}\Omega=\sqrt{p_j}E_{ij}$ and $E_{ij}^*\Omega=\sqrt{p_i}E_{ji}$, whence $S(E_{ij})=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$. The maps $JX=X^*$ and $\Delta X=\rho X\rho^{-1}$ satisfy $J\Delta^{1/2}E_{ij}=\sqrt{p_i/p_j}\,E_{ji}$ and $\Delta E_{ij}=(p_i/p_j)E_{ij}$. Thus $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ on a basis, so uniqueness of the polar decomposition gives the stated modular data.

For $X\in\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$, $$\Delta^{it}L_A\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}X,$$ because $\Delta^{-it}X=\rho^{-it}X\rho^{it}$ and the final right factor $\rho^{it}$ cancels $\rho^{-it}$. Hence $\sigma_t(A)=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}$.

For $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, functional calculus gives $\rho^{it}=Z^{-it}e^{-i\beta tH}$; the scalar factor cancels in conjugation. Substituting $t=-s/(\beta\hbar)$ into step 3.1 yields $\sigma_{-s/(\beta\hbar)}(A)=e^{isH/\hbar}Ae^{-isH/\hbar}=\alpha_s(A)$. Here $\beta\hbar$ has units seconds, so the modular parameter is dimensionless.

At $z=t+i\beta\hbar$, write $U=e^{itH/\hbar}$. Since $U$ commutes with $e^{\pm\beta H}$, $$F_{A,B}(t+i\beta\hbar)=Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta H}A e^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)e^{\beta H}\right) =Z^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(Ae^{-\beta H}\alpha_t(B)\right) =\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\rho\alpha_t(B)A\right).$$ The middle equality cycles $e^{\beta H}$ past the trace, and the last cycles $A$ past the trace. The lower boundary is $F_{A,B}(t)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A\alpha_t(B))$. Thus [F3] gives the physical-time $\beta$-KMS condition with width $\beta\hbar$.
