citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von
Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$, and define
$$M_\perp:=\{T\in\mathcal S_1(H):\operatorname{Tr}(Tx)=0 \text{ for every }x\in M\}.$$
Equip the coset space $Q:=\mathcal S_1(H)/M_\perp$ with the quotient norm.
Then the trace pairing
$$\Psi:M\to Q^*,\qquad (\Psi(x))([T])=\operatorname{Tr}(Tx),$$
is a well-defined isometric bijection, and $Q$ is a Banach space. Thus $Q$ is
an isometric predual of $M$, and its dual unit ball is weak-star compact.
Every vector functional $x\mapsto\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$ and every positive
functional in $Q$ preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in
$M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

**Assume the ultrafilter lemma.**  If $X$ is a real or complex normed space,
then its closed dual unit ball $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology
$\sigma(X^*,X)$.  Completeness of $X$ is not required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

Assume AC. For a bounded self-adjoint operator $T$ on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique isometric unital star-homomorphism $C(\sigma(T))\to\mathcal B(H)$, $f\mapsto f(T)$, sending the coordinate function $z$ to $T$, with range $C^*(I,T)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$ with
pole set $S$, and let $\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in
$\Omega$. Then

$\int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{a\in S}n(\Gamma,a)\operatorname{Res}(f,a),$

where only finitely many terms are nonzero.

Assume countable choice. If $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f\in L^1$, then
$$g(x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi$$
is bounded and continuous, equals f almost everywhere, and equals the specified value at every Lebesgue point of f.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a positive self-adjoint injective operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, the unbounded Borel functional calculus defines $A^{it}$ as a unitary on all of $H$. For every $\xi\in H$, the map $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Fix $|\lambda|=1$ with $\lambda\ne-1$. Write $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, set $\alpha=(1+\lambda)^{-1}$, and note $\alpha+\bar\alpha=1$. Because $\Delta$ is positive, its spectrum lies in $[0,\infty)$; $-\lambda\notin[0,\infty)$, so $(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}$ is a bounded spectral multiplier.

First let $x'\in M'$ be a positive contraction. In the linear-second notation $(u|v)=\langle v,u\rangle$, define $\psi(y)=(x'\Omega|y\Omega)=\omega(x'y)$ and $\psi_x(y)=\omega(\alpha xy+\bar\alpha yx)$ for $y\in M$ and $x=x^*\in M$. Since $x'$ commutes with $M$, $0\leq\psi\leq\omega$, and $\psi$ is normal by its rank-one trace-class representation. Each $\psi_x$ is self-adjoint. For fixed $y$, both $x\mapsto\omega(xy)$ and $x\mapsto\omega(yx)$ are normal matrix-coefficient functionals, so $x\mapsto\psi_x$ is continuous from the weak-star topology of $M_{\rm sa}$ to the pointwise topology of $M_*^{\rm sa}$. The self-adjoint unit ball of $M$ is weak-star closed; [F3]–[F4] make it compact. Hence $V=\{\psi_x:x=x^*,\ \|x\|\leq1\}$ is compact and convex.

Suppose $\psi\notin V$. The pointwise topology on $M_*^{\rm sa}$ has a base of finite evaluation conditions, so there are self-adjoint $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in M$ for which $q=(\psi(a_j))_{j=1}^m$ is outside the compact convex set $K=\{(\phi(a_j))_{j=1}^m:\phi\in V\}\subset\mathbb R^m$. Choose $0<r<\operatorname{dist}(q,K)$, put $U=K+B(0,r)$, choose $u_0\in U$, and set $C=U-u_0$. The open convex neighborhood $C$ of $0$ is absorbing; its gauge $p(v)=\inf\{s>0:v\in sC\}$ is finite and sublinear, and convexity and openness give $C=\{v:p(v)<1\}$. With $v_0=q-u_0\notin C$, $p(v_0)\geq1$. On the line $\mathbb Rv_0$ define $f(tv_0)=t\,p(v_0)$. Positive homogeneity gives $f\leq p$ for $t\geq0$; for $t<0$ the inequality $p(v_0)+p(-v_0)\geq0$ gives the same domination. By [F5], extend $f$ to a real linear $L$ on $\mathbb R^m$ with $L\leq p$. Then $L(k-u_0)<1\leq L(q-u_0)$ for every $k\in K$. Writing $L(z)=\sum_j c_jz_j$ and $y_0=\sum_jc_ja_j\in M_{\rm sa}$ gives $\psi(y_0)>\sup_{\|x\|\leq1,\ x=x^*}\psi_x(y_0)$.

Fix $|\lambda|=1$, $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$, $-\pi<\theta<\pi$. For $n\geq1$ let $E_n=1_{[1/n,n]}(\Delta)$. On $E_nH$, $\Delta$ and its inverse are bounded. Apply [F8] to each scalar matrix coefficient of $$f_n(z)=\frac{e^{i\theta z}}{\sin(\pi z)}\Delta^{-z}E_nxE_n\Delta^z$$ around the rectangle $-1/2\leq\operatorname{Re}z\leq1/2$, $|\operatorname{Im}z|\leq R$. On $E_nH$, $\log\Delta$ is bounded, so $f_n$ is norm-meromorphic with simple poles at integers; the rectangle encloses only $0$, with residue $E_nxE_n/\pi$. On the horizontal sides, the norm is at most $2e^{|\theta|R}n^2\|x\|/(e^{\pi R}-e^{-\pi R})$, which tends to zero. On the right vertical side, $z=it+1/2$ gives $\sin(\pi z)=\cosh(\pi t)$, $e^{i\theta z}=e^{-\theta t}e^{i\theta/2}$, and $\Delta^{-z}E_nxE_n\Delta^z=\Delta^{-1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_nxE_n\Delta^{it}\Delta^{1/2}$. On the left side, $z=it-1/2$ gives $\sin(\pi z)=-\cosh(\pi t)$ and the corresponding factors $\Delta^{1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_nxE_n\Delta^{it}\Delta^{-1/2}$ and $e^{-\theta t}e^{-i\theta/2}$. Substitution in the oriented contour formula therefore gives $$E_nxE_n=\Delta^{1/2}E_n\widetilde xE_n\Delta^{-1/2}+\lambda\Delta^{-1/2}E_n\widetilde xE_n\Delta^{1/2},\qquad \widetilde x=e^{-i\theta/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Delta^{-it}x\Delta^{it}\,dt.$$ The scalar weight is integrable because $|\theta|<\pi$. For fixed $\xi\in H$, the orbit $t\mapsto\Delta^{-it}x\Delta^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous: writing $U_t=\Delta^{-it}$, $\|U_txU_t^*\xi-U_sxU_s^*\xi\|\leq\|x\|\|(U_t^*-U_s^*)\xi\|+\|(U_t-U_s)xU_s^*\xi\|,$ and each term tends to zero as $t\to s$ by [F10]. Its norm is at most $\|x\|\|\xi\|$. Define the integral as the norm limit of ordinary vector integrals over finite intervals; the integrable scalar weight makes the tails Cauchy. The resulting linear map has norm at most $\|x\|$ times the weight's $L^1$ norm, so it is a bounded operator. This contour identity has the normalization fixed by the residue $E_nxE_n/\pi$.

The last strict inequality is impossible. Positivity and $0\leq\psi\leq\omega$ imply $\psi(y_0)\leq\psi(|y_0|)\leq\omega(|y_0|)$. For $n\geq1$, let $x_n=f_n(y_0)$ by [F6], where $f_n(s)=s/(|s|+1/n)$. Each $x_n$ is self-adjoint with $\|x_n\|\leq1$ and commutes with $y_0$. The positive functions $g_n(s)=s^2/(|s|+1/n)$ increase to $|s|$, so $x_ny_0=y_0x_n=g_n(y_0)\uparrow|y_0|$. Normality gives $\psi_{x_n}(y_0)=\omega(g_n(y_0))\uparrow\omega(|y_0|)$, contradicting the strict separator. Therefore $\psi=\psi_x$ for some self-adjoint contraction $x$.

Apply the same residue calculation to $g_n(z)=e^{i\theta z}\Delta^{-z}E_n/\sin(\pi z)$, whose residue at $0$ is $E_n/\pi$. On the right vertical side its multiplier is $2e^{-\theta t}e^{i\theta/2}\Delta^{-1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_n/(e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t})$; on the left it is $-2e^{-\theta t}e^{-i\theta/2}\Delta^{1/2}\Delta^{-it}E_n/(e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t})$. Including the opposite orientations of the two vertical sides and using $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$ yields $$\Delta^{1/2}(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}E_n=e^{-i\theta/2}\left(\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Delta^{-it}\,dt\right)E_n.$$ This follows by factoring $\Delta^{-1/2}(\Delta+\lambda)=\Delta^{1/2}+\lambda\Delta^{-1/2}$ from the vertical-side integral. Define the strong integral vectorwise as in step 1.4. The bounded spectral multiplier on the left and the integrable weight on the right allow $n\to\infty$ strongly, so the identity holds with $E_n$ omitted. In particular the scalar factor has no additional $i$: at $\lambda=1$ and $\Delta=I$ both sides equal $1/2$.

For every $y\in M$, $\psi=\psi_x$ and $\alpha+\bar\alpha=1$ give $$(x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega|y\Omega)=\omega(x'y)-\alpha\omega(xy)=\bar\alpha\,\omega(yx)=(S_0y\Omega|\bar\alpha x\Omega).$$ The antilinear-adjoint definition therefore puts $\bar\alpha x\Omega$ in $D(F)$ and gives $F(\bar\alpha x\Omega)=x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega$, or $\alpha F(x\Omega)=x'\Omega-\bar\alpha x\Omega$. Since $x=x^*$, $Sx\Omega=x\Omega$; hence $x\Omega\in D(\Delta)$ and $F(x\Omega)=\Delta x\Omega$. Thus $x'\Omega=(\alpha\Delta+\bar\alpha)x\Omega=(\Delta+\lambda)x\Omega/(1+\lambda)$. Replacing $x$ by $x/(1+\lambda)$ proves $(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}x'\Omega\in M\Omega$. For a general $x'\in M'$, write $x'=h_1+ih_2$ with $h_j=h_j^*$. If $c\geq\max(1,\|h_1\|,\|h_2\|)$, each $(I\pm h_j/c)/2$ is a positive contraction, so $x'$ is a complex linear combination of positive contractions. Linearity extends the inclusion to all of $M'\Omega$. Uniqueness follows because $\Delta+\lambda$ is injective and $\Omega$ is separating.

Let $x'\in M'$ and $x\in M$ satisfy $x'\Omega=(\Delta+\lambda)x\Omega$. For $y_1,y_2\in M$, commutation, $\Delta=FS$, $S(y\Omega)=y^*\Omega$, and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}=\Delta^{-1/2}J$ give $$(y_1\Omega|x'y_2\Omega)=(y_2^*y_1\Omega|x'\Omega)=(Sx\Omega|S(y_2^*y_1\Omega))+\lambda(y_1\Omega|y_2x\Omega)=(y_1x^*\Omega|y_2\Omega)+\lambda(y_1\Omega|S(x^*S(y_2\Omega)))=(\Delta^{-1/2}JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|y_2\Omega)+\lambda(y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$ If $y_1\Omega,y_2\Omega\in(\Delta+1)^{-1}M'\Omega$, then both lie in $D(\Delta^{1/2})\cap D(\Delta^{-1/2})$. Since $JxJ$ is bounded with adjoint $Jx^*J$, $$(\Delta^{-1/2}JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|y_2\Omega)=(JxJ\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega),$$ and self-adjointness of $\Delta^{-1/2}$ gives $$(y_1\Omega|\Delta^{-1/2}Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{-1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$ Therefore $$(y_1\Omega|x'y_2\Omega)=(\Delta^{1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{-1/2}y_2\Omega)+\lambda(\Delta^{-1/2}y_1\Omega|Jx^*J\Delta^{1/2}y_2\Omega).$$

The space $\Delta^{-1/2}M'\Omega$ is dense: $F(y'\Omega)=y'^*\Omega$ and $F=J\Delta^{-1/2}$ give $\Delta^{-1/2}M'\Omega=JM'\Omega$, which is dense by cyclicity of $\Omega$ for $M'$. In particular each $y'\Omega$ belongs to $D(\Delta^{-1/2})$. Fix $\xi\in D(\Delta^{1/2})\cap D(\Delta^{-1/2})$ and put $\eta=(\Delta^{1/2}+\Delta^{-1/2})\xi\in H$. Choose $y_n'\in M'$ so that $\eta_n:=\Delta^{-1/2}y_n'\Omega\to\eta$ in $H$. Step 3.1 at $\lambda=1$ supplies $y_n\in M$ with $y_n\Omega=(\Delta+1)^{-1}y_n'\Omega$. The spectral calculus gives $$y_n\Omega=q(\Delta)\eta_n,\qquad \Delta^{1/2}y_n\Omega=a(\Delta)\eta_n,\qquad \Delta^{-1/2}y_n\Omega=b(\Delta)\eta_n,$$ where $q(\lambda)=\sqrt\lambda/(1+\lambda)$, $a(\lambda)=\lambda/(1+\lambda)$ and $b(\lambda)=1/(1+\lambda)$ for $\lambda>0$. These three multipliers are bounded. The identities follow by multiplying their scalar functions on the domain of $\Delta^{-1/2}$; moreover $\lambda^{1/2}q(\lambda)=a(\lambda)$ and $\lambda^{-1/2}q(\lambda)=b(\lambda)$ are bounded, so $q(\Delta)\eta_n$ belongs to both required domains. Applied to $\eta$, the same identities give $q(\Delta)\eta=\xi$, $a(\Delta)\eta=\Delta^{1/2}\xi$ and $b(\Delta)\eta=\Delta^{-1/2}\xi$. Thus convergence of $\eta_n$ in $H$ implies $y_n\Omega\to\xi$ and $\Delta^{\pm1/2}y_n\Omega\to\Delta^{\pm1/2}\xi$. This proves density of the core from step 4.1 in the joint graph norm, without treating $\Delta^{-1/2}$ as a bounded operator.

Both sides of the identity in step 4.1 are continuous in those graph norms: the left side is bounded by $\|x'\|\|\xi_1\|\|\xi_2\|$, and the right side by $\|x\|$ times the products of the indicated $\Delta^{\pm1/2}$ norms. Passing to the approximating sequences of step 5.1 proves the displayed form identity for every $\xi_1,\xi_2\in D(\Delta^{1/2})\cap D(\Delta^{-1/2})$.

If $y$ satisfies the form identity of step 6.1, compression to $E_nH$ and comparison with step 1.4 show that $v_n=E_n(y-\widetilde x)E_n$ satisfies $\Delta_n v_n+\lambda v_n\Delta_n=0$, where $\Delta_n=\Delta|_{E_nH}$. The spectra of $\Delta_n$ and $-\lambda\Delta_n$ are disjoint compact sets: $\sigma(\Delta_n)\subset[1/n,n]$ and $-\lambda$ is not positive real. Choose a contour $\Gamma$ enclosing $\sigma(\Delta_n)$ and excluding $\sigma(-\lambda\Delta_n)$. For $z\in\Gamma$, multiplying the Sylvester equation by $(z-\Delta_n)^{-1}$ on the left and $(z+\lambda\Delta_n)^{-1}$ on the right gives $$(z-\Delta_n)^{-1}v_n=v_n(z+\lambda\Delta_n)^{-1}.$$ The spectral theorem and scalar residue formula give $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma(z-\Delta_n)^{-1}\,dz=I$ and $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\Gamma(z+\lambda\Delta_n)^{-1}\,dz=0$. Integration yields $v_n=0$.

The projections $E_n$ increase strongly to $I$ because $\ker\Delta=0$. Thus $E_n(y-\widetilde x)E_n=0$ for all $n$ implies $y=\widetilde x$ by taking matrix coefficients and passing to the strong limit. Applying this to the form identity of step 6.1 proves the resolvent-core formula $$Jx^*J=e^{-i\theta/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}\,dt.$$ The displayed scalar factor is determined by step 1.4; for $\lambda=1$ and $\Delta=I$ the integral gives $x/2$, as required by the form identity.

Fix $x',y'\in M'$, let $\lambda=e^{i\theta}$ with $-\pi<\theta<\pi$, and use step 3.1 to choose $x\in M$ with $x'\Omega=(\Delta+\lambda)x\Omega$. Since $(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}x'\Omega=x\Omega$, step 2.2 gives
$$y'J\Delta^{1/2}(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}x'\Omega=e^{i\theta/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}y'J\Delta^{-it}x'\Omega\,dt.$$
The left side is $y'J\Delta^{1/2}x\Omega=y'x^*\Omega=x^*y'\Omega$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. Conjugating the operator identity of step 8.1 by the antiunitary $J$ gives
$$x^*y'\Omega=e^{i\theta/2}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}Jy'\Omega\,dt.$$
Equating these expressions and cancelling their common nonzero scalar gives, for each $-\pi<\theta<\pi$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{e^{-\theta t}}{e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t}}\Bigl(J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}Jy'\Omega-y'J\Delta^{-it}x'\Omega\Bigr)\,dt=0.$$
The first summand is bounded by $\|x'\|\|y'\|$ and norm-continuous by the conjugation-orbit estimate in step 1.4 applied to $x'$ and $Jy'\Omega$; the second is bounded by the same constant and norm-continuous by [F10] applied to $x'\Omega$, followed by the fixed bounded maps $J$ and $y'$. For any $\eta\in H$, let $c(t)$ be its scalar coefficient. If $|\operatorname{Re}z|\leq r<\pi$, then $|c(t)e^{-zt}/(e^{\pi t}+e^{-\pi t})|\leq C e^{-(\pi-r)|t|}$ for a fixed $C$. For difference quotients with $|h|\leq\delta<\pi-r$, the integral formula for $e^{-ht}-1$ gives the integrable bound $C|t|e^{-(\pi-r-\delta)|t|}$. By [F11], dominated convergence differentiates the integral in $z$ on every such compact substrip, so its Laplace transform is holomorphic on $|\operatorname{Re}z|<\pi$. It vanishes on the real interval $(-\pi,\pi)$. A scalar holomorphic function with zeros accumulating at an interior point is identically zero: its Taylor series at that point either has a first nonzero coefficient, which would make the zero isolated, or all coefficients vanish and it is zero in a neighborhood; the set of points with a zero neighborhood is then open and closed in the connected strip. Evaluating at $z=is$ shows the Fourier transform of that $L^1$ coefficient is zero for every $s\in\mathbb R$.

By [F9] the scalar coefficient in step 9.1 vanishes almost everywhere; continuity makes it vanish everywhere. Since this holds for every $\eta\in H$, $$J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}Jy'\Omega=y'J\Delta^{-it}x'\Omega\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$ For fixed $t,x'$, apply this identity with $y'_2$ and then with $y'_1y'_2$. It gives $$(y'_1J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}J)y'_2\Omega=y'_1y'_2J\Delta^{-it}x'\Omega =(J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}J)y'_1y'_2\Omega.$$ The vectors $M'\Omega$ are dense, so $J\Delta^{-it}x'\Delta^{it}J$ commutes with every $y'_1\in M'$. Thus it lies in $M''=M$. At $t=0$, $JM'J\subseteq M$, hence $M'\subseteq JMJ$.

To prove the reverse inclusion, fix $x,y\in M$ and $x'\in M'$. Step 10.1 gives $Jx'J\in M$. Using commutation of $x'$ and $y$, the identities $F=S^*=JSJ$, $S(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$, and $(JxJ)^*=Jx^*J$, we obtain $$(x'^*\Omega|yJx\Omega)=(y^*\Omega|x'Jx\Omega) =(y^*\Omega|J(Jx'J)x\Omega) =(y^*\Omega|JS(x^*Jx'^*J\Omega)) =(y^*\Omega|F(Jx^*Jx'^*\Omega)) =(Jx^*Jx'^*\Omega|Sy^*\Omega) =(x'^*\Omega|JxJy\Omega).$$ Since $x'^*\Omega$ ranges over the dense subspace $M'\Omega$, this implies $yJx\Omega=JxJy\Omega$. For $y_1,y_2\in M$, it follows that $y_1JxJy_2\Omega=y_1y_2Jx\Omega=JxJy_1y_2\Omega$. Density of $M\Omega$ then gives $JxJ\in M'$. Therefore $JMJ\subseteq M'$, and step 10.1 yields $JMJ=M'$.

The inclusions $J\Delta^{-it}M'\Delta^{it}J\subseteq M$ from step 10.1 and $JMJ=M'$ from step 11.1 imply $\Delta^{-it}M'\Delta^{it}\subseteq M'$ for every $t$. Replacing $t$ by $-t$ and conjugating gives equality. Taking commutants and using $M''=M$ gives $\Delta^{it}M\Delta^{-it}=M$.

For $x'\in M'$, write $x'=JxJ$ with $x\in M$ by step 11.1. Since $J\Omega=\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$, direct substitution gives $JS_0J(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega=F_0(x'\Omega)$. Thus $F_0=JS_0J$, so graph closure gives $\overline{F_0}=JSJ=F=S^*$. Steps 3.1, 11.1–12.1, and this closure identity establish all stated conclusions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standard modular data of a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ with unit cyclic-separating vector $\Omega$. Let $F=S^*$, where $S$ is the closure of $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$, and let $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. For every $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda\ne-1$,
$$(\Delta+\lambda)^{-1}M'\Omega\subseteq M\Omega.$$
The modular conjugation and operator satisfy
$$JMJ=M',\qquad \Delta^{it}M\Delta^{-it}=M\quad(t\in\mathbb R),\qquad \overline{F_0}=F=S^*.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and write its polar decomposition as $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. The preceding Tomita-operator lemma ensures this closure and polar data are well defined, with $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective. For $x\in\mathcal B(H)$ and dimensionless $t\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sigma_t(x):=\Delta^{it}x\Delta^{-it}.$$
Set $\omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$. The powers $\Delta^{it}$ are the bounded unitary imaginary powers from the unbounded Borel functional calculus. At this definition stage $\sigma_t$ is defined on $\mathcal B(H)$; preservation of $M$ is established by a separate theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in its first argument, let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra, and let $\Omega$ be a unit vector that is cyclic and separating for $M$. Define $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ on $M\Omega$ and $F_0(x'\Omega)=x'^*\Omega$ on $M'\Omega$. Let $S=\overline{S_0}$ and $F=S^*$. Then $S$ is a densely defined closed antilinear involution, its polar decomposition is $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ with $J$ antiunitary and $\Delta$ positive self-adjoint and injective, and
$$J=J^*=J^{-1},\qquad J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1},\qquad J\Delta^{it}J=\Delta^{it}\ (t\in\mathbb R),\qquad F=J\Delta^{-1/2}=\Delta^{1/2}J,\qquad J\Omega=\Omega,\qquad \Delta\Omega=\Omega.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator whose spectral projection valued measure $E$ is supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $\xi\in H$, put $\mu_\xi(B)=\langle E(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$. Define
$$D(A^{1/2})=\left\{\xi\in H:\int_{(0,\infty)}\lambda\,d\mu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\right\}.$$
For $z\in S=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq1\}$ and $\xi\in D(A^{1/2})$, define $A^{-iz/2}\xi$ by the unbounded Borel functional calculus for the function $\lambda\mapsto \exp(-iz\log(\lambda)/2)$. This vector is defined, strongly continuous in $z$ on $S$, and satisfies
$$\|A^{-iz/2}\xi\|^2\leq\|\xi\|^2+\|A^{1/2}\xi\|^2.$$
The map $z\mapsto A^{-iz/2}\xi$ is norm-holomorphic on the open strip $S^\circ$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a concrete von
Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space $H$, and define
$$M_\perp:=\{T\in\mathcal S_1(H):\operatorname{Tr}(Tx)=0 \text{ for every }x\in M\}.$$
Equip the coset space $Q:=\mathcal S_1(H)/M_\perp$ with the quotient norm.
Then the trace pairing
$$\Psi:M\to Q^*,\qquad (\Psi(x))([T])=\operatorname{Tr}(Tx),$$
is a well-defined isometric bijection, and $Q$ is a Banach space. Thus $Q$ is
an isometric predual of $M$, and its dual unit ball is weak-star compact.
Every vector functional $x\mapsto\langle x\xi,\xi\rangle$ and every positive
functional in $Q$ preserves suprema of bounded increasing positive nets in
$M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, and let
$\mathcal S_1(H)$ be its trace-class operators with trace norm $\|\cdot\|_1$
and trace $\operatorname{Tr}$. Finite-rank operators are dense in
$(\mathcal S_1(H),\|\cdot\|_1)$. For every bounded linear functional
$\Phi:\mathcal S_1(H)\to\mathbb C$, there is a unique $X\in\mathcal B(H)$ such
that
$$\Phi(T)=\operatorname{Tr}(TX)\qquad(T\in\mathcal S_1(H)),$$
and the correspondence is isometric:
$\|\Phi\|=\|X\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\ne\{0\}$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space. Use the predual $M_*=Q$ of [[lem-qsmx-von-neumann-predual]]; its elements are the normal linear functionals, and the induced topology $\sigma(M,Q)$ is the ultraweak topology. A **normal state** on $M$ is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:M\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$, $\omega(a)\geq0$ for every positive $a\in M$, and
$$\omega\!\left(\sup_i a_i\right)=\sup_i\omega(a_i)$$
for every increasing net $(a_i)$ of positive elements with $0\leq a_i\leq C I$ for a common finite $C$ and supremum taken in $M$.
An automorphism of $M$ is **normal** when it preserves the suprema of all such bounded increasing positive nets.
A **point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter automorphism group** is a family $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ of bijective unital complex-linear maps $M\to M$ preserving multiplication and adjoints, with $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$, $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$, and $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(x))$ continuous for every $x\in M$ and every normal linear functional $\varphi\in Q$.
For dimensionless $t$ and dimensionless $\beta>0$, the normal state $\omega$ satisfies the **upper-strip $(\alpha,\beta)$ KMS condition** when, for every $A,B\in M$, there is a bounded scalar function $F_{A,B}$ on $S_\beta=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\}$ that is continuous on $S_\beta$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies
$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+i\beta)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be a positive self-adjoint injective operator with spectral projection valued measure $E$ supported on $(0,\infty)$. For $t\in\mathbb R$, the unbounded Borel functional calculus defines $A^{it}$ as a unitary on all of $H$. For every $\xi\in H$, the map $t\mapsto A^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\sigma_t(M)=M$. Each $\sigma_t$ is conjugation by the unitary $\Delta^{it}$, so it is complex-linear, multiplicative, adjoint-preserving and bijective, with inverse $\sigma_{-t}$. The spectral calculus gives $\Delta^{i(s+t)}=\Delta^{is}\Delta^{it}$, hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=\sigma_{s+t}$ and $\sigma_0=I$. To check normality, let $0\leq a_i\uparrow a$ be a bounded increasing net in $M$. Unitary conjugation is an order isomorphism of $\mathcal B(H)$: if $b$ bounds every $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}$, then $\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ bounds every $a_i$, so $a\leq\Delta^{-it}b\Delta^{it}$ and $\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}\leq b$. Thus $\Delta^{it}a_i\Delta^{-it}\uparrow\Delta^{it}a\Delta^{-it}$ in $\mathcal B(H)$. By [F2] the limit is in $M$, hence is also the supremum in $M$. By the definition in [F7], each restriction is a normal $*$-automorphism.

For $A,B\in M$, both $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ lie in $D(\Delta^{1/2})$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$ and $\|Sx\Omega\|=\|\Delta^{1/2}x\Omega\|$. Define $$F_{A,B}(z)=\bigl(\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega\,\big|\,\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega\bigr),$$ where $(u|v)=\langle v,u\rangle$ is linear in its second argument. By [F3], both vectors $A^*\Omega$ and $B\Omega$ belong to $D(\Delta^{1/2})$; [F4] then makes each vector factor bounded and continuous on the closed strip. The first is anti-holomorphic as a vector-valued function of $z$ and enters the first, conjugate-linear slot, while the second is holomorphic in the second slot. Hence $F_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous on the strip and holomorphic inside.

By [F8], $t\mapsto\Delta^{it}\xi$ is norm-continuous for every $\xi\in H$. For fixed $x\in M$ and $\xi,\eta\in H$, the coefficient $\langle\sigma_t(x)\xi,\eta\rangle$ is therefore continuous. If $T$ is finite rank, $\operatorname{Tr}(T\sigma_t(x))$ is a finite sum of such continuous coefficients. For arbitrary trace-class $T$, choose finite-rank $T_n\to T$ in trace norm by [F6]; uniformly in $t$, $|\operatorname{Tr}((T-T_n)\sigma_t(x))|\leq\|T-T_n\|_1\|x\|$. Thus every element of the predual $Q$ evaluates continuously on $\sigma_t(x)$, which is point-ultraweak continuity.

Since $\Delta^{it}\Omega=\Omega$ and $\Delta^{it}$ is unitary, $$\omega(\sigma_t(x))=\langle\Delta^{it}x\Omega,\Omega\rangle=\langle x\Omega,\Delta^{-it}\Omega\rangle=\omega(x).$$ So $\omega$ is invariant under $\sigma_t$ and under $\alpha_t=\sigma_{-t}$. Also $\omega(I)=\|\Omega\|^2=1$ and $\omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2\geq0$, so $\omega$ is a state; because $\Omega$ is separating for $M$, this same identity shows that $\omega$ is faithful. By [F5], $\omega$ is a normal vector functional on $M$. Hence it is a faithful normal state as asserted.

For real $t$, unitarity of $\Delta^{it/2}$ and the identity $\Delta^{-it}B\Omega=\sigma_{-t}(B)\Omega$ give $$F_{A,B}(t)=(A^*\Omega|\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=(\Omega|A\Delta^{-it}B\Omega)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)).$$ This is the lower boundary in [F7].

At $z=t+i$, $\Delta^{i\overline z/2}A^*\Omega=\Delta^{it/2}J A\Omega$ and $\Delta^{-iz/2}B\Omega=\Delta^{-it/2}J B^*\Omega$, because $Sx\Omega=x^*\Omega$ and $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$. By [F2], $J$ commutes with $\Delta^{it/2}$; antiunitarity gives $(Ju|Jv)=(v|u)$. Therefore $$F_{A,B}(t+i)=(\Delta^{-it/2}B^*\Omega|\Delta^{it/2}A\Omega)=(B^*\Omega|\Delta^{it}A\Omega)=\omega(B\sigma_t(A)).$$ Invariance from step 2.2 changes the last expression to $\omega(\sigma_{-t}(B)A)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)$, the upper boundary in [F7].

Steps 2.2–3.1 provide the bounded continuous strip function with both required boundary values for each $A,B\in M$. By [F7], $\omega$ is upper-strip $(\alpha,1)$ KMS. Step 1.1 gives the asserted point-ultraweakly continuous automorphism group, and [F2] gives $JMJ=M'$. No norm-continuity assertion on all of $M$ is made.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\geq1$, let $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^n$, and let $\rho$ be a positive-definite Hermitian matrix, meaning $\langle\rho v,v\rangle>0$ for each nonzero $v\in\mathcal H$, with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Write $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}=M_n(\mathbb C)$ with inner product $\langle X,Y\rangle_{\rm HS}=\operatorname{Tr}(Y^*X)$, linear in the first argument, and let $M_n(\mathbb C)$ act on $\mathcal H_{\rm HS}$ by left multiplication. For $\Omega=\rho^{1/2}$, the standard modular data are
$$JX=X^*,\qquad \Delta X=\rho X\rho^{-1},\qquad \sigma_t(A)=\rho^{it}A\rho^{-it}\quad(A\in M_n(\mathbb C),\ t\in\mathbb R).$$
The vector state of $\Omega$ is $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$. If $H=H^*$ has energy unit joules, $\beta>0$ has unit joules$^{-1}$, $\hbar>0$ has unit joule-seconds, and $\rho=e^{-\beta H}/Z$ with $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$, then the physical-time dynamics
$$\alpha_s(A)=e^{isH/\hbar}Ae^{-isH/\hbar}\quad(s\text{ in seconds})$$
satisfies
$$\alpha_s=\sigma_{-s/(\beta\hbar)}.$$
On the finite-dimensional C$^*$-algebra $M_n(\mathbb C)$, $\omega$ is a $\beta$-KMS state for $\alpha$ in the physical-time convention of the stated KMS definition, with strip width $\beta\hbar$ seconds. If $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$, then $k_B$ has units joules per kelvin and $T$ has units kelvins.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root convention that its inner product is linear in the first argument, and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$ ([[def-qc-density-operator]]). If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

The trace is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]), and the spectral definition makes the expression independent of the eigenbasis. The term for a zero eigenvalue is defined to be $0\ln0:=0$. The default unit is nats, using the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]); the entropy in bits is $S_2(\rho):=S(\rho)/\ln2$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B$, both marginals $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$ are density operators.

derivations.claim: By [F1], the input is a positive trace-one endomorphism on its finite tensor product. Apply [F5] to each bipartite grouping of a finite multipartite density operator; this makes every one-factor and two-factor marginal used in the Definition a density operator. Repeated partial traces use [F4] to retain the stated tensor-factor order.

Each such density operator has finitely many eigenvalues in $[0,1]$, so the finite entropy sum in [F2] is a real number, including when some eigenvalues vanish. The relative entropy clause is defined on exactly the two support cases in [F3]. Therefore $I(A:B)$ and $I(A:C\mid B)$ are finite real-valued functions on the stated density operators, and $D$ has the extended-real domain specified in the Definition.

All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad
\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $H_A,H_B,H_C$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $\rho_{ABC}$ be a density operator on their ordered tensor product. Write $\rho_{AB},\rho_{BC},\rho_B$ for its marginals using the partial traces in [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. Then
$$S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})\ge S(\rho_B)+S(\rho_{ABC}),$$
where $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho)$ with $0\ln0:=0$ as in [[def-it-von-neumann-entropy]].

Let $H_A,H_B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces, let $d=\dim H_B\ge1$, and let $A,B$ be non-negative operators on $H_A\otimes H_B$. Then

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_B A\|\operatorname{Tr}_B B)\le D(A\|B).$$

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: By [A1], the left side of the first assertion is the displayed four-entropy difference. Apply [F1] to the given state with the same factor order; the resulting inequality is exactly $I(A:C\mid B)_\rho\ge0$.

By [F3], choose a finite Kraus list $K_1,\ldots,K_q$ with $\sum_aK_a^*K_a=I_d$; because $d\ge1$, this identity rules out $q=0$. Let $\mathcal E=\mathbb C^q$ with orthonormal basis $(f_a)$ and define $V:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e\otimes\mathcal E$ by $Vx=\sum_aK_ax\otimes f_a$. Orthogonality of the $f_a$ gives $\langle Vx,Vy\rangle=\sum_a\langle K_ax,K_ay\rangle=\langle x,(\sum_aK_a^*K_a)y\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$, so $V^*V=I_d$. The coordinate formula [F4] then gives $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal E}(VXV^*)=\sum_aK_aXK_a^*=\Phi(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$.

The isometry $V$ maps each positive-eigenvalue eigenspace of $X\ge0$ onto the corresponding eigenspace of $VXV^*$, with the same eigenvalue; the orthogonal complement of $\operatorname{ran}V$ is in the kernel. Hence $\operatorname{supp}(VXV^*)=V(\operatorname{supp}X)$, and likewise for $Y$. Because $V$ is injective, support inclusion holds for $X,Y$ exactly when it holds for $VXV^*,VYV^*$. If it fails, both relative entropies are $+\infty$ by [F5]. If it holds, the support-restricted spectral logarithms satisfy $\log(VXV^*)=V(\log X)V^*$ and $\log(VYV^*)=V(\log Y)V^*$ on the corresponding supports. The trace identity in [F6] therefore yields $D(VXV^*\|VYV^*)=D(X\|Y)$.

Apply [F2] to $R=VXV^*$ and $S=VYV^*$, which are positive semidefinite because $V$ is linear and $X,Y\ge0$. By step 1.2 their partial traces are $\Phi(X),\Phi(Y)$, and by step 2.1 their relative entropy equals $D(X\|Y)$. Thus $D(\Phi(X)\|\Phi(Y))\le D(X\|Y)$, including when the right side is $+\infty$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ on a Hilbert space $H$, define its support subspace in either finite or infinite dimension by
$$\operatorname{supp}\rho:=(\ker\rho)^\perp,\qquad \ker\rho:=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}.$$
It is closed; write $P_\rho$ for its orthogonal projection, whose existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]].

Fix the positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K, as in the approved QSM quantities design and [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]]). For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

The spectral-moment identification in the preceding cross-log clause is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, so that the state is supported on the space where $-\log\sigma$ acts. Outside that domain, $C$ denotes only the displayed nonnegative double sum.

Let $H=H^*$ act on a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\geq1$, $\beta>0$, $k_B>0$, $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$, and $Z=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})$. Put $\sigma=e^{-\beta H}/Z$, $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, and $S(\rho)=-k_B\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, with $0\log0=0$. Then every density matrix $\rho$, including rank-deficient matrices, satisfies
$
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho H)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality if and only if $\rho=\sigma$. Moreover $S(\sigma)=k_B(\log Z+\beta\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H))$, so $F_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma H)-TS(\sigma)$. This is finite-dimensional mathematical optimization; actual preparation is a separate postulate.

For nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ and a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B$, both marginals $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$ are density operators.

Let $V,W$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $W$, let $V\otimes W$ be their tensor product with the inner product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], and let $\operatorname{tr}$ denote the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

(a) For every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$ there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. For $\|\Psi\|=1$ the reduced density $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$ holds exactly when $k=1$, i.e. exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector; mixed-state separability is not decided by this criterion.

(d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb C^q$ in the standard basis $e_j$, $0\le j<q$, define $S e_j=e_{j+1\ {\rm mod}\ q}$ and $D e_j=e^{2\pi i j/q}e_j$. The $q^2$ unitaries $S^aD^b$, $0\le a,b<q$, satisfy $q^{-2}\sum_{a,b=0}^{q-1}(S^aD^b)^*R(S^aD^b) =q^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(R)I_q\qquad(R\in M_q(\mathbb C)).$ Indeed, averaging over $b$ cancels each off-diagonal matrix unit because its phase is a nontrivial $q$-th root sum, and averaging the surviving diagonal units over $a$ gives their arithmetic mean times $I_q$; for $q=1$ the formula is the identity. Applying this one-site twirl on each factor in $Y\setminus X$ yields the normalized partial trace of [F1]. Each twirl is an average of unitary conjugations, so it is unital, positive, and contractive. The formula is unchanged when an extra identity factor is added, since its normalized trace is $1$; hence $E_X$ is consistent on $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$. Contractivity extends it uniquely to the completion, and its range remains in the closed finite-dimensional subalgebra $\mathcal A_X$.

Enumerate $Y\setminus X=\{z_1,\ldots,z_k\}$ and write $E_{z_j}$ for the one-site twirl. The commuting twirls satisfy $B-E_X(B)=\sum_{j=1}^k E_{z_1}\cdots E_{z_{j-1}}\bigl(B-E_{z_j}(B)\bigr).$ For any $C\in\mathcal A_Y$, the average formula gives $\|C-E_{z_j}(C)\|\le\sup_{V_z}\|C-V_z^*CV_z\|=\sup_{V_z}\|[C,V_z]\|$, where $V_z$ ranges over the one-site unitaries. Each preceding twirl is contractive and commutes with conjugation by $V_z$, so its term in the displayed sum is at most $\sup_{V_z}\|[B,V_z]\|$. The triangle inequality and the finite sum over sites give the stated bound.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $d\ge1$, the site set $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, its max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$, and the local spin algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of the uniformly finite-dimensional spin system. A finite interaction is a family $\Phi(Z)=\Phi(Z)^*\in\mathcal A_Z$ indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$. For a finite $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define

$$H_\Lambda^\Phi:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z),\qquad \tau_t^{\Lambda,\Phi}(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda^\Phi/\hbar},$$

where $\hbar>0$, $A$ is embedded in a common finite local algebra, and the finite sum is a self-adjoint matrix. When a path $\Phi_s$, $s\in[0,1]$, is used, each $\Phi_s(Z)$ is $C^1$ in matrix norm and the derivative is taken term by term.

For $r\ge0$ put $F(r)=(1+r)^{-d-1}$. The admissible weights used here are

$$F_a(r):=e^{-ar}F(r)\quad(a>0),\qquad F_\rho(r):=(1+r)^{-\rho}\quad(\rho>d).$$

For an admissible weight $G$, define the weighted interaction norm

$$\|\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma}\frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{\substack{Z\subset\Gamma\ {\rm finite,\ nonempty}\\x,y\in Z}}\|\Phi(Z)\|.$$

The derivative norm of a path is

$$\|\partial\Phi\|_G:=\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\sup_{x,y\in\Gamma} \frac{1}{G(d_\infty(x,y))} \sum_{Z\ni x,y}|Z|\,\|\partial_s\Phi_s(Z)\|.$$

A finite-volume spectral band is a nonempty selected subset $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\subseteq\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})$ together with the orthogonal projection onto the sum of its eigenspaces. It may be specified by an interval $I_\Lambda(s)$ with smoothly varying endpoints, in which case $\Sigma_\Lambda(s)=\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\cap I_\Lambda(s)$. The band is uniformly isolated with gap $\gamma>0$ along a specified finite-volume exhaustion when

$$\operatorname{dist}\!\left(\Sigma_\Lambda(s),\sigma(H_\Lambda^{\Phi_s})\setminus\Sigma_\Lambda(s)\right)\ge\gamma$$

for every volume in that exhaustion and every $s\in[0,1]$. For spectral-flow arguments, the selected eigenvalues must also form a locally fixed spectral cluster: for each $s_0$, a contour in the resolvent set encloses exactly the selected eigenvalues for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $s_0$. In finite dimension this implies that its projection is $C^1$ when the Hamiltonian path is $C^1$. This cluster condition holds, for example, for the first $r_\Lambda$ eigenvalues counted with multiplicity when the integer $r_\Lambda$ is fixed along the path and the gap after them stays open. Uniform distance between the selected and unselected spectra alone does not prevent an interval from changing membership discontinuously. A ground band is such a band containing the lowest eigenvalue or a finite-volume cluster of lowest eigenvalues; no uniqueness is implicit.

For physical units, take interaction terms and Hamiltonians in joules, time in seconds, and $\hbar$ in joule-seconds. The path parameter $s$, lattice distance, and admissible weights are dimensionless; the interaction norm therefore has energy units and the derivative norm has energy units per dimensionless path parameter.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $f$ be meromorphic on $\Omega$ with
pole set $S$, and let $\Gamma$ be admissible for the residue theorem in
$\Omega$. Then

$\int_\Gamma f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\sum_{a\in S}n(\Gamma,a)\operatorname{Res}(f,a),$

where only finitely many terms are nonzero.

derivations.claim: Define $\chi(\omega)=e\exp(-1/(1-(\omega/\gamma)^2))$ for $|\omega|<\gamma$, and $\chi(\omega)=0$ otherwise. The exponential tends to zero faster than every power at the endpoints, so $\chi$ is real, even, smooth, compactly supported in $[-\gamma,\gamma]$, and $\chi(0)=1$. Define $w(t)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int\chi(\omega)e^{-it\omega}\,d\omega$. By [A1], [F3], and the sign/scale conversion stated in [F3], $w$ is Schwartz, real and even, its Fourier transform $\widehat w(\omega)=\int w(t)e^{it\omega}dt$ equals $\chi(\omega)$, and $\int w=1$. For $t>0$ put $W_\gamma(t)=\int_t^\infty w(v)\,dv$; for $t<0$ put $W_\gamma(t)=-\int_{-\infty}^t w(v)\,dv$; set $W_\gamma(0)=0$. Evenness and unit integral make $W_\gamma$ odd with one-sided limits $W_\gamma(0^\pm)=\pm\frac12$. For every $N$, a Schwartz bound $|w(v)|\le c(1+|v|)^{-N-2}$ on either tail gives $|W_\gamma(t)|\le c'(1+|t|)^{-N-1}$; hence $W_\gamma\in L^1$ and has the stated tail estimate. Integration by parts on the two half-lines, accounting for the jump of size $1$ at zero and using $W_\gamma'=-w$ away from zero, gives $-\widehat w(\omega)=-1-i\omega\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)$. Thus $\widehat W_\gamma(\omega)=i(1-\chi(\omega))/\omega$ for $\omega\ne0$, so it equals $i/\omega$ for $|\omega|\ge\gamma$.

Fix $s_0$. By the locally fixed spectral-cluster hypothesis and [F2], choose a finite union of positively oriented contours $\Gamma$ surrounding exactly the selected eigenvalues and staying a positive distance from the remaining spectrum, with the same selected eigenvalues enclosed for nearby $s$. For $s$ near $s_0$, $\|H_\Lambda(s)-H_\Lambda(s_0)\|$ is small; factoring $zI-H_\Lambda(s)$ through $zI-H_\Lambda(s_0)$ and using the norm-convergent Neumann series keeps every $z\in\Gamma$ in the resolvent set. The contour projection $P_\Lambda(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_\Gamma(zI-H_\Lambda(s))^{-1}\,dz$ is therefore $C^1$, since the inverse matrix is $C^1$ in $s$.

In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H_\Lambda(s)$, write its eigenvalues as $E_m$ and the band indicator as $p_m\in\{0,1\}$. Differentiating $P^2=P$ gives $P'_{mn}=0$ when $p_m=p_n$. Differentiating $HP=PH$ gives $P'_{mn}=(p_m-p_n)H'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)$ when $p_m\ne p_n$; the denominator has magnitude at least $\gamma$. The integral defining $D_\Lambda$ converges in norm because $W_\gamma\in L^1$; it is self-adjoint because $W_\gamma$ is real and each conjugated $H_\Lambda'$ is self-adjoint. Dominated convergence, using continuity and boundedness of $H_\Lambda'(s)$ on the compact interval and the integrable majorant $2\sup_s\|H_\Lambda'(s)\||W_\gamma(t)|$, shows $D_\Lambda(s)$ is norm-continuous. Its matrix entries are $(D_\Lambda)_{mn}=H'_{mn}\widehat W_\gamma(E_m-E_n)=iH'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)$ across the band gap. Hence $i[D_\Lambda,P_\Lambda]_{mn}=(p_n-p_m)i(D_\Lambda)_{mn}=(p_m-p_n)H'_{mn}/(E_m-E_n)=P'_{mn}$ across the gap, and both sides vanish within either band block. This proves the identity in every matrix entry.
