citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Use the finite local matrix algebras and isometric factor inclusions of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]] and [[lem-qsm-local-spin-inclusions-isometric]]. Identify $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with its image in every larger finite-region algebra. The directed union

$$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}:=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$$

is the algebra of **strictly local observables**. Its norm is $\|A\|=\|A\|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ for any finite localization region $\Lambda$ of $A$; isometric inclusions make this independent of the chosen region. The **quasi-local spin algebra** is the norm completion

$$\mathcal A:=\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\,\|\cdot\|}.$$

The C*-algebra structure on this completion has product and adjoint extended continuously from the finite local matrix algebras. Countable Choice is assumed for the published existence theorem for metric completions; [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]] supplies the full extension argument using the finite C*-identity of [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]].

**No global Hilbert tensor product is selected.** “Quasi-local” means norm completion of the directed algebra of finite-region observables; it does not mean a chosen representation as operators on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space. A local operator $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ may have more than one localization region. Disjoint finite local factors commute in their common finite tensor algebra.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Cauchy-sequence completion. For the local spin system of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], the normed $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and its completion $\mathcal A$ of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]] are well defined; $\mathcal A$ is a unital complex C*-algebra and $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is norm dense in it. If $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and $B\in\mathcal A_\Delta$ for disjoint finite regions $\Lambda,\Delta$, then $AB=BA$.

Use the lattice $\Gamma=\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge1$, the finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, the local matrix algebras $\mathcal A_\Lambda$, and the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. For finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z=\max_{x,y\in Z}d_\infty(x,y)$; for finite nonempty $X,Y\subset\Gamma$, write $\operatorname{dist}_\infty(X,Y)=\min_{x\in X,y\in Y}d_\infty(x,y)$.

A **uniformly bounded finite-range interaction** is a family $\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_Z$, indexed by finite nonempty $Z\subset\Gamma$, such that $\Phi(Z)^*=\Phi(Z)$ and there are an integer $M\ge1$, a finite $R\ge0$, and $\kappa<\infty$ satisfying

$$\Phi(Z)=0\quad\text{if }|Z|>M\text{ or }\operatorname{diam}_\infty Z>R,\qquad\kappa:=\sup_{x\in\Gamma}\sum_{Z\ni x}\|\Phi(Z)\|<\infty.$$

The norm in this sum is the operator norm in the local matrix algebra $\mathcal A_Z$. If a model lists several terms with the same support, first add them in that local algebra; the resulting single operator is $\Phi(Z)$, and $\kappa$ uses its norm. Thus no multiplicity is implicit.

For a finite region $\Lambda\subset\Gamma$, define the **free-boundary finite-volume Hamiltonian** by summing only terms whose complete support lies inside $\Lambda$; terms meeting $\Lambda$ but extending outside it are omitted:

$$H_\Lambda:=\sum_{\varnothing\ne Z\subseteq\Lambda}\Phi(Z)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda.$$

It is a finite sum of self-adjoint matrices. For a fixed scale $\hbar>0$ and any finite $\Omega\supseteq\Lambda$, embed $H_\Lambda$ in $\mathcal A_\Omega$ by the canonical factor inclusion and define

$$\alpha_t^\Lambda(A):=e^{itH_\Lambda/\hbar}Ae^{-itH_\Lambda/\hbar}\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Omega,\ t\in\mathbb R).$$

These actions are compatible as $\Omega$ increases, because the extra tensor factors carry the identity. On $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ this is the ordinary finite matrix Heisenberg dynamics.

In physical SI bookkeeping, when $\Phi(Z)$ is interpreted as an energy, $\Phi(Z)$, $\kappa$, and $H_\Lambda$ have units J, $t$ has units s, and $\hbar$ is the adopted reduced Planck constant with units J s. The mathematics below uses only $\hbar>0$ and asserts no measured parameter value.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C*-identity condition [A1] below. Let $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z^d,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$ and let $\mathcal A$ be its norm completion as in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. These assumptions give the conditional unital C*-algebra structure supplied by [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. Let $\Phi$ be a uniformly bounded finite-range interaction of [[def-qsm-bounded-finite-range-interaction]].

For any increasing finite exhaustion $(\Lambda_n)_{n\ge1}$ in the convention of [[lem-qsm-boundary-dynamics-cauchy]]—that is, each $\Lambda_n$ is finite, $\Lambda_n\subseteq\Lambda_{n+1}$, and $\bigcup_{n\ge1}\Lambda_n=\mathbb Z^d$—the free-boundary finite-volume maps $\alpha_t^{\Lambda_n}$ converge in norm on every local observable, uniformly for $t$ in compact intervals. Their limit is independent of the exhaustion and extends uniquely to a strongly continuous one-parameter group $\alpha_t$ of maps $\alpha_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$. Here “one-parameter group” means $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal A}$ and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$. Each $\alpha_t$ is a bijective complex-linear unital $*$-homomorphism (a $*$-automorphism), with inverse $\alpha_{-t}$. Strong continuity means $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ is norm-continuous for every fixed $A\in\mathcal A$. This result does not assert that an infinite-volume Hamiltonian is an element of $\mathcal A$ or a bounded operator on a preselected infinite tensor-product Hilbert space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If $Y$ is Banach,
then $\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is Banach for the operator norm.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

derivations.claim: Each interaction term is an orthogonal projection of norm one. The interaction is self-adjoint, has support size two, range one and per-site sum $\kappa=2$. It satisfies the finite-range hypotheses in [F2], so its thermodynamic dynamics $\alpha_t$ exists. This conclusion requires no choice of a finite-volume ground state.

Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb Z$. It is countable under [A1], by enumerating finite tuples and taking their ranges. Complete the finitely supported complex functions on $\{+1,-1\}\times\mathcal F$ for their linear-first sum inner product, obtaining $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\{+1,-1\}\times\mathcal F)$ by [F3]. Denote its orthonormal basis by $|\sigma,F\rangle$. Define $$\pi(Z_j)|\sigma,F\rangle=\sigma(-1)^{\mathbf1_F(j)}|\sigma,F\rangle,\qquad \pi(X_j)|\sigma,F\rangle=|\sigma,F\triangle\{j\}\rangle.$$ Here $X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference. These operators are self-adjoint unitaries, anticommute at the same site and commute at distinct sites. Thus they give the usual local Pauli matrix representations, including $Y_j=iX_jZ_j$. On a finite region $\Lambda$, decompose $\mathcal H$ into the subspaces with fixed $\sigma$ and fixed finite $F\setminus\Lambda$; each has the $2^{|\Lambda|}$ basis vectors indexed by $F\cap\Lambda$ and is a standard matrix representation of $\mathcal A_\Lambda$. Therefore $\|\pi(A)\|=\|A\|$ locally. These compatible representations extend by norm continuity and [F3] to a unital contractive $*$-representation of $\mathcal A$.

For $F\in\mathcal F$, put $w(F)=|\{j\in\mathbb Z:\mathbf1_F(j)\ne\mathbf1_F(j+1)\}|$. This number is finite, is zero exactly when $F=\varnothing$, and is at least two otherwise: a nonempty finite set has both a left and a right boundary. More precisely it is twice the number of finite interval components of $F$. Define the diagonal operator $$K|\sigma,F\rangle=w(F)|\sigma,F\rangle,\qquad D(K)=\left\{\xi:\sum_{\sigma,F}w(F)^2|\xi_{\sigma,F}|^2<\infty\right\}.$$ Finite-support vectors make the domain dense and the quadratic form is nonnegative. If $\xi$ lies in the adjoint domain with $K^*\xi=\zeta$, testing on each basis vector gives $\zeta_{\sigma,F}=w(F)\xi_{\sigma,F}$, so $\xi\in D(K)$. Conversely that square-summability condition makes the adjoint identity hold by sum Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus $K=K^*$ on exactly this domain.

Set $U_t|\sigma,F\rangle=e^{itw(F)}|\sigma,F\rangle$. It is a unitary group. For each $\xi$, dominated convergence with majorant $4|\xi_{\sigma,F}|^2$ proves strong continuity. For $\xi\in D(K)$, $|e^{itw}-1|/|t|\le w$ and [F4] show its norm derivative at zero is $iK\xi$. Conversely, if that norm derivative exists, its coordinates must be $iw(F)\xi_{\sigma,F}$, whose square sum is finite, so the exact generator domain is $D(K)$. The kernel has basis $|+,\varnothing\rangle,|-,\varnothing\rangle$. Every other diagonal energy is at least two and energy two occurs for a singleton $F$. For $0<\lambda<2$, the diagonal inverse $(w(F)-\lambda)^{-1}$ is bounded by $\max(1/\lambda,1/(2-\lambda))$ and maps into $D(K)$ since $w/(w-\lambda)$ is bounded. The same diagonal argument excludes negative real and nonreal spectrum. Consequently $\sigma(K)\subseteq\{0\}\cup[2,\infty)$, with excitation gap exactly two.

The representation is covariant for the actual dynamics in step 1.1. Every interaction term is diagonal in the Pauli $Z$ basis, and these terms commute. Finite-volume conjugation of a local observable therefore depends only on the finitely many bonds meeting its support. In particular the evolution of $Z_j$ is constant. On $X_j|\sigma,F\rangle$ the phase of $U_t\pi(X_j)U_t^*$ is $e^{it(w(F\triangle\{j\})-w(F))}$; the energy difference involves only the two bonds adjacent to $j$. It is exactly the phase from every finite-volume Hamiltonian containing these bonds. The local Pauli matrices generate every finite matrix algebra, so the covariance identity holds for every local $A$, and the norm completion gives $$\pi(\alpha_t(A))=U_t\pi(A)U_t^*\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$ This verifies the relation to the thermodynamic dynamics rather than choosing an unrelated diagonal operator.

Let $\Omega=(|+,\varnothing\rangle+|-,\varnothing\rangle)/\sqrt2$. It is a unit zero-energy vector fixed by $U_t$, so its state $\omega(A)=\langle\pi(A)\Omega,\Omega\rangle$ is a positive-energy ground state. Its finite restrictions have density $$\rho_\Lambda=\tfrac12|+\cdots+\rangle\langle+\cdots+|+\tfrac12|-\cdots-\rangle\langle-\cdots-|,$$ with the empty-region density one; these are the consistent equal mixture of the two product phases. This representation is cyclic. Given finite $F$ and $\sigma\in\{+1,-1\}$, choose $j\notin F$ and let $P_{\sigma,j}=(I+\sigma Z_j)/2$. Then $$\sqrt2\,\pi\left(\prod_{i\in F}X_i\,P_{\sigma,j}\right)\Omega=|\sigma,F\rangle.$$ Thus every displayed basis vector is generated by a local observable, proving cyclicity and identifying the gap in step 3.1 as a gap of the state's own ground representation.

In the two product vectors $Z_i$ has respective expectations $+1$ and $-1$, whereas $Z_iZ_j$ has expectation one in each for $i\ne j$. Hence the equal mixture has $\omega(Z_j)=0$ and $\omega(Z_iZ_j)=1$. For every integer $r\ge1$ its connected $Z_0,Z_r$ correlation is therefore one. No finite $C_0$ and positive $\mu$ can satisfy $1\le C_0e^{-\mu r}$ for all $r$. The two product vector states are distinct positive-energy ground states, so uniqueness fails exactly where needed. This gives a gapped degenerate counterexample without altering any assertion about transport of an entire gapped ground band.

Step 1.1 computes each bond projection norm one; step 6.1 gives correlation exactly one for every r≥1.

Step 3.1 proves the resolvent on 0<λ<2 and an eigenvalue at 2; step 6.1 includes r=1 and arbitrarily large integer r.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: For a nonzero vector, reshape its coefficient array as a matrix with row index $i_1$ and column index $(i_2,\ldots,i_N)$. By [F1] this gives an exact finite sum of products of a first-site coefficient and a residual coefficient array. Reshape the residual array at site $2$ with row index $(a_1,i_2)$ and remaining sites as column index, apply [F1] again, and store the resulting left coefficient array as the entries of $A_2^{i_2}$ with virtual indices $(a_1,a_2)$. Repeating this finite operation through site $N-1$ leaves a final array defining $A_N^{i_N}$; every SVD factorization is exact, so the original coefficient of each ordered product-basis vector is the displayed matrix product. For $N=1$ take the coefficients as scalar matrices. For the zero vector take all bond dimensions equal to $1$ and set the first site matrices to zero. Thus all finite vectors admit the stated representation.

For any integer $q\ge1$ and positive semidefinite $Y\in M_q(\mathbb C)\otimes M_D(\mathbb C)$, the amplification is $({\rm id}_{M_q}\otimes\mathcal E)(Y)=\sum_{i=1}^d(I_q\otimes A^i)Y(I_q\otimes A^{i*})$. Each summand is positive semidefinite, so every amplification is positive and $\mathcal E$ is completely positive. The displayed definition also fixes its exact input and output spaces and makes no trace-preserving or unitality assertion.

The map $\Gamma_L$ is linear and its image is a finite-dimensional subspace of $(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes L}$. By [F2], choose an orthonormal basis $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ of that image and define $P_Lv:=\sum_{a=1}^s\langle v,u_a\rangle u_a$. Orthonormality gives $P_L^*=P_L$ and $P_L^2=P_L$, and $v-P_Lv$ is orthogonal to every $u_a$. Thus $h_L=I-P_L$ is the orthogonal projection onto the complement, with $\langle h_Lv,v\rangle=\|h_Lv\|^2\ge0$ and kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$.

Fix a finite open MPS made from the same tensor and a block of $L$ consecutive sites. For each fixed physical-basis configuration outside that block, contraction of the outside tensors leaves a row $\alpha$ on the left and a column $\beta$ on the right. With $X=\beta\alpha$, direct coordinates give $\operatorname{tr}(XA^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})=\sum_{u,v}\beta_u\alpha_v(A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})_{vu}=\alpha A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L}\beta$, so that block slice is $\Gamma_L(X)$. The outside basis configurations are orthonormal, so the full vector is a sum of outside basis vectors tensored with block vectors in $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$; the corresponding $h_L$ therefore annihilates it. Each term in $H_{N,L}$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.3, and their sum annihilates the MPS. If that vector is nonzero, zero is an eigenvalue and the minimum possible energy, so the vector is a zero-energy ground state. The zero vector is annihilated but supplies no eigenstate: for example, if all tensor matrices vanish, then $\Gamma_L=0$, $h_L=I$ and $H_{N,L}=(N-L+1)I$, whose ground energy is positive. No uniqueness or positive-gap conclusion for a nonzero MPS follows from this argument.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $N\ge1$ and $d_1,\ldots,d_N,D_0,\ldots,D_N\ge1$ be integers. Give each site $j$ the Hilbert space $H_j=\mathbb C^{d_j}$ with standard inner product $\langle x,y\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{d_j}x_i\overline{y_i}$, linear in its first argument, and its fixed ordered standard basis $(|i_j\rangle)_{i_j=1}^{d_j}$. Tensor products use the ordered product basis and the product inner product. For every site and physical index choose a matrix $A_j^{i_j}\in M_{D_{j-1}\times D_j}(\mathbb C)$, a boundary column $\ell\in\mathbb C^{D_0}$, and a boundary column $r\in\mathbb C^{D_N}$. Here $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb C)$ is the space of $m$-by-$n$ complex matrices and $A^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. The associated finite open matrix product state (MPS) is the vector

$$|\psi_A\rangle:=\sum_{i_1=1}^{d_1}\cdots\sum_{i_N=1}^{d_N}\ell^*A_1^{i_1}\cdots A_N^{i_N}r\,|i_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|i_N\rangle\in H_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H_N.$$

The dimensions $D_j$ are the bond dimensions; the virtual indices between adjacent matrices are matrix indices summed in their product. The zero vector is allowed. A nonzero vector is normalized by division by its norm, and normalization is defined only when $\langle\psi_A,\psi_A\rangle>0$. Every vector in a finite tensor product of these site spaces has an exact open MPS representation.

For a translation invariant tensor, let $d,D\ge1$ and use one family $A^i\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ for every site. Its transfer map is the completely positive linear map

$$\mathcal E:M_D(\mathbb C)\to M_D(\mathbb C),\qquad \mathcal E(X):=\sum_{i=1}^d A^iXA^{i*}.$$

Here complete positivity means that for every integer $q\ge1$, the amplified map $\operatorname{id}_{M_q}\otimes\mathcal E$ sends positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices; a matrix is positive semidefinite when it is Hermitian and has nonnegative quadratic form on every vector.

The tensor is injective at length $L\ge1$ when the matrices $A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L}$, over all $i_1,\ldots,i_L\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, span the full vector space $M_D(\mathbb C)$. No injectivity or transfer-spectrum condition is assumed by this definition.

For each block length $L\ge1$, define the blocked boundary map

$$\Gamma_L:M_D(\mathbb C)\to(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes L},\qquad \Gamma_L(X):=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_L=1}^d\operatorname{tr}(XA^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})\,|i_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|i_L\rangle,$$

where $\operatorname{tr}(Y):=\sum_{a=1}^D Y_{aa}$. Let $P_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, set $h_L:=I-P_L$, and, for $N\ge L$, define the open-chain parent Hamiltonian

$$H_{N,L}:=\sum_{j=1}^{N-L+1}I^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes h_L\otimes I^{\otimes(N-j-L+1)}.$$

Each local term is positive semidefinite with kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, and $H_{N,L}$ annihilates every finite open MPS formed from the same translation invariant tensor. Every nonzero such vector is a zero-energy ground state of $H_{N,L}$. This definition asserts no uniqueness of that ground state and no spectral-gap bound.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$, the countable site set $\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^d$ of [[lem-qsm-integer-lattice-countable]], and one finite spin dimension $q\ge1$, where $q$ is a positive integer (so $q\in\mathbb N$ and $1\le q$, by [[def-natural-numbers]] and [[def-nat-order]]). For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. A **localization region** for $T$ is any finite $\Lambda$ for which $T\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ under these inclusions; a localization region need not be minimal.

The ordinary operator norm makes each local matrix algebra a nonzero unital complete C*-algebra, and every positive normalized complex-linear functional is uniquely a trace pairing with a density matrix, by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]]. This includes the empty region, whose Hilbert space is $\mathbb C$. This definition does not posit an infinite-dimensional tensor-product Hilbert space.

Use the finite local matrix algebras and isometric factor inclusions of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]] and [[lem-qsm-local-spin-inclusions-isometric]]. Identify $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with its image in every larger finite-region algebra. The directed union

$$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}:=\bigcup_{\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma,\ |\Lambda|<\infty}\mathcal A_\Lambda$$

is the algebra of **strictly local observables**. Its norm is $\|A\|=\|A\|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ for any finite localization region $\Lambda$ of $A$; isometric inclusions make this independent of the chosen region. The **quasi-local spin algebra** is the norm completion

$$\mathcal A:=\overline{\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}^{\,\|\cdot\|}.$$

The C*-algebra structure on this completion has product and adjoint extended continuously from the finite local matrix algebras. Countable Choice is assumed for the published existence theorem for metric completions; [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]] supplies the full extension argument using the finite C*-identity of [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]].

**No global Hilbert tensor product is selected.** “Quasi-local” means norm completion of the directed algebra of finite-region observables; it does not mean a chosen representation as operators on an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space. A local operator $A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ may have more than one localization region. Disjoint finite local factors commute in their common finite tensor algebra.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, $D=\dim H\ge1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. With composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity and the induced operator norm, $\mathcal B(H)$ is a nonzero unital complex C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. In particular it is complete, $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$, $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$, $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$ and $\|I\|=1$. The matrix $\|A\|^2I-A^*A$ is positive semidefinite and has a positive square root in $\mathcal B(H)$.

Every complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal B(H)\to\mathbb C$ that is positive, meaning $\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ for all $B$, has a unique positive semidefinite matrix $\rho$ such that $\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ for all $A$. It is bounded and satisfies

$$|\omega(A)|\le\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\|A\|\quad(A\in\mathcal B(H)),\qquad \|\omega\|=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho)=\omega(I).$$

Consequently the canonical states of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]] are exactly the trace pairings of density operators of [[def-qc-density-operator]]; for a positive functional, normalization $\omega(I)=1$ is equivalent to norm one. The result includes zero positive functionals, nonfaithful densities and $D=1$; it makes no infinite-dimensional density representation assertion.

Let $\mathcal A$ be the unital quasi-local spin C*-algebra of [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]], whose C*-structure uses Countable Choice as in [[lem-qsm-quasilocal-completion]]. An **infinite algebraic state** is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ satisfying $\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$.

For each finite region $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$, the restriction $\omega|_{\mathcal A_\Lambda}$ is a finite-matrix state. By [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], every positive normalized functional on a finite matrix algebra is represented by a unique density matrix. Define its **local density matrix** $\rho_\Lambda$ by

$$\omega(A)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

where $\rho_\Lambda=\rho_\Lambda^*\ge0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}\rho_\Lambda=1$. For $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, put $\Delta=\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda$ and use the configuration-basis factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_\Delta$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]]. If $T\in\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$, define its **partial trace over $\Delta$**, $\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, by its matrix coefficients

$$\langle \operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)e_s,e_{s'}\rangle:=\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle\qquad(s,s'\in S_\Lambda),$$

where $e_s$ and $e_t$ are the configuration basis vectors of $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ and $\mathcal H_\Delta$. The finite sums depend linearly on $T$, so they define a linear map $\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}\to\mathcal A_\Lambda$ with a unique output matrix for each $T$. Expanding both configuration-basis traces gives its pairing identity

$$\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda\!\left(A\operatorname{Tr}_\Delta(T)\right)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'}\!\left((A\otimes I_\Delta)T\right)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A_\Lambda),$$

with the common value given by

$$\sum_{s,s'\in S_\Lambda}\sum_{t\in S_\Delta}\langle A e_{s'},e_s\rangle\langle T(e_s\otimes e_t),e_{s'}\otimes e_t\rangle.$$

The pairing identity determines this matrix uniquely: if $D\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$ pairs to zero with every $A$, taking the configuration-basis matrix units $A=E_{ji}$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(E_{ji}D)=\langle D e_j,e_i\rangle=0$ for every $i,j$, so $D=0$. The local densities are **consistent** when $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. No density operator on a globally chosen Hilbert space is part of this definition.

This agrees with the canonical state convention of [[def-state-on-a-c-star-algebra]]: the finite restrictions have norm one by [[lem-qsm-finite-matrix-cstar-and-state-duality]], giving $|\omega(A)|\le\|A\|$ on the dense local algebra and hence on its completion; evaluation at the norm-one identity gives $\|\omega\|=1$. Conversely a canonical state has local restrictions with density matrices of trace one, since the finite norm formula and continuity on the dense local algebra imply $\|\omega\|=\omega(I)$. No global density representation is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice for the norm completion in [[def-qsm-quasilocal-spin-algebra]]. Let $\{\rho_\Lambda\}$ be positive trace-one matrices, one on each finite-region algebra $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ of [[def-qsm-local-spin-algebras]], such that for every $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$ their partial traces agree: $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$. There is a unique infinite algebraic state $\omega$ on $\mathcal A$ whose restriction to each $\mathcal A_\Lambda$ is $A\mapsto\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda}(\rho_\Lambda A)$.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: The finite coefficient sum defining $\mathcal E_O(X)$ is complex-linear in both $O$ and $X$. For $O\ge0$, write its spectral decomposition as $O=\sum_\alpha|v_\alpha\rangle\langle v_\alpha|$, absorbing the square roots of the nonnegative eigenvalues into $v_\alpha$, and put $v_{\alpha,I}=\langle v_\alpha,e_I\rangle$. Then $O_{I,J}=\sum_\alpha v_{\alpha,I}\overline{v_{\alpha,J}}$, so with $K_\alpha:=\sum_J\overline{v_{\alpha,J}}A^J$ the insertion map satisfies $\mathcal E_O(X)=\sum_\alpha K_\alpha X K_\alpha^*\ge0$ whenever $X\ge0$. Diagonalizing $\ell$ by [F7] and expanding $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_O(\rho))$ as a weighted sum of nonnegative diagonal expectations shows $\omega_k(O)\ge0$. For $O=I_{d^k}$, $O_{I,J}=1$ if $I=J$ and $0$ otherwise, so the insertion sums over all length-$k$ words and equals $\mathcal E^k$. The fixed-point equations and $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\rho)=1$ give $\omega_k(I)=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E^k(\rho))=1$. Thus each contiguous-block functional is positive and normalized.

Tensor-factor order in the definition gives $\mathcal E_{O\otimes P}=\mathcal E_O\circ\mathcal E_P$ for consecutive blocks: expanding both sides gives the same ordered product $A^{J_O}A^{J_P}X(A^{I_P})^*(A^{I_O})^*$. Inserting an identity site on the right composes with $\mathcal E$ on the input, which leaves $\rho$ fixed; inserting one on the left composes with $\mathcal E$ on the output, which leaves the trace pairing with $\ell$ fixed. Repeating these identities shows that the value is independent of the chosen containing interval and that restrictions to nested finite regions agree. A positive observable remains positive when identity factors are inserted, so the local functionals on arbitrary finite regions are positive and normalized as well. The empty-region convention is consistent because every local functional assigns one to the identity.

By [F2]–[F4] each local positive normalized functional has a unique trace-one density $\rho_\Lambda$. For nested regions, step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}_{\Lambda'}((O\otimes I)\rho_{\Lambda'})=\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\rho_\Lambda)$ for every $O\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$. Applying the defining partial-trace pairing [F5] shows $\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'}))=\operatorname{tr}_\Lambda(O\rho_\Lambda)$ for all $O$. Taking $O$ to be each matrix unit makes every matrix entry of the two matrices equal, so the density family is consistent.

Apply [F6] to the consistent finite-region density family from step 3.1. Its hypotheses hold by [A1], [F2], [F3], and the positive trace-one property just proved. It yields a unique infinite algebraic state on the specified quasi-local algebra, with exactly these local restrictions and no chosen global Hilbert-space representation. This establishes that the transfer contractions in the Definition are well defined.

Input an integer $N\ge1$, nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_1,\ldots,H_N$ with fixed ordered orthonormal bases, a normalized vector $\psi\in H_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H_N$ with exact coefficients in those bases, and integer rank caps $D_k\ge1$ for $1\le k<N$. For $N=1$ the cap list is empty. The algorithm performs the following exact finite procedure.

1. Set the current remainder to $\psi^{(0)}:=\psi$, the retained left space before the first cut to $S_0:=\mathbb C$, and an empty list of site tensors and discarded squared norms.

2. For each $k=1,\ldots,N-1$, reshape the current remainder as a matrix whose row index is the retained left index in $S_{k-1}$ together with the physical basis index in $H_k$, and whose column index is the ordered product basis of $H_{k+1}\otimes\cdots\otimes H_N$. Compute an exact singular value decomposition. Order the positive singular values nonincreasingly. Within each repeated positive singular value, form a deterministic orthonormal basis of its left singular subspace by projecting the row-coordinate standard basis vectors in lexicographic order and applying Gram–Schmidt, discarding zero residuals; obtain the corresponding right singular vector as $M^*u/s$ for singular value $s>0$. Retain the first $m_k:=\min(D_k,r_k)$ positive singular directions, where $r_k$ is the number of positive singular values, and record $\delta_k:=\sum_{j=m_k+1}^{r_k}s_{k,j}^2$ from this current unnormalized remainder. Reshape the retained left singular vectors into a site tensor $A_k^{i_k}$ with left index in $S_{k-1}$ and right index in $S_k:=\mathbb C^{m_k}$; pass the retained singular values times the adjoints of the retained right singular vectors as the next current remainder $\psi^{(k)}$. Since the input has norm one and $D_k\ge1$, every current remainder is nonzero and each $m_k\ge1$.

3. After the last cut, reshape the remaining array as the final site tensor $A_N^{i_N}$, use outer bond dimensions $D_0=D_N=1$ with scalar boundary columns $\ell=r=(1)$, and return the resulting unnormalized open MPS $\phi=\psi^{(N-1)}$, the list $(\delta_1,\ldots,\delta_{N-1})$, and the bond dimensions $(m_1,\ldots,m_{N-1})$. For $N=1$, return $\phi=\psi$ and empty lists with the same scalar boundaries. If $\|\phi\|^2=0$, return a norm-zero flag and do not normalize. Otherwise an optional normalized copy is $\phi/\|\phi\|$; the returned $\phi$ and discarded norms always refer to the unnormalized sweep output.

All coefficients and SVDs are exact mathematical objects; no floating-point threshold is used. The tie rule fixes a choice even when a rank cap cuts through a degenerate singular-value subspace.

where $\operatorname{tr}(Y):=\sum_{a=1}^D Y_{aa}$. Let $P_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, set $h_L:=I-P_L$, and, for $N\ge L$, define the open-chain parent Hamiltonian

$$H_{N,L}:=\sum_{j=1}^{N-L+1}I^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes h_L\otimes I^{\otimes(N-j-L+1)}.$$

Each local term is positive semidefinite with kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, and $H_{N,L}$ annihilates every finite open MPS formed from the same translation invariant tensor. Every nonzero such vector is a zero-energy ground state of $H_{N,L}$. This definition asserts no uniqueness of that ground state and no spectral-gap bound.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex-inner-product spaces with the tensor-product convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]]. For every $\Psi\in H\otimes K$ there are an integer $r\ge0$, positive numbers $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, and orthonormal families $u_1,\ldots,u_r\in H$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_r\in K$ such that

$$\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j u_j\otimes v_j,\qquad \|\Psi\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j^2.$$

For $\Psi=0$ take $r=0$ and the empty sum. For any chosen ordered pair of orthonormal bases, the construction below obtains the $s_j$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient matrix of $\Psi$ in their ordered product basis.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Since $\|\psi\|=1$ and every cap $D_k\ge1$, each current remainder has a positive singular value and the algorithm retains at least one; hence its subsequent remainders are nonzero and every retained bond dimension is positive. For each cut $k$, let $P_k$ be the orthogonal projection on the full tensor product onto the retained left Schmidt subspace at that cut tensored with the remaining right factors; set $P_0=I$. The current remainder before cut $k$ is $\psi^{(k-1)}=P_{k-1}\psi$. Its support in the first $k$ sites lies in the previous retained space tensored with $H_k$, so every positive left Schmidt vector retained by the next SVD lies in that previous space tensored with $H_k$. Hence $\operatorname{ran}P_k\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_{k-1}$, $P_kP_{k-1}=P_{k-1}P_k=P_k$, and the next remainder is $\psi^{(k)}=P_k\psi$.

Across cut $k$, the coefficient matrix of an exact MPS factors as $L_kR_k$ by summing over its $D_k$-dimensional virtual index. Its matrix rank is therefore at most $D_k$. By [F3]–[F4], the Schmidt rank is the number of positive singular values, so it is at most $D_k$. Writing the Schmidt expansion as $\psi=\sum_{j=1}^q s_j u_j\otimes v_j$ gives $q\le D_k$, $p_j:=s_j^2>0$, and $\sum_jp_j=1$. Expanding the partial trace in [F5] gives $\rho_{1\cdots k}=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, so these $p_j$ are exactly its positive eigenvalues.

Put $\varepsilon_k:=\psi^{(k-1)}-\psi^{(k)}=(P_{k-1}-P_k)\psi$. This vector lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_{k-1}$ and is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}P_k$. For $j>k$, nesting gives $\varepsilon_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_{j-1}\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_k$, so $\langle\varepsilon_k,\varepsilon_j\rangle=0$. Thus the discarded components from different cuts are pairwise orthogonal.

At cut $k$, [F3] identifies the squared norm removed by the orthogonal Schmidt projection with the sum of squared discarded singular values, exactly $\delta_k$ by [F1]. Since $\psi-\phi=\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\varepsilon_k$, orthogonality from step 2.1 gives $\|\psi-\phi\|^2=\sum_k\|\varepsilon_k\|^2=\sum_k\delta_k$. For $N=1$ both sides are zero, so the equality also covers the empty sweep.

For every $x>1$, apply [F8] to $\log$ on $[1,x]$; [F6]–[F7] give $\log x=(x-1)/c\le x-1$ for some $c\in(1,x)$. For $0<x<1$, apply [F8] on $[x,1]$ to get $-\log x=(1-x)/c$ for some $c\in(x,1)$, hence $\log x\le x-1$; equality holds at $x=1$. Apply this inequality to $x=(q p_j)^{-1}$, multiply by $p_j>0$, and sum: $\sum_jp_j\log((q p_j)^{-1})\le\sum_j(1/q-p_j)=0$. The logarithm product law [F6] then gives $\log q-S(\rho_{1\cdots k})=\sum_jp_j\log(qp_j)\ge0$. Since $q\le D_k$ and $\log$ is increasing, $S(\rho_{1\cdots k})\le\log q\le\log D_k$. The zero-eigenvalue convention in [F5] includes rank-deficient reductions.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $N\ge1$ and $d_1,\ldots,d_N,D_0,\ldots,D_N\ge1$ be integers. Give each site $j$ the Hilbert space $H_j=\mathbb C^{d_j}$ with standard inner product $\langle x,y\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{d_j}x_i\overline{y_i}$, linear in its first argument, and its fixed ordered standard basis $(|i_j\rangle)_{i_j=1}^{d_j}$. Tensor products use the ordered product basis and the product inner product. For every site and physical index choose a matrix $A_j^{i_j}\in M_{D_{j-1}\times D_j}(\mathbb C)$, a boundary column $\ell\in\mathbb C^{D_0}$, and a boundary column $r\in\mathbb C^{D_N}$. Here $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb C)$ is the space of $m$-by-$n$ complex matrices and $A^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. The associated finite open matrix product state (MPS) is the vector

$$|\psi_A\rangle:=\sum_{i_1=1}^{d_1}\cdots\sum_{i_N=1}^{d_N}\ell^*A_1^{i_1}\cdots A_N^{i_N}r\,|i_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|i_N\rangle\in H_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H_N.$$

The dimensions $D_j$ are the bond dimensions; the virtual indices between adjacent matrices are matrix indices summed in their product. The zero vector is allowed. A nonzero vector is normalized by division by its norm, and normalization is defined only when $\langle\psi_A,\psi_A\rangle>0$. Every vector in a finite tensor product of these site spaces has an exact open MPS representation.

For a translation invariant tensor, let $d,D\ge1$ and use one family $A^i\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ for every site. Its transfer map is the completely positive linear map

$$\mathcal E:M_D(\mathbb C)\to M_D(\mathbb C),\qquad \mathcal E(X):=\sum_{i=1}^d A^iXA^{i*}.$$

Here complete positivity means that for every integer $q\ge1$, the amplified map $\operatorname{id}_{M_q}\otimes\mathcal E$ sends positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices; a matrix is positive semidefinite when it is Hermitian and has nonnegative quadratic form on every vector.

The tensor is injective at length $L\ge1$ when the matrices $A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L}$, over all $i_1,\ldots,i_L\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, span the full vector space $M_D(\mathbb C)$. No injectivity or transfer-spectrum condition is assumed by this definition.

For each block length $L\ge1$, define the blocked boundary map

$$\Gamma_L:M_D(\mathbb C)\to(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes L},\qquad \Gamma_L(X):=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_L=1}^d\operatorname{tr}(XA^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})\,|i_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|i_L\rangle,$$

where $\operatorname{tr}(Y):=\sum_{a=1}^D Y_{aa}$. Let $P_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, set $h_L:=I-P_L$, and, for $N\ge L$, define the open-chain parent Hamiltonian

$$H_{N,L}:=\sum_{j=1}^{N-L+1}I^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes h_L\otimes I^{\otimes(N-j-L+1)}.$$

Each local term is positive semidefinite with kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, and $H_{N,L}$ annihilates every finite open MPS formed from the same translation invariant tensor. Every nonzero such vector is a zero-energy ground state of $H_{N,L}$. This definition asserts no uniqueness of that ground state and no spectral-gap bound.

Fix integers $d,D\ge1$ and a translation invariant tensor $A^1,\ldots,A^d\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ with transfer map $\mathcal E(X):=\sum_iA^iXA^{i*}$. A matrix is positive semidefinite when it is Hermitian with nonnegative quadratic form on every vector. Let $\rho,\ell\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ be positive semidefinite matrices satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1,\qquad \mathcal E(\rho)=\rho,\qquad \mathcal E^*(\ell)=\ell,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\ell\rho)=1,$$

where $\mathcal E^*(Y):=\sum_iA^{i*}YA^i$, equivalently the trace-pairing adjoint determined by $\operatorname{tr}(Y\mathcal E(X))=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal E^*(Y)X)$. For a contiguous block of $k\ge1$ sites, write $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)$ and $J=(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ for physical multi-indices, let $e_I$ be its ordered standard product basis, put $O_{I,J}:=\langle Oe_J,e_I\rangle$ for $O\in M_{d^k}(\mathbb C)$, and set $A^I:=A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_k}$. Define the transfer insertion map and local expectation by

$$\mathcal E_O(X):=\sum_{I,J}O_{I,J}A^JX(A^I)^*,\qquad \omega_k(O):=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_O(\rho)).$$

For any finite nonempty $\Lambda\subset\mathbb Z$ and local observable $O\in\mathcal A_\Lambda$, embed $O$ into the interval $[\min\Lambda,\max\Lambda]$ by inserting identities at missing sites and evaluate the same formula. For the empty region set $\omega_\varnothing(cI):=c$. These definitions give compatible positive normalized local functionals. Their unique density matrices $\rho_\Lambda$ obey $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(\rho_{\Lambda'})=\rho_\Lambda$ whenever $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$. Assume Countable Choice. The transfer-generated infinite-chain state is the unique infinite algebraic state $\omega$ on the norm-completed quasi-local spin algebra whose restriction to every finite region is the defined local functional. No infinite tensor-product Hilbert space is selected.

For observables $O_A\in M_{d^a}(\mathbb C)$ and $O_B\in M_{d^b}(\mathbb C)$ on two fixed consecutive blocks, with $g\ge0$ identity sites between the blocks, the connected correlation is

$$\omega(O_A\otimes I^{\otimes g}\otimes O_B)-\omega(O_A)\omega(O_B).$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[lem-complex-polynomial-growth-and-minimum-modulus]], [[lem-dalembert-minimum-modulus-descent]].

Let $T$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space whose characteristic polynomial splits over $F$. If the elementary divisors of $V_T$ are $(x-\lambda)^e$, then $T$ has a Jordan canonical form with one block $J_e(\lambda)$ for each elementary divisor. The multiset of blocks is unique, and conversely each Jordan block yields its corresponding cyclic primary module. The zero space has empty lists.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$. Choose an ordered basis $\mathcal B$ and define

$$\chi_T(x):=\chi_{[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}}(x).$$

Matrices representing the same endomorphism in different ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial. Hence $\chi_T$ is independent of $\mathcal B$. When $V=\{0_V\}$, the empty ordered basis gives $\chi_T=1$.

Let $T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$, and let $\lambda\in\sigma_F(T)$. The **algebraic multiplicity** of $\lambda$ is the largest natural number $m\geq1$ such that $(x-\lambda)^m$ divides $\chi_T(x)$ in $F[x]$. This largest exponent exists because $\lambda$ is a root, the factor theorem gives one factor $x-\lambda$, and the nonzero polynomial $\chi_T$ has finite degree and unique factorization.

The **geometric multiplicity** of $\lambda$ is

$$\dim_F E_\lambda(T).$$

The eigenspace is a nonzero subspace of the finite-dimensional space $V$, so this dimension is defined and is at least $1$.

Let $T$ be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, and let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue. Then

$$\dim E_\lambda(T)\le \operatorname{mult}_{\chi_T}(\lambda).$$

derivations.claim: Define the linear functional $\varphi(X):=\operatorname{tr}(\ell X)$ and the rank-one map $P(X):=\rho\,\varphi(X)$. Since $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, $\rho\ne0$; the pairing normalization $\varphi(\rho)=1$ gives $P^2=P$. The fixed-point equations give $\mathcal EP=P$ and $P\mathcal E=P$, since $\varphi(\mathcal E(X))=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal E^*(\ell)X)=\varphi(X)$. Hence $M_D(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C\rho\oplus\ker\varphi$ is an $\mathcal E$-invariant direct sum, $\mathcal E$ is the identity on $\mathbb C\rho$, and $P$ is zero on $\ker\varphi$. If the restriction of $\mathcal E$ to $\ker\varphi$ had eigenvalue $1$, it would have a nonzero eigenvector $X$ there. Since $\varphi(X)=0$ and $\varphi(\rho)=1$, $X$ and $\rho$ would be linearly independent eigenvectors of $\mathcal E$ for $1$, so $\dim E_1(\mathcal E)\ge2$. But [F7]–[F8] identify the Statement's simple-root hypothesis with algebraic multiplicity one, and [F9] bounds this geometric multiplicity by the algebraic multiplicity. This contradiction shows that the restriction has no eigenvalue $1$. Therefore $\mathcal E^g-P$ is zero on $\mathbb C\rho$ and equals $(\mathcal E|_{\ker\varphi})^g$ on the invariant complement.

Use $\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Xv\|$ on $M_D(\mathbb C)$ and the induced norm $\|\Phi\|:=\sup_{\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1}\|\Phi(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ on its linear maps.
If $\ker\varphi=\{0\}$, then $\mathcal E=P=I$ and $\mathcal E^g-P=0$ for every $g\ge0$; for every allowed $r$, take $K_r=0$.
Otherwise the restriction is a finite-dimensional complex endomorphism of positive dimension $m$. Its characteristic polynomial is monic of degree $m$ by [F7]. By [F4] it has a root $\mu$. Write this characteristic polynomial as $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^m c_kx^k$. Since $p(\mu)=0$, the identities $x^k-\mu^k=(x-\mu)\sum_{t=0}^{k-1}x^{k-1-t}\mu^t$ give $p(x)=(x-\mu)h(x)$ with $\deg h=m-1$. Induction on degree therefore shows that this characteristic polynomial splits into linear factors over $\mathbb C$. Now [F5] gives a similarity to finitely many Jordan blocks $J_s(\lambda)=\lambda I+N$ with $N^s=0$. Every such $\lambda$ belongs to $\sigma_{\mathbb C}(\mathcal E)\setminus\{1\}$, since an eigenvector of the restriction is also an eigenvector of $\mathcal E$ and step 1.1 excludes $1$ from the restricted spectrum; hence $|\lambda|\le q$.
If $q=0$, all Jordan powers of the restriction vanish for sufficiently large $g$, so $\mathcal E^g-P=0$ for those $g$. Since every allowed $r>q=0$ is positive, the finitely many remaining quantities $\|\mathcal E^g-P\|r^{-g}$ have a finite maximum; take this maximum as $K_r$ to obtain the required bound for all $g$.
If $q>0$, fix $r>q$. For a block with $\lambda\ne0$ and $g\ge s$, the binomial expansion gives $J_s(\lambda)^g=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom gj\lambda^{g-j}N^j$. For every fixed $j$, $g^j(|\lambda|/r)^g$ is bounded because the ratio of consecutive terms tends to $|\lambda|/r<1$; hence each matrix entry is bounded by a constant times $r^g$. Blocks with $\lambda=0$ vanish for $g\ge s$, and all finitely many smaller $g$ are absorbed into the constant. In the maximum-coordinate norm of the Jordan basis, the norm of the block-diagonal power is bounded by a constant times $r^g$, since there are finitely many blocks and each has finitely many entries; the zero action of $\mathcal E^g-P$ on $\mathbb C\rho$ adds only a one-dimensional zero block. The fixed change-of-basis map and its inverse have finite induced norms, so submultiplicativity transfers this bound to the stated superoperator norm: $\|\mathcal E^g-P\|\le K_r r^g$ for a finite $K_r$ and every $g\ge0$.

By [F1]–[F2], the transfer contraction for the two blocks with a gap of $g$ identities is $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_{O_A}\mathcal E^g\mathcal E_{O_B}(\rho))$. The product of the separate expectations equals $\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_{O_A}P\mathcal E_{O_B}(\rho))$, since $P(X)=\rho\operatorname{tr}(\ell X)$. Subtracting gives $C_g=\operatorname{tr}(\ell\mathcal E_{O_A}(\mathcal E^g-P)\mathcal E_{O_B}(\rho))$.

Diagonalize $\ell\ge0$ using [F6] as $\ell=\sum_j t_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ with $t_j>0$. For every matrix $X$, $|\operatorname{tr}(\ell X)|=|\sum_jt_j\langle Xu_j,u_j\rangle|\le\operatorname{tr}(\ell)\|X\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. The block insertion maps are finite sums of matrix multiplications, so their induced norms in step 2.1 are finite; submultiplicativity gives $|C_g|\le\operatorname{tr}(\ell)\,\|\mathcal E_{O_A}\|\,K_r\,\|\mathcal E_{O_B}(\rho)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,r^g$. All factors before $r^g$ are finite and independent of $g$, so their product is an admissible $C$. This proves the claimed exponential clustering bound, including Jordan blocks and the case $q=0$.

The dimensions $D_j$ are the bond dimensions; the virtual indices between adjacent matrices are matrix indices summed in their product. The zero vector is allowed. A nonzero vector is normalized by division by its norm, and normalization is defined only when $\langle\psi_A,\psi_A\rangle>0$. Every vector in a finite tensor product of these site spaces has an exact open MPS representation.

For a translation invariant tensor, let $d,D\ge1$ and use one family $A^i\in M_D(\mathbb C)$ for every site. Its transfer map is the completely positive linear map

$$\mathcal E:M_D(\mathbb C)\to M_D(\mathbb C),\qquad \mathcal E(X):=\sum_{i=1}^d A^iXA^{i*}.$$

Here complete positivity means that for every integer $q\ge1$, the amplified map $\operatorname{id}_{M_q}\otimes\mathcal E$ sends positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices; a matrix is positive semidefinite when it is Hermitian and has nonnegative quadratic form on every vector.

The tensor is injective at length $L\ge1$ when the matrices $A^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L}$, over all $i_1,\ldots,i_L\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, span the full vector space $M_D(\mathbb C)$. No injectivity or transfer-spectrum condition is assumed by this definition.

For each block length $L\ge1$, define the blocked boundary map

$$\Gamma_L:M_D(\mathbb C)\to(\mathbb C^d)^{\otimes L},\qquad \Gamma_L(X):=\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_L=1}^d\operatorname{tr}(XA^{i_1}\cdots A^{i_L})\,|i_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|i_L\rangle,$$

where $\operatorname{tr}(Y):=\sum_{a=1}^D Y_{aa}$. Let $P_L$ be the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, set $h_L:=I-P_L$, and, for $N\ge L$, define the open-chain parent Hamiltonian

$$H_{N,L}:=\sum_{j=1}^{N-L+1}I^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes h_L\otimes I^{\otimes(N-j-L+1)}.$$

Each local term is positive semidefinite with kernel $\operatorname{im}\Gamma_L$, and $H_{N,L}$ annihilates every finite open MPS formed from the same translation invariant tensor. The product of all vertex operators is $I$, because each edge has two endpoint incidences counted modulo two. The product of all face operators is $I$, because the closed surface has two incident face sides at each edge. Therefore any simultaneous joint eigenvalue assignment has an even number of violated vertex constraints and an even number of violated face constraints.

The image of $\partial_1$ is the even-parity subspace of $\mathbb F_2^V$: every edge boundary has even parity, while for a fixed vertex $v_0$, a path to each $v\ne v_0$ has boundary $v+v_0$, and these vectors span that subspace. A vertex coefficient vector lies in $\ker\partial_1^T$ exactly when it is orthogonal to this even-parity subspace; this orthogonal complement consists of the constant vectors and has dimension one. Rank-nullity gives $\operatorname{rank}\partial_1^T=|V|-1$, the number of independent vertex stabilizers. A face 2-chain is in $\ker\partial_2$ exactly when its coefficients agree across adjacent faces; dual-graph connectedness makes this kernel the one-dimensional constant subspace, so $\operatorname{rank}\partial_2=|F|-1$, the number of independent face stabilizers. Choose independent generators $S_1,\ldots,S_r$ from those commuting involutions and set $\Pi=2^{-r}\prod_{j=1}^r(I+S_j)$. This is an orthogonal projection. Independence of the vertex and face support vectors implies that its $2^r$ Pauli terms are distinct and only the all-identity term is the identity matrix. Every other Pauli term has trace zero because at least one tensor factor is $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$, each of which has trace zero. Thus $\operatorname{Tr}\Pi=2^{-r}2^{|E|}>0$, so the common $+1$ eigenspace is nonzero and has dimension $2^{|E|-r}$. The positive Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on that eigenspace, proving frustration freeness and identifying the ground space.

Put $m=\min(\{J_v\}\cup\{K_f\})$. The dimension found in step 2.1 is $2^{|E|-|V|-|F|+2}$. By [F2], under [A1], $|V|-|E|+|F|=2-2g$, so $|E|-|V|-|F|+2=2g$. Therefore the ground-space dimension is $2^{2g}$.

Both $W$ and $U$ are nonzero and have smaller dimension, so induction decomposes them into irreducibles. Let $\pi:H\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be any irreducible representation and choose $0\ne v\in V$. Define the linear map $\Phi:\mathbb C[H]\to V$ by $\Phi(\sum_h a_h h)=\sum_h a_h\pi(h)v$. By [F1], $\ker\Phi$ has an invariant complement $W$ in $\mathbb C[H]$; then $\Phi|_W$ is onto and injective, so $W\cong V$ is an irreducible summand of $\mathbb C[H]$. For each irreducible representation $\pi$, choose any positive-definite inner product and average it as $\langle v,w\rangle_H:=\sum_{h\in H}\langle\pi(h)v,\pi(h)w\rangle$. This is positive definite and is $H$-invariant by reindexing the finite sum, so $\pi(h)$ is unitary and $\chi_\pi(h^{-1})=\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$. For two irreducibles $\pi,\sigma$, define $P(T):=|H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}\sigma(h)T\pi(h^{-1})$ on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V_\pi,V_\sigma)$. Reindexing gives $\sigma(k)P(T)\pi(k^{-1})=P(T)$ for every $k$, so $P(T)$ intertwines the group actions; if $T$ already intertwines, every summand equals $T$. Hence $P$ is a projection with image exactly $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V_\pi,V_\sigma)$.

The trace of $T\mapsto\sigma(h)T\pi(h^{-1})$ on $\operatorname{Hom}(V_\pi,V_\sigma)\cong V_\sigma\otimes V_\pi^*$ is $\chi_\sigma(h)\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$, so $\operatorname{tr}P=|H|^{-1}\sum_h\chi_\sigma(h)\overline{\chi_\pi(h)}$; because $P$ is a projection on a finite-dimensional space, this trace equals $\dim\operatorname{im}P$. An endomorphism of an irreducible complex representation is scalar: it has an eigenvalue $\alpha$, and $T-\alpha I$ has nonzero invariant kernel, so irreducibility forces $T-\alpha I=0$. $e_\uparrow,e_\downarrow$, let $V_N=V^{\otimes N}$ in left-to-right site
order, and let $V_a=V$ be an auxiliary copy. For $u\in\mathbb C$, define
$R_{aj}(u)=uI_{aj}+iP_{aj}$ on $V_a\otimes V_N$, where $P_{aj}$ swaps the
auxiliary factor and site $j$. Define
$$T_a(u)=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad t(u)=\operatorname{tr}_a T_a(u),$$
where products mean composition with the rightmost factor acting first, and
$\operatorname{tr}_a$ is the ordinary finite-dimensional trace over $V_a$.
For distinct sites $j,k$, $P_{jk}$ swaps those two tensor factors. Define the
oriented cyclic shift by
$$U(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_N)=v_N\otimes v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{N-1}.$$
The spectral parameter $u$ is dimensionless. All operators in this definition

derivations.claim:
At $u=0$, every factor is $R_{aj}(0)=iP_{aj}$, so
$t(0)=i^N\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a1})$. On an elementary chain
tensor $e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_N}$, start the auxiliary factor at
each basis vector $e_a$ in turn. The swaps pass $e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_N}$
successively to the auxiliary factor and shift the preceding entries one site
right; the auxiliary trace retains exactly the term with $e_a=e_{j_N}$. The
output is therefore $e_{j_N}\otimes e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-1}}$.
These tensors form a basis, hence $\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a1})=U$.
As $U$ permutes a basis, it is invertible, proving the first identity and
invertibility of $t(0)$.

Differentiate the finite product defining $T_a(u)$ and use
$R'_{aj}(0)=I_{aj}$. For each $m$, let
$D_m=\operatorname{tr}_a(P_{aN}\cdots P_{a,m+1}P_{a,m-1}\cdots P_{a1})$,
with the factor $P_{am}$ omitted. Following the auxiliary basis vector
through the remaining swaps and taking its trace gives, for $2\le m<N$,
$$D_m(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_N})= e_{j_N}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{r=1}^{m-2}e_{j_r}\right)\otimes e_{j_m}\otimes e_{j_{m-1}}\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{r=m+1}^{N-1}e_{j_r}\right).$$
An empty tensor block in this display is omitted.
For $m=N$ the same calculation gives
$e_{j_{N-1}}\otimes e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-2}}\otimes e_{j_N}$;
for $m=1$ it gives
$e_{j_1}\otimes e_{j_N}\otimes e_{j_2}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{N-1}}$.
In each case this is exactly $UP_{m-1,m}$ applied to the input, with
$P_{0,1}:=P_{N,1}$. Since the elementary tensors form a basis,
$D_m=UP_{m-1,m}$ as operators. Thus
$t'(0)=i^{N-1}\sum_{m=1}^N UP_{m-1,m}$.

From step 1.1, $t(0)^{-1}=i^{-N}U^{-1}$. The definition of $U$ shows
$UP_{m-1,m}U^{-1}=P_{m,m+1}$ for $2\le m\le N$, while
$UP_{N,1}U^{-1}=P_{1,2}$. Therefore
$t'(0)t(0)^{-1}=i^{-1}\sum_{m=1}^N P_{m,m+1}=-i\sum_{m=1}^N P_{m,m+1}$.
Multiplication by $i$ proves the claimed logarithmic-derivative identity.

The spectral parameter $u$ is dimensionless. All operators in this definition

Let $t(u)$ and $U$ be the transfer matrix and cyclic shift defined by the
ordered monodromy construction. Use the periodic convention
$P_{N,N+1}:=P_{N,1}$. Then
$$t(0)=i^N U,\qquad i\,t'(0)t(0)^{-1}=\sum_{j=1}^N P_{j,j+1}.$$
In particular, $t(0)$ is invertible. The derivative is with respect to the
dimensionless complex parameter $u$.

For the ordered periodic monodromies
$$T_a(u):=R_{aN}(u)\cdots R_{a1}(u),\qquad T_b(v):=R_{bN}(v)\cdots R_{b1}(v),$$
the finite-dimensional operator identity
$$R_{ab}(u-v)T_a(u)T_b(v)=T_b(v)T_a(u)R_{ab}(u-v)$$
holds on $V_a\otimes V_b\otimes V_N$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb C$.

derivations.claim:
Put $s=u-v$. Since $P_{ab}^2=I$ and the mixed terms cancel,
$R_{ab}(s)R_{ab}(-s)=-(s^2+1)I$; hence $R_{ab}(s)$ is invertible for
$s\ne i,-i$. By [F3],
$T_b(v)T_a(u)=R_{ab}(s)T_a(u)T_b(v)R_{ab}(s)^{-1}$. The factor $R_{ab}$
acts only on the finite auxiliary space $V_a\otimes V_b$, so the ordinary
finite trace over that space is cyclic even with operator-valued coefficients
on $V_N$. Also $\operatorname{tr}_{ab}(T_a(u)T_b(v))=t(u)t(v)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}_{ab}(T_b(v)T_a(u))=t(v)t(u)$, by expanding each auxiliary
matrix in matrix units. Taking $\operatorname{tr}_{ab}$ therefore proves
$[t(u),t(v)]=0$ whenever $u-v\ne\pm i$.

Each entry of $t(u)$ is a polynomial in $u$, because it is the trace of a
finite product of matrices whose entries are linear polynomials. Thus every
entry of $[t(u),t(v)]$ is a polynomial in $(u,v)$. For each fixed $v$, it
vanishes for every $u$ except at most $v+i$ and $v-i$; a one-variable
polynomial with infinitely many zeros is zero. This holds for every $v$, so
$[t(u),t(v)]=0$ for all complex $u,v$, including the two singular
differences.

By [F2], $t(0)$ is invertible; hence $M(u)=t(0)^{-1}t(u)$ is analytic near
$0$ and $M(0)=I$. Choose a submultiplicative matrix norm. Continuity of $M$
gives a neighborhood of $0$ where $\|M(u)-I\|<1$, and there define
$\log M(u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}(M(u)-I)^n/n$, a convergent matrix power
series. Step 2.1 implies $t(u)$ commutes with $t(w)$ and every $t(v)$; since
$t(0)$ is invertible, $t(0)^{-1}$ commutes with them as well. Thus $M(u)$,
$M(w)$, and each $t(v)$ commute. Their logarithmic power series preserve
these commutations. Comparing the convergent two-variable Taylor coefficients
proves the coefficient matrices commute pairwise and with every $t(v)$.

derivations.claim:
Fix $u\in\mathbb C$. Differentiate $[t(u),t(v)]=0$ from [F3] with
respect to $v$ at $v=0$; the entries are polynomials, so this gives
$[t(u),t'(0)]=0$. Also $[t(u),t(0)]=0$. Since $t(0)$ is invertible by [F2],
multiplying $t(u)t(0)=t(0)t(u)$ on the left and right by $t(0)^{-1}$ shows
$[t(u),t(0)^{-1}]=0$. Therefore $t(u)$ commutes with
$t'(0)t(0)^{-1}$.

Substitute [F2] into step 1.1 and multiply by the scalar $iJ$. The sum
$\sum_jP_{j,j+1}$ therefore commutes with every $t(u)$, and so does
$H_N=J\sum_jP_{j,j+1}+cI$, since scalar multiples of the identity commute
with all endomorphisms.

Each $P_{j,j+1}$ is a real permutation matrix with $P_{j,j+1}^2=I$;
therefore $P_{j,j+1}^*=P_{j,j+1}^{-1}=P_{j,j+1}$, so the real linear
combination $H_N$ is Hermitian. On the ordered basis
$|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle,|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle,
|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$ of $V\otimes V$,
the swap $P$ fixes the first and fourth vectors and exchanges the middle two.
Direct multiplication of the displayed Pauli matrices gives
$$\begin{aligned} \tfrac12(I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z)|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle&=|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle,\\ \tfrac12(I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z)|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle&=|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle,\\ \tfrac12(I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z)|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle&=|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle,\\ \tfrac12(I+X\otimes X+Y\otimes Y+Z\otimes Z)|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle&=|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle. \end{aligned}$$
These four vectors form a basis, so the displayed Pauli operator equals $P$.
