Fix a finite dimension $d\geq1$, a positive constant $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, a Hermitian matrix $H\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ in joules, and a finite family $L_1,\ldots,L_m\in M_d(\mathbb C)$ with units ${\rm s}^{-1/2}$, where $m\geq0$. On dimensionless matrices $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, define the **finite Gorini–Kossakowski–Sudarshan–Lindblad (GKSL) generator**

$$\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_{a=1}^{m}\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right),$$

where $[A,B]=AB-BA$, $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$, and $A^*$ is the conjugate transpose. Each summand has units ${\rm s}^{-1}$ times the units of $X$. An empty sum when $m=0$ is zero. The resulting $\mathcal L$ is a linear map on the matrix space used in the finite-channel definition [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]].

For a compact time interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ whose coordinate is time in seconds, continuous functions $H:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $L_a:I\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ with $H(t)=H(t)^*$ define the corresponding **continuous finite GKSL family** $\mathcal L_t$ by the same formula at each $t$. A propagator for this family means a family of linear maps $\Lambda(t,s)$, $s\leq t$ in $I$, satisfying $\partial_t\Lambda(t,s)=\mathcal L_t\circ\Lambda(t,s)$ and $\Lambda(s,s)=\operatorname{id}$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

These are finite-dimensional mathematical definitions. They do not assert that a physical system follows this generator or that a microscopic bath has a Markovian limit.

Let $\mathcal L$ be a finite GKSL generator on $M_d(\mathbb C)$, $d\geq1$, with the units and conventions of [[def-qsm-dt-gksl-definition]]. For a bounded operator $A$ on a complex Banach space, write $e^{tA}:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}t^nA^n/n!$ for the operator-norm convergent series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]]. Then $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ is a finite channel for every $t\geq0$. The family satisfies $T_0=\operatorname{id}$, $T_{t+s}=T_t\circ T_s$, and is norm-continuous. derivations.claim: Let $J=\sqrt{\gamma}Z$, which is Hermitian and has units seconds$^{-1/2}$, so $J^*J=\gamma I_2$. Substitution of $H=0$ and this jump into [F2] gives $J\rho J^*-\frac12\{J^*J,\rho\}=\gamma(Z\rho Z-\rho)=\mathcal L(\rho)$. By [F3] and [F1], this generator produces a finite channel semigroup. The exponential series and its derivative converge uniformly on compact time intervals by the factorial norm bound, so $\dot\rho_t=\mathcal L(\rho_t)$ for $\rho_t=T_t\rho(0)$.

Since $H=0$, $e^{-\beta H}=I_2$ and $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}I_2=2$, so the faithful Gibbs density is $\sigma_\beta=I_2/2>0$. Multiplication gives $Z\rho(0)Z=\begin{pmatrix}p&-z\\-\overline z&1-p\end{pmatrix}$. Thus the generator equation is $\dot p=0$ and $\dot z=-2\gamma z$; integrating these scalar equations with the given initial values yields $\rho(t)=\begin{pmatrix}p&e^{-2\gamma t}z\\e^{-2\gamma t}\overline z&1-p\end{pmatrix}$. Hence the Gibbs density is not the unique stationary density, and this initial state does not converge to it, refuting both conclusions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, $H=H^*$ with energy unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, and let $\sigma=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ be the stationary Gibbs density from [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]]. Let $A=A^*$ and $B=B^*$ be matrices, let $T>0$ be finite in s, let $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless; $h(t)B$ has unit J. Put $U_0(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ for time $t$ in s, $\alpha_t(A)=U_0(t)^*AU_0(t)$, and $B_t=\alpha_t(B)$. Let $W_\epsilon$ solve
$$W_\epsilon'(t)=\frac{i\epsilon h(t)}{\hbar}B_tW_\epsilon(t),\qquad W_\epsilon(0)=I,$$
and set $U_\epsilon(t)=U_0(t)W_\epsilon(t)$ and $\rho_I(t)=W_\epsilon(t)\sigma W_\epsilon(t)^*$. Then $U_\epsilon$ solves $i\hbar U_\epsilon'(t)=(H-\epsilon h(t)B)U_\epsilon(t)$, $U_\epsilon(0)=I$, and $\rho_\epsilon(t):=U_\epsilon(t)\sigma U_\epsilon(t)^*$ satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\epsilon(t)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))$. Define
$$R_{AB}(u)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[\alpha_u(A),B]\right),\qquad C_T=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^T|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds.$$
Then $W_\epsilon(t)$ is unitary and, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(A))+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds+r_\epsilon(t),\qquad |r_\epsilon(t)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}}2.$$
The initial Gibbs matrix is fixed as $\epsilon$ varies. The result is an exact finite-time first variation with a controlled remainder, not a static derivative of a re-prepared Gibbs family. $C_T$ and $\epsilon$ are dimensionless, and $R_{AB}$ has units $[A][B]/(\mathrm J\,\mathrm s)$.

Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

derivations.claim: Since $h_{j,j+1}$ and $q_{j+1}$ are self-adjoint, $[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}]^*=-[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}]$. Thus $j_{j,j+1}=(i/\hbar)[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}]$ is self-adjoint.

The Heisenberg derivative is $\dot q_j=(i/\hbar)\sum_k[h_{k,k+1},q_j]$. By [A1], only the existing bonds immediately to the left and right of $j$ can contribute. The left contribution is $(i/\hbar)[h_{j-1,j},q_j]=j_{j-1,j}$ when that bond exists, and is zero by the open-boundary convention otherwise.

For the right contribution, [A2] gives $[h_{j,j+1},q_j]=-[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}]$, so $(i/\hbar)[h_{j,j+1},q_j]=-j_{j,j+1}$ when that bond exists. If it is absent at the open right endpoint, both terms are zero by convention.

Combining steps 1.2 and 1.3 proves $\dot q_j=j_{j-1,j}-j_{j,j+1}$. Summing over $j\in\Lambda_L$ cancels every existing open-chain or periodic bond once with each sign, so $\dot Q_L=0$, equivalently $[H_L,Q_L]=0$.

Use the finite open or periodic chain and bond-current definition in [[def-qsmx-lattice-current-and-limits]]. Each $j_{j,j+1}$ is self-adjoint, and with $\dot q_j:=(i/\hbar)[H_L,q_j]$ the exact local identity
$$\dot q_j=j_{j-1,j}-j_{j,j+1}$$
holds at every site. Consequently the total charge $Q_L:=\sum_{j\in\Lambda_L}q_j$, where $\Lambda_L$ is the open-chain site set or periodic site set from the definition, is conserved: $[H_L,Q_L]=0$. The current orientation is from $j$ to $j+1$, so positive outgoing current lowers the charge at site $j$.

Under the finite-dimensional unitary dynamics of [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]], let $P_E$ be the orthogonal spectral projection of $H$ for its distinct energy $E$. For every density matrix $\rho$,

$$\frac1T\int_0^T U(t)\rho U(t)^*\,dt\longrightarrow\sum_E P_E\rho P_E$$

in trace norm as $T\to\infty$. The diagonal energy blocks, including all blocks within degenerate eigenspaces, remain. This is Cesaro convergence of the averaged state; pointwise convergence of $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$ is not asserted.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

derivations.claim: The lattice-current definition fixes $J_L=\sum_jj_{j,j+1}$, and the local-current lemma gives $J_L=J_L^*$. Subtracting its real mean $\omega(J_L)$ preserves self-adjointness, so $J$ is a matrix observable in $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$.

On $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ define $(A,B)_\rho:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A^*B)$, linear in its second argument. It is positive definite: if $(A,A)_\rho=0$, then $\rho\ge cI$ for some $c>0$ in finite dimension, so $0=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A^*A)\ge c\operatorname{Tr}(A^*A)$ and hence $A=0$. The invariance $[\rho,H]=0$ gives $(\alpha_t(A),\alpha_t(B))_\rho=(A,B)_\rho$ by cyclicity of the finite trace, so $\alpha_t$ is unitary on this finite-dimensional Hilbert space of matrices.

Write $H=\sum_E E P_E$ over its distinct eigenvalues. Then $\alpha_t(J)=\sum_{E,F}e^{it(E-F)/\hbar}P_EJP_F$. For $E\ne F$,
$$\left|\frac1T\int_0^T e^{it(E-F)/\hbar}\,dt\right|\le\frac{2\hbar}{T|E-F|}\longrightarrow0,$$
while for $E=F$ the coefficient is $1$. The sum is finite, so $M_TJ:=T^{-1}\int_0^T\alpha_t(J)\,dt$ converges in matrix norm to $PJ:=\sum_E P_EJP_E$. This block map is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal N:=\{A:[H,A]=0\}$ in $(\cdot,\cdot)_\rho$: $PJ\in\mathcal N$, and each off-diagonal block of $J-PJ$ has zero weighted trace pairing with a block-diagonal matrix because $\rho$ is block diagonal. It is the same energy-block projection as the density-matrix dephasing in [F3]; [F3] states the density-matrix version, while the explicit finite expansion here proves the observable version used.

Since $J=J^*$, $(\alpha_t(J),J)_\rho=\omega(\alpha_t(J)J)$. Norm convergence in step 2.1 therefore gives
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\,\omega(\alpha_t(J)J)\,dt=\operatorname{Re}(PJ,J)_\rho=\|PJ\|_\rho^2,$$
because $J-PJ$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal N$ and $PJ\in\mathcal N$.

Set $S:=\operatorname{span}\{Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\}\subseteq\mathcal N$, and let $P_S$ be its orthogonal projection. Then $P_SJ=P_SPJ$, so $\|PJ\|_\rho^2\ge\|P_SJ\|_\rho^2$. The Gram matrix $G$ is positive definite by linear independence and the positive-definite inner product. Writing $P_SJ=\sum_a c_aQ_a$, orthogonality gives $Gc=v$, so $c=G^{-1}v$ and $\|P_SJ\|_\rho^2=c^*Gc=v^*G^{-1}v$. Together with step 3.1 this proves the bound.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Use the finite open or periodic chain and bond-current definition in [[def-qsmx-lattice-current-and-limits]]. Each $j_{j,j+1}$ is self-adjoint, and with $\dot q_j:=(i/\hbar)[H_L,q_j]$ the exact local identity
$$\dot q_j=j_{j-1,j}-j_{j,j+1}$$
holds at every site. Consequently the total charge $Q_L:=\sum_{j\in\Lambda_L}q_j$, where $\Lambda_L$ is the open-chain site set or periodic site set from the definition, is conserved: $[H_L,Q_L]=0$. The current orientation is from $j$ to $j+1$, so positive outgoing current lowers the charge at site $j$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Under the finite-dimensional unitary dynamics of [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]], let $P_E$ be the orthogonal spectral projection of $H$ for its distinct energy $E$. For every density matrix $\rho$,

$$\frac1T\int_0^T U(t)\rho U(t)^*\,dt\longrightarrow\sum_E P_E\rho P_E$$

in trace norm as $T\to\infty$. The diagonal energy blocks, including all blocks within degenerate eigenspaces, remain. This is Cesaro convergence of the averaged state; pointwise convergence of $U(t)\rho U(t)^*$ is not asserted.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Use its finite-range spin algebra $\mathcal A$, strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$, and invariant state $\phi$ obtained from consistent local densities. Let $V=V^*\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\phi(V)=0$, and define
$$X_T=\int_0^T\alpha_t(V)\,dt,\qquad G(t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_t(V)).$$
If $G\in L^1([0,\infty))$, then
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\phi(X_T^2)}{2T}=D:=\int_0^\infty G(t)\,dt\ge0.$$
For a finite list of centered self-adjoint observables $V_1,\ldots,V_m$, if each symmetrized covariance $G_{ab}(t)=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_a\alpha_t(V_b))+\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_b\alpha_t(V_a)))$ is absolutely integrable on $[0,\infty)$, then $D_{ab}=\int_0^\infty G_{ab}(t)dt$ is a real positive semidefinite matrix. For a velocity observable measured in m s$^{-1}$, $D$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; for general $V$, its units are $[V]^2$ s. The result is a variance of a time-integrated observable, not a joint classical trajectory or a universal transport law.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
(Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything

companion page.

the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$

(The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval

derivations.claim: In the classical alternative fix $T>0$ and use Lebesgue measure on $[0,T]$ for the Bochner integral. For each $n\ge1$, let $J_n:[0,T]\to L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ take the value $J(kT/n)$ on $[kT/n,(k+1)T/n)$ for $0\le k<n$ and the value $J(T)$ at $T$. Each $J_n$ is a measurable simple function. Uniform continuity of $J$ on $[0,T]$ gives $\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\to0$, and hence $\int_0^T\|J_n(t)-J(t)\|_2\,dt\to0$. Thus $J$ is strongly measurable (an almost-everywhere limit of measurable simple functions), and $\int_0^T\|J(t)\|_2\,dt<\infty$ because $J$ is bounded. By the definition of the Bochner integral as the $L^1$-norm limit of integrals of simple functions, $J$ is Bochner integrable. The Bochner integrals of $J_n$ are the left-endpoint Riemann sums for $J$; they converge both to the Bochner integral by the $L^1$ approximation and to the norm-Riemann integral by [F6]. Hence these integrals agree. The expectation functional $\Lambda(Y):=\mathbb E[Y]=\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}$ is bounded since $|\Lambda(Y)|=|\langle Y,1\rangle_{L^2}|\le\|Y\|_2\|1\|_2=\|Y\|_2$. Applying the bounded-linear-map clause of [F6] gives $\mathbb E[X_T]=\int_0^T\mathbb E[J(t)]\,dt=0$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)=\mathbb E[X_T^2]$.

The spatially normalized current convention is fixed by [F1]. In the quantum alternative, [A1] and [F2] apply to the exact $\alpha_t$, invariant state $\phi$, and centered self-adjoint $V$ in the Statement, so the supplier gives the variance identity and limit. The evenness asserted in the Statement follows from $C(-t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_{-t}(V))=\operatorname{Re}\phi(\alpha_t(V)V)=\operatorname{Re}\overline{\phi(V\alpha_t(V))}=C(t)$, using invariance and self-adjointness. In the classical alternative, continuity of the inner product makes $(s,t)\mapsto\mathbb E[J(s)J(t)]=C(t-s)$ continuous on $[0,T]^2$. Riemann sums for $X_T$ converge in $L^2$, so continuity of the inner product makes the expectations of their squared norms converge to $\mathbb E[X_T^2]$; each squared-sum expectation is a product Riemann sum for this continuous kernel. Thus [F3] gives $\mathbb E[X_T^2]=\int_0^T\int_0^T C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$, which equals $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)$ by step 1.1. The integrand is symmetric because $C$ is even. The diagonal has zero area: it lies in strips of width $\delta$ and area at most $2T\delta+\delta^2$, tending to zero, so a bounded continuous integrand contributes zero there. Off the diagonal the two triangular restrictions are continuous; on a grid meeting the diagonal their upper-lower gap is bounded by the kernel oscillation away from the diagonal plus twice its supremum times the diagonal-strip area. Hence the product of the triangular indicator with the kernel is Riemann integrable. Each section has at most one jump and is therefore Riemann integrable. For the upper triangle, $g(t):=\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds$ satisfies $|g(t)-g(t\prime)|\le T\omega_C(|t-t\prime|)+\|C\|_\infty|t-t\prime|$, where $\omega_C(\delta):=\sup_{|u-v|\le\delta}|C(u)-C(v)|\to0$; hence its outer integral is continuous. The lower triangle has the same estimate with reversed limits. Splitting the square into its two triangles and applying [F3] to each gives $2\int_0^T\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds\,dt$.

For the classical alternative, apply [F4] to $\varphi(s)=t-s$ on $[0,t]$. It gives $\int_t^0 C(u)\,du=-\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds$; reversing the oriented endpoints yields $\int_0^t C(t-s)\,ds=F(t)$, where $F(t):=\int_0^t C(u)\,du$. By [F7], $F'=C$; the product rule gives $(tF(t))'=F(t)+tC(t)$, a continuous derivative. Applying [F5] to $tF(t)$ and using $F(T)=\int_0^T C(u)\,du$ yields $\int_0^T F(t)\,dt=\int_0^T(T-u)C(u)\,du$. Thus step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Var}(X_T)/(2T)=\int_0^T(1-u/T)C(u)\,du$.

In the classical alternative, put $K:=\int_0^\infty|C(u)|\,du<\infty$. For $T>R>0$, the difference between step 3.1 and the improper integral is bounded by
$$\left|\int_0^T(1-u/T)C(u)\,du-\int_0^\infty C(u)\,du\right|\le\frac{R}{T}K+2\int_R^\infty|C(u)|\,du.$$
First choose $R$ so the tail is arbitrarily small, then let $T\to\infty$; this proves the classical limit. The quantum limit is supplied by [F2].

In the classical alternative every finite-time variance is nonnegative, so its limit is nonnegative; in the quantum alternative nonnegativity is part of [F2]. The limit therefore has the stated sign in either case.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Assume Countable Choice and the finite-matrix C$^*$-identity hypothesis used by [[thm-qsm-dt-algebraic-kubo]]. Use its finite-range spin algebra $\mathcal A$, strongly continuous automorphism group $\alpha_t$, and invariant state $\phi$ obtained from consistent local densities. Let $V=V^*\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\phi(V)=0$, and define
$$X_T=\int_0^T\alpha_t(V)\,dt,\qquad G(t)=\operatorname{Re}\phi(V\alpha_t(V)).$$
If $G\in L^1([0,\infty))$, then
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{\phi(X_T^2)}{2T}=D:=\int_0^\infty G(t)\,dt\ge0.$$
For a finite list of centered self-adjoint observables $V_1,\ldots,V_m$, if each symmetrized covariance $G_{ab}(t)=\tfrac12(\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_a\alpha_t(V_b))+\operatorname{Re}\phi(V_b\alpha_t(V_a)))$ is absolutely integrable on $[0,\infty)$, then $D_{ab}=\int_0^\infty G_{ab}(t)dt$ is a real positive semidefinite matrix. For a velocity observable measured in m s$^{-1}$, $D$ has units m$^2$ s$^{-1}$; for general $V$, its units are $[V]^2$ s. The result is a variance of a time-integrated observable, not a joint classical trajectory or a universal transport law.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
(Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$.

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything

the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a real vector space ([[def-vector-space]]) with a norm $\|\cdot\|$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) whose metric $d(x,y):=\|x-y\|$ is complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]). Let $a<b$ be reals ([[def-interval]]) and let $g:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). For endpoints $c,d\in[a,b]$, set $\int_c^c g:=0_X$ and, when $c>d$, set $\int_c^d g:=-\int_d^c g$; for $c<d$ use the Riemann-sum construction below on the restriction to $[c,d]$. Then:

1. **Integral.** For every sequence of tagged partitions of $[a,b]$ whose mesh tends to $0$, the Riemann sums $\sum_i(t_{i+1}-t_i)\,g(s_i)$ converge in $X$; the limit, written $\int_a^b g$, is independent of the sequence, and
$$\Bigl\|\int_a^b g\Bigr\|\;\le\;(b-a)\sup_{t\in[a,b]}\|g(t)\| .$$
2. **Fundamental theorem.** The curve $G:[a,b]\to X$, $G(t):=\int_a^t g$, is well defined, satisfies $\|G(t)-G(s)\|\le(t-s)\sup_{[s,t]}\|g\|$ for $a\le s\le t\le b$, and is differentiable with $G'=g$ on $[a,b]$ in the one-sided sense at the endpoints.
3. **Linearity.** For continuous $g,h:[a,b]\to X$ and reals $\alpha,\beta$: $\int_a^b(\alpha g+\beta h)=\alpha\int_a^b g+\beta\int_a^b h$; and for $a\le c\le b$, $\int_a^b g=\int_a^c g+\int_c^b g$.
4. **Bounded linear images.** If $Y$ is a normed real vector space and $T:X\to Y$ is linear with $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for some $C<+\infty$ and all $x$, then $T\circ g$ is continuous and $T\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b (T\circ g)$; in particular, for every real-linear functional $\Lambda:X\to\mathbb R$ with $|\Lambda x|\le C\|x\|$, $\Lambda\bigl(\int_a^b g\bigr)=\int_a^b\Lambda\circ g$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$), let $F$ be its integral function
(The integral function $F(x) := \int_a^x f$ of an integrable $f$), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

citations.quote:
Fix either a finite open chain with sites $\{1,\ldots,L\}$, $L\ge2$, or a periodic chain with sites $\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z$, $L\ge3$, and denote its site set by $\Lambda_L$. Let $\mathcal H_L$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space. For each site $j$, let $q_j=q_j^*$ be a bounded charge observable, with physical unit $\mathsf Q$. For each oriented nearest-neighbor bond $(j,j+1)$, let $h_{j,j+1}=h_{j,j+1}^*$ be an energy operator in joules. Require $[h_{k,k+1},q_j]=0$ whenever $j\notin\{k,k+1\}$, and require local charge conservation $[h_{j,j+1},q_j+q_{j+1}]=0$. On an open chain set $H_L=\sum_{j=1}^{L-1}h_{j,j+1}$; on a ring set $H_L=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z}h_{j,j+1}$ with periodic indices. For an open chain define the absent boundary currents $j_{0,1}=j_{L,L+1}=0$. Use $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. These finite local data may be realized on a tensor-product spin space or on a finite fixed-particle site space, provided the stated commutation conditions hold.

The oriented bond current from $j$ to $j+1$ is
$$j_{j,j+1}:=\frac{i}{\hbar}[h_{j,j+1},q_{j+1}].$$
It has unit $\mathsf Q\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The total current is the sum over existing bonds, $J_L:=\sum_{(j,j+1)}j_{j,j+1}$, and its Heisenberg evolution for $t\in\mathbb R$ is $J_L(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_Le^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. For finite inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$, define $\rho_{\beta,L}:=e^{-\beta H_L}/\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H_L})$ and $\omega_{\beta,L}(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_{\beta,L}A)$. Write $J_L^\circ:=J_L-\omega_{\beta,L}(J_L)I$ and $J_L^\circ(t):=e^{iH_Lt/\hbar}J_L^\circ e^{-iH_Lt/\hbar}$. Define the real, connected, symmetrized correlation per site by
$$C_L(t):=\frac{1}{L}\operatorname{Re}\,\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ\right)=\frac{1}{2L}\omega_{\beta,L}\!\left(J_L^\circ(t)J_L^\circ+J_L^\circ J_L^\circ(t)\right).$$
The correlation has unit $\mathsf Q^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}$ per site.

This definition assigns no transport coefficient by itself. Any proposed finite-volume or thermodynamic transport quantity must additionally state its time cutoff, frequency regulator (for example $e^{-\eta t}$ with $\eta>0$ in seconds$^{-1}$), spatial normalization, and the exact order in which $L\to\infty$, the time cutoff tends to infinity, and any regulator is removed. Existence of those limits is not part of this definition.

Use the finite open or periodic chain and bond-current definition in [[def-qsmx-lattice-current-and-limits]]. Each $j_{j,j+1}$ is self-adjoint, and with $\dot q_j:=(i/\hbar)[H_L,q_j]$ the exact local identity
$$\dot q_j=j_{j-1,j}-j_{j,j+1}$$
holds at every site. Consequently the total charge $Q_L:=\sum_{j\in\Lambda_L}q_j$, where $\Lambda_L$ is the open-chain site set or periodic site set from the definition, is conserved: $[H_L,Q_L]=0$. The current orientation is from $j$ to $j+1$, so positive outgoing current lowers the charge at site $j$.

Take the finite-chain data of the current definition on $\mathcal H_L$ and identify $\mathcal H:=\mathcal H_L$. Let $H=H^*$ have energy unit joules, let $\hbar>0$ have unit joule-seconds, and let $\rho$ be a positive-definite trace-one matrix satisfying $[\rho,H]=0$. Define $\omega(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ and $\alpha_t(A):=e^{iHt/\hbar}Ae^{-iHt/\hbar}$. Let $J_L$ be the total lattice current of the finite-volume current definition and center it with respect to this same $\rho$, setting $J:=J_L-\omega(J_L)I$. With no identification of $H$ and $H_L$, the estimate below is an abstract bound for this observable under $\alpha_t$. Its lattice-transport specialization further takes $H=H_L$; then the Gibbs density $\rho_{\beta,L}$ in that definition is stationary and is an admissible choice of $\rho$. More generally, $\rho_{\beta,L}$ can be used with another $H$ exactly when it also satisfies $[\rho_{\beta,L},H]=0$. Then $J=J^*$, as established by the local continuity result. For $m\ge1$, let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$ be linearly independent conserved matrices, $[H,Q_a]=0$. Put
$$G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Q_a^*Q_b),\qquad v_a:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Q_a^*J).$$
Then $G$ is positive definite, the finite Cesàro limit exists, and
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\,\omega\!\left(\alpha_t(J)J\right)\,dt\;\ge\;v^*G^{-1}v\;\ge0.$$
This is a finite-dimensional persistent-correlation bound. It does not identify a thermodynamic Drude weight or assert that either volume/time order of limits exists.

derivations.claim: Each $h_{j,j+1}$ acts only on the span of $|j\rangle,|j+1\rangle$, so it commutes with every $q_k$ outside those two sites and with $q_j+q_{j+1}$. The definition [F1] therefore applies. By [F2], each bond current is self-adjoint, so $J_3=J_3^*$. Direct multiplication gives $H_3=-g(S+S^*)$ and $J_3=(ig/\hbar)(S-S^*)$. Since $S$ is unitary, $S$ commutes with $S^*$; hence $[H_3,J_3]=0$, and $J_3\ne0$.

In the Fourier basis of the three-cycle, $H_3$ has eigenvalues $-2g,g,g$, while $J_3$ has eigenvalues $0,\sqrt3g/\hbar,-\sqrt3g/\hbar$ in the corresponding order. The two states with energy $g$ have equal Gibbs weight, so $\omega_{\beta,3}(J_3)=0$. Positive definiteness of $\rho_{\beta,3}$ and $J_3\ne0$ give $c:=\omega_{\beta,3}(J_3^2)>0$.

Because $[H_3,J_3]=0$, Heisenberg evolution fixes $J_3$ for all $t$. Thus $J_3^\circ=J_3$ and $C_3(t)=c/3$ is a positive constant. Therefore $\int_0^\infty|C_3(t)|\,dt=+\infty$, refuting the statement.

In the finite Mazur bound [F3], choose the single conserved operator $Q_1=J_3$. Then $G_{11}=v_1=c$, so the lower bound on the Cesàro average of the unnormalized autocorrelation $\operatorname{Re}\omega_{\beta,3}(\alpha_t(J_3)J_3)$ is $c>0$. The per-site convention in the definition gives $C_3(t)=\frac13\operatorname{Re}\omega_{\beta,3}(\alpha_t(J_3)J_3)$, so the Mazur contribution for the Cesàro average of $C_3$ is $c/3$, equal to the constant correlation found in step 3.1. This remains a finite-volume obstruction only; no thermodynamic Drude weight is inferred.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Take the finite-chain data of the current definition on $\mathcal H_L$ and identify $\mathcal H:=\mathcal H_L$. Let $H=H^*$ have energy unit joules, let $\hbar>0$ have unit joule-seconds, and let $\rho$ be a positive-definite trace-one matrix satisfying $[\rho,H]=0$. Define $\omega(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$ and $\alpha_t(A):=e^{iHt/\hbar}Ae^{-iHt/\hbar}$. Let $J_L$ be the total lattice current of the finite-volume current definition and center it with respect to this same $\rho$, setting $J:=J_L-\omega(J_L)I$. With no identification of $H$ and $H_L$, the estimate below is an abstract bound for this observable under $\alpha_t$. Its lattice-transport specialization further takes $H=H_L$; then the Gibbs density $\rho_{\beta,L}$ in that definition is stationary and is an admissible choice of $\rho$. More generally, $\rho_{\beta,L}$ can be used with another $H$ exactly when it also satisfies $[\rho_{\beta,L},H]=0$. Then $J=J^*$, as established by the local continuity result. For $m\ge1$, let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$ be linearly independent conserved matrices, $[H,Q_a]=0$. Put
$$G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Q_a^*Q_b),\qquad v_a:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Q_a^*J).$$
Then $G$ is positive definite, the finite Cesàro limit exists, and
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\,\omega\!\left(\alpha_t(J)J\right)\,dt\;\ge\;v^*G^{-1}v\;\ge0.$$
This is a finite-dimensional persistent-correlation bound. It does not identify a thermodynamic Drude weight or assert that either volume/time order of limits exists.

citations.quote:
Let $r\geq1$, let $H_1=\mathbb C^r$ with ordered orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let
$\mathcal F_-(H_1)=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{r}\bigwedge^k H_1$ be its finite-mode
fermionic Fock space. Let $\mathcal A_r$ be the unital *-algebra generated
by its annihilation and creation operators; it is finite-dimensional. Let
$c_j,c_j^*$ be those operators in this basis, satisfying
$$c_ic_j+c_jc_i=0,\qquad c_ic_j^*+c_j^*c_i=\delta_{ij}I,\qquad c_i^*c_j^*+c_j^*c_i^*=0.$$
A state is a complex-linear functional $\omega$ on $\mathcal A_r$ such that
$\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(X^*X)\geq0$ for every $X\in\mathcal A_r$. Define
the gauge automorphism $\gamma_\theta$ by
$\gamma_\theta(c_j)=e^{-i\theta}c_j$ and
$\gamma_\theta(c_j^*)=e^{i\theta}c_j^*$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R$; the CAR
relations are preserved, so these assignments extend to a one-parameter
family of algebra automorphisms. A state is gauge invariant when
$\omega(\gamma_\theta(X))=\omega(X)$ for every $X$ and every $\theta$.

For a gauge-invariant state, define its one-particle covariance matrix
$C\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ by $C_{ji}:=\omega(c_i^*c_j)$. A finite
gauge-invariant state is quasifree when $C=C^*$, $0\leq C\leq I$, and its
normally ordered moments obey the following rule: for $p\neq q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1})=0,$$
and for $p=q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_p}\cdots c_{j_1})=\det\!\left[\omega(c_{i_a}^*c_{j_b})\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}=\det\!\left[C_{j_bi_a}\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}.$$
The empty moment is $\omega(I)=1$. The inequalities $0\leq C\leq I$ mean
$\langle Cv,v\rangle\geq0$ and
$\langle(I-C)v,v\rangle\geq0$ for all $v\in H_1$. Moments of words not
in normal order are obtained by reordering with the displayed CAR relations.

For a Hermitian one-particle matrix $h=h^*$, a real chemical potential $\mu$,
and $\beta>0$, define
$$d\Gamma(h-\mu I):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{r}c_i^*(h-\mu I)_{ij}c_j,\qquad Z:=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}\right),\qquad \rho:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}.$$
The finite grand Gibbs state has covariance
$$C=(I+e^{\beta(h-\mu I)})^{-1}.$$
Here $h$ and $\mu$ are in joules, $\beta$ is in inverse joules, and $C$ is
dimensionless. The existence and uniqueness of the state for every
Hermitian contraction $C$, and the displayed finite Gibbs covariance formula,
are established by an earlier finite-dimensional result.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

In the occupation basis for the eigenmodes, define $w_j(0):=1-
u_j$ and $w_j(1):=

u_j)+

For the Gibbs assertion, diagonalize $h=W\operatorname{diag} (\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_r)W^*$ by [F3], and set $d=W^*c$ in column notation. The unitary $\Gamma_-(W)^*$ changes the occupation basis to these eigenmodes. On the occupation vector $|m\rangle$ it gives $$d\Gamma(h-\mu I)|m\rangle=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{r}(\epsilon_j-\mu)m_j\right)|m\rangle.$$ Therefore the positive exponential has eigenvalues $\prod_j q_j^{m_j}$ , where $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}>0$ , and its finite trace is $$Z=\prod_{j=1}^{r}(1+q_j)\in(0,\infty).$$ The normalized density is a product Bernoulli density with occupation probabilities $p_j=q_j/(1+q_j)=(1+e^{\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)})^{-1}$ .

The density $ho_D$ is diagonal in the occupation basis, so its state is invariant under the global gauge rotation. For a normally ordered monomial, repeated creation or annihilation indices give zero by the CAR. If the distinct creator and annihilator index sets differ, the monomial changes an occupation vector and has zero diagonal expectation. If the sets agree at $S$ , the CAR relations reorder the product to its permutation sign times $\prod_{j\in S}c_j^*c_j$ ; its product-state expectation is that sign times $\prod_{j\in S}
u_j$ . The determinant of the diagonal two-point matrix has exactly the same value: it is zero for unequal index sets and, for equal sets $S$ , is the permutation sign times $\prod_{j\in S}
u_j$ . Thus $ho_D$ obeys the quasifree moment rule with diagonal covariance $\operatorname{diag}(
u_1,\ldots,
u_r)$ . Moreover, every $c_i$ is a linear combination of the eigenmode annihilators and every $c_i^*$ is the corresponding conjugate linear combination. Expanding a normal-ordered product and using multilinearity of the determinant carries the Wick rule to covariance $V\operatorname{diag}(
u_1,\ldots,
u_r)V^*$ . The unitary $\Gamma_-(V)$ commutes with total particle number, so it preserves gauge invariance. Hence $ho_C$ has the required covariance and moments.

The CAR relations reorder any word in the generators into a linear combination of normally ordered monomials. These monomials determine the functional on the full finite matrix algebra: the vacuum projection is $P_0=\prod_{j=1}^{r}(I-c_j^*c_j)$ , and for any two occupation subsets $S,T$ , the operator obtained by creating the modes in $S$ , applying $P_0$ , and annihilating the modes in $T$ is a nonzero scalar multiple of $|S\rangle\langle T|$ . Expanding $P_0$ and reordering with CAR expresses each such matrix unit as a linear combination of normally ordered monomials. Since these matrix units span the full algebra, no two states can have the same stated moments unless they are equal. This proves uniqueness of $\rho_C$ .

The product density in the eigenmode basis obeys the determinant moment rule proved in step 2.1. Its covariance is $W\operatorname{diag}(p_1,\ldots,p_r)W^*$ by the convention [F1], and the finite spectral calculus [F3] identifies this matrix with $(I+e^{\beta(h-\mu I)})^{-1}$ . Uniqueness from step 3.1 identifies the Gibbs density with $\rho_C$ . All sums are finite-mode sums; no infinite-mode implementability or thermodynamic limit is involved.

Let $r\geq1$, let $H_1=\mathbb C^r$ with ordered orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let
$\mathcal F_-(H_1)=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{r}\bigwedge^k H_1$ be its finite-mode
fermionic Fock space. Let $\mathcal A_r$ be the unital *-algebra generated
by its annihilation and creation operators; it is finite-dimensional. Let
$c_j,c_j^*$ be those operators in this basis, satisfying
$$c_ic_j+c_jc_i=0,\qquad c_ic_j^*+c_j^*c_i=\delta_{ij}I,\qquad c_i^*c_j^*+c_j^*c_i^*=0.$$
A state is a complex-linear functional $\omega$ on $\mathcal A_r$ such that
$\omega(I)=1$ and $\omega(X^*X)\geq0$ for every $X\in\mathcal A_r$. Define
the gauge automorphism $\gamma_\theta$ by
$\gamma_\theta(c_j)=e^{-i\theta}c_j$ and
$\gamma_\theta(c_j^*)=e^{i\theta}c_j^*$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R$; the CAR
relations are preserved, so these assignments extend to a one-parameter
family of algebra automorphisms. A state is gauge invariant when
$\omega(\gamma_\theta(X))=\omega(X)$ for every $X$ and every $\theta$.

For a gauge-invariant state, define its one-particle covariance matrix
$C\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ by $C_{ji}:=\omega(c_i^*c_j)$. A finite
gauge-invariant state is quasifree when $C=C^*$, $0\leq C\leq I$, and its
normally ordered moments obey the following rule: for $p\neq q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1})=0,$$
and for $p=q$,
$$\omega(c_{i_1}^*\cdots c_{i_p}^*c_{j_p}\cdots c_{j_1})=\det\!\left[\omega(c_{i_a}^*c_{j_b})\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}=\det\!\left[C_{j_bi_a}\right]_{a,b=1}^{p}.$$
The empty moment is $\omega(I)=1$. The inequalities $0\leq C\leq I$ mean
$\langle Cv,v\rangle\geq0$ and
$\langle(I-C)v,v\rangle\geq0$ for all $v\in H_1$. Moments of words not
in normal order are obtained by reordering with the displayed CAR relations.

For a Hermitian one-particle matrix $h=h^*$, a real chemical potential $\mu$,
and $\beta>0$, define
$$d\Gamma(h-\mu I):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{r}c_i^*(h-\mu I)_{ij}c_j,\qquad Z:=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}\right),\qquad \rho:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}.$$
The finite grand Gibbs state has covariance
$$C=(I+e^{\beta(h-\mu I)})^{-1}.$$
Here $h$ and $\mu$ are in joules, $\beta$ is in inverse joules, and $C$ is
dimensionless. The existence and uniqueness of the state for every
Hermitian contraction $C$, and the displayed finite Gibbs covariance formula,
are established by an earlier finite-dimensional result.

Let $r\geq1$ and let $C=C^*$ be an $r\times r$ matrix with
$0\leq C\leq I$. There is a unique finite density operator $\rho_C$ on
$\mathcal F_-(\mathbb C^r)$ whose state is gauge-invariant quasifree with
covariance $C$ in the convention
$C_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_Cc_i^*c_j)$. If $h=h^*$, $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
and $\beta>0$, then the finite Gibbs density
$$\rho_{h,\beta,\mu}:=\frac{e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)}}{\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta d\Gamma(h-\mu I)})}$$
is quasifree and equals $\rho_C$ for
$$C=(I+e^{\beta(h-\mu I)})^{-1}.$$

All Hilbert spaces in this item are nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$. A density operator $\rho$ on $H$ is a Hermitian positive semidefinite endomorphism with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Its dimensionless von Neumann entropy, in nats, is

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\log\lambda_j,$$

where $\lambda_j$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$, the logarithm is natural, and $0\log0:=0$. For any positive semidefinite endomorphisms $X,Y$ on one finite-dimensional $H$, let $\operatorname{supp}X:=(\ker X)^\perp$. Define

$$D(X\|Y):=\operatorname{Tr}(X\log X)-\operatorname{Tr}(X\log Y)$$

when $\operatorname{supp}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Y$, taking each logarithm spectrally on its positive support and setting zero-eigenvalue contributions to zero; set $D(X\|Y):=+\infty$ otherwise. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional quantum relative entropy in nats.

For a density operator $\rho_{AB}$ on the ordered product $H_A\otimes H_B$, define $\rho_A:=\operatorname{Tr}_B\rho_{AB}$ and $\rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{AB}$, where in orthonormal product bases $\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B R\bigr)_{ii'}=\sum_jR_{(i,j),(i',j)}$ and the first factor is retained. Define

$$I(A:B)_\rho:=S(\rho_A)+S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{AB}).$$

For a density operator $\rho_{ABC}$ on $H_A\otimes H_B\otimes H_C$, define

$$\rho_{AB}:=\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_{BC}:=\operatorname{Tr}_A\rho_{ABC},\qquad \rho_B:=\operatorname{Tr}_A(\operatorname{Tr}_C\rho_{ABC}),$$

where each partial trace contracts the indicated tensor factor and retains the other factors in their displayed order.

$$I(A:C\mid B)_\rho:=S(\rho_{AB})+S(\rho_{BC})-S(\rho_B)-S(\rho_{ABC}),$$

using the partial traces in the displayed factor order. For any fixed positive conversion factor $k_B$ with units J/K, the corresponding physical entropy is $S_{\mathrm{phys}}(\rho):=k_BS(\rho)$; no numerical value of $k_B$ is specified here.

Let $I$ and $\mathcal F_\pm(\ell^2(I))$ be as in
[[def-qsm-identical-particle-fock-sectors]]. Define
$$
\Omega_B:=\{m:I\to\mathbb N_0:m\text{ has finite support}\},\qquad \Omega_F:=\{m:I\to\{0,1\}:m\text{ has finite support}\}.
$$
For either statistics choice, write $|m|=\sum_jm_j$. If $m\in\Omega_B$, choose the elementary tensor $x_m$ containing $m_j$ copies of each mode $j$ in the fixed order and set
$$
|m\rangle_B:=\sqrt{\frac{|m|!}{\prod_jm_j!}}\,P_+^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
If $m\in\Omega_F$, list its occupied modes increasingly in the fixed enumeration, let $x_m$ be their elementary tensor and set
$$
|m\rangle_F:=\sqrt{|m|!}\,P_-^{(|m|)}x_m.
$$
For $|m|=0$, both vectors are the vacuum. These vectors form orthonormal bases and define unitary identifications $\mathcal F_+(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_B)$ and $\mathcal F_-(\ell^2(I))\cong\ell^2(\Omega_F)$.

On the finite-support span $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ of the bosonic basis, define
$$
a_j|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j}|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,\qquad a_j^\dagger|m\rangle_B=\sqrt{m_j+1}|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_B,
$$
where the annihilation term is zero when $m_j=0$. Their maximal closed extensions have domains
$$
D(a_j)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}m_j|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad D(a_j^\dagger)=\left\{c:\sum_{m\in\Omega_B}(m_j+1)|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},
$$
and $a_j^\dagger=a_j^*$. On $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, they satisfy
$[a_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}I$, $[a_i,a_j]=0$, and $[a_i^\dagger,a_j^\dagger]=0$.

On the fermionic basis define
$$
c_j|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}m_j|m-\mathbf1_j\rangle_F,\qquad c_j^\dagger|m\rangle_F=(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}m_i}(1-m_j)|m+\mathbf1_j\rangle_F.
$$
These operators are bounded on the full fermionic Fock space and satisfy
$\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}I$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$. These are mathematical sector relations; they do not select a physical species or imply a spin-statistics theorem.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Fix an integer $r\geq1$,
an action scale $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and
the finite-mode Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$. In Schrödinger
coordinates, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ be the Schwartz space
$$\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^r):\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^r}|x^\alpha\partial^\gamma f(x)|<\infty\text{ for every }\alpha,\gamma\in\mathbb N_0^r\}.$$
Here $\mathbb N_0$ denotes the nonnegative integers,
$x^\alpha=\prod_jx_j^{\alpha_j}$, and
$\partial^\gamma=\prod_j\partial_{x_j}^{\gamma_j}$.
Use the dense domain $\mathcal D:=\mathcal U^{-1}\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ and
define on it the operators $Q_j$ and $P_j$ by transporting multiplication
by $\sqrt{\hbar}\,x_j$ and differentiation $-i\sqrt{\hbar}\,\partial_{x_j}$
through $\mathcal U$. Thus, for $f\in\mathcal S$,
$(Q_j\mathcal U^{-1}f)=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt{\hbar}\,x_jf)$ and
$(P_j\mathcal U^{-1}f)=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt{\hbar}\,\partial_{x_j}f)$.
Use the commutator convention $[A,B]=AB-BA$ on common invariant domains.
These quadratures satisfy $[Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I$ on $\mathcal D$
and have units $\sqrt{\mathrm{joule}\cdot\mathrm{second}}$. Each product
Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian; all its derivatives and
polynomial multiples remain a polynomial times that Gaussian and are bounded
on $\mathbb R^r$. Thus the complete product Hermite family lies in
$\mathcal S$, so $\mathcal D$ is dense. The finite-mode Fock-to-Schrödinger
supplier establishes completeness and the quadrature actions used here.
Reorder the quadrature column to grouped order
$R_g:=(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)^T$.

A finite positive quadratic canonical operator is specified by a real
symmetric matrix $G\in M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ with
$x^TGx>0$ for every $x\neq0$, and a real constant $c$. The coefficient
$G$ has units of inverse seconds and $c$ has units of joules. On $\mathcal D$
define the symmetrically ordered operator
$$H_{G,c}^{(0)}:=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}G_{ab}(R_{g,a}R_{g,b}+R_{g,b}R_{g,a})+cI.$$
The real multiplication and derivative operators preserve Schwartz space,
so this finite sum maps $\mathcal D$ into $\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)$.
Integration by parts makes each $Q_j,P_j$ symmetric on $\mathcal D$. For
$f,g\in\mathcal D$, symmetry and invariance of $\mathcal D$ give
$\langle R_{g,a}R_{g,b}f,g\rangle
=\langle R_{g,b}f,R_{g,a}g\rangle
=\langle f,R_{g,b}R_{g,a}g\rangle$; the same identity with $a,b$
interchanged proves that each symmetrized summand is symmetric. Since
$G_{ab}=G_{ba}\in\mathbb R$, the finite sum is symmetric. Its quadratic
coefficients are strictly positive in the stated matrix sense. The statement
does not yet assert that this symmetric operator is self-adjoint.

In grouped coordinates set
$$J_g:=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_r\\-I_r&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad D_\omega:=\operatorname{diag}(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r,\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r).$$
A finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ consists of matrices
$U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ and positive angular frequencies $\omega_j>0$ in
inverse seconds such that, with $^*$ denoting conjugate transpose and $^T$
transpose without conjugation,
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
$$S_g:=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\\operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_g^TJ_gS_g=J_g,\qquad S_g^TGS_g=D_\omega.$$
This certificate is explicit finite-dimensional data. No claim is made here
that every positive $G$ has such a certificate; the theorem on this page
uses it as a stated hypothesis. Each term in $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ has units of
joules because $Q_j$ and $P_j$ have units $\sqrt{\mathrm{joule}\cdot\mathrm{second}}$.

A finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ consists of matrices
$U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ and positive angular frequencies $\omega_j>0$ in
