Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and the finite-mode Fock conventions of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Let $U,V\in M_r(\mathbb C)$ obey
$$UU^*-VV^*=I_r,\qquad UV^T=VU^T,$$
where $^*$ is conjugate transpose and $^T$ is transpose without conjugation.
On the finite Hermite core define
$$a'_j=\sum_k(U_{jk}a_k+V_{jk}a_k^*).$$
Then the $a'_j$ satisfy $[a'_j,(a'_k)^*]=\delta_{jk}I$ and
$[a'_j,a'_k]=0$ on that core. The real matrix
$$S_g=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(U+V)&-\operatorname{Im}(U-V)\\ \operatorname{Im}(U+V)&\operatorname{Re}(U-V)\end{pmatrix}$$
is symplectic in grouped coordinate order $(Q_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_1,\ldots,P_r)$.
There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order. The transformed vacuum
$M\Omega$ has finite mean number
$$\sum_j\|a_jM\Omega\|^2=\operatorname{tr}(VV^*).$$
No infinite-mode implementability assertion is made.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator is defined on a compact interval $[0,T]$ with $0<T<\infty$. Its coefficient path $K:[0,T]\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ has Lebesgue-integrable entries and is symmetric, $K(t)=K(t)^T$ for every $t$; an almost-everywhere symmetric integrable path is understood through a symmetric representative. In the displayed interleaved quadrature order put
$$H_t=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}K_{ab}(t)(R_aR_b+R_bR_a)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r),$$
with no linear or scalar term. The path $U:[0,T]\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ consists of unitary Schwartz automorphisms, has $U(0)=I$, and for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ its trajectory $U(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in each Schwartz seminorm $p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta g(x)|$ and satisfies $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)f=H_tU(t)f$ almost everywhere. Absolute continuity in a seminorm means the finite disjoint-interval condition for the seminorms of the increments. The construction below proves existence, uniqueness and continuity of the inverse path in the same pointwise Schwartz topology. Precisely, $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is the set of all endpoint operators $U(T)$ for this integrable-coefficient class, over all such $T$ and $K$. Piecewise-smooth coefficient paths are included and yield the same endpoint set, as proved below; the definition does not restrict the admissible propagators to that subclass.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $r\ge1$, fix a positive real action-scale parameter
$\hbar>0$, and let $H=\mathbb C^r$ with orthonormal basis
$e_1,\ldots,e_r$, and let $\mathcal F_s(H)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^{\otimes_s n}$
be the bosonic Fock space with vacuum $\Omega$ and creation and annihilation
operators $a_j^*,a_j$ from
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For
$N=(n_1,\ldots,n_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, set
$$|N\rangle:=\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(a_j^*)^{n_j}}{\sqrt{n_j!}}\Omega.$$
Let $g_N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r g_{n_j}(x_j)$ be the normalized product Hermite
function from [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-multidimensional-oscillator-completeness]].
Then $(|N\rangle)_N$ and $(g_N)_N$ are complete orthonormal families, and the
map $\mathcal U|N\rangle=g_N$ extends uniquely to a unitary
$$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^r).$$
On the algebraic finite-particle span, $\mathcal U a_j\mathcal U^{-1}$ and
$\mathcal U a_j^*\mathcal U^{-1}$ are respectively
$(x_j+\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ and $(x_j-\partial_{x_j})/\sqrt2$ on product
Hermite functions. In particular the quadratures
$$Q_j=\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j+a_j^*),\qquad P_j=-i\sqrt{\hbar/2}(a_j-a_j^*)$$
act there as multiplication by $\sqrt\hbar x_j$ and as
$-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j}$, respectively. These are core identities;
they do not assert that a finite number cutoff preserves the canonical
commutation relations.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval. If for every compact $B\subset J$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then throughout $J$, $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), with Hilbert adjoint $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$
([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]).

**The absolute value.** The operator $T^*T\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact, since it
is the composite of the compact $T$ with the bounded $T^*$
([[lem-compositions-with-a-compact-operator-are-compact]]); it is self-adjoint,
because $(T^*T)^*=T^*T^{**}=T^*T$ ([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]); and it
is positive, because
$$\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\langle Tx,Tx\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\ge0$$
for every $x\in H$ ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]).
The **absolute value** of $T$ is the unique compact self-adjoint positive
operator
$$|T|:=(T^*T)^{1/2}$$
with $|T|^{2}=T^*T$, whose existence and uniqueness are the preceding square-root
lemma ([[lem-positive-square-root-of-a-compact-positive-operator]]). It satisfies
$$\||T|x\|^{2}=\langle|T|^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle T^*Tx,x\rangle=\|Tx\|^{2}\qquad(x\in H),$$
so in particular $\bigl\||T|\bigr\|=\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]) and
$\ker|T|=\ker T$, since $\||T|x\|=\|Tx\|$ for every $x$.

**The singular values.** By the spectral theorem for $|T|$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-compact-self-adjoint-operators]]) the nonzero
eigenvalues of $|T|$ form a finite or countably infinite set of positive reals,
each with finite multiplicity, and for every real $\varepsilon>0$ only finitely
many of them exceed $\varepsilon$; positivity rules out negative eigenvalues and
$0$ already corresponds to the kernel. The **multiset of positive singular
values of $T$** is the multiset of positive eigenvalues of $|T|$, counted with
multiplicity ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]).

**The ordered singular-value sequence.** The **distinct** positive singular
values are listed with positive labels in *decreasing* order $\mu_1>\mu_2>\cdots$ as follows:
if the multiset of positive eigenvalues is empty (equivalently $|T|=0$,
equivalently $T=0$), the list is empty; otherwise $\mu_1:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$
is an eigenvalue of $|T|\}$, a maximum and not merely a supremum, because a
supremum value not attained would be an accumulation point different from $0$;
having chosen $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_k$, put $\mu_{k+1}:=\max\{\lambda>0:\lambda$ is an
eigenvalue of $|T|$ and $\lambda<\mu_k\}$ whenever that set is nonempty, and stop
otherwise. Each step is legitimate by the finiteness-above-thresholds property
above, and an infinite list satisfies $\mu_k\to0$ (otherwise its decreasing
limit would be a nonzero accumulation point). Writing $d_k$ for the multiplicity
of $\mu_k$ (a positive integer), the **zero-padded singular-value sequence** is
$$s_1\ge s_2\ge s_3\ge\cdots$$
where $s_1=\cdots=s_{d_1}=\mu_1$, $s_{d_1+1}=\cdots=s_{d_1+d_2}=\mu_2$, and so
on; if the multiset is finite with total multiplicity $r=d_1+\cdots+d_m$, one
sets $s_n:=0$ for every $n>r$, and if $T=0$ one sets $s_n:=0$ for every
$n\ge1$. The number $s_n$ is written $s_n(T)$ and called the $n$-th **singular
value** of $T$.

**Zero-based domain and positive labels.** Set $s_0(T):=\|T\|=s_1(T)$.
Thus the numerical sequence is the function $n\mapsto s_n(T)$ on all of
$\mathbb N$, including zero. The positive-labelled tail $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$
is the multiplicity-counting list constructed above. The auxiliary initial
value $s_0$ is not an additional entry of the eigenvalue multiset, does not index
a singular vector, and is excluded from multiplicity counts and singular-value
sums, which use $n\ge1$. The full sequence satisfies
$s_0\ge s_1\ge s_2\ge\cdots$ and tends to zero. This preserves the page's
positive rank labels while giving convergence statements a zero-based domain.

**Rank and the finiteness of the list.** The map $\Phi:\operatorname{ran}|T|\to\operatorname{ran}T$
given by $\Phi(|T|x):=Tx$ is well defined and linear, because $|T|x=|T|x'$ forces
$x-x'\in\ker|T|=\ker T$ and hence $Tx=Tx'$; it is injective, because $Tx=0$ gives
$x\in\ker T=\ker|T|$ and $|T|x=0$; it is surjective onto $\operatorname{ran}T$
because $T=\Phi\circ|T|$; and it is isometric, $\|Tx\|=\||T|x\|$. Hence
$\operatorname{ran}T$ is finite-dimensional if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}|T|$ is finite-dimensional; in that case the linear
bijection $\Phi$ gives
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T=\dim\operatorname{ran}|T|$
([[def-dimension]]). Consequently, whenever $T$ has finite rank, the positive
singular values with multiplicity number exactly
$\dim\operatorname{ran}T$, the rank of $T$, and all later $s_n$ vanish, so the
sequence is **zero-padded**. If $T$ does not have finite rank, the multiset of
positive singular values is infinite and countable
([[def-countable]]) and $s_n>0$ for every $n$, with $s_n\downarrow0$; in
particular finite rank of $T$ is characterised by the eventual vanishing $s_n=0$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, and conversely such eventual vanishing forces finite rank. The sequence $(s_n)$ is numerical data only: no orthonormal system is
selected here, and the zero padding is *not* an indexing of any family of
vectors. The unordered multiset determines $(s_n)$ uniquely, so $(s_n)$ is well
defined, and $s_1(T)=\||T|\|=\|T\|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint positive operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ is a
nonnegative real for every $x$. Then there is a compact self-adjoint positive
operator $S\in\mathcal B(H)$ with $S^{2}=T$, and it is unique: if
$R\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact and positive
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]) with $R^{2}=T$,
then $R=S$. The root acts by multiplication by $\sqrt\lambda$ on each positive
eigenspace $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, $\lambda>0$, and by zero on
$\ker T$; in particular $S$ is the operator denoted $\sqrt T$ or $T^{1/2}$.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the certificate's matrices give a unitary $M$ satisfying $M^*R_gM=S_gR_g$ on the common transported Schwartz core. By [F3], we may take this implementer to preserve Schwartz space: its normalized metaplectic implementer has that property, and multiplying by a scalar phase leaves $M^*R_gM$ unchanged.

Conjugating each symmetrically ordered term of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ by $M$ replaces $R_g$ by $S_gR_g$ . Collecting the finite sums gives $$M^*H_{G,c}^{(0)}M=\frac14\sum_{a,b}(S_g^TGS_g)_{ab}(R_{g,a}R_{g,b}+R_{g,b}R_{g,a})+cI.$$ By [A2] this is the diagonal quadratic with coefficient $D_\omega$ on the same core.

On the finite Hermite core put $a_j=(Q_j+iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ and $a_j^*=(Q_j-iP_j)/\sqrt{2\hbar}$ . The relation $[Q_j,P_j]=i\hbar I$ gives $Q_j^2+P_j^2=2\hbar(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)$ by direct multiplication. Consequently the diagonal quadratic is $\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(a_j^*a_j+\tfrac12 I)+cI$ . Write $g_{\mathbf n}\in L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ for the product Hermite basis and set $\phi_{\mathbf n}:=\mathcal U^{-1}g_{\mathbf n}\in\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)$ . Then $\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}=g_{\mathbf n}$ , and the diagonal quadratic has eigenvalue $E_{\mathbf n}=c+\sum_j\hbar\omega_j(n_j+\tfrac12)$ . Denote this diagonal differential expression on $\mathcal S$ by $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ , and its Fock-space transport on $\mathcal D$ by $T_\omega^{(0)}:=\mathcal U^{-1}\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}\mathcal U$ .

Put $\epsilon_j=\hbar\omega_j$ and let $A$ be the maximal diagonal multiplier in the basis $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ with eigenvalues $\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ . By [F5], $A$ is self-adjoint on the domain where $\sum_{\mathbf n}|\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j|^2|f_{\mathbf n}|^2<\infty$ . The diagonal operator with eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}$ is $A+c_0I$ , where $c_0=c+\tfrac12\sum_j\epsilon_j$ . Its domain is the same: for real $x,c_0$ , $|x+c_0|^2\leq2|x|^2+2|c_0|^2$ and $|x|^2\leq2|x+c_0|^2+2|c_0|^2$ , and each coefficient sequence $(f_{\mathbf n})$ is in $\ell^2$ . For $g\in D((A+c_0I)^*)$ , [F7] says that boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle(A+c_0I)f,g\rangle$ and boundedness of $f\mapsto c_0\langle f,g\rangle$ imply boundedness of $f\mapsto\langle Af,g\rangle$ . Thus $g\in D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $(A+c_0I)^*g=Ag+c_0g$ . Conversely, every $g\in D(A)$ satisfies this adjoint identity, so $T=A+c_0I$ is self-adjoint. Finite Hermite truncations converge in its graph norm, because the tail of $\sum_{\mathbf n}(1+|E_{\mathbf n}|^2)|f_{\mathbf n}|^2$ tends to zero. Thus finite Hermite sums are a core for $T$ in the graph norm of [F8].

For $\psi\in\mathcal D$ , put $f=\mathcal U\psi\in\mathcal S$ . The coordinate expression $\widetilde T_\omega^{(0)}$ sends $f$ to an $L^2$ function. Integration by parts against each Schwartz Hermite function gives $\langle T_\omega^{(0)}\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle =E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle$ ; equivalently, this is the $L^2$ pairing of the differential expression on $f$ with $g_{\mathbf n}=\mathcal U\phi_{\mathbf n}$ . Boundary terms vanish because both functions are Schwartz. For every finite set $F$ of occupation indices, orthogonal projection therefore gives $\sum_{\mathbf n\in F}|E_{\mathbf n}\langle\psi,\phi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2 \leq\|T_\omega^{(0)}\psi\|^2$ . These coefficients are square-summable, and completeness of $(\phi_{\mathbf n})$ from [F4] identifies their vector with $T_\omega^{(0)}\psi$ . Hence $\mathcal D\subseteq D(T)$ and the diagonal expression is $T$ on $\mathcal D$ . The finite Hermite sums from step 4.1 lie in $\mathcal D$ because [F1] places each $g_{\mathbf n}$ in $\mathcal S$ , and are graph-norm dense in $D(T)$ ; so the graph closure of this restriction is $T$.

By step 1.1, $M$ and $M^*$ preserve Schwartz space, and by step 2.1 $H_{G,c}^{(0)}=M T_\omega^{(0)}M^*$ there. Step 5.1 gives graph closure $T$ for the diagonal restriction. Conjugation by the unitary $M$ carries the graph and its closure in $\mathcal F_s\oplus\mathcal F_s$ to the graph and closure of $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ , so $H=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}=MTM^*$ . This is self-adjoint because $T$ is self-adjoint and $M$ is unitary.

Set $q_j=e^{-\beta\epsilon_j}=e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}$ . Since $\beta>0$ and every $\omega_j>0$ , $0<q_j<1$ ; the mode set is finite, so $q_*<1$ and $\sum_jq_j<\infty$ . Apply [F5] to the diagonal number-energy operator $A$ to get $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ . On the occupation basis, $T$ has eigenvalues $E_{\mathbf n}=c_0+\sum_j\epsilon_jn_j$ , so the spectral exponential has positive eigenvalues $e^{-\beta E_{\mathbf n}}=e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_jq_j^{n_j}$ by [F9]. Thus $e^{-\beta T}=e^{-\beta c_0}e^{-\beta A}$ on the occupation basis; [F10] and the trace-class conclusion for $e^{-\beta A}$ from [F5] show that $e^{-\beta T}$ is positive trace class. Its eigenvalue sum is $e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty$ by [F5], so [F6] identifies that sum with its trace. By steps 6.1 and 5.1, the vectors $M\phi_{\mathbf n}$ form a complete orthonormal eigenbasis for $H$ with the same eigenvalues; equivalently $e^{-\beta H}=M e^{-\beta T}M^*$ . The unitary invariance in [F10] makes $e^{-\beta H}$ trace class with the same eigenvalue sum, and [F6] gives the same trace. Finally, $$e^{-\beta c_0}\prod_j(1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j})^{-1}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\frac{e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j/2}}{1-e^{-\beta\hbar\omega_j}}=e^{-\beta c}\prod_j\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}.$$ Every factor is strictly positive and finite, proving $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ . The only infinite-dimensional Hilbert space used here is the bosonic Fock space for the stated finite number $r$ of modes.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $r\geq1$,
$\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $\beta>0$ in inverse joules, $c\in\mathbb R$ in
joules, and let $G=G^T$ be a strictly positive real $2r\times2r$ matrix
whose entries have units of inverse seconds. Assume $(U,V,\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_r)$
is a finite diagonalization certificate for $G$ as defined earlier, with
each $\omega_j>0$ in inverse seconds. Let $H_{G,c}^{(0)}$ be the symmetric
quadratic operator on the stated Schwartz domain. Then its graph closure
$H:=\overline{H_{G,c}^{(0)}}$ exists and is self-adjoint, and its finite-mode
Gibbs partition sum is
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H})=e^{-\beta c}\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left[2\sinh\!\left(\frac{\beta\hbar\omega_j}{2}\right)\right]^{-1}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \sinh x:=\frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{2}.$$
The matrix $G$ acts on the finite grouped quadratures; the bosonic Fock
space remains infinite-dimensional at each $r\geq1$. This conditional
finite-mode conclusion neither proves that every positive $G$ has a
diagonalization certificate nor asserts infinite-mode implementability,
interacting depletion bounds, or superfluidity.

Assume [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $I$ be finite or countably infinite with a specified enumeration, let $m\in\Omega_\pm$ be the occupation configurations of [[lem-qsm-fock-occupation-basis-and-car-relations]], and let $\epsilon_j\in\mathbb R$ be finite mode energies. For each finite-support configuration put
$$
E(m):=\sum_j\epsilon_jm_j,\qquad N(m):=|m|=\sum_jm_j.
$$
These are finite sums. On $\ell^2(\Omega_\pm)$, define the real diagonal multipliers
$$
D(H)=\left\{c:\sum_mE(m)^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Hc)_m=E(m)c_m,
$$
$$
D(N)=\left\{c:\sum_m|m|^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (Nc)_m=|m|c_m,
$$
and, for $\mu\in\mathbb R$,
$$
D(K_\mu)=\left\{c:\sum_m|E(m)-\mu|m||^2|c_m|^2<\infty\right\},\quad (K_\mu c)_m=(E(m)-\mu|m|)c_m.
$$
Each is self-adjoint on its displayed domain. No equality between $D(K_\mu)$ and $D(H)\cap D(N)$ is asserted.

For $\beta>0$, set $q_j=e^{-\beta(\epsilon_j-\mu)}$. In the bosonic case assume
$$
0<q_j<1,\qquad q_*:=\sup_jq_j<1,\qquad \sum_jq_j<\infty;
$$
Here $q_*=0$ by convention when $I$ is empty; for nonempty $I$ the displayed supremum is unchanged. In the fermionic case assume $q_j>0$, $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and only finitely many gaps $\epsilon_j-\mu$ are negative. Define the positive diagonal multiplier $G_{\beta,\mu}$ by $G_{\beta,\mu}|m\rangle=e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}|m\rangle$. Then $G_{\beta,\mu}$ is trace class, with
$$
\Xi_B=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1-q_j)^{-1}<\infty,\qquad \Xi_F=\operatorname{Tr}G_{\beta,\mu}=\prod_j(1+q_j)<\infty.
$$
Thus $\rho_{\beta,\mu}=\Xi^{-1}G_{\beta,\mu}$ is a positive trace-class operator of trace one. Its finite-mode marginals are independent: bosonic occupation $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$ has law $(1-q_j)q_j^{n_j}$, and fermionic occupation $n_j\in\{0,1\}$ has probabilities $(1+q_j)^{-1}$ and $q_j(1+q_j)^{-1}$. In particular
$$
\mathbb E_BN_j=\frac{q_j}{1-q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_B(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1-q_j)^2},\qquad \mathbb E_FN_j=\frac{q_j}{1+q_j},\quad \operatorname{Var}_F(N_j)=\frac{q_j}{(1+q_j)^2}.
$$
The total number has finite mean and variance under the stated mode conditions. The trace hypotheses alone do not imply finite energy moments or differentiability in $\beta,\mu$.

For an additional compact-parameter envelope, the corresponding response identities hold. For fixed $\mu$, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be a nonempty open interval. If for every compact $B\subset J$ a summable $(a_m)$ satisfies $(1+|E(m)-\mu|m||^2)e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}\le a_m$ for all $m$ and $\beta\in B$, then throughout $J$, $-\partial_\beta\log\Xi=\mathbb E(K_\mu)$ and $\partial_\beta^2\log\Xi=\operatorname{Var}(K_\mu)$. If $(\beta,\mu)$ varies over an open set and a summable compact-parameter envelope dominates $e^{-\beta(E(m)-\mu|m|)}(1+|E(m)|^2+|m|^2)$, then at fixed $\beta$, $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(N)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(N)$ and $\partial_\mu\mathbb E(E)=\beta\operatorname{Cov}(E,N)$. These stronger moment envelopes are additional hypotheses, not consequences of trace-class normalization.

For a finite mode set $J$, the canonical fixed-number coefficients are defined by
$$
\prod_{j\in J}(1-ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})^{-1}=\sum_{N\ge0}Z_{B,N}(J)z^N,\qquad \prod_{j\in J}(1+ze^{-\beta\epsilon_j})=\sum_{N=0}^{|J|}Z_{F,N}(J)z^N.
$$
Each coefficient is the sum of the Boltzmann weights over the corresponding number sector; for a countable mode set it is the increasing limit over finite mode sets and is finite under the stated grand-trace hypotheses. A fixed-number law is the grand law conditioned on total number, so its occupations are generally coupled. The oscillator specialization uses the actual one-particle Hermite basis and diagonal domain of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]], not a formal differential eigenfunction list.

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to the reduced finite mode set $\{2,\ldots,r\}$ with $\epsilon_k=\hbar\omega_k$ . Its factors satisfy $q_k=e^{-\beta\epsilon_k}\in(0,1)$ , and the set is finite, so the hypotheses $q_*<1$ and $\sum_{k=2}^rq_k<\infty$ hold. Its occupation partition sum is $\prod_{k=2}^{r}(1-q_k)^{-1}$ ; adding each oscillator's zero-point energy $\hbar\omega_k/2$ multiplies this by $e^{-\beta\sum_{k=2}^r\hbar\omega_k/2}$ , giving $\prod_{k=2}^{r}[2\sinh(\beta\hbar\omega_k/2)]^{-1}$ . If $r=1$ , the reduced set is empty and its sum and product are both $1$ .

For each $k\geq2$ , put $x_k=\beta\hbar\omega_k>0$ . Its one-mode occupation sum is $$\sum_{n_k=0}^{\infty}e^{-x_k(n_k+1/2)}=\frac{e^{-x_k/2}}{1-e^{-x_k}}=\left[2\sinh(x_k/2)\right]^{-1},$$ which is positive and finite. If the first occupation is restricted to $0\leq n_1\leq N$ and the remaining modes are summed, the resulting partial sum is $$(N+1)\prod_{k=2}^{r}\left[2\sinh(x_k/2)\right]^{-1}.$$ This tends to $+\infty$ as $N\to\infty$ ; when $r=1$ the product is empty and the same partial sum is $N+1$ . Hence $Z_\beta=+\infty$ .

Removing mode $1$ changes the occupation Hilbert space and leaves only the finite product over $k\geq2$ . The full system has an additional countably infinite zero-energy occupation degeneracy, so its positive Gibbs weights cannot be normalized. The finite positive-frequency theorem does not apply at $\omega_1=0$ , and the omitted-mode product is the partition sum of a different model.

citations.quote: Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

derivations.claim: Regard $B=iA$ as a complex matrix on $\mathbb C^{2N}$. Since $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$ and $A$ is real, $B^*=(-i)A^{\mathsf T}=iA=B$. By [F1], $B$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. Complex conjugation sends an eigenvector of eigenvalue $\epsilon>0$ to an eigenvector of eigenvalue $-\epsilon$, because conjugating $iAz=\epsilon z$ gives $-iA\overline z=\epsilon\overline z$. Thus nonzero eigenvalues occur in opposite pairs.

Fix a unit eigenvector $z=u+iv$ for $\epsilon>0$, with real vectors $u,v$. The vectors $z$ and $\overline z$ belong to distinct eigenspaces of the Hermitian matrix $B$, so $\langle z,\overline z\rangle=0$. Expanding this equality gives $\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2$ and $u\cdot v=0$; $\|z\|=1$ then gives $\|u\|=\|v\|=1/\sqrt2$. From $Az=-i\epsilon z$, comparison of real and imaginary parts gives $Au=\epsilon v$ and $Av=-\epsilon u$. Therefore $e_1=\sqrt2u$ and $e_2=-\sqrt2v$ are orthonormal and $Ae_1=-\epsilon e_2$, $Ae_2=\epsilon e_1$, which is the displayed block in this basis.

Choose an orthonormal basis in each positive eigenspace of $B$; [F1] supplies these finite-dimensional bases. Together with their complex conjugates, the chosen vectors are orthonormal: conjugation preserves orthonormality, and every positive eigenspace is orthogonal to every negative eigenspace of the Hermitian matrix $B$. Hence the real planes from step 2.1 are mutually orthogonal. On the zero eigenspace, $Az=0$, so the real and imaginary parts of each vector lie in the real kernel of $A$. The real and complex kernels have equal dimension because row reduction of the real matrix $A$ has the same pivots over $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$; this dimension is $2N$ minus twice the total number of positive eigenvectors, hence even. Choose a real basis of $\ker A$ and successively subtract projections onto earlier vectors and normalize each nonzero residual; this gives an orthonormal real basis. Pairing consecutive vectors gives zero blocks. The resulting real orthonormal basis gives the required $O$.

Since $O$ is orthogonal, $(OAO^{\mathsf T})^{\mathsf T}(OAO^{\mathsf T})=OA^{\mathsf T}AO^{\mathsf T}=\bigoplus_{r=1}^N\epsilon_r^2I_2$. Thus the singular-value multiset from the Statement has two entries $\epsilon_r$ for each block $r$, including its two zero entries when $\epsilon_r=0$. This identifies every positive block value once per real two-plane and completes the multiplicity assertion.

derivations.claim: For every site, $\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}=X_jY_j=iZ_j$, so $ih\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}=-hZ_j$. For $j<N$, $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=Y_jZ_jX_{j+1}=iX_jX_{j+1}$, so $iJ\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=-JX_jX_{j+1}$. Summing exactly these terms gives the open-chain $H_N$ of [F1], with no $j=N$ bond.

For any paired indices $a<b$ with coefficient $c$, setting $(A_N)_{ab}=2c$ and $(A_N)_{ba}=-2c$ contributes $(i/4)(2c\gamma_a\gamma_b-2c\gamma_b\gamma_a)=ic\gamma_a\gamma_b$ by [F2]. Applying this to $c=h$ on $(2j-1,2j)$ and $c=J$ on $(2j,2j+1)$ yields $H_N=(i/4)\gamma^{\mathsf T}A_N\gamma$.

By [F3], choose a real orthogonal $O$ with $OA_NO^{\mathsf T}$ in the displayed $2\times2$ blocks, and put $\eta=O\gamma$. Since $O$ is real and orthogonal, [F2] gives $\{\eta_a,\eta_b\}=2\delta_{ab}I$. Define $b_r=(\eta_{2r-1}+i\eta_{2r})/2$. Direct expansion using these anticommutators gives $\{b_r,b_s^*\}=\delta_{rs}I$, $\{b_r,b_s\}=0$, and $b_r^*b_r=\tfrac12I+\tfrac{i}{2}\eta_{2r-1}\eta_{2r}$. Using the matrix expression from step 2.1, substitution into the block expression gives $H_N=\sum_r\epsilon_r(b_r^*b_r-\tfrac12I)$.

The projections $n_r=b_r^*b_r$ commute by the CAR in step 3.1 and are simultaneously diagonalizable: diagonalize $n_1$ using [F5], restrict the remaining commuting Hermitian matrices to its invariant eigenspaces, and continue through the finite list. Their joint eigenvalues lie in $\{0,1\}^N$. If a joint eigenspace has occupancy $0$ in coordinate $r$, $b_r^*$ maps it isometrically into the eigenspace with that bit changed to $1$, since $\|b_r^*\psi\|^2=\langle\psi,(I-n_r)\psi\rangle=\|\psi\|^2$; when the bit is $1$, $b_r$ is the inverse isometry. Hence all $2^N$ joint eigenspaces have the same positive dimension. Their orthogonal sum is $\mathcal H_N$, whose dimension is $2^N$, so each eigenspace is one-dimensional. The resulting ordered occupation basis identifies the $b_r$ representation unitarily with the finite fermionic Fock occupation basis.

In that occupation basis, $\sum_r\epsilon_r b_r^*b_r$ is the diagonal finite-mode Hamiltonian with energies $\epsilon_r$. Apply [F4] with mode set $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, chemical potential $0$, and $q_r=e^{-\beta\epsilon_r}$ to obtain trace $\prod_r(1+e^{-\beta\epsilon_r})$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and let $\mathcal H_N=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes N}$ with the product inner product linear in its first argument. At each factor use
$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$
For $1\le j\le N$, $X_j,Y_j,Z_j$ denote these matrices on factor $j$ and $I_2$ on every other factor. For real $h,J$ measured in joules define the finite open-chain matrix
$$H_N(h,J)=-h\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}X_jX_{j+1}.$$
The upper limit $N-1$ is the open-boundary convention: no term couples site $N$ to site $1$. Put $S_0=I_{\mathcal H_N}$ and $S_{j-1}=Z_1\cdots Z_{j-1}$ for $j>1$. The ordered Majorana operators are
$$\gamma_{2j-1}=S_{j-1}X_j,\qquad \gamma_{2j}=S_{j-1}Y_j\qquad(1\le j\le N).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, use the open-chain Hilbert space and Hamiltonian $H_N(h,J)$ of the ordered Majorana definition, and let $\beta>0$ have units $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$ while $h,J$ have units joules. Define the real skew matrix $A_N\in M_{2N}(\mathbb R)$ by $ (A_N)_{2j-1,2j}=2h$ for $1\le j\le N$, $(A_N)_{2j,2j+1}=2J$ for $1\le j<N$, the opposite entries by skew-symmetry, and all other entries by zero. Let $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_N\ge0$ be its real orthogonal block energies, including zero values. Then
$$H_N(h,J)=\frac{i}{4}\gamma^{\mathsf T}A_N\gamma=\sum_{r=1}^N\epsilon_r\left(b_r^*b_r-\frac12I\right)$$
for the transformed Majorana modes $b_r$ in the Proof, and its finite Gibbs trace is
$$Z_N(\beta;h,J):=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal H_N}(e^{-\beta H_N(h,J)})=\prod_{r=1}^N2\cosh\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon_r}{2}\right).$$
Every zero mode contributes a factor two. The chain is open throughout; no periodic Jordan–Wigner parity boundary term is included.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ and let $m_{\mathbb T}$ be its normalized Borel probability measure, so in the angle coordinate its integral is $\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_0^{2\pi}F(k)\,dk/(2\pi)$, obtained from the normalized one-dimensional torus by $k=2\pi x$. On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}=u_1\overline{v_1}+u_2\overline{v_2}$ and $\|u\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$, linear in the first argument. Define
$$\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\left\{x=(x_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}:x_j\in\mathbb C^2,\ \sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\|x_j\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2<\infty\right\},\quad \langle x,y\rangle_{\ell^2}:=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\langle x_j,y_j\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}.$$
Define $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$ to be the vector space of pairs of Borel-measurable functions $f=(f_1,f_2):\mathbb T\to\mathbb C^2$ with $\int_{\mathbb T}(|f_1|^2+|f_2|^2)\,dm_{\mathbb T}<\infty$, modulo equality $m_{\mathbb T}$-almost everywhere, with inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}:=\int_{\mathbb T}\bigl(f_1\overline{g_1}+f_2\overline{g_2}\bigr)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$
These pairings are linear in the first argument. The square-summable-family supplier gives the scalar $\ell^2$ norm and pairing used coordinatewise. The $L^2$ space is the pair of scalar $L^2$ quotient spaces with the displayed sum inner product and completeness convention. Let $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\{x\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):\{j:x_j\ne0\}\text{ is finite}\}$. Define the linear map
$$\mathcal F_0x(k)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}x_j e^{ijk},\qquad k\in\mathbb T,$$
componentwise, from $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$. Its values are continuous finite sums and therefore belong to this $L^2$ space. Then $\mathcal F_0$ preserves inner products on finitely supported sequences and has a unique extension to a surjective linear isometry (a unitary map) $\mathcal F:\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)\to L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$.

On $\mathbb C^2$ use $\langle u,v\rangle_{\mathbb C^2}=u_1\overline{v_1}+u_2\overline{v_2}$ and $\|u\|_{\mathbb C^2}^2=|u_1|^2+|u_2|^2$, linear in the first argument. Define

Define $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$ to be the vector space of pairs of Borel-measurable functions $f=(f_1,f_2):\mathbb T\to\mathbb C^2$ with $\int_{\mathbb T}(|f_1|^2+|f_2|^2)\,dm_{\mathbb T}<\infty$, modulo equality $m_{\mathbb T}$-almost everywhere, with inner product
$$\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}:=\int_{\mathbb T}\bigl(f_1\overline{g_1}+f_2\overline{g_2}\bigr)\,dm_{\mathbb T}.$$
These pairings are linear in the first argument. The square-summable-family supplier gives the scalar $\ell^2$ norm and pairing used coordinatewise. The $L^2$ space is the pair of scalar $L^2$ quotient spaces with the displayed sum inner product and completeness convention. Let $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):=\{x\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2):\{j:x_j\ne0\}\text{ is finite}\}$. Define the linear map
$$\mathcal F_0x(k)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}x_j e^{ijk},\qquad k\in\mathbb T,$$
componentwise, from $c_{00}(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)$ to $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$. Its values are continuous finite sums and therefore belong to this $L^2$ space. Then $\mathcal F_0$ preserves inner products on finitely supported sequences and has a unique extension to a surjective linear isometry (a unitary map) $\mathcal F:\ell^2(\mathbb Z;\mathbb C^2)\to L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C^2)$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set**
of $T$ is
$$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$
where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on
$H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is
$\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator
$$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used
throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of
[[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$.

**The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently
$T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for
$x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$.

**Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph
theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with
$R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$.
The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since
$\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$.
Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$
where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with
continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$
and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets
to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed.
No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here.

For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Throughout, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$ is written
$\lambda_n$ ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]), and
$\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R$ is the copy of the integers
([[def-integers]]).

**The torus.** Let $q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T:=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ be the
canonical projection of the quotient of the additive group $\mathbb R$ by its
subgroup $\mathbb Z$, carrying the quotient topology
([[def-quotient-topology]], [[def-topological-space]]); we write
$[t]:=q(t)=t+\mathbb Z$. Thus $[s]=[t]$ exactly when $s-t\in\mathbb Z$. The map
$q$ is continuous ([[def-continuous-map-top]]), and $\mathbb T$ is a compact
Hausdorff space homeomorphic to the Euclidean unit circle.

**Fundamental domain.** Every class has exactly one representative in $[0,1)$:
for $t\in\mathbb R$ the integer part $n=\lfloor t\rfloor$ satisfies
$n\le t<n+1$, so $t-n\in[0,1)$ represents $[t]$ ([[lem-integer-part]]); and if
$s,t\in[0,1)$ satisfy $s-t\in\mathbb Z$, then $|s-t|<1$ forces $s=t$.
Consequently the map $[0,1)\to\mathbb T$, $t\mapsto[t]$, is a bijection.

**Topological checks.** The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and maps onto $\mathbb T$, so the quotient is compact by [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. The map $t\mapsto(\cos 2\pi t,\sin 2\pi t)$ is continuous by [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], and is constant on quotient fibres by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]. It induces a continuous map $\varphi:\mathbb T\to S^1$ by [[thm-quotient-universal-property]]. The bijection of $[0,2\pi)$ with the circle in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], together with the unique representatives in $[0,1)$, makes $\varphi$ bijective. The Euclidean circle is Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]], so the compact-to-Hausdorff clause of [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]] makes $\varphi$ a homeomorphism. In particular $\mathbb T$ is Hausdorff.

The map $q$ is open: for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R$, its saturation $q^{-1}[q[U]]=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb Z}(U+k)$ is open. The images under $q$ of rational-endpoint open intervals form a countable base: if $q(t)\in V$ with $V$ open, choose such an interval containing $t$ and contained in $q^{-1}[V]$. Its image is an open neighbourhood contained in $V$.

**The measure.** For a Borel set $E\in\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) the preimage $q^{-1}[E]$ is a Borel subset of
$\mathbb R$, because $q$ is continuous
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]), hence Lebesgue
measurable ([[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). Define

$$m_{\mathbb T}(E):=\lambda_1\bigl(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)\bigr) ,$$

the value at $q^{-1}[E]$ of the same-ambient restriction of $\lambda_1$ to $[0,1)$
([[def-restriction-of-a-measure]]).

This is a measure on $\mathcal B(\mathbb T)$ by [[prop-restriction-is-a-measure]]:
the assignment $E\mapsto\lambda_1(q^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1))$ is the composition of the
restriction measure with the inverse image along $q$, and inverse images preserve
the empty set, complements and countable unions, while countable additivity is
that of $\lambda_1$. It is a **probability measure**:
$m_{\mathbb T}(\mathbb T)=\lambda_1([0,1))=1$
([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]). Thus
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T})$ is a probability measure space
([[def-measure-space]], [[def-measure]]).

**The integral.** For a Borel measurable $F:\mathbb T\to[0,+\infty]$, define

$$\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}:=\int_{[0,1)}F\circ q\,d\lambda_1 .$$

The defining integral is meaningful because $F\circ q$ is Borel
([[thm-composition-with-borel-functions-preserves-measurability]],
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). The assignment agrees with
$E\mapsto m_{\mathbb T}(E)$ on indicators, and it is additive and homogeneous on
finite nonnegative simple functions; for a sequence $0\le F_0\le F_1\le\cdots$
with $F_n\uparrow F$ pointwise the identity passes to the limit because
$F_n\circ q\uparrow F\circ q$ and monotone convergence holds for $\lambda_1$
([[thm-increasing-simple-approximation-of-a-nonnegative-measurable-function]],
[[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]). For real or complex integrable
$F$ the integral is defined by decomposition into nonnegative parts or into real
and imaginary parts, and it is linear
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]],
[[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]). In particular
$\int_{\mathbb T}1\,dm_{\mathbb T}=1$, and the same formula holds with $[0,1)$
replaced by any half-open interval $[a,a+1)$ or $(a,a+1]$, by the periodicity of
$q^{-1}[E]$ and the translation invariance of $\lambda_1$
([[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]).

**Translation invariance.** For $y\in\mathbb R$ the map
$\tau_y:\mathbb T\to\mathbb T$, $\tau_y([t]):=[t+y]$, is well defined (if
$s-t\in\mathbb Z$ then $(s+y)-(t+y)\in\mathbb Z$) and continuous, because it is
induced by the continuous map $t\mapsto q(t+y)$ from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb T$. This composite is constant on the fibres of $q$, since $q(t)=q(s)$ implies $q(t+y)=q(s+y)$ ([[thm-quotient-universal-property]]). It preserves
$m_{\mathbb T}$: write $y=n+r$ with $n=\lfloor y\rfloor$ and $r\in[0,1)$, put
$A:=q^{-1}[E]$ and use that $A-n=A$ and that
$A\cap[0,1)=\bigl(A\cap[0,r)\bigr)\cup\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)$ while
$A\cap[r,r+1)=\bigl(A\cap[r,1)\bigr)\cup\bigl((A\cap[0,r))+1\bigr)$, so that

$$m_{\mathbb T}(\tau_y^{-1}E)=\lambda_1\bigl((A-y)\cap[0,1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[r,r+1)\bigr)=\lambda_1\bigl(A\cap[0,1)\bigr)=m_{\mathbb T}(E),$$

the middle equality by translation invariance of $\lambda_1$. Hence
$(\mathbb T,\mathcal B(\mathbb T),m_{\mathbb T},\tau_y)$ is a measure-preserving
system for every $y$, and the published integral-invariance theorem gives
$\int_{\mathbb T}F\circ\tau_y\,dm_{\mathbb T}=\int_{\mathbb T}F\,dm_{\mathbb T}$
for every measurable $F\ge0$ and every integrable $F$
([[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]],
[[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]). This is the
**normalized Haar integral** of $\mathbb T$; abstract Haar theory is not
invoked.

**The finite torus.** For a natural $n\ge1$ put
$\mathbb T^n:=\mathbb R^n/\mathbb Z^n$ with the quotient topology of the
canonical projection $q_n$, and define

$$m_{\mathbb T^n}(E):=\lambda_n\bigl(q_n^{-1}[E]\cap[0,1)^n\bigr),\qquad \int_{\mathbb T^n}F\,dm_{\mathbb T^n}:=\int_{[0,1)^n}F\circ q_n\,d\lambda_n .$$

Coordinatewise integer parts give unique representatives in $[0,1)^n$, and the continuous quotient map sends the compact cube $[0,1]^n$ onto $\mathbb T^n$. Compactness of the cube follows from [[thm-heine-borel-r]] and [[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]], and compactness of its image follows from [[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]. Preimages of Borel sets are Borel; disjoint preimages and countable additivity make the displayed set function a measure, and the box formula gives total mass one. The integral identity follows from indicators, increasing simple approximation and decomposition exactly as in one dimension. For translation invariance, discard the integer parts of the translation vector, split each coordinate of $[0,1)^n$ at its fractional part, and translate the resulting $2^n$ disjoint half-open boxes by integer vectors to partition the translated cube. The periodic preimage set is unchanged by these integer vectors; finite additivity and Lebesgue translation invariance give the same measure. Applying the indicator identity, simple approximation and decomposition gives the integral formula on any translated cube. The coordinate projections induce a continuous bijection
$\Phi:\mathbb T^n\to(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^n$ by the universal property. Its
domain is compact by the preceding check, while its codomain is a finite
product of Hausdorff spaces and hence Hausdorff ([[lem-products-preserve-t0-t1-and-hausdorff]]); the continuous-bijection
theorem therefore makes $\Phi$ a homeomorphism. Thus $\mathbb T^n$ carries the
finite product topology ([[def-product-topology]],
[[thm-finite-products-of-compact-spaces]],
[[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), and its characters
$x\mapsto\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, are defined on this compact
Hausdorff space: replacing representatives by integer vectors leaves the exponential unchanged by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]] and the trigonometric period. Finite products of the countable base above form a countable rectangular base. Hence every product-open set is a countable union of Borel rectangles. Conversely coordinate projections are continuous, so Borel rectangles are Borel in the product. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb T^n$. On a product $A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1}$ of Borel subsets
of the factors, the defining fundamental-domain formula and repeated application of [[thm-lebesgue-product-measure-agrees-with-euclidean-lebesgue-on-borel-sets]] give
$m_{\mathbb T^n}(A_0\times\cdots\times A_{n-1})=\prod_jm_{\mathbb T}(A_j)$, so
$m_{\mathbb T^n}$ agrees on every measurable rectangle with the product measure
$m_{\mathbb T}\times\cdots\times m_{\mathbb T}$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]); both are probability measures,
and uniqueness of the product measure on sigma-finite spaces identifies them
on the entire Borel sigma-algebra
([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
Fubini's theorem then computes iterated integrals of $L^1$ functions on
$\mathbb T^n$
([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]).

derivations.claim: Let $S_+f$ have coordinates $(S_+f)_j=f_{j+1}$ and let $S_-f$ have $(S_-f)_j=f_{j-1}$. Reindexing gives $\|S_\pm f\|=\|f\|$ and $\langle S_-f,g\rangle=\langle f,S_+g\rangle$, so $S_-^*=S_+$ and $S_+^*=S_-$ by [F6]. The Fourier-unitarity fact [F2] makes $\mathcal K$ a Hilbert space, so the bounded shifts and their bounded linear combinations have Hilbert adjoints under [F6]. With $B=2hI-2JS_-$, $B^*=2hI-2JS_+$; the block formula $A_\infty=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&B\\-B^*&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ then gives $A_\infty^*=-A_\infty$. By [F3] and the triangle inequality, both $B$ and $B^*$ have bound $2(|h|+|J|)$, whence $\|A_\infty x\|^2=\|Bv\|^2+\|B^*u\|^2\le4(|h|+|J|)^2\|x\|^2$. Thus $A_\infty$ and $K_\infty=iA_\infty$ are everywhere-defined bounded operators by [F4]. Finally $\langle iA_\infty x,y\rangle=i\langle x,A_\infty^*y\rangle=\langle x,-iA_\infty^*y\rangle$, so $K_\infty^*=-iA_\infty^*=iA_\infty=K_\infty$ by [F6].

For a finitely supported sequence, $\mathcal F(v_{j-1})(k)=e^{ik}\widehat v(k)$ and $\mathcal F(u_{j+1})(k)=e^{-ik}\widehat u(k)$ by reindexing the sums. Therefore $\mathcal F A_\infty\mathcal F^{-1}$ is multiplication by $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2(h-Je^{ik})\\-2(h-Je^{-ik})&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$; boundedness and density extend the identity to all of $\ell^2$. Multiplication by $i$ gives the displayed $M(k)$.

Put $a(k)=2i(h-Je^{ik})$. Then $M(k)=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&a(k)\\\overline{a(k)}&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ and $M(k)^2=|a(k)|^2I$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2-|a(k)|^2$, so its two eigenvalues are $\pm|a(k)|=\pm2\sqrt{h^2+J^2-2hJ\cos k}$, including the double zero when $a(k)=0$.

Let $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ lie outside the union of the two bands in the Statement. By step 3.1, $\epsilon(k)=|a(k)|$ for every $k$, so $d(k):=|\lambda^2-|a(k)|^2|$ is continuous and strictly positive on $\mathbb T$. For each $k_0$, the open set $U_{k_0}:=\{k:d(k)>d(k_0)/2\}$ contains $k_0$. Compactness from [F7] supplies a finite subcover $U_{k_1},\ldots,U_{k_m}$, whence $d(k)>c:=\min_{1\le r\le m}d(k_r)/2>0$ for every $k$. The matrix identity $(M(k)-\lambda I)(M(k)+\lambda I)=(|a(k)|^2-\lambda^2)I$ therefore gives the pointwise inverse $(M(k)+\lambda I)/(|a(k)|^2-\lambda^2)$. This inverse matrix field is continuous and its operator norm is uniformly bounded because $\|M(k)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2(|h|+|J|)$ and $d(k)\ge c$. Multiplication by it is an everywhere-defined bounded two-sided inverse for $\mathsf M-\lambda I$, and its negative is an inverse for $\lambda I-\mathsf M$. Conjugating by $\mathcal F$ puts $\lambda$ in the resolvent of $K_\infty$ by [F5]. Thus the spectrum is contained in the two bands.

Fix $k_0\in\mathbb T$. When $a(k_0)\ne0$, the vectors $w_+=(a(k_0)/|a(k_0)|,1)/\sqrt2$ and $w_-=(-a(k_0)/|a(k_0)|,1)/\sqrt2$ are unit eigenvectors of $M(k_0)$ with eigenvalues $\pm\epsilon(k_0)$ by step 3.1; when $a(k_0)=0$, $M(k_0)=0$ and either standard unit vector is an eigenvector. For either eigenvalue $\lambda$, set $\delta_n=\min(\pi/2,1/n)$ and let $I_n=\{k_0+[t]:-\delta_n<t<\delta_n\}$, an open arc of angular length $2\delta_n$ and measure $m_{\mathbb T}(I_n)=\delta_n/\pi>0$ by [F7]. Put $\psi_n(k)=\mathbf1_{I_n}(k)w/\sqrt{m_{\mathbb T}(I_n)}$ using the corresponding fixed eigenvector $w$. Then $\|\psi_n\|_2=1$ and continuity of $M$ gives $\|(\mathsf M-\lambda I)\psi_n\|_2\le\sup_{k\in I_n}\|(M(k)-M(k_0))w\|\to0$. If $\mathsf M-\lambda I$ had a bounded inverse, these unit vectors would have residual norms bounded below by the reciprocal inverse norm, a contradiction. By [F5] and the unitary equivalence in step 2.1, every band value lies in the spectrum of $K_\infty$.

Steps 4.1 and 4.2 give both inclusions, so the spectrum is exactly $\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb T}\{-\epsilon(k),\epsilon(k)\}$. Since $\cos k\in[-1,1]$, step 3.1 gives $\min_k\epsilon(k)^2=4(h^2+J^2-2|hJ|)=4(|h|-|J|)^2$. The minimum is attained at $k=0$ when $hJ\ge0$ and at $k=\pi$ when $hJ<0$. Taking the nonnegative square root gives $\Delta_{\mathrm{bulk}}=2\bigl||h|-|J|\bigr|$, which vanishes exactly for $|h|=|J|$. This concerns the one-particle convolution operator only.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.
Assume Countable Choice.
For real $h,J$ measured in joules define the finite open-chain matrix $$H_N(h,J)=-h\sum_{j=1}^N Z_j-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}X_jX_{j+1}.$$
its finite Gibbs trace is $$Z_N(\beta;h,J):=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathcal H_N}(e^{-\beta H_N(h,J)})=\prod_{r=1}^N2\cosh\!\left(\frac{\beta\epsilon_r}{2}\right).$$
Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

derivations.claim: At $h=0$, an $X$-basis configuration $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_N)\in\{-1,1\}^N$ has energy $-J\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}s_js_{j+1}$. Each bond contributes at least $-J$, with equality exactly when $s_j=s_{j+1}$. Since the open chain is connected, all bonds attain equality exactly for the two constant configurations; for $N=1$ the empty bond sum leaves its two basis configurations degenerate as well.

At $J=0$, a $Z$-basis configuration $s\in\{-1,1\}^N$ has energy $-h\sum_js_j$. If $h>0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=1$; if $h<0$, each site uniquely minimizes its term by taking $s_j=-1$. Thus the unique minimizing $Z$-configuration has the orientation stated in the Example.

For $\beta>0$, [F2] gives the stated product trace for the exact $H_N$ of [F1] and its open-chain energies. The trace itself is the ordinary trace of the finite matrix exponential on the $2^N$-dimensional space.

For an endomorphism $C$ of $\mathcal H_N$, use the operator norm $\|C\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup\{\|C\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}:\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H_N}=1\}$ from the finite product inner product. The entries of $-\beta H_N(h,J)$ are polynomials in $\beta,h,J$. On each compact set of complex parameter triples this matrix has a finite uniform operator-norm bound $C$. Define its complex-parameter exponential by $\exp(-\beta H_N)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(-\beta H_N)^m/m!$; the summands have norm at most $C^m/m!$, so the series converges uniformly on each such compact set. The matrix exponential power series is holomorphic in its entries (that is, locally represented by convergent complex power series), so composing it with the polynomial matrix entries makes each matrix entry, and its finite trace, holomorphic in $(\beta,h,J)$. Their restrictions to $\mathbb R^3$ are real-analytic in the sense defined in the Statement. For real parameters, [F3]'s spectral exponential agrees with this series by applying the scalar exponential series to each real eigenvalue $\lambda_r$ of the Hermitian $H_N$; hence $Z_N=\sum_re^{-\beta\lambda_r}>0$. This proves analyticity for each fixed finite $N$ only; it gives no conclusion about the existence or analyticity of a limit as $N\to\infty$.

citations.quote: A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$
The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and $$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$ for every $v\in V$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is $H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor indices.
A function $T:V\to W$ is **linear** when $$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$ for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or **linear transformation**.
The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$** is the matrix $[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is $[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$.
there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$.
This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace.

If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by $$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

derivations.claim: For each basis vector $f_b$, prescribe $\rho_{\rm out}f_b:=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{\rm out}}(\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\rm in}}\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)})f_a$. The product basis in [F3] supplies the matrix entries of $\rho$, and [F4]–[F6] give a unique linear extension from the prescribed images; its matrix is exactly the displayed formula.

Since $\rho$ is self-adjoint by [F1]–[F2], its matrix satisfies $\overline{\rho_{(i,b),(i,a)}}=\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)}$, so $\rho_{\rm out}$ is self-adjoint. For every $y\in H_{\rm out}$, expansion in $(f_a)$ gives $\langle\rho_{\rm out}y,y\rangle=\sum_i\langle\rho(e_i\otimes y),e_i\otimes y\rangle\ge0$ by [F2]–[F3]. Its trace is $\sum_a(\rho_{\rm out})_{aa}=\sum_{i,a}\rho_{(i,a),(i,a)}=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F1] and [F7]; hence $\rho_{\rm out}$ is a density operator by [F1].

For every endomorphism $B$ of $H_{\rm out}$, define $I_{\rm in}\otimes B$ on the product basis by $(I_{\rm in}\otimes B)(e_i\otimes f_b):=e_i\otimes Bf_b$; [F3]–[F6] give its unique linear extension. For arbitrary $x,y$, expansion in the chosen bases shows this map sends $x\otimes y$ to $x\otimes By$, so it is independent of those bases. Finite matrix multiplication gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{\rm out}B)=\sum_{i,a,b}\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)}B_{ba}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(I_{\rm in}\otimes B))$. The right side is therefore basis-independent. If a second choice produced $\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}$, then $\operatorname{tr}((\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})B)=0$ for all $B$; taking $B$ to be the matrix unit with sole nonzero entry in row $b$, column $a$ gives $\operatorname{tr}((\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})B)=(\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})_{ab}$, so every entry of the difference is zero. Thus the endomorphism is basis-independent.

By [F8] and step 1.2, the eigenvalues of $\rho_{\rm out}$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so each term of the finite spectral sum is real, including zero eigenvalues by convention. The eigenvalue multiset is basis-independent, and multiplying by the fixed real $k_B$ preserves finiteness and basis-independence.
