Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future causal vectors form
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $\xi$ be a smooth vector field
on $M$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **Lie
derivative of the metric along $\xi$**, written $\mathcal L_\xi g$, is the
smooth symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field obtained by the flow definition of
[[def-lie-derivative-of-a-tensor-field]] applied to $g$: for the local flow
$\Phi_t$ of $\xi$,

$$\mathcal L_\xi g:=\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*g .$$

The field $\xi$ is a **Killing field** of $(M,g)$ (an **isometry generator**,
or a **Killing vector**) when

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0 .$$

The equivalent local characterization

$$\mathcal L_\xi g=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nabla_a\xi_b+\nabla_b\xi_a=0,$$

where $\nabla$ is the metric-selected connection of $g$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]) and
$\xi_b:=g_{bc}\xi^c$ is the lowered field, is proved in
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]] clause (a); the definition
itself asserts neither direction. Whether a given metric has Killing fields is
a property of that metric: neither existence nor uniqueness of a Killing field
is asserted here, and a general metric has none beyond the trivial field
$\xi=0$.

Let $(M,g,N_0)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], and let
$\nabla$ be its unique torsion-free $g$-compatible connection supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Fix a nonempty
connected open set $O\subseteq M$. A **selected stationary thermal carrier** on
$O$ consists of a smooth future timelike vector field $\xi$ and a smooth
positive scalar field $T:O\to(0,\infty)$, where $T$ is measured in kelvins,
such that $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$ in the sense of
[[def-gr-killing-field]]. Equivalently, the criterion is
$\nabla_{(a}\xi_{b)}=0$ by
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]. The round brackets mean
symmetrization with factor $1/2$. The choice of $\xi$ specifies the thermal congruence; no
coordinate chart or universal observer field is selected.

Set $N_\xi:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and $u:=\xi/N_\xi$. Then
$g(u,u)=-1$. In the length-coordinate convention $x^0=ct$, $u$ is
dimensionless and $cu$ is the physical four-velocity, with $c>0$ in
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. For a fixed Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in
$\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, define the inverse-temperature vector
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$, with units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, and the Killing-normalized
temperature field $T_K:=N_\xi T$. Thus $\beta=\xi/(k_BT_K)$; this definition
does not assert that $T_K$ is constant.

For a smooth chemical-potential scalar $\mu:O\to\mathbb R$ in joules, put
$\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$, a dimensionless scalar. Define the rest-space metric,
derivative, acceleration, expansion and shear by
$$h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+u_au_b,\qquad D:=u^a\nabla_a,\qquad a_b:=u^a\nabla_au_b,\qquad \theta:=\nabla_au^a,\qquad \sigma_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}u_{d)}-\frac13\theta h_{ab}.$$
Here $a$, $\theta$ and $\sigma$ have inverse-length units; the physical
proper acceleration is $c^2a$. The smooth tangent-bundle structure used by
the cited GR suppliers assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]; no stronger choice principle is part of this
definition.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

A **piecewise $C^1$ curve** in $M$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with a finite subdivision such that, in local charts on each closed piece, its coordinate representative is $C^1$ on the interior and its derivative extends continuously to both endpoints. The endpoint values of this extension are the corresponding one-sided derivatives.

Use the chartwise regularity convention of [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]] and the finite path operations of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]]. Refining a piece into finitely many chart pieces is allowed. No nonzero-velocity hypothesis is imposed: constant segments and pauses are admissible. A singleton parameter interval is interpreted as a constant curve.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
(Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$,
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$ earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Use SI dimensions and the signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Take the geometric data of
[[def-tgr-stationary-thermal-carriers]]: $O$ is a nonempty connected open domain in a
smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$, $\nabla$ is the
Levi–Civita connection, and $\xi$ is a smooth future-directed timelike Killing
field with dimensionless components in physical length coordinates $x^0=ct$
and $x^i$ measured in metres. Put $N:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and
$u:=\xi/N$, so $g(u,u)=-1$. Its smooth
tangent-bundle data carry the supplier's explicit foundational assumption
[[def-countable-choice]] ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$); no stronger choice principle
is added here.

Let $A$ be a smooth real one-form on $O$: for each $x\in O$, $A_x:T_xO\to\mathbb R$
is linear, and in every smooth chart $(x^a)$ its coefficients $A_a$ are smooth
and obey the covector transformation law $A'_i=A_a\,\partial x^a/\partial y^i$
on an overlapping chart $(y^i)$. The coefficients have units tesla metres.
Define $F$ in each chart by
$$F_{ab}:=(dA)_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a.$$
This prescription defines a global smooth antisymmetric covariant two-tensor:
under a change of chart $x=x(y)$ the chain rule gives
$$F'_{ij}=F_{ab}\,\frac{\partial x^a}{\partial y^i}\frac{\partial x^b}{\partial y^j},$$
since the only additional term is
$A_a(\partial_i\partial_jx^a-\partial_j\partial_ix^a)=0$. Thus $F=dA$ is a two-form;
its components have units tesla. A global gauge compensator is a smooth real
function $\Lambda_\xi$ on $O$ satisfying
$$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi,\qquad (\mathcal L_\xi A)_a:=\xi^b\partial_bA_a+A_b\partial_a\xi^b$$
in every smooth chart. This defines the Lie-derivative coefficients globally:
under $x=x(y)$, put $J^a_i:=\partial x^a/\partial y^i$ and
$K^i_a:=\partial y^i/\partial x^a$. Substitution of
$A'_i=A_aJ^a_i$ and $\xi'^i=K^i_a\xi^a$ gives
$$ (\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=\xi^b(\partial_bA_a)J^a_i+\xi^bA_aK^j_b\partial_jJ^a_i+A_cJ^c_j(\partial_iK^j_b)\xi^b+A_bJ^a_i\partial_a\xi^b. $$
Differentiating $J^c_jK^j_b=\delta^c_b$ and using
$\partial_jJ^a_i=\partial_iJ^a_j$ cancels the two middle terms, leaving
$(\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=(\mathcal L_\xi A)_aJ^a_i$. The units of
$\Lambda_\xi$ are
tesla metres. No global compensator is assumed to exist for an arbitrary
smooth $A$. Define contraction by $(\iota_\xi F)_a:=\xi^bF_{ba}$.
When a global smooth compensator $\Lambda_\xi:O\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi$ is supplied as additional data, set
$$\Psi_\xi:=\xi^aA_a-\Lambda_\xi,\qquad \Phi_\xi:=-c\Psi_\xi.$$
Thus $\Psi_\xi$ has units tesla metres and $\Phi_\xi$ has units volts.
These two scalars are defined only for such supplied compensated data;
the trajectory, mass shell, transport and ansatz below require no compensator.

Let $c>0$ be the speed of light, let $m>0$ be a particle rest mass in
kilograms, let $q\in\mathbb R$ be its charge in coulombs, and put
$M:=mc^2>0$ joules. A charged massive Lorentz trajectory is a $C^2$ curve
$x:J\to O$, where $J$ is an open real interval, parametrized by physical
length $s_m=c\tau$ in metres, with future unit tangent
$w:=dx/ds_m$, $g(w,w)=-1$, energy four-vector $P:=Mw$, and equation
$$\nabla_wP^a=cqF^a{}_bw^b,\qquad F^a{}_b:=g^{ac}F_{cb}.$$
In particular $g(P,P)=-M^2$ and $P$ is future directed. This is a conditional
definition of curves satisfying the equation; it makes no existence claim.

The future massive shell for this definition is the subset
$$\mathcal P_M^+(O):=\{(x,P)\in TO:g_x(P,P)=-M^2,\ P\text{ future directed}\}.$$
On the full tangent bundle $TO$, define charged transport as the vector field
whose integral curves, with parameter $\lambda=s_m/M$, satisfy
$$\frac{dx^a}{d\lambda}=P^a,\qquad \nabla_{dx/d\lambda}P^a=cqF^a{}_bP^b.$$
In a smooth chart its expression is
$$\mathcal L_{F,q}:=P^a\partial_{x^a}+\left(-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}P^bP^c+cqF^a{}_bP^b\right)\partial_{P^a}.$$
The restriction of this field to $\mathcal P_M^+(O)$ is justified by
[[lem-tgr-charged-liouville-preserves-mass-shell]]. For any smooth real scalar
$\zeta$ and smooth vector field $\beta$ with components in inverse joules,
define the dimensionless charged exponential ansatz on the shell by
$$f(x,P):=\exp\!\left(\zeta(x)+g_x(\beta(x),P)\right),\qquad \beta_b:=g_{bc}\beta^c.$$
The equation $\mathcal L_{F,q}f=0$ means that the derivative of this function
along the restricted charged transport vector field vanishes.

Under a smooth gauge change $A\mapsto A+d\chi$, with $\chi$ in tesla square
metres, a supplied compensator changes by
$\Lambda_\xi\mapsto\Lambda_\xi+\xi(\chi)$. These definitions fix the sign
convention for $F$, the Lorentz force, and the potential terms used on this
page.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

derivations.claim: In any smooth chart, the definitions give $(\iota_\xi F)_a=\xi^b(\partial_bA_a-\partial_aA_b)$ and $\partial_a\Psi_\xi=A_b\partial_a\xi^b+\xi^b\partial_aA_b-\partial_a\Lambda_\xi$. By [A1] and [F1], $\partial_a\Lambda_\xi=\xi^b\partial_bA_a+A_b\partial_a\xi^b$. Substitution yields $(\iota_\xi F)_a=-\partial_a\Psi_\xi$. Since this calculation holds in every chart, it proves the stated one-form identity.

The scalar $\Psi_\xi=\xi^aA_a-\Lambda_\xi$ is global and smooth because it is the contraction of globally defined smooth fields minus a global smooth scalar. Thus step 1.1 gives $\omega=-d\Psi_\xi=d(-\Psi_\xi)$ globally, which is exact by [F2].

Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold, meaning a topological $n$-manifold equipped with a maximal smooth atlas, and let $\omega\in\Omega^1(M)$ be a smooth real one-form, meaning a smooth section of the cotangent bundle $T^*M\to M$. Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ be a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ curve with $\gamma(0)=\gamma(1)$: there is a finite subdivision $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=1$ such that on each closed piece a chart contains the curve image, its coordinate representative is $C^1$ on the piece interior, and its derivative extends continuously to the endpoints. At a piece endpoint, use the corresponding one-sided derivative as the tangent. On each piece, pair this tangent $\dot\gamma(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ with $\omega_{\gamma(t)}\in T^*_{\gamma(t)}M$. Define the oriented period by

$$\operatorname{Per}_\gamma(\omega):=\sum_j\int_{t_j}^{t_{j+1}}\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))\,dt,$$

where $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=1$ is any admissible chartwise subdivision with the regularity specified above. The covector-vector pairing is intrinsic, and additivity makes this value independent of further subdivision. No invariance under homotopy is asserted by this definition.

For the complex [[def-de-rham-cochain-complex]], put $Z^k(M)=\ker(d:\Omega^k(M)\to\Omega^{k+1}(M))$ and $B^k(M)=\operatorname{im}(d:\Omega^{k-1}(M)\to\Omega^k(M))$. A form is **closed** if it belongs to $Z^k$ and **exact** if it belongs to $B^k$.

If $\omega=d\eta$, then $d\omega=d^2\eta=0$ by [[thm-the-exterior-derivative-squares-to-zero]], so $B^k\subseteq Z^k$. In particular $B^0=0$, since $\Omega^{-1}=0$. The zero form is both closed and exact in every degree.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
(Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim: Fix the finite subdivision from [F1]. On each chartwise $C^1$ piece choose a chart containing the piece, write its coordinate curve as $x(t)$ and $\widetilde\phi=\phi\circ x^{-1}$. By [F2] the coordinate coefficients of $\omega$ are $\partial_i\widetilde\phi$; applying [F3] to $\widetilde\phi\circ x$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\phi\circ\gamma)(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on that piece. This derivative is continuous and therefore integrable by [F4].

Apply [F5] on each subdivision interval to $h=\phi\circ\gamma$. By [F1] the period is the sum of those integrals, so it equals the sum of the increments $\phi(\gamma(t_{j+1}))-\phi(\gamma(t_j))$. The internal endpoint terms cancel, and the remaining increment is $\phi(\gamma(1))-\phi(\gamma(0))=0$ because $\gamma$ is closed. Thus the period is zero.

Let $O$ be a nonempty connected open subset of a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, with its Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$ and length-coordinate convention $x^0=ct$. Let $\beta$ be a smooth future-directed timelike Killing vector field on $O$, with components in $\mathrm{J}^{-1}$, and fix $k_B>0$ in $\mathrm{J\,K}^{-1}$. On $O$ define

$$T:=\frac{1}{k_B\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}},\qquad u:=k_BT\,\beta,\qquad \varpi_{ab}:=-\frac12(\nabla_a\beta_b-\nabla_b\beta_a).$$

Thus $T$ is in kelvins, $g(u,u)=-1$, and the covariant two-form $\varpi$ has units $\mathrm{J}^{-1}\mathrm{m}^{-1}$. For a smooth chemical-potential scalar $\mu:O\to\mathbb R$ in joules, set $\zeta:=\mu/(k_BT)$ and $\alpha:=-\zeta$, both dimensionless. These fields are defined only on the region where $\beta$ is future timelike; no thermal state or material realization is part of this definition.

Let $O$ be a connected open set in a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian
four-manifold, let $u$ be a smooth future unit timelike vector field on $O$
($g(u,u)=-1$), and let $T:O\to(0,\infty)$ be smooth. Define
$\beta:=u/(k_BT)$, $h_{ab}:=g_{ab}+u_au_b$,
$D:=u^a\nabla_a$, $a_b:=u^a\nabla_au_b$,
$\theta:=\nabla_au^a$ and
$\sigma_{ab}:=h_a{}^ch_b{}^d\nabla_{(c}u_{d)}-\theta h_{ab}/3$ as in
[[def-tgr-stationary-thermal-carriers]]. Then $\beta$ is a Killing field of
$g$ (equivalently $\nabla_{(a}\beta_{b)}=0$ by
[[def-gr-killing-field]] and
[[thm-gr-killing-and-on-shell-matter-identities]]) if and only if
$$DT=0,\qquad \theta=0,\qquad \sigma_{ab}=0,\qquad h_a{}^b\nabla_b\log T=-a_a.$$
No hypersurface-orthogonality or vanishing-vorticity condition is assumed.

Use SI dimensions and the signature $(-,+,+,+)$. Take the geometric data of
[[def-tgr-stationary-thermal-carriers]]: $O$ is a nonempty connected open domain in a
smooth oriented, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$, $\nabla$ is the
Levi–Civita connection, and $\xi$ is a smooth future-directed timelike Killing
field with dimensionless components in physical length coordinates $x^0=ct$
and $x^i$ measured in metres. Put $N:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and
$u:=\xi/N$, so $g(u,u)=-1$. Its smooth
tangent-bundle data carry the supplier's explicit foundational assumption
[[def-countable-choice]] ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$); no stronger choice principle
is added here.

Let $A$ be a smooth real one-form on $O$: for each $x\in O$, $A_x:T_xO\to\mathbb R$
is linear, and in every smooth chart $(x^a)$ its coefficients $A_a$ are smooth
and obey the covector transformation law $A'_i=A_a\,\partial x^a/\partial y^i$
on an overlapping chart $(y^i)$. The coefficients have units tesla metres.
Define $F$ in each chart by
$$F_{ab}:=(dA)_{ab}:=\partial_aA_b-\partial_bA_a.$$
This prescription defines a global smooth antisymmetric covariant two-tensor:
under a change of chart $x=x(y)$ the chain rule gives
$$F'_{ij}=F_{ab}\,\frac{\partial x^a}{\partial y^i}\frac{\partial x^b}{\partial y^j},$$
since the only additional term is
$A_a(\partial_i\partial_jx^a-\partial_j\partial_ix^a)=0$. Thus $F=dA$ is a two-form;
its components have units tesla. A global gauge compensator is a smooth real
function $\Lambda_\xi$ on $O$ satisfying
$$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi,\qquad (\mathcal L_\xi A)_a:=\xi^b\partial_bA_a+A_b\partial_a\xi^b$$
in every smooth chart. This defines the Lie-derivative coefficients globally:
under $x=x(y)$, put $J^a_i:=\partial x^a/\partial y^i$ and
$K^i_a:=\partial y^i/\partial x^a$. Substitution of
$A'_i=A_aJ^a_i$ and $\xi'^i=K^i_a\xi^a$ gives
$$ (\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=\xi^b(\partial_bA_a)J^a_i+\xi^bA_aK^j_b\partial_jJ^a_i+A_cJ^c_j(\partial_iK^j_b)\xi^b+A_bJ^a_i\partial_a\xi^b. $$
Differentiating $J^c_jK^j_b=\delta^c_b$ and using
$\partial_jJ^a_i=\partial_iJ^a_j$ cancels the two middle terms, leaving
$(\mathcal L_\xi A)'_i=(\mathcal L_\xi A)_aJ^a_i$. The units of
$\Lambda_\xi$ are
tesla metres. No global compensator is assumed to exist for an arbitrary
smooth $A$. Define contraction by $(\iota_\xi F)_a:=\xi^bF_{ba}$.
When a global smooth compensator $\Lambda_\xi:O\to\mathbb R$ satisfying
$\mathcal L_\xi A=d\Lambda_\xi$ is supplied as additional data, set
$$\Psi_\xi:=\xi^aA_a-\Lambda_\xi,\qquad \Phi_\xi:=-c\Psi_\xi.$$
Thus $\Psi_\xi$ has units tesla metres and $\Phi_\xi$ has units volts.
These two scalars are defined only for such supplied compensated data;
the trajectory, mass shell, transport and ansatz below require no compensator.

Let $c>0$ be the speed of light, let $m>0$ be a particle rest mass in
kilograms, let $q\in\mathbb R$ be its charge in coulombs, and put
$M:=mc^2>0$ joules. A charged massive Lorentz trajectory is a $C^2$ curve
$x:J\to O$, where $J$ is an open real interval, parametrized by physical
length $s_m=c\tau$ in metres, with future unit tangent
$w:=dx/ds_m$, $g(w,w)=-1$, energy four-vector $P:=Mw$, and equation
$$\nabla_wP^a=cqF^a{}_bw^b,\qquad F^a{}_b:=g^{ac}F_{cb}.$$
In particular $g(P,P)=-M^2$ and $P$ is future directed. This is a conditional
definition of curves satisfying the equation; it makes no existence claim.

The future massive shell for this definition is the subset
$$\mathcal P_M^+(O):=\{(x,P)\in TO:g_x(P,P)=-M^2,\ P\text{ future directed}\}.$$
On the full tangent bundle $TO$, define charged transport as the vector field
whose integral curves, with parameter $\lambda=s_m/M$, satisfy
$$\frac{dx^a}{d\lambda}=P^a,\qquad \nabla_{dx/d\lambda}P^a=cqF^a{}_bP^b.$$
In a smooth chart its expression is
$$\mathcal L_{F,q}:=P^a\partial_{x^a}+\left(-\Gamma^a{}_{bc}P^bP^c+cqF^a{}_bP^b\right)\partial_{P^a}.$$
The restriction of this field to $\mathcal P_M^+(O)$ is justified by
[[lem-tgr-charged-liouville-preserves-mass-shell]]. For any smooth real scalar
$\zeta$ and smooth vector field $\beta$ with components in inverse joules,
define the dimensionless charged exponential ansatz on the shell by
$$f(x,P):=\exp\!\left(\zeta(x)+g_x(\beta(x),P)\right),\qquad \beta_b:=g_{bc}\beta^c.$$
The equation $\mathcal L_{F,q}f=0$ means that the derivative of this function
along the restricted charged transport vector field vanishes.

Under a smooth gauge change $A\mapsto A+d\chi$, with $\chi$ in tesla square
metres, a supplied compensator changes by
$\Lambda_\xi\mapsto\Lambda_\xi+\xi(\chi)$. These definitions fix the sign
convention for $F$, the Lorentz force, and the potential terms used on this
page.

Let $O$ be a connected domain with the stationary Lorentzian data, potential
$A$, field $F=dA$, Killing field $\xi$, lapse $N=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}$, future
unit stationary observer $u=\xi/N$, and charged transport on the future mass
shell from [[def-tgr-charged-liouville-data]]. Let $m>0$, $q\in\mathbb R$,

$\mu:O\to\mathbb R$. Define $f(x,P)=\exp(\zeta+g(\beta,P))$. Without any global
potential-symmetry assumption,
$$\mathcal L_{F,q}f=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \beta\text{ is Killing and }d\zeta=-cq\,\iota_\beta F.$$

constants $T_K>0$ and $\mu_K\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$NT=T_K,\qquad \beta=\frac{\xi}{k_BT_K},\qquad N\mu+q\Phi_\xi=\mu_K.$$
With $E_{\rm loc}:=-g(P,u)$ and
$H_\xi:=-g(P,\xi)+q\Phi_\xi$, the same exponent then has both forms
$$\zeta+g(\beta,P)=-\frac{E_{\rm loc}-\mu}{k_BT} =-\frac{H_\xi-\mu_K}{k_BT_K}.$$

conditional deductions from the displayed smooth data; no equilibrium state,
particle ensemble, or physical realization is asserted to exist.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The displayed definitions give $u=k_BT\beta$ and $k_BT=(-g(\beta,\beta))^{-1/2}$, so $u=\beta/\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}$ is future unit timelike and $\beta=u/(k_BT)$. Applying the exact equivalence [F2] to this $u$ and $T$ gives the four displayed kinematic conditions if and only if $\beta$ is Killing. No hypersurface-orthogonality or zero-vorticity condition is added.

In the Killing subcase of the Statement, fix any constant $T_*>0$ kelvins and set $\xi:=k_BT_*\beta$. This is a smooth future-timelike Killing field with dimensionless components. Its lapse is $N_\xi=k_BT_*\sqrt{-g(\beta,\beta)}=T_*/T$, so $\xi/N_\xi=u$ and $N_\xi T=T_*$. Therefore these fields satisfy the stationary thermal-carrier hypotheses of [F4], and [A3] supplies its massive-shell ansatz. That theorem states that stationarity is equivalent to $\beta$ being Killing and $d\zeta=-cq_{\rm SI}\omega$. Since this subcase already has $\beta$ Killing, its differential condition is exactly $d\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\omega$ by [A1]. This identifies the transport equation as the charged stationarity condition, without assuming stationarity in the separate solvability argument below. The only inherited set-theoretic premise is $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ in [F9]; no stronger choice principle is invoked.

Since $q_{\rm eff}\ne0$, any global solution of $d\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\omega$ gives $\omega=d(\alpha/q_{\rm eff})$, which is exact by [F5]. Conversely, if $\omega=d\psi$ for a global smooth $\psi$, choosing $\alpha=q_{\rm eff}\psi$ solves the equation, and $\mu=-k_BT\alpha$ is a smooth global chemical-potential scalar with the stated units. Thus the scalar transport equation has a global solution exactly when $\omega$ is exact. This is a solvability result and does not itself assert that the supplied fields are stationary.

If $\xi=k_BT_*\beta$ has the global compensator in the Statement, [F8] gives $\iota_\xi F=-d\Psi_\xi$. Since $\beta=\xi/(k_BT_*)$, we get $\omega=-(k_BT_*)^{-1}d\Psi_\xi$, an exact one-form; [F7] then forces every period to vanish. This stronger potential-symmetry condition is separate from the obstruction hypotheses.
If any closed curve has $\operatorname{Per}_\gamma(\omega)\ne0$, [F7] contradicts the exactness forced by step 1.3. Hence no global smooth charged chemical scalar can solve the transport equation.

In the rotating Minkowski model, $\partial_{x^0}$ and the smooth rotation generator $\partial_\phi=-y\partial_x+x\partial_y$ are Killing because the metric is invariant under time translations and rotations. Their constant linear combination $\beta$ is Killing and $g(\beta,\beta)=-b^2+b^2\Omega^2r^2=-b^2(1-\Omega^2r^2)$. Also $g(\beta,\partial_{x^0})=-b<0$, so it is future-directed in the stated time orientation wherever it is timelike. Thus its future-timelike domain is exactly $1-\Omega^2r^2>0$. Substituting this norm into [F1] gives the stated temperature; when $\Omega=0$ the norm is $-b^2$ for every $r$.

The image of $I_0\times\Sigma$ in $D$ is compact, so $p_\mu$ and $p_{\mu\mu}$ are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Since $N$ is continuous and positive on compact $\Sigma$, its image has a minimum $N_{\min}>0$; also $dV_h(\Sigma)<\infty$. The one-variable mean value theorem and uniform continuity of $\partial_r f$ make the difference quotients of $f$ converge uniformly in $x$ to $\partial_r f=p_\mu(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(k_BT_0)$. For these quotients $q_h$, the estimate $|\int_\Sigma q_h\,dV_h-\int_\Sigma\partial_r f\,dV_h|\le dV_h(\Sigma)\sup_x|q_h(x)-\partial_r f(r,x)|$ tends to zero. Applying the same uniform difference-quotient argument to $\partial_r f$, whose derivative is $\partial_r^2 f=p_{\mu\mu}(T_0/N,(r-q\Phi)/N)/(N k_BT_0)$, gives $\partial_{\mu_0}^2W_{\rm hs}=\int_\Sigma p_{\mu\mu}/(N k_BT_0)\,dV_h$. Let $n\ge2$, let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, and let $g$ be a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. Write $\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$ for its oriented metric volume form. Let $\nabla$ be its Levi-Civita connection, the unique torsion-free, metric-compatible connection. Let $\phi=(g,\psi)$ denote a smooth section of a specified field bundle $\pi:E\to M$, including the metric and any other dynamical fields $\psi$ that are smooth tensor fields with the pullback action of spacetime diffeomorphisms. An admitted field family is a smooth map $\Phi:P\times M\to E$ with $\pi(\Phi(p,x))=x$, where $P$ is a finite-dimensional smooth parameter manifold; for $v\in T_pP$, $\delta_v\phi$ is the derivative of $\Phi$ along any smooth parameter curve with initial velocity $v$. A **finite-jet Lagrangian $n$-form** is a smooth spacetime $n$-form $\mathcal L(\phi)$ whose coordinate coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many spacetime derivatives. It is **diffeomorphism-covariant** when pullback by every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ satisfies $\mathcal L(\Psi^*\phi)=\Psi^*\mathcal L(\phi)$.

A **chosen covariant first-variation decomposition** is data consisting of an Euler–Lagrange expression $E_\phi[\eta]$, the $n$-form linear in a field variation $\eta$ left after spacetime derivatives have been moved off $\eta$ by integration by parts, and a covariant $(n-1)$-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, also linear in $\eta$, such that
$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$$
for every admitted smooth finite-dimensional family of fields. Here covariance means that for every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ and field variation $\eta$,
$$E_{\Psi^*\phi}[\Psi^*\eta]=\Psi^*E_\phi[\eta],\qquad \theta(\Psi^*\phi;\Psi^*\eta)=\Psi^*\theta(\phi;\eta).$$
The choice of $\theta$ is part of the data and need not be unique. A solution has $E_\phi=0$; a linearized solution $\delta\phi$ at $\phi$ has $\delta E_\phi[\delta\phi]=0$.

A **stationary solution with generator $\xi$** is a solution $\phi$ and a fixed smooth spacetime vector field $\xi$ such that $\mathcal L_\xi\phi=0$. Thus $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$, so $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$. A **bifurcate Killing horizon** is a pair of smooth null hypersurfaces generated by this Killing flow: $\xi$ is nonzero, null, tangent and normal on each hypersurface away from their transverse intersection $B$, and $\xi=0$ on $B$. Fix a compact, oriented, boundaryless, spacelike embedded codimension-two submanifold $B\subset M$. Choose a future-directed unit timelike normal $u$ and a chosen unit spacelike normal $n_B$ along $B$, orthogonal to each other, and define the binormal $\epsilon_{ab}=2u_{[a}(n_B)_{b]}$, so $\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon^{ab}=-2$. Orient $B$ compatibly with the spacetime orientation and this normal frame so that, on $B$, $(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{ab a_3\ldots a_n}=\epsilon_{ab}(dA_B)_{a_3\ldots a_n}$; here $dA_B$ is the positive volume form of the induced metric with that orientation. The horizon is **nondegenerate** when the fixed normalization of $\xi$ gives a constant $\kappa>0$ on $B$ with $\nabla_a\xi_b=\kappa\epsilon_{ab}$ there; $\kappa$ is its surface gravity. Variations keep $\xi$ and the embedded surface $B$ fixed.

For such data define the **Noether current** $(n-1)$-form
$$J_\xi:=\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\phi)-\iota_\xi\mathcal L.$$
Choose a smooth covariant $(n-2)$-form $Q_\xi$ on a neighborhood of the admitted field data and define the residual constraint form $C_\xi:=J_\xi-dQ_\xi$. Require $C_\xi=0$ on the selected solution and, for each admitted linearized perturbation used below, require its fixed-$\xi$ variation $\delta C_\xi=0$. These are explicit on-shell and linearized-constraint conditions; no existence or global exactness of $Q_\xi$ follows merely from closure of a presymplectic current. The pullback of $Q_\xi$ is required to be globally compatible on the integration region.

Boundary data consist of a specified smooth solution space $\mathcal S$, with specified falloff, a family of closed codimension-two surfaces $S_R$ approaching the asymptotic boundary, and finite oriented smooth singular hypersurface chains $C_R$ with $\partial C_R=S_R-B$. With a fixed boundary-term convention, define the charge-variation one-form by
$$\alpha_\xi(\delta\phi):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}\bigl(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)\bigr).$$
Require this limit to exist and be globally integrable: there is a smooth Hamiltonian charge $H_\xi$ on the specified solution space with $d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi=\alpha_\xi$, where $d_{\mathcal S}$ is the exterior derivative on that solution space. This exactness, and the chosen boundary formula itself, are hypotheses. Other boundary actions or falloff conditions can add terms and require a separately stated charge formula.

Adopt the $c=1$ action-unit convention: time is measured as length, $[\hbar]=\text{action}$, and $[k_B]=\text{energy}/\text{temperature}$; neither $\hbar$ nor $k_B$ is set to $1$. Normalize the flow parameter of the fixed generator $\xi$ in length units. Then its Lie action and $\nabla\xi$ have units $L^{-1}$, and the surface gravity $\kappa$ in $\nabla_a\xi_b=\kappa\epsilon_{ab}$ has units $L^{-1}$. The spacetime integral of $\mathcal L$ has units of action, so if $\mathcal L=\ell\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$, then $[\ell]=\text{action}\,L^{-n}$. Since curvature has units $L^{-2}$, the Einstein--Hilbert normalization $\ell_{\rm EH}=R/(16\pi G)$ in $n$ spacetime dimensions has $[G]=L^{n-2}\,\text{action}^{-1}$. Thus the curvature derivative $P^{abcd}$ used below has units $[P]=\text{action}\,L^{2-n}$, and the downstream functional $-(2\pi k_B/\hbar)\int_B P^{abcd}\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon_{cd}\,dA_B$ has entropy units $k_B$. The integrated Noether charge and $H_\xi$ have energy units, consistent with $\hbar\kappa\,\delta S_W/k_B$.

When SI units are restored for the $n$-dimensional Einstein--Hilbert normalization $c^3R/(16\pi G)$, $[G]={\rm m}^{n-1}{\rm kg}^{-1}{\rm s}^{-2}$ and $[A_B]={\rm m}^{n-2}$, so the area expression is $S_W=k_Bc^3A_B/(4G\hbar)$. In four spacetime dimensions this is the usual SI Newton constant in ${\rm m}^3{\rm kg}^{-1}{\rm s}^{-2}$ and horizon area in ${\rm m}^2$; the SI acceleration surface gravity is $\kappa_{\rm acc}=c^2\kappa_{\rm geom}$.

derivations.claim:
Differentiating the coordinate curvature tensor and using that the
variation of a connection is a tensor gives
$$\delta R^a{}_{bcd}=2\nabla_{[c}\delta\Gamma^a{}_{d]b},\qquad \delta\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12g^{ae} (\nabla_b\delta g_{ec}+\nabla_c\delta g_{eb}-\nabla_e\delta g_{bc}).$$
Substitute these identities into $P^{abcd}\delta R_{abcd}$, use the
Riemann symmetries of $P$, and apply the product rule to move derivatives
off $\delta g$. The part of the resulting potential that contains a
derivative of $\delta g$ is
$$2(\mathbf E_R^{bcd})\nabla_d\delta g_{bc},\qquad (\mathbf E_R^{bcd})_{a_2\ldots a_n} :=P^{abcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{a a_2\ldots a_n};$$
all other curvature terms have no derivative of $\delta g$. For each finite
matter-jet term the repeated identity
$$A^a\nabla_a(\delta T)=\nabla_a(A^a\delta T) -(\nabla_aA^a)\delta T$$
moves its finitely many derivatives off the varied tensor slots. Iterating
that identity $r$ times writes a term with $r$ derivatives of a variation as
a divergence whose coefficients multiply variations of covariant jets of
orders $0$ through $r-1$, plus an Euler term with no derivative on the
variation. The connection-variation terms are included when those jets are
varied as tensors. This supplies a covariant first-variation potential
linear in the variations of covariant tensor slots.

By [A2], covariance and the first-variation identity with variation $\mathcal L_\zeta\phi$ give $\mathcal L_\zeta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\mathcal L_\zeta\phi]+d	heta(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)$. By [F2], $\mathcal L_\zeta\mathcal L=d(\iota_\zeta\mathcal L)+\iota_\zeta(d\mathcal L)$; since $\mathcal L$ is an $n$-form on an $n$-manifold, $d\mathcal L=0$. Subtracting gives $dJ_\zeta=-E_\phi[\mathcal L_\zeta\phi]$, so the current is closed on a solution and the assumed canonical local primitive is compatible with the on-shell identity. For a tensor $T$, [F1] gives $$(\mathcal L_\zeta T)^{a_1\ldots a_p}{}_{b_1\ldots b_q}=\zeta^e
abla_eT^{a_1\ldots a_p}{}_{b_1\ldots b_q}-\sum_{i=1}^p(
abla_e\zeta^{a_i})T^{a_1\ldots e\ldots a_p}{}_{b_1\ldots b_q}+\sum_{j=1}^q(
abla_{b_j}\zeta^e)T^{a_1\ldots a_p}{}_{b_1\ldots e\ldots b_q}.$$ For each $r\ge1$ let $D^r\psi:=
abla_{(a_1}\cdots
abla_{a_r)}\psi$, and set $D^0\psi:=\psi$. Naturality of the Levi-Civita connection gives $D^r\psi[\Phi_t^*g,\Phi_t^*\psi]=\Phi_t^*(D^r\psi[g,\psi])$ along the local flow $\Phi_t$ of $\zeta$. Differentiating shows that the total variation of this jet, including the variation of the connection, is $\mathcal L_\zeta(D^r\psi)$; applying [F1] to the whole jet tensor shows that it contains only $\zeta$ and $
abla\zeta$. Thus every covariant tensor-slot contribution to $	heta(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)$ contains only $\zeta$ and $
abla\zeta$, even when the finite matter-jet order exceeds one. The metric slot contributes $2\mathbf E_R^{bcd}

abla_b\zeta_c+
abla_c\zeta_b)$. Since $\mathbf E_R^{bcd}$ is antisymmetric in $c,d$, $\mathbf E_R^{bcd}
abla_d
abla_c\zeta_b=	frac12\mathbf E_R^{bcd}[
abla_d,
abla_c]\zeta_b$, a curvature-times-$\zeta$ term. Therefore the sole second-derivative term in $J_\zeta$ is $2\mathbf E_R^{bcd}
abla_d
abla_b\zeta_c$; $-\iota_\zeta\mathcal L$ contains only $\zeta$.

Apply the defining integration-by-parts construction of the canonical
local representative to the term in step 2.1. The product rule gives
$$2\mathbf E_R^{bcd}\nabla_d\nabla_b\zeta_c =2\nabla_d(\mathbf E_R^{bcd}\nabla_b\zeta_c) -2(\nabla_d\mathbf E_R^{bcd})\nabla_b\zeta_c.$$
In form components, the second-derivative part of
$(d(X^{cd}\nabla_{[c}\zeta_{d]}))_{a_2\ldots a_n}$ is
$$-(n-1)P^{pqcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{pq[a_3\ldots a_n} \nabla_{a_2]}\nabla_{[c}\zeta_{d]}.$$
Antisymmetrizing $p,q$, $c,d$, and the form slots, then exchanging the
curvature-derivative index pairs of $P$, gives
$$2P^{abcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{a a_2\ldots a_n} \nabla_d\nabla_b\zeta_c,$$
which is the second-derivative term in step 2.1. Thus the coefficient and
sign of $X$ are fixed as stated. The remaining
terms in the product rule, the curvature commutator, and the other terms of
$J_\zeta$ contain at most first derivatives of $\zeta$. Repeatedly apply
$$A^a{}_b\nabla_a\zeta^b=\nabla_a(A^a{}_b\zeta^b) -(\nabla_aA^a{}_b)\zeta^b$$
to the lower-order terms in the canonical construction. Each step lowers
the derivative order on $\zeta$ by one, so the residual potential term is
linear in $\zeta$, denoted $W^c\zeta_c$. This proves the canonical formula.
The stipulated Lagrangian and potential changes contribute respectively
$\iota_\zeta\mu$ and $\mathbf Y(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)$ to the charge;
an exact charge change contributes $dZ$. This gives the full stated class.

Let $n\ge2$, let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, and let $g$ be a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. A **finite-jet Lagrangian $n$-form** is a smooth spacetime $n$-form $\mathcal L(\phi)$ whose coordinate coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many spacetime derivatives. It is **diffeomorphism-covariant** when pullback by every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ satisfies $\mathcal L(\Psi^*\phi)=\Psi^*\mathcal L(\phi)$.

A **chosen covariant first-variation decomposition** is data consisting of an Euler–Lagrange expression $E_\phi[\eta]$, the $n$-form linear in a field variation $\eta$ left after spacetime derivatives have been moved off $\eta$ by integration by parts, and a covariant $(n-1)$-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, also linear in $\eta$, such that
$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$$
for every admitted smooth finite-dimensional family of fields. Here covariance means that for every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ and field variation $\eta$,
$$E_{\Psi^*\phi}[\Psi^*\eta]=\Psi^*E_\phi[\eta],\qquad \theta(\Psi^*\phi;\Psi^*\eta)=\Psi^*\theta(\phi;\eta).$$
The choice of $\theta$ is part of the data and need not be unique. A solution has $E_\phi=0$; a linearized solution $\delta\phi$ at $\phi$ has $\delta E_\phi[\delta\phi]=0$.

A **stationary solution with generator $\xi$** is a solution $\phi$ and a fixed smooth spacetime vector field $\xi$ such that $\mathcal L_\xi\phi=0$. Thus $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$, so $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$. A **bifurcate Killing horizon** is a pair of smooth null hypersurfaces generated by this Killing flow: $\xi$ is nonzero, null, tangent and normal on each hypersurface away from their transverse intersection $B$, and $\xi=0$ on $B$. Fix a compact, oriented, boundaryless, spacelike embedded codimension-two submanifold $B\subset M$. Choose a future-directed unit timelike normal $u$ and a chosen unit spacelike normal $n_B$ along $B$, orthogonal to each other, and define the binormal $\epsilon_{ab}=2u_{[a}(n_B)_{b]}$, so $\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon^{ab}=-2$. Variations keep $\xi$ and the embedded surface $B$ fixed.

For such data define the **Noether current** $(n-1)$-form
$$J_\xi:=\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\phi)-\iota_\xi\mathcal L.$$
Choose a smooth covariant $(n-2)$-form $Q_\xi$ on a neighborhood of the admitted field data and define the residual constraint form $C_\xi:=J_\xi-dQ_\xi$. Boundary data consist of a specified smooth solution space $\mathcal S$, with specified falloff, a family of closed codimension-two surfaces $S_R$ approaching the asymptotic boundary, and finite oriented smooth singular hypersurface chains $C_R$ with $\partial C_R=S_R-B$. Differentiate $J_\xi$ at fixed $\xi$. Since $\mathcal L_\xi\phi=0$ on the stationary background and $\theta$ is linear in its variation argument,
$$\delta J_\xi=\theta(\phi;\delta(\mathcal L_\xi\phi))-\iota_\xi\delta\mathcal L =\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\delta\phi)-\iota_\xi\bigl(E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)\bigr).$$
The first equality uses that the coefficient variation of $\theta(\phi;0)$ is zero; the second uses $\delta(\mathcal L_\xi\phi)=\mathcal L_\xi\delta\phi$ because $\xi$ is fixed. Covariance of $\theta$ identifies $\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\delta\phi)=\mathcal L_\xi\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$. Since $E_\phi=0$, Cartan's identity [F1] yields $\delta J_\xi=d(\iota_\xi\theta)$.

By [A1], $C_\xi=J_\xi-dQ_\xi$ and $\delta C_\xi=0$. Differentiating this identity gives $\delta J_\xi=d(\delta Q_\xi)$ because $d$ is independent of the field variation and the spacetime coordinates. Combining with step 1.1 gives $d(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta)=0$. This conclusion uses the explicit constraint-variation premise; it is not inferred from the closure of a presymplectic current.

Apply [F2] to $\alpha=\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta$ on $C_R$. By step 2.1 and $\partial C_R=S_R-B$,
$$0=\int_{C_R}d\alpha=\int_{S_R}(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta)-\int_B(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta).$$
On $B$, $\xi=0$, so $\iota_\xi\theta=0$. Taking the limit in the first term is permitted by the boundary convergence assumption in [A1], and its value is $\delta H_\xi$ by the specified definition of the Hamiltonian variation. Hence $\delta H_\xi=\int_B\delta Q_\xi$.

By [F3], the charge used here is in the representative class required by [L1]. Apply [L1] to the right-hand side of step 3.1. This gives $\delta H_\xi=(\hbar\kappa/(2\pi k_B))\delta S_W$, with all field variations taken at fixed generator and fixed background $\kappa$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $M\ne\{0\}$ be a concrete von Neumann algebra on a complex Hilbert space. Use the predual $M_*=Q$ of [[lem-qsmx-von-neumann-predual]]; its elements are the normal linear functionals, and the induced topology $\sigma(M,Q)$ is the ultraweak topology. A **normal state** on $M$ is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:M\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(I)=1$, $\omega(a)\geq0$ for every positive $a\in M$, and
$$\omega\!\left(\sup_i a_i\right)=\sup_i\omega(a_i)$$
for every increasing net $(a_i)$ of positive elements with $0\leq a_i\leq C I$ for a common finite $C$ and supremum taken in $M$.
An automorphism of $M$ is **normal** when it preserves the suprema of all such bounded increasing positive nets.
A **point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter automorphism group** is a family $(\alpha_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}$ of bijective unital complex-linear maps $M\to M$ preserving multiplication and adjoints, with $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$, $\alpha_s\alpha_t=\alpha_{s+t}$, and $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(x))$ continuous for every $x\in M$ and every normal linear functional $\varphi\in Q$.
For dimensionless $t$ and dimensionless $\beta>0$, the normal state $\omega$ satisfies the **upper-strip $(\alpha,\beta)$ KMS condition** when, for every $A,B\in M$, there is a bounded scalar function $F_{A,B}$ on $S_\beta=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq\beta\}$ that is continuous on $S_\beta$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies
$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+i\beta)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

derivations.claim:
The rescaled maps satisfy
$\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_1}\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_2}
=\alpha_{\tau_1/\lambda+\tau_2/\lambda}
=\widetilde\alpha_{\tau_1+\tau_2}$ and
$\widetilde\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}_M$. For each $X\in M$ and normal
linear functional $\varphi$, the map
$\tau\mapsto\varphi(\widetilde\alpha_\tau(X))
=\varphi(\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(X))$ is continuous because it is the
composition of the continuous map $t\mapsto\varphi(\alpha_t(X))$ with
$\tau\mapsto\tau/\lambda$. Thus $\widetilde\alpha$ is a
point-ultraweakly continuous one-parameter group.

For each $A,B\in M$, choose the strip function $F_{A,B}$ supplied by
[F1] and define $G_{A,B}(z)=F_{A,B}(z/\lambda)$. Since $\lambda>0$, the
map $z\mapsto z/\lambda$ sends the closed strip of width $\lambda\theta$
bijectively to $S_\theta$ and its interior to the interior. Therefore
$G_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous on the closed rescaled strip and
holomorphic inside.

For real $\tau$, the boundaries are
$G_{A,B}(\tau)=\omega(A\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(B))
=\omega(A\widetilde\alpha_\tau(B))$ and
$G_{A,B}(\tau+i\lambda\theta)
=\omega(\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(B)A)
=\omega(\widetilde\alpha_\tau(B)A)$. These are precisely the required
upper-strip boundary values at width $\lambda\theta$.

The hypotheses require theta>0 and lambda>0; zero strip width or zero rescaling is excluded.

Steps 1.2–2.1 map the closed strip, including both boundary lines, and verify each boundary value.
The premise is explicit in A1; step 1.2 uses the supplied function separately for each fixed A,B and does not assert a uniform choice beyond the hypothesis.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and an inertial
chart of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and
[[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]. Use signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinates
$x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres, and coordinate time $t$ in seconds as in
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. Greek spacetime indices run
from $0$ to $3$; spatial indices run from $1$ to $3$ and are contracted with
the Euclidean spatial metric. The coordinates $x^a$ have unit metre and
$\partial_a:=\partial/\partial x^a$ has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$.

The positive constants $c$, $h$ and $e_{\rm SI}$ have the exact SI defining
values; write $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$. The magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ has SI unit
$\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ and is experimentally determined under the current SI;
no exact numerical value or current estimate for it is adopted. Put
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ when that symbol is used. These are SI
normalization inputs, not empirical claims about a selected QFT model.

For a species with rest mass $m_{\rm rest,SI}>0$ in kilograms define its
inverse-length mass parameter

$$\mu:=\frac{m_{\rm rest,SI}c}{\hbar}\quad[\mathrm m^{-1}].$$

For a spatial wave vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, with each component in
$\mathrm m^{-1}$ and the Euclidean norm, define
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k):=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, with
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Here $\omega_\mu$ is the temporal wave number, not the
SI angular frequency; the corresponding SI angular frequency is
$c\omega_\mu$. Energy and momentum are $E=\hbar c\omega_\mu$ in joules and
$\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. With
$p=(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k)\in\mathbb R^4$ and
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^4$, the phase convention is

$$p\mathbin{\circ}x:=\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x=-\eta(p,x).$$

For a selected local action represented on a chart region
$\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ by
$$\frac{S}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathcal U}\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}(x)\,d^4x,\quad d^4x:=dx^0dx^1dx^2dx^3,$$
the natural Lagrangian density $\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. Since $x^0=ct$, the corresponding SI Lagrangian density is
$\mathcal L_{\mathrm{SI}}:=\hbar c\,\mathcal L_{\mathrm{nat}}$ and has unit
$\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. This unit conversion alone does not identify a
Lagrangian density with the model's Hamiltonian energy density.

For canonical engineering dimensions in this four-dimensional normalization,
use the formal field symbols $\phi_{\rm n}$ and $\psi_{\rm n}$ in the selected
scalar and Dirac kinetic terms, assigning them length degrees $-1$ and
$-3/2$, respectively. These are the dimensions fixed by those free kinetic
terms, not exact scaling dimensions of interacting fields: anomalous
dimensions, when present, are separate quantities. These symbols do not
assert pointwise field maps or operator fields; a model supplies its field
space and regularity. Let $A^\mu_{\rm SI}=(\varphi/c,\mathbf A)$ and
$F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}$ use the component convention of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]], namely
$F_{0i}=-E_i/c$ and $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$, with
$F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu$ only when a potential is
supplied. Define the normalized photon potential and field strength by

$$a^\mu:=\frac{A^\mu_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}},\qquad f^{\mu\nu}:=\frac{F^{\mu\nu}_{\rm SI}}{\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}}.$$

They have length degrees $-1$ and $-2$, respectively. The EM supplier is used
only for SI units and tensor components: no classical Maxwell equation,
Lorentz-force law, or classical-to-quantum identification is adopted here.

For any separately declared SI charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}$ in coulombs put

$$q_{\rm n}:=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}.$$

It is dimensionless. For the positive exact SI elementary charge use
$e_{\rm n}:=e_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$ and define the rationalized
dimensionless coupling $\alpha:=e_{\rm n}^2/(4\pi)$. Since $\mu_0$ is
measured, these formulas do not assign an exact numerical value to
$e_{\rm n}$ or $\alpha$. If the model uses minimal coupling, its convention is
$D_\mu=\partial_\mu-iq_{\rm n}a_\mu$; for an electron with
$q_{\rm SI}=-e_{\rm SI}$ this reads $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+ie_{\rm n}a_\mu$.
Bare, renormalized-at-scale, and measured effective charges are separately
labelled model parameters; applying the conversion to one label does not
identify it with either of the others or specify a running law.

In a supplied four-component spinor representation, let
$\gamma^a\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^4)$, $a=0,1,2,3$, be
dimensionless linear maps satisfying
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}:=\gamma^a\gamma^b+\gamma^b\gamma^a
=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$, where $I_4$ is the identity map. Set $\beta:=\gamma^0$
and $\alpha^i:=\beta\gamma^i$; then $\beta^2=I_4$ and
$\gamma^i=\beta\alpha^i$. For a supplied four-component spinor $\psi$ write
$\bar\psi:=\psi^\dagger\beta$. The effective Clifford metric is $-\eta$.
A supplied free Dirac model may use
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi=0$ for its model-supplied spinor field
$\psi$; that model supplies its field domain and regularity. The phase and
Clifford choices are conventions; this item proves no representation or field
equation.

For the autonomous evolution convention, assume Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]: every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice
function. Let a selected model supply a complex Hilbert space $\mathscr H$
as in [[def-hilbert-space]] and a time-independent complex-linear Hamiltonian
$H:D(H)\to\mathscr H$ with a specified dense linear domain
$D(H)\subseteq\mathscr H$ and SI energy
unit joules. Require self-adjointness as in
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]: $H=H^*$,
including equality of domains and values. Here $y\in D(H^*)$ precisely when
there is a $z\in\mathscr H$ such that
$\langle Hx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(H)$, and
$H^*y=z$; density makes $z$ unique.

The published mathematical supplier
[[lem-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cc-arbitrary-hilbert-spectral-calculus]]
then supplies the spectral measure $E_H$ on the Borel subsets of
$\mathbb R$. This is a normalized projection-valued measure as in
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]: its values are bounded orthogonal
projections, $E_H(\mathbb R)=I$, $E_H(B\cap C)=E_H(B)E_H(C)$, and it is
countably additive in norm on every vector. For $\xi\in\mathscr H$ put
$\nu_\xi(B):=\langle E_H(B)\xi,\xi\rangle$, a finite positive measure.
The spectral integral of $\lambda$ represents $H$, on exactly the domain
$D(H)=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,d\nu_\xi(\lambda)<\infty\}$.
For real $t$ in seconds define the autonomous evolution by bounded Borel
functional calculus,
$$U(t):=\exp(-itH/\hbar):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda).$$
The spectral variable $\lambda$ carries unit joule. This exponential is a
bounded operator on all of $\mathscr H$, even when $H$ is unbounded; it
does not mean an operator power series on arbitrary vectors. The supplier
gives a strongly continuous unitary group: $U(0)=I$,
$U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$ and $\|U(t)\xi-U(t_0)\xi\|\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ for
each $\xi\in\mathscr H$. A model may restrict it to a declared
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$. Each $U(t)$ is a surjective complex-linear map
satisfying $\langle U(t)\xi,U(t)\zeta\rangle=\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle$
for all $\xi,\zeta\in\mathscr H$; write $U(t)^*:=U(t)^{-1}$. The exponent
is dimensionless because $\hbar$ has unit $\mathrm{J\,s}$. For any
model-supplied complex-linear operator $O:D(O)\to\mathscr H$, with specified
linear domain $D(O)\subseteq\mathscr H$, define its Heisenberg conjugate by
$$O_H(t):=U(t)^*O\,U(t),\quad D(O_H(t)):=\{\xi\in\mathscr H:U(t)\xi\in D(O)\}.$$
The model supplies the Hamiltonian and operator domains; the spectral supplier
justifies this evolution only for those data and hypotheses. This dictionary
constructs no model-specific Hamiltonian or field representation and does not
adopt a physical dynamics law. Where a free-field
module uses an inner product linear in its second variable, convert to the
repository's first-variable-linear pairing by
$\langle u,v\rangle_{\rm FF}=(v,u)_{\rm root}$.

For precision about domains, let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space with
inner product linear in its first variable and let
$\mathscr D\subseteq\mathcal H$ be a dense complex linear subspace. A **weak operator-valued distribution
on the common domain $\mathscr D$** means a complex-linear assignment
$g\mapsto\Phi(g)$ for $g\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^4)$, where each
$\Phi(g):\mathscr D\to\mathcal H$ is linear and, for every
$u,v\in\mathscr D$, the scalar map
$g\mapsto\langle\Phi(g)u,v\rangle$ is a continuous complex-linear functional
on the test-function space with the topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]], hence a distribution as in [[def-distribution]].
This definition gives no pointwise field $\Phi(x)$ and no product
$\Phi(x)\Phi(x)$; a product or extension needs a separate construction. It
asserts only matrix-element continuity and the stated linear maps; all further
operator properties, locality, local observable algebras, graded locality,
and gauge-specific potential behavior must be supplied by a constructed
model. Test-function units can be chosen so a specified smeared observable is
dimensionless; there is no universal test-function unit asserted here.

Primitive data for a selected model include its species and rest masses,
declared charge parameters, regulator geometry, couplings, state and any
constructed measurement data. Vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonians, regulator
eigenvalues, distributions, correlations and outcome probabilities are
derived only when their constructions supply the required domains and
well-definedness. This dictionary neither constructs an interacting
four-dimensional QED Hilbert space nor asserts pointwise field products,
scattering, an LSZ limit, asymptotic completeness, or removal of a regulator.

The future mass shell is
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p): (p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\}.$$

parameterization. The scalar shell pairing is

$$d\nu_\mu(p_\mu(\mathbf k))= \frac{d^3\mathbf k}{(2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)},\qquad H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C),$$

R^4)$ define its pointwise shell Fourier restriction by

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, an inertial length-coordinate chart
$x=(x^0,\mathbf x)$, $x^0=ct$, and coordinates measured in metres, as specified
by [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write
$\Box=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. The mass-shell parameter $\mu\ge0$ has
unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ has the same unit. For a
massive species, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the separately
admitted massless branch of the mathematical free-field construction. Thus
$\hbar c\omega_\mu$ is physical energy and $\hbar\mathbf k$ is physical
momentum. The natural-unit action is written $S/\hbar$.

The scalar one-particle space is
$\mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, where
$H_\mu^+=\{(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),\mathbf k):\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3,\ \omega_\mu(\mathbf k)>0\}$ and
$d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$; at $\mu=0$ the
measure-zero apex $\mathbf k=0$ is omitted. These are the shell conventions
of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]].

For a smooth real classical scalar $\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$
with the canonical free-field length degree $-1$, adopt
$$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4}\left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n}+\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$
For a smooth commuting classical Dirac spinor
$\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ with canonical free-field length
degree $-3/2$, put $\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}=\psi_{\mathrm n}^\dagger\beta$ and
use the Clifford convention
$\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\}=-2\eta^{ab}I_4$ from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Adopt
$$\frac{S_D}{\hbar}=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\bar\psi_{\mathrm n}(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}\,d^4x.$$
The smooth classical variables in these functionals commute; no Grassmann
algebra or path-integral construction is being adopted. These formulas specify
local action densities: for arbitrary smooth global fields the total
integrals need not converge. Only compactly supported variations are used;
the action difference under such a variation is an integral over a compact
set and is finite for smooth fields. With these variations on the fixed
background, the intended Euler–Lagrange equations are
$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi_{\mathrm n}=0$ and
$(i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}=0$, conditional on the exact
mathematical supplier recorded as [L1] below.

As the physical interpretation of this selected free model, assign the real
scalar species to the bosonic symmetric Fock representation and assign the
Dirac field to the particle/antiparticle CAR representation on
$\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. Choose the zero-particle Fock
vectors as the scalar and Dirac vacuum states. This is an adopted species and
statistics assignment. The CCR/CAR and operator properties of the specified
representations are mathematical model consequences; they do not prove a
general spin-statistics theorem or establish that nature realizes this model.

The scalar construction is the Schwartz-smeared field
$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f)$ on the finite-particle
domain, with the future-shell phase
$p\circ x=\omega_\mu x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$, exactly as in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. The Dirac construction is the bounded
spacetime-smeared CAR field of
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], using the positive and negative
projections of the specified free Dirac matrix. In that carrier,
$\mathcal H_D=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k/(2\pi)^3;\mathbb C^4)$,
$h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$, and
$P_\pm(\mathbf k)=(I_4\pm h_D(\mathbf k)/\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))/2$; the
particle and antiparticle one-particle spaces are the closed ranges
$\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$. These carriers state their
mathematical hypotheses and construction domains; their draft status is not an
independent physics or proof approval.

Tong's lecture notes and Srednicki's book draft provide independent
presentations of the scalar and Dirac free-field formulations. Their formal
mode notation supplies context for this adoption, not a proof of the
operator-domain claims and not evidence that the adopted model describes
nature.
