supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the fields, Fock spaces, vacua, coordinate conventions, and natural/SI
normalizations adopted in [[post-qft-free-field-model]]. For an open spacetime
region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, a scalar test is a real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$ and a Dirac test is a
$F\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb C^4)$. These are compactly supported smooth test
functions on the fixed inertial Minkowski chart.

For scalar tests use the bounded Weyl operators
$$W_\mu(f)=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f),$$
where $K_\mu$ is the future-shell restriction and
$W_{\rm Segal}$ is the unitary generated by the closed Segal field, with the
normalization and phase convention of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the scalar bounded observable algebra
$\mathfrak A_s(O)$ to be the norm closure of the unital $*$-algebra generated
by these $W_\mu(f)$. The real smeared field is symmetric on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and its self-adjoint closure has the exact multiplier
domain supplied by [[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]] and
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]].

For Dirac tests, $\Psi(F)$ is the bounded smeared CAR field of
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]. Define $\mathfrak A_D(O)$ as the norm
closure of the unital algebra generated by products containing an even number
of these field operators and their adjoints, with all test supports in $O$.
“Even” here means even field parity, or equivalently an even number of odd
CAR field generators in each product. The even algebra is the selected local
Dirac observable algebra; an odd charged field is not included as a commuting
local observable.

The selected vacuum states on bounded operators are the vector states
$\omega_s(A)=\langle\Omega_s,A\Omega_s\rangle$ and
$\omega_D(B)=\langle\Omega_D,B\Omega_D\rangle$. For the scalar Fock space,
define the total number, Hamiltonian, and physical momentum components by
$$N_s=d\Gamma_s(1),\qquad H_s=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu),\qquad P_{s,j}=\hbar\,d\Gamma_s(k_j).$$
Here $d\Gamma_s$ acts on the $n$-particle sector by summing the displayed
one-particle multiplier over its $n$ arguments. Their maximal domains are
the square-integrability domains of those sector sums; in particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
These physical components have one-particle momentum $+\hbar k_j$, as in
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. The mathematical spatial generators in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] and [[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]] use
$G_{s,j}=d\Gamma_s(-k_j)$ with the positive-exponent convention;
thus $P_{s,j}=-\hbar G_{s,j}$. For a translation increment
$a=(a^0,\mathbf a)$ in length coordinates, the scalar translation unitary
is the sectorwise phase
$\exp(i(a^0H_s/(\hbar c)-\sum_j a^jP_{s,j}/\hbar))$.
Changing the sign does not change the maximal domain, since the squared
sector multiplier is unchanged. This also follows directly from
[[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]] with multiplier $k_j$. For the Dirac Fock space, let $H$
and $P_j$ be the mathematical translation generators of
[[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]]. Their one-particle
multipliers are respectively $(\omega_\mu,\mathbf k)$ for particles and
$(\omega_\mu,-\mathbf k)$ for antiparticles, and the sector multiplier is
their sum. Define the physical Dirac Hamiltonian and momentum by
$H_D=\hbar cH$ and $P_{D,j}=\hbar P_j$, using the positive SI constants from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Their exact domains are unchanged by these
nonzero scale factors; their multipliers have units joules and momentum,
respectively.

For any of these self-adjoint operators $A$, a normalized state
$\Psi\in D(A)$ has model mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and variance
$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2$.
This requires the second spectral moment but does not require
$\Psi\in D(A^2)$. Products of unbounded operators use their composition
domains.

If a signed charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}\in\mathbb R$ measured in coulombs is supplied, the intended
Dirac charge-number operator is $Q_{\rm SI}=q_{\rm SI}(N_p-N_{\bar p})$.
Here $\Pi_p$ and $\Pi_{\bar p}$ are the orthogonal projections onto
$\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$; on the $n$-particle sector,
$N_p$ and $N_{\bar p}$ are the sums of the corresponding projections over
the $n$ tensor factors. Its candidate maximal direct-sum domain is
$$D(Q_{\rm SI})=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge0}\left\|q_{\rm SI}\sum_{r=1}^n(\Pi_p-\Pi_{\bar p})^{(r)}\Psi_n\right\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
This is a candidate definition only; no self-adjointness or proved-domain
claim is asserted here.

Measurements in this model are assigned only when a state and a normalized
finite bounded Kraus instrument have actually been constructed. For such an
instrument, the adopted outcome probabilities and positive-probability
conditional states are exactly those of
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]. They are model probabilities,
not observed outcomes. The field definitions are test-smeared: neither
$\Phi_\mu(x)$ nor $\Psi(x)$ is a pointwise operator supplied here, and the
smearing results do not define coincident products or a diagonal restriction.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the proper
orthochronous Poincare group
$G=\mathbb R^4\rtimes SO^+(1,3)$ in the coordinates of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. Give $SO^+(1,3)$ the matrix subspace topology
from $M_4(\mathbb R)$ and $G$ the product topology on
$\mathbb R^4\times SO^+(1,3)$, with the group law below. A unitary
representation of this topological group is a homomorphism into the unitary
operators on $H_\mu$; it is strongly continuous when each orbit map
$g\mapsto U_\mu(g)h$ is norm-continuous for $h\in H_\mu$. For
$g=(a,\Lambda)\in G$, define
$$f_g(x)=f(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),\qquad [U_\mu(g)h](p)=e^{ip\circ a}h(\Lambda^{-1}p).$$
Then $f_g\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$, $U_\mu(g)$ is a well-defined unitary
on $H_\mu$, $g\mapsto U_\mu(g)$ is a strongly continuous representation, and
$$K_\mu f_g=U_\mu(g)K_\mu f \qquad(f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)).$$
The group product convention is
$(a,\Lambda)(b,\Gamma)=(a+\Lambda b,\Lambda\Gamma)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], let $\mu\ge0$, let
$H_\mu$ and $K_\mu$ be as in [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]], and form
$\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$ with vacuum $\Omega$ and finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ define on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$
This is a complex-linear map of test functions into operators
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\to\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. For real $f$ it is symmetric
and equals $\sqrt2\,\Phi_{\rm Segal}(K_\mu f)|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}$, where the Segal field of
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]] is
$\Phi_{\rm Segal}(h)=\overline{(a^\dagger(h)+a(h))/\sqrt2}$.
Thus its Weyl unitary is
$W_\mu(f):=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f)$ and, for real $f,g$,
$$W_\mu(f)W_\mu(g)= e^{-i\,\operatorname{Im}\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2}W_\mu(f+g).$$
For every real $f$ the vacuum Weyl expectation is
$$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2 =e^{-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2}.$$
Here the inner product is second-variable-linear as fixed in
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The vacuum has zero one-point function and
two-point function
$$\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle_2 =\langle K_\mu\overline f,K_\mu g\rangle_2,$$
which obeys $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(\overline f)\Phi_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle_2=\|K_\mu f\|_2^2\ge0$ for every complex test $f$ (ordinary diagonal positivity holds for real tests); higher vacuum moments of ordered real smeared
fields obey the CCR pairing recursion and hence the free-field Wick pairing
rule. The field is a weak operator-valued tempered distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$: every matrix coefficient $f\mapsto\langle\Psi,\Phi_\mu(f)\Theta\rangle_2$ for $\Psi,\Theta\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on Schwartz space. Its adjoint satisfies $\Phi_\mu(f)^*|_{\mathcal D_{\rm fin}}=\Phi_\mu(\overline f)$, and its normalized vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by these fields.

The relative-coordinate two-point tempered distribution is
$$W_\mu(z)=\int_{H_\mu^+}e^{-ip\circ z}\,d\nu_\mu(p),$$
understood by pairing with Schwartz tests. Its translation-invariant bidistribution is the shell integral of $e^{-ip\circ x}e^{ip\circ y}$; on product tests it is the displayed vacuum covariance.

For $g=(a,\Lambda)$, let $f_g$ and $U_\mu(g)$ be the affine test pullback
and one-particle action of [[lem-qft-scalar-poincare-action]]. Their Fock
lifts implement the same covariance for $\Phi_\mu$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$
and for the bounded Weyl operators.

For translations, the joint spectral measure on Fock space is the
second-quantized multiplier measure with one-particle vector
$(\omega_\mu(\mathbf k),-\mathbf k)$. Its support is contained in the closed
future cone $\{(E,\mathbf P):E\ge|\mathbf P|\}$; the vacuum is an eigenvector
at $(0,\mathbf0)$. These are conditional mathematical model deductions.
No point field, empirical observation or measurement claim is made.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume both the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Fix a

Use a smooth, oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with its metric-selected Levi-Civita connection $\nabla$, as defined in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. write $i:\mathcal H\hookrightarrow M$ for the inclusion. A generator $\chi$
here is a smooth section of $i^*TM$ with $\chi_p\in T_p\mathcal H$
nonzero and null at each $p\in\mathcal H$. For a smooth tangent field $X$
on $\mathcal H$ and a smooth vector field $V$ along it, define

ambient tangent bundle and its metric-selected connection. The prescription

[[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. In particular,

ambient extension. If $\chi$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient field

$\nabla_\chi\chi=(\nabla_{\widetilde\chi}\widetilde\chi)|_{\mathcal H}$;

$\nabla_\chi\chi=\kappa_{\rm geom}\chi$. When the flow parameter has length units, $\kappa_{\rm geom}$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; the corresponding acceleration-unit quantity $\kappa_{\rm acc}:=c^2\kappa_{\rm geom}$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. By [A2], $\Delta_W^{it}=U(\Lambda_W(-2\pi t))$. Since
$\alpha_t=\sigma_{-t}$, we have
$\alpha_t(X)=\Delta_W^{-it}X\Delta_W^{it}
=U(\Lambda_W(2\pi t))XU(\Lambda_W(2\pi t))^*$ for $X\in M$. Thus
$\alpha_t$ is the future-boost action with rapidity $2\pi t$; the minus
sign in the adopted modular identity is essential for this direction.

Put $\rho=c^2/a$ and differentiate the curve in the Statement. Then
$\dot\gamma_a(\tau)=(c\cosh(a\tau/c),c\sinh(a\tau/c),0,0)$ and
$\ddot\gamma_a(\tau)=(a\sinh(a\tau/c),a\cosh(a\tau/c),0,0)$. Direct
contraction with $\eta$ gives
$\eta(\dot\gamma_a,\dot\gamma_a)=-c^2$ and
$\eta(\ddot\gamma_a,\ddot\gamma_a)=a^2$; also
$\dot x^0=c\cosh(a\tau/c)>0$. Therefore $\tau$ is proper time, the curve
is future timelike with proper acceleration magnitude $a$, and its boost
rapidity is $a\tau/c$.

Let $\lambda=2\pi c/a>0$, which has seconds as its unit by [F3]. Then
$\tau/\lambda=a\tau/(2\pi c)$ and, by step 1.1,
$\widetilde\alpha_\tau=\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}$. Apply [F1] and [F2] with
dimensionless width $\theta=1$: $\omega_W$ has the required bounded
continuous upper-strip functions on width $\lambda=2\pi c/a$ seconds for
every $A,B\in M$. By [F3],
$\beta_U=\lambda/\hbar=2\pi c/(a\hbar)$ and
$T_U=(k_B\beta_U)^{-1}=\hbar a/(2\pi c k_B)$. The displayed units give
$[\beta_U]=\mathrm{J^{-1}}$ and $[T_U]=\mathrm K$. No density matrix or
detector statement is used.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

State maps and geometric currents have the types and units in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]]: a formal marker density $n$ is $\mathrm{marker\,m^{-3}}$; entropy density $s$ is $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; a $C^1$ entropy current $S^a$ has components $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-3}}$; and its physical flux is $cS^a$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Its geometric divergence $\nabla_aS^a$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,m^{-4}}$, so $c\nabla_aS^a$ is entropy production per physical volume per second. The symmetric stress tensor $\mathsf T^{ab}$ has components in pascals in length coordinates; it is a tensor, not an observer-independent array of energy densities. The state-function energy density $\varepsilon$ and the observer projection $\mathsf T^{ab}u_a u_b$ remain distinct unless a material model identifies them.

The constant $c$ supplies the spacetime length/time conversion. In a branch with dynamical Einstein gravity, $G$ is an independent coupling parameter in $\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$. The Boltzmann constant $k_B$ has units $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ and is used when a statistical entropy/temperature calibration is adopted. Planck's constant $h_{\rm P}=2\pi\hbar$ has units $\mathrm{J\,s}$; $\hbar$ is used only in a quantum branch. Under the current SI definition, $c$, $h_{\rm P}$ and $k_B$ have exact defining numerical values; this metrological fact does not make them derived predictions of a thermodynamic or gravitational model. $G$ is experimentally adjusted and carries measurement uncertainty. The roles of these quantities as primitive model inputs are framework-specific. The local energy function, pressure, temperature and chemical potential in [[def-tgr-local-fluid-state]] are derived from the supplied state function; no particle mass or universal equation of state is derived from gravity alone.

For a smooth Killing field $\xi$ on an open domain, meaning $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$ by [[def-gr-killing-field]], restrict attention to a domain where $\xi$ is future timelike and choose a positive normalization at infinity or at a specified wall/observer. Define the lapse $N_\xi:=\sqrt{-g(\xi,\xi)}>0$ and unit observer $u_\xi:=\xi/N_\xi$. For a supplied proper-temperature scalar $T>0$ in kelvins, define the Killing-normalized temperature field $T_\xi:=N_\xi T$. It is not assumed constant; if a separate equilibrium argument proves constancy on its stated domain, denote that value by $T_K$. The finite matter charge and its side-flux convention are those in [[lem-tgr-killing-energy-normalization]] and [[def-tgr-spacelike-current-slab]]; their charge-balance clause retains its explicitly conditional finite-slab hypotheses. This charge is not a general gravitational energy.

Keep covector types separate. A mechanical momentum covector $p_a$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$; its Killing energy is $E_\xi(p):=-c\,p_a\xi^a$ in joules. An energy-valued covector $\pi_a$ already has units joules and pairs as $E_\xi(\pi):=-\pi_a\xi^a$, without another factor of $c$. An inverse-length wave covector $k_a$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ and pairs as $E_\xi(k):=-\hbar c\,k_a\xi^a$. For a specified charged stationary gauge, charge $q$ has coulombs and a potential covector $A_a$ in length coordinates has units $\mathrm{V\,s\,m^{-1}}$; when a global stationary potential is actually defined, $\Phi_\xi:=-cA_a\xi^a$ has volts and $q\Phi_\xi$ has joules. A charged energy or chemical-potential convention requires its stated gauge and reference; no global potential, electrochemical equilibrium, or constancy is asserted here.

When $T_K>0$ is supplied, distinguish the inverse-temperature vector $\beta^a:=u_\xi^a/(k_BT)=\xi^a/(k_BT_K)$, with units $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, from the scalar $\beta_K:=1/(k_BT_K)$, also in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a quantum statistical model, let $\mathcal A$ be a unital complex $C^*$-algebra: an associative complex algebra with nonzero identity $1$, a complete norm satisfying $\|AB\|\leq\|A\|\,\|B\|$, and a conjugate-linear involution $A\mapsto A^*$ satisfying $(A^*)^*=A$, $(AB)^*=B^*A^*$, and $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Its elements represent bounded observables. Let $\{\alpha_t:t\in\mathbb R\}$ be bijective complex-linear maps $\alpha_t:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$ preserving multiplication and involution, with $\alpha_t(1)=1$, $\alpha_0=\operatorname{id}$, and $\alpha_{s+t}=\alpha_s\circ\alpha_t$; require $t\mapsto\alpha_t(A)$ to be norm-continuous for every $A\in\mathcal A$. A state is a bounded complex-linear functional $\omega:\mathcal A\to\mathbb C$ with $\omega(1)=1$ and $\omega(A^*A)\geq0$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$. For $b>0$ in the chosen flow-parameter units, define $S_b:=\{z\in\mathbb C:0\leq\operatorname{Im}z\leq b\}$. The state $\omega$ satisfies the KMS condition at width $b$ when for every $A,B\in\mathcal A$ there is a function $F_{A,B}:S_b\to\mathbb C$ with $\sup_{z\in S_b}|F_{A,B}(z)|<\infty$, continuous on $S_b$ and complex-differentiable at every point of its interior, such that

$$F_{A,B}(t)=\omega(A\alpha_t(B)),\qquad F_{A,B}(t+ib)=\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)\quad(t\in\mathbb R).$$

This all-observable boundary-value definition uses no separately declared analytic subalgebra. With the quantum statistical calibration $\beta_K=(k_BT_K)^{-1}$, a physical-time parameter $t$ in seconds has KMS width $b_t=\hbar\beta_K$ seconds. If the flow parameter is length $\lambda=ct$, use the reparameterized group $\widetilde\alpha_\lambda:=\alpha_{\lambda/c}$; its KMS width is $b_\lambda=c\hbar\beta_K$ metres. These are unit and parameter-convention assignments only. This definition introduces no Hilbert-space operator $H_K$ and does not identify the abstract automorphism flow or its strip width with the finite matter charge $H_\xi$ of [[lem-tgr-killing-energy-normalization]]. This item asserts neither the existence of an observable algebra or flow for a given thermodynamic-gravity model nor the existence of a KMS state or equilibrium.

On a specified smooth embedded null hypersurface $\mathcal H\subset M$,
write $i:\mathcal H\hookrightarrow M$ for the inclusion. A generator $\chi$
here is a smooth section of $i^*TM$ with $\chi_p\in T_p\mathcal H$
nonzero and null at each $p\in\mathcal H$. For a smooth tangent field $X$
on $\mathcal H$ and a smooth vector field $V$ along it, define
$\nabla_XV:=(i^*\nabla)_XV$ by [[def-pullback-connection]], applied to the
ambient tangent bundle and its metric-selected connection. The prescription
is independent of frames by
[[thm-pullback-connection-is-well-defined-and-functorial]]. In particular,
$\nabla_\chi\chi$ is a vector field along $\mathcal H$ and needs no chosen
ambient extension. If $\chi$ is the restriction of a smooth ambient field
$\widetilde\chi$, the same theorem gives
$\nabla_\chi\chi=(\nabla_{\widetilde\chi}\widetilde\chi)|_{\mathcal H}$;
thus this convention also covers the supplied ambient Killing generators.
The generator may admit a scalar $\kappa_{\rm geom}$ defined by
$\nabla_\chi\chi=\kappa_{\rm geom}\chi$. When the flow parameter has length units, $\kappa_{\rm geom}$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$; the corresponding acceleration-unit quantity $\kappa_{\rm acc}:=c^2\kappa_{\rm geom}$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. This definition does not assert a horizon exists, that $\kappa$ is constant, or that a temperature law follows. The formula $T_K=\hbar c\kappa_{\rm geom}/(2\pi k_B)$ requires a specified quantum/semiclassical model, and an area-entropy formula requires a separate thermodynamic identification. Assume both the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice. Fix a
massive real scalar species with rest mass $m_{\mathrm{rest}}>0$ in kilograms.
Use four-dimensional affine Minkowski spacetime with metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and length coordinates
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, where $x^0=ct$ and $c>0$ has units
$\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Set $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest}}c/\hbar>0$ in
$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, where $\hbar>0$ is in $\mathrm{J\,s}$. The future shell,
one-particle space, and measure are
$$H_\mu^+=\{(p^0,\mathbf p):(p^0)^2-|\mathbf p|^2=\mu^2,\ p^0>0\},\qquad \mathcal H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu),\qquad d\nu_\mu=\frac{d^3\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^3\,2\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2+\mu^2}}.$$
Take the scalar Hilbert space to be the bosonic symmetric Fock space
$\mathcal H=\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_\mu)$ and its unit zero-particle vector
to be $\Omega$.

For an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ and real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$, define
$$K_\mu f(p)=\int_{\mathbb R^4}f(x)e^{i(p^0x^0-\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf x)}\,d^4x, \qquad W_\mu(f)=W_{\mathrm{Segal}}(\sqrt2\,K_\mu f).$$
Let $\mathfrak A_s(O)$ be the operator-norm closure of the unital
$*$-algebra generated by all these bounded Weyl unitaries, and set
$W_R=\{x\in\mathbb R^4:x^1>|x^0|\}$ and
$M(W_R)=\mathfrak A_s(W_R)''\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$. Here
$\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$ denotes the bounded linear operators;
$\mathcal S'$ is the set of bounded operators commuting with every member of
$\mathcal S$, and $\mathcal S''=(\mathcal S')'$. Thus $M(W_R)$ is a concrete
von Neumann algebra in the chosen double-commutant convention.

For dimensionless rapidity $s\in\mathbb R$, define the future-directed boost
by
$$\Lambda_W(s)(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) =(x^0\cosh s+x^1\sinh s,\ x^0\sinh s+x^1\cosh s,\ x^2,\ x^3).$$
Use its scalar Fock implementation: on the one-particle space
$[u_\mu(\Lambda)\psi](p)=\psi(\Lambda^{-1}p)$, and on the $n$-particle
symmetric sector $U(\Lambda)=u_\mu(\Lambda)^{\otimes_s n}$, with the vacuum
sector fixed. The QFT Fock pairing is linear in its second argument; for the
modular definitions use the equivalent first-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_1:=\langle v,u\rangle_2$. Thus the vacuum vector state
is $\omega_W(X)=\langle X\Omega,\Omega\rangle_1
=\langle\Omega,X\Omega\rangle_2$. Assume explicitly that $\Omega$ is cyclic and separating for
$M(W_R)$, meaning $\overline{M(W_R)\Omega}=\mathcal H$ and
$X\Omega=0$ for $X\in M(W_R)$ implies $X=0$. The Tomita operator is the
closure of $S_{W,0}(X\Omega)=X^*\Omega$ on $M(W_R)\Omega$; write its polar
decomposition as $S_W=J_W\Delta_W^{1/2}$, in the standard modular-data
convention.

As an additional model interface, adopt
$$\Delta_W^{it}=U(\Lambda_W(-2\pi t))\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).$$
This geometric identity and cyclic-separating property are explicit adopted
assumptions for this selected model. The abstract Tomita–Takesaki theorem
supplies modular automorphisms and their KMS property, but this carrier does
not use it as a proof that the modular unitaries equal spacetime boosts. No
tensor-product factorization of the continuum Hilbert space across the wedge
and its complement is assumed.

derivations.claim:
Let $\psi_{z,N}=\sqrt{1-z}\sum_{n=0}^N z^{n/2}
|n\rangle_R\otimes|n\rangle_L$. Orthogonality gives, for $M>N$,
$\|\psi_{z,M}-\psi_{z,N}\|^2=(1-z)\sum_{n=N+1}^M z^n
\le (1-z)\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}z^n=z^{N+1}\to0$.
Thus the partial sums converge in $\mathcal H_R\otimes\mathcal H_L$ to
$\psi_z$. Also $(1-z)\sum_{n=0}^N z^n=1-z^{N+1}$, so continuity of the
norm gives $\langle\psi_z|\psi_z\rangle
=(1-z)\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^n=1$.

The product-basis coefficients are
$\langle m,k|\psi_z\rangle=\sqrt{1-z}\,z^{k/2}\delta_{mk}$.
Substitution in the defining partial-trace sum gives
$\langle m|\rho_R|n\rangle
=(1-z)\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^k\delta_{mk}\delta_{nk}
=(1-z)z^n\delta_{mn}$. Therefore the eigenvalues are exactly
$p_n=(1-z)z^n$, they are positive, and their sum is one by step 1.1.

Put $a_n=nz^n$ for $n\ge1$. Since
$a_{n+1}/a_n=z(1+1/n)\to z<1$, choose $q$ with $z<q<1$; for all
sufficiently large $n$, $a_{n+1}\le q a_n$, so $a_n\to0$ and the tail
$\sum a_n$ is bounded by a geometric series. Differentiating
$\sum_{n=0}^N z^n=(1-z^{N+1})/(1-z)$ gives
$\sum_{n=1}^N n z^{n-1}
=\bigl(1-(N+1)z^N+Nz^{N+1}\bigr)/(1-z)^2$. Since $Nz^N\to0$,
taking $N\to\infty$ gives $\sum_{n=0}^\infty n z^n=z/(1-z)^2$. Hence
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty n p_n=z/(1-z)$, and
$-\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n\ln p_n
=-\ln(1-z)-(\ln z)\sum_{n=0}^\infty n p_n
=-\ln(1-z)-z\ln z/(1-z)$. The series converges because
$\sum z^n$ and $\sum n z^n$ converge for $0<z<1$. In particular,
$\sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n|\ln p_n|
=|\ln(1-z)|+|\ln z|\,z/(1-z)<\infty$.

Step 2.1 shows that the coefficient formula in the Example gives
$\rho_R|n\rangle=p_n|n\rangle$ with $0<p_n<1$ and $\sum_n p_n=1$; hence
$\rho_R$ is bounded and nonzero. Step 1.1 gives $P_z\ne0$. Every element of
$V_z$ therefore has a unique form $cP_z$, so $\mathcal R_z(cP_z)=c\rho_R$
defines a linear map from $V_z$ to $W_z$. On $P_z$ its matrix coefficients
are exactly those of the rank-one coefficient formula in the Example; thus
$\mathcal R_z(P_z)=\rho_R$ and the displayed rank-one diagram commutes. The
asserted reduction is confined to this rank-one input. The continuum
postulate [F1] instead defines a scalar Fock representation and a right-wedge
von Neumann algebra; no map identifying those two constructions is defined
or used here. Consequently this example proves the stated oscillator
identities but no continuum wedge factorization or density-matrix claim.

derivations.claim: Put $\tau=\chi u$, $\kappa=k/\chi$, $x_H=\chi U_H$, and $\lambda=Ak>0$. In the length coordinate $\tau$, the map $x(\tau):=\ell(\tau/\chi)$ satisfies $x(\tau)=x_H+\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)$, since $\lambda U_\kappa(\tau)=-\chi A e^{-\kappa\tau}$. By [F1], $U_\kappa$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,0)$; the positive affine map $y\mapsto x_H+\lambda y$ is a smooth diffeomorphism from $(-\infty,0)$ onto $(-\infty,x_H)$. Since $u\mapsto\tau=\chi u$ is also a positive linear diffeomorphism, $\ell$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism from $\mathbb R$ onto $(-\infty,\ell_H)$, with smooth inverse $u_\ell(x)=\chi^{-1}U_\kappa^{-1}((x-x_H)/\lambda)$. Differentiating the supplied coordinate formula gives $\ell'(u)=\chi\lambda e^{-\kappa\chi u}=\chi Ak e^{-ku}$ and hence $U'(u)=Ak e^{-ku}>0$. If $\operatorname{supp}g\subseteq[a,b]$, then $\operatorname{supp}f_g\subseteq[\ell(a),\ell(b)]\subset(-\infty,\ell_H)$, so the zero extension is smooth and compactly supported. Thus $J(f_g)$ is defined by [F1]–[F2].

The map $(u,v)\mapsto(\ell(u),\ell(v))$ is a smooth diffeomorphism, so [F4] transports the two-variable test pairing with Jacobian $\ell'(u)\ell'(v)$. Since $\ell=\chi U$, the regularized identity $\chi^2[-(4\pi)^{-1}(\chi s-i\epsilon)^{-2}]=-(4\pi)^{-1}(s-i\epsilon/\chi)^{-2}$ shows that the positive unit scale cancels in the boundary distribution, giving the stated seconds-coordinate kernel. Positivity is the supplied Fock norm identity $W(g,g)=\|h_{f_g}\|_2^2\ge0$ from [F1].

On the finite-particle domain, the left vacuum annihilates every creation term and the right vacuum is annihilated by every annihilation operator. Commuting the annihilation part of the leftmost $J(f_{g_1})$ through the later fields, [F3] replaces each commutator by its scalar two-point contraction; the term with the annihilator reaching the right vacuum vanishes. Hence
$$M_n(g_1,\ldots,g_n)=\sum_{j=2}^n M_2(g_1,g_j)\,M_{n-2}(g_2,\ldots,\widehat{g_j},\ldots,g_n).$$
The base cases are $M_0=1$ and $M_1=0$. Induction gives zero for odd $n$ and the stated sum over pair partitions for even $n$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) with metric-selected connection
$\nabla$ ([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]]), whose existence and
uniqueness are supplied by
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; that theorem also
extends $\nabla$ to a derivative on tensor fields commuting with contractions
and annihilating $g$ and $g^{-1}$. Let $U\subseteq M$ be open and let
$X,Y,Z$ be smooth vector fields on $U$; brackets are those of
[[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]], and contractions those of
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]].

**(a) The curvature operator.** The **curvature operator** of $\nabla$ is the
assignment

$$R(X,Y)Z:=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z .$$

The right-hand side is a smooth vector field on $U$: $\nabla_YZ$ is smooth
because $\nabla$ is an affine connection
([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]), $[X,Y]$ is smooth, and
$\nabla_X(\cdot)$ and $\nabla_{[X,Y]}(\cdot)$ preserve smoothness. The
assignment is defined for the given smooth fields; that its value at a point
depends only on the values of $X,Y,Z$ at that point, so that $R$ is a smooth
tensor field of type $(1,3)$, is the content of
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a), and
likewise the algebraic symmetries used below are proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]].

**(b) Component functions.** Let $(V,x)$ be a smooth chart of $M$ and let
$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ be the Christoffel symbols of $\nabla$ in this chart,
characterized by $\nabla_{\partial_b}\partial_c=\sum_a\Gamma^a{}_{bc}\partial_a$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]); the coordinate fields
commute, so $\nabla_{\partial_c}\partial_d$ and $\nabla_{\partial_d}\partial_c$
are obtained from the same symbols. The **components** of the curvature in the
chart are the smooth functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ on $V$ defined by

$$R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=\sum_a R^a{}_{bcd}\,\partial_a .$$

The first index is the output slot, the second is the differentiated slot and
the last two are the two directions of the loop; indices are $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$
and the Einstein summation convention of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] applies.

**(c) Lowered tensor, Ricci tensor, scalar curvature, Einstein tensor.** On
the chart domain define, using the inverse metric
$g^{ab}$ of [[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]],

$$R_{abcd}:=\sum_e g_{ae}R^e{}_{bcd},\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_{bd}:=\sum_{a,c}g^{ac}R_{abcd},\qquad S:=\sum_{b,d}g^{bd}\operatorname{Ric}_{bd},\qquad G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}-\tfrac12 S\,g_{ab}.$$

The fields $R_{abcd}$, $\operatorname{Ric}_{ab}$, $S$ and $G_{ab}$ are called
the **Riemann tensor with lowered indices**, the **Ricci tensor**, the
**scalar curvature** and the **Einstein tensor** of the metric-selected
connection. Tensoriality of $R$ is proved in
[[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]] clause (a).
Lowering its output slot with the smooth metric and contracting with the
smooth inverse metric are intrinsic tensor operations
([[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] clauses (b)-(c),
[[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]]). Thus these formulas give smooth
fields of types $(0,4)$, $(0,2)$, $(0,0)$ and $(0,2)$, respectively,
independent of the chart. Symmetry of $\operatorname{Ric}$ and $G$ is proved
separately in [[thm-gr-curvature-algebraic-symmetries]] clause (d).

signature $(-,+,+,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in
each tangent space, and a time orientation selects the future timelike cone.
A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with tangent consistently future- or
past-directed and causal; $J^\pm(p)$ denote points reachable from or reaching
$p$ by such curves. Strong causality means every point has arbitrarily small
neighborhoods that each causal curve meets in a connected parameter
interval. Global hyperbolicity means strong causality and compact causal
diamonds $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$. Fix a real scalar Klein-Gordon operator
$P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+V$, where $\nabla$ is the Levi-Civita connection
and $V$ is a prescribed smooth real scalar of dimension $\mathrm{m^{-2}}$ in
length coordinates. Use the canonical field length degree
$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ used for the framework's free scalar field, so its
two-point distribution and subtraction kernel have length degree
$\mathrm{m^{-2}}$. Supply the free-field $*$-algebra $\mathcal A_P$ and its
real test-function smearing map $\Phi:C_c^\infty(M;\mathbb R)\to\mathcal A_P$;
smearing uses $d\mathrm{vol}_g$. This is model input, not a field-algebra
construction claim. In the massless minimally coupled collapse
specialization, [[post-tgrx-free-collapse-scattering]] specifies bosonic
Fock quantization, the smeared field operators, and the positive normalized
state convention. A **state** $\omega$ is a positive normalized linear
functional on $\mathcal A_P$, so $\omega(A^*A)\ge0$ and $\omega(1)=1$.
Its two-point distribution $W_\omega\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$, in the
test-density convention, is defined by the pairings
$W_\omega(f,h)=\omega(\Phi(f)\Phi(h))$ for compactly supported smooth real
tests $f,h$, extended complex linearly. Require
$P_xW_\omega=P_yW_\omega=0$ and
$\operatorname{WF}(W_\omega)=\mathcal C_g^+$, where $\mathcal C_g^+$ consists
of pairs $(x,\xi;y,-\zeta)$ with nonzero future-null covectors $\xi,\zeta$
that are equal at a coincident point or are the metric-dual tangents, with a
common positive scale, along one nonconstant future-directed null geodesic;
the two base points need not be ordered along that geodesic. This is the
positive-frequency Hadamard convention in [[def-qftx-wavefront-hadamard]],
whose definition fixes this relation without a base-point order.
$\operatorname{WF}$ records nonzero cotangent directions in which localized
Fourier transforms fail rapid decay. The
framework's massless, minimally coupled collapse scalar is one
specialization; its Schwarzschild and scattering assumptions are not imposed
on this general contract.

For each open convex normal neighborhood $U\subset M$ (an open set such that
for every $p\in U$ the exponential map at $p$ restricts to a diffeomorphism
from a star-shaped open neighborhood of $0\in T_pM$ onto $U$), supply a
locally covariant Hadamard singular bidistribution $H_\mu$ for $P$. The scale
$\mu>0$ is fixed and has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. “Hadamard singular
bidistribution” here means the prescribed local, state-independent singular
part determined by $(g,P,\mu)$, with
$W_\omega-H_\mu\in C^\infty(U\times U)$. The parametrix pieces, the
bidifferential operators below, and their resulting coincident values must be
compatible on overlaps. This is supplied data: the definition proves no
parametrix construction or general existence theorem.

Supply a finite-order bidifferential operator $D_{ab}(x,y)$ which maps a
smooth biscalar on $U\times U$ to a smooth covariant symmetric two-tensor at
$x$; any coefficient bitensors and parallel transports needed to define its
indices are part of the supplied operator. Also supply a smooth, symmetric,
state-independent local curvature tensor $C_{ab}[g;\mu,\mathbf c]$, where
$\mathbf c$ is the fixed list of finite renormalization conditions. “Local”
means determined by the values of $g$, $P$, and their derivatives at the
point, through finitely many curvature contractions; it has no state or
distant-geometry dependence. Require local covariance: whenever
$\psi:(M,g)\to(M',g')$ is a smooth embedding with $\psi^*g'=g$, preserves the
time orientation, and has causally convex image (every causal curve segment
in $M'$ with endpoints in the image stays in the image), the assigned local
prescription on $(M,g)$ is the pullback of the one on $(M',g')$. Require
conservation,
$\nabla^aT^{\mathrm{ren}}_{ab}=0$, with the index raised using $g^{ab}$.

Define the renormalized stress tensor by
$$T^{\mathrm{ren}}_{ab}[g,\omega](x):=\lim_{y\to x}D_{ab}(x,y)\bigl(W_\omega-H_\mu\bigr)(x,y)+C_{ab}[g;\mu,\mathbf c](x).$$
The limit is taken inside a convex normal neighborhood. It exists because
$W_\omega-H_\mu$ is smooth and $D_{ab}$ has finite order. In SI units and
length coordinates $x^0=ct$, the normalization of $D_{ab}$ is part of the
chosen scalar-field prescription and its output, as well as $C_{ab}$, has
stress-energy units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. No pointwise product of the
singular distributions $W_\omega$ and $H_\mu$ is taken.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: For $|x|<1$, the power series $P(x):=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n$ converges absolutely because it is termwise bounded in absolute value by the geometric series in [F5]. Its radius is therefore at least $1$, and [F6] gives $P'(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^{n-1}=1/(1-x)$. The difference quotient for $\log$ in [F4], with increment $-h$, gives $\frac{d}{dx}[-\log(1-x)]=1/(1-x)$. Both functions are differentiable on $(-1,1)$ and hence continuous there by [F8]: at a differentiability point, the difference quotient is bounded near the point, so multiplying it by the increment shows that the function increment tends to zero. Since both functions vanish at $0$ by [F3], [F7] applied to their difference yields $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}x^n/n=-\log(1-x)$ for every $|x|<1$.

Write $d:=\dim H$. For any endomorphism $T$, let $M:=\max_{i,j}|T_{ij}|$ in the fixed orthonormal basis. For $x=\sum_jx_je_j$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] applied in these coordinates to $(T_{ij})_j$ and $(\overline{x_j})_j$ gives $|(Tx)_i|=|\sum_jT_{ij}x_j|\le(\sum_j|T_{ij}|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_j|x_j|^2)^{1/2}\le\sqrt dM\|x\|$ for each $i$, hence $\|Tx\|\le dM\|x\|$. Thus $T$ is bounded, so the operator norm [F9] is defined and finite, with $\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le dM$. For any endomorphisms $S,T$, [F9] then gives $\|STx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Tx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\|$ for every vector $x$. Taking the supremum over unit $x$ proves $\|ST\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.

Put $A_0:=A(t_0)$ and let $\lambda_{\max}$ and $\lambda_{\min}$ be its largest and smallest eigenvalues. They satisfy $0<\lambda_{\min}\le\lambda_{\max}$ by [F1] and the hypothesis. Set $c:=2\lambda_{\max}$, $B:=I_H-A_0/c$, and, for $t\in U$, $B_t:=I_H-A(t)/c$. The eigenvalues of $B$ lie in $[1/2,1-\lambda_{\min}/c]$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $B$, writing its eigenvalues as $b_j$, [F9] gives $\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\max_j|b_j|$: for $x=\sum_jx_je_j$, $\|Bx\|^2=\sum_j|b_j|^2|x_j|^2\le(\max_j|b_j|)^2\|x\|^2$, with equality on an eigenvector for a largest $|b_j|$. Hence $q:=\|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}<1$ by [F1]. Choose $r$ with $q<r<1$. By [F8], every entry of $A(t)-A_0$ tends to zero as $t\to t_0$. Since there are finitely many entries, $M(t):=\max_{i,j}|(A(t)-A_0)_{ij}|\to0$, and the matrix bound in step 1.2 gives $\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}\to0$, so choose a neighborhood $V\subseteq U$ of $t_0$ where $\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c<(r-q)/2$. For every unit vector $x$, the inner-product norm triangle inequality [F11] and [F9] give $\|B_tx\|\le\|Bx\|+\|(A(t)-A_0)x\|/c\le q+\|A(t)-A_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c<r$ for $t\in V$; taking the supremum proves $\|B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}<r$. Since $B_t$ is self-adjoint, each eigenvalue $\beta$ satisfies $|\beta|\le\|B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}<r<1$. For $t\in V$, the scalar identity in step 1.1 applied to these eigenvalues, the product law [F10], and spectral calculus [F1] give $\log A(t)=(\log c)I_H-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}B_t^n/n$, with convergence in operator norm because repeated application of step 1.2 gives $\|B_t^n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|B_t\|_{\mathrm{op}}^n<r^n$ and $\sum r^n/n\le\sum r^n<\infty$.

For $t$ sufficiently near $t_0$, put $E:=A(t)-A_0$, $Z:=-E/c$, and $z:=\|Z\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Then $B_t=B+Z$. The supremum definition gives $z=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$, so $z\to0$ as $t\to t_0$; shrink the neighborhood so that $q+z\le r$. Distributivity writes $(B+Z)^n=B^n+S_n+R_n$, where $S_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}B^j ZB^{n-1-j}$ contains the terms with exactly one $Z$, and $R_n$ contains all terms with at least two $Z$ factors. The submultiplicative bound in step 1.2 gives $\|S_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le nq^{n-1}z$. For $R_n$, each word with exactly $k$ factors $Z$ has norm at most $q^{n-k}z^k$, and there are $\binom nk$ such words, so $\|R_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_{k=2}^n\binom nkq^{n-k}z^k\le\binom n2z^2(q+z)^{n-2}\le\binom n2z^2r^{n-2}$. The middle bound follows from $\binom nk\le\binom n2\binom{n-2}{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$.

Substituting the series of step 2.1 into $G(A):=\operatorname{tr}(A\log A)$, and using step 3.1, yields
$$G(A_0+E)-G(A_0)=(\log c)\operatorname{tr}E-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\operatorname{tr}(EB^n)+\operatorname{tr}(A_0S_n)}{n}+R(E),$$
where $|R(E)|\le C\|E\|^2$ for a constant $C$ independent of sufficiently small $E$. Indeed, the omitted terms are $\operatorname{tr}(A_0R_n)$, $\operatorname{tr}(ES_n)$, and $\operatorname{tr}(ER_n)$; for each orthonormal basis vector $e_i$, the $i$th coordinate of $Te_i$ is $\langle Te_i,e_i\rangle$ and [F12] gives its magnitude at most $\|Te_i\|\|e_i\|=\|Te_i\|\le\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by [F9], since $\|e_i\|=1$, so [F2] gives $|\operatorname{tr}T|\le d\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ with $d=\dim H$, and the bounds in step 3.1 make their series after division by $n$ bounded by constants times $z^2\sum_{n\ge2}nr^{n-2}$, $z^2\sum_{n\ge1}q^{n-1}$, and $z^3\sum_{n\ge2}nr^{n-2}$, respectively. Each geometric derivative sum is finite by [F5]–[F6], and step 3.1 gives $z=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$.

The linear matrix-log term read from the series in steps 2.1 and 3.1 is
$$L(E):=\frac1c\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}B^jEB^{n-1-j}.$$
Its series converges in operator norm because the $n$th summand has norm at most $q^{n-1}\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}/c$. The remainder in the logarithm series is bounded by $\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\binom n2 z^2r^{n-2}/n=(z^2/2)\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(n-1)r^{n-2}=O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$, so $L(E)$ is the full first-order term of $\log(A_0+E)$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis of $A_0$, write $A_0e_i=\lambda_i e_i$ and $b_i:=1-\lambda_i/c$. Then
$$L(E)_{ik}=\frac{E_{ik}}c\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1n\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}b_i^jb_k^{n-1-j}.$$
If $b_i\ne b_k$, the inner sum is $(b_i^n-b_k^n)/(b_i-b_k)$, so its coefficient is
$\frac1c\frac{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(b_i^n-b_k^n)/n}{b_i-b_k}=\frac{\log(1-b_k)-\log(1-b_i)}{c(b_i-b_k)}=\frac{\log\lambda_i-\log\lambda_k}{\lambda_i-\lambda_k},$
where step 1.1 evaluates the series and [F10] gives $\log\lambda_j=\log c+\log(1-b_j)$, while $\lambda_i-\lambda_k=c(b_k-b_i)$. If $b_i=b_k$, the coefficient is $c^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_i^{n-1}=1/(c(1-b_i))=1/\lambda_i=\log'(\lambda_i)$ by [F4] and [F5]. Defining $\log^{[1]}(x,y):=(\log x-\log y)/(x-y)$ for $x\ne y$ and $\log^{[1]}(x,x):=1/x$, we have $L(E)_{ik}=\log^{[1]}(\lambda_i,\lambda_k)E_{ik}$: this is the divided-difference derivative of the matrix logarithm.

In a fixed basis, [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\sum_{i,j}X_{ij}Y_{ji}=\sum_{i,j}Y_{ji}X_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$, so trace is cyclic. Since $A_0$ commutes with $B$ and $Z=-E/c$, cycling each term gives $\operatorname{tr}(A_0S_n)=-(n/c)\operatorname{tr}(A_0B^{n-1}E)$. Thus the $A_0S_n$ terms in step 4.1 sum to $\operatorname{tr}(A_0L(E))$. In the eigenbasis used in step 4.2, $L(E)_{ii}=E_{ii}/\lambda_i$, so $\operatorname{tr}(A_0L(E))=\sum_i\lambda_iL(E)_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}E$. The remaining linear terms in step 4.1 are $\operatorname{tr}(E\log A_0)$ by the spectral series in step 2.1. Therefore $G(A_0+E)-G(A_0)=\operatorname{tr}(E(\log A_0+I_H))+O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$.

By [F8], for $h\to0$ the path increment is $E=A(t_0+h)-A_0=hA'(t_0)+o(h)$ entrywise. The finite-coordinate bound in step 2.1 gives $\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O(|h|)$. Dividing the expansion in step 5.1 by $h$ makes its $O(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2)$ remainder tend to $0$ and its linear term tend to $\operatorname{tr}(A'(t_0)(\log A(t_0)+I_H))$. This is the stated derivative.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $A,B:H\to H$ be non-negative operators. For such an operator $A$, set $\operatorname{supp}(A):=(\ker A)^\perp$, where $\ker A$ is the kernel of a linear map ([[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]); this extends the density-operator support convention in [[def-qc-density-operator]]. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, define

$$D(A\|B):=\operatorname{tr}(A\ln A)-\operatorname{tr}(A\ln B).$$

Here $\ln A$ is defined spectrally on the positive eigenspaces of $A$ with $0\ln0:=0$, and $\ln B$ in the cross term is restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(B)$; the support condition ensures that $A$ vanishes on $\ker B$, so the omitted kernel contributes zero. If $\operatorname{supp}(A)\nsubseteq\operatorname{supp}(B)$, set $D(A\|B):=+\infty$. In particular, $D(0\|B)=0$. For density operators this is the finite-dimensional **quantum relative entropy**. The logarithms are natural, so the value is in nats; the base-two value is $D_2(A\|B):=D(A\|B)/\ln2$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root convention that its inner product is linear in the first argument, and let $\rho$ be a density operator on $H$ ([[def-qc-density-operator]]). If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by

$$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

The trace is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]), and the spectral definition makes the expression independent of the eigenbasis. The term for a zero eigenvalue is defined to be $0\ln0:=0$. The default unit is nats, using the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]); the entropy in bits is $S_2(\rho):=S(\rho)/\ln2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For

$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with a fixed orthonormal basis, let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, and let $t_0\in J$. Let $\operatorname{tr}$ be the finite-dimensional trace, and let $\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|=1}\|Tv\|$ be the operator norm. For $t\in U$, define $\log A(t)$ by applying the natural logarithm to the eigenvalues of $A(t)$ in its spectral decomposition and set $G:U\to\mathbb R$ by $G(t):=\operatorname{tr}(A(t)\log A(t))$. Then $G$ is differentiable at $t_0$ and

$$G'(t_0)=\operatorname{tr}\!\left(A'(t_0)(\log A(t_0)+I_H)\right),$$

where $I_H$ is the identity endomorphism of $H$ and $A'(t_0)$ is obtained by differentiating the matrix entries in the fixed basis.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space. Let $\rho,\sigma:H\to H$ be self-adjoint linear maps with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one, and suppose every eigenvalue of $\sigma$ is strictly positive. Define $K_\sigma:=-\log\sigma$ by spectral calculus, and for any self-adjoint $\tau:H\to H$ with nonnegative eigenvalues and trace one define $s(\tau):=-\operatorname{tr}(\tau\log\tau)=-\sum_{\lambda_j(\tau)>0}\lambda_j(\tau)\log\lambda_j(\tau)$, with the zero-eigenvalue term $0\log0:=0$ and natural logarithms, so the entropy is in nats. Define the modular-energy difference relative to $\sigma$ by $\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma):=\operatorname{tr}((\rho-\sigma)K_\sigma)$. Then

$$D(\rho\|\sigma)=\Delta_K(\rho,\sigma)-(s(\rho)-s(\sigma)).$$

For any nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$ with $H=H_A\otimes H_B$, partial tracing both states over $H_B$ cannot increase relative entropy:

$$D(\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\rho\|\operatorname{Tr}_{B}\sigma)\le D(\rho\|\sigma).$$

The identity and inequality are finite-dimensional mathematical statements; no Hamiltonian, physical energy, physical units, continuum limit, or gravitational entropy is assumed.

Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. derivations.claim: Let $m>0$ be the smallest eigenvalue of $\sigma$ from [F3]. Since $\rho$ is entrywise continuous at $0$, its finite matrix difference $T(\varepsilon):=\rho(\varepsilon)-\sigma$ tends to zero in operator norm: in a fixed orthonormal basis, if every entry of $T$ has magnitude at most $M$, then for a unit vector $x$ $\sum_j|x_j|^2=1$ makes each coordinate of $x$ have magnitude at most $1$, and each coordinate of $Tx$ has magnitude at most $dM$, and therefore $\|Tx\|\le d^{3/2}M$, where $d=\dim H$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that $\|T(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}<m/2$ for $|\varepsilon|<\delta$. For each $v\in H$, $\langle\sigma v,v\rangle\ge m\|v\|^2$ by spectral decomposition, while [F5] and [F6] give $|\langle T(\varepsilon)v,v\rangle|\le\|T(\varepsilon)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|v\|^2$. Hence $\langle\rho(\varepsilon)v,v\rangle>(m/2)\|v\|^2$ for nonzero $v$. Thus $\rho(\varepsilon)$ is positive definite near $0$ and [F1] applies.

Apply [F1] to $\rho$ at $0$: $\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}s(\rho(\varepsilon))\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0)(\log\sigma+I))$. Because $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\varepsilon))=1$ on the whole interval, in the fixed basis [F4] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0))=\sum_i\rho'_{ii}(0)=\lim_{h\to0}\sum_i(\rho_{ii}(h)-\rho_{ii}(0))/h=\lim_{h\to0}(1-1)/h=0$; the finite sum commutes with this limit. Therefore $\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}s(\rho(\varepsilon))\right|_0=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0)\log\sigma)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0)K_\sigma)$, as claimed.

The identity [F2] holds for every $\rho(\varepsilon)$ in the path. Its right-hand side is differentiable at $0$ by linearity of trace and step 2.1, so differentiating gives $\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}D(\rho(\varepsilon)\|\sigma)\right|_0=\operatorname{tr}(\rho'(0)K_\sigma)-\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}s(\rho(\varepsilon))\right|_0=0$. The additional twice continuously differentiable hypothesis ensures the differentiability required here.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$.
